articles.title: Mind the Gap: British Producer-Financier Phil Hunt Is Bringing Head Gear Stateside
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 5:43am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Head Gear Co-founder and CEO Phil Hunt Phil Hunt, Hana Holmes The AFM got a welcome boost ahead of this year’s market when British producer-financier Head Gear unveiled plans to launch a U.S. operation, promising to invest $120 million in production in its first year of operation. Head Gear COO Samantha Allwinton will run the U.S. division as director of operations. For Phil Hunt , who launched Head Gear in 2002 with film financier (and oil industry exec) Compton Ross, setting up stateside has been a dream “for 25 years.” In the U.K., Head Gear has developed a reputation as the “producer’s producer,” working at every stage of financing and production — from presales and packaging to gap and bridge funding — to support about 30 films a year, including Talk to Me , Danny and Michael Philippou’s Australian horror breakthrough that grossed more than $90 million worldwide; Ali Abbasi’s Oscar-nominated “reality horror” film The Apprentice , about the making of Donald Trump ; and Molly Manning Walker’s art house crossover hit How to Have Sex. Related Stories Movies 'Exotic' Takes Us to Polish Pole Dance Camp to Tell a Female Story of Self-Discovery and Body Confidence Movies Producers Push for Year-End Passage of Trump-Backed Federal Film Incentive: AFM Head Gear also is active on the sales side through its international operation, Bankside Films, whose AFM slate this year includes the AI-themed sci-fi comedy Almost You , starring Juno Temple, Joey King and James McAvoy from Ted Lasso director Matt Lipsey. Bankside is selling the project, now shooting in Scotland, worldwide, co-repping the U.K. and North America with UTA Independent Film Group. Speaking with THR ahead of the market, Hunt explains why he’s bullish about the U.S., with or without a federal tax credit, the impact of the creator economy on indie film and what he’s learned from taking on Trump – and Julie Andrews . Why Head Gear USA, and how will it work? I’ve wanted a U.S. business for about 25 years. It took that long to find the right person to run it. Now the timing is right as well: more U.S. producers need financing, and a federal tax credit could bring a lot more production into the country. We’re putting about $120 million into U.S. film and TV in the first year. We’re not just a lender. We help producers package the project, build the financing plan, handle the business affairs and collect the money after release. We behave like a small studio. We decide whether a film goes into production, and we deliver about 35 films a year to our regular sales agents and buyers. Whether we like it or not, the U.S. leads the rest of the world on global distribution of English-speaking movies. Being there is often not an option. But we’re a British company with the culture we have built over the past quarter of a century, and that means we uphold key principles. We’re transparent and do what we say we’re going to do — while bringing a great punk rock style. ‘Talk to Me,’ which Head Gear backed, was a breakout hit, earning more than $90 million worldwide. Matthew Thorne/A24 How does the federal tax credit fit into your U.S. expansion plans, and what if it doesn’t pass? If it passes, a U.S. production gets cheaper to make and lenders can borrow against the credit, the way we already do in the U.K. and Europe. That’s why we’re setting up now, so we’re ready the day it lands. If it doesn’t pass, we’re still going to be investing heavily in U.S. movies. Nothing much changes that desire to open up there for the past 25 years. What are the biggest lessons you take from the past year’s indie successes and failures? The films that worked were made for a price that makes sense; good cast, clear idea, a budget the market can pay back. The ones that failed mostly cost too much for what they were. People priced the film on hope, not on what buyers actually pay. Second lesson: The old safety nets are gone. Revenue is down and costs are up. If your plan only works when everything goes right, it won’t work. Third: Be honest early. When a producer tells us the problem on day one, we can usually solve it together. Those are the people we make films with again and again. What has been the biggest disruption in traditional indie financing, and how has that changed how you put projects together? Presales stopped covering what they used to. Streamers buy fewer films from independents and pay less for the ones they do buy. So there’s a bigger gap between what a film costs and what’s guaranteed up front. Gap is the new equity. Investors like us now fill part of what used to be covered by sales. That means we build the film around the money from the start. We look at cast, genre and budget together, before the script is locked. We stay with low-cost, high-concept projects: action, thriller, horror. We also watch how much we have riding on any one genre or sales agent at a time. Head Gear scored a cross-over arthouse hit with ‘How to Have Sex’ from Molly Manning Walker Courtesy MUBI mk2 Films/Nikos Nikolopoulos How was Almost You financed? It’s a mix. Tax credit money from the U.K., a lender borrowing against it [us], some money from sales to territories, and equity from the producers and partners. Bankside came on early with the cast, which helped make the sales numbers believable. How is the creator economy affecting indie film? Creators have something indie films have always struggled to buy: an audience that already knows them. That matters more than ever because marketing a small film is hard and expensive. A creator with millions of followers brings people before the film is released. But a big following doesn’t automatically turn into cinema tickets. Watching a free video is very different from paying to see a film. The ones who will make it work are the creators who treat a film like a real production: proper script, proper budget, proper distribution plan. I’m interested in that. I’m not interested in a follower count on its own. But most of all it’s about great storytellers, whether they are from the creator economy or not. What’s been the biggest surprise for you, and which title (whatever the commercial success) are you most proud of? There’s a lot that I’m surprised that failed so badly, but on a more positive note: from a commercial perspective, it’s got to be Talk to Me . No one knew that it was going to do the incredible business it did. It changed global strategies for many distribution companies. On a more controversial note, it’s got to be The Apprentice , which talked to me in many ways. I’m always fascinated at the power movies can have globally. It was really the story of Frankenstein, how a monster was made. It’s the original horror — Trump is Frankenstein. It was almost “reality horror.” We got a cease and desist from Trump on the day of the film’s world premiere in Cannes, and of course we threw it in the bin … The way all the filmmakers went about making and releasing it is truly punk rock. Sebastian Stan as Donald Trump in ‘The Apprentice.’ Pief Weyman/Rich Spirit What project did you learn the most from, in terms of your approach to the business? It’s got to be my second feature, Chunky Monkey , which I made in 2000 in the early days of my producing career. The great Greg Cruttwell wrote and directed it, and I was the sole producer — in the days when there was only one producer credit. Some folk called it a cult movie, others were disgusted by it. [The comedy features, among other things, a Julie Andrews-lookalike prostitute and the obscene use of Chunky Monkey ice cream.] Particularly offended were Rogers & Hammerstein, EMI, Julie Andrews, Unilever and the original creator of the Chunky Monkey comic strip [Pauline Comanor], all of whom tried to sue us and totally failed. [Comanor] claimed Ben & Jerry stole the name from her. Unilever, who bought the ice cream manufacturers, were incensed about the nature of our depiction of “finding another pleasurable” use for the ice cream. EMI was being forced by the very conservative Rogers and Hammerstein [estate] to withdraw its signed agreement with us. We rerecorded “The Hills Are Alive With the Sound of Music” with our Black Jesus singing and the pink panther playing the bongos. Julie Andrews just didn’t get our love note to her … I got more column inches over the period of a month than any studio movie. It was a David and Goliath story that stole the front page of many newspapers. The film was harmless, and it just shows you how people react without really reviewing the facts. While the film made no money, it was pirated a lot and got a cult following and put me on the map as a producer. I made sure everyone in the industry knew me after that. I realized then this business is all about marketing.” THR

articles.title: ‘Tangled’ Takes Ciudad de la Luz From Up-and-Coming Studio to Production Must-Stop
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The morning sun hits Studio Ciudad de la Luz. Publicity For the team at Studio Ciudad de la Luz, 2026 is the year it went from an up-and-coming shoot destination to a top-tier must-stop for major international productions. In Alicante, this large-scale film and TV hub was born from the vision of Spanish filmmaker and screenwriter Luis García Berlanga, who in 2005 set out to reindustrialize the Spanish audiovisual sector. That initial seven-year phase culminated in 63 projects, including J.A. Bayona’s The Impossible and Francis Ford Coppola’s Tetro . Studio Ciudad de la Luz reopened in 2023 with a renewed intention to set itself apart from its rivals. Boasting state-of-the-art facilities, it has six climate-controlled stages, interconnected in pairs, and two indoor, floodable pits that come in at over three metres deep. Among its signature draws is the outdoor water tank, a 100-by-80-meter facility with wave-generation systems, water cannons, slides, a seawater pumping system and partial fill-and-drain capability. The backlot totals 14.8 hectares of space with natural horizon, power, water and telecommunications, over 4,000 square meters of workshop space and 7,000 square meters of storage space, with three production support buildings hosting dressing rooms, make-up, hair, offices and services. Related Stories Movies 'Exotic' Takes Us to Polish Pole Dance Camp to Tell a Female Story of Self-Discovery and Body Confidence Movies Producers Push for Year-End Passage of Trump-Backed Federal Film Incentive: AFM And from 2023 to 2025, this production eden was a well-kept secret. Among some of their projects during that time period were Venom: The Last Dance with Tom Hardy, generating 35 million euros and 570 contracts, as well as The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon , which shot in the aforementioned water tank, the French Netflix shows Nero and Under Paris , as well as Alberto Rodriguez’ Los Tigres and Alejandro Amenabar’s El Cautivo , which had an estimated economic impact of eight million Euros. But the word is officially out. This year, the studio has found industry consolidation in two projects of significant scale: Disney’s live-action Tangled and the permanent establishment of The Good Film Studios Spain , helping Ciudad de la Luz absorb some of the most technically and logistically demanding shoots with newfound confidence. Ciudad de la Luz is currently the only facility in Europe that allows indoor, outdoor and aquatic filming on the same site. That kind of versatility — paired with a warm-weather climate, competitive incentives and an experienced local crew — is attracting the eyeballs of producers across the globe. A shot from the outdoor water tank at Studio Ciudad de la Luz. Publicity Michael Gracey’s Tangled , produced by Kristin Burr, has emerged as a case-in-point example of what’s possible at this production behemoth. The original 2010 animation, following Rapunzel’s team-up with a local outlaw, the devilish Flynn Rider, was a smash hit that swiftly accrued nearly $600 million at the global box office. Set for a 2028 theatrical release and starring Teagan Croft, Milo Manheim and Kathryn Hahn, the new era of Tangled was shot at Studio Ciudad de la Luz over 10 months from February to October this year and involved the intensive use of stages, on-site exteriors and locations across the region of Valencia. Its direct economic impact on Ciudad de la Luz is currently over 40 million euros, with more than 1,000 professionals mobilized on the project. A whopping 2,500 local contracts were generated by the arrival of this Hollywood production, lending help to the studio’s 90 percent occupancy in 2026. Gracey argues that fellow U.S. execs should consider booking that flight to Alicante. “There’s an extraordinary level of passion and dedication here,” he says ahead of the American Film Market. “That energy comes across on screen.” The filmmaker, best known for his work on The Greatest Showman (2017) and Better Man (2024), said his crew was able to combine exterior and interior stages, “and it feels real,” he adds. “You don’t notice the transition.” He sings the praises of the local crews and scenery here in southeast Spain. The region certainly gives Los Angeles a run for its money, attracting more than 300 days of sunshine a year and diverse landscapes such as beaches, mountains, salt flats and protected natural areas. With the bustling Spanish town of Alicante, an international airport, and hotel capacity of over 70,000 beds in the surrounding area, Gracey lauds the no-fuss environment: “The people, the locations and the spaces have been fantastic. Having the city only 15 minutes away is a real advantage.” Burr even hails it as her “favorite location.” She explains: “The stages are among the most spectacular I’ve ever worked on [and] I’m extremely impressed by the level of dedication we’ve seen on the sets. I’m very demanding when it comes to production design, and I think this is some of the best I’ve seen in my career.” As vocal advocates of Studio Ciudad de la Luz, Gracey and Burr are in good company. Top producer Miriam Segal founded the Good Films Collective in 2007, established to develop and finance “intelligent, inclusive and commercially ambitious independent films.” Now, her joint venture with the Spanish government and Canadian-U.S. outfit Orogen Media, The Good Films Studios Spain has set up a permanent home at Studio Ciudad de la Luz, bringing with it an investment of 19.8 million Euros from the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT) and private partners. With the arrival of Segal’s Spanish branch here in Alicante — a long-term commitment eyeing 20 international features over the next 10 years — her company has evolved from rising production outfit to integrated studio business. “It’s the best crew I’ve worked with anywhere in the world,” says Segal, known for The Infiltrator (2016) with Bryan Cranston and The Postcard Killings (2020) with Jeffrey Dean Morgan. The Good Films Studios Spain have set their first film out of the Alicante hub: People of the Book , directed by Michael Haussman and based on the novel of the same name written by Pulitzer Prize-winning author Geraldine Brooks. The cast includes Ziad Bakri, Rania Ben Fattoum, Ankido Hussen, Luca Ferrini, Giorgia Sinicorni, Pasquale Esposito and Jose Luis Ferrier, who filmed in the studio’s outdoor water tank, as well as on their stages and workshops. It isn’t just the expansive facilities drawing the industry’s most prolific producers and crews, but the territory’s expertly trained ecosystem of graduates. The Film Trades School initiative, developed in collaboration with the country’s leading film school, Escola Superior de Cinema i Audiovisuals de Catalunya (ESCAC), has upskilled thousands of students across more than 30 specialisms, including set construction, lighting, camera, sound, VFX, green filming, costume, production, who are able to come and hone their craft at Studio Ciudad de la Luz. Regional and national tax incentives continue to be a real weapon in the team’s arsenal. A non-repayable grant of 25 percent on production and post-production expenditure is available in Valencia for a maximum relief of 1.5 million Euros per project. At the country-wide level, Spanish productions and co-productions can claim 30 percent of the first million and 25 percent on the remainder back, capped at 20 million Euros per production. For foreign shoots in Spain, it’s the exact same, but the minimum spend in the country must total at least one million Euros. Ciudad de la Luz and the region of Valencia are hopeful they’ve consolidated their position as a real and competitive option in the league of Europe’s most demanding production destinations. And the knock-on effect so far is palpable: “When the Region of Valencia believes in itself,” begins Marián Cano, the regional minister for industry, tourism, innovation and trade, “it can compete with anyone to attract top-level projects.” THR

articles.title: ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: Nicholas Hoult Delivers Adrenalized Big Finance Payback That Entertains Despite Its Tonal Mishmash
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Nicholas Hoult in 'How to Rob a Bank.' Megan Schoenbachler/Amazon MGM Studios If the midterm elections were not indication enough that Americans are feeling the pinch and hitting back at a system heavily rigged to favor obscene wealth and unchecked power, high-octane action specialist David Leitch ’s How to Rob a Bank offers further evidence. A kinetic heist thriller in which we root for the thieves — Mark Bianculli’s script name-checks Point Break , swapping Ex-Presidents for animal masks — the good-looking movie doesn’t reconcile its twin identities as a crime caper with a satirical edge and a poignant social justice fantasy. But a strong ensemble keeps things moving. Related Stories Movies David Leitch's 'How to Rob a Bank': First Reactions Movies How David Leitch Made 'How to Rob a Bank' on a Budget -- and Around Nicholas Hoult's Torn ACL Following up on the breezy insouciance of The Fall Guy , Leitch directs with his foot planted firmly on the accelerator, reassembling his trusty core team of DP Jonathan Sela, production designer David Scheunemann, composer Dom Lewis and editor Elísabet Ronaldsdóttir. If the early action overloads on YouTube interface and quippy content creation, that’s amply justified in the script, though it’s a relief when the movie takes time to breathe and allow the characters some depth. How to Rob a Bank The Bottom Line Now is the winter of our collective discontent. Release date : Friday, Nov. 13 Cast : Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz, Anna Sawai, Rhenzy Feliz, Pete Davidson, John C. Reilly, Christian Slater, Paul Sparks, Tati Gabrielle, Young Mazino, Alessandra Frugoli Director : David Leitch Screenwriter : Mark Bianculli Rated R, 2 hours 2 minutes Nicholas Hoult plays underdog antihero Ryan, aka “The Wolf,” who leads a close-knit crew of Pittsburgh bank robbers and fronts their popular online videos in a furry lupine mask. “Content is king,” he says in voiceover narration, explaining that an audience is more powerful than a gun. Their YouTube show is widely known by the acronym HTRAB and the catchphrase, “Who’s hungry?” It plays not only tightly edited footage of their daring bank escapades, providing tips for a growing number of copycat robbers across the country, but also their “pay it forward” philosophy of tossing cash at bank employees and customers, distributing larger sums to charities like schools, churches and hospitals. At a time when the American Dream is accessible only to the top wealth bracket, these bad guys are good guys, and they make it look easy. Says Ryan: “You’re more likely to live your entire life under the poverty line than get caught stealing your way out from under it.” The HTRAB crew includes Ryan’s partner Emi ( Anna Sawai ), the getaway driver and strategist, an expert at creating diversions to keep law enforcement occupied; combat vet Vince ( Pete Davidson ), who found that after he fought for his country in Afghanistan, his VA health insurance was not prepared to fight for him the same way; and tech wizard Hugo (Rhenzy Feliz), who shapes the YouTube content. Like many of their millions of followers — burdened by student debt and shrinking job opportunities, the goal of home ownership and medical coverage remaining out of reach — Ryan & Co. share a common bond of having run out of options. Bankrupted by medical bills and predatory money-lending policies, he and Emi struggle to accept tragedy that might have been forestalled with more available means. Hugo and Vince, who’s up against a ticking clock, are just desperate to provide for their families. While the robberies are diverting enough and the YouTube inserts splashed with pop-up graphics, the fun wears a bit thin, which makes the shift into trauma and pathos a welcome one, even if the transition might have been smoother. Basically, it turns into a different movie. The cast compensates for any shortage of fluidity, however, notably Hoult and Sawai, whose sexy body language counters the lacerating sorrow and anger left by a devastating loss; and Davidson, who curbs his comedy instincts to show uncustomary shadings. His final scene in the movie is intensely moving, in what’s arguably the actor’s best performance since The King of Staten Island . Feliz, best known for Marvel’s Runaways and HBO’s The Penguin , is given less to do, but his sparky personality makes him a magnetic presence. Having pulled off 15 bank robberies over three months and triggered a 400 percent increase in similar operations nationwide, the HTRAB bandits remain frustratingly elusive to the FBI. Nearing retirement and unwilling to go out on a failure, veteran agent John West ( John C. Reilly ) refuses to accept his team’s lack of leads. He recruits coding genius Reagan (Zoë Kravitz) to examine the hours of YouTube material for clues and patterns. An associate professor at Carnegie Mellon, Reagan is now serving time under house arrest on a hacking charge. She’s resistant at first, reluctant to break her routine of bong hits and junk food, not to mention sympathetic to the robbers’ cause. But West wins her over with an exchange that will wipe her slate clean. Reagan is a very cool character who gives Kravitz plenty of room to inject sly humor and irreverent attitude, even just via the low-key running joke of her constant eating in every scene. Initially looking to hunt down a deadbeat ex-boyfriend, she developed a tracking program called FYPOS (“Fuck You Piece of Shit”) designed to locate people via their social media activity. That becomes an essential tool in the FBI investigation. But after giving Reagan an intriguing setup, Bianculli’s script runs out of ideas for the character, relegating her to observer status for much of the climactic stretch. Reilly is put to better use as an old-school agency man set on doing his job, but with enough misfortune behind him to understand what drives Ryan and his crew. The chaotically plotted penultimate act involves West closing in during the “big finish” that the HTRAB team have been carefully plotting for months. That involves their agenda getting personal as they hit heavyweight financial institution Vitality Trust. That monolith is run by David Walton (Christian Slater), an arrogant asshole whose merciless loan scheme was designed to reap huge profits once the borrowers had been bled dry. The volatile mob of HTRAB followers gathered in the blocks surrounding VT inevitably recalls the wealth inequality protests of 2011 that began near Wall Street and spread to cities across the country, including Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles and Seattle. That brings a stirring “power to the people” sentiment, even as Ryan’s determination to complete their plan seems doomed once the Feds know their identities. But the movie keeps a few tricks up its sleeve for a satisfying coda. The narrative’s plot holes and contrivances don’t reward close inspection, but as an avenging underdog fairy tale pieced together from the shards of the American Dream, it’s fast-paced, entertaining and surprisingly emotional. That’s due in no small part to the soulful qualities the principals bring to their roles. Sela’s muscular camerawork, Lewis’ pulse-racing score and Ronaldsdóttir’s punchy editing all play vital parts, as do the energizing needle drops. These range from the pounding dubstep beats of “Victory Lap,” by Fred Again, Skepta and PlaqueBoyMax through the garage revival of The Hives, the alternative rock of Jane’s Addiction and the gorgeous, whispery vocals of Billie Eilish. The use of Radiohead’s haunting anti-corporate anthem “Karma Police” over one heartbreaking scene is a master stroke. How to Rob a Bank is not without flaws; there are times in the early action when it risks repeating the far-too-pleased-with-itself flashiness of Leitch’s numbing 2022 assault on the senses, Bullet Train . But there’s unexpected heart and a finger on the zeitgeist here that at least ensure it’s never dull — a mainstream commercial anti-capitalist movie in these rollercoaster times is a rare thing. Full credits Release date: Friday, Nov. 13 Production companies: 87North Productions, Imagine Entertainment, Amazon MGM Studios Distribution: Amazon MGM Cast: Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz, Anna Sawai, Rhenzy Feliz, Pete Davidson, John C. Reilly, Christian Slater, Paul Sparks, Tati Gabrielle, Young Mazino, Alessandra Frugoli Director: David Leitch Screenwriter: Mark Bianculli Producers: Brian Grazer, Jeb Brody, Allan Mandelbaum, Kelly McCormick, David Leitch Executive producers: Ben Ormand, Mark Bianculli Director of photography: Jonathan Sela Production designer: David Scheunemann Costume designer: Jocelyn Pierce Music: Dom Lewis Editor: Elísabet Ronaldsdóttir Sound designers: Pat Haskill, Ryan Nowak, Gregorio Gomez Stunt designer: Greg Rementer Casting: Mary Vernieu, Lindsay Graham Ahanonu Rated R, 2 hours 2 minutes THR

articles.title: ‘GTA 6’ vs. Hollywood: Industry Braces for “Biggest Entertainment Launch in History”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 6:16am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Amazon MGM’s new season of 'Rings of Power' and Lionsgate's latest 'Hunger Games' installment are bowing right as 'Grand Theft Auto VI' is poised to dominate the entertainment landscape. Illustrated by Cat Sims Logo text Are gamers who have waited 13 years to return to Vice City really going to spend their time in Panem, Middle-earth, and the Underworld instead? The massively anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI , coming Nov. 19, will land amid a slew of expensive and high-profile movies and returning TV shows dropping within several days of each other. Most of them offer their own escapist fantasy worlds that will compete in the attention economy with a title that’s expected to be the biggest video game launch in history. Season three of Amazon-MGM’s The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is rolling out episodes over three weeks beginning Nov. 11 and Johnny Depp’s comeback vehicle Ebenezer lands Nov. 13. Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens the day after GTA 6 launches on Nov. 20 along with the fourth season of the studio’s Paramount+ hit Yellowjackets . The same day, Disney rolls out the third season of Percy Jackson and the Olympians . Five days down the road comes Amazon MGM’s limited series Blade Runner 2099 . “It’s going to be a watershed moment for not only the gaming industry but also all the folks in the media and entertainment industry who are going to have to deal with the fact that eyeballs are going to be leaving their environments to go play GTA 6 ,” said Bart Spiegel, global media, entertainment, gaming and sports leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers. It’s indeed tough to overstate the earthquake GTA6 is expected to create in terms of entertainment spending, distraction hours and pop culture noise. The Rockstar Games project has a first-year sales forecast of 45 million copies and $3.2 billion in sales — a figure which would top all-time box office champ Avengers: Endgame . A whopping 29 percent of U.S. gamers expect to purchase the title and one economist suggested, rather wildly, that the game would cost the U.S. economy $1 billion in lost productivity due to PTO requests. Other video game publishers have run for the hills and surrendered November to Rockstar’s sun-drenched, pastel-colored 800-pound gorilla. “I think GTA 6 will be the biggest entertainment launch in history,” predicts Geoff Keighley, gaming industry producer and entrepreneur behind The Game Awards . “Not just as a game in terms of dollars it will make — this will easily trump Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three — but how much it will impact moviegoing, streaming, and the way people spend their time. Hollywood should look at the hours as closely as the dollars because GTA 6 is going to be some people’s entertainment plan for the rest of the year, basically. The entertainment industry has never really seen something like this before.” While the game’s core mission will likely take around 80 hours to complete — which alone is a massive amount of hours for one title — the title is also an open world environment where players tend to return again and again, and insiders assume the game will allow some kind of online multiplayer mode as well. “So this is not just about opening weekend,” Keighley says. But for Hollywood, which is accustomed to largely owning the entertainment attention economy, particularly around the holidays, the impact of GTA 6 seems almost certainly to be felt — if difficult to measure. Spiegel noted streaming is likely to take the biggest hit because a console game directly competes for viewing hours on living room TVs. Last year’s fourth quarter streaming numbers were rather strong, he noted, but he suspects GTA 6 could put a real dent in the year-over-year comps. The live urgency of sports viewing, however, will be safer from erosion than entertainment programming. “But trust me, if that game gets boring, GTA 6 is going on pretty soon,” he quipped. Behind the scenes, streamers are increasingly aware GTA 6 is coming and that Jason and Lucia might rob some of their viewers. “Everybody is rumbling about how big this game is going to be,” says a representative working with one potentially impacted streaming title. On the film side, a major exhibitor executive said it’s “tough to know” the effect on films like Ebenezer and Sunrise on the Reaping. “ It’s hardly come up in internal discussions, but anyone in the industry who’s ever been a gamer — or who lives with someone who is — knows it’ll have some impact,” he said. “Hunger Games presales are strong, which might point to it being solid counter programming. Ebenezer presales are dire, but I doubt GTA6 is the main reason. We’ll have to see how walkup sales go.” Future box office heavy hitters like Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three , which open “Dunesday” Dec. 18. Such titles would seem to fall outside the game’s blast radius, but perhaps not. Spiegel has noted the game’s “pull could last through December.” While hardcore gamers will rush out and play GTA 6 the first few weeks, others will hold off until they have more free time during the December holidays, while some kids (with rather permissive parents) won’t even be unwrapping the presumably Mature-rated game until Christmas. Music will be disrupted, too, with the game’s 34-song soundtrack already at 26 million monthly listens on Spotify and a 30-track original score by Justice coming Dec. 11. One as-yet-unappreciated aspect of the game’s gravitational pull will be on social media, where you’re already starting to see anticipatory videos (such as a boyfriend getting his girlfriend a kitten so she won’t bother him while playing the game, or another boyfriend who seemingly wrote up a contract pledging a list of compromises if his girlfriend doesn’t, yes, bother him while playing the game). But social media is also massive part of entertainment marketing — not just direct advertising but fan-generated content that helps programs generate buzz and become part of the cultural conversation. But what happens if GTA 6 becomes all anybody is talking about? “It’s going to take over live streaming and clips and content creators,” Keighley says. “Barbenheimer worked because you could go see Barbie and Oppenheimer , and you only needed five or six hours. People will still go see other things, but I think the entertainment value has to be extremely high.” This story appeared in the Nov. 12 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Next Gen 2026: 35 Rising Hollywood Executives Under 35
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Next Gen execs were photographed Oct. 26 and Oct. 30 at PMC Studios in Los Angeles. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Nobody ever said that Hollywood careers come easy. But right now, with consolidation and layoffs decimating the middle rungs of entertainment’s steep corporate ladder and studio remits changing with each earnings report, dream jobs have never been more difficult to land, much less retain. Such trends aren’t slowing the ascent of THR ’s Next Gen class of 2026, who join such illustrious alumni as Donna Langley, Ari Emanuel, Kevin Feige and Peter Rice. In fact, this group is too busy forging new paths through the chaos — whether that’s bringing Gen Z back to cinemas (as indie producer Christian Vazquez did with both Primetime and You Can See Everything ) or fortifying the streaming ecosystem amid endless churn (see Claudia Shin and Louie Hayes, behind the Apple TV Emmy darling Widow’s Bay and the Prime Video breakout Sterling Point , respectively.) Meet the 35 executives and reps, each of them 35 years old or younger, who should be atop your call list, if they aren’t already. Alyssa Altman, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion RK Films, senior vp LOGLINE Championing rom-coms like Anyone But You and Netflix’s upcoming 13 Going on 30 update. THE ARC Altman got a unique view of the industry when she would join her father, Steve, who rented out lighting, camera and grip equipment: “I grew up doing my homework in grip trucks, and I just loved being on set.” Her dad’s rom-com adoration rubbed off during their weekly trips to the movies, where films like Love Actually made an early impression. Altman studied journalism at Emerson but caught the producing bug while moonlighting on college TV projects. After time at Gersh, she became then-Universal exec Jeff Kirschenbaum’s assistant and followed him to RK Films. While the company focused on bigger IP plays, she endorsed the script for Anyone But You (“That was my baby”), Sony’s Sydney Sweeney-Glen Powell feature that became a rare theatrical comedy hit. Up next: Amazon MGM’s tennis rom-com Love Love and Netflix’s Millie Bobby Brown-led Just Picture It . PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Andy Cohen. My favorite way to de-stress after a long day is to watch and listen to the soothing sound of people fighting on Bravo.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “The fact that movies geared towards women do great theatrically. Every time it happens, people act like it’s an anomaly. Women are starved for content and it’s not a coincidence.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “When I was an assistant at Universal, we set up a screening for an A-list star who specifically requested popcorn from the Universal Studios theme park. I had to sneak into the park through the back lot and bring it back before he arrived.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Sally Albright from When Harry Met Sally . She isn’t afraid to speak her mind, is a hopeless romantic, and has strong opinions on how she orders her food.” Jenna Berger, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Marvel Studios, director of production development LOGLINE Berger is serving as co-producer, and Kevin Feige’s right hand, on Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars . ’Nuff said. THE ARC An L.A. native with industry parents, Berger grew up wanting to make movies. “I had this theory that everybody who didn’t want to make movies was lying to themselves and secretly did,” she says. So, shortly after graduating from University of Pennsylvania with a double major in English and film, she landed a gig at The Mark Gordon Co. Still, it was Marvel that was making some of her favorite films — she saw Spider-Man: Homecoming four times in the theater — but the company felt impenetrable … until it wasn’t. In 2019, Berger scored a position, rising to junior exec before finding herself the solo exec on the Marvel TV series Ms. Marvel , where she earned a supervising producer credit and honed her creative leadership, talent development and production expertise. “It was the best crash course in figuring out how this company worked and making something worthy of the Marvel name,” she says. The higher-ups took note, which is why Berger now oversees some of the studio’s most ambitious films. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Kermit the Frog. Because my job is to bring amazingly talented people together to make something special amid total chaos … which sometimes means convincing everyone the show must go on before the set falls down around us.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “David Heyman. To get to work on Bond and Harry Potter?! A dream. Would love to trade places for a day … or forever.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Having a sneeze attack while leaving a voicemail for Aaron Sorkin on behalf of my boss.” Natalie Berkus, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion LuckyChap, senior vp TV LOGLINE Developing (and producing) your future TV obsessions, including Andrew Garfield’s Wild Things . THE ARC Rather than follow her agent dad and comedy writer mom into the business, Berkus arrived at University of Michigan eager to be a lawyer. “Then I rushed the law fraternity and didn’t get in,” she says. “I mean, I whiffed it and was like, ‘Shit, now what do I do?’ ” The answer, it turns out, was to parlay her love of TV into a series of PA gigs on shows like The Mindy Project before talking her way into a job as the writers assistant on Girls and, later, with Lena Dunham and Jenni Konner’s company. From there, she logged six years at Imagine Entertainment, where she was intimately involved in a slate that included The ’Burbs and the upcoming Siegfried and Roy series starring Garfield and Jude Law for Apple TV. But LuckyChap came calling a year ago, and the L.A. native and new mom to daughter Roonie jumped at the opportunity to work at the Margot Robbie-led hit factory. In that time, she has built a roster of 10 to 15 projects, including a Life Is Strange series for Amazon Prime Video. Still, Berkus doesn’t take herself too seriously. “If I had to brand myself, I’d say I like to bring a levity to this business,” she says, “because I think sometimes, especially now, things can get really stressful and we lose sight of the fact that ultimately this is just one big party.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Nina Rosenstein, who does all of the HBO comedy specials. We’ve never met, but Nina, girl, if you’re reading this, let’s link and get our Freaky Friday moment started!” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “That having unapproachable girlboss ‘I’m smarter than you’ energy is cool. It’s not, it’s lame! Normalize the quiet power in validating others and having a fun vibe.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Nowhere are you crazy!! No more of these!!” Mandi Brooksbank, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Netflix, senior manager, business affairs, scripted series LOGLINE Helps mold Netflix’s scripted slate, brokering deals with top talent like Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media. THE ARC As a kid in Reno, Nevada, Brooksbank figured she was destined for Broadway. While most her age were on the playground, she was busy with casino shows, doing dinner theater (and playing the harp) in vintage Hollywood glam. “It was entertainment or bust,” she recalls with a laugh. Later, she’d speedrun undergrad at USC and law school at Southwestern, finishing both in five years. Since then, she’s built a Hollywood résumé that includes stints at CAA, Donaldson Callif Perez and eOne. Now in her fifth year at Netflix, Brooksbank helps steer the streamer’s scripted series unit, striking deal after deal with TV’s biggest names. It’s a high volume affair, with Brooksbank managing a slate that includes The Altruists , Ransom Canyon and Sirens , among many others. “I’m the third child in a family of six,” she says of her negotiating chops. “They all have big personalities, so they prepared me well for Hollywood.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Miss Piggy.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Women directors’ second and third films. We talk about breaking through, but what about career longevity?” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “When I was considering law school, Patti Felker encouraged me to see being a woman as an advantage in negotiations, particularly the ability to read people, adapt and adjust your approach to the person across the table without losing sight of what you’re there to accomplish.” Barry Buren, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion CAA, TV talent agent LOGLINE Makes deals for A-listers including Pedro Pascal, Matthew Rhys, Steven Yeun and Eddie Redmayne. THE ARC Hollywood has Orlando’s Central Florida Talent agency to thank for putting Buren on his path. After the New Jersey native graduated a semester early from nearby Rollins College, he picked up a gig at the model/talent agency to stay near friends who were still in school. Though he imagined he might become an engineer someday, he accepted an L.A.-based relative’s offer to live with her while giving Hollywood a try. As luck would have it, agenting stuck, and after a stint at Gersh, the avid golfer joined CAA in 2014. Today, the married rep is entrusted by actors including Josh Hartnett, Charlie Hunnam and Hannah Waddingham. Earlier this fall, client (and double Emmy winner) Rhys gave Buren a shout-out from the Emmy stage. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Serving coffee to people in an order determined by seniority and annual earnings. It was my first introduction to the Hollywood hierarchy, and I learned very quickly that even caffeine has a pecking order.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Being on a call with 15 people to schedule another call with 15 people, only to discover that the one person who actually needed to be there wasn’t invited.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Lorne Michaels. To have spent five decades at the intersection of comedy, culture, and discovering talent is pretty remarkable.” Winnie Carrillo Montiel, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Amazon MGM, film executive, production & development LOGLINE Oversees films that range from bro-y actioners ( The Wrecking Crew ) to weepy love stories ( Honeymoon With Harry ). THE ARC Carrillo Montiel’s career in entertainment began with a clerical error. As an Emerson undergrad, she was mistakenly admitted as a screenwriting major instead of the literature and publishing program she had applied to. She ended up staying the course, eventually doubling down by attending graduate school at USC’s famed Peter Stark Producing Program. While there, she landed a temp job in MGM’s film group, which she did by day, leaving classes for night. Ultimately, it was the studio’s then-president Jonathan Glickman who helped push through the Guatemala City native’s visa sponsorship to land her her first full-time Hollywood gig. “He just made me promise that I wouldn’t get my green card and leave,” she remembers. “This was almost a decade ago and I’m still here. So, I really kept my promise.” Carrillo Montiel has since survived several regime changes, not to mention an acquisition, to land at her current spot on Amazon MGM’s film team, where she has overseen such films as The Sheep Detectives and an upcoming slate with projects from Dan Fogelman ( Honeymoon ) and Michael Showalter (a Serendipity reimagining). One of her proudest accomplishments is shepherding Angel Manuel Soto’s The Wrecking Crew , explaining, “Latinos are often put in a very specific box, and we are only hired to tell Latino-specific stories. I’m always looking for opportunities to elevate talent that I think are just great filmmakers.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Unlimited budgets.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “I was advised to look for an American husband as I was told it would be impossible for me to earn a work visa in this industry.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Cold calling very specific animal experts in Russia and Brazil to attempt to track down recent sightings of extremely large species of bears and snakes.” Margaret Clark, 32 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion 20th Television, director of development LOGLINE Manages a roster of overall deals (Liz Meriwether, Drew Goddard) and development projects, including the Hulu hit Furious . THE ARC Technically speaking, Clark was discovered at the Panera on South Beverly Drive. Now, she’s working on Pagans , the Steven Yeun-led supernatural drama series that sparked a major bidding war won by Netflix. When she’s off the clock, Massaro’s often either walking her golden retriever or baking. TALENT I’D DIE TO WORK WITH “Zach Cregger or Megan Park.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Carl from Up , for many reasons but most importantly because I also have an adopted golden retriever obsessed with squirrels like Dug.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Bringing my dad to the Porject Hail Mary premiere and getting a photo of him standing next to the back of Ryan Gosling’s head.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “How female executives throughout both film and TV are being pushed out of decision-making roles.” Erick Mendoza, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Untitled, manager LOGLINE In early on writers and filmmakers like Primetime ’s Ajon Singh and Lurker ’s Alex Russell. THE ARC In high school, Mendoza spent an hour on the 405 each way from his home in Inglewood to Brentwood School as part of the Young Eisner Scholars program that helps place talented kids from around L.A. at elite private schools. There, he learned Hollywood was a career path, as many of the school’s parents were agents, lawyers and execs, including Dawn Ostroff, then head of The CW, where he interned. USC and the UTA mailroom came next before he settled at management firm Grandview. “My first day, I’m building my desk from an Amazon box, but also got to attend the big staff meeting,” he recalls. Lurker ’s Russell was an early client (he won two Indie Spirits this year). His list also includes Kalos Chu, a former DreamWorks Animation assistant who sold the elite university pitch Imposter to HBO in a bidding war. Mendoza was also behind The Waffle House Index ’s splashy sale to Apple from Andrew Nunnelly, with Inde Navarrette starring. And Ajon Singh hit it big with his spec Primetime , which became the A24 movie starring Robert Pattinson. MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “ Curb Your Enthusiasm , season nine, episode nine. I’m somewhere in the background.” TALENT I’D DIE TO WORK WITH “Alex Garland.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Sorting through fan mail for the Vampire Diaries cast. People sent some gnarly stuff.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D LOVE TO TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “CEO of LEGO … my nephews would find that very cool.” Samantha Militante, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion FX, vp current series LOGLINE Guides FX series including Adults to a bigger and far buzzier season two. THE ARC Militante’s love of TV began with Filipino soap operas, which she spent her Orange County childhood devouring with her mom and grandma. Initially, it was a way to learn their language. “Then I just fell in love with the bonkers storytelling,” she says, following that passion all the way to Chapman, where she got her film school degree in three years and managed to squeeze in roughly 10 internships in the process. “It was aggressive,” she jokes, but it set her on a path, ultimately landing at Gersh, where she’d meet her future husband (and fellow Next Gen honoree) Louie Hayes. In fact, it was Hayes who first jumped to FX and later put Militante, then just his friend, up for a job. In the decade since, she’s been intimately involved in projects like Reservation Dogs , What We Do in the Shadows and the zoomer hit Adults . Despite her “current” executive title, the self-proclaimed foodie has also, at various points, been deployed to develop new shows, oversee a doc slate and work with short-form content. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “When the stand-in on a Wendy’s shoot called in sick, I was the only brown person on set, so naturally I got promoted from PA. Ate a lot of hamburgers that day. No spit bucket.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Riding a private jet for the first time to go to a film festival. Also, getting on this list with my husband.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “There is such a thing as stupid questions.” IT WAS FROM … “My internship supervisor when I asked about my pay.” Sam Rabinowitz, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion WME, talent agent LOGLINE Confidant of A-listers Teyana Taylor, Austin Butler, Nicolas Cage and Dwayne Johnson. THE ARC Rabinowitz’s early education in the art of the cold call came from a college-era internship selling life insurance for Northwestern Mutual. “It was amazing prep for this whole business because it’s just rejection every day,” says the Cornell grad, who entered Hollywood via another internship (at Paradigm) before ultimately landing in the WME mailroom and working his way up to assistant, going into the office seven days a week. In those days, the Rochester, New York, native lived so cheaply that he didn’t have Wi-Fi at his apartment, and would go to a nearby Starbucks for Wi-Fi so that he could stream shows like Dwayne Johnson’s Ballers . Now, Rabinowitz is on Johnson’s team, as he is for Taylor (who just directed her first movie, Paramount’s Get Lite ), Butler (filming Joe Kosinski’s Miami Vice ’85 ) and Cage (starring in the next season of True Detective ). In recent years, he also signed Dave Bautista, now starring in Amazon’s God of War , and helped Will Poulter go from well-regarded actor to TV producer on Apple’s Beat the Reaper . His roster also includes Lukas Gage, who just wrapped on the Prison Break revival , and Michael Gandolfini , who just shot a role in Daniels’ untitled Universal movie. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “George Costanza.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Getting a Vitamin D deficiency from spending every hour of daylight in the mailroom.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “The Fountain Room.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “It’s a relationship business.” Claudia Shin, 33 Image Credit: Courtesy of Subject Chum Films, senior vp film and TV LOGLINE Guides projects including Emmy darling Widow’s Bay for Hiro Murai’s busy production shingle. THE ARC How did a biomedical engineering major at Yale end up at one of Hollywood’s coolest production companies? For Shin, the story began with the Spike Jonze film Her . The 2013 movie inspired the Pasadena native to take a film class. Before long, she was taking on a second major in film and, later, landing a gig in UTA’s mailroom. “I thought I’d just start it off in Hollywood, and then really one job led to another and I never left,” she says. While working at Paramount TV Studios, she reconnected with Atlanta director-producer Murai, a client of a former UTA boss, and they hit it off. When Murai launched his first production company, Super Frog, Shin was his first hire. She’s worked with Murai ever since (now at his Chum Films), through season one of Amazon Prime’s Mr. & Mrs. Smith to FX’s The Bear and Apple’s Widow’s Bay , which Shin produced. When she’s not on set, you can find her taking coffee meetings at her climbing gym, doing karaoke in Koreatown or traveling the world with her partner. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Calvin from Calvin and Hobbes .” IF I HAD ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Teleportation powers, so that I can be on set and sleep in my own bed.” Alix Taylor, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Gloria Sanchez, head of TV LOGLINE Oversees a slate of nearly a dozen upcoming projects, including adaptations of Dream State and Prep . THE ARC Raised two blocks from her public library in Atlanta, Taylor was a self-proclaimed “psychotic reader.” In fact, she says, “We’d joke that when my mom was working, she’d drop me there and that was my day care.” Fittingly, she became a comparative literature major at Brown, though Taylor thought she, like her mom, would ultimately pursue a career in the art world. There were a few internships and early gigs, but in the end, Hollywood proved more alluring. After a quick stint with producer Nathan Kahane, Taylor found her way to Amazon’s comedy team, where she worked on series like Undone , Modern Love and Overcompensating before jumping to Will Ferrell’s company to run the TV division three and a half years ago. She’s since built a considerable slate, with projects in various stages of development, including several adaptations and one idea loosely inspired by Taylor’s time interning at Christie’s. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Jane from Broadcast News — but not in a depressing way.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Spending every Friday afternoon at my boss’ house turning on and off all the lights to check for burned-out bulbs.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Dramaturgically, this feels like a trap.” Christian Vazquez, 30 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Indie producer LOGLINE Lance Oppenheim’s right hand on You Can See Everything and Primetime . THE ARC If you were a firefighter in the mid-aughts and flashed your badge at Long Beach’s Regal movie theater, they’d usher you in for free. Such was the experience of Vazquez and his two siblings thanks to their firefighter dad, an immigrant from Mexico. Vazquez was a driven student and track athlete, and ultimately made his way to Harvard, where he met Oppenheim, who asked for his help producing his senior thesis film. That film became the Sundance darling Some Kind of Heaven , about the Villages retirement community in Florida. Spermworld and the HBO docuseries Ren Faire followed, but nothing compares to this year’s Elizabeth Holmes doc, a box office hit and an Oscar contender. The latter came just weeks after their first narrative feature, the Robert Pattinson starrer Primetime . Vazquez, a hands-on producer who never misses a day on set, has been out of town working on HBO’s Neighbors for the rollout of both films. His firefighter dad (now retired) has attended the premieres in his place, and has been introducing himself to talent, including Nathan Fielder. TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Danny McBride.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Never ask someone to do something you wouldn’t do yourself.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Shelley ‘The Machine’ Levene.” Allie Veneris, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Brillstein, manager LOGLINE Navigating the careers of Cara Delevingne, whom she put in Club Kid , as well as Phil Dunster and Reacher spinoff star Maria Sten. THE ARC The Huntington Beach native grew up as a sports enthusiast who loved softball and golf. She studied film editing at Boulder before a friend suggested becoming a rep: “I was way too extroverted to be an editor,” she says with a laugh. The revelation led to an internship at Brillstein and then stints at Gersh, 360 and Authentic. Amid the strikes, she returned to Brillstein and has leaned into a personal passion for music and sports. The latter space fueled recent wins, like Sophie Nélisse booking Heated Rivalry a month after Veneris set up a general with creator Jacob Tierney. Ted Lasso breakout Dunster — Veneris’ frequent companion for Dodgers and Arsenal games — is not only joining the How to Train Your Dragon live-action franchise but has moved into writing and producing, as has longtime client Jessica Rothe, who leads the TIFF horror favorite River . Thanks to her obsession with online trends, Veneris jumped to work with gymnast-turned-content creator Livvy Dunne — making her acting debut on Fox’s Baywatch reboot — and would not rest until Cara Delevingne landed Club Kid , the Cannes sensation from former viral comedian Jordan Firstman. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “A mix of Liz Lemon ( 30 Rock ), Sutton Brady ( The Bold Type ) and Jimmy from Hacks .” IF I HAD ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH … “To have the attention span of someone who has never heard of TikTok.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Kristen Stewart … and any or all members of Blackpink.” Paige Wandling, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Range, manager LOGLINE Reps hot TV talent Shailene Woodley and Fallout ’s Ella Purnell. THE ARC A hostessing gig at a small Malibu restaurant gave Wandling her earliest brushes with Hollywood notables. “If I thought they could be someone, I would Google them,” she says. “Oh! That’s David Ellison. Oh my God, that’s Nicole Avant and Ted Sarandos.” The Pepperdine grad would have many more such brushes when she moved from ID PR to CAA, where she worked for David Bugliari, whom she’d later follow to Range. After getting a tip from an assistant friend that Woodley had parted ways with her manager, she spent the next year working sources for intel that could woo the actress. One such piece of intel paid off when she learned an actress had dropped out of Michael Mann’s Ferrari . Wandling helped coordinate a meeting between the actress and the filmmaker. Woodley got the part and signed with Range, with Wandling attending the Emmys this to watch her client win for Paradise . The Minneapolis native and former competitive dancer has also guided the careers of Purnell, Gabrielle Union and Furious star Lola Petticrew, who landed the co-lead in the upcoming Assassin’s Creed . MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Finding six dozen sunflowers the Saturday before Oscars Sunday for a client who wanted to decorate a fellow nominee’s hotel room with them.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “The most important thing about any job in representation is to ‘anticipate the need.'” IT WAS FROM … “Publicist Leah Chang.” Caroline Warner, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Apple TV, domestic programming executive LOGLINE Supports some of the streamer’s most ambitious TV bets, from Ascension to Disclaimer . THE ARC “I’ve always been obsessed with TV,” says Warner, who received a script from Charmed for her 10th birthday. The New York native parlayed that passion into a series of internships — at Katie Couric’s short-lived talk show, Piers Morgan Live and at Showtime — while still at Yale and, later, a post-grad gig in the WME mailroom. But after a job at Chernin, she was debating a career pivot, beginning with business school. It was her dad who advised her to try one more gig before deciding. That job was at Apple TV+, where Warner was the fourth-ever hire. Rising through the ranks, she’s now working with Alfonso Cuarón for the second time on his upcoming series Ascension and, already mother to a rescue dog named Winston, is expecting her first child. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Dream: Rory Gilmore. Reality: Paris Geller.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “I feel like this is a cliche but I’d be lying if I said anyone other than Jeff Probst!” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “I had to babysit a puppet for four days on my first business trip. It was awesome.” This story appears in the Nov. 12 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Entertainment 360 Buys Influencer Firm Brigade As It Expands In Creator Economy
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All November 11, 2026 7:04am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'How Long Gone' podcasters Jason Stewart and Chris Black are among Brigade's clients. Roger Kisby/Getty Images Entertainment 360 has accelerated its drive into the creator economy by acquiring Brigade, the creative management firm focused on digital talent. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the acquisition brings elite digital tastemakers, including Substack writers, podcasters and influencers, to the Los Angeles-based talent management company run by a collective of partners as it moves beyond traditional film and TV representation. Brigade founder Max Stein will become a partner at Entertainment 360 and bring his team and clients with him to help the combined company tap a growing influencer universe and manage and monetize celebrity creators coveted by brand marketers. “The ways audiences discover and engage with entertainment have changed, and so have the needs of the talent building careers today,” the Entertainment 360 partners said in a statement. “Max recognized this evolution early and he and his exceptional team have built a remarkable business representing exactly the kind of original, forward-thinking talent we have always sought to work with. Bringing Brigade into 360 expands what we can offer our clients and strengthens our ability to create extraordinary opportunities for artists across an increasingly diverse entertainment landscape.” Entertainment 360 will look to Brigade to help sign digital talent fostered by Stein and others to brand deals and partnerships, and new business opportunities in publishing, podcasts and traditional media. “I’ve always been drawn to people with a singular point of view, whose work and ambitions don’t fit neatly into one category,” said Stein in his own statement. “Our clients have built remarkable careers by following their own taste and instincts, and our job has been to help them turn those ideas into lasting businesses. Entertainment 360 shares that philosophy and brings an extraordinary depth of experience, relationships, and resources. Joining forces gives our clients access to many more opportunities, while allowing us to preserve the personal approach that has always defined Brigade.” The Brigade acquisition comes as YouTube stars, podcasters and other digital creators increasingly rise to the fore in Hollywood and a fast-shifting entertainment ecosystem. Brigade’s clients include fashion writer Leandra Medine Cohen; Feed Me

articles.title: Comedy Duo Kate Berlant and John Early to Co-Host 2027 Spirit Awards
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All November 11, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kate Berlant and John Early Sela Shiloni (2) Comedy duo Kate Berlant and John Early have been tapped to co-host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards . The comedians, actors and longtime creative collaborators will serve as emcees for the 42nd edition of the awards, which honor independent storytelling across film and TV. The show is set to take place March 6 at the Hollywood Palladium for a second consecutive year after moving from its longtime home on the beach in Santa Monica. “If there’s one thing we don’t need, it’s another predictable awards show,” said Juan Devis, president of Film Independent. “Kate and John are two of the funniest, strangest and most brilliantly unpredictable performers working today. They embody everything we love about independent storytelling: originality, fearlessness and a healthy disregard for convention. We’re excited to shake things up, break a few rules and have some fun along the way.” Related Stories Movies Two Films Share Top Jury Prize at 50th San Francisco Frameline Festival Movies Film Independent Spirit Awards Launches New Honor for Environmental-Themed Films Named After Robert Redford Added the co-hosts in a joint statement: “We’ve always been obsessed with awards shows, and we’re so honored we get to host the coolest one. Tune in to see if we choke under pressure!” Berlant and Early’s comedy collaborations include the sketch series 555 and the Emmy-nominated comedy special Would It Kill You to Laugh? In addition, Berlant’s has appeared in Sorry to Bother You, Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood, Don’t Worry Darling and The Bear. She has also starred in her one-woman show KATE and her comedy specials Cinnamon in the Wind and Parmesan . Early is known for his breakout role in the series Search Party, as well as his stand-up special Now More Than Ever. He recently made his feature directorial debut with Maddie’s Secret, in which Berlant also appears. Nominations for the 42nd annual awards show will be announced Dec. 2. A nominees brunch will take place Jan. 9 at The London West Hollywood. This year’s ceremony will introduce the best International first feature and digital creator sward categories. In addition, filmmaker Roman Coppola will bring serve as the creative consultant, a newly created role. Past Spirit Awards hosts include Ego Nwodim, Aidy Bryant, Hasan Minhaj, Megan Mullally and Nick Offerman, Aubrey Plaza, Nick Kroll and John Mulaney, Kate McKinnon and Kumail Nanjiani, Fred Armisen and Kristen Bell, Andy Samberg and John Waters. THR

articles.title: Peacock Overhauls Mobile App for Vertical Video Era in Effort to “Win Another Hour Per User, Per Month”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All November 11, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Peacock Peacock mobile users might want to check their app store for updates — the NBCUniversal streaming platform is undergoing its largest mobile revamp ever. Peacock mobile 2.0 (it’s probably well beyond 2.0, but stick with us here) is designed to, in part, “win another hour per user, per month,” Matt Strauss , chairman of NBCUniversal Media Group, told a small group of reporters including The Hollywood Reporter on Tuesday. Peacock has been profitable for two straight quarters now, and it’s part of Strauss’s job to keep it that way. To accomplish that reasonable-sounding goal, NBCU is overhauling Peacock’s smartphone display and functionality for the vertical video craze, which it boasts as having been early money on, as well as the Comcast entertainment brand’s fandoms and its sports content. Peacock users who use the app on both their TV and smartphone double the engagement of those who only sign in on their television. As John Jelley, the group’s senior vice president of product and UX (user experience), sees it, today’s opportunity is on the smaller of the two screens. “Every streamer today is really a sea of sameness on the homepage. Because they’ve taken a TV experience and largely ported it over, they are expecting the user to do the sorting,” Jelley said. “We see an opportunity to recognize what a fan is trying to accomplish in that session and make the next most useful action easier to find.” “We recognize that we have to start thinking of ourselves less as a streaming platform and more of an entertainment platform,” Strauss said. “How do we super serve our franchises and our fandoms where the best experience is on our app?” To those ends, “conversational AI search” will help users find what they want even if they don’t know how to directly express it. Short clips that lead to full episodes will expedite and elongate engagement, and franchise/fandom hubs can be a one-stop shop for fans of the Bravo-verse, for one standout example. There will also be games (like Law & Order: Clue Hunter and Public Eye ) and a membership program “giving eligible subscribers exclusive rewards, benefits and activities tied to the movies and shows they enjoy,” per the official announcement. One particularly cool idea is adaptive live viewing. Peacock plans to expand its live vertical video tests to The Voice live simulcasts, NCAA basketball games and, in a clear direct response to the rise of YouTube Golf, you guessed it: golf. A “dynamic video player” will switch between vertical and horizontal video playback automatically depending on the device orientation, keeping key action in frame. NBA games will soon get the same treatment, with “easy access to player stats” and “deeper game information sitting directly underneath the live feed in a dual screen view,” the executives say. Finally, these days, you cannot talk about vertical video without discussing microdramas . Jelley discusses them frankly, because he says that’s how his users speak about them. “When we talk to users about microdramas, they’re not embarrassed by them. They don’t feel that they’re something they’ll just do in private,” Jelley said. “They’re watching them at home at different moments of the day, they’re watching them on the commute. We are very committed to premium long-form content, and that has a massive place not only on the phone, but also on TV. But this is really another modality.” THR

articles.title: ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy Elevate Peacock’s Overly Familiar Southern-Fried Thriller
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Daniel Fienberg Plus Icon Daniel Fienberg Chief Television Critic TheFienPrint Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Meghann Fahy (left) and Rose Byrne in ‘The Good Daughter.' Mark Hill/PEACOCK Logo text We all have our television pet peeves and, for me, red flags abound in Peacock ‘s new limited series, The Good Daughter . Adapted by Karin Slaughter from her book of the same name, The Good Daughter is interchangeable, in terms of title, plot or structure, with a dozen recent limited series — most conspicuously, Amazon’s The Better Sister and Netflix’s His & Hers . The Good Daughter The Bottom Line A strong cast makes up for familiar irritations. Airdate: Thursday, November 12 (Peacock) Cast: Rose Byrne, Meghann Fahy, Brendan Gleeson, Olivia Williams, Harper Steele, Michael Dorman, Audrey Grace Marshall, Drew Cheek Creator: Karin Slaughter Director: Steph Green It’s a story set in and filmed in the Deep South, but its central cast is populated by actors from Australia, Ireland, Massachusetts and basically anywhere other than the Deep South, leading to a succotash of colorful and, to put it politely, inconsistent accents. Related Stories TV 'O.J.'s Accomplice' Has Its Own 'The Jinx' Hot Mic Moment TV Matthew Weiner Out as Showrunner of Eddie Murphy Peacock Series After Clash With Producers And it’s a story instigated by a school shooting and pushed forward by multiple instances of sexual violence, all propping up a mystery that’s barely mysterious — at least until the characters all sit down to explain everything in a series of weakly staged monologues. That The Good Daughter is so full of tropes I find tedious or annoying and yet somehow ends up being compulsively entertaining is a tribute to Slaughter’s gift for characterization and dialogue, the confident hand of series director Steph Green, and particularly the committed, emotionally exposed and often funny performances from leads Meghann Fahy , Rose Byrne and Brendan Gleeson . The Good Daughter begins with a double dose of trauma, the better to winnow away squeamish viewers. First, in flashback, devoted sisters Sam (Audrey Grace Marshall) and Charlie (Drew Cheek) witness a horrible act of violence perpetrated on their doting mother (Olivia Williams’ Gamma), perhaps the latest retaliation against their father (Gleeson’s Rusty), a defense attorney prone to rubbing people the wrong way. Their lives will never be the same. Jump to the present. Charlie (Fahy) has grown up to follow in her father’s footsteps, working out of his ramshackle office in the same Georgia town populated by people who still hate him and don’t feel too kindly toward her. She’s separated from hubby Ben (Michael Dorman, endearingly normal in a show populated by broad portrayals) and making various self-destructive choices, including a one-night stand with Huck (Jake McDorman), whose ponytail and scruff let you know he’s a bad idea. Charlie and Huck accidentally swap phones, which leads her to discover that he’s a high school teacher. In the process of returning his phone, she is present when Kelly (Shayna Benardo, an impressively grounding force) shows up and shoots and kills the well-liked principal and a freshman. Rusty, who has a bad cough and a history of heart problems, and likes to wear — for reasons that are never explained — a red clown nose, shows up to represent Kelly, whose cognitive issues haven’t stopped the local powerbrokers from eyeing the death penalty. Sensing everything is going astray, Rusty also calls elder daughter Sam (Byrne), now a patent lawyer in New York City and left with a permanent limp and partial blindness stemming from the incident with her mother. Sam hasn’t seen or talked to Charlie in 10 years, but she quickly finds herself back in Pikeville, caught up in the mystery of the shooting, as well as several additional mysteries from her family’s past. If you just look at the bones of the series, The Good Daughter is beyond rudimentary, with a crime in the present and a crime in the past that just coincidentally happen to be directly connected. The story can barely even decide what twists are supposed to be surprising and, as a result, nothing is really “guessable” or revelatory. Instead, The Good Daughter works best as a dirtied-up — though confusingly racially whitewashed — version of To Kill a Mockingbird , with Rusty as a lawyer doing noble things in a disreputable way, constantly looking like he slept at his desk, bottle in hand, eschewing Atticus Finch’s seersucker and moral rectitude. He stands up to threats from his adversaries that are violent and gory rather than ominous and insinuated, investigating cases in which the rape and persecution of the handicapped and impoverished play out on the surface rather than being buried in euphemism. It almost certainly works better on the page than on the screen, where we’ve seen too many versions of these generic rednecks in their generic pick-ups and these generic drawling, obfuscating lawmen to take them seriously. Green and the series’ cinematographers are able to embed in the rundown streets of Pikeville and take us into the “holler,” capturing this community within a community. But when every main cast member talks like the closest they’ve ever been to a holler was a quick drive-through during rehearsal, the verisimilitude suffers. What holds the show together is Slaughter’s grasp on the characters and their relationships. When Sam, Charlie and Rusty talk, it’s in a vernacular that mixes in-jokes, deeply felt family history, snooty literary references (lots of Flannery O’Connor and Emily Dickinson), amusingly unsnooty pop culture references (from Die Hard to Buffy the Vampire Slayer ), and an awareness of how to hurt or heal the people they know best. Byrne, Fahy and Gleeson don’t talk like they come from the same place, but the energy among them gives the series its energy and its authenticity. Sure, Fahy is doing a variation on her bad sister character from Netflix’s Sirens , but she’s tremendous at playing these open books of damage. A little too much of Byrne’s performance consists of actorly takes on disability, but she makes those notes of artificiality pay off. Everything Sam does is a put-on; her attire, hair and speech are defined in opposition to the place she left behind and hoped never to return to, with aspects of her natural self returning as she spends more time in Pikeville. It’s easy to buy them as sisters, in both the parts evoking pain and the parts where they bicker humorously. Plus, it’s easy to see the toll taken by trauma and time because Byrne and Fahy are well-matched by Marshall and Cheek. Gleeson isn’t as convincing in the flashback segments, and his Southern-ish intonations kept reminding me of somebody I couldn’t quite place, but he makes Rusty rascally and flawed. Like the actors, the characters are occupying roles — the city mouse, the bad girl, the folksy country lawyer — but when they’re together, they can be themselves. It’s a nice touch that one of the few characters who doesn’t have a public role to play, Rusty’s longtime assistant Lenore, is played by Harper Steele — you know her from the documentary Will & Harper — who isn’t an actor and comes across not as studied but as gentle and natural. For five episodes, Green maintains the flow between past and present smoothly, and is able to modulate most of the agonizing parts of the story so that they feel tense but not exploitative. Too bad the finale collapses under the weight of all its over-explaining. I never quite cared who did what and why, but Fahy, Byrne and Gleeson at least made it possible to care about the people to whom these things were happening. THR

articles.title: Benson Boone Set to Perform at NHL’s 2027 Winter Classic in Salt Lake City (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 8:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Singer Benson Boone performs at the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Festival at T-Mobile Arena on Sept. 19, 2026. Kayla DeLaura/WireImage Benson Boone is set to headline the entertainment portion of the National Hockey League’s 2027 Discover Winter Classic, The Hollywood Reporter has exclusively learned. The annual outdoor hockey game is scheduled for New Year’s Eve in Salt Lake City, Utah. The Utah Mammoth, who joined the league as an expansion team in 2024, will host their first-ever edition of the Winter Classic at Rice Eccles Stadium against the Colorado Avalanche. The Mammoth become the 32nd NHL franchise to participate in the outdoor event — a regular-season game for the teams. Related Stories TV Where to Watch the 2026 NASCAR Cup Series Championship Race Live Online Business Bob Iger's Son to Call Games for Lakers G League Team Boone, fresh off his Wanted Man tour, is set to perform during the first intermission of the game during a performance presented by Ticketmaster, according to a release. The pop star is known for his energetic performances, which often include a flip — or two.
