articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In Read the full story By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt ‘Sinners’ Breakout Miles Caton Joins Denzel Washington Thriller At Amazon MGM/UA Aaron Paul To Play Music Mogul Jimmy Iovine In Universal’s ‘Snoop’; Giovanni Ribisi Also Set ‘SNL’ Alums Bobby Moynihan, Aristotle Athari & Taran Killam Team On Collectibles Podcast ‘On Display’ – Watch The First Episode View All November 9, 2026 9:47am Add us as a Google Preferred Source EXCLUSIVE: Today, Saturday Night Live alumni Bobby Moynihan , Aristotle Athari and Taran Killam launched On Display , a new podcast birthed out of their shared passion for collectibles. The trio loves collecting everything from comic books to action figures and movie memorabilia. Each week on the podcast, they’ll be joined by a celebrity guest to talk about their cherished items and hobbies, while sharing their own personal fandoms. The show brings together comedy, nostalgia and often-heartfelt stories about personal obsessions, and what certain prized possessions really mean to both the hosts and their guests. Related Stories Late Night TV Milwaukee Brewers Make Surprise "Weekend Update" Appearance After World Series Win With Returning 'SNL' Alum Bobby Moynihan Podcast Comedians Leslie Liao & Jason Cheny Team With All Things Comedy On 'Happy Fun Times' Podcast On Display premiered today at 9 a.m. PT. New episodes will go out weekly on Mondays across YouTube and wherever else podcasts are found. The first season will feature 12 episodes, with five or six already shot. Watch a special preview above and the full first episode below. Watch on Deadline The pod is produced by StudioTen42 , in association with the comedian-owned podcast network All Things Comedy . Billy Rosenberg and Drew Eller are exec producing for ATC, alongside Guy Robinson for StudioTen42, and Andy Smith for high-end collectibles company, Sideshow , which is the show’s sponsor. Athari came to the idea for On Display after connecting with Andy Smith, who works in PR at Sideshow, during his time working on the film M3GAN 2.0 . Through Smith, he learned that Killam is a passionate collector who lost a collection he’d spent decades building — featuring some irreplaceable items — when his house burned down in the devastating Palisades Fire of January 2025. On Saturday Night Live for just one season, from 2021-2022, Athari hadn’t overlapped there with either Moynihan, who did nine seasons from 2008-2017, or Killam, who was on for six seasons from 2010-2016. After learning about what had happened to Killam, he began working with Sideshow to help him rebuild his collection. Then, he leaned that Moynihan is an avid collector, as well, leading to initial discussions amongst the trio about On Display . Killam told Deadline, “Hosting this podcast is beyond fun. Being a collector my entire life has directly informed what I do for a living. It’s been great interviewing other accomplished collectors and learning how it informs their own professional process. It’s also really great to see lots of really cool toys.” Moynihan commented, “I love talking about things I love with people I love while people who love things watch this thing we hope they love because we also love…it.” Athari added, for his part, “I feel immensely fortunate to share my affinity for collecting ephemera with friends and transform that shared passion into a creative and entertaining endeavor. Apparently, the only difference between collecting and hoarding is having a podcast.” Moynihan is repped by UTA, OPE Partners and Jackoway Austen Tyerman; Athari by CAA, Stride Management and Gang, Tyre Ramer; and Killam by UTA and Ziffren Brittenham. articles.title: ‘Hope’ Composer Michael Abels Played Even The Gross-Out Comedy Parts Like A Thriller – Sound & Screen Film
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In Read the full story By Fred Topel Fred Topel More Stories By Fred ‘Project Hail Mary’ Composer Daniel Pemberton Built “A Language From The Ground Up” Using New Instruments – Sound & Screen Film ‘Alien: Earth’ Composer Jeff Russo Used An Aztec Death Whistle For His Xenomorph Theme – Sound & Screen TV ‘All Her Fault’ Composer Jeff Beal Used Music To Give Mystery Series’ Duplicitous Characters The Benefit Of The Doubt – Sound & Screen TV View All November 9, 2026 10:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Director Na Hong-jin’s Hope took Cannes by storm , after which it opened in South Korea over the summer and came to the U.S. this fall. In it, the police and locals of Hope Harbor find they are facing an alien threat. But, even when the film takes surprising comedic directions, the music never lets on that it’s funny. Speaking at Deadline’s Sound & Screen Film, composer Michael Abels referenced a scene in which a man recounts his alien encounter while going to the bathroom in minute detail. Related Stories News Deadline Launches Its Contenders London Streaming Site Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Tonys, Guilds & More “There’s a very long discussion of bowel habits and the music during that all plays it very tense, but it’s pretty funny,” Abels said. “It’s the type of comedy where it’s the situation that’s funny. In that sort of situation, it helps when the music plays it straight. You just let the audience realize, this is pretty funny.” Abels said if the music lets on that it’s comedic, “then you feel like you’re forced to laugh and that’s not funny anymore. I don’t think there’s any funny music in the film.” Humor extended to Abels’ relationship with Na, who understands English but spoke in Korean through a translator. “He’d speak in these long paragraphs in Korean,” Abels said. “Then about one minute or two minutes into what he was saying, the translator would burst out laughing. Then I just had to pray that by the time the translation got to me, I would get the joke.” He did pass the Na test, at least. “I think that I laughed at the right time and he said, ‘Oh, you’re Korean’s getting better,’” Abels said. “So my Korean got a little better. I’m not sure how.” Michael Abels conducts at Sound & Screen Film JC Olivera for Deadline Director Na asked Abels to score Hope based on Abels’ work with Jordan Peele. Abels said Na used his horror movie scores as temp tracks. “The first part of the film is actually much more textural sort of score and you think it’s going this one way,” Abels said. “Then it suddenly turns into this big action movie with all this pounding chase music.” As the film begins, officer Beom Seok (Hwang Jung-min) investigates the destruction left in the wake of a creature. When the creature (Cameron Britton) finally reveals himself, it’s only the beginning. Three other aliens (Michael Fassbender, Alicia Vikander and Taylor Russell) are involved in the second half of the movie. “The first part of it really demands keeping the audience on the edge of the seat and you’re not sure what’s going to happen,” Abels said. “You just realize the aliens might be the good guys. The humans aren’t that smart in spite of they’re trying to be smart. articles.title: Son Lux Says Its ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Score Reflected The Islamic Faith – Sound & Screen Film
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In Read the full story By Fred Topel Fred Topel More Stories By Fred ‘Project Hail Mary’ Composer Daniel Pemberton Built “A Language From The Ground Up” Using New Instruments – Sound & Screen Film ‘Alien: Earth’ Composer Jeff Russo Used An Aztec Death Whistle For His Xenomorph Theme – Sound & Screen TV ‘All Her Fault’ Composer Jeff Beal Used Music To Give Mystery Series’ Duplicitous Characters The Benefit Of The Doubt – Sound & Screen TV View All November 9, 2026 11:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source There are not many Muslim action movies, so Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is already unique. Its music reflects the disparate elements at play in the film, too. Son Lux wrote the score for the Orion Pictures / Amazon MGM Studios film, as well the song “Now I’m Listening,” which singer-songwriter Bilal performs with them. The band members Rafiq Bhatia, Ian Chang and Ryan Lott spoke about reflecting the movie’s themes in the music in a virtual Q&A for Sound & Screen Film. Your Mother stars Mahershala Ali as Latif, a devout Muslim hit man. Bassam Tariq wrote and directed; many of Son Lux’s inspirations came from Tariq, they band said. Related Stories News Deadline Launches Its Contenders London Streaming Site Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Tonys, Guilds & More “A big part of the Islamic faith is that there’s this unknowable, ineffable feeling,” Chang said. “That was something that was very important to Bassam, he told us from the beginning, this kind of almost mystery with something that needed to be communicated in a way that was both dealing with mystery and the majesty of the unknowable.” Tariq also encouraged Son Lux to utilize a vocal choir in the music. Lott said it led the band “to really investigate the power of the human voice both individually and also collectively. We found the soul of the score upon his urging to investigate more aggressively the use of the human voice.” A choir sings “Now I’m Listening” at Sound & Screen Film JC Olivera for Deadline The human choir more specifically incorporates Sufi Zikr chants. Bhatia said Son Lux drew from real men facing violence. “Some of the most unforgettable ones were these Chechen rebels that were preparing for battle and doing chanting Zikr and doing breath work,” Bhatia said. With vocalization, Son Lux could repeat words and phrases. This also reflected Islamic philosophies. “In Islamic artwork and architecture, there is this idea of infinite geometry of these patterns that repeat endlessly to give an expression to the otherwise inexpressible, to communicate infinity,” Bhatia said. “Even if you truncate the Islamic creed and you just say ‘La ilaha,’ ‘There is no god.’ Or ‘La ilaha il,’ ‘There is no god but,’ if you take that and repeat it as an infinite pattern, that expression of doubt made infinite is actually its own expression of the infinite and the unknowable.” Lott also credits Bilal with bringing their song to life. articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In Read the full story By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas The Hunt For The Next ‘Obsession’ Continues At AFM, Where A24’s ‘Elden Ring’ & New Films With Jeremy Renner, Idris Elba, Gillian Anderson & Renée Zellweger Hit The Market: Hot List + Analysis Jonathan Bailey & Bill Nighy To Star In Love Story ‘Insomniac City’ For Director Dominic Cooke — AFM Al Munteanu’s German Outfit BriskPace Confirms Leadership Team View All November 9, 2026 11:32am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Alex Proyas and Antonio Banderas Courtesy/Jesus Chacon EXCLUSIVE : I, Robot and Dark City filmmaker Alex Proyas is taking over directing duties on Cortés , the historical epic starring Oscar nominee Antonio Banderas as Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés. Filming began in Paris and Spain a few weeks ago with French filmmaker Paul Mignot announced at the time as helming the project. Proyas has subsequently taken over. According to the production, “Mignot remains attached to the project in another capacity.” No reason was given for his directing exit. The AI-enabled film, written by Oscar nominee Nicholas Kazan ( Reversal of Fortune ) and produced by Marco Weber is co-financed and co-produced by Utopai Studios and Ex Machina Studios. Related Stories News The Hunt For The Next 'Obsession' Continues At AFM, Where A24's 'Elden Ring' & New Films With Jeremy Renner, Idris Elba, Gillian Anderson & Renée Zellweger Hit The Market: Hot List + Analysis Casting Adam Devine & Chloe Fineman Set For Michael Diliberti Crime Comedy 'Miami PI' - AFM It marks Proyas’ highest-profile movie since he made big-budget Lionsgate action pic Gods Of Egypt a decade ago. The announcement comes as the companies head into the American Film Market ( AFM ), where sales partner K5 International, under the Ex Machina sales label, will be looking to sell the project to buyers in Europe, Latin America, Australia and New Zealand. Utopai Studios controls distribution rights throughout the rest of the world, including North America and Asia. Set in 1519, “ Cortés begins in Cuba, where a restless soldier hungry for glory seizes command of an expedition to the Yucatán and sails without permission. After landing on the coast of what is now Mexico, he meets Marina, an enslaved Indigenous woman and gifted linguist who becomes indispensable to his advance. As Cortés turns fragile alliances, faith and fear into instruments of conquest, Marina watches him transform from a daring outlaw into a self-anointed messiah.” Proyas said today: “ Cortés is one of cinema’s great untold stories — a tale of ambition, conquest and betrayal, told through the eyes of the extraordinary woman who helped shape the course of history. Nicholas has written a script of remarkable scale and intimacy, exploring a man of profound contradictions — visionary and ruthless, charismatic and monstrous, capable of extraordinary courage and unspeakable cruelty. With Antonio, we have an actor who can inhabit every facet of that complexity. My collaboration with Marco and the Ex Machina team on Heaven has opened up exhilarating new possibilities for cinematic storytelling, allowing us to bring this extraordinary world to life on a scale and with a visual ambition that would once have been unimaginable.” The filmmaker, also known for movies The Crow and Knowing , most recently produced the 2023 thriller Mercy Road starring Luke Bracey and Toby Jones and is is on production on Ex Machina project Heaven , which is due for release in 2027. He’s also been in post on comedy musical R.U.R. in recent years. Watch on Deadline Mignot’s previous credits include the historical feature Vaincre ou Mourir . He has also directed campaigns for BMW, Porsche, Audi, Lexus, Jeep, L’Oréal, Louis Vuitton, and Emporio Armani. ‘Yellowstone’s Cole Hauser Preps FBI Action Thriller ‘Pale Horse’ With Eye To Star ‘Godzilla’ Stalks $32M U.S. Bow, Best For Live-Action Foreign-Language Pic 10½-Year Prison Sentence; Survivor Speaks Out, Rips Channel 4 De Niro Targets Elon At ‘Musk’ Documentary Screening On GOP Spending Spree Read More About: Comments

articles.title: James Gunn Releases Statement Following Departure As DC Studios Co-Head
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In Read the full story By Justin Kroll Justin Kroll Film Editor @krolljvar More Stories By Justin Robert Pattinson & Nicholas Hoult Round Out James Bond Screen Tests Teyonah Parris To Co-Star With Denzel Washington In Christopher McQuarrie’s Thriller For United Artists Nicholas Galitzine Eyeing Ichabod Crane Role In Sony’s ‘Hollow’ Starring Sydney Sweeney View All November 9, 2026 11:33am Add us as a Google Preferred Source James Gunn Theo Wargo / Getty Images Following the news that he and Peter Safran would no longer be co-running DC Studios following the Skydance-Warner Bros. merger, James Gunn has spoken out about his time running the studio. The lengthy statement which Gunn dropped on his social media platforms goes into detail how proud his four years were touching on all the projects made while also touching on his partnership with Safran, who he described as “the smartest most competent person” he’s know. Gunn also touched ono how trying the four years had been and how he had grown to “dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job.” The statement comes after Skydance chose to replace Gunn and Safran with veteran exec Latcham as the president and chief creative officer of DC Studios. Gunn and Safran will continue to produce on various DC projects and returning to their full-time creative work. They’re currently in post on the Superman sequel, Man of Tomorrow which will open in theaters on July 9, 2027. Related Stories News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In News John Constantine Movie From 'Evil Dead Wrath's Francis Galluppi In Development At DC Gunn released the statement on his social media platforms and you can read it in full below: Watch on Deadline “Oh, boy. What a four years.” “Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios. When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri, I used to write and draw my own comics with a mix of DC Comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn’t know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn’t pass up the unique opportunity. I’m glad I took the job.” “There have been so many highs along the way – releasing Superman and Clayface, making Peacemaker, reading the scripts to The People Vs, the entire process of Man of Tomorrow, which thus far has been the best filmmaking experience of my life, and numerous other moments.” “The highest of the highs have been all the talented and wonderful people I’ve worked with and grown to love: the DC Studios crew, our talented collaborators, our casts and crews, and the boisterous and hilarious fans. And the best part of all has been working with Peter Safran, the smartest and most competent person I know. You’ve been the best partner a person could ask for, and, more so, a truly good friend.” “But what only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years (Jenn, I love you and I’m sorry and you don’t need to feel guilty for being the happiest of all people that I’m no longer doing this job). And the thing my ADHD hyperfocus has had the most difficulty with has been dividing my time between projects I’m incredibly passionate about and the ones I’m not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head.” So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking. That’s not to say Peter and I are immediately done with DC or superheroes. We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we’ve just been engaged on another DC project which I’m writing, and we’ll see where it goes after that. And, of course, the characters we set up will live on. Thank you so very, very much for embracing the characters and stories we’ve put on screen. Love and gratitude, James Gunn View this post on Instagram ‘Yellowstone’s Cole Hauser Preps FBI Action Thriller ‘Pale Horse’ With Eye To Star ‘Godzilla’ Stalks $32M U.S. Bow, Best For Live-Action Foreign-Language Pic 10½-Year Prison Sentence; Survivor Speaks Out, Rips Channel 4 De Niro Targets Elon At ‘Musk’ Documentary Screening On GOP Spending Spree Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Camerimage Founder Marek Zydowicz on AI, Aronofsky and Why “Cinematographers Are Artists, Not Technicians”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 7, 2026 4:11pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Marek Żydowicz Camerimage Camerimage , the world’s premier festival devoted to the art of cinematography, turns 34 this year, and it arrives in Torun, Poland, Nov. 7-14, with its founder in both a combative and reflective mood. Marek Zydowicz, who launched the event in 1993 to champion cinematographers and other below-the-line artists the industry treated as mere technicians, is fielding questions on a thorny set of issues. Among them: the rise of generative AI , which gets its own debates and workshops this year; the squeeze on budgets and theatrical releases; and the decision to honor Darren Aronofsky , an outspoken AI adopter, with the festival’s director award. Related Stories Movies PÖFF Stands With Ukraine: A Look at Films Featured at Tallinn Made Despite, and Because of, the War Oscars 2027: Int'l Films in Focus 'Hold Onto Me,' Cyprus' First Oscar Hopeful, Stars a Newcomer and a 'Dogtooth' Actor in a Very Personal Father-Daughter Drama Joe Walker, the editor behind Dune and 12 Years a Slave , is also being feted and will chair the Main Competition jury, while Polish cinematographer Janusz Kaminski, whose Disclosure Day is screening in contention, receives THR ’s Visionary award . Speaking to THR ahead of this year’s fest, Zydowicz said Camerimage will remain open to a “diversity of techniques and technologies” but draws the line at fully AI-generated films. In a wide-ranging conversation, Zydowicz spoke about the festival’s growing ambitions, the reason why Poland seems to produce so many great cinematographers, and why the human eye will never be replaced. Why are there so many extraordinary Polish cinematographers? What’s the secret? A full answer would require going quite far back into the history of Polish cinema, and even further, to the period when Poland was partitioned. For 123 years, paintings and graphic works depicting the most important events in our nation’s history sustained our hopes of regaining independence and stirred our imaginations and dreams. After the second World War, this tradition of depicting the past played an enormously important role in laying the foundations of the Lodz Film School. Artists working under communist censorship often drew on the same ways of expressing what could not be said openly as their predecessors had in the nineteenth century. Sometimes the dialogue between characters told one story while the images suggested another. This encouraged the development of an extraordinary sensitivity and a search for ways of using composition to smuggle forbidden content and aesthetics into films. Technological limitations and Poland’s isolation from the most progressive developments in Western culture made it necessary to find original solutions of our own. During those difficult times, Polish filmmakers absorbed different cinematic traditions, both those that reached us legally and those that were banned and smuggled in from Western Europe and America. The relationship between the director and the cinematographer became an important factor in the creation of original forms of cinematic imagery. Many outstanding filmmakers taught in Lodz, and later at other Polish film schools as well. The film school taught the history of painting, and not only Polish painting. Over successive generations, an exceptionally strong artistic tradition emerged from this. That is what we see today in the diversity of Polish cinematographers’ work: from Hollywood productions to independent and art cinema around the world. Why did you choose Darren Aronofsky for your director honor this year? Do you expect a debate around his embrace of AI in production , which is still a very controversial subject in the industry? I do expect that discussion, because AI is an important and contentious subject, and Darren has shown that he wants to explore it professionally. Our award recognizes over thirty years of his filmmaking. His body of work provokes, unsettles and asks us to confront aspects of human nature from which we might prefer to look away. His films can be difficult to watch, but it is often precisely that discomfort that makes us look more closely at ourselves and others. His artistic achievements deserve awards. Think of the intensity with which Requiem for a Dream conveys the experience of addiction, or the way Black Swan draws us into its protagonist’s increasingly disturbed perception of reality. The Fountain explores love, mortality and spiritual longing through an extraordinarily ambitious visual imagination. It is a film I admire enormously, also for the risks it took and the resistance it encountered. The Whale , made on an entirely different scale, finds another way to bring us close to suffering and the desire for human connection. Darren Aronofsky Courtesy of Camerimage Darren moves between intimacy and spectacle, tenderness and brutality, sometimes bringing religious imagery into stories about deeply personal struggles. His films encourage audiences to question their own values and to notice people whose pain might otherwise go unseen. This combination of formal boldness and concern for human beings is one of the most important reasons we are honouring him. His interest in AI is a separate discussion, although it also reflects his continuing curiosity about the tools available to filmmakers. We are not presenting this award as a judgement on how he uses the technology. I do, however, appreciate his willingness, as an established artist, to explore unfamiliar territory. That curiosity has been evident throughout his career. We should discuss his experiments openly, including the disagreements they provoke. What is Camerimage’s policy towards AI — would you accept AI-generated work in your selection? We do not accept productions generated entirely by AI. Our selection focuses on the art of cinematographers. Of course, to understand AI as a tool for creating moving images, we watch films made entirely with AI. Personally, I am in favour of hybrid films in which the live actors appearing in them decide for themselves how far AI may intervene in the images being created. Within cinematography, we are open to a diversity of techniques and technologies, but always with respect for artists’ personal rights. A film may use extensive visual effects and digital post-production, or it may be made with very limited resources and rely almost entirely on techniques achieved on set, but it should always respect the wishes of the people lending their likenesses and voices. We value the cinematographer’s creative contribution to telling a story through film. Advanced digital techniques have long been part of that process. AI will, in time, find its proper place in this process. Everyone will use it. The only question is how. For now, curiosity about the future does not change our principles for selecting films for the festival competitions. The subject remains open, and we want to discuss it with a view to bringing about legal regulations, for example at European Union level, that will make AI safe for our industry. Explain the reasoning behind your other honoree, Joe Walker. Joe Walker is an outstanding editor whose work we have admired and presented for many years. His collaborations with Denis Villeneuve, including Sicario , Arrival , Blade Runner 2049 and the Dune films, demonstrate the expressive possibilities of editing on very different scales. He has helped give these films their distinctive rhythms and their ability to make an audience understand something before it is explained in words. In Arrival , the organization of time is fundamental to the way we experience the story. In Dune , the editing helps maintain the connection between a vast, complex world and the characters moving through it. Zendaya in Dune: Part Three. Courtesy of Everett His work with Steve McQueen, from Hunger to 12 Years a Slave and Widows , reveals an equally extraordinary sensitivity to performance, the duration of shots and silence. We are interested in how his editing gives images the power to affect us and shape the relationship between what we see and what we feel. This makes his contribution particularly relevant to a festival devoted to visual storytelling. We are delighted to honour him in Torun and give audiences the opportunity to speak with him about his films after their screenings. He has also agreed to chair the Main Competition jury. The eye of an editor with his experience and sensitivity brings a valuable perspective to a competition that means so much to us. THR is honoring Poland’s own Janusz Kaminski with its Visionary award this year . How would you sum up his contribution to the art of cinematography? We could easily devote the rest of this interview to Janusz’s contribution and still leave a great deal unsaid. He is one of the greatest cinematographers in the history of cinema. He created images that have become part of our shared cinematic memory in Schindler’s List and Saving Private Ryan . I am very interested in his search for the right form for the story contained in a screenplay. He chooses an approach to imagery that will fully convey its emotional truth. THR Visionary Award Winner Janusz Kaminski Gabriel Olsen/FilmMagic/Getty Images Our festival recognized The Diving Bell and the Butterfly , for which Janusz received the Golden Frog. It is a beautiful, painful and deeply moving film, with an extraordinary ability to bring us into another person’s experience. The cinematography is inseparable from that achievement. It reminds us that we should appreciate Janusz’s work beyond his collaboration with that brilliant and iconic master of cinema, Steven Spielberg. This year, I invited another of their films, Disclosure Day , to the Main Competition. Janusz’s unsettling cinematography, with frequent halation creating a sense of the presence of something unknown and alien, is crucial to the film as a whole. Janusz is a “visionary”, and his images have a profound effect on audiences and young filmmakers. Camerimage has traditionally championed the cinematographer as an artist in their own right, rather than simply a technical collaborator. Do you think the industry is doing enough to recognize the creative contribution of cinematographers, particularly during awards season? I would say both yes and no. Cinematography awards are presented in several places around the world. At the same time, most mainstream media coverage of films names only directors and actors, leaving out the cinematographers. The term “below the line” has an established meaning in the organization of a production, but it says very little about the artistic role of the people it describes. A cinematographer helps determine how we experience a film’s story and how closely we connect with its characters. They create the atmosphere of every frame on screen and the emotions and feelings of the characters. They are an artist, not a technician operating a camera. Our role is to help people understand and appreciate the artistry involved in this work, and to ensure that these artists have appropriate working conditions. Awards season is one opportunity to do this, but the conversation should continue throughout the year. What are the biggest challenges you see facing cinematographers and other below-the-line artists at the moment? Financial pressure is certainly one, particularly when filmmakers are expected to do more with fewer resources. There is also considerable anxiety about AI and what it may mean for people’s livelihoods. I understand those concerns, although I do not believe that an artist’s contribution can simply be replaced by a generated image. A cinematographer brings a lifetime of observations, relationships, emotions and experiences of the world to their work. All of this can inform a decision made on set in a fraction of a second. It has a decisive influence on the power of the moving image being created. Technology will change working methods, but I am certain that the human perspective which gives films a spiritual dimension remains indispensable. Younger filmmakers face a particular kind of pressure because they have grown up amid an almost constant influx of images and information. They are also entering a world in which it will become increasingly difficult to judge how an image was made and whether it records something that actually happened. I am cautious about generational labels, but these conditions are worth recognizing. My generation grew up with different constraints, so I would not pretend that our experiences are the same. Every generation has to understand its own circumstances and find a way to navigate them. There are also encouraging changes, including the growing participation of women in film productions dominated by men for decades. Jolanta Dylewska, who won our Golden Frog in 2011 and returns to the Main Competition this year [as the cinematographer of Through the Wall ], is one of the artists who helped break down those barriers. It is wonderful to see so many women creating outstanding work today. How would you describe the identity of Camerimage in 2026? Our identity remains rooted in the idea I set out at the first edition of the festival in 1993: Let us recognize excluded and marginalised artists, the cinematographers whom the industry largely treats as technicians. We want audiences to discover what images contribute to their experience of film. TorunCamerimage is a spiritual spa for film artists, who can talk here, free from pressure, about the language of the moving image and its significance in the contemporary world and in the future. There are occasional incidents and attempts to exert aggressive pressure on us as organisers, and on me as the founder and director of TorunCamerimage, but never between our guests. We will remain independent, respecting artistic and humanistic values. How has it changed over more than 30 years of operation, and what do you want the festival to become in the future? The most obvious change is the scale. We began in Torun, with a venue that was not a professional cinema. We searched for a suitable location in Poland and returned to Torun, whose authorities decided, together with the Polish government, to build the European Film Center Camerimage at a cost of around $200 million. The festival has grown, with an average annual attendance of around 70,000 across its events. Around 1,000 film school students and some 800 cinematographers from around the world attend, along with several hundred other creative professionals from our industry. In recent years, we have welcomed guests from more than 80 countries. Alongside the film studio, the European Film Center Camerimage will have an education centre, an exhibition and trade fair centre of around 4,000 square metres dedicated to presenting filmmaking techniques and technologies, and a large screening auditorium with more than 1,600 seats, capable of accommodating a wide variety of projection technologies. The complex will be completed by the House of Cinema, with several cinemas, including an IMAX-type auditorium, and the David Lynch’s World of Imagination. David gave me more than a dozen shipping containers of artefacts from Twin Peaks . I am working on the exhibition design that I agreed with David and that we intended to realise together. What advice do you have for a first-time Camerimage attendee? Come with a plan, but leave room to change it. Choose the films and events you particularly want to attend, remembering that schedules will overlap and some screenings may be full. An unexpected alternative may turn out to be the most valuable experience of your entire visit. We have seen this many times. Be active. Talk to the artists and other audience members. Take part in the Q&As after screenings and in workshops at Camerimage Film Studio. The festival continues beyond the screening room, as people share impressions, disagree, get to know one another and sometimes find the beginnings of a future collaboration. A little spontaneity and courage can take you a long way at TorunCamerimage. THR

articles.title: Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan Apologize for Laughing at “Insensitive Joke” About Charlie Kirk on ‘I’ve Had It’ Podcast
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All November 7, 2026 7:08pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan Theo Wargo/Getty Images I’ve Had It podcast hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie “Pumps” Sullivan have released an apology statement for laughing at a joke about Charlie Kirk on the Thursday episode of their show. “On Thursday’s show, we laughed at a joke about Charlie Kirk. It was an insensitive joke, and we should not have laughed. We regret it, and we apologize,” they wrote in a statement shared on the I’ve Had It podcast Instagram Saturday. “Whatever our political differences, there is nothing funny about gun violence. We’ve long supported common-sense gun safety reform. To that end, we’ve made a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety, the largest gun violence prevention organization in America.” Related Stories TV Pete Davidson Makes Shocking Charlie Kirk Joke at Kevin Hart Roast News The Widow and the Firebrand: How Candace Owens Turned a Conservative Succession Into a Crusade Against Erika Kirk During the Thursday episode of the podcast, the hosts read posts made by online users amid the 2026 midterm results. They read one that said, “We’re digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again,” and they both laughed. (That segment of the Thursday episode has since been cut out, but was reshared online.) “We’ll keep using our platforms to fight for the safety of all Americans,” Welch and Sullivan’s joint statement concluded. Kirk died in September 2025 after being fatally shot while speaking at a college event in Utah County, Utah. On Thursday, in response to a video of the cut clip from I’ve Had It on X , Cash App announced they were no longer sponsors of the podcast. “We do not condone violence of any kind, and we are no longer sponsors of this podcast,” Cash App wrote. Boll & Branch, a luxury bedding company, also said they would not “advertise with the I’ve Had It podcast and will not in the future.” Chewy additionally put out a statement noting they “do not sponsor or support the I’ve Had It podcast. We unequivocally condemn violence in all forms. The comments made by the hosts do not reflect Chewy’s values or what we stand for as a company.” Nov. 7, 7:45 p.m. Updated to include Chewy’s statement. THR

articles.title: Emma Stone Joins Druski During His ‘SNL’ Hosting Debut
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All November 7, 2026 8:53pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Emma Stone and Druski on 'SNL.' Screenshot Logo text Druski made his Saturday Night Live debut with an assist from his upcoming co-star Emma Stone . He kicked off his first-ever monologue by acknowledging that his appearance marked the first time an online content creator hosted the show. “It is a dream to be hosting Saturday Night Live . Apparently, people are saying I’m the first internet content creator, social media influencer, only make you laugh on your phone, TikTok and YouTube and Instagram star to host this show,” he said. “Woo. People say a lot of things about me, honestly.” Related Stories TV 'SNL' Writer Jimmy Fowlie Pays Tribute to Sister Christina Downer After Police Arrest Two for Her Murder TV Druski Signs Deal With Netflix, Sets Church Comedy 'Collect & Praise' “Some people say I look like a lesbian. I don’t know how true that is,” Druski joked. “Some people say I’m on Ozempic. Could be lies, could be truth to that.” Druski, whose real name is Drew Desbordes, admitted that SNL would not be “holding me back from saying anything.” He said there were only a few rules to follow: No cussing and no “whiteface,” which he both joked he couldn’t promise to. (More on that later.) “But honestly, this is a huge moment for me growing up as a fat kid from the suburbs. Why y’all laughing? My teachers never believed in me, so I just wanna say… Yeah, I’m just lying. I just wanted to say that because rappers be saying that type of stuff,” he joked, before thanking his family, who was in the audience, for supporting his dreams. “I’m so grateful. When I first started my career, I let them, let me turn my dreams into a full-blown movie convention. Every day I think about how could I possibly repay y’all,” he began, as one of his family members offered, “Some money!” The comedian recounted the growth his career has seen in recent years, noting, “I am living proof you can bet on yourself and make your dreams come true.” He added, “I just finished filming my first ever movie with Emma Stone, and she is here right now!” The Oscar winner then entered the stage, and the two recounted their time working on The Catch together. “Emma, what’s going on? I’m actually playing her love interest in the new movie that we just did,” he said. Stone responded, “Oh, I’m sorry. OK, yeah. I think you might have misread that in those scenes because we weren’t love interests in the film, but now it is actually starting to make more sense to me why you kept looking at me like that through all these scenes.” “That’s probably why we ain’t kiss either,” Druski added, before also telling the actress he loved her work in Bugonia . “Oh my God, thank you, really?” Stone said. The comedian replied, “No, I just wanted to be the first Black guy to say it.” Druski and Stone are set to appear in Universal Pictures’ rom-com The Catch , which will be directed by Dave McCary, Stone’s husband who was also as a segment director on SNL in the 2010s. The film hits theaters on May 21, 2027. Druski's monologue! pic.twitter.com/RnaI5AkQpb — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) November 8, 2026 Elsewhere in the episode, the show spoofed on the success of Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything with a fresh take on its origins. As the skit went, before Fielder and Oppenheim signed on to direct the project, Druski was originally attached to the doc. Jane Wickline appeared in the sketch as Elizabeth Holmes while Ben Marshall portrayed Holmes’ husband, Billy Evans. SNL poked fun at the close-up shots featured in You Can See Everything , with Druski and Wickline recreating the infamous moment from the doc where Fielder and Holmes converse about whether the latter was trying to deceive the filmmaker. They also spoofed on Fielder’s decision to bring in an actress to portray Holmes later in the doc, with Druski himself stepping into the role of the disgraced Theranos CEO, prosthetics and all. Druski said, “I just need to find somebody who can truly embody her character,” before a a shot of Druski dressed up as Elizabeth Holmes was shown. “I’m always being real,” he said, as Wickline repeated, “I’m always being real.” They continued to repeat the phrase to one another, as Druski offered, “I could do this all day, bitch. You don’t scare me.” Dru Can See Everything pic.twitter.com/lqIQEHK4VZ — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) November 8, 2026 Texas senator-elect James Talarico also joined the often-political cold open to call for a shift in SNL ‘s cold opens. The sketch began by recounting the success Democrats found in the 2026 midterms, with Talarico joing by the end of the bit. “People want something new; they want something different,” Talarico said. “I’m talking about SNL’s cold opens,” he said turning to James Austin Johnson’s Trump to ask him how long he’d do the bit. “Infinity,” he said. In more political spoofing, Jeremy Culhane portrayed Elon Musk during the Weekend Update segment to break down the midterm results. Trump breaks down the midterm election results pic.twitter.com/1yy2ug6Aak — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) November 8, 2026 As he said in his monologue, Druski is the first creator to ever host SNL . He was joined by The Strokes as the night’s musical guest. He got his beginning in the industry via his online presence, where he built a name for himself performing sketches online. Druski has since expanded his career into television ( Grown-ish ) and film ( House Party ), and hosted the BET Awards this June. On Monday, it was announced Druski signed a multi-year deal with Netflix , which will first see him star in the “semi-scripted” comedy series Collect & Praise . Jalen Brunson , Dakota Johnson , Shane Gillis and Inde Navarrette have already hosted season 52. Next up, John Mulaney will host the Nov. 14 episode alongside Phoebe Bridgers. THR

articles.title: James Talarico Crashes ‘SNL’ Cold Open, Apologizes for Texting Us So Much
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All November 7, 2026 9:35pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source James Talarico on 'Saturday Night Live.' Logo text James Austin Johnson was born for this moment — Donald Trump spinning as he is roundly defeated by Democrats — and he rose to meet in Saturday Night Live ’s cold open. But it was a Democratic politician who stole the show from Trump’s 2026 defeatism tour, as Texas senator-elect James Talarico made a surprise appearance as himself at the end of the sketch. “I’m James Talarico, the guy who’s been texting you every day asking for five dollars,” the popular Texas politician said as he came out on stage to gasps and cheers from the audience, with Trump mumbly meta-jibing behind him, “In this economy, who can blame you?” Related Stories TV Emma Stone Joins Druski During His 'SNL' Hosting Debut TV After 2026 Midterms, Bill Maher Asks Trump, "Donnie, Are You OK?" Talarico a moment later invoked the iconic “Live from New York” with Johnson. Talarico drubbed his Republican opponent Ken Paxton by 12 points in the most expensive race in the history of the United States Senate, in part on the back of the grassroots fundraising campaign he was self-mocking on SNL . The result turned a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time in over 30 years. Before Talarico showed up in Studio 8H, Johnson had been reveling in his presidential character’s anti-moment. “I didn’t even say it was rigged,” Trump said of the election tallies. “I accepted the results, which is even scarier in a way. It’s like, ‘What the hell is he planning?'” He then said he only cared about his newly redesigned White House ballroom, before allowing under his breath, “Oh my God, I hate my life.” Trump breaks down the midterm election results pic.twitter.com/1yy2ug6Aak — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) November 8, 2026 Talarico’s cold-open surprise cameo echoed moments like Kamala Harris’ 2024 turn-up, in which she played opposite her celebrity impersonator Maya Rudolph ahead of the election, while Hillary Clinton and Sarah Palin also made unexpected appearances as White House candidates more than a decade ago. A senator or senator-elect, however, is rarer, and the moment both reflected and reinforced the emergent media celebrity of the new class of Congressional Democrats, many of them in their 30s or early 40s. Johnson’s Trump, at least, is not a fan. “The next few years are going to be horrible,” he said, pausing a comic beat. “It’s not that they’re Democrats; it’s that they’re Millennials.” He then lamented the return of generational staples like “adorkable” and the show New Girl . The president and the Republican party were handed several heaping platters of whoopings in the midterms, as Democrats gained at least 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate. Voters rejected both Trump’s policies and personality as they voted for a wide range of change, especially on the economy. Johnson — who told The Hollywood Reporter last year that “I don’t want to call what I’m doing Shakespeare, but I am trying to find the deeper forms of Trump, who is a rich text” — went full Hamlet Saturday with a digression about when New Girl started finding good storylines (it involved Winston and the cat). Johnson has been been appearing (or crashing) the cold open as the president seemingly every week since Trump’s return to office, and writers gave Talarico one of the best lines of the sketch in letting him…question that choice. “People want something new; they want something different,” Talarico said, appearing to be talking about electoral politics , before the comic pivot. “I’m talking about SNL’s cold opens,” he said turning to Trump to ask him how long he will continue doing this shtick. “Infinity,” Johnson’s Trump said. They don’t want to talk about it, but we have to talk about it. Johnson’s Trump also engaged in what might be a bon voyage to Colin Jost’s Pete Hegseth; with the defense secretary rumored to be leaving the administration, it could end Jost’s well-regarded impression run too. “Do I look like a person who gets less crazy when backed into a corner?” Jost asked as he walked onto the sketch, adding, “I live a YOLO life: you only lose often.” He then sashayed off, backside first, playing to the new Trumpian rumpian obsession. The sketch began with Sarah Sherman’s Chuck Schumer and Kenan Thompson’s Hakeem Jeffries taking credit for victories that were only partly their doing and then describing their post-midterm plan. “As our first order of business we are going to march right up to Donald Trump, look him right in the eye and say, ‘Knock it off buster,'” Thompson’s Jeffries said, mocking a perceived ineffectuality of current Congressional Democratic leadership. As they rhetorically asked who was responsible for pulling off all the wins, Johnson’s Trump appeared and took upside-down credit: “Me,” he boasted. Talarico’s appearance on SNL provides a bookend — and a bit of sweet revenge — for the Texas politician after broader threats by FCC chair Brendan Carr led ABC and Jimmy Kimmel in September to move an appearance of Talarico’s on Jimmy Kimmel Live! off broadcast television to YouTube, a decision both Kimmel and the candidate condemned. The ostensible reason that Carr would take issue was because Talarico was a candidate, triggering an equal-time provision, even though both Republican and Democratic candidates have long appeared on late-night shows. With Talarico officially a senator-elect, all of that is moot. Druski hosted the Nov. 7 episode. THR

articles.title: Druski Embodies Elizabeth Holmes in ‘You Can See Everything’ Spoof on ‘SNL’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All November 7, 2026 9:51pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Druski as Elizabeth Holmes on 'SNL.' Screenshot Logo text You really can see just about everything on Saturday Night Live — even Druski dressed up as Elizabeth Holmes . During the comedian’s SNL debut , the show spoofed on the success of Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything with a fresh take on its origins. As the skit went, before Fielder and Oppenheim signed on to direct the project, Druski was originally attached to the doc. Jane Wickline appeared in the sketch as Elizabeth Holmes while Ben Marshall portrayed Holmes’ husband, Billy Evans. Related Stories TV James Talarico Crashes 'SNL' Cold Open, Apologizes for Texting Us So Much TV Emma Stone Joins Druski During His 'SNL' Hosting Debut “We’re so glad you’re here,” Wickline’s Holmes said, as Marshall’s Evans added, “It’s really important to us that people find out who Liz really is, you know.” “I just want people to see me as an ordinary person. Can you do that, Druski?” the faux Holmes asked. Druski replied, “Based on what I’ve seen so far, I’m gonna go ahead and say no. Y’all got some of the weirdest, freakiest vibes I have ever seen.” SNL poked fun at the close-up shots featured in You Can See Everything , with Druski and Wickline recreating the infamous moment from the doc where Fielder and Holmes converse about whether the latter was trying to deceive the filmmaker. And while Fielder and Oppenheim’s doc “was a three-hour cinematic epic,” the show joked that “Druski’s tape was released on Instagram Reels in a 1,000 part series titled ‘Crazy White Lady Skit.'” Dru Can See Everything pic.twitter.com/lqIQEHK4VZ — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) November 8, 2026 Referencing the comedian’s own popular mock audition show Coulda Been Love , he even had Marshall’s Evans perform a song of his own. “My name is Billy and I make eight figures, can’t believe I’m here with all my –” he said before being cut off. In one of the most jaw-dropping parts of the sketch, Druski himself transformed into Elizabeth Holmes, prosthetics and all. The moment was prefaced with an SNL voiceover that said, “And just like Fielder, Druski used reenactments to better understand his subjects.” Druski himself added, “I just need to find somebody who can truly embody her character.” Cut to a shot of Druski dressed up as Elizabeth Holmes. “I’m always being real,” he said, as Wickline repeated, “I’m always being real.” They continued to repeat the phrase to one another, as Druski offered, “I could do this all day, bitch. You don’t scare me.” During his monologue as host, Druski warned the SNL audience he couldn’t promise that he wouldn’t do whiteface. “Listen, I know y’all think SNL gonna water me down tonight, but no, they are not holding me back from saying anything,” he said earlier in the episode. “They said, number one, no cussing. I cannot promise that. Number two, no whiteface. I also can’t promise that. That’s about half the show right there.” In another moment in full Elizabeth Holmes drag, Druski told Wickline, “I’m going to show you one of the most famous comedy videos in all of history,” which cut to a viral video of Druski dancing. Earlier in the episode, Emma Stone crashed the comedian’s monologue, as the two are set to co-star in the Universal Pictures rom-com The Catch , which hits theaters on May 21, 2027. “Emma, what’s going on? I’m actually playing her love interest in the new movie that we just did,” he said. Stone responded, “Oh, I’m sorry. OK, yeah. I think you might have misread that in those scenes because we weren’t love interests in the film, but now it is actually starting to make more sense to me why you kept looking at me like that through all these scenes.” In another surprise appearance, Texas senator-elect James Talarico joined the often-political cold open to call for a shift in SNL ‘s cold opens. “People want something new; they want something different,” Talarico said. “I’m talking about SNL’s cold opens,” he said turning to Trump to ask him how long he will continue doing this shtick. “Infinity,” James Austin Johnson’s Trump said. THR

articles.title: Elon Musk Is Portrayed on ‘SNL’: “The Worst Thing South Africa Has Ever Done”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All November 7, 2026 10:58pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk on 'SNL' Weekend Update with Colin Jost. Logo text Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars to get humiliated at the polls, but at least he came away with an SNL parody. Jeremy Culhane played the mogul in an appearance with Weekend Update’s Colin Jost as he tried to make sense of his bruising electoral losses. The actor offered a persuasive impression of the mogul’s halting speeches and nonsensical attempts to change the subject with talk of a future that won’t happen. “Imagine,” Culhane’s Musk ended a sentence several times non-sequiturishly. A few days after his major campaign investments came up fruitless (and in a week when his Cybertruck was officially deemed a failure , compounding the injury), comic Musk sought to change the subject “You’re in the news because you wasted half a billion dollars on the midterms… almost all the candidates you backed lost,” Jost said. Related Stories TV Druski Embodies Elizabeth Holmes in 'You Can See Everything' Spoof on 'SNL' TV James Talarico Crashes 'SNL' Cold Open, Apologizes for Texting Us So Much “I’m in the news because my car did a flip… it was like a freaking Hot Wheel,” Musk replied with a Buttheadian enthusiasm. Jost pointed out the irony that “you moved to Texas because California was run by Democrats” and now Texas would be too. “How does that make you feel?” Jost asked. “Bad,” Musk said, before cluelessly changing the topic back to a car flip and barrage of so-you-know-uhs the mogul is known for. (In real life, Musk tried to turn the losses into vindication for the conspiracy theories that he was involved in rigging the 2024 election.) The show’s writers piled on when they had Musk ask Grok to treat him to an “epic vulgar-roast” (Culhane’s coinage for what Musk considers a major burn) and the AI chatbot came back with, “You’re the worst thing South Africa has ever done;” “When you’re on TV it feels like a episode of ‘Hate on the Spectrum’;” and “If you have 100 more kids, maybe one of them will talk to you.” Musk has been in the pop-cultural spotlight this fall with Alex Gibney’s four-hour investigative documentary , which deconstructs the myth of mogul and makes a case he is far more dangerous than caricaturist appearances in Hollywood productions may suggest. Musk has recently has been buying up spectrum, spending $1 billion on Skydance and taking flack for allegedly turning off Starshield and potentially endangering Ukrainian lives. The character had recently been played by Mike Myers, as in a cold open appearance a year ago as he maniacally bellowed “Legalize Comedy” behind portrayals of Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and other appearances in which he did an unhinged air-pounding two-first dance. That impression had a lot of scenery-chewing swings (and more than its share of Mike Myers being Mike Myers), while Culhane Saturday night was more effectively restrained and on-point, leaving the possibility he might be reprising the character on future SNL episodes. Gibney’s film notes how Musk has been savvy at doing cartoonish enough behaviors that people tend to underestimate him, a point that was underscored even in the sketch when, after he went off one more time about a vulgar epic-roast and a car flip, Jost said “I cannot believe you’re the richest person in the world.” SNL has a tricky relationship with the mogul. Five years ago, Musk himself hosted in an appearance that prompted a boycott from multiple cast members, led to Chloe Fineman crying and is now seen as a bad choice to cuddle-ify a toxic figure. The appearance Saturday could be seen the show’s attempt to atone for that misstep, though some critics will say it further turns Musk into a colorful media character at the expense of his status as a graver threat. Elon Musk is at the Update desk to comment on his tough week pic.twitter.com/9LAVmxFuD1 — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) November 8, 2026 THR

articles.title: Camerimage Opens With a Robot, an AI Reckoning and a Minute of Silence for Kraków
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 8, 2026 2:29am Add us as a Google Preferred Source AI-friendly director Darren Aronofsky received the 2026 Director Award at Camerimage Camerimage The AI elephant in the room took center stage on Saturday at the opening night of the 34th Camerimage Film Festival. Instead of avoiding the divisive issue of artificial intelligence , the Polish fest, the world’s leading festival for the celebration of the art of cinematography, doubled down. For the opening address, in place of festival director Marek Żydowicz, Camerimage sent a humanoid robot, called “Edward Warchocki,” on stage. The slightly tottering, Polish-speaking android addressed the crowd before Żydowicz joined it for an extended back-and-forth about the role of AI in cinema. The “hopes and threats” of the technology, Żydowicz stressed , would be a major talking point throughout the seven-day event in Toruń. Related Stories Movies Camerimage Founder Marek Zydowicz on AI, Aronofsky and Why "Cinematographers Are Artists, Not Technicians" Movies PÖFF Stands With Ukraine: A Look at Films Featured at Tallinn Made Despite, and Because of, the War The Camerimage opening ceremony featured a humanoid robot called Edward. Camerimage The theme ran through the three-hour ceremony at the city’s Jordanki Culture Centre, which was regularly interspersed with video messages from Francis Ford Coppola, Gal Gadot, Christopher Nolan, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Steven Spielberg and Ben Affleck, each weighing in on AI in entertainment. Few filmmakers are as closely associated with the debate as Darren Aronofsky , who was honored with Camerimage’s honorary Award for Director . A vocal advocate of generative AI in filmmaking since launching his AI studio Primordial Soup last year , the Requiem for a Dream and Black Swan helmer said it was his third visit to the festival and that he hoped to keep coming back. “The reason I come back is because there are very rarely film festivals that celebrate the collaboration of everyone,” he said. “They’re very focused on not just the flashy names and that’s really incredible because it honors everyone who makes films possible for people like me.” Other honorees included Karolina Gruszka, one of Poland’s most acclaimed film and stage actresses, who received the Marshal of the Kujawy Pomorze Region Film Award. Gruszka, who appeared in David Lynch’s last feature, Inland Empire (which was shot in Poland) paid tribute to the late director as a “master investigator” of stories. Polish cinematographer Janusz Kamiński, longtime Spielberg collaborator and two-time Oscar winner (for Schindler’s List and Saving Private Ryan ) received The Hollywood Reporter ’s Visionary Award for contributions to cinematography. The festival also paid tribute to the late great Polish director Andrzej Wajda ( Man of Iron , Ashes and Diamonds ), a century after his birth and a decade after his death, with a performance by the Polish Radio Choir – Lusławice giving an a cappella reinterpretation of the music from Wajda’s most important films. Poland’s Senate has declared 2026 “The Year of Wajda.” The night’s opening film — Luca Guadagnino ’s OpenAI origin story Artificial , starring Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever — continued the AI theme. Guadagnino and cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed took the stage to discuss the film and the issues it raises. When it comes to cinema, said Sayeed, AI was “just a tool, like any other.” Guadagnino, who shot Artificial on 35 mm and has shown no interest in using AI for his work, said the real issues raised by Artificial are about “what they call the tech oligarchs, the tech bros” and the unprecedented levels of power, “economic power and political power” they have acquired over our lives. Simon Rich’s script, he said, offered “an unprecedented setup for showing how very few people control societies.” Neon is releasing Artificial in the U.S. on Dec. 25. The Camerimage festivities were overshadowed by events elsewhere in the country. The ceremony began with a minute’s silence for the victims of a mass shooting in Kraków earlier in the day. According to reports, at least six people were killed and more than a dozen injured when a gunman, suspected of far-right ties, drove into the city’s historic Main Market Square and opened fire. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three more bodies were later found at the suspect’s home, making it Poland’s deadliest shooting in decades. Local politicians scheduled to speak at the opening acknowledged the severity of the attack before the program began. Camerimage runs through Nov. 14. THR

articles.title: To Make a Doc About a Nomadic Cyclist, the ‘Perfect Road’ Filmmakers Spent 3 Months in a Campervan
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All November 8, 2026 3:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Perfect Road' film still Courtesy of Elk Film For their documentary Perfect Road , Danish directors and cousins Adam and Christian Bonke followed nomadic cyclist Maximilian Schnell on an extreme journey across some of Europe’s highest mountain passes. The film documents his journey, offers a character study and serves up a meditation on modern life and our priorities and life choices. Elk Film and Dogwoof produced Perfect Road , with Andreas Dalsgaard , Anna Godas, Oli Harbottle, Miriam Nørgaard serving as producers. Jonatan Mose served as cinematographer, with editing handled by Martin Anthon. Related Stories Movies Janusz Kaminski, the Polish Cameraman Who Taught Hollywood How to See Movies Camerimage Opens With a Robot, an AI Reckoning and a Minute of Silence for Kraków Perfect Road , which world premiered at Zurich, is now screening at the 30th anniversary edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ) in Estonia. It shows how the road brings freedom and adventure, but also grueling physical and mental challenges. And that is not only true for Schnell but also the directors and their cinematographer. “We ended up living in a campervan for three months,” recalls Adam Bonke. “It was three grown-up men in a not so big campervan with a lot of equipment. And then we had a small a smaller car, like a satellite, that we could send out on the tiny roads where the campervan couldn’t go.” Adds Christian Bonke: “It was such a headache because you had to put water into the car, you had to empty the toilet. So when we were done shooting for the day, we had to take care of all that.” ‘Perfect Road’ Courtesy of Elk Film The filmmakers considered various strategies for capturing footage. Initially, they wanted to use several different camera people over the course of the three-month adventure. “But then our DP was kicked out by his girlfriend,” Christian Bonke tells THR . “So he said, ‘I’m going to do all three months. This is perfect for me.’ And Adam and I took turns.” It may not have been a holiday or super-comfortable, but Adam Bonke tells THR : “It was comfortable enough.” And it allowed the filmmakers to get a better feel for Schnell’s life choices. “He said, ‘I’m trading comfort for freedom,'” the co-director explains. “I think that’s that’s such a nice thing to say and really frames the film perfectly.” The Danish filmmaker duo actually still fondly looks back at the experience shooting Perfect Road . “We often talk about how we miss those days. It was so beautiful,” says Christian Bonke. “You felt embraced by nature. And after meeting Max, we were completely hit by how conventional and boring [traditional life can be] and how many constraints our lives had at home. So we could get a little glimpse of living his way.” THR

articles.title: Janusz Kaminski, the Polish Cameraman Who Taught Hollywood How to See
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Janusz Kamiński Gabriel Olsen/FilmMagic/Getty Images Like pretty much every great cinematographer, Janusz Kamiński is Polish. As much as any single artist of his generation, he has also taught Hollywood how to see. Kamiński, winner of THR ‘s 2026 Visionary Award for excellence in cinematography, presented at the Camerimage festival on Saturday, grew up in Ziębice, a small town where, as he remembers it, the world was gray. “Although we didn’t feel it was bleak, it was bleak,” Kamiński says. “No billboards. No advertisements. The streets were dark. People dressed in darker tones.” In winter, the houses were heated with coal, and the smoke from every chimney stayed in the air. “The air had this thickness in it, like a fog, because of the coal particles.” Related Stories Movies To Make a Doc About a Nomadic Cyclist, the 'Perfect Road' Filmmakers Spent 3 Months in a Campervan Movies Camerimage Opens With a Robot, an AI Reckoning and a Minute of Silence for Kraków But there was a lot of longing in that gray. “Poland is a very lyrical country, to some degree,” he says. “There’s that melancholy, that certain wish for something else.” Theater troupes passed through, and the local cinema promised a world beyond the town. “We were exposed to work that we didn’t experience in real life, but we wanted to experience,” Kamiński says. “The primary reason I left home is because of the theater and movies, and a life of color.” Kamiński left Poland as a political refugee in 1981, dreaming of American movies. He spoke no English. Landing in Chicago, he spent two years learning the language and then enrolled part-time at Columbia College. In an introductory filmmaking class, he found himself in a group of five. “We had to each pick: One would be the writer, one the actor, one the director, one the producer, and one the cinematographer,” he recalls. “We literally picked straws. I got cinematography. I was 22.” It was love at first sight. “I found out I really enjoyed creating images. It was just fascinating for me to see the flickering image on 16 mm black and white,” he says. “Just that mystery: Will it be in focus? Will it be properly exposed? Will it have a story?” A professor told him he was good at it and should keep going. “This is not a sad story, but it was the first time anyone every told me I was good at something,” says Kamiński. “In Poland, when I grew up, nobody’s parents said that kind of thing. It was: You have food, you eat, you’re good.” All his classmates at Columbia wanted to direct, so Kamiński shot their movies. He loaded a station wagon with equipment every weekend and made student films, and picked up commercial work as a camera assistant, an electrician and a grip. One commercial spot a month would pay $250. “My rent was $280, so I was doing good,” he says. “I had a job, and for an immigrant, it’s essential that we support ourselves, because there was no mommy, no daddy, no cousins.” ‘Schindler’s List’ Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection In the early days, The Hollywood Reporter came to his aid. Back then, in the back of the magazine, THR ran lists of movies going into production, including location shoots. “That’s how I got my first jobs, through The Hollywood Reporter ,” says Kamiński. “I’d look at that films listed and I wouldn’t call on a Tom Cruise movie, but if it was something like Bambis from Hell , I’d call the producer up and say ‘Hi, my name is Janusz Kamiński. I’m a cinematographer. Would you like to look at my work? I got my first two features from that.” Kaminski knew Chicago would not get him to Hollywood. “Most of the movies that would originate in California would come into Chicago and use secondary crew members,” he says. “I don’t want to be secondary.” His girlfriend filled out an application to the American Film Institute, and he was accepted. “That was 1986/87. I moved to California, another place I’d never been to. I had no car.” He rented a place within walking distance of campus. A classmate’s husband, a cinematographer, was shooting a movie for Roger Corman and needed a key grip. Kamiński took the job. “Meanwhile, the gaffer quit. So I said, I like lighting. Let me. So I became the gaffer.” He kept shooting second unit and small independent films while he finished school. The real break came through his demo reel. A friend of a friend was Diane Keaton’s assistant. “He shows my demo reel, my student film demo reel, to Diane Keaton and, suddenly, I have a job shooting for Diane Keaton.” The film was Wildflower, a period TV movie with Patricia Arquette and Beau Bridges. Steven Spielberg saw it and offered Kaminski another TV gig, Class of ‘61, a pilot Spielberg was producing. The show, about West Point cadets on the eve of the Civil War, didn’t get picked up. But Spielberg liked what he saw. When the pilot wrapped, the two men met. “He says, ‘I’d like you to film my next movie. I’m doing a black and white movie called Schindler’s List. Would you be interested?’” Spielberg first went off to do Jurassic Park . “It took him eight to nine months to finish editing,” Kamiński recalls. “All that time I knew I had a job coming with Steven Spielberg. But nobody believed me. Only when I shot the movie, it became reality.” With Spielberg, Kamiński went home to Poland. The film he shot there, full of the gray light and smoky streets he had grown up in, changed how Hollywood shot history. He says the two of them barely discussed the visual style beforehand. “We knew it would be shot in Poland and be black-and-white, but we didn’t have a deep, in-depth conversation about how we’re going to make this movie,” he recalls. “We just wanted to strip away anything that would take us away from the story, so there was no crane, no dolly and no Steadicam. I brought in the idea of using handheld.” ‘ Saving Private Ryan ‘ Photofest Schindler’s List won Kamiński his first Oscar for Best Cinematography. Saving Private Ryan won him a second. The script for that film, he points out, contained one sentence about the landing at Normandy: “Now the troops land at Normandy. That’s it. So as a cinematographer, you have to create the language that corresponds to the story, to the emotions, to the sets and the locations.” What he and Spielberg came up with, all handheld, drained of color and chaotic, rewrote the language of the war movie. Shooting Julian Schnabel’s The Diving Bell and the Butterfly , Kamiński took another phenomenal visual approach to depict the story of a man with locked-in syndrome, only able to see the world through a single functioning eye. In the film, won Camerimage’s Golden Frog honor in 2007, the lens shifts sharply in and out of focus, blurring most of the field of vision while some details pop with intense clarity. “The script, and the book it was based on, are great,” says Kamiński, but provided little guidance. “The whole description is: ‘The hero returns from darkness, from being unconscious for the last two weeks, and starts seeing the world through one eye.’ That’s it.” Samantha Morton and Tom Cruise in ‘Minority Report’ 20th Century Fox Film Corp. All rights reserved./Courtesy Everett Collection Despite certain aesthetic preferences — ”I do like strong light, particularly backlight, I like characters in half-light, going into and out of the shadows. I like smoke” he says — Kamiński does not have a signature look. His approach is film follows function. Cold blues and metallic shadows to evoke the tech-dystopia of Minority Report . Retro pastels and smooth tracking shots to make the 60s swing in Catch Me If You Can . Grainy, handheld shots of muted oranges and browns in Munich to give the story the feel of a 1970s conspiracy thriller. The Kamiński/Spielberg collaboration, which now stretches over 30 years and more than 20 films, has to count as one of the most significant artistic collaborations in American cinema history. His work with Kamiński marks the second phase of Spielberg’s career, as the director moved from glossy, classical Hollywood imagery, sharp lights and bright colors, to a grittier, more naturalistic style, appropriate to the more mature, morally-ambivalent stories he wanted to tell. Kamiński does not claim credit for the director’s evolution. “Steven was not ready to do Schindler’s List until he was ready,” he says. “He was moving that way and I entered his life at the right point where he was able to accept the aesthetics I gave him and embrace them. I think what he saw in me was someone new with a new point of view, someone who wasn’t biased by Hollywood, with a fresh approach. He saw me as a partner. And I saw him as a partner.” ‘ Disclosure Day ‘ Universal Pictures and Amblin Entertainment The partnership continues on Spielberg’s latest, Disclosure Day , which has Kamiński working in a different register. “As I’m getting older, things are becoming more simplistic,” he says. “I want to go slightly more reserved, relaxed.” For the film, a sci-fi thriller about aliens, but set in the present day, he says he aimed for “something more naturalistic, more contemporary.” In one scene, in a safe house, a gray, very direct light comes through the window, slightly green, with a little flare in the background. “It’s got austerity in the images,” Kamiński says, “and that comes from growing up in Poland, with the images from my childhood.” Next up is another collaboration with Spielberg, on an untitled Western, the director’s first, which Spielberg hopes to shoot next year. Kamiński is already imagining the landscape, drawing, as always, from the world he grew up in. “We used to go to this region in the Sudeten Mountains, where it was just beautiful, rolling hills, looked like parts of Montana,” he says. “The lay of the land, the snow on the ground, the fog.” All these elements exist in America too, he acknowledges, but “those who shoot American movies tend to come from somewhere else, and we see these same things differently. That’s why there’s room in this profession for men and women from different countries who bring different aesthetics to American movies.” THR

articles.title: ‘The Invisible Guest’ Remake Director Danial Rifki on Suharto-Era Fear and Why His New Thriller Is About ‘How to Fight Back’
articles.full_text: × Nov 7, 2026 7:21pm PT ‘The Invisible Guest’ Remake Director Danial Rifki on Suharto-Era Fear and Why His New Thriller Is About ‘How to Fight Back’ By Jenny S. Li Plus Icon Jenny S.
