articles.title: ‘3 Body Problem’ Director Derek Tsang Boards DEA True-Crime Series ‘Group 41’ From Zhang Yimou’s ‘Shadow’ Producer Jonah Greenberg (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: × Nov 7, 2026 1:50am PT ‘3 Body Problem’ Director Derek Tsang Boards DEA True-Crime Series ‘Group 41’ From Zhang Yimou’s ‘Shadow’ Producer Jonah Greenberg (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘3 Body Problem’ Director Derek Tsang Boards DEA True-Crime Series ‘Group 41’ From Zhang Yimou’s ‘Shadow’ Producer Jonah Greenberg (EXCLUSIVE) 5 hours ago Stephen Chow Told Japan to Stop Aping Kung Fu, Says Boss of Film Fund Behind Kore-eda Hirokazu’s ‘Look Back’ 11 hours ago Why ‘Suits’ Japan Swapped Drugs for Cash: NBCUniversal, TBS Format Chiefs on Localizing Hits at Taiwan Creative Content Fest 12 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images/Salty Pictures “3 Body Problem” and “Better Days” filmmaker Derek Tsang is attached to direct and executive produce “ Group 41 ,” a true-crime drama series about the first Asian-American squad at the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). The project, from Jonah Greenberg ’s Salty Pictures, is at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. The 10-episode series, with 45-minute episodes, opens in New York in 1986. While the DEA has its sights set on Colombian cocaine cartels and the city’s “Five Families” of the Mafia, a scrappy crew of Asian-American agents teams up with a hard-charging Irish prosecutor nicknamed “The Dragon Lady.” Together they form DEA Group 41, which becomes the first squad to chase the No. 4 heroin pouring into the U.S. through a network few had noticed. Related Stories Sundance Hires Tracy Brady as Marketing, Communications Chief Over the next decade, the underfunded unit grows into an elite international task force. Its targets include Johnny Kon, a Hong Kong boss whose billion-dollar triad spans five continents; Johnny “Onionhead” Eng, a brutal Chinatown gangster; and Khun Sa, a warlord in the Golden Triangle with a 20,000-strong narco-army. The show explores immigration, prejudice and what the American Dream costs, with stories from both sides of the law. Greenberg, a former managing director of CAA’s China office whose producing credits include Zhang Yimou’s “Shadow,” wrote the source book with Marc Iserlis and Aidan Swift, who are also producers and writers on the series. Greenberg says shows about present-day law enforcement can be great, but surveillance technology now gives cops the upper hand. “Back in the 1980s when you went undercover, you went deep. And all the bad guys carry guns, and the danger to cops and informants is real,” Greenberg says. The crimes, and the agents who solved them, were largely overlooked at the time, he adds. “It simply wasn’t considered as sexy to work Chinese cases in the 1980s. People were busy watching ‘Miami Vice’ (myself chief among them!) and watching Rudy Giuliani convict the Italian mobsters,” Greenberg says. Neither the media nor even the DEA made Asian cases a priority, according to Greenberg. “So it’s an underdog story. It’s literally the war on drugs we actually won but which no one knows about.” He also sees room for several seasons across the 10-year saga, with Khun Sa looming over the whole show as a Colonel Kurtz-like final target, giving the series what Greenberg calls a “save the best for last” advantage. The source material, a 180-page nonfiction book titled “The Incredible Story of D.E.A. Group 41 & The Rise and Fall of the Asian Heroin Trade,” will be published next year. Greenberg says the team has the trust and cooperation of the real people involved. Taiwan’s Each Other Films, co-founded by co-producer Tiffany Yu-chia Chen, is on board as co-production partner, and former CAA TV co-head Adam Berkowitz of Lenore Entertainment Group serves as executive producer. After seven years of development, the next steps are to find a writer-showrunner and possibly attach cast before pitching to platforms next year. Greenberg says what has kept him with the project is a wish to tell stories about people driven by purpose, pointing to Cathy Palmer and the agents of Group 41, who took apart a heroin pipeline running from Southeast Asia to the U.S. “‘Serpico’ was always a foundational film for me and well, maybe nobody liked the guy, but he lived by a certain code. And that’s what interests me,” he says. At TCCF, the team wants to learn how incentives in Taiwan and elsewhere in the region could offset the budget, and to explore distribution in Asia, so that production, financing and perhaps even distribution are lined up efficiently before pitching to U.S. platforms. articles.title: bringing backGirls
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Peter White Peter White Executive Editor, Television @peterzwhite More Stories By Peter ‘Call Her Daddy’s Alex Cooper Officially Moves To CAA After Leaving UTA ‘The Terminal List’ Franchise Continues At Amazon With ‘Savage Son’ Danielle Steel’s ‘The Whittiers’ In The Works As Series From Cottage Industry Entertainment & Fox Entertainment Studios View All October 13, 2026 12:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source HBO Girls is coming back. HBO has ordered a limited run of five episodes of Lena Dunham ’s hit comedy with the majority of the original cast confirmed to return. Watch the announcement video below. Related Stories News Lena Dunham Has Idea For ‘Girls’ Movie, Jokingly Tries To Force HBO Max’s Hand News Animated Comedy Series ‘Merrick & Treves’ From ‘Archer’ Team Lands Two-Season HBO Order Dunham will reprise her role as Hannah, Allison Williams returns as Marnie, Jemima Kirke is back as Jessa, Zosia Mamet comes back to play Shoshanna, and Andrew Rannells — who recurred as Elijah in the first three seasons before joining the cast as a regular in Season 4 — also is back. There is, however, no sign of Adam Driver, who played Hannah’s boyfriend Adam. Dunham wrote in her recent memoir Famesick that Driver was “verbally aggressive” during filming of the show. Production will begin next year, which will be 15 years after its premiere and 10 years after the Season 6 finale. Watch on Deadline Dunham, who also created Netflix’s Too Much , which premiered last year, long has talked about wanting to return to the Girls universe. Last year, she told Variety that if she had something “really specific” such as millennial women becoming mothers or stepping into menopause, she would “always want to work with those people again.” In that interview, she also suggested Mamet’s Shoshanna was divorced from the New York mayor, Williams’ Marnie is on her third marriage, Jessa is unvaccinated and lives on a boat in Croatia, and Driver’s Adam is a cult theater actor living in Berlin, while Dunham’s own Hannah teaches at Bard and has a son and a chef girlfriend. Dunham created, wrote and directed the series and will exec produce the return alongside Judd Apatow, and Ilene S. Landress and Michael P. Cohen for Good Thing Going. Williams, Kirke, Mamet and Rannells serve as co-executive producers. Jenni Konner, who served as co-showrunner and was a close creative partner to Dunham during Girls , is not returning. In Famesick , Dunham wrote that she hasn’t spoken to Konner since 2018. Dunham said: “We always said we would only return to Girls if there was a specific story we were burning to tell. I’ve missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn’t quite picture them in the present day. Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking, it’s pretty hard to get them to stop. … It’s rare that you get the chance to return to something that changed your life with the gift of hindsight and a whole new level of gratitude and understanding. I love these girls (and boy), our friends at HBO and all the people who have continued to discover the show and remind us afresh why we do this, which is the joy of being together … and the chance to wear yellow mesh…” Amy Gravitt, EVO, Head of HBO & HBO Max Comedy Programming, added: “We’re thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one’s 20s to the milestone of turning 40. To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa, and Elijah is a massive understatement, but we know fans — old and new — will be happy to see how they’ve grown and relieved to see that they’re still the Girls we knew way back when.” ‘Godzilla’ Stalks $30M-$33M Domestic Bow, Best Ever For Foreign-Language Pic ‘Grey’s’ Spinoff Pushed To 2027-28; Shoot Moves To N.M. articles.title: died at age 52
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Denise Petski Denise Petski Senior Managing Editor More Stories By Denise ‘Melania, The Series’ Gets Prime Video Release Date & Trailer Ella Langley, Tim McGraw, Miranda Lambert Among Performers For CMA Awards More Details Revealed About ‘Ellen DeGeneres Show’ EP Matthew Wright’s Sudden Death View All November 4, 2026 10:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Matthew Wright on 'The Ellen DeGeneres Show' The Ellen DeGeneres Show via YouTube UPDATED: More details have been revealed about the sudden death of Ellen DeGeneres Show executive producer Matthew Wright . A GoFundMe page created for the family was updated to reveal that Wright “died suddenly but peacefully in his sleep on Friday, October 30.” Wright was 52. No other details about his death were shared. PREVIOUS, November 2: Ellen DeGeneres is mourning the loss of Matthew Wright, who worked as an executive producer on The Ellen DeGeneres Show for 16 years and appeared frequently on the show. Wright died Friday, October 30, “in an unfathomable tragedy” while he was working remotely in Los Angeles, according to a GoFundMe for his family. He was 52. No details about the cause of his death were shared. Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries News Sandy Frank Dies: Legendary Distributor & ‘Name That Tune’ Producer Was 97 “In an unfathomable tragedy, Matt Wright passed away Oct 30th while working remotely in Los Angeles. His husband, father, sister and niece are in New York, desperate to be reunited for a proper goodbye. We’re asking for all of his friends, who Matt loved so fully, to help the family at this time. As many of you know, Matt and Justin were both laid off this summer. And the unexpected costs of getting Matt home, a funeral and a memorial are impossible for the family to bear,” the GoFundMe continued. “If Matt has ever made you laugh, said an encouraging word right when you needed it, or ordered one too many appetizers for the enjoyment of the whole table, now is the time to repay the favor. Please donate what you can and share this with anyone who’s been in the orbit of Matt’s huge heart. And when you’re at dinner and see a sunset, know that Matt is looking down, loving you, but wildly disappointed in what you ordered.” DeGeneres shared a tearful video, saying: “He was an amazing guy. He was funny. God, he made me laugh. He would surprise me with things that he did all the time. He was smart. He was kind. He was the part of our show that — I mean, everyone loved him. I loved him. And it’s just shocking — it’s shocking,” she said. “We’re gonna miss him. He is and always will be the glue to our entire family at the ‘Ellen Show.’” Wright was a regular presence on the show, appearing frequently in a recurring segment called “Strong Opinions with Matt”. You can watch one of the segments here: Wright also was a producer on several episodes of DeGeneres’ Ellen’s Game of Games in 2017-18 and her 2009 special Ellen’s Bigger, Longer & Uncut. He began his TV career as a producer on the 2002-06 SoapNet series Soap Talk. Andy Lassner, who also served as an EP of the Ellen DeGeneres Show , shared photos of him and Wright on the Jennifer Hudson Show set that were taken on Thursday, the day before Wright’s death. Lassner said Wright had stopped by the set to visit. “We are all in shock. He was a brilliant producer and an even better human being,” Lassner wrote. “The way he looked after his mom, flying back and forth from Los Angeles to New York practically every weekend before she died, showed what an incredible son he was. He gave that same depth of love to his friendships. My heart breaks for his husband, Justin, his family, and all of us who loved him. I was so lucky to work beside Matt for so many years and to call him my friend. We should have had so much more time with him.” Wright’s survivors include his husband Justin Fusella. articles.title: Netflix’s Radford Studio Acquisition Moving Ahead Despite Streamer’s Sunset Blvd Landlord Throwing Shade On Deal
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Netflix’s Radford Studio Acquisition Moving Ahead Despite Streamer’s Sunset Blvd Landlord Throwing Shade On Deal Ken Ziffren Offers Optimistic View On Industry, Even When It Comes To AI & Federal Tax Credit Legislation Nithya Raman Wins L.A. Mayor Race As Karen Bass Concedes View All November 6, 2026 6:41pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Radford Studio Center Getty Images / Netflix Netflix didn’t end up owning the legendary Warner Bros lot after losing out earlier this year to David Ellison for the Burbank studio, but the streamer is still ploughing ahead to take control of Radford Studio Center in the next several months. Despite some recent shade thrown by Netflix’s current Sunset Blvd landlord, the long-rumored $400 million plus purchase of the 55-acre Studio City production facility by the Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters -run company is coming together on schedule. Netflix did not respond today to Deadline’s request for remarks on the status of the Radford acquisition. However, a source close to events said “the deal is progressing on the agreed upon timetable and with the agreed upon sets of milestone dates.” Related Stories Trailers 'The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth' Trailer: More Plot Details Emerge In Latest Look At Fincher-Tarantino-Pitt Team-Up Executives Emily Feingold Heads To Walt Disney As EVP Comms; Succeeds Retiring Studio Vet David Jefferson What exactly that timetable and those milestone dates are has been left vague. Late this summer, the streamer was granted more time to look into the bones of Radford and see what the true shape of the place is. Still, even with big layoffs, Peter Rice taking over as Content chief from the fired Bela Bajaria , declining engagement and an ailing stock (which dipped to $63.4 today), the desire at the upper echelon of Netflix for a sprawling studio lot of their own to cement the company’s industry dominance is stronger than ever. Watch on Deadline With Hudson Pacific CEO Victor Coleman announcing on a November 5 earnings call that Netflix “had not closed the transaction” on Radford, a real estate monsoon of sorts swelled up this week. Undercutting his own remarks, Coleman added, “they are not deciding to close it until sometime maybe later in the year, or not.” At present, there haven’t been any required filings with the SEC or L.A. County by Netflix for Radford Still, while the endgame has never really been in doubt since this summer, the fact is negotiations for Radford have been moving in ebbs and flow, I’m told. “They haven’t signed on the dotted line, that will all likely happen later this year,” a L.A. real estate insider added of where talks between Netflix and the Goldman Sachs-led group that took over the 98-year-old Radford when Hackman Capital Partners defaulted on a $1.1. billion loan early this year. “It’s a priority, sure. Remember with renovations and new builds, there’s a lot to put in place too.” (L-R) Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters, WBD CEO David Zaslav and Netflix-co-CEO Ted Sarandos tour the Warner Bros lot in late 2025 Joe Pugliese and John Nowak for Warner Bros. Discovery A December 17 stroll around the WB lot by Sarandos and Peters with then WBD CEO David Zaslav when the streamer looked certain to buy the joint wetted the Netflix’s CEO beaks. However, beyond those maters of the universe moments, it has also long been clear to Netflix’s execs that they needed a full service L.A. space of their own for both offices and production – which led to the start of talks with Goldman in April. As it is, the global HQ of the global streamer right now is a rented hodgepodge of Hudson Pacific-owned Sunset structures and venues that the Netflix has outgrown. With leases on the ICON building and others until 2031, Netflix is one of Hudson Pacific’s biggest customers. Netflix’s office building in Hollywood, California Robyn Beck/AFP via Getty Images Outside pricey California, Netflix has been building out from renter to owner itself the past few years. Leaning into incentives offered in other states, the streamer has Netflix Studios Albuquerque, a108-acre campus with 12 soundstages and more in New Mexico. In New York, there’s the six soundstages of Netflix Studios Brooklyn. Next door in New Jersey, the massive nearly 300-acre Netflix Studios Fort Monmouth studio is under construction at a cost of more than $1 billion. The projected 12 sound stages are expected to come online in staggered openings next year and in 2028. Add to all that, just outside London, the streamer’s UK hub of Longcross Studios with its five sound stages A CBS hub over the decades and once dubbed Republic Studios way back in the day, Radford has “22 stages, 210,000 square feet of office space and 172,737 square feet of support space,” according to its specs. The site of where Seinfeld, Gunsmoke , and The Mary Tyler Moore Show were shot, Radford has a number of current tenants who would obviously need to have their leases bought out if Netflix took over. After buying Radford in 2021 off what was then ViacomCBS for $1.85 bilion, Hackman and its partners planned to pour big bucks into upgrades and revamps. That all fell apart for the company, who own the likes of the 25-acre Television City on Fairfax and other venues around the world, as production in the home of Hollywood took a downward dive around 2023. Very quickly, once hard to get soundstage space became plentiful — and often empty. That won’t change overnight at Radford once Netflix takes over, but it will send a very clear message to a town eager for good news and jobs. ‘Godzilla’ Stalks $30M-$33M Domestic Bow, Best Ever For Foreign-Language Pic ‘Grey’s’ Spinoff Pushed To 2027-28; Shoot Moves To N.M. articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Justin Kroll Justin Kroll Film Editor @krolljvar More Stories By Justin Teyonah Parris To Co-Star With Denzel Washington In Christopher McQuarrie’s Thriller For United Artists Nicholas Galitzine Eyeing Ichabod Crane Role In Sony’s ‘Hollow’ Starring Sydney Sweeney Maya Hawke Boards ‘Magic: The Gathering’ Movie From Legendary And Hasbro View All November 6, 2026 7:33pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult Getty/Getty After weeks of wondering who could be up for the mystery James Bond screen test, Deadline has not only found out who the actor is, another suitor was also added to the mix. While not confirmed, insiders tell Deadline that Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult joined Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner in recent screen tests to play the next 007 . While it was recently reported that four actors tested, insiders say a fifth test was added at the 11th hour (though it is unknown which actor was that last addition). articles.title: Toei CEO Fumio Yoshimura Talks Global Expansion, GenAI Adoption & Entry Into Games
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz ‘The Remarried Empress’ Sets Disney+ Record As Most Viewed Local Original Launch Ever ‘Dune’ Star Chang Chen Introduces Six Rising Taiwanese Actors In Golden Horse & TCCF Showcase Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah Unpacks TAICCA Partnership: “Taiwan Has Creative Talent, Technology & Government Support” View All November 6, 2026 11:55pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Toei CEO Fumio Yoshimura speaks at TCCF TAICCA Fumio Yoshimura, CEO of Japan’s Toei Co, explained how the studio is working with local partners to globalize its long-established IP, as well as innovating in areas including GenAI and gaming, in a keynote Forum session at Taiwan Creative Content Fest ( TCCF ). In 2023, the 75-year-old studio launched an ambitious $2BN ‘Toei New Wave’ plan to boost its international revenue’s share of total income from 30% to 50% by 2033, which included upgrades to its studio facilities in Tokyo and Kyoto. Since then the company has embarked on several international co-productions and partnerships, started exploring GenAI technology and moved into production of games. Related Stories News 'Dune' Star Chang Chen Introduces Six Rising Taiwanese Actors In Golden Horse & TCCF Showcase News Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah Unpacks TAICCA Partnership: "Taiwan Has Creative Talent, Technology & Government Support" Yoshimura started the session by explaining how the company has been introducing its popular IP to international markets. The latest series in one of its oldest franchises, Kamen Rider Zetz , is currently streaming in Taiwan and other international markets, with India a particular focus. Watch on Deadline “In 2025, we held an event to introduce Kamen Rider to India consumers. We got a very good response and signed a contract with a Disney affiliate to distribute the content. Due to its population size and the growth of its middle-class, we see India as a promising market,” Yoshimura said. Kamen Rider was one of the first franchises that Toei globalized, working with U.S. partners to produce an English-language verskon, Mighty Morphin Power Rangers , more than 30 years ago, with the franchise now handled by toymaker Hasbro. Both the Kamen Rider and Power Rangers franchises have been extended to toys, merchandising and live events. In other IP extensions, Toei recently teamed with Sony’s Anyplex Inc and Godzilla VFX house Shriogumi Inc to launch a Kamen Rider anime label. Other recent localization efforts include the Voltes 5 franchise, which was first launched as an anime in Japan in 1977 and became a cultural phenomenon in the Philippines where its themes of resistance against a repressive empire got it banned by the Marcos regime. In 2023, Philippines broadcaster GMA produced a live-action remake, Voltes V: Legacy , which became a ratings hit in the Philippines and also aired in Japan. “Simply exporting content limits its reach, so in order to break through constraints, we are producing remakes and localisations,” Yoshimura explained. After getting started with remakes, Yoshimura said the studio is now also working on local productions based on original stories: “We’re developing local content from scratch, working with local talent to release locally and then sell globally. We believe this local first model will generate more sustainable long-term revenue than the traditional export model.” Among recent productions, Toei worked with Taiwan’s Lou Lou Film Studio on Dear Stranger , directed by Tetsuya Mariko and starring Hidetoshi Nishijima and Gwei Lun-mei, which screened on the festival circuit last year. More recently, the company worked with Taiwan’s Wowing Entertainment Group on horror film The Rope Curse 4: Kuntilanak , directed by Liao Shih-Han and starring Lee Kang-sheng. Yoshimura identified Taiwan as another key market for Toei’s global expansion, due to cultural similarities and the popularity of Japanese IP in Taiwan. “Data shows that Japanese films had a 26% share of Taiwan’s box office last year, the second highest share after Hollywood with 41%,” Yoshimura said. “Taiwanese audiences have a strong interest in Japanese content.” Toei has also partnered with Thailand’s M Studio on a slate of Thai-language remakes and local features, and is currently working with both M Studio and Korea’s Showbox on a horror feature based on Japanese manga The Long Hair In The Attic , by artist Junji Ito. The studio has also stepped into assisting the growing number of international productions now shooting in Japan, encouraged by Japan’s incentives scheme, including U.S. indie action thriller Iris, created by and starring Dani Swan ( The Matrix Resurrections ). In addition to providing facilities, Toei helped with casting for the film and assisted on the incentives application. On the tech front, Yoshimura explained that the company is expanding the Virtual Production and motion capture facilities at its studios in Tokyo and Kyoto and also starting to use AI in workflows. “We’re also experimenting with GenAI image generation,” Yoshimura said. “The Toei team is performing tests on practical AI applications daily; building tools to assist junior producers in estimating production budgets, and using AI in background artwork. However we believe human creativity remains the core of everything we do.” Microdrama is another area that Toei has stepped into – producing Everyday Host Club , a 24×3-minute anime series, and a 30-episode short-form vertical drama, Meshimori Onna , made for smartphone screens. Gaming is another new area for Toei as it explores how to expand its IP across borders and formats. “Gaming is a global entertainment medium and delivering games to users worldwide aligns perfectly with our global expansion strategy,” Yoshimura said. Toei plans to launch its first game, Hino , developed by UnGloom Studio, in spring 2027, followed by Debug – Nephemee and Killa later next year. All the games will be distributed across platforms and consoles including Steam, Nintendo and Xbox. The session entitled ‘Survival Strategies for Global Enterprises: Japan’s Toei on IP, Globalization, and Business Mindset’ took place as part of TCCF’s Forum section, which also includes sessions on Japan’s K2P Film Fund, Indonesian studio MD Entertainment’s scaling strategy, as well as panel discussions on co-production, mircodrama, AI adoption and IP exploitation. articles.title: How A Mistake In Warner Bros. Contracts Helped Eleven Film & Jack Thorne Land ‘Lord Of The Flies’ TV Rights — Thessaloniki
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Magenta TV’s Cypriot-Set Thriller ‘Brothers’ Wasn’t Allowed To Shoot In The Country. The Producers Explain Why: “The Reasons Were Political” ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: More Plot Details Emerge In Latest Look At Fincher-Tarantino-Pitt Team-Up Oscar Micheaux Film And Media Institute To Launch Theatrical Roadshow Program For Independent Filmmakers View All November 7, 2026 3:40am Add us as a Google Preferred Source David McKenna as Piggy in 'Lord of the Flies' BBC/Eleven/Lisa Tomasetti “It’s the only thing I’ve ever done that I’d describe, without feeling embarrassed, as hard work,” Joel Wilson of Eleven Film said when discussing his role as an executive producer on Jack Thorne’s Lord of the Flies adaptation. Wilson was speaking on a panel at the Thessaloniki Film Festival, where the series is screening this weekend. Wilson added: “It was genuinely physically tough and psychologically rigorous. But the creative process was the most joyful one I’ve ever been involved in.” Related Stories News Thessaloniki: Walter Thompson-Hernández's 'If I Go Will They Miss Me' Among Titles Set For International Competition News Thessaloniki: Adaptation Of Ioanna Karystiani's 'Swell' Among 2026 Agora Works In Progress Titles The four-part series, based on William Golding’s novel of the same name, launched on the BBC in the UK in February and started streaming on Netflix in the U.S. in May. Adolescence co-creator and Emmy winner Thorne adapted the book for the screen. Wilson told the audience in Thessaloniki that the process began many years earlier, when he unsuccessfully contacted Golding’s estate to enquire about purchasing the Lord of the Flies TV rights. Watch on Deadline “I hadn’t done very much, and they politely told me to come back later,” Wilson joked. “So I did, again and again. Eventually, we made Sex Education , and our reputation had grown since the first time I’d called them.” Wilson added that he later developed a relationship with the agent who owned the stage rights to the book, whom he called “every six months”, and later tipped him off about a potential quirk in the book’s copyright contracts that could open the door for a TV adaptation. “Warner Bros. owned the rights and had tried to remake it several times without success,” Wilson explained. “It was unclear in the original contract whether Warner Bros. owned the film and television rights or only the film rights because the idea of making Lord of the Flies for television wouldn’t have been considered at the time.” Wilson said the Golding family retained the TV rights and, miraculously, around the same time, Thorne, whom he had worked with before, mentioned his interest in adapting the book. “I’d offered him another project he didn’t want to do, and said, ‘If you don’t want to do that, how am I ever going to get you to work with me again?’” Golding said of the conversation he had with Thorne. “He responded, ‘If you can get the rights to Lord of the Flies , I’ll do that.’ It’s one of the only moments in my life I’d genuinely describe as serendipitous. I nearly fell off my chair and said, ‘I’m speaking to the family about it now. Can I email them on Monday with Jack Thorne— Lord of the Flies in the subject line? He said, Absolutely.” Wilson explained that with Thorne attached, the project quickly picked up momentum. “We then pitched it to the BBC. It was the first time this had happened to me, though it seems to happen to everyone else: We went in and said, ‘Jack wants to make Lord of the Flies . Are you in?’ They said, ‘Yes, please,’” Wilson recalled. “There wasn’t even a script, but the vision was very clear, and they greenlit it.” Marc Munden ( The Mark of Cain, National Treasure ) directed the series, with Wilson executive producing alongside his Eleven colleague Jamie Campbell and Thorne. Hans Zimmer provided music for the series, which was nominated for two Emmys. “I think we managed to do exactly what we set out to do: protect the vision Jack and Mark had, which relates so closely to the original novel,” Wilson said of the series. “I’m glad to say Judy, William Golding’s daughter, was delighted with it. That was one of the most important things, because the book was so precious to her.” The 2026 Thessaloniki Film Festival runs until November 15. ‘Godzilla’ Stalks $30M-$33M Domestic Bow, Best Ever For Foreign-Language Pic ‘Grey’s’ Spinoff Pushed To 2027-28; Shoot Moves To N.M. articles.title: Paul Howard Dies: Son Of Three Stooges’ Moe Howard, Keeper Of The Flame Was 91
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘The End Of Oak Street’ Gets HBO Max Streaming Release Date ‘Buena Vista Social Club’ Sets Broadway Closing; West End Production Announced For 2027 Kimmarie Johnson Dies: ‘Beverly Hills, 90210’ & ‘Dude, Where’s My Car?’ Actor Was 50 View All November 7, 2026 6:34am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Moe Howard, Paul Howard circa 1940s Courtesy C3 Entertainment Paul Howard , the only son of The Three Stooges ‘ Moe Howard and the last surviving son of the comedy team’s classic line up – Moe, brothers Curly and Shemp, and Larry Fine – died this week. He was 91. The death was confirmed by a spokesperson for C3 Entertainment, the owner of The Three Stooges license and brand. An exact date or cause of death was not specified. Howard, who lived on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, had acted as a guardian of his father’s legacy, often interacting with fans over the years and, in the words of C3, providing “a unique, firsthand view of the man behind the iconic bowl cut and timeless slapstick comedy.” Related Stories News Kimmarie Johnson Dies: 'Beverly Hills, 90210' & 'Dude, Where's My Car?' Actor Was 50 News More Details Revealed About 'Ellen DeGeneres Show' EP Matthew Wright's Sudden Death Both Moe Howard and Larry Fine died in 1975; Moe’s brothers Shemp and Curly died in 1955 and 1952, respectively. Watch on Deadline “He connected directly with generations of The Three Stooges fans at various conventions and events over the years, sharing personal stories, family memories, and insights into the life of Moe Howard and the Stooges’ enduring impact on American pop culture,” the announcement stated. In 2015, Paul Howard hosted an acclaimed 9-part docuseries Hey Moe, Hey Dad! , a series that served as an intimate, definitive tribute to the legacy of The Three Stooges, featuring rare archival footage, personal family accounts, and interviews with the families of Moe Howard, Larry Fine, Curly Howard, Shemp Howard, and latter Stooge Curly Joe DeRita, as well as interviews with well-known celebrity fans including Whoopi Goldberg, Billy West, and Leonard Maltin. The docuseries is available on The Three Stooges+ YouTube channel. Moe Howard, Larry Fine, Curly Howard, 1936 Everett Collection The Three Stooges, of course, were the beloved comedy troupe active from the early 1920s through 1970 who starred in nearly 200 film shorts that featured their slapstick, cartoonishly violent humor. Moe Howard and Larry Fine were part of the act throughout its existence, with either of Howard’s brothers Samuel “Shemp” Howard and Jerome “Curly” Howard taking the role of third stooge at various times during the act’s prime years. After the deaths of Shemp and Curly in the 1950s, comics Joe Besser and “Curly Joe” DeRita filled in during the 1960s. The C3 statement concluded, Paul Howard’s “devotion to preserving his family’s history leaves a lasting imprint on the global Stooges community. He will be remembered fondly for his dedication to honoring his father’s memory and the joy he brought to fans worldwide.” Howard is survived by daughter Jennifer and nephew Jeffrey. ‘Godzilla’ Stalks $30M-$33M Domestic Bow, Best Ever For Foreign-Language Pic ‘Grey’s’ Spinoff Pushed To 2027-28; Shoot Moves To N.M. articles.title: Magenta TV’s Cypriot-Set Thriller ‘Brothers’ Wasn’t Allowed To Shoot In The Country. The Producers Explain Why: “The Reasons Were Political”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Magenta TV’s Cypriot-Set Thriller ‘Brothers’ Wasn’t Allowed To Shoot In The Country. The Producers Explain Why: “The Reasons Were Political” ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: More Plot Details Emerge In Latest Look At Fincher-Tarantino-Pitt Team-Up Oscar Micheaux Film And Media Institute To Launch Theatrical Roadshow Program For Independent Filmmakers View All November 7, 2026 6:43am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Magenta TV’s Brothers. Magenta TV. Nicosia, the capital of Cyprus, is at the center of Brothers, the new 6-part series by Simon Farmakas, but producers Fenia Cossovitsa and Alexandra Hoesdorff revealed this afternoon during a panel in Thessaloniki that the show couldn’t shoot in the city. Cossovitsa and Hoesdorff were joined on the panel by Faye Tsitsipi, Deputy Director of Content Management at MagentaTV, which will broadcast the series in Greece. The show follows an unorthodox Turkish Cypriot and a hard-headed Greek Cypriot detective who unexpectedly join forces with a European bank auditor in her fight to bring down a politically corrupt network. Related Stories News Thessaloniki: Walter Thompson-Hernández's 'If I Go Will They Miss Me' Among Titles Set For International Competition News Thessaloniki: Adaptation Of Ioanna Karystiani's 'Swell' Among 2026 Agora Works In Progress Titles The series was shot across several European countries, including Germany, Luxembourg, and Greece, but not Cyprus. When asked why the production was spread so widely across Europe, Farmakas told the audience in Thessaloniki that the producers were “forced” to do so on political grounds. Watch on Deadline “In August 2025, we submitted the project to the Ministry of Culture in Cyprus for the equivalent of a cash rebate. It was five or six months of long discussions explaining what the project would be,” she said. Hoesdorff added: “We had a meeting in Cannes, and we had a Zoom call with everyone. They had read the presentation and the first episode, so they knew what the project was about. That’s very important.” Cossovitsa continued to say that “in December 2025, we were told—and it’s important to say this was communicated verbally, not in writing—that they couldn’t commit to the project. This happened just before we started production.” Cossovitsa said the series was already in pre-production. She said reasons the Ministry of Culture in Cyprus turned the project down were “political, obviously.” Cossovitsa continued to suggest that the Cypriot government was unwilling to support a project that predominantly represented Turkish Cypriots. “You can’t make people disappear,” she said. “You can’t pretend that, on the other side of the no man’s land, there isn’t the Turkish-occupied part. You can’t say there are no Turkish detectives. You can’t leave out the Turkish flag, because when you go to Nicosia, it’s there. We couldn’t make them disappear. That was the request.” Hoesdorff said the decision from the Cypriot government put the production in a “very difficult situation” financially. “One has to understand that Cyprus has very high tax credits. Moving everything to Greece made a huge logistical and financial difference,” she said. “So we had to become very creative—more creative than usual—to solve the huge gap we suddenly faced.” Brothers is currently in post. Farmakas is the showrunner. His previous credits include Sunrise in Kimmeria (2018). Tsitsipi said Brothers will likely land on MagentaTV in the next year. articles.title: Apple TV Renews ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ for Season 3
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All November 6, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jesse Burgess in Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars Kristin Silady Logo text As the Michelin Guide continues to expand to new cities, so must its television series. Apple TV has given the official green light to season three of its culinary docuseries, Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars . The series, which comes from executive producer Gordon Ramsay , takes cameras around the globe and into the kitchens of the chefs fighting for the most prestigious accolade in restaurants: a Michelin star. Some chefs are going for their first, some are going for more and many are just trying to hold onto their cred. Hosted by TopJaw frontman and co-founder Jesse Burgess , the first two eight-episode seasons are streaming on Apple TV now. “I’m absolutely delighted that Apple TV audiences and chefs from all around the world have truly embraced Knife Edge,” Ramsay said in a statement. “Taking viewers on the journey towards Michelin stars is like climbing aboard an epic rollercoaster. You’d better hold on tight, because it’s one hell of a ride.” Related Stories TV Toni Collette to Lead Apple TV Dramedy 'Lenni' TV 'Monarch: Legacy of Monsters' Eyes Season 3 Shakeup -- If It's Renewed What distinguishes the show, easily Apple TV’s most ambitious entry into the popular food space, is the access its been given by The Michelin Guide. After all, this is an institution that prizes itself on secrecy, deploying its undercover diners to restaurants the world in hopes of getting an accurate reporting of a typical dining experience. “What I love most about making Knife Edge is that, however much time I spend in restaurants around the world, I’m constantly surprised by the extraordinary people and stories we discover,” said Burgess. “Behind every restaurant is a very personal journey, and for the chefs we follow, a Michelin Star can represent years of sacrifice, obsession and an enormous amount of hard work.” Knife Edge has been a unique entry into the Apple TV catalog, marrying travel, culinary competition and docudrama. It’s been enough to attain a 100 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes and earn a nomination at the BAFT Television Awards. The series is produced by Apple TV by Studio Ramsay Global, a Fox Entertainment Company. Executive producers are Ramsay, Lisa Edwards, Lorraine Charker-Phillips and Jill Greenwood, with James Callum serving as the series director. The season two finale dropped on the steamer Friday. THR

articles.title: ‘Stranger Things’ Spinoff Series ‘Other Worlds’ Set in the 1950s Ordered by Netflix
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All November 6, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Noah Schnapp as Will Byers and Winona Ryder as Joyce Byers in 'Stranger Things.' Courtesy of Netflix Logo text Stranger Things is returning to Netflix . The streamer has officially ordered a live-action prequel series to its massive sci-fi hit (see announcement video below). Titled Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure , the new series will be set in the 1950s, with production taking place in New Mexico. Original series creators and showrunners The Duffer Brothers will serve as co-creators, but have otherwise handed over creative duties to longtime Stranger Things writer Kate Trefry, who also penned the Stranger Things: The First Shadow stage play, and Golden Globe-winning director Joe Wright ( Atonement ), who will helm the first three episodes. Related Stories Business Netflix Taps Mattel's Roberto Stanichi to Lead Consumer Products and Experiences Movies 'La Bola Negra' Ups Planned Theater Count Heading Into Netflix Film's Widest Weekend Yet (Exclusive) The series will feature an all-new cast and story. Details are being kept under wraps, but the title, 1950s New Mexico setting, and one hint by the Duffers in their statement (“watch the skies”) sure do suggest the show has a UFO/aliens/outer space theme. “We’ve been dreaming of Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure for many years now, and to see it become a reality is surreal and exhilarating,” said Matt and Ross Duffer in a statement. “We’re so grateful to our incredible team of collaborators: our showrunner Kate Trefry, who has been in the trenches with us since season two and wrote Stranger Things: The First Shadow ; and our director, Joe Wright, a brilliant artist whose work we’ve long admired. We can’t wait for you to see what they’re cooking up. It’s Stranger Things , but also thrillingly fresh, with a new setting, new heroes and villains, and new… actually, we’re not allowed to say any more. Now, on to casting. In the meantime — watch the skies, nerds!” Last year, Duffers signed a deal to officially jump from Netflix to Paramount as part of a four-year deal with the studio which covers film, TV and streaming projects. “ Stranger Things has always belonged to the fans, and their passion made it a worldwide phenomenon,” said Netflix scripted head Jinny Howe. “Today, on Stranger Things Day, we’re honored to partner again with Matt and Ross Duffer and Kate Trefry to give fans a new dimension of this universe to step into. Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure takes us to the 1950s with new heroes and all the heart, mystery, and spectacle of the original series.” Added Trefry: “The Duffer Brothers gave me my first paying job in Hollywood, and it has been a joy and a fever dream ever since. Now, it is my insane honor and privilege to be bringing this new chapter of Stranger Things to life alongside them and our incredible director Joe Wright. With the support of Netflix and 21Laps, we have had the time of our lives returning to all the horror, wonder and mystery of the flagship, while also telling a wholly new story, one we hope will blow your minds and break your hearts all over again.” Executive producers include The Duffer Brothers via Upside Down Pictures, Shawn Levy and his 21 Laps company, and Paul Dichter, Shelley Meals, Andrea Sperling and Pavlina Hatoupis. Stranger Things debuted in 2016 and became Netflix’s biggest show, delivering 1.2 billion views globally during its first four seasons. The show aired its series finale earlier this year. THR

articles.title: ‘Buena Vista Social Club’ to Close on Broadway in January
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All November 6, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Broadway company of 'Buena Vista Social Club.' Matthew Murphy Buena Vista Social Club will play its final performance Jan. 17 after close to two years on Broadway . The musical, inspired by the titular Cuban band, took home five Tony Awards in 2025, including a special Tony for its onstage band. While the show is closing in January, producers say it is on track to recoup before closure, making it the second musical of the 2024-2025 to announce recoupment. The show also has a touring production, and currently has productions in Puerto Rico and Mexico City. In 2027, the musical will open in London’s West End. Buena Vista Social Club is the first show on Broadway to feature a score sung entirely in Spanish. The story is based on the creation of the Buena Vista Social Club’s 1997 album, which was made up of legends in the 1950s Cuban music scene and toggles between the creation of the album and the past. The musical opened on March 19, 2025, at the Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre, after starting previews in February 2025. The musical is still commanding high attendance, though its grosses have gradually fallen from the highs of 2025. It is the second musical of its season to recoup, following Just In Time , which is still running. The show features a book by Marco Ramirez, direction by Saheem Ali and choreography by Patricia Delgado and Justin Peck. Lead producer Orin Wolf also hinted at a possible film deal. “From our very first trip to Cuba to meet the musicians who created this masterpiece, I knew we had something truly special, something to cherish. I am in awe of what Marco R., Saheem, Patricia, Justin, David, Marco P. and Dean have created artistically, bringing this extraordinary music to life on stage and presenting the first Broadway score performed exclusively in Spanish,” said Wolf. “I am deeply grateful for the time we’ve had on Broadway – and the speed with which the team has created three more productions. We are thrilled the Broadway production is on schedule to recoup as we look ahead to an exciting tour, special engagements in Mexico and Puerto Rico, the film and so much more.” In addition to the onstage band, the cast of Buena Vista Social Club currently includes Gina Torres (Omara), Rick Negron (Compay), Mel Semé (Ibrahim), Jainardo Batista Sterling (Rubén), Isa Antonetti (Young Omara), Da’Von T. articles.title: ‘an open field’ Is a Deeply Personal Story of Loss, Grief and Compassion (Exclusive Netflix Trailer)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All November 6, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'an open field' Courtesy of Netflix In March 2019, a Boeing 737 MAX crashed in Ethiopia just six minutes after taking off from the airport in the country’s capital, Addis Ababa. It had 157 people on board, and all of them died. Among them was Max Thabiso Edkins . His older brother Teboho Edkins decided to make a film about the experience of grief and mourning that his family and the local community went through. The result is the very personal 38-minute short film an open field , directed by Edkins and produced by his father, Don Edkins, and Carine Chichkowsky. The film is now going global, hitting Netflix on Dec. 1, about a year after its world premiere at the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam ( IDFA ) 2025, where it won the best short documentary award. Related Stories Business Netflix Taps Mattel's Roberto Stanichi to Lead Consumer Products and Experiences Business Dark Slope to Open New Virtual Production Stage in Vancouver (Exclusive) The title of the movie becomes clear when you watch it. In an open field, the filmmaker finds out that dozens of nearby villagers immediately converged on the crash site to help. Some even stood vigil for a month to protect and preserve the area. Years later, they continue to mourn alongside family members who visit the site, including Edkins and his father, also making the film a story about collective grief and compassion. “Boeing’s widely criticized response to the crash stands in sharp contrast to the community’s enduring compassion,” highlights a synopsis. “Both a personal essay on loss and an exploration of the potential healing power of collective mourning, Edkins’s film is a quiet testament to humanity – moments of warmth, resolve, grief, fear, patience, and simple acts of kindness.” Indeed, the film feels like a cinematic attempt to connect with a late brother and son’s spirit. In that sense, an open field is a family film. And it may be set in a far-away place for many viewers, but it transcends borders, given that the plane’s passengers came from more than 30 countries and that anyone who has lost a loved one has faced the burden of that loss. ‘an open field’ Courtesy of Netflix an open field is a South Africa-France-Germany production by Day Zero Film and Video Productions in South Africa, Day Zero Films UG in Germany and Survivance in France. The cinematographer is Jide Akinleminu, the editor is Anne Fabini. The film, shot in color and black-and-white, features dialogue in both English and Amharic. “This is a delicate and personal work and about something fundamental to being human,” says director Teboho Edkins. “I hope that the film can find its way to as many people as possible, and that something in it might resonate with them. Having Netflix bring the film to its global audiences is very meaningful to me, and I’m grateful for their support as it makes its way out into the world.” THR can now exclusively premiere a trailer for an open field ahead of its Netflix debut. THR

articles.title: Romanian First-Ever Country of Focus at AFM, ‘Fjord’ Director Cristian Mungiu to Attend
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 6, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Fjord, Sebastian Stan, 2026. Neon/Courtesy Everett Collection In a surprise move, the American Film Market , traditional home to mainstream cinema in all its schlocky glory, is going upscale arthouse. At next week’s AFM — Nov. 10-15 at the Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles — there will be a focus on Romanian cinema. AFM has named Romania its first-ever country of focus. National film industry group Creative Romanian Filmmakers (CRFM) will bring over a delegation of filmmakers, producers and production companies to present their latest movies and to meet with industry execs to discuss shooting in Romanian and international co-production opportunities. Related Stories Movies 'an open field' Is a Deeply Personal Story of Loss, Grief and Compassion (Exclusive Netflix Trailer) Movies 'Elsinore' to Close Camerimage Festival “Romania has been part of the AFM community for many years, and we’re proud to recognize its contributions to global cinema as our first-ever Country of Focus,” said Jackie Brenneman, President & CEO of the Independent Film & Television Alliance (IFTA), which produces the AFM. “Together with Creative Romanian Filmmakers, we look forward to showcasing the country’s exceptional talent and opportunities for international collaboration.” “Since 2016, Creative Romanian Filmmakers has brought Romanian producers to the world’s most important film markets and festivals, and the American Film Market has always been a key stop on that journey,” added CRFM managing director Mihai Lupu. “Being named Country of Focus this year is a milestone for our entire industry – an invitation to buyers, sales agents and producers to discover Romanian stories, talent and locations, and to build lasting partnerships with us.” The delegation will include Cristian Mungiu , attending with his Palme d’Or winning drama Fjord , starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve . Fjord is Romania’s official entry for the Oscar in the best international feature category and is seen as a shoo-in for the Academy long-list, being announced Dec. 15. “This year, a Romanian film was awarded at every major festival,” noted Mungiu. “I believe Romanian films have real potential in international markets – not only at festivals, but with a wider audience. In this sense, Fjord ’s awards-season campaign and its North American theatrical release look promising.” Mungiu also put in a pitch for his country as a shooting location, noting that “not only is the Romanian cash rebate working again, we have also started a conversation with the Romanian authorities about providing upfront cash-flow financing for the rebate, and we hope to see concrete results as early as 2027.” At AFM, Mungiu will take part in a panel, “Beyond the New Wave: Romania as Your Next Production Partner,” on Saturday, Nov. 14, from 4:00–5:00 PM on the Constellation Stage at the Fairmont Century Plaza. Mungiu will be joined by Valentin Savu, General Manager, Romanian Office for Film and Investments in Culture, Alma Bacula, Head of Production & Partner, Icon Films, and leading producers Iuliana Tarnovetchi, Gabriel Popescu and Ionuț Ionescu to discuss opportunities for filming in Romania, and partnering with local producers to accessing the country’s filming incentives. AFM will showcase four Romanian films with screenings at the AMC Century City 15: Comatogen by Igor Cobileanski, Gone Guy by Andrei Dascalescu, Grounded by Ligia Ciornei and The Circle by Valeriu Andriuta. Romanian companies participating in the event at AFM include Augmented Films, Bullsrecords, Idea Film, Nomad Films Global, Profesional Film Partners, Quantum Media Creative, Frame Film, Mavish Ask, Negrea Visuals, Sýmbolon and Tarnovski Marketing Consultancy. At the Fairmont Century Plaza, Romanian companies will have dedicated exhibition space in suites 1005 and 1037 for meetings. THR

articles.title: How John Summit Is Turning Arenas Into the “World’s Biggest Nightclub” for CTRL ESCAPE Tour
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content John Summit during his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour. Gautthiierr “I’m always about doing things first and really breaking the mold and breaking barriers, especially in the DJ world,” John Summit says. That mentality spawned the 32-year-old DJ’s idea to embark on his first-ever arena tour. For any DJ, organizing a global arena tour is a tall order, as their home away from home is typically nightclubs and music festivals. While Summit has become a fixture in those spaces in recent years, he also saw an opportunity for something bigger. Following one-off shows at New York’s Madison Square Garden and Los Angeles’ Kia Forum, Summit admits he didn’t even want to flirt with the idea of a full arena run initially because there are a limited number of DJs capable of pulling off a tour on a similar scale to massive mainstream pop acts. Related Stories Music Singer Jackson Wang Signs With WME (Exclusive) Music With 'The Girl of Your Dreams,' Ashe Finds Her Sweet Spot: "I'm A Really Solid Version of Myself" Sure, a handful of DJs such as The Chainsmokers and Kaskade have launched their own versions of arena and stadium tours. Still, Summit considers his multi-country CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour a particularly unique and ambitious opportunity, as he’s the sole headliner on each date, and it’s strictly a DJ set rather than mixed in with pop performances. John Summit during his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour. Julian Bajsel “There’s been DJs who’ve played arenas, but to this scale and this level, this is a very ambitious tour and it’s not something I technically have to do because obviously the clubs and festivals and everything has been working so well,” Summit tells The Hollywood Reporter . “But because I did those one-off shows and they worked out super well, I knew that I had the confidence to actually take the show on the road.” Luckily for Summit, the tour’s visual concept came easily as his sophomore album CTRL ESCAPE already had a theme centered around breaking out of the corporate 9-to-5 “matrix.” The notion was personal for Summit, as he left his job as a CPA in 2019 to follow his passion for music — and it clearly worked out. “The fans can relate as well too because you’re going to that show; they probably all worked their 9-to-5 during the day to then be able to afford the ticket at night,” Summit says. “So it’s going to be that show is their way of breaking out of that.” It was important for Summit to build a world that his fans could truly escape into, so he leaned on his creative director, Alex Alvga, who also worked on his sophomore album and other shows, to channel the corporate-to-rave transformation that originated in his “LIGHTS GO OUT” music video. John Summit during his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour. Jamal Eid “We used the music video to drive the whole rollout of the album, and from there we just built the whole narrative,” Alvga tells THR . “Then for the arenas, we just wanted to keep building on that.” The attention was in the detail, from Summit’s mixing table looking like an old computer monitor to the speakers having a ’90s computer casing around them, to backup dancers wearing corporate attire dancing in cubicle-like structures. “We have a lot of stuff that plays into that same aesthetic that we’ve been playing up until now, because of course the best thing as a fan is just when everything feels cohesive,” Alvga says. But the team didn’t slack on lighting, automation, lasers, pyro and practical effects either, a necessity for what is essentially a massive dance party. Summit delivers several immersive moments throughout the show, from dropping 1,200 employee performance review papers over the crowd to a fired/hired bit with audience members who aren’t dancing enough. All these elements are key components for the narrative Summit aims to tell during his four-act performance. “I can’t really think of any DJs who really do an actual story throughout a set,” the DJ says. Alvga says it “starts with a control, then we go into the escape section and then we go into the Experts Only section,” which is act three and will feature Summit in the crowd at the much more intimate B stage. “By that moment in the show, the narrative already explains the workers have escaped. Now it’s time to party and have fun,” the creative director says of the fourth and final act, titled “release.” With the visuals, design and story set, the last — and arguably the most important — piece of the puzzle is the music. John Summit during his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour. Julian Bajsel When it comes to his other shows, Summit often finalizes the set hours before taking the stage and “it’s not even an official set list because I get on stage and I switch it up,” he says. However, with a tour of this scale, there’s much more at play behind the scenes. “Honestly, the biggest challenge for me is getting the music done ahead of time and then not going full improv with it,” Summit says. Thankfully for his team, this DJ found his perfect mix. “I know how I’m going to start, I know I’m going to finish [and] I know the big moments in the middle,” he says, while also weaving in moments “to get a little spicy with it and creative.” As Summit sets out on this new chapter, he’s excited to learn and grow with each show. As for his fans, he hopes that by the end of the night, “the phones are down, you’re dancing, you’re in the moment.” John Summit during his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour. Gautthiierr Fans will also need to be locked in so they don’t miss potential surprises, special guests and an outfit change or two. “I’m starting in my [accountant] suit and I guarantee you I won’t be finishing it in the suit,” Summit quips. However, despite having a group of backup dancers, don’t expect Summit to debut a whole dance routine. “I’ll do my typical fist bump, don’t worry,” he says with a laugh. “But no breakdancing or anything. I’m not going to go full Tate McRae or anything.” That’s the fans’ responsibility — lest they get fired by the boss on the first day now. He says, “It’s kind of cool to turn an arena into the world’s biggest nightclub for a night.” THR

articles.title: Meet the British Foodie Demystifying the Michelin Guide’s Secrets
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All November 6, 2026 8:28am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jesse Burgess in 'Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars.' Apple TV Jesse Burgess is a chef whisperer. If you’re interested in food and have a penchant for scrolling, you may already know this from one of his many vertical clips. The 35-year-old English foodie, host and co-founder of media platform TopJaw, forged a reputation for charming London’s culinary luminaries into opening up not just about their work but the restaurants, bars and Sunday roasts that they adore. And, just as informative, the spots that they think are overrated. Interviewing chef after chef after chef for going on 10 years, Burgess has honed another rather novel skill. He can talk about fine dining without a ring of pretension. “This guy properly reads the fucking room,” says Gordon Ramsay , several times a TopJaw guest. “Jesse understands what he does and doesn’t know. He talks from a viewer’s perspective and lets you in on the secret, what’s going on … where a critic would have the tendency to slide toward being an asshole.” Related Stories TV Apple TV Renews 'Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars' for Season 3 TV Toni Collette to Lead Apple TV Dramedy 'Lenni' An asshole was the last thing Apple TV needed when casting its ambitious culinary series, Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars . The word Michelin already evokes thoughts of white tablecloths, comical price tags, foams, fermentations and microgreens applied via tweezers. (And, you know, the whole tire manufacturing part of the business.) To preemptively deflate perceived elitism, many associated with the project say there was ultimately only one choice to be its face. Gordon Ramsay and Jesse Burgess Photo by Dave Benett/Getty Images for Studio Ramsay “I’d heard about the show, because they had already filmed quite a bit of it without a host, flying to chefs all around the world,” says Burgess, over lunch this past summer in East Hollywood. “I didn’t think I had a hope in hell of getting the job.” The series was being produced by Studio Ramsay Global, so it was Ramsay who suggested Burgess fly out to do a screen test during the first season’s Sweden shoot. “We had a long list of A-listers lining up to present the show, and Apple wanted some of their own talent, but Jesse, from my side, was the running favorite from day one,” says Ramsay. “What makes him special is his vulnerability in these situations” It’s a unique situation in which Burgess found himself. Ostensibly another cooking competition, Knife Edge , which concludes its second season on Nov. 6, follows chefs from around the world as they strive to earn, maintain or up their count of stars in the storied Michelin guide. They punch walls. They weep. They hemorrhage money. They make very appetizing meals. But in lieu of having Burgess exhaustively interview them, he’s almost the translator of their work — narrating the trials of operating a restaurant and describing meals as he eats them with the relatable manner of a thoughtful guy at the pub who just really wants to tell you about his burger. Most episodes include one of Michelin’s many international galas where the stars are announced and presented. Maintaining a distance from the hopeful chefs like he’s Jane Goodall, Burgess takes it all in from the backs of different ballrooms as careers are made and hearts are broken. His empathy and everyman quality make him suitable for this job, but he doesn’t claim to have ever had ambitions for a traditional career in entertainment. Burgess just likes travel and eat and talk about both. Chatting over our respective plates of Somali chicken and grilled fish at East Hollywood Pan-African bistro Foods From Afar (his selection), Burgess traces his curiosity back to his mother’s career as cabin crew on Britannia Airways and then private jets. View this post on Instagram “To me, her life was just so exciting,” he says, recalling how he’d wait for her return and edible souvenirs. “I had Beluga caviar because she’d flown to Russia, Danish pastries from Copenhagen, Stollen from Cologne. She hates me telling these stories because she reckons she wasn’t allowed to take the food out of the country. She thinks that someone’s going to come and arrest her or something.” In 2015, Burgess made eating his business. He partnered with his friend Will Warr and founded TopJaw. The digital media brand originally just focused on YouTube and on London, because they couldn’t afford to go very far, with Burgess in front of camera and Warr largely behind the scenes. Growth was slow and incremental. It took four years before they hit 10,000 subscribers. But when they began posting travel videos, things accelerated quickly. One in particular, 48 Hours in Paris , went viral. It’s since logged 2.6 million views. Unfortunately, this mitzvah was the eve of lockdown. Restaurant content wasn’t a viable plan in 2020, and the guys thought of hanging it up. But when restrictions loosened, a shift back to the U.K. and, pivotally, a focus on Instagram grew the business so that it could be Burgess’ full-time pursuit by 2023. Today, they have almost 1.9 million followers across platforms. They produce travel videos in cities around the world now, but, in world culinary capital of London, TopJaw has arguably become the most valuable resource for recommendations. He’s not just interviewing chefs anymore, either. Every few clips there’s another luminary: Matt Damon, Florence Pugh (twice), Kate Winslet, Theo James. The singer Jessie Ware, who hosts food podcast Table Manners with her mother Lennie, recently mocked Burgess’ rising profile by referring to him as “Mr Michelin” in her visit to TopJaw. (The calls for talent participation, by the way, are almost exclusively incoming.) Knife Edge has already been renewed for a third season , and Burgess will be there to chronicle the professionals he admires succeed and fail — and to eat their food. But when I ask him the obvious question, if this is another paver in the path from content creator to traditional TV host, the suggestion seems to leave him a little indifferent. “There’s so much that I want to do in that world, and I don’t think I’m necessarily attracted to doing more TV,” he says. “There’s a lot of green grass on both sides. Plus, making videos on the internet is awesome.” So is getting to travel and eat for a living. Jesse Burgess in Apple TV’s Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars . Apple TV THR
