articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All November 2, 2026 11:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Grace Amber Conway of Great Britain Photo by Pau Barrena/Getty Images The new flag football league from the NFL and TMRW Sports will officially launch next summer, and now it also has a name: Premier Flag. The league and the sports media company (which is also behind the TGL golf league) announced the new branding Monday. Premier Flag will get underway well ahead of the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, where the sport will be prominently featured. The NFL views flag football as a major growth engine, not only to get people interested in the full contact version of the game, but as a sport worth playing and watching in its own right. The inaugural season will be played in a purpose-built flag football stadium, the location of which is to be announced. Similarly, media rights for the first season are still being discussed, though the summer window gives it an opening, with only Major League Baseball as significant summertime competition (and a possible lockout may interrupt the next baseball season). “Flag football is exploding in popularity, and Premier Flag is establishing itself as the destination for the world’s top women and men competing at the highest level of the sport. The Premier Flag brand represents where flag football is headed – elite, global and accessible – while setting a professional standard for the sport’s growing ecosystem,” said Brendan Donohue, president of flag football for TMRW Sports. “When we launch next summer, fans will have the opportunity to see these amazing athletes perform at their best, supported by Premier Flag’s world-class training, strength and conditioning, nutrition and coaching programs.” “Premier Flag represents an exciting step forward in the continued evolution of flag football,” added Brian Flinn, NFL senior VP of global flag football. “Together with TMRW Sports, we’re building a global platform to showcase the world’s top flag football players and to engage fans in a premium experience, with the Premier Flag Showcase during Super Bowl LXI week providing an exciting first look at that vision. The launch of Premier Flag creates a new professional opportunity for the world’s best players and establishes the pinnacle of the sport’s growing global pathway.” The NFL and TMRW Sports officially announced the league earlier this year, with all 32 team owners invested alongside institutional investors and celebrity investors like Silver Lake, Ariel Investments/Project Level, Bessemer Venture Partners, Blue Pool Capital, and Dynasty Equity, as well as Tom Brady, Peyton Manning, Serena Williams, Billie Jean King, Joe Montana and Alex Morgan. In fact, Morgan’s TOGETHXR media and content company will provide social content strategy and production for the league, with Pivot Brand Group creating the brand name, positioning and visual identity of Premier Flag. articles.full_text: × Nov 2, 2026 9:48am PT Utopai Studios Names Former Disney AI Leader Hans Ku as Chief Product Officer By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Utopai Studios Names Former Disney AI Leader Hans Ku as Chief Product Officer 1 hour ago Cate Blanchett-Backed Group and Collection of Hollywood Stars File Brief in New York Times-OpenAI Lawsuit: Hollywood Has ‘Proven Infrastructure’ to License Content 3 days ago AI Vocal Modifier Voicemod Inks Disney Deal to Add Star Wars, Marvel Soundboards to Platform 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Utopai Studios Utopai Studios , the AI-focused entertainment studio, has hired former Disney AI leader Hans Ku as its chief product officer, tapping a Hollywood studio veteran as the company tries to grow its content slate. Ku will focus on the studio’s product, engineering, research and business development teams, scale the startup’s AI tech and its AI production platform PAI across its film and TV slate and determine how the company builds its proprietary technology. He will report to CEO Cecilia Shen. Related Stories Appetite for Agatha Christie Shows No Signs of Slowing 50 Years After Her Death: 'She Has Such Enduring Appeal' Mediawan's Pierre-Antoine Capton on Buying Reese Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine and Doubling Down on Hollywood Amid Consolidation (EXCLUSIVE) Ku was previously Disney’s vice president of AI and engineering in its office of technology enablement, where he worked on expanding AI tools across the company and researching AI-native production pipelines. He also helped connect Disney and OpenAI team members during the short-lived $1 billion deal to license Disney characters for OpenAI’s Sora video generator. “Hans knows what it takes to move emerging technology from experimentation into an organization operating at global scale,” Shen said in a statement. “From developing tools for animators early in his career to helping lead Disney’s collaboration with OpenAI on Sora, Hans has consistently worked at the intersection of creative ambition and emerging technology. He brings that experience to a studio where filmmakers and technology teams develop tools together on active productions. That combination is critical to where Utopai Studios is going next. We are building a global studio for a new era of entertainment, and Hans will be central to scaling the technology and infrastructure that make that possible.” Ku, who also worked at Walt Disney Feature Animation and DreamWorks Animation, said Utopai “has the opportunity to build something fundamentally different” due to the close collaboration between its studio and product sides. “We can take what we learn from real productions, turn those lessons directly into better products and workflows, and then bring those capabilities to filmmakers and studios around the world,” Ku said in a statement. “My focus is on building PAI alongside filmmakers, giving them better tools to explore ideas, refine their work, and bring their creative vision to the screen while keeping creative decisions in their hands.” Utopai has tried to cement itself as a premier production studio in the AI age, raising $60 million last month at a $1 billion valuation. It has also amassed an extensive slate of projects, both AI-generated and AI-enabled, including an Antonio Banderas-led live-action film “Cortés” and an AI-assisted animated feature-length adaptation of “ The Most Serious Fart ,” a 2023 children’s book written by “Not Another Teen Movie” screenwriter Mike Bender . It also partnered with the Chinese production company Huace to produce a fully AI-generated adaptation of “Journey to the West: The Lost Five Hundred Years,” an origin story of the 1592 Chinese mythological book. “Cortés,” “The Most Serious Fart” and the live-action feature “Half Moon’ are set for release sometime next year. articles.title: John Goodman Says ‘Digger’ Was ‘Killed’ by Critics ‘Before We Even Opened’ and ‘It Hurt’
articles.full_text: × Nov 2, 2026 10:23am PT John Goodman Says ‘Digger’ Was ‘Killed’ by Critics ‘Before We Even Opened’ and ‘It Hurt’ By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest John Goodman Says ‘Digger’ Was ‘Killed’ by Critics ‘Before We Even Opened’ and ‘It Hurt’ 41 minutes ago Jennifer Lawrence Says ‘Absolutely F—ing Not’ to Transforming Into X-Men’s Mystique Again 3 days ago Jessica Lange Hints at Acting Retirement: ‘I Feel Like I’m Coming to an End… It Doesn’t Seem Easy to Get Things Made Anymore’ 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Seoju Park /© Warner Bros. /Courtesy Everett Collection John Goodman is finally speaking out about “ Digger ” flopping with critics and at the box office. During an appearance on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast, the actor said all of the negative pre-release buzz for the movie effectively killed its chances of making money at the box office. “Digger” cost north of $160 million to make and only earned $15 million in its domestic box office debut. The movie has yet to cross $50 million worldwide after one month in theaters. Related Stories The Muppets Turn 50 This Year but They Nearly Didn't Get Made at All: 'It Was a Real Study in Perseverance' What's Driving Spanish TV? Spanish Drama Originals on Platforms, Renewals and Crossover Genres “People are talking. It hurt. It kinda killed us before we even opened. [The headlines like]: ‘This will only make $5.’ It was good reason for people to avoid it,” Goodman said about the response. “I am proud of it. I had a ball doing it. It was a good six months out of my life. It is a huge swing. It’s going to be around for a long time.” When asked if he still cares about what critics and audiences think of his work after so many years as a professional actor, Goodman responded: “Unfortunately I have to say that I am. I have to be very honest. I used to be less so. Maybe I am getting old and pathetic and it’s like, ‘Don’t hit me again!’ I put so much into this film and here you go. I am over it now. I am proud I did it.” However, Goodman noted that “everything I have done for the Coen Brothers flopped initially… so who cares, man? I still have people coming up to me in the streets asking me about ‘Barton Fink’ and ‘Big Lebowski.'” Goodman starred opposite Tom Cruise in “Digger,” directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu. Cruise plays an oil tycoon who is faced with the end of the world after one of his rigs in Antartica malfunctions and sends ice caps hurtling towards Europe. Goodman stars as the U.S. president. The movie strongly divided critics (53% on Rotten Tomatoes) and needed an estimated $350 million just to break even in theaters. It will now go down as one of the most costly studio flops in Hollywood history by losing Warner Bros. around $250 million in theaters. Amid the movie’s disastrous box office run, various Hollywood celebrities rallied around Cruise and the movie. Neil Young posted on his website that “Digger” is “the best film I have ever seen.” Mandy Patinkin agreed, hailing Cruise’s latest as an “instant classic” and “one of the greatest pieces of film I have ever seen in my entire life.” Anne Hathaway, Jane Fonda, Ben Affleck and more also sung the movie’s praises, with Affleck condemning the public bashing of the movie. “Everybody wants to celebrate this bomb as if it’s the most exciting thing to happen. And you think like, it’s a pretty ambitious, interesting movie made by interesting people who have talent,” Affleck said in his own “Happy Sad Confused” interview last month. “Everybody wants to count the money, what it lost or whatever. To me, I just think, if you punish movies that take risks, guess what you’re going to get? A bunch of shitty homogenized movies. You cannot do something interesting without taking a big swing. And that means you’re going to sometimes look bad.” Watch Goodman’s full interview on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast below. articles.title: John Turturro on Nearly Robbing Someone to Practice for ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,’ Fighting to Save His 2005 Musical ‘Romance & Cigarettes’ and the Knicks Championship
articles.full_text: × Nov 2, 2026 10:46am PT John Turturro on Nearly Robbing Someone to Practice for ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,’ Fighting to Save His 2005 Musical ‘Romance & Cigarettes’ and the Knicks Championship Awards Circuit Podcast: Turturro discusses his new role in the Sony Pictures Classics drama, plus the success of Apple TV's 'Severance' and more. By Clayton Davis Plus Icon Clayton Davis Chief Awards Editor byClaytonDavis Latest John Turturro on Nearly Robbing Someone to Practice for ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,’ Fighting to Save His 2005 Musical ‘Romance & Cigarettes’ and the Knicks Championship 31 minutes ago ‘Obsession’ Breakout Inde Navarrette to Receive Rising Star Award at Palm Springs Film Awards (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Joel Coen’s ‘Jack of Spades,’ With Josh O’Connor and Patsy Ferran, Lands at Netflix for Fall 2027 2 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Primož Korošec John Turturro never actually picked a pocket on the subway, but he came close. “I had my hand, like, right, sort of almost in the bag,” he tells Variety . “But then I felt like, well, then I would have to give it back, and I could get arrested.” That is about as far as the star of “ The Only Living Pickpocket in New York ” was willing to take his homework, which he did under Apollo Robbins, the sleight-of-hand artist Turturro describes as part concert pianist, part psychologist. The rest of the practice happened on set, where he spent the shoot lifting things off the crew and occasionally getting caught. “The whole idea is that you don’t feel it,” he says. “It’s kind of a magic trick.” Related Stories Gersh Launches Victoria House, Expanding Into Scripted Films, True Crime and International Co-Productions (EXCLUSIVE) The Muppets Turn 50 This Year but They Nearly Didn't Get Made at All: 'It Was a Real Study in Perseverance' The film, written and directed by Rian Johnson regular Noah Segan, runs a tight 90 minutes and puts Turturro at the center as Harry, an aging thief caring for his disabled wife in a city that no longer has much use for him. Steve Buscemi, his co-star across “Miller’s Crossing,” “Barton Fink” and “The Big Lebowski,” and Giancarlo Esposito are along for the ride. Turturro, who has been a caretaker and a guardian himself, says the restraint is the point. “When someone goes for your jugular, sometimes you can recoil,” he says. “But when someone opens their heart up and offers it to you, it allows you space to enter.” It has been a strange and lovely year for him. The Knicks fan who fell for the 1969-70 and 1973 teams watched his franchise finally win another championship, and he is still shaking his head about it. He is 69 and looks a decade or two younger. Turturro is the only person in this awards conversation who has won best actor at Cannes, earned Emmy nominations for “The Night Of” and the Apple TV sci-fi drama “Severance” and never once heard his name read on Oscar nominations morning. “That’s the cherry on top of the cake,” he says of the accolades. “That’s not why you do it.” Turturro has a screenplay of Philip Roth’s “Sabbath’s Theater” waiting for people brave enough to make it. And he is still chasing the film he has wanted to make for years, an adaptation of Susan Sheehan’s Pulitzer Prize-winning “Is There No Place on Earth for Me?,” a book about mental illness and the families it splinters that he knows, he says, “really well personally.” “As you get older, time is precious,” he says. “I believe in the audience, and I believe in the young audience, too.” On this episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast , Turturro discusses his new role in the Sony Pictures Classics drama, why he’s still proud of “Romance & Cigarettes,” the 2005 musical he had to buy back and release himself after a studio regime change, and more. Listen below! The conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity. John Turturro in “The Only Living PIckpocket in New York” Courtesy of MRC II Distribution Company Have you ever actually pickpocketed anyone? I did a lot when I was practicing with Apollo Robbins. He’s a magician and a pickpocket, and he basically gave me a course. He’s kind of a psychologist. He understands how someone approaches another person, from the social sphere to the personal to the intimate. What he can do with his hands is like a concert pianist. He gave me exercises and things to do. I didn’t really pickpocket anyone on the subway, but I came close. I had my hand almost in someone’s bag. But then I thought, well, I’d have to give it back, and I could get arrested. I practiced a lot on set, constantly trying to do it with the crew. Sometimes you’d get caught. The whole idea is that you don’t feel it. It’s kind of a magic trick. Noah Segan was an actor before becoming a director. What’s different about working with someone who understands what it’s like to be in front of the camera? It helps, but I’ve worked with a lot of actor-directors, and they’re all different. He’s not cynical. He’s an open-hearted fellow. He wrote the script, and what I brought to it was my offering. He was very open to things. He gave me a playlist of songs he listened to, and I used a lot of them on the set. He was really delicate. The cinematographer, Sam Levy, who was Harris Savides’ assistant, brought in these old lenses from the ’70s. We did tests with them, and that’s why the movie has that kind of ’70s vibe. We wanted to find the most intimate way to shoot it without an extreme amount of cutting. You and Steve Buscemi have worked together for more than 30 years. How much of that chemistry comes from friendship versus acting? You have a history. I have a history with Giancarlo, too, but not as long as with Steve. There’s a comfort zone and a shorthand. You can build off that and take advantage of it. They’re both wonderful actors, and that makes the fabric of the film really rich. Harry is caring for his disabled wife in a city that doesn’t really need him anymore. The film is deeply emotional but never sentimental. How did you find that balance? There was something innately resonant in the film when I read it. You’re of a certain age, so you’ve experienced success and failure. You know what it is to be surrounded by loss. My phone is surrounded by a lot of ghosts. And being a husband, a son and a father, there are always regrets and mistakes you make, even when you try your best. I know from being a caretaker myself, a guardian, sometimes in extreme situations, that it’s not a celebrated thing. You can be upset, but you’re giving to someone else. You’re putting your attention on the other person, and you’re doing it for them. It’s not about you. The film creeps up on you emotionally. I’ve seen it a few times and seen the effect it has on people. Rian Johnson told me it gets him every time. There’s a restraint that allows you to feel something. When someone goes for your jugular, sometimes you can recoil. But when someone opens their heart up and offers it to you, it allows you space to enter. I’m from the Bronx. I grew up watching John Starks and Patrick Ewing walk off without a ring. And you’re on an Oscar run the year the Knicks finally win the championship. Do you feel like you can do anything now? I loved the team when I was a kid, in ’69 and ’70, and they went again in ’73. That was my team, and I became a loyal Knicks fan. The afterglow hasn’t left. I love the way they did it. There’s a kind of chemistry. They’re almost overachievers, most of them on the team, and that made everything even sweeter. The way they kept coming back, led by our fearless captain, Jalen Brunson. This little guy with incredible footwork and smarts, and how he can read a game. It felt like one of the few real team victories. This was a team, a real team victory, and that’s beautiful in life because people don’t celebrate the collective. It really takes the collective to accomplish things. It’s the same way when you do a movie. Everything has to work together, because one thing can really mess it up. It’s been a lovely year. What can I say? You’ve won best actor at Cannes for “Barton Fink,” earned Emmy nominations for “The Night Of” and “Severance” and never received an Oscar nomination. Does that register with you? This has been a very rich time for me, a wonderful career. I didn’t know I was going to work with all different kinds of people who would give me different opportunities. I’ve worked with so many great directors, so I’m very appreciative of the career I have. Accolades, I’ve gotten some things. That’s the cherry on top of the cake. That’s not why you do it. My objective is to tell a story and reach you, whether it’s through comedy, drama or both. To move you, to make you identify with the plight of the character. I’m competitive mostly with myself. Would it be nice to be acknowledged? Yes. If it gets more people to see the movie, that’s even better. I’m a huge fan of “Romance & Cigarettes.” Do you ever think about getting back behind the camera? With “Romance & Cigarettes,” we had a great distributor lined up. It was United Artists, but United Artists and MGM got bought by Sony. Bingham Ray was the person who greenlit it. When the new people came in, Joel and Ethan Coen were my executive producers, and they had final cut. They said, “When you see the movie, it’s a new comedy. Please see it with an audience.” But they had a couple of old geezers who saw it, and they just didn’t understand the movie. So I got stuck in limbo with a film we’d tested and were preparing for an 800-theater release. I fought to get it back and put together some money, including some of my own, to distribute it. We got a tremendous response from critics, and in some countries it played for a really long time. That’s something I’m quite proud of. There are exceptional things in that movie. “Severance” introduced you to a generation that might not know your earlier work. What do you think has made the series resonate? We never know. I think the success was the execution by Ben Stiller, and Dan Erickson posed the question about having your brain split. Something about that resonated post-COVID, even though we shot it during COVID. You don’t know what’s going to resonate with people. It’s a wonderful group of people, and I’ve gotten to work with Christopher Walken, which was sort of my idea. Shows like this pose a question, and I’m interested in how you answer it. How do you survive this inside and outside? You have a screenplay of Philip Roth’s “Sabbath’s Theater” and have been trying to adapt Susan Sheehan’s Pulitzer Prize-winning book “Is There No Place on Earth for Me?” What keeps those projects alive for you? I have the rights and the screenplay for “Sabbath’s Theater,” which is pretty wild, racy, about sex and death. I just have to find people who will be brave enough to do it. We tested it with an audience as a play, and it played really well. I’ve also wanted to do “Is There No Place on Earth for Me?” for many years. It’s about mental illness, and I have a lot of experience with that, unfortunately. But it’s not what you would think, because it has the whole person in it. It’s not just the disease. It’s the family and the labyrinth of the mental health system, which I know really well personally. I was going to do it as a miniseries, but it’s a difficult subject because people always want a story where someone gets better. The idea is that someone can find a level of peace, and that the family can stay together. A lot of families are splintered by it and very isolated. These are real people who suffer. They have tremendous dimension and capacity for manipulation, lust, ambition and rage. They’re full human beings. That’s something I would love to get a crack at. You’re 69, and you look 40. Has the way you decide which projects are worth your time changed? I always was sort of picky, maybe stupidly at times. I tried to save my money when I first started, because I’d done interesting plays, and I would turn things down. In those days, you could make a nice living in a middle-sized film, and I never did big films until 2000 or so. As you get older, time is precious, and the things I really want to do, I don’t want to give that up. I have confidence in the audience. Sometimes the gatekeepers can help you, or they’re an obstacle, but I think audiences are hungry to see different kinds of things. I really do. I believe in the audience, and I believe in the young audience, too. Variety’s “Awards Circuit” podcast, hosted by Clayton Davis, Jazz Tangcay, Emily Longeretta and Michael Schneider, who also produces, is your one-stop source for lively conversations about the best in film and television. Each episode, “Awards Circuit” features interviews with top film and TV talent and creatives, discussions and debates about awards races and industry headlines and much more. Olympics, 75th Show Anniversary in 2029 (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Inside NBC News’ Bid to Break Out From Election-Night Pack 4 hours ago Fox News ‘Viewer Fatigue’ Captures Notice of Fox CEO Murdoch, Who Vows to Press Forward 5 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Versant Look for MS NOW to offer a little red and purple as it chronicles what may be a blue splash on Election Night. The Versant Media-backed news outlet will hold forth from special watch parties of its own design in Houston, Texas and Atlanta, Georgia, where it will offer followers in those states a chance to hang out at a Members Lounge and meet up with other subscribers to the network’s new subscription streaming service. Related Stories ‘Death in Paradise’ Gets Its First International Adaptation in Croatia, Promises 'Murder Mystery, Humor, Warmth and a Strong Sense of Place’ (EXCLUSIVE) Skoop Media Launches New Crime Label Dutch Noir: ‘Range, Scale and Attitude’ (EXCLUSIVE) “Our MS NOW Members Lounges let us bring our growing MS NOW community together IRL, especially in these huge moments when politics and culture dominate the national moment,” says Marcus Mabry, senior vice president of content strategy at MS NOW, in a statement sent via email. “They’re a powerful extension of the connection our Members have already found with our journalists and each other.” The gatherings, held at Atlanta’s Painted Pin, a boutique bowling alley and entertainment venue in the city’s Buckhead neighborhood, and Houston’s Rooftop Cinema Club, represent a way for MS NOW to burnish its nascent streaming property, which launched in September. In October, a lounge was featured at the Power to the People concert in Maryland. He was 52. “In an unfathomable tragedy, Matt Wright passed away Oct 30th while working remotely in Los Angeles His husband, father, sister and niece are in New York, desperate to be reunited for a proper goodbye. We’re asking for all of his friends, who Matt loved so fully, to help the family at this time. As many of you know, Matt and Justin were both laid off this summer. And the unexpected costs of getting Matt home, a funeral and a memorial are impossible for the family to bear,” the GoFundMe reads. “If Matt has ever made you laugh, said an encouraging word right when you needed it, or ordered one too many appetizers for the enjoyment of the whole table, now is the time to repay the favor. Please donate what you can and share this with anyone who’s been in the orbit of Matt’s huge heart. And when you’re at dinner and see a sunset, know that Matt is looking down, loving you, but wildly disappointed in what you ordered.” Related Stories Gersh Launches Victoria House, Expanding Into Scripted Films, True Crime and International Co-Productions (EXCLUSIVE) ORF-Enterprise Boards ‘Crème de la Crème’ – About a Sperm Bank Business – Produced by Whatever Pictures and a 'Playful and Irreverent' Series DeGeneres posted a tearful video on Monday, calling Wright “the glue to our entire family.” Wright had worked on “The Ellen DeGeneres Show” from 2006 until it ended in 2022. “He was an amazing guy. He is and always will be the glue to our entire family at the ‘Ellen Show.'” View this post on Instagram Fellow “Ellen DeGeneres Show” executive producer Andy Lassner shared photos of him and Wright on the “Jennifer Hudson Show” set that were taken on Thursday, just “hours” before Wright’s death. “We are all in shock. articles.title: Driven Unveils Original Programming Slate, Including Series Starring Tom Nelson, Emelia Hartford and Tanner Foust (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: × Nov 2, 2026 11:01am PT Driven Unveils Original Programming Slate, Including Series Starring Tom Nelson, Emelia Hartford and Tanner Foust (EXCLUSIVE) By Jennifer Maas Plus Icon Jennifer Maas TV Business Writer @jmaasaronson Latest Driven Unveils Original Programming Slate, Including Series Starring Tom Nelson, Emelia Hartford and Tanner Foust (EXCLUSIVE) 7 minutes ago Sega’s ‘Sonic the Hedgehog’ to Launch Lingokids Games (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Future Games Show Sets Its First Live, In-Person Event During Gamescom 2027 (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Driven Automotive enthusiast-centric interactive streaming platform Driven has unveiled its initial original programming slate beginning with “Art of Speed” starring renowned engine builder Tom Nelson. First announced last December , Driven comes from car-enthusiast co-founders including longtime producer Michael George, “Top Gear USA” host Tanner Foust and “Gran Turismo” actor Emelia Hartford. Related Stories What's Driving Spanish TV? Spanish Drama Originals on Platforms, Renewals and Crossover Genres ‘Death in Paradise’ Gets Its First International Adaptation in Croatia, Promises 'Murder Mystery, Humor, Warmth and a Strong Sense of Place’ (EXCLUSIVE) Additional original series include programs starring automotive talent like Hartford (“Gran Turismo”), Foust (“Top Gear USA”), Ben Collins (“Top Gear”), Ant Anstead (“Wheeler Dealers”), Jenson Button (Formula 1 World Champion), Tom Nelson (renowned car builder), Antron Brown (award-winning drag racer) and more. Per Driven, this starting lineup will “anchor a library of content from established and emerging creators, and complement conversations in dedicated communities where enthusiasts can connect, discuss their interests, share projects, and exchange knowledge.” Driven unveiled its original series lineup ahead of its upfront presentation to advertisers, which is scheduled for Nov. 3 at SEMA in Las Vegas. According to the company, the platform’s initial beta program has brought in more than 15,000 users over the last few months and “helped shape the platform’s technology, features and community experience, with members continuing to influence its development.” The ad-supported, subscription-free platform is available on iOS, Android, web, Apple TV, Google TV, and Amazon Fire TV, with additional connected-TV platforms planned. “We built Driven to bring premium storytelling and authentic car culture together,” Driven CEO Michael George said. “Enthusiasts want to go deeper into the people, the craft and what’s really at stake. These four originals deliver that – without fabricated timelines, fake ticking clocks, or manufactured drama. The ambition, setbacks, and breakthroughs are real. Driven is giving those stories a home, and look forward to sharing them with our audience.” Additional series premiering exclusively on Driven in early 2027 will include “Pikes Peak” (starring Tanner Foust, Jenson Button and Ant Anstead), “Queen of the Mountain” (starring Emelia Hartford) and “Go or Go Home” (starring NHRA champion Antron Brown). Descriptions for each series, provided by Driven, can be found below. ART OF SPEED Six 1-hour episodes. Starring Tom Nelson. Created and Directed by Michael George. Produced by Emelia Hartford. Executive Produced by Michael George, Matt Swanson and Tom Lofthouse. The man behind the most powerful street cars on earth, and the over five years it took to build them. Tom Nelson left street racing to build a company around what he understood better than anyone: horsepower. Nelson Racing Engines became the place you go when 1,000 horsepower is the starting point, and the cars that roll out of his Chatsworth shop have gone on to Hollywood, to magazine covers and to the kind of owners who want something nobody else has. Art of Speed was shot over five years inside that shop. Each episode follows one build from a bare block to the first time its owner turns the key, including Maximus, the twin-turbo Charger built for Furious 7, and F-Bomb, David Freiburger’s 1,500-horsepower Camaro. The engines are the easy part. The hard part is everything around them: the deadlines, the customers, the physics, and a builder who has never once accepted the number on the dyno as the final answer. It ends in Iceland, with a machine on roads it was never meant for. PIKES PEAK Three 1-hour episodes. Starring Tanner Foust, Ant Anstead and Jenson Button. Directed by Tom Lofthouse and Dan Hack. Produced by Jake Cardew and Ed Sanders. Executive Produced by Michael George and Tom Lofthouse. One hundred days to build a car. One mountain to prove it. A customer handed Radford Motors a million dollars and told them to build whatever they wanted. Ant Anstead decided to race it up America’s deadliest road before delivering it. One hundred days on the clock, a company that had never raced anything, and a car nobody had driven in anger. Ant and Jenson Button put Radford’s name on it. Joe Scarbo and Martin Jung built it. Tanner Foust, who has raced almost everything with wheels, agreed to take it up 12.42 miles of mountain with no barriers where it matters, in a car that was still being finished the week it shipped. No insurance if it crashes. No second attempt if it fails. Pikes Peak: A Race to the Clouds follows the whole thing, from a bare chassis in a California shop to practice mornings above the treeline, through the breakages, the all-nighters and the clashes, to a result nobody saw coming: Radford’s first race ever, and a win. QUEEN OF THE MOUNTAIN One 90-minute documentary. Starring DRIVEN co-founder Emelia Hartford. Featuring Jeff Zwart, Tanner Foust, Betim Berisha, and Robin Shute. Executive Produced by Michael George and Tom Lofthouse. 12.42 miles. 156 corners. One run. The mountain decides. A year ago Pikes Peak sent DRIVEN co-founder Emelia Hartford home before the summit. So she built a car to go back: a brand new Corvette ZR1, 1,064 horsepower to the rear wheels, a cage she welded herself, and a crew she moved to Colorado for a month. Race week nearly broke the program. Her carbon wheels were banned mid-week, the car failed tech, and two days out she was tearing it apart to re-weld the cage while the coolant boiled over. Then the green flag. Ten minutes and eleven seconds later, she was the fastest woman ever up Pikes Peak, in the fastest rear-wheel-drive production car the mountain has seen, on her first run to the top in the race’s 104th year. Queen of the Mountain tells the story behind that time, featuring Jeff Zwart, the champion who coached her corner by corner, Tanner Foust, Betim Berisha, and Robin Shute, the veterans who know what fast really costs up there, and the question none of them can quite answer: why this road, at this price, every June. Emelia’s answer is already in. Just wait till next year. GO OR GO HOME Three 30-minute episodes. Starring Antron Brown. Directed by Ben Carter. Produced by Lisa Hughes Kennedy. Executive Produced by Michael George and Tom Lofthouse. A season inside NHRA drag racing, where runs last under four seconds and every driver says goodbye to their family before strapping in. Top Fuel dragsters are the fastest accelerating machines on earth. Go or Go Home spends a season with the people who drive them and the people who pay for them: four-time champion Steve Torrence, who nearly died twice before he ever sat in a race car. Antron Brown, racing toward the win most drivers want, at Indy. And the young drivers and family-run teams trying to stay on the track against billionaire budgets. Shot across Bristol, Sonoma, Charlotte and the U.S. Nationals at Indianapolis, with full access to the pits and the homes behind them. The results are in there. What stays with you is the rest of it: fathers and sons, the money it takes, the fear nobody talks about, and the hour between rounds when a crew tears an engine down to nothing and rebuilds it. articles.title: Chelsea Frei Directing & Starring In Horror-Comedy ‘Get Off Your Phone’ With Maria Bakalova & Jon Rudnitsky
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor Read the full story By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Thriller ‘Games We Play’, With ‘Riverdale’ Star Casey Cott, Heads To AFM & Gets North American Release Hockey’s Hollywood Moment Hits AFM As Liam Neeson Will Play Legendary Coach In ‘Believe 13’ About Bond With Injured High School Star Brittany O’Grady To Star In Thriller ‘State Of Emergency’ For ‘House Of The Dragon’ Director Greg Yaitanes & FilmNation — AFM View All November 2, 2026 9:07am Add us as a Google Preferred Source From left: Chelsea Frei, Maria Bakalova and Jon Rudnitsky EXCLUSIVE : Principal photography has wrapped on satirical horror comedy Get Off Your Phone , the feature directorial debut of Chelsea Frei ( The Paper ). Frei wrote the screenplay and stars alongside Oscar nominee Maria Bakalova ( The Apprentice) and Jon Rudnitsky ( Saturday Night Live ). The film “follows Daniela (Frei), a canceled influencer who retreats to rural Wisconsin with her boyfriend, Jackson (Rudnitsky), in hopes of disconnecting from the digital world. But when a mysterious stranger, Rada (Bakalova), enters their lives, their attempt to unplug takes an unsettling turn.” Related Stories News 'Mayday' Review: Kenneth Branagh Steals The Show From Top Gun Ryan Reynolds In Skydance & Apple's Wild Buddy Action Comedy That Should Have Been In Theaters Casting Melissa McCarthy 'Margie Claus' Sets Fall 2027 Release, Rounds Out Cast With Songs By Meghan Trainor Pic is produced by Phiphen Pictures ( The Stalemate ), Framehound ( Mountains ), and Doom and Gloom, with Molly Conners, Amanda Bowers, Andi Matichak, Emma Thorne, Gillian Williams and Frei serving as producers. Watch on Deadline The producers say the “social satire with psychological horror and dark comedy explores the increasingly blurred boundaries between our digital identities and the people we are when no one is watching.” Frei commented: “I started writing Get Off Your Phone during the pandemic, when my screen time had reached truly alarming levels. I think we’re all a little addicted to our phones, and I wanted to take that obsession to the extreme. I’m so grateful to Framehound and Phiphen for believing in this story and helping me make it a reality.” Bakalova is repped by CAA, Untitled Entertainment, Insight Management & Production and Yorn, Levine, Barnes, Krintzman. Frei is repped by Paradigm and Untitled. articles.title: Utopai Studios Names Former Disney AI Exec Hans Ku Chief Product Officer
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor Read the full story By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Elon Musk’s SpaceX Reportedly Talking With EchoStar About A Boost Mobile Deal Hello Sunshine Lays Off Half Of Staff In Wake Of Acquisition By Reese Witherspoon And Mediawan Reddit Shares Plunge 30% After Company Says Its Q3 Search Traffic Was “Down Meaningfully” View All November 2, 2026 9:08am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Hans Ku Courtesy EXCLUSIVE: Hans Ku , a former Disney , DreamWorks and Yahoo exec, has been named Chief Product Officer at Utopai Studios . In his new post, Ku will lead product, engineering, research and business development. He will aim to increase the scale of the technology behind the emerging firm’s film and TV slate along with expanding the company’s cinematic storytelling engine. Ku most recently had been VP of AI & Engineering in Disney’s Office of Technology Enablement. He played a key role in Disney’s connection with OpenAI around the well-funded start-up’s generative video offering, Sora. At the end of 2025, Disney swung a deal with OpenAI to license characters for use on Sora in exchange for a $1 billion equity investment. The arrangement was later undone after Sora was shuttered. Related Stories Legal WME Urges "Ethical & Responsible" AI In NYT Copyright Battle With Sam Altman News Reddit Shares Plunge 30% After Company Says Its Q3 Search Traffic Was "Down Meaningfully" Prior to his AI stint at Disney, Ku also worked at Walt Disney Deature Animation, where he created a system to help traditional animators online. As an exec at DreamWorks Animation, he also created the DreamColor display in collaboration with HP, which netted him a Scientific and Engineering Award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. Watch on Deadline In addition to those entertainment-oriented roles, Ku has also been an entrepreneur and a product exec at Tubi, Yahoo and TikTok predecessor Flipagram. Utopai Studios, founded in 2022, recently raised $60 million in funding at a $1 billion valuation. It is among the firms benefiting from the industry’s gradually increasing willingness to embrace AI (albeit within certain parameters) after the technology had initially set off alarms about job losses. “Hans knows what it takes to move emerging technology from experimentation into an organization operating at global scale,” said Cecilia Shen, CEO and co-founder of Utopai Studios, in a statement. “From developing tools for animators early in his career to helping lead Disney’s collaboration with OpenAI on Sora, Hans has consistently worked at the intersection of creative ambition and emerging technology. He brings that experience to a studio where filmmakers and technology teams develop tools together on active productions. That combination is critical to where Utopai Studios is going next. We are building a global studio for a new era of entertainment, and Hans will be central to scaling the technology and infrastructure that make that possible.” Utopai “has the opportunity to build something fundamentally different because the studio and the technology are growing together,” Ku said. “We can take what we learn from real productions, turn those lessons directly into better products and workflows, and then bring those capabilities to filmmakers and studios around the world. My focus is on building PAI alongside filmmakers, giving them better tools to explore ideas, refine their work, and bring their creative vision to the screen while keeping creative decisions in their hands.” Fox Revenue Leaps 22% To $4.57B; Fueled By World Cup, Political Ads, Tubi Liam Neeson Set As Hockey Coach Who Bonds With Injured Teen Star In ‘Believe 13′ ‘You Can See Everything’ Bosses ‘Clayface’ With $11.4M Weekend Win Michigan Bombshell Creates One Of Midterm Cycle’s Memorable TV Moments Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Lexington Film Office Launches Workforce Development Initiative With Location Managers Guild
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor Read the full story By Katie Campione Katie Campione Senior TV & Labor Reporter @katie_campione More Stories By Katherine Josh Holloway To Guest Star As Colter Shaw’s Reluctant Partner In Season 4 Of CBS’ ‘Tracker’ ‘Percy Jackson’ Season 3 Trailer Introduces New Gods & Bigger Threats In Quest To Save Annabeth From The Titan’s Curse Fiona Cauley & Inevitable Foundation Are Making The Disabled Community “The Main Character” In New Digital Series ‘Talking Sh*t’ View All November 2, 2026 9:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The city of Lexington, Kentucky, is looking to expand its local well of production experts. FilmLEX , the city’s official film and entertainment office, has partnered with the Location Mangers Guild International for a workforce development initiative, “From Page to Place: The Art of Location Management.” The two-day workshop is aimed at a wide range of skill levels, including college and high school students, emerging talent and local crew members. The event will take place November 6 and 7, and attendees will have access to LMGI professionals including Andrea Keener ( Killers of the Flower Moon , Captain America: Brave New World) , Todd Christensen ( The Hunger Games, Sicario ), Mike Fantasia ( Top Gun: Maverick, Killers of the Flower Moon ), and Dennis Muscari ( Oppenheimer, Breaking Bad ). Over the course of the two days, participants will engage in industry discussions, hands-on training, mentorship and networking. Related Stories News IATSE Taps Jillian Arnold As Union's First Labor & Technology Intelligence Officer News Hollywood Unions Warn U.S. Film & TV Production Is On The Brink In Latest Economic Report “It’s a tremendous privilege to partner with the Location Managers Guild International and have some of the industry’s most respected professionals helping us cultivate the next generation of talent right here in Central Kentucky,” Lisa Brin, Head of FilmLEX, said in a statement. “This is an exciting first step in strengthening the dynamic local production workforce and laying the foundation for long-term industry growth in Central Kentucky – one that we are deeply invested in.” Watch on Deadline Per FilmLEX, students from eight regional colleges and universities will participate, including University of Kentucky, Asbury University, Bluegrass Community & Technical College, Centre College, Eastern Kentucky University, Kentucky State University, Midway University, Transylvania University, as well as area high schools. Adds Danny Finn, President of the Locations Manager Guild International: “The future of our industry depends on investing in the next generation. Location professionals connect storytelling with the communities that make it possible and partnerships like this one with FilmLEX help introduce new talent to our craft while building the local workforce needed to sustain production for years to come.” The latest workshop is part of a broader initiative to strengthen the area’s local production workforce and build the necessary infrastructure to support a robust film and television industry in Central Kentucky. A major part of that effort is to build a deeper pool of skilled production professionals across a range of disciplines, including location management, producing, assistant directing, production design, editorial and on-camera talent. Lexington ’s convention and visitor’s bureau launched FilmLEX two years ago to promote Kentucky ’s incentive program, which launched in 2022, and help producers on the ground. The official announcement of FilmLEX called Lexington “a modern, mid-size city rich in history and resources for the filmmaking community. The area boasts abundantly diverse landscapes and real-life backdrops that serve as a façade for any genre — from bustling, urban cityscapes to quaint small towns frozen in time; and from rolling bluegrass hills and lush forests to castles, battlefields and abandoned rickhouses [used to store bourbon]. Lexington’s four seasons create mood and personality all year round with best-in-class hospitality and a warm and welcoming spirit.” Local celebrities Steve Zahn and Rick Gomez, who founded Macaroni Art Productions in Midway just outside of Lexington, have long been supporters of bolstering the state’s filming infrastructure and have thrown support behind FilmLEX in the past. These efforts at the local level are in addition to the state’s own initiatives to encourage production to relocate to Kentucky. Via the Kentucky Entertainment Initiative Program, the state offers a fully refundable, non-transferable tax credit ranging from 30% to 35%. The program has an annual funding cap of $75 million and per project cap of $10 million. articles.title: Fiona Cauley & Inevitable Foundation Are Making The Disabled Community “The Main Character” In New Digital Series ‘Talking Sh*t’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor Read the full story By Katie Campione Katie Campione Senior TV & Labor Reporter @katie_campione More Stories By Katherine Josh Holloway To Guest Star As Colter Shaw’s Reluctant Partner In Season 4 Of CBS’ ‘Tracker’ ‘Percy Jackson’ Season 3 Trailer Introduces New Gods & Bigger Threats In Quest To Save Annabeth From The Titan’s Curse Fiona Cauley & Inevitable Foundation Are Making The Disabled Community “The Main Character” In New Digital Series ‘Talking Sh*t’ View All November 2, 2026 9:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Fiona Cauley on 'The Tonight Show' Photo by: Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images Comedian Fiona Cauley is calling the disabled community to the front of the class, er, stall in her new digital series Talking Sh*t . No more hiding in the wings. Produced by Inevitable Foundation ‘s newly launched digital arm, the satirical web series is designed to foster discussions about disability, which might otherwise feel forbidden, in a way that’ll disarm the audience and welcome them in, rather than push them away. Think Ziwe or Between Two Ferns , Cauley and Inevitable Digital co-founder Richie Siegel tell Deadline. Shot inside an ADA bathroom stall, the show has guests answer Fiona’s pressing questions about disability and share the occasional awkward moment. Because what better place to have a chat than the ultimate hot seat? Related Stories News Inevitable Foundation Reveals 2026 Accelerate Fellows Casting 'A Quiet Place's Millicent Simmonds Co-Writes, Will Star In Crime Thriller 'Grace' For Inevitable Studios “This is often such a taboo subject that no one knows how to talk about,” Cauley said. “The fact that you can get people to relax and exhale a little bit, and be like, ‘OK, we can engage with this as people, and it’s not off limits,’ is wonderful. This topic and this community can often feel off limits.” Watch on Deadline The series, which launched October 29 on Cauley’s YouTube channel, is already generating some buzz. In the lead up to the premiere, content from the series had already garnered over 4 million views. Cauley didn’t just bring her comedy and her social following to the project, she also brought the guests. She says that Season 1 — featuring guests including Bill Nye, Shapel Lacey, Robby Hoffman and more — “kind of ended up being me riffing with my friends while interviewing them.” Season 1 guests also include Adam Ray, Lisa Gilroy, Brad Williams, Jeremiah Watkins, Steve Furey, and Matt Taylor. In the interview below, Cauley and Siegel explain how the series came together and give viewers a taste of what to expect from what they hope will be the next satirical talk series to take the internet by storm. DEADLINE: Can you tell me a little bit about what inspired the series? SIEGEL: Yeah. Do you want me to start, Fiona? Does that work? CAULEY: Yes. SIEGEL: I’ve watched Rick Glassman’s podcast for probably the last year or so. He’s a very funny comedian. I think it’s objectively fair to describe his humor as autistic, because he is autistic. It’s basically three-hour, long-form sketch comedy. CAULEY: Yeah, it’s called Take Your Shoes Off . Definitely worth watching. SIEGEL: He has a two-hour episode, for example, with Michael Cera and Paul Rudd. I won’t tell you what happens, but it’s just batsh*t crazy, basically. Fiona was on one of the episodes, probably seven or eight months ago. She was telling the story — and correct me if I’m misremembering this — of how she has a genetic condition that’s progressive, and her siblings have it, too. As she got older, her mom thought she was making fun of her siblings as she started developing symptoms. I was just like, ‘That’s an insane story.’ I wanted to see if there was anything we could do with it. We originally thought, ‘Is this a TV show? Something around Fiona’s life?’ We reached out to her team, had lunch and initially started talking about a movie idea, which is kind of where this started. Inevitable has Inevitable Studios, which is a more traditional film and television production company. We have a development fund, and we’ve been developing a number of projects over the last year and a half. The conversation started there. We’re still working separately on developing some sort of rom-com based on Fiona’s life, which we’re very excited about. Then we started thinking about the digital space and what to do there. My co-founder, Marisa [Torelli-Pedevska], and I were having lunch, and one of us came up with the idea of a talk show in a bathroom, kind of like Between Two Ferns or something like that. We were like, ‘Who could we do this with?’ We were already talking to Fiona, so we thought, ‘Oh, we should just ask Fiona.’ DEADLINE: Fiona, what were your thoughts? CAULEY: I was like, ‘This is really unique. I haven’t seen anything like it.’ I kind of like how doing it in a accessible bathroom levels the playing field, you know? Walk into my space, kind of thing. When Inevitable Studios first reached out, they sent me an article about the company and its mission. I thought it was really beautiful. They were trying to give a voice to disabled creators and actors, and talk about disability without making you feel like you’re supposed to feel sad for the person. I had never seen anything like that, and I think that’s exactly what we’re doing. It’s been cool because we were like, ‘All right, it’s an interview in a accessible stall. What’s the overall purpose of this?’ We decided it has to be funny. We went in with a lot of stuff planned out to ask, and it kind of ended up being me riffing with my friends while interviewing them. It took on a life of its own, but I think it’s fun and sort of educational. It points out all these knowledge gaps that, for the most part, people don’t know about disability. I don’t blame them, but now it’s time to learn. DEADLINE: I really like what you said about the show’s mission of talking about disability without feeling like you have to feel bad for the person and using comedy to make the conversation more disarming. Can you talk about navigating those conversations with your friends and finding moments to make them educational, while carrying out that mission? CAULEY: To be fair, as a comedian, that is kind of my own mission. That’s what I’ve been trying to do. Before I did comedy, I created a web series in 2019 called Capable . They were short, five-minute videos that were supposed to be funny, but also had sincere moments about being young and disabled and people just not understanding. I realized pretty quickly, once I was diagnosed and understood what was happening with my body, that we all have a very two-dimensional concept of disability. It’s so much more complicated than that. People get very upset about my speech and the fact that I’m not paralyzed but use a wheelchair. Some people think I’m not disabled enough, or they’re so uncomfortable that they can’t look at me. There’s no sweet spot. I’m learning. I come from a pretty broken home, so comedy was always used to talk about things or dance around the hard topics. SIEGEL: Can I just add something, Katie? Part of it for us is that we have this weird structure where we have a nonprofit at the top as the parent company, where the mission lives. But increasingly, through both Inevitable Studios and Inevitable Digital, we’ve been working to create commercial entertainment to carry out that mission. On the spectrum of ‘Let’s get a bunch of people in a room and put up a PowerPoint and have a really serious conversation’ to ‘Let’s host a talk show in the bathroom,’ we’re moving this way in terms of what we think can be effective. As Fiona was saying, there’s a version of this where other disabled people find it funny and really enjoy it, and I think that’s great. There’s also a version where it expands the conversation and drives some awareness. Even with the word ‘education,’ the version we mean is: If you want it, it’s there. We’re not trying to lecture anyone or force anyone to believe anything. We’re trying to bring you into this world. Through osmosis, you might walk away thinking, ‘Maybe I won’t use the accessible stall next time, because if I’m not disabled and I use it, maybe I’m blocking someone else from using it.’ There’s a part in the Robbie episode where Fiona talks about how flight attendants putting their coats and luggage in the closet that’s supposed to hold wheelchairs makes her life way harder. Those little moments build up over time. But it’s through this ridiculous container — a talk show in a bathroom. DEADLINE: Once you had the idea for this, how did you figure out who your guests would be, and what were the initial conversations you wanted to have? SIEGEL: I’ll add one little bit about the premise from more of a business perspective. We had this idea and a vision for how we wanted the show to play out. We needed to find a partner who wasn’t just talent and could host the show, but who also brought an audience. One of the really exciting parts about working with Fiona was that, for a number of years, she’d been building a massive audience on social media. They show up to her shows. Our idea was that if we just opened an Instagram account tomorrow, it would start with zero followers. We could make the show and have someone host it, but no one would see it. We’d waste all our time. The idea was to be smart about who we partnered with — someone who could bring distribution and an audience. I don’t think we would have gotten anywhere near the guests we got in Season 1 if Fiona hadn’t texted these people, because they’re her friends. That was a key part of the partnership: What are we each bringing, and is it complementary and valuable? But, yeah, no Fiona, no guests, is one easy answer to that question. DEADLINE: Fiona, how did you decide whom you were going to text or who you wanted to have on the show? CAULEY: I wanted a variety of people: people I’ve become friends with who I know I’m the only disabled person they know, people who are very invested in the disabled community, and then we had Brad Williams, who’s disabled himself. I wasn’t even sure if I was allowed to call him disabled when we started our interview. He was like, ‘Yeah, what? Of course.’ I was trying to offer a range of perspectives so viewers felt seen. I didn’t want to have a bunch of experts. I wanted people I had a good dynamic with, so we could bounce off each other. I’d say the biggest guest this season is Bill Nye the Science Guy. I met him in France, because we were both on a panel for a drug for my disease. I was doing comedy, but I found out Bill is really involved in ataxia research because his family — his dad and sister — had or have a form of ataxia. He feels really close to it. I think it might surprise people. There are more celebrities like that out there who are very invested in research and disability, because disability affects a ton of people — I think more than we’re aware of. SIEGEL: I think the stats now are that up to one in four people in America have a disability, and most people usually know someone or have someone in their family who does. But something Fiona is getting at, and that we’ve thought about for a long time, is this paradox: It’s technically the largest minority in the country, but it’s an invisible group of people for so many reasons. Part of our work is figuring out how to close the gap between the scale and the numbers and the awareness. The Bill episode was great, because it’s very funny to see a man in a bow tie in a bathroom stall on a talk show. DEADLINE: I’m interested in the idea you bring up about filling those knowledge gaps and having a range of people on the show to illustrate different understandings. Fiona, you said you weren’t even sure if you could call another guest disabled, and earlier you talked about what ‘disabled enough’ means. How do you navigate that conversation throughout the series? CAULEY: Man, that’s becoming a really big conversation, especially right now, and it’s so hard because I don’t know that we talk about it too much…It feels like there’s a hierarchy within disability. SIEGEL: I think something we’ve thought about is how to separate the idea that there are probably a lot of people with disabilities who wish they didn’t have the disease or condition that causes their disability from the idea that, regardless of what they have, they should still be treated as humans and have access to public spaces. Those things get conflated a lot, but I think there’s some separation there. There’s a great bit in the Brad episode where Fiona asks, ‘What’s the best disability?’ Brad says a guy once came up to him and said, ‘You and me are just alike,’ and the guy was missing one small part of one finger. I think the point Brad is making is that there’s a big difference there. That person can call himself what he wants, but being a little person is a very different experience from having a little piece of a finger missing. I think that’s what he’s trying to get at. We also posted the teaser last Thursday and got hundreds of comments on it. It was fascinating to see people saying, ‘I have an invisible disability, so when I walk out of the accessible stall, I get weird looks sometimes because people don’t think I need it.’ There’s all this complexity around what’s invisible and what’s visible. CAULEY: I relate to that, because mine used to be invisible. I needed the grab bars, because I didn’t have the balance, but I could walk. My little brother has what I have, but he’s in the walking stage right now. People don’t realize he’s disabled. They just think he’s drunk, so they’re very judgmental of him. He won’t park in the accessible spot, because he doesn’t want the looks. I remember thinking, ‘Oh my God, I can’t wait until I’m in a f*cking wheelchair so people will see something is wrong, and I won’t have to explain.’ DEADLINE: That’s kind of what I was thinking, too, in terms of invisible illness and invisible disabilities. Even without having that exact conversation directly in the show, showing a range of discussions about a range of people experiencing a range of disabilities inherently does that. To your point, people often judge: Are you allowed to use the accessible parking space? Are you disabled enough to do that? CAULEY: Yeah. Even now, I’ll park in an accessible spot, and people just see that I’m not an old lady and come up and say, ‘You can’t park here.’ I’m like, ‘Wait till you see my ride, dude. You’re gonna freak out.’ Disability can affect young people, too. It doesn’t matter. SIEGEL: Especially with where we are in the world right now, there’s been this thing — if you want to talk about hierarchy — of litmus tests and ‘Prove it.’ Even Disneyland has changed the rules around who can use the fast lanes, and that’s had really weird implications. CAULEY: I have a joke about this, but it’s just a real thing that happened. For my bachelorette party, I went to Dollywood because I thought cutting the lines would be cool. I hadn’t been to an amusement park as a disabled person, and they made me take a whole quiz to prove I was disabled enough for the fast pass. For real. DEADLINE: Oh my God! CAULEY: Yeah. I’m in a wheelchair. What are you talking about? SIEGEL: I think one of the underlying, subliminal messages of the show is just: Give people what they need to enjoy their life. If it’s this bathroom, this chair or this ramp, there are so many basic parts of access that are a struggle for people in this community. One of the questions Fiona asks in almost every episode is, ‘Could I get into your house if you invited me over?’ It’s such a simple question. There’s a great response in the episode with Adam. He says, ‘Well, you walk in,’ and she goes, ‘You lost me at walk in .’ No one even registers that they started the sentence that way. That’s the space we’re trying to play in [for disability awareness], rather than making a PSA about building a ramp, which has its own purpose somewhere else. I think you can get farther and do better with this version, which is much less on the nose. DEADLINE: What are you looking forward to about premiering the show? CAULEY: I’m excited for everyone to see it, obviously. I’m really excited, and I hope it does well online. I hope the disabled community feels like they’re the main character — like they’re being talked about in a fun way instead of a sad way. I hope everyone enjoys it and maybe looks at the world a little differently. Just keep humanizing everyone. I don’t know. What about you, Richie? SIEGEL: We’ve been working on this for about five months. On the one hand, that’s a lot of time. On the other hand, it’s so fast to go from an idea to a fully released thing. I’m excited for people to see what we’ve been working on together and the real collaboration that it was. This wouldn’t exist in the way it does, or reach the people it reaches, without Fiona playing such a huge role. I’m excited to see how close to the line we can get comedically while still maintaining the goal of the show. There are some fun moments that give it a good run for its money in terms of what can be talked about and how Fiona can navigate all of that. As she said, I’m excited for people to have a fun time watching and maybe think about something differently afterward. Maybe the next day they won’t give someone a dirty look. Those little things add up. It goes back to what Fiona said: Disabled people are human. That’s at the core of so much of our work, and of this show, too. I’m excited for a lot of people to see it. It’s already happening and will only happen more. The release is this moment where it’s out in the world and it’s not ours anymore. I also hope it finds a home on the internet, in an internet culture where Between Two Ferns , Ziwe and some of these other things exist. This space is so underdeveloped. I hope we’re not just the first entrant, but also the best entrant into that space, and maybe we can make more of them. articles.title: ‘Percy Jackson’ Season 3 Trailer Introduces New Gods & Bigger Threats In Quest To Save Annabeth From The Titan’s Curse
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor Read the full story By Katie Campione Katie Campione Senior TV & Labor Reporter @katie_campione More Stories By Katherine Fiona Cauley & Inevitable Foundation Are Making The Disabled Community “The Main Character” In New Digital Series ‘Talking Sh*t’ Lexington Film Office Launches Workforce Development Initiative With Location Managers Guild Indiana Hoosiers’ Historic National Championship Run To Be Chronicled In Upcoming Doc ‘Misfits’ From Tom Brady’s Shadow Lion View All November 2, 2026 9:42am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The war between the Greek gods and the Titans is looming in the first full-length trailer for Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3. The trailer, which debuted on Monday, makes clear that in order to save the world from that apocalyptic clash, Percy ( Walker Scobell ) is going to need all the help he can get. That likely means the son of Poseidon will have to join forces with Thalia (Tamara Smart), daughter of Zeus. But, it’s not going to be easy to recruit her, and in the meantime Percy has some demigods to save. We finally get footage of Levi Chrisopulos and Olive Abercrombie , who will play the children of Hades, Nico and Bianca di Angelo. This opens up the main quest for Season 3, based on the third book in Rick Riordan’s bestselling series, The Titan’s Curse. While rescuing the siblings, Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries) is captured by Luke’s forces and taken to the titan Atlas at an enemy stronghold in California, where she is forced to bear the weight of the sky in place of goddess Artemis or Luke. Related Stories News Disney+ & Netflix Hoover Up Non-English Acquisitions As Fervor For Japanese & Korean Content Continues - Ampere News Jay Z & Apple Make It Official! Hova's Headlining The Super Bowl Halftime Show “Victory will require sacrifice,” Zeus ominously says over the climax of the trailer. Watch on Deadline The trailer also includes a first glimpse of Kate McKinnon as Aphrodite and Ming-Na Wen as Hera, as well as new looks for the rest of the gods, including Lin-Manuel Miranda as Hermes, Courtney B. Vance as Zeus, and Adam Copeland as Ares. Also joining Season 3 are Jennifer Beals as Demeter and Hubert Smielecki as Apollo. Audiences also get to see a look at one of the several monsters that Percy & co. will encounter on their mission to save Annabeth: Talos, the giant bronze automaton prototype in the Junkyard of the Gods. Watch it above. Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3 premieres November 20 on Disney+ . Created by Rick Riordan and Jonathan E. Steinberg, Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3 is executive produced by Steinberg, Dan Shotz and Craig Silverstein, alongside Rick Riordan, Rebecca Riordan, The Gotham Group’s Ellen Goldsmith-Vein and Jeremy Bell, Bert Salke, James Bobin, Jim Rowe, Albert Kim, Sarah Watson and Tamara Becher-Wilkinson. Jet Wilkinson serves as an executive producer on the last two episodes of the season. Other new cast members include Holt McCallany in a recurring guest role as the legendary Titan Atlas, David Costabile as Dr. Thorn and Jesse L. Martin as Annabeth’s mortal dad Frederick Chase, as well as Dafne Keen as Artemis and Saara Chaudry as Zoë Nightshade . articles.title: Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor Read the full story By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor Devin McRae Forms Own Law Firm After More Than A Decade At Early Sullivan Wright Gizer & McRae WME Urges “Ethical & Responsible” AI In NYT Copyright Battle With Sam Altman View All November 2, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source California Governor Gavin Newsom at Xavier Becerra rally on Nov 1, 2026 in LA Getrty The day before his successor as California’s governor is elected in the high stakes midterms, Gavin Newsom is going out with a bang. A more than billion dollar film and television bang,to be precise. Related Stories News What To Watch For As Networks Cover Midterm Election Night: More Data, More Coverage & More Competition News Trump Celebrity Supporters: Famous Folks In Favor Of The 47th President In what would be termed a seismic November surprise in any other normal election year, potential POTUS contender Newsom is proposing hiking the Golden State’s $750 million tax incentive film and TV program to more than $1 billion. Newsom’s big move would make California’s heavily subscribed big and small screen tax credits the largest capped program in the United States. While Georgia’s media tax incentive has long been uncapped, hiking California’s investment (which is what the California Film Commission -run tax credits program has lucratively proved to be) to $1 billion could leave New York (and its bulging production) in the bicoastal dust. Watch on Deadline “At least $1 billion in tax credits means more investment flowing into our economy and more opportunity across the industry,” the term-limited Newsom said Monday morning. “Through this expansion, we will maintain the momentum and success of our historic expansion last year. But states can’t shoulder the cost alone, which is why I am calling on Congress to back up an expanded tax credit by passing national film and TV tax credit legislation already on the table.” Donald Trump Getty Images The much hyped bipartisan federal plan , backed by strange bedfellows of Donald Trump, Newsom, Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA), the Hollywood guilds, studios, streamers and MAGA loyalists, remains on the procedural back burner until at least after tomorrow’s midterms and the aftermath. Still, within Newsom’s announcement today lies some pretty shiny baubles for an ailing West Coast industry that has seen production crater and over 50,000 jobs directly lost over the past six years. Backed by influential state Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur, who literally reps Hollywood, the latest plan from Newsom has some long and much desired changes to the way money is handed out to productions in California. If enacted just under a year and a half after CA’s tax credits were raised from $330 million annually to $750 million, Newsom’s revamped billion dollar baby also promises to: 🎬 Expand the tax credit eligibility to above-the-line expenditures and make above the line compensation a qualified expenditure to ensure the creative industry’s leading talent stay here in this state, subject to appropriate funding caps. 🎬 Extend the tax credit sunset from five to 10 years to provide more predictability and support long-term production investment. 🎬 Introduce an incentive for companies that commit to at least two distinct qualifying productions in California by providing a 5% boost in tax credits. 🎬 Increase independent film funding to $100 million annually , up $26 million from the current program, to strengthen California’s independent film sector and support a broader range of productions and creative talent. Now, coming back to reality, it’s extremely unlikely that lame-duck Newsom would be able to get the increase through the legislature in Sacramento before he leaves office in January 2027. However, with poll-leading former California attorney general and U.S. health secretary Xavier Becerra poised to replace his old boss as governor, Newsom’s big bucks bet has a pretty good shot at becoming law and cementing his Hollywood legacy. During the about-to-conclude campaign, both Becerra and GOP gubernatorial rival Steve Hilton , as well to a lesser extent L.A. mayoral candidates Nithya Raman and Karen Bass , have laid out proposals of their own to juice up the state’s film and TV tax credits program. Also, a $10 million, post-production tax credit was signed into law by Newsom in September. Echoing Becerra’s previously released blueprint, it is worth noting that Newsom’s plan today insists on capping the incentives — which is clearly intended on helping Hollywood, but also not busting the state’s current theoretically balanced budget of $352 billion. Still, not a bad move for the home of Hollywood, that needs a jolt to get back in the ring. Not a bad move at all for an always-camera-ready CA pol like Gavin Newsom with DC ambitions and donor coffers to fill. BTW – Successful recipients of the next round of CA’s film and TV tax credits should know before Thanksgiving if they and their productions made the big bucks cut. With an anticipated $1.08 billion spend in the state, the latest big screen round was made public on October 7. The sequel to Michael , Lionsgate’s blockbuster Michael Jackson biopic, as well as New Line’s Friday sequel Last Friday and a new project from indie filmmaker Mike Mills , were all in the winner’s circle, so to speak.
