In Lithuanian director Vildziunas’ ( Songs for a Fox , Seneca’s Day ) sixth feature, which recently premiered at the Warsaw International Film Festival , philosophical and sci-fi riddles may prove not to be as hard to solve as the mystery of human connection. Watch the Dice-Ching-O-Mat trailer here. Sh*t Happens Director: José María Cabral Section: Official Competition You may mainly think of the Dominican Republic as a great destination for a holiday. But you may want to think again when you hear about the dark comedy cinematic export it is bringing to Tallinn for its world premiere. Flush away all the negativity and potty like a rockstar with Sh*t Happens ! “When science fails, trust your gut. Just don’t ask what the ‘miracle cure’ is made of,” reads a logline for the new film from Cabral, who has seen three of his films submitted for the best international feature film Oscar race, namely The Projectionist , an homage to pre-digital cinema as seen through the lens of an old-style traveling cinema owner, Woodpeckers , about an impossible romance between inmates at adjacent male and female prisons, and the thriller Checkmate . ‘Sh*t Happens’ film still – PÖFF – H 2026 In case you haven’t noticed yet, this movie is different. It tells the story of the people in a wealthy Dominican household. “Verónica (Lizbeth Santos) controls every bite eaten by her sickly daughter Isabella, while Raúl (Fele Martínez), a frustrated biotechnologist, experiments with homemade cures. Only Abi (Cindy Galán), the young nanny, can still make the girl smile,” explains a synopsis. “Then Raúl develops a microbiotic treatment with a secret ingredient as astonishing as its results. Isabella’s gut stabilizes, her strength returns – and soon the household’s other illnesses begin clearing up too.” And word spreads. A remedy nobody can quite explain becomes the one thing everyone wants. But then the miracle takes an unexpected turn. You are likely smelling that you are in for a very different game of thrones. The trailer only gives you a minimal tease for the film. Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag Director: Vesa Kuosmanen Section: Doc@PÖFF International Competition Finnish filmmaker Kuosmanen’s documentary Just Animals , which screened at Tallinn in 2023, is a portrait of an animal rights activist facing her own limits when she realizes that the utopia she has always fought for will never quite be as she imagined. His new doc also features compelling real-life characters and also has a provocative title, Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag . But it focuses on a very different story – one of a community’s cultural memory. ‘Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag,’ courtesy of PÖFF Courtesy of PÖFF Jolanda, a retired archivist, stood on a stage in the late 1970s alongside his friend Mummo in Finland’s first drag show, Happy Gays , which drew much attention and big audiences. Mummo was one of the first openly gay men in Finland, but then the AIDS crisis hit, causing fear and violence. In 1988, Mummo was killed in his home. More than 30 years later, Jolanda opens up his own archive and invites a new generation of drag artists to bring Happy Gays back to the stage. The re-enactments bring up painful memories, but also an inappropriate and humorous side of Jolanda. The film mixes archive footage from the 1980s, staged reconstructions and contemporary footage from rehearsals featuring young people for whom drag is more a form of self-expression than for the pioneers. “This contrast gives rise to both humor and a sense of recognition,” the PÖFF website teases. “The freedom enjoyed by today’s youth has been built on the shoulders of people whom no one has ever thanked. This warm and heartfelt film … reminds us that Pride began, in part, out of fear, and that one small show was once a tiny step towards resistance and freedom.” The Mystery Package Director: Silje Evensno Jacobsen Section: Doc@Just With that time of year nearing, PÖFF is also serving up a slice of holiday season spirit in the form of a mystery package. Well, actually, The Mystery Package . The cinematic surprise comes courtesy of Norwegian filmmaker Silje Evensno Jacobsen, who you can actually see in the documentary. ‘The Mystery Package,’ courtesy of PÖFF It’s not a mystery what the film is about. Just take a look at this synopsis: “Nine-year-old Edle and six-year-old Brage have racked their brains their whole lives: why has their family been receiving a bunch of strange presents every Christmas from an anonymous sender for the past 20 years? With their filmmaker mother and close relatives, who are all, naturally, suspects themselves, the children become fearless detectives.” What will they encounter on their unusual but heart-warming journey? “They leave no ink-stained handwriting unchecked, no suspicious person uninterrogated, no post office security footage unwatched, and no snowball unturned,” the festival website promises. That leaves one key question to be answered: “Will the anonymous benefactor be found before Christmas is over?” While you wait for the answer, check out the trailer for The Mystery Package . THR

articles.title: Edinburgh Film Festival Toasts Bollywood With ‘Kuch Kuch Hota Hai’ Anniversary Event at 2028 Edition
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 3:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kajol, Shahrukh Khan in 'Kuch Kuch Hota Hai' Courtesy of Everett Bollywood is coming to the Edinburgh International Film Festival . EIFF on Friday confirmed that a special 30th anniversary celebration of the legendary Indian film Kuch Kuch Hota Hai (1998) will screen as part of the 2028 edition. Partly filmed in Scotland, the beloved cult favorite — and Karan Johar’s directorial debut, following the love triangle between Rahul Khanna ( Shah Rukh Khan ), Anjali Sharma ( Kajol ) and Tina Malhotra (Rani Mukerji) — will return to the cinema to celebrate its enduring legacy as a landmark of Indian cinema, with Johar and other guests in attendance. Related Stories Movies From 'Sh*t Happens' to an Erotic Photographer Being Confronted by His Daughter: Offbeat Films at Tallinn Movies Jamie Dornan Boards 'Nostalgie,' Starring Aidan Gillen as Washed-up Pop Star, as Executive Producer (Exclusive) Johar was invited to mark Kuch Kuch Hota Hai ‘s anniversary at the 2028 EIFF during a meeting he hosted in the Mumbai offices of his production company, Dharma Productions, earlier this week with the First Minister of Scotland, John Swinney, and Screen Scotland’s interim executive director, David Smith. The meeting, said EIFF, was focused on Scotland’s potential as a destination and partner for Indian film and television production, co-production, talent development and cultural exchange. Kuch Kuch Hota Hai was the first major Indian production to film extensively across Scotland, including Eilean Donan Castle, Glen Coe, Tantallon Castle and Inchmahome Priory. Swinney said: “It was a pleasure to meet Karan Johar in Mumbai […] I look forward to welcoming him to Edinburgh. During my visit to India, I met with people from the Indian film industry, including representatives from Dharma Productions, to discuss opportunities for future collaboration between Scottish and Indian filmmaking. Scotland’s screen industry has tremendous potential as a creative partner for Indian film and television, offering the infrastructure, expertise and world-class filming locations to support a wide range of productions.” EIFF CEO and festival director Paul Ridd said his team is always thinking about the future and what’s next. “So we jumped at an opportunity like this,” he said, “to plant the seeds for a celebration of a legendary, much-loved film at our festival, a film featuring Scotland and some of the most iconic stars of Bollywood cinema on screen. We can’t wait for what promises to be something truly special for our 81st edition in 2028. But in the meantime, watch this space for more news of our 80th next August.” The 80th Edinburgh International Film Festival is set to run Aug. 12-18. THR

articles.title: Christina Hendricks, Accidental DJ, Has Music Lovers Lining Up
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All October 30, 2026 6:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source DJ Christina Hendricks at Sid's Bar. Eric Garcia The queue outside of the auditorium snaked nearly 200 people long. This wasn’t an unusual sight for the South Pasadena concert hall from bookers and promoters Sid the Cat. Their year-old destination, housed inside a 19th Century elementary school, has already hosted Sylvan Esso, Mike D, Death Cab for Cutie and Jenny Lewis side hustle Nice as Fuck. But on the October Saturday in question, the stage was empty. Instead, the crowd was there for actress Christina Hendricks at the venue’s bar. Most would expect Hendricks, the instantly recognizable redhead from Mad Men , Drive and Good Girls , to be there performing a one-woman show. Maybe some experimental theater. Perhaps she’s just joined the legion of celebrities with their own line of spirits. But they clearly don’t know Hendricks, because she was there to DJ. “Everyone who knows me says, ‘Oh yeah, this makes perfect sense,’” Hendricks tells The Hollywood Reporter . “Because I’ve been doing this since junior high, making playlists and forcing them upon people. This is my favorite thing.” Related Stories Movies 'Ancestors' Invites You to a Cinematic "Séance," Led by Éanna Hardwicke, That Mixes Dream, Reality and Memory (Exclusive TIFF Clip and Chat) TV Naomie Harris and Christina Hendricks Filming BBC Legal Drama 'Reputation' Rumblings of “DJ Christina Hendricks” began earlier in 2026 after she made two appearances at San Diego listening bar Part Time Lover. Her debut was a bit of a fluke at the coaxing of her close friend, the harpist and DJ Mary Lattimore. She suggested Hendricks bring some of her own records down from Los Angeles. She’d show her the ropes and they’d share billing. Hendricks says she balked for a split second before she recognized the kind of wish fulfillment that was on the table. Each played for two hours. Hendricks proved a quick study and Part Time Lover asked her back. But with Lattimore busy, she decided to go it alone. She was getting comfortable with the gear, and it felt like a relatively low-pressure scenario. Hendricks at Sid’s Bar. (Photo credit: Eric Garcia ) “When we started walking towards the venue, my husband went, ‘I think there’s a line out front,’” says Hendricks, who’s married to cinematographer George Bianchini. “I said, ‘Oh no, sweetie, that must be for restaurants and stuff.’ As we got closer, he was like, ‘No, I’m pretty sure that’s a line for you.’ That’s when I started feeling pressure.” If she’s still feeling pressure, it appears to be eclipsed by the kick she’s getting out of all of this. At Sid’s Bar, a former classroom in the 140-year-old building, Hendricks looked gleeful as she navigated a playlist that meandered between Shoegaze, Chillwave, Electronic and Indie Sleeze. The crowd, which appeared to lean heavy on 30-to-50-somethings, nodded in approval. And when Hendricks transitioned from Washed Out to The Knife, this geriatric millennial, for one, felt very seen. The free show marked Hendricks’ first gig in Los Angeles County, so the audience naturally skewed a little industry. Mad Men creator Matthew Weiner was in the crowd, as was Hendricks’ longtime body double and stand-in, Becky Stockton. Johnny Jewel, the artist and music producer who scored Hendricks vehicle Lost River , was there, as were colleagues of Bianchini. Many filtered in and out during the four-hour set, though the bar remained at capacity until she closed with “Protest Song” by Broken Social Scene. Hendricks says she’s still getting used to different crowds and isn’t sure what to think when people don’t dance. “I’m trying to not let how people react determine whether they had a good time or not,” she says. “As an actor, hopefully you’re making people feel something and telling a story. But it’s someone else’s story. With this, I’m not just the performer but the director and the editor at the same time. I’m in the room with the audience, so they’re a part of it as well. I’ve realized that it’s just a different way to tell a story.” Attendees and a few lookie-loos at Hendricks’ set. (Photo credit: Eric Garcia ) Recently wrapping two acting projects — the third season of Apple TV+ drama The Buccaneers and BBC miniseries Reputation , in which she stars opposite Naomie Harris — Hendricks says she’s leaning into DJing as much as she can. On Halloween, she’ll return to San Diego for another set at Part Time Lover. And, throughout November, she’ll be part of a guest DJ series on KCRW, programming an hour of music each week. For the first two weeks, which she’d already submitted when we spoke, her intention is to stick to what she’s been spinning live. Then she plans to stretch herself a little more. A “sad girl dreamy hour,” an A guitar-focused set and a dark, moody jazz playlist are all on the table. When I remind Hendricks that it’s almost awards season and invites for her to DJ Hollywood parties are probably already being drafted, she says she’s game. “I’d love that,” says Hendricks. “The nice thing about all of this is that each time I do it, I get more calls — offers to come and do stuff, people saying they’ll help teach me new things — and I’m saying yes. Let’s do it all.” THR

articles.title: Eric Karson, Director of ‘The Octagon’ and Producer of ‘Lionheart,’ Dies at 86
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 6:41am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Director Eric Karson at work on 1980’s ‘The Octagon.’ American Cinema Releasing/Courtesy Everett Collection Eric Karson, the martial-arts movie specialist who directed Chuck Norris in The Octagon and produced the Jean-Claude Van Damme-starring Lionheart , has died. He was 86. Karson died Aug. 24 of natural causes while in hospice care in Henderson, Nevada, his brother Gil Karson told The Hollywood Reporter . Karson also directed Olivier Gruner in his first movie, Angel Town (1990), and produced his second film, Nemesis (1992), and the French kickboxer considered Karson a mentor. Related Stories Critic's Appreciation Patrick Stewart's Career Was a Rare and Thrilling Marriage of the Prestigious and the Populist Movies Patrick Stewart, 'Star Trek' Captain and 'X-Men' Superhero, Dies at 86 The son of a TV writer, Karson was working for Los Angeles-based American Cinema Productions when he was offered the chance to make his feature directorial debut on The Octagon (1980). Written by Leigh Chapman of Dirty Mary Crazy Larry fame at the dawn of the ninja movie craze, the film stars Norris as Scott James, a retired karate champion who takes on a band of assassins led by his estranged foster brother (Tadashi Yamashita). At Imperial Entertainment, Karson directed Van Damme in Black Eagle (1988), then reunited with the Belgian martial artist on Lionheart (1990), directed by Sheldon Lettich. With his turn as Lyon Gaultier, who deserts the French Foreign Legion and becomes a street fighter to raise money for his murdered brother’s family, Van Damme became a leading man in the U.S. One of four kids, Karson was born in Phoenix on March 5, 1940. His father was Lee Karson, who created the 1956-59 CBS-ABC program The Gale Storm Show (also known as Oh, Susanna ), set on a ship à la The Love Boat ; he also wrote for shows including The Restless Gun , Wagon Train and The Detectives . His mother, Mary, was a theater actress turned homemaker. The family moved to L.A. in the 1950s and lived in a house next door to John Wayne on Highland Avenue in Hancock Park. Karson, who started out as an actor, graduated from Cal State Northridge and began his directing career on commercials and documentaries in Australia. Back in L.A., he handled spots for The Peterson Co., a leading production house back then, and served as a vp before getting his big break on The Octagon . Karson also directed the action flick Opposing Force (1986), starring Lisa Eichhorn and Tom Skerritt , and appeared onscreen as a CIA chief in Black Eagle and as a doctor in Lionheart . In addition to his brother, a musician who also has worked as a film editor, survivors include his other siblings, Lisa and Michael; his wife of two decades, Tara; his nieces, Sylvia and Jackie Lee; and his nephew, Josh. THR

articles.title: Goldman Sachs Thinks the Sports Boom Isn’t Going Anywhere
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 7:35am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jaydon Blue of the Dallas Cowboys rushes against the Arizona Cardinals during the preseason NFL game at State Farm Stadium on Aug. 22 in Glendale, Arizona. Christian Petersen/Getty Images Within most media companies, sports remain core to their larger content strategy. Premium entertainment isn’t going anywhere, of course, but if you ask Ted Sarandos or Mike Cavanagh or Josh D’Amaro about their content mix, sports will be at the center of it. “These events break through,” Sarandos said on the company’s last earnings call. “They drive new membership, they add fuel to our ad revenues.” It’s with that backdrop that Goldman Sachs is releasing a new report focused on sports investing … and the bank is predicting that the sports economy is only going to go up from here. “We increasingly hear from our clients a continuation of a theme that started with our first paper two years ago, which is this really high level of interest in participating in this explosion that we’re seeing in the sports ecosystem,” says Goldman Sachs partner Nicole Pullen Ross. “When you think about the trajectory of growth within sports, our expectation is that we’ll see growth within the sports ecosystem grow to you know over $600 billion by 2030, that’s 44 percent growth.” Indeed, the new Goldman report notes a number of things contributing to that explosive growth, from continually rising media rights deals (the bank estimates global sports media rights will hit $67 billion this year); institutional capital buying into teams; and all the ancillary opportunities around entertainment and live events and IP. “Streaming is now 20 percent of the market for media rights and those contributions of how advertisers are thinking about reaching the consumer in a real-time way is one of the drivers of what we’re seeing,” Ross says. “We’re very analytical in terms of thinking about the value and what the data suggests. One of the things that we saw was the expectation that media rights growth would continue, and the participation was becoming much broader in terms of in terms of the value of the consumer and that live entertainment part of the formula.” Goldman also dug into some more sector-wide (and in some cases economywide) trends: Institutional investors are buying into teams as league change their roles to give owners more liquidity, and sports team owners, like many business owners, are exploring how artificial intelligence can improve efficiency and create more personalized fan experiences. But the report also digs into the ancillary opportunities in sports, particularly around athlete-centric brands (athlete-led studios and consumer brands, etc) shortform content, and opportunities like VR tickets to games. “In an increasingly fragmented media landscape, sports owners are leveraging the power of storytelling to capture and retain a fan base with an increasingly short attention span,” the report states. “Rather than relying solely on traditional broadcasts, they use narrative-driven content to sustain the appeal of live games while capturing younger demographics.” “When you consider the brands that the athletes have and the longevity of their lives post-career, there is an opportunity one for the athlete to want to invest in their brand and those relationships while they’re still playing, but also the opportunity for them to transition that into areas of focus for their business interests,” Ross says. “So the creativity is around how can we make the athlete more relatable? How can we get more fans to engage? Particularly the younger audience, and how can we use technology as a way to do that? Some of the shortform engagement is an example of that, and so that creativity around making additional ways available to increase engagement and participation is one of the things that we heard from clients and the creativity that they’re using to to make sure that they are having points of differentiated connectivity across their across their attendee base. ultimately, teams want to win, owners want to win.” THR

articles.title: Jaalen Best Wanted to Be a Pro Athlete. Now He’s Playing ‘The Greatest’ Boxer Onscreen
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Jaalen Best Photograph by Juan Veloz This story might sound familiar: a rising student discovering who he is as he juggles his love for both the court and the stage. However, this isn’t High School Musical . It’s the beginning of Jaalen Best’s trek to Hollywood, which started his junior year at East Carolina University in 2019 and led him to his breakout role, portraying legendary boxer Muhammad Ali . After stumbling into an intro to acting class, the 28-year-old quickly caught the professor’s attention. “She would tell me how great I was at improv and how I had a face for television and I should consider moving out to a bigger city or state and pursuing acting,” Best recalls. Related Stories Movies 'Ali G: Who Iz I?' Extends Theatrical Run as Amazon MGM Says Movie "Delivered Against Our Goals" (Exclusive) Movies Sacha Baron Cohen's 'Ali G: Who Iz I?' to Stream on Prime Video Days After Brief Theatrical Stint But he wasn’t ready to hear that yet. “I’m like, ‘I’m a basketball player. This ain’t happening.'” Best later got another acting push from his then-girlfriend, who convinced him to audition for his hometown production of Pocahontas in Clinton, North Carolina. Though skeptical at first, he decided to give it a real shot, landing the role of Pocahontas’ father, Chief Powhatan. “I would wake up early at 5 a.m., and I would do basketball practice for the first three hours of my day, finish classes, and then I would drive an hour and a half to my hometown and do two-hour rehearsal,” he says. Despite the chaotic schedule, Best eventually came to a realization while on stage: “I was having more fun than basketball.” While recounting this period of his life with The Hollywood Reporter over Zoom earlier in October, Best playfully acknowledges the similarities to the beloved Zac Efron-led Disney movie, with one exception: “I wasn’t the star player. I was riding the bench and just getting my opportunity,” he quips. Much like how Troy Bolton moved away to college to pursue his dreams, Best made the decision to move to Los Angeles post-college to follow his own. Jaalen Best in The Greatest . Prime Video The first few years in Tinseltown proved challenging, as Best was one of thousands who came to the city with the same goals. But after years of background work, occasional guest roles and finding new talent representation, he finally got the audition he had been longing for in 2023. “There were maybe seven or eight auditions,” he recalls, referring to the months-long audition process for the role of Muhammad Ali in Prime Video ‘s The Greatest , which premieres Nov. 4. “It also was during the [actors] strike as well, so a lot of it was completely delayed and being pushed back.” As months drew by between auditions and no confirmed offers, Best sought other roles. He later got offered a six-month contract with Days of Our Lives , but admits he was still holding out hope for The Greatest . That’s when his team flagged producers on the biopic of his pending soap opera booking and “instantly they’re like, ‘OK, we’re sending him to L.A. to do a network test,'” the actor recalls. A day after the test, as he headed back to the airport, Best receives a call that The Greatest creator Ben Watkins wants to meet at his office. “I walk in and I shake his hand, and he’s just telling me, ‘Hey, there’s a couple of executives that don’t think you can hold up the voice, and they think you just practiced really well, and you just wowed us at these auditions.'” In that moment, a confused Best was willing to do whatever’s necessary to prove he’s meant for the role. “[Watkins’] like, ‘I’m going to put you on camera and I’m going to ask you some things, and I just want you to talk back,'” the actor says. “We do that, and then he wants me to repeat some phrases, like Muhammad Ali’s favorite line, ‘I am the greatest.'” After repeating a variety of phrases, the showrunner gives Best one final line: “Jaalen, you got the role.” “I’m so locked into repeating the phrases and making sure I’m giving, I’m like, ‘Jaalen, you got the role.’ And I say it in [Muhammad’s] dialect,” he recalls. “And [Watkins’] like, ‘No, Jaalen. You got the role.’ I started to say it again, and I’m like, ‘Wait, what?’ And then they bust in, and it’s like this moment.” The Greatest Prime Video Before Best could fully celebrate, he had to get one more blessing from Muhammad’s wife, Lonnie Ali, before officially stepping into the ring. After meeting her in Louisville, Kentucky, a nervous Best was on the flight home when he “got a text from Ben basically saying, Lonnie sent a message saying, ‘He’s the one in more ways than you know.'” Below, Best opens up to THR about honoring Ali with his performance; the advice he got from Michael B. Jordan, who served as an executive producer on The Greatest ; and what he can’t live without. Playing such an iconic figure, how did you navigate honoring him with your performance, but also bringing your own portrayal to the screen? When I got the role, I started going down this deep dive on him, and I tried to gather my own perspective of what I believe he displayed to not just me but to the people. And people would tell me so many stories as well. Every time someone has an Ali story, I stop everything I’m doing and I listen in because I think it’s important to see how he affected people just off of one meeting, whether he just put his fist up or whether he just threw air punches at them or whatever the case is. It’s very beautiful to be able to rely on real connections that he made with people. I can’t ever be Ali, but I needed to get as close as possible to him. And it’s great because I feel like the look that I had, I’ve always grown up being told, “Hey, you remind us of a young Muhammad Ali,” and that never registered to me until I got in the training process. My body was naturally kind of shaped like his in a way. … And sometimes, I would just wear these white boots every single time I would train because he always wore his white boots. And my trainer would also give me footage to break down at night for homework. So on top of me doing all my studying, I broke down every punch and every movement and the rhythm of his bounces in the ring, and then I would be able to show up the next day and replicate all of that. So all of these things just allowed me to truly get to a place where I felt like I was embodying him and just really just showing up as him. And I started to rely on my own instincts and I would just say, “You know what? No more watching the movies, no more watching this.” Michael B. Jordan and Jaalen Best. Jason Mendez/Getty Images for Prime Video With Michael B. Jordan serving as an executive producer on the show, how much did you get to chat and learn from him? He’s a mentor for me. I call him Big Bro. He calls himself Big Bro. So it’s definitely something that has allowed me to feel much more of a personal connection to him as opposed to just business. Him looking out for me in terms of trying to make sure that I have a great, long career with incredible success. You hear him all the time say he wants the younger generation to be better than him, and he’s always coming with that energy when he comes to me, and I think that’s incredible. He’s somebody I can constantly look up to and see the greatness that he’s doing. I tell him, “Thank you for the blueprint and for showing us the way and continuing to lead us, especially as Black men who just want to be successful and help our community and just be a face of the world and the industry in a positive way and lead with great influence.” For those who are just getting to know you with your role in The Greatest , what do they need to know? I’m just a regular guy. I love just being inside, watching TV. Sometimes it’s hard to get me out of this room. I love going to parks and I love riding horses. I love doing just anything that people would say is boring. And then I just picked up tennis, so I’m learning tennis. I’m just trying to have fun. What’s something you absolutely cannot live without? I’m learning to relax a little bit on the coffee. I’ve been going a little crazy lately. I just love the taste of it so much. Sometimes I was literally, it’s so wild, two o’clock in the morning, I’m waking up and I’m processing, oh, should I chill off the coffee for tomorrow? Should I try to go the day without coffee? But I’m just constantly in this battle with myself because I feel like I sometimes would just order two different cups because I want to try a different coffee, but I don’t want to sacrifice to not get my favorite. *** The Greatest premieres Nov. 4 on Prime Video. THR

articles.title: Russell Brand Treated Consent as “an Obstacle to Remove or Ignore,” Prosecution Tells Jury in Rape Trial’s Closing Arguments
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 8:10am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court on Oct. 30, 2026. Courtesy of Getty The prosecution has made its closing arguments in Russell Brand ‘s highly publicized rape and sexual assault trial in London, saying his defense is “a lot of half-truths, but spun into lies.” The jury, made up of eight men and four women, will now deliberate. The judge will only accept a unanimous verdict on each count. As The Hollywood Reporter has covered in detail, the presenter and comedian (also star of St Trinian’s and Forgetting Sarah Marshall ) is accused of three counts of rape and three charges of sexual assault. He was initially accused of indecent assault, which was reduced to a count of attempted indecent assault by the judge on Tuesday. Six women allege offenses dating from 1999 to 2009, and Brand denies the allegations vehemently. Related Stories Movies Edinburgh Film Festival Toasts Bollywood With 'Kuch Kuch Hota Hai' Anniversary Event at 2028 Edition Movies From 'Sh*t Happens' to an Erotic Photographer Being Confronted by His Daughter: Offbeat Films at Tallinn London’s Southwark Crown Court has heard from the complainants, one of whom says she was raped by Brand in a Bournemouth hotel room after the Labour Party conference in 1999. Another alleges Brand pulled her into a nearby toilet and orally raped her at a bar in Soho in 2004 and a separate accuser says she was anally raped by the star at his Hampstead home in 2009, after the two had consensual vaginal sex. Brand is also said to have attempted to drag an MTV colleague into a bathroom at work in 2001, and exposed himself while traveling with a complainant in a car, telling her to “suck it.” Over the last three weeks, the jury has watched police interviews with all of the complainants, whose identities have been kept anonymous during the trial. Their testimonies have been cross-examined, witnesses — including Brand’s former personal assistant, Helen Berger — have been called to the stand, and Brand himself gave evidence just this week. He revealed he hadn’t persuaded anyone to testify on his behalf, but his wife, Laura, did take the stand on Thursday and told the room that Brand is a “caring and kind, wonderful father” to their three children. The defendant himself maintained : “I know what ‘no’ means… Consent is a fundamental, essential and necessary and in many ways more important than sex itself.” Lead prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told the jury in her closing argument on Friday that these six women do not know each other. None of them “sought the limelight” or “any kind of publicity,” she said. “None of these women has anything to gain — except perhaps some closure.” She urged the jury: “Listen to their accounts, how many said he was nice, then there was a personality change, a pivot.” She said these women have told the court: “[Brand] didn’t listen when I said no, he didn’t listen, he didn’t care… In the rape cases, he just kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim and ejaculated.” All of the accusers have since moved on with their lives, but the trial has forced them to “relive what has happened to them” and describe intimate details to the court, Karmy-Jones also said. They are not “jealous women spurned,” as one complainant was made out to seem, she continued, and it doesn’t matter that the complainants “can’t remember” what they wore. She also said Brand seemed to “remember lots now” despite initially not being able to recollect many of the encounters in his police interviews. Brand’s defense is “a lot of half-truths, but spun into lies,” said Karmy-Jones. At this moment, per Sky News coverage , proceedings were briefly interrupted by the snoring of a member of the public who had fallen asleep in the gallery. Karmy-Jones also said that Channel 4’s Dispatches , a documentary built from allegations against Brand that kickstarted the 2023 police investigation, was not a “magic force” that caused the women to “recast” memories of “happy consensual fun.” Instead, these women “have realized they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth.” Karmy-Jones asked the jury to sit in silence for 20 seconds — the same length of time one woman alleges her encounter with Brand, as he attempted to pull her into the toilet, lasted. The prosecution also described Brand’s wife as “undoubtedly lovely” but said Laura Brand was not in touch with the defendant at the time the alleged encounters took place. Karmy-Jones quoted one of Brand’s earlier statements: “Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself,” before asking the jury: Does that ring true?” She pulled a quote from Brand’s 2007 autobiography My Booky Wook . He wrote: “Now if I want something — whether it’s a job or a woman — I will determinedly, resolutely, remove anything that’s in the way, until I possess the object of my desire.” Karmy-Jones said consent was maybe “just an obstacle to be removed, or perhaps to ignore,” for Brand. Brand had a “tendency” to “swiftly make things sexual,” said Karmy-Jones, wrapping up. Court has ended for the week. The defense’s closing arguments will take place on Monday. THR

articles.title: Matthew Weiner Out as Showrunner of Eddie Murphy Peacock Series After Clash With Producers
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All October 30, 2026 8:23am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Matthew Weiner ANTHONY HARVEY/AFP/Getty Images Matthew Weiner has exited Eddie Murphy ‘s Peacock series The Chairman following a clash with producers, The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed. Murphy is among the producers. Weiner ( Mad Men ) was the project’s showrunner. The reason given for his departure was “creative differences.” A new showrunning team is already in place, we’re told, and will be announced soon. The writers room has been shuttered for two weeks amid the transition. THR reached out to Weiner for comment did not immediately respond back. Related Stories TV Alexander Brothers Case Is a "Microcosm for a Lot of Questions about Sexual Assault," Says Doc Director Business Peacock's Hot Streak: Two Quarters of Profit After Years Of Losses Variety first reported the news of Weiner’s exit. The Chairman is being produced by Universal Television and David Glasser’s ( Yellowstone ) 101 Studios, which has a first-look film and television deal at NBCUniversal. The show also stands out as the first project from Chris McCarthy under his overall deal with NBCU. (McCarthy followed his buddy Taylor Sheridan over from Paramount.) The plot of The Chairman remains under wraps . The Chairman will be Murphy’s first TV series regular role since NBC’s Saturday Night Live , which launched his comedy career. He served as a cast member on the sketch comedy series for four seasons from 1980 to 1984. Murphy is often credited with having saved the struggling SNL — he even hosted it once as a cast member when movie star Nick Nolte fell sick. (And then twice more as planned.) Murphy later went on to star in dozens of films, including the Beverly Hills Cop franchise, 1996’s The Nutty Professor , 1998’s Doctor Dolittle , 2003’s The Haunted Mansion , 2003’s Daddy Day Care , 2008’s Meet Dave and 2023’s You People . Murphy’s also voiced multiple characters, such as Donkey in the Shrek franchise and Thurgoode Orenthal Stubbs in The PJs . In 2007, he was nominated for an Academy Award for best supporting actor for Dreamgirls . Weiner has won nine Emmy awards, mostly for his iconic AMC series Mad Men . He was also a writer and executive producer on The Sopranos . Other credits include The Romanoffs , Becker and Are You Here . In 2017, Kater Gordon, an Emmy-winning writer for Mad Men , accused Weiner of sexual harassment . Gordon said that while working late one night, Weiner told her she owed it to him to let him see her naked. She was let go from the series a year later. Weiner has repeatedly denied Gordon’s allegations, telling the New York Times in October 2018, “I have reasons I don’t believe that I said it, if that makes sense, but I really don’t remember saying it.” For its part, 101 Studios has gone through numerous showrunner shuffles itself, mostly on Sheridan shows. THR

articles.title: Canadian Rock Icon Bryan Adams Takes Aim at Trump, Says His Protest Song Gets Standing Ovations in Red States (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Seth Abramovitch Plus Icon Seth Abramovitch Senior Writer SethAbramovitch Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 8:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bryan Adams Christopher Polk/Billboard/Getty Images He never says him by name — not in the songs and not in this interview. But there can be no mistaking who Bryan Adams is taking aim at in his recent musical output, a string of Canadian protest songs like “51st State” and his latest, the plaintive “Lake Ontario.” Adams has Donald Trump on the brain. Both of those songs appear on How’s It Goin’ , a Canadian concept album which drops Nov. 6 and features a dozen new tracks about Adams’ homeland. Related Stories News Russell Brand Treated Consent as "an Obstacle to Remove or Ignore," Prosecution Tells Jury in Rape Trial's Closing Arguments Movies Edinburgh Film Festival Toasts Bollywood With 'Kuch Kuch Hota Hai' Anniversary Event at 2028 Edition It’s the 17th studio album for the rocker — whose catalog of indestructible hits includes “Summer of ’69,” “Run to You” and “(Everything I Do) I Do It for You” — and easily his most politically pointed, having found a new muse in the deterioration of relations between his homeland and the United States. Since returning to the White House, Trump has placed punishing tariffs on Canadian goods, repeatedly threatened to make Canada the “51st state” and even ordered Lake Ontario renamed “Lake America” in U.S. federal records, inflaming tensions with the country’s longtime ally north of the 49th parallel. Adams, for one, has had enough. He checked in with The Hollywood Reporter from a tour stop in Las Vegas — he’s in the middle of a five-show run at the Wynn — to share where his head is at these days. It’s firmly grounded in the waning months of 2026, about as far as you can get from the summer of ’69. I’ve lived in L.A. for 25 years, but I grew up in Montreal. I’m still very much a proud Canadian. And I’ve got to say, listening to “Lake Ontario,” I got a little choked up. Wow, that’s super nice. Now wait till you hear the rest of the album. Half my family is still there, and it’s been a really rough couple of years. You put those dark feelings into these angry, beautiful words that really helped me process it a bit. I mean, it’s not even angry. It’s not? It’s not angry. It’s stating the facts. I’m just commenting on current affairs and feeling the temperature in the room, basically. Do you live in Canada? Yeah. So you might not be angry, but I know people there are very angry. No, I mean, listen, I might be angry, but I don’t think the songs are angry. I think there’s a lot of irony in there. And they’re heartfelt and funny. But it’s helping process what feels like a betrayal. You say it in the song : We’ve had so many years of peace and harmony, and it just takes “one dude” — and I’m wondering if “dude” was the original word you wanted to use — to fuck it all up. Yeah, “dude” was the original word. There are other expletives you could put in there, but I consider myself respectful as well, even under the circumstances. But the thing I really wanted to say is that if you have that much power, why would you not want to channel it for good? You could do so much good in the world with that much power, and it’s just not happening. So I think that’s the thing that perplexes me more than anything. Put Canada aside for one second and just look at the global situation. It’s baffling. How did the idea for the album come to you? Did it come out of this frustration? It started out that I was asked to write a song for a documentary on Canada, about Canada’s East Coast. When I write, I don’t just focus on one thing. I just start writing. Looking back on my notes, I noticed there were a few things I had that were potentially interesting. So I went down and finished that one, then I finished another one, and then I started getting into the current affairs thing. Before I knew it, I had three or four songs that seemed like part of a concept album. So I just kept going, and the whole album was written and recorded in three months. “51st State,” that was the first song on the album that was quite political. How did people react to it? We debuted that song in St. Louis on our tour this summer, and we weren’t sure how it was going to go down in America. But the first night we did it, standing ovation. Second night we did it, standing ovation. Got into Texas, into the red states, standing ovation. And I suddenly thought to myself, I’m not sure that the people in this country, in America — I’m in Las Vegas at the moment — I’m not sure everybody agrees with what’s going down. And that was the way of testing the temperature in the room, because if you play it live, you can see automatically what people think. We were getting just full-on cheers. Well, we’ll see in a few days what people really think, with the Nov. 3 election. It’s not worth predicting it at all. I’m just writing my truth. I want to bring up this viral thing that happened, and I return to it whenever I want to smile. It’s when that drunk guy came onstage during “Summer of ’69,” and you let it happen, and then you continued the song without missing a single beat. Not only is it funny, but it says something about you, I think. Which is? A lot of people would have been angry, would have been reactive, would have said, “Get this guy off the stage!” But you let the universe just happen. That’s me. That’s what I’m getting at. I feel that I saw the real you at that moment. Well, that’s nice. I think that’s actually very much what I am like. I let the universe do its thing. And when I saw that guy coming, I mean, I could have easily backed off, but I saw him coming and just thought, “Go for it, have a crack.” As he climbed onto the stage, he whacked his head. And I remember that moment, thinking, “He’s not going to make it all the way up here.” But he did. Oh dear. I’m glad somebody filmed it. Since we’re on the subject of “Summer of ’69.” I’m just curious, how much of those lyrics are true? Do you remember your summer of ’69? Did you really have a band with friends? The song is obviously bittersweet, and it’s a song of nostalgia, but it’s not about the year. Someone told me it’s about another kind of 69. I was like, “There’s no way.” Well, it’s just a metaphor. It’s about first love. It’s about first figuring out where you’re going, what you’re doing, and it’s about reflecting on how that summer went. But there’s no double entendre in there. Oh, of course there is. OK then! My friend is right. I was like, “Are you crazy? No, it’s about the summer of 1969!” Nowhere in the song do I say [1969]. Where did you get your first real six-string? My father. Well, I’m glad he got it for you. Same here. THR

articles.title: Bobby Wright, ‘McHale’s Navy’ Actor, Singer and Son of Kitty Wells, Dies at 84
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All October 30, 2026 8:34am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bobby Wright on 'McHale's Navy' Courtesy Everett Collection Bobby Wright, the singer and son of country music legend Kitty Wells who played the radio operator Willy Moss on the popular ABC comedy McHale’s Navy , died Tuesday at his home in Madison, Tennessee, his family announced . He was 84. McHale’s Navy , starring Ernest Borgnine , Joe Flynn and Tim Conway , aired for four seasons (1962-66), and Wright appeared on all 138 episodes of the show that was set on the U.S. Navy boat PT-73 in the Pacific during World War II. He also appeared with the rest of the cast in the features McHale’s Navy (1964) and McHale’s Navy Joins the Air Force (1966). Related Stories Critic's Appreciation Patrick Stewart's Career Was a Rare and Thrilling Marriage of the Prestigious and the Populist Movies Patrick Stewart, 'Star Trek' Captain and 'X-Men' Superhero, Dies at 86 Wright recorded for Decca, ABC and United Artists Records from 1967-79 and had 21 singles on Billboard’s Hot Country Songs chart, with the gentle “Here I Go Again” peaking at No. 13 in 1971. His other singles included “Lay Some Happiness on Me,” “Everybody Needs a Rainbow,” a cover of Terry Jacks’ “Seasons in the Sun,” “Lovin’ Someone on My Mind” and “I’m Turning You Loose.” One of three kids, John Robert Wright Jr. was born on March 30, 1942, in Charleston, West Virginia. His father was Johnnie Wright, who toured the South in an act called Johnnie & Jack, with Wells often performing with them. At age 8, he sang with his parents on the country music program Louisiana Hayride out of Shreveport and played guitar. He and his family moved to Nashville in 1958 when his folks became headliners at the Grand Ole Opry, and he graduated from Madison High School, where he played baseball, basketball and football. Wright came to Hollywood to audition for director Peter Tewksbury ( Father Knows Best , My Three Sons ) for a role on television as a Southern youngster who could play the guitar. The show didn’t move forward, but his screen test was seen by a producer on McHale’s Navy (he was billed as John Wright on the show). While the comedy was still in production, he gave music another try and worked with his mom on one of her 1965 albums. After McHale’s Navy ended, Wright played a robber on a 1966 episode of CBS’ Pistols ’n’ Petticoats , a short-lived Western that starred Anne Sheridan, and showed up in the 1974 film Catch the Black Sunshine , starring Ted Cassidy and Chris Robinson . Wright, who also played bass, trumpet and drums, appeared with his parents and sisters, Ruby and Carol Sue, on the syndicated Kitty Wells Johnnie Wright Family Show for years and toured with his parents until they retired from the road in 2007. Survivors include Carol Sue; his children, LeAnn and Kamela; his grandchildren, Austin, Cassidy, Shelby and Dalton; his great-grandchildren, Hayden, Pazlee, Remi, Fletcher and Axel; his nieces and nephews, Kitty, John Jr., David, Corrie and Stephanie; and his former wife, Brenda. Wells, a member of the Country Music Hall of Fame, was country’s first female superstar, racking up nearly three dozen Top 10 hits from 1952-65, including the No. 1 smash “It Wasn’t God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels.” THR

articles.title: Emerging Arab Directors Given a Pathway Toward Filmmaking Careers by Expanded Pitching Platform at Sharjah Film Festival
articles.full_text: × Oct 30, 2026 7:37am PT Emerging Arab Directors Given a Pathway Toward Filmmaking Careers by Expanded Pitching Platform at Sharjah Film Festival By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest Emirati Filmmakers on Building a Local Cinema Ecosystem: ‘We Have a Long Way to Go’ 16 minutes ago Sharjah Film Festival Partners With UAE’s Media Authority in Push to Assist Emerging Filmmakers 4 days ago Egyptian Cinema Eyes Its Next Act as Industry Veterans Call for Better Scripts, Wider Distribution 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "Kot Kot Kot" (Courtesy of Boubaker Boukhari) The 13th edition of the UAE’s Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth is expanding its pitching platform for its second iteration. Six projects were selected this year, up from the three that took part during its inaugural program. The expansion is part of SIFF’s effort to build a pathway for emerging filmmakers beyond training and exhibition. As festival director Sheikha Jawaher bint Abdullah Al Qasimi told Variety ahead of this year’s edition, learning how to make a film is only part of the equation, “getting that film produced and seen is a completely different challenge.” This year’s projects bring together filmmakers from across the Arab world and diaspora, with the principal goal of finding financing and production partners from Sharjah and beyond. Related Stories ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says the Show Was a ‘Big Undertaking’ as Co-Star Acknowledges He Could Be ‘Difficult’ to Work With ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested an Intimacy Coordinator Because of 'Uncomfortable' Age Gap With Montana Jordan: 'He Was a Baby!' Here are the six short film projects presented at this year’s pitching sessions: “The Black Hole” (Mike Mo Elsherif, U.S. Produced by JohnBen Lacy) Palestinian-American filmmaker Mike Mo Elsherif’s “The Black Hole” follows a Gazan refugee living in the U.S. who develops a mysterious illness as he searches for answers about his family in Gaza. El Sherif describes the film as a “visceral exploration of the complex ways in which our bodies store and process trauma throughout our lives, highlighting the deep connection between physical sensations and emotional experiences.” The film is part of a trilogy of shorts. The first installment, “Maqluba,” screens in the Arabic short films competition at SIFF following stops at Woodstock, BlackStar and El Gouna, while “Goodbye Habibi,” now in post-production, was financed by FilmLab Palestine, the Islamic Scholarship Fund, the Doha Film Institute and the Kentucky Arts Council. Currently in the financing stage, the project was developed through screenwriting lab The Front Porch Lab, under Louisville-based nonprofit 502 film, as well as The New Harmony Project, a writing organization. Partially privately financed, “The Black Hole” is seeking further funding in Sharjah ahead of a winter 2027 shoot in Louisville, Kentucky. Elsherif describes the project as “a psychological study of a Palestinian grappling with the heartbreak and dehumanization he witnesses every day,” and a search for healing amid the devastation of his homeland. “Kot Kot Kot” (Boubaker Boukhari, UAE) “Kot Kot Kot” follows a young girl grappling with the loss of her mother. Her father gives her a chick that she raises into a hen with which she grows deeply attached, only for it to suddenly disappear one day. The film grew from a story Boukhari’s mother told him as a child, which he had largely forgotten until his young nephew recounted it years later at a family gathering. “The emotion and wonder in his voice made me realize that this was a story worth telling again,” Boukhari tells Variety . Currently in production, the independently-produced UAE project has been self-financed and is seeking funding to complete post-production, particularly in music, sound design, sound effects and sound recording. Boukhari has also signed Tunisian co-producer Alaeddin Abou Taleb of Key Production Films, whose credits include the Tanit d’Or-winning stop-motion short “Diaspora” at the Carthage Film Festival. Completion is planned by the end of 2026. Illustrator Nadia Zilanova, whose international work includes commissions for the New York Times and publishing houses, recently joined the project to create and color the film’s backgrounds “in a distinctive visual style.” “The Last Call” (Saleh Mohammed, UAE) UAE-based filmmaker Saleh Mohammed’s “The Last Call” begins with an unexpected phone call from a number connected to a forgotten memory, sending its protagonist on an emotional journey through the past, unresolved feelings and unanswered questions. Mohammed says the film explores “the things we leave unsaid and the moments we fail to appreciate until they are gone.” The director described the visual approach of his film as “restrained,” allowing the film to reflect “on how a single moment can change a life and how we sometimes recognize the value of someone’s presence only after they are gone.” The screenplay is complete and the project is in pre-production, with location scouting underway and casting and crew assembly next. Mohammed is seeking financing and sponsorship, as well as potential co-producers and industry partners to help move the film into production. “In a world where communication is constant, genuine connection can sometimes be the thing we overlook most,” Mohammed says. He is also using SIFF to build relationships with festivals and distributors ahead of the film’s eventual release. Mohammed, who began his career as a theater actor and director, also co-stars in Khalid Al Mahmood’s “The Mangrove House,” the opening film of this year’s festival. “Lucky Shot” (Salah Al Hadhrami, Oman. Screenwriter Dalila Al-Dar’iya) Omani filmmaker Salah Al Hadhrami’s “Lucky Shot” centers on Amjad, a boy from a working-class neighborhood whose passion for football fuels dreams of a life beyond his modest circumstances. An unexpected turn of events forces him to choose between those ambitions and temptation that could change his future. Written by Omani filmmaker, writer and actor Dalila Al-Dar’iya, the 12-15 minute narrative short is in development, with initial approaches made to potential cast members. The independent project has yet to secure production financing and is seeking backers and co-producers in Sharjah and elsewhere in the region, with a tentative 2027 shoot dependent on funding. “I believe that simple stories can carry the profoundest human messages,” Al Hadhrami says. For the director, the film is less about football itself than the moment when an unexpected opportunity becomes “a true test.” The goal, above all, Al Hadhrami shares, is “to tell an authentic story that transcends geographical and cultural boundaries, one that resonates with the audience’s emotions. We hope to find partners who believe in this message and will help bring the film to the screen.” “My Uncle Saman” (“Saman 3my”) (Aljouri Abdelaziz Alzarooni, UAE. Creative Producer Shahad Al Ali) Emirati writer-director Aljouri Abdelaziz Alzarooni’s “My Uncle Saman” follows three young men on their way to their uncle’s long-awaited wedding. The groom, who is close enough in age to feel more like a cousin, sends them on a quick errand that turns into a string of misadventures, leaving the trio at risk of missing the wedding altogether. The comedy short is in development and has yet to secure financing or attach a production company. Alzarooni is seeking financing and production partners at SIFF, along with collaborators in areas including cinematography, sound and post-production. She says the pitch has already generated interest from potential partners, with discussions now underway. The young director says potential partners expressed strong enthusiasm for the project’s “fresh and distinctive approach to Emirati storytelling.” “‘My Uncle Saman’ is rooted in the natural humour, relationships, and everyday experiences of Emirati families, and I want to bring that authenticity to the screen in a way that audiences everywhere can connect with,” Alzarooni says. Alzarooni is also eyeing eventual support from potential distributors, broadcasters, streaming platforms and industry mentors as her search to secure financing continues. “Tomato Merchant” (Thoraya Farzaneh, UAE. Produced by Sayed Mousavi) UAE-based filmmaker Thoraya Farzaneh makes her directing debut with “Tomato Merchant,” about an elderly man who spends his day selling tomatoes in a quiet neighborhood and refuses to leave until they are all sold. As repeated attempts are made to persuade him to go home, the reason for the insistence gradually becomes clear. Farzaneh, who has spent the past several years working as an assistant director and writing scripts, says she waited until she felt ready to direct a story of her own. “I feel this is the right moment to take that step and share one of my stories with the world.” The independent short has received funding from the RAK Art Fund, supported by the Sharjah-based Al Qasimi Foundation, while FANN – Media Discovery Platform, the parent organization of the festival, will provide post-production support following its SIFF pitch. Now in pre-production, “Tomato Merchant” is set to shoot in the UAE in early November, with completion targeted for January. Farzaneh is using SIFF to explore festival and distribution opportunities for the finished film. Producer Sayed Mousavi says, “This film reminds us that kindness often begins with the simple choice to be patient.” “Tomato Merchant” Courtesy of Thoraya Farzaneh Charli xcx Cancels ‘Music, Fashion, Film’ Show in Arizona Due to Illness: ‘It Breaks Me That I Can’t Be With You’ Charli xcx Announces U.K. and Europe ‘Music, Fashion, Film’ Tour Dates, With Audrey Hobert Opening Charli xcx Brings Out Chappell Roan for ‘Boom Clap’ at Los Angeles Concert Madonna Opens MTV Video Music Awards With Sabrina Carpenter and Charli xcx, Plus Sombr, Debi Mazar and More Elton John, Charli xcx, Burna Boy and More Set Shows at New Apple Music Hall in London Charli xcx Joins Martin Scorsese’s ‘What Happens at Night’ With Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...

articles.title: Emirati Filmmakers on Building a Local Cinema Ecosystem: ‘We Have a Long Way to Go’
articles.full_text: × Oct 30, 2026 7:58am PT Emirati Filmmakers on Building a Local Cinema Ecosystem: ‘We Have a Long Way to Go’ By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest Emirati Filmmakers on Building a Local Cinema Ecosystem: ‘We Have a Long Way to Go’ 32 minutes ago Emerging Arab Directors Given a Pathway Toward Filmmaking Careers by Expanded Pitching Platform at Sharjah Film Festival 52 minutes ago Sharjah Film Festival Partners With UAE’s Media Authority in Push to Assist Emerging Filmmakers 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "The Mangrove House" (Courtesy of Faradees) Two Emirati filmmakers are bringing distinctly local stories to the 13th edition of the Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth, with Khalid Al Mahmood ’s musical “The Mangrove House” and Abdulrahman Al Madani ’s family drama “Oug,” the only Emirati films in competition. Both filmmakers have longstanding ties to SIFF. “The Mangrove House,” which world premiered as the festival’s opening film, was pitched at SIFF’s inaugural Film Pitching Session last year as Al Mahmood was seeking post-production support. FANN – Media Discovery Platform, SIFF’s parent organization, subsequently came aboard to back the film. For Al Madani, “Oug” marks the third film he has screened at the festival, following “Nagafa,” which played at SIFF in 2015, and “Laymoon” in 2019. Related Stories ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says the Show Was a ‘Big Undertaking’ as Co-Star Acknowledges He Could Be ‘Difficult’ to Work With ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested an Intimacy Coordinator Because of 'Uncomfortable' Age Gap With Montana Jordan: 'He Was a Baby!' “Oug” Courtesy of Abdulrahman Al Madani Their return comes as Emirati filmmakers see renewed momentum around a local industry that has weathered significant ups and downs over the past two decades. Al Mahmood, who made his first film while a university student in the U.S. in 1999, recalls returning to a UAE where filmmaking was virtually nonexistent, just as an early community of filmmakers was beginning to take shape. Annual screenings of locally made films, which later took shape as the Emirates Film Competition, became “a school where we came together and critiqued our films,” he explains. “More and more festivals popped up,” including the Dubai Intl. Film Festival and Abu Dhabi Film Festival. Al Madani entered the industry shortly before much of that festival ecosystem disappeared and remembers the “privilege” of having an abundance of platforms before “the plug was pulled, and then we didn’t know where to go next.” Abu Dhabi Film Festival remains defunct, while Dubai, which held its last edition in 2017, is set to return in December 2027. Khalid Al Mahmood, Abdulrahman Al Madani Courtesy of Essie Assibu, Muhammad Reda The loss pushed Al Madani and many Emirati filmmakers of his generation beyond the UAE. In the decade that followed, he made shorts that traveled internationally, an experience he describes as a “wake-up call” that taught him not to solely rely on platforms at home. Institutional support across the emirates is now growing. “Oug” received a grant from the UAE Ministry of Culture, a significant shift from a period Al Madani describes as having virtually “zero support.” “We have a long way to go, but I think this is a good start,” he acknowledges. “People feel like they can go and apply somewhere [local] to get funding.” For Al Mahmood, however, much of the UAE’s film infrastructure remains geared toward attracting international productions rather than sustaining local filmmakers. “What’s missing to me is just the infrastructure to be able to make films in the country,” he argues. Distribution presents another challenge. This year Al Madani launched Meylas Aflam, a screening initiative aimed at giving Emirati shorts a life beyond their initial festival runs. “We screen our film once, then what?” he asks. Meylas Aflam has held four sold-out screenings this year, with local audiences staying for discussions that have run as long as an hour. The response challenges what Al Madani calls a “misconception that our audience is not prepared for our stories.” His films on YouTube have drawn millions of views, he adds, with viewers responding to stories from their own environment “told truthfully, and without sugarcoating.” ‘The Mangrove House’ Al Mahmood’s “The Mangrove House” is a musical about two deaf brothers and their sister trying to raise money for a competition. The project originated with Emirati writer and editor Ayesha Alameri, whose brother is deaf and whose family uses sign language at home. Al Mahmood admits that when Alameri first brought him the screenplay, he expected the kind of story about living with a disability he had seen before. “Usually the stories are all sad, and it’s going to be a sob story,” he recalls. Instead, what appealed to him was precisely what the screenplay avoided. “There’s no pity. I didn’t feel like they were anything less than any other character.” That approach grew out of Alameri’s own conversations with her brother. When the two watched films and videos featuring deaf characters, she remembers him asking why their stories “always have to be sad.” Alameri’s original screenplay ran 23 pages, leaving Al Mahmood with a story he felt was too long to produce affordably as a short but not developed enough for a feature. He concentrated the film around one section of the script and then proposed another departure from its original form, asking, “Why not? Let’s do a musical.” That decision also gave Al Mahmood an opportunity to root the film more firmly in the UAE, weaving local instruments, clothing and even songs playing with the names of different fish into the story. “I always felt like I need to introduce something from this part of the world, something that’s rooted here,” he explains. “If it’s not the landscape, it’s the clothing, something.” ‘Oug’ Al Madani draws “Oug” from experiences around him. The title translates as “the defect,” referring to the blame directed at women whose marriages have yet to produce children. The idea grew out of conversations with married women he knew who faced intrusive questions about when they would have children, including a relative who undertook diets, exercise and other measures. “I was telling her, what about your husband? Does he have to do anything?” Al Madani recalls. “So this question stuck.” Set largely during a shopping trip to IKEA, the film follows a couple (Sarra’a Abdulaziz, Yaser Al Neyadi) as those pressures surface in a confrontation with the husband’s mother (Huda Al Ghanem). “I wanted it to be completely in a public setting,” Al Madani explains. “They are fighting, but they have to remain composed also. So I felt like it makes it much stronger.” He also resisted reducing the mother-in-law to a straightforward villain, instead portraying a family in which each character is responding to different expectations. That includes the husband, whose vulnerability culminates in an emotional breakdown. When Al Madani filmed the scene, he recalls crew members reacting to the sight of an Emirati man in kandura and ghutra, traditional clothing, crying onscreen. “I didn’t realize I was doing a thing,” he admits. “I was just staying true to the story.” The film’s international run has produced other unexpected reactions. At Denmark’s Odense Film Festival, where “Oug” premiered last year, Al Madani remembers audience members expressing surprise that its hijab-wearing women were the dominant personalities rather than passive figures. “I was not trying to break stereotypes,” he stresses. “I’m just portraying the truth of my environment, and somehow that broke so many stereotypes.” For both filmmakers, the next challenge is moving beyond shorts. Al Mahmood has an early-stage feature project he describes only as “very artistic,” while Al Madani has spent the past year developing a feature screenplay and identifies funding as the principal obstacle to making that transition. “This is my seventh short film. So I am ready,” Al Madani says. “My next project has to be a feature.” He argues that he is hardly alone. “There’s a community of filmmakers who have done countless short films,” he adds, “and we need to move on to the next step.” Emirati Filmmakers on Building a Local Cinema Ecosystem: ‘We Have a Long Way to Go’ Patrick Stewart Dies: Marvel, Kevin Feige Praise ‘X-Men’ Icon For Bringing ‘Charles Xavier to Life With Grace, Intelligence and Humanity’ Mexico City Grand Prix 2026: Here’s Where to Watch F1 Online for Free How ‘Up Again’ Director Captured the Rise of a Teenage Figure Skating Champion: ‘The Technical Conditions Were Extremely Challenging’ Taylor Sheridan’s ‘The Last Cowboy’ Sets Season 7 Premiere Date on CMT (EXCLUSIVE) Mohammad Rasoulof, Shahrbanoo Sadat Push Back on Idea of Separate Oscar Category for Exiled Filmmakers as Cate Blanchett’s Displacement Film Fund Hits Tokyo Loading comments...

articles.title: Dominic Cooke to Direct ‘John Daniel,’ Real-Life Story of Woman’s Friendship With Baby Gorilla in Post-WWI England, as Cornerstone Boards Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: × Oct 30, 2026 8:00am PT Dominic Cooke to Direct ‘John Daniel,’ Real-Life Story of Woman’s Friendship With Baby Gorilla in Post-WWI England, as Cornerstone Boards Sales (EXCLUSIVE) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Dominic Cooke to Direct ‘John Daniel,’ Real-Life Story of Woman’s Friendship With Baby Gorilla in Post-WWI England, as Cornerstone Boards Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 31 minutes ago Tahmima Anam’s New Novel ‘Good Books’ Being Adapted for TV With Pacesetter, Kudos and ‘Emily in Paris’ Writer (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Disney+ Strikes Landmark Content Deal With U.K.’s Channel 4 That Streamer Says Is Among Its ‘Most Significant’ Globally 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Supplied Acclaimed British theater director Dominic Cooke , behind the recent stage spin-off “Game of Thrones: The Mad King,” is to helm his first film since 2020’s Benedict Cumberbatch-starring spy thriller “The Courier.” “John Daniel,” which has been acquired for worldwide sales by Cornerstone ahead of the American Film Market, is based on the extraordinary true story of an unlikely friendship between a fiercely independent Englishwoman and a baby gorilla in the aftermath of WWI. With a screenplay written by Alexi Kaye Campbell (“Woman in Gold”), the film is inspired by original home movie footage and photographs recorded by locals in Uley, Gloucestershire between 1918-22. Related Stories ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says the Show Was a ‘Big Undertaking’ as Co-Star Acknowledges He Could Be ‘Difficult’ to Work With ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says He Was the ‘Most Happy’ About the Show Ending: I Wasn’t ‘Going Home and Crying All Day’ “John Daniel” is a Genesius Pictures production, in association with Edward Film Company and produced by BAFTA nominee Debbie Gray (“Good Luck to You Leo Grande,” “Mrs Lowry & Son”). The film is currently in pre-production, with principal photography scheduled to begin in the U.K. in mid-2027. According to the filmmakers, motion capture and VFX will be used to “deliver a photoreal performance” of the gorilla, with visual effects by Axio World, led by Loris Mantello (“Avengers: Infinity War,” “Prehistoric Planet,” “The Lion King”) and Maoris Creantor (“The Lion King,” “Fast & Furious 9,” “The Matrix Resurrections”). Set in 1918 in the Cotwolds village of Uley, still raw from the losses of WWII, “John Daniel” follows Alyce Cunningham, who has built a solitary life behind a wall of wit and stoicism. As per the synopsis, that changes when her reckless nephew impulsively rescues a baby gorilla from the window of a London department store and, ignoring her protests, leaves her no option but to take him in. Mischievous and endlessly curious, John Daniel, as she reluctantly names him, slowly wins her over, and as he becomes part of village life, from the school classroom to the village pub, he brings joy back to the grieving community. When fear and suspicion threaten to drive him out, Alyce must decide how far she will go to protect the animal who has opened her heart. “The moment I read this beautiful script by Alexi, I knew I wanted to be part of it,” said Gray. “It’s an extraordinary true story about a gorilla, but at its heart it’s a story of love, hope and human connection in the aftermath of war. At a time when the world can feel increasingly divided, this film reminds us of our capacity to heal, unite and find compassion again.” Added Cooke: “I am delighted to be attached to direct John Daniel – a beautiful, funny and profound story. Alexi’s script gets to the heart of the strange, necessary bonds between humans and animals. It shows how we sometimes need to surrender control in order to feel fully alive. I couldn’t be happier to be working with such committed and driven producers as Debbie Gray and the team at Cornerstone to bring this moving and hopeful true story to life.” “John Daniel” marks the third feature from Cooke following “The Courier” and his 2017 directorial debut “On Chesil Beach,” based on Ian McEwan’s Booker Prize-nominated novella and starring Saoirse Ronan and Billy Howle. Cooke is represented by UTA and Casarotto Ramsay & Associates. articles.full_text: × Oct 30, 2026 8:21am PT ‘Blindspot Berlin,’ a Beta Film TIFF Standout With ‘All Quiet’ Star Albrecht Schuch, Seals Deal for Spain with Filmin (EXCLUSIVE) The deal for the counter-terror police task force thriller comes ahead of the series’ Spanish premiere at the South International Series Festival in Cádiz By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest South International Series Festival: ‘American Hostage,’ Ronan Bennett, Great European Series and Andalusia’s TV Build 3 days ago Lula’s Election Win: How Fan Accounts for Taylor Swift, Billie Eilish and More Helped Him to a Historic Victory and Defeat for Trump 4 days ago ‘Killing a Bear,’ From Movistar Plus and Arte France: a Real-Event Inspired Murder-Mystery Whose Victim Is a Pyrenean Brown Bear 7 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Blindspot Berlin (Courtesy of Neuesuper/Hubert Mican) “ Blindspot Berlin ,” a buzzy counter-terror police unit thriller led by “All Quiet on the Western Front” star Albrecht Schuch has been licensed by Beta Film to Spain’s upscale SVOD platform Filmin. Backed by Germany’s ARD, Europe’s biggest public broadcaster as well as rbb, NDR, and HR, “Blindspot Berlin’s” Spanish deal was announced Friday on the eve of the six-part series screening in main competition at Cadiz’s South International Series Festival. Related Stories ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says He Was the ‘Most Happy’ About the Show Ending: I Wasn’t ‘Going Home and Crying All Day’ ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested an Intimacy Coordinator Because of 'Uncomfortable' Age Gap With Montana Jordan: 'He Was a Baby!' The news comes as “Blindspot Berlin” launches Oct. 30 on ARD’s streaming service, with linear broadcasts on Nov. 1 and Nov. 6. The series will be made available on Filmin in early 2027. A true crime thriller, the heavily researched “Blindspot Berlin” charts German police efforts to prevent Berlin’s Dec. 19 2016 Christmas market terror attack which killed 13 and injured dozens. A standout world premiere at TIFF Primetime, where it was one of only two European series to make its cut, it turns on Detective Lieutenant Frank Laudlin (Schuch) and Iraq-born rookie police officer Isra Al-Husseini (Bayan Layla, “Elaha”), based out of Düsseldorf State’s Criminal Police H.Q., who race at first to dismantle ISIS recruiting young Germans. Planting an informant, Murat Cem (Tamer Tıraşoğlu, “Unfamiliar,” “Manta Manta”), their concern soon turns, however, to a threatened terror outrage on German soil, inspired by 2015’s Paris attacks. Yet as Laudlin’s task force closes in on a key suspect, its efforts are undermined by the very German institutions meant to support them. Schuch is well known for his performances in “All Quiet on the Western Front,” “Bad Banks,” “Berlin Alexanderplatz” and “System Crasher.” Layla was selected this year as one of this year’s German Films Face to Face talents. The ensemble cast also includes Wael Alkhatib (“Sun and Concrete”), Jeanne Goursaud , star of “Exterritorial” and “Barbarians”), Bernd Hölscher (“The Captain,”) and Sina Martens (“From Hilde, with Love”). Tense from the get-go thriller, fuelled by an atmospheric electronic score and co-created, co-written and directed by David Nawrath (“Your Honor,” “Atlas”), “Blindspot Berlin” is produced by Neuesuper (“8 Days”), one of Germany’s most ambitious production houses. Much of the series is set in claustrophobic corridors, backrooms and basements, endowing it with the sense of a labyrinth that its anti-terror agents have to navigate. It also adopts the multiple POVs of Laudlin, Al-Husseini and Cem, meaning viewers are often one step ahead of Maudlin and certainly German top-flight security officials who deam their prime suspect an ”improbable threat” and pull his monitoring. “Blindspot Berlin” records all the decisions made before the tragic event and the “systemic failures and human errors that led to this catastrophe,” Nawrath told Variety . “So many things went wrong. There were so many crazy situations we didn’t have time to show them,” added co-writer David Marian. “From the moment we watched the first episodes, we had no hesitation in acquiring the series for Filmin. It is an outstanding example of how to craft a thriller based on true events while remaining entirely faithful to the real story, said Jaume Ripoll, co-founder and CCO of Filmin. He added: “Its technical excellence, exceptional performances, and direction that revives the very best of the European thriller tradition make ‘Blindspot Berlin’ one of Filmin’s flagship series for the first quarter of 2027.” “‘Blindspot Berlin’ turns a chapter of recent German history into a gripping, character-driven thriller with universal appeal. Its combination of true-crime urgency, outstanding performances, and a story about the consequences of institutional failure makes it a powerful proposition for international audiences,” said Christian Gockel, Beta Film EVP international operations Spain and Portugal. “Filmin recognized that potential. We are proud that ‘Blindspot Berlin’ already premiered at TIFF and Hamburg, and will now celebrate its Spanish premiere at the South International Series Festival in Cádiz. We are confident that the series will continue to engage audiences around the world,” Glockel continued. Beta Film is a producer/distributor of many of the continent’s biggest titles such as “Babylon Berlin,” “Gomorrah,” “Borgia,” “Sisi” and evergreen “Rex.” Founded in 2007, Filmin has grown to one of the highest-profile Spanish SVOD services, acquiring select upscale series and independent and auteur films, as it has begun to produce its own original series, such as Serielizados-selected “Segunda Temporada” as well as acquiring the distribution business of top Spanish arthouse/crossover producer-distributor Elastica Films. ‘Percy Jackson and the Olympians’ Debuts New Season 3 Footage at Lucca Comics as Stars and Creator Tease the Show’s ‘First Real Bad Guy’ ‘Monarch: Legacy of Monsters’ Eyes Season 3 Renewal at Apple TV With New Writers, Showrunner 25 In-the-Know Gifts for Women: Mahjong Boards, ACOTAR Merch, Nathan Fielder Lingerie and More Emerging Arab Directors Given a Pathway Toward Filmmaking Careers by Expanded Pitching Platform at Sharjah Film Festival Annecy Winner ‘The Violinist’ Found Its Italian Co-Producers at Tokyo Market, Director Ervin Han Tells Anime Co-Production Panel David Bowie’s Immersive ‘Stage’ Concert Experience: Director Brett Morgen on the Show, the Artist and the Archive (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...
