articles.title: Russell Brand Takes the Stand in Rape Trial: “I Know What ‘No’ Means”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 28, 2026 4:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand outside Southwark Crown Court on Oct. 28. Courtesy of Getty Russell Brand took the stand for the first time in his ongoing rape and sexual assault trial on Wednesday and revealed that no one else has agreed to testify on his behalf. At London’s Southwark Crown Court, the prosecution has completed presenting its case and Brand’s defense team, led by Ian Winter, is now set to detail its arguments for the jury. The prosecution ran the court through all of the charges against the TV host and comedian, also star of St. Trinian’s and Forgetting Sarah Marshall . He is accused of three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault, with six women alleging offenses dating from 1999 to 2009. The final charge was reduced from indecent assault to attempted indecent assault by the judge, Justice Bennathan, on Tuesday afternoon. Related Stories Movies Jafar Panahi Facing Five Years' Imprisonment in Iran After Being Sentenced in Absentia Movies 'Men in Black' Director Barry Sonnenfeld Joins Short Film 'Serenity,' Set in Funeral Home, as Exec Producer (Exclusive) Among the claims is a woman who says Brand raped her in a Bournemouth hotel room in 1999 following one of his comedy gigs. Another says he grabbed her breasts and pushed her into a toilet in a bar in Soho, where he orally raped her in 2004. A separate woman alleges Brand anally raped her at his home in Hampstead in 2009, after consensual vaginal sex. Brand vehemently denies any criminal wrongdoing. According to Sky News coverage , there was a “significant shift” in the courtroom on Wednesday as Brand took the stand as the defense’s first witness. After taking his oath, his barrister began probing Brand on the “sea of change” brought about in his life after marrying U.S. pop superstar Katy Perry in 2010. “It did,” replied the defendant. “Staggering fame.” Brand was asked about the documentary that prompted the police to first investigate him in 2023 . Made by Channel 4’s Dispatches and followed by allegations in The Sunday Times , the program accused Brand of rape and assault . “It was devastating,” he told his barrister, who then asked: “Were you able to persuade a single person with relevant evidence to come to give evidence on your behalf?” Brand replied: “I have not.” When Winter asked if anyone “would touch him with a bargepole,” Brand said, “No.” He added: “My entire life has been consumed by these allegations. I have devoted myself to these matters.” Winter took Brand through various statements from the complainants, some of whom he remembers meeting and others whom he says he has no recollection of. Winter asked Brand, “Is that something that you normally do? Speak during sex?” His client replied, “Yes … I believe I would have been saying: ‘Am I doing this right, do you like this, is this OK?” Brand said when asked for his opinion on consent: “Consent is a fundamental, essential and necessary, and in many ways more important than sex itself.” He discussed the first complainant, saying he remembered meeting her at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. He told the court he found her “loquacious” and “interesting,” and when asked if there was any truth in her claim that Brand raped her that night in a hotel room, the defendant said: “No.” The prosecution, cross-examining Brand, then suggested he “just didn’t care whether she was interested in having sex with you or not.” Brand refuted that and told them he cared “very much.” He added: “I know what ‘no’ means.” The third complainant says Brand groped her breasts in a bar before pulling her to the toilets and forcing her to perform oral sex on him. He does remember meeting her, he told the court. He said a friend introduced him to the woman, telling him “something like, ‘There’s a bird here who really wants to meet you mate.'” Brand told the court that he would have said to this woman upon meeting her: “‘You’re really, really beautiful.'” “Is there any question you just grabbed her breasts?” Winter said to Brand. “Absolutely not,” he replied, saying the act does not turn him on because it’s “disgusting behavior.” He remembers speaking to the complainant for less than a minute before going to the bathroom to “fool around.” Winter said: “As far as you’re aware, is there any question that she did not consent to going into the cubicle with you?” Brand told him: “There’s absolutely no question.” Winter also asked: “Did your penis enter her mouth at all whilst in the cubicle?” His defendant said, “No.” On the allegation that he anally raped another woman at his North London home in 2009, Brand said after a “memorable” sexual encounter he was “excited and enthusiastic” to see her again. The woman said they had consensual vaginal sex in his bedroom, which Brand recalls. When asked if he had then anally raped her, Brand said: “No.” He was asked if she told him to stop, to which he replied: “No.” The trial could last up to six weeks. THR

articles.title: Peter Medak, Director of ‘The Ruling Class’ and ‘The Changeling,’ Dies at 88
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All October 28, 2026 5:39am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Peter Medak J. Quinton/WireImage Peter Medak, the Hungarian-born director who guided Peter O’Toole in The Ruling Class , George C. Scott in the classic ghost story The Changeling and Gary Oldman in the crime thriller Romeo Is Bleeding , died Tuesday in Los Angeles, his family announced. He was 88. Medak made his feature directorial debut on the erotic Negatives (1968), featuring Glenda Jackson in one of her first films, and followed that with the black comedy A Day in the Death of Joe Egg (1972), starring Alan Bates and Janet Suzman in an adaptation of Peter Nichols’ play. Related Stories TV Kevin Bleyer, Emmy-Winning 'Daily Show' Writer, Dies at 54 in Car Crash TV Susan Saint James, 'Name of the Game,' 'McMillan & Wife' and 'Kate & Allie' Star, Dies at 80 He also helmed the British gangster drama The Krays (1990), with Gary Kemp and brother Martin Kemp, both members of Spandau Ballet, as real-life British gangsters; Let Him Have It (1991), featuring Christopher Eccleston and Tom Courtenay in another true story, about a controversial hanging; and Zorro: The Gay Blade (1981), starring George Hamilton. For television, Medak worked on multiple episodes of Homicide: Life on the Street , Hart to Hart and Shelley Duvall ‘s Faerie Tale Theatre and on installments of Breaking Bad , The Wire , Space: 1999 , Magnum, P.I. , Law & Order: SVU , St. Elsewhere , Chicago Hope , House and Cold Case . With Medak calling the shots, O’Toole picked up the fifth of his eight career best actor Oscar nominations for his turn as a British nobleman who believes he’s Jesus Christ and then Jack the Ripper in the dark comedy The Ruling Class (1972). Based on a play by Peter Barnes, who also wrote the screenplay, the film played in competition at Cannes. Martin Scorsese, Steven Spielberg, Guillermo del Toro and Alejandro Amenábar are among those who admire his Changeling (1980), about a grieving composer (Scott) caught in a supernatural mystery involving his new home. Spielberg, in fact, screened the film several times for his crew on Poltergeist to help set the tone for that horror classic, Medak noted in a 2018 interview . “He said, ‘This is what it should be.’ It was a great compliment coming from him, and I know he even has his own 35mm copy of The Changeling , and so does Martin Scorsese,” he said. “It’s lovely to have that, to be on their lists of the greatest ghost stories of all time.” Oldman scored high marks for his performance as a corrupt New York homicide detective involved with a vicious hitwoman (Lena Olin) in Romeo Is Bleeding (1993). In his review for Rolling Stone , Peter Travers wrote that Medak “keeps the action stylish, sexy and fiendishly funny. The film rarely makes a lick of sense, but it’s compulsively watchable.” Alas, Medak also is famous for directing the lamentable Ghost in the Noonday Sun (1974), a comedy about bumbling 17th century pirates that starred the combustible Peter Sellers and Spike Milligan. “Oh, it was probably the biggest nightmare of my life,” he said in a 2007 interview for the DGA. Even though the film nearly torpedoed his career, he chose to revisit the experience by helming the 2018 documentary The Ghost of Peter Sellers . Peter Medak (center) with actors Janet Suzman and Alan Bates on the set of 1972’s ‘A Day in the Death of Joe Egg.’ Courtesy Everett Collection Medak was born on Dec. 23, 1937, in Budapest, Hungary. In 1956, he fled to England during his country’s uprising against the communists, and his aunt, an opera singer, helped him quickly land a job with the Associated British Picture Corp. He started out as an editor, cameraman and assistant director and helped out Fred Zinnemann on The Sundowners (1960). A stint as a second A.D. on The V.I.P.s (1963), starring Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton , led to him in 1963 to sign a seven-year contract at Universal Studios to direct for television in Hollywood and London. After many months of false starts, he made his helming debut with a 1965 episode of ITV/Universal’s Court Martial , starring Bradford Dillman and Peter Graves. He had quite the start to his film career. “My first three movies‚ Negatives , Joe Egg and Ruling Class , were just total perfection for me to make as a young director,” he said in a 2020 interview . In 1973, Medak was asked to direct Death Wish , but when he insisted that Henry Fonda be cast as the lead, Paramount turned to Michael Winner, who hired Charles Bronson for the role of vigilante Paul Kersey. On King’s Road in London that year, he ran into Sellers, who invited him to direct Ghost in the Noonday Sun. “Peter was a nightmare,” he recalled. “It was his project, which he developed for two years before me, and I realized about a month before shooting that he’s never read the script. If you can believe it.” The film was shot on location in Cypress, and its pirate ship broke down daily and had to be towed back to the harbor. Meanwhile, the mercurial Sellers fired the producers and faked a heart attack to get time off. (Days later, Medak was stunned to see a newspaper photo of his star dining with Princess Margaret.) The film was so bad, Columbia Pictures never released it; it finally made its way to VHS in the early ’80s. Medak didn’t direct another feature until The Odd Job (1978), starring Monty Python member Graham Chapman. “I was basically punishing myself unconsciously for not making the greatest success of a film with Peter Sellers and Spike Milligan,” he said. “But it wasn’t my fault. Peter’s terrible, insane, destructive behavior on that film [was the reason it failed].” Medak’s résumé also included the features The Men’s Club (1986), La voix humaine (1990), Pontiac Moon (1994) and Species II (1998) and the 1997 telefilm The Hunchback of Notre Dame , starring Mandy Patinkin as Quasimodo. And his love of music of all genres provided him with opportunities to direct early music videos for artists such as Peter Gabriel and Pink Floyd. Survivors include his children, Christopher, Joshua, Karen and Cornelia, and his grandchildren, Sacha, Marlowe, Ryden, Oliver and Anders. He was married to Catherine Marie La Kermance from 1963 until her death by suicide in 1972; to English actress Carolyn Seymour (she’s the wife of O’Toole’s character in The Ruling Class ) from 1973 until their 1984 divorce; and to opera singer Julia Migenes from 1988 until their 2003 divorce. “If it’s in your blood, directing, you never stop,” he said. “And it doesn’t matter that you’re alone in your mind, dreaming or imagining things, you’re always making a movie.” THR

articles.title: How “Toxically Optimistic” Zainab Johnson Found a Fan (and Hype Woman) in Michelle Obama
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All October 28, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Zainab Johnson Netflix “Washington, DC, make some noise for Zainab Johnson .” The intro itself isn’t an original way to start Johnson’s latest special, Netflix’s Toxically Optimistic , but the individual speaking as she takes the Howard Theatre stage marks a comedy first. That’s Michelle Obama riling up the audience. Johnson, the actress and stand-up who saw her comedy profile surge with 2023’s Hijabs Off , didn’t just get the former former First Lady to introduce her special. The Obamas’ Higher Ground produced the hour, out Oct. 27, a first for their ever-expanding company. So how did Johnson get into business with the Mrs. Obama? By accidentally kind of snubbing her a few years back. Related Stories TV Angry Golf Bros Tried to Ruin Heather McMahan. She Released a Hulu Special Instead Movies Harvey Keitel Threw 'Bad Lieutenant' in the Trash Before Giving One of His Greatest Performances Johnson was in Detroit for a show in late 2024, not far from where Kamala Harris was stumping for her presidential run. Obama was set to attend the rally, so when her team engaged Johnson about meeting her there, Johnson jumped in a car and headed that way. “But I didn’t know how political rallies work,” says Johnson. “I thought you just pull up, park and walk in. No, they shuttle you from a mall that’s ten miles away. I get there and realize I only have enough time to turn around if I’m going to make it to my show. I tell her people that I’m so sorry. And they’re like, ‘Are you sure? Because Michelle is really looking forward to meeting you.’ I know this sounds crazy, but I gotta go be a professional comedian.” Fortunately for Johnson, she’d get another chance a few weeks later —an encounter that’s since proven quite fruitful. Speaking during a recent episode of The Hollywood Reporter podcast I’m Having an Episode (listen to the complete interview on episode on Spotify , Amazon Music , Apple ), Johnson talked about finding a champion in Mrs. Obama, confusing U.K. audiences with a bit about her decision to buy a gun and the billboard she recently spotted that told her all she needed to know about TV’s backslide into defaulting to white actors. So how did you meet Mrs. Obama after this near-miss? In 2024, when Kamala Harris was campaigning, I was in Atlanta when Michelle was there for this bipartisan “Get out the vote” thing. A lot of powerful women in Hollywood were in this room — Kerry Washington, Shonda Rhimes — and I had just had this encounter with these celebrity girls. I was like, “Hey y’all, I’m a fan!” They looked at me like I was dirt. I will not say their names because I’m a huge fan of theirs. I don’t want the world to turn on them. So, I sat down, like, “I don’t know how I got in this room, but let me sit my ass down.” As soon as Michelle walks in the room, everybody flocks to her. She turns, sees me and she says, “Zainab Johnson!” She pulls me up to hug her. She turns me around to Shonda Rhimes, like, “Did you see this girl’s special? It’s fantastic!” She just starts raving about me. In my mind, I’m like, “My God, this is crazy.” Please tell me the women who blew you off were watching as all of this happened. Yes, they saw it. Right after they see Ms. Michelle fawning over me, they come back and apologize. It’s like a high school movie. Like a Mean Girls short starring Zainab Johnson, Michelle Obama and three beautiful, famous girls that will remain nameless. This is the first comedy special produced by the Obamas. I picture you walking into a general meeting, someone handing you a bottled water and Michelle and Barack just hanging out in a conference room. But I’m guessing that’s not how it happened. It’s so far off, not that I haven’t been to Higher Ground for some meetings been offered a wonderful bottle of water. So let’s fast forward to the top of 2026. My team and I decide I’m doing this special. I don’t care if I’m producing it or funding it myself. I’m not gonna wait on anybody to give me permission to put this out. But I had this idea as I was watching Sheng Wang’s special. I’ve always liked how Ali Wong sets the table for him. I thought, “Dang, if somebody were to introduce me, who would I want it to be? What if I got Michelle Obama to do it?” So I called my managers and said, “I’m gonna ask Michelle Obama to introduce my special.” Just voice of God. That’s all I need. I don’t need her to show her face. I don’t need her to produce it. I’m gonna do this thing all by myself. Which is not what happened. Maybe like a week or so later, I’m out to dinner with my friend, and, Michelle’s team, I get a text from them. “Hey, she’s recording the intro right now.” Simultaneously, I get a phone call from my managers. “Yes, she’s recording it. They want to produce the special. How do you feel about that?” I’m having all of the emotions. So they’re like, “Hello?” My friend who’s at dinner with me is asking what’s happening because she can see my face is stunned. And I’m like, “I would absolutely love that.” So then managers start screaming. And when I tell my friend, she says something so interesting to me. She asked how did this happen? “I just asked her to intro me.” She said, “You know what? That’s God, the universe, whatever you want to call it, telling you you can ask for more.” Something I learned about you in this special is that you bought a gun, at your friend’s suggestion, when you moved into a new house. How did the experience of buying a gun compare to how you thought it would be? When they were like, “Get a gun,” I’m thinking we gonna go get a gun with no serial number. I’m thinking we’re getting a back alley gun, right? No. When you go the legal route in California, you have to take classes, you have to get certified, then you have to go to the gun range with a with a certified person. I had to take a test. This used to be in my set, because this this set has come a long way. But I used to talk about how in California, you take a 20-question multiple choice test. I got two of the questions wrong, and they still gave me the gun. That you can get up to five questions wrong and they still give you a gun. That margin of error is crazy to me. And that bar is significantly lower in many other states. When I was touring this through the South, they were like, “Girl, just go to a Walmart! A gas station! Just make sure you have your driver’s license.” Then it was “Girl, you don’t even need that! Just make sure you got the money.” So this went through several incarnations, but you performed an early version at Edinburgh Fringe. This made me wonder how the U.K. audience responds to gun material versus a U.S. audience? The headline of one British paper’s review was “U.S. comic targets gun culture.” It was a bit different in Edinburgh, but I would not have described that show as “she takes on guns.” What’s interesting is that I didn’t just tour it in the U.K., I toured it in Paris. I brought it to Australia, a lot of places where civilians are unfamiliar with day-to-day gun ownership. I remember I would cold open the show with, “I got a gun.” A lot foreign audiences, they would feel confirmed about America with Donald Trump, like, “Yup! We knew it.” Slowly, they’d see some of the material that’s in the special now and they’d be like, “Well, if everybody who has a gun is like you, I guess it’s OK?” With a lot of people, I’m able to get them to see how I’m seeing things. The Edinburgh audience is an older audience. So when I would be like, “I got a gun,” they would be like “ha ha ha” and literally reach for their partner. Then I’d say, “I mean, I don’t have it on me. I don’t think they would have let me through customs.” Then they would understand, OK, this is gonna be a fun time. During a recent interview, you said that the only person that relates to Black women are other Black women. Knowing that, but also knowing that your audience is much broader, I’m curious how some material played. There’s one bit, during which you recount the potential outcomes of a scary encounter walking down a sidewalk. Predicting your possible death, you say, “I’m a Black woman in America. I’ve got to solve my own murder.” It’s a horrifying statement, because it’s very honest, but you play it for laughs. How did that one land on the road? Yeah, I gotta solve my own murder before I go. That’s painfully true, but that’s comedy, right? You bring levity. I’ve toured this hour in different places and when I drop that line, sometimes I would get a standing ovation. Sometimes I would liberate people in the room. Not just Black women. People who have that awareness and understand that truth. And sometimes, I would bring a really laughing crowd down to a sobering reality. It’d be like, “Wait, my God, that’s terrible.” I’m proud that I was able to convey that. It’s such a powerful thing, to convey that in between the absurdity. I’m happy that it landed and I’m happy that it made the final cut. You’re also an actress, and we’ve been talking a lot at work about how TV opportunities have been cratering for people of color. It’s like Hollywood has completely abandoned this push that, for a little while, actually seemed like it was gaining traction. So as you navigate that part of your career, what are the conversations you’re having about opportunities? What does your team say? The talks have been the same, which is, “There’s so little work.” I’m getting the same amount of enthusiasm and willingness to meet with me and pitch an idea. But that last part? The willingness to spend money, to invest, that’s the part. But entertainment is whatever the world is exhibiting at the moment. This might sound crazy, but I haven’t seen this in a very long time. I was driving up La Brea and I saw a billboard for a procedural show. All five of the cast were just cis white people. I I haven’t seen that in years. It’s very back. And I think I know the show you’re referring to. I couldn’t believe it. I almost had to avoid a traffic accident. Am I seeing what I think that I’m seeing? We’re back in the nineties with Friends . We’re back in those conversations. I think we’re in a time that we can call a regression. We are regressing. It’s scary and it’s sad. This is not specific to the show we’re talking that we will not name. But I think it’s all gonna prove to be very boring. THR

articles.title: Comedy Legend George Schlatter Sets Doc Release With Freestyle Digital Media (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 28, 2026 6:05am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Producer George Schlatter made an appearance at the Newport Beach Film Festival premiere of his doc 'Sock It to Me: The Legend of George Schlatter.' Tiffany Rose/Getty Images for Newport Beach Film Festival Freestyle Digital Media, the digital film distribution division of Byron Allen ’s Allen Media Group, has picked up the North American VOD rights to Sock It To Me: The Legend of George Schlatter . The feature documentary about Schlatter, the creator of Rowan & Martin’s Laugh-In , the groundbreaking comedy variety hour that launched on NBC in 1968, will debut on digital platforms from Dec. 8. Laugh In launched the careers of Goldie Hawn and Lily Tomlin and gave birth to late-night television, including Saturday Night Live. Schlatter also created and produced the NBC reality series Real People from 1979 that featured an 18 year-old Byron Allen in his first TV gig as a regular co-host. Recalling a seven-decade career as a prolific TV producer and director, Sock It To Me uses archival footage and interviews with stars like Hawn, Tom Hanks, Tomlin, Martin Short, Billy Crystal, Jay Leno, Jimmy Kimmel, Lionel Richie, Lisa Ann Walter, Berry Gordy and Byron Allen to explore how Schlatter, now 96, changed TV comedy. “People have been asking me to write an autobiography, and I’ve always said have somebody else write it. They then explained to me that it wouldn’t be an autobiography, so here we are,” Schlatter said in a statement. “It’s a full circle moment to work with Byron Allen’s company to get this documentary out into the world. You bet your sweet bippy I’m excited for audiences to see it and remind them of the power of laughter!” Written and directed by Chris Coronado, Sock It To Me was produced by Coronado, Greg Myers and Dayna Winston. Since 2016, Coronado has served as creative director at George Schlatter Productions, overseeing the creative development and production of documentary and entertainment projects. Freestyle Digital Media negotiated the deal to acquire Sock It To Me directly with the filmmakers and George Schlatter Productions. THR

articles.title: On Air Fest Sets Initial Talent Lineup for 10th Anniversary Edition in Brooklyn
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 28, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Megan Rapinoe, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, Audie Cornish, Ari Shapiro and Sam Sanders. Getty Images On Air Fest will soon be on air in Brooklyn, New York. The sound and storytelling festival mounted by On Air Presents has revealed the initial lineup of headliners and talent set to take the stage at venues including the Wythe Hotel and Arlo Williamsburg from Feb. 23-25, 2027, organized under a theme of “10 Years On…” to mark a milestone 10th anniversary. The first drop of names includes headliners Megan Rapinoe, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, Audie Cornish & Ari Shapiro, Dan Harris, Anthony Fantano, On the Media, One Song, World Café and more across live podcasts , conversations, performances, parties and events focused on the future of storytelling. There will be live recordings of Why Are You Like This with Megan Rapinoe , CNN’s Chasing Life with Dr. Sanjay Gupta , and 10 Percent Happier with Dan Harri s, CNN’s Engagement Party with Audie Cornish and Ari Shapiro , WNYC’s On The Media with Brooke Gladstone and Micah Loewinger, and WXPN’s World Café with Raina Douris. Also booked to make appearances are music critic Anthony Fantano, The Sam Sanders Show’s Sam Sanders, One Song hosts Diallo Riddle and Blake “LUXXURY” Robin, and Chameleon’s Josh Dean. Leon Neyfakh and Sayre Quevedo are set to discuss narrative podcasting in a conversation centered on Death of an Artist and Reaching Out , while actor and comedian Connor Ratliff will host a main stage. Kicking things off on Feb. 23 will be the Podcast Business Summit presented with Bloomberg at Wythe Hotel. Hosted by Bloomberg reporter Ashley Carman, the invite-only daytime gathering is expected to host leaders across media, technology, advertising, publishing and podcasting. Later that night, the Podcast Academy will present the Ambies, an awards show to honor excellence in podcasting at Arlo Williamsburg. Additional programming and talent names will be announced in coming weeks and months. Previous participants at On Air Fest have included Anderson Cooper, Malcolm Gladwell, Seth Meyers, Norah Jones, Wyclef Jean, Bon Iver’s Justin Vernon, Audie Cornish, Jad Abumrad, Terry Gross, Francis Ford Coppola, Ira Glass and more. More intel on tickets and scheduling can be found here . THR

articles.title: ‘Transplant’ Creator Joseph Kay Sets Overall Deal at Netflix
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 28, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Joseph Kay Courtesy of Netflix Netflix has signed an exclusive overall deal with Joseph Kay, the creator and showrunner of the medical drama Transplant , which landed on NBC stateside. As part of the deal, Kay will develop and write new TV series for Netflix in Canada, starting with an untitled new family drama. He most recently worked with Netflix as a consulting producer on North of North season 2, the Arctic-set comedy also on the CBC and set to return on Nov. 5. Also for Netflix, he co-executive produced the upcoming adaptation of Carley Fortune’s bestselling novel, This Summer Will Be Different. Transplant, which ran for four seasons, was a medical procedural about a Syrian refugee working as a doctor in a Toronto trauma unit. The drama centered on Dr. Bashir “Bash” Hamed (Hamza Haq, Quantico ), a Syrian doctor with battle-tested skills in emergency medicine who fled his country with his younger sister, Amira (Sirena Gulamgaus). Together they struggled to build a new life in Canada while Bash strived to rebuild his career in medicine. Transplant was produced by Sphère Média Plus, in association with CTV and NBCUniversal International Studios. “I am beyond grateful and thrilled to partner with this incredible company. I have huge admiration for Netflix’s entire team, and for their unsurpassed drive to tell great stories and connect with audiences around the world,” Kay said in a statement on Wednesday. His TV writing credits include Ransom, This Life and Republic of Doyle. “Joe is a seasoned and gifted creator and showrunner, who is also adept at supporting other writers. We have loved working with him on our shows so far and we are thrilled to expand our relationship,” Danielle Woodrow and Tara Woodbury, directors of content at Netflix Canada, said in their own statement. Kay is represented by Dustin Alpern and Conrad Sun at Sundust Management. The overall deal was negotiated by Casey Chisick of Cassels Brock & Blackwell LLP. THR

articles.title: Sundance Sets Legacy Screenings Including Films by Christopher Nolan, Justin Lin and Alfonso Cuarón
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 28, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A still from Justin Lin's 'Better Luck Tomorrow.' Courtesy of Sundance Institute As Sundance prepares to write a new legacy in Boulder, Colorado in 2027 and beyond, the film festival is bringing some hits from its past to the new home. Sundance Institute today revealed the lineup for the Legacy program for next year’s festival, and it includes works by filmmakers including Christopher Nolan, Alfonso Cuarón , Justin Lin , Stacy Peralta, Julie Taymor, Barbara Hammer, Patricia Cardoso and Tom Kalin. While old will be new again, there’s also something fresh for the lineup once known as From the Collection: Letterboxd joins as a co-presenter of the Legacy program with additional details for onsite activations to come. Related Stories Movies Alfonso Cuarón Reflects on Making 'Harry Potter': "Two of the Most Beautiful Years of My Life" 'Awards Chatter' Podcast John Leguizamo on 'The Odyssey,' Non-Traditional Casting and Being Uninvited From 'Spider-Man: Homecoming' Plucked for the Legacy program — curated as a home to showcase “groundbreaking independent cinema including archival and restoration screenings of fiction and nonfiction works as well as special events” — will feature brand-new restorations of the 2002 Sundance version of Lin’s Better Luck Tomorrow , a digital 4K restoration of Peralta’s Dogtown and Z-Boys , a 35th anniversary screening of Taymor’s Fool’s Fire , Hammer’s Nitrate Kisses , a 25th anniversary screening of Cardoso’s Real Women Have Curves, a star making turn for America Ferrera, a 35th anniversary screening of Kalin’s Swoon , and a 25th anniversary screening of a 4K restoration of Cuarón’s Y tu mamá también, a star making turn for Diego Luna and Gael Garcia Bernal. (Top left to right): Better Luck Tomorrow and Dogtown and Z-Boys ; (middle left to right): Fool’s Fire, Nitrate Kisses and Real Women Have Curves ; (bottom left to right): Swoon and Y tu mamá también . Legacy screenings will include director appearances and select cast members in attendance. Courtesy of Sundance Institute Sundance has also set a special two-part session on the final weekend of the festival dubbed “ Sundance Film Festival presents: Cinema Interruptus featuring Memento .” It will feature a 4K restoration and communal discussion for Nolan’s 2000 effort, Memento, starring Guy Pearce, Carrie-Anne Moss and Joe Pantoliano. “We’re excited to kick off the festival season in earnest with this first 2027 Sundance Film Festival announcement, revealing some of our Legacy programming,” explained Eugene Hernandez, who serves as director of the Sundance Film Festival and public programming. “Each year we honor the legacy of our founder Robert Redford and the history of the Sundance Film Festival by looking back at just a few of the films and filmmakers who have shaped our history. Our first festival in our new home in Boulder, Colorado will bring change, but as we evolve, we’ll keep at our core what we celebrate: our rich history.” Added Kim Yutani, director of programming: “Revisiting and becoming newly acquainted with films from our previous lineups in a theatrical setting, in community, and with some of the talent behind the films is a rare treat — even more so when these projects have been restored. We’re really looking forward to welcoming back these artists and know that audiences will enjoy the opportunity to complement the new films we will soon be announcing with these classics.” The Sundance Film Festival will take place in Boulder from Jan. 21–31. Additional Legacy programming will be announced in the coming weeks. THR

articles.title: Environmental Media Association and Its Awards Show to Become Part of Nonprofit United by Nature
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All October 28, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The 2025 Environmental Media Awards Gala. Amy Sussman/Getty Images for The Environmental Media Association It’s a new era for the Environmental Media Association, as the Hollywood sustainability group is becoming a part of nonprofit United by Nature. EMA has been active in the industry for nearly 40 years, creating conversation through educational initiatives, industry partnerships and events like the Impact Summit and its signature EMA Awards Gala. United by Nature — an organization focused on building the next generation of America’s conservation movement — plans to build upon these programs and relationships, as well as host the first United by Nature Awards in April 2027 to coincide with Earth Month. Related Stories News 'The Wild Robot,' 'The Daily Show' Among Winners at Environmental Media Awards News Stars Talk L.A Wildfires, Home Rebuilds and What to Do With Your Tesla at EMA Impact Summit “Environmental progress requires a bigger coalition that’s more reflective of communities across America,” Benji Backer, founder and CEO of United by Nature, said in a statement. “EMA proved how powerful storytelling can shape culture, unite people and drive meaningful outcomes for nature. Together, we’re building upon that impact by reaching new audiences and inviting people of all backgrounds to protect the outdoors they love.” Debbie Levin, the former CEO of EMA who will now serve as chief visionary officer of United by Nature, said, “EMA has always believed in the extraordinary power of entertainment and storytelling to inspire environmental action. For more than three decades, we’ve worked alongside the entertainment community to make sustainability part of the cultural conversation. We’re proud of the legacy we’ve built, and we’re excited to work with United by Nature to reach new audiences and continue making sustainability more accessible and engaging.” United by Nature’s inaugural takeover of the awards event will continue to celebrate the entertainment industry’s environmental leadership, while also expanding to recognize the individuals and organizations across music, sports, podcasts and universities that inspire positive change. Past EMA honorees include Billie Eilish, Michael Bloomberg, Jane Fonda, Ted Turner, Natalie Portman, Matt Damon and Laura Dern. The EMA Green Seal will also become the United by Nature Green Seal, which recognizes industries that take meaningful steps to reduce their environmental footprint. Wildwood , the animated fantasy film from Laika Studios, is the first movie to be awarded the United by Nature Green Seal; the movie joins nearly 3,000 other productions recognized for their sustainability efforts. THR

articles.title: TikTok Wants to Help Its Users Find Their Next Must Eat
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 28, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Photo Illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images TikTok ‘s U.S. joint venture is leaning hard into the food creator community, launching a new product called Must Eat that is meant to boost food creators, as well as restaurants, all in service of helping its users find that next must visit place to grab a bite. The company officially rolled out Must Eat at a reception held at Undercote in New York City Tuesday evening, with Adam Presser, the CEO of TikTok’s U.S. business, hosting food creators in the lounge. “The first time that I came across FoodTok was actually before I joined the company, it was in the pandemic,” Presser told the attendees. “I came across the feta cheese pasta trend … So we were lucky enough to be able to get a block of feta cheese at that time, and we made the recipe, and it was incredible. And it was that first experience of being able to be watching videos, consuming content, and then translating that into real life experiences. And that journey has only continued on TikTok. “The ‘lunch in my city’ trend has really driven a lot of momentum,” he continued. “I know some of the creators here have made content around that trend. I have tried it out, it’s fantastic. And over the last several years, we’ve just seen more and more people have this experience of discovering something on the platform and driving their in-real-life experience. I saw a stat last year: More than 27 million Americans went to an independent restaurant, cafe, or store in the U.S. that they had discovered for the first time on TikTok.” So, Must Eat. The product is launching in New York, Los Angeles and the Bay Area, highlighting places in two categories: “Everyday Eats” and “Elevated Dining” featuring restaurants that have connected with TikTok food creators. TikTok also partnered with OpenTable to enable reservations at selected locations. The product, an expansion of “Must GO” (focused on travel), is an example of how TikTok U.S. is trying to carve its own path forward, now 10 months or so into its new ownership structure. For Presser, it is also a chance to bring his own imprint onto one of the biggest creator platforms in the country. “I am an L.A. native, and probably like most people that grew up in L.A., I had dreams of working in entertainment, but any hope of working in front of the camera were quickly dashed — I think it was around the eighth grade play. I was assigned the role of lighting director,” he quipped Tuesday, noting that he went on to work in the music industry and later as an executive at Warner Bros. Discovery before joining TikTok some four and a half years ago. “It was the first time that I really had the experience of realizing that you didn’t have to be at the top of the charts or on the big screen to be a star,” he said. “That it could be anybody with a voice, and a phone, and a vision, a creative perspective, and a platform like TikTok that could bring people’s voices to the world and have people discover the incredible, talented people that had something to say. So it is truly a dream come true.” THR

articles.title: Free IP and Fresh Eyes: How Hollywood Is Reinventing the Classics
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content East of Eden, A Tale of Two Cities, Sense and Sensibility photo illustration THR Staff/Nicholas Brawley Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’ s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it. *** East of Eden showrunner Zoe Kazan has had her eye on adapting John Steinbeck’s family saga since she first read it at 15. “Somebody has to put the thing on screen that I see in my head,” she told The Hollywood Reporter . And after “a good 20 years” of carrying that feeling, the opportunity to translate the story to screen finally came to fruition, with Kazan’s vision unfurling as an eight-episode Netflix limited series. Related Stories TV 'Transplant' Creator Joseph Kay Sets Overall Deal at Netflix TV 'Nobody Wants This' Star Condemns Adam Brody's Gaza "Genocide" Comments Hollywood has never been shy about mining the classics, with Pride and Prejudice , To Kill a Mockingbird and Little Women among the staples of film and TV’s page-to-screen catalog. This year, Kazan’s dip into the classic canon is joined by the likes of Christopher Nolan, who has taken on Homer’s The Odyssey , Emerald Fennell’s adaptation of Emily Brontë’s Wuthering Heights , and new versions of Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility and Charles Dickens’ A Tale of Two Cities . Steinbeck, Austen and Dickens come with name recognition, a built-in audience and, as Sense and Sensibility screenwriter Diana Reid puts it, “free IP.” But the prestige and name recognition only get a project so far with audiences desperate for something fresh. This year, the writers behind Netflix’s East of Eden , Focus Features ’ Sense and Sensibility and MGM+ ’s A Tale of Two Cities used that audience demand to do something different: leave the novels’ worlds intact and rebuild the people inside them. For Kazan, that meant re-reading Steinbeck’s Cathy. For Daniel West, it was giving Dickens’ Lucie a pulse. Reid let the Dashwood sisters Marianne and Elinor each grow into a bit of the other. And while a famous novel might spark initial curiosity, it offers no inherent road map once development begins. So rather than reimagining these books through a modern lens, each writer chose to lean into the ways the stories already transcend time. “You don’t need to spoon-feed the audience the modernity of it,” West says. Why a Classic Novel Already Has Appeal Esmé Creed-Miles stars as Marianne Dashwood and Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility. Courtesy of Focus Features Reid is the first to admit the commercial logic of adapting a classic. “I think they are classic for a reason,” she says. But the appeal runs deeper. In an era of surface-level connection, she argues, audiences crave something that feels substantial. “There’s nothing more satisfying as an audience than encountering someone who’s superficially very different from you — they live in another time, they have different values and customs, they dress in a bizarre way — and then realizing that emotionally you have the same inner life.” She also knows she won’t be the last to take on Austen. “It’s nice to be part of such a big catalog. On one hand it’s an honor, and on the other it takes pressure off, because it’ll be one of many. It doesn’t need to be definitive.” West’s pitch for A Tale of Two Cities , a four-part series that premiered on MGM+ last month, started with what he calls a “unicorn”: a book with a huge cultural footprint that, by his account, hadn’t had a major screen adaptation in nearly 40 years. He and star and executive producer Kit Harington had been talking about adapting Dickens’ 1859 novel for roughly a decade, noting that there “hasn’t really been a seminal TV or film adaptation” of the story. “It was done quite a lot in the first half of the 20th century, but then it petered out. So a large part of the draw was the opportunity: There was this huge built-in audience that already knew the book, or at least knew of it,” he says. “The story itself is incredibly timely,” he adds. “It’s about a disenfranchised, broken society that is pushing back and reaching a crisis point. Within that, there’s a very personal, intimate love story.” Kazan has a personal tie to East of Eden — her grandfather, Elia Kazan, directed the 1955 film — but part of her motivation for making a series was to tell more of the novel than that film did. Though Steinbeck’s book was published in 1952, she says, “there’s this beautiful continuum between us and the past,” which is part of what makes revisiting a classic so appealing. Looking backward and forward at the same time, she adds, “is a profound part of what makes us human.” “It’s the opposite of AI. It’s not regurgitation, not spitting back up what we’ve already digested,” she says. “It’s why we should read these books. They’re like a bow shot across time from one human to another.” Rethinking the Novels’ Protagonists Mirren Mack as Lucie Manette in A Tale of Two Cities . Marcell Piti/Federation Studios/MGM+ Still, none of the three writers treated an established title as a safety net. Instead, their adaptations declined to modernize the novel’s setting and embraced finding new ways into the protagonists. While developing A Tale of Two Cities , West and his producers considered a contemporary reimagining early on before dropping it. “The issues these characters are dealing with, the injustice and the way it bleeds into vengeance and cruelty, already feel very 2026,” he says. What he changed instead was characterization. In Dickens’ novel, heroine Lucie Manette is “prone to a lot of weeping” and “quite a lot of fainting,” West says. “She’s not the most compelling heroine in large passages of it. So we made some fundamental changes. We made her much more intentional.” He wanted Lucie to be “the central pivot of the entire story” and “the investigative force” of the opening episodes, pushing against the walls of “buttoned-up Georgian London.” “That was a fairly big modernization from the book,” he says. Of Mirren Mack, who plays Lucie in the series, he adds: “Lucie is the central component of the whole thing, the sun at the center of the solar system, and then an actor arrives who delivers all of that and more and elevates it through her own interpretation.” He also replaced Jarvis Lorry and Miss Pross — who he felt were “serving a similar purpose” and were too “big and colorful” for the series’ taut, volatile tone — with a new character, Hester (Sharon Duncan-Brewster). “She isn’t a proxy father figure to Lucie. She’s an inherited family member, almost an inherited stepmother. … As the story goes on, they discover that they mean a lot to each other and are more than just inherited relations. They really are family, but they come to that on their own terms. That gives them a larger emotional distance to travel.” Thérèse Defarge (Roxane Duran) marks another departure. “We wanted to see somebody become, for want of a less anachronistic word, radicalized,” West says. “She starts as part of her community. She has a warmth and generosity. Because of what happens to her within the story, we see that crack begin to metastasize into something really sinister and ugly, and by the end, murderous. When we meet her in episode one, she’s a completely different person from what we see at the very end of the show.” From left: François Civil as Charles Darnay and Kit Harington as Sydney Carton in A Tale of Two Cities . Marcell Piti/Federation Studios/MGM+ Dickens’ book centers on a couple, but West wanted to “intensify that” and “twist it slightly into much more of a triangle and make it more live and more complex” between Sydney Carton (Harington), Lucie (Mack) and Charles Darnay (François Civil). “That way we don’t really know which way Lucie is going to go until she does, toward the back end of the story. I also wanted both men to be equally attractive, equally intriguing and volatile, each speaking to a different side of her, so we really feel the pull, the tension and the dilemma she’s wrestling with.” Kazan’s re-reading centered on Cathy Ames ( Florence Pugh ), the character who first hooked her in Steinbeck’s story. Writing the series, which released on Netflix on Oct. 1, she realized something she hadn’t anticipated: Cathy “is almost always telling the truth.” A fresh perspective also helped Kazan see the story as a love story between brothers Adam (Christopher Abbott) and Charles (Mike Faist), one that Cathy interrupts. “By watching Chris and Mike interact, I understood how much these characters loved each other,” she says. Respecting the Literary Blueprint — and Knowing When to Change It Creative liberties, the writers insist, aren’t changes for the sake of it. Reid describes her approach as “respect rather than reverence.” Her biggest liberty is a duel between Herbert Nordrum’s Colonel Brandon and Frank Dillane’s John Willoughby, which Austen mentions but keeps offstage. “Hearing about things secondhand in a novel is not so confusing, but on screen, hearing a character describe it isn’t very interesting,” she says. “You need to see it to reveal the drama.” Austen’s voice also served as a guide for balancing drama with wit. “When I read the book, I made a note of the lines that made me laugh, and a lot of those ended up verbatim in the film. Jane Austen’s just really funny,” Reid says. Cathy “is almost always telling the truth,“ Kazan says. Kirsty Griffin/Netflix Kazan’s challenge was the opposite: too much book. She was only interested in adapting it as a series because “the book is simply too big,” and even with seven episodes, “half is not in our series.” For A Tale of Two Cities , West’s key structural decision was genre. “I always wanted it to be a thriller: a very taut, limited story,” he explains. “Four episodes felt like the perfect length to keep the pace and stakes up, and to never let any of the characters settle. I really wanted to make sure that all the characters, whether they’re in London or Paris or moving between the two, are always in a state of agitation. Their feet are never quite on solid ground, so we feel the jeopardy and the volatility of their world.” Why We Keep Going Back Left to right: Mike Faist, Christopher Abbott and Florence Pugh in Netflix‘s East of Eden. Courtesy of Netflix Asked why classics keep returning, each offers their own perspective. West points to archetypes and longevity. A Tale of Two Cities , he says, “is the archetypal sacrificial story,” with “strong parallels in that act of sacrifice to the Bible and all the stories that form the basis of our narratives and our emotional map of the world.” Classics “still feel timeless, and they still feel as resonant today,” West adds. “The key thing for us as creatives is to find a new way of telling those classic stories, an angle and something new to say about them. That doesn’t mean reinventing the wheel. It just means giving yourself the license to look at them with fresh eyes.” Reid returns to the idea that classics are “classics for a reason.” She explains that “when an audience doesn’t feel patronized” and an adaptation allows “the classic to exist in its own time, that makes for incredibly powerful viewing.” Kazan sees adaptations as a way to lower the barrier for new readers. “One thing these adaptations can do is make a general audience feel they have access to East of Eden , The Odyssey , Wuthering Heights .” While they have differing ideas about what keeps the classics coming back, all three writers share the same hope: that viewers will pick up the book. Classics haven’t disappeared from school reading lists, but students are reportedly reading significantly fewer full-length books than in past decades. “As long as we don’t ban and burn these books, everybody will continue to have access to them,” Kazan says. “There are so many books I came to as an adult that changed my life, and if I’d read them in high school, I wouldn’t have cared or understood. The most important thing is to let kids feel they can have pleasure in reading.” There’s already evidence that these adaptations are sending people back to the page. Since the series’ Oct. 1 debut, sales of East of Eden have risen nearly 200 percent across all formats, according to publisher Penguin Classics. The novel also hit No. 1 on Amazon’s bestsellers list — 74 years after it was published. The Economist reports that U.S. sales of The Odyssey have quadrupled this year, while Wuthering Heights topped Britain’s bestseller list. “Anything that can nudge people back toward bookshops and toward discovering those works again can only be a good thing,” West says. “The reason the work of classic storytellers like Dickens, Shakespeare and Austen still resonates is that they’re saying something about the human condition, about what we’re all struggling with, yearning for and reaching for.” “It would be amazing if people went back to the book,” Reid says. If Sense and Sensibility “could make Austen and the classics feel less intimidating, and encourage people to see themselves in it and find emotional truth in a story they thought was too remote, that would be amazing!” “It would be amazing if people went back to the book,” Sense and Sensibility screenwriter Reid says. Courtesy of Focus Features THR

By Marc Malkin Plus Icon Marc Malkin Senior Editor, Culture and Events marcmalkin Latest Jennifer Lopez to Release New Single ‘Proof of Love’: ‘It’s a Happy Dance Song’ That Also Addresses ‘Pain and Grief When Someone’s Gone’ (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Actors on the Verge of Losing SAG-AFTRA Health Insurance Find Support via ‘One Job Away’ Instagram Campaign: ‘The System Is Not Working’ 2 days ago Owen Thiele on His New Tinder Campaign, ‘Adults’ Season 3 and the ‘13 Going on 30’ Sequel (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Swan Gallet Jennifer Lopez is getting close to releasing new music. The multi-hyphenate tells me she was inspired to write and record again when her kids, twins Max and Emme Muniz with ex-husband Mark Anthony, left for college. “They take up such a big part of your brain for so long, and when they’re gone, which is devastating and sad and scary, you’re facing a life that’s totally different now, and you’re like, ‘What am I going to do with this space and this time?’ For me, I just went back in the studio. I’ve written some of the best songs that I’ve ever written, and I’m really excited,” Lopez tells me. “It’s a very happy era album. It’s some of the most joyous, beautiful songs that have just a tad of a tear in them.” Related Stories Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’ The first new song, “Proof of Love,” will be included as a bonus track on the first-ever vinyl release of her 2011 album “Love?” in November. “It’s really a beautiful song about this kind of duality,” Lopez says. “It’s this happy dance song, and these are the things that are the proof of love. articles.full_text: Oct 28, 2026 5:00am PT Josh O’Connor Is a Reluctant Boxer in First-Look Clip of National Theatre Live’s ‘Golden Boy’ Ahead of Cinema Release (EXCLUSIVE) By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Josh O’Connor Is a Reluctant Boxer in First-Look Clip of National Theatre Live’s ‘Golden Boy’ Ahead of Cinema Release (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Amelia Dimoldenberg’s Final ‘Chicken Shop Date’ Series to Screen in Theaters 1 day ago Meghan Markle to Co-Host ‘Junior MasterChef Australia’ 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Josh O’Connor may be in the James Bond conversation, but his next on-screen role is a filmed version of his most recent play, “Golden Boy.” After its sold-out run at London’s Almeida Theatre, National Theatre Live is bringing “Golden Boy” to the big screen starting Nov. 5. In Clifford Odets’ acclaimed play — directed by Sam Yates — O’Connor stars as Joe Bonaparte, “a gifted young violinist with a future in music, until a chance at fame and fortune lures him into the brutal world of professional boxing,” according to its synopsis. “He must confront what he’s willing to sacrifice, who he’s willing to become and how to find his place in a world that demands he choose a side.” Related Stories Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’ In the exclusive first-look clip above, O’Connor artfully grapples with his longing to return to music, hugging a past version of himself playing the violin as his face bleeds from a boxing injury. Filmed during a performance at the Almeida Theatre, “Golden Boy” features a live string quartet alongside O’Connor and fellow cast members Hayley Squires and Daniel Mays. “Golden Boy” marked O’Connor’s return to the London stage after five years, in which he’s catapulted to worldwide fame. He’s an Emmy winner for his portrayal of King Charles in Netflix’s “The Crown,” and has earned acclaim for his film roles including “La Chimera,” Luca Guadagnino’s “Challengers,” “Knives Out: Wake Up Dead Man” and Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day.” “Golden Boy” is coming to theaters worldwide starting Nov. 5. articles.title: Latvian Oscar Submission ‘Ulya’ Sells Wide Ahead of Opening Tallinn: ‘This Film Is a Blockbuster’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: × Oct 28, 2026 5:07am PT Latvian Oscar Submission ‘Ulya’ Sells Wide Ahead of Opening Tallinn: ‘This Film Is a Blockbuster’ (EXCLUSIVE) 'Ulya' has closed sales to a North America and France, while now the second most-watched film in Latvian history, notes director Viesturs Kairiš By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Latvian Oscar Submission ‘Ulya’ Sells Wide Ahead of Opening Tallinn: ‘This Film Is a Blockbuster’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago ‘Barbara Forever’ Director Brydie O’Connor on Celebrating a Lesbian Icon Who Did It All – and Getting Support From Christine Vachon 1 day ago ‘Good Girls’ Director on Life in Girls’ Correctional Center in Poland: ‘It Damages You Even More’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Ulya,' Courtesy of Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival International distributors continue to fall for “ Ulya .” The Latvian Oscar submission for Best International Feature Film has closed North America (New Mountain Films), France (Destiny), Italy (Invisible Carpet), Slovakia (ASFK), former Yugoslavia (Five Star Distribution), Estonia (Hea Film), Lithuania (GPI), MENA (Teleview), Finland (Cinema Orion), Poland (1989) and Brazil (Belas Arte). Related Stories Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’ The black-and-white film, directed by Viesturs Kairišs , will open the 30th edition of Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival . It premiered at Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section. Produced by Ego Media (LV), Allfilm (EE), Staroń Film (PL) and Tremora (LT), it’s sold by B-Rated International. Inspired by the life of legendary basketball player Ulyana Semjonova, born in 1952, “Ulya” is not a typical biopic. “I don’t think I could ever make a nice, typical biopic. My interest lies in arthouse films. I wasn’t really thinking about sports either. I wanted to tell a Werner Herzog-esque story about a giant girl living in the countryside,” Kairišs told Variety . Semjonova was known for her size; she stood at seven feet tall. But it also made her a bit of a recluse. “I’ve been wondering how to get into her head. I wanted it to be very, very subjective. To stick to her point of view, we used what we called ‘crazy cameras’ and slightly out-of-focus shots. Finding the landscape of her inner soul was a very concrete task.” It was not Kairišs who came up with the idea of making a film about Semjonova. It was the long-held dream of his lead, Kārlis Arnolds Avots . “When I became the artistic director of the Dailes Theatre, I was looking for actors and he was outstanding. During our first meeting, when I asked him to join our ensemble, he said: ‘You know, I would like to play Ulyana Semjonova.’ Then I forgot all about it,” recalled Kairišs. “In theatre, it’s not unusual for men to play women. It goes back to Shakespearean times. A few years later, he played in my film ‘January’. At one point, while I was resting, I heard Kārlis talking to our DP, explaining this idea to him again. That’s when I realized: It’s a film!” Other collaborators still needed convincing, though. “Everyone wanted us to make a standard biopic. I understand it. It could be a good film, but it wouldn’t be my film. We set out to make a film about a girl and we just had to believe in it.” As proved by a photograph of Semjonova with Kārlis Arnolds Avots, added at the end of the film, she actually gave them her blessing. She passed away in January, 2026. “She trusted us. It must have been strange to have us come over and say: ‘And a boy will be playing you.’ But it quickly became clear why it made sense,” said Kairišs. “I actually saw Kārlis yesterday. He’s been filming [the Viking series] ‘Bloodaxe,’ so he has a long beard and he’s really big right now. But he always felt close to her somehow. He knew how it felt to be treated as a ‘giant’.” Or simply as an outsider. To Kairišs’ surprise, “Ulya” has managed to connect with all kinds of viewers, regardless of their size. “Everyone is struggling with something they want to hide, but it’s probably the best part of who they are,” he said. “We had incredible reactions everywhere in Latvia. This film is a blockbuster – we’re already the second most-watched film in history. It was the same at Cannes, Rome and Los Angeles. None of my previous films have received this kind of response. Even my daughter said to me: ‘It’s about me, too.’ We touched upon something that’s very modern and very universal.” Kairišs added: “There’s so much pressure today to look the same and like the same things. We live in times that try to kill all the difference. Everyone struggles with their identity or feels like a ‘freak’. We just have to learn to trust this freak and embrace it as the best thing about us, rather than trying to get rid of it.” Viesturs Kairišs and actor Kārlis Arnolds Avots Courtesy of Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival Secuoya Studios Taps Carla Gómez to Lead Latin American Development as Regional Expansion Accelerates (EXCLUSIVE) HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Music Will Be ‘As Far Away as Possible’ From the Movies; Hans Zimmer Says ‘I Can’t Write Like John Williams’ ‘Girls’ Shocker: Lena Dunham Sets Revival at HBO With Allison Williams, Zosia Mamet, Jemima Kirke Returning ‘Industry’ Season 5 Casts Ben Platt, Russell Tovey ‘Lanterns’ Episode 7 Hits 7 Million U.S. Viewers in Three Days as Season Reaches Average of Nearly 19 Million Globally ‘Harry Potter’ HBO Series Casts Its Arthur Weasley, Moaning Myrtle, Colin Creevey Loading comments...

articles.title: Jennifer Lawrence Says Playing Katniss Again After 11 Years in ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Was ‘Crazy,’ ‘Unbelievable’ and ‘So Beautiful’
articles.full_text: × Oct 28, 2026 6:38am PT Jennifer Lawrence Says Playing Katniss Again After 11 Years in ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Was ‘Crazy,’ ‘Unbelievable’ and ‘So Beautiful’ By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest Jennifer Lawrence Says Playing Katniss Again After 11 Years in ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Was ‘Crazy,’ ‘Unbelievable’ and ‘So Beautiful’ 2 hours ago Barry Keoghan Undergoes Skin-Tightening Cosmetic Treatment in Video Posted Months After He Called Out Online Abuse Over ‘How I Look’ 17 hours ago Jennifer Lawrence Did Not Start Her Beauty Brand Because of Hollywood Instability: ‘A Smarter Exit Plan Would Be Signing Up for a Big Franchise’ 22 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source ©Lions Gate/Courtesy Everett Collection Jennifer Lawrence appeared on the latest episode of the “Call Her Daddy” podcast and spoke out for the first time about what it was like to reprise Katniss Everdeen for the first time in 11 years. The Oscar winner is back as her iconic “Hunger Games” character in the upcoming prequel movie “Sunrise on the Reaping,” in theaters Nov. 20 from Lionsgate. “It was unbelievable,” Lawrence said about reprising Katniss. “It was so crazy. It was the same crew. It was the same AD, who I’ve worked with a million times because I love him. And with Josh [Hutcherson] and Woody [Harrelson] … it was so emotional. Josh and I didn’t walk to the bathroom without our arms around each other. It was so beautiful. And Woody, obviously, came through the window of my hotel room uninvited. It wouldn’t be the same if he listened to boundaries or used a door.” Related Stories Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’ Variety reported last December that Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson were returning as Katniss and Peeta Mellark for a scene in “Sunrise on the Reaping.” Lawrence has now let it slip that Woody Harrelson will also be back as Haymitch. The new prequel movie centers on a young Haymitch (played by Joseph Zada) as he competes in the 50th Hunger Games. Book readers know that Suzanne Collins’ “Sunrise on the Reaping” novel ends with a flash-forward epilogue featuring Katniss, Peeta and Haymitch, so it appears the film adpatation is following suit. Lawrence told Variety during her “No Hard Feelings” press tour in 2023 that she was “totally” open to reprising her “Hunger Games” role of Katniss Everdeen should the right opportunity arise. She added at the time, “If Katniss ever could ever come back into my life, 100 percent.” As Katniss, Lawrence headlined four “Hunger Games” movies between 2012 and 2015. The franchise (which also includes the Rachel Zegler-led 2023 prequel “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes”) has grossed $3.3 billion to date at the worldwide box office. “What made me nervous was how it could negatively affect my acting career and my personal life,” Lawrence said on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast about her biggest concern with joining the franchise when she was 20 years old. “The one thing I was always sure of when I was younger was that I wanted to be a mom, and this looked so different then doing some indies. ‘Twilight’ had just come out and everybody saw what that was. It was more like… how is this going to change my life and my acting career?” Watch Lawrence’s full interview on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast in the video below. articles.title: Oscar Contender ‘Shame and Money’ Acquired in North America by Oscilloscope (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: × Oct 28, 2026 7:00am PT Oscar Contender ‘Shame and Money’ Acquired in North America by Oscilloscope (EXCLUSIVE) By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest Oscar Contender ‘Shame and Money’ Acquired in North America by Oscilloscope (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago BAFTA Names Hilary Rosen as Chair 23 hours ago David Bowie Immersive Concert Experience ‘Stage’ From Brett Morgen to World Premiere at Berlin Film Festival 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Vicky Bane, Schuldenberg Films Oscilloscope Laboratories has acquired North American rights to Visar Morina ’s “ Shame and Money .” The film won the Grand Jury Prize in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at the Sundance Film Festival, which qualifies it to compete for the Oscar for international feature film under new Academy rules . Oscilloscope is planning a theatrical release in early 2027. The film, which stars Astrit Kabashi, Flonja Kodheli, Kumrije Hoxa, Fiona Gllavica and Alban Ukaj, was co-written by Morina with Doruntina Basha. Related Stories Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’ The film centers on a couple in their 40s who live with their extended family in rural Kosovo making a modest living on their farm. Following a familial dispute, their livelihood is lost. They are forced to move to Pristina where the pressure to provide for their family weighs heavily on the parents as they do their best to find work and a place to stay. Morina said: “In times when the majority of people worldwide are finding it increasingly difficult to make ends meet, I believe we need a kind of class consciousness, and I hope our film makes a small contribution toward that.” Oscilloscope president Dan Berger said, “Visar’s has drawn a portrait of a family that is subtle, searingly real and ultimately humane. We feel as one with the characters and their struggles, fully signed on for this indictment of an economic system constructed to keep too many people down.” The producers are Fabian Altenried, Sophie Ahrens and Kristof Gerega from Schuldenberg Films (“Objet a,” “Strange River,” “Life Is Not a Competition but I’m Winning”), along with Pia Hellenthal (“Searching Eva”) and Morina. Rights have also been acquired via international sales agency The Yellow Affair for France (Arizona Distribution), Indonesia (Falcon), Spain (Mirror Audiovisual), Switzerland (Trigon) and Filmarti (Turkey) with further deals expected to close soon. Eksystent Filmverleih released the film theatrically in Germany in September. “Shame and Money” has won a plethora of awards since Sundance including the Cinemasters Jury Prize at FilmFest Munich, best film and best actor at Prifest Kosovo and four awards at ODA Film Festival – best movie, actress, actor and script. “Shame and Money” is Morina’s third feature, following “Exile” and “Babai.” He is represented by Cinetic Media. ‘Harry Potter’ HBO Series Casts Its Arthur Weasley, Moaning Myrtle, Colin Creevey Bill Maher’s Embarrassing Karoline Leavitt Interview on ‘Real Time’ HBO Max to Revamp Harry Potter Film Rewatch Podcast Into Companion Series for New TV Show (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Oh, Mary!’ Set for HBO With Cole Escola Reprising Lead Role in Filmed Stage Play Javier Bardem to Star in Drama Series ‘The Spread’ at HBO From Bill Dubuque, Sean Sansiveri ‘The Birds’ Reboot: Sarah Snook to Lead HBO Limited Series Take on Hitchcock Classic Loading comments...

articles.title: Peter Medak, Director of ‘The Changeling’ and ‘The Krays,’ Dies at 88
articles.full_text: × Oct 28, 2026 7:18am PT Peter Medak, Director of ‘The Changeling’ and ‘The Krays,’ Dies at 88 Medak also worked extensively in television, directing episodes of "Breaking Bad" and "The Wire." By Anna Tingley Plus Icon Anna Tingley Latest Peter Medak, Director of ‘The Changeling’ and ‘The Krays,’ Dies at 88 1 hour ago As NFL Expands Globally, Marriott Bonvoy Taps Cooper Kupp, Jerry Rice and More for City Travel Guides 20 hours ago Joy Behar Returns to ‘The View’ After Nearly a Month Away: ‘I Dislocated My Shoulder’ and the Pain Was ‘Worse Than Childbirth’ 24 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Peter Medak , the Hungarian-born director and actor best known for films including “ The Changeling ,” “ The Krays ” and “The Ruling Class” died Tuesday in Los Angeles. He was 88. Over a career spanning six decades, Medak directed 27 feature films, moving between psychological horror, black comedy and crime dramas. His 1980 supernatural thriller “The Changeling,” starring George C. Scott, won eight Genie Awards including best motion picture. He also directed the 1990 British gangster drama “The Krays,” for which he received the Evening Standard Award for best director. Related Stories Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’ Born in Budapest in 1937, Medak spent part of World War II in hiding with his family. Under Hungary’s Communist regime, his father was imprisoned and Medak was barred from attending school. He fled to England during the Hungarian Revolution of 1956 and began working in the British film industry, eventually serving as assistant director before moving to Hollywood. He made his feature directorial debut with 1968’s “Negatives,” starring Glenda Jackson. His 1972 satire “The Ruling Class,” starring Peter O’ Toole, competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes and earned an Oscar nomination for Toole. Other credits include “A Day in the Death of Joe Egg,” “Let Him Have It” and the Gary Oldman-led “Romeo Is Bleeding.” Medak also worked extensively in television, directing episodes of “Homocide: Life on the Street,” “The Wire,” “Breaking Bad” and “House.” His 2018 documentary “The Ghost of Peter Sellars” revisited his troubled production of the 1970s comedy “Ghost in the Noonday Sun.” He is survived by his four children, Christopher, Joshua, Karen and Cornela, and five grandchildren. articles.title: Versant Expands Suite of FAST Channels With 4 New Selections From CNBC, E!, Oxygen
articles.full_text: × Oct 28, 2026 7:45am PT Versant Expands Suite of FAST Channels With 4 New Selections From CNBC, E!, Oxygen By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Versant Expands Suite of FAST Channels With 4 New Selections From CNBC, E!, Oxygen 1 hour ago Politico Plans Live Video Coverage of Midterm Elections 16 hours ago ‘60 Minutes’ Audience Sinks to Surprising Low Without Football 17 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Versant Versant may best be known for the cable channels that provide the bulk of its revenue, but the company continues to build out new-media extensions. The owner of MS NOW, CNBC and USA is launching four new free ad-supported streaming networks based on programming franchises from CNBC, Oxygen and E! . When these new options debut, Versant will have a portfolio of 13 FAST outlets. The new quarter consists of Snapped, a program that chronicles the life of a women charged with murder and which began airing on Oxygen in 2004; Botched, a selection from E! that examines the highs and lows of plastic surgery; Oxygen Murders of America, a true-crime documentary series; and CNBC Ambition, which offers stories of entrepreneurship, innovation, wealth creation, and success and relies on a bevy of primetime series that previously aired on the business-news cable outlet. Related Stories Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’ All four new channels will be available on Prime Video in the U.S. beginning October 27, with staggered launches on The Roku Channel starting November 3. articles.title: Fox News Ratings Sink a Staggering 27% in October, but It Still Has Much a Larger Audience Than CNN or MS NOW
articles.full_text: × Oct 28, 2026 8:10am PT Fox News Ratings Sink a Staggering 27% in October, but It Still Has Much a Larger Audience Than CNN or MS NOW By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Fox News Ratings Sink a Staggering 27% in October, but It Still Has Much a Larger Audience Than CNN or MS NOW 14 minutes ago Elmo Is Going as Meryl Streep’s Evil Fashion Editor Miranda Priestly for Halloween This Year 18 hours ago Trump Says ‘Artificial Intelligence’ Is ‘a Very Bad and Inaccurate Name,’ and That He Wants to Officially Ban the Term ‘AI’ 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Fox News In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, Fox News lost more than a quarter of its overall viewing audience in the month of October, according to new data. That said, the network remains the most-watched news outlet on cable, well ahead of rivals CNN and MS NOW . For October 2026, Fox News is on track to post its lowest-rated month in total-day viewers since December 2023, according to preliminary figures from Nielsen, first reported by Status. FNC averaged 1.1 million total viewers for the month, down 27%, and 98,000 viewers in the key 25-54 demographic coveted by advertisers, a drop of 32%. Related Stories Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’ The ratings decline comes amid a continuation of the drop-off in TV viewers overall — but Fox News has been losing viewers at a double-digit clip as CNN and MS NOW have been slightly up in recent months. As Variety has reported, Fox News on many nights draws a bigger live audience than one or more broadcast TV networks. But its viewership is steadily eroding: In the third quarter of 2026, Fox News saw total-day viewership decline 16%, and viewership in the 25-54 demo fall 24%. Both CNN and MS NOW saw small gains in overall audience for Q3. In primetime, Fox News averaged about 2 million total viewers (down 28% year over year) in October, with viewers in the 25-54 demo falling 36% to 183,000, according to the Nielsen data. “Fox & Friends” had its second consecutive month below 1 million total viewers and under 100,000 in the key demo, with October representing its lowest overall viewers since July 2015 (and its lowest in the 25-54 demographic since June 2001). Meanwhile, progressive rival MS NOW saw its daytime audience rise 16% to 588,000 total viewers in October, and CNN viewership was up 3% to 402,000 viewers over the same timeframe, according to the preliminary Nielsen figures. Variety has reached out to Fox News for comment. Some observers detect a worrisome sign in Fox News’ ratings decline that conservatives are tuning out at rates faster than CNN or MS NOW as the fight for control of the Senate and House of Representatives will be up for grabs on Election Day next week, Nov. 3. President Donald Trump — whose feelings about Fox News historically run hot and cold — recently complained that the network has not been backing Republicans strongly enough. “Fox spends more time defending Dumocrats, and putting on their views versus their Republican opponent, than at any time in the History of FoxNews,” Trump wrote in an Oct. 19 post on Truth Social. “It’s ridiculous!
