A logline for the first season reads: “There is nothing special about Harry Potter — or so his Aunt Petunia tells him. But when a mysterious letter of admission to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry arrives, it opens the door to a hidden world of magic, friendship and adventure. Yet behind Hogwarts’ enchanted walls lie dark secrets. Harry must find the courage to prove himself against the darkest wizard of all.” HBO’s Harry Potter is written and executive produced by Francesca Gardiner. Mark Mylod will executive produce and direct multiple episodes of the series for HBO in association with Brontë Film and TV and Warner Bros. Television. The series is executive produced by J.K. Rowling, Neil Blair, and Ruth Kenley-Letts of Brontë Film and TV, David Heyman of Heyday Films, Laura Neal, and Jon Brown. THR

articles.title: David Bowie Returns to Berlin With Immersive Event
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 5:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Bowie JTE Photo ©Blackout David Bowie is coming back to Berlin. Oscar-nominated documentary filmmaker Brett Morgen ( Moonage Daydream , On the Ropes ) will present the world premiere of Stage , his new immersive David Bowie concert experience, at the 2027 Berlinale . Morgen designed the immersive concert around original camera footage from Bowie’s 1978 Isolar II World Tour, which the director discovered while doing research for his 2022 documentary on Bowie, Moonage Daydream . The tour features Bowie performing material from Heroes , the landmark album he wrote and recorded while living in Berlin. Like Moonage Daydream , Stages was created with the cooperation of the David Bowie Estate. Bowie, a genre- and gender-bending icon of pop music , and one of biggest rock stars in history, died in 2016 , aged 69. Related Stories TV HBO's 'Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone' Casts James and Lily Potter, Charlie Weasley Business Hilary Rosen Named BAFTA Chair Stages features a three-screen presentation combining large-scale projections of the recovered and restored footage alongside transparent LED screens and a lighting design from Patrick Woodroffe, who has lit and designed tours for everyone from ABBA and The Police to Adele and Michael Jackson. He also lit Martin Scorsese’s Rolling Stones’ concert documentary Shine a Light , which opened the Berlinale in 2006. Paul Massey, the Academy Award-winning sound mixer of Bohemian Rhapsody (and 11-time Oscar nominee), created a special sound mix for Stages to give the audience the experience of being at the center of a live David Bowie concernt. Stages will have its world premiere at Berlin’s Uber Arena on Feb. 14, on the first weekend of the Berlinale. Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle called the event “a dream come true” for the festival. “The Berlinale is a place where cinema, art, and new forms of storytelling intersect,” she said. “To have this world premiere [of Stages ] in Berlin, a city so closely connected to David Bowie, makes the experience especially meaningful.” Morgen was Oscar-nominated for his 1999 boxing documentary On The Ropes and has directed several acclaimed docs, including Cobain: Montage of Heck (2015), on Kurt Cobain, the Emmy-winning Jane (2017) on the primatologist Jane Goodall, and The Kid Stays in the Picture (2002), on legendary Paramount producer Robert Evans. Morgen will attend the Berlinale and be a headline contributor to the European Film Market’s talks program. The 77 th Berlin International Film Festival runs Feb. 10-21, 2027. THR

articles.title: ‘Babel’: THR’s 2006 Review
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ray Bennett Plus Icon Ray Bennett View All October 27, 2026 6:16am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Brad Pitt in 2006's 'Babel.' Everett On Oct. 27, 2006, Paramount unveiled Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Babel in theaters following its premiere in competition at the Cannes Film Festival in May. The feature, starring Brad Pitt, Cate Blanchett and Gael Garcia Bernal, was nominated for seven Oscars at the 79th Academy Awards, including best picture. It walked away with one win, in the original score category. The Hollywood Reporter’s original review is below: Tense, relentless and difficult to watch at times, Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Babel is an emotionally shattering drama in which a simple act of kindness leads to events that pierce our veneer of civilization and bring on the white noise of terror. Iñárritu and screen writer Guillermo Arriaga involve six families, most of them not known to one another, in four countries on three continents in their story of random fate and the perils of being unable to communicate. Brad Pitt, Cate Blanchett and Gael Garcia Bernal give committed ensemble performances alongside seasoned character performers and nonactors as the story ranges from Morocco to San Diego to Tokyo. The film, which also features exceptional work by director of photography Rodrigo Prieto, production designer Brigitte Broch, editors Stephen Mirrione and Douglas Crise and composer Gustavo Santaolalla, is headed for major prizes and large, appreciative audiences. As with his previous films, Iñárritu tells his story using scenes out of order so that the pieces fall together in a jagged form that heightens the tension. It starts in the Moroccan desert, where a man buys a Winchester rifle from a neighbor to help keep the jackals away from his herd of goats. A Japanese hunter had gifted the neighbor with the rifle in gratitude for his work as a guide. The rifle is entrusted to the goat herder’s two young sons, who end up firing it from a mountainside at a coach filled with Western tourists just to see how far the bullet would go. The bullet, however, strikes an American named Susan (Blanchett) who is traveling with her husband Richard (Pitt) in attempt to patch up their marriage following the death of a child. Four hours from the nearest hospital, the coach takes a detour to a remote village, where a local man offers shelter while the other tourists argue over whether to stay or leave. Desperate, Richard phones the U.S. embassy pleading for help and also calls home in San Diego, where their longtime maid Amelia (Adriana Barraza) is caring for their other two children. With Susan bleeding and near death in the desert, he begs Amelia to remain with the kids as he tries to get help. Amelia’s son, however, is getting married across the border and, having exhausted attempts to find another sitter, she decides to take the kids with her to the wedding in a car driven by her friendly but hot headed nephew Santiago (Bernal). As Richard fights to keep Susan alive with the help of a wise and calm old Moroccan woman and a veterinarian, the shooting escalates into an international incident with security forces believing terrorists to be responsible and hunting for the perpetrators. Meanwhile, in Tokyo, a young deaf-mute woman named Chieko (Rinko Kikuchi) is grappling with the loss of her mother by suicide, fighting with her equally bereft father (Koji Yakusho) and trying to deal with the frustrations of adolescence. The filmmakers succeed brilliantly in weaving these stories together, taking time to explore depth of character and relationships. The suspense builds throughout as everyone involved becomes lost in a place they don’t understand with people they don’t know if they can trust. Several astonishing Tokyo sequences replicate what it might be like to be deaf-mute, and equal imagination is applied to scenes at night in the wasteland of the Mexico-California border and the barren mountains of Morocco. — Ray Bennett, originally published on May 24, 2006. THR

articles.title: The NFL’s Biggest Dramas This Season Are In the Broadcast Booth
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 7:07am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Troy Aikman is in the final year of his ESPN deal. Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images The NFL might be the undisputed king of TV content, but it is off-the-field drama that has dominated much of the conversation around the game this season so far. In particular, it was a widely reported altercation before the Los Angeles Rams-Buffalo Bills game at SoFi Stadium earlier this month … in the ESPN broadcast booth. To recap: ESPN’s lead play-by-play announcer Joe Buck signed a rich new contract with the company, but his longtime analyst partner Troy Aikman has not, resulting in reported bad blood between the boothmates. On-air, of course, viewers would have no clue (Buck and Aikman have continued to deliver a broadcast worthy of their decamillion dollar contracts), but the dispute has become fodder, and Aikman has not been willing to shy away from discussing it. The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback appeared on The Mike Fisher Show on Friday, where he was almost melancholy about what his future holds in media. “I never had any interest in going into television, it was just by happenstance that I even got into it,” Aikman said, recalling the outreach from Fox Sports . “I don’t know that if they hadn’t hired me, I would have gotten an opportunity anywhere else. And here I am, 25 years later, and now as I’m into my last year at ESPN, I’m realizing that this is something that could very well be taken away from me, and so for the first time, I’m realizing how much I really do, and I’ve always enjoyed it. “Until you risk having something taken away from you, I think sometimes you tend to maybe take things for granted,” he continued. “And so for the first time probably in my career, I’m realizing, you know, this is a great profession, it’s been a great ride for me, and I hope that it’s not over.” Joe Buck and Troy Aikman will also lead ESPN’s coverage of the Super Bowl this year. Julio Aguilar/Getty Images As the faces of Fox and ESPN’s NFL coverage, Aikman and Buck have been staples on Sundays (and more recently Mondays) for years. The looming end of that is ripping through sports, media and the league itself. And the situation comes as Disney is set to host its first Super Bowl since 2006, with Buck and Aikman set to lead the game from the booth (they have also been a big part of its marketing). But with their rich deals, nothing can be assured, and in the TV business, any opportunity to get a better deal or sign talent that could make a difference is typically taken fast. At a conference room in the InterContinental Barclay Hotel in Midtown Manhattan last week, NFL executive VP and chief media officer Hans Schroeder was asked about the Buck-Aikman-ESPN impasse. Schroeder, who is responsible for managing the league’s relationships with its media partners, said that it had “no concern” with the situation. “I don’t know if you watched the game on Monday night. It was an incredible game. An incredible game, and incredible coverage by Joe and Troy, just like they always do,” Schroeder told assembled journalists in the room, adding that the league was proud of Disney’s coverage, including its numerous altcasts with the Manning brothers, Pat McAfee and Star Wars , and with all the effort going into next year’s Super Bowl. “I think the fans are deserving of first-class game production, which Joe and Troy have — I think going back to ’02 or something was their first year — a history of doing that as well as anyone, and I think you’ll continue to see them do that as well as anyone.” Suffice it to say, it is not the story that the league or Disney want to be talking about right now. And yet, the ESPN broadcast booth drama underscores what has been perhaps the most tumultuous and uncertain year ever for NFL broadcasters. At CBS, Tony Romo’s preseason arrest for operating a vehicle while intoxicated (OWI) led to his eventual ouster from the network’s broadcast booth. His replacement, JJ Watt, was named the permanent successor last week when he was given a multiyear contract extension, with Skydance Sports chief David Berson praising him as “insightful, entertaining, passionate, meticulous in his preparation, and the ultimate teammate.” Greg Olsen is in the final year of his deal at Fox, and is looking for a new home, while current NFL names like Travis Kelce and Sean McVay have bubbled up as potential TV talent in chats with agents and network execs. A senior NFL source told THR that the league doesn’t micromanage the personnel decisions of its broadcast partners, and that it isn’t involved in the calls being made when it comes to talent. But that doesn’t mean the league doesn’t have any say. Sources at both the league and its rights partners paint the conversation around broadcasting as an ongoing conversation, with the league always interested in improving coverage of the game. More precisely, the league’s NFL deals require a quality of production from its partners that includes an A-team broadcast booth that can deliver a broadcast worthy of the league and its viewers (“first-class production,” as Schroeder said). It might be a mushy benchmark, but it does mean that more out there ideas like the Manningcast, the McAfeecase or animated altcasts remain secondary considerations, and that the main booth needs to have seasoned or otherwise A-list talent (like Tom Brady, who made his broadcast booth debut for Fox). The drama matters, because the NFL matters. While no real fans will turn off their NFL games because of some broadcast booth drama, the entire situation is a rare speed bump for what is otherwise the most reliable bet in all of TV. And yet: The broadcast booths may change, but there’s no reason to think that the NFL will ever become less relevant, or less watched. THR

articles.title: Susan Saint James, ‘Name of the Game,’ ‘McMillan & Wife’ and ‘Kate & Allie’ Star, Dies at 80
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All October 27, 2026 7:11am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Susan Saint James Susan Saint James Susan Saint James, the Emmy-winning actress who delighted TV viewers with her light-hearted turns on The Name of the Game , McMillan & Wife and Kate & Allie before quitting at the peak of her powers, has died. She was 80. Saint James died Monday of pancreatic cancer, her family announced. Survivors include her third husband, Dick Ebersol, the former Saturday Night Live executive producer and head of NBC Sports whom she married in November 1981. The couple soldiered on after losing their youngest child, 14-year-old son Teddy, in a 2004 plane crash. Related Stories Movies Hubert de la Bouillerie, 'Woodstock' and 'Witches of Eastwick' Film Editor, Dies at 75 TV Alan Dysert, 'All My Children' Actor, Dies at 75 Saint James was someone who was “generous with her time and energy, which she valued more than money, and instinctively drawn to whoever needed lifting up,” her family said. “She taught her children to pause, be kind and look out for other people.” On the big screen, she went on the run with Peter Fonda in Outlaw Blues (1977); played the lustful target of Dracula in Love at First Bite (1979), starring George Hamilton; executed a heist with fellow suburbanites Jessica Lange and Jane Curtin in How to Beat the High Cost of Living (1980); and portrayed George Segal ’s wife in Carbon Copy (1981). A contract player at Universal, Saint James portrayed the frequently kidnapped editorial assistant Peggy Maxwell for three seasons (1968-71) on the stylish 90-minute NBC drama The Name of the Game . ( THR took a look back at the series in 2018). Peggy worked at Howard Publications for all three of the rotating characters on the “wheel” series — Tony Franciosa as hotshot reporter Jeff Dillon, Gene Barry as kingly publisher Glenn Howard and Robert Stack as FBI agent turned magazine editor Dan Farrell. Six months after The Name of the Game ’s final episode, Saint James was back on another 90-minute wheel series, McMillan & Wife , which began in rotation with Columbo and McCloud as part of the NBC Mystery Movie franchise. Like Peggy, Saint James’ Sally McMillan also got into trouble and helped solve crimes, here with her husband, San Francisco police commissioner Stewart “Mac” McMillan ( Rock Hudson ). She appeared on the show for five seasons through 1976, when she left in a contract dispute (Hudson stuck around the final sixth season). Saint James returned to series television in 1984 by reuniting with Curtin for the CBS sitcom Kate & Allie . On that show, two childhoods friends now divorced — Saint James’ free-spirited Kate McArdle and Curtin’s more by-the-books Allie Lowell — raise their kids (three in all) in a Greenwich Village brownstone they share. When Kate & Allie was canceled in 1989 after the sixth season — it was nominated three times for the Emmy for outstanding comedy series — Saint James decided to pretty much shut down her acting career. She told People magazine in 2002 that she was tired of being “one of those people juggling knives and melons and then [saying], ‘Toss me in a razor blade.’” Saint James received an Emmy in 1969 for her work in the first season of The Name of the Game , then added noms in 1970 and ’71. She also was nominated for McMillan & Wif e in 1972, ’73 and ’75 and for Kate & Allie in 1984 and ’85. Susan Saint James (right) and Jane Curtin on a 1984 episode of ‘Kate & Allie.’ Courtesy Everett Collection One of four kids, Susan Jane Miller was born in Los Angeles on Aug. 14, 1946. She and her family moved in 1958 to Rockford, Illinois, after her father, Charles, was named president of The Testor Corp., maker of tools and accessories for model kits, and the Hobby Industry Association of America. Her mother, Constance, was a schoolteacher. Saint James attended the Woodlands Academy of the Sacred Heart for high school and lived and modeled in France for about three years. Inspired by Paula Prentiss, she moved back to California to try acting when she was 20 — she lived at the Hollywood Studio Club — and quickly scored a part alongside Franciosa in the 1966 NBC/Universal TV movie Fame Is the Name of the Game . Directed by Stuart Rosenberg, who would soon helm Cool Hand Luke , it served as the pilot for The Name of the Game . Created by Jennings Lang, the series sported a budget of $400,000 an episode, the largest of its day (Universal’s Black Tower stood in for Howard Publications headquarters). It was canceled after its third season, during which the temperamental Franciosa was fired. In 1967, Saint James appeared in a failed pilot for a crime show called Ready and Willing that starred Jack Weston and Joe Flynn and in the George Peppard feature P.J. A year later, she showed up on the pilot episode of ABC’s It Takes a Thief , starring Robert Wagner, leading to a recurring role as the crook/love interest Charlene “Charlie” Brown. She also made three other films at Universal that were released in 1968: Jigsaw , starring Bradford Dillman ; What’s So Bad About Feeling Good? , starring Peppard and Mary Tyler Moore ; and the sequel Where Angels Go … Trouble Follows! , starring Rosalind Russell. When McMillan & Wife , created by Leonard Stern, bowed in September 1971, Saint James had just turned 25 while Hudson was closing in on 46. In a 1971 interview with Bobbie Wygant, Saint James described Sally McMillan, the daughter of a cop, as “Peggy Maxwell grown up.” “She’s still just as nutty and just as goofy, but she’s married to Rock Hudson, and they live a very sophisticated life, they have a very nice house,” she continued. “She can’t get anything done, she doesn’t do anything right, she gets him involved in all her terrible happenings. It’s kind of a comedy mystery.” Susan Saint James and Rock Hudson, stars of ‘McMillan & Wife.’ Courtesy Everett Collection At the start of the final season, Sally is killed in a plane crash with her and Mac’s never-seen son. Saint James moved to Connecticut in 1983 to star in Kate & Allie , which taped in New York City. The sitcom, created by Sherry Coben , debuted in March 1984 as a six-episode midseason replacement series but was quickly renewed for a full season in the fall. She and Curtin went head to head for outstanding lead actress in a comedy series at the Emmys in 1984 and ’85, with the former SNL star winning both times. As The New York Times wrote in 2007, “Jane Curtin’s Allie, the ex-wife of a cheating Connecticut doctor, is truly miserable, and so the better character.” When the sitcom ended after 122 episodes in March 1989, Saint James was 43 and would soon become pregnant with Teddy. She didn’t quit acting entirely, appearing on episodes of The Drew Carey Show , Law & Order: SVU , Suits and Upload and onstage in Connecticut in The Miracle Worker , but she focused on being an active volunteer with the Special Olympics and launching a business selling baby-gift baskets. Saint James, who had dated rocker Stephen Stills in the late ’70s, got together with Ebersol when she was about to host Saturday Night Live in October 1981. “She comes to New York, we met on a Sunday, I was in love with her by Monday, we were living together in a hotel by Tuesday, and she did the show on Saturday,” Ebersol said in a 2009 interview . “We were married six weeks later.” After she hosted, Ebersol took her out to dinner that night, and their photograph while kissing soon appeared in The New York Daily News with the headline, “When Dick Ebersol Books a Host, He Doesn’t Fool Around … On Second Thought, He Does.” When Kate & Allie became a hit, Ebersol left Saturday Night Live in April 1985 to raise the kids. On Nov. 28, 2004, a private plane carrying Ebersol and he and Saint James’ sons Charlie and Teddy crashed in snow and fog during an attempted takeoff from Montrose Regional Airport in Colorado (the Ebersoles owned a home in nearby Telluride). Charlie pulled his injured dad through a hole in the middle of the plane, but Teddy was killed — his body was discovered underneath the wreckage 24 hours later — as was the pilot and steward. Less than three weeks after the crash, Saint James recorded an interview with Tim Russert for the Today show to thank those who had reached out to her and her family. “If you know anybody that loses somebody, call them on the phone,” she said. “People always say, ‘I know you don’t want to be bothered.’ You can’t be bothered enough. It’s just fantastic, and I just want them to know that.” Her family on Tuesday called what she did in the immediate aftermath of Teddy’s death her “defining act … she delivered his eulogy as a note to each of her other children and her husband, giving them words to heal. Even in the deepest grief of her life, she put everyone else first.” In addition to her husband and Charlie, survivors include another son, William, whom she also had with Ebersol; her son and daughter, Harmony and Sunshine, whom she had with her second husband, makeup artist (and manager) Tom Lucas; her sister, Mercedes; a niece, actress Christa Miller ( Shrinking ); seven grandkids; and her beloved service dog, Lola. Her first husband was screenwriter Richard Neubert; they were married from 1967-68. “She never met a stranger,” her family noted. “Every person she met became the most important person in the room at that moment, from a fellow board member to the clerk at the shoe store, who usually walked away knowing her entire life story.” THR

Days after the crash she sat with Tim Russert to thank the people who had reached out and to tell them the family was okay.” Saint James became a television fixture in the late 1960s with NBC’s “The Name of the Game,” an anthology drama in which she played research assistant Peggy Maxwell. The role earned her three Emmy nominations, including a win for supporting actress in a drama series in 1969. She went on to star alongside Hudon in “McMillan & Wife,” playing Sally McMillan, the wife of a San Francisco police commissioner, from 1971 to 1976. Her performance earned her three additional Emmy nominations. In 1984, Saint James returned to series television in “Kate & Allie,” starring alongside Curtin as two divorced mothers who decide to raise their children together in a Manhattan apartment. The sitcom ran for six seasons on CBS, earning Saint James two more Emmy nominations. Her film credits include “Outlaw Blues” (1977), the vampire comedy “Love at First Bite” (1979) and “How to Beat the High Cost of Living” (1980). Born Susan Jane Miller in Los Angeles on Aug. 14, 1946, Saint James grew up in Rockford, Ill., before pursuing modeling and acting. She largely retired from Hollywood following the conclusion of “Kate & Allie” in 1989, though she made occasional television appearances, including on “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” and “Suits.” Outside acting, she was a longtime advocate for the Special Olympics. She received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2008. She is survived by her husband, former NBC executive Dick Ebersol, four children and seven grandchildren. articles.title: ‘Miraculous: Tales of Ladybug & Cat Noir’ Sets Global Season 7 Rollout on Disney, TF1 and Globo
articles.full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 6:49am PT ‘Miraculous: Tales of Ladybug & Cat Noir’ Sets Global Season 7 Rollout on Disney, TF1 and Globo By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest ‘Miraculous: Tales of Ladybug & Cat Noir’ Sets Global Season 7 Rollout on Disney, TF1 and Globo 1 hour ago France Riots Put Hollywood Shoots on Alert as Curfews Disrupt Movie Theaters: It ‘Has Now Been Flagged as a Problem Area’ 4 days ago Charli xcx Joins Martin Scorsese’s ‘What Happens at Night’ With Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence (EXCLUSIVE) 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Miraculous Corp “Miraculous: Tales of Ladybug & Cat Noir,” the blockbuster French animated series, is gearing up for a global rollout of its seventh season across Disney , France’s TF1 and Brazil’s Globo . Miraculous Corp , the joint venture between Mediawan and ZAG, has unveiled a staggered release schedule for the 26-episode season, which will premiere on Globo in Brazil on Oct. 30, followed by TF1 in France on Nov. 1 and Disney Channel across Europe, the Middle East and Africa on Nov. 14. Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart In the U.S. and Latin America, the new season will debut on Disney Channel on Nov. 20 before launching on Disney+ the following day. The rollout comes as “Miraculous” enters its second decade with a growing international footprint. The series outperformed 850 school-age and preschool children’s programs tracked worldwide, according to audience demand data from Parrot Analytics covering June 21 to Sept. 18. It also ranked fourth among all television series globally during that period, making it the only children’s show to crack the top 10. “Season 7 comes at a moment of strong momentum for ‘Miraculous,’ and this coordinated rollout reflects the continued strength of our longstanding broadcast partnerships,” said Maria Doolan, Miraculous Corp’s head of content partnerships and distribution. “We value the collaboration that has helped the series reach audiences across key markets and are excited to build on that foundation as we bring Season 7 to viewers across their platforms.” Produced in collaboration with Disney Kids & Family, Brazil’s Globosat, Italy’s KidsMe and France’s TF1, the new season will continue to follow the adventures of Marinette and Adrien, two Parisian teenagers who transform into superheroes Ladybug and Cat Noir. In Season 7, Marinette’s decisions begin to have greater consequences for both her personal life and her responsibilities as Ladybug, as shifting friendships and relationships complicate her efforts to protect Paris. The new episodes will also introduce new superpowers and more enemies. Since its launch, “Miraculous” has grown into one of France’s biggest international animation franchises, spanning six seasons distributed in more than 150 countries, along with television specials, a feature film, video games, live events and consumer products. While the animated show is about to return on the air, a live-action series in currently in development at See-Saw Films , the Oscar and Emmy-winning powerhouse behind “Slow Horses.” which is part of Mediawan. articles.title: Errol Morris Is Sitting on a Secret Elizabeth Holmes Interview (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Larry Busacca/Getty “I have this problem ,” shares Errol Morris , the Oscar-winning documentary filmmaker behind “The Thin Blue Line,” “The Fog of War” and countless other renowned docs. You see, the 78-year-old can’t seem to screen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s docu-phenomenon on Elizabeth Holmes , “You Can See Everything.” He claims to have contacted the appropriate parties but has thus far been rebuffed. “Can you get me a screener?” he pleads. (I cannot.) Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart What Morris did do, however, was finally watch Alex Gibney’s 2019 documentary on Holmes and her sham blood-testing company Theranos — “The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley” — for the very first time. Morris, who’s directed “probably 1,000” commercials for various companies, was hired by Holmes in 2015 to shoot a series of ads for Theranos that depicted the “founder” staring wide-eyed into the camera that have attracted criticism for contributing to her mythmaking . Morris says he doesn’t know how Gibney got ahold of extra footage from the ads to use in “The Inventor,” but that’s not all: Morris exclusively revealed to Variety that he actually conducted a two-hour Interrotron interview with Holmes that he’s contemplating releasing in light of the renewed interest around the infamous grifter. So, I understand you have not seen “You Can See Everything,” but recently watched Alex Gibney’s documentary on Elizabeth Holmes, “The Inventor,” for the very first time. I never really wanted to see it until recently for a variety of different reasons, and I was quite surprised to find out that I was in it. He used outtakes from your Theranos ads, right? Well, what’s really not known about any of this is, yes, I did all the advertising for Theranos, but I did it at a time when Elizabeth Holmes was on the front cover of Forbes and many other magazines. She was riding high, and this was before everything collapsed. Did I have any reason to believe that she was a fraud? I did not. Did that change as time went on? It did. I had tried very hard, over a number of years, to do a documentary on Elizabeth Holmes and it would have happened except that she was under indictment. There was massive litigation going on. You wanted to interview Holmes for a documentary? I asked her, at a certain point, if I could film an interview with her — and this is at the height of her success — and I did film a two-hour interview with her, which is not very well-known if it is known at all. And I just watched that. I am sincerely interested in putting that out as an unedited film. You should. If anything, it gives you a comparison of Elizabeth before and Elizabeth after , which I think is interesting in and of itself. I noticed that the Gibney film begins and ends with my interview with Elizabeth Holmes. This two-hour interview you conducted with Holmes has not been seen by anyone other than yourself? Well, myself and the people in my office, but yes, for all intents and purposes, it has not been seen by anyone. Let me ask you a fast question: Why do you think [“ You Can See Everything ”] has proven so popular? I think it touches on a lot of different things that fascinate the culture — grifters, self-delusion to the point where the person created a persona that incorporated a fake Yoda voice, true crime and Silicon Valley megalomania channeled through the prism of Nathan Fielder’s brand of awkward comedy that pits, to borrow from John Ganz, a neurotic against a psychotic. Well, it’s hard for me to tell you about the film having not yet seen it, but I can tell you what I think about Elizabeth Holmes having spent a considerable amount of time with her. I was interviewed by John Carreyrou recently for an article that subsequently appeared in The New York Times, and he was questioning me about something I’d said to him many, many years ago when I was considering making a documentary about Elizabeth Holmes and had asked him if he would participate in that documentary. Some people see these stories as an on/off switch of she’s innocent or she’s guilty, she’s lying or she’s telling the truth. And when you’re investigating a crime, part of that investigation has to be if the person is guilty or innocent, since the criminal justice system works in such a way that you are looking for some kind of result. But what interests me is: To what extent was she self-deceived? To what extent did she believe in her own bullshit? Carreyrou understandably wants to tell you that she knowingly committed fraud, is guilty, should have been convicted and is in prison, as she should be. I keep wondering about the psychology of self-deception because part of me believes that she believes in Theranos and that she could achieve the results as promised. Aren’t there, say, serial killers who are convinced that what they’re doing is right and just? And isn’t it more about the people you hurt along the way? Yes, it is. You could say that lots of people in Silicon Valley misrepresent or out-and-out lie about what their technology can achieve, but in this case it involved medical results and people whose lives are directly affected by those medical results, and that in itself makes it different. One example of a lie would be that she’d claimed Theranos had a Department of Defense contract and its blood-testing technology was being deployed on the battlefield, none of which was true. Now, we can get into a philosophical discussion of the nature of lying and what is a lie, and did she lie in a very clear sense? Yes. Many, many times. Did she see them as lies? That is of interest to me. I want to ask you about something you’d said during a Reddit Q&A after Holmes’ house of cards collapsed: “When everything fell apart, I was shocked because I believed in Elizabeth Holmes. I feel, rightly or wrongly, that most of the television programs and movies about her have missed the mark. Did she do bad things? Most assuredly. The question remains, why?” You then drew a comparison between her and Joan of Arc. Probably the Robert Bresson “Joan of Arc,” which is one of my very favorite films. But Elizabeth Holmes wasn’t burned at the stake. She’s serving some time in prison for defrauding people. The nature of her punishment is not similar to being burned at the stake, and if you thought that’s what I meant by it, I did not. You were drawing that comparison in regard to their self-deception. One thing I can say about Joan of Arc: Do I think that God was speaking to her? I have a confession to make: I don’t believe in God. Do I think that God exists? No, I don’t! Do I think that God was directly communicating with Joan of Arc? I don’t! Do I think she thought that God was directly communicating with her? She did! She went to the stake on the basis of it. That’s your comparison. Going back to those Theranos promos you shot with her— —Don’t call them promos! I was hired as a commercial director, and I’ve shot probably 1,000 commercials. In the Gibney documentary, it is mentioned that Elizabeth Holmes and Patrick O’Neill, who was her CCO, had hired me because of the many Apple commercials I’d directed for Steve Jobs. If I had known how much of my interview was being used [by Gibney], or even if it was being used at all, I’m not sure what I would have said. I knew it was being used, but I never really wanted to watch [“The Inventor”]. Maybe I’d just had enough of it. How did Gibney get ahold of the footage? This I do not know. I really don’t know. And I’m not being coy or cagey. I do not know. I know the commercials you shot for Holmes and Theranos have garnered quite a bit of criticism for contributing to her mystique, but I found Holmes quite creepy in those commercials. How do you feel about people’s perception of those commercials? People have never seen my long interview that I did with Elizabeth Holmes. I’ve heard that I have been accused of representing a fraud — knowingly — and this is just not true. I’ll join a lot of other people who were on the Theranos board at the time that I was doing this series of commercials. Are you sure you want to join Henry Kissinger? I’m joking. I actually interviewed Henry Kissinger just before he died. Is that going to go anywhere? It might. I have so much stuff that I do nothing with. I’d heard a very funny story about how BP approached you to direct an ad for them following the Deepwater Horizon oil spill and that you proposed a wild idea that they turned down. I believe that’s true! And what was that idea? You tell me and I’ll tell you if it’s real! That Mel Gibson would be standing on a BP oil platform and say something to the effect of, “If anyone knows about a public relations disaster, it’s me.” That’s it! And of course, they said no. Fortunately, enough people have said yes over the years, but I can’t tell you how many people have said no. I once said to my producer for commercials, “You know, I get all these commercials, but I’ve never gotten diarrhea or erectile dysfunction commercials. What’s wrong with me?” I once got a Depend commercial, and my ideas for incontinence/Depend commercials were by and large rejected. What was one of those ideas that you really liked? Thank you for asking. I had just done a long interview with Janis Karpinski, who’d just been demoted in connection with Abu Ghraib — and this interview has never seen the light of day — so there’s this lady general inside a tank in a war zone. Shells are exploding all around. The tank is on maneuvers. We see the face of the lady general inside the tank. She has an enormously pinched expression. She is fidgety, edgy. And then, you hear the sound of running water, and the expression on her face changes to one of total relaxation and pleasure. And then we cut outside and we see the artillery exploding. Depend . That is hilarious. The guy who was producing the commercials to Depend put his face two inches away from mine and said, “THERE IS NOTHING, NOTHING FUNNY ABOUT INCONTINENCE!” And I said, “I guess I beg to differ.” I’m with you on that one. By the way, why did your two-hour Elizabeth Holmes interview never come out? Because the company fell apart and she was prosecuted… but I can’t really answer it. The clearest answer is that I’d moved on. But now I feel pretty strongly that this is an interesting document — not because I’m trying to prove something about Elizabeth Holmes, but it does provide some kind of evidence of what she was like when everything was going her way. And what is your takeaway after watching the interview? That she was a true believer. Loading comments... articles.title: ‘Every Contact Leaves a Trace’ Director on Why She Hired a Detective: ‘I’m Trying to Reconstruct a Life Story’
articles.full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:03am PT ‘Every Contact Leaves a Trace’ Director on Why She Hired a Detective: ‘I’m Trying to Reconstruct a Life Story’ By Will Tizard Plus Icon Will Tizard Contributor @willtizard1 Latest ‘Third Land’ Director on the Risks of Chronicling the Lives of Iranian Refugees in Turkey: It Was ‘Extremely Tense and Frightening’ 2 hours ago Latvian Filmmaker Who Witnessed Last Days of the Soviet Union Portrayed in ‘Podnieks on Podnieks’ 12 months ago Albania’s Soviet-Tinged Propaganda Archives Reveal a Passion for the Cinematic, says Docmaker Roland Sejko 12 months ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "Every Contact Leaves a Trace" (Courtesy of Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival) U.S. artist and documentarian Lynne Sachs has often screened her past films at Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival , but she’s finally made it in person this year, serving on the First Lights jury, which evaluates docu debuts. Sachs says she’s been impressed by Ji.hlava films that span the globe while showcasing the full range of filmmaking approaches and perspectives. “There are about 24 movies to see. It’s kind of revelatory. Already I’ve seen two films here, one from Argentina and one from Congo and they really couldn’t be more different. They make you think about the documentary paradigm.” Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart A case in point, she says: “Positionality.” Whose perspective is an audience seeing and is the filmmaker’s role visible or even known? It’s something Sachs has made crystal clear in her newest film, “Every Contact Leaves a Trace,” screening at Ji.hlava in its Czech premiere. Sachs herself is clearly onscreen, investigating, making connections, doubting herself, and occasionally seeking help from a youthful niece and nephew as she goes through old business cards, some decades old, wondering at who gave them to her and what traces of lives contacting hers can still remain. The film is a kind of detective story that eventually enlists the actual analyses of forensic investigators as Sachs follows leads to track down people whose names remain in her box of hundreds of carefully preserved business cards – a good number she admits have lost all meaning to her. “I actually hired a detective at one point,” she confesses. Some left burning impressions on her and she has always wondered what became of the card giver – such as an artist whose work touched her years ago or a fellow artist filmmaker who was later canceled over allegations of impropriety. One card was from a Syrian woman whose family discouraged her from sitting for an on camera to share her experiences as a refugee – so Sachs settles for filming a tribute to the woman’s cooking skills. Sachs says she is also uneasy about terms that have come into common use for people in docus. Rather than say “protagonists” or “characters,” she much prefers “on camera participants.” Or maybe “visible collaborators who are the people in front of the camera.” “We’re offered the chance to tell our story by the person behind the camera. What I don’t know is, who is the person behind the camera?” In the case of “Every Contact,” it’s clear to all who is filming and inquiring as Sachs visibly, sometimes awkwardly, tracks down people who once met her but certainly never expected her to appear again at their doorstep with a camera. It’s a role she has not always put onscreen so clearly, she says. “I’m trying to reconstruct a life story of life experience from the interactions I’ve had with people…people who left a mark.” Since the film came out, Sachs says, people have offered her their own collections of old business cards. “I say, ‘Oh, no!’ This combination of cards only goes back to one person. You’re the person who had that dentist. You’re the person who met that psychoanalyst. Or potential friend on a bus.” As Sachs investigation progressed, she says, “I was most drawn to the cards that presented the biggest obstacles.” Some card donors may be impossible to find now. And others presented a different challenge: At times figures from your past have made lasting impressions – but that doesn’t always mean that was mutual. The process of recounting past encounters is one fraught with traps, says Sachs, as human minds tend to re-enact them in the mind, often editing, sometimes finding specific moments deeply burned in. As Sachs enlists the help of family on her quest, one suggests that it’s not usually even up to us to choose which memories will stay with us and which we’ll lose. Sachs discovered through her docu detective work that sometimes she did not need to fly across time zones to track down someone she once knew who might not even remember her or feel they shared an important interaction, she says. “I don’t need to prove I did or didn’t,” says Sachs. “I need to deal with the residue.” Jennifer Coolidge to Return for ‘The Watcher’ Season 2 ‘Decision to Leave’ Cinematographer Kim Ji-yong on Chasing Natural Light for Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’: ‘This Is the One Where We Worried, Debated and Planned the Most’ CAA’s Roeg Sutherland Says It’s Too Soon to Predict Fallout From Netflix Firings, Thinks Recent Mergers Represent ‘Opportunity’ for Industry Netflix Says 67% of Surveyed Members Want to Visit Korea as Busan’s Creative Asia Puts Locations in Focus How Netflix’s Messy Transition Will Rock Hollywood: Looking at You, NBCU ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ ‘Squid Game’ Stars Fete Netflix’s Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases ‘Tantara,’ ‘All of Us Are Dead’ Season 2 Loading comments...

The series will debut on November 23, just ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday its subject helped spur. “Billy Bob Thornton is a captivating storyteller with a unique ability to bring history to life. ‘The Mayflower ‘offers a fresh and thought-provoking perspective on one of the most familiar chapters in American history, giving viewers a richer understanding of the people, conflicts and events that shaped our nation’s beginnings,” said Lauren Petterson, president of Fox Nation, in a statement. The series traces the Pilgrims’ Atlantic crossing aboard the Mayflower, the alliance forged between English settlers and the Wampanoag people, and the conflict that ultimately pushed what were once colonies of Britain toward forming an an American identity. Kudos to Billy Bob Thornton for helping to bring this vital story from America’s past to life,” said Philbrick in a prepared statement. Thornton joins a growing list of top creatives who have done work for Fox Nation , including Martin Scorsese, Kevin Costner and Kelsey Grammer. articles.title: Christina Applegate Tells MS Community ‘I’m Still Your Warrior’ After Being Misdiagnosed: ‘I’m Going to Speak Out on Your Behalf Forever’
articles.full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:31am PT Christina Applegate Tells MS Community ‘I’m Still Your Warrior’ After Being Misdiagnosed: ‘I’m Going to Speak Out on Your Behalf Forever’ By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest Christina Applegate Tells MS Community ‘I’m Still Your Warrior’ After Being Misdiagnosed: ‘I’m Going to Speak Out on Your Behalf Forever’ 30 minutes ago ‘Call of Duty’ Movie Will Be About the ‘Cost of War and Having to Be a Warrior,’ Says Director: ‘These Are Not Comic Books or Cartoon Characters’ 17 hours ago Robert Pattinson Praises Steven Soderbergh for Stepping in to Finish ‘Batman 2’ Filming for Matt Reeves: ‘Completely Selfless’ 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Gilbert Flores/Variety Christina Applegate returned to the “MeSsy” podcast one week after revealing she was misdiagnosed with MS to tell listeners that she will never stop advocating and fighting for those impacted by the disease, even if she does not have it herself. The Emmy winner said people in the MS community are still “my people.” “Even though I don’t have this disease, I’ve fallen in love with everyone that we know, our listeners, our friends that have MS,” Applegate said to podcast co-host on the show Jamie-Lynn Sigler, who was diagnosed with MS in 2001 (via Entertainment Weekly ). “I’m still your warrior, and I’m still going to speak out on your behalf forever and ever. Despite not having MS. I still feel like part of this community. No matter what, I love you.” Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Applegate originally revealed she had been diagnosed with MS in 2021, and retired from acting after the finale of her hit series “Dead to Me” the next year. She then become a fierce advocate for people with the disease — which causes damage to the central nervous system — and co-founded the “MeSsy” podcast as a way to share her experience and spread awareness. On the latest episode, Applegate continued to share the symptoms she faces of a now un-diagnosed illness, explaining: “I actually timed it today, it took me 10 minutes to be able to move off my pillow and get out of the bed and stand up, at which point I almost couldn’t walk to the bathroom, and now a walker is sitting next to my bed because of what’s going on. I don’t know what’s going on. This is what I’m still living with, and I never had that before. I was able to sit up and stuff.” After taking a seven-month break from the podcast, Applegate returned to the program on Oct. 21 and broke down in tears while telling listeners that new technology led to the discovery that she was misdiagnosed with MS . “This may come as great news, but to me, I’m back at square one,” Applegate said. “It’s hard to say that [my doctor] came into my room and she said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS.’ You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I’m better. I haven’t gotten better … If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways. So I’m back at square one, that I don’t know what’s going on with me.” Applegate added that “it’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down” after becoming such a big advocate for the MS community. She said that she’s still in a “state of shock,” adding: “It’s a mindfuck, for sure.” Listen to the latest episode of the “MeSsy” podcast in the video below. ‘Hatchet’ Movie: Netflix and Derek Cianfrance to Adapt Gary Paulsen’s Survival Book (EXCLUSIVE) How Netflix’s Messy Transition Will Rock Hollywood: Looking at You, NBCU Netflix Sets Release Date for Rob Lowe Documentary ‘The Outsider’ ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ ‘Squid Game’ Stars Fete Netflix’s Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases ‘Tantara,’ ‘All of Us Are Dead’ Season 2 Box Office: ‘La Bola Negra’ Scores $277,500 From Four Theaters as Netflix Reports Grosses for First Time Ever Lego’s ‘Heartlake the Musical’ Heads to Peacock in the U.S., Tencent in China Amid Global Sales (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...

articles.title: Netflix Grapples With Digital-Ad Squeeze Amid Widening Glut of Streaming Commercials
articles.full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:40am PT Netflix Grapples With Digital-Ad Squeeze Amid Widening Glut of Streaming Commercials By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Netflix Grapples With Digital-Ad Squeeze Amid Widening Glut of Streaming Commercials 32 minutes ago Billy Bob Thornton Examines Mayflower Voyage in Fox Nation Documentary Series 42 minutes ago Lisa Ling Signs With CAA 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Illustration: Michael Starbuck/Variety VIP+ Netflix blazed a path in the streaming era that many of its media rivals have tried to follow. As it has tried to navigate Madison Avenue, however, the company has found bumps in the road. The streaming giant last week rolled back its projections for advertising revenue, calling for $2.7 billion instead of $3 billion by the end of 2026. At a time when marketers have been moving their dollars from linear TV to streaming video by the millions, the disclosure was surprising. Netflix co-CEO Greg Peters cited “some delays in the rollout and partner integrations” for some of its new advertising products as a primary culprit for the pared-back estimates. Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Media buyers, however, say Netflix has for months held lofty expectations that are out of sync with the general advertising market. These executives say Netflix’s pricing for inventory remains too high, the process for accessing some of its inventory is too removed from the rest of the market, and that the company’s interest in selling ad-supported sports events like Christmas Day games for NFL football has not been matched with a sales executive who is versed in the nuances of such telecasts. “There’s an existing marketplace, and there’s an existing way of working, and a lot of these digital players think that they can just come in and sell, and it’s not that easy,” says one media buying executive with knowledge of the current market. Netflix declined to make executives available for comment. The streamer for years vowed never to sully its viewing experience with commercials, but media economics, and increased competition from services like Amazon’s Prime Video, HBO Max and Disney+ have not let it hold to those convictions. And just as Netflix has made a concentrated foray into ad sales, the market for streaming inventory has been undermined by a glut of supply. Amazon has loads of ads to sell, and traditional media outlets do as well. The sheer tonnage of streaming inventory available has given advertisers the upper hand in negotiations. To be sure, streaming is soaring. The volume of ad commitments put toward streaming in the most recent “upfront” video market rose a whopping 30%, according to consultancy Media Dynamics, hiking to about $17.2 billion, compared with about $13.2 billion in the 2025 market. But a rising swath of digital inventory, spurred by the rise of cheap FAST channels and increased inventory on mainstream streamers, has weakened the media companies’ stance. The cost of reaching 1,000 viewers, a key metric in these annual negotiations that is known as a CPM, is under clear pressure. Streaming CPMs during the upfront fell 4.9%, to $25.90 from $27.75, according to Media Dynamics. This upfront marked the third year in which media companies agreed to what is known as “rollbacks,” or reductions in the rate of change in pricing they seek for the viewers they deliver. “Free ad-supported TV channels are attracting accelerating audiences especially among increasingly challenged lower per capita income households,” says Pivotal Research Group analyst Jeff Wlodarczak in a recent research note. Other media companies are likely to face these pressures. Simply put, more streaming inventory is purchased via programmatic means, or via algorithms that seek out particular audience characteristics, such as expectant mothers or first-time car buyers. This digital automation of advertising inventory has made it harder for media companies to prove that such video opportunities are “premium,” or better than what else is available in the market. Some companies have tried to create new ways to stand out. Before its acquisition by Skydance, Warner Bros. Discovery burnished its ability to help advertisers identify specific settings and emotions present in its programming library. So a marketer might look for a scene set in an airport, grocery store or theme park, or seek out shows that made viewers feel a sense of mystery, curiosity or adrenaline. Paramount had touted a concept called a “streaming fixed unit” that gives advertisers who buy it the same ad placement in the premieres of new episodes of top shows such as “Tulsa King”. When an advertiser buys the unit, it is also buying a guarantee that Paramount will run the ad in a fixed place, such as the first spot in a commercial break, for the first seven days after the episode debuts. Netflix isn’t the first new-tech streaming purveyor to face challenges upon turning to the ad market. Amazon infamously pressed advertisers to pay more for “Thursday Night Football,” then untested as a stand-alone on the Prime Video platform, than they did for Fox’s Sunday-afternoon NFL games, some of the medium’s costliest properties. Media buyers pushed back , and Amazon is believed to have retreated from some of its highest price demands. To be sure, Netflix has something many advertisers want: Programing that gets attention. Blue chip marketers ranging from Coca-Cola to Anheuser-Busch and State Farm have turned logistical somersaults to link their products with programs like “Stranger Things,” “The Gentlemen” and “Running Point,” often with stand-out placements in and commercials liked to the series. The challenge, of course, is that the number of sponsorships available hinges on Netflix’ programming slate. “We’re still growing, our ads business is growing over 80% this year. And I think noting that if you are sufficiently aggressive with your product road map, you’re going to occasionally be behind some milestones,” Peters said, adding: “General demand remains very strong, the breadth of advertisers continues to expand, and ultimately, advertisers want our new products and features, and that’s a big mechanism of growth for us. So we are very focused on getting those out to them as quickly as we possibly can.” Getting more ad dollars into its funnel may require a little savvy. Buyers feel Netflix’ initial decision to focus on creating a stand-alone suite of ad-tech may have crimped some of its efforts. “They were trying to build their own walled garden, their own tech,” says the buying executive. “It is just going to slow down adoption, because you’re making it harder for us to work with you in the ways that we’re used to working.” Perhaps Netflix has heard this complaint. The company has struck deals in recent months to allow its programmatic ad inventory to be purchased via Amazon and Yahoo platforms. Last week, the company unveiled an expansion of its interaction with Trade Desk, a demand-side platform that functions as one of the bigger programmatic marketplaces. With sports the only programming format that truly lures the sizable and simultaneous crowds advertisers covet, Netflix may want to beef up its expertise. Too often, the buying executive notes, Netflix has been slow to reveal pricing terms or inventory packages it sought around sports properties. “There was confusion about even just basic things. Are you requiring a match spend on entertainment? When are you sending out plans? When are we negotiating pricing?” this buyer says. “They’re being too difficult to work with, and it just makes things harder.” Boosting ad sales may come as a distraction as Netflix executives fret about their service’s ability to keep subscribers and boost the number of hours they spend with the platform. Ted Sarandos , Netflix’s co-CEO, described a scenario under which Netflix had to work harder to develop relationships with producers, directors and other members of the creative community. A new executive, Peter Rice, formerly of Fox and Disney, has come aboard to focus on just that. The ad revenue will remain equally important, argues Dan Salmon, an analyst at New Street Research. “We expect mis-execution in the ad business to be added to the investors’ #1 concern about continued slumping engagement,” he says in a recent research note. articles.title: ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama
articles.full_text: × Oct 27, 2026 7:44am PT ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama Docmaker Jelena Maksimović's first fiction feature is a narratively sparse but atmospherically throbbing exercise, playing in competition at Tokyo following its Venice Orizzonti premiere. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama 30 minutes ago ‘Love Language’ Review: Chloë Grace Moretz Sells Words of Affirmation in an Old-School Romcom With Gen-Z Trappings 3 days ago ‘Clayface’ Review: DC Comics Horror Movie Is Good, Gross Fun, With No Franchise Homework Required 6 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Paul Spengemann Amid the turmoil of mass student protests in the streets of Belgrade, two young people are bonded by a rash act of rebellion, despite their outwardly incompatible ideologies. The premise of Serbian writer-director Jelena Maksimović ‘s “ Until the Day Ends ” portends a tidy political parable — a sort of “why can’t we all get along” homily for an age, and particularly a generation, of vastly polarized beliefs. The execution, thankfully, is flintier and more complicated than that. The film’s teachings, if any, are ambiguous, and learned on the run: Maksimović’s first fiction feature is most memorable for its galloping formal restlessness, moving at the breathless pace of its characters as they evade authority and chase a glimmer of hope in their joint resistance. Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Having made an impression on the docfest circuit with her two nonfiction features “Taurunum Boy” (2019) and “Homelands (2020), Maksimović brings a street-level, vérité -style grit to the lean narrative of “Until the Day Ends” that feels authentically keyed into the reality of current youth unrest in Eastern Europe. The film is set against a surge of real-life anti-government demonstrations in Serbia in early 2025, triggered by the tragic deaths of 16 people the previous year, following the collapse of a train station canopy in Novi Sad. But if the honest performances of a mostly non-professional ensemble contribute to a docudrama spirit, the filmmaker and her DP Paul Spengemann embrace an aesthetic of epic escapism, with roving, kinetic camerawork punctuated with enough bursting lens flare to make Janusz Kaminski blush. It’s an attention-grabbing approach that promises bigger things from Maksimović, and is propelling the film some distance on the international festival circuit. A premiere last month in Venice’s Horizons program has since been followed with berths in Vienna, Hamburg and, now, the main competition in Tokyo. The film opens on a virtuoso long take, roaming through the shadowed, disheveled hallways of a university building that, ahead of the revolution, has become something of a campsite for displaced, rebellious students; insurgent streaks of red disrupt the general gloom of the mise-en-scène. Through this faintly apocalyptic scene, we follow 20-year-old Lena (riveting newcomer Lena Trifunović), a firebrand student activist who is all in on the protests, unwavering in her anti-authoritarian conviction. That may earn her the admiration of her college comrades, but at home, she’s seen as an idealistic naif — mocked, in particular, by her older brother Milan (Miodrag Dragicevic), who is staunchly right-wing in his sympathies. Milan’s similarly inclined friends join in the teasing, but one does so with a little less gusto: 22-year-old Stefan (Andrija Krivokapić) is a working-class punk who goes with the flow of his social group, but doesn’t seem wholehearted in his pro-government stance. Perhaps sensing his lack of commitment, Lena taunts him back. This hint of connection between them is later made concrete when, at the demonstration, the two are complicit in an act of defiance — throwing a cobblestone at a policeman, badly injuring him — and must skip town for the night. As they flee, their mutual attraction deepens, but they must also parse their political differences. There’s no great capitulation or come-to-Jesus moment here, however. “Until the Day Ends” isn’t an outright romance, or a tale of a proud, gathering storm of resistance; rather, it finds human emotions and obligations sometimes messily at odds with social and political ideals. Narratively, the momentum crests at the protest, abetted by Maksimović’s most dynamic cinematic trickery — which extends to a shot from the perspective of the errant, offending stone. As a more intimate two-hander in the second half, the film is less urgent, but kept compelling by the push-pull chemistry between its two punchy young leads, playing characters who are alike in their combative vulnerability, but little more than that. Trifunović, in particular, is a real find, unpredictable in her coiled-up physicality and alternately commanding and petulant presence. Lena bristles with angry, frustrated optimism, recognizable to anyone who has ever, at one point or another, felt alone in trying to change the world. ‘Until the Day Ends’ Review: Two People Connect Across a Political Divide in a Striking Serbian Youth Drama Reviewed at Soho Screening Rooms, London, Aug. 20, 2026. articles.title: Parallax Films Boards Sales On ‘Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting’ Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Rolf de Heer & Fellow Tokyo Jury Members Talk Festival ‘A-List’ Ratings, Co-Production & How To Judge Films Parallax Films Boards Sales On ‘Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting’ Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi Pledges Support For Japanese Film At Tokyo Fest Opening View All October 26, 2026 4:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting Parallax Films EXCLUSIVE: Parallax Films has boarded international sales for Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting , directed by Chinese artist-filmmaker Qiu Jiongjiong, which is receiving its world premiere in the main competition section of Tokyo International Film Festival. Qiu is known internationally for his debut narrative feature A New Old Play , which won the Special Jury Prize at the 2021 Locarno Film Festival. Rooted in the folklore of China’s Sichuan province, Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting unfolds through four separate feasts spanning four millennia, that “bring the living and the dead, gods and ghosts, to the same table”. The word “fuxi” in its title is a Sichuan expression meaning “the joy of the belly”. Related Stories News Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi Pledges Support For Japanese Film At Tokyo Fest Opening News How TIFFCOM Is Building On Cannes Recognition To Strengthen Global Networks, Co-Production & Japanese IP Parallax describes the film as a “handcrafted mythic fantasy” referencing Qiu’s unique style of filmmaking that combines painting, theatre and cinema. “Rather than reproducing reality, Qiu uses hand-painted scenic flats, handmade props and theatrical staging to give physical form to his imagination, creating a cinematic universe entirely his own,” Parallax explains. ( See here for the trailer of the film.) Watch on Deadline The cast includes Lee Kang-sheng, Taiwanese filmmaker Tsai Ming-liang’s longtime leading actor, playing two grandmothers in different chapters of the film, marking his first female roles on screen. He is joined by actor-filmmaker Lee Hong-chi, whose directorial debut Love Is A Gun won the Lion of the Future award at Venice, and Annie Chen, known for her role in Netflix series Born For The Spotlight . Produced by David Tang, Ningyuan Ding and Zhao Jin, Fuxi is a co-production between Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. The project received support from international film funds and project markets including Hong Kong-Asia Film Financing Forum (HAF), MPA APSA Academy Film Fund, Red Sea Fund, Doha Film Institute and Network of Asian Fantastic Films (NAFF) at Korea’s Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival. The film’s visual world also extends beyond the screen in Fuxi: A Feast For The Universe , Qiu’s large-scale solo exhibition at A4 Art Museum in Chengdu. Bringing together paintings, sets, props and installations, the exhibition translates the film’s imagined universe into a new spatial narrative. The deal for world sales on Fuxi extends Parallax’s relationship with Qiu, with the company also representing his seven previous films, which include A New Old Play, experimental documentary shorts and documentary features. Season 4 of the period drama, co-showrun by creator Julian Fellowes and Sonja Warfield, the series tackles the results of growth in industry, accumulation of mass wealth and drastic societal changes as well as new inventions that sped civilization along to where it is today. Related Stories News Everything We Know About ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 So Far News ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 Trailer Hints At Tension In Russell Marriage Plus Situation That “Requires” Agnes Van Rhijn “To Take Leave” Of Her Manners For the full release schedule of The Gilded Age Season 4, read on. When does The Gilded Age Season 4 premiere? Watch on Deadline Season 4 of the period drama premieres Sunday, November 1. How many episodes are in Season 4 of The Gilded Age ? Do they arrive weekly or all at once? There will be eight episodes in the fourth season of The Gilded Age . After the first one premieres Sunday, November 1 in the popular 9 p.m. slot on HBO and HBO Max , new episodes will come out one per week through December 20. See the full release schedule below: Sunday, November 1: Episode 1 Sunday, November 8: Episode 2 Sunday, November 15: Episode 3 Sunday, November 22: Episode 4 Sunday, November 29: Episode 5 Sunday, December 6: Episode 6 Sunday, December 13: Episode 7 Sunday, December 20: Episode 8 (FINALE) Who is in the cast of Season 4 of The Gilded Age ? Most of the core ensemble will return for Season 4. Louisa Jacobson portrays Marian Brooke, niece of Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) and Ada Brooke now Forte (Cynthia Nixon, who married the Reverend Luke Forte (Robert Sean Leonard) only to have him pass away from cancer. Carrie Coon and Morgan Spector will be back as the ambitious social climber Bertha Russell and her railroad tycoon husband George Russell, though their relationship hit some rough waters in Season 3. Harry Richardson plays their son Larry Russell, and Taissa Farmiga portrays their daughter Gladys, who married the Duke of Buckingham (Ben Lamb) in Season 3 through arrangement by her mother. L-R: Denée Benton and Jordan Donica in ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 Karolina Wojtasik/HBO Denée Benton stars as Peggy Scott, a journalist and writer who met her match in Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica) last season. Audra McDonald portray’s Peggy’s mother Dorothy, and John Doughlas Thompson portrays her father Arthur Scott. Blake Ritson plays Agnes van Rhijn’s son Oscar. Kelley Curran plays Enid Winterton, formerly known as Turner because she served as Bertha’s maid. Ashlie Atkinson plays Mamie Fish, socialite who is close with Mrs. Astor (Donna Murphy). Ben Ahlers plays Jack Trotter, formerly the van Rhijn footman and now a man of means since his clock invention patent was sold. Also on the van Rhijn household side, Debra Monk plays Agnes’ lady’s maid Ms. Armstrong. Taylor Richardson plays Bridget. Kristine Nielsen plays Mrs. Bauer who cooks for Ada and Agnes. Simon Jones plays the van Rhijn butler, Bannister. Celia Keenan-Bolger plays Mrs. Bruce, housekeeper for the Russell family. Erin Wilhelmi plays Adelheid Weber, Gladys’ lady’s maid. Douglas Sills portrays Chef Borden, who cooks for the Russells. Jack Gilpin is the Russell butler. George Russell’s secretary Richard Clay (Patrick Page) and New York Globe publisher T. Thomas Fortune ( Sullivan Jones ), will not appear in the rotation of Season 4.

articles.title: Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max BAFTA Names New Chair Stephen & Simon Cornwell Take On Chairmen Roles At ‘Night Manager’ Producer The Ink Factory As Michele Wolkoff Upped To President Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK View All October 26, 2026 5:01pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Daisy Haggard and Bella Ramsey in the upcoming 'Maya' Channel 4 Disney and Channel 4 have struck a landmark UK content deal that will also see the Channel 4 linear network become available on Disney+ , a UK first. In one of the biggest deals of its kind in UK TV history, shows like Channel 4 stalwart Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins and upcoming Bella Ramsey-starrer Maya will drop on Disney+ at the start of next year in the UK and Ireland. From there, Disney+ EMEA general manager Karl Holmes told Deadline there will be a “regular tempo” of new Channel 4 shows entering the Mouse House, although he wouldn’t put an exact figure on this. Related Stories Cancellations and Renewals 'Coven Academy' Renewed For Season 2 By Disney News Nicola Coughlan's 'I Am Helen' Trailer Shows Dark Side Of Modern Relationships As Toxic Masculinity Takes Its Toll From the start of next year, Disney+ UK and Ireland subs will be able to watch these shows day-and-date plus hundreds of hours of on-demand content like Russell T. Davies’ Tip Toe and Nicola Coughlan’s Big Mood. And in a UK first, Channel 4’s linear channel will also become available in its entirety on Disney+. Watch on Deadline Speaking alongside Holmes, Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra claimed the Gogglebox network and Disney+ don’t have much overlap in terms of audience and the deal can be complementary. Channel 4 already licenses Disney content like Abbott Elementary , The X Files and Scandal for its VoD player. “From our perspective, people develop viewing habits in different places,” said Dogra. “There are a number of services they may use to discover content, and we need to make sure Channel 4 is available on those platforms.” Holmes said Disney+ viewing skews younger than public service broadcasters like Channel 4, adding that around 40% of Disney+ viewing over the past year has come from 16-34 year olds. “There is a genuinely complementary relationship here,” added Holmes. “We’re not competing with free-to-air partners; we’re helping them reach a broader audience.” The news comes more than a year after Disney+ kicked off a strategy of partnering with local European networks by striking a content-swapping deal with ITV that has seen shows like The Bear and The Kardashians head to ITVX, while Love Island and Mr Bates vs the Post Office went in the opposite direction. This preceded Disney deals with the likes of Germany’s ZDF and Spain’s Atresmedia. Netflix has simultaneously struck a high-profile pact with France’s TF1 that was recently talked up by Ted Sarandos. Holmes said the Disney-Channel 4 pact is broader in scope than Disney-ITV and his team learned from the latter when executing the former. “One clear lesson is that a focus on shows that are current, big, bold and buzzy – and available day-and-date – works particularly well with our audience,” he added. “That’s what we’ve prioritised in this collaboration. We’d like to build on it further in the future.” For Dogra, who has been in post less than a year, the deal is the latest landmark agreement she has helped mastermind following the once-in-a-generation ads deal inked with Paramount (now Skydance) UK network 5 . She has talked up collaboration opportunites including putting Channel 4 shows on BBC iPlayer , while downplaying the idea of a BBC-Channel 4 merger. While the Paramount deal “gives us scale from an advertising perspective,” today’s agreement “allows us to maximise our impact by reaching as many people as possible across the UK and Ireland, including people who may not currently be using Channel 4 services,” Dogra added. “The premise is that we need to lean into the wider ecosystem,” said the CEO, a former Sky and Warner Bros. Discovery executive. “We’re not going to build scale in every area ourselves, so we need to work with like-minded organizations.” More details on the Disney-Channel 4 deal will be incoming in due course.
