articles.title: Kore-eda Hirokazu Explains Why He Never Films Children Crying – and What Ken Loach and Hou Hsiao-hsien Taught Him
articles.full_text: Oct 24, 2026 1:40am PT Kore-eda Hirokazu Explains Why He Never Films Children Crying – and What Ken Loach and Hou Hsiao-hsien Taught Him By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Kore-eda Hirokazu Explains Why He Never Films Children Crying – and What Ken Loach and Hou Hsiao-hsien Taught Him 4 hours ago Vino G. Bastian, Pevita Pearce, Faradina Mufti, Indra Jegel Lead ‘Miracle in Cell No. 7’ Director Lee Hwan-kyung’s Indonesian Father-Son Drama ‘Gasigogi’ (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Kartik Aaryan’s ‘Captain India’ Set Amid Houthi Conflict in Yemen (EXCLUSIVE) 11 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Lim Japanese auteur Kore-eda Hirokazu , whose films are known for their natural performances from child actors, said there is one thing he has decided never to put on screen: a child crying. “It’s not that I can’t, or that it’s difficult. I don’t shoot it,” the Japanese director said at an In Conversation event at the the Singapore International Film Festival on Saturday. “The ideal is that after viewers finish watching, they remember that child’s smile and cry.” Related Stories Meta’s Almost $10 Billion Legal Costs Take Huge Toll on Q3 Earnings, Wall Street Shrugs Skydance Stock Drops 2.7% on First Day of Trading After Paramount-WBD Merger Close The festival presented Kore-eda with its Cinema Honorary Award at the National Museum of Singapore before an onstage conversation with festival chair Boo Junfeng, the filmmaker behind “Apprentice.” Introduced in 2014, the award is the festival’s top honor and recognizes lasting contributions to Asian cinema. Previous recipients include Im Kwon-taek, Garin Nugroho, Jafar Panahi and Deepa Mehta. Popular on Variety Kore-eda said his methods with children have grown more flexible. Through “Shoplifters” and the films he made abroad, “The Truth” and “Broker,” he did not hand children scripts. Instead, he rewrote dialogue around the personality and vocabulary of the children he met at auditions, so that they only spoke lines they could say with conviction, and then fed them lines on set or described a situation and let them talk freely. On “Monster,” he gave the young cast scripts, judging that the subject was risky enough that separating the children from their roles was safer. He now decides child by child and film by film, he said. Two directors shaped that approach. Hou Hsiao-hsien , Kore-eda said, joins in when children are playing in a scene, slips out once the camera is rolling and lets them keep going – a trick Kore-eda now uses himself. From Ken Loach , he took a lesson about judgment. In Loach’s “Kes,” a boy discovers the bird he has raised dumped in a trash can after his brother kills it, and the young actor’s reaction looks nothing like a performance. When Kore-eda met Loach about 20 years ago, while he was making “Nobody Knows” and wrestling with similar questions, Loach told him he had only instructed the boy to go and look for the missing bird. Asked how he had weighed the ethics of that, Loach said he understood the risk but was confident that his relationship with the boy could repair any hurt. Kore-eda said the lesson was that Loach was weighing each shot as he went. “I keep it firmly in mind that judging things that way – it worked on the last shoot so it will work this time, or a method that worked with the last child will work with this one – is the most dangerous thing in directing children,” he said. He never gets angry with children or rushes them, he said, and he doesn’t lie to them. “The ideal is that a child ends the day saying, ‘Today’s shoot was fun, I’m looking forward to tomorrow,’” he said. Some children simply won’t listen, he added, in which case he turns that into the role. During auditions for “Like Father, Like Son,” one boy answered every question, including his name and where he was from, with “Why?” Staff thought communication was impossible, but Kore-eda was drawn to him and wrote a character who answers everything with “Why?” Kore-eda called himself a fan of Hou rather than someone he was influenced by, but the Taiwanese director also changed how he approaches a scene. Hou read the script for Kore-eda’s 1995 debut “Maborosi,” which won the Golden Osella in Venice, and introduced him to a composer, so Kore-eda showed him the finished film. Hou critiqued it severely, he said. “I was deflated. But what he told me was absolutely right.” Kore-eda said he had drawn up a meticulous blueprint and that his crew did professional work to realize it, but he failed to update the plan on set. Hou asked whether he had storyboarded every scene and shot it exactly as drawn. He had. “Where you shoot a scene from – you go into the location, feel the space, see the light falling there, and that’s when you first decide how the actors move,” Kore-eda recalled Hou telling him. “Once the actors’ movements are decided, only then do you decide the camera position. You have to do it in that order. You know that, you made documentaries.” “Now I’m truly grateful he said that to me, but at the time it really got to me,” Kore-eda said. “I swore I’d never draw storyboards again.” Kore-eda said he sees his two 2026 films, “Sheep in the Box” and “Look Back,” as a return to his roots. “Sheep in the Box,” which competed in Cannes, follows a couple whose 7-year-old son died two years earlier and who take in a humanoid robot built from his data. Despite the AI element, Kore-eda said, the film is about grief work. “It’s a story about how to properly say goodbye to the dead, so I feel it actually ended up closest to what I tried to do in my debut,” he said. “Look Back,” his live-action adaptation of Fujimoto Tatsuki’s manga about two girls bound by a love of drawing manga, played in competition at Venice and opens in Singapore on Oct. 29 after playing at the festival. On it, he said, he went back to the documentary thinking of his early films, treating the camera as an eye and simply asking where to watch the subject from. “So I think the second half of my career probably starts next year,” he said. Kore-eda said he writes best on long flights and in spare hours at hotels abroad, and has been writing on his current trip from London to Thailand and Singapore. He hopes to be shooting one project around this time next year at the earliest, or the year after if that proves difficult. Thirty years after he started making films, the growing number of career awards leaves him uneasy, he said. “I feel like I still have about half my career left, and yet it kind of feels like I’m being told it’s time to graduate,” he said. Kore-eda said he has little interest in AI, even though “Sheep in the Box” features a child brought back through generative AI. At a producer’s suggestion, he let an AI read his script for the first time. “At first it told me, ‘This is wonderful, it’s a sure thing for the Cannes Film Festival,’” he said. He ended the exercise after concluding the AI had probably never had a film experience big enough to change its life. Kore-eda said he never tries to work out what audiences want, citing advice from a senior colleague he admired in his television days, when ratings were treated as everything. “He told me, ‘If you think of them as viewers, it won’t reach anyone,’” Kore-eda said. “He said to picture one person’s face and make it for them.” Asked what dish he would choose for the afterlife, a nod to his 1998 film “After Life,” Kore-eda said he probably wouldn’t eat anything once he was dead. His last meal before dying, though, is already decided: the tenzaru soba at Sunaba, a noodle restaurant in Tokyo’s Akasaka district, where a senior producer took him when he was a young assistant director who had gone days without going home. “The soba I ate there was the best I’ve had in my life, and it still is,” he said. “I want to eat that one more time at the end.” Telly Awards Adds Microseries Competition Track, With Dozens of New Categories (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Sin Filtro’ Producer JK Media Producing First Original Microdramas Shot in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision’s ViXMicrO (EXCLUSIVE) Vidio Teams With ReelShort for First Indonesian Short-Drama Partnership COL Group, Virtue Asia and V47 Entertainment Launch Inside Microdramas, Vertical Entertainment Upfront Generative AI, Microdramas to Take Center Stage at Busan Market Raindance to Launch U.K.’s First Major Vertical Festival and Market (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...

articles.title: Jay-Z Brings Out Blue Ivy Carter, DJ Khaled and John Legend During the First of Two Nights at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium
articles.full_text: Oct 24, 2026 1:42am PT Jay-Z Brings Out Blue Ivy Carter, DJ Khaled and John Legend During the First of Two Nights at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium By Steven J. Horowitz Plus Icon Steven J. Horowitz Senior Music Writer speriod Latest Jay-Z Brings Out Blue Ivy Carter, DJ Khaled and John Legend During the First of Two Nights at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium 4 hours ago Slayyyter Cancels Remaining European and U.K. Tour Dates to Recover From Laryngitis 19 hours ago Former Eminem Employee Pleads Guilty to Stealing and Selling Unreleased Music 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Roc Nation “Can I take you to my home for a second?” asked Jay-Z as he led into “Empire State of Mind” during the first of two headlining shows at Inglewood, California’s SoFi Stadium. Thus, he did, as he’d been doing for the past hour-and-a-half, bringing Brooklyn to Los Angeles as he traced the corners of his vast discography, the backbone of a career that stretches 30 years with countless hits to match. Jay touched down on the West Coast for an invigorated set Friday night as part of his yearlong “Jay-Z 30” celebration, which began with a one-off headlining show at Philadelphia’s Roots Picnic in late May. What followed were three back-to-back sold-out nights at Yankee Stadium, plus shows in London and Paris, and a robust eight-episode HBO docuseries breaking down the finer points of his catalog. Given all the chatter that Jay may have booked himself for Super Bowl 2027 as the Halftime Show performer — which would make sense, considering a year of unusually high activity nearly a decade after he released his last album — it was hard not to consider Friday’s concert as a test run for what could potentially be the biggest performance on the biggest stage this coming February. (After all, the Super Bowl is taking place in the same venue where he performed.) Related Stories How David Ellison Won the Battle: Timeline of Paramount's Rocky Road to Acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery David Zaslav Bids Farewell to Warner Bros. Employees in Video on Eve of Skydance Merger Close: 'It's Been a Great Honor to Be Alongside All of You' As he’s consistently shown, Jay was in mint condition as he ran through hit after hit after hit at SoFi across a two-hour set, toggling the setlist of previous shows while keeping the focus centered on the electricity between himself, the audience and his band. Fans have, of course, come to expect high-wattage surprise stars: At his Yankee Stadium shows, he coronated the 25th and 30th anniversaries of “The Blueprint” and “Reasonable Doubt,” respectively, with cameos from his wife Beyoncé, Rihanna, Eminem and his daughter Blue Ivy Carter , to name just a few. Popular on Variety Blue Ivy Carter plays the keys with her dad Jay-Z at the first of two shows at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium pic.twitter.com/7h5kZzNA1p — Variety (@Variety) October 24, 2026 His SoFi show, meanwhile, felt pared-down with purpose. There were few guest stars throughout the night, with Blue Ivy playing the keys on “The Story of OJ” and “Dead Presidents,” a shift from when she tickled the ivories on “Feelin’ It” at Yankee Stadium. Scarface came out for “This Can’t Be Life” as well as his own classic “Mind Playing Tricks on Me.” John Legend and DJ Khaled emerged for the night’s closer, “God Did,” a song that originally also featured Fridayy, Lil Wayne and Rick Ross. (As an aside, having witnessed the very rare performance of “This Can’t Be Life,” I can’t help but note that Scarface’s verse is one of the most moving I’ve ever heard on a rap song. Listen if you haven’t, immediately .) Amid the talking points surrounding Jay’s potential Halftime Show has been the question of whether or not he can carry a performance of that magnitude without bringing out guests. And by the sheer propulsion of the evening, plus the hits lining it, Jay once again reinforced that he’s the star of his own show, no matter which direction it points. At 56, he is a seasoned veteran, one of the few hip-hop acts who can book stadium shows across the world after such long periods of dormancy. Consider him an elder statesman, if you will, but the bravado and showmanship that he continues to exhibit feel like more than a decent justification for his continued relevance, despite what any detractor on the Internet might deign to claim. Jay-Z brings out Scarface for “This Can’t Be Life” in Los Angeles pic.twitter.com/bp2BwcLKI1 — Variety (@Variety) October 24, 2026 Jay comes from a time when success was predicated mainly on skill, with business acumen running hand in hand alongside it. It’s why he managed to build an empire around his own talents, and why fans continue to show up by the thousands to behold them. The SoFi show was no exception, a dexterous display of lyrical acuity and magnetism that jolted to life with opener “Hovi Baby” and gave way to tracks like “Izzo (H.O.V.A.)” and “Run This Town.” Many of the visuals were the same as his Yankee Stadium shows, right down to the opening shot of Beyoncé shaving his head, yet they still felt elevated and unique to his performance, building out the world of tracks like “Song Cry” and “Lucifer.” It’s likely that Jay will pull out all the stops for the final night of his “Jay-Z 30” tour on Saturday night. (Fans clocked Beyoncé, Kelly Rowland and Michelle Williams having a Destiny’s Child reunion in one of the SoFi suites on Friday.) But if his first performance was any indication, Jay is up to the task, no matter how big the platform. Check out the full setlist below: Hovi Baby Izzo (H.O.V.A.) articles.title: El Gouna Takeaways: ‘Safe Exit’ Wins Top Prize, Arab TV Seeks New Talent and Egyptian Filmmakers Push Boundaries
articles.full_text: Oct 24, 2026 3:23am PT El Gouna Takeaways: ‘Safe Exit’ Wins Top Prize, Arab TV Seeks New Talent and Egyptian Filmmakers Push Boundaries By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest El Gouna’s CineGouna Expands Industry Push: ‘We Want to Give Every Filmmaker a Chance’ 18 hours ago British Filmmaker Joanna Hogg on the Struggle to Turn Personal Stories Into Fiction: ‘Each Time I’m Learning From Scratch’ 23 hours ago Egyptian Screenwriter Mariam Naoum on the Struggle for Arab Series to Find Buyers: ‘We’re Suffocating Inside’ 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mohammed Hammad (Courtesy of Alessandro Levati/Getty Images) Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival wrapped its ninth edition Friday after nine days of screenings, industry activity and a closing night that spread its top prizes across the Middle East and beyond. Mohammed Hammad ’s “ Safe Exit ,” a psychological drama about a young Coptic security guard in Cairo confronting trauma rooted in religious violence, won the Golden Star for best narrative feature. Ahmed Hassouna’s “Citizen Osama,” following a Gaza photojournalist balancing his work with family life amid war, took both the Golden Star for documentary and best Arab documentary. Anders Davidsen’s “Stolen Memories,” in which the discovery of childhood photographs leads an 18-year-old to question his past, won the Golden Star for short film. Rakan Mayasi ’s Bekaa Valley-set “ Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep ” was named best Arab narrative, while Marie Rose Ousta’s “One Day Born,” about an 11-year-old boy living under the constant threat of warplanes in Lebanon, took best Arab short. Jordan’s Rakeen Saad won best actress for Zaid Abu Hamdan’s “Boomah,” while Jovan Ginić took best actor for Miroslav Terzić’s “3 Weeks After.” Popular on Variety Here are five takeaways from this year’s festival. CineGouna, the Industry Platform, Is Becoming the Main Event “We want the industry to be our hero,” El Gouna co-founder and executive director Amr Mansi told Variety ahead of this year’s festival. The ninth edition made good on that ambition. More than 320 projects applied to CineGouna Funding, with 19 selected projects ultimately receiving more than $350,000 across 40 awards, while participants held more than 140 one-on-one meetings with companies, institutions and international festivals. The activity extended beyond financing. CineGouna now encompasses Funding; Forum, a program of panels, masterclasses and industry discussions; Market, which connects filmmakers with companies and institutions; and Emerge, its initiative for young and emerging talent. This year also brought Egyptian Voices, a development program for Egyptian filmmakers, and an inaugural Series lab for Arab television projects into the fold. CineGouna is becoming as central to El Gouna’s identity as the films it screens. Arab TV Is Searching for a Development Pipeline CineGouna’s expansion into television also highlighted a wider problem confronting Arab television: there’s an abundance of talent, but opportunities to develop and sell new shows are sorely lacking. Veteran Egyptian screenwriter and producer Mariam Naoum, who spearheaded the six-week CineGouna Series development lab, told Variety there are “great, great talents” in the region, but only “three or four platforms,” leaving creators competing for limited outlets. Producer and screenwriter Haitham Dabbour similarly noted that fewer platforms make buyers more cautious, while director Mariam Abou Ouf warned that the business is “approaching a deadlock.” The six projects selected for the inaugural lab came to El Gouna to pitch their series and meet potential industry partners, with the aim of moving the projects closer to production. Displaced Filmmakers Need More Than a Platform War and displacement continue to shape filmmaking across the Arab world, affecting not only the stories reaching screens but the filmmakers trying to build careers. The first Safe Harbour MENA, launched with the International Film Festival Rotterdam and the International Emerging Film Talent Association, brought four filmmakers displaced within the region into a program of training, project development and industry networking. The initiative reframed support less as simply offering filmmakers a platform to tell stories about displacement than giving them the professional connections needed to continue working. “Citizen Osama’s” double win offered a potent reminder of the circumstances confronting filmmakers in the region: director Ahmed Hassouna remains in Gaza. Egyptian Filmmakers Are Pushing for More Creative Freedom “Safe Exit’s” top prize landed amid a broader conversation at El Gouna about an Egyptian industry in transition. Producer Mohammad Mashish pointed to a younger generation with “more freedom than before” and audiences increasingly exposed to international cinema, but argued that the industry needs more time for development and screenwriting. Producer-distributor Ziad Srouji put the challenge more succinctly: “Specificity travels, generic does not.” Muhammad Mustapha, whose documentary “Big Boys Don’t Cry” premiered at El Gouna, similarly argued for models that lower financial risk while allowing filmmakers to take greater artistic risks. The tension is increasingly clear: Egyptian filmmakers are looking outward while asking for enough room to make work rooted firmly at home. El Gouna Looks Beyond El Gouna One of the festival’s most locally significant launches will take place largely after its guests have gone home. Cinema on Wheels is taking three shorts from this year’s lineup on a free screening tour through Hurghada, Minya, Qena, Luxor and Aswan before concluding in Cairo, accompanied by discussions with audiences. “We’re always exploring ways to increase the reach of El Gouna Film Festival beyond just its duration and the town of El Gouna,” artistic director Andrew Mohsen explained. For a festival built in an affluent Red Sea resort, the effort to bring its programming to audiences elsewhere in Egypt significantly expands its reach. articles.title: Morelia Film Festival Prizes: ‘Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building,’ an ‘Expression of Pure, Unbound Beauty,’ Wins Top ‘Ojo’ Award
articles.full_text: Oct 24, 2026 5:52am PT Morelia Film Festival Prizes: ‘Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building,’ an ‘Expression of Pure, Unbound Beauty,’ Wins Top ‘Ojo’ Award Guillermo del Toro, Alfonso Cuarón, Carlos Reygadas, Jonás Cuarón, Diego Luna, Gael García Bernal, Demián Bichir, Diego Boneta and Luis Gerardo Méndez were among some of Mexico's most outstanding filmmakers and actors who attended the festival this year By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest Cinépolis Distribution Lands ‘5 More Minutes,’ a Time-Warping Thriller Starring ‘Talk to Her’ Lead Javier Cámara (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago ‘Black Shine, From ‘State of Silence’ Director Santiago Maza, ’ Delves Into the Aftermath of a 2006 Mining Tragedy That Buried 63 Miners 2 days ago Todd Haynes’ ‘De Noche’ Mexican Co-Producer Península Boards Pimienta Films’ Stop-Motion ‘Insectario’ by Sofia Carrillo (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building. Courtesy of Bruno Santamaría Razo Bruno Santamaría Razo’s fiction debut “Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building”(“Seis meses en el edificio rosa con azul”) has clinched the top Ojo award at the 24 th Morelia Film Festival (FICM), which wraps Oct. 25. Hailed by Variety as a “lush, poetic film rooted in memories,” it became the first Mexican feature to compete at Cannes’ Critics Week in 20 years. Morelia’s international jury, led by J.A. Bayona (“Society of the Snow”), praised the coming-of-age film for “courageously exploring the past, embracing pain and transforming it …into an expression of pure, unbound beauty.” Popular on Variety Related Stories Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden Revenues Climb 11% to $390 Million Thanks to ‘Harry Potter’ Tour, Increased Production (EXCLUSIVE) Meta’s Almost $10 Billion Legal Costs Take Huge Toll on Q3 Earnings, Wall Street Shrugs Drawing on the filmmaker’s own experiences, the drama traces back to a defining moment in his childhood: the year he turned eleven and when his father was diagnosed with HIV. “Six Months…” also nabbed the Audience Award for fiction films, a strong indication of its box office potential. Alejandro Ramírez, Cinépolis CEO and FICM president, described the festival’s 24th edition as a particularly Mexican celebration as it welcomed some of Mexico’s finest filmmakers and actors, including Guillermo del Toro , Alfonso Cuarón , Carlos Reygadas, Jonás Cuarón, Diego Luna , Gael García Bernal, Demián Bichir, Diego Boneta and Luis Gerardo Méndez. With James Gray in town to present his crime drama “Paper Tiger” and J.A. Bayona serving as jury president, the festival has enjoyed a standout edition, he noted. Bayona also presented “Beyond Society,” a three-part documentary about the making of “Society of the Snow.” “I think the films this year represent the wide diversity of Mexican cinematic imagination,” festival director Daniel Michel observed. “There are many different and fascinating stories covering the breadth of experiences in our country which, we hope, will find a home in cinemas, as well as a large spectatorship. We’re also very proud to represent very different regions; Mexico is not a country one can easily summarize, but, rather, a vast territory with many differences which, I believe, our official selection has tried to gather in a single place.” Meanwhile, Joaquin del Paso’s “The Garden We Dreamed,” which turns on a Haitian family traveling north in search of a better future, snagged two awards: a Special Mention and Best Cinematography for its DP, Gökhan Tiryaki. “Sad Girlz,” a buzz film at the fest, was recognized as the best fiction debut with the Casa Wabis-Escine award, lauded by the jury for its “genuine performances” and “impeccable exploration of a young modern teen’s life, with all its complexities and contradictions.” The rest of the awards were quite evenly distributed. Santiago Maza, whose “Black Shine” competed among the short films , won the ECAM award, a scholarship for a Master’s degree in distribution from the prestigious Madrid Film School (ECAM). Nicolas Pereda snapped up the Best Director award with his a bsurdist comedy “Everything Else Is Noise,” which also snagged his lead Teresa Sanchez (“Flies”) a Best Actress Ojo prize for her performance as Tere, a cello musician-composer in whose apartment her colleague Rosa arranges her first television interview. Sam Louwyck won the Best Actor prize for his portrayal of a gay hairdresser in Nathalia Acevedo’s “Beauty Salon,” where his salon serves as a refuge for marginalized people. Noted Michel: “We’re also very pleased to have had directors from very different backgrounds and identities who have brought their perspectives and very singular ideas on filmmaking to our festival.” Next year, the festival will be moving its dates back to the last week before the Day of the Dead. FICM is already gearing up for its 25th anniversary, promising a landmark edition with major guests, bold retrospectives and a stellar lineup. Among the highlights of the 10-day festival: “ Naza ” Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary “Naza” – which means collateral damage – played to a packed Teatro Matamoros after which it unsurprisingly won an audience award. Unlike its reception at the 83rd Venice Film Festival, where it won the Special Jury Prize and received a record-breaking standing ovation, it was met with stunned silence as the credits rolled. Presenting the documentary beforehand was festival VP Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Batel who underscored the importance of the screening to help audiences understand such a complex conflict. He noted that the Israeli filmmakers have been unable to return to their country after being accused of treason, adding that such accusations by a “criminal government” are a source of pride for those working toward peaceful solutions. He reaffirmed the festival’s commitment to peace, dialogue and ending violence worldwide, calling for an end to the ongoing genocide against the Palestinian people. Film critic Alonso Díaz de la Vega, also spoke, describing Naza as a “deeply moving” film that exposes not only the genocide in Gaza but also the global implications of military technology, artificial intelligence and surveillance. “The most important thing this screening can inspire is not silence, but the words ‘Free Palestine,’” Díaz de la Vega concluded. The film opens in select theaters in Mexico on Oct. 22. Guillermo del Toro Rules At the festival to present the 3D re-release of his much-lauded “Pan’s Labyrinth,” the anti-authoritarian theme of his Oscar-winning fable hit home even harder this time, given the rise of right-wing governments across the region and the world at large. Speaking to hordes of mostly young fans at his Masterclass and later at a press conference and multiple one-on-one interviews, the indefatigable filmmaker reflected on the current state of affairs in the world. He grew emotional at the presser when he said: “The state of our species and society today goes beyond anything we could have imagined back then. But I recognize the same sadness and despair. It pains me deeply to see one, two, or three generations fail the next. We’re handing down a world in ruins, morally, socially and spiritually fractured, with the very fabric that once allowed us to tell fables and parables falling apart.” French-Mexican Alliance As part of the partnership established in 2003 between FICM and Cannes Critics’ Week, this year’s edition presented a selection of eight films and one short that screened at the sidebar last May. Ava Cahen, artistic director of the Cannes Film Festival’s parallel section, led the screenings, which included such titles as Aina Clotet’s “Viva,” Alexander Murphy’s “Tin Castle” and Zou Jing’s “A Girl Unknown.” Toasting Mexico and France’s 200 years of diplomatic relations this year, French ambassador to Mexico Delphine Borione awarded Alfonso Cuarón the insignia of Officer of the Order of Arts and Letters during the fest to honor his “extraordinary contribution to contemporary cinema, singular vision, artistic reinvention and role in bringing Mexican culture to global audiences.” Calling Cuarón “one of the greatest filmmakers of our time,” she praised his universal vision and the cultural ties his work has forged between Mexico and France. “To speak to the world, one must never stop being oneself,” she said, reflecting on his films, from “Y Tu Mamá También” to “Roma.” Reflecting on France’s deep influence on his filmmaking, Cuarón described cinema as “not a narrative art, but a musical art” – a rhythmic, organic creation with its own heartbeat and a direct image of time. He closed by addressing France’s current political turmoil, expressing hope that young people’s calls for change would be heard rather than co-opted by opportunism. Quoting French writer Pascal Quignard, he concluded: “I do not believe art can ever be negative. It ignores negation because it ignores time.” 24 th Morelia Film Festival ‘Ojo’ Winners: Best Feature Film “Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building,” Bruno Santamaria Razo Special Mention “The Garden We Dreamed,” Joaquin del Paso Premio Casa Wabis – Escine Best Debut Feature “Sad Girlz,” Fernanda Tovar Best Director Nicolás Pereda, “Everything Else is Noise” Best Screenplay Joaquín Ruano, “Us” Best Cinematography Gökhan Tiryaki, “The Garden We Dreamed” Best Actress Teresa Sánchez, “Everything Else is Noise” Best Actor Sam Louwyck, “Beauty Salon” Best Documentary “Forensita,” Pablo Vaca Special Mention “The Lost Mariachis,” Francisco Ohem Best Fiction Short “Cuerda Manual,” Gustavo Obregon Special Mention, Fiction “Albatross,” Amandine Thomas Best Documentary Short “Voces en el bosque,” Teresa Camous Guerrero, Arturo López Pio Special Mention, Documentary “Nadie recuerde ese film,” Andrés Pulido Esteva Best Animated Short “Cuna de lobos,” Emilia Schettino Bustamante Special Mention, Animated Short “Cartas a los perdidos,” Adriana Monteforte Lahera International Audience Award “Naza,” Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. articles.title: TitledMiami Vice '85
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Justin Kroll Justin Kroll Film Editor @krolljvar More Stories By Justin Tony Lipp And Dara Gordon Join Entertainment 360 As Partners Cory Michael Smith Joins Scarlett Johansson In ‘Scapegoat’ At Square Peg And A24 Denzel Washington And Christopher McQuarrie Team On New Thriller At United Artists And Amazon MGM Studios View All April 22, 2026 2:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Michael B Jordan; Philip Michael Thomas and Don Johnson in 'Miami Vice'; and Austin Butler Juan Veloz/Michael Buckner for Deadline/Everett Universal Pictures’ upcoming Miami Vice movie officially has its Tubbs and Crockett as well a title, as Michael B. Jordan and Austin Butler are set to star in Miami Vice ’85 with Joseph Kosinski directing. The film will be shot for Imax and is set to bow on August 6, 2027. The film explores the glamour and corruption of mid-’80s Miami in an all-new version of Miami Vice , inspired by the pilot episode and first season of the landmark Universal Television series that influenced culture and set the style in everything from fashion to filmmaking. Related Stories News Universal Dates Joseph Kosinski’s ‘Miami Vice’ For Late Summer 2027 Casting Austin Butler In Early Talks To Play Sonny Crockett In ‘Miami Vice’ Movie At Universal Deadline reported last fall that Jordan and Butler were in talks to star in the pic, but it was not expected to begin production until fall of 2026, so there was no rush to close deals. Insiders add that the film only recently had its budget greenlighted, and deals for Jordan and Butler closed soon after the studio gave the thumbs up. The film will be produced by Dylan Clark and his Dylan Clark Productions and Kosinski. Nightcrawler Oscar nominee Dan Gilroy is writing the script , based on characters created by Anthony Yerkovich from the series executive produced by Yerkovich and Michael Mann. Eric Warren Singer wrote an earlier draft of the screenplay. Watch on Deadline EVP Production Development Sara Scott and Creative Executive of Production Development Christina Hoffrogge will oversee the project for Universal.

On Friday, the Golden Globe nominee teased the “really funny” script from the 2018 film’s co-writer Adele Lim, revealing the filming is taking place in New York City for the one-hour drama series, which got a series order from HBO earlier this month. “Well, I mean, the first movie is based on the book by Kevin Kwan,” she explained on Today . “And he actually has a whole bunch of books in the Crazy Rich Asians world, and so a lot of it follows that. I could tell you that we’re all excited to be coming back. It’s filming here in New York where I live, so I’m thrilled about that. And I think it’s really funny. Chu Shares ‘Crazy Rich Asians’ Series Update: “It’s A Real Thing” Wu confirmed that production starts next year on the eight-episode series, and she’s read a script. “It’s very funny. articles.title: ‘Clayface’ Takes Shape As No. 1 With $23M-$25M; ‘You Can See Everything’s Wild Ride Continues With $19M – Box Office Update
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony Leslie Bibb Boards Amazon MGM Studios’ ‘Upgraded 2’ Opposite Camila Mendes Wayfarer Studios Sets Six For Coming-Of-Age Feature Drama ‘The Alchemy Of Being Okay’ ‘Game Of Pets’: Animated Pic Based On ‘Bad Guys’ Author’s Book Series In Works With Rideback, Foundation Media & Amazon MGM Studios View All October 23, 2026 4:31pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tom Rhys Harries as Matt Hagen in 'Clayface' Warner Bros./Courtesy Everett Collection UPDATED FRIDAY PM: Right now, Warner Bros/DC’s R-rated Clayface is puffing its chest with a $9.5 million Friday (including previews) and an estimated $23M-$25M opening weekend at 3,458 theaters. If that comes to be it’s a solid start in the vicinity of other mid-October genre movies like Smile ($22.6M opening) and last year’s Black Phone 2 ($27.2M). But it still remains to be seen what type of blood transfusion audiences give Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes this weekend as the A24 documentary You Can See Everything is coming on strong with a $5.8M Friday, up 5% from a week ago, and what’s looking to be an awesome $19M+ second weekend after its wide expansion from 855 locations to 2,655. Related Stories News How A24 Spurred A Meme Craze & Got The Many To Watch ‘You Can See Everything’; Documentary Opens To $15M Milestone Reviews Deadline’s Reviews Of This Week’s Box Office Openers: ‘Clayface’, ‘Wildwood’ & More That will get the 10 -day total for the doc to $44.6M . Some rivals think a $20M+ second weekend remains a possibility. But at a $19M second frame, You Can See Everything is up 22% from its opening. Obsession was +39% in its second weekend (though that was during a Memorial Day weekend). Watch on Deadline ‘You Can See Everything’ A24 At this point in time, Clayface is keeping himself together for a No. 1 finish atop the domestic charts after great audience scores (93% on RT) and solid reviews (75%). RelishMix says, “Convo runs positive for Clayface with a felling that James Gunn has finally cracked the code on how to make a villain movie, without Batman holding its hand. Fans see the trailer like a masterclass in restraint, ‘the zero-dialogue approach and letting dread do the talking is working.’ There’s affection bubbling up for Batman: The Animated Series with comments pitching Mr. Freeze, Scarecrow and Poison Ivy follow-ups. Viewers are also spinning Clayface against Spider-Man villain universe, ‘This as the blueprint nobody asked Sony to copy but should have.’ plus, ‘No Dialogue, only horror sounds, and some eerie song playing in the background, THIS is what a horror teaser should be like.'” ‘ Wildwood ‘ Fathom’s theatrical release of Laika’s stop-motion Wildwood is also coming in where it was expected: at $11M+ in third place after a $4.2M Friday (including previews). That’s much better than the Portland, OR studio’s previous movie, 2019’s The Missing Link ($5.9M), which United Artists/Annapurna handled at the time. Travis Knight’s previous Laika movie, Kubo and the Two Strings, released by Focus Features, opened to $12.6M in 2016 and legged out to $48M domestic. Paramount/Legendary’s Street Fighter is fourth at 3,575 theaters with a second Friday of $2.7M and a three-day of $9.5M , -79%, for a 10-day cume of $47.8M . In No. 5 is Black Bear’s $2.5M domestic acquisition of period sex comedy Wicker , with a first Friday (plus previews) of $2.4M and a 3-day of $6M+ at 1,471 locations. This is a great start for Black Bear and an upscale female movie. Audience score on RT is excellent at 94% on par with critical score of 93%. Outside the top 5 is Sony/Spyglass/TSG’s Klara and the Sun from Taika Waititi and starring Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams. The movie isn’t looking good at a $300,000 Friday at 880 locations for what’s looking like a 3-day of $900K . Critics refuse to be emotionally moved with 55 reviews at 23% Rotten. UPDATED FRIDAY AM after Thursday PM exclusive: Warner Bros/DC’s Clayface came in exactly where we spotted it: at $3.5M in previews. We understand the fanboys who showed up last night enjoyed it too with 4 1/2 stars on PostTrak and a 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Meanwhile, A24’s You Can See Everything ends its first week with $25.6M , compared to Street Fighter ‘s $38.3M. The three-hour Nathan Fielder-Lance Oppenheim documentary bested Street Fighter and was the No. 1 movie on Monday ($2.5M), Wednesday ($2.6M) and Thursday ($2.2M). Tuesday was strong with $2.6M. Black Bear’s Sundance pickup Wicker is off to a solid specialty start with $620K in previews, and that’s with 92% reviews and 93% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Pic is booked at 1,471 locations. Previews are above Conclave ($491K, $6.6M opening) and not far from The Social Reckoning ($617K previews, $5M opening), and similar to The Roses , another Olivia Colman movie ($606K, $6.2M opening). Taika Waititi’s feature take of Klara and the Sun is in limited release this weekend in under 1,000 locations. Previews were shiny with $85K at 782 sites from showtimes that began at 4 p.m. Here are this week’s grosses: Street Fighter (Par) 3,575 theaters, Wk $38.3M/Wk 1 You Can See Everything (A24) 855 theaters, Wk $25.6M/Wk 1 Other Mommy (Uni) 3,370 theaters, Wk $11.1M (-70%), Total $47.6M/Wk 2 Whalefall (Dis) 3,065 theaters, Wk $10.8M/Wk 1 Sense and Sensibility (Focus) 2,545 theaters, Wk $10.2M/Wk 1 PREVIOUSLY, Thursday PM EXCLUSIVE: Peter Safran and James Gunn’s DC entry into lower-budget genre movies, Clayface , is off to a solid start in previews Thursday night with an estimated $3.5 million , if not more. Domestic weekend forecasts are between $20M-$25M, which if that occurs would deliver the newly combined Paramount-Warner Bros its second back-to-back No. 1 opener at the box office after last weekend’s Street Fighter ($31M). Previews started at 2 p.m. today for the James Watkins-directed Clayface , which though based on the Batman villain is a stand-alone story about babyfaced Hollywood actor Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), who in reaching for the stars falls short, kisses the wrong girl at the party, and — oops — there goes his face. The screenplay by Mike Flanagan in December 2024 got Gunn and Safran excited, and it was off to the races to make this movie, which is coming in at a net production cost of $44M before P&A, shot in the UK. In regards to preview comps, Clayface ‘s money is higher than the R-rated Sony/Marvel movie Kraven the Hunter ($2M previews, $11M dismal opening), and not far from the pre-Covid PG-13 DC spinoff Birds of Prey ($4M previews, $33M opening). Next to horror films, Clayface ‘s cash is similar to Blumhouse Atomic Monster’s Other Mommy ($3.6M previews, $27.8M opening) and ahead of 2022’s Smile ($2M previews, $22.6M opening). The hope is that the DC movie isn’t frontloaded tonight, as all eyes are on the potential hold of A24 documentary You Can See Everything following its great midweek business and fantastic $15.6M opening last weekend. The documentary co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim about Theranos architect Elizabeth Holmes expands to 2,600 locations Friday after bowing in 855 sites. Clayface glides into the weekend with a 76% certified fresh Rotten Tomatoes critics score, which is higher than The Flash (63%), Supergirl (52% Rotten), Joker Folie à Deux (31%), Shazam: Fury of the Gods (49%), James Wan’s Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom (33%) and almost as good as Birds of Prey (79% certified fresh). ‘V for Vendetta’ Warner Bros. Pictures Note this isn’t the first time in DC movie history that it has ventured into low- to midsized-budget fare. In the early aughts there was DC/Vertigo’s The Losers, in 2010, which cost $25M before P&A and opened to $9.4M and finaled at $23.5M domestic. There was also the Josh Brolin-Megan Fox 2010 fantasy western Jonah Hex, which bombed with a $5.3M opening, $10.5M stateside final next to its $47M production cost. And there was the Wachowskis’ R-rated 2005 feature take of the DC Vertigo title V for Vendetta, which yielded a No. 1 $25.6M North American opening off a $50M production cost. Its final domestic take was $70.5M, and $134.7M global. We’re hearing that previews for the Fathom release of Laika’s stop-motion animated title Wildwood is around $1M . The hope is that the Travis Knight-directed movie can break double-digits in its opening. The 100% certified fresh critical score and 98% with audiences on RT will certainly help. We’ll have more preview grosses in Friday AM. Tonight’s numbers are per distribution sources. articles.title: All The Songs In ‘Klara And The Sun’: Violent Femmes & More
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi Everything We Know About Universal’s ‘Miami Vice ’85’ Movie So Far All The Songs In ‘Klara And The Sun’: Violent Femmes & More All The Songs In Laika’s ‘Wildwood’: From Portugal. The Man To The Decemberists View All October 23, 2026 4:34pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Mia Tharia and Jenna Ortega star in 'Klara and the Sun' Sony 3000 Pictures Taika Waititi ’s Klara and the Sun , based on the book by Kazuo Ishiguro, stars Jenna Ortega as the titular robotic Artificial Friend. The film follows Klara as she wishes for a charge or owner to claim her from the Friend Store, where she gets a limited amount of time in the front alcove to show off and garner attention. Then she is chosen by Josie (Mia Tharia), whose mother Chrissy ( Amy Adams ) is reluctant to purchase an older model of the product when the newer ones are being sold at Fancy Friends down the street. But Klara and Josie’s bond is solid from the moment they meet eye contact. Though Josie is “lifted,” or genetically enhanced, she is also gravely ill, and Klara does her best to cheer her up as well as her mother. The film also features Natasha Lyonne, Aran Murphy, Steve Buscemi and Rachel House. articles.title: Awards Season Heats Up With ‘The Only Living Pickpocket In New York,’ ‘Fatherland’ & More – Specialty Preview
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill Abramorama Takes North America Rights, Sets Release For John David Coles Doc ‘The Choice’ Mayor Zohran Mamdani And Neon Set Free NYC Screenings Of ‘Once Upon A Time In Harlem’ Elon Musk Steps In With $1 Billion Equity Investment For Debt-Laden Skydance — Report View All October 23, 2026 5:30pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: 'The Only Living Pickpocket in New York', 'Wicker', 'Fatherland' and 'A Talent for Murder' Sony PIctures Classics/Black Bear Pictures/Mubi/Bleecker Street The weekend feels awards-y with John Turturro tugging the heartstrings in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , Olivia Colman ( Wicker ) and Helen Mirren ( A Talent For Murder ) in the house, and Hans Zischler and Sandra Hüller playing Thomas Mann and his daughter on a road trip ( Fatherland ). The A24 You Can See Everything phenomenon goes wide, and Netflix expands its TIFF audience award-winner La Bola Negra . Sony Pictures Classics opens the Turturro-starring Pickpocket by Noah Segan in limited release on six screens in New York (AMC Lincoln Square, Angelika Film Center, Bam Rose) and Los Angeles (AMC Burbank, AMC Grove, Laemmle Royal). He plays Harry Lehman, an aging pickpocket who plies his trade with ever-diminishing returns in a drastically changed New York. Related Stories Reviews Deadline’s Reviews Of This Week’s Box Office Openers: ‘Clayface’, ‘Wildwood’ & More News ‘Clayface’ Takes Shape As No. 1 With $23M-$25M; ‘You Can See Everything’s Wild Ride Continues With $19M – Box Office Update Turturro took the Zurich Film Festival’s Golden Eye Award for his performance in the film — Segan’s directorial debut. Steve Buscemi as Harry’s regular fence; Tatiana Maslany as his estranged daughter; and Will Price as the arrogant, heat-packing scion of a Manhattan crime family also star. A favorite out of Sundance where it premiered, the film is Rotten Tomatoes Certified Fresh at 97% . See Deadline’s review , which calls it mesmerizing. Watch on Deadline Mubi is out with Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , also limited, at four theaters in New York (Film Forum, Film at Lincoln Center) and Los Angeles (AMC Burbank, Laemmle Royal). World premiered at Cannes to critical acclaim and the Best Director award for Pawlikowski. At 91% Certified Fresh on Rotten Tomatoes, see Deadline review . In the summer of 1949, at the height of the Cold War, Nobel Prize-winning writer Thomas Mann (Zischler) and his daughter Erika (Hüller) embark on a challenging and emotional road trip across a Germany in ruins, from U.S.-dominated Frankfurt to Soviet-controlled Weimar. Mann, who had returned home after 16 years in exile in the U.S., faced not only a divided fatherland but also a deep fracture within his own family. Pawlikowski picks up here where he left off with his award-winning Ida and Cold War , exploring themes of identity, family, love and guilt amid the turmoil and confusion of post-war Europe. Mubi also debuts Making Marie Antoinette , the late filmmaker Eleanor Coppola’s behind-the-scenes documentation of her daughter Sofia Coppola directing 2006 film Marie Antoinette . Premiered at Telluride, Deadline review here . Opens on 20 screens nationally including NY and L.A. Moderate/wide Bleecker Street, in partnership with longtime collaborator LD Entertainment, releases Anton Corbijn thriller A Talent For Murder on 876 screens with Helen Mirren starring as celebrated crime novelist Patricia Highsmith. World premiered at TIFF, see Deadline review. Based on Joanna Murray-Smith’s acclaimed 2014 play Switzerland , the film follows a young literary agent from New York (Alden Ehrenreich), who travels to Switzerland on a mission to convince the famously reclusive Highsmith to write one final installment in her iconic Ripley series. What begins as a seemingly straightforward assignment soon takes an unexpected turn. Black Bear launches Wicker , the Sundance breakout from Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, at 1,471 theaters. A lusty comedic fable about sex, marriage and social convention centered around a lonely Fisherwoman (Colman), who commissions a wicker husband from the local Basketmaker (Peter Dinklage). Her unexpected romance with the creation (Alexander Skarsgård) sparks jealousy and threatens the village’s social order. The Tailor’s Wife/bullying local queen bee (Elizabeth Debicki) sets out to sabotage the romance. Rotten Tomatoes Certified Fresh at 92% with critics. Audience score of 93%. Deadline review here .

articles.title: Billy Corgan Backs Marilyn Manson Over Sex Abuse Claims, Citing Inside Knowledge Of Case: “I Personally Didn’t Feel He Was Guilty”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Billy Corgan Backs Marilyn Manson Over Sex Abuse Claims, Citing Inside Knowledge Of Case: “I Personally Didn’t Feel He Was Guilty” Nick Reiner Poised To Receive Trust Fund Cash For Defense In Parents’ Murder Case; Lawyer Insists Money Deal Needs “To Get Resolved As Quickly As Possible” Joe Perry Bows Out Of Hollywood Vampires Doc Screening As Aerosmith Ramps Up For Hollywood Bowl Gigs View All October 23, 2026 7:11pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source (L-R) Marilyn Manson & Smashing Pumpkins' Billy Corgan; Hall of Justice in Los Angeles Getty Images “I personally didn’t feel he was guilty of the things he was being charged with,” Billy Corgan says of his old friend Marilyn Manson , who was accused of sexual abuse, domestic violence and more by Evan Rachel Wood and other women. “Ultimately the fact (is) that the D.A. didn’t pursue,” the Smashing Pumpkins leader added. “So, basically, the person that I knew, and the way it all kind of went down, even though it was an elongated process, was commensurate with the person that I knew,” Corgan went on to say on a just released episode of the New York Times podcast Popcast. “I don’t want the world to tell me who my friends are and who I should associate with.” Related Stories Legal Nick Reiner Poised To Receive Trust Fund Cash For Defense In Parents' Murder Case; Lawyer Insists Money Deal Needs "To Get Resolved As Quickly As Possible" Books The Smashing Pumpkins Release Latest 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping' Album Track, 'Black Stars' It is a fact that back in January 2025, newly sworn in L.A. District Attorney Nathan Hochman closed the four-year long probe his office and the Sheriff’s department had been conducting into Manson. “We have determined that allegations of domestic violence fall outside of the statute of limitations, and we cannot prove charges of sexual assault beyond a reasonable doubt,” Hochman said of the much accused shock rocker born Brian Warner. Watch on Deadline At the time , current The Shards star Wood, who had been engaged to Manson during their tumultuous 2007 – 2010 relationship, stated that she and her lawyer were told by “Deputy District Attorneys and the Sheriff deputies who investigated the case that there was compelling evidence to support our claims, but that the statute of limitations prevents many of those crimes from being prosecuted.” Writing online, Wood, who had testified before California’s state Senate on sexual and domestic violence and was a booster of the non-retroactive statute of limitations extending 2024 Phoenix Act, tersely noted “violent crimes should not have an expiration date.” In his Popcast appearance, Corgan didn’t address the specifics of why the D.A. dropped the case and never mentioned Wood, Game of Thrones actress Esmé Bianco ( who settled her sexual assault and battery claims with the ‘Beautiful People’ singer in 2023), or other Manson accusers by name. He did however pull back the Gen X rockstar curtain a bit in offering his POV. “The other thing that people should know, and it may gets lost in the gloss here, is Manson’s wife, Lindsay, is a twin, and her twin is Ashley, and Ashley is married to James Iha of the Pumpkins,” the Grammy winning guitarist explained to Popcast hosts Jon Caramanica and Joe Coscarelli. “So, Manson’s basically a part of our family. Anybody in that situation struggles with the accusations, the seriousness of the accusations.” “I also knew the inside baseball of the case. I knew certain people who were involved, and so you make those evaluations.” View this post on Instagram Despite the Popcast sit-down proving wide-ranging on a number of professional and personal subjects, Corgan, who had Manson as a guest at his birthday party earlier this year, did not elaborate on the aforementioned “inside baseball” nor who the other individuals involved were besides obviously Manson himself. Shifting his perspective somewhat, Corgan went on to say of Manson and the very high profile situation: “If he’s guilty or anybody in that situation is guilty, they should go to jail. I’m not saying I have any moral supremacy here. I’m saying it’s a case by case basis. This kind of witch mob thing bothers me.” In the aftermath of allegations from Wood and then others, Manson was dumped by CAA as a client and lost acting roles in American Gods and Creepshow . From 2020 to 2025 and beyond, Manson has decried the claims from various women as “horrible distortions of reality. Even though he was ordered in late 2024 to pay Wood nearly $327,000 in legal fees from suing her for defamation in 2022 , the now 57-year old Manson has insisted that his past relationships were “entirely consensual with like-minded partners.” As he has for many years, accusations and otherwise, Manson is out playing gigs to a loyal fanbase. He will be playing L.A.’s Wiltern on Halloween and on November 1, with a show at London’s Wembley Stadium set for May next year. This weekend finds Manson on-stage at Fort Worth’s Texas Motor Speedway on October 24. JC Olivera/PMC/Parisa Taghizadeh/Warner Bros./Courtesy Everett Collection In DC Studios ‘ Clayface , Tom Rhys Harries’ titular shape-shifting Batman villain takes multiple forms, including a surprising familiar face. Following murmurs of a cameo, director James Watkins confirmed that Aaron Paul makes a brief appearance in the DCU movie as Matt’s (Harries) father, who raised him in the slums of Gotham City. “He has a real brief Easter egg kind of moment,” Watkins told Entertainment Weekly . Related Stories Reviews ‘Clayface’ Review: DCU Molds Batman Villain’s Origin Story Into Fun, Scary Body Horror Trailers ‘Clayface’ Trailer: DC Studios’ Batman Bad Guy Gets His Close-Up While flashbacks of Paul as Matt’s father were ultimately cut from the film, the Breaking Bad alum makes a quick appearance in the action-packed Club Vesuvius scene, in which Matt shape-shifts into multiple people to take on Szabo’s (David Dencik) goons before taking has dad’s form to kill Jimmy “One Nut” (Enzo Squillino Jr.), the gangster who took his father’s life years before. Watch on Deadline “In terms of trying to figure out the character, it was, How much is Matt defined by his past and how much is he an everyman?” the director explained. “At one point, we were looking at it and thinking, Is it the ‘sins of the father’?” Watkins continued, “But actually, as we worked on the script, I thought that notion of revenge was more universal and more relatable to all of us. But when he discovers the groundbreaking nanotech research of Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), Matt convinces her to restore his face to its former glory, only to result in terrifying side effects and a bloody quest for revenge. articles.title: Karoline Leavitt Compares Katie Zacharia’s Abrupt Exit As Trump’s Press Secretary To ‘The Apprentice’: “He’s Known For … Moving On From People”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Karoline Leavitt Compares Katie Zacharia’s Abrupt Exit As Trump’s Press Secretary To ‘The Apprentice’: “He’s Known For … Moving On From People” FCC’s Sole Democrat Calls On Broadcast Lobby To Push Back On Trump-Backed Chairman’s Regulatory Threats Over Election Coverage Donald Trump Lashes Out At NBC News Reporter As She Presses Him On Why He Supports Ad That Has Been Condemned By Democrats And Republicans View All October 23, 2026 8:16pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Karoline Leavitt Getty Images Karoline Leavitt appeared on HBO’s Real Time with Bill Maher on Friday and was questioned about the short stint of her successor as Donald Trump ‘s White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia. After doing just one briefing that lasted 14 minutes, Zacharia was ousted last Friday, after less than a week in the job. Leavitt told Maher that “it’s a tough job” and one of the “hardest” in Washington. “That pressure in that room is enormous,” Leavitt said. “The press are vicious, and you know I give her credit for standing up there. And as the president said, it wasn’t a good fit, and that’s okay. I wish her well, and we’re on to the next. And he has a lot of options.” Related Stories News FCC's Sole Democrat Calls On Broadcast Lobby To Push Back On Trump-Backed Chairman's Regulatory Threats Over Election Coverage News Donald Trump Lashes Out At NBC News Reporter As She Presses Him On Why He Supports Ad That Has Been Condemned By Democrats And Republicans Maher, though, said that that “sometimes you give up a home run at the first inning. They don’t usually go to the bullpen that quick.” Watch on Deadline Leavitt responded, “Look, I mean, the president did have a hit show called The Apprentice , where he’s known for, you know, moving on from people. So hey, it’s in his nature to do that type of thing, I guess.” Earlier, Maher quipped that Zacharia’s tenure was shorter than the dinner he had with Trump last week that lasted for four hours. At that sitdown at the White House, Maher was joined by Stephen A. Smith and Kid Rock. The HBO host credited Trump with listening to him as he challenged him on certain issues, like ICE, degrading Ukraine’s Starlink access, as well as telling the president that Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth “is dragging you down.” “There are so many moments where he gets it,” Maher said. “Like I said to him, ‘You know, when you said the Supreme Court, they’re voting against me? You know that’s not how the Supreme Court is supposed to work, right? They’re not voting for or against you. You appoint them and they make decisions.’ And he went, ‘Yeah, I took that one too personally.'” Maher added, “He gets it and then he doesn’t get it. Now I’m an optimist. I prefer to think of the president as half sane.” In response, Leavitt tried for a bit of whataboutism, telling Maher that Trump is “very sane. He’s a lot more, I think we can agree, he is far more sane than the last one. We had a mental patient.” “He’s far more energetic,” Maher said. But Maher returned to what happened during the dinner with Trump. “We have a nice conversation and he goes, ‘You’re my enemy. Pass the peas.’ I mean, he will say that, ‘You’re my enemy,’ and then a minute later, we’re just talking normally, and we don’t act like enemies.” Maher also told Leavitt that he was worried over what Trump will do if the midterms go bad for Trump and Republicans. “We know he likes vengeance,” he said. Leavitt, though, said that she doesn’t “worry about the president. Look, he loves our country very much, and he wants to make it right.” She even suggested that he would work with Democrats, noting that he has worked with D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser. During her tenure, Leavitt was known for her steadfast defense of the president, even if that meant delivering regular lectures to the media on their coverage of the administration. Even though she was highly praised for her performance, it didn’t stop the fall in Trump’s approval rating, which has dropped to an average of 38.8% from 50.5% at the start of his term, per Real Clear Politics. Maher pressed Leavitt on Trump’s recent moves to waive sanctions on Russia, calling it “unconscionable,” along with “basically putting a knife in the back of [Ukraine’s president] Zelensky.” Maher asked, “Is there anything that could make you, because a lot of Republicans now say we’ve had enough, make you not be loyal to whatever he was doing?” Leavitt, who is soon to become a commentator for Fox News, gave no indication that there was anything. “He was my boss, but to me, he’s also a friend, and he gave me the opportunity of a lifetime.” Quentin Tarantino Surprises At AFI Fest, Shows First 17 Minutes Of ‘Cliff Booth’ Inside BBC Cuts: Service Closures Begin, But Worse Could Be To Come ‘Clayface’ Shaping Up At $23M-$25M; ‘See Everything’ Wide-Eyes $19M Casey Bloys’ New DTC Team Is All HBO Max Execs; Par+’s Jane Wiseman Out Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Quentin Tarantino Wraps His AFI Fest Q&A By Showing Crowd First 17 Minutes Of ‘Cliff Booth’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Peter Berg’s Powerful True WWII Story Takes Four Star Players From The Glory Of The Football Field To The Hell Of The Battlefield – AFI Fest ‘Wicker’ Review: Olivia Colman And Peter Dinklage Turn Alexander Skarsgård Into A Sexy Basket Case In Comic Fable That’s Pure Delight ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Review: Sacha Baron Cohen’s Signature Prankster Returns In Outrageous Form With Something To Offend Everyone View All October 23, 2026 11:37pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth in 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' Netflix Quentin Tarantino surprised the crowd during a Q&A and screening of his 10-time Oscar-nominated Once Upon a Time in Hollywood on Friday night at AFI Fest in Los Angeles by screening the first 17 minutes of its sequel The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth . It marks the first public look at the film, a follow-up to Hollywood that Tarantino scripted and David Fincher directed. Brad Pitt revises his Oscar-winning role as Booth, a stuntman and sidekick to Leonardo DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton in the original 2019 film. Related Stories Trailers ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: Brad Pitt Revisits The Character That Won Him An Oscar In David Fincher’s Latest News ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’: New Photos Of Film Starring Brad Pitt, Elizabeth Debicki, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II & More Netflix is gearing up for the Cliff Booth theatrical release November 25 in Imax before hitting the streamer beginning December 23. Watch on Deadline “Well, I could talk a little bit about The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , or I could show you the first 17 minutes,” Tarantino said at the end of his special-event Q&A session at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood. He had just been asked about the film and how it came about, and if he had anything else to say before the conversation wrapped. He then stood up as the crowd began to figure out what was coming. Here’s the moment: Quentin Tarantino reflects on the decision to revisit Cliff Booth as he introduces the first 17 minutes of ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ at AFI Fest pic.twitter.com/0flrYw0J73 — Deadline (@DEADLINE) October 24, 2026 Cliff Booth fast-forwards to 1977 from the original film’s 1969 timeline. The new logline: Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s great and, sometimes, not so good. The pic also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Peter Weller, Matt Groove, JB Tadena, Corey Fogelmanis and Karren Karagulian. Buzz for the film has been building since it was announced in 2024 that Pitt and Fincher were teaming on the project that Tarantino originally wanted to direct. Fincher said earlier this week that he had to cut 60 pages from Tarantino’s script, after he said the first draft he read was 230 pages. “It was essentially two movies,” Fincher told Empire . The final cut of the film, Fincher said, has a runtime of around 2 1/2 hours. During tonight’s AFI Fest event, Tarantino also talked about his upcoming play The Popinjay Cavalier , which will premiere in London’s West End next spring. Sacha Baron Cohen will star in the director’s first stage play, which begins previews February 23 and opens March 18 at the Phoenix Theatre. Quentin Tarantino on his debut stage play, which stars Sacha Baron Cohen and will open on the West End next year pic.twitter.com/jMUAJpEuCN — Deadline (@DEADLINE) October 24, 2026 Patrick Hipes contributed to this report. articles.title: Inside The BBC Cuts: Painful Service Closures Begin, But Worse Could Be To Come
articles.full_text: “The world needs the BBC more than ever. It might be a different size and shape. It’s not going to be a so-so Netflix or a me-too YouTube. It’s going to be a better BBC.” That was the message Matt Brittin left ringing in the ears of BBC staff when concluding a town hall last month. The director general was attempting to lift the gloom after being beset with questions from anxious employees about job losses, service reductions, and general retrenchment. He has an uneviable task. Brittin is grappling with a financial crisis that is precipitating some of the most painful cuts in the BBC’s history. He is also attempting to cement the BBC’s position as Britain’s premium media brand in an era of unprecedented competition. Related Stories News International Insider: Turmoil At Netflix; MIA Market Report; Patrick Brammall Interview News Trump Ordered By Judge To Sit For Deposition In $10B Lawsuit Against The BBC These two objectives are not obviously compatible, but Brittin’s pitch to staff is that they are not incompatible. It’s why, when he announced the closure of linear networks BBC Three , BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra on Tuesday, he said the decisions were necessary to both “respond to immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world.” Watch on Deadline It’s not an easy sell to an unsettled workforce that is all too aware that worse is yet to come. The BBC must save £500 million ($670M) by 2028 after hemorrhaging more than two million licence fee payers since 2020. Despite relentless internal memos about layoffs and content cuts since the summer, the BBC has only announced £200M of its half-billion goal. In other words, it’s not even halfway through the cuts. Closing BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra may seem substantial, but the reality is that switching off these services in spring 2027 will only save around £10M, according to two insiders. In the case of BBC Three, the network spectrum from which the channel broadcasts will continue to be an expense because it also houses CBBC, the children’s network that airs between 7AM and 7PM. Deadline can reveal that BBC leaders did discuss merging CBBC with the corporation’s other children’s network, CBeebies. The BBC would have banked a more significant saving alongside the closure of BBC Three, but executives dismissed the idea because they did not wish to call into question the corporation’s commitment to kids’ public service media. CBBC series ‘The Worst Witch’ starred Bella Ramsey A senior insider, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the closure of CBBC was deemed too “politically dangerous” when the BBC is negotiating its funding settlement and charter with the UK government. A second source added that Lisa Nandy believes BBC children’s services should be protected — perhaps unsurprising after her first visit to the BBC as culture secretary involved meeting Hacker T Dog, CBBC’s resident puppet. BBC Sounds Under Threat? That the BBC even contemplated CBBC’s future is revealing of the agonizing decisions facing Brittin as he attempts to put the broadcaster on a surer financial footing. Speculation internally has turned to the future of another service: BBC Sounds, the radio and podcast streaming service launched in 2018. Deadline hears that the BBC has held tentative discussions about whether Sounds could be folded in with iPlayer to create a single streaming service for video and audio, not unlike Netflix and YouTube. A BBC insider said it is symptomatic of the BBC “having to dig much deeper and be more radical to find savings.” Although no decisions have been made and Sounds is not under immediate threat, there are signals that point in this direction. During an internal all-staff call earlier this month, Brittin said he wanted iPlayer to be an “entertainment destination,” and asked Manon Dave, a product designer, to demonstrate a reimagined iPlayer where audio and video dovetailed. A further clue came this week, when BBC content chief Kate Phillips merged TV and audio commissioning teams in comedy and arts. Somewhat counterintuitively, BBC Media Tech, the division that powers online platforms, is among the hardest hit by the cuts. The unit must save £102M by next year , but the talk is that a smaller team will focus on fewer products, which also fits with the emerging narrative around a single streaming service. BBC News BBC The BBC has announced around 1,200 job cuts in recent months, which is 800 shy of its intended target. Some think the BBC could exceed 2,000 redundancies. On-screen presenters like health editor Hugh Pym have decided to leave and will not be replaced as BBC News contributes at least £51M to the savings pot. Staff morale is low amid the drip-drip of redundancy announcements, which follows the BBC’s workforce contracting by 10% since 2020. The BBC is also navigating fraught negotiations over a staff pay deal, with the corporation infuriating unions by bundling in changes to terms and conditions, such as curbing cab usage for night shift workers . Many think industrial action is likely. “There’s a lot of anger and bitterness,” said one insider. “If we all took work-to-rule [industrial action] and refused to do overtime, and turned our phones off for our lunch break, it would cause them a real headache.” Another spoke of a “f**k it feeling” internally: “The longer cuts get drawn out, the more uncertain everything feels. You think, God, do I really want to be sticking around for whatever this might end up being?” A former Google executive, Brittin is trying to inject more Silicon Valley spirit and speed into the BBC’s culture. He is known to be disarmingly direct in meetings, unapologetically taking team members to task if they do not support their assumptions with audience data. “I’d like us to celebrate activity less, and outcomes more,” he told colleagues this month. BBC Three Not Mourned The closure of BBC Three, BBC Scotland, and Radio 4 Extra has not provoked significant backlash. When BBC Three was first taken off air in 2016, campaigners rallied to save the channel and two producers, Hat Trick boss Jimmy Mulville and Avalon co-founder Jon Thoday, made a serious offer to acquire the network. A decade on, Thoday is unmoved by the switch-off. “I don’t think the BBC should have got rid of BBC Three in the first place. I don’t think they should have brought it back in the second place. And I’m not going to lose any sleep over them getting rid of it now,” said Thoday, who produces HBO’s Last Week Tonight with John Oliver . “All I hope is that the cancelation of BBC Three for the second time results in the BBC increasing its spend on content for young people. It’s really important that the BBC increases and leads on comedy investment and lets comedy bring young viewers to the BBC.” A former BBC executive added that the “terrible” decision to reinstate the channel in 2022 had harmed BBC Three, which was hit by low linear ratings for flagship shows. “It killed it,” they said. RuPaul’s Drag Race UK, The Rap Game and I Kissed a Girl/Boy have all been cancelled recently, meaning there is space for a creative refresh of the brand on iPlayer. The BBC has committed to increasing investment for younger audiences, but offered no detail on the value and scope of this ambition. ‘RuPaul’s Drag Race UK’ airs on BBC Three BBC/World of Wonder Perhaps the most ominous thing for the BBC is that it is not in control of what comes next. Funding talks with the government are progressing slowly, despite Westminster press briefings about enthusiasm for a so-called “Netflix tax,” which would involve charging consumers extra for subscription streaming services to help pay for the BBC. Ministers like this idea, and the BBC has not dismissed the solution, but there are those at the corporation who are skeptical that it will solve its funding crisis. The protracted talks leave the BBC with no visibility over its finances beyond the end of next year, an extraordinary situation for any organization that relies on £3.9 billion of public income. The BBC expects the government to publish its policy position before the end of the year. As director-general Matt Brittin looks to forge a “sovereign” streaming service from a smaller BBC, clarity can’t come soon enough. Read More About: 2 Comments

articles.title: Anika Rashaun Dies: ‘Real World’, ‘The Challenge’ Alum Was 34
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘The Notebook’ Musical Plans West End Premiere Jonathan Groff Returning To Broadway In Solo Play ‘The Amish Project’ ‘The Imaginary Invalid’ Broadway Review: Molière Gets Clowned By A Winning Bill Irwin View All October 24, 2026 6:08am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Anika Rashaun Anika Rashaun Instagram Anika Rashaun , the Reality TV star who appeared and competed on MTV’s The Real World and The Challenge and later became a professional matchmaker, advice columnist and dating coach, died October 1 of breast cancer. She was 34. Rashaun’s death was announced by friends on social media. Cyndi Rich wrote on Facebook , “Anika shined so bright. Being close to that light as one of her closest friends was a true blessing. She is a vibrant soul. I’ll love her and treasure the 16 years of memories forever.” Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries Obituaries Michael Gray Dies: ‘Shazam!’ Star Was 75 In a Substack tribute , Rashaun’s friend Tiara Ramos wrote that Rashaun was diagnosed with stage 4 breast cancer last summer. “My world already feels dulled and blurred without her,” Ramos writes. “The urge to pick up the phone and FaceTime her is a reflex I can’t shake. Knowing the pain her husband, her parents, her loved ones, and her community are feeling right now makes me sick. I am angry. I am heartbroken. I am devastated.” Watch on Deadline Rashaun first appeared at age 24 on MTV’s The Real World Seattle: Bad Blood in 2016 and, the following year, returned to take part in The Challenge: Invasion of the Champions . For The Real World 2016-2017 “bad blood” season, in which Real World housemates were eventually joined by people they considered nemeses, Rashaun was paired with her ex-boyfriend Will. The synopsis for that season notes, “Ex-lovers Anika and Will go together like oil and water: The yin yang pair dated for three years, and during that time Anika was constantly annoyed that Will couldn’t match her dominance.” After the season ended, Rashaun, a New York City native, moved to Los Angeles and, building on the social media following she attained through the series, built a lifestyle brand that would eventually include matchmaking and dating advice. She remained cordial with Will, though lost touch after the show. In 2017, Rashaun returned to the MTV universe for The Challenge: Invasion of the Champions. She was eliminated in the third episode. Theo King-Bradley, who appeared in both of Rashaun’s seasons on Real World and The Challenge , posted a tribute on Instagram (see it below). “I’ve been doing everything else to keep my mind off the fact that you’re not here. I’ve genuinely been sad as hell since hearing you passed. I’m sad I didn’t get to see you one last time. But the last time and conversation we had with each other I can cherish and play it back in my mind to smile.” After her stint on The Challenge , Rashaun returned to her career as dating coach and lifestyle podcast host. According to her Instagram, she attended school to become a licensed marriage and family therapist. Rashaun married her boyfriend Kyle Rehn on Valentine’s Day this year. Complete information on survivors was not immediately available.
