articles.title: ‘Apart,’ Set in Cyprus and Apartheid South Africa, “Challenges the Idea of ‘Us’ and ‘Them'” (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 23, 2026 1:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Apart' Courtesy of PÖFF Can a young woman forced to leave a divided Cyprus in the 1970s find belonging and even love in an arranged marriage in Apartheid South Africa, especially when a secret from her past threatens to change everything? With Apart , South African Cypriot writer-director Stelana Kliris ( Find Me Falling , Committed ) has created a deeply personal film about displacement, belonging, borders, both the ones that are physical and those that are in our hearts, and human connections. And it is inspired by the real experiences of her refugee parents. The movie, world-premiering at the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF), stars Leem Lubany ( Omar , Rock the Kasbah ), Luca Pasqualino ( Rivals , The Musketeers ) and Girley Jazama ( Under the Hanging Tree , The White Line ). Related Stories Movies 'Biermann' Director Explains Why His Doc About a German Political Singer Is a Film for the Trump Era Business Nobody Knew This Game Existed, and Now It's a Hot 2027 Title “In 1974, when Turkey invades Cyprus, young Eleni (Lubany) leaves her homeland through an arranged marriage and finds herself in Apartheid South Africa, swapping one divided country for another,” reads a synopsis for the film. “There, a new life with Nico (Pasqualino) slowly turns into love, until an unexpected friendship forces her to confront a secret from her past.” Shot in Cyprus with a story that goes between Cyprus and South Africa, Apart brings a turbulent time in the 1970s to life, with a focus on a female perspective. The filmmaker’s Find Me Falling became the first Cypriot film to premiere on Netflix. Apart will open Tallinn’s Critics’ Picks section. “With this very personal and ambitious film, Stelana Kliris has delivered a deeply moving cinematic ode to humanity, a film that will stay with you long after the final frame,” the festival website teases. With cinematography by Simon Sarketzis and editing by Emilios Avraam, Apart is being sold by Reinvent Yellow Sales. The producers are Kliris, Susan Simnett, Jamie Harvey and Ioanna Bolomyti. “It has always fascinated me that people like my parents, who emigrated from Cyprus to South Africa, left one divided place for another, and I wanted to translate this into a film that challenges the idea of ‘us’ and ‘them,’ and, whilst the central narrative is fictional, the individual events around it are from real events,” Kliris says. “This is an intimate, character-driven film with a specific set of aesthetics that represents not just the two locations, but two distinct periods, 1970s South Africa interwoven with flashbacks to the Cypriot past, and while war and Apartheid serve as the backdrop, our story of love, friendship and identity provides for a more human, intimate experience.” THR can now exclusively premiere the trailer for Apart . Prepare for a touching journey through time and across the globe to get a first glimpse of the challenges and emotions the protagonists experience. THR

articles.title: Judge Orders Trump to Testify Under Oath in BBC Defamation Lawsuit
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 23, 2026 1:55am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Donald Trump at a midterm rally in Kansas, Oct. 19, 2026. Courtesy of Getty Logo text A U.S. judge has told Donald Trump that he must answer questions in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC or face sanctions. If the President does not sit for a deposition under oath by Dec. 11, the most extreme outcome might include the dismissal of the entire suit, according to the BBC . Last year, Trump sued the British broadcaster over claims that a BBC Panorama documentary was doctored to make it appear as though Trump, during his Jan. 6, 2021 speech outside the White House, had urged his followers to attack the Capitol. Related Stories Business Nobody Knew This Game Existed, and Now It's a Hot 2027 Title TV 'MobLand' EP Teases What Season 3 Holds for Tom Hardy as 'Laird' Star Peter Sarsgaard Shares How He Feels About Playing a "Malevolent U.S. Billionaire" The 33-page document, brought in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida last December, alleges that the BBC made “a false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump.” A BBC spokesperson told The Hollywood Reporter as news of the lawsuit broke: “While the BBC sincerely regrets the manner in which the video clip was edited, we strongly disagree [that] there is a basis for a defamation claim.” Ten months later, Trump cancelled a previous deposition set for Oct. 16, citing “matters of national importance.” A lawyer for the BBC said in court that Trump was actually campaigning in Georgia and had “prioritized that” over answering questions. U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett said Trump must sit for the deposition by Dec. 11 or he’ll face sanctions, unless this “discovery period” — described by the BBC as the phase where both sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence — is extended. All of this came about when a leaked BBC memo from an independent advisor, a man named Michael Prescott, concluded that the doc Trump: A Second Chance? “seemed to be taking a distinctly anti-Trump stance.” In the speech, Trump said: “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol, and we’re going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women.” However, in the Panorama edit, he was shown saying: “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol … and I’ll be there with you. And we fight. We fight like hell.” The two clips stitched together were, in actuality, more than 50 minutes apart. THR

articles.title: Kim Kardashian Read Every Page of Her Authorized Biography. Here’s What She Pushed Back On.
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Illustrated By Christopher Hughes Jonathan Van Meter, the legendary magazine writer and editor, has spent much of his career getting unusually close to famous women. His intimate profiles on cultural powerhouses like Oprah Winfrey, Jennifer Aniston, Jodie Foster, Liza Minnelli and Lady Gaga, to name a few, have appeared in the pages of Esquire , Vanity Fair , New York and Vogue , among scores of other glossies. I have known Jonathan for more than 30 years, since we were both came of age in New York magazine publishing during its last golden age, the early 1990s. He is a gifted reporter, a superb raconteur and, as anyone who knows him will attest, a man with very strong feelings about practically everything. Related Stories Beyond the Book "Respect Rather Than Reverence": Inside the Making of a Grittier 'Sense and Sensibility' TV 'Fourth Wing' Author Breaks Silence on Casting, Esther McGregor and Emilio Sakraya to Star as Violet and Xaden So when he told me during the pandemic that he intended to devote the next several years to writing a biography of Kim Kardashian , I was intrigued — and skeptical. Kardashian might be the most extensively documented woman of her generation. Between reality television, social media and a bottomless tabloid appetite, what could possibly remain to discover? And how would a writer who specializes in emotional complexity get beneath the exquisitely managed surface of someone who has built a billion-dollar-scale public identity around revealing herself while simultaneously giving almost nothing away? The result is Citizen Kim , an authorized biography that took five years to report and write. Van Meter spent time in Kardashian’s homes, accompanied her to photo shoots, watched her conduct business and interviewed dozens of people from across her life. He also discovered that access has its own complications. Kardashian read the manuscript, objected to some passages and, according to Van Meter, ultimately accepted almost all of them. He, meanwhile, found himself increasingly protective of his subject — a predicament he discussed with his therapist. I am aware that one old friend interviewing another about the hazards of getting too close to your subject carries its own set of ironies. We talked anyway, about the handshake deal that got him in the door, Kim’s infamous sex tape, the people he didn’t get to talk to him (Kanye West, Ray J and Paris Hilton, who canceled 17 times) and whether a biographer can fall in love with his subject and still find a way to tell the truth about her. You’re in the thick of your press tour right now. How’s it going? I did three interviews this morning: Dutch, German, German. For some reason, the fucking Germans love this book. But there’s no book tour, no in-person events, no book party. It’s all Zoom and podcasts. I put on some lip balm, throw on a nice shirt and sit down in my office. What’s interesting is seeing what people take. The Daily Mail paid the U.K. publisher a lot of money for an excerpt and cherry-picked everything remotely scandalous. It was the opposite of the book I was trying to write. But the publisher had the right to do it. Are there still people who simply refuse to take her seriously? Every day. Some people hear you’re writing about Kim Kardashian, and their face sinks. When Vanity Fair ran an excerpt and collaborated with me on Instagram, a ton of comments came into my feed. I’d never really studied them. There’s a group that says, “She’s only famous because of a sex tape. It’s not that deep, bro.” They don’t want analysis of any kind. When Kim finally followed me on Instagram, people started sending messages asking me to get their clothing lines to her. She hadn’t even followed me during the five years I was writing the book. Clockwise: Magazine writer and editor Jonathan Van Meter. Lady Gaga spotted leaving Chez André in 2010 in Paris (Van Meter is second from left). From left: Van Meter, Renée Zellweger and artist Ross Bleckner in 2005. Kendall Jenner ran out of gas in Beverly Hills in 2016, the year that Van Meter wrote about Kendall for her first Vogue cover and in the process met Kris Jenner and Kim Kardashian. Jason Schmidt/Marc Piasecki/Filmmagic/Fameflynet.uk.com/Splashnews.com/Lisa Mauceri/Filmmagic Why Kim? You could have chosen any number of subjects. I wrote a Vogue cover story about her in 2019. When it came out, she called me from Bali, at three in the morning, and said, “There’s no better feeling in the world than when someone gets you.” I said, “I’m going to write a book about you someday.” Then the pandemic happened, I drank for three months, I sobered up, and I thought, “What am I going to do? Why not a book about Kim?” I talked to my agent, Todd Shuster, and began texting her. There was never any resistance. I could tell she was game. Eventually I said I was coming to L.A. for three months in the summer of 2021. And I started going to her house. Nothing was ever signed. She stayed committed for five years. I thought it would take two years, and so did she, but she never bailed. That seems extraordinary for somebody so famously controlling of her image. What were the ground rules? My agent talked to her lawyer. We called it the Todd Summit because they were both named Todd. The only precondition was that Kim got to read the book for fact-checking. Nobody said, “You can’t talk to these people,” or, “She won’t discuss that.” We just jumped in. It made me wonder whether the idea that she’s controlling about everything is wrong. Maybe this is how she is. But “fact-checking” can mean different things to different people. What happened when she disliked something? She did her homework. She went through it page by page: “Page 33, this is wrong. That was 2002.” Then we had a Zoom with two people who work for her and another long phone call. That’s when she said things like, “This part, really? Do we have to?” And I’d say, “We do.” What was she most upset about? The number one thing was the way I wrote about her father. She kept saying, “There’s just a tone.” And when I looked again, I thought, “You know what? She’s right.” It was a little snarky. He’s been dead for so long that he had stopped feeling like a real person to me. To her, he’s still alive in her mind. She also thought the sex tape material went on too long, and the Damon Thomas [Kardashian’s first husband] material made her squirm. But she read a couple of other chapters [about her earlier years] and cried because they were so true to her experience as a 13-year-old. She said it made her give that little girl some grace. In the end, she accepted the material she had objected to. I cut two sentences for her because they concerned her safety. “She wanted to be famous so badly, she got exactly what she wanted, and she loves it.” Jonathan Van Meter, on Kardashian (pictured in ninth grade) @kimkardashian/Instagram. Has her family read it? A couple of months ago, Kim called me late at night. She’d been at Khloé’s house, where Khloé told her Kris had flipped out on camera while they were filming the show. She was yelling, “Why did Kim drag us all into this? Why is my affair from 30 years ago in the book?” Two days later, Kris was fine. But it’s going to be on the show. Kim said to her mother: “All this stuff gets written about us, and then a guy comes along who gets us and wants to explain us. Why wouldn’t you want that?” That’s the closest I got to an answer about why she did the book. So why did she take that risk in the first place? Was she looking for legitimacy? I think that’s the simplest answer. She’d been written about for years through scandal and gossip, and here was somebody who wanted to really explain her. But in 2020, that felt more urgent than it does now. People increasingly understand that her criminal justice work is real, that she studied law seriously. There are still people who hear you’re writing a biography of Kim Kardashian and look at you as though you’ve lost your mind. It’s in the first line of the book: You can tell a lot about a person when you say you’re writing a book about Kim Kardashian. She has documented so much of her own life already. What could you discover that wasn’t already splashed across television or Instagram? Her life is so self-mediated. Nobody had really told it from a writer’s perspective. She understood that: “I know this book is from your point of view. It’s your book.” The challenge was vulnerability. Her childhood friends said she never showed it, even as a little girl. You couldn’t tell how she felt about difficult things. What she did intuit was how journalism works. Most people outside the business don’t understand the difference between “off the record” and “on background.” Kim did. She’d say, “I’ll tell you this whole weird, crazy, dark story, and then we can decide what words I want to come out of my mouth. I want you to know it and I want you to write about it, but I don’t want it coming from me.” It took until the summer of 2024, when I spent time with her in Malibu, before she really cracked open. What changed in Malibu? The visits were open-ended, and she was alone. Before that, I’d interview her while she worked out, or she’d call while getting her hair dyed. We’d talk at photo shoots, with a whole glam squad around. I estimate we spent something like 50 hours together going back to 2019. She could be completely open, but there was a boundary. In Malibu, it was just, “Come over.” We’d hang out in the living room. Most of the time she was in sweats, without makeup. Once she had just had a needling procedure and her face was bruised. Another time she came down the staircase in this gold outfit, fully made up, from a child’s dinosaur-themed birthday party. I asked what she was dressed as. She said, “Cleopatra.” Tell me about your first real dinner together. Casa Vega, in the Valley. She drove herself up in a Range Rover, wearing a full-length black leather coat and boots. We sat down, and she was just like every other girl. She ordered a strawberry daiquiri, took three sips, and I asked if I could finish it. Then she noticed girls at another table filming her. They eventually approached us, pretty aggressively. She handled it like a pro. I was struck by how normal she could be in a situation that was completely abnormal. Paris HIlton and Kardashian in 2006. Van Meter noted that Hilton canceled their interview 17 times over about four months: “Eventually I thought the cancellations were more interesting than whatever she’d tell me. Kim was so mad when I told her. It seemed to stir up some ancient irritation between them. The creation turning on the creator.” Chris Polk/Filmmagic For Bragman Nyman Cafarelli You also saw her deal with her daughter North when she was upset. There was a Vogue shoot, and North had imagined that she and Kim would wear matching dresses. When they didn’t, she had a meltdown. Kim took her away. Later she told me they’d laid on the bed together for about 15 minutes without talking. She just held her until she calmed down, then explained things to her. I remember thinking, “My mother never did that for me.” It made me feel Kim trusted me with something parents don’t necessarily want outsiders to see. I know you grew up in relatively modest circumstances in Atlantic City. Were you surprised by the scale of Kim’s life? I walked into her house one day and saw a woman mopping floors way off in the distance. It reminded me of The Crown , where you occasionally see somebody vacuuming Buckingham Palace. There’s always somebody cleaning, a chef, nannies, assistants. But I never felt the grossness I’ve sometimes felt around very rich people. It felt warm. At the same time, there are gates into Hidden Hills and then another gate and armed security. It’s a bubble. How much of the apparent domestic normalcy survives the machinery around her? Both things exist. You go through a gate into Hidden Hills, then through another gate at her house, and there’s armed security. But the family lives nearby, and the kids ride their bikes between houses. In Malibu, she told me she bought the house next door so the employees could work and park over there. She was trying to get the chaos out of her home. And there were odd, unguarded moments. At a photo shoot, I looked up from my phone and she was completely naked while people helped her change. Neither of us flinched. At another shoot, she was texting like a chainsaw, but she still heard every word of the conversation happening around her. You watched her work up close. How much of the business is actually Kim and how much is the team around her? I went to see her one day when she was shooting two back-to-back covers — one of them was Vogue Hong Kong. We were in the glam room, and she was directing everything: the air-conditioning, the music, the makeup. And at the same time, she was on the phone with Tyra Banks, trying to persuade her to appear in a Skims campaign with other supermodels. Tyra was feeling insecure. Kim spent hours lovingly talking her into it. I thought, “That’s Anna Wintour plus an advertising agency plus the model in the shoot.” She was wearing seven hats at once. Skims isn’t just underwear. It’s a platform and a fashion company and a very strange conglomeration of things. It’s also an empire that was launched by a sex tape. How do you think that happened? Do you see her as someone exploited by a humiliating episode or someone who brilliantly capitalized on it? Both. I think she was humiliated by it and at some point decided to capitalize on something beyond her control. We talked about its effect on her life almost from the beginning. But she can’t really talk about exactly how it happened. Ray J and Kim were together for years, filming all kinds of things, including sex. Somehow footage ended up with Vivid. I don’t know how that happened, and Kim is never going to tell. Ray J has claimed that Kris Jenner was involved in arranging its release. If that turned out to be true, wouldn’t it change your understanding of their entire origin story? No, it wouldn’t! And I still don’t believe Kris had anything to do with it. But you didn’t interview Ray J. No. Nor Kanye West, arguably the most important creative influence on her transformation into a fashion icon. Wasn’t that a significant hole in your reporting? Kim initially said, “Of course he’s going to talk to you.” But as his behavior grew more troubling, I didn’t think it would be ethical to interview somebody in the middle of a mental health crisis. Years ago, I profiled someone who was high out of her mind, and I thought, “This is like date rape. There’s no consent here.” I promised myself I’d never let that happen again. When he tipped into raging antisemitism, I thought it might ruin the book. He was central to her life, and suddenly he was a pariah. But Kim managed to separate herself from that, and in a way his absence kept the focus on her story. Later someone said that if you get him on the phone, he’ll talk for seven hours. I didn’t need seven hours straight from Kanye West. Was there anyone who turned you down? Paris Hilton. Late in the process, I told Kim I should talk to her. Kim checked and said Paris agreed, but I had to go through her publicist. That was unusual: With everybody else, Kim just sent a text. I sent questions, connected with Paris’ assistant, and then the interview was canceled 17 times over about four months. Eventually I thought the cancellations were more interesting than whatever she’d tell me. Kim was so mad when I told her. It seemed to stir up some ancient irritation between them. The creation turning on the creator. What did the interviews with her sisters reveal to you about the family? Kourtney took about nine months to talk to me. At one point, her assistant asked if we could do it while they filmed the show, which I didn’t think Kim would appreciate. Khloé jumped right in. Kim told her she didn’t have to get glammed up, and of course she got fully glammed up. I became convinced that what you see on the show is mostly real. Kim and Kourtney can be wicked to each other. Kim and Khloé are genuinely close. Kendall and Kylie are so much younger that Kim has almost maternal pride in them. She once said to me, “My mom made all of her mistakes on me.” By the time she got to Kylie, she’d perfected it. I know you spent a whole lot of time with their grandmother MJ. She was one of the warmest people I’ve ever met. She told me the history of the maternal side of the family going back to Arkansas. Again and again these women would divorce a shitty man and open a store. Kim’s mother is Kris, Kris’ mother is MJ, and before that there was Lou Ethel and Tiny. You begin to see a family history of women making their own way. So who’s the head matriarch now — Kris or Kim? It’s already shifting to Kim. In Malibu in 2024, she said to me, “I’m the one who pushes everybody. It’s me. It’s not my mom.” Did the family help you understand her or did they mostly reinforce the version of themselves we already know? I first spent time with the family years earlier when I profiled Kendall. We drove around Calabasas and Hidden Hills, played miniature golf and ran out of gas. Kris cooked dinner one night. I asked where I could have a cigarette, and she said, “Come with me.” We picked up our vodka drinks and smoked by the pool. I thought, “I love this woman.” That experience made me receptive to Kim before I really knew her. It was the opposite of what people assume about the family. Doesn’t that suggest you’d already lost some journalistic distance even before you started the book? Maybe. But I was also trying to get past a kind of reflexive contempt. When the book was announced, people would visibly recoil. Some people simply don’t want any serious analysis of Kim. But you don’t have to like her to recognize her enormous effect on the culture. Anna Wintour blurbed your book. When Vogue first put Kim on the cover, readers canceled their subscriptions. What finally brought Anna around? Probably some combination of Kanye’s relentless campaign, realizing that magazines were in trouble and that people like Kim had millions of followers, and recognizing that the world was changing. Hollywood got Kim sooner. They could see that Kris and Kim are powerful and make money. But people like Graydon Carter and Maureen Dowd thought it was nonsense. Every time Maureen Dowd dropped Kim’s name into her column without actually writing about her, I thought, “What are you doing?” It felt like using her for clicks. But Kim doesn’t care. It just doesn’t mean anything to her. The subtitle calls Kim “The Woman Who Created the Future.” What does that mean? That subtitle was suggested to me, and at first I said, “That’s not right.” Then weeks went by, and I thought, “Actually, hmm.” As a teenager, she was selling things on eBay before anybody had heard of eBay. She had a blog with members — essentially followers — and posted videos of herself talking about dating. She was an early adopter of every single one of these things. People only look at what happened after 2007. Everything before she was famous was the stuff I cared about most. Isn’t that also a future of relentless materialism and everyone making themselves the center of the universe? Isn’t that what people don’t like about her? Yes, but I don’t

articles.title: Jonathan Groff to Return to Broadway in Solo Play ‘The Amish Project’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All October 23, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jonathan Groff attends The 78th Annual Tony Awards at Radio City Music Hall on June 08, 2025 in New York City. (Photo by Michael Loccisano/Getty Images) Michael Loccisano/Getty Images Jonathan Groff is returning to Broadway this season in the solo play The Amish Project. The play, written by Jessica Dickey, is a fictional exploration of a schoolhouse shooting in an Amish community, and how the community learns to provide forgiveness and compassion. Sarna Lapine will direct the show, which is slated to begin performances Feb. 10, 2027, at the Broadhurst Theatre. The play debuted at the New York International Fringe Festival and was developed at the Cherry Lane Theatre before premiering Off-Broadway at the Rattlestick Playwrights Theater in 2009. It has since had productions at regional theaters across the U.S. and around the world. The play is typically performed as a one-woman show, with the main actor playing multiple characters. Groff will perform the play as written. Related Stories Lifestyle Tom Hanks Sets Broadway Return in 'This World of Tomorrow' Lifestyle Daniel Kaluuya to Make U.S. Stage Debut in New Branden Jacobs-Jenkins Play This marks the third Broadway project for Groff in recent years, following his Tony-nominated run in Just In Time from March 2025 to 2026 and his Tony-winning role in Merrily We Roll Along in the 2023-2024 season . He comes to the project after making his Royal Shakespeare Company debut in As You Like It this past fall. He recently completed production on Lin-Manuel Miranda’s feature adaptation of Octet , as well as the independent film Trust the Man , which he stars in opposite Daniel Radcliffe. The subject matter of the play struck a chord with Groff, who grew up nearby in Amish country. “20 years ago this month, an unimaginable tragedy happened in a one room Amish schoolhouse in Lancaster, Pennsylvania and Jessica Dickey wrote an astounding work of art in response. Sarna Lapine sent me The Amish Project last year and I was floored by the urgency and potent poetry of Jessica’s writing as she dives headfirst into the many aftershocks of this horrific event and explores the idea that sometimes the most radical human act is forgiveness. I am profoundly grateful to be bringing Jessica’s play to Broadway alongside Sarna and this incredible team,” Groff said. Robert Ahrens and Tom Kirdahy, producers of Just In Time , are producing the play. THR

articles.title: ‘Clueless’ Inspired Kim Kardashian to Buy This Priceless Monet
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Storm Off the Coasts of Belle-Ile, by Claude Monet, 1886. Oil on canvas. Says Kardashian of another Monet she purchased: This is “the first real piece of art that I bought — myself. Because in Clueless, they called the girls ‘a Monet’ if they look good from afar, but up close they’re just a mess.” Leemage/Corbis Via Getty Images/ One day in early February 2022, I was hanging out at Kim’s office as she tried to cram two cover shoots into one day. Between the shoots, Kim was back in her glam room, getting RE-glammed with different hair and new makeup, this time to shoot the cover of Vogue Hong Kong. Kim was effusive and bossy, running her multibillion-dollar business in a bathrobe, two gay men pulling at her hair and face. At one point, as she was helped into and then out of a complicated, totally sheer Schiaparelli tulle dress — it was pretty much nothing but scaffolding — I looked up from my phone and she was entirely naked. Neither of us flinched. Lately, she and I had been playing a little game of “Guess What Happened in 1995?” because we kept being surprised by the astonishing number of cultural and technological shifts — to say nothing of her own complicated personal circumstances — that unfolded in that one year. Once she was dressed and sitting back in her chair, I said to Kim, “You know what else happened in 1995?” She looked at me expectantly. The movie Clueless came out (her favorite film). When it was first released, Kim and her father (and a group of Kim’s friends and their fathers) all went to see it together. “We were dying at every reference,” she told me. “It was so me in high school. … I had pretty much every outfit that the girls wore in Clueless . … I was still into Contempo Casuals and shopping at Judy’s at the Century City Mall. … Like, when I saw that movie, I couldn’t believe it. Clueless is still, to this day, my favorite movie. It really resonated.” Related Stories Lifestyle Kim Kardashian Read Every Page of Her Authorized Biography. Here's What She Pushed Back On. Beyond the Book "Respect Rather Than Reverence": Inside the Making of a Grittier 'Sense and Sensibility' Clueless , inspired by Jane Austen’s Emma , stars Alicia Silverstone as Cher Horowitz, a ditzy but well-meaning rich girl living in the ultraprivileged bubble of her Beverly Hills high school. “I just wanted this fake world that you would see in a comedy of manners about the turn of the century,” director Amy Heckerling said in an interview, adding, “Positivity fascinates me — I don’t understand it … so I started to think about a character that would be so happy and sure things would work out.” A character like Kim. Clueless was written and directed in 1994, right as Kim was entering her freshman year at Marymount High School, and right as her family was becoming a fixture in the inescapable O.J. Simpson news cycle. Heckerling’s highly tuned antennae capture such a specific moment of Beverly Hills youth culture; it’s hard to believe something of Kim’s life wasn’t absorbed from the ether. Cher goes to the mall and shops at Contempo Casuals and Fred Segal. She is obsessed with her closet, the organization of which puts even Kim to shame. Cher’s iconic yellow plaid outfit evoked Kim’s Catholic school girl uniform as imagined by Donatella Versace. Kim and Kourtney and their friends carpooled to school, blasting hip-hop in a white BMW, while Cher drives her friends in a white Jeep Wrangler. Cher famously volunteers to be “captain of the Pismo Beach disaster relief” effort, while Kim spent Coastal Cleanup Day scouring the Santa Monica beaches for trash. All of the scenes in the ostentatiously enormous house where Cher lives with her strict, attorney father (who happens to look exactly like O.J. lawyer Robert Shapiro) were shot in a 10,000-square-foot house in Encino, just down the road from Robert Kardashian’s 11,000-square-foot former home on Mandalay Drive, which, much like the fictional Horowitz residence, features a grand double staircase. As their homes become the prep site for a big trial, Kim and Cher both take an interest in their father’s legal work. Ripped straight from the headlines, Cher calls her brother-in-law Josh a “Kato” — as in Kato Kaelin, one of the minor witnesses in the O.J. trial — meaning “freeloader.” Amy Heckerling’s 1995 hit Clueless , starring Stacey Dash (left) and Alicia Silverstone, is Kardashian’s favorite film: “It was so me in high school. … I had pretty much every outfit that the girls wore in it. I was still into Contempo Casuals and shopping at Judy’s at the Century City Mall.” ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Much of the infamous slang from the film — the texture that provides the crackling authenticity — came from Heckerling’s impeccable ear for the way people really talk (gay men, stoners, rappers), but there was another source, one with surprising proximity to Kim. “I have to give props to the UCLA linguistics department,” said Heckerling. “They published a list of slang words and phrases, and Monet came from that.” (As Cher explains to Dionne: “She’s a full-on Monet. It’s like a painting, see? From far away it’s OK, but up close it’s a big ol’ mess.”) You could literally throw a rock from Kim’s high school parking lot at Marymount across Sunset and it would land on the UCLA campus. Seniors at Marymount often walked over to hang out in the quad. All of which is to say, some of the ’90s slang collected by the students at UCLA may very well have been uttered by Marymount students. In Kim’s glam room, as she was explaining why Clueless is her favorite movie — indeed, the impact it had on her teenage years — she said, “And that’s the reason I bought my Monet.” I stared at her and blinked a couple of times. “The first real piece of art that I bought — myself — was a Monet. Because in the movie they called the girls ‘a Monet’ if they look good from afar, but up close they’re just a mess.” I was still staring and blinking, trying not to let on how extravagantly implausible this sounded. Kim bought a Monet not because she had visited the famous Water Lilies at l’Orangerie in Paris or under the art world tutelage of Kanye West. She bought a Monet for the same reason she kept the box of chicken McNuggets from her first date with TJ Jackson — a piece of high school nostalgia. A sketch of Kardashian’s Tadao Ando-designed concrete house in Palm Springs on her Instagram. @kimkardashian/Instagram She continued: “I was in Italy, and it was being auctioned, and I was with Kim Jones [creative director of Fendi], and we were doing our Fendi/Skims fitting in Rome. I really wanted this Monet painting because it’s a gray Monet — a pretty landscape, but gray. … I really wanted it for my Tadao Ando house in Palm Springs, which is all concrete. And I’m bidding and I’m bidding, and it was the first auction that I ever did, so I didn’t really know how they worked. But you get really into it. So Kim Jones is there with me and he’s like, “GET IT!” So I bid on it. I win. And I went over what my budget was because you’re in the moment.” And then, in true Cher Horowitz fashion, a blunder straight out of a comedy of manners: “So, I got it. It’s delivered. And it’s like … THIS big. Like, a postcard. I didn’t think to check the dimensions! I thought it was going to cover a whole wall! I’m going to put it in my Ando when it’s done,” she says, laughing. “Like in the powder room.” Excerpted from Citizen Kim by Jonathan Van Meter. Copyright 2026. Reprinted by permission of Viking, an imprint of Penguin Random House, LLC. This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Meghan Markle Says She’s Kept Her Children From Her Father “to Protect Them” In Wake of Child Abuse Image Allegations
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 23, 2026 6:38am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Duchess of Sussex in April this year. Courtesy of Getty Meghan Markle is “deeply distressed” by the news that her father, Thomas Markle, is being investigated for possessing child sex abuse images, and has revealed she’s kept her children from him “for one reason: to protect them.” In a report by Rupert Murdoch-owned tabloid The Sun on Thursday, the Duchess of Sussex’s father, now 82, is said to have been reported to authorities by his own son, Thomas Markle Jr., who told police there were “hundreds, if not thousands” of illegal images in Markle’s Philippines home, the British outlet said. Related Stories News Judge Orders Trump to Testify Under Oath in BBC Defamation Lawsuit Movies 'Apart,' Set in Cyprus and Apartheid South Africa, "Challenges the Idea of 'Us' and 'Them'" (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer) The elder Markle, who was forced to leave the property in May and return to the U.S. after a blood clot led to the amputation of his left leg, is also reportedly being probed by the FBI about the “stash of vile content packed into storage boxes.” The Duchess’ father has told The Daily Mail that the allegations are “a bunch of lies.” He said: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.” Now the Duchess — who has been estranged from her father since she married Prince Harry in 2018 — has released a bombshell statement to the U.K. press , in which she says she first learned of the allegations that same year. “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” began Markle. She continued: “In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.” Markle added that she hopes “it can now be understood, that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families. Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.” The Hollywood Reporter has reached out to reps for the Duchess. Thomas Markle Jr., 60, told The Sun : “When I found this material, I was horrified and I had no option but to report my dad. I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now. I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.” Markle Sr. has given multiple interviews to the press about his daughter over the years, including in a Channel 5 documentary titled Thomas Markle: My Story , which aired in 2020. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex moved back to the U.K. just last month and have even been making some public appearances, despite King Charles’ assertion that the pair are “private citizens” and not working royals. Their decision to come back to Britain shocked the nation and has not come without hurdles: Harry and Meghan were forced to move seven-year-old Archie and five-year-old Lilibet to a different school after just a few days due to security concerns over the commute. THR

articles.title: Why Judd Apatow Puts Himself in (Most of) His Documentaries
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All October 23, 2026 6:42am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Judd Apatow and Maria Bamford in 'Paralyzed by Hope: The Maria Bamford Story.' Netflix Right now, Netflix’s stock price (NFLX) is a joke — just not the funny, ha-ha kind. Simultaneously, the Netflix Is a Joke branding is bringing subscribers four documentaries on four comedy entities — Martin Mull (Oct. 7), Norm Macdonald (Oct. 16), Maria Bamford (Oct. 23) and SCTV (Oct. 30) — this month. Judd Apatow, a comedy legend in his own right, directed two of them: he made Norm’s solo and Maria’s with Neil Berkeley, who also co-directed Martin’s (with Bob Saget; Jason Hehir directed the SCTV documentary). (To proactively clear any confusing, the Netflix Is a Joke festival is not happening this month. Robbie Praw, Netflix’s vice president of standup and comedy formats told THR that Netflix Is a Joke is “more than a festival — it’s an ecosystem and lens for how we think about stand-up comedy,” adding, “These documentaries are part of that and take it further: Honoring four comedy icons… and keeping the conversation going all year round.”) The individual films are as different as the individuals they chronicle. Apatow ( Knocked Up , The 40-Year-Old Virgin ) often inserts himself as an on-screen supporting character in his documentaries — like his prior Mel Brooks and Garry Shandling films — as he does again with Paralyzed By Hope: The Maria Bamford Story . The first voice we hear after the Paralyzed by Hope title screen is Apatow’s. The first face we see in its present-day footage is Apatow’s. It’s not a vanity thing. Apatow believes the camera following him is “a way to make [the film] more personal,” and in cases like the Shandling doc, to show “what it was like to be his friend and mentee,” he told The Hollywood Reporter . It’s a user-experience thing: as a viewer, Apatow likes to know to whom a documentary’s subjects are talking at any given time. “Those conversations are very intimate, and the obsession with eliminating the idea that someone asks a question sometimes takes away a level that reveals something about the subject,” Apatow said. “If I’m talking to Mel Brooks, he’s talking in a specific way because it’s me … It’s being honest with the audience that this isn’t exactly normal.” Neil Berkeley ( Gilbert , Harmontown ) is not famous, which can also work to one’s advantage. When making his Gilbert Gottfried doc, Berkeley just moved in with the comedian (a la Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything — except, you know, nothing at all like what goes down in You Can See Everything ). “I’m not in my movies. I’ve always been very against that. Not for any other reason other than, who wants to see me in this movie?” Berkeley said. His Paralyzed By Hope colleague is “a known commodity,” Berkeley added, so Apatow being on screen “makes sense.” The differing approaches, which converged somewhat in Paralyzed By Hope , are equally legit, Netflix’s vp of original documentaries Adam Del Deo, told THR . It is what we don’t see that makes for the best biographical documentaries, he said. “What we(‘ve) found is this,” Del Deo explained. “To create this authenticity, it’s about filmmakers building trust and getting intimacy with the subjects. In doing that, there’s ability to dig deeper into their lives, what makes them tick, and it creates this relatability.” ‘Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald.’ Netflix Apatow made Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald the Berkeley way. “The approach there was to do a found-footage documentary about Norm because he’s such an unreliable narrator. You don’t really know when he’s telling the truth or trying to be provocative or just making things up for fun in a very Bob Dylan-esque way,” Apatow said. “So, we made the decision to just arrange moments from his life and career, and let the audience decide what it all adds up to.” Also: Norm died in 2021, so it necessitated a different format. The “brilliance” of the Macdonald doc , Berkeley said, stems from his theory that “the best documentaries feel like their subjects … that movie feels like everyone these days’ experience with Norm Macdonald.” If you don’t get that, just search Norm’s name on YouTube. You can easily spend hours spiraling down through a rabbit hole of material and stories, laughing the whole time. And when you finally come up for air, you still won’t know who was the real Norm Macdonald and what was one big joke on all of us. No one will fault Apatow for switching his styles up — probably. When it’s your money financing the film, as Apatow says he did “for years” for the Bamford doc, pretty much anything goes. Paralyzed By Hope features two different scenes in which Apatow forks over some of that sweet, sweet Girls money to Bamford. At their on-screen meet cute, Apatow hands Bamford $500 cash just to pitch her on her own documentary. The scene was real, Apatow said. “She did say to me, ‘Bring $500.’ I knew she wasn’t kidding,” Apatow said. “She’s very into talking about money. She’s very transparent… She’s been in Debtors Anonymous for decades even though she never went bankrupt.” And she won’t for at least a few more years: the film effectively ends with Apatow handing Bamford a satchel full of cash. He’d eventually be reimbursed by Netflix. Knowing Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos’ strong affinity for Bamford’s comedy, Apatow figured that would happen. “We thought somehow this is going to land at Netflix. I don’t know how, but,” Apatow said. “The whole roll of the dice was at the end of the day, will Ted [Sarandos] like this enough? And we showed it to him, and he loved it the way only a mega, mega Maria fan would love it.” Who Is Martin Mull? wouldn’t have happened without Sarandos either. “The only reason that got finished is we got through a sizzle [reel] and a deck, and Martin had died, and they sent it to Ted, and Ted called the producers and was like, ‘Why didn’t anyone tell me about this? Why didn’t Bob [Saget] tell me about this?’ And he was kind of upset. He said, ‘In case you didn’t know, my first date in high school was a Martin Mull concert,'” Berkeley told THR . “So really, Ted was like the reason that movie is in the world at all.” (Sarandos appears in both docs, and fun fact, owns a dozen Martin Mull paintings.) Del Deo might take slight exception to that innocent statement. “I’ve learned a lot from [Ted] around comedy,” Del Deo said of his final boss Sarandos. “He’s a student of it. But when it comes to programming, those decisions are left up to the documentary team, and these were just great stories.” Three of the four great stories are available now on Netflix; the SCTV documentary premieres one week from today. THR

articles.title: Alexander Brothers Case Is a “Microcosm for a Lot of Questions about Sexual Assault,” Says Doc Director
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All October 23, 2026 6:50am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A still from Peacock’s ‘The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers.’ Courtesy of Peacock Ahead of their sentencing next week in a federal sex-trafficking case, a Peacock documentary is casting a fresh light on the sordid story of the Alexander brothers. The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers , which premieres on Sunday, arrives just as brothers Tal, Oren and Alon Alexander — two of them onetime stars in the flashy world of luxury real estate — face potential life sentences. After being accused of drugging and raping dozens of women in a federal trial earlier this year, they were convicted of sex trafficking, while two of them are still awaiting trial for a state case in Florida. The three-part documentary follows the brothers’ rise from their privileged youth in Miami to reaching the highest echelons of high-end real estate, first at Douglas Elliman and then at their own brokerage, called Official. And it tracks them through their rapid downfall after news broke that two women had filed civil suits against Oren and Alon alleging rape and assault, after which dozens of women came forward with their own grisly accusations. (The brothers have maintained that they never drugged and raped anyone.) The Wolves of Real Estate director Emma Schwartz is no newbie to stories of sexual abuse and violence: She executive produced and co-directed The Fall of Diddy for HBO Max, which tracked accusations surrounding Sean “Diddy” Combs. Still, she says, even with her track record in telling tricky pop-culture investigations with the production company Maxine (she also worked on Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV ), “this one was definitely one of the harder ones” in terms of finding subjects willing to go on camera, she told The Hollywood Reporter . In the interview, Schwartz also discussed a lingering mystery in the brothers’ story, the details of the case that stick with her and the questions that she hopes viewers ask after watching the documentary. The story has been covered pretty intensely in the press. What more did you feel that a documentary could bring to the story? I think a lot of the stories that we like to focus on at Maxine are taking a big look at the story. The day-to-day coverage only tells you part of it. And even the articles that went through a dozen accounts in the summer of 2024, they were sort of part of the buildup of a story. And what you can do with a documentary is you can look at the entirety. How did it begin? What happened before? You can look outside of the walls of a criminal case. You’re right, there were reporters at trial writing articles a number of days, but that only told you part of the story. And part of what we can also do is help raise these bigger questions. Why is it that it takes women so long to come forward? What systems do we have in place to enable women to feel safe coming forward? How much does power and wealth play into the way the justice system goes after cases like this? And so I think there’s a lot of bigger questions that you can see in context in a documentary that you might not understand or see [otherwise]. But beyond that, I think there are really unique accounts that we have from individuals that were not necessarily in the public domain that have not been out there that help you understand people’s relationships with the brothers, the kind of power that they wielded and so much more. Was the process of finding subjects for this project simple or complex? Look, I don’t think anyone who’s done a documentary would ever tell you that it’s an easy thing. Certainly not documentaries that investigate people who are powerful, but I think this one was definitely one of the harder ones. There was a sort of cone of silence around the brothers and people who knew them and a lot of fear still from a lot of the women who, while they had come forward, not a lot of them wanted to actually share that publicly. Even if you look at the trial, a number of women testified under a pseudonym. They wanted to testify, but they didn’t want their name plastered all over the Internet. And I can understand that, right? So this was a really difficult story to get people to speak publicly and it took a lot of fits and starts and there were people that wanted to and then didn’t want to. And that’s part of the process. But I do think in the end, we were able to find people across the eras and in different facets of the brothers’ lives to, at least I hope, tell a fulsome account of both what happened and our best understanding of how some of this may have happened. What surprised you most as you were working on this documentary? There’s always a lot of surprises along the way, and you get to a point where you almost can’t remember what was surprising anymore. But I think one thing I keep coming back to was the way in which the brothers committed so much to writing, so much about the way that they thought about women and the way that they, in their own words, hunted women, preyed on women, and thought of women as something where you could get your return on investment, almost like property. That kind of language is sort of searing. And while we may never understand why people commit sexual assault or exactly what leads to any particular situation, there was clearly this mentality that women were less than, and that they were pretty brazen in how they talked about women, at least among their friends, quite openly. I mean, even messages that never made it in the doc, I still remember. Oh really? There’s this one that was at trial. I mean, I don’t know, it’s all really inappropriate and uncomfortable to say, but there was an exchange with this one woman where she texts Oren and she says, “I woke up with a dick inside of me. That’s not okay.” And he’s like, “Oh, I’m sorry.” And then she’s like, “You have to ask consent before you do that.” And he says, “I used my fingers first.” I mean, I can’t forget that one, and that was part of the evidence at trial. So I think it really was a lot of those messages that stood out. It seems like an interesting challenge as a filmmaker to be in the trial and be able to witness that, but not be able to put it on camera. So how did you look to convey what you saw and witnessed through the film? Yeah, that was an incredible challenge. A lot of documentaries, especially ones in certain states, you have the footage, you have the testimony. We had transcripts, we had court sketches, and then we did obviously have an interview with Lindsey who had testified at trial and journalists who were there. I remember the first cutdown we did of the trial was outrageously long because we’re like, “There were so many things.” But in trying to help people understand what happened at trial, we’re not prosecutors putting on evidence, we’re trying to give you the essence of what happened and not every single detail. And so part of that was laying out the patterns, laying out some of the messages, laying out some of the accounts, laying out videos. The thing about rape and sexual assault is, not always, but more often than not, it’s not like there are witnesses. There’s not someone who saw the bloody knife in a murder, right? And oftentimes they’re very difficult cases because it’s him and it’s her. But in this one instance, there was a woman who didn’t even remember what had happened to her. She had been 17 at the time, and she testified at trial that they seemed to have found her because they found this video on one of the brother’s hard drives. And it was a video in which she was clearly intoxicated, not just with alcohol, but drugs, and Oren engaging in various sex acts and recording it, which resulted in a charge of sexual exploitation of a minor because she was 17 at the time. And so the public never saw that, which thank God, we don’t need to see that, but those 12 jurors had to watch that seven-minute video. And for those seven minutes, it was like a ghost town. It was silent. I think that silence speaks volumes to the intensity of what they were watching. It’s horrible. Were there any parts of the story that you were unable to crack in time to deliver this documentary? One of the things that a lot of people raised was the brothers had friends around them, there were allegations involving the brothers and sometimes a friend, and nobody else was charged with a crime, so what happens to those people is there liability, there’s a lot that remains uncertain about all of those things. But look, with any story, there’s always questions, there’s always things that you wish you could answer and sometimes your job is to lay out the best that you can and raise those questions and hopefully that provokes more from other people. Beyond the specifics of this story, is there any larger message that you hope the series leaves viewers with? Yeah absolutely, and thank you for that question. I think sometimes the timing gods work in your favor here, which is to say that I think we always felt going into this story that as a society, even in the wake of #MeToo, that we had not really reckoned with these questions of what is appropriate behavior? What is predatory? How do we make women feel safe coming forward with sexual assault? And what is the appropriate adjudication and justice for that kind of behavior? We’ve seen really in the last week that these are very live question in our public dialogue and with young people, when you look at all of the conversations around the Jane Doe from Cornell, there are—again, these are different cases — but there are certain themes. Themes about does a woman realize it’s sexual assault right away? In the case of Jane Doe it took her weeks to come to that realization. In the case of some of these women, it took years. The guys at the fraternity said everything that happened, it was consensual. That was at the core of the brothers’ argument — they were playboys, they were not predators. Yes, they had a lot of sex, but that was consensual. And so these are questions that I think we are still reckoning with and that I hope in telling these stories we continue to ask ourselves what should be okay? And try to continue to come to places where more women can feel safe to come forward. I think a big reason people in general participated but especially the women participated was that, I think someone said, “I just hope this never happens again.” They wanted people to learn. And look, we don’t learn from everybody’s experiences perfectly but if somebody can, then I think hopefully we’ve done something. So certainly I think this is a microcosm for a lot of questions about sexual assault, about the way power functions, about the justice system, that we can all learn from, I hope, and go through that journey. Anything else you want to add? The one thing I will just throw out here and this might be a little wonky but I think is really important here is the reason why these women were even able to file these civil lawsuits, it took two women to snowball into these floodgates of dozens of women, but that only happened because there was a special law in New York called the Adult Survivors Act which you no doubt know about, but it had a time window to allow women to come forward with just civil claims that were outside the statue of limitations. That doesn’t exist anymore. And in most states, there are time windows on sexual assault, on when a survivor of sexual assault can come forward and can actually lead to some sort of criminal case. So I think there’s a lot of questions around the system we have today and whether it is designed to, what we know from research is the reality of when people come forward or how people come forward. Which is often not right away and often can take years. So I think there are real questions about whether any of those systems will be reconfigured or repealed. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. THR

articles.title: Tony Dokoupil Has a Question: Will You Watch His New Podcast? (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 23, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Great Question' with Tony Dokoupil. CBS News Tony Dokoupil is launching a podcast, and if you happen to watch the video version and look very, very closely, there’s a chance you could spot Salvador Dali’s phone number. Dokoupil, the anchor of the CBS Evening News , is now almost 11 months into the job, and to hear him explain it, he is just beginning to find his rhythm and footing in the high-profile role. So that makes for an opportune moment to expand the Evening News to digital platforms with a wholly original podcast extension: Great Question with Tony Dokoupil . It will be available in video form (on YouTube and all the other podcast platforms), shot in his office, alongside audio versions. “You’re going to get to see my dad’s mugshot on the shelf behind me [he was arrested for smuggling marijuana in 1992], and my great uncle’s pioneering gay advocacy journal that he came out with called Michael’s Thing on the shelf behind me, and all my old Newsweek covers and a bunch of books I like,” Dokoupil says, noting all the paraphernalia, before landing on his favorite: “I rescued a Rolodex from the dump when Newsweek was on the brink of folding.” And yes, it has Dali’s phone number. Great Question will be built off of the foundation of the Evening News , but it will also be its own thing. The premise? Twice per week, on Mondays and Wednesdays, Dokoupil will focus on one “great question,” looking to journalists or experts to help answer it. “When I think of the Evening News , I think of our beat as being the story of America one day at a time, which is why I always have that sign off, ‘that’s another day in America,’ and even though we have this amazing team and these global resources and we put out a jam-packed show, there are still things we couldn’t get to the bottom of, and so every day starts with new questions,” Dokoupil explains. “Over the course of a week, there’ll be things that we didn’t get to or that are lingering, and the hope of the podcast is you’ll be able to distill that into the biggest, most urgent, most pressing, most important, or just most interesting question, and then you try to match that to a guest.” Watch the trailer: Among those guests will be author and podcast host Malcolm Gladwell to discuss whether America needs more police and 60 Minutes contributor Gianna Toboni talking about the death penalty. Episodes will focus on why America kids seem so bad at math, if gambling apps are trying to addict us, and other tough or interesting questions. The show “is an effort to capture that curiosity and have a format where I’m asking a question that is genuinely occurring to me in the moment that I genuinely want to know the answer to, and I don’t know what’s going to happen next,” he says. But for Dokoupil the show is also a chance to show his voice, and to help a digitally-native audience that might not watch the Evening News understand who he is as a journalist and as a person. “There are people who watch traditional TV and they love it, they love the product, they grew up with it, they’re still into it, and that’s a great audience,” Dokoupil says. “There’s another group of people who are more online who genuinely believe that people on TV are just getting things fed into their earpiece, and they’re basically robots with hair pieces on. That is a real meaningful part of the population.” “And I think part of the advantage of a podcast is when you’ve been around as long as I have, and you have stories from the field and the things you’ve learned, giving people an opportunity to hear you talk at length with somebody else who knows a lot, who’s been around, and have a genuine conversation — it just exposes new people to who you are as a journalist,” he continues. “What excites you? What interests you? And it deepens that one-on-one relationship, which is what works on television, and is also I think what works in podcasts .” Dokoupil hopes that it gives viewers a little slice of who he is outside of those 30 minutes every weekday, and outside of other things he does for CBS, like last week’s town hall with Vice President JD Vance, or next month’s midterm election coverage, which he will co-anchor with Norah O’Donnell. And it comes as he says he has finally found his footing at the Evening News . “At the beginning, I felt like Mr. Smith Goes to Washington , I was naively walking into this new neighborhood, and it took me a little while to realize all the ways in which it’s not the morning show,” he recalls, adding that “a lot of people didn’t know my work or who I was. “Different people are watching, and they have different ideas about what works, and everything I think flows from that.” he adds. “But now, 10 months in, I understand it, I love it.” A big part of that has been finding his voice in the anchor chair, and refining the stories the show covers. “I think when we launched, we were pretty heavy on politics. And politics are important, we cover it every night, sometimes with two beats, sometimes with even more, but it’s not everything,” he says. “And I think we’ve found a mix that’s right for us. I also think the sound of the show has changed in a way that’s been great. I write or revise every single word that comes out of my mouth… I think now people can tell when they’re hearing it, it’s really me.” And now Great Question will, hopefully CBS News thinks, bring that voice to new places, in a digital expansion that is unusual for an evening news anchor. “I believe in the form. I like podcasts myself, so there’s that,” Dokoupil says. “But also, you know, I’ve been doing the Evening News for 10 months now, almost a year, we’re in a good rhythm with the show, we like the direction of the show, we feel the momentum, and we realize we had the resources and the space to fit a podcast in, and it would give us the opportunity to pursue the longer questions and answers that are often the most exciting part of journalism.” THR

articles.title: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Nicholas Galitzine and Bill Skarsgard in Peter Berg’s Technically Impressive, Emotionally Hollow Netflix War Drama
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All October 23, 2026 7:05am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'The Mosquito Bowl' Kane Skennar / Netflix The Mosquito Bowl , Peter Berg ’s new World War II drama for Netflix, sets the tone right away with a famous Herbert Hoover quote. “Older men declare war,” it goes. “But it is youth that must fight and die. And it is youth who must inherit the tribulation, the sorrow, and the triumphs that are the aftermath of war.” It is a statement eternal in its truth and devastating in its poignancy, one well worth keeping in mind any time the specter of battle is raised. It is also, you may have noticed, the theme of more or less every single war movie ever made. It would take some really sharp and distinctive execution to make it feel fresh again — and as admirable as The Mosquito Bowl often is in its craft, its storytelling falls well short of that bar. Related Stories Movies Friday Night Fights: Peter Berg Returns to Football ... and War Movies Peter Berg's Netflix War Movie 'The Mosquito Bowl' to Premiere at AFI Fest (Exclusive) The Mosquito Bowl The Bottom Line Looks good but says little. Venue: AFI Fest Release date: Friday, Oct. 30 Cast: Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgard, Ray Nicholson, Tom Francis Director: Peter Berg Screenwriters: Peter Berg, Mark L. Smith Rated R, 2 hours 6 minutes The premise, at least, had potential. Adapted from the book of the same title by Buzz Bissinger (whose Friday Night Lights also spawned a Berg film), The Mosquito Bowl leads up to a legendary football game played between two Marine divisions while stationed at Guadalcanal on Christmas Eve in 1944. One would expect the sports angle to add a welcome new spin on the usual war-drama storylines — and it does, though not nearly as much as you’re probably guessing, given how little of the 126-minute run time the match actually takes up. Its leads are a quartet of elite college football players who’ve joined the Marines after the 1941 bombing of Pearl Harbor, and all are played by hot rising stars du jour: the ubiquitous but apparently un – typecast – able Nicholas Galitzine as thoughtful Brown alum John McLaughry; Ray Nicholson as charming Purdue alum turned promising NFL draftee Tony Butkovich; Tom Francis and Bill Skarsgard as anxious David Schreiner and wild Bob Bauman, both graduates of University of Wisconsin (though only David maintains a grudge against Tony for beating them in a pivotal game). But if that Hoover epigraph suggests a well-trod path, the rest of the film confirms it has no intention of straying from it. The central themes are all ones you could guess based on the logline alone. War forges unbreakable bonds of brotherhood. War makes men out of boys, but destroys their minds and bodies in the process. War is hell, as opposed to football, which represents youthful idealism, except that football is also a little bit like war if you think about it: “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in the history of football,” one character declares. The Mosquito Bowl ’s great saving grace — the thing that might nevertheless make it worthwhile for people who simply enjoy war movies — are its technical elements. (Well, maybe aside from the dull gray-brown-blue color palette that seems to aim for “serious and gritty” and lands right back at “produced by Netflix.”) Combat sequences, set in the Pacific theater and filmed in Australia, look expansive and authentic, weaving around hundreds of soldiers running and shouting and shooting at once. Berg, working with DP Jacques Jouffret, favors close shots that force us to experience battle much like our heroes do, as confusing, terrifying bursts of mayhem. Pinned in place by the machine guns we hear thundering all around, we watch in horror as a friend gets struck down by a bullet mid-conversation, or flamethrowers wave wildly in the periphery. But that’s often all we get. Other soldiers, friendlies and enemies alike, are glimpsed through trees or plumes of smoke. Updates get passed around like rumors. What lurks over the next ridge or the next nightfall is anyone’s guess. Given that commitment to their perspective, I suppose you could argue that these scenes dragging on for quite a while is part of the idea, too: The guys who’d previously hoped to be home in time for the Fourth of July — of 1942 — are learning the hard way that fighting rarely goes so quick or easy. But as the minutes stretch on, it starts to seem that The Mosquito Bowl is primarily interested in showing off how skilled Berg and his team are at producing action set pieces, be they ones of battle or boot camp or football, and only secondarily interested in its plot or characters. This impression is not diminished by a script, from Berg and Mark L. Smith, that barely bothers to build any connective tissue between said set pieces. Even the titular Mosquito Bowl finally arrives with almost no build-up at all. No sooner has one Marine complained about low morale than a sergeant has assigned two others to organize a football game; no sooner has that order gone out than we’re watching them line up to play it. Logically, the necessary pieces are all accounted for; it’s not as if we need to watch Bob and David recruiting teammates to surmise that that must have happened at some point. But in its constant rush to get to the good stuff, The Mosquito Bowl keeps shortchanging the emotional beats required to make them land. Personalities are sketched only in the margins, mostly via brief snippets of chatter between rounds of gunfire. Character development happens offscreen, or possibly doesn’t exist at all — it’s hard to tell if anyone’s changing when everyone’s so vaguely conceived to begin with. The big ideas we’re meant to take to heart are reduced to disingenuous platitudes. While The Mosquito Bowl does not completely ignore the nastier undercurrents of the military culture and mindset, it’s so invested in the idea of wartime service as an act of noble self-sacrifice that it refuses to engage with them directly. So even as Bob announces in boot camp that “This recruit is here to learn how to kill Japanese people, sir!” the film never stops to reexamine his eagerness or his motives. It introduces such details only to gloss by them completely on the way to a straightforwardly heroic ending. This refusal to look directly at the shadows is all the more aggravating given how often The Mosquito Bowl pats itself on the back for being clear-eyed. In quieter moments, the film zooms out into a placid view of the globe from space, or zooms into bittersweet details like a seagull walking along a corpse-strewn beach — reminders to maintain a sense of perspective about our place in this vast and indifferent universe. In moments of grand emotion, it often freezes into black-and-white snapshots (sometimes pulled from actual archives) to emphasize that what we’re watching really happened. But in the rest of its run time, it forgets that just because something is true doesn’t mean you can’t make it ring false. Full credits Venue: AFI Fest Distributor: Netflix Production companies: Imagine Entertainment, Film 44 Cast: Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgard, Ray Nicholson, Tom Francis Director: Peter Berg Screenwriters: Peter Berg, Mark L. Smith Producers: Peter Berg, Brian Grazer, Alex Gayner Executive producers: Ezra Emanuel, Buzz Bissinger, Jeb Brody Director of photography: Jacques Jouffret Production designer: Philip Ivey Costume designer: Liz McGregor Editors: Jon Otazua, Garret Donnelly Music: Explosions in the Sky Casting director: Rachel Tenner Rated R, 2 hours 6 minutes THR

articles.title: Jamie Lee Curtis, Téa Leoni and Tim Daly Lead NBC’s Refreshing and Witty Sitcom ‘Newlyweds’: TV Review
articles.full_text: Oct 23, 2026 6:15am PT Jamie Lee Curtis, Téa Leoni and Tim Daly Lead NBC’s Refreshing and Witty Sitcom ‘Newlyweds’: TV Review By Aramide Tinubu Plus Icon Aramide Tinubu Latest Jamie Lee Curtis, Téa Leoni and Tim Daly Lead NBC’s Refreshing and Witty Sitcom ‘Newlyweds’: TV Review 36 minutes ago ‘Other Desert Cities’ Broadway Review: Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Ed Harris and Allison Janney Lead a Resounding Family Drama 4 days ago Netflix’s ‘Victorious’ Spinoff ‘Hollywood Arts’ Is a Bland Copy of Shows From a Past Era: TV Review 1 week ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Nicole Weingart/NBC Sitcoms aren’t what they used to be. Though a select few on network television, like “Abbott Elementary” and “Ghosts,” pay homage to comedies of the past while tapping into present-day culture, sitcoms today rarely feel truly universal. NBC ’s “ Newlyweds ,” co-created by Jamie Lee Curtis and (the since-fired) Gail Lerner, is fun and refreshing, speaking to a collective audience across generations. Set in present-day Los Angeles, “Newlyweds” begins with a blind date. James ( Tim Daly ), a reserved college professor, sits anxiously in a restaurant, awaiting Jeanie ( Téa Leoni ), a free-spirited middle school teacher who is trying to decide whether she even wants to meet James. After individually deciding to bail on the dinner, the pair run into each other by the valet, and their mutual attraction, despite their vastly different personalities, leads to a spicy evening together. The duo initially believes that they are just having a fling, especially when James’ work sends him to Norway for a month. However, the couple’s connection continues to blossom, and they end up marrying in Las Vegas just six weeks after meeting. Despite their whirlwind romance, neither James nor Jeanie anticipates how different their lives are. Jeanie is enmeshed with her adult children, Poppy (Emma Meisel) and Lolo (Ignacio Diaz-Silverio), who still live at home. Meanwhile, James’ meddling ex-wife, Claudia (Jamie Lee Curtis), remains an aggravating fixture in his otherwise buttoned-up existence. Across the 13-episode first season (critics received three episodes for review), the pair immerse themselves in a newlywed bubble while trying to embrace the chaotic family and friends who orbit them — often infiltrating their private moments. Real-life couple Leoni and Daly work wonderfully as a later-in-life couple, invigorated by this new romantic chapter as they navigate long-held histories, patterns and preferences. Though the duo forms a gentle, tenderhearted center, the ensemble as a whole elevates “Newlyweds,” allowing it to stand above so many recent middling entries in the sitcom space. While all of the episodes provided have their amusing moments, Episode 3, “We’ll Never Have Paris,” is the best of the bunch. During the episode, Jeanie and James’ mini-moon plans are constantly interrupted by Claudia and Jeanie’s children. James even tries to comfort a distraught Poppy after a breakup. Still, the banter between Claudia and Arvid (Bill O’Neill), aka Milky, James’ Norwegian-born teaching assistant, consistently stands out throughout the show. As Claudia, Curtis is perfectly biting and obnoxious, willing to insert herself into her ex-husband’s life for sport, stomping on his feeble boundaries. However, it’s O’Neill’s turn as Arvid that elevates the series. Like Sean Hayes’ Jack McFarland in “Will & Grace,” O’Neill has perfect comedic timing, throwing himself into every aspect of the character’s physical comedy with energetic vibrancy. What’s more, because the couple moves between two worlds — Jeanie’s modest city bungalow with all its warmth and Gen Z angst, and James’ museum-like suburban estate — viewers see how differently the pair live, and the shenanigans they get into when forced outside their respective comfort zones. These days, it’s rare to actually laugh out loud to sitcoms, which is why “Newlyweds” is already off to a stellar start. The cast works like a well-oiled machine, and the characters feel tangible, as if the audience lives next door. Interestingly, Lerner, who co-created the series with Curtis and served as showrunner for the first six episodes, was recently fired because of “creative differences,” and “The Conners” co-creator Bruce Helford has been brought in to replace her for the duration of the season. Whether the show builds on its already solid foundation or collapses in on itself will be fascinating to watch. For now, “Newlyweds” feels refreshing and enjoyable. Director Pam Fryman also executive produces (pilot only). “Newlyweds” is produced by Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group.
