articles.title: Despite Hudson Williams, Canadian Witch Mystery ‘Yaga’ Is No ‘Heated Rivalry’: TV Review
articles.full_text: Oct 23, 2026 6:30am PT Despite Hudson Williams, Canadian Witch Mystery ‘Yaga’ Is No ‘Heated Rivalry’: TV Review By Alison Herman Plus Icon Alison Herman TV Critic aherman2006 Latest Despite Hudson Williams, Canadian Witch Mystery ‘Yaga’ Is No ‘Heated Rivalry’: TV Review 32 minutes ago ‘The Gilded Age’ Team on Paramount Merger Parallels and Going From Budget Cuts to a Season 3 Breakout: ‘You’re Part of a Very Fortunate Minority’ 23 hours ago Olivia Cooke on Returning to ‘Slow Horses,’ On-Set Injuries and That Shocking Finale Cliffhanger: ‘I Want a Showdown!’ 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of AMC+ The witchy thriller “ Yaga ” is a Canadian production that co-stars Hudson Williams, now hot enough off of “Heated Rivalry” to earn a “with” before his name in the credits. That’s about where the similarities with the hockey-themed megahit end, though not for lack of trying: “Yaga” — which airs on streaming service AMC+ in the States — painfully strains for the eroticism and insight into sexuality that came so easily to “Heated Rivalry,” resulting in an eight-episode season that’s often cringe without ascending into camp. But other blunders are all “Yaga”’s own. Choppy pacing, poor casting and facile feminism all combine to make “Yaga” a misfire, one viewers in search of seasonal scares should overlook in favor of alternatives. Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ Adapted by creator Kat Sandler from her play of the same name, “Yaga” introduces itself as a missing persons mystery centered on Williams’ Henry Park, a billionaire heir whose concerned parents send family fixer Rapp (Noah Reid) to track down somewhere in rural British Columbia. But the story’s real interest is right there in the title: Sandler wants to rework the Baba Yaga myth of cannibal witches in chicken-legged huts for the modern day. (“Yaga” foreshadows this project with Slavic covers of various pop standards, a legitimately fun detail.) Unfortunately, the show can’t muster a take more interesting than platitudes like “a witch is just someone society has decided they’re afraid of,” coming more than a decade after touchstones like “The Witch” and “American Horror Story: Coven” advanced similar ideas in a more artful way. Popular on Variety “Yaga” could deliver excitement in other areas, and tries to. Rapp quickly discovers Henry and his lookalike roommate Logan (also Williams, minus colored contacts and plus a prosthetic nose), both college students, had an uncommonly close relationship with their professor Katherine (Carrie-Ann Moss), an anthropologist known as the “bone lady” for her academic interest in ossified remains. When he meets Katherine in a hotel bar, not realizing she’s about to be a person of interest, Rapp’s idea of a come-on is asking for sexy facts about bones. Such clumsy and futile attempts at chemistry are not the fault of Moss, who’s pretty much the only person in the ensemble to project the earthy, seductive vibe “Yaga” is clearly going for. Rapp himself is part of the problem: Reid’s performance renders him a loudmouth bro whose effect on the town’s women, including but by no means limited to Katherine, utterly baffling. (At times, the question of Rapp’s inexplicable attractiveness is more pressing than that of Henry’s whereabouts.) There’s also a clash between the gorgeous, haunting atmosphere implied by the scenery, all fog-bound waters and shady forests, and the buddy-cop banter between Rapp and his quasi-partner Carson (Clark Backo), a local police officer he mocks for being mannish — or even, gasp, gay! “Yaga” can’t manage the ramp-up from such crass comments to the eerie and metaphysical, with the elements forming a discordant clash rather than a smooth blend. If there’s an archetype more overdone than the witch who’s actually a misunderstood outcast, it’s the rich guy who’s secretly into sinister sex stuff. Sure enough, the ghost of Jeffrey Epstein begins to haunt “Yaga” as Rapp and Carson start to uncover what Henry and Logan have been up to — namely, house parties suffused with bisexual lighting and the occasional chicken sacrifice. Rather than alluring or even disgusting, the details of Henry and Logan’s trysts are almost juvenile in their attempts to provoke; the particulars of who’s sleeping with who, and under what circumstances, are filled with over-the-top and unconvincing details, jumping the shark from the salacious to the outright criminal in the blink of an eye. By the time “Yaga” arrives at its inevitable reversals of perpetrator and victim, whatever spell (get it?) the show’s cast on the audience has long since been broken. Already offputting, Reid’s performance of Rapp’s dawning realizations — flipping from dismissive skepticism to feverish belief with little in between — grows less grounded by the minute. To be fair, the fault here lies equally with the scripts, which dump information without first creating suspense. Perhaps there’s a reason most horror dramas don’t have quick, 30-minute episodes, though the prospect of an even longer “Yaga” is not an enticing one. The first two episodes of “Yaga” are now streaming on AMC+, with remaining episodes airing weekly on Fridays. articles.title: You Can See Everything, Except Outside North America: Inside A24’s Staggered International Release Strategy for Nathan Fielder’s Hit Elizabeth Holmes Doc
articles.full_text: Oct 23, 2026 6:30am PT You Can See Everything, Except Outside North America: Inside A24’s Staggered International Release Strategy for Nathan Fielder’s Hit Elizabeth Holmes Doc By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest You Can See Everything, Except Outside North America: Inside A24’s Staggered International Release Strategy for Nathan Fielder’s Hit Elizabeth Holmes Doc 31 minutes ago Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones Support ‘Normal People’ Author Sally Rooney After U.K. Book Ban: She’s a ‘Writer, Not a Terrorist’ 2 days ago The Beatles Immersive Experience, Featuring Sets and Props From Sam Mendes’ Biopics, Set for Liverpool 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of A24 A24 ’s “ You Can See Everything ” has become one of the year’s biggest box office surprises, opening to a staggering $15.6 million in the U.S. and generating a frenzy of headlines, spoilers, memes and online chatter. But for audiences outside North America, catching Nathan Fielder’s three-hour documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes — now expected to be a major player in awards season — has become a frustrating waiting game. Despite the film’s blockbuster debut — the second-biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary, behind “Fahrenheit 9/11” — A24 isn’t releasing it in the U.K. and Australia until Nov. 20, more than a month after its U.S. bow. Sony Pictures, which recently acquired the film for several international territories, including Germany, Latin America and South Korea, has yet to announce its release plans. Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ As one producer jokingly put it in a message to Variety : “You Can See Everything, unless you live outside N. America.” Popular on Variety The frustration was palpable at the BFI London Film Festival, where excited speculation was mounting that the documentary would be unveiled as the surprise screening on Oct. 16. With co-director Lance Oppenheim in town earlier that week (for his other film, “Primetime”) and a special BAFTA screening having taken place that afternoon, many festivalgoers were convinced “You Can See Everything” was heading to the Royal Festival Hall. Instead, the surprise screening turned out to be Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky.” The delay raises a broader question about A24’s international release strategy at a time when social media can turn a film into a global cultural event overnight. Because “You Can See Everything” isn’t alone among the studio’s titles that make non-U.S. audiences sit tight, something that has been widely lamented online. Oppenheim’s Robert Pattinson starring “Primetime” released in the U.S. on Sep. 25, becoming A24’s third biggest opening with $19.2 million after “Backrooms” and “Civil War.” U.K. previews kick off on Oct. 28, just days before it gets VOD launch in the U.S. (like “You Can See Everything,” Sony picked up the film for numerous other territories). Back in 2022, A24’s megahit and Oscar winner “Everything Everywhere All at Once” released in the U.K. a full two months after bowing in the U.S. And then there’s another of 2026’s most hotly-anticipated titles, “Club Kid,” which is suffering a similar fate. Jordan Firstman’s acclaimed directorial debut and Cannes breakout lands in cinemas in the U.S on Nov. 6. In the U.K.? Jan. 8, 2027. There are, of course, several factors at play. A24 — which wouldn’t comment on its release strategy for this article — only self-distributes outside North America in a couple of territories, notably the U.K./Ireland and Australia/New Zealand, and even then many of its titles go through a third party (the films named above were all handled solely by A24). There’s also the long-held sense that having an advanced U.S. campaign is extremely beneficial to help test the waters and serve as a momentum-building ice-breaker for the overseas trip. “But for a film that is so spoiler-heavy as ‘You Can See Everything,’ a month is extraordinary,” notes one Brit doc publicity veteran. It should be noted that last Christmas’ extremely buzzy A24 release “Marty Supreme” came out in the U.K. less than a week after the U.S. and grossed in excess of $22 million, the studio’s biggest success on British shores to date. But perhaps “You Can See Everything” is a very unique case. After all, very few people outside of the inner A24-Fielder-Oppenheim circle knew anything about it before its shock Telluride screening. As one insider notes, “The film really didn’t exist in the world until six weeks ago.” A24 has had a tight turnaround to get it into U.S. cinemas since then. Perhaps a simultaneous or near-simultaneous launch in the U.K. — where it has an office overseeing local productions but no dedicated distribution team — was a step too far (especially given it’s gearing up to release “Primetime” as well). There’s also the possibility that simply few expected “You Can See Everything” — a documentary almost as long as “Oppenheimer” and about a disgraced and overexposed Silicon Valley founder who has already been the center of a hit TV drama — to become such a theatrical juggernaut. Was the power of Fielder and this stunt release underestimated? Not so — at least not among those who know documentaries — claims the publicity vet. “Within the very rarefied documentary world, the minute it was announced, everyone knew it was going be huge,” they say. “Maybe A24 isn’t plugged in as much, but as soon as Elizabeth Holmes’ face popped up, everyone was just like, ‘Well that’s just blown ‘NAZA’ out.'” In terms of timing, to launch in the U.K. on the same date as the U.S. would have seen “You Can See Everything” go up against fellow new releases in the video game adaptation “Streetfighter” and animated feature “Forgotten Island” (and not, unlike America, the closest potential rival in terms of audiences, “Sense & Sensibility”). That said, the U.K. is about to go into school half-term holidays, not generally suited, at least when it comes to more mainstream-focused cinemas, for arthouse-focused indies. “If someone had tried to get us to put a 3-hour doc in our cinemas just ahead of half term, we probably wouldn’t have even answered their calls,” says one exhibition exec, who admits his audiences tend to lean much more towards the popcorn titles. “This is just the wrong type and shape of film for us during that period, which is more horror classics and family fun.” The exec suggests that a post-holiday early November release might have been more strategic, but then that would put “You Can See Everything” firmly on the heels of “Primetime.” A month-long delay to see a film the entire internet appears to be talking about might be excruciatingly frustrating — especially for those desperately now trying to avoid the spoiler-filled articles and posts littering social media. But the wait and anticipation do appear to have done wonders for pre-sales. According to a report in The Guardian earlier this week, tickets at London’s Picturehouse Central cinema went on sale before its U.S. opening, with the demand forcing the chain to put on additional screenings. It was a similar situation at Cineworld, which has added more screenings at its major Leicester Square site and expanded bookings elsewhere after the initial batch of tickets sold out. Variety has since heard that Australia’s Palace Cinemas — which operates in 25 locations across the country — has just broken the record for single-day pre-sales with “You Can See Everything.” Such was the demand for tickets for Fielder’s wild, genre-flipping documentary that sales doubled that of the previous record holder: “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour.” ‘Billions’ and ‘John Wick 3’ Star Asia Kate Dillon Says Acting Jobs Have ‘Diminished’ and They’re in Need of Customer Service Work Loading comments...

articles.full_text: Oct 23, 2026 6:45am PT The Gotham Group and Toonstar Team Up for New Animated Series By Isabelle Farina Plus Icon Isabelle Farina Latest ‘Ebenezer’ Creates a Real Venmo Profile for Scrooge, Which Hands Out Money and Accepts It, Too 13 hours ago Lucia Aniello, Mike Flanagan, Karyn Kusama, Boots Riley and Lesli Linka Glatter Among Mentors for DGA Women’s Steering Committee 18 hours ago ‘The Holiday’ Returning to Theaters for 20th Anniversary 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Gotham Group and Toonstar The Gotham Group and Toonstar are partnering to produce up to 12 new original animated series for kids. The partnership aims to create quality animation and family entertainment that will be launched on direct-to-audience platforms. Toonstar is a tech-powered animation studio building entertainment franchises. Founded by Disney, Warner Bros. and DreamWorks veterans Attanasio and Luisa Huang, the studio produces and distributes digital-first, creator-led series. The L.A.-based studio is repped by WME and law firm Hansen Jacobson. Toonstars investors include Founders Fund, Greycroft, Snap and GFR. Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ “When I first started talking with John and Luisa, we connected immediately,” founder and CEO of The Gotham Group Ellen Goldsmith-Vein said. “They’re creatives first. They love animation, they have great creative instincts and they understand how to produce for a digital-first audience. That’s where the opportunity is right now, and it’s why creators need new ways to reach audiences.” Popular on Variety “Ellen and Gotham have spent three decades finding and championing incredible animation talent and IP,” John Attanasio, co-founder and CEO of Toonstar, said. “Together, we can help those artists and storytellers create the next generation of beloved kids’ franchises directly with audiences.” In a statement, Matt Shichtman, head of Emerging Technologies at The Gotham Group, said, “Animation creators can now produce at a pace and scale once limited to the largest studios, with distribution support and analytics that help them understand and respond quickly to audience preferences.” The partnership is the latest addition to Toonstar’s network of development partners that includes Fox Entertainment, HarperCollins and Penguin Random House. WME represented both The Gotham Group and Toonstar in this deal. articles.title: Luke Evans on His New ITV Drama ‘The Party,’ Starring in ‘The Rocky Horror Picture Show’ on Broadway and Whether He’ll Return as Bard in ‘The Hunt for Gollum’
articles.full_text: Oct 23, 2026 6:45am PT Luke Evans on His New ITV Drama ‘The Party,’ Starring in ‘The Rocky Horror Picture Show’ on Broadway and Whether He’ll Return as Bard in ‘The Hunt for Gollum’ By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ 2 hours ago Prince William Declares His Love for Christopher Nolan Movies and ‘The Traitors’ in Surprise Appearance on ‘The Graham Norton Show’ 4 hours ago Amy Winehouse West End Musical in Development (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source World Productions Luke Evans is among the rare cadre of British actors who regularly balance Hollywood blockbusters with more modest British dramas. Not to mention the actor, who has starred in movies as diverse as “The Hobbit” trilogy and the live-action “Beauty and the Beast” opposite Emma Watson, also recently came off a five-month stint Broadway stint as Frank-N-Furter earlier this year, for which he was nominated for a Tony. His latest project is “The Party,” an adaptation of a psychological thriller by Elizabeth Day, which he also co-produced, for ITV . (The five-part series, which is repped for global sales by ITV Studios, is currently available to watch on ITVX). The show deals with class, hidden sexuality and the nature of both romantic and platonic love all wrapped up in a tense drama. Popular on Variety Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ Evans, who first came across Day’s novel as a lockdown read during the Covid pandemic, was instrumental in bringing the series to screen and in getting Sarah Solemani to adapt it (Solemani also plays his wife, Lucy, in the show). Evans sat down with Variety to talk about the differences between the novel and the series, his recent experiences on Broadway and whether Tolkien fans can expect him to reprise his role as Bard the Bowman in Andy Serkis’s upcoming feature “The Hunt for Gollum.” How much did you and Sarah discuss the changes between the source material and the screenplay? When you bring somebody on who has the capability of someone like Sarah, you have to let them run with it, and it was exciting and also daunting to know what she was going to change, but also we knew things would change. The fact that Lucy is pregnant adds another major layer of weight to what is going on in Martin’s head, and also that you know they had a physical relationship, and I think that informs something more about how messed up the life Martin has chosen to live is. There is a love there, and I think that’s another reason why we expanded on their relationship. You see much more of Lucy and Martin together because you want to see that they are a functioning, if slightly unconventional, relationship. I know couples like Martin and Lucy. The other big difference is that Martin in the screen version serves time and he doesn’t in in the novel. What was the thinking behind that change? Putting him into detention to pay the price for someone else, it’s a scar that — he’s tarnished for life. He has a criminal record and lives his life knowing he didn’t do it, I mean it’s huge. It’s massive. What did you want to bring to the character of Martin? Sarah and I had very, very long Zoom calls where she just asked me lots of questions about my upbringing, and of course I started saying I can relate to Martin. I’m a gay man. I’ve come from a very working-class background, and I was presented with opportunities that I took that put me in very alien situations where I didn’t feel comfortable or an insider, but I kept watching, learning, adapting, and trying to fit in. I basically spent my whole life doing that, and that’s who Martin is. I talked about the fact I’m an only child, a very religious background, and Sarah took a lot of those ideas from my life or real things that happened to me and turned them into Martin’s story. So of course, there are slight parallels, which is interesting and it works. Elizabeth revisits the characters in another book, “One of Us.” Does the show lend itself to potentially being returning series? Yeah, absolutely. There is closure for sure within this arc, of course there needs to be, but there are lots of unanswered questions. “One of Us” came out during the end of the shoot, which was exciting and teased us with lots of new ideas. Who knows? As well as “The Party,” there have been a number of shows recently, like Richard Gadd’s “Half Man” and Russell T Davies’ “Tip Toe,” that have explored male relationships and homophobia. Do you think there’s a reason these stories are being told now? As much as we live in a more progressive society, and I think we’re very lucky — I’ve just been in New York and America for seven months, and of course, New York is this little world of its own where everybody can do what the hell they want, and everybody’s accepted — I know that’s not how the country is. I feel that we have progressed in the United Kingdom very far when it comes to equality and it comes to being yourself and an acceptance of each and every one of us. But it’s not by a long shot safe. What we have right now is not safe. You only have to look at the politics, and you have to look at the parties, and some of them, what they’re saying, it’s scary. And I think those kinds of whispers of threat to your life and your existence and your authenticity and your identity can suppress people and can make people hide away, and I do think people do. In my industry I know for a fact that happens. I couldn’t because I was already an openly happy gay man before my movie career began, and so I knew it would become a public knowledge/gossip column idea for a period of my career because I knew people would find out and there was nothing I could do about it and I had to accept it. And then we’re talking about Martin’s industry and the political world, and on top of why Martin suppresses it or hides is because Ben has chosen a certain life, and for Martin to be in Ben’s life, Martin has to be a certain way also. On the other end of the spectrum, you recently played Frank-N-Furter in the Broadway revival of “The Rocky Horror Picture Show.” How was that? It was nuts. It was not what I was expecting. In a wonderfully colorful, big way. It delivered on so many levels I wasn’t expecting. I absolutely loved it. Probably one of the hardest things I’ve ever done. After not doing a musical for 18 years, to set foot on a Broadway stage with a Broadway audience in six-[inch] stiletto boots, eight times a week, was a cross-country marathon, I would say, but I loved it, and it was so rewarding. And then to get a Tony nomination, it was — it just kept delivering. Tim Curry, who originated the role and of course played him in the iconic film adaptation, died just after you finished the show. Had you spoken to him about it? I wrote a letter to him two weeks before I finished the show, and I sent it to him, and his team gave it to him, and he said he was very appreciative of the letter, and then two weeks later I finished the show, and a day after that he died. I was part of that final show that was associated with him and him with us. And he was in my mind every day. I had a picture of him in my dressing room, and so I’m just so grateful I sent the letter and that I was part of that incredible show. It was magical. Another cult project you’ve been involved with of course is Peter Jackson’s Tolkien adaptations, having starred as Bard the Bowman in “The Hobbit” trilogy. Are you returning for Andy Serkis’ sequel, “The Hunt for Gollum”? Well, if I’m correct, Bard is a human. I don’t think he would have been born, or is he dead? Is it in between? It’s in between. But how far after “The Hobbit” is it? I think there’s approximately 60 years between “The Hobbit” and “The Lord of the Rings” and “The Hunt for Gollum” will be set in between – so Bard could come back. Yeah, I think Bain, my son, could be in it. But I think Bard doesn’t. Take me back to Wellington. I’d love to go! articles.title: Banijay Entertainment’s Frédéric Balmary on U.S. Ambitions, Netflix and the Battle for IP: It’s ‘One of Our Big Fights’
articles.full_text: Oct 23, 2026 6:56am PT Banijay Entertainment’s Frédéric Balmary on U.S. Ambitions, Netflix and the Battle for IP: It’s ‘One of Our Big Fights’ By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest ‘Galileo,’ Toplining Elio Germano, Boarded by Fandango, Kicking Off Sales at Rome’s MIA Market (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Sebastian Koch, Toni Servillo Set for Oscar Winner Gabriele Salvatores’ Chess-World Noir ‘The Lüneburg Variation’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mary Sullivan Fresh off its merger, the Banijay /All3Media behemoth, now known as Banijay Entertainment, is eyeing an expansion into U.S. scripted production as Netflix looks to ramp up its slate of American hits amid a major shake-up of its content leadership. Speaking at Rome’s MIA Market, Banijay Entertainment chief business officer Frédéric Balmary said in an interview with Variety that the group, which ranks as the world’s largest independent studio, looks to capitalize on Netflix’s renewed focus on U.S. programming, while continuing to grow its English-language scripted business, bolstered by the merger with All3Media, and its roster of talent including George Kay and Sam Mendes. Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ Balmary also discussed the growing global appetite for European dramas, the U.K.’s role as a bridge between Hollywood and Europe, and the financial pressures facing U.S. studios and streamers. He stressed the importance of retaining IP, echoing CEO Marco Bassetti’s call for European producers to hold their ground when it comes to negotiating terms of trade. “Retaining IP is really one of our big fights at the moment,” Balmary said. Popular on Variety Talk to me about the ongoing growth in English-language dramas output at Banijay. Well, the English language market is certainly growing, and that was also one of the rationales of the merger deal between All3Media and Banijay. At Banijay we were already growing in the U.K. scripted market with a few acquisition we’ve done in past years, like The Forge Entertainment and the other British companies we invest in. But All3 has incredible talents in the scripted sphere, from [“Lupin’ creator] George Kay to Sam Mendes, to many others. We’ve always said that our business is based on talent and IP, and the growing English market is really where we want to be, in order to follow the market. Not only in production, also in distribution. Marco Bassetti recently hinted to an expansion in the U.S. scripted space. Can you tell me more? We are already there, but not as a studio. We’ve done the “Ripley” series and these kinds of things, though more on the packaging side. Today it’s really a growing area. From its last earnings call, it’s clear that Netflix is looking for more U.S. hits. I think that was part of Marco’s vision in saying maybe we will also follow that growth area and be more active in that space in the U.S. How do you see the prospects for European scripted dramas now, given these latest developments at Netflix, but also following the merger between Paramount and Warner Bros.? The latest Netflix call underlined the growth in terms of viewers of content coming from non-English language countries. We are quite strong in that space. With Italy, of course, Groenlandia being one of the most successful scripted Italian companies. But also in Spain, where we have the company Pokeepsie that just made “Drawn Together” on Amazon that was a fantastic success because they are number one worldwide. We want to continue to invest in that space, flying the European flag with more local stories that can travel globally. Do you think that in macroscopic terms we could be looking at a shift towards a greater amount of high-end TV content productions being shot in the U.S.? Maybe. Yes and no. I think Netflix and the Hollywood studios are all under financial pressure. So they will also look at finding the best balance between finance and creative on high-end things. I think the U.K. is maybe a good bridge between the two. We can produce high-end and premium scripted, as we already do. But we want to continue to grow in that space. We produced “House of Guinness,” which is renewed for season two. We produced “War,” just released on HBO, also a great success. “The Wanted Man” is coming soon on Apple, made with George Kay again. So I think there will be a balance, and that’s also why we really want to invest in the English language market. Bassetti in an impassioned keynote here at MIA underlined the importance of what he called the “European production model.” Can you elaborate on that? We fight a lot for that. Retaining IP is really one of our big fights at the moment, and we are really convinced it’s crucially important for us. And I think the U.K. model works very well, often allowing you to retain 50% of the IP. This allows us to invest in creativity, and our business is based on creativity. Marco said it: ‘we invested one billion euros over the last four years in creativity, because it’s the root of our business. It’s where everything starts. To be able to have the ability to invest in creativity, we need to retain IP. And that’s where the European model sits. articles.title: ‘Ali G: Who Iz I’ Star Morgana Robinson on Sacha Baron Cohen Not Letting Her Break Character as ‘Me Julie’ and Why Film Doesn’t Mock Working Class
articles.full_text: Oct 23, 2026 7:00am PT ‘Ali G: Who Iz I’ Star Morgana Robinson on Sacha Baron Cohen Not Letting Her Break Character as ‘Me Julie’ and Why Film Doesn’t Mock Working Class By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest You Can See Everything, Except Outside North America: Inside A24’s Staggered International Release Strategy for Nathan Fielder’s Hit Elizabeth Holmes Doc 30 minutes ago Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones Support ‘Normal People’ Author Sally Rooney After U.K. Book Ban: She’s a ‘Writer, Not a Terrorist’ 2 days ago The Beatles Immersive Experience, Featuring Sets and Props From Sam Mendes’ Biopics, Set for Liverpool 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Variety via Getty Images After more than a decade out of the limelight and away from his wardrobe of high-visibility, low-practicality clothing, Sacha Baron Cohen ‘s Ali G is back with his first film in almost 25 years. This time, alongside the satirical would-be bad boy himself leading “Ali G: Who Iz I” comes his long-suffering girlfriend Julie (constantly referred to by Ali as “Me Julie”). Played by British comic and impressionist Morgana Robinson, Julie is seen in the trailer to the film — released Oct. 23 by Amazon MGM — heavily pregnant while Ali first explains to a doctor that her bump is “probably wind or a big poo” and later with him as, when asked what type of father he wants to be, he replies “absent.” Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ For Middleton, who played Pippa Middleton in “The Windsors,” the experience making “Ali G: Who Iz I” was the most insane she’s ever had, one that required her, on the insistence of Cohen, to stay in character off set. “He was training me like Rocky,” she says. But for all the silliness of the film (Morgana claims it’s half-silly — ”laugh-out loud funny, but with a message”), “Ali G: Who Iz I” has also come under significant fire, accused of using outdated racist stereotypes and mocking the working class. In the U.K., there have also been calls for cinemas to boycott the film. Popular on Variety Speaking to Variety , a wildly entertaining Morgana claims that Julie — who she describes as “the heart of the film” — is much more than what’s been seen in the trailer, adding that the “Who Iz I” actually takes aim at Ali G’s out-of-date views and attitude. But she also laughs about the shock and surprise of finding people in America who didn’t know Ali G and could be duped by the joke and reveals the real — and painful — struggles of trying not to laugh during each scene, because “there is no take two.” How’s the “Ali G: Who Iz I” press tour been? I’m in a bowl of jelly, to be honest. It is a bit knee-knocky. It’s on a rather grand scale, but it’s been amazing, especially on the red carpet and turning up in character. Most carpets are quite serious affairs with serious questions. Was turning up as Julie and, I guess, ad lobbing a bit quite fun? I find it a bit of a comfort. It’s like a very solid bra. I feel supported and not so exposed. They can look a bit serious, can’t they? And if you look a bit silly, it’s fine. So how silly is this film? It’s half-silly. It gets less silly as you go on. But it’s got all the feels. It’s outrageous. It’s very funny. It’s terrifying. It’s uncomfortable. It’s heartbreaking. It’s confusing. But it’s laugh out loud funny, but with a message. We haven’t had Ali G on screens for a very long time. How does he rank to the Ali G of old? He hasn’t changed particularly much, apart from you know his beard’s a bit longer. But how does he sit into today’s society? I think that’s sort of the reason they made this —what happens when you take a very dated character and drop him in into today’s society, into the world that we live in today that’s a very different place. Does he manage to survive that? I might let you wait and see. But what I will say is that I think a lot of questions have been asked, and I think they get answers. So how did how did this film find you? How did you become Julie? There was a very rigorous, full-on casting situation, and there were waves of auditions. There was like the first wave of auditions was a sort of like, “Hi, can you come in and have an improv with Sasha? Can you be funny? Can you go toe to toe with him? Can you hold your own?” And then the second, once you’ve passed that, was, “We throw you into the jaws of a shark with a with a real interview with a real person. Can you be believable?” I guess what they were looking for was a balance between someone who could be funny, but also someone who you know could feel real. Otherwise, I guess they don’t have a film. But I think it took them about a year to cast. This film took us all by surprise when it was announced. So much must have been done in secret. Oh yeah, I like the word ‘clandestine.’ It’s an odd it’s an odd fish, isn’t it? I mean, I’ve never done anything like this with real people. It was was crazy. Sometimes we were in the desert in Palm Springs. We stayed in these random hotels, all of us, but no one knew what we were doing there. So it was all sort of cloak and dagger and lying about what we were doing. You’d be doing makeup in your hotel room, and some days I’d come back and I’d have a bob and I’d be not pregnant. Then the next morning, I’d be eight months pregnant, walking out the lobby. Then I’d be in the bar having a glass of wine. And the concierge was just so confused. Previous mockumentaries from Sasha, whether with Ali G or Borat or Bruno, have all relied on people not understanding that it’s a joke. But I’d be surprised if there’s anyone now who doesn’t know. Was it all scripted or were you actually meeting real people who had no idea that this was a joke? Every single person, apart from me and him and the guy who plays his dad, are all real people. It think Borat is well known in America, but Ali G isn’t. But I think the people on the team scouted for people, and they had to pass a sort of certain test of who they know and what they know. That must be quite some scouting. I’m really surprised that someone who’s not been cut off from the world for the last 20 years wouldn’t just see Ali G and know that a joke was coming a mile off. Was it a surprise to you that some people out there were still duped by it? The whole thing is ridiculous. The whole thing is shocking and surprising. I don’t know where to begin. But the script was a constantly evolving thing. It wasn’t like, “Here is the script. You may read it.” It was like, “Here it is and it’s different from yesterday.” So you’re in your room waiting to come on set and 10 minutes before someone runs in going, “Hey Morgana, this has totally changed.” You’re like, “This is chaos. This is ludicrous. They’re never going to believe this. We can’t pull this off. This is impossible.” And I don’t know what happens, but [Cohen] sort of hypnotizes people. it’s like a magic trick. Morgan Robinson. Photo: Lou Rolley Did you struggle not to laugh? Because obviously you can’t start again. You literally have to stay in character or the whole thing’s ruined, right? There’s no take two. So that actually stops you from laughing a lot of the time. I did corpse twice in the entirety of filming. One was when I had to peel a banana with my toes, and the other one was something that happens later, but I don’t want to spoil it. So I did it twice, but I sort of managed to look away and stifle it. I bit so hard on my cheek. That’s one way of doing it. You can sometimes turn it into a cough. Or it can come out as a sort of twitch. But yes, it’s very hard. And after each scene, are you and Sasha able to have a laugh or do you stay in character? He will not let you break character. So we’re in character for eight hours. It’s exhausting. Normally, when you’re acting, you’re like, that was a very big take, is it lunch break? But here you’re eating lunch in character or whatever you’re doing because they’re watching. It’s wild. I remember when we first started filming, I hadn’t seen Sasha since the audition and I got to the lot to do the first rehearsals and talk and read the script. I was like, “Oh, hi Sasha, it’s Morgana, I haven’t seen you for six months.” And he’s like, “In character! All day I want you in character! I never want to hear you speaking as Morgana! It’s always me Julie!” Then he’d march me down to the mall and be like, “Go and have an argument with some people and buy some socks and then come back and then call up your mother and have a conversation as me Julie and eat that bento box as me Julie. How would she use chopsticks?” He’s mad. So you were Julie constantly, if there was a camera on you or not? He was training me like Rocky. All day long, running up and down those steps, all sweaty. How then did it feel then at the end of all that to finally put Julie to bed? I think I lost my marbles a little bit for a while, but I think I found them again. I think it’s sort of like sort of slow release PTSD. I can’t believe we fucking did that. I cannot believe that. I mean.. so I get kidnapped. What? Yeah, I get kidnapped. That’s an actual thing. That’s not even the bad bit. That’s just in the second act. I get kidnapped. But more happens. What can you say? I get my minge out. You’ll probably have to change that because no one knows what a minge is in America. So all these years, I’ve been doing these cute little cult things, like Vic and Bob, and no one’s watched it. Really, all you need to do is just go to Hollywood and get your fanny out. You know, I’m 44. I’ve got to pay the mortgage. The last major thing that Sasha did was Borat 2, which obviously has that scene in a hotel room with Maria Bakalova and Rudy Giuliani. Does it reach those levels? Yes, indeed. But with well-known individuals who are going to be made to feel ashamed of their actions afterwards? No, they’re not politicians. Not in my scenes anyway. When the first trailer came out, there was a lot of noise – some good, some bad. There were quite a few negative comments with regards to the scenes with Julie, with a lot of people saying it was mocking working class women and was quite derogatory. What did you think when you know saw those comments? I found it difficult. So I just stopped reading them entirely. People have their opinions, and that’s absolutely fine. I am a character actress and I play all sorts of people. I play every class, everything and so I feel like that’s what my job is. But think the hard things to read online was when they got really nasty. I get it. But in terms of those claims about the film mocking the working class, is that something that you would remotely agree with? I think she’s a well thought out character. She’s got heart. She’s got soul. She cares very much for her baby. She’s got amazing morals. She loves her family to pieces. She would die for them, as you will see. It’s not just one note. There’s more to her than what you see in the trailer. The film is much more layered. I think they probably designed the trailer a little bit to get people talking. You said that the story is about dropping Ali G, this outdated character, in today’s world. There have also been accusations about him being this tired racist caricature. But it sounds like that’s actually part of the film — is that the case? It’s sort of all about that, really. How’s Sasha to work with? He’s kind of like a giant kid who’s had too much sugarish. Sometimes it’s like trying to wrangle a hurricane. It’s chaos, but in a wonderful way and I think that shows in the work he makes. It’s just not normal, but it’s exciting, you know, and it’s interesting, and exhilarating and also terrifying. All those things. There’s so much adrenaline going around in your in your body. That’s his gift to you. I always felt like in today’s world of social media and everybody knowing everything because it’s all been videoed and posted everywhere, you just couldn’t get away with this kind of stuff anymore. But the fact that they were able to find people that had no idea and keep that joke going is phenomenal. I know it’s crazy. I think this will probably be the last one. ‘Billions’ and ‘John Wick 3’ Star Asia Kate Dillon Says Acting Jobs Have ‘Diminished’ and They’re in Need of Customer Service Work Loading comments...

articles.full_text: Oct 23, 2026 7:01am PT Meghan Markle ‘Deeply Distressed’ by Allegations Her Father Possessed Child Sex Abuse Images By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest ‘Nobody Wants This’ Creator Erin Foster on Adam Brody’s Support for Palestine: ‘I Disagree With Him, and That’s OK’ 3 hours ago ‘The Notebook’ Musical Sets West End Run at Newly Renamed Judi Dench Theatre 7 hours ago Charli xcx Joins Martin Scorsese’s ‘What Happens at Night’ With Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence (EXCLUSIVE) 18 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Pool Meghan Markle has shared a statement saying she is “deeply distressed” by allegations that her estranged father, Thomas Markle, possessed child sex abuse images. A report in The Sun claimed on Friday that child sex abuse images had allegedly been found in Thomas Markle’s former home in the Philippines by his son, Thomas Markle Jr. Variety has not been able to verify if there is currently an investigation underway. Thomas Markle vehemently denied the allegations to the Daily Mail, calling them “a bunch of lies” and adding: “I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.” Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ In a statement shared with Variety , the Duchess of Sussex said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.” She claimed that in 2018, a letter about her father was sent to the Metropolitan Police as well as Royalty and Specialist Protection and was “subsequently shared” with her. Popular on Variety “It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.” Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018, when he failed to walk her down the aisle at her wedding. She was escorted by King Charles instead. Thomas Markle has never met her and Prince Harry ‘s two children. Last year, she sent a letter to him while he was in the hospital getting his left lower leg amputated due to a blood clot. “Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan concluded. Representatives for the Metropolitan Police, the FBI and local police in The Philippines did not immediately respond to Variety ‘s request for comment. Variety has made attempts to reach Thomas Markle and Thomas Markle Jr. According to the BBC , the undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, Nicholas Ty, confirmed that “the matter is currently being investigated” by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force. The national police are in possession of Thomas Markle’s computer, Philippines interior minister Jonvic Remulla told the outlet, to conduct a digital forensic examination. Meghan and Prince Harry recently moved back to the U.K. after living in California for six years. Speaking to GQ about the move, Prince Harry revealed that he still has hopes of reconnecting with his father, King Charles, and brother Prince William. “Some people don’t want it to work out. I want it to work out,” Harry said. “With everything else that’s going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile — that’s the key point.” ‘Billions’ and ‘John Wick 3’ Star Asia Kate Dillon Says Acting Jobs Have ‘Diminished’ and They’re in Need of Customer Service Work Loading comments...

A network spokesperson confirmed Thomas’ departure, which was first reported by Variety . Thomas has served as EP since 2021. Related Stories News Gayle King Will Stay At ‘CBS Mornings’ As She Renews Deal With Network News Tony Dokoupil Asserts ‘CBS Evening News’ Will Be Independent From Its Corporate Owner: “I Report For You” “For five years, I’ve tried to make this show something she and everybody on this team want to be a part of. Want to watch. Want to learn from,” Thomas wrote in a note to staffers. She wrote that she had been “thinking about this for a while and, frankly, I’m tired y’all.” Jon Tower will run CBS Mornings on an interim basis after Thomas departs at the end of the month, wrote Tom Cibrowski, president and executive editor of CBS News . Watch on Deadline Cibrowski wrote, “Morning television moves fast. It demands grace under pressure, sharp instincts, and the ability to pivot at a moment’s notice. Shawna does all of that with a calm confidence and a great sense of humor. Morning television is also a tight-knit family. Behind the scenes, Shawna’s leadership creates space for collaboration, creativity, and trust – and on screen, that translates into something viewers can feel.” The news of Thomas’ departure comes a day after the announcement that Gayle King renewed her deal to remain as co-host and at the network. Executives also indicated that co-host Nate Burleson would remain, while the show’s traditional slot for a third co-host has been vacant since Tony Dokoupil departed to become anchor of CBS Evening News . CBS Mornings averaged 1.9 million viewers in the fourth quarter of last year, behind NBC’s Today with 2.9 million and ABC’s Good Morning America with 2.7 million, according to Nielsen. During Thomas’ tenure, the show underwent a revamp, with a new title from CBS This Morning , while taking on some of the elements of the network’s long-running Sunday Morning . Thomas wrote that the CBS Mornings team “has made me more thoughtful, empathetic and expanded my personal definition of storytelling. I’ve had the privilege of helping to make 10 (now 12!) hours of television each week that goes out free to people everywhere. articles.title: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Peter Berg’s Powerful True WWII Story Takes Four Star Players From The Glory Of The Football Field To The Hell Of The Battlefield – AFI Fest
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Wicker’ Review: Olivia Colman And Peter Dinklage Turn Alexander Skarsgård Into A Sexy Basket Case In Comic Fable That’s Pure Delight ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Review: Sacha Baron Cohen’s Signature Prankster Returns In Outrageous Form With Something To Offend Everyone AFI Fest Opens Tonight: President & CEO Bob Gazzale On Why It Matters In The Oscar-Season Deluge Of Film Festivals – The Deadline Interview View All October 23, 2026 12:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Mosquito Bowl Netflix There have been so many films about WWII, both during and after, so many different takes and personal stories told, that now 81 years since it ended it is hard to imagine finding a fresh way to say anything new, but with his film adaptation of Buzz Bissinger’s best seller, The Mosquito Bowl : A Game Of Life And Death In World War II , filmmaker Peter Berg has done just that with a powerful and ultimately poignant portrait focusing on four very young star college football players who enlist after the bombing of Pearl Harbor and go on to fight the bruising Battle Of Okinawa. In less than three months they go from a football field to a very different battlefield where the score is sadly measured in lives lost, not points won. Related Stories News Jenna Ortega Plans To "Be Off The TV For A While" After 'Wednesday' Casting 'The Watcher' Season 2 Adds Madelaine Petsch, Evan Adams, Owen Painter & Quintessa Swindell The team of Berg and Bissinger seems appropriate here since both gave us that classic of Texas football, Friday Night Lights, and now find a new uniquely moving connection to the sport and the young men who played it. In the Netflix film, The Mosquito Bowl, which had its World Premiere Thursday night at AFI Fest in Hollywood, this true story of the transition of young star players who signed up to serve their country in its darkest hour becomes one of the most effective anti-war films I have ever seen, one that never resorts to preaching or false patriotic rah-rah posturing. Watch on Deadline It achieves its true strength by putting us directly into the center of the hell of war, a visceral experience so intense and unrelenting it seems we are there and, like those who were on the front lines, a feeling there is no way out. Make no mistake, despite the premise, this is not a football movie, it is a war movie putting us right in harms way into the thick of battle, a film about the unforgiving nature of combat, and in that way makes you think twice about the price of it all and, 86 years later, about the cost now of wars being waged that never should have been started. Ultimately this is a human story, but fair warning, Berg whose films have included Lone Survivor, Deep Water Horizon, and other tales of valor and courage against all odds, does not hold back in showing the true horrors of the fight, in this case a noble one. After the attack on Pearl Harbor, four of America’s greatest college football stars — John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Bob Bauman (Bill Skarsgård), Tony Butkovich ( Ray Nicholson ) and David Schreiner ( Tom Francis ), in their late teens or early twenties put country over fame and enlist in the Marines. They were like others who experience glory in sports who had to face a nightmare, a violent unforgiving battlefield for which they had little time to prepare. Berg’s screenplay, written with Mark L. Smith introduces us to four men, putting the focus on them to tell a larger story. We move from 1941 college ball to training at Parris Island in South Carolina, right into the front lines in the Pacific Theater. The story is essentially told through the eyes of Galitzine’s McLaughry, an impressive young man with deep talents that will take him far in life if he can survive a war with no timetable for its end. Each of the others we follow along the way are distinctive personalities, with Nicholson’s vibrant Tony Butkovich a massive star player you feel could withstand hits from any direction; Skarsgard’s Bob Bauman a little more loose with a devil-may-care attitude; and Francis’ Scheiner a more shy and humble type of All American. In the telling of this particular tale in WWII these four represent many others, but it is smart of Berg and Bissinger to zero in on just a few, because in addition to all the shooting and explosions and sounds and sights of carnage all around them, we have time to see their humanity, their fortitude, and heroism, their bonding, all of which makes the inevitable loss of young lives all that much more emotional. The bulk of this film is war, but as it was for 64 college players who gathered one afternoon , there is a brief respite from it all in the Mosquito Bowl, an organized game that would take them back to earlier times. For a moment they were all boys again, superstar players, tossing the ball, hitting the end zone. It wasn’t just relief for them, it is also for the audience now watching it unfold because it shows how time was fleeting. What is to come afterwards is when their world is on fire as the fierce Battle Of Okinawa Island takes them , and us, back to sad reality. In actual numbers 14 of the young men playing that game that day would die on Okinawa, three of them were among the four Marines we get to know so well. In terms of filmmaking this is one of Berg’s most impressive outings. He shot in sequence, not the usual course in production, and it clearly helped the actors build their brotherhood and camraderie in authentic fashion. The use of tight camera lens and handheld against a 360 degree background that takes in the whole environment the characters are experiencing is very effectively employed. Thanks to the exceptional cinematography of Jacques Jouffret we are right in their faces. Shout out also to editors Jon Otazua and Garret Donnelly, as well as the music score from Explosions In The Sky, a regular contributor to Berg’s films. The four main stars, Galitzine, Skarsgard, Nicholson, and Francis are completely believable as football stars suddenly thrust into the life of a Marine with little time to train before being shipped out knowing it might be a one way ticket. It is a fine ensemble in a movie well worth seeing not as just another war movie but rather one that should make any leader think hard about the human price paid everytime they start one. Producers are Berg, Brian Grazer, and Alex Gayner. Title: The Mosquito Bowl Festival: AFI Fest – World Premiere Distributor: Netflix Release Date: October 30, 2026 (Theatrical); November 25, 2026 (streaming) Director: Peter Berg Screenplay: Peter Berg and Mark L. Smith Cast: Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson, Tom Francis, Brent Comer, Jack Ingram, Ella Newton, Peter Berg, Dominic Bogart, Lola Bond, Stacy Clausen, Billy Smith, Steven Sammut, Blake Erickson, Claudia Ware, Pat McAfee Rating: R Running Time: 2 hours and 6 minutes ‘Top Gun’, ‘Picket Fences’ And ‘Alien’ Star Dies At 93; Career In Photos ‘Clayface’ Solid $3.5M Thursday Previews; Can He Scare Off Elizabeth Holmes? articles.title: U-KNOCK 2026 Brings Korean Content Companies To Hollywood For Investment & Global Partnerships
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Partner Content Add us as a Google Preferred Source U-Knock 2025 U-KNOCK U-KNOCK 2026 will connect Korean content and technology companies with U.S. investors and entertainment partners on November 4–6, 2026, at The Biltmore Los Angeles. The program is hosted by South Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and organized by the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA). Now in its third year, U-KNOCK builds on relationships with international investors and Hollywood studios, emphasizing deal-making and long-term partnerships. Key programs include the International Content Investment Forum on November 5 and one-on-one investment and business meetings on November 6. Related Stories News Human Imagination, Directable AI: How Asian Directors Wrap Kling AI Into Their Workflows News DJI Unveils Osmo Pocket 4P In Cannes, Redefining Pocket-Sized Cinematic Imaging The November 5 forum, themed “What Makes Content Last,” will bring together Korean and U.S. leaders in media, finance and technology to examine how cultural success becomes enduring commercial value. Discussions will explore IP monetization, global franchise expansion and emerging business models driven by AI, digital platforms and evolving investment strategies. U.S. participants include The Raine Group; Shamrock Capital; Atwater Capital; J.P. Morgan Global Corporate Bank; Amblin Entertainment; and Anonymous Content, who all bring perspectives across entertainment finance, investment and production. From Korea, speakers will include global transmedia company CJ ENM; YLAB, which develops webtoon universes and screen adaptations; character-IP company IPX (formerly LINE FRIENDS); creator-focused comedy label MetaComedy; Moneygraphy, the original-content media outlet from financial platform Toss; and bemyfriends, a provider of direct-to-consumer fandom business solutions. Together, they will examine how stories travel across formats, how content models evolve and how global fan communities can support sustainable businesses. Five Korean companies will then present at the Korean Company Showcase. Modhaus, the company behind K-pop group tripleS and Web3 fan-participation platform COSMO, will appear alongside YN Culture & Space (YN C&S), known for its LED-wall virtual production and advanced production infrastructure; Klleon, which develops real-time multilingual interactive digital humans; Contents First, operator of Tappytoon and its global audience of more than 14 million readers; and Studio Eon, which uses an Unreal Engine-based pipeline to produce science-fiction animation. The companies will present their business models and plans for North American expansion. On November 6, the five showcase participants will be joined by seven more companies for one-on-one business meetings. The full 12-company delegation spans original story IP in drama, film, animation and web novels, as well as generative AI, interactive entertainment and fan platforms. Meetings are intended to connect the companies with North American investors, buyers, studios and other potential business partners. The additional participants include Big Ocean ENM, with crime procedurals Flex X Cop and Another Heaven, the latter in development; EO Content Group, developing action-espionage series TEAM-K; and Mstoryhub, whose webtoon IP includes The Remarried Empress. LOCUS is developing Kkokdu, a 3D family fantasy feature inspired by Korean funeral traditions. RECOV combines K-pop touring, merchandise and VIP services, while JIRO brings AI content-production platform Dropshot AI and AI-generated K-pop idol IP SEORIA. Draftify’s PlaySquad rounds out the lineup with playable livestreaming that lets viewers influence gameplay. U.S. and international investors, buyers and production executives interested in attending the International Content Investment Forum or requesting one-on-one meetings with the 12 participating Korean companies can register and submit meeting requests at www.uknockglobal.com . ‘Top Gun’, ‘Picket Fences’ And ‘Alien’ Star Dies At 93; Career In Photos ‘Clayface’ Solid $3.5M Thursday Previews; Can He Scare Off Elizabeth Holmes? articles.title: Donald Trump Wanted Google Maps To Change Name Of Atlantic Ocean
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Fremantle Global Entertainment Exec Chris O’Dell Retires After 19 Years At ‘Got Talent’ Maker Donald Trump Wanted Google Maps To Change Name Of Atlantic Ocean Zee Studios Sets Release Date For Omung Kumar’s ‘Silaa’ View All October 23, 2026 1:54am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Donald Trump and Sundar Pichai Getty President Donald Trump ‘s continuing desire to name parts of the world after himself or the U.S. almost made it to the oceans. During a rally in South Carolina, Trump told supporters he had called Google CEO Sundar Pichai to ask about changing the name of the Atlantic Ocean on Google Maps . “I only like two oceans: The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. I’m not going to put either Trump or America on any other ocean but these two, so we seriously looked at the Atlantic Ocean, and I called Google Maps, who were really great with the lake,” said Trump. “I said: ‘Sundar, I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean.'” Related Stories News Trump Ordered By Judge To Sit For Deposition In $10B Lawsuit Against The BBC News Politico Corrects Susie Wiles Story After Trump Official's Threat, But Media Outlet's Attorney Warns White House Of "Unconstitutional Retaliation" Trump claimed the Google boss responded, “No, no, no. This time I’m not doing it. Oceans are different, sir. They cover a lot of countries. Please don’t ask us to do that.” Watch on Deadline Trump’s “proposal” now appears to be on the back burner. “So I’ll probably pass. Should I pass it?” the President asked his supporters. “I think let’s keep it the Atlantic Ocean.” The “lake” Trump referenced was Lake Ontario, which Trump has renamed Lake America amid the trade war between his administration and Canada. Google Maps currently displays the water as ‘Lake Ontario (Lake America)’ and also uses the same phrasing for the Gulf of Mexico. Trump has also pondered renaming the Strait of Hormuz, writing on social media last month: “Should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? articles.title: Ryu Murakami Dies: Japanese Author & Filmmaker, Best Known For ‘Almost Transparent Blue’, Was 74
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Mayor Zohran Mamdani & Neon Partner On Free ‘Once Upon A Time In Harlem’ Screenings Across NYC Apple’s Fleetwood Mac Doc Lands Title & Release Date The Lede Company Acquires Lauren Winslade’s London-Based Agency Aisle 8 View All October 23, 2026 2:07am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ryu Murakami Marc GANTIER/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images The Japanese writer and filmmaker Ryu Murakami has died. He was 74. Murakami’s publisher, Gentosha, announced his death today in a lengthy statement on their website. “Author Ryu Murakami passed away at his home on October 17, 2026, at the age of 74. We hereby express our deepest condolences and share this news,” the statement read. “The funeral was held as a private family service. In accordance with the family’s wishes, they are declining all condolence visits, monetary offerings, floral tributes, telegrams, and other gifts.” Related Stories Obituaries Tom Skerritt Dies: 'Top Gun,' 'Picket Fences,' 'Alien' Actor Was 93 Obituaries George Fenton Dies: 'Gandhi', 'Cry Freedom' & 'The Blue Planet' Composer Was 76 Born in Nagasaki Prefecture in 1952, Murakami made his writing debut in 1976, while still a university student, with Almost Transparent Blue , which won both the 19th Gunzo New Writers’ Award and the 75th Akutagawa Prize. Watch on Deadline The book became a hit, selling more than 3.5 million copies across its hardcover and paperback editions. In 1980, he received the 3rd Noma Literary Newcomer’s Award for Coin Locker Babies . Murakami also wrote and directed several film adaptations of his own works, including Tokyo Decadence , which explores the lives of women in Tokyo during the bubble economy, and Kyoko , the story of a young Japanese woman’s relationship with a Cuban-American serviceman stationed in the country. In 1994, he published A World Five Minutes Later , set in an alternate reality where Japan did not surrender in World War II. In 1997, he won the 49th Yomiuri Literary Prize for In the Miso Soup . He has been at RTL-owned Fremantle since 2007 and left just shy of 20 years of service on October 9. During that time he has worked on shows such as Got Talent , Idol , X Factor and The Price Is Right , and worked closely with major UK talent such as Ant & Dec and Simon Cowell. O’Dell, who was as most recently Head of Global Entertainment Production, announced his retirement on LinkedIn and this was subsequently confirmed by a Fremantle rep. He’s also the third long-serving Fremantle exec to depart this year following the exit of International and Commercial COO Bob McCourt in July and formats boss Vasha Wallace in August . “It’s been amazing working with Chris, who is loved by all at Fremantle and beyond,” said Crompton. “The legacy of all the fantastic shows Chris has worked on is a testament to his breadth of knowledge, experience and leadership. We wish him all the best in his retirement, and he will be greatly missed.” O’Dell began his career in regional TV in the UK and then moved to become a series producer at London Weekend Television, where he worked on the original Blind Date . He went on to become Head of Entertainment Series at ITV Studios predecessor Granada, and then had spells at Objective Television and IMG Media before joining Fremantle in 2007. “I have also been very fortunate to work with some fabulous on-screen talents, including Cilla Black, Bruce Forsyth, Simon Cowell, Ant & Dec, Bradley Walsh, Matthew Kelly, Tess Daly and countless other stars, both in the UK and around the world,” wrote O’Dell on LinkedIn. “Just as importantly, I have been a part of some wonderfully talented teams. I’m sure I’ll miss it, but I’m also sure it’s time for me to start a new chapter. “I want to thank anyone who has ever helped me over the years. In a front-page story on Friday, the Rupert Murdoch-owned tabloid newspaper claimed that Thomas Markle is being investigated over child abuse images after being reported to the FBI by his own son. Thomas Markle has denied the allegations, telling The Daily Mail that it was “a bunch of lies.” He added: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me.” Related Stories News 'SNL UK' Cold Open Features Face-Off Between Prince William & Harry: "Oh Look, It's The Woman From 'Suits'" News 'SNL UK' Cold Open Lampoons Harry & Meghan's Return: "Don't Tell Me You've Spent All Your Netflix Money Already!" In her statement, which was shared with Deadline, Markle said she became aware of unspecified allegations against her father in 2018. Markle said she decided at that time to deny him access to her children so she could “protect” them. Watch on Deadline The Duchess of Sussex said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed. “In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. “I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families. Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.” Thomas Markle Jr. told The Sun that he discovered a stash of “hundreds” of images and videos on computers and a cellphone at his father’s home in the Philippines. “When I found this material I was horrified and I had no option but to report my dad. I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now,” he said. “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.” ‘The Sun’ front page Thomas Markle Sr. denied his son’s account, claiming that the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines. “Those computers were boxed up in Mexico and put on a cargo ship which took months to get to the Philippines. I kept asking Tom for my computers but he wouldn’t give them to me,” he said. The Sun story goes into detail about what was discovered and the nature of the images, reporting that they included toddlers “either captured nude or engaged in horrifying sex acts.” Markle Sr., who won an Emmy for his work in the camera and electrical department on ABC’s General Hospital , is currently in a rehab centre in Florida after having his leg amputated below the knee following a blood clot. articles.title: Jonathan Groff Returning To Broadway In Solo Play ‘The Amish Project’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Jonathan Groff Returning To Broadway In Solo Play ‘The Amish Project’ ‘The Imaginary Invalid’ Broadway Review: Molière Gets Clowned By A Winning Bill Irwin Neil DeGrasse Tyson, Bill Nye & Mae Jemison Join Broadway’s ‘Galileo’ Musical As Co-Producers View All October 23, 2026 6:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jonathan Groff, Jessica Dickey, Sarna Lapine Chad Meyer/Production Tony Award winner Jonathan Groff will return to Broadway this winter in The Amish Project , a solo play written by Jessica Dickey and directed by Sarna Lapine. Performances begin Wednesday, February 10, 2027, at the Broadhurst Theatre. Producers Robert Ahrens and Tom Kirdahy announced the show and its star today. An official opening night is yet to be announced, and the design team will be announced shortly. Coming off two very successful big-cast Broadway projects – Merrily We Roll Along and Just In Time – Groff will now go solo in The Amish Project , a play described by the production as “a deeply moving solo play about the astonishing power of compassion in the face of unimaginable loss.” Related Stories News 'The Imaginary Invalid' Broadway Review: Molière Gets Clowned By A Winning Bill Irwin News Neil DeGrasse Tyson, Bill Nye & Mae Jemison Join Broadway's 'Galileo' Musical As Co-Producers The synopsis: “When tragedy shatters a close-knit Amish community, what follows is an extraordinary act of grace that challenges everything we think we know about forgiveness. Inspired by true events that unfolded just minutes from where Groff grew up, The Amish Project is an intimate portrait of a place and a community channeled through a single performer. Written by acclaimed playwright Jessica Dickey ( The Rembrandt, The Convent) and directed by Sarna Lapine ( Call Me Izzy, Sunday in the Park with George ), this remarkable story invites us to reflect on how, even in the darkest of hours, our shared humanity endures.” Watch on Deadline Said Groff, “Twenty years ago this month, an unimaginable tragedy happened in a one room Amish schoolhouse in Lancaster, Pennsylvania and Jessica Dickey wrote an astounding work of art in response. Sarna Lapine sent me The Amish Project last year and I was floored by the urgency and potent poetry of Jessica’s writing as she dives headfirst into the many aftershocks of this horrific event and explores the idea that sometimes the most radical human act is forgiveness. I am profoundly grateful to be bringing Jessica’s play to Broadway alongside Sarna and this incredible team.” The Amish Project debuted to critical acclaim at the New York International Fringe Festival and was developed at the Cherry Lane Theatre before premiering Off Broadway at the Rattlestick Playwrights Theater in 2009. It has since become Dickey’s most-produced play, with productions at the Guthrie Theater (Minneapolis), Milwaukee Rep, American Theater Company (Chicago) and City Theatre (Pittsburgh), among others at theaters around the world. Producers Ahrens and Kirdahy said in a statement, “We are honored to bring Jessica Dickey’s stirring and luminous play to Broadway, under the direction of the visionary Sarna Lapine. There is nothing quite like experiencing the singular Jonathan Groff live, and his humanity, generosity and gift for storytelling make this a deeply transporting night of theater that we are proud to share with audiences.” Playwright Dickey said, “I wrote The Amish Project in the heartbreak of my twenties, grappling with how to make a meaningful life as an artist in a world capable of such violence. The play launched my writing career and changed my life. To return to it now, all these years later, when its questions feel as urgent as ever, is profoundly moving. And to do so alongside Jonathan Groff, whose personal connection to this story is matched by his staggering talent, and the extraordinary Sarna Lapine, with the steadfast belief and care of Robert Ahrens and Tom Kirdahy, is a gift I could never have imagined. I can’t wait for Broadway audiences to see it—I’ll be the playwright in the back laughing and crying.” Director Lapine said, “When I first read Jessie’s play, I was blown away by it. She has channeled something extraordinary about a community, a community in mourning, a community in conversation. It is a piece that stays with you for days, weeks, months, years after you’ve sat with it. Like the framework of a well-built one-room schoolhouse, the writing is precise, lean, and strong, illuminating resilience in the face of fragility, and asks, how does one forgive the unforgivable?” ‘Top Gun’, ‘Picket Fences’ And ‘Alien’ Star Dies At 93; Career In Photos ‘Clayface’ Solid $3.5M Thursday Previews; Can He Scare Off Elizabeth Holmes? Lang, who plays Colonel Miles Quaritch in James Cameron’s Avatar franchise, has signed on to star in The Mercy Rider , a modern-day Western thriller which Edel will direct from a script by Richard Julian. articles.title: Peacock’s Hot Streak: Two Quarters of Profit After Years Of Losses
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 22, 2026 4:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Comcast president Mike Cavanagh Kevork Djansezian/Getty Images Peacock , the marquee NBCUniversal streamer, on Thursday delivered its second consecutive profitable quarter on the back of 48 million subscribers, up from 41 million in the year-earlier period but flat quarter-to-quarter. As Comcast, led by Brian Roberts and Michael Cavanagh, reported its third-quarter financials, Peacock posted a pre-tax profit of $261 million, which followed a $189 million profit in the most recent second quarter and a $217 million year-ago loss. Peacock’s maiden second-quarter profit was lifted by FIFA World Cup games, which contributed $440 million in incremental media revenues. The third quarter included $224 million of incremental advertising revenue from the FIFA World Cup as the final games were shown at the start of the latest financial quarter on Peacock and NBCUniversal’s Spanish language Telemundo service. Comcast’s content and experiences businesses reported revenue of $10.5 billion, up 6.5 percent from a year ago, and adjusted EBITIDA up 29 percent to $1.8 billion. Media revenue rose 13 percent to $5.35 billion, with adjusted EBITDA of $769 million. Studios revenue fell 1.1 percent to $2.96 billion, with adjusted EBITDA of $402 million. The latest quarter saw contributions to Universal from Christopher Nolan’s epic The Odyssey , Minions & Monsters and the breakout horror pic Obsession for Focus Features. Peacock, the streaming service of Comcast’s entertainment unit NBCUniversal, saw revenue come to $1.8 billion in the most recent quarter, up from $1.4 billion of revenue in the prior-year period after recent subscription price increases and lower programming costs. As Comcast continues to face a broadband division downturn, the media conglomerate posted third-quarter revenue down 6 percent to $29.29 billion, compared with $31.19 billion in the year-earlier period. Net income attributable to Comcast rose 3.5 percent to $3.44 billion, against $3.33 billion in the same period of 2025. Comcast did manage to trim its broadband losses to 376,000 subscribers during the third quarter, an improvement from 475,000 broadband customer losses a year-ago. The latest results from Comcast follows a separation from Versant, the cable TV-focused spinoff from NBCUniversal that runs CNBC, MS NOW, USA, Golf Channel and other assets. On a morning analyst call, Cavanagh said the Versant separation transaction would be completed by the middle of 2027, and “we’re well into the execution phase,” including building out standalone companies. “While there is still significant work ahead, we have a clear path to completion and remain focused on creating two companies with the strategic flexibility, financial strength and leadership to compete and grow independently,” he added. Cavanagh also welcomed so far holding Peacock’s subscriber base at around 48 million over the last two quarters amid rate increases. As to future profits or losses for the the streaming platform, he added: “The quarters ahead can get lumpy, depending on when rates kick in for different properties.” To continue growing Peacock, NBCUniversal will be bundling the streamer with rival platforms, as with a recently announced multiyear deal between NBCUniversal and YouTube to bring Peacock to YouTube premium subscribers. “We are interested in doing this with others as well. Different bundles will be different for different types of partners, but we’re looking to make them additive to the business,” Cavanagh told analysts. CFO Jason Armstrong also warned Comcast would take a “significant” restructuring charge at over $1 billion in the fourth quarter as the media conglomerate continues to refocus its mobile business around convergent cable and Internet products to fend off competition in broadband from wireless providers like Verizon and T-Mobile. Brian L. Roberts, co-CEO of Comcast, on the call touted the ongoing transformation efforts around connectivity and convergence products at the media conglomerate. “In broadband, while the market’s super competitive, we’ve got a very intelligent remaking of our relationship with our customers, using technology to our advantage.” THR
