articles.title: John C. Reilly, Penny Lane Board Short Doc ‘Stalin Boys’ as Executive Producers (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 21, 2026 5:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Stalin Boys' Courtesy of Pipsqueak Productions/Amplify Pictures Nonfiction filmmaker Penny Lane ( Confessions of a Good Samaritan ) and Academy Award-nominated actor John C. Reilly have boarded the short documentary film Stalin Boys as executive producers. Directed by Ora DeKornfeld and Bianca Giaever, the film follows Malachi, a middle school student in Marathon, Texas, who is obsessed with Joseph Stalin . Yes, THAT Joseph Stalin! When he hears about the Texas History Day competition, he writes a play about the late Soviet dictator and enlists his friends Cayden, Lyric and Jurem to play fearful civilians and loyal henchmen. Related Stories Business Audiovisual Women Leadership Program Unveils Participants, Sets Tallinn Partnership Business Netflix Stock and Price Targets Drop as Wall Street Debates If the Streamer Can Flip the Script “In a school of 11 students in a town of about 400, the boys grapple with a dark chapter of history and confront questions of power and legacy in their own lives,” a synopsis teases. The film debuted on The New York Times Op-Docs earlier this month and is eligible for the Academy Award for Documentary Short Film category. Veteran doc director Lane, whose subjects have ranged from Kenny G in Listening to Kenny G to Flaco the owl in Wild Inside , was drawn to what she described as the Little Miss Sunshine -esque blend of whimsy and heart. “I never imagined the words, ‘Screw National History Day!’ could make me laugh so hard and feel as much pain at the same time,” said Lane. “I’d also never thought to ask, ‘What was Stalin’s favorite color?’ but I’m glad to have met Malachi and discover he knows the answer.” Giaever lauded Lane as “a documentary icon,” adding: “Her work taught us that documentaries can be funny, playful, and absurd, while still tackling difficult topics.” Reilly will support the filmmakers’ campaign to bring Stalin Boys to classrooms and audiences nationwide. “I loved this short film,” the star said. “I loved it so much I lent my name to it as an executive producer. It reminded me of my own very imaginative and inspired childhood obsessions as a theater kid. I found the kids to be a wonderful inspiration to us all with their commitment to and enthusiasm for their vision. I also was deeply moved by the teachers who supported and guided them to realizing their visions. It takes caring people like these teachers to shepherd today’s young people if we want a better future for our world.” Concluded Reilly: “I hope everyone watches this film and remembers that big lives always start small and even tiny dusty towns in the middle of nowhere can produce people who can shape a brighter future for us all.” DeKornfeld said about Reilly: “John has spent his career playing people who are funny and heartbreaking in the same breath, which is exactly who these boys are. He immediately understood this film is about what’s possible when teachers encourage kids to follow their interests, as weird as they may be. We could not have asked for a better champion to help us get it in front of the audiences who need it most.” The filmmakers learned about the story while visiting their friend Crawford Hunt, who had been recruited to teach history at the school. They spent a week with the boys and their teachers during rehearsals for the state competition. Stalin Boys , which you can watch here, premiered at the Big Sky Documentary Film Festival and won the Audience Award and a Special Jury Award at the 2 026 SXSW Film & TV Festival. In July, the film also won the Academy Award-qualifying Documentary Grand Prize at Indy Shorts. It screens later this month at AFI Fest in Los Angeles. Stalin Boys was edited by Natalie Ancona, with an original score by Elori Saxl. The Pipsqueak Productions film was produced by Alejandra Vasquez and Amplify Pictures. For Op-Docs, Alexandra Garcia is the executive producer and Yvonne Ashley Kouadjo the producer. The short was supported by Southern Methodist University’s Narrative Now Initiative, Mountainfilm and The Economic Hardship Reporting Project. DeKornfeld directed the Emmy-nominated short USA v SCOTT , The Grandfather Puzzle and several episodes of the Netflix original series Explained . She is currently in production on a feature documentary about journalistic fixers in Mexico. Giaever is an independent filmmaker, radio journalist and the creator and host of the podcast Constellation Prize . Her upcoming documentary series Free Help premiered at the Tribeca Film Festival and will be available next year. THR

articles.title: Interscope Unveils Exec Promotions Following Shake Up
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All October 21, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michelle An, Laura Carter and Ramon Alvarez-Smikle. courtesy of Interscope Interscope revealed a suite of promotions on Tuesday, a week after the record label and parent company Universal Music Group underwent a round of layoffs and executive departures as part of UMG’s previously-announced cost-savings measure that started in 2024. Longtime Interscope exec Michelle An has been named president and Chief Creative Officer at the label, Interscope said, adding that An would both IGA’s pop/rock division as well as have a broader role across the whole roster to help artists “shape the worlds around their music, from visual identity and storytelling to brand development and long-term career strategy.” “IGA has always been defined by original voices and by the teams who back those voices with taste, conviction and care,” John Janick, Chairman and CEO of Interscope Capitol, said in a statement. “Michelle has one of the clearest creative instincts in the business. She helps artists make the world around their music feel bold, fully realized and unmistakably their own.” Laura Carter and Ramon Alvarez-Smikle, meanwhile, have been named co-presidents of Urban at the label. The two are well-respected hip-hop marketing executives, and Interscope said the duo “will bring A&R, marketing innovation, digital strategy and audience development closer together for IGA Urban’s artists.” “Laura and Ramon bring complementary strengths to IGA Urban,” Janick said. “Laura has earned deep trust through her artist relationships, creative judgment and commitment to developing talent. Ramon brings cultural instinct, deep digital expertise and a sharp understanding of how artists build audiences and communities. Together, they will connect A&R, marketing and digital strategy around each artist’s vision, helping IGA Urban artists move with more clarity, momentum, and impact.” Interscope’s pop/rock and urban divisions were impacted by last week’s restructuring as Sam Riback, Interscope’s co-president and head of pop/rock A&R, as well as Nicole Wyskoarko, the label’s head of urban A&R, both departed. THR

articles.title: Sacha Baron Cohen Gets Real About Backlash, Death Threats and Resurrecting Ali G
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Sacha Baron Cohen was photographed Oct. 14 at PMC Studios Los Angeles. Styling by Artistic & Fashion Director Alison Edmond Paul Smith sweater; Ali G’s jewelry. Paul Smith sweater; Ali G’s jewelry. Photographed By Beau Grealy Sacha Baron Cohen insists his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I? , is the last guerrilla comedy of its kind that he’ll make. He’s adamant. No more Borat. No more Bruno. No more Ali G. They’re too hard, he says, too risky. He’s tired of hoodwinking people to expose their prejudices, and he’s even more tired of the death threats that periodically follow. There are easier ways to make money in this business, and eventually his luck will run out. The trouble with his declaration, however impassioned, is that he has been making it for years. He’d routinely say he was done before he made the 2020 Borat sequel, which, incidentally, earned two Oscar nominations, and he was even more insistent afterward. And each time he says it, he believes it to be true. He wants it to be true, he tells me. So, why are we here, I ask, discussing an Ali G revival? “Because I’m terrified of where our society is headed, and the way I can comment on that is through my comedy,” he says. “I wanted to show the extremism on both sides of the political spectrum and the danger of virtuous violence.” There’s a level of seriousness that belies the 90-minute comedy film he’s made, which features an imbecilic white rapper who speaks in Caribbean-British slang and a contraption that shoots bullets out of one’s rear end. Recognizing this, he adds: “And obviously we wanted to make the funniest film that’s ever been made.” His longtime collaborators have other theories about his return. Anthony “Ant” Hines, who’s been working with Baron Cohen since The 11 O’Clock Show , where the Ali G character originated, believes his pal had missed the adrenaline rush, just as he had. “It’s a visceral buzz you get from making a movie this way,” Hines says, “and nothing comes close to it.” Dan Mazer, whose friendship with Baron Cohen dates back to secondary school in the U.K., wasn’t particularly surprised to get the call about dusting off Ali G, in part because they’ve never stopped talking about the character. In fact, whenever they got together, they’d often slip into Ali G’s voice, he says, and imagine what patently absurd things he would be saying or doing in different situations. “I also think it’s a knowledge that Sacha is the Michael Jordan of this sort of filmmaking,” says Mazer. “And yeah, Michael Jordan went off and tried to play baseball, and you go, ‘OK, you’re a pretty good baseball player,’ but he’s not the Michael Jordan of baseball. And Sacha is the Michael Jordan of this, and to an extent, we all are. We invented this genre, and nobody else has matched what we’ve done.” Whatever the reasoning may be, Ali G is back, rolling into theaters Oct. 23 before landing on Amazon Prime Video soon after. And like plenty else that Baron Cohen has done, it’s already prompted a full-blown meta-outrage cycle, complete with a campaign to boycott the film. With each new trailer or PR stunt posted to social media come fresh accusations of an outdated caricature and of cultural appropriation — the latter a central plot point in the film, in which Ali G’s progressive nemesis (also played by Baron Cohen) attempts to cancel him on those very grounds. Some in his camp have speculated that it’s more of a coordinated attack by pro-Palestinians who are critical of Baron Cohen’s past support of Israel. (Though he’s been quiet about Israeli politics and the conflict in Gaza in recent years, Baron Cohen is a prominent Jew who has sounded the alarm about the surge of antisemitism on social media, reportedly telling TikTok executives in 2023 that what was happening on their platform was “creating the biggest antisemitic movement since the Nazis.”) Colton Dunn, an Emmy-winning Ali G superfan and one of three Black writers hired on the film, is aware of the cultural appropriation claims. “But we knew where we were coming from, and we dealt with it all in the movie,” he says, “and at the heart of it, Sacha and the movie want to defeat evil and hate. That’s the intention behind it.” Still, the internet has suggested the backlash has Amazon spooked. Courtenay Valenti, Amazon MGM Studios’ head of film, streaming and theatrical, offers this: “We want to be in business with exceptional storytellers who have distinctive creative visions, and Sacha is exactly that. He has always been fearless in his comedy, with a unique ability to tap into the cultural conversation in ways that are both provocative and entertaining.” Over cappuccinos in the garden of the Chateau Marmont, Baron Cohen lets loose on the mounting backlash, his battles with studios and the $3 million day that nearly derailed his film. Paul Smith robe; Wander socks; stylist’s own slippers; Ali G’s own jewelry, glasses, hat. Photographed By Beau Grealy In 2021, you allegedly performed as Ali G at The Comedy Store in Australia. How soon after did you explore the idea of another film, and what did those early conversations entail? During the pandemic, our family moves to Australia, and when they lock down in Australia, you cannot leave where you are. My ex [Isla Fisher] is from Perth, so we applied to go there. She’s rejected. I find out that you have to show that there’s a financial benefit to Western Australia to be allowed in. You have to apply to the police. So I say, “Listen, I’m doing a stand-up tour. It’s going to create 300 jobs. It’s going to bring tens of millions of dollars into Western Australia.” Obviously I had no intention of doing it. But then the police accept me. We spent 14 days in lockdown, and at the end, a police car turns up, an inspector comes out, and she says, “I am in charge of your stand-up tour.” So, you had to do a stand-up tour. I did, and I had the police watching me. I ended up doing a 90-minute show, and what was interesting was that people really loved seeing Borat and Bruno, but when Ali G came out, there was a different response. It was as if people believed he was real. There’s going to be a lot of amateur psychology in this interview, but my observation was that because Ali G existed before I existed as a public figure — for five or six years, I didn’t give an interview [as myself] — people thought Ali was real and therefore there was this different response to him. So, I felt, “Hold on, is there a movie in this character?” I came back to America at the end of 2021 and started talking with the team about it. We all felt Ali by himself wouldn’t be a satirical movie because he was from a bygone era — this relic from another period who’s unaware that he is deeply problematic. But what if we brought in another character, an ultraprogressive extremist [also played by Baron Cohen] who’s his rival and make it a thriller like The Fugitive ? We had in our mind this line that goes, “We have a cultural appropriator on the loose,” from that famous speech in The Fugitive . That felt funny to me. In the revisionist history of the film, you had ended Da Ali G Show because you couldn’t come to financial terms with HBO. It left me wondering if there were any conversations or interest, from either side, about doing more? Oh, yes. HBO wanted to carry on. I said no because at that time, in Britain, I think a lot of comedians were snobs about doing multiple seasons. So, there was no expectation or desire to do 15 seasons — to do the American way. I’m very friendly with Larry David, and I’m jealous of him that he can do Curb again and again. I probably would’ve had a much easier life if I just carried on doing Da Ali G Show . Paul Smith sweater, pants; Wander socks; Doucal’s boots; Ali G’s own jewelry, glasses. A decade ago, you said of this type of filmmaking: “It’s a young man’s game. You have to be prepared for a small amount of risk, and my philosophy was always: ‘Well, if something bad happens, I’m single and everyone’s going to be all right if I end up in hospital for two weeks.’ Now that I’m married with kids, it’s more difficult to justify.” So, did you find a way to do it differently, or did you just say, “Fuck it”? I’m never cavalier. These movies are dangerous to make, but we try to limit the risks and keep everybody safe. But even physically, they’re incredibly demanding. So, the final scene of this film is an eight-hour continuous scene that takes place over 12 locations. It’s a continual shot. There’s gunfire in it. There’s a medical procedure. There are drones, there are explosions, and it’s taking place in the desert. On the way to shooting it, I bumped into one of the great stuntmen and he said, “You will go to hospital if you make this movie,” because I explained I’m wearing a prosthetic head in a fat suit. He said, “You’ll be so dehydrated you’ll be in hospital for two weeks.” You hear that and think what? That I have to fix the problem. So, I had an endurance specialist who does the Tour de France be by my side during the scene and they’re measuring my weight. I think I had 11 liters of Pedialyte. And listen, a number of people went to the hospital for dehydration, including the bodyguard. There were dangers in the scene as well. One of the people grabbed a gun and almost did something very dangerous. These really are the hardest movies to make, but I suppose I made it because I’m scared of this world of conspiracies and lies that are spread by social media and now by AI. If we don’t have these shared facts, then democracies crumble and we can’t have a tolerant society. And to make people laugh is therapy. As I read your own quote back to you just now, you were laughing. Why? Because I’m always surprised at my own idiocy. I’m very bad at looking into the future and imagining how I will feel. So, for example, the naked fight in Borat 1 , we get to set and Ken Davitian, who’s not conventionally attractive, is naked, and he’s going to sit on my face. And I say, “I’m not going to do this!” At that point, Larry Charles, the director, said, “So why did you write it?!” I continually make these decisions that are very bad for my own health and sanity. You are making this film in a very different moment, culturally and comedically. Do you derive some masochistic pleasure from that kind of challenge? I’ll tell you, in the script, there was a moment where Ali G is canceled, and the way we wanted to do that was that I, Sacha, should be canceled in the real world and the idea was to use the footage of me being canceled and stick it into the movie. And we did actually get some of the second bit, but we didn’t have the money to open up the movie and put the footage in. That was the intention, though. I’m told you get a fair number of death threats, which now come from both the left and the right. When have you decided something wasn’t worth it? I was about to do a scene [in Borat 1 ] and we had a cop who had his gun on his thigh and I said, “Why is your gun on your thigh?” He goes, “Well, I need to be really fast to draw in this area.” I said, “Well, how close are you to me?” And he said, “I’ll be with you within three minutes.” I realized that was not a good thing to do, so I pulled that scene. I will never do a scene if I think I’m actually going to die. Thom Sweeney shirt; Ali G’s ring, sunglasses. Photographed By Beau Grealy You’ve filmed in a bulletproof vest, so you’ve clearly anticipated the possibility of being shot? Yes, on Borat 2 , there was a scene at a gun rights rally that I knew there was a risk of getting shot. But I felt it was an important film to be made. Is there anyone who says to you, “Hey, Sacha, I know this seems noble to you, but maybe it’s not necessary”? Yes. Who? Your children? I don’t talk about my children. But my brothers tell me that. And my mom and some of my team as well, because there are much easier options. I made a movie called Ladies First . I shot it in three months. It came out. A lot of people saw it [on Netflix]. And it’s as financially beneficial as making something that takes years, and there’s absolutely zero risk. There must be some masochistic nature to me, but I don’t think it’s just that. I want to give the fans who’ve been loyal for the last 28 years something that they’ve never seen before. I want to give them the most ambitious movie I’ve ever made, which is a three-character movie. [Baron Cohen also plays a former Mossad agent.] It is my version of the Avengers. I’ve always assumed that you were like Tom Cruise, after the same adrenaline rush that he is as he jumps out of planes. I don’t think that’s the reason I do it. You don’t? Your collaborators seem to … No. The first [for-hire] movie I did, Talladega Nights , I walked into my trailer and there was a bed there. I realized I’d never been in a trailer before, and I go, “Hold on, this is a paid job where I can go to sleep?!” I couldn’t comprehend how relatively easy it was, and it was great fun. But as you’ll probably deduce from this interview, I’m not very self-aware. Paul Smith sweater; Ali G’s jewelry. Photographed By Beau Grealy I don’t know that I buy that. OK. Do I enjoy it when something works? Yes. Am I upset when something doesn’t work? Yes. So, for example, this final scene is an eight-hour continuous shot over multiple locations and no one had ever done that before. Normally we shoot a scene or two scenes a day. Here, we put probably 40 scenes together and shot them continuously. I had a variety of line producers and assistant directors refuse to schedule it. And there are 400 or so beats that must all go perfectly, because you’re dealing with real people and if anything doesn’t feel quite right, they will stop and say, “Hold on, this isn’t real.” Of course. So gunfire, the squibs have to go off perfectly. A medical procedure happens. That body that we use has to be believable. Then a fire breaks out during the first part of the scene. As we’re driving to the second location to kidnap somebody with these real people, I find out that location four is surrounded by fire, and it’s being evacuated, and we have to pull the scene. And each time we run it, it’s $4 million and we’re insured for $1 million, and I personally have to pay $3 million. So, we shut down production and we have a discussion, which is that it’s completely idiotic that we’re trying this. And everyone is telling you it’s not possible? Yes, and I’ve lost $3 million that day. Obviously it was my money, which is a very stupid idea. But you ultimately got it? We got it. We had some of the team that worked on the Oscars because I was like, “What is a movie or a TV show where nothing can go wrong? It’s the Oscars.” And even there, sometimes something’s going wrong! I said to them, “OK, this is the Oscars, it’s just taking place over 50 miles in 12 locations. And it has gunfire and blood.” But at the end of all of it, if you look at the behind-the-scenes footage, I’m not jumping up and down. I’m content. The Ali G film, which has Baron Cohen playing three different characters, suffered multiple shutdowns and a change of studios. Michael Legato © 2026 Amazon Content Services With 2020’s Borat 2 , you’ve said that several of the places you pitched were concerned by the political content and the idea of running it before the election. How did this pitch compare? Well, the desire was always to have this come out a few days before either a presidential election or the midterms. A lot of my movies have come out around those times. Borat 1 came out almost 20 years to the day, on November 3, 2006, just before the midterms. It’s a time for people to think about the choices that they’re about to make. But this movie is more about the dangers of extremism on both sides. I get that, but you’re also operating in an extremely risk-averse climate. I can’t imagine there weren’t any concerns … Well, Hollywood is a superficial place. Noooo. I know. ( Laughter. ) But I pitched this after Borat 2 had won two Golden Globes and had Oscar nominations and was the most watched movie ever on Amazon. That’s enough to convince studio heads to buy it. And everyone tried. It was somewhere else first, no? Yes. Amazon and Universal were the final contenders. We ended up going with Universal but, in the end, the movie took so long that we went back to Amazon. And it was actually great because we’d had an incredible experience there with the last one. We really did. And that movie [ Borat 2 ] also was at Universal and ended up at Amazon. So, this one moved because — It was taking too long. You have to understand the basis of this kind of movie is that we have to find people who don’t know who I am, which becomes harder and harder. I think our research department interviewed 5,000 doctors to get one [for a single scene]. Then we had a number of other things that kept on shutting it down. The fire. The writers strike. I ended up doing another movie in the middle. Baron Cohen was joined by 300 Ali G look-alikes who followed him around London for a viral promo stunt Oct. 11. Jeff Spicer/Getty Images Amazon came aboard a third of the way through. What did their notes look like? For better or worse, maybe for worse, I’m a final-cut producer and director. So, you’re saying it didn’t much matter what their notes were? Well, executives can have really fantastic notes. And they can have terrible notes. But I always listen to the audience and I’m really guided by that. You were once asked about comparisons between you and Andy Kaufman, to which you said, “In a way, he’s more of an artist than I am in that I don’t think he cared what the audience thought — and deep down, I really want to make the audience laugh. And that’s why I fight to get jokes to be funny … I’ll go to war with whatever studio has been stupid enough to pay me money to make a movie.” Again, you’re laughing … I can’t believe how honest I was. What did those fights look like on a film like this? If something is funny, then I will go to war for it. And the studios know that because I make it clear when we do these movies, which makes me not very studio-friendly in some ways because my allegiance is to the audience. And I go to every single screening and I record the laughter and I grade the jokes and I have a few people that I’ve trained to grade them too, and then I cut the jokes within a frame. It’s obsessive and very intricate, but it’s designed to deliver really funny movies. Some people find me incredibly arrogant because they’ll come up and say, “You know that movie, Borat 2 , wasn’t funny.” And I’ll say, “You’re entitled to your opinion, but you’re wrong. I have 5,000 people laughing at these jokes and I can show you they are empirically funny.” While the vast majority of the Ali G cast are unsuspecting nonactors, Baron Cohen and his onscreen partner, played by Morgana Robinson, are the exceptions. Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios You said that you’re not studio-friendly, but, as you noted, this is a superficial business and if your model can put butts in seats … Yes, it’s about money. But I’m also a great supporter of the Oscars and other awards ceremonies because, however absurd they are, it creates another incentive for studio heads to make quality projects. Because studio heads do want to win Oscars and they want to get nominated. And we’ve been very lucky in that the Academy and the Globes and some other organizations have recognized our work. In fact, I was sitting at that table [pointing to another table in the Chateau garden] in 2006 having done Borat , and Sean Penn came and sat at the table and he said, “Why don’t you do an Oscar campaign for your performance in Borat ?” I said, “That’s absurd. They’ll never give me an Oscar nomination.” And he said, “They will.” So, we went to Fox at the time and they said, “Listen, we’ll pay for one Oscar campaign, but it’s either writing or acting.” At the time, I was actually winning some of the acting awards, to my great surprise, but I spoke to the team and we decided to push the writing. [The 2006 film was nominated for best adapted screenplay.] So, we gave up the acting campaign. Also, I was about to make Bruno and I didn’t want to go on a baby-kissing tour, which would destroy my next movie. Me doing this kind of stuff [an interview as himself] destroys the ability to make another one. I know, I know. I’m sorry. There we go. Look what you’ve done. You’ve ruined me. As you anticipated, it didn’t take long for people to start lodging complaints. One criticism, which mirrors a plotline in the film, is that Ali G uses the character as a cover for enforcing racial stereotypes. What do you say to that? Well, I’ll repeat what I’ve said for many years, which is that Ali G is a white cultural appropriator who steals from the musical artists that he admires. The reason Ali G says “West Side” is not because the Afro-Caribbean community in London was saying “West Side.” Nobody there was. It’s because Tupac Shakur, who he admires, is saying “West Side.” And so he is funny because he is delusional. He lives this boring, white middle-class life in a suburban town, and he deludes himself that he’s living in Compton, and that is the absurdity of Ali G. The core joke is that a white moron, possibly the stupidest man in the world, is interviewing a white expert or high-status politician, and that white expert or high-status politician believes that this imbecile played by me is real and that leads to comedy. And in my belief, it slightly undermines the power of the establishment. So it was fundamentally an anti-establishment character where we’re pricking the assuredness of the establishment by saying, “Listen, these people aren’t that smart. They believe that Channel 4 or HBO could have sent one of the most stupid people in the world to interview them.” Baron Cohen as Bruno in 2009 in Berlin. Sean Gallup/Getty Images What do you make of the argument that not everybody recognizes the absurdity and so the stereotypes being presented can have dangerous ramifications? Everyone is entitled to their own view. And a lot of the stuff on social media is orchestrated, and not necessarily orchestrated by people who really believe in what they’re saying. We’ll get to that. But when I did Da Ali G Show in America, the first people who gravitated to it were the Black hip-hop community. The first GQ Award that I was given was given to me by Method Man and Redman. I did a series of adverts for the NBA directed by Spike Lee, who’s not naive about racial issues. They recognized these characters, these white cultural appropriators, and they found them funny. So, this notion of it being problematic hadn’t been raised for 20 years. OK, but you seemed to know it would be this time around? Yes. I knew, and I wanted to make sure that this was an anti-racist movie, which is why we were so concerned with having absolutely brilliant Black writers on board and consulting with brilliant Black cultural commentators. As I believe you were referencing, there was a pretty sizable social media campaign to boycott the movie, and some have speculated that the campaign is tied to your pro-Israel stance — Well, I haven’t said anything about Israel. [Baron Cohen voiced his support for Israel and the hostages immediately after the Oct. 7 attacks but has been quiet on the Gaza war and Israeli politics in the years since.] I think people are being portrayed as things that they are not on social media and it’s problematic. We are in a world where people can’t distinguish between facts and lies, and that’s something that I’ve spent a lot of the last few years trying to fix. For example, I co-founded a group called Stop Hate for Profit with the NAACP and Color of Change and the ADL and certain other civil rights groups to stop the misinformation and incitement of racism on social media. So, I’m not surprised that prominent Jews are being targeted. I knew that this was going to happen. The level of organization is surprising, but this is a trend of Jews being portrayed in certain ways and trying to be silenced. You’ve been vocal about the rise of antisemitism, broadly speaking. Have you felt any difference in your own Hollywood career after Oct. 7? No, not really. I mean, maybe it’s because I don’t do much, but I haven’t. Well, you’re about to make your West End debut in a Quentin Tarantino play, which feels like a big leap, going from this film, in which you’re in complete control as the writer, director and star, to being a puppet in Tarantino’s theater. How did that come together? I’ve never had a career plan, but I have this kind of no-brainer rule, which is if one of the best directors in the world asks me to do something, I’ll say yes, even if it’s instinctively the wrong project. So when Martin Scorsese says, “I’m doing a kid’s film, will Sacha play the villain in it?” And I read the book and the character’s not that interesting. I actually had a lot of arguments with [screenwriter John] Logan about it [ Hugo ]. But I say yes because I want to learn how to make better films. And so if Quentin comes along and says, “I want to do a play,” I say yes. Then I actually read the play and I thought it was fantastic. And I felt, why not? So currently, I’m doing nine hours of sword-fighting training a week. And I would just clarify, rather than be a puppet, Quentin did suggest that there would be some element of collaboration. As Borat, sporting a mankini in Cannes in 2006. Anthony Harvey – PA Images/PA Images via Getty Images Have you seen it yet? A little bit, yes. But Quentin and I have been talking about doing a project for at least 20 years. We talked about doing The Scarlet Pimpernel about 20 years ago. Borat came out and Quentin and I would have dinner monthly and I almost did a part in [his 2012 Western] Django Unchained . In the end, I had to drop out because I ended up doing Les Misérables . But I came very close to doing a scene with Kerry Washington. I even had a prosthetic chin made because Quentin was very adamant that I would resemble this character he’d liked from the ’40s. Ant Hines, one of your longtime collaborators, suggested you’ve tussled with Amazon in the promotion of this new film. “We’re giving Amazon panic attacks on the daily,” he told me. “They’re used to Timothée Chalamet eating some chicken wings; they’re not used to 300 Timothée Chalamets attempting to take part in the London Marathon, which is a thing they shut down.” This is why it’s best not to talk to somebody like Ant. ( Laughs. ) You know, they’ve actually been great in terms of the marketing. But it’s not a traditional process when you work with me and you’re marketing a movie. You did end up with 300 Ali G look-alikes following you around London. That had to be validating, if a little overwhelming. The really concerning thing was that these fans were coming out with catchphrases that I’d completely forgotten. I was like, “Wait a minute. I recognize that … What is that from?” And they’d go, “It’s you!” And some of them were doing better Ali G impressions than me. There was one guy there, an Ali G impersonator, and I had to explain, like, “Listen, you’ve been doing this at weddings and bar mitzvahs every week for the last 20 years. I haven’t been doing this.” I’ve actually had that happen before. We did a movie called Bruno , and Jonah Hill was one of the writers. And in the writers room, he was doing impressions of Bruno, and they were better than Bruno. Then when I started shooting the movie, I realized that I was doing an impression of Jonah Hill doing an impression of me. In any genre, there’s always an “It” person, and at various points, you’ve employed those people shortly before they reached that status: Jonah, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg and, most recently, Nathan Fielder, who worked on your Showtime series, Who Is America? What do you think of what Nathan has done in the eight years since you worked together? Oh, I think he’s a comic genius and he reinvented the genre that I, I suppose, created or developed. And he had a rule, really, which was to not do anything that I had done. But he’s a brilliant, brilliant mind, and absolutely hilarious. I think his documentary [ You Can See Everything ] is going to be huge, so I’m very excited for him. But it’s been an honor to have all of these incredible people come and work with me. Seth and Evan, the story with them was, it was the Ali G Show , and they came in with an idea for Bruno — instead of Girls Gone Wild , it was Boys Gone Wild . I said, “OK, you’re hired, but I’ve only got enough money for one writer, so unless you want to share a hotel room and a bed and a wage, I can only hire one of you and it’s going to be Seth.” They came back and said, “We’ll split the wage.” And basically they would write in a double bed in the Best Western hotel we were in. They had beers all around them. They were smoking and they’d write in bed. That’s fantastic. For you, what do the incoming calls look like these days? I think they’re kind of what comes in to everyone. I get the traditional comedies, kernels of comedy ideas, and then dramas. Is one genre more appealing than the other right now? No. I want to do stuff that challenges me. So again, I’m not doing Borat 3 , which also would be incredibly challenging. Again, this movie I just did is the most challenging movie I’ve ever done, but I’m not doing more. Until the next one … No, no, I really have had enough. I know you don’t believe me. I do not. Oh, I really pray that in six years’ time, you don’t come to me and quote me to myself. This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Disney and Netflix Are Courting Creators. YouTube Is Playing Hardball to Keep Them
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 21, 2026 6:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Texas-based sports creators Dude Perfect inked a wide-ranging partnership with Disney that will span entertainment, sports, consumer products and experiences. Illustrated by Neil Jamieson On Sept. 23, YouTube gathered a couple hundred of its top creators at Pier 57 in New York City for its annual “Made on YouTube” event. The showcase is where YouTube reveals new initiatives for its creator community, giving attendees a sneak peek at what the video platform has been cooking up in its Skunk Works, like new AI video editing tools. But this year, YouTube wasn’t the only platform on their minds. Netflix, Disney+, Tubi and others are aggressively cutting deals for top creators, in some cases securing wholly original programming or day-and-date releases with YouTube, offering millions of dollars in the process. The Google-owned video platform is not taking it lying down, launching a carrot-and-stick approach to try and keep its place as the primary home for top talent. “It’s a very good time to be in the creator business,” says Adam Wescott, CEO of Home Game Studios, noting the demand for their work. With creator-owned studios proliferating nationwide, it’s a battle that could portend the future of streaming entertainment. It started with kids and family content. Netflix, seeking to bolster its kids programming, inked deals for YouTube native content from CoComelon , Ms. Rachel and Mark Rober. It worked, with all three becoming among the most watched programs in the category. The streamer subsequently ordered originals from them and began to reach out to creators in other genres, spanning food (Nick DiGiovanni), talk ( Good Mythical Morning with Rhett & Link) and teen content (Alan Chikin Chow). Rich Greenfield, the LightShed analyst, believes Netflix has committed upward of $1 billion on creator and podcast programming over the next three years (still, admittedly, a very small slice of its $20 billion annual content budget). But Netflix only started the current war. Disney has long worked with creators, but recent months have seen wide-ranging deals with the likes of Dhar Mann, Dude Perfect and Like Nastya as it seeks out family-friendly and on-brand creators who can live on Disney+. And the company recently hosted a creator event at the El Capitan Theater and Disney Studios Lot, with some 350 creators to further forge those relationships. Tubi, the Fox-owned streaming service, has inked deals with dozens of creators for both originals and library fare. YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Dhar Mann at YouTube Brandcast at David Geffen Hall on May 14, 2025 in New York City. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for YouTube There’s already hope in the creator community that Skydance is about to follow them, with new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz having served as the CEO of Maker Studios. But why are these other streamers so eager to get in the creator business? Multiple sources paint a picture built around audience, money and speed. The larger studio platforms and streamers desperately want to have a product that appeals to the younger, digitally native audience that religiously watches creator content on YouTube. “I think creators really do value, in the right circumstances, the elevation and amplification of being on a main channel platform like a traditional media company,” says Akshay Mehta, the CEO of Lighthouse Studios, a creator entertainment studio. “Creators are creatives fundamentally. They just discovered that in the last 15 years, for a lot of people, the best way to be creative is to go make stuff on YouTube.” The money certainly helps. Multiple sources on the creator side stress that they need funding to help pursue some of the ideas they have, and such places as Netflix, Tubi and Disney are helping them do that. The big streamers are funding original shows and offering help to break into areas like consumer products or live experiences (that was a key piece of Disney’s Dude Perfect deal). Streamers also are banking that creators can not only bring their audience with them but fill their libraries with content that is, frankly, dramatically less expensive than traditional fare and that is produced at a more rapid clip. “These platforms have seen this shift, and they can’t ignore it,” says Nic Paul, the president of the creator services company Spotter. “They all have subscriptions, they all have ad-supported products, even at Netflix, the ad-supported product is becoming a lot more of the focus. There’s a lot of churn. Everyone is like, how do I create enough content fast to keep audiences engaged? Because if you think about it, Stranger Things on Netflix, I’ve got to wait a year plus for a season, and creators are obviously very fast at putting out IP.” Indeed, one top creator who has a deal with a streaming platform says they told their new partner that they can produce an hour’s worth of programming at perhaps 10 percent of the cost (or less!) of a traditional comedy, drama or unscripted concept, all at a faster pace. But what has surprised creators more than anything is how hard YouTube is fighting back. The platform is a juggernaut, and it would be just fine if it lost top creators to other places. But it is waging a multipronged effort — with both incentives and threats — to try and convince creators to make YouTube their primary home. Many of the incentives focus on brand deals, with YouTube significantly increasing its resources in the space. Some creators see YouTube’s brand deals as a way to subsidize or pay for content that they want to make, given that YouTube does not pay to license content in the same way platforms like Netflix do. “Given the cultural phenomenon that YouTube creators are, and this sort of juggernaut that they are in the culture out there, of course other streaming platform services have taken note,” YouTube CEO Neal Mohan told the Big Technology podcast after Made on YouTube when pressed on the dispute, adding that even as MrBeast produces his Beast Games for Prime Video, he still keeps YouTube as his home base. “And, frankly, I think that’s flattering to our creators.” But YouTube also has played hardball, with one creator telling THR that they were “shocked” at the platform’s approach. On the one hand, some of the threats are reasonable: YouTube selects a handful of creators to appear onstage at its annual Brandcast upfront event, a high-profile stage that can lead to major deals. And it has supported Emmy campaigns for creators in certain categories. Those would stop for creators who shift their allegiances to other platforms. (Netflix and Disney already have promised to bring creators to their own upfronts next year and fund some Emmy efforts, according to sources.) And they have even suggested that creators may not be eligible for YouTube Select, an ad program for its very top creators. That caught some creators off guard, as it was seen as an objective program based on reach and scale and is built around videos on YouTube. “That was never their approach in the past,” says Wescott. “It was always about supporting creators and reminding them why YouTube was their home.” Lilly Singh has spoken out candidly about the difference between working in the traditional Hollywood system vs. the creator-driven YouTube economy. Mathew Tsang/Getty Images The platform still plays that game, though even there the tone has become somewhat combative, as one creator notes to THR . Earlier in October, comedian Lilly Singh returned to YouTube after a years-long hiatus, once again creating original content after working in Hollywood. In an interview YouTube posted to its blog , she did not hold back. “Hollywood has real systemic issues, especially for women and people of color. Over the past few years, I received countless notes that weren’t about improving the project, but about making it ‘more palatable,” ‘more marketable,’ or ‘less niche.’ That is fundamentally anti-creative. Our job is to tell our stories unapologetically,” Singh said. “On YouTube, there are no gatekeepers demanding I make my brain baby more palatable for the masses. That authenticity is why my channel worked in the first place.” Message received. But why is YouTube seem so interested in keeping creators on-platform? Especially because, as Mohan notes, it’s a good thing for the ecosystem when others are interested? “On the surface, YouTube should not care. Creators are not launching their careers on Netflix or Disney+,” LightShed analyst Greenfield wrote on Oct. 9. “We suspect YouTube is concerned because the top 20-50 creators have an outsized importance to its major brand advertising commitments each year. Most brands only know a select group of high-profile creators. If brands start to see those creators appearing on Netflix… does a brand start to ask why it is paying YouTube for creators it can find in a curated, brand-safe environment elsewhere?” Advertising is at the heart of the battle, with the ad-supported Tubi competing with Netflix and Disney (each of which is leaning into ads) for creator deals. Creators, of course, are used to working with brands. “A dirty little secret of our space is 90 percent of the revenue is brand endorsements, influencer marketing,” Wescott notes. Still, none of the creators (or those who worked with top creators) suggest that they will completely leave YouTube, even if they may still cut deals to develop original ideas elsewhere. And it isn’t just out of loyalty to the platform that made them or that funds them (Instagram and TikTok, they note, pay basically nothing). “I think you’ll be hard pressed to find a successful YouTube creator who’s willing to walk away from that platform, because it’s what they know, it’s where their audience is, it’s where they grew their business, and it’s where they have the most direct control,” says Wescott. “You’re still playing on someone else’s playground, but YouTube is not telling you what to post on your channel. The other guys are going to have some sort of opinion on what you create on the original side.” For an ambitious creator, it may mean taking a more strategic approach to how, when, and where they choose to produce content. “I’m distributing on [YouTube], I’m paying for everything, I’m getting paid, which is amazing, but now I’ve got to start thinking like a CEO and be like, wait, hold on, strategically, what is my distribution? Where is my next thing coming from?” says Paul. It’s a question that will be felt across the entertainment world. This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: The Emancipation of Charli D’Amelio: How the TikTok Queen Took Back Her Life
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nancy Jo Sales Plus Icon Nancy Jo Sales View All October 21, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Charli D’Amelio was photographed Oct. 5 at PMC Studios in Los Angeles. Artisitic & Fashion Director Alison Edmond Prada dress, top, jewelry. Photographed by Emman Montalvan Charli D‘Amelio — the reigning queen of TikTok — loves to dance. Whenever a new song comes on at this photography studio in L.A., Charli is shimmying her shoulders, shaking her hips. Now she stamps and turns like a flamenco dancer, swishing the skirt of her ruffly black gown. “So pretty, stunning,” says Emman Montalvan, the photographer snapping her. “Gorg!” With her glossy black hair and sparkly smile, Charli is gorg. She’s the girl next door drawn by Disney; she’s the bright and shiny face of social media , making it all seem benign. “This is her before she becomes jaded,” Montalvan observes. “Nothing calculated. Natural. She reminds me of when Britney Spears was young.” Related Stories THR Cover Story Sacha Baron Cohen Gets Real About Backlash, Death Threats and Resurrecting Ali G Business Instagram Lines Up Donatella Versace, A$AP Rocky, Finneas, Chloé Zhao as This Year's Creator Awards Judges (Exclusive) Rihanna’s “Breakin’ Dishes” begins to play. Charli mouths the words: “I don’t know who you think I am —” “Are you having fun?” I ask, finding myself smiling. Because when Charli is happy, you feel happy — which is no doubt part of her appeal. You want to believe that a life spent dancing around in fabulous clothes and opening yourself up to a dizzying 160 million-plus followers (the second most on TikTok) really is as wonderful as it looks. But a flicker of annoyance crosses Charli’s brow, as if the question touches a nerve. Maybe that’s because of how the algorithms are always demanding she offer up the semblance of a perfect life, the performance of joy, no matter the reality. “Are you having fun?” she asks, flashing her diamond bracelet smile. Then she’s running gleefully down the hallway of the studio, followed by her social media manager, Alexa Davis, who films her nearly constantly with a DJI Osmo Pocket. When Charli’s having fun, there’s someone there to capture it. *** Coming off a 10-month run in Broadway’s & Juliet — in which she sang and danced in the ensemble cast, earning some good reviews — Charli moved into a house in Valley Village, California, all by herself, earlier this year. The place represents something more than just a first home: At 22, Charli has separated herself professionally and financially from the family with whom she built her extraordinary career. “I’m figuring out who I want to be,” she tells me, “and that’s what I’m really excited for.” Photographed by Emman Montalvan For years, Charli and her parents, Marc and Heidi D’Amelio, and her older sister, Dixie, seemed inseparable. They moved to L.A. together, signed with the same talent agency, started businesses, starred in a Hulu reality show. Charli was always the main attraction, the engine of an empire — consisting of brand partnerships, media ventures, a clothing line and more — all built on the image of a close-knit family. Now, amid public speculation that her parents mismanaged her money — which her father has denied — she’s trying to find out who she is apart from them. (None of the D’Amelios responded to requests for comment.) The new place is her first house of her own. It doesn’t quite look like what you’d expect of a young woman who earns an estimated $18 million a year annually, according to Forbes . It’s a modest, almost nondescript two-story house on a tree-lined street, with a gate and security door, but nothing that screams “TikTok star.” But then you get to the secluded backyard with its shimmering pool, immaculate lawn and big stone grill, and you see the dance studio with the neon sign: RED BULL DANCE YOUR STYLE. Red Bull, one of Charli’s sponsors, built it for her. She grew up promoting brands; now even her backyard comes with one. “This is a very much a home,” Charli says, her voice soft and gentle as ASMR. She’s sitting cross-legged on the oversized wraparound couch in her big, open living room — her “safe space,” she tells me. She’s wearing Levi’s and a long-sleeved black Prada top (she’s an official friend of the house, so there’s Prada, Prada everywhere around her). Seventeen silver studs and hoops glint at her ears. “Sometimes I just fall asleep here,” she says sleepily. “It’s so comfy, it’s a slippery slope.” She spends a lot of time alone, just being on her phone or watching her giant, wall-mounted TV. On the couch, there’s a pillow that says: JUST A GIRL WHO LOVES ORCAS. Charli says she likes the way they always win in a fight with sharks. “Lame of a life as it may be sometimes, I love just to be at home and do nothing,” she says. “I’m surrounded by a lot of peace, which is something it took me a long time to realize I need to be comfortable.” She’s been a bit of a “hermit” over the past year, she says, retreating from a life in which almost everything she did was potentially something to be shared. “I took my first break off of social media” between October and February, “which was a really tough decision — I was always told, ‘If you take a break, you can never come back’ — but I think mentally I was just in a place where I needed to stop working and figure out who I was. Photographed by Emman Montalvan “I started working full-time when I was 15,” she continues, “and once I started, it was, ‘OK, this is my life now.’ But the other side of it was, ‘This is all I’ve ever known.’ And I think it took me, really for the first time, taking a step back and being like, ‘Who am I? What am I? Do I have a favorite color? Do I have a favorite anything?’ I realized I didn’t really know anything about myself, and so I had to sit with the hard truth of like, ‘Who am I at night when everyone leaves and no one cares that I’m Charli D’Amelio,’ you know?” Her dog, Rebel, a 12-year-old chocolate lab, stares up at her worshipfully. The bloodshot eyes of the internet noticed, of course, when Charli took a break — not just from social media but seemingly from the family that had been so central to her identity. She hasn’t appeared publicly with her parents or her sister for about a year, adding to speculation of a rift. In May, the gossip website Deuxmoi published allegations that Marc and Heidi had mismanaged Charli’s money. In June, Marc took to TikTok to deny these claims. “So a website said … we took money and put it offshore,” said Marc, sounding frustrated. “I wouldn’t even know how to do that. Come on, dude. This was never about money, it was about having this crazy, awesome experience with my family.” And then in September, appearing on creator Quenlin Blackwell’s YouTube cooking show, Feeding Starving Celebrities, Charli was asked how much money she had made from a certain item of merch. “Mmm, ain’t that the question,” she responded, deadpan. “Wouldn’t I like to know.” The moment went viral, becoming a GIF. “Charli D’Amelio family drama” trended on TikTok. *** Photographed by Emman Montalvan Charli was just your average upper-middle-class girl, growing up in Norwalk, Connecticut, when TikTok made her famous overnight. She’d been dancing competitively for nearly a decade when, in May 2019, at age 15, she began posting videos of herself doing popular routines, “just like everybody else was doing.” “My dream in life was to be a backup dancer,” she says. “I was like, ‘I want to go to the University of Nevada at Las Vegas and join their dance team,’ because they’d won nationals. I’m a very type A person. I had a vision board — I had a whole plan. But then the plan went sideways.” Five months after she started posting on TikTok, she had a million followers. By November 2020, she’d become the first TikTok creator to reach 100 million. Why her? Even Charli can’t explain it. “I think it was a mix of things,” she says. “Happy accident.” People watched her videos repeatedly to learn the choreography. “Also, when I started, I got just as much hate as I got love, so people were talking, arguing with each other.” Enragement, as they say, drove engagement. People argued about Charli’s looks, her dancing, whether she deserved her fame. In 2019, she drew criticism for performing the viral “Renegade” dance to K Camp’s song “Lottery” without crediting its 14-year-old Black creator, Jalaiah Harmon. (Charli and pop star Addison Rae later performed the original choreography with Harmon, giving her proper credit.) Then COVID-19 drove young people inside, where they were more often on their phones, and what better way to distract oneself from a pandemic than watching pretty Charli D’Amelio dance? For a generation of girls, Charli represented the ultimate social media success story. You didn’t need a Hollywood agent — you could become famous in your bedroom, just by being yourself. The catch: Once being yourself became your job, you might never get to stop working. Charli was about to become one of the most famous teenagers in the world while remaining remarkably powerless over her own life, she says: “I was a child, which I didn’t really get the significance of at the time, but I can see it very clearly now.” In summer 2020, Charli moved with her family into a rented mansion in the Hollywood Hills. The relocation was her idea; she felt “there was a lot more I could be doing,” though she’d already appeared in a Super Bowl commercial and an ABC special. She and her family signed with UTA as a package. Marc came from the apparel industry and had an unsuccessful run as a Republican candidate for the Connecticut State Senate in 2018; Heidi was a former model and personal trainer; and Dixie, three years older than Charli, was an aspiring singer. The family seemed to envision a Kardashian-esque enterprise, with Charli as its teenage Kim. Marc and Dixie launched their own TikTok accounts after Charli went viral. Everyone had a part to play in Charli’s newfound fame. Photographed by Emman Montalvan There’s a family story here that predates TikTok: A gifted child gets flooded with opportunities, and the adults around her see ways to capitalize on her appeal. Their involvement in her career, no matter how well-meaning, also gives them a say in her image and her decisions. In the pilot episode of The D’Amelio Show (2021-2023), the family sits down to hear the business plan for the upcoming year. Greg Goodfried, a former UTA agent who became their manager, holds forth enthusiastically. On the floor are 23 binders — 23! — containing proposals for a slew of new business ventures. Charli looks scared. “Where is the binder where she gets to be a kid?” Heidi asks. “I still have those binders,” Charli tells me wryly. “Twenty-three major projects in a year were agreed to. I had just turned 16.” (Goodfried did not respond to requests for comment.) Photographed by Emman Montalvan *** “I’m always grateful. I know I’m very lucky,” Charli says. “I don’t know what doing this without them would have looked like; I don’t know if I would have had this life.” It’s a refrain she returns to, almost as if she fears that questioning what happened will be mistaken for ingratitude. One of the peculiar cruelties of fame for young women is that they must be grateful for it, no matter how much it hurts. But lately she’s been reassessing what it meant to be a working child in the entertainment industry. “I was the youngest in every room I was in,” she says. “I was surrounded by people who were the best in the business, so you trust because that’s all you have — these people who are supposed to be guiding and helping you. But people are selfish, and that’s the sad reality. “And people have bad intentions, too,” she adds. “You can’t be a trusting person. I’ve learned that the hard way.” Rebel presses her nose against Charli’s knee. Charli pats it. “There are not a lot of rules and regulations when it comes to people who do what I do,” says Charli. “I didn’t start learning about and getting involved in my financials until I was about 21. I’m very fortunate to be able to be living the life that I am, but I’ve also been working nonstop since I was 15, so I should have stuff to show for it.” The laws protecting children in film and television evolved over decades in response to cases of exploitation. But the business of children making money on social media has grown faster than the rules protecting them. When parents are also business partners, who is looking out for the child? Are the rumors true, I ask, about her parents mishandling her money? “No, they’re not true,” Charli says. “I wouldn’t say that they stole my money.” There’s a long pause. “I think we did a lot of things as a family,” she says carefully. Photographed by Emman Montalvan *** Recently, Charli has been watching The D’Amelio Show for the first time. “It’s kind of like watching something I never lived,” she says. “It’s almost as if I’m figuring out what has happened in my life over these last few years. I was so disconnected in so many ways.” I mention how flat and monotone she seems onscreen, nothing like the person talking to me now. “I was like that. For years,” she says. “I kind of stopped talking. I stopped having a personality. I stopped doing much of anything because I had so much scrutiny from the outside world. It’s taken me to now to realize maybe I was dissociating through a lot of it.” All 28 episodes of The D’Amelio Show come with mental health trigger warnings. Charli and Dixie are seen struggling with the unceasing abuse that comes with online fame. At one point, a viral post predicts Charli’s death. Grown men make vulgar, sexualized videos about her when she’s still a teenager. “It’s a scary world, and it was hard on me,” she says. Her experience wasn’t so different from that of millions of girls negotiating a world of constant comparison and judgment — it was just on a much larger scale. Charli was the smiling face of a platform that amplified those pressures, twerking and twirling like the girl in The Red Shoes who couldn’t stop dancing. To many of her fans, she represented the fantasy: beauty, popularity, incredible clothes, a seemingly perfect family, wealth that came from doing what she loved. Behind it was a girl overwhelmed by scrutiny. Adolescent girls had always been judged on their looks and popularity; what was new was the technology that could make the judgment relentless, public and profitable. Charli was both a victim of social media culture and one of its most effective advertisements. “Have you ever seen The Matrix ?” I ask. “Is that the one where Keanu Reeves goes like this?” she says, doing the move where he dodges bullets in slow motion. I tell her about the main character, Neo, who discovers his world is a simulation controlled by machines. “And then when he wakes up, he starts fighting back. You should watch it.” “I love that, you’re giving me homework,” she says with a little laugh. Charli had suffered from anxiety even before TikTok. “I was a kid when I started having severe anxiety,” she says. In third grade, bullies pulled her hair and shoved her into a bathroom stall, breaking two of her fingers. “That was the same age I started having anxiety, so maybe they are connected,” she says. “I never really thought about that before.” On her reality show, her anxiety becomes a storyline. She describes having up to 15 panic attacks a day; viewers see her sob and break down in response to online hate. “But then I would get hate for showing my feelings,” she says. “You’re not allowed to be upset, you’re not allowed to cry, you’re not allowed to have any emotion, you can’t be angry.” Part of the concept of the show was to expose the dark side of influencer fame — even as it made its underage star more famous. But while the show urged viewers who were struggling to seek treatment for their mental health, Charli feels she didn’t always get the help she needed. “I went untreated for most of my life,” she says. “I had a life coach” from ages 16 to 19, “but I didn’t have a therapist. I probably should have had a therapist. I wasn’t medicated at all, even though I had ADHD, which I didn’t get diagnosed with until I was 18.” She was later also diagnosed with OCD and trichotillomania, a hair-pulling disorder associated with OCD and anxiety. Her life was work. Due to her professional commitments, she dropped out of high school at 16, though friends back home in Connecticut made sure she went to prom. Meanwhile, she was having experiences some kids dream of, such as winning season 31 of Dancing With the Stars (along with her dance partner Mark Ballas) in 2022, when she was 18. Her mother, Heidi, also competed that year. She came in eighth place. *** Matt Winkelmeyer/Kca2021/Getty Images for Nickelodeon/Tyler Golden/Hulu Charli has been seeing a therapist lately. “I told my therapist,” she says, “one thing I don’t want to be is another statistic. I don’t want to be another kid who got thrown into Hollywood and let that ruin their life.” The cautionary tales of child stardom, from Judy Garland to Britney Spears, have found a new breeding ground online. Charli’s generation doesn’t need studio executives to make them famous anymore, but the disappearance of the old gatekeepers hasn’t made children any less vulnerable to exploitation. I ask what finally made her reconsider how she wanted to move forward? “This is probably going to sound really crazy,” Charli says, “but I was doing Broadway” — & Juliet, a gig she’d chosen herself — “and it was the easiest thing I had ever done. And I did a good job. I showed up every day with a smile on my face, and I loved every second of it. And it reignited something in me, this love that I used to have” for dancing, performing. She had moved to New York — without her family — and was living in Columbus Circle to be near the theater. After years of being the star, it felt like a “relief” to be part of an ensemble of dancers, some of whom became friends. For the first time in her life, she was on her own, and it felt good. But then, when her run ended in September 2025, she says she became “the most depressed I’d ever been.” She rarely left her apartment and “didn’t see another human for a few months.” She went off social media and decided it was time to “take a look at myself.” Her team continued pitching projects that felt uncomfortably familiar. She started saying no. In December, she parted ways with Goodfried, her former manager. She doesn’t have a replacement manager yet, “but I’m OK with that,” she says. “I like it. I’m in charge. Now I say what I’m doing and not doing.” She sits up a little as she says this, her drowsy voice suddenly more alive. She also separated herself from the D’Amelio family business. Now, she oversees her own finances. For most 22-year-olds, independence means getting a job and supporting oneself; for Charli, it has meant taking command of an empire she helped build before she was old enough to vote. The internet took note again when she and her parents unfollowed one another on Instagram. Marc said on TikTok that he now communicates with Charli “through her lawyer.” As for Dixie, Charli says, “I mean, that’s my sister. I’m going to love her till the day I die. But there are times where you’re figuring stuff out.” Charli’s still making TikToks, still dancing around, smiling, in cool clothes; and she’s vlogging more on her YouTube channel, which has around 9 million followers. “Sometimes I want to record my entire day,” she says. “And sometimes I talk about whatever people are asking for. People like to feel included.” She’s still looking for ways to monetize her platform, still promoting Dunkin’, which has named two drinks after her: The Charli (2020) and The Charli Cold Foam (2021). Charli isn’t trying to bring down TikTok or renounce the fortune that brought her here. She isn’t trying to escape the machine. She just wants to be the one at the controls. “I’m taking the last few months of 2026 to work on getting to a place where I’m doing things I’m really proud of,” she says. She has a major project to announce in November, something that “I hold dear to my heart.” She continues: “Because of being told so often I didn’t deserve where I was, I felt that way for a really long time. But I’m at the point now where I can see that, like, I’ve lived a pretty amazing life, and I’m getting what I feel is like my second chance to do this the way that I want to do it. “I love what I do,” she says. “I love the person that I’m turning out to be.” Charli’s publicist, Nicole Perez-Krueger, comes in the room and says it’s time to stop. Charli’s dinner guests are arriving — her social media manager, Davis; her day-to-day manager, Alison Scoon; her stylist, Carlee Barrow; her agent, Ali Berman, and Berman’s 7-year-old daughter, June. They really are her friends, Charli says. They bring the sides. Charli’s going to grill them steak. “How do you do your TikToks and stuff?” June asks. “I just dance what I feel and say what I feel,” Charli says with a smile. Her social media manager is filming again. This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Noel Clarke Pleads Not Guilty to Sexual Offense Charges
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 3:19am PT Noel Clarke Pleads Not Guilty to Sexual Offense Charges By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest Noel Clarke Pleads Not Guilty to Sexual Offense Charges 4 hours ago Sacha Baron Cohen Defends Bringing Back ‘Problematic’ Ali G Amid Controversy: He’s ‘Designed to Expose’ Prejudice 21 hours ago BBC Three Among Linear Services Set to Close as Broadcaster Looks for Savings 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images Noel Clarke has pleaded not guilty to six sexual offense charges. Appearing at Westminster Magistrates Court in London on Wednesday morning, the actor, writer and director entered not guilty pleas in relation to all the charges, which include two charges of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism and one charge of exposure. The charges relate to alleged offenses that took place between 2007 and 2016 involving five women. Related Stories CMA's 'Celebration of Dolly Parton' Special Slates 20 Performers, Including Ella Langley, Lainey Wilson, Molly Tuttle and Reba McEntire As well as a long-running role on “Doctor Who” as dimension-hopping hero Mickey Smith, Clarke won critical acclaim for his teen dramas “Kidulthood,” “Adulthood” and “Brotherhood.” Popular on Variety He also co-wrote Sky drama “Bulletproof” with Ashley Walters, which ran for three seasons. It was cancelled in spring 2021 after The Guardian published an article containing multiple sexual misconduct allegations, which Clarke denied at the time. Clarke eventually brought a libel claim against the newspaper, which he lost last year after the judge, finding in favor of The Guardian, held that the paper’s reporting was “substantially true.” Justice Steyn also found Clarke to lack credibility as a witness. The actor was ordered to pay £3 million ($4 million) of the paper’s legal costs. Last month, Clarke was charged by London’s Metropolitan Police after the U.K.’s Crown Prosecution Service (similar to a D.A.) gave authorization having reviewed a file of evidence. He will next appear in court on Nov. 18. articles.title: ‘When I Existed,’ a Cannes Market Standout, Swooped On for World Sales by M-Appeal and Now Bound for Tallinn Black Nights (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 4:04am PT ‘When I Existed,’ a Cannes Market Standout, Swooped On for World Sales by M-Appeal and Now Bound for Tallinn Black Nights (EXCLUSIVE) By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest ‘When I Existed,’ a Cannes Market Standout, Swooped On for World Sales by M-Appeal and Now Bound for Tallinn Black Nights (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom 6 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source When I Existed (Courtesy of M-Appeal) Berlin-based M-Appeal has boarded “ When I Existed ,” a buzzy, feel-good second-chance drama comedy and Kafkian social satire which proved a standout at the Cannes Market’s Ventana Sur Goes to Cannes showcase, marking an auspicious debut for Uruguay’s Alejandro Damiani and Martin Avdolov. A select but discerning sales agent of Latin American movies, M-Appeal has picked up international sales on “When I Existed” (“Cuando yo existía”) just weeks before the feature’s world premiere in the Critics’ Picks Competition at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival . Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately The feature debut of writer-directors by Damiani and Martin Avdolov, “When I Existed” unfolds its humane modern parable when Silvio Bertolini retires after spending 40 years building Uruguay’s foremost gates construction company. Popular on Variety Attempting to draw his pension, and with his credit cards frozen, he discovers that the National Pension and Retirement Fund, also his bank, register him as deceased. Sent from pillar to post – to the bank’s Accounts, Payments and Claims treading dark puddled basement corridors and joining seemingly interminable lines. He meanwhile reconnects with old friends from his sculling boat club of youth, and re-awakes – but is it too late? – to what it really means to be alive: Spending time with his wife who hopes retirement will open a new chapter in their life together. Driving “When I Existed” is a notably modulated performance from César Troncoso, star of “The Pope’s Toilet” and “The Eternaut,” as Silvio, ranging from smiling containment of a reasonable man to outraged anger, paralysis from anxiety, wistful regret and lovelorn solitude. Silvia Kutica (“Avellaneda’s Moon,” “Argentina, Land of Love and Revenge”) plays Silvio’s now increasingly estranged wife of 40 years. “When I Existed” is lead produced by Federico Cetta for Uruguay’s El Cielo Cine who describes as “a story of reinvention built around the things that truly matter.” Structured as near any film of ambition these days an as international co-production, “When I Existed” is co-produced by David Matamoros at Barcelona’s Doce Entertainment and Andrés Rosenblatt at Montevideo’s Metropolis Films as co-producers. Matías Burgos at Moon Ideas, also based out of Montevideo, serves as associate producer. “This story speaks to us in a world where we have the constant feeling that time is slipping away between obligations we don’t always choose,” said Avdolov. “What do we do with the time we have? Today we need small acts of resistance against a logic that tends to make everything increasingly automatic and artificial. For me, making this film has something of that.” “What won us over about ‘When I Existed’ was its rare mix of humor and humanity,” said M-Appeal founder Maren Kroymann. She added: “Silvio is a charming man who struggles to accept retirement, while his wife has been waiting for this moment, hoping they can finally enjoy life together. Their story is both touching and deeply relatable, reminding us how easily we can get caught up in our habits and lose sight of what matters most. It’s a film that makes you laugh, moves you, and reminds us that it’s never too late to reconnect with the people we love.” ‘When I Existed,’ Broken Down by Damiani and Avdolov “When I Existed” is shot with unusual elegance but sense of humor by Manuel Branaa, a camera operator on J.A. Bayona’s Netflix smash-hit “Society of the Snow.” This is caught in the the lateral tracking shot with which it opens, crossing a dark granite stone tomb taking in the red and yellows of flowers left on it. Asethetically, it’s a highly pleasing composition, but the flowers are wilting. Drawing a counterpoint between the open expanses of marshlands, where Silvio catches up with his boat club best friends of youth, the charcoal grey and black corridors and barred doors and windows of the National Pension and Retirement Fund’s labyrinthine office conveys a sense of claustrophobia – that of a man caught not only in a bureaucratic system but his own self-absorption. “When I Existed” delves into “the nature of the system, the ego, bureaucracy, technological trends, the dangers of alienation, and the erosion of humanity,” said Damiani and Avdolov. “We poured our souls into even the smallest details – things that might go unnoticed by others, but which, to us, made the work feel complete and purposeful,” they added. Damiani has worked for years in advertising, as a copywriter and designer, wining Uruguay’s fist Golden Lion, then in VFX rising to Creative Director at top Uruguayan VFX house Aparato. Avdolov has transitioned to filmmaking from a career as a novelist (“Violeta Corazón,” “Camba”), short-story writer and author of the non-fiction “El Corazón Creativo” (“The Creative Heart”). “When I Existed” is born from the deepest fear any human being can have: how are we supposed to live? No one teaches you that,” Damiani told Variety . It is also semi-autobiographical. “Working on ‘When I Existed’ made us realize how much of ourselves we poured into the film’s protagonist,” they added. “For many years, we had channeled our energy and creativity into other people’s projects. Following the pandemic – and having passed the age of 40– we decided to commit ourselves to our own meaningful projects. We see this film as a reminder that we are not here to live someone else’s life; Damiani’s 2016 short, “M.A.M.O.N. (Monitor Against Mexicans Over Nationwide),” went viral, hitting over 13 million views on YouTube. El Cielo Cine Of features, “El Cielo Cine” has produced with Argentina 2025’s well-received adopted son drama “Emi,” directed by Ezequiel Erríquez, and Santiago Giralt’s 2023 “Norma,” a later-life self-discovery tale starring and co-written by Mercedes Morán (“Neruda,” “My Sad Dead”) which scored a best comedy Platino Award nomination.
