articles.title: Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 4:05am PT Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says 3 hours ago ‘Deadstream’ Directors Joseph and Vanessa Winter to Helm Horror Movie ‘Future Me’ as Longevity Pictures, Spooky Pictures and Image Nation Studios Ink Multi-Picture Deal (EXCLUSIVE) 22 hours ago Raj Singh and Italy’s RP1 Holding Launch €100 Million Film Fund to Boost Country’s Struggling Indie Ecosystem 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "The Monster of Florence" (Courtesy of Emanuela Scarpa/Netflix) Investment in content production destined for Italy’s film TV and streaming industries dropped 7.4% to €2 billion ($2.24 billion) in 2025, compared with the previous year, with the scripted sphere suffering most amid uncertainty over government support of the country’s tax credits and the ongoing transition in viewership from linear to streaming. That is the main takeaway from a report issued on Wed. by Italian TV producers’ association APA during Rome’s MIA market, which is dedicated to international TV series, animation, feature films and documentaries. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately After reaping the rewards of a protracted growth spurt, Italian producers in 2025 faced a forced slowdown as the country’s right-wing government dithered with ongoing regulatory modifications to tax incentives for domestic film and TV production. The domestic tax credit modifications impasse did not impact Italy’s international production rebates which remained firmly in place. Popular on Variety “This situation hinders producers’ ability to plan, increases financial burdens, and shrinks profit margins,” the report pointed out. “It negatively impacts all companies — especially smaller ones — by straining liquidity and limiting their capacity for future investment,” is added. Hopefully, there is some relief in sight with the new tax credit now in place. The so-called application “window” to apply has been reopened. The report underlined that unscripted content remains the backbone of Italian broadcasting programming, with an output of over 17,000 hours of original, first-run content, being churned out by Italian producers last year. Independent production accounts for 59% of these titles. Unscripted offerings from streaming platforms in Italy have also expanded, with a 51% increase in the number of titles and a 30% rise in total hours. Within Italy’s unscripted sphere, the factual genre has seen the most significant growth, up 36% in terms of number of hours, with the number of domestic factual titles adapted from international formats doubling. Game shows are also gaining ground on linear networks, both in early evening and prime time slots. As for scripted originals, the number of titles in 2025 grew 9% to a total 101 shows produced for the current season. But this growth is driven primarily by 74 smaller domestic series for linear networks, that don’t tend to travel, while the number of Italian originals served up by streamers last year stands the same as 2024 with 27 titles, most of which are, similarly, “local for local” product. The report underlined that Italian scripted content continues to reach broad and demographically diverse audiences. In the linear broadcasting sphere, Lux Vide’s “Sandokan,” a modern take on the classic pirate tale adapted from Italian author Emilio Salgari’s iconic book series, and BiBiFilm’s “La Preside,” about a feisty female principal of a school in a crime-ridden Naples neighbourhood, both drew a hefty average of over 4.6 million viewers per episode. In the streaming space, Picomedia’s Naples-set prison drama “The Sea Beyond” is still a big hit on state broadcaster RAI’s streaming and linear outlets, as is Aurora TV’s period drama “Il Paradiso delle Signore.” The standout Italian original on Netflix is serial killer series “ The Monster of Florence ,” pictured above, directed by genre specialist Stefano Sollima that launched from the 2025 Venice Film Festival and garnered 9.7 million global views in its first week in October 2025. Meanwhile, as in the rest of the world, the market share for linear television (both free-to-air and pay-TV) is steadily shrinking in Italy while global platforms continue to grow. The streaming segment, which accounted for 21% of the market in 2020, has now reached 43% in the Italian market and “is set to surpass linear television in value in the short-to-medium term,” the report said. Also in line with global TV trends, microdramas are starting to gain traction in Italy with ReelShort, DramaBox, NetShort, and DramaWave already among the country’s top fifteen entertainment apps in terms of user spend, the report said. And the first original Italian microdrama production has been released, titled “Tutto in una notte,” produced by Fascino PGT, with its 54 episodes distributed on Italian platform WittyTV and on social media. articles.title: ‘Glee’ Reboot Officially Set at Disney+ and Hulu
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 5:00am PT ‘Glee’ Reboot Officially Set at Disney+ and Hulu By Selome Hailu Plus Icon Selome Hailu Latest ‘American Horror Story’ Renewed for Season 14 18 hours ago Elizabeth Holmes Mania: ‘You Can See Everything’ Drives 186% Viewership Spike for Amanda Seyfried’s ‘The Dropout’ (EXCLUSIVE) 19 hours ago ‘Lioness’ Season 3 Closes With 9.7 Million Viewers in Seven Days, a Series High and the No. 5 Paramount+ Finale Ever (EXCLUSIVE) 19 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Everett Collection To quote Finn Hudson, “The show must go all over the place, or something.” He was right: “ Glee ” is back. Disney+ and Hulu have greenlit a reboot of Ryan Murphy ‘s famous (and infamous) musical dramedy series. “Glee” premiered on Fox in 2009 concluded in 2015 after six seasons of following a group of show choir members from Lima, Ohio as they dealt with the highs and lows of high school and beyond. It was a massive cultural phenomenon that is especially remembered for the blunt, sometimes controversial ways it tackled topics such as sexuality, race, disability, mental health and more — as well as its covers of songs like “Don’t Stop Believin’,” “Teenage Dream,” “River Deep, Mountain High” and “Smooth Criminal,” among others. The series remains popular today, as does its music, which averages 4.1 million monthly listeners on Spotify. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately The original cast included Lea Michelle, Cory Monteith, Matthew Morrison, Jane Lynch, Dianna Agron, Chris Colfer, Darren Criss, Amber Riley, Naya Rivera, Heather Morris, Kevin McHale, Jenna Ushkowitz, Harry Shum Jr., Chord Overstreet, Mark Salling and more. Popular on Variety Details about the new “Glee” are scant; Disney shared nothing aside from the fact that the series is being produced by 20th Television and will air on Hulu and Disney+. Casting information is not yet known, though it can safely be assumed that several of the original stars will return. “I’ve been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members,” Murphy recently said in an interview with Entertainment Tonight, in which he confirmed that he’d just written a reboot script with collaborators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan. “It’s very sweet, and they all had a lot of questions, but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea.” Murphy’s comments came weeks after Michele expressed to E! News that she’d be happy to join a “Glee” reboot: “I love ‘Glee.’ I will always love ‘Glee.’ I love Ryan Murphy. It just holds such a special place in my heart for me… I will follow Ryan wherever he goes.” Speaking to Bustle recently, Colfer pointed out that rebooting “Glee” would be complicated following Rivera’s death, but that he would consider it: “It was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya [Rivera] is gone. But I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no. So I don’t know, but hopefully I’ll have more information and I can actually think about it.” Rivera died in 2020 at age 33, tragically drowning in a lake while saving her young son who had fallen into the water. She was the third death among the “Glee” cast: Monteith died from an overdose in 2013, while the show was still on the air, and Salling died by suicide in 2018 after pleading guilty to possession of child pornography. articles.title: Netflix Stock Deflates to Two-Year Low. What Will It Take to Revive Revenue Growth?
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 5:06am PT Netflix Stock Deflates to Two-Year Low. What Will It Take to Revive Revenue Growth? By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Netflix Stock Deflates to Two-Year Low. What Will It Take to Revive Revenue Growth? 2 hours ago Ted Sarandos Addresses Netflix Content Exec Purge: ‘I Know That We Could Do Better’ 17 hours ago Netflix Q3 Revenue Meets Wall Street Estimates, Forecasts Q4 Slowdown and Says It Will Miss Ad Sales Target for the Year 18 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Netflix Shares of Netflix hit a two-year low after the streamer’s Q3 2026 earnings report revealed an ongoing softening in top-line growth and a miss on advertising revenue for the full year. The stock was down -7% in premarket trading Wednesday, to under $64/share, a decline of nearly 30% year-to-date to the lowest point since August 2024. Netflix’s Q4 revenue guidance was slightly below Wall Street expectations, and the company said ad sales for 2026 are now expected to be $2.7 billion, $300 million lighter than previously forecast, because of the slower-than-expected rollout of “some ad product capabilities.” Related Stories CMA's 'Celebration of Dolly Parton' Special Slates 20 Performers, Including Ella Langley, Lainey Wilson, Molly Tuttle and Reba McEntire So how does Netflix recharge audience engagement (and therefore keep revenue pointed up) after a drop-off in viewing, particularly in the U.S. ? Popular on Variety To Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, the answer is better execution on its core model — that the company needs to crank up its buffet of buzzy, must-watch TV shows and movies. Last week he dismissed content chief Bela Bajaria, who’s being replaced by Peter Rice, as part of a larger overhaul of content leadership . On the Q3 earnings call, Sarandos praised Bajaria but said “I know that we could do better.” Ahead of its Q3 earnings, Netflix also laid off 1,000 workers , 6% of its headcount, which execs have framed as giving it the ability to invest more into growth areas. But some on Wall Street believe Netflix needs to do more than churn out TV and movie hits — that it needs a strategy to capture viewing of short-form video content, which is being soaked up by platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram. “[W[e think the Street should remain skeptical of a long-term strategy that simply sees NFLX double down on its legacy core strength (premium TV, films, and increasingly, live events), while NFLX remains largely absent from the fastest areas video entertainment growth (e.g., mobile, short-form),” New Street Research analyst Dan Salmon wrote in an Oct. 20 research note. YouTube continues to make significant viewing share gains with an “all content types, all formats” approach on connected TV, Salmon wrote. While it doesn’t make sense for Netflix to adopt a straight user-generated content approach, he said, “we believe bold thinking is increasingly needed to address these long-term threats to NFLX mindshare with younger audiences.” Pivotal Research Group’s Jeff Wlodarczak similarly cited concerns for Netflix that short-form entertainment “is doing to streaming what streaming has done to traditional Pay TV,” as younger consumers spend an ever-increasing amount of time on social media platforms. Following Netflix’s Q3 earnings report, Wlodarczak reduced his subscriber forecasts and increased programming cost forecasts, leading to a $5 reduction in his year-end 2026 target price on the stock to $65. Meanwhile, Netflix once touted the addition of videogames as an extension of its core service as a promising growth driver — but games weren’t mentioned at all in its Q3 earnings, except that the company noted in its shareholder letter that it teamed up with Take-Two Interactive to unveil a sneak peek in August of highly anticipated title “Grand Theft Auto VI.” But all of that said, with over 325 million global subscribers, Netflix remains well positioned to keep its core streaming business humming along nicely, albeit at a somewhat less rapid clip, according to MoffettNathanson analyst Robert Fishman. “We continue to believe Netflix has significant headspace to push monetization of its leading SVOD scale, which should lead to compounding profits for years to come,” Fishman wrote in a research note. MoffettNathanson forecasts Netflix earnings per share to reach $3.85 in 2027 (down from $4.00 previously), growing by 21% in 2028 to $4.65 (vs. $4.80 previously). The analyst reiterated a “buy” rating on Netflix stock but lowered his 12-month price target by $10 to $90/share. Also bullish on the long-term strategy was Wedbush Securities analyst Alicia Reese, who wrote in a note that “the details suggest Netflix isn’t beholden to industry headwinds; it is in control.” She noted, “Churn and pricing held up, ad demand is intact, Netflix is expanding its valuable live-events inventory, and it plans to preserve its content strategy rather than duking it out with YouTube on short-form.” “Importantly, management’s tone underscored its intent to shift toward a platform model as it broadens its licensing partnerships and add-on deals, in addition to reaccelerating its ad rollout,” Reese wrote. Because Netflix still has “significant potential” to expand ad revenue, Wedbush analysts reiterated their “outperform” rating on Netflix but lowered the price target on the stock from $90 to $80/share. articles.title: Neiman Marcus’s Luxe 2026 Holiday Offerings Include $180,000 ‘Star Wars’ Experience
articles.full_text: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. For “ Star Wars ” fans with $180,000 to spare, Neiman Marcus is offering something even harder to come by than a vintage lightsaber: a look inside the famously guarded world of Lucasfilm. The luxury department store has unveiled its annual Fantasy Gifts collection , headlined by a one-of-a-kind “Star Wars” experience that includes private access to Lucasfilm and Industrial Light & Magic, custom lightsabers and four VIP tickets to an upcoming “Star Wars” world premiere and afterparty. The six-figure package arrives ahead of the franchise’s 50th anniversary in 2027, when Disney and Lucasfilm will release Shawn Levy’s highly anticipated “Star Wars: Starfighter.” Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately Des Willie The experience begins at One Letterman in San Francisco’s Presidio, home to Lucasfilm and Industrial Light & Magic, the visual effects company George Lucas founded in 1975. Guests will receive private, behind-the-scenes access to the studios where some of Hollywood’s most recognizable cinematic worlds have been brought to life, along with a visit to an active Lucasfilm production. Also included is a one-of-one replica of an “Ahsoka” Season 2 lightsaber hilt prop signed by Lucasfilm president and chief creative officer Dave Filoni, as well as a private consultation to design a pair of custom-assembled lightsabers. The experience culminates in four VIP tickets to an upcoming Star Wars world premiere and afterparty, offering the opportunity to celebrate alongside the franchise’s cast and creators. Lucasfilm also prepares to celebrate half a century since the release of George Lucas’s original 1977 film. The anniversary comes amid a new theatrical chapter for the franchise, with “The Mandalorian & Grogu” slated for May 2026 and Levy’s “Starfighter,” starring Ryan Gosling, set to arrive in theaters in May 2027. The “Star Wars” package is the centerpiece of Neiman Marcus’ 2026 Holiday Book, which is celebrating its own milestone: 100 years since the retailer introduced its now-famous holiday catalog. This year’s edition, titled “Grand Gestures,” continues the Fantasy Gifts tradition that began in 1959, when Stanley Marcus started offering customers elaborate, sometimes outrageous presents that money could buy — provided they had enough of it. And while a $180,000 trip inside the “Star Wars” universe may be the most obvious draw for Hollywood obsessives, the rest of this year’s lineup is similarly ambitious. For fashion and jewelry collectors, Neiman Marcus is offering a six-day trip through Venice, Florence and Milan hosted by the Buccellati family, featuring private museum and atelier visits and a design session with Andrea Buccellati to create a bespoke piece of high jewelry. Another package, offered in partnership with Verdura, takes guests to New York City for a private tour of the jeweler’s historical collection and a fitting for a custom Maltese Cross cuff set with emeralds, sapphires and diamonds, followed by dinner at Orso and producer house seats to a Broadway show. Dolce & Gabbana is contributing a Carretto Siciliano foosball table, complete with hand-painted Sicilian artwork, solid wood construction and a screen-printed glass playing field. A fragrance experience with Saujet and Lalique includes a trip to Alsace, France, where guests will stay at Villa René Lalique, participate in a perfume masterclass and receive an exclusive first-edition crystal fragrance trunk. For those who prefer being on the water, another gift includes a fully loaded electric Arc Sport wake boat, personalized equipment and private lessons with world champion wakesurfer Austin Keen. And in perhaps the most sentimental offering of the bunch, customers can work with Neiman Marcus’ corporate chef to refine a cherished family recipe, which will then appear on the retailer’s restaurant menus nationwide for a full year. “The 2026 Fantasy Gifts continue to redefine extraordinary luxury through one-in-a-lifetime experiences, unparalleled access, and boundless imagination,” Darcy Penick, president and chief commercial officer of Exemplar Luxury Group, Neiman Marcus’ parent company, said in a statement. This year’s holiday campaign, dubbed “Holiday Fantasy,” also features supermodel Natasha Poly in imagery shot by director and photographer Alexandre Bassard at Neiman Marcus’ Beverly Hills store. The retailer is rolling out additional in-store events, holiday dining experiences and gift guides across its locations and digital channels. A portion of every Fantasy Gift purchase will benefit the Heart of Neiman Marcus Foundation through a corporate donation. The retailer is also continuing its seasonal fundraising campaign for Boys & Girls Clubs of America. Loading comments...

articles.title: Jake Tapper Sketches Work Outside CNN: Graphic Novel Probes Life of ‘Butcher’ Klaus Barbie
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 6:00am PT Jake Tapper Sketches Work Outside CNN: Graphic Novel Probes Life of ‘Butcher’ Klaus Barbie By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Starz Gets Back on Verizon Fios After New Carriage Pact 20 hours ago Atlanta Hawks Strike Streaming Alliance With Amazon’s Prime Video 23 hours ago Meet Kate DePetro, Fox News’ Social-Media Ambassador to Younger Viewers 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Top Shelf/Elliott O'Donovan Many of the stories, interviews and analyses Jake Tapper presents to his followers on CNN rely heavily on moving pictures, courtesy of his employer. A new project from the anchor and author will substitute still images — that Tapper drew himself. Tapper has spent the past three years working on a graphic novel, and much of his time was spent drawing every panel. “ The Butcher : The Decades-Long Hunt for Klaus Barbie, One of the World’s Most Notorious Killers,” will publish on June 1, 2027, from Top Shelf Productions. The illustrated novel examines the story of Klaus Barbie, the Nazi figure known as the “Butcher of Lyon” who escaped Germany and avoided capture for decades, until Nazi hunters and journalists tracked him down. Tapper, who first became interested in the story while visiting France with his family, used source material in four different languages to chronicle the pursuit for Barbie in excruciating detail. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately “It’s just this fascinating story about this young Nazi who comes to Leon, France, terrorizes the city, and then pops up years later in South America in Bolivia,” says the CNN anchor during a recent interview. “He also helped support a right-wing government in South America before eventually being captured.” In what may be a surprising twist, the journalist presents eyebrow-raising information about who helped Barbie escape Europe. Popular on Variety Graphic novels are a favored medium of younger readers who not only read coming-of-age tales or longer stories involving fictional characters, but also memoirs that deeply probe cultures or perspectives that may not turn up in more mainstream media formats. Top Shelf, Tapper’s publisher, has released graphic novels such as “From Hell” by Alan Moore and Eddie Campbell, “They Called Us Enemy” by actor George Takei, and the “March” trilogy co-written by Congressman John Lewis. Tapper may best be known for anchoring “The Lead” and “ State of the Union ” on CNN as well as some special news events, but he has long juggled his news job with a suite of other activities. He has written eight books, including three novels. What people may not know about him is that he has been drawn to comics and cartooning for most of his life. As a child, he avidly read Charles Schulz’ “Peanuts” and Walt Kelly’s “Pogo,” as well as super-heroes like Batman and Superman. His home office contains strips of “Little Orphan Annie,” “Doonesbury” and “Zippy the Pinhead.” Some of his work has been seen in Roll Call, the college paper at Dartmouth when he attended, and even in a local paper, The South Street Star, where he grew up. For a period of time, he drew a fresh piece for CNN’s “State of the Union” “It’s a very American art form,” he says of the medium. “There’s just a brilliance. It’s not filmed, but it’s not written. It’s somewhere in between.” Still, CNN viewers haven’t seen the end-of-show political cartoons he once drew in several years. “The truth of the matter is that I stopped doing it because the best political cartoons are really hard hitting, and I just, as an anchor, I just couldn’t do cartooning the way that it deserves to be done,” Tapper says. “I had to hold back. I had to pull punches. I had to run towards silly and inoffensive as opposed to hard hitting and brutal. And it just wasn’t as good. I wasn’t happy with it.” He’s had a lot of time to work on “The Butcher.” Tapper, who says he draws less frequently now, has been tough on himself. “After I finished the 250th page, I went back and redrew 100 pages because I’m like, those are awful. And I need to redraw them.” The recent practice has helped him regain some of his skill, he says, but “I’m still going back and tweaking.” One reason he embraced Top Shelf as his publisher is because he admired other graphic novels they have produced and he liked the fact that the editors there challenged him, with notes that could be “absolutely brutal.” Tapper embraced them. “I didn’t want it to be fast,” he says of the project. “I wanted it to be good.” He hopes the new graphic novel will have appeal. “It’s obviously a very serious topic, but it’s kind of a suspenseful book about how they track down this mass murderer who’d gotten away with it,” he says. “And then it gets into the politics of it, but in a very accessible way, about all the people that let this guy get away. I think anybody who’s interested in in a mystery, anybody who’s interested in World War II, anybody who’s interested in just a good yarn” will find something in the project. Tapper even worked with the daughter of Allan Ryan a former U.S. Department of Justice official who investigated how Barbie was able to avoid punishment for so long. He places Ryan in the graphic novel, where he serves as a sort of narrator. Tapper knows that some people may be surprised by his work in the medium, but believes the tale will win them over. “It’s not about 2026 politics at all,” he says. “It’s just a true story.” NFL on Sling TV 2026: Here’s How to Watch Minnesota Vikings vs. Chicago Bears Game Live Online Disney and NFL Team Up on Apparel Collection, Pairing Each of the League’s 32 Teams With Beloved Franchise Characters NFL Season 2026-2027 Livestream: Here’s Where to Watch Pro Football Games Online X Launches ‘NFL Gametime,’ a Football Feed Placed Alongside ‘For You’ and ‘Following’ Tony Romo Suggests He’d Like to Return to CBS’ NFL Coverage After No Contest Plea Netflix Taps ‘Friday Night Lights’ Director Peter Berg for NFL Gameday Openers, the First Narrated by Kyle Chandler Loading comments...

articles.title: Young Audiences Want to Redefine Modern Storytelling, New Study Shows
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 6:30am PT Young Audiences Want to Redefine Modern Storytelling, New Study Shows By Mya Copeland Plus Icon Mya Copeland Latest Young Audiences Want to Redefine Modern Storytelling, New Study Shows 33 minutes ago ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Screenwriter on Book-to-Screen Changes and Why Jane Austen Is So Adaptable: ‘She’s Almost Like Shakespeare’ 2 days ago Betty McGuire, ‘Growing Pains’ Actress, Dies at 100 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy Everett Collection Begone the days of 30-year-olds playing high schoolers! Gen Z and Gen Alpha want to see themselves depicted accurately on screen. A study from the Center for Scholars & Storytellers at UCLA found that young viewers are often not consulted about what they want to see on screen — even in projects about and for them. Over the past five years, CSS’s annual Teens and Screens Report has worked to change that by providing data about what young people really want to see. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately The 2026 report reveals a broad definition of what a “story” is and where to find it, coupled with an appetite for traditional media and in-person experiences. This year’s study surveyed more than 1,500 adolescents aged 10-24. Popular on Variety Among the interesting findings: YouTube (72.9%) ranked as the top medium for storytelling, with nearly four out of five respondents saying that short-term videos can tell a story. 16.8% said they would not cast an influencer in a project, while almost 40% said they would most prefer to cast an unknown actor. Gen Alpha and Gen Z are split on AI: 27.4% of respondents at age 19 identified “doom” as their dominant emotion toward its portrayals in media, while 44.2% of 10 to 13-year-olds described it as “fascinating.” 55% want to see more neurodivergent characters on screen. Friendship is key: 57.3% want to see more platonic relationships represented. “Adults are making stories that they think are going to resonate with young people, but they’re not really talking to a lot of young people to do it,” CSS founder and CEO Yalda T. Uhls, Ph.D., tells Variety about the findings. Uhls is a professor in UCLA’s psychology department who spent nearly two decades as a senior executive at studios like MGM and Sony before pivoting to psychology research of media and young adults. Since launching the Teens and Screens Report, Uhls has seen industry executives and researchers make a concerted effort to integrate the study’s findings. Uhls highlights that individuals from across the industry at CAA, Disney and UTA will attend a summit on Oct. 22 to listen and inform their work. “Our assumptions based on what we thought were stories when we were younger can’t hold,” Uhls says. “They’re not holding, and we need to really talk to young people, do research like this to make sure that these stories are everywhere and they’re consuming it all the time. Make sure that hopefully, if the people we work with that are in the industry — who have the real cultural power, they’re the ones making content that goes all over the world — if they’re really paying attention to our work about what young people need and want and care about, they’re gonna not only probably make content that will resonate and that these young people will see more, but also, it’ll just hopefully create a more empathetic and kind world.” In her work with CSS and the study, Uhls challenges her gut instincts on young people’s take on entertainment. She was surprised to hear participants say they think short-form content like Instagram Reels can tell stories. “So many adults look down on this medium,” Uhls says, but younger audiences “see stories everywhere. They see media. They’re looking for something that they can relate to that resonates with them. And if they don’t see it in a traditional piece of content storytelling in TV, books or movies, they’re going to go elsewhere, and they are going elsewhere.” Uhls describes these young audiences as “way more discerning” than executives might realize. “They like to discover someone new, but yet at the same time, with ‘Obsession’ and ‘Backrooms,’ there’s a different kind of storytelling that’s learned on YouTube really, and maybe TikTok and other things too. So, from a filmmaker perspective, it’s not that they want the stories on those platforms to be translated into mainstream content, but certainly the style and the thinking of their issues and what they do seems to be something Gen Z loves.” But this group Uhls surveys isn’t monolithic, something she stresses is important to remember. She recalls working on her dissertation and realizing that assumptions based only on Los Angeles teens did not ring true across the country. She has two things she hopes executives take away from the study’s findings: “Listening to young people and diverse young people from all over the country is one. And then the second thing is they’re way more nuanced than we give them credit for. They’re way more sophisticated than we give them credit for. Sometimes they say really wise and brilliant things.” CSS will host its sixth annual Teens & Screens Summit on Oct. 22 at the UCLA Meyer and Renee Luskin Conference Center. The event features panels and discussions with industry leaders, researchers and youth activists. Barack and Michelle Obama’s production company Higher Ground Productions will be honored with CSS’s second annual Greg Berlanti Social Impact Award at the event. articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 6:51am PT Sharjah Film Festival Unveils Lineup With ‘Gohan,’ ‘Monster Mia,’ Emirati Talent By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest ‘Big Boys Don’t Cry’ Director Muhammad Mustapha Talks Masculinity Ahead of El Gouna Premiere: ‘The Only Emotion Men Are Allowed to Express Is Anger’ 1 day ago Egyptian Star Mona Zaki Reflects on Three Decades of Reinvention as El Gouna Honors Her Career: ‘Art Is About Freedom’ 2 days ago 10 Films to Track at El Gouna, From Cannes and Berlin Standouts to Rising Arab Filmmakers 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "Monster Mia" (Courtesy of Arx Anima, Peng! Boom! Tschak!, Arxlight Pictures, Arx Anima MD) The Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth will bring films from Thailand, Brazil, India, Italy and across the Arab world to the UAE for its 13th edition, with a lineup featuring international festival titles, emerging filmmakers and Emirati talent. Running Oct. 26-Oct. 31, SIFF’s Green Carpet program includes Chayanop Bunprakob, Baz Poonpiriya and Atta Hemwadee’s Thai drama “ Gohan ,” Fabrizio Cattani’s Italian feature “Forever With You” and Verena Fels’ Austrian-German animated film “ Monster Mia ,” all receiving their Middle East premieres. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately “Gohan” follows a stray dog as he passes through the lives of three owners over more than a decade, while “Forever With You” follows two friends whose search for a missing dog leads them deep into the woods and into unexpected danger. “Monster Mia” follows a 12-year-old girl who finds herself at a school full of monsters. Poonpiriya previously directed Thai box-office hit “Bad Genius” and Sundance prize winner “One for the Road.” Popular on Variety Elsewhere in the lineup, Juan Cabral’s Argentine feature “Risa and the Wind Phone” receives its Gulf premiere. Cabral’s previous feature, “ Two/One ,” premiered at Tribeca and was released by Mubi across select international territories. Indian filmmaker Ravi Nimbalkar’s “87 Rupees Ink Pen” also receives its Middle East premiere, while Brazilian director Celia Catunda’s animated feature “My Grandfather Is a Nihonjin” arrives in Sharjah after premiering at Annecy in 2025. The animation selection extends to David Súkup, Patrik Pašš, Leon Vidmar and Jean-Claude Rozec’s Czech-French-Slovak-Slovenian stop-motion feature “ Tales From the Magic Garden ,” another 2025 Annecy selection. Local talent features in the shorts program. Abdulrahman Al Madani’s “Oug,” part of the Arabic short-film competition, follows an Emirati couple facing family and social pressure to have children. The film received the Gulf Capital-ADMAF Visual Arts Award in 2025 and has since screened at Denmark’s Odense Intl. Film Festival. Young filmmakers also get their own space through SIFF’s Child & Youth Made Films and student competitions, with selections spanning live-action and animation. The wider festival program counts 71 films from 38 countries selected from a pool of 1,802 submissions representing 72 countries, with a further eight films screening out of competition. Morning screenings at VOX Cinemas City Centre Al Zahia are reserved for school-aged and university students, while evening screenings are open to the public. Workshops introduce young participants to stop-motion and flipbook animation, alongside workshops on cinematography, production management and content creation. Italy, this year’s country of honor, is represented in the workshop program with “The Italian Eye – Photography Through Light, Color & Composition” and “Tell a Story in Five Shots – Inspired by Italian Cinema.” The festival’s panel lineup turns to what happens once filmmakers have industry-ready work. “Film Festivals Decoded: What Happens After You Press Submit?” brings together festival programmers and directors to discuss the selection process, submissions and how festivals build their programs. Moderated by Saudi Cinema Assn. CEO Hani Al Mulla, the panel features Rotterdam Arab Film Festival artistic director Rosh Abdelfattah, American Intl. University Kuwait executive director of alumni affairs and strategic events Alia Al Azzeh, and Alexandria Short Film Festival head Mohamed Mahmoud. Another panel, “How Do I Get My Next Film Made? From Idea to Financing,” will focus on pitching materials, development labs, producers, financing and co-production opportunities. The festival’s Industry Hub and pitching sessions will run alongside the public program, giving emerging filmmakers opportunities to present projects and connect with industry professionals. SIFF opens Oct. 25, with screenings beginning Oct. 26 and continuing through Oct. 31, ahead of the closing ceremony on Nov. 1. articles.title: Empire Founder Ghazi Launches Supply Chain, New Rights Management/ Distribution Company for Independent Music
articles.full_text: Oct 21, 2026 7:00am PT Empire Founder Ghazi Launches Supply Chain, New Rights Management/ Distribution Company for Independent Music By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Music Industry Moves: Barbara Cane, BMI’s VP of Worldwide Creative, to Retire After Five Decades 16 hours ago Cleo Sol Announces First-Ever North American Arena Tour Dates 24 hours ago Bob Buziak, Former President of RCA Records and Sony’s Tristar Music Group, Dies at 83 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ghazi , founder of the indie label and distribution giant Empire , has announced the launch of his newest company, Supply Chain, an independent B2B cloud-based distribution company for the global music industry, which encapsulates technology, distribution, operations, and commercial connectivity. Alongside the launch, the company announced two senior leadership appointments, with Craig May joining as SVP of marketing and Kristy May as SVP of business affairs. Supply Chain’s international headquarters are based in Amsterdam, one of Europe’s most-connected music and technology hubs. According to the announcement, the company’s goal is a huge one: to build the infrastructure that independent music runs on. “Its mission is to deliver the technology, expertise and commercial access needed to operate, grow and compete globally, in service of a broader vision of a world where independent music has the power to shape its own future,” the announcement reads. “The platform gives independent music businesses neutral, enterprise-grade infrastructure without requiring them to give up control of their catalog, data, client relationships or commercial choices.” Supply Chain launched in beta in 2025 and is now operational globally. Supply Chain is working with a variety of clients across the industry ecosystem, including a launch partnership with Beatport-owned Ampsuite, to power infrastructure expansion. Popular on Variety “There needs to be a fully fleshed-out rights management system that is also culturally nuanced,” Ghazi tells Variety. “The needs of an independent label in Brazil are not the same as an artist in India, which are not the same as a private equity company that’s invested $500 million in catalogs. Supply Chain can manage contracts, master royalties, publishing royalties, merch royalties, split payments and more. “It’s been a labor of love for five years,” he continues. “I wanted to build something as scale-able and as future-proof as possible. It introduces a lot of operational efficiencies and reduces tech friction, and when you do all that, you’re allowing creativity to flourish. Our software is built for independents and it’s designed to connect and serve the independent community.” Beatport CEO Matt Gralen says, “Ampsuite offers the most complete set of tools for the labels that power Beatport, but we are always looking to provide more and respond to evolution in the industry. In Supply Chain, we have a partner that offers advanced features out of the box and the ability and ambition to build for the future of the business.” How to Watch the Chiefs vs. Colts Live Online NFL TV Favorites Like Joe Buck, Troy Aikman, Greg Olsen, Kirk Herbstreit Could Play for New Teams Next Season NBC Sends Football on Cross-Country Trip to Count Down to NFL Kickoff CAA Names Dasha Smith as Chief Operating Officer, Joins Agency From NFL U2 to Play Halftime Show for NFL’s Thanksgiving Eve Game in What League Calls ‘a New NFL Holiday Tradition’ NFL Season 2026-2027 Livestream: Here’s Where to Watch Pro Football Games Online Loading comments...

articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart Kari Skogland To Direct Vigilante Crime Thriller ‘Vigilant’ From ‘Severance’ Star Ólafur Darri Ólafsson Christie Brinkley Opens Personal Archive With Never-Before-Seen Home Movies For ‘Uptown Girl’ Docuseries Lance Armstrong On Schwinn Bicycles Documentary ‘No Hands’: “It’s An Incredible American Story” View All October 21, 2026 2:03am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kari Skogland & Ólafur Darri Ólafsson David Leyes, Jonatan Gretarsson EXCLUSIVE: Kari Skogland will direct Vigilant , a vigilante crime thriller based on a Skúli Sigurðsson novel and adapted for TV by Severance star Ólafur Darri Ólafsson . The project is a big-ticket European co-production and has been greenlit by Icelandic production company ACT4 alongside German broadcaster ZDF and its distribution division ZDF Studios . Iceland’s Siminn is also on board. ZDF Studios will sell the English-language show internationally. Zero Gravity is handling U.S. sales. Vigilant follows a female journalist who is approached by a self-styled vigilante who is waging a violent campaign against sexual predators. The reporter initially sees him as a voice for the voiceless, but soon begins to suspect a darker truth. As her reporting fuels a nationwide debate, the series explores whether violence can ever be justified when the justice system fails. Related Stories News Buyers Move For German Crime Drama 'SOKO' As ZDF Studios Brings Classic & YA Series To Cannes News Icelandic Drama 'Elma' Set For Siminn Bow As Glassriver Debuts 'NCU' At MIPCOM Ólafur is a partner in ACT4 and starred in Severance . He has adapted Sigurðsson’s novel ‘Stóri bróðir’ (‘Big Brother’ in English) for TV. Víkingur Kristjánsson, Anita Briem, Teitur Magnússon and Anna Gunndís Guðmundsdóttir are co-writers, meaning a powerhouse Icelandic creative team. Watch on Deadline “Skúli’s novel had a profound impact on me when I first read it,” Ólafur said. “Beneath the thriller, I found a story asking difficult questions about justice, anger and what happens when people lose faith in the systems meant to protect them. “I’m incredibly proud of the scripts we’ve created, and I can’t wait to see Kari bring this world and these characters to life with her extraordinary vision, alongside the incredible cast and creative team we’ve assembled.” Skogland’s many directing credits include The Handmaid’s Tale , The Walking Dead and Vikings . She will also executive produce the six-part series. “ Vigilant captivated me from the first page,” she said. “The characters walk their own lines of morality that continually makes the audience question their own moral position. Everyone’s damage is exposed at some point, their fragility and strength are tested in this fantastic landscape for thought-provoking performance opportunities, all while wrapped in a nail-biting thriller.” “ Vigilant is exactly the kind of premium international drama that resonates across borders: a compelling thriller rooted in a highly relevant societal dilemma,” said Rodrigo Herrera Ibarguengoytia, Director Drama, ZDF Studios. “The series combines Iceland’s distinctive storytelling tradition with universal themes that will connect with audiences worldwide.” Production kicks off on October 29 in Iceland, where the drama is set. ZDF will have the show for Germany and Iceland’s Siminn, which has an IPTV and streaming service, has local rights. Bayona, Javier Bardem & Laurent Bouzereau Partner On Movistar Plus Doc About Life Of Legendary Spanish Cinematographer Néstor Almendros View All October 21, 2026 2:24am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Hiam Abbass Deadline Hiam Abbass is set to receive the European Film Academy ’s honorary award for European Achievement in World Cinema. Abbass will be handed the award at the 39th European Film Awards on 16 January 2027 in Athens. She will be the ceremony’s honorary guest. Abbass was born in Nazareth, the child of a Palestinian family that was forced into exile in 1948. She began her acting career at the Palestinian National Theatre El-Hakawati in East Jerusalem, which was often closed by the Israeli authorities. During a theatre tour through Europe, she decided to leave Palestine for London and has been living in Paris since the late 1980s. She has since acted in over 100 films, including Satin Rouge by Raja Amari, Paradise Now by Hany Abu-Assad, The Visitor by Tom McCarthy, and Denis Villeneuve’s Blade Runner 2049 . Watch on Deadline Abbass has been nominated twice for European Film Awards, in both cases for her performance in films directed by Eran Riklis: She was nominated for the People’s Choice Award 2005 for Syrian Bride and for European Actress 2008 for Lemon Tree , which won her an Asia Pacific Screen Award. Her daughter Lina Soualem’s documentary Bye Bye Tiberias , which returns to her home village Deir Hanna and explores her bold choices and her bond to her family, was also nominated for the European Film Awards 2024. Alongside her work as an actress, Hiam Abbass also directs. Her film Inheritance was screened at Gijón, São Paulo, and Venice Days (2012). articles.title: Jane Tranter Calls For “Stories That Change The Lack Of Empathy In Our World” & Reveals How James Gandolfini Influenced Bad Wolf
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Jane Tranter Calls For “Stories That Change The Lack Of Empathy In Our World” & Reveals How James Gandolfini Influenced Bad Wolf Prime Video Adds Sony LIV To Indian Offer Ex-Disney, NBCU & Bloomberg TV Execs Among New Advisory Board At Storyboarding Platform Pzaz View All October 21, 2026 3:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jane Tranter on stage at the MIA Market in Rome MIA The Other Bennet Sister producer Jane Tranter has launched an impassioned plea for TV makers to search out stories that “that will make our world a more empathetic place.” In a keynote talk at MIA Market this week, the Bad Wolf Production CEO and co-founder used the example of a “farmer in his 70s” who had identified with Mary, the outcast protagonist of BBC period drama The Other Bennet Sister played by the 30-year-old Ella Bruccoleri. “Being able to make a drama in 2026 that features a woman who some people in society doesn’t think should be an acceptable face of a woman,” said Tranter. Related Stories News 'Industry' Star Myha'la Claims "Unconscious Racial Bias" Is Baked Into 'The Traitors' News International Insider: 'Doctor Who' Regeneration Underway; MIPCOM Preview; Busan Takeaways “She doesn’t look like what people want her to look like, she doesn’t sound like what people want her to sound like and she doesn’t behave like society wants a woman to behave like and yet she is her own woman. Watch on Deadline “In 2026, stories about people being accepted for who they choose to be are the kind of stories I will keep making until someone carries me out in a wooden box. I really urge you to look for those stories. We have to tell stories that change the lack of empathy in our world. Look into yourselves and go and tell your own stories that will make our world a more empathetic place.” The Other Bennet Sister is an adaptation of former BBC executive Janice Hadlow’s novel of the same name. The BBC series, which plays on BritBox in the U.S., tells the story of Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice from the viewpoint of Mary, the overlooked sister from the Bennet family, before telling the tale of her journeys to London and the Lake District. A three-part Christmas special has been ordered. As one of the most experienced execs working in scripted having led the BBC’s drama before launching Bad Wolf, Tranter has made shows such as Doctor Who and Industry . While she acknowledged funding high-end dramas is challenged, she said demand for major series remains strong. “If someone says to you, ‘You can’t make period dramas, no one’s buying them… You can’t make fantasy, no one is buying it.’ You can’t make a drama set in finance. Make it. Just find a way to make it,” she said. As such, Tranter’s Sony-owned Bad Wolf is also known for productions such as Industry , His Dark Materials and Doctor Who , making it one of the UK’s most prolific drama producers across genres of the past decade. James Gandolfini’s influence Earlier in her talk at the Excelsior Westin Hotel in Rome, Tranter played the audience an extended clip of The Night Of , the HBO drama starring Riz Ahmed about a man who is accused of murdering a woman after a one-night stand. Based on a BBC series, Criminal Justice , the series was big hit in 2016 and earned five Emmy wins. She recalled how the HBO production became challenged when James Gandolfini, who had championed the project, unexpectedly passed away while away on holiday in Italy in 2013. He had played Ahmed’s defense lawyer in a pilot and was an exec producer on the show, and his passing left Tranter, then new to the U.S. system having only recently moved from the UK, and series creator Steven Zaillian at a crossroads. “I got really lucky that Steven took on the show, and then I got even luckier that James Gandolfini came in to play the role of John Stone,” she said. “And then James unexpectedly died and the whole project got put on hold for a while. Then, as in life sometimes happens, one door closes and another opens. John Turturro, who is the most brilliant actor and the nicest of men, came in, and so we continued making The Night Of .” Tranter revealed that her experience producing The Night Of also influenced her decision to launch a major production studio in Wales, where the Bad Wolf era of Doctor Who was filmed. “After Jim’s death, I continued to work with a lot of his crew,” she explained. “He was very, very loyal, and his crew were very loyal to him. so a lot of his Sopranos [crew] worked on The Night Of , and I got to know and understand a lot of them from New Jersey. I understood what it was like to work within the community, and I began to think of Wales and the passion of the crews that I had worked with in my time.” Earlier this month, Deadline revealed the production companies vying to become the next producer on Doctor Who when it returns in 2028. Bad Wolf and showrunner Russell T. Davies both dramatically exited in June. Tranter was not quizzed on the current Doctor Who situation on stage. articles.title: Tokyo Film Festival Chiefs Talk Balancing Blockbusters & Arthouse; Launching International Films In Japan
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz How TIFFCOM Is Building On Cannes Recognition To Strengthen Global Networks, Co-Production & Japanese IP Tokyo Film Festival Chiefs Talk Balancing Blockbusters & Arthouse; Launching International Films In Japan Disney Appoints Carol Choi As Asia Pacific President Following Luke Kang’s Retirement View All October 21, 2026 3:24am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Godzilla Minus Zero Toho It’s an exciting time for Japanese cinema, with franchise hits from Demon Slayer to Godzilla stomping around the world, and Japanese arthouse titles taking the spotlight at major film festivals including Venice, Toronto and Cannes. This year’s Tokyo International Film Festival, taking place in the Hibiya-Ginza district of the city from October 26 to November 4, aims to take full advantage of the momentum and help expand the international profile of Japanese films. Under incoming Festival Director Takeo Hisamatsu, and Programming Director Shozo Ichiyama, the festival is also positioning itself as a launchpad for international films in Japan. Related Stories Commentary We Can See Oscar Possibilities For A24's Hit Documentary 'You Can See Everything' - And That Includes An Acting Category News 'La Bola Negra' Directing Duo Los Javis Reveal How Spanish Sensation Became "The Journey Of Our Lives" Hisamatsu, who previously held senior posts at Warner Bros Japan and local studio Shochiku, headed the festival from 2017-2021 and returned earlier this year when Hiroyasu Ando stepped down after seven years at the helm. While Ichiyama has been strengthening the festival’s competitions, Gala and World Focus line-ups, Hisamatsu says he wants to bolster the glamour quotient at the festival, especially as it gears up for its 40th edition next year. Watch on Deadline “We want to combine art and entertainment and make the festival as multifaceted as possible,” says Hisamatsu, sitting down with Deadline at the festival’s office in the historic Togeki Building in Ginza. “This should be a festival for cinephiles, for general film fans, and also for people who maybe only visit a cinema once or twice in a year. Everyone should be able to find something they want to see.” While describing this year’s pre-anniversary edition as a time for evaluation, he envisages a line-up that includes Japanese films, Hollywood and other international titles, awards contenders, and every genre and format from live action and animation to documentary and short films. The U.S. studios have not been promoting heavily at Asian film festivals in recent years, but Hisamatsu hopes to lure them back: “Japan is still a big market – last year our box office hit a record and surpassed pre-pandemic revenues. Now is a good time to reboot the popularity of Hollywood films in Japan.” Hisamatsu is also engaging with international organisations, including the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences ( AMPAS ), which is bringing a delegation of executives, including Academy CEO Bill Kramer, to participate in a busy schedule of panels and networking events at the festival. Several awards season contenders, including Wild Horse Nine , La Bola Negra , animated feature Wildwood , and Christian Mungiu’s Cannes Palme d’Or winner Fjord , are screening across the festival’s Gala, World Focus and Special Screenings sections. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Searchlight Pictures However, the festival toppers stress that this doesn’t mean any attention will be taken away from Japanese titles. “One of our major goals is to introduce Japanese films to international markets,” says Hisamatsu. The festival will open with a Japanese film – Zeze Takahisa’s Sukiyaki , about the historic song that topped the Billboard charts and remains one of the world’s best-selling tunes – while Takashi Yamazaki’s Godzilla Minus Zero , the highly-anticipated sequel to Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One , will play as the Centerpiece Film. Korean filmmaker Yang Sang-ho’s zombie thriller Colony will close the festival. Three Japanese films have been selected for the festival’s main Competition section: The Canary’s Lullaby , directed by Akira Ikeda; Yukiko Mishima’s Two Cigarettes, Three Nights ; and Akira Yamamoto’s The Intertwining . Ichiyama, the festival’s Programming Director, explains that The Canary’s Lullaby is a Japan-Taiwan co-production, partly filmed on Taiwan’s Kinmen Island, and The Intertwining is based on a Japanese novel but has Korean elements, demonstrating the more international outlook of Japan’s new generation of directors. With major festivals including Cannes, Venice and Toronto, all of which take place before Tokyo, hoovering up Japanese titles over the past few years, Ichiyama says his focus has been on discoveries, as the festival requires world premieres for the Japanese films in competition. “These three filmmakers are not so well known internationally, but they’re all extremely promising, and have the potential to go to European film festivals in the future,” he says. Takeo Hisamatsu [L] & Shozo Ichiyama [R] Other world premieres in the Competition line-up include Indonesian filmmaker Garin Nugroho’s Red Before Dawn , set in a newly independent Indonesia in the 1940s, which Ichiyama describes as “a big-budget epic drama”; Macedonian filmmaker Milcho Manchevski’s social satire Sister Brother Manhole Cover ; and two Chinese-language titles Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting , from Qiu Jiongjiong, and Wang Jianyong’s The Night That Binds Us . Also in the line-up of 15 competition titles is Rubaiyat Hussain’s The Difficult Bride , which world premiered in the Horizons section of this year’s Venice film festival and marks the first ever Bangladeshi film selected for Tokyo main competition. “We saw it in Venice and sent the the invitation very quickly,” says Ichiyama. “We usually see two or three interesting films from Bangladesh in one year, and this one is outstanding.” Rounding out the competition are Heysel 85 , from Romanian filmmaker Teodora Ana Mihai, joining Tokyo Competition for the third time following Traffic and La Civil ; Until The Day Ends , from Serbian filmmaker Jelena Maksimović; Double Freedom , from Argentina’s Lisandro Alonso; Even If Hell Came , from Italy’s Samuele Rossi; Portuguese filmmaker Sérgio Graciano’s Memories Of Prison ; Singaporean animation Magic Atlas from Sun Xun, and Trees Are Watching from Iranian-Kurdish filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi. ‘Heysel 85’ Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer is heading the main competition jury, which also includes Tokyo and New York-based producer Alex Lo, Korean producer Oh Jungwan, French colorist Yov Moor and Japanese actress Makiko Watanabe. An Australia Spotlight will screen De Heer’s 2022 The Survival Of Kindness ; Natalie Erika James’ body horror Saccharine , and Vee Shi’s hybrid documentary Time And Tide . Other talent attending the festival include Cate Blanchett , in town to celebrate the Japan premieres of five short films supported by the Displacement Film Fund (and who is also a producer on Alpha Gang , recently added to Special Screenings); as well as Iranian director Mohammad Rasoulof and Japanese filmmaker Mipo O, both recipients of this year’s Kurosawa Akira Award. Filmmakers including Ilya Khrzhanovsky ( DAU ), Teodora Ana Mihai ( Heysel 85 ), Zeze Takahisa ( Sukiyaki ), Shahrbanoo Sadat ( No Good Men ) and Yukiko Sode ( All The Lovers In The Night ) will deliver talk sessions and masterclasses. Tokyo has two other competition sections – Asian Future, focused on emerging Asian directors, and Nippon Cinema Now, which aims to present an overview of the current state of contemporary Japanese film. Nippon Cinema Now will screen eight titles, from both new and established directors, and has introduced two new awards for Best Film and a Special Jury Prize. Asian Future, programmed by Kenji Ishizaka, will screen 10 world premieres from Japan, Korea, Philippines, India, Turkey, Kazakhstan, Indonesia and Iran. This year also sees the return of the festival’s non-competitive section dedicated to Southeast Asian cinema, Crosscut Asia, held in partnership with the Japan Foundation, which stopped running during the pandemic period. Now titled Crosscut Asia+, the section will screen three recent festival hits, Four Seasons In Java , Filipiñana and Becoming Human , along with a selection of retrospective titles. ‘ Iron Boy ‘ Other major sections include Animation, which will screen Cannes Un Certain Regard special jury prize winner Iron Boy , among other titles; Women’s Empowerment, including recent festival breakouts Lovers In The Blue Night , from India’s Anupama Roy, and A Girl Unknown , from China’s Zou Jing; Japanese Classics, including a Kenji Mizoguchi retrospective; and the Youth and Asian Students Film Conference sections. Taking place towards the end of the year, Tokyo Film Festival has always been in a good position to present a “best of fests” round-up for local audiences, and this year aims to double down on efforts to connect international films with Japanese buyers, both directly at the festival and through the TIFFCOM contents market taking place a few metro stops away. “Especially in World Focus, we’re showing many films that played in Berlin, Venice and Cannes, several of which have still not found a Japanese distributor,” Ichiyama says. “Japan has many strong, independent buyers, but with the current weakness of the Japanese yen, they’ve not been so eager to travel to Venice and Toronto or acquire new films. We can present those titles here in theatres with local audiences and Japanese subtitles.” With many screenings already sold out, filmmakers and industry can expect packed houses and attentive audiences for these films. As Hisamatsu observes, Japan continues to be one of the world’s top theatrical markets, and while anime and Godzilla may be pulling the biggest crowds, Tokyo Film Festival is one time of year at least when movies of all genres, languages and budget levels will be reaching audiences on a big screen. The festival kicks off on Monday, October 26, with an opening ceremony and screening of Sukiyaki, and runs until Wednesday, November 4, while TIFFCOM is taking place October 28-30 at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center in Hamamatsucho. articles.title: How TIFFCOM Is Building On Cannes Recognition To Strengthen Global Networks, Co-Production & Japanese IP
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz How TIFFCOM Is Building On Cannes Recognition To Strengthen Global Networks, Co-Production & Japanese IP Tokyo Film Festival Chiefs Talk Balancing Blockbusters & Arthouse; Launching International Films In Japan Disney Appoints Carol Choi As Asia Pacific President Following Luke Kang’s Retirement View All October 21, 2026 3:27am Add us as a Google Preferred Source TIFFCOM 2025 TIFFCOM At this year’s Marché du Film at the Cannes film festival, it would be no exaggeration to say that Japanese content and creators were everywhere you turned. Designated ‘Country of Honour’ at the market, Japan was involved in a slew of panels, workshops and labs; played a prominent role in Cannes flagship programs, including Cannes Animation, Co-Production Day, and Producers Network; and also launched the Japan IP Market, a three-day initiative co-hosted by the Marché and Japan’s leading contents market TIFFCOM . The Marché decided to shine a spotlight on Japan in recognition of the strength of its content and intellectual property (IP), as well as recent efforts – by the Japanese government, local studios, and independent filmmakers and producers – to engage with the rest of the world. As Deadline noted at TIFFCOM two years ago, Japan was once reliant on its huge domestic market, but is now actively seeking co-production, collaboration and exports, focusing its efforts on North and South America, Europe, and the rest of Asia. Related Stories Executives Amazon MGM Studios Elevates Julie Rapaport & Alana Mayo In Film Division Reorg News 'Lizard Music' Starring Dwayne Johnson And Directed By Benny Safdie To Tune Up Christmas Day 2027 Via Amazon MGM All these efforts are being supported by the Japanese government, which last year launched the ‘Content Industry Growth Investment Support Program’, branded as IP360, which aims to expand overseas sales of Japanese content (across film, anime, games and music) to $126BN (JPY20 trillion) by 2033. Watch on Deadline “Historically, sectors including Japanese anime and live-action content have been optimized for the domestic market, lacking an industrial structure designed to expand into global markets,” explains TIFFCOM CEO Yasushi Shiina. “At Cannes this year, as the Country of Honour, the public and private sectors joined forces to showcase Japan’s key strengths, including anime and manga. In doing so, we built networks with international producers, distributors, and other industry professionals, driving strong momentum toward transforming the sector into an IP-driven industry that generates global revenue. “Following this, TIFFCOM will leverage the home-ground advantage of being hosted in Japan to promote Japanese IP alongside a diverse array of participants. For international attendees as well, we aim to make TIFFCOM a platform where they can connect directly with Japanese partners and unlock new business opportunities.” Yasushi Shiina [L] & Kaori Ikeda [R] A key program within TIFFCOM is the Tokyo IP Market: Adaptation & Remake (TIPM), an initiative that the Cannes IP event was also based on, which brings together publishers and production companies holding rights to Japanese manga, audiovisual works, novels and games. This year, the number of participating IP holders has expanded from six to ten companies, including content giants such as Amuse Creative Studio, Kadokawa, Nippon Animation, Shochiku and Toei . TIPM organizes a series of one-on-one meetings between the rights holders and international producers, mostly from North America, Europe and the rest of Asia. In addition, eight of these companies will hold an open pitch event, with audiovisual support from Imagica Group, to present their flagship IP. “We co-organized the Japan IP Market in Cannes – the Cannes edition of TIPM – with the Marché du Film, and the event generated an exceptionally strong response,” explains TIFFCOM managing director Kaori Ikeda. “Thanks to this success, the Tokyo edition is seeing an increasing number of leading producers attending from Europe and Hollywood. We’re excited to offer everyone in Tokyo this premier opportunity to connect with high-quality Japanese IP.” Another key TIFFCOM track is the Tokyo Gap Financing Market (TGFM), which presents projects with Asian elements and at least 60% of their funding in place, that are seeking to complete their budgets through co-production, sales, distribution and other forms of investment. This year, the event has selected 24 projects including Vincci Cheuk’s Hong Kong-Japan co-production 38.83 ; Boo Junfeng’s multi-territory co-production Trinity ; François-Marc Baillet’s animated feature Back To Tomioka ; five projects selected through a partnership with Canada’s Frontières genre market, and three in partnership with Italy’s Cinecitta ( see here for the full list of selected projects ). In addition, TGFM talk sessions will introduce Japan’s various support schemes – including grants for international co-productions from Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs (Bunka-cho) – alongside funding from Canada and Brazil. Japanese producers have been co-producing with their East Asian neighbors in Taiwan and South Korea for quite some time but have recently been venturing further afield into Southeast Asia and Europe. “Two factors are driving this,” says Ikeda. “First, production volume is increasing across Asia as a whole, including Southeast Asia, and production capabilities are also rising. “Second, opportunities to build networks with one another at film festivals and markets across Asia are expanding. Platforms such as TGFM are facilitating mutual introductions, leading to an increasing number of co-production projects with Southeast Asia. Japan also recently joined the new Asian Producers Alliance with the Agency for Cultural Affairs as the representative member.” In Europe, co-productions between Japan and France have been the most common, but Ikeda observes that projects with Italy have also increased following the signing of an official Japan-Italy co-production treaty in 2024. Recent co-productions involving Japan include Sleep No More , from Indonesian filmmaker Edwin, which premiered at this year’s Berlinale; Ria , from the Philippines’ Arvin Belarmino, which won the Heart of Eurasia Award at Busan film festival, and Boo’s upcoming Trinity , which has around ten co-producers across Europe and Asia. Trinity , Ria and Janus Victoria’s Japan-Philippines co-production Diamonds In The Sand were all selected for various editions of TGFM. ‘Ria’ Meanwhile, TIFFCOM’s conference program will present around 20 sessions organized along thematic lines: intellectual property (IP), artificial intelligence (AI), Japanese TV, Asian Series & Films, market trends and co-production. Key sessions include an ‘Unlocking the Global Potential of Japanese IP’, with speakers from Credeus ( Kokuho ), Amazon MGM Studios and Netflix’s One Piece ; an AI-themed keynote with AGBO ’s Chris Brearton and Dominic Hughes; and the annual session by the Association of Japanese Animations, presenting data on the anime industry. Leading Japanese broadcasters Nippon TV and TBS will host sessions on their international activities; an Anime Co-Production Conference will feature speakers including Ervin Han ( The Violinist ), and a “Beyond Country of Honour” session has speakers from Toho and K2 Pictures, along with TIFFCOM’s Shiina and Cannes Marché Head of Industry Programs Alexandra Zakharchenko. Last year’s TIFFCOM had more than 4,600 attendees from 46 countries and regions, an increase of 13% from the previous year, while international participation rose by 10%. As of two weeks before this year’s edition, Ikeda says that visitor registrations – mostly buyers and producers – were up about 10% on the same point last year. “East Asia continues to drive strong participation, led by Taiwan and South Korea, as well as a dedicated pavilion from Thailand,” Ikeda says. “Some companies from China, including streaming platforms, will also take part. And in a notable new trend, we are also seeing increasing participation from companies offering AI and data analytics solutions.” TIFFCOM is taking place October 28 to 30 at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center in Hamamatsucho district, which is just a few train stops away from Tokyo International Film Festival’s main venues in Hibiya-Ginza. The festival is running from October 26 to November 4. articles.title: BBC Scraps TikTok Generation TV News Bulletin ‘The Catch Up’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake BBC Scraps TikTok Generation TV News Bulletin ‘The Catch Up’ Judi Dench Laments “Waste Of Goodwill & Talent” In ‘Cats’: “Oh God, I Can’t Bear It” BBC Three To Be Switched Off For Second Time, As BBC Confirms TV & Radio Network Closures View All October 21, 2026 4:08am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'The Catch Up' BBC EXCLUSIVE : The BBC has canceled The Catch Up , a nightly news bulletin that was aimed at the TikTok generation. The BBC has canned The Catch Up as part of the planned closure of BBC Three , the youth network that will be switched off for a second time in spring 2027. BBC Three ‘s brand will be retained on iPlayer. The Catch Up was launched in 2022 and was pitched as an attempt to “bring back” 16- to 24-year-old viewers to traditional news bulletins. Its debut coincided with BBC Three being restored to linear TV, a decision that was reversed on Tuesday. Related Stories Acquisitions The BBC & MHz Choice Board Sweden's Latest 'Wallander' Series News BBC Three To Be Switched Off For Second Time, As BBC Confirms TV & Radio Network Closures The two- to four-minute news bulletin was designed to provide young viewers with a roundup of the day’s headlines in an accessible format, complete with graphics and a conversational tone. Watch on Deadline Tuesday’s bulletin was hosted by BBC journalist Ben Henley-Washford and featured a report on BBC Three’s demise as a linear television network. “The BBC has announced it is closing BBC Three,” Henley-Washford said. “Not just yet, though. They said the TV channel, along with BBC Scotland’s channel, will close in the spring as the corporation continues to make £500 million pounds worth of savings by 2028.” He did not mention that The Catch Up would be discontinued. When The Catch Up launched, then editor Amanda Goodman told Press Gazette : “We want to create relatable news for young people that doesn’t necessarily sound like the BBC, or the BBC they think exists at present.” BBC News was not on TikTok in 2022, but this has changed. The BBC News account now has 16.5 million followers and more than 1 billion likes. A BBC News spokesperson said: “The BBC is the UK’s leading news publisher for 16-34 year olds in the UK – reaching around half of 16–34-year-olds each week across its BBC News platforms, including youth-focused offerings such as Newsbeat , as well as Newsround for a younger audience. “Further to this, there are significant and growing numbers of young people accessing BBC News across our social channels – including TikTok, Instagram and YouTube. London’s Metropolitan Police said in September that Clarke had been charged with two counts of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism, and one count of exposure. The alleged offenses took place between 2007 and 2016, involving five women. Clarke appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday. He pleaded not guilty to all the charges and will next appear at Southwark Crown Court on November 18, according to BBC News . Watch on Deadline Detectives had been investigating Clarke for a year, arresting the actor on September 25, 2025. He has not worked in the entertainment industry in any substantial on-screen capacity for years. He played Mickey Smith in Doctor Who , while his last series on UK television was ITV’s Viewpoint in 2021. Clarke created hit indie movie Kidulthood and had roles in other productions, including Star Trek Into Darkness and Bulletproof. articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim , Melanie Goodfellow October 21, 2026 4:50am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sara Ishaq’s ‘The Station’ Watermelon Pictures EXCLUSIVE: The Station , the debut narrative feature from Yemeni-Scottish filmmaker Sara Ishaq, has been picked up for North America by Watermelon Pictures . Watermelon will release the film theatrically later this year. The Station debuted in the Critics’ Week competition at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. The official synopsis reads: Set against the backdrop of war-torn Yemen, The Station follows Layal, who runs a women-only petrol station where the rules are simple: no men, no weapons, no politics. A rare sanctuary of safety and solidarity, the station becomes a vibrant gathering place where women from every walk of life come together with humor, resilience, and hope. When Layal’s younger brother faces forced enlistment, she reunites with her estranged sister to save the one life they still can, embarking on an emotional journey that balances warmth, wit, and quiet defiance in the face of extraordinary circumstances. Related Stories News Dark Sky Films Takes U.S. Rights To Prize-Winning Emirati Horror 'The Vile' News Qatar's Doha Film Festival To Open With Yemeni Female-Focused Drama 'The Station' Manal Al-Mulaiki, Abeer Mohammed, Rashad Khaled, and Saleh Al-Marshahi star in the film. The film was produced by Screen Project and Georges Films, and co-produced by One Two Films, KeplerFilm, Barentsfilm, Setara Films, The Imaginarium Films, and ZDF Das kleine Fernsehspiel – ARTE. Jon Kilik ( Babel ) serves as executive producer. The move has been on the cards for some time with co-creator Ryan Murphy regularly discussing its potential return over the last few months as he promotes FX series The Shards. Related Stories News Ryan Murphy “Just Finished” Writing ‘Glee’ Reboot Script, Says Original Cast Is “Enthusiastic” News ‘Glee’ Co-Creator Ryan Murphy Says “Maybe We Should Revisit That Show” For A Reboot As “It’s Come Back Around” “That show is interesting because it’s come back around. So many young people now watch it. And I’m like, ‘Maybe we should revisit that show,’” he said in July. Less than two months later, Murphy revealed that he had just finished a reboot script for the musical comedy series, which originally ran for six seasons on Fox between 2009 and 2015. Watch on Deadline Murphy co-created the series with Ian Brennan and Brad Falchuk. While Murphy was behind The WB’s Popular and FX’s Nip/Tuck, Glee marked Murphy’s first major broadcast breakthrough, winning his first Emmy for directing the pilot episode. The former journalist revealed last month that he had been in touch with “around ten of the original cast members” of the show, although no casting was announced as part of the series order. The show featured the likes of Chris Colfer, Jane Lynch, Kevin McHale, Lea Michele and Matthew Morrison as well as Dianna Agron, Cory Monteith, Amber Riley, Mark Salling, Naya Rivera and Darren Criss. A number of these stars have since passed including Monteith, who died in 2013, and Rivera, who died in 2020. Colfer told Bustle earlier this month, “It was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya [Rivera] is gone. But I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no.” Set at William McKinley High School in Lima, Ohio, it followed the members of the New Directions, a glee club competing in the show choir circuit, while dealing with social issues. Each episode featured a musical performance. The reboot comes from 20th Television, which produced the original. The show, which won six Emmys including for Murphy and Lynch as well as guest stars such as Neil Patrick Harris and Gwyneth Paltrow, currently streams on Hulu and Disney said that it currently draws around 4M monthly listeners on Spotify, highlighting its current relevance.
