articles.title: Fox Sports Soccer Announcer John Strong Is the New Voice of the Westminster Dog Show (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All October 19, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source John Strong and his doggies Courtesy John Strong Logo text Fox Sports ‘ lead soccer play-by-play announcer John Strong is now sitting — and presumably staying — in the big chair. Strong has been named the new in-venue show announcer for the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show , The Hollywood Reporter has learned, which returns to New York City in early 2027 with its 151st installment. Strong, who has called the FIFA World Cup and Major League Soccer (MLS), succeeds Michael J. LaFave as the “Voice of Westminster.” LaFave put 25 years into the role. As announced in May, the Westminster dog show will stream on Netflix . The Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show is the second-longest continuously held sporting event, behind only the Kentucky Derby. Related Stories Movies Edward Berger Talks Filmmaking in a Streaming Age: "The Movie Industry Needed Netflix to Wake Up" Business Netflix Earnings Preview: Not the Time to Chill Strong is no new pup here — he’s called the play-by-play for the Masters Agility Championship and hosted the Best of Breed competition the past seven years for Fox. “As the legacy of Westminster continues, we are overjoyed to welcome John back to the show in this exciting new role,” said Dr. Donald Sturz, president of The Westminster Kennel Club. “John has called some of the world’s most historic sporting moments, including some of Westminster’s very own. We know he will bring his signature flair, expert commentary and genuine love of dogs to every moment leading up to Best in Show.” “I am humbled and honored to step into this prestigious role for The Westminster Kennel Club,” added Strong. “I look forward to honoring the legacy of Westminster and celebrating the future of this beloved sporting event while lending my passion for dogs and live sports experience to the world’s top canine competitors.” “Bark! Bark!” said the dogs, probably. (But actually, they probably didn’t — these pooches are very well-behaved.) For the first time, the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show’s evening group judging and Best in Show competition will stream live on Netflix from Madison Square Garden on Feb. 1-2. The daytime breed competitions at the Jacob K. Javits Convention Center will stream live on The Westminster Kennel Club’s website and YouTube channel. The Javits competitions begin on Jan. 30; the 14th annual Masters Agility Championship will be taped and streamed on Netflix at a later date. THR

articles.title: CNN Shocker: Christiane Amanpour to Exit News Channel Next Year
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 19, 2026 8:26am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Christiane Amanpour Photo by Sean Gallup/Getty Images CNN is losing one of its highest-profile anchors and correspondents next year. Christiane Amanpour will scale back her work at CNN over the next few months, and leave the channel entirely next June. CNN CEO Mark Thompson shared the news in a note to staff Monday morning. “Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” he wrote. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.” Amanpour has been with CNN for 43 years, becoming perhaps its most famous foreign correspondent, and a staple of its lineup. Why Amanpour is leaving is not clear, but the announcement comes just weeks after Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner bros. Discovery, bringing CNN into its fold. Thompson will continue to lead CNN for the time being, though longer-term anything could happen. “After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” she said in a statement. “I will end my daily shows across CNN and PBS at the end of this year, while continuing to maintain a weekly show on CNN through May and working on a smooth transition through June. Amanpour had publicly expressed concern with the takeover, saying at an event in May that “Clearly I’m concerned, and I’m not sure how much I’m allowed to say about a corporate thing that’s under way, but I am obviously, as a person, as a journalist with a record, concerned, and I’m concerned based on what’s happened to the other things that [Ellison has] taken over already, like CBS News.” For now, she will gradually pull back on her CNN International show this year bfore it ends next May. She will continue to host her podcast The Ex Filed, which she co-hosts with her ex-husband and former U.S. diplomat and Assistant Secretary of State Jamie Rubin. The podcast is not produced by CNN. “I want to thank all the amazingly talented people I’ve worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews,” she continued. “From my very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukrain and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much, as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor.” You can read Thompson’s note to staff below. Dear all, I’m writing today with news about a CNN icon – and our dear friend and colleague – Christiane Amanpour. After more than 43 years at CNN, Christiane has decided that the time is right to begin a new chapter. Early in 2027, she will scale back her CNN International show, Amanpour, to once a week. The program will conclude in May, and she will leave CNN at the end of June. Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months. Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally. Christiane has been a household name around the world for decades. Yet she began more than 40 years ago not as one of the biggest stars in CNN’s history, but as a news desk assistant in our Atlanta newsroom. Famously, one of her bosses told her back then that she didn’t have what it took to become a foreign correspondent – or to hold any on-air role at all. Boy, did she prove him wrong! It would be impossible to list all of her reporting triumphs, exclusive interviews, awards and broadcasting firsts, or the many other accomplishments that have made her one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere. We will make sure to share and celebrate them all before she departs next year. In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship. Mark THR

articles.title: Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close By Mia Galuppo Plus Icon Mia Galuppo Senior Entertainment Reporter miagaluppo Follow Sign Up View All October 19, 2026 8:38am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Dan Lin Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images for American Cinematheque Dan Lin is out as Netflix ‘s film chief, sources tell The Hollywood Reporter . The news comes as the streamer cuts from its uppermost ranks and implements layoffs that will affect roughly 1,000 people, the company’s biggest cut since 2022. Prior to Lin, chief content officer Bela Bajaria was exited, along with VP of film Doug Belgrad and a series of high-ranking television executives. It is unclear who will assume Lin’s role, but the understanding is that Peter Rice, who took over the chief content officer post, will be in charge of finding new leadership. Netflix did not immediately reply for comment. Lin joined Netflix in 2024, taking over from then film chief Scott Stuber. Under Stuber, Netflix became known as the place where name filmmakers could land big budgets and paydays as the traditional studios implemented more cost-conscious spending practices. During this time, the streamer consistently ended up with best picture nominations, but top awards have notoriously evaded Netflix films. Lin, who was hired by Bajaria, was brought in to curb spending while (ideally) increasing the quality of the entire film slate, not just the titles from big-name directors. Under Lin, the streamer‘s movies division was reorganized by genre , with deputies like Kira Goldberg and Niija Kuykendall handling films that fell under categories like sci-fi, rom-com and family film. Netflix began offering more mid-size films that have been ignored by theatrical players, including big book adaptations like Remarkably Bright Creatures and People We Meet on Vacation , as well as mid-budget action films like Apex and The RIP. (This is not to say that Netflix’s Lin tenure was without big swings — see: Greta Gerwig‘s Narnia movie due out next year or David Fincher’s The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth — but the offerings no doubt slowed.) Lin came from his production company Rideback, which minted the $1 billion grossing Aladdin and was involved in the hit It movies as well as The Lego Movies . He departed the company when he joined Netflix, leaving partners at the helm who found another $1 billion hit with last summer’s live-action Lilo & Stitch . Presumably, he could return to Rideback now that his Netflix tenure is up. As of late, the streamer hasn’t been able to capture audience interest, at least at the rate co-CEO Ted Sarandos would like, with viewership and subscriber growth stagnant. Under Rice‘s leadership, Netflix will focus on “creating big, buzzy hits,“ as Sarandos wrote in his memo to staff. THR

articles.title: ‘Carrie’ Star Alison Thornton Knows Exactly How You Feel About Her Polarizing Character
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close Alison Thornton Jenna Berman Logo text Alison Thornton is fully embracing the divided online discourse provoked by her polarizing character in Prime Video ‘s Carrie . The Vancouver native actress, who is in the midst of continued press for Mike Flanagan ‘s series adaptation of Stephen King’s classic, which was released on Prime Video on Oct. 7, knows her Chris Hargensen villain role has given viewers moral whiplash. “Some people hate Chris, some people forgive Chris, some people want to give her a hug, and some people cheer when she dies,” Thornton tells The Hollywood Reporter, laughing. Related Stories Beyond the Book Inside Tubi's Plan to Build an R.L. Stine Cinematic Universe TV Amazon Orders Tennis Drama 'Rally' From Julie Plec and Andre Agassi The 27-year-old actress has an array of onscreen credits already, including Girlfriends’ Guide to Divorce , Dare Me and School Spirits . However, her portrayal of the tragic villain in Flanagan’s adaptation of King’s Carrie felt like a stroke of destiny. Thornton revealed that the iconic author was a “huge deal” in her household while growing up. “My mom is the biggest Stephen King fan, and I grew up reading a lot of his books . … I had actually read Carrie twice before even auditioning,” she shares. Despite being familiar with the story of the bullied teen with telekinetic powers, reading the script for Flanagan’s take on the horror caught the actress off guard, realizing how his expanded version added new layers of depth to the ensemble of characters originally introduced in the 1974 novel and its previous film adaptations. Flanagan’s Carrie marks the first time the novel has been reimagined for the small screen with the cast also including Summer H. Howell and Samantha Sloyan. The role of Chris Hargensen has been portrayed by Nancy Allen, Emilie de Ravin and Portia Doubleday in previous screen versions of the book, but in Flanagan’s Carrie , viewers see a more developed Chris, and chronicling how her internal conflicts leads her to a path of tragic disaster. Thornton has been navigating the whirlwind of attention surrounding her role at the heart of the show’s intense discourse. “The response has been incredible. I love seeing people argue about the characters, about who’s morally wrong and who’s morally right. All the conversations around redemption and kindness versus cruelty are exactly what we wanted,” she says. Throughout Flanagan’s eight-episode series, each of the characters are placed at the center of a complex moral debate, continually forced to choose between kindness and cruelty. As their interpersonal dynamics fray, a constant tug-of-war between power and vulnerability not only shapes the characters’ individual choices, but also profoundly impacts their ultimate journeys and tragic fates. Thornton’s Chris journey is one that reflects a tragic spiral and fate. But the series’ choice to humanize the villain without excusing her actions was intentional, Thornton explains. “Reasons are not excuses,” she says. Though she even admits, “If I knew her, I’d want to give her a hug and also yell at her.” In a chat with THR , Thornton reflects on the divisiveness over her character, the parallel journey of Chris and Carrie and responds to those Christine theories. It’s been a little while since the show came out. What have you made of the response, and how are you feeling now that it’s out there for audiences to watch? It’s so wild that the show is finally out, because we shot it over a year ago. The response has been incredible. I love seeing people argue about the characters, about who’s morally wrong and who’s morally right. All the conversations around redemption and kindness versus cruelty are exactly what we wanted. Some people hate Chris, some people forgive Chris, some people want to give her a hug, and some people cheer when she dies. (Laughs.) I love the debate around her. The conversation is really meaningful to me. Take me back to the start. Were you familiar with the Carrie book and the other adaptations? What did you think of the story overall? I was very familiar with Carrie going into this. Stephen King is a huge deal in my household. My mom is the biggest Stephen King fan, and I grew up reading a lot of his books. I’d seen the Brian De Palma movie and the 2013 movie, and I had actually read Carrie twice before even auditioning, so I went in thinking I knew exactly what it was going to be. Then I read Mike [Flanagan]’s scripts, and seeing how much time we had with the characters and how three-dimensional everyone was, I was blown away. I was also a fan of Mike Flanagan, so I was over the moon to be in the Flanniverse and the Stephen King universe. The characters aren’t necessarily what I was expecting from the book, which was such a treat to play. Everyone is so layered. In the show we get to learn Chris’s home dynamic. Her mother is no longer in the picture, and her father is there but not a loving, present figure. Can you talk about the Chris we first meet and how this family dynamic has impacted her? The family dynamic is a huge reason for the choices Chris makes. Working with Michael Trucco and Heather Graham was a dream. One thing I thought was so important is that Chris has truly been shielded from facing any consequences her whole life. Her dad has always covered everything up for her, so I don’t think she understands what adult repercussions look like, and I don’t think she understands how much damage she can actually cause, to other people and to herself. Working on the family dynamic and seeing Michael’s portrayal of John Hargensen, I saw just how ruthless he was. They have a winner mentality, and they view cruelty and being mean as power. There were so many moments in the scripts, and in things we found on the day, where the only time Chris feels affection from her dad is when she’s making fun of Brooklyn or being cruel to someone else. That was so interesting to me: her lack of good role models and her lack of emotional support at home. In the very first scene where we meet Chris and John, Chris doesn’t get breakfast from her dad. She ends up getting a burrito from Sue (Siena Agudong). She really doesn’t have any parental figures at home, which is tragic for her. “She’s such a product of how she was raised, which of course doesn’t justify anything she does, because she does really unforgivable things,“ Thornton says of her villain character. Jenna Berman At school, Chris projects a strong, unfazed persona. She has popularity, power and a following, while Carrie is the complete opposite, someone who can easily become a target. The saying is hurt people hurt people. Do you think Carrie is just a bystander Chris chooses to project her hurt and anger onto, and that it could easily have been someone else? Why Carrie and why not Brooklyn? I love that question, because I really don’t think it has anything to do with Carrie herself. As you said, it’s just bad timing for Carrie. I love that Carrie and Brooklyn look kind of similar, and that Brooklyn is off limits. I think a lot of Chris’s reason for targeting Carrie is how vulnerable she is and also the threat of losing Sue. Carrie enters the picture, and Sue gravitates toward her and shows her all this warmth. I think Chris is really envious of that, especially since she’s losing her support system at home, and Sue has been the only parent and healthy role model Chris has ever had. When that gets threatened, Chris thinks, “I need to push this girl as far away from our friend group as possible and hopefully get Sue back.” There’s also something interesting in Summer’s beautiful portrayal of Carrie and how optimistic she is. She’s so wholesome and genuinely kind, and people start gravitating toward her. Carrie gets more and more popular throughout the show, and I think that’s really threatening to Chris because of how she was raised. She’s been taught that you get power from making people afraid of you and being cruel. Chris has such a sinister view of the world, so seeing this girl come in and truly embody kindness, and that being enough to give her power, is so threatening to Chris’ identity. She can’t handle it. So there are a lot of reasons Chris is unaware of for why she chooses to bully Carrie, but none of them have to do with Carrie herself. Despite being different, Carrie and Chris have more in common than they may think. Both of their parents project their own faults onto their kids, yet Carrie and Chris turn out differently. Carrie wants to escape and be free from her mom, whereas Chris internalizes that cruelty and uses it against others. Do you think Chris could ever see that similarity, that they’re two sides of the same coin? I don’t think Chris has the perspective to see that. She’s so caught up in her own pain and her own world. But I love the parallel between them. One thing I thought was so cool in the scripts is that, as you said, they both lose their emotional support at home in the first episode. They both discover power early on: for Carrie it’s telekinesis, and for Chris it’s social media and bullying. They’re both then influenced by outside forces to do the wrong thing: for Carrie it’s Emaline (Thalia Dudek), and for Chris it’s Billy (Arthur Conti). They’re on a parallel track the whole time. I think one of the most interesting conversations around the show is: once you discover you have that power, whatever it may be, do you use it for good or for bad? I don’t think Chris is old enough or has the maturity to see the tragedy that they could actually have been friends, that they’re quite similar and could have helped each other out. That’s such a shame. The characters all have a choice between kindness and cruelty, yet they all seem to take the more destructive path. Chris takes the cruel path, but it doesn’t always seem solid. There are moments, like with Billy holding the rock over the freeway or wanting to hit Carrie with his car, where she shows hesitance and that there’s still a moral compass there. What did you make of her internal conflict? I think there are many moments in the show where Chris hesitates. One of my favorites is the trench sequence at the construction site. I really don’t think Chris knows how far she’s going to take it. She’s discovering this power as she goes, and she’s being influenced by Billy, who at that point is the only person validating her and giving her any kind of attention. He likes it when she’s cruel, so she plays that up around him, especially once Sue has exited Chris’ life. Chris really needs someone to say, “Hey, you’re OK, you’re enough. All of these dark thoughts, acting on them is the wrong choice.” Billy (portrayed by Arthur Conti) “is the only person validating her and giving her any kind of attention,“ Thornton says of their dynamic. Prime Video I also love how many moments there are where I think Chris is about to apologize. I think she’s about to apologize in the principal’s office. I think she wants so badly to apologize when she’s alone with Carrie in the bathroom. The internal conflict she’s facing is that she wants everything to go away and go back to normal, but she’s also hearing her dad’s voice in her head, the idea that the Hargensens don’t lose, and that if she apologizes, she’s admitting defeat. Combine that with her never actually being held responsible for any of her actions, and it’s a perfect storm. She’s so stubborn that she can’t make things right, which is also very sad to me. There’s something really scary about being at that age, where you don’t really understand the consequences yet, or how much damage you can do through cruelty. She’s facing all of that at the same time, which is unfortunate for her. It does not end well. You mentioned how she wants to go back to normal, but there’s a new normal that she’s unwilling to accept. She has one identity crisis, which will probably be one of many she’d have in life, but it’s so tragic to her that she thinks, “Everything’s over. I can’t handle it.” I think she really needed the promise of going to Duke and getting out of Chamberlain, getting away from her mom and her dad. She needed that so much, especially with Sue. When that falls apart, she’s just like, “Well, I don’t know what to do now. It’s done.” “I saw just how ruthless he was. They have a winner mentality, and they view cruelty and being mean as power,“ Thornton says of Chris‘ father (portrayed by Michael Trucco). Prime Video You brought up the bathroom scene with Carrie. In that moment, Carrie genuinely wants to understand and seems to give Chris the chance to explain so they can move on. It could have been the moment everything changed for the better. Can you talk more about that scene? I love that scene so much. Episode six was the last episode we shot, so we’d been building toward it the whole time. Summer and I kept calling it the real mediation, because the parents hijack the actual mediation. The scene felt so complicated and layered to me. Carrie’s question, “Why me?” is such a fair question, and no one has really asked Chris that. It’s the only scene where Chris and Carrie are alone together, and I think it catches Chris off guard. I don’t think she’s thought about it: why, genuinely, did you do this? At that point she’s dug herself into such a deep hole that I don’t think she can process anything clearly. Carrie does get through to her for a second. Chris is actually reflecting for the first time and almost apologizes, and then at the last minute she pulls back. I remember reading it and wanting to shake her and say, “Come on, you’re so close! You could have fixed everything.” It’s my favorite scene in the show, I think, because it’s when Chris doubles down. After that, it’s the point of no return for her. There’s a scene where it alternates between Chris and Carrie in the car. Carrie is happy and free, allowing herself to be a normal teenager for the first time, lifting the car without even knowing it. In contrast, we see Chris completely breaking down, hiding it from Sue while Sue drives. If she could just show that part of herself, I’d imagine people would be there for her more than she thinks. I totally agree. Chris has unfortunately been taught that vulnerability is weakness. If she could open up to the people around her and lean on Sue. … I think she could benefit from some therapy and just talking about her feelings. She’s such a product of how she was raised, which of course doesn’t justify anything she does, because she does really unforgivable things. That scene is so interesting to me, too, because from Chris’ perspective, that was supposed to be her night, her at her most powerful, running this party. It wasn’t supposed to end with Carrie on top. Chris doesn’t really witness that, but once again it’s the parallel between them. They’re on very similar tracks. They’re two sides of the same coin, essentially. “Working with Michael Trucco and Heather Graham was a dream.“ (Pictured from left: Trucco, Thornton and Heather Graham.) Prime Video With all the characters in the show, there’s an exploration of losing control, taking control and relinquishing control, and Chris experiences all of those. What was Chris’ relationship with control like to you, and how did it shape the path she’s on? She’s seemingly losing control and trying to take it back, but in the wrong way. Chris has always been someone who has had control and power, just because of her family circumstances, and she loses it really quickly in the first episode. I think that’s a big reason she makes the “Carrie Red” account. It’s the only power she has. Bullying Carrie is a new kind of power she finds, essentially the only control in her life. The more followers she gets and the more people send posts to “Carrie Red,” the more she realizes she’s having a pretty large impact, and that feels good, especially since she doesn’t have power in any other part of her life at that moment. As you said, she’s grasping for these morsels of power and control, and she finds them in really destructive places. Do you think her friendship with Sue would have been repairable? We see the moment on the “Carrie Red” social media account where Chris reveals Sue‘s big secret yet we also see Chris learn Sue is the one to betrayed her by recording her admission of being behind the social media account. I would hope so, but I feel like the scars would have been so deep that it would have taken so much work. I think they could use years apart. They have a really co-dependent, really toxic friendship. I do think Chris addresses Sue’s betrayal by posting the photo of Sue’s pregnancy test. It’s a little bit of revenge and a cry for help at the same time. But the damage is so deep in that friendship that I think they should probably separate for a while and see who they are without each other. Chris needed support and love from other people, and she was very dependent on Sue for that. She needed other healthy friendships and role models in her life, too. “They have a really co-dependent, really toxic friendship,“ Thornton says of Chris and Sue (portrayed by Siena Agudong). Prime Video The final scene between Chris and Carrie where Chris is about to die, she attempts to apologize to Carrie. Do you think she was genuinely saying sorry in that moment, or was it an act of desperation to save herself? I think Chris is genuinely sorry. I think of the conversation she has with Billy right before the car flips, when she looks at him and says, “What did we do?” She’s facing so much guilt and remorse, and she’s being forced to see the impact of her actions. In those final moments, she knows what’s going to happen. She knows there’s nothing she can do, and there’s no point in fighting. She just wants to make things as right as possible before she dies. So I think it’s genuine remorse. The show ends on a cliffhanger, and there’s been a lot of online discussion and conspiracy theories about the story’s connections and where it could lead. One is that Chris’ soul possesses Billy’s car at her death and turns it into Stephen King’s famous killer car, Christine. Have you heard that? Do you have thoughts? I’ve heard that one, and I really like it. It’s so exciting. The evil car, of course. I trust Mike Flanagan. Whatever he thinks for season two is in his hands. But I do love the conspiracy theories. I love seeing people say, “They’re wearing the same necklace! What does that mean?” People keep sending me screenshots of conspiracy theories asking, “What is this?” And I’m like, “I don’t know. I didn’t notice that either.” (Laughs.) I do think the Christine connection makes the most sense. I could play a car for a few hours in hair and makeup, easy! I’m so here for it! This show’s version of Chris is one where we can humanize her and understand how she became this deeply broken person, but we can also still not excuse a single thing she does. After playing her, do you feel protective of her? What do you make of playing a character that people can be conflicted over? She’s polarizing.I have very complicated feelings. What I was really holding on to is that reasons are not excuses. We see her reasoning, and I understand her decision-making, and she’s also making the wrong choices. When I was playing her, the only way to play her was to have so much empathy for her. If I knew her, I’d want to give her a hug and also yell at her. I feel so bad for her. I really think her death is a tragedy, and it’s a tragedy also because she’ll never be able to make things right. My interpretation is that I would have loved to see her go to juvie, get some therapy, do community service and then actually get on a better path. I was never cheering for her to die. There are moments in the show where I’m like, “What are you doing? Please stop. This is cruel.” But, again, reasons are not excuses. And I love that she’s polarizing. It’s so fun. I imagine things are still very Carrie -focused right now, but what are you working on, and what roles and stories are you hoping to tell? I imagine this feels like a big chapter in your career, and hopefully one of many. I can’t say too much. I do have a movie coming out soon called And Love Knocked , but there are a few things on the horizon that I can’t share yet. Carrie was a dream project with dream collaborators: the cast, Mike Flanagan, Stephen King. It was such a dream role and such a pivotal chapter in my life, and it was a masterclass to work with everyone. Right now I’m just in Carrie world and reveling in that. We shall see! Mike Flanagan is known for having his staple ensembles and teaming with the same actors in different projects. Is there another story he could take on that you’d love to be part of? I would love to work with him on anything! He’s such an incredible director and a great guy, and I’d love to keep working with him. The cast of actors he works with are all so phenomenal. I keep saying I would love a Pet Sematary remake, because it’s my favorite Stephen King book, so I’m putting it out there! About those Christine rumors: “I could play a car for a few hours in hair and makeup, easy! I’m so here for it!“ Jenna Berman THR

articles.title: Foo Fighters, Weezer, Sublime Join KROQ’s 2026 Almost Acoustic Christmas Lineup
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All October 19, 2026 8:55am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Dave Grohl of Foo Fighters. Daniel Boczarski/Getty Images for Harley-Davidson Foo Fighters , Weezer and Sublime are among the recording acts that will be on the lineup for this year’s KROQ Almost Acoustic Christmas. Interpol, Joyce Manor, Julia Wolf, Almost Monday and The Linda Lindas also will be headliners at this year’s event, which will take place Dec. 12 at the Kia Forum in Los Angeles. KROQ, the legendary alternative rock station in Los Angeles that’s owned by Audacy, is bringing the event back to Southern California for its 35th year. The annual event also gives back to the local community, with proceeds benefiting Para Los Niños and Al Wooten Jr. Youth Center. Related Stories Music Young Miko Gets Flirty With L.A. During Her Late Checkout Tour Music Miley Cyrus Returns to the Stage With Emotional and Cathartic Hollywood Bowl Show Founded in 1980 in Skid Row, Los Angeles, Para Los Niños partners with children, youth, and their families through integrated education, wellness, support and advocacy to address individual and systemic barriers and create pathways to success. The Al Wooten Jr. Youth Center in Los Angeles hosts free after-school and low-cost summer programs, through which it revitalizes and empowers communities in crisis by providing a safe, nurturing environment committed to good citizenship and academic excellence. “Almost Acoustic Christmas has always been about the bands and their connection with our listeners,” said Kevin Weatherly, senior vp programming at KROQ. “That’s what makes this show so special, and we’re incredibly grateful to the artists who take the time to be part of it. Celebrating 35 years of this together is pretty amazing. And to be able to give back to two great organizations supporting local youth makes it that much more meaningful.” Tickets go on sale at noon Oct. 30. THR

articles.title: Locarno Golden Leopard Winner Sho Miyake Gets First North American Retrospective, 14-City Tour (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 7:00am PT Locarno Golden Leopard Winner Sho Miyake Gets First North American Retrospective, 14-City Tour (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Locarno Golden Leopard Winner Sho Miyake Gets First North American Retrospective, 14-City Tour (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Ju Ji-hoon, Choo Young-woo Return for Netflix’s ‘The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call’ Seasons 2 and 3 6 hours ago Selena Gomez Reveals Vaping Nicotine Changed Her Voice: ‘It’s Not Worth It’ 6 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bitters End Japanese director Sho Miyake , whose “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” won the Golden Leopard at Locarno in 2025, will get his first North American retrospective at New York’s Metrograph from Nov. 7–17. It is one stop on a Japan Foundation tour of 14 cities in eight countries. The Metrograph program, titled “Unspoken Gestures: The Films of Sho Miyake,” is co-organized and presented by the Japan Foundation. Miyake will attend in person over the opening weekend, and select encore screenings will follow the main run. Related Stories Olivia vs. Olivia: Predicting the Grammys' Album of the Year Contenders... and Why Rodrigo and Dean Are at the Front of the Race Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound The series brings together eight of Miyake’s own titles. They include his 2012 debut feature “Playback,” which premiered at Locarno, and “The Cockpit” (2014), a 64-minute film that watches producer-rapper OMSB and his collaborator Bim make a track in a small suburban Tokyo apartment. “And Your Bird Can Sing” (2018) screens with the 2016 short “August 8th,” and “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” is paired with the 2016 short “Nagahama.” Boxing drama “Small, Slow but Steady” (2022) and “All the Long Nights” (2024) round out the lineup. Popular on Variety Miyake has also picked two films that influenced his work as carte blanche selections: David Elfick’s 1973 surf film “Crystal Voyager” and Aoyama Shinji’s 2007 drama “Sad Vacation,” the final part of Aoyama’s “Kitakyushu Saga,” starring Asano Tadanobu. He will introduce both on Nov. 8, after Q&As following “Small, Slow but Steady” and “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” the day before. “For a long time now, Sho Miyake has been one of international cinema’s best-kept secrets, each of his films landing quietly but forcefully amid the cacophony of contemporary film culture. With this retrospective, we’re giving the man a microphone and calling on New York audiences to attend the voice of an essential Japanese film artist,” said Metrograph programmer Edo Choi. The tour opens on Nov. 3 in Washington, D.C., where the Japan Information & Culture Center at the Embassy of Japan will screen “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” and Miyake will join the Q&A remotely. Oklahoma follows from Nov. 9–11, with screenings at the University of Oklahoma’s Meacham Auditorium in Norman and the Oklahoma City Museum of Art. Miyake will also teach a masterclass for a university screenwriting class that is closed to the public. Los Angeles hosts the program Nov. 13–15 at the Japan Foundation, Los Angeles, UCR Arts at the University of California, Riverside, and the American Cinematheque’s Los Feliz Theatre. The lineup there adds King Vidor’s “The Patsy” (1928) and Tony Scott’s “Deja Vu” (2006). Toronto runs Nov. 17–19 at TIFF Bell Lightbox, the Fox Theatre and Paradise Cinema, with Miyake’s 2010 film “Good for Nothing” and Jacques Demy’s “Bay of Angels” (1962) on the bill. In the new year, the tour heads to Paris, Toulouse, Rome, Turin, Madrid, Zurich, Cologne, London and Derby, and wraps in February 2027. Miyake will travel to every city except Washington. In a joint statement, Inoue Ryo and Rokkaku Akinaru of the Japan Foundation pointed to Miyake’s own description of a director’s job as “taking on the responsibility of creating images of humanity.” “We, too, are among the audience members who were once struck and moved by his gaze. We sincerely hope to bring that sense of wonder and emotion to as many viewers as possible in theaters around the world,” they said. Miyake made “Playback” while still in his mid-twenties. Murakami Jun plays an actor nearing 40 who wakes up on the way to a hometown wedding wearing his old school uniform. His friend Hamaguchi Ryusuke compared the film to “a modern-day reincarnation of [John Cassavetes’s] ‘Opening Night.’” “Small, Slow but Steady” stars Kishii Yukino and is drawn from the life of deaf boxer Ogasawara Keiko. “All the Long Nights,” adapted from Seo Maiko’s novel, pairs Matsumura Hokuto and Kamishiraishi Mone as co-workers who form a bond. “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” adapts two manga by Tsuge Yoshiharu and stars Kawai Yuumi, Takada Mansaku, Shim Eun-kyung and Tsutsumi Shinichi. articles.title: Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 7:00am PT Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE) Kicking in from December, the deal sees 18 wide-ranging Globo titles, including International Emmy Winner 'India – A Love Story,' hitting Netflix in Brazil or worldwide By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom 4 days ago ‘The Castle’ Shapes Up as Another Hit From ‘La Bola Negra’ Producer Movistar Plus 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Credit: Alile Dara Onawale - Globoplay When the going gets tough, the tough get together: Brazil’s Globo , Latin America’s biggest media company, has struck an 18-title licensing deal with Netflix , led by one jewel in Globo’s crown, Walter Salles ’ Academy Award winner “ I’m Still Here .” Kicking in from December, the agreement sees titles rolling out on Netflix through mid-2027. The wide-ranging deal also takes in “India – A Love Story,” created by Glória Perez, the doyenne of Brazilian telenovela writers, and directed by Marcos Schechtman, which won the 2009 International Emmy for Best Telenovela. Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Todd Rundgren Slams Taylor Swift, Says She ‘Ruined Music’ and Is ‘the Apotheosis of Mediocrity’ Also in the mix is “Vitória,” directed by notable film-TV helmer Andrucha Waddington (“Under Pressure,” “Emergency 53”) and starring Academy Award nominee Fernanda Montenegro (“Central Station”) in a lauded central performance as an 80-year-old battling to expose a drug racket on Copacabana. Popular on Variety Rights details vary. Sold worldwide by Goodfellas in theatrical deals, “I’m Still Here” has been licensed just for Brazil. Netflix has closed the U.S. and Latin America, a telenovela heartland, on “India – A Love Story.” Created by Leandro Soares and directed by João Fonseca and Regis Faria, seven seasons of “Vai Que Cola,” Brazil’s biggest pay TV comedy series hits, running over 2013-26, has been acquired by Netflix in Brazil. “Vitória,” in contrast has been bought for the world. The Globo original productions will be made available on Netflix, dubbed and subtitled in multiple languages. The package is comprised by 14 films, three telenovelas and a series. “We hope this agreement is just the first step in a long partnership between two companies that share the ambition, creative craftsmanship and commitment to take Brazilian culture even further”, said Elisabetta Zenatti, VP of Content at Netflix Brazil. “It makes us proud to see interest in Brazilian productions growing across different markets,” said Pedro Garcia, Globo’s Director of Rights. “For decades, we have been dedicated to sharing the richness of our culture with the world. By combining that experience with Netflix’s global scale, we take another step toward bringing Brazilian creativity to new audiences, expanding the presence and strengthening the recognition of Brazilian film and television abroad.” Several broader market trends are also at work. “The deal is a reflection of a wider trend in streaming,” said Guy Bisson, Ampere Analysis executive director. “Licensing spend is growing while original production spend is flat,” he added. “Content owners can no longer afford to keep their own content in long windows of exclusivity or in perpetuity given the challenge of customer acquisition in a saturated market so we’re seeing more content enter the market again and windows shortening. Courtesy of Netflix Why Globo Is Important to Netflix? “Both companies say the move underscores the power of Brazilian content to entertain audiences around the world,” Globo and Netflix noted in a press statement Monday. Globoplay co-produced “I’m Still Here” and saw it gross a remarkable $36.5 million worldwide, racking up $17 million in box office gross outside Brazil, including $6.2 million for Sony Pictures Classics in the U.S. Globo announced at Mipcom that Globoplay Original “Red Blood,” a teen werewolf-vampire love triangle thriller, has sold at the BBC. Equally, Netflix has seen a surge in international audiences’ passion for Brazilian fiction, movie “Caramelo” reigning s Netflix No. 1 non-English film in the world over Oct. 6-19 last year. “Rulers of Fortune,” and “Radioactive Emergency,” also hit the Netflix Global No. 1, Non-English show spot, over Nov. 3-9, 2025 and March 23-29 this year. As a streaming service , Netflix reigns supreme in Latin America, where it has 63.8 million subscriptions forecast for 2026, which will increasing to 73.7 million by 2031, María Rúa Aguete, Head of Media and Entertainment at Omdia, announced at Mipcom. Brazil is said to have more Netflix subscribers than any other country in the world outside the U.S. at a time when international revenue growth is increasingly vital to Netflix’s fortunes. Globo can supply some of its drivers. articles.title: Nathan Fielder Says Elizabeth Holmes Called Him From Prison Right Before ‘You Can See Everything’ Release to Tell Him Repeatedly: ‘I Trust You’
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 7:20am PT Nathan Fielder Says Elizabeth Holmes Called Him From Prison Right Before ‘You Can See Everything’ Release to Tell Him Repeatedly: ‘I Trust You’ By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest Nathan Fielder Says Elizabeth Holmes Called Him From Prison Right Before ‘You Can See Everything’ Release to Tell Him Repeatedly: ‘I Trust You’ 2 hours ago Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Billy Evans Admits ‘She Looks Insane’ in ‘You Can See Everything’ Trailer but Defends Making the Doc: ‘Make Up Your Own Mind’ 3 days ago Ben Affleck Says Bullying ‘Digger’ Will Only Lead Studios to Make More ‘S—ty Homogenized Movies’: Don’t ‘Punish Movies That Take Risks’ 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jc Olivera / Justin Sullivan Nathan Fielder revealed in a new interview with Wired magazine that Elizabeth Holmes called him from prison right before the theatrical release of his new documentary, “ You Can See Everything .” The call marked the first time the director and his documentary subject had spoken in half a year. Ex-Theranos CEO Holmes is currently in federal prison after being convicted for fraud. “She had not called me in over six months. I had not heard from her in any way… she asked how I was doing,” Fielder said about their conversation. “I asked her if she had seen any stuff about the film coming out and how she felt about it. She told me she had seen some stuff, but most things she just isn’t seeing, so she’s heard things, but she hasn’t really read anything. And then, at the end, she said to me – ‘I trust you.’ I said, ‘OK, thanks.’” Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'The Life of a Showgirl' Spends 15th Week at No. 1 on Albums Chart Olivia vs. Olivia: Predicting the Grammys' Album of the Year Contenders... and Why Rodrigo and Dean Are at the Front of the Race Fielder continued, “We talked about some other stuff. She talked about her kids, and then some updates that are not really my place to share. But then after that, she said again, at the end of the call— ‘I trust you.’ And I don’t know what she meant by that.” Popular on Variety “You Can See Everything,” directed by Fielder and “Primetime” helmer Lance Oppenheim, follows Holmes and her partner Billy Evans in their final weeks before Homes’ 11-year prison sentence begins. The filmmakers moved in with the couple 34 days before Holmes went to prison. Fielder told Wired that he got involved with the project after hearing that Holmes and Evans had tried and failed to pitch a documentary about them to A24, explaining: “Months later, I heard that that had happened. So I called A24 and said, ‘Well, could I meet her?’ That was the start of it all.” But why would Holmes allow Fielder to come into her home? That’s a question that still has Fielder puzzled considering his previous work, be it “Nathan for You” or “The Rehearsal,” should’ve made it clear to Holmes that bringing Fielder on board would not produce anything straightforward or conventional. “This is part of the mystery that, like, doesn’t make sense to me,” Fielder said. “I asked her that on, I think, one of the first days we shot. I still don’t fully understand it. That really messed with my head. Also, I got the sense very early that she hadn’t seen a lot, but she had seen some of what I did, and she had talked to people who had seen what I did. Billy had seen more. I think she found the clip that she said she saw funny. But you know, her relationship to that … to what’s funny? I don’t even know. She said her favorite movie is ‘Elf,’ the Will Ferrell movie.” Evans appeared on the “All-In” podcast the day before “You Can See Everything” opened in theaters and explained the couple’s rationale behind letting Fielder and Oppenheim into their home. Mainly, they wanted people to get to know Holmes up close and personal so they could decide for themselves if she is a bad person or not. “It was to have people see who she is,” Evans said. “I have gone through this consistent experience with the people who love me most, from my grandmother to my best friends. They’d hear I knew [Elizabeth Holmes] or I was falling for this person and now we’re going to have a kid… in the beginning, every single one of these people thought I was crazy. ‘Do you know who she is?’ I would tell them, ‘I understand why you feel that way but just meet her.’ And they would meet her and spend time with her and see her in a totally natural environment, like going on a hike or helping a friend. Every opinion of her would radically shift. That was the intention of the film. To help scale that up and allow other people to sit with her and make up their own minds.” The decision is backfiring for Holmes, however, since “You Can See Everything” is only amplifying the backlash against her. Even before the movie screened for press, A24 dropped a chilling teaser trailer that had many viewers disturbed by Holmes’ demeanor and claims that she did not do anything wrong at Theronos. The movie has since turned into a box office hit by grossing $15 million in its domestic debut, which is the biggest launch for a documentary in decades. “You Can See Everything” is now playing in theaters nationwide. Head over to Wired’s website to read Fielder’s interview in its entirety. articles.title: ‘Smallville’ at 25: Tom Welling and Michael Rosenbaum on Clark Kent and Lex Luthor’s Origin Story, the Journey to Superman and That Final Moment
articles.full_text: Dan Doperalski for Variety A little more than 25 years ago, on Oct. 16, 2021, “ Smallville ” premiered on The WB. Created by Alfred Gough and Miles Millar, and based on the DC Comics character, the show set out to do something that’s now common practice but was then novel: tell the origin story of an iconic character, enriching the character’s mythology along the way. On the show, an immediate hit for the network, Tom Welling and Michael Rosenbaum played, respectively, a high-school-aged Clark Kent and his eventual nemesis Lex Luthor in the fictional town of Smallville, Kansas. One of the inventions of “Smallville” is that Clark (who yearns to be ordinary) and Lex (who lives under the thumb of his controlling zillionaire father) are, for a time, best friends, before the inevitable happens, as Lex succumbs to his darker instincts. “I felt like I had the liberty to just do what I wanted to do, and be real, and grounded,” Rosenbaum said in a recent interview. “I mean, seeing Lex and Clark as friends — and then obviously we know what happens with the relationship, but I thought it was really fascinating. It had never been done.” As opposed to their characters, Welling and Rosenbaum remain close: They host a “Smallville” rewatch podcast called “TalkVille,” and the night before they came to the Variety office, Welling, who doesn’t live in Los Angeles, had stayed at Rosenbaum’s house. They’ve been celebrating the show’s 25th anniversary, and in their most extensive conversation together about the show’s legacy, they filmed a “How Well Do They Know Each Other?” video, answering questions about one another and about “Smallville.” During the game, they flopped on things like the show’s premiere date (somehow, Welling’s first answer was Oct. 14 , 1992 , before he switched it to that same date in 2002) and its ratings, which broke records for The WB. The correct answer was that 8.4 million total viewers tuned in live, but Rosenbaum wrote “12 million, Beeyotch,” and Welling wrote “1 trillion,” then trying to explain by saying, “Well, I mean, worldwide.” Rosenbaum harangued him. “You know how much a trillion is? A trillion is like, a lot of billions,” he said. “Dude, if we had those ratings, we’d still be on the air. Good lord.” As they reminisced, they talked about the guest stars who’d appeared on “Smallville” over its 10 seasons, some already well known, others new to the business. One of them, in a loving tribute to Superman ’s long history, was Christopher Reeve, who appeared twice on the show as billionaire scientist Dr. Virgil Swann, Clark’s mentor. Well before superhero movies became ubiquitous, Reeve had his breakthrough role as Clark Kent in the 1978 “Superman” film, a blockbuster, and played him three more times in its sequels. In 1995, however, Reeve, a competitive equestrian, had a devastating accident, breaking his spine while riding, and becoming paralyzed for the rest of his life. (He died in 2004.) Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Bumps 'Choosin' Texas' Out of No. 1 on Hot 100; 'Encore' Tracks Fill Four Out of Five Top Slots Taylor Swift to Perform at Academy Museum Gala Dan Doperalski for Variety Welling said he’d filmed the scenes with Reeve in New York, and they bonded. “We talked a lot about what it meant to play the character,” he said. “He said he was really happy that they chose me to play the role, which I thought was cool.” Popular on Variety The “Smallville” production wanted to make things easy for Reeve, Welling said, with him filming his part of the scene and then leaving. “But he wanted to stay for my coverage, where they filmed me speaking — I mean, he totally didn’t need to do that,” Welling said. “We laughed a lot; he was very funny, and it got to the point where he was being told to leave. And he wouldn’t leave! His nurse was like, ‘If you don’t leave, I’m going to call the police, and I’m going to take you out of here.’ And he turned to me, and he goes, ‘They’re always telling me what to do,’ which is really funny, just considering the whole situation.” In “Smallville” lore, Clark landed on Earth as a toddler from the planet Krypton during a meteor shower that took a toll on the town, and he had super-strength, super-speed, X-ray vision, and was growing into all the abilities we associate with the character of Superman. The meteor rocks also infected Smallville and its population, which gave the show its engine for the case-of-the week format of its early seasons — and brought in a lot of guest stars, one of whom was Amy Adams in Season 1. Dan Doperalski for Variety Welling picked Brian Austin Green as his favorite (“because I watched ‘Beverly Hills, 90210’”), and Rosenbaum selected Adams “because it’s memorable and she became a big movie star, and she was really cool,” writing her name in cursive on the game’s whiteboard. “That’s respect,” Welling told Rosenbaum. “You’re an elegant man, Michael.” “TalkVille” has re-familiarized them with the show, so they had no problem remembering Adams’ episode. “‘Crave’ — she was a girl who craved to get thinner, right?” Rosenbaum asked. Welling replied, “She took kryptonite to get skinnier. And she took it too far.” Rosenbaum: “Yeah. She devoured people.” As the show’s central character, Welling appeared in every episode of “Smallville.” But Rosenbaum left after Season 7, following a contract dispute with Warner Bros. Television, the show’s producer. “I mean, do I get into it?” Rosenbaum wondered, looking to Welling, who then backed him up. “There’s a point in the show where the actor’s contract comes up for renewal, and the idea is that, based on the success of the show, the contract will be increased,” Welling said. “And that wasn’t happening.” Rosenbaum said he was already itching to do other things when the impasse occurred. “It was like, ‘Hey, we want you to come back for three years — we want you to sign a three-year deal, and give you no increase in pay,’” he recalled. “And anybody who works in any business, it’s like, ‘Oh, I’m an integral part of this show, or this business,’ or whether you work at Kmart or whatever. And you’re like, ‘I’m part of the success, and don’t I need to get rewarded?’ So I said, ‘Yeah, no thanks.’ And that was it.” Dan Doperalski for Variety Rosenbaum did return for the “Smallville” series finale, though, which aired on May 11, 2011 — with a full head of hair they had to cover with a bald cap. (He shaved his head to play Lex for the seven seasons he was on the show.) He’d called the then-showrunners Brian Peterson and Kelly Souders (Gough and Millar had also left after the seventh season) to say he wanted to come back one last time. Rosenbaum remembered thinking to himself, “You should come back and wrap it up for the fans — I think the fans will love it. And I didn’t realize how much I would love it, and I’m glad I did it.” Lex was a last-minute addition, and they had Rosenbaum for only one day, so Peterson and Souders had to scramble to explain where Lex had been for all those years, filming one last scene in the Luthor Mansion. (Additionally, in a flash-forward, Lex becomes president, portending ominous showdowns between Lex and Clark far in the future.) For Rosenbaum, it was an emotional return. “I was in the makeup trailer with Natalie, our makeup artist, who was like a mother to me,” he said. “I go, ‘All right, well, that’s it!” And I gave her a hug, and I just go, ‘Oh man. Oh, shoot. Here I go!’ I just started crying, and she cried, and we hugged it out, and that was it. It was bittersweet.” Throughout “Smallville,” Gough and Millar had a “no flights, no tights” ethos about the character, which Welling felt so strongly about that he had it in his contract. “We toed the line a few times, don’t get me wrong, but they couldn’t do it without me saying, ‘All right, this one will be all right.’” But in the finale’s last shot, after he’s been alerted to yet another crisis, Clark bounds up to the Daily Planet rooftop. As he prepares to take off, he rips open his shirt — revealing the classic imagery of the Superman suit. Welling remembers it well. “We didn’t even do a rehearsal on it, because we didn’t want anyone to see it if it wasn’t right,” he said. He’d wanted assurance that there wouldn’t be a full suit, and the head of wardrobe told him, “No, no, no — it’s too expensive.” “We got to set that day, and they had given me just a T-shirt, with no sleeves to wear underneath the shirt. Because they didn’t have the money to put the suit on, and they weren’t going to see it anyway.” Welling had been inspired by the conclusion of Kiefer Sutherland’s “24,” when Jack Bauer goes on the run and says his final goodbyes to his closest colleagues. Welling pitched that idea to the writers, he said, because he liked the idea of it as an ending to Clark’s story. “We can’t go with him,” Welling said. “But he’s out there.” As they reflected on “Smallville,” both Welling and Rosenbaum said they wished they’d appreciated it more at the time. “You’re on a hit show, and you’re doing all these things,” Rosenbaum said. “And sometimes you should really enjoy it, and embrace it. And I did; I think we both did. But if I could go back and do it again, I would’ve just been like, ‘Remember, this is fun . We’re getting paid to do this!'” Welling feels the same way. “I didn’t really have anybody who I knew to be like, ‘Hey buddy, you know this is cool, right?’” On Rosenbaum’s popular podcast “Inside of You,” “we talk about mental health, facing adversity, loss, all those things,” he said. He thinks a number of its listeners are “Smallville” fans. “The fans have stood by me, I think, for almost everything we do,” he said, crediting Gough and Millar — who’ve gone on to, among other projects, create “Wednesday” for Netflix – for how good the show was, and for creating the “family atmosphere” among the cast and crew. “Al and Miles,” Rosenbaum said, “it came down to them, and they chose us.” “I mean, we’re lucky,” he added. “People are like, ‘Well, do you think you’ll ever do anything as big as “Smallville?”’ I’m like, ‘Probably not!’” “But we were on one of the biggest shows ever, and isn’t that enough? It’s always, ‘What’s next? What are you doing?’ It’s like, ‘Hey dude, I’m content. I’m happy. And we kicked some ass for a while.” ©CW Network/Courtesy Everett Collection Loading comments... articles.title: Christiane Amanpour to Exit CNN in June After 43 Years
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 8:16am PT Christiane Amanpour to Exit CNN in June After 43 Years By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Christiane Amanpour to Exit CNN in June After 43 Years 46 minutes ago CBS News Correspondent Jan Crawford Apologizes for Post on Abdul El-Sayed That Sparked Social-Media Ire 22 hours ago Odell Beckham Jr. Taps Range Sports for Off-Field Opportunities 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Vintiner for Variety Christiane Amanpour , who parlayed a job as a news assistant on CNN ‘s foreign desk into a years-long globe-trotting assignment for the news giant, plans to step away from the media company in June. “After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said in a statement Monday. She added that she “looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.” Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Graham Norton Shoots Down ‘Conspiracy Theory’ That Taylor Swift’s ‘Opalite’ Video Was Shot Before She Came on His Show Amanpour’s exit is announced just as CNN comes under the control of a new owner, Skydance , which is grappling with billions of dollars in debt and perceptions that it may want to skew its news operations toward a particular view on politics and other issues. Popular on Variety Amanpour, 68 years old, has hosted both an evening program for CNN’s international channel since 2009 and a show for PBS, “Amanpour & Company,” since 2017. She left CNN briefly for an ill-fated run at ABC News, where she was named moderator of the Sunday program, “The Week,” in 2010. Low ratings undermined her efforts there, and she returned to CNN in 2012. “Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” said Mark Thompson, CEO of CNN, in a statement. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.” CNN employs many journalists, correspondents and anchors, but few of them are as tied to the news outlet’s overall brand as Amanpour. Perhaps only Wolf Blitzer and Anderson Cooper enjoy similar status among present staffers. After securing a role in eastern Europe in 1986, she made a reputation for herself by covering conflicts in Bosnia, Iraq and Afghanistan. From 1992 to 2010, she worked as CNN’s chief international correspondent. “I will end my daily shows across CNN and PBS at the end of this year, while continuing to maintain a weekly show on CNN through May and working on a smooth transition through June,” Amanpour said in her note Monday. She indicated that she expects to continue working on an independent podcast, “Ex-Files,” which she leads along with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, former official at the U.S. State Department. articles.title: Dan Lin Out as Netflix Film Chief
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 8:25am PT Dan Lin Out as Netflix Film Chief By Matt Donnelly Plus Icon Matt Donnelly Chief Correspondent @MattDonnelly Latest Dan Lin Out as Netflix Film Chief 46 minutes ago Harry Styles ‘Together, Together’ Tour Doc Coming From John Wilson, Universal Pictures Content Group (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago How Netflix’s Messy Transition Will Rock Hollywood: Looking at You, NBCU 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images for Netflix Dan Lin has been dismissed as Netflix ‘s head of film after almost three years, multiple sources tell Variety . Even if expected, it’s a significant shoe to drop following a layoff bloodbath last week at the streamer. Roughly 1,000 employees got the chop, capped by the shock firing of chief content Bela Bajaria. Lin was let go at the start of the weekend, two sources added, and will address his teams throughout the day on Monday. The executive attended Saturday’s Academy Gala, and was spotted Sunday evening at a tastemaker screening for “La Bola Negra” on the Netflix campus. Related Stories Graham Norton Shoots Down ‘Conspiracy Theory’ That Taylor Swift’s ‘Opalite’ Video Was Shot Before She Came on His Show Todd Rundgren Slams Taylor Swift, Says She ‘Ruined Music’ and Is ‘the Apotheosis of Mediocrity’ A Netflix spokesperson had no immediate comment on the matter. It’s unclear who will replace Lin, though an announcement is expected in the coming days. Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, the former heads of the Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group, have been widely speculated to be speaking with the streamer about a possible role at the company. Popular on Variety Netflix is embarking on a major creative restructuring after months of headlines citing engagement problems and stock stagnation — all in the aftermath of its defeated bid for Warner Bros. — namely in hiring the seasoned film and TV executive Peter Rice to replace Bajaria. In the days leading up to his ouster, Lin watched as layoffs claimed his right hand Doug Belgrad and the film vertical’s indie head Sheroum Kim. Lin’s ascension to the top Netflix film job turned heads in 2024. The accomplished producer sat atop a thriving self-made business in Rideback. That production house is best known for building the animated “Lego” film franchise, Stephen King’s “It” adaptations and the “Sherlock Holmes” movies. He departed Rideback to replace longtime film lead Scott Stuber. In a June sit-down with The New York Times, Lin said that he greenlit or acquired 88 movies for Netflix up to that point, with the standouts being “Apex,” “Emelia Perez,” “Here Comes the Flood,” “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” and Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew.” More to come … Jack Dunn contributed to this post. articles.title: Egyptian Star Mona Zaki Reflects on Three Decades of Reinvention as El Gouna Honors Her Career: ‘Art Is About Freedom’
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 9:00am PT Egyptian Star Mona Zaki Reflects on Three Decades of Reinvention as El Gouna Honors Her Career: ‘Art Is About Freedom’ By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest 10 Films to Track at El Gouna, From Cannes and Berlin Standouts to Rising Arab Filmmakers 3 days ago El Gouna’s Amr Mansi on CineGouna Expansion, New Partnerships and Making ‘the Industry Our Hero’ 3 days ago El Gouna Artistic Director Andrew Mohsen Puts ‘Discovery’ First: ‘We’re Trying to Draw Attention’ to Overlooked Films 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Alia Rady The 9th edition of El Gouna Film Festival (Oct. 15-23) may be celebrating Mona Zaki ’s past, but the Egyptian film star is far more interested in what she’s yet to do. Honored with the festival’s Career Achievement Award at the opening ceremony, Zaki, who has already built a career spanning more than three decades, hasn’t even turned 50. Sitting down with Variety on the shores of the Red Sea, she speaks about that prolific career less as a completed body of work than a continuous process of reinvention. That ongoing transformation has required her to repeatedly shed audiences’ expectations of who Mona Zaki should be. “I get bored easily with myself,” she shares. Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Bumps 'Choosin' Texas' Out of No. 1 on Hot 100; 'Encore' Tracks Fill Four Out of Five Top Slots Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Looking back, Zaki says two lessons in particular stand out: learning the power of saying “no” and finding the confidence and willingness to express herself, both personally and emotionally. The latter, she confides, was something acting itself helped teach her. Popular on Variety “You just have to open up,” she reflects. “Your emotions are important to be heard, and it’s okay. Part of your healing is saying what you feel.” Zaki entered the industry young, first in theater, before moving into television and, ultimately, the silver screen. Early on, she became closely associated with the “girl next door,” an image that increasingly felt at odds with both the woman she was becoming and the kinds of characters she wanted to explore. “I started to kind of feel like I’m going there doing the same thing in every different project,” she recalls. “How boring is that? I needed to shift.” That turning point came with Yousry Nasrallah’s 2009 drama “ Scheherazade, Tell Me a Story ” (Ehky Ya Shahrazad), written by the late Wahid Hamed, which saw Zaki take on the role of a television host whose program examines the experiences of women navigating romance, health, everyday life, and the expectations placed upon them by Egyptian society. The departure from Zaki’s familiar screen persona drew intense backlash, with audiences questioning what had happened to the “girl next door” they had come to know. The response shook her enough that she turned to Hamed with concerns about facing the film’s promotional tour. He encouraged her to stand behind a choice she had made out of love for the work, advice that helped Zaki confront the resistance to seeing her move beyond the roles that had defined her early career. For Zaki, the experience marked the beginning of a struggle that has followed her throughout her career, that of finding roles that allow women to address subjects Egyptian cinema has historically treated as difficult or off-limits. “Censorship, talking about taboos, things that are not okay most of the time, especially for women to talk about,” remain among the challenges she continues to face. “I’m still living in that struggle even now. It can be very difficult to find a meaningful script.” While she believes the landscape has advanced over more than 30 years, Zaki remains deeply frustrated by the gap between the talent of Egypt’s actresses and the opportunities afforded them. “It breaks my heart that most of them are not taking the chances they deserve and the topics they would love to talk about and the rights they want to stand for.” Her own connection with audiences is something she has learned to negotiate over time. “It’s a relationship. You work on it like any other relationship in your life,” she explains. Part of that relationship, she believes, means establishing boundaries around her freedom to evolve as an artist. “I have the right not to feel bored and sick of myself doing the same thing because I’m not corporate, I’m an artist,” she stresses. “Art is about freedom, it’s about change, it’s about trial and error.” With each role, Zaki starts by building a life for the character beyond what exists in the script. She works with an acting coach on every project, drawing on different techniques to construct the character’s history. One of the most important parts of that process, she explains, is imagining a character’s life before the audience ever meets her. Zaki might close her eyes and picture the woman she’s playing at seven years old, in her childhood home with her mother, building memories and emotional associations that will never appear on screen but are critical to the performance. “I don’t have to say it, but I can make people feel it the way I felt it.” That method was put to a different test with “ El Sett ,” Marwan Hamed’s biopic of Umm Kulthum. This time, Zaki was building a character from the life of one of the Arab world’s most revered cultural figures, with decades of history and public memory with which to contend. She plunged into what she calls “crazy research,” watching every piece of footage she could find and repeatedly listening to a rare two-hour radio interview that became one of her most important references. “The whole internal emotions are the imagination of the writer and me.” While the facts of Umm Kulthum’s life are immutable, Zaki still had to find the woman behind them. To bridge that gap, Zaki imagined the parts of Kulthum’s life no archive could relate: the emotions, relationships and private struggles that might have shaped her from childhood. The character stayed with Zaki long after cameras stopped rolling, and she found it difficult to sever that connection after filming wrapped. “I came out of the project feeling that I’m a 70-year-old woman. I’m serious, this was not a joke.” For months, she had taken on not only the physical transformation into Kulthum, but also the emotions and experiences of a woman decades older than herself. Fully returning to Mona Zaki proved disorienting. “I think my whole face changed after that,” she recalls. “I couldn’t accept myself in the mirror.” Some of Kulthum has proven difficult to shake. “I’m trying to get rid of her,” Zaki muses. “I only have a few leftovers, gladly. Honestly, I don’t want to feel like I’m 70 and I’m not there yet.” Asked what she looks for in a role now, after more than three decades of acting, Zaki doesn’t hesitate. “Reality. Honesty. That would just take my heart.” Charlamagne tha God on Mental Health, Social Media and Prioritizing Real-Life Connection: ‘You Got to Constantly Weed Out Your Garden’ Loading comments...

articles.title: Ticketmaster Goes All-In on AI, Names Ex-Amazon Exec as Chief Technology Officer
articles.full_text: Oct 19, 2026 9:00am PT Ticketmaster Goes All-In on AI, Names Ex-Amazon Exec as Chief Technology Officer By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Anna Faris Says ‘It Hurts’ After ‘Mom’ Creator Chuck Lorre Admits His ‘Reluctance to Hire’ Her Was Proven ‘Correct’ After She Exited the Show 3 days ago CNN and Google Strike Multiyear Partnership to Embrace Generative AI 4 days ago Trump Says Execution of Fort Hood Shooter by Firing Squad Will Not Be Livestreamed 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Ticketmaster Bot attacks have plagued Ticketmaster for years, so to combat it, the ticketing service is shaking up its executive ranks and going all-in on AI. Ticketmaster has hired Jim Freeman as its chief technology officer, filling a slot left vacant since February after its London-based chief technology officer, Carlos Alvarez-Coch, departed ahead of a deposition in the U.S. government’s antitrust trial against parent company Live Nation. It has also appointed Rachel Smith, a veteran of Block (owner of music service Tidal), to be its first senior vice president of data science and machine learning, and Disney and Stripe product veteran Chuck Mortimore as its next senior vice president of product. Related Stories Todd Rundgren Slams Taylor Swift, Says She ‘Ruined Music’ and Is ‘the Apotheosis of Mediocrity’ Taylor Swift's 'Encore' Edition Boosts 'The Life of a Showgirl' Back to No. 1 for First Time Since January, Adding a 13th Week on Top As part of the AI push, Ticketmaster has also brought on the team from Raige.ai, an AI startup the company acquired in July. The team will boost Ticketmaster’s adoption of AI tools across the company while also building out the platform’s AI infrastructure. Popular on Variety “Reliable, secure and personalized experiences depend on how effectively we use technology and data,” Saumil Mehta, Ticketmaster’s global president, said in a statement. “Jim, Rachel, Chuck and the Ragie.ai team will help us move faster, build better tools and deliver better outcomes for fans, artists, venues and clients.” Freeman’s remit as chief technology officer will tackle all things AI: building AI tools, using the technology to power fan experiences and ensuring its adoption across Ticketmaster’s organization. Freeman joined the company after a stint as senior adviser at Permira, though he formerly worked as a vice president at Amazon to build and launch Prime Video and its respective device and distribution partnerships. Smith’s work will include an expanded focus on data science and analytics, including tightening integration between data and the company’s broader product development, while Mortimore will help lead product strategy to help combat the company’s bot issues and ensure fans have easier access to both their accounts and their tickets.
