Television where Aguirre-Sacasa and Berlanti are under overall deals. Related Stories News KJ Apa Asked 'Riverdale' Showrunner Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa For 'Afterlife with Archie' Cameo: "I Don't Know Who I'd Play" News Disney+ And Hulu To Stream Pave Studios True-Crime Podcasts 'Clues' And 'Mother Knows Murder' Penned by Aguirre-Sacasa based on the Archie Comics characters, Afterlife with Archie turns the all-American town of Riverdale into a zombie-overrun apocalypse — where the only thing scarier than the undead is trying to survive your teenage years. When a supernatural spell from a certain teen-witch backfires, unleashing an army of the possessed dead upon Riverdale, Archie and his friends must fight to stay alive, testing the friendships, romances, and loyalties that have always held them together. Watch on Deadline Afterlife with Archie is executive produced by Aguirre-Sacasa and Jimmy Gibbons via Muckle Man; Greg Berlanti, Sarah Schechter, Leigh London Redman via Berlanti Productions; and Jon Goldwater via Archie Comics Studios. “ Afterlife with Archie has always been about more than just zombies — it’s about the friendships, loyalty and humanity that make Riverdale worth fighting for,” said Ayo Davis, president, Disney Kids & Family. “Roberto, Greg, Sarah and Jon have such a deep appreciation for these characters, and they’ve built something that’s equal parts thrilling and heartfelt. Fans are going to fall hard for this new version of the gang … and maybe scream a little too.” This is Aguirre-Sacasa, Berlanti Prods. and Warner Bros. TV’s third live-action Archie Comics series adaptation — and the first to launch on the outlet it was originally sold to. Riverdale was initially set up at Fox before moving to the CW, Chilling Adventures of Sabrina started at the CW before relocating to Netflix. Riverdale spawned a short-lived spinoff series on the CW, Katy Keene. Afterlife with Archie also marks Warner Bros. TV’s first series for Disney+, which has been increasingly opening up its slate to outside studios. “The world of ‘Archie’ and Riverdale is the gift that keeps on giving,” said Channing Dungey, Chairman and CEO, Warner Bros. Television Group and WBD US Networks. “To bring Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa’s incredible story to life with our partners at Berlanti Productions, ArchieComics and Disney+ is a thrill for all of us at WBTVG.” Aguirre-Sacasa, a film, TV and comic book writer, had written Archie Comics’ two best-selling horror series, Afterlife With Archie and Chilling Adventures Of Sabrina , when he was named the publisher’s Chief Creative Officer in March 2014. Twelve years later, he continues in his role while also expanding his TV footprint — and the Archie TV universe which launched with the 2017 Riverdale. “This was the comic book that started it all. Before there was a Riverdale, before there was a Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, there was Afterlife with Archie , which I collaborated on with the best horror artist in the business, Francesco Francavilla,” Aguirre-Sacasa said. “Getting to turn Afterlife into a TV series for the amazing team at Disney+ with our incredible partners at Berlanti Productions, WB and, of course, Jon (Goldwater) and his Archie family is truly a full-circle moment — and the ultimate dream project for me. Time to say a prayer for Archie, Betty, Veronica and the whole gang, ‘cause THE ZOMBIES ARE COMING!!!!” Berlanti Prods. and WBTV also have the upcoming Scooby-Doo! live-action series at Netflix, the HBO drama pilot How To Survive Without Me , Stillwater , based on the Skybound comic books, which has a series commitment at Amazon , as well as All American , which just launched its eighth and final season on the CW. “We are so happy to reunite with Roberto on this exciting series that takes us back into the Riverdale world that we so love, and we are thankful to Disney+ and WBTV for giving us the opportunity to revisit some of our favorite characters in a unique and thrilling way,” Berlanti and Schechter said. “A special thank you to Jon Goldwater for letting us continue to play within the beloved ‘Archie’ universe and trusting us to bring Archie’s various stories to life.” Aguirre-Sacasa is repped by WME and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern. Berlanti is repped by CAA and Felker McGinnis & Ryan. Schechter and Goldwater are repped by CAA. articles.title: Christiane Amanpour To Leave CNN In 2027 After 43 Years With Network
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Jon Ossoff Makes L.A. Fundraising Swing In Midterm Final Stretch Christiane Amanpour To Leave CNN In 2027 After 43 Years With Network CBS News Correspondent Jan Crawford Apologizes For X Comment On Michigan U.S. Senate Candidate Abdul El-Sayed View All October 19, 2026 8:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Christiane Amanpour David Buchan/PMC Christiane Amanpour will depart CNN next year, with plans to scale back her schedule at the end of this year before exiting in June. The network’s chief international anchor on Monday wrote in a memo to staffers, “After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” She added, “From my very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much, as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor.” (Read her full memo below.) Related Stories News Jon Ossoff Makes L.A. Fundraising Swing In Midterm Final Stretch Politics CBS News Correspondent Jan Crawford Apologizes For X Comment On Michigan U.S. Senate Candidate Abdul El-Sayed Amanpour also said that she would end her PBS show, Amanpour & Company , by the end of this year, along with her daily CNN International series. She will maintain a weekly CNN show through May, she said, and will continue to do a podcast, The Ex Files , a Global production. Watch on Deadline Mark Thompson , chairman and editor in chief of CNN, wrote in his own memo, “Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months. Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.” (Read his full memo below.) Amanpour’s departure comes amid the closing earlier this month of Skydance Paramount’s deal to acquire CNN’s parent company, Warner Bros Discovery. Thompson is remaining in place as leader of the news network, while Skydance CEO David Ellison has promised editorial independence. Amanpour has been outspoken about coverage of Donald Trump. In 2023, she publicly criticized the network’s town hall with Trump as he was campaigning for a return to the White House. Amanpour said that she shared her views with then-CEO Chris Licht. In her note to staffers on Monday, she wrote, “Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.” Here is Amanpour’s complete memo: “After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years! I will end my daily shows across CNN and PBS at the end of this year, while continuing to maintain a weekly show on CNN through May and working on a smooth transition through June. I want to thank all the amazingly talented people I’ve worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews. From my very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much, as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor. I will be continuing my successful podcast the Ex-Files with Global and look forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.” Here is Thompson’s note to staffers: Dear all, I’m writing today with news about a CNN icon – and our dear friend and colleague – Christiane Amanpour. After more than 43 years at CNN, Christiane has decided that the time is right to begin a new chapter. Early in 2027, she will scale back her CNN International show, Amanpour , to once a week. The program will conclude in May, and she will leave CNN at the end of June. Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months. Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally. Christiane has been a household name around the world for decades. Yet she began more than 40 years ago not as one of the biggest stars in CNN’s history, but as a news desk assistant in our Atlanta newsroom. Famously, one of her bosses told her back then that she didn’t have what it took to become a foreign correspondent – or to hold any on-air role at all. Boy, did she prove him wrong! It would be impossible to list all of her reporting triumphs, exclusive interviews, awards and broadcasting firsts, or the many other accomplishments that have made her one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere. We will make sure to share and celebrate them all before she departs next year. In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship. articles.title: Lance Armstrong On Schwinn Bicycles Documentary ‘No Hands’: “It’s An Incredible American Story”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart ‘Tall Tales & Murder’ Scores New International Deals As Season 2 Takes Shape Cineverse Boards Genre-Bending Holiday Film ‘Ralph’s Perfekt Christmas’ From ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ To Scottish Indie Boss: Kevin McKidd On Ferryman Films & His New Show ‘The Only Suspect’ View All October 19, 2026 8:37am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Lance Armstrong narrates 'No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company' Schwinn Doc LLC EXCLUSIVE: No Hands : The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company documents the extraordinary tale of the titular bike brand with Lance Armstrong serving as both an interview subject and narrator. Armstrong tells Deadline about this rags-to-riches-to-bankruptcy tale and how things could have been different for the iconic brand if he had been on board a Schwinn as he raced the Tour de France , in turn creating a boom in the U.S. market for road bicycles. “It doesn’t have the greatest ending for the family, but it’s an incredible American story,” he says of the feature documentary. “It’s the story of an immigrant. It’s the story of starting from scratch. It’s also the story – and I love thinking about this – of the importance of the bicycle on American culture, and I think sometimes that’s lost on people.” Related Stories News Tour De France: Tadej Pogacar Dominates Race For Record-Tying Fifth Win News Paramount's 5 Pacts With WBD's TNT Sports For Tour De France Highlights Unfeatured Films founder Daniel Clarke directs the film, which comes from the people behind The Lego Brickumentary , narrated by Jason Bateman, and Loopers: The Caddie’s Long Walk , which was narrated by Bill Murray. Watch on Deadline “There are a few brands in the history of whatever that have really owned the category, or, said another way, have named the category,” Armstrong says of Schwinn. And the feature doc duly shows how ingrained in U.S. culture Schwinn became as it got to a point of making over a million bikes a year. “Schwinn equals bike, bike equals Schwinn,” Armstrong said of its glory years. He got involved in No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company via Jim Packer , the Lionsgate exec who is an EP on the documentary, which uses AI to bring historical pictures and sequences to life. Deadline has a first look at the trailer (see below) as the film embarks on a festival run. No Hands recounts how Ignaz Schwinn traveled from Germany to the U.S. and, in 1895, he and Adolph Arnold launched the iconic bike brand, setting a manufacturing base in Chicago. Different generations will get misty-eyed over various models Schwinn produced, from the humble safety bike to the Sting-Ray, which took its design cues from American muscle cars, to sleek race bikes such as the Paramount. Armstrong, a veteran of the world’s biggest bike races, has his own memories: “I did the [1989] Junior World Champs on a Paramount, and to this day, for whatever reason, I still think that’s the best riding bike that I’ve ever ridden.” The film shows how Schwinn was cutting edge in many ways. The brand leaned into what would now be called influencer marketing, with the likes of Roy Rogers, Frank Sinatra and Joan Crawford seen aboard their bikes. It pioneered having its own stores – nowadays the A-list bike brands have their own concept stores – and it had groundbreaking designs and detailing. Having gotten generations of people onto two wheels, it had huge influence on BMX, mountain biking and cutting-edge design, but did not capitalize on these trends as they changed the face of cycling. Armstrong’s succinct take captures it: “They were innovative until they weren’t.” He rode a Trek bicycle in multiple editions of the Tour de France and cycling’s other blue ribband events. As U.S. audiences saw their man in the Yellow Jersey, sales at the likes of Trek and Specialized exploded. But Schwinn had been left in their dust, filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 1992. The Schwinn brand continued under new ownership after the bankruptcy and the No Hands filmmakers said they have no relationship with the current Schwinn Bicycle Company. “There’s a world where, somehow, they had agreed to offshore production, or got into the carbon game, and if they had done that in those early years…if that was a Schwinn instead of a Trek [I was riding], we would 100% be having a very different conversation,” Armstrong says. Sadly for Schwinn, that was not the case, but the rise and fall story takes in how a family business became a cultural icon. No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company opens with scenes from film and TV that reference Schwinn, underlining how it became shorthand for cycling. Director Clarke says his film “is the love letter to Schwinn that generations of kids deserve.” He adds: “The documentary feature explores Schwinn’s storied history, from the iconic Sting-Ray to its widespread influence in the worlds of BMX and mountain biking. “Through the accounts of fans, collectors, cycling pioneers and the Schwinn family themselves, No Hands tells the story of a brand that changed cycling forever and survived through the struggles of American manufacturing, family drama, fads and business forces that ultimately led to its bankruptcy.” Armstrong was keen to get involved. “I watch probably an unhealthy amount of documentaries, so there’s just my general interest in the category, and then obviously I had a touchpoint here, I have a lot of history with this brand.” Having been the subject of numerous docs, this was new for Armstrong in that here, he is narrating and being interviewed, and the doc isn’t focused on him. “I thought it was a fun thing to try. You hope the audience appreciates it. I think the film is great. I enjoyed the hell out of being a little bit involved in the process, obviously sitting for the interview, but then just getting in the studio and recording the narration.” While No Hands is a family story, a business story, a sports story and a story about moments in history, ultimately, it taps into the simple and timeless joy of riding bicycles, with which Schwinn is synonymous. The simple premise is: you never forget your first bike. In the film, Armstrong talks about the excitement and freedom that a first bike can bring. Decades later, the fire lit by his first steed, a brown Schwinn Mag Scrambler, still burns bright. “It’s not lost on anybody, my history with the bicycle, with the sport, with all of the races, with the Tour, all of the things associated with it,” he says. “Still to this day, at 55 years old, if I can wake up and go for a bike ride … and it borders on sounding a little corny, but when I talk about how that makes me feel, how that is still an escape for me, in many ways, it is like church.” No Hands comes from Tiburon Productions and Gem Pictures in association with Brookwell McNamara Entertainment and KSQD Media, and is produced by Human Design. Packer is an EP alongside Chris Brown, David Brookwell, Carl Cramer, Khristian A. Howell and George K. Howell. articles.title: Dan Lin Axed As Netflix Film Boss; Stock Slumping Streamer Set To Unveil Earnings Tuesday
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony How A24 Spurred A Meme Craze & Got The Many To Watch ‘You Can See Everything’; Documentary Opens To $15M Milestone ‘Street Fighter’ Rings Up No. 1 $51M+ WW Opening, Largely Driven By Fans – Global Box Office Update ‘Street Fighter’ Socks $31M, ‘You Can See Everything’ Has 2,000+ Sellouts With $15M Docu Milestone – Sunday Update View All October 19, 2026 8:38am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Dan Lin Getty Images Dan Lin is out as film boss at Netflix in what has been largely speculated for weeks. Insiders at the streamer have denied that Dan Lin and even Bela Bajaria were on the chopping block, but here we are. At Saturday night’s Academy Museum Gala cocktails, we caught up with Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos and asked if more cuts were coming. In what seemed like a polite dodge, he just winked and stepped away. Interpret that as you may. Lin’s firing comes in the wake of Netflix making 1,000 pink-slips given their recent slow growth, and minimal overall viewership spike. Wall Street is bracing for what is expected to be a downer quarter from the OTT service. At the time of this post, Netflix shares were trading at $69.76, -1% at the time of this report. The 52-week share high on Netflix was $124.86. Related Stories Acquisitions Netflix Strikes Deal With Globo For Brazilian Fare Including 'I'm Still Here' & 'India - A Love Story' Cancellations and Renewals Ju Ji-hoon & Choo Young-woo Return To 'The Trauma Code: Heroes On Call' With Seasons 2 & 3 In Production At Netflix Many were shocked when the ax swung last week and it missed Lin’s head, landing on his lieutenant co-head of film, Doug Belgrad. It was seen that Belgrad was an extra layer at the top of Netflix’s film brass that could easily be let go, dollar wise. Lin was expected to be safe until Bajaria’s replacement arrived on Oct. 26, Peter Rice. It was at that point in time that the exec was going to assess the situation. Watch on Deadline All of this boils down to: Netflix, what is it you exactly want? All of streaming has turned into basic cable as we get farther away from Covid. They looked to Lin in April 2024 post Scott Stuber in order to ratchet down the quantity of features and at a lower cost. Lin did exactly what they asked, steering away from overpriced $200M-plus, non downstream features like Red Notice, The Irishman and The Electric State . However, he had a no-nonsense approach to filmmakers. He had no problem reportedly pushing back on prestige content creators like Greta Gerwig and Ben Affleck. During the Lin regime, one source told us that relationships with filmmakers were fraying. Recently, The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth filmmaker David Fincher opted not to renew his longtime exclusive contract with the streamer. During Lin’s run Netflix saw their most viewed movie of all-time, Sony’s Kpop Demon Hunters (325.1M global views). However, that was greenlit under the previous Stuber administration. Lin and Belgrad’s bragging rights include War Machine ($80M production cost, 147M views), animated movie Swapped (144.9M views, which broke into the streamer’s top 10 of all-time), The Rip ($100M production cost, 136M views), Happy Gilmore 2 (135.1M), Apex (129M), Thrash (100M views) and People We Meet on Vacation ($14M production cost, 77.1M). Still there wasn’t a consistent reseeding of the Top 10 Most Popular list like there was during the Stuber era. The Mike and Pam Of It All After being passed over by Skydance for top jobs at the new Paramount Warner Bros. post-merger, we hear that former WB Motion Picture Bosses Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy are in the home stretch this week of finalizing the payout of their WB contracts by David Ellison. Until they’re closed, they can’t entertain any job offers. Those close to De Luca tell us he’d have no problems reporting into Rice if offered the job, however, Netflix would need to make a fire-breathing commitment to theatrical. The notion of a 45-day theatrical window to streaming isn’t a prospect that De Luca (and Abdy) could make to the filmmakers they’ve worked with, i.e. Ryan Coogler, Paul Thomas Anderson, Ridley Scott. The notion that the duo are bound to raise capital for their own feature operation seems like the more practical future for them. All this smoke over De Luca and Abdy heading to Netflix came about due to a friendly lunch with Sarandos. This has morphed into gossip that Sarandos was full-on courting the duo. If Sarandos and Rice bring the filmmaker-friendly duo in, the question is whether they’ll put any guardrails on them. When it came to De Luca and Abdy justifying the lofty costs for Anderson’s One Battle After Another, Coogler’s Sinners, Tom Cruise’s Digger and so on, David Zaslav didn’t blink an eye. Will Sarandos allow them the same greenlight independence he granted Stuber? Or will he expect them to count coins like Lin? Riddle us that, Mr. Sarandos. “Netflix isn’t a place where they talk about film,” says one creator who has worked with them, “They’re all about the process, the algorithm and breaking the code, which still makes Lin a good workhorse for them as he’s also about process.” There’s a rumor out there, and that is despite the notion that De Luca and Abdy are always joined at the hip, historically they haven’t been. Some believe there’s a world that Abdy could entertain an offer sans De Luca from Netflix once her WB contract is paid out. “Sure, there is a world where that could happen,” says one source with knowledge of the situation. Still, there’s no solid definite word out there as to who might fill Lin’s vacancy. No interview process going on as of yet. A rival studio boss complimented over the weekend, “I think you’ll be surprised as to who Peter Rice selects.” But still, no matter how the greenlight process is improved at Netflix, there’s a new sign of the times for the streamer. “If you want to know where the young crowd is looking, Meta just introduced Muse. People are heading back to cinemas, and streaming has become basic cable,” said one Netflix vet, “They can change shuffle as many executives as they want, and it still won’t make a difference.” Sources in the know have confirmed Lin’s firing to us. articles.title: Edward Berger Says Movie Biz “Needed Netflix To Wake Up” But Studios Can Now “Inspire” The Streamer
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Ju Ji-hoon & Choo Young-woo Return To ‘The Trauma Code: Heroes On Call’ With Seasons 2 & 3 In Production At Netflix Rafe Spall On Playing An Amnesiac Super Sleuth In ‘The Death Of Sherlock Holmes’: “This Is A Clean Slate” Hudson Williams, Zach Galifianakis & Jay Baruchel Set For ‘The Assembly’ Season 2 At Canada’s CBC View All October 19, 2026 8:48am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Edward Berger Violeta Sofia The movie business “needed Netflix to wake up”, according to Edward Berger , but the Oscar-winning All Quiet on the Western Front director predicted it could be the Hollywood studios inspiring the streaming service in years to come. Related Stories News Netflix Dismisses Dan Lin As Film Boss Before Peter Rice Arrives Executives Netflix Names Peter Rice As Chief Content Officer Speaking today during a fireside chat at the MIA Market in Rome, Berger offered an assessment of how Netflix, which greenlit Oscar winner All Quiet , had impacted Hollywood with its global streaming model. “The movie business needed Netflix to wake up,” he said. “They needed a real disruptor. They had probably become complacent and thought, ‘Okay, let’s do this because it was successful [before]’.” Netflix last week underwent its largest round of layoffs since 2022 – around 1,000 – incidentally the same year World War II pic All Quiet released. With Paramount and Warner Bros. recently becoming one under the Skydance banner and David Ellison promising to make 30 films a year, the wheel could be turning the other way. Watch on Deadline Berger didn’t comment directly on the market, but noted: “Maybe we are now entering a period where the relationship works the other way around, with Netflix being inspired by the movie business. I think the two worlds are additive.” Berger recalled how Sasha Bühler, Netflix’s Director of Film for German-speaking Europe at the time All Quiet was on the market, gave him a simple assessment of how the streamer would handle the film . “She said, ‘If the movie’s great, we’ll support it. If it’s not, we won’t.’ That’s so scary, but I really love that,” he added. Berger called his experience with All Quiet and Netflix “singularly great, with no stress at all.” He praised the streamer for giving “a considerable amount of money for a German film – money we could not have raised in that environment through local or international sales,” coming just as the Covid-19 outbreak was beginning. “Without that support, we might not have been able to make the movie,” he added. The film ultimately won the Best International Film category at the 2023 Oscars. Bühler, who helmed it for Netflix, exited the streamer in August this year, as we revealed at the time. How an Italian actor changed ‘ Conclave ‘ Conclave director Berger charmed a room of Italian delegates today at the MIA Market with a humorous tale from the set of the Oscar-nominated pic, which filmed in Rome. He and his team were searching for a male Italian actor over the age of 65 who spoke English. “The list was very short,” he recalled to laughs from the room. Sergio Castellitto was recommended to play Cardinal Tedesco, and soon given the role. It quickly became clear that Castellitto’s English was limited, but this led to an unexpected change of direction for the movie. Castellitto began changing lines from English into Italian, and with just days to go before filming, the decision was made to add the language. “We had an all-English cast and Sergio was speaking basically only Italian,” he laughed. Ralph Fiennes, who was leading the cast as Cardinal Thomas Lawrence, then decided he would need to quickly learn Italian, so he could respond naturally. “No one was going to go and say, ‘We’re going to stop the film,'” said Berger. It has been a busy few years for Berger, with another bustling period coming up. We were first with the news that Berger had given the World War Z sequel impetus by being attached as director, with Brad Pitt returning to star. The original film, released in 2013, was based on Max Brooks’ bestselling 2006 novel World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War . Pitt, Dede Gardner and Jeremy Kleiner are producing the sequel on behalf of Plan B Entertainment. Berger will also executive produce. Dennis Kelly will write the script. Berger is also attached to direct the untitled Lance Armstrong movie package starring Austin Butler as the disgraced cyclist, with Apple winning a heated auction . He will also direct Itamar Moses’ Netflix pic Stradivarius . Berger is headlining this year’s MIA Market in Rome alongside the likes of Jane Tranter. The event begins today and runs through October 23. articles.title: Ari Emanuel Pitches Brother Rahm as Centrist Democratic President and Says He Isn’t Too Worried About AI: “It Doesn’t Have Taste”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 17, 2026 1:44pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ari Emanuel Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC/Getty Images Ari Emanuel , TKO Group executive chair and CEO and executive chairman of WME Group , was in London on Saturday to discuss his memoir , entitled Roll the Calls , published by Penguin Random House. And to no one’s surprise, he didn’t hold back, including on issues like AI, politics in the age of Donald Trump — and his brother Rahm’s potential White House run. In a conversation with Tina Brown , former editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair and The New Yorker , which was organized by Intelligence Squared, he also touched on such details as his early days in the CAA mailroom all the way to the super-agent and Hollywood power broker he is today. The title of the event: “An Evening With the Dealmaker Who Reshaped Hollywood.” Related Stories TV 'The Diplomat' U.K. Prime Minister on the Operatic Way He Learned of His "Shocking" Season 4 Storyline TV Patrick Brammall Is Poised to Join the Ranks of Australia's Great Exports Emanuel, who has represented the likes of Larry David, Martin Scorsese and Oprah Win­frey, famously also served as the inspiration for Ari Gold, portrayed by Jeremy Piven, in the TV drama Entourage . Asked about his work as the agent to big names, he said: “What I say to people is: ‘You pay me 10 percent for my opinion. You’ll listen to my opinion. You don’t want to follow it, don’t follow it! Now I have gotten fired for giving my 10 percent. I’m OK with that. I’ve re-signed the people that have fired me, a couple of them, but you’re paying me for my opinion.” Emanuel connected that to the rise of AI. “In this day of AI, that’s more important than anything — your opinion, your taste,” he offered. “AI doesn’t have taste, and taste only comes with time and knowledge of situations.” Curiosity and ideas matter more than ever in the age of AI, he argued. “AI is just an average, a very good average,” Emanuel said. “There is something so important that people are missing here. It is not the answer. Curiosity is important, judgment is important, taste is very important. It has no taste. As much as there are scary things about AI, those are qualities that you own that are only human.” Will AI enhance creativity? “Yeah, it will,” the agent offered. “It will add [for] a great creative mind, such as Marty Scorsese. They will be able to implement taste and creativity. My wife’s a fashion designer. She works with AI, but she’s the one who has the taste, and she’s giving it the ideas.” Brown asked if he was concerned about AI’s “absence of morality.” His take: “It’s something that has to come into it. I’m not sure how,” or how that will be possible without stifling technological opportunities. Which of his many deals of the past gave him the biggest headache? “The hardest deal was probably the UFC deal,” Emanuel told the London crowd. “I had been representing UFC for 25 years. It was on Fox. …. We thought Fox was going to buy it – easy.” Another option, Warner, was downsizing at the time. “So those two were out, and then it was us against the Chinese because they had a lot of money coming into the entertainment space,” the super-agent recalled. “But [UFC boss] Dana [White] didn’t want to go to them, and then all of a sudden something horrible happened. I blame all of you from Britain because you guys didn’t elect the right person at the time. Brexit happened, and the banking system fell apart, and so we had to buy the business [when] the banking system kind of went haywire.” In short, “it was just one headache after another, but we got it done,” he concluded. Emanuel also described UFC and other sports and live experiences as events that can bring a politically divided world together. “I’d rather talk to the other side,” as a Democrat, he said. “Sports is a common ground.” Continuing the talk about politics, Brown asked if MAGA wasn’t “the biggest cult going.” Emanuel replied: “I don’t want to be in MAGA. And I don’t want to be in the DSA [Democratic Socialists of America]. When the moderator suggested that UFC may have become the biggest sport associated with the Trump era, asking if it could last beyond it, Emanuel offered: “Yeah, I think it’s going to outlast me.” The agent didn’t let Brown drag him into speculating about Trump’s political future and future directions. “I talked to him about four weeks ago,” he said. “This Ukraine [policy] thing is upsetting.” And he added: “I think after Congress is back, I’m going to call him because I got some stuff I have to talk to him about. I plan on having a conversation.” Asked about his hopes for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Emanuel said: “Let’s hopefully get the Senate and the House.” He also expressed support for his brother, Rahm Emanuel, as the centrist Democratic candidate in the next presidential election. He said: “All kidding aside, I don’t think there’s a better candidate in the world who could be president and cares more about the world, the United States, helping kids and will fight the fight.” THR

articles.title: ‘The Diplomat’ U.K. Prime Minister on the Operatic Way He Learned of His “Shocking” Season 4 Storyline
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All October 17, 2026 4:11pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Rory Kinnear in 'The Diplomat.' Idris Solomon/Netflix Logo text [The following story contains spoilers from the first four episodes of The Diplomat season four, through “Pagliacci.”] Rory Kinnear couldn’t leave The Diplomat without one more surprise. The actor, who has spent the past four seasons playing wild-card British prime minister Nicol Trowbridge, resigns midway through the Netflix political thriller’s latest season, announcing the move in a shocking moment at the end of episode four. Trowbridge steps down after an unusually surreal episode for The Diplomat , in which he imagines that former adviser Margaret Roylin (Celia Imrie), who dies early in season three, is still alive and chiming in on his latest actions. He also hallucinates that the U.S. officials with whom he’s meeting are laughing at and mocking him and sings an aria as he thinks of himself as both a king and a clown (donning both costumes). Related Stories Business Ari Emanuel Pitches Brother Rahm as Centrist Democratic President and Says He Isn't Too Worried About AI: "It Doesn't Have Taste" TV Patrick Brammall Is Poised to Join the Ranks of Australia's Great Exports Despite the trippy scenes leading up to Kinnear’s final scene, which comes just one episode after viewers learn that U.K. foreign secretary Austin Dennison (David Gyasi) has died in a helicopter crash, Diplomat showrunner Debora Cahn says there were grounded, real-life reasons for this season’s shake-up in the British government. “By the time we got to this season, Rory had been prime minister for a period of time where the actual U.K. had like five different people at 10 Downing Street,” Cahn tells The Hollywood Reporter . “And it felt like there was this essential part of being a diplomat, which is that you’re always learning the cast of characters from scratch. You either outlast the people that you’re working with, or you’re sent to a different country. And I wanted to see our team going through the struggle of just when you think you know where the ground is under your feet, it completely changes. You’ve built all these relationships, and suddenly you have nothing.” Cahn was also interested in showing what it would mean for Keri Russell ‘s American ambassador to the U.K. to no longer have to work with someone like Trowbridge. “I also really wanted to play with the dynamic of like, you think you’re working with somebody who’s difficult and they’re the problem, and then they leave, and it turns out you were the problem or both of you were the problem,” she says. Cahn gave Kinnear a heads-up that his character would be resigning at some point in season four, but the specifics around his departure didn’t emerge until the actor received an unusual request while he was boarding a flight to Lithuania. “I got a message from Deb saying, ‘Do you think you’d be able to sing this?’ And she sent me the aria,” Kinnear recalls. “And I thought, ‘Why on earth would I be required to do that?’ And I said, ‘I think I could, but how did you know I could sing?’ And she said, “Do you remember it? I think it was at the beginning of season two, there was a funeral in St Paul’s Cathedral, and the whole congregation was asked to sing a hymn and I could hear your voice.’ I thought, ‘Interesting.’ And she’d obviously held on to that for two and a half seasons and brought it back. So I thought, ‘OK, how does that fit into why he might be resigning?'” Trowbridge’s resignation is immediately preceded by Russell’s Kate blackmailing him by telling the newly appointed British foreign secretary Robyn Palmer (Abigail Marlowe), as Trowbridge looks on, about Roylin’s involvement in the carrier ship attack that kicked off the series and how Trowbridge “tried to kill” Roylin when he learned what she’d done. The risky move is, unsurprisingly, Hal’s (Rufus Sewell) idea and though Kate initially resists his “mafioso”-like approach to foreign policy, she ends up doing what he suggested. “I just think [Trowbridge] makes her crazy. I think he pushed her buttons,” Russell says of why Kate threatens him after he said, in part, that she and Hal won’t be invited to Dennison’s funeral. “He knew how to get her riled up and make it personal, and it’s too fresh. She’s doing something she doesn’t want to do anyway. She doesn’t believe in it, and then he’s attacking her when she hasn’t processed something.” The shake-up also meant Gyasi and Kinnear would be leaving the Netflix series on which they’d been central castmembers for the past few years, a disappointing development for Cahn and the show’s remaining cast. “We wanted to keep Dave Gyasi and Rory Kinnear forever,” Cahn says. “I wish I could see them every day. It’s a bummer when the company shifts in some way. We’ve had the luxury of bringing a lot of people in, and sometimes the story is ejecting people out on the other end, and it sucks.” Sewell adds that Dennison’s death and Trowbridge resigning are “tremendously shocking.” For Kate, though, Russell says the loss of Dennison, with whom she had a close relationship (the show teased the possibility of a romance early on, culminating in a passionate kiss in season three) is “really hard.” “I think what that does to Kate is really hard, especially at this moment when her morals are being put to the test because he was such a moral character, so I think that fuels all of those doubts,” she says. “And then you have Hal on the other line going, ‘This is what you got to do. You got to do this.’ It’s an enormous loss for the show, for a lot of people who loved him, too. But it’s good storytelling ultimately.” Kinnear, while sad that he won’t get to keep working with his Diplomat colleagues, is confident the bonds he’s forged with them will continue after he’s left the show. And he’d be happy to return in a guest capacity. “I’d be fascinated to see where Trowbridge does end up,” he says. “There are so many different roles that a retired politician finds themselves in, and I’m sure he wouldn’t spend the rest of his life lying low.” Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter , Kinnear opens up about why Trowbridge resigns; how his character feels about Dennison’s death, as the two had a complicated relationship; and the experience of filming his final episode. What was your reaction when you found out that this is what would be unfolding for your character? I got a heads up from Deb that at some point during the series, Trowbridge will be resigning, and I’ve already felt pretty lucky to have stayed on for as long as I have, given the nature of British politics over the last six or seven years. To finally receive the script, to see, as is typical of Debora’s writing, the psychological acuity she was going to bring to it, and how much she wanted to explore his inner life at the point of his greatest crisis. I sort of knew then that it was going to be a real gift for me as as an actor to be able to to bring that to life. How do you feel about about having to leave the show and the people that you were working with for a number of seasons? Well, luckily, when you do a job for as long as this has been — a lot of the time we were hosting our American friends in London, and then luckily they got to return the favor when we were filming in New York — we’re in and out of each other’s lives to such an extent that we knew that we had formed these lifelong friendships. So while it’s obviously sad that I won’t be able to get to go to work with them. I know that I’ll still be able to hang out with them whenever they’re in town or I’m in their town. To have been able to be part of a series that is so smart, so funny, so dramatic, so psychologically aware and so incredibly well-written and -cast is one thing. But to have left with a load of lifelong friends is far too great. What was it like filming that very surreal episode in which Trowbridge resigns, with the Margaret Roylin hallucinations? That’s such a different approach for this show. What was exciting about it was that you knew that it was a new flavor. Shows like this, they constantly have to reinvent themselves or show new aspects of themselves, and a character that has loomed as large as Trowbridge has over the four seasons, to be able to get into what really sort of drives him, what makes him tick and to see what what it meant to him to be prime minister, to see what losing that meant to him, what destruction it wreaked him, and how he thought he might be seen both as a king and as a clown and that he’d sort of straddled both roles in his prime ministership, and that we get to see them played out for for real, as it were, within this kind of wild dream life. We never really get a concrete explanation from Trowbridge about why he resigned. How much do you think Kate’s blackmail threat prompted his resignation? What do you think it was really due to? Well, I mean, I do think that most politicians have a sort of self-awareness about how they how they can present themselves or how they can operate and what constitutes a line in the sand for something they wouldn’t be able to to go on with. And I think knowing how compromised he would be, particularly in his relationship with America, and how complicated he had been with that, with this new information in their hands, I think he knew: There’s nothing I can do without feeling I’ll be limping on. I won’t be able to do it with the gusto that I feel like I’ve been able to operate for as long as he has been prime minister. I also think events catch up with people, and it caught up with him what happened with Roylin and at the very beginning of season one, and sometimes people’s appetite goes for the the hurly burly of politics, and I think everyone knows that you’re a long time retired and resigned once you leave it so you keep on going, keep on going because there’s nothing quite like it in terms of the status that you’re afforded, in terms of the decisions you get to make, in terms of just the day-to-day excitement of it, but when it’s time to to step away, it must be sort of crashingly obvious, and I think that’s why he leaps to resignation. We also find out at the end of the previous episode that Austin Dennison (David Gyasi) has died. How does Trowbridge feel about that? He and Dennison had a complicated relationship. That’s, I think, definitely another reason that pushes him towards the resignation. They had come up together. They had been adversaries together, but they had found a use for each other as well in the highest echelons of politics. So, to have lost Roylin, to then lose Dennison. Those were the good cop and bad cop on his shoulder, or the devil and the angel on his shoulder, throughout his time. So, I think he felt completely settled as to where he would turn. Lydia obviously provides some support, ballast and encouragement, determination for him. But without Dennison and without Roylin, there was there was an instability to how he saw himself. Do you have a favorite memory or scene from playing Nicol Trowbridge in The Diplomat ? Driving up in that Jag outside the big country house, in the first [season], you thought, oh yeah, this is going to be fun. This show’s got something about it. Getting to film in St Paul’s Cathedral, getting to film in all those amazing locations. We’re up in the foreign office, and there were times where you felt — I see why people in the top echelons of power try and cling on because traveling in big motorcades or helicopters, all the ceremony of it, you can see how it can go to people’s heads and become quite addicted. I’ve made sure that I kept my feet on the ground, but you could see, particularly with a Netflix-style budget affording you. I’m sure it’s not all as quite as grand and as glamorous, being prime minister, but it certainly felt it at times. And I always remember turning the corner dressed in full crown and coronation robes and singing an aria straight down the camera, and I don’t think the crew had any idea what was going on or why I was doing that or dressed like that. THR

articles.title: Miley Cyrus Returns to the Stage With Emotional and Cathartic Hollywood Bowl Show
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All October 17, 2026 4:17pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Miley Cyrus performs at the Hollywood Bowl. Kevin Mazur / Getty Images Fans of all ages packed in close at the Hollywood Bowl Friday to witness a rare experience in today’s music landscape: A full-fledged Miley Cyrus solo concert. The 33-year-old pop star, going by just Miley these days, has been open about the tolls that performing live takes on her mental health and wellness. As a result, it’s been a near-decade since her last large-scale world tour, and four years since her last major concert. Even during Friday’s performance, the singer was honest about the fact she wasn’t sure if she’d ever do a show of this scale again, attributing her desire to do these shows in part due to her late godmother, country music icon Dolly Parton, who died earlier this this year. Related Stories Music Harry Styles Debuts Unreleased Song at MSG to Honor Liam Payne on Second Death Anniversary Music Miley Cyrus Tearfully Pays Tribute to Dolly Parton With "Jolene" Performance at Hollywood Bowl: "Me and Dolly, We Are Eternal" “For me, performance can’t be everything because the curtain closes and the lights go down, and I have to go back home and be happy with who I am,” the pop star told the crowd. “I really appreciate you all honoring that and respecting and celebrating and supporting and encouraging me, finding this balance in my life where I can really have everything that I’ve ever wanted.” Dubbed Bass Persuades Live at the Hollywood Bowl, Friday’s concert, the first of two this weekend, was held in support of her latest album Bass Persuades . Her fans have been patiently waiting for the day she’d return — the 1.5 million people that joined the queue for the roughly 36,000 tickets across the two nights are serving as proof. Miley Cyrus performs at the Hollywood Bowl. Kevin Mazur / Getty Images The singer kicked off the night with material from Bass Persuades , unsurprisingly, given the show’s name. She took the stage after one of what would be several pre-recorded, black-and-white videos of the star spoke directly to the crowd. “‘Hello.’ A voice greets me that sounds more like a mirror. ‘Make a record.’ Oh, that’s very specific for an angel,” pre-recorded Cyrus said to the crowd. “You will stand on that same stage held by the people, the sound and the desire that’s carried you all the way to your destiny. And sitting behind you is the rest of your life, but nothing waits forever.” Cyrus reiterated many times that she was grateful to her fans for being understanding about where she’s at in her career. “I didn’t know that if live performance was going to be a part of my future, if this was something that I wanted to dedicate and devote myself to, because that’s what it really is,” she said. “Tonight, it isn’t just the night for us, but it’s all the preparation of everyone that is behind the scenes that you’ll never get to see that make this show possible.” The 18-song set — which included two surprise guests in the form of The Flaming Lips’ frontman Wayne Coyne, a collaborator of the pop star, and her fiance Maxx Morando, another collaborator — included both new and old hits, but the experience was admittedly different for each. Miley Cyrus performs at the Hollywood Bowl. Kevin Mazur / Getty Images Cyrus clearly felt the most passionate about the newer material, belting the words to the songs from Bass Persuades , while tending to let the backtrack and the crowd lead on some of her older hits like “Party in the USA” and “We Can’t Stop.” Her Hannah Montana movie track “The Climb” received one of the biggest reactions of the night, with the entire crowd singing along. Her 2013 hit single “Wrecking Ball” took on a new arrangement for the show, skipping the iconic shift into the chorus. Sure, the hits were lighter on Cyrus’ live vocals, but they were still endlessly enjoyable and emotional for both the singer and the crowd. Cyrus could have stood onstage with a laptop playing music videos, a la Justin Bieber’s Coachella headlining set, and the sold-out crowd, would’ve still likely counted the night as a success. The most emotional moment of the evening came in the form of a tribute to Parton, who Cyrus has often referred to as Aunt Dolly. As the pop star’s godmother, Parton has been close with Cyrus her entire life. The singer broke down in tears speaking about the country music pioneer as the intro to Parton’s iconic song “Jolene” played in the background. She told a story of her experience seeing Parton at the Hollywood Bowl before covering “Jolene.” Later in the show, during “Wrecking Ball,” her Aunt Dolly’s favorite song, she clutched a small photo of Parton in a heart-shaped frame to her chest. Miley Cyrus performs at the Hollywood Bowl. Kevin Mazur / Getty Images Friday’s performance was cathartic for the audience, and clearly for Cyrus, who’s seemingly found the balance for her life as a pop star that she’s been looking for. She told the crowd she was excited to perform at the iconic venue all day, but she’d been equally excited to have acquired a new fish that day. These Hollywood Bowl performances were as much for Cyrus as they were for the crowd. “Being able to create a life that I get to wake up every day and have those joys that give me meaning and purpose — I’m proud to be a person that those kinds of things bring me just as much joy as performing for almost 18,000 people here tonight,” she told the crowd midway through the show. “Being able to live a life in true harmony and have everything that I’ve ever wanted… Every dream that I’ve been able to conjure and make a reality, I’m experiencing here today. October 16th. This is like a new holiday in my life.” She didn’t, of course, forget the fans. “It’s been 20 years of us on this journey, this evolution and this metamorphosis. You all, you have not skipped a beat. I am so, so appreciative of your support,” she said. “It’s been steadfast, and it’s been deeply felt. The appreciation I have for you is never forgotten on show days.” Cyrus, preparing to launch into her 2013 anthem “We Can’t Stop,” finished her speech with more gratitude. “Because of you, I get to have the life that is everything I could have ever imagined. I have love, I have animals, I have all of you, I have music, I have creativity. I have someone else, and I just love my life. It’s the most beautiful. Thank you all for making it that way.” Cyrus returns for the second and final night of Bass Persuades Live at the Hollywood Bowl on Sunday, Oct. 18. THR

articles.title: Gene Schwam, Hollywood Publicist to Elvis Presley, Judy Garland and Julie Andrews, Dies at 96
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 17, 2026 4:35pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Gene Schwam Courtesy of the Schwam family. Gene Schwam, the veteran Hollywood publicist who worked with the likes of Elvis Presley , Judy Garland , Julie Andrews , Barbara Eden and Blake Edwards , has died. He was 96. Schwam died Friday in Los Angeles following a brief illness. In 1954, he was working with fellow publicist Stanley Cowan making $35 per week, when he decided to leave the company and found his own agency. Alongside Adeline Hanson, they opened Hanson & Schwam Public Relations in 1955. The firm began by representing restaurants and musicians, though their roster quickly expanded into the wider entertainment industry. Nancy Wilson and Lou Rawls were among those represented by the agency, which additionally handled publicity for the Cocoanut Grove nightclub. Related Stories Movies Michael Forest, Actor in Roger Corman Movies and 'Star Trek,' Dies at 97 Music Mark Pucci, Longtime Music Publicist and Blues Advocate, Dies at 79 Schwam also worked with Lenny Bruce, Cyd Charisse and Gene Barry. His work with Andrews and Eden were central to his career as a publicist, and he formed a close friendship with Edwards; the publicist character in his 1981 film S.O.B. was inspired by Schwam. He is also the creator of Humanity 101, an initiative of Arizona State University’s Project Humanities that promotes compassion, empathy, forgiveness, integrity, kindness, respect and self-reflection. The veteran publicist reflected on his career in conversation with The Hollywood Reporter ‘s Chris Gardner in April 2021, noting, “There’s a mistake people make when they think it’s about who you know in Hollywood, but it isn’t about that — it’s about who knows you.” He also shared some secrets to success: “Begin with the end of the game and work your way backward,” Schwam said. “Figure out what it is that we want to do, such as win an Oscar, then we figure out how to get there.” Schwam added, “I’ve always felt that success of the personal service business is referrals. It’s not getting on the phone or going online. It’s always been someone saying, ‘Hey, Gene, I have a friend who is writing a book, would you be interested in working with them?’” He is survived by his wife, Myrna Schwam; his daughter, Stephanie Schwam Adams; his stepchildren, Adam London, Greg London and Linda London; and four grandchildren. THR

articles.title: South Africa’s Oscar Entry ‘Variations on a Theme’ Was Written With Microsoft Excel
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 18, 2026 12:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Variations on a Theme' Courtesy of IFFR Ouma Hettie is an octogenarian goat herder in South Africa’s Kamiesberge. When she falls victim to a scam promising reparation for her father’s unpaid service during World War II, her family becomes more involved than she would like them to. Welcome to the world of Variations on a Theme ( Variasies op ‘n Tem ) from writers/directors Devon Delmar and Jason Jacobs ( Carissa ), which won the Tiger Award at this year’s International Film Festival Rotterdam and just screened at the 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival (LFF). Related Stories TV 'The Diplomat' U.K. Prime Minister on the Operatic Way He Learned of His "Shocking" Season 4 Storyline Business Ari Emanuel Pitches Brother Rahm as Centrist Democratic President and Says He Isn't Too Worried About AI: "It Doesn't Have Taste" “A poetic and distinctive visual style infuses playfulness into this insightful study of a woman’s resilience and a community that exists close to the land,” the LFF website said about the film. Delmar, who also edited the film, came to London for LFF snd talked to THR about the musicalness of Variations on a Theme and how it may well be the only movie ever to be written on Microsoft Excel. The film has a rhythmic dance vibe, a sense of an underlying choreography that you just feel while experiencing it – without necessarily being able to explain that feeling. And that is all by design. “It all starts with Jason being a very perceptive and observant person,” Delmar tells THR . “He is from this village you see in the film. He was born there, went to school there, and then came back after living in Cape Town to live with his grandmother.” The duo actually made a short film there a few years ago, ”and I have become part of this community in some way as well,” he explains. And the place has its own pace. “Anyone would be able to observe the routine, the rhythm of this space,” Delmar says. “If you sit in a corner for long enough, you’ll start to notice the routines and the rhythms that occur naturally. ‘Here comes Mr. So and So with his goats when the sun is setting,’ and so on. The routines are very ingrained into the space, and it’s very beautiful to observe the musicality of the space within that rhythm.” That’s also where the title Variations on a Theme comes from. The repetition of everyday life also “harmonized, to use a musical term again, with the awareness that the exploitation that’s happening there in 2026 is merely history repeating itself,” the filmmaker tells THR . “What’s happening with villagers being scammed out of money is exactly what happened in the 1940s to [the protagonist’s] father, who was being exploited by the government at the time, which is exactly what happened to the people who were colonized going back several generations.” Highlights Delmar: “So this idea of repetition became very important to our way of thinking, and then it was very natural to incorporate that into the structure of the film to show this repetition and the cycle of violence, and the daily routines of this woman.” One possibly surprising tool to map out shots for the film to ensure the visual representation of this repetition and cycle was Microsoft Excel. Yeah, really! “I’ve joked that it’s the only film ever, potentially, to be written on Microsoft Excel,” says Delmar. “Because we have five story days, so we has five columns and then 30 shots that repeat like clockwork.” And the filmmaker keeps the surprises coming. “We were borrowing from an Estonian composer called Arvo Pärt,” Delmar explains. He’s the big guy in Tallinn in terms of music, and he wrote music very formulaically. He came up with these almost formulas or equations for his music. He would work on a very small kernel of an idea or a seed, but once he unleashes that little seed, it manifests the most unbelievably beautiful and spiritual music.” That served as an inspiration for Variations on a Theme . “We were interested in how we could contain the film into one core idea, and then almost press play on it and let it unfold,” Delmar explains. “It’s like an origami thing you do, and then a pop-up book appears.” THR

articles.title: ‘What Belongs to Others’ Wins Top Warsaw Film Festival Award
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 18, 2026 2:10am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'What Belongs to Others' Courtesy of Warsaw International Film Festival The 42nd edition of the Warsaw International Film Festival is wrapping up on Sunday after its winners were unveiled during a Saturday night awards ceremony. The top honor, the Warsaw Grand Prix in the international competition of the Polish fest, went to Grzegorz Dębowski for What Belongs to Others . The film follows a Polish burglar who assumes the identity of a dead stranger’s girlfriend, with unexpected results. The jury said it awarded the top honor to the film “for its precise and delicate storytelling, its exceptional performances, and its complex portrait, devoid of judgment, of a flawed and elusive woman who undergoes a transformation as she slips into a stranger’s identity and life, and therein finds the possibility of her own.” Related Stories Movies South Africa's Oscar Entry 'Variations on a Theme' Was Written With Microsoft Excel TV 'The Diplomat' U.K. Prime Minister on the Operatic Way He Learned of His "Shocking" Season 4 Storyline The Warsaw best director award went to Chinese filmmaker Cai Chengjie for Suzhou Quartet , which the jury lauded as “an original and ambitious concept brought to life through striking cinematography and daring experimentation with narrative form.” The “visually captivating and richly layered meditation on life and mortality” tells the story of four people who meet by chance in a small noodle shop, only to find they are long-lost acquaintances. Meanwhile, the Warsaw festival also gave a special jury award to Maria Dębska for her performance in Through the Wall , directed by Maciej Sobieszczański, about two young political prisoners during the Stalinist terror in Poland who fall in love The jury lauded the actress for “a remarkably precise and emotionally truthful portrayal [and] for creating a complex character with great sensitivity and without exaggeration.” It added that the honor is also “for a role that stays with the audience long after the film ends.” Meanwhile, a special jury mention went to Bloody Men , directed by Jens Sjögren, with the jury saying it “captures with remarkable authenticity the chaos caused by domestic violence and the challenges faced by children growing up with a single parent struggling with personal difficulties and making decisions that repeatedly put the entire family’s safety at risk.” Also at Warsaw, the main award in the Competition 1–2 program, dedicated to directors’ first and second fiction features, went to Lorin Terezi’s Agia . “It is rare for a fiction feature debut to feel so complete,” the jury said. “Its structure recalls a Greek tragedy, offering a glimpse into a disappearing world. A subtle story of a young woman rebelling against patriarchal tradition and a world in which family honor is valued above life itself. Agia wants to live on her own terms and make her own decisions.” A special mention in the 1-2 program went to Urša Menart’s Everything That’s Wrong With You , “a touching portrait of a young woman desperately trying to find an honest human connection in a world full of emotional uncertainty, white lies and cheating German boyfriends.” The Warsaw documentary competition saw the award go to Jonas Spriestersbach’s Meanwhile in Namibia , which explores how the German government, instead of paying reparations for its occupation of Namibia in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, offers development cooperation programs. “The director demonstrates an amazing ability to frame reality with extraordinary precision, letting the images slowly unfold and reveal the unsettling and absurd contradictions of human behavior,” the jury said. “The film addresses moral complexity without simple judgments, allowing viewers to construct their own meaning.” María Molina Peiró’s Like Any Other Mortal received a special mention in the doc program. articles.title: ‘Imperium,’ ‘Concrete Land’ and ‘9 Temples to Heaven’ Win BFI London Film Festival Awards
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 18, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Imperium' Courtesy of BFI London Film Festival The 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival (LFF) is wrapping up Sunday night with the U.K. premiere of Jesse Eisenberg ’s star-studded The Debut , following the afternoon unveiling of this year’s award winners. The 2026 honors were led by Sergei Loznitsa ‘s Imperium , which won the best film award in the official competition, and Asmahan Bkerat’s Concrete Land , which was named the winner of the Grierson Award in the LFF documentary competition. Imperium brings together Italian footage from the early 1970s that was shot across what was then the USSR. The result is a look at the diversity of the country in contrast with official Soviet portrayals and productions from the same era. Related Stories Movies South Africa's Oscar Entry 'Variations on a Theme' Was Written With Microsoft Excel TV 'The Diplomat' U.K. Prime Minister on the Operatic Way He Learned of His "Shocking" Season 4 Storyline “ Imperium is an extraordinary film that explores the Soviet Union in the early 1970s from a rich archive with a wide-ranging perspective that looks at life in a country with an extraordinary social and cultural landscape that has rarely been seen,” the LFF jury said. “The film is richly evocative and emotionally engaging on all levels, giving us a visually arresting perspective of life before the Soviet Union was broken apart.” Palestinian-Jordanian director Bkerat’s Concrete Land tells the story of a Palestinian Bedouin family displaced in Jordan. The young filmmaker told THR in a recent interview that the family featured in the film helped her discover her love for documentary filmmaking. ‘Concrete Land’ Courtesy of Asmahan Bkerat “This was a beautifully observed portrait filmed with mastery and confidence,” highlighted the LFF jury. “In image creation, sound design, scene building and, most importantly, the deep and trusting relationship with the films’ characters, the filmmaker proved themselves a worthy recipient of the Grierson award. It takes a tremendous cinematic skill and maturity to bring the audience to feel so close to each and every character of this remarkable family, across generations and in a very different part of the world, yet the warmth we feel for each is profound. In a noisy and often polemical world, it was refreshing, humbling and deeply relevant to see the quiet resilience and dignity of this family in the face of the erasure of their culture and traditions. This is filmmaking which never gets in the way of itself and will surely take its place in the annals of observational greats.” A special mention in the doc competition was awarded to Queer Edward II from director Theo Rollason , who recently discussed their archival look behind the scenes of Derek Jarman’s Edward II film set, against the backdrop of anti-LGBTQIA+ legislation in 1980s Britain, with THR . “This was a spirited and tightly constructed portrait of Jarman as both an artist and an activist,” the jury noted. “Along with the luscious making-of footage, the integration of wider political archive was skilfully and heart-fully done, making it a fitting and timely tribute to Jarman in its defiant call for tolerance and against prejudice.” Meanwhile, 9 Temples to Heaven , directed by Sompot Chidgasornpongse, won the Sutherland Award in the first feature competition. In the road movie, which is Thailand’s international Oscar feature film submission, a prophecy prompts an aging grandmother to embark on a nine-temple pilgrimage with her children and grandchildren. “An accomplished first feature paving his own path in the well-established tradition of filmmaking in the Southeast Asian region,” said the jury about the winning project. “The film is visually outstanding, spiritual, and meditative, where a story about life and death transcends borders and generations.” ‘9 Temples to Heaven’ Cannes A special mention in the first feature program went to Bertil Nilsson’s MASC , following Robin as he moves through temporary jobs and tentative relationships in search of a place to belong. The jury called the filmmaker “a strikingly original new voice in British cinema, using innovative storytelling, notable performances, and artistically crafted scenes. We were impressed by Bertil’s highly unique concept coupled with capable new talent and a humorous script.” Finally, Aman , from director Rahul Roye, received the Short Film Award in the LFF short film competition. It follows a trans man whose journey takes an unexpected turn on the eve of his gender-affirming surgery, when he discovers that he is pregnant. “We were deeply impressed by Aman ’s accomplished filmmaking, tackling knotty themes through authentic and nuanced characters we felt compelled to follow,” shared the LFF jury. “We were struck by the film’s painterly cinematography and expansive and assured storytelling, which guided us through the world with care. Aman ’s finely drawn narrative is made all the more engrossing by the film’s refusal to provide easy answers to the complexities it presents us with.” ‘Aman’ Elizabeth Hobbs’ Daughters of the Late Colonel received the short film special mention. The film sees two middle-aged sisters finding themselves at a loss after the death of their ill-tempered and controlling father. Said the Short Film Competition jury: “We would like to give a special mention to Daughters of the Late Colonel for its singular and inventive visual style, and its deft balance of humor, pathos and provocation.” Voting for the LFF Audience Awards closes on Wednesday. articles.title: James McAvoy Says ‘Split’ Is The Only Film That ‘Really Consistently Pays Me’
articles.full_text: Oct 17, 2026 4:21pm PT James McAvoy Says ‘Split’ Is The Only Film That ‘Really Consistently Pays Me’ By Payton Turkeltaub Plus Icon Payton Turkeltaub Latest Quentin Tarantino Confirms He’s ‘Written a Script’ for His Tenth Film, But Won’t Pursue It Yet Because He Wants to ‘Live a Little’ 13 hours ago James McAvoy Says ‘Split’ Is The Only Film That ‘Really Consistently Pays Me’ 14 hours ago ‘Musk’ TikTok Ad Account Permanently Suspended Ahead of Documentary’s Wide Release 19 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source ©Universal/courtesy Everett / Everett Collection James McAvoy has starred in films including “Speak No Evil,” “Atonement” and “X-Men: First Class,” but he recently revealed the “only” film he still consistently receives residuals from is M. Night Shyamalan’s 2016 horror “ Split .” “You get the odd check for, you know, a couple 100 quid here or sometimes you get checks for, like, 25 cents and you’re like, ‘It literally costs more to post this than it did for me to cash it,’” McAvoy said during a recent episode of the Happy Sad Confused podcast. “But the only one that really consistently pays me is ‘Split.’” “I think it was made for like $6 million or something like that? And let’s say they spent 30 advertising it. In our first weekend, we made 40, so we were in profit,” McAvoy continued. “Our first residual check came at the end of the first weekend. It was bonkers.” Popular on Variety In “Split,” three girls are kidnapped by a man with a diagnosed 23 distinct personalities (McAvoy). “They must try to escape before the apparent emergence of a frightful new 24th,” per the film’s official description. Anya Taylor-Joy, Haley Lu Richardson and Jessica Sula starred alongside McAvoy. The film, which cost just $6 million to make, went on to gross $138.29 million domestically and $140.16 million internationally for a $278.45 million worldwide total. McAvoy also spoke about Shyamalan and his experience working with the director. “I very consciously took from many of the directors that I worked with, and subconsciously as well, but the thing I took away from him is his preparedness,” McAvoy said. “He made that film, and [sequel] ‘Glass,’ on incredibly modest budgets, and very focused on how he would maximize his day and maximize his shots and maximize what he got out of the story by just being incredibly well-prepared and being able to share that and communicate that with the crew.” ‘Beast in Me’ Renewed for Season 2 With Claire Danes Returning Produced by J.A. articles.title: Quentin Tarantino Confirms He’s ‘Written a Script’ for His Tenth Film, But Won’t Pursue It Yet Because He Wants to ‘Live a Little’
articles.full_text: Oct 17, 2026 4:59pm PT Quentin Tarantino Confirms He’s ‘Written a Script’ for His Tenth Film, But Won’t Pursue It Yet Because He Wants to ‘Live a Little’ By Payton Turkeltaub Plus Icon Payton Turkeltaub Latest Quentin Tarantino Confirms He’s ‘Written a Script’ for His Tenth Film, But Won’t Pursue It Yet Because He Wants to ‘Live a Little’ 13 hours ago James McAvoy Says ‘Split’ Is The Only Film That ‘Really Consistently Pays Me’ 14 hours ago ‘Musk’ TikTok Ad Account Permanently Suspended Ahead of Documentary’s Wide Release 18 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images Quentin Tarantino has long said he’ll be retiring after his tenth feature film, but fans shouldn’t worry yet. While the “Pulp Fiction” director confirmed he’d finished penning the script for his final project, he won’t be getting much further with it until his newly opened play, “The Popinjay Cavalier,” closes. Tarantino made the statement on a recent episode of “The Graham Norton Show,” where he joined the host alongside fellow guests Ellen DeGeneres, Colin Farrell and Gemma Chan. It was his first appearance on the show in more than a decade. “I’ve written a script that I really like, but I want to do the play and see who I am; then I’ll then go back and spend time with my family and live a little and then see what I want to do,” Tarantino said. Popular on Variety He also gave audiences more insight into “The Popinjay Cavalier,” which he said started as a screenplay before the director realized “it really worked as a play.” “I think it will be thrilling,” he said. Starring Sacha Baron Cohen, “The Popinjay Cavalier” will open at London’s Phoenix Theatre next March, following previews in late Feb. The play, described as a “swashbuckling comedy,” is set to run for three months, closing on June 13. “I’m keen with anticipation to give the West End a great night out,” Tarantino said in a statement when the show was announced. Tarantino’s most recent release remains “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which came out in 2019 and starred Brad Pitt, Leonardo DiCaprio, Margot Robbie, Margaret Qualley and more. Pitt won the Oscar for best supporting actor that year, as did Barbara Ling and Nancy Haigh for best production design.
