articles.title: Ryan Gosling’s Zero-G Stunts on ‘Project Hail Mary’ Broken Down by the Space Epic’s VFX Supervisors
articles.full_text: Oct 18, 2026 12:28am PT Ryan Gosling’s Zero-G Stunts on ‘Project Hail Mary’ Broken Down by the Space Epic’s VFX Supervisors Oscar-winning supervisor Paul Lambert and co-supervisor Mag Sarnowska also talked at Turin’s View Conference about how ESA star maps, Greig Fraser’s cinematography and puppetry shaped the Ryan Gosling space epic By Davide Abbatescianni Plus Icon Davide Abbatescianni Latest ‘The Angry Birds Movie 3’ Unpacked by VFX Supervisor, Including Red’s Redesign and Character-Effects Automation: ’He’s Similar by Choice’ 23 hours ago ‘Toy Story 5’ Co-Director Kenna Harris on Going From Jessie Superfan to Pixar Filmmaker — and the Two-Week Rewrite That Reshaped the Sequel 2 days ago ‘The Mandalorian and Grogu’ VFX Veteran Hal Hickel on Rotta’s Redesign, Phil Tippett and Jon Favreau’s ‘Less James Bond, More Jackass’ Approach 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ryan Goslng's zero-G stunts in 'Project Hail Mary' explained at View Conference, Oct. 16, 2026 Courtesy of View Conference For Oscar-winning VFX supervisor Paul Lambert Lambert, of all the huge challenges presented by Ryan Gosling space epic “ Project Hail Mary ,” the most daunting was creating convincing zero gravity. “Zero-G was probably my personal biggest concern going into the movie,” he said at View Conference in Turin, Italy, drilling down on its VFX. “We tried very hard to convince the production to use the vomit comet,” he added, referring to aircraft maneuvers that briefly generate weightlessness. But the spacecraft sets were too elaborate to recreate onboard, so Gosling performed on wire rigs, including a rotating harness. Removing the wires was only the beginning. When a suspended body still appeared to be hanging rather than floating, VFX artists adjusted the position of Gosling’s legs, arms or torso and added drifting objects to reinforce the illusion. Lambert said the actor was committed to performing his own stunt work, including demanding spacewalk material. Popular on Variety Other experiments were deliberately hands-on. Fraser used an infrared-modified camera, programmable IR lights and water running in front of the lens to develop some of the film’s stranger imagery. “It was literally a mad science lab,” Lambert recalled. Burning fireballs, liquids, lasers and ferrofluid were also filmed to provide starting points for the microscopic effects. The DP returned during postproduction to work with ILM’s Helios virtual-camera system on the sequence near Adrian. Artists tracked Gosling’s on-set performance and recreated it within digital environments, allowing Fraser to choose new camera positions without discarding the original acting. Across those techniques, the supervisors’ ambition remained consistent: to make even the most elaborate effects obey a recognizable physical logic while ensuring Rocky felt as present beside Gosling as any human scene partner. The visual effects team behind “Project Hail Mary” started its journey through space, however, by making an unexpected discovery: much of the sky would look surprisingly familiar. Rather than fill Ryan Gosling’s interstellar adventure with colorful nebulae, Lambert and co-supervisor Mag Sarnowska used astronomical data, practical puppetry and carefully controlled cinematography to keep its science-fiction imagery grounded in reality. “We had visions of all these beautiful nebulae, but in the end, the skies were pretty much as we see them today, from Earth,” Lambert told View Conference in Turin on Friday, describing research conducted for directors Phil Lord and Christopher Miller ’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s novel. The team drew on data from the European Space Agency’s Gaia mission to map the stars between Earth and Tau Ceti, some 11.9 light-years away, while studying NASA footage and raw images from the International Space Station to establish how cameras behave in orbit. Exposure became a guiding principle. “If you were to take a movie camera up to space and try to shoot something, you wouldn’t see the stars,” Lambert explained. Near the brightly illuminated planet Adrian, background stars were therefore largely absent. Farther from Tau Ceti, where the light was weaker, a hypothetical high-sensitivity camera could reveal them. “Rather than simply choosing when to show stars with dramatic effects, we wanted their visibility to follow the actual lighting and exposure conditions,” Lambert said. DP Greig Fraser extended that philosophy into the film’s texture. Digitally captured footage was printed onto Kodak film and scanned back: 5254, with silver retention, for a relatively smooth, subdued Earth, and grainier 5203 for space. Two months of virtual-production exploration before filming also allowed Fraser and the directors to test lighting, camera movements and the scale of spacecraft interiors. Rather than dictate final shots, those sessions let the filmmakers experiment with digital environments and camera positions early, with the resulting camera data helping guide the physical shoot and subsequent VFX work. Rocky, the alien companion performed by James Ortiz and a team of puppeteers, posed a different problem: making a physically present character indistinguishable from his digital counterpart. Sarnowska described three practical versions, including an animatronic and a smaller reference puppet. Framestore scanned the physical creation and studied hours of performance footage, reproducing the puppeteers’ movement when the cramped spaceship sets made practical operation impossible. “Our full CG Rocky got really good at mimicking the puppeteers,” Sarnowska said. “In the end, half of the Rocky shots were puppet and the other half CG.” She added that the team sometimes struggled to distinguish the versions during internal reviews. The effects crew also rebuilt Rocky’s transparent xenonite barriers digitally to remove reflections, hide operators and maintain the complicated play of light through the set. For Rocky’s sonar-based point of view, the filmmakers also experimented with printing the images onto different film formats, ultimately using 10mm and 16mm for selected shots to give them a more organic texture, to bring a larger credibility to a moving tale of interstellar friendship which proved one of this year’s box office hits. articles.title: Roger Deakins on Instinct, Experience and Not Knowing What Is a Cinematographer: ‘I Still Can’t Answer That’
articles.full_text: Oct 18, 2026 1:38am PT Roger Deakins on Instinct, Experience and Not Knowing What Is a Cinematographer: ‘I Still Can’t Answer That’ By Callum McLennan Plus Icon Callum McLennan Latest Roger Deakins on Instinct, Experience and Not Knowing What Is a Cinematographer: ‘I Still Can’t Answer That’ 4 hours ago A Cyclops on Strings and Samantha Morton Reshaping Faces by Hand: How Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ Made Its Monsters Real 5 days ago Sony Pictures Imageworks’ Michelle Grady and ILM’s Janet Lewin on Bad Bosses and Changing Studio Culture: ‘Culture Is What You Tolerate’ 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Roger Deakins Courtesy of Lionsgate Walking through Turin with his wife and creative partner James Ellis Deakins, Roger Deakins found himself thinking about Giorgio de Chirico. The Italian painter, one of his favorites, had drawn inspiration from the city’s vast squares, long arcades and unusual arrangements of light and shadow. Deakins was noticing the relationship for himself. It’s characteristic of a man who has spent much of his life looking at the world, yet remains somewhat at a loss to explain precisely how he sees it. “Somebody asked the other day, what is a cinematographer? I mean, I still can’t answer that,” he says. Popular on Variety It’s an uncommon admission from someone whose images have helped define contemporary cinema, from “No Country for Old Men” to “Blade Runner 2049” and “1917.” But for Deakins, the work is too dependent on the circumstances of a story, and the people telling it, to be reduced to any one method. “It’s your emotional reaction to things that’s important,” he says. Technical considerations can be discussed, but the decisions that shape an image ultimately arise from something inexplicable. Perhaps his relationship with looking began as something more personal. As a young man, Deakins, born in the southern English resort of Torquay, discovered that the camera offered a kind of confidence, a way of approaching a world in which he hadn’t always felt comfortable. “I was kind of hiding behind the camera to a certain degree,” he recalls. “I had confidence because there was something between me and reality.” He could scarcely have imagined where that camera would take him. Only in retrospect has he come to appreciate the significance of experiences whose importance wasn’t apparent at the time. “If you don’t experience things, then what have you got to contribute?” It’s a conviction he shares with Ellis Deakins, his wife and essential collaborator on every project since they met on Michael Apted’s “Thunderheart.” For her, experience gives a filmmaker more than a collection of visual references. It provides different ways of understanding the people and specifics of a story. “If you’re going to tell a story, having had many different experiences gives you many different points of view,” she says. “You’re able to actually add more to the story.” Deakins worries that cinema can become too inward-looking, with filmmakers drawing inspiration primarily from other films. “I rarely, if ever, do that,” he says of referencing earlier movies. “You bring all the things that you experienced in your life to something.” Their Team Deakins podcast often explores the myriad routes people have taken into filmmaking. There is no repeatable path, just as there is no formula for a good image. James encourages the aspiring to experiment, examine their photographs and footage, and ask themselves why something works or doesn’t. It’s how they develop an eye, or what Roger calls a personal sensibility. Deakins, however, is less inclined to analyze his own. When asked about the relationship of shapes and forms in his still photography, he struggles to explain what draws him to a composition. He tends to see the whole image, he says, rather than its individual elements. Ellis Deakins is more definite. Looking at his photographs, she notices how shapes intersect and contrast. “You may not be aware of it, but you are interconnecting shapes,” she tells him. “But I know it’s instinctual.” The distinction between conscious intention and instinct becomes more intriguing when we discuss Andrew Dominik ’s “The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford.” Much of the film contrasts light and dark, yet the scene depicting Robert Ford’s murder takes place in a bar housed in a tent, surrounded by snow, its interior swathed in flat, even light. The violence, and Casey Affleck’s Robert Ford, seem jarringly exposed. Was the contrast deliberate? Deakins considers the question. The appearance arose partly from the circumstances of the set: the tent, the snow outside, the whiteness of the surroundings. Whether the scene had been staged there for its visual effect or because of its historical circumstances, he cannot entirely say. But there were choices to be made. They could have introduced stronger shadows, allowing the light to fall on only part of the tent. Instead, they chose to preserve the evenness of the illumination. “I think it was a very conscious decision to have almost a sort of documentary feel about it, as opposed to the rest of the film.” He thinks the scene is stronger for it. How much is planned varies from one director to the next. With Sam Mendes on “Jarhead,” he worked largely handheld, responding to actors as they performed. With Joel and Ethan Coen, the process was often meticulously planned. Different ways, he suggests, of reaching the same place. The common concern is what matters in the scene, and where the audience should be as that part of the story unfolds. For James, that requires entering someone else’s imagination. She recalls her early work as a script supervisor, when understanding what a director wanted meant learning to see through another person’s eyes. It is a reminder that, however personal Deakins’ instincts may be, the images are not made in isolation. His way of seeing must always attempt to meet the director’s vision, the actors’ performances and the needs of the film. Harrison Ford once described what it feels like to work with Deakins. Discussing “Blade Runner 2049” alongside Ryan Gosling, Ford observed that Deakins’ approach to lighting proceeds from the story, leaving an actor feeling supported. It’s a quality Deakins himself describes as the product of collaboration. He particularly misses the intimacy of operating a camera with a director standing beside him, rather than watching from a monitor elsewhere. After a take, the director might turn and ask, “How was that for you?” “Then there was that sense of trust,” he remembers. He misses, he says, that “intense collaboration and trust.” He and Ellis Deakins are careful to distinguish digital technology from the working habits it can encourage. They have always embraced whatever technology best serves the storytelling, and have a long and fruitful history of shooting digitally. But Roger remembers the particular discipline of working on low-budget film productions, when stock and time were precious and rolling the camera was consequential. “You kind of had to figure out what was the essence of the scene and what was the shot that was going to give you that.” Finding the essence of a scene does not always mean moving closer or showing more. Ellis Deakins points out that holding back from an actor can itself create a feeling, leaving the audience uneasy because they want a closer view. Deakins recalls admiring Andrei Tarkovsky’s long takes. “They would hold shots, and the shot would become something else. It would be saying something else.” He finds another kind of patience in his still photography, where a single image can hold the viewer’s attention indefinitely. And he has spent a lifetime fishing. A couple of days before our conversation, he had been out in his boat off the Devon coast catching mackerel. Enough for supper, anyway. “You never know what might happen,” he says, “and you’ve got to sort of change your approach constantly to adapt to the sort of tide and the weather and the way the fish are running.” He acknowledges the parallels with filmmaking, without wanting to make too much of them. Both involve waiting, observation and a willingness to respond to the world as it is rather than impose a fixed plan. At View Conference in Turin, I later spot the partners attending a number of technical talks themselves. For all their insistence that filmmaking depends on instinct and experience rather than formulas, they remain curious about what others are making and discovering. There is something fitting about seeing Deakins, whose work is so often studied and dissected by others, sitting among the audience, still looking and listening. During our conversation, he had recalled a remark by the photographer Raymond Depardon: if he knew how to take a good photograph, every photograph he took would be good. I had also mentioned “Moby-Dick,” the novel Deakins chose to take to the island on a recent episode of “Desert Island Discs.” Did he identify more with Ishmael, the observer, or Captain Ahab, the obsessive pursuer? “I’m definitely Ahab,” he replied. “Isn’t Ahab the captain?” Ellis Deakins asked. “Yeah, he goes down with a whale.” “A crazy captain,” she said. “Searching for something he doesn’t really understand, fighting something he doesn’t really understand,” Deakins replied. “I’ve always felt an affinity with Ahab for sure.” Netflix Says 67% of Surveyed Members Want to Visit Korea as Busan’s Creative Asia Puts Locations in Focus What’s New on Netflix in October 2026 ‘Bridgerton’ Spinoff, Centered on Lady Violet, Ordered by Netflix Netflix Lays Off 6% of Employees, Eliminating About 1,000 Jobs in Biggest Cutbacks to Date Madrid’s Iberseries & Platino Industria Pivots Toward More B2B Activities Where the Hot Button Issues of AI and Microdramas Also Take Center Stage Netflix Film VP Doug Belgrad Is Out Amid Layoffs Loading comments...

articles.title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Weekend Update Takes Jab at Shane Gillis: ‘You Stupid F—ing C—’
articles.full_text: Oct 18, 2026 1:45am PT ‘SNL U.K.’ Weekend Update Takes Jab at Shane Gillis: ‘You Stupid F—ing C—’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest ‘SNL U.K.’ Weekend Update Takes Jab at Shane Gillis: ‘You Stupid F—ing C—’ 4 hours ago ‘I Play Rocky’ Surprise Screens at London Film Festival 2 days ago Russell Brand Trial: Second Woman Alleges He Was a ‘Wild-Eyed Maniac’ as He Tried to Pull Her Into Bathroom 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Screenshot courtesy Sky/SNL UK “SNL U.K.” didn’t hold back from criticizing its American counterpart on Saturday night’s Weekend Update, roasting Shane Gillis ‘ controversial hosting appearance. After cracking jokes about everything from U.S. President Donald Trump’s recently fired press secretary to ridiculous claims that King Charles might be Muslim, co-host Ania Magliano turned her attention to Gillis. The comedian caused quite the stir last weekend for making misogynistic comments in his opening monologue as well as dropping the f-bomb live on air, which is not allowed per NBC guidelines. “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” Gillis said during his monologue. “You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial bait-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look! You’re not allowed to look.” Popular on Variety Magliano riffed on this by saying: “A ride operator at Munich Oktoberfest was praised for giving out free cycling shorts to female riders. Wearing the gym shorts will protect women from being upskirted, but it does make them vulnerable to something much worse.” A photo of Gillis during his monologue then appeared on screen, sparking laughter from the live audience. Magliano then took aim at Gillis’ accidental f-bomb, subtly pointing out the fact that “SNL U.K.” is allowed to swear on air. “Last week on ‘SNL,’ comedian Shane Gillis also caused controversy by dropping the f-bomb,” she said. “Oh, Shane. You’re not allowed to say that, you stupid fucking cunt.” Watch the full clip below. articles.title: James Austin Johnson’s Trump Stops by ‘SNL U.K.’ for Meeting With Burnham and Zelenskyy: ‘You Don’t Have One Guy Who Can Play Trump?’
articles.full_text: Oct 18, 2026 2:23am PT James Austin Johnson’s Trump Stops by ‘SNL U.K.’ for Meeting With Burnham and Zelenskyy: ‘You Don’t Have One Guy Who Can Play Trump?’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest ‘SNL U.K.’ Weekend Update Takes Jab at Shane Gillis: ‘You Stupid F—ing C—’ 4 hours ago ‘I Play Rocky’ Surprise Screens at London Film Festival 2 days ago Russell Brand Trial: Second Woman Alleges He Was a ‘Wild-Eyed Maniac’ as He Tried to Pull Her Into Bathroom 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Screenshot courtesy Sky/SNL UK Donald Trump made his first appearance on “ SNL U.K.,” courtesy of “SNL” cast member James Austin Johnson . Saturday night’s cold open recreated U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham (George Fouracres) meeting with Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy (Freddie Meredith) to reaffirm Britain’s support in their war with Russia. “We need America to restore the Starlink internet. Without it, we are vulnerable to drone strikes,” Meredith’s Zelenskyy said. “Also, it is very difficult to stream ‘Celebrity Traitors.’ I’m very behind, no spoilers, but I think Richard E. Grant is going to go all the way.” Replied Fouracres as Burnham, “Well, I can promise you now that I’ll raise all of this with President Trump at the first opportunity.” Popular on Variety Johnson then appeared with his spot-on Trump impression, marking the first crossover between the “SNL U.K.” and “SNL” casts. “Did somebody say Richard E. Grant?” he said. “President Trump?!” Fouracres’ Burnham exclaimed. “That’s right, you say my name and I appear,” Johnson’s Trump sad. “I got the idea from my very close friend Beetlejuice, the late, great Beetlejuice. It’s one of the two ways I am like him, the other is sex pest — alleged, they can’t prove he did that stuff.” When asked why he’s in the U.K., Johnson as Trump said he’s been in town “to see my favorite comedian” who is “performing live at high court in the role of defendant,” referencing the Russell Brand trial. Johnson’s Trump then explained that he is hoping to do a job swap with Burnham. “I take over the U.K., you take over America,” he said. “I tell ya, that place is a real mess, you’re going to hate it. It’s an awful, awful job. It’s a terrible place full of disgusting people, I don’t know what the hell happened. C’mon, job swap with me!” Fouracres as Burnham replied, “I can’t swap jobs with you now, cocker! I’ve barely gotten started. People don’t even hate me yet!” Johnson’s Trump then went on a rant about things he could fix in Britain, including that M&S have too many variations of Percy Pigs. “And how about British comedy, folks? What a bad situation, it’s not doing well,” he continued. “‘SNL U.K.,’ you’re telling me you don’t have a guy — the whole cast, you don’t have one guy who can play Trump? What an awful situation. Some of these people went to RADA! What is that, the Royal Academy of Dogshit Actors? Ooh, you can say shit on this one! That felt really good.” Johnson as Trump finally gave up on the job swap, saying: “Fine, I’ll go home. And Zelenskyy, let me know if you need anything, anything at all. Provided it’s not help with war.” Added Fouracres as Burnham, “Sorry Zelenskyy, me old mocker. But as dire as things might be, what matters most is that we all be nice to this insane man.” Watch the full sketch below. articles.title: Sergei Loznitsa’s ‘Imperium’ Wins Best Film at BFI London Film Festival
articles.full_text: Oct 18, 2026 6:00am PT Sergei Loznitsa’s ‘Imperium’ Wins Best Film at BFI London Film Festival ‘9 Temples to Heaven,’ ‘Concrete Land’ and ‘Aman’ also take top prizes as the festival wraps its 70th edition. By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Mahershala Ali Cries Recalling ‘Moonlight’ Scene, Keeps Quiet on ‘Spider-Verse’ at London Talk: ‘I’ve Got to Be Careful’ 23 hours ago ‘Renoir’ Producers Join Asia-Europe Co-Production Panel at Tokyo Market as Japanese Accelerator Atmovie Global Track Partners With Ties That Bind 1 day ago Indonesian Zombie Franchise ‘Zona Merah: Dead City’ Unveils Teaser, Takes Outbreak Into the City 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim Sergei Loznitsa’s “Imperium,” which revisits the Soviet Union of the early 1970s through footage shot by Italian cameramen, has won the best film award at the 70th BFI London Film Festival competition. The prizes were unveiled Sunday as the festival drew to a close. The competition jury was led by filmmaker Sam Pollard, whose credits include “MLK/FBI” and “Citizen Ashe,” and also featured “Life of Jorge Luis Borges” filmmaker Mariano Llinás and DDA chief strategy officer Julie La Bassiere. “The film is richly evocative and emotionally engaging on all levels giving us a visually arresting perspective of life before the Soviet Union was broken apart,” the jury said. Popular on Variety In the first feature competition, the Sutherland Award went to Thailand’s Oscar submission “9 Temples to Heaven,” the first fiction feature from Sompot Chidgasornpongse. The film reflects on faith, kinship and the passage from life to death. Actor Amir El-Masry (“Giant,” “Limbo”) presided over that jury, joined by “Moonglow” producer Alemberg Ang and sales, distribution and awards strategist Rosa Bosch. “An accomplished first feature paving his own path in the well-established tradition of filmmaking in the Southeast Asian region,” the jury said. Bertil Nilsson’s “Masc” received a special mention in the same section. The debut tracks Robin, who drifts between short-term jobs and uncertain relationships while looking for somewhere he fits. The jury singled out Nilsson as a fresh British talent with an unusual concept and a funny script. The Grierson Award for documentary went to Asmahan Bkerat’s feature directorial debut “Concrete Land,” which spends time with several generations of a mixed-race family in Jordan as they resist displacement and hostility. “Santosh” director Sandhya Suri headed the documentary jury, alongside Melbourne International Film Festival senior programmer Kate Fitzpatrick and BAFTA and Emmy-winning producer Andee Ryder. “In a noisy and often polemical world it was refreshing, humbling and deeply relevant to see the quiet resilience and dignity of this family in the face of the erasure of their culture and traditions,” the jury said. Theo Rollason’s “Queer Edward II,” assembled entirely from archive material, earned a special mention. It goes behind the scenes of Derek Jarman’s “Edward II,” set against the anti-LGBTQIA+ laws Britain passed in the 1980s, and the jury praised it as a portrait of Jarman the artist and Jarman the activist. Rahul Roye’s “Aman” won the Short Film Award. The film centers on a trans man who learns he is pregnant the night before his gender-affirming surgery, upending his sense of who he is as a man and as a father. It is streaming free on BFI Player until Oct. 25. Writer-producer Helen Simmons (“100 Nights of Hero”) led the shorts jury, which also included comedian Leo Reich and script editor Jack Casey. “We were struck by the film’s painterly cinematography, and expansive and assured storytelling, which guided us through the world with care,” the jury said. Elizabeth Hobbs’ “Daughters of the Late Colonel,” about two middle-aged sisters left adrift after the death of their domineering father, took a special mention for its inventive visual style. Audience voting for the festival’s best feature film and best British discovery prizes closes Oct. 21, with winners to be named later. articles.title: Michael Forest Dies: Actor In Roger Corman B-Movies, ‘Star Trek’s Apollo Was 97
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Suspends Val Chmerkovskiy For TikTok Referencing Will Smith Oscar Moment; Dancer Responds, “Instinct Was To Defend My Wife” Miley Cyrus Tearfully Remembers Dolly Parton At Hollywood Bowl Concert, Performs ‘Jolene’ Harry Styles Pays Tribute To Liam Payne With New Song At Madison Square Garden Concert View All October 17, 2026 6:42am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Forest in 'Ski Troop Attack' (1960) Getty Michael Forest , a prolific and longtime character actor who appeared in the B movies of Roger Corman, lent his voice to numerous anime projects and guest starred in scores of TV series from The Adventures of Rin Tin Tin, The Twilight Zone and The Dick Van Dyke Show to Silk Stalkings, daytime soaps and a memorably outsized role on Star Trek , died October 14. He was 97. Sparks most recently resided at an assisted living facility in Sparks, Nevada. His death was announced on Facebook by his friend James A. Brown. Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries Obituaries Bernie Orenstein Dies: Writer-Producer On ‘Sanford & Son,’ ‘That Girl,’ ‘Kate & Allie’ & More Was 95 Among the actor’s numerous TV roles was a favorite among Star Trek fans: Forest played the giant Greek god Apollo in the memorable 1967 episode “Who Mourns for Adonais?” Watch on Deadline Other notable TV roles include a former boyfriend of The Dick Van Dyke Show ‘s Laura Petrie (Mary Tyler Moore) who gets set up for a date with Rose Marie’s ever-single Sally Rogers (Laura doesn’t know he has become a priest. That same year – 1964 – Forest played a member of an alien biker gangs in The Twilight Zone episode “Black Leather Jackets.” Just a sampling of his many other TV credits in the 1950s, ’60s and ’70s includes appearances on episodes of Z orro, Have Gun – Will Travel, Maverick, Ben Casey, The Outer Limits, Gunsmoke, Gomer Pyle: USMC, I Spy, Mission: Impossible, Gilligan’s Island, Get Smart, The Rookies and Who’s The Boss. Forest also was a busy voice and dubbing actor, appearing in hundreds of animated films lending his skills to hundreds of The 1990s and 2000s saw Forest largely pivoting to voice work and dubbing for animated series and video games including entries in the Power Rangers and Dynasty Warriors franchises, World of Warcraft and various anime projects. Michael Forest as Apollo in 1967 Star Trek episode ‘Who Mourns for Adonais?’ On the big screen, Forest appeared in such drive-in notables as 1959’s Beast From Haunted Cave and Roger Corman’s The Saga of the Viking Women and Their Voyage to the Waters of the Great Sea Serpent (1958), Ski Troop Attack (1960) and sword-and-sandal adventure Atlas (1961). Decades later he played a pilot in the Tom Hanks 2000 film Cast Away, among other late career appearances. Over the years he appeared in the soaps As The World Turns, Days of Our Lives and The Young and the Restless. In 2013, Forest reprised his Apollo role for the fan-made web series Star Trek Continues . Born Gerald Michael Charlebois on April 17, 1929, in Harvey, North Dakota, Forest moved to Los Angeles in 1955 and met director Corman through an acting class, leading to their collaborations that began in the late 1950s. Forest was preceded in death by his wife, the actress Diana Hale, who passed away in 2022. articles.title: Pro Wrestler Benjamin Satterley Cause Of Death Determined

The death was classified as natural. The cause of death was first reported by The New York Post and has been confirmed by other media outlets. Satterley, who over the years wrestled for AEW and WWE under various names including Pac, Bastard, Adrian Neville and Neville, died September 27, one day after he was featured (as Pac) at AEW’s All Out pay-per-view from Chicago. He had lost the AEW National Championship to Andrade El Idolo. Related Stories Obituaries Wrestler Benjamin Satterley Dies One Day After Match: AEW Star Known As “Pac” Was 40 News Michael Forest Dies: Actor In Roger Corman B-Movies, ‘Star Trek’s Apollo Was 97 His death was announced by AEW in a statement reading, “A native of Newcastle upon Tyne, England, Satterley began his wrestling career in 2004 and went on to perform for wrestling organizations all over the world, captivating fans with innovative high-flying moves and incredible in-ring ability. Pac signed with All Elite Wrestling in 2019 and held multiple AEW Championships and competed in some of the most memorable matches in AEW history. Our condolences go out to Satterley’s family, friends and fans.” Watch on Deadline Satterley was known as “The Man that Gravity Forgot” for his signature finishing move, a corkscrew shooting star press off a top rope. He won multiple championships throughout his career. Bronchial asthma, or simply asthma, is, according to the Cleveland Clinic, a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways that causes the breathing tubes in the lungs to swell, narrow, and produce extra mucus. articles.title: ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Suspends Val Chmerkovskiy For TikTok Referencing Will Smith Oscar Moment; Dancer Responds, “Instinct Was To Defend My Wife”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Miley Cyrus Tearfully Remembers Dolly Parton At Hollywood Bowl Concert, Performs ‘Jolene’ Harry Styles Pays Tribute To Liam Payne With New Song At Madison Square Garden Concert Pro Wrestler Benjamin Satterley Cause Of Death Determined View All October 17, 2026 12:30pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Val Chmerkovskiy and Jenna Dewan Greg Doherty/Getty Images for iHeartRadio UDPATED with Chmerkovskiy response: Val Chmerkovskiy is being suspended from Dancing with the Stars for a week after he posted a controversial TikTok message that seemed to reference Will Smith’s 2022 Oscar slap. In a statement released today, producer BBC Studios said, “The well-being of everyone who works on Dancing with the Stars is non-negotiable. Val’s social media post was inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show. As a result, he will not participate in next week’s show.” Chmerkovskiy sparked the controversy the day after the show’s first “Super Bowl Night,” during which judge Carrie Ann Inaba offered a withering critique of the performance of Chmerkovskiy’s wife, DWTS dance pro Jenna Johnson. Wrote Chmerkovskiy in the since-deleted post, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night.” Related Stories News 'Dancing With The Stars' Scores 9-Year Ratings High Among Adults 18-49 On Super Bowl Night News 'Dancing With The Stars' Recap: Super Bowl Night Sends Home A Fan Favorite In a response to the suspension, Chmerkovskiy issued a statement through his rep, acknowledging his “poor decision” and “bad judgment,” saying he hadn’t thought through his TikTok comment before posting. Watch on Deadline Chmerkovskiy’s statement reads: “Hi everyone. As you may have seen in the news, I won’t be in the ballroom this week. “In a moment where my instinct was to defend my wife, I made a poor decision to reference a meme to ‘keep my wife’s name’ out of the conversation, without stopping to think through what else that reference could imply, which was genuinely never my intention. Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was. “The last thing I want is to become a distraction from an important week or from the incredible work my dance partner Jenna Dewan is putting in. “Please send Carrie Ann, Jenna, and the whole DWTS family lots of love during Dedication Night. I’ll be watching and cheering everyone on!!” Chmerkovskiy’s scrutinized post came in response to Inaba’s on-air critique of a lift move made by Johnson, in which she read the definition of a lift and suggested Johnson should know better. The Fresh Prince comment referred, unintentionally or not, to the infamous 2022 Oscar-night moment when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock across the face after the latter made a joke about Smith’s wife Jada Pinkett Smith. Chmerkovskiy’s TikTok comment was widely interpreted to suggest, however jokingly, that he had considered taking action similar to Smith’s, though the dancer later said he hadn’t thought that far. In any case, the joke was apparently lost on Inaba, who on Thursday posted a since-deleted message on Instagram saying, “So this is what we are doing now?” Her post showed photos of Chmerkovskiy and Smith, and in the text of her message she thanked the New York Post and Entertainment Weekly “for bringing this to my attention.” After he posted the TikTok, Chmerkovskiy apologized, writing on Instagram, “I want to apologize from the bottom of my heart for my recent post. I have reached out to Carrie Ann to apologize directly and personally, and I also want to apologize publicly as I understand my words affect so many outside of our internal DWTS family. I should have never made the reference that I did and I deeply regret it. I recognize that I am in a fortunate position to have a platform and to be a role model to some, and I need to treat that with more care by actively pausing to think before I post to ensure what I am sharing aligns with who I am, and who I want to be for you all.” Chmerkovskiy’s celebrity partner Jenna Dewan is apparently aware of the pro’s temporary suspension and will dance with pro Alan Bersten next week in a performance dedicated to her mother. Bersten had been paired with Giada De Laurentiis this season; the duo were eliminated in Week 3. ‘Street Fighter’ Slays $31M; Elizabeth Holmes Doc Milestone $12M+ J.K. The actress, who played recovering addict Jill Kendall on the CBS sitcom, defended her co-stars as “an incredible cast of women” after Lorre wrote in his memoir Sitcom that he “ was, in fact, right ” about his reluctance to cast Anna Faris in the lead as Christy Plunkett. “I was there for seven years, but there [were] eight seasons,” she told E! News . “I came on in the second season, but I had seven wonderful years of working with an incredible crew and an incredible cast of women, who were, all of us, just as beautifully flawed as our characters on the show were.” Related Stories News Anna Faris Was “Hurt” By Chuck Lorre’s Comments About Her ‘Mom’ Exit: “Yikes” Books Chuck Lorre Q&A On The Care & Feeding Of Sitcom Stars & Why A WGA Strike Doomed Democracy Pressly continued, “And I think I just really thoroughly enjoyed being able to go to work with girlfriends every day. The mom in Mom would be, and should be, Anna Faris.” Lorre added: “As the years went by, it became apparent that my initial reluctance to hire Anna was, in fact, correct. After six years, she left the show for mysterious reasons that were not mysterious to anyone on the show.” Premiering in 2013, Faris starred in the first seven seasons of Mom as Christy, a recovering alcoholic who struggles to maintain a job, her family and her sobriety as her mom Bonnie (Allison Janney), who’s also in recovery, moves in with her. Faris left the show in 2020 to “pursue new opportunities,” leaving Janney as the sole lead for the eighth and final season, which ended in 2021. View this post on Instagram Following Lorre’s comments, Faris shared her response Thursday on Instagram. “Yikes. Yes, I read a few things. I really didn’t see that coming. Of course it hurts. Chuck gave me a job I loved, and for seven years I never took a day of it for granted. I’m proud of what we made together, and nothing changes how grateful I am for those people and those years,” she wrote. “I’ve been sober for a year and a half. I was on a show about recovery, and then I lived it. Now I’m healthy, I’m working, and I’m happier than I’ve been in a long time,” Faris continued. “If anyone reading this is where I was, I hope that’s useful. It gets better. I’m proof.” In addition to Faris and Janney, Pressly starred in the series alongside Mimi Kennedy, Beth Hall and Kristen Johnston, playing their supportive group of friends from Alcoholics Anonymous. ‘Street Fighter’ Slays $31M; Elizabeth Holmes Doc Milestone $12M+ J.K. The Golden Globe nominee recently revealed that he pitched a Star Trek series about “young Picard ” that was titled Mutiny On the Stargazer , noting that he nearly “made” the limited series. “That was a whole idea I had I pitched to the Star Trek people as well, and we nearly did it,” said McAvoy on the Happy Sad Confused podcast. “I’ve got a whole story about an early Picard. All I really want to do in my career is play young versions of Patrick [Stewart].” Related Stories News Premiere Episodes Of ‘Star Trek: Picard’, ‘Discovery’, ‘Lower Decks’, ‘Strange New Worlds’ & More Available For Free In Honor Of Star Trek Day News James McAvoy Recalls Being Bullied On The Set Of HBO’s ‘Band Of Brothers’ The interview came after McAvoy took over the role of Professor Charles Xavier from Stewart in the X-Men prequel movies First Class (2011), Days of Future Past (2014), Apocalypse (2016) and Dark Phoenix (2019). Stewart originated the live-action role in X-Men (2000), reprising him in the sequels X2 (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006), X-Men Origins: Wolverine (2009), The Wolverine (2013), Logan (2017) and Days of Future Past, and again in the upcoming MCU title Avengers: Doomsday, premiering Dec. 18 in theaters. Watch on Deadline McAvoy continued, “I had this whole story of a young Picard that I love. I pitched, it was like a one-off standalone season … when he took over as captain of the Stargazer and what actually happened, and the secret he’s been holding his entire career. I just pitched it to them, talking to them, and they were into it, but we had logistical issues that meant we couldn’t do it. But I love that story that I just got to bed and think about it at night.” Running for seven seasons in syndication from 1987 to 1994, Stewart starred in Star Trek: The Next Generation as Captain Jean-Luc Picard , commanding officer on the USS Enterprise-D. He reprised the role in Star Trek: Picard, running for three seasons from 2020 to ’23. Picard’s first command was explored in author Michael Jan Friedman’s six-part Star Trek: Stargazer book series, which was published between 2002 and 2004. ‘Street Fighter’ Slays $31M; Elizabeth Holmes Doc Milestone $12M+ J.K. articles.title: El Gouna Unveils Third Cohort Of CineGouna Emerge Program’s Rising Stars
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie El Gouna Unveils Third Cohort Of CineGouna Emerge Program’s Rising Stars Strand Releasing Takes North American For Hanaël El Yousfi’s TIFF-Selected ‘The Daughters Of Abraham’ Egypt’s El Gouna Kicks Off MENA Fall Film Festival Season With Local Breakouts, Oscar Contenders & Emerging Talents View All October 18, 2026 5:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R Abdallah Dnewar, Razan AlSoghayer, Omar Rammal L-R Asmahan Bkerat, Rama Abd courtesy El Gouna Film Festival EXCLUSIVE : Egypt ’s El Gouna Film Festival has announced the third cohort of emerging talents from across the Arab world selected for its Rising Stars program. They are Egyptian director Abdallah Dnewar, Saudi Arabian writer-director Razan AlSoghayer, Palestinian filmmaker Omar Rammal, Palestinian Jordanian director-producer Asmahan Bkerat and Syrian DoP, editor and director Rama Abdi. Launched in 2024 , the initiative is part of El Gouna’s CineGouna Emerge program aimed at nurturing the next generation of MENA film professionals. CineGouna Emerge in turn is a strand of El Gouna’s CineGouna industry program alongside the Forum talks lineup, Funding project showcase, Market and new Series focus. Related Stories News Egypt's El Gouna Kicks Off MENA Fall Film Festival Season With Local Breakouts, Oscar Contenders & Emerging Talents Books Sally Rooney Will "No Longer Supply" Her Books To UK After Palestine Action Proscribed Terrorist Organization “This year’s Rising Stars are already leaving their mark, each in their own corner of the industry,” said Hayat Aljowaily, Director of CineGouna Emerge & International Engagement, who spearheaded the Rising Stars program. Watch on Deadline Cairo-based Dnewar produced the critically acclaimed Rotterdam-selected animated short My Brother, My Brother , and Locarno-selected Khufu , and been a script consultant on several short films. He is currently Head of Specials at Egyptian media company Zest. There, he oversaw the Eish Short Film Competition, a joint initiative between the El Gouna Film Festival and United Nations World Food Programme (WFP). Based between Saudi Arabia and The Netherlands, AlSoghayer’s work explores womanhood, memory, friendship, patriarchy and growing up within a rapidly changing society. Drawing from personal experience and everyday life, she creates intimate, nostalgic stories rooted in Saudi culture and the complexities of change. Her debut short Son Of Badriyah plays in this edition of El Gouna. West Bank-born Rammal has carving out a unique path between digital storytelling and independent cinema, with his visual style and deeply human storytelling racking up hundreds of millions of views across digital platforms. He made waves this year with Everyday in Gaza , which won the best short documentary award in the 2026 edition of Italy’s David di Donatello awards. His debut fiction short, Kentucky Gaza makes its MENA premiere at the El Gouna, having premiered in the International Competition at Clermont-Ferrand in France. He is currently developing his first feature film. Bkerat ,whose work explores themes of displacement, identity, and cultural heritage, is currently on the festival circuit with her debut feature documentary Concrete Land , which premiered at the Locarno Film Festival and won the Insights Audience Award at VIFF (Vancouver). It recently played to sold-out screenings at the BFI London Film Festival and is now on a major festival tour, including Dok Leipzig, IDFA, and Doha. She is currently producing the feature documentaries If These Stones Could Talk and Landwards , and is in early production on her next directorial feature. Damascus-based Abdi began her filmmaking journey in 2018, working across commercial, journalistic and cinematic productions as a camerawoman and director. In 2022 she directed her first short Fish Dance , and is now working on her first feature-length documentary House Number 7 , which she is presenting in the CineGouna Funding project showcase. Through the program, this year’s Rising Stars will connect with industry leaders and take part in the festival’s main activities, from panel discussions and media engagements to the red carpet. The experience is curated to give each of them the visibility their work has earned. “What we offer them is not a beginning, but a moment of recognition: a chance to be seen, to be heard, and to find one another,” said Aljowaily. “Our role is simply to bring them into the same room, and into the light, at a moment when their work is ready to be seen. Amr Mansi, Co-Founder and Executive Director of El Gouna Film Festival added: “We need to ensure that stories from this region are shared with the rest of the world. We strongly believe that our participants will be the dominant voice in telling these stories.” Andrew Mohsen, Artistic Director of El Gouna Film Festival, emphasized the fact that the participants are fully integrated into the festival program. “What makes Rising Stars meaningful is that it does not stand apart from the rest of the festival,” he said. “Many of these filmmakers are here with projects they are pitching at CineGouna Funding, or with films that are competing, or have competed, in our official selection. The program recognizes talent we are already invested in, and whose work we have watched grow from one edition to the next.” ‘Street Fighter’ Slays $31M; Elizabeth Holmes Doc Milestone $12M+ J.K. articles.title: London Film Festival: Sergei Loznitsa’s ‘Imperium’ & Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s ‘9 Temples To Heaven’ Among Big Winners — Full List
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac ‘Dear William:’ Film Adaptation Of David D. Magee’s Memoir Underway Rita Coburn & Jeffrey Wright To Bring Their Feature Doc ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel With A Cause’ To London BFI & Chanel Filmmaker Award: ‘Ish’ Director Imran Perretta Among 2026 Winners View All October 18, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source '9 Temples to Heaven' Sompot Chidgasornpongse. Ukrainian filmmaker Sergei Loznitsa’s latest feature Imperium has won the Best Film Award in the Official Competition at this year’s London Film Festival . The winners were announced this afternoon, the last day of the LFF . The LFF Official Competition jury was led by documentary filmmaker Sam Pollard. Discussing why they chose Imperium, the jury described the picture as an “extraordinary film that explores the Soviet Union in the early 1970’s from a rich archive with a wide-ranging perspective that looks at life in a country with an extraordinary social and cultural landscape that has rarely been seen.” Related Stories Reviews 'Klara And The Sun' Review: Taika Waititi's Latest Is A Curiously Flat Dystopian Comedy-Drama - London Film Festival Festivals 'Cameron Winter At Carnegie Hall' Review: Paul Thomas Anderson's Concert Movie Captures The Grandeur And Intimacy Of An Esoteric Event - London Film Festival The jury added: “The film is richly evocative and emotionally engaging on all levels, giving us a visually arresting perspective of life before the Soviet Union was broken apart. Our jury is immensely proud to honour such a powerful and singular piece of work.” Watch on Deadline Thai filmmaker Sompot Chidgasornpongse won the coveted Sutherland Award in the First Feature Competition with 9 Temples To Heaven. The film, which debuted at Cannes, follows Sakol, who, after hearing a prophecy that his elderly mother may die soon, sets out on a one-day pilgrimage to nine temples as a remedy. Kissada Kamyoung and Palme d’Or winner Apichatpong Weerasethakul ( Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives ) produced the film alongside co-producers Thomas Hakim and Julien Graff of petit chaos, the company behind Payal Kapadia’s award-winning All We Imagine as Light. Discussing their decision, the first feature jury, led by Amir El-Masry, said the film was an “accomplished first feature paving his own path in the well-established tradition of filmmaking in the Southeast Asian region. The film is visually outstanding, spiritual, and meditative, where a story about life and death transcends borders and generations.” Elsewhere, Concrete Land , directed by Asmahan Bkerat, won the Grierson Award in the Documentary Competition, and Rahul Roye’s Aman won the Short Film Award. The LFF ends this evening with a screening of The Debut , directed by Jesse Eisenberg. ‘Street Fighter’ Slays $31M; Elizabeth Holmes Doc Milestone $12M+ J.K.
