articles.title: Austin Abrams Still Won’t Admit Which Was Tougher to Shoot, ‘Whalefall’ or ‘Resident Evil’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Brian Davids Plus Icon Brian Davids Writer PickYourBrian Follow Sign Up View All October 16, 2026 3:48pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for 20th Century Fox Logo text The autumn of Austin Abrams marches on with Whalefall , his second one-man genre exercise in the span of a month. The belle of the fall’s emotional survival tale joins Resident Evil in theaters as the latter continues to build on its $324 million worldwide box office gross. In Whalefall , co-written and directed by Brian Duffield , Abrams plays college student Jay Gardiner, who reluctantly returns home to California’s Central Coast a year after his estranged father, Mitt (Josh Brolin), responds to his terminal mesothelioma diagnosis by taking his own life at sea. Related Stories Movies Josh Brolin Talks the Personal Side of 'Whalefall' and the "Undeniable" Script for 'Sicario 3' Movies 'Street Fighter' Socks Away $4M in Previews as 'You Can See Everything' Takes $1.7M In a decision partly influenced by his mother (Elisabeth Shue) and two sisters (Jane Levy and Emily Rudd) having to visit an empty grave, Jay sets out to find his father’s remains on the ocean floor near Monastery Beach. The underlying hope is that the gesture will help him resolve their lingering differences stemming from his overly strict seafaring upbringing. But the plan goes belly-up almost immediately when a sperm whale pursuing a squid also swallows Jay, ensnaring him in its multichambered stomach. Like Resident Evil , Whalefall gives its protagonist just an hour to accomplish his goal, which in this case means escaping the whale’s innards before his oxygen tank runs dry. When The Hollywood Reporter last caught up with Abrams for Resident Evil , he refused to declare which film ended up being the more backbreaking ordeal. He certainly didn’t complain about splitting his head open during an elevator leap in Resident Evil ‘s third act or act fazed by nearly being crushed to death by a 150-pound blood bag in act two. But now that I’ve seen Whalefall , it seems that the only thing worse than actually being inside a whale’s stomach is pretending to be inside one. Yet Abrams still won’t kvetch about being crammed into a tiny whale-stomach set with a camera crew, while a half-dozen crew members surrounding the practical gut, wielding a gimbal, tossed him around like a wet rag doll. Duffield — who is also collaborating with Resident Evil filmmaker Zach Cregger on the upcoming Siren Head — believes his film takes the prize for putting their shared leading man through the wringer, given that his extremities weren’t restricted in Resident Evil . Abrams, meanwhile, continues to straddle the fence in gentlemanly fashion. “[The ability to move my limbs] was the nice part about Resident Evil . But they both have their perks and [pitfalls],” he tells THR in support of Whalefall ’s Oct. 16 theatrical release. To prepare for a scuba diver’s worst nightmare, Abrams earned the necessary certifications. He also visited a sperm whale sanctuary on a Caribbean island. Although the trip didn’t guarantee any face time with the wild animals, Abrams lucked out when they emerged for him, something they hadn’t done in the previous nine days. “It was beautiful. It was peaceful. It was the opposite of what you think it would be. You immediately know and feel how gentle and loving they are,” Abrams recalls. He also walked around his neighborhood in full scuba attire just to get used to the extra weight. While his neighbors weren’t alarmed enough by the unusual sight to call security, Abrams wasn’t as lucky during filming at Radford Studios in Studio City. “There’s a point where Jay gets visibly more distressed and blown-up looking,” Abrams shares. “I remember walking around the lot during that time and having security called on me just because I looked so fucked up.” Abrams, who generally avoids sharing too much about himself on a personal level, does reveal that his family is a little irked by how often his characters die in movies, a pattern that began with his first film, 2011’s Ticking Clock . A couple of years later, in his major studio debut, Abrams worked alongside Ryan Gosling in Gangster Squad until his shoeshine boy character caught a bullet during a mob ambush near a newsstand. (Brolin also stars in the 2013 crime pic, but didn’t share the screen with his future Weapons and Whalefall co-star.) Unintentionally, Abrams took a page out of Gosling’s playbook while preparing for his consecutive shoots on Whalefall and Resident Evil in 2025. Ahead of filming Peter Jackson’s The Lovely Bones in 2007, Gosling arrived to set with a beard and 60 extra pounds. Only 26 at the time, Gosling felt he needed to sell the appearance of a grieving father to two teenagers and a 4-year-old. Jackson was so thrown by Gosling’s unexpected character decisions that he recast him with Mark Wahlberg. Post- Whalefall , with little time to prepare for Resident Evil ‘s shoot in Prague, Abrams also adopted the “it’s easier to ask forgiveness than to get permission” approach to his own unannounced weight gain. He wanted his medical courier, Bryan, to look ill-equipped to handle a zombie outbreak, and seeking approval beforehand might’ve led financiers and producers, who typically want the most physically appealing lead actor possible, to discourage the idea. (Even Keanu Reeves’ beard nearly cost John Wick its financing.) Luckily, Cregger loved Abrams’ surprise choice. “I wanted Bryan to be a dude you look at and think he won’t be able to get out of this,” Abrams says. “I just had a strong impulse that I needed to do it. If you say you want to look a little bit different, it’s hard for people to imagine it. So it just felt like something that needed to be done, and I just went with it.” Below, during a conversation with THR , Abrams also discusses the careful handling of a particular letter in Whalefall . *** Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in Brian Duffield ‘s Whalefall . 20th Century Studios I previously asked you which movie made you suffer more, and you chose to be Switzerland about it. But now that I’ve seen Whalefall , there’s no question it was more unbearable than Resident Evil . Are you willing to cop to it now? ( Laughs .) No, man. You said it, not me. Your Whalefall director, Brian Duffield , wasn’t proud of it, but he immediately took credit for his movie being the more punishing of the two. He did? He said, “The fact that Austin can move his arms and legs freely in Resident Evil gives Whalefall the edge.” That was the nice part about Resident Evil . But they both have their perks and [pitfalls]. I’m curious about your family’s response to these two new movies. Has it been hard for them to watch their baby boy in such precarious situations? I don’t know. I imagine to some degree it could be, but I also feel like everyone takes it okay. I feel like they’d prefer if I died less in some of them, but other than that, I think they do alright. Yeah, that has been a pattern in your work. The Line was especially brutal. Yeah, man. It’s been that way from the beginning. I don’t know why. It’s funny you say that because I’m about to reference the first major one. Go ahead! (L-r) Director Brian Duffield and Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner on the set of Whalefall . Jennifer Clasen/20th Century Studios Well, the first thing that struck me about Whalefall was how different you looked as Jay, especially since you shot it right before Resident Evil . Then I read that you gained weight for Bryan in Resident Evil . Given how little time you had in between, did you microwave tubs of Häagen-Dazs once you got to Prague and gorge yourself? ( Laughs .) Oh man. Yeah, you just do whatever you can. I wanted Bryan to be a dude you look at and think he won’t be able to get out of this. I didn’t want him to look like someone who runs laps in his free time or something like that. So it was a close period of time, but there wasn’t really any science to it. You just do whatever you can to get where you need to go. The Häagen-Dazs method? I don’t know. Just pure ice cream is preferable. It was a bold move not to tell Zach Cregger you were packing on some pounds. There’s a famous story involving your shoe-shine customer, Ryan Gosling. [ In Gangster Squad , Gosling’s character urged Abrams’ young shoeshiner to go home, but he didn’t listen and fell victim to mob-related gunfire. ] ( Laughs .) Shoe-shine customer, that’s funny. He showed up on a Peter Jackson set 60 pounds heavier from drinking melted Häagen-Dazs, only he didn’t tell Jackson he was doing it. So that’s the reason why Mark Wahlberg is now the one who starred in The Lovely Bones . Yeah, but I just had a strong impulse that I needed to do it. So I just went from there. If you say you want to look a little bit different, it’s hard for people to imagine it. So it just felt like something that needed to be done, and I just went with it. Most importantly, Zach loved the choice. I hope so. He said so. ( Laughs. ) Yeah. By all accounts, you were a great sport when filming inside each whale stomach, but was there a day where you needed to be let out early because it was just too much? I don’t know if we had that situation. The nature of the movie meant welcoming whatever difficulty came with it. When something is welcomed, it makes it less difficult. You don’t want to get out of any difficulty. You want to keep it there [for the sake of the scene]. Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in Brian Duffield’s Whalefall . 20th Century Studios I read that you walked around your neighborhood in scuba gear to get used to the weight. Did your neighbors give you any weird looks or call the police about some guy loitering in scuba apparatus? I can’t remember if there were any funny looks or not. This is a little different from what you’re talking about, but there’s a point where Jay gets visibly more distressed and blown-up looking. I remember walking around the lot during that time and having security called on me just because I looked so fucked up. Before filming, you traveled to a Caribbean island to get in the water with some real sperm whales, and they appeared for you, something they don’t always do for people. Were you trembling with fear? Or was it more peaceful than it sounds? Man, it was beautiful. It was peaceful. It was the opposite of what you think it would be. You immediately know and feel how gentle and loving they are. Also, if they’re not interested in you, they’ll just dive back down. They can very easily avoid you if they want to, at least in this circumstance. But it was just an immensely moving experience, and I’m super grateful. You don’t know if any whales are going to be around, and you also don’t know if they’re going to have any interest in hanging out for a little bit. So I got really, really lucky with that. You and Josh Brolin knew each other from Weapons , but given how intense Jay and Mitt’s scenes are, did you avoid socializing before the scene work? [ Brolin was also in Gangster Squad , but he and Abrams didn’t share the screen .] Thankfully, there was already a level of love and trust from knowing one another beforehand. When it comes to the work and their relationship, there’s a certain point where it’s not necessarily helpful to be palling around together. Sometimes it’s important and useful to strip that stuff away, and sometimes it’s not. It’s whatever feels the most useful, and hopefully it is. But yeah, there was certainly less [socializing] than there’d normally be. It’s always different when you’re working and doing whatever you need to do to lend a feeling to the scene. So that’s my answer or non-answer to that. (L-R): Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner and Josh Brolin as Mitt Gardiner in Brian Duffield’s Whalefall . 20th Century Studios There was an early cut of the movie where Mitt’s letter to Jay was at least partially visible, but then the studio urged Brian to remove any glimpse. Are you ever going to reveal what Jay’s letter said? Unh-unh. Good. Keep that secret for the rest of your life. Yeah. Maybe I’ll tell people personally. That’s cool, but don’t tell people like me. We don’t deserve it. ( Laughs .) It’s richer this way. I really feel that way. If you put your own interpretation on it, that’s potentially going to be more meaningful and interesting than whatever was written. You’re also projecting whatever you wish a family member had said to you if they’d written you a letter before they died. That’s valuable. So there’s value in the not knowing. Austin Abrams as Bryan in Zach Cregger ‘s Resident Evil . Dušan Martinček/Sony Pictures Can we speed-round some Resident follow-ups in our waning moments? Oh boy. Whatcha got for me? The internet believes the Sundress Woman was actually the farmer’s wife. That would explain why she was relatively close to the farm in the first place. Do you believe that to be true? That’s shown in there. You must be referring to the photo of the farmer and his wife. I looked up the actor (Andrea Miltnerová) who plays the Sundress Woman, and compared her with the woman in that photo. While I’m 99.9 percent certain it’s the same person, I hesitate to call that confirmation. All I’m saying is that it’s in there. I read a draft of the script, and in the second phone call with Michelle (then known as Ashley) in the car, Bryan eventually tells her straight up that he wants to have a kid with her, only she couldn’t hear him because of bad cell service. Did you ever shoot that version? Unh-unh. No. The Paul Walter Hauser character, Paul, used to be a woman named Pauline, and she went with Bryan to the rat sewer before getting consumed by them. Bryan then mowed down her rat-infested body. Do you know why Zach dropped any version of that? I don’t know what you read. It must have been a very early draft. Yeah, you found an early one. The dog also bit Bryan first and caused his infection, not the little girl. Yeah, yeah, yeah. There’s certain parts of these that I’m remembering, but the one with Pauline and the rats, I don’t remember that. The syringe originally broke inside the lab, but Zach happened to shoot another version with it outside in case he changed his mind in post. Did he let you find out about that switch when you watched it for the first time? We talked about that. That was something we’d been talking about. *** Whalefall is now paying in movie theaters nationwide . THR

articles.title: John Amos’ Daughter Sues Brother for Wrongful Death Over Actor’s Death
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Winston Cho Plus Icon Winston Cho View All October 16, 2026 4:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source John Amos Brent Lewis/The Denver Post via Getty Images Logo text John Amos ‘ daughter is suing her brother and people in his orbit over the death of their father for elder abuse and wrongful death. The daughter, Shannon Amos, faults her brother, Kelly Christopher Amos, for delaying medical care while isolating the actor from his family and friends in the years leading up to his death. The lawsuit seeks a court order that, if granted, would bar K.C. Amos from inheriting from John Amos’ estate and to void the current will, plus unspecified damages. John Amos, 84, died in 2024 of natural causes. For years, his children have been engaged in an acrimonious battle over the actor’s care and finances. The lawsuit chronicles the last years of John Amos’ life. Around 2019, K.C. Amos started to keep his father from family and friends by shuffling him around various locations while monitoring his communications, manipulating the actor into believing that his family and friends were trying to exploit him, according to the complaint. For a three month period in 2023, all attempts by John Amos’ family to contact the actor were blocked, the lawsuit says. They were told to reach out to K.C. Amos. On multiple occasions, John Amos was left alone in unsafe and unsanitary conditions, including in hotels filled with trash, drug paraphernalia and soiled diapers, according to the complaint. Around this time, he was treated for an infection in his feet caused by maggots — one of numerous hospitalizations, prompting a call from Adult Protective Services over his care, the filing says. In an email to Shannon Amos, Elizabeth Bowling, a caregiver for John Amos, wrote of the actor’s living conditions, “The smell was horrid. There were no clean dishes. Mold had began to grow in the sink. Garbage bags/garbage laying where it was left. Food was left out on the counters and on the stove dried up. Counters and tables covered with gunk and what looked like marijuana and empty beer and liquor bottles around. No fresh food in the fridge.” During this period, the lawsuit says, John Amos missed treatments for prostate cancer and other health issues while continuing to do Cameo and low budget commercial appearances at the direction of his son. The matter was later referred to adult protective services in Colorado, the lawsuit claims, though John Amos was subsequently moved to Tennessee, where K.C. Amos struck a movie deal for his father. In August 2024, John Amos started to exhibit “obvious signs of a serious medical emergency,” the lawsuit claims. Despite this, Shannon Amos says her father’s his caregivers neglected to seek treatment for 13 hours. The actor was later brought to a hospital in Inglewood, where he died four hours after arriving. Shannon Amos accuses her brother of hiding their father’s death, which she discovered in October when it was reported in the media. The passing was announced by K.C. Amos, who allegedly had his father cremated without telling family members, according to the complaint. After John Amos’ death, K.C. Amos allegedly transferred substantial funds from his father to his personal bank accounts, the filing says. He later filed instated himself as sold owner of his father’s production outfit, Step and One Half Productions, securing control over the actor’s name and business interests, Shannon Amos claims. He also obtained exclusive access to John Amos’ roughly $6,300 SAG-AFTRA monthly pension and residuals while cutting the rest of the family out. The lawsuit challenges the current will. It claims that John Amos was tricked into signing documents that benefited K.C. Amos at the expense of other family members. A previous version of the will executed in 2020 accounted for beneficiaries that K.C. Amos didn’t think was appropriate, according to the complaint, which notes that the document “disappeared” days after it was signed. Another will was executed a year later that gave K.C. Amos power of attorney. In addition to K.C. Amos, the lawsuit names Belinda Foster, secretary for Step and One Half Productions, plus three companies formed by K.C. Amost. Two of them list Foster as a principal. One was formed in Colorado, weeks after law enforcement requested John Amos’ bank records. The other two were formed in California, roughly two months before the actor died. Shannon Amos alleges they were used to take over her father’s business interests. The legal action was filed in August in California state court. A petition had been filed in probate court asking for an emergency court order to freeze John Amos’ estate. The legal action was later withdrawn. THR

articles.title: Timothy Busfield Child Sex Abuse Case Dismissed Over Prosecutorial Misconduct
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All October 16, 2026 4:09pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Timothy Busfield Steven Ferdman/Getty Images The child sexual abuse case against Timothy Busfield has been tossed out by the judge overseeing the proceedings as he accused prosecutors of misconduct and violating grand jury statutes as the case began to move through the justice system. The charges of sexual assault involving two minors that were filed earlier this year in New Mexico against Busfield stem from time on the set of the TV series The Cleaning Lady , episodes of which he directed, between 2022 and 2024. The 69-year-old thirtysomething and Field of Dreams star, who went on to a prolific career as a director on television shows, is accused of sexually assaulting twin boys who appeared in several seasons of the show. Related Stories Movies Anna Paquin and Melissa Gilbert Call for Protection of Child Actors After Hayden Panettiere's Death: "Where Is the Collective Outrage?" TV Melissa Gilbert Believes Husband Timothy Busfield Will Be Exonerated of Child Sexual Abuse Charges Throughout his career as an actor and director, Busfield has faced multiple accusations from women of on-set groping and sexual assault; the outcomes of these accusations have varied from out-of-court settlements to dismissal of charges against him. He has been married to actor Melissa Gilbert since 2013. The 2026 accusations stem from a call placed to police in Albuquerque by a University of New Mexico physician who examined the boys and alerted them to allegations of abuse. After police had a difficult time finding him, a media frenzy followed and the actor was eventually arrested after he surrendered himself. The Bernalillo County District Attorney’s Office in New Mexico charged Busfield with four counts of criminal sexual contact of a child and he was released under his own recognizance ahead of the trial. An attorney for the actor has said that the charges are bogus and that the accusations come from the parents of the children who were looking for vengeance against Busfield for recasting the boys in the fourth season of the Fox series after they aged out of their roles. An investigation by Warner Bros. into the incident produced no evidence, and Busfield has passed a polygraph test regarding the allegations, his attorneys have told the court. But on Friday, it was the actions of prosecutors earlier this year during the grand jury process that sank the case — for now, at least. Judge Joseph Montano of the Second Judicial District Court of New Mexico in Albuquerque said prosecutors “failed to act in a fair and impartial manner” — but he did not close the door on future charges, leaving Busfield exposed to further legal action from New Mexico prosecutors. In his dismissal of the case, Judge Montano said that the state didn’t call certain witnesses after the grand jury asked to hear from them and failed to properly instruct jurors on procedures. In his conclusion, the judge lambasted prosecutors for failing to “act in a fair and impartial manner” and for violating grand jury statutes that are “designed to protect the structural integrity of our grand jury system.” The Hollywood Reporter reached out to the New Mexico Office of the Second Judicial District Attorney on Friday to discuss the grand jury proceedings and ask about plans for re-filing the case against Busfield, but did not immediately hear back. The New York Times reported that prosecutors are undecided as of Friday afternoon about refiling the charges. Nancy Laflin, a spokeswoman for the Second Judicial District Attorney’s Office of New Mexico, said in a statement sent to the outlet on Friday that her office “is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed.” Since the accusations against Busfield went public, he was dropped by talent agency Innovative Artists. THR

articles.title: How ‘You Can See Everything’ Exacts Hollywood’s Revenge on Big Tech
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder speak onstage at the 'You Can See Everything' premiere during the 64th New York Film Festival at Alice Tully Hall, Lincoln Center on Sept. 30, 2026 in New York. Cindy Ord/Getty Images for FLC [No spoilers! ] Life may be too short for long-term grudges, as the quote goes, but it’s still lengthy enough to dole out some justice. This weekend, A24 brings out Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything , the Elizabeth Holmes doc that is already creating a major stir with filmgoers after previously dazzling critics. The opening follows the releases last weekend of Mus k , The Social Reckoning and the New York Film Festival premiere of Artificial . All four films contend with the tech alphas trying to remake our lives in their image. And they exact a kind of revenge at once inevitable and improbable. You know the alpha types — those talkers on CNBC or in your college WhatsApp group saying there’s a solution for everything, even to things you didn’t know were problems. Actually, they don’t say there’s a solution — they say there’s a solve, w hich should tip you off right there. Never get involved in a land war in Asia, and never trust anyone who seamlessly turns a verb into a noun. He’s probably trying to sell you something from behind his puffer jacket. Far from the usual stake-less Hollywood gaze, these docs and fact-based dramas center three figures deeply relevant to our current landscape: Elon Musk , Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman . (Add any more of them and we might think it’s a Donald Trump state dinner.) The fourth figure, You Can See Everything ’s Holmes along with her husband Billy Evans, is less relevant, but the pair embody a Silicon Valley attitude that survives and dominates even as one half of it sits in a Texas prison: that with a little pluck and a lot of smooth talk anything can be achieved, reality be damned. But it’s not just filmmakers’ decision to center these figures that matters: it’s how they take them on. Musk s pends four hours meticulously deconstructing the ways its subject got his power and the surveillance and even alleged potential-election rigging he is using it for. Reckoning shows a Meta intent on stoking our rage and divisions for its own profiteering. Artificial , which arrives in theaters on Christmas, may be the most searing of the lot. Ostensibly a procedural account of Sam Altman’s rise to power at OpenAI, Luca Guadagnino’s drama (complete with an Oscar-level performance from Andrew Garfield) brutally takes apart how Altman hustled investors and even his own staff — including the engineering prodigy Ilya Sutskever. Sutskever joined and made possible OpenAI’s breakthrough science after Altman reassured him everything would be done all human-centric and responsible. Whoops. Audiences may justifiably seethe at how Sutskever’s safety-first mindset gets steamrolled by Altman’s slick accelerationism (as happened in real life). But we also might want to take heart in how the very fact that we’re watching this account represents its own kind of triumph, as the safety concerns Sutskever worried would be silenced are being megaphoned into the very theater in which our rage curdles. Winning the P.R. war isn’t the same as winning the Wall Street one, of course. But it doesn’t stand apart from it either — not least because companies need some pretty heavy consumer adoption to pull off their financial coup. Even as Musk rolled out to theaters nationwide, homepages told of how Musk’s SpaceX appeared to manipulate Starshield such that it limited Ukraine’s ability to ward off Russian attacks, the man becoming in real-time the policy oligarch Gibney’s film intimates. In all these movies you can’t help sensing a kind of authorial revenge. Aaron Sorkin, sitting down to tell us how mad he is at what Zuckerberg has done in the 15 years since he last visited with him, with not much Zuckerberg can do to respond. Or Gibney, by his own telling, shines a light on the power Musk is gaining over all our lives, with little recourse but to lash out scatologically on the social platform he owns. (X, TikTok, Meta and YouTube all at first denied ads for the film; the latter two, at least, came to their senses.) Altman, meanwhile, was left to simper that “I don’t think they’re going for accuracy,” which he did to Vanity Fair on the day of the Artificial premiere, clearly worried that accurate is exactly how we’ll perceive it. In all of this we have a collection of great dramas — if you haven’t booked your ticket to hoot and gasp at YCSE , go do so now — but also the latest turn in a greater meta-drama, lowercase m, between artists and Silicon Valley, a bow-shot from human storytellers to the masters and sellers of computer code. Tech leaders thought that the magic of LLMs had rid us of all that professional wordsmithing for good. These writers and creators come to say not so fast. After all these years of hearing about (and sometimes already living the idea of) AI coming for Hollywood jobs, some of the people who work at them finally get to say their piece, with everyone listening. This sudden storyteller leverage is literalized by, well, Fielder’s face, which, to every Holmes or Evans desperate fib, subtly contorts into skepticism or disbelief, giving that not only does he know he is being fed con-ish hooey, but also that he and co-director Lance Oppenheim have the power to cast it as such the minute they enter the edit room. What’s more, Holmes and Evans seem to know it too. At one point Evans stomps in to a Fielder secondary interview to try to stop it. You could almost smell the algorithmic impotency in the face of human vitality. In that moment vibrates the larger, call it…trans-cinematic message of the four films — “Engineers may live in our screens and even addict our brains, but the storytellers have something even more powerful: they can make us feel.” The people shaping these four narratives are all singing the same chorus — that much of what they do (and human thought generally) can’t be outsourced to a machine. “I’m not particularly charismatic or good-looking,” Artificial screenwriter Simon Rich told the NYFF audience, “but as a last-ditch effort to warn mankind I wrote this movie.” (Lisa Kudrow and Michael Patrick King’s latest season of The Come back also boldly trafficked in this Hollywood vs the Machines theme.) Perhaps the most surprising part of this filmmaker uprising is that it’s also turned Hollywood studios into something they haven’t been in a long time, possibly since the 70’s and all those Vietnam protest movies: the good guys. Amazon thought it could silence the protest voices by dropping Artificial . Instead it just sidelined itself. And now Neon (which picked up Artificial ), Sony ( The Social Reckoning ), HBO ( Musk ) and A24 ( You Can See Everything ) are all out there proudly putting the tech industry in check. Not for nothing do these four studios also have some of the smallest Silicon Valley involvement. (Though an A24 making deals with Google DeepMind, a Sony that produces hardware and an HBO now bankrolled by Larry Ellison shows how such entanglements also aren’t easily escapable in 2026.) AI will generate plenty of memeslop and cost-cutting; anyone who comes out of these movies thinking the great automation battle has been won in Hollywood, let alone the world, is either naive or self-deceiving. But it would be equally misguided to emerge into the daylight and think the films won’t matter at all, that a strong injection of anti-oligarchal humanity won’t course through the collective blood or change social views — that a long-term grudge, really, won’t be settled in some very productive ways. That grudge quote, by the way, comes from Elon Musk, who (ironic contrasts with his own lawsuit-happy pedigree aside ) now has been grudgily victimized himself — and by the very truth-seekers and storytellers he thought he’d dispatched when he bought Twitter. Talk about a good solve. Related Stories Movies 'Street Fighter' Socks Away $4M in Previews as 'You Can See Everything' Takes $1.7M Movies 'Street Fighter' Eyes Box Office Victory as Buzzy Elizabeth Holmes Doc Heads for Strong Launch THR

articles.title: Angie Nixon Says Black Republican Byron Donalds “Doesn’t Support Black People”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All October 16, 2026 5:37pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon speaks during a campaign event at the St. John Missionary Baptist Church on September 28, 2026 in Boynton Beach, Florida. Nixon faces incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody (R-FL) in the November 3rd general election, one of several Florida races that are heating up Joe Raedle/Getty Images Florida is becoming one of the bigger enigmas of the already-puzzling 2026 election season. Democrats are showing themselves to be surprisingly competitive. Democrat David Jolly is running neck-and-neck with Trump-approved Republican Byron Donalds in two of three recent polls for the governor job. And Jacksonville legislator and DSA member Angie Nixon , having upset moderate Democrat Alex Vindman in the primary, now is at least keeping it close against Republican incumbent Ashley Moody. All of which is startling in a state that went for Donald Trump by 13 points just two years ago and hasn’t elected a Democratic governor since 1994. Related Stories News Half a Scaramucci: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Ousted After One Briefing Business BBC Asks Judge to Force Trump to Sit for Deposition in His Own Lawsuit Against Broadcaster Now Nixon is turning up the heat on Republican candidates. On an upcoming episode of Crooked Media’s YouTube show Long Play, Nixon lets it fly against the Republican gubernatorial candidate. “Byron Donalds doesn’t support Black people,” she tells hosts Jennifer Palmieri and Errin Haines on camera in an early cut of the episode, which debuts Monday. Haines then follows up by asking Nixon to explain what she means when she says that Donalds is “going to bring back the worst parts of our history.” Nixon replies, “I mean, he is someone who said that Black people were better off during the Jim Crow era.” The race has grown contentious but seems to be reaching a new level of fervor as it heads into the final two weeks. Nixon has said at rallies that she wants to keep funding the police, referring to a common anti-DSA knock, because she wants Moody, Ron DeSantis and Trump locked up. For his part, vice president J.D. Vance said recently at a rally, addressing Nixon, “Get the hell out of here, you don’t belong in America.” (Nixon in the episode: “They don’t have anything to run on but cruelty.”) Meanwhile, Donalds has been criticized by Jolly for not extending leniency to young people that he was shown when he was arrested on drug charges as a young man and given the opportunity of a diversion program; a hot-button new ad has a retired U.S. General calling Donalds “weak” and a “hypocrite” for it. (Palmieri and Haines discuss the ad in the new episode.) Launched earlier this year , Long Play examines the divisions and shifting political alignments in various Southern states. After concluding its first season with trips to Georgia, Texas and other Southern states, the show kicks off its second season ahead of the midterms with a Florida episode. Five flagship and three bonus episodes are planned, straddling both sides of the midterms and set in Texas and Georgia, where close Senate races are unfolding, among other states. The overall goal remains to recalibrate perceptions of the region as a GOP stronghold, which principals say is far too simplistic and out of date. In Florida, Donalds has looked to court the Black vote to gain the governorship. “You’ve been faithful to that [Democratic] party, have they been faithful to you?,” he recently told an audience at HBCU Florida A&M. Donalds would be Florida’s first Black governor, though has struggled to gain support of large numbers of Black voters, even losing 17 counties in August’s primary to white opponents. As for the Senate, flipping a Florida seat blue (the seat Nixon is seeking is currently held by Moody, who was appointed two years ago when Marco Rubio was named Secretary of State), is a nice-to-have for Florida Democrats but not seen as essential in retaking control of the Senate. Nixon says on the show that she thinks a win for her is viable. “So, honestly, there’s a whole bunch of polls,” says Nixon, as she seeks to become both the first Black senator and first female Democratic Senator in Florida’s history. “There are some ranging from tied to seven points. Recently, one was two, I was two points down, like, yesterday. And so the only poll that matters is the Election Day poll.” In an email, Palmieri said that “My takeaway is neither party can ever write off Florida. It’s too big, too dynamic to take for granted…any outcome is possible.” Added Haines: “The 2026 midterm cycle has been unpredictable — and Florida is arguably one of the biggest examples of that unpredictability.” Palmieri, a former Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama comms exec who also cohosted Showtime staple The Circus , and Haines, editor-at-large for The 19th, co-host the show with contributions from former NOLA mayor Mitch Landrieu. Circus producer Left/Right produces, and Crooked Media fixture Jon Favreau exec produces. A companion podcast will also be released. THR

articles.title: Jacob Elordi Thought He Was Having a Mental Breakdown Until He Saw a John Cassavetes Film: “Made Me Feel a Lot Less Insane and Alone”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 16, 2026 6:56pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jacob Elordi at 'The Dog Stars' world premiere at London's Odeon Luxe Leicester Square on Aug. 20, 2026. Stuart C. Wilson/Getty Images Jacob Elordi thought he was going crazy until he saw a classic John Cassavetes film . “I probably made three movies that I thought were pretty bad when I was young, and I had hopes and dreams of being this kind of terrific, ferocious stage actor. So I was pretty not fond of myself at that time,” explained the Australian actor during an event presented by Cartier Cinema Club at Santa Monica’s Aero Theatre on Friday. “And I watched this movie and it was one of the first times that I saw the creative process of an actor sort of fleshed out in detail. The movie made me feel a lot less insane and alone.” Related Stories Movies 'Coyote vs. Acme' Snags No. 2 With $15.4M as 'Spider-Man' Nears 'Avatar 2'; 'Dog Stars' Put to Sleep Movies 'The Dog Stars' Review: Jacob Elordi and Margaret Qualley in Ridley Scott's Subdued but Pleasingly Soulful Dystopian Western It proved to be such a pivotal experience in his creative life that Elordi handpicked that film — 1977’s Opening Night starring Gena Rowlands as a renowned actress teetering on the edge of a breakdown as she inches closer towards big Broadway opening night — for Friday’s screening, which marked the first stateside Cartier Cinema Club event after the initiative’s launch last month at the Venice Film Festival. The luxury house created the initiative to honor the spirit of cinema while paying tribute to artists who make big-screen work. Cartier ambassador Elordi not only selected the film, he sat for a 30-minute discussion about it alongside Oscar-winning filmmaker Sean Baker and moderator Kim Morgan. Like Rowlands’ character, Myrtle Gordon, Elordi thought he, too, “was having some form of mental breakdown.” But he was able to exhale once he saw how the storyline played out. Rowlands stars alongside Cassavetes, Ben Gazzara, Joan Blondell, Paul Stewart, Zohra Lampert and others. “This movie showed me that what was actually happening was hopefully the artistic process, the process of creating to a character. You can’t just learn the lines and say the lines. It showed me all the stuff that was going on inside that I thought was sort of my body and mind breaking down [but] was actually a part of the acting process,” explained the Oscar nominated Frankenstein star. Elordi revealed that he watched Opening Night last week in preparation for today’s event, and he had some similar thoughts to those from his first watch, notably because he’s about to start another new movie shortly that has thrown him for a loop. (Though he didn’t name the project, he’s due to start shooting Ari Aster’s Scapegoat alongside Scarlett Johansson, Jude Law, Ella Purnell and Caleb Landry Jones.) “I’m getting ready to do a movie now and I’ve been kind of throwing myself on the floor and wondering, should I just drink a lot of vodka? Or should I smash a window? What do I need to do to get to this point?” he wondered aloud. “And me re-watching the film now after making over 10 movies or something like that, again, it invited me back into the creative process and what it means. You can be searching for a character and not know that you’re searching for it. It starts happening in your toes and your knees and your chest. And that’s why I picked this movie because it always makes me feel less crazy and more like I’m actually a part of a process of filmmaking that’s been happening for a long time.” Morgan, a screenwriter known for work on Nightmare Alley directed by her husband Guillermo del Toro, then asked Elordi if that’s because he’s so absorbed by Rowlands performance. He is and was. “Yeah. I mean the amount of times that I just want to throw myself on the floor and cry and scream and tell the director to go fuck themselves and just drink and drink and drink. It makes me feel a lot less alone as an actor.” "I probably made three movies that I thought were pretty bad when I was young, and I had hopes and dreams of being this kind of terrific, ferocious stage actor. So I was pretty not fond of myself at that time," explained Jacob Elordi during an event presented by Cartier Cinema… pic.twitter.com/eNpowE9jkU — Chris Gardner (@chrissgardner) October 17, 2026 That said, Elordi drew laughs when he said that he had no clue how Rowlands’ pulled off any of her scenes on the big screen, particularly the ones where she was really throwing herself around and acting under the influence. “I don’t know how you do that and not look like a ham because everything she does is so big and so expressive, but it’s all completely contained in truth inside her. I’ve watched that scene so many times. You can spin around in circles until you’re dizzy, you can get drunk, you can do all kinds of things, but I don’t know how she does that. I don’t know how she does anything. She’s a genius.” Baker then weighed on on Cassavetes’ filmography and how inspired he is by the entirety of his work. “You get asked often as an independent filmmaker, ‘What is your favorite Cassavetes?’ And it really depends on the day because, first off, they’re all masterpieces. They deal with very personal, universal issues and struggles that we all go through. So it really depends on where you are in your life,” he explained. “It’s where I am in my life and that’s how I gravitates towards a certain title. I said Husbands back in the day because I think that was my guy film. Then when I started exploring genre cinema, I was more drawn towards The Killing of a Chinese Bookie .” Later, when he started working more with actors and honing his craft as a filmmaker, Baker then leaned more toward A Woman Under the Influence and Opening Night , he said. “I can go on forever about him. He’s basically the godfather of U.S. indie cinema and had really just in many ways I think showed us how to do it.” Morgan closed the conversation by asking both Elordi and Baker if they take inspiration from the many risks Cassavetes took throughout his career. “I think all artists should take risks,” said the Anora auteur in answering first. “Obviously he did throughout his entire career, which may be hurt in the moment. He was always ahead of his time, but it also proves one very important thing — that cream rises. We’re here 50 years later talking about this film and celebrating this film? That proves that taking risks, staying true to your own, not compromising, and making art that’s a little unsafe is worth it.” Baker’s words generated an enthusiastic round of applause. “[Cassavetes] said something like, ‘I’d love to be part of the studio system and have my rent paid and my family good, but I just can’t do it. I’d love to, but I just can’t do it.’ And that’s my favorite thing about these movies. There was no other story he could have told. It made him too ferocious and angry or upset. There was no other way that he could have made movies,” Elordi added in closing. “In movies now, we need a lot of that. Something that you can’t deny, something that you have to do, no matter if it sends you broke, hungry, tired, jobless, you’ve got to make that movie that you have to make. And that’s exactly what we do.” THR

articles.title: Miley Cyrus Tearfully Pays Tribute to Dolly Parton With “Jolene” Performance at Hollywood Bowl: “Me and Dolly, We Are Eternal”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Nicole Fell , McKinley Franklin October 16, 2026 9:48pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Dolly Parton and Miley Cyrus perform onstage during the 61st Annual Grammy Awards. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for The Recording Academy Miley Cyrus broke down in tears at her Hollywood Bowl performance Friday night during a moving tribute to her godmother, the late Dolly Parton . The singer projected a photo of the country music icon as the beginning notes of her iconic song “Jolene” played. The Grammy winner told the crowd that one of the things that inspired her to play the venue was the memory of the only time she was able to sit and enjoy a Parton show at the Hollywood Bowl. She recalling telling her “Aunt Dolly” that for once, she just wanted to sit in the crowd and enjoy her like everyone else. Cyrus began, “If she had it her way, and she was playing a show, I’d be standing right beside her in a matching costume. And so when I was coming to the show at the Bowl to see her, I said, you know, ‘I would love a night where I can just experience you. I can just enjoy you like the rest of the world has gotten to.'” Related Stories Music Reba McEntire Reveals She Missed a Call From Dolly Parton Before Her Death: "I'll Never Know Why She Called" Movies Dolly Parton's '9 to 5' Comedy Returning to Theaters to Support Late Icon's Foundation The “Flowers” singer said her godmother responded by saying, “Okay, Miley,” but Cyrus joked “that never means okay.” Instead of having Cyrus onstage to perform alongside her, Parton instead opened the show with “The Best of Both Worlds,” Cryus’ hit track from Hannah Montana : “All of a sudden, Dolly enters, but I hear ‘The Best of Both Worlds.’ Yeah, Dolly opened performing Hannah Montana.” “But that’s just not the end of that story,” she continued. “And she goes, like a proud aunt, ‘I don’t know if y’all know this, but my goddaughter is Hannah Montana, and she’s actually here tonight, but she’s sitting out in her seat. She didn’t want anyone to bug her. She said she just wanted to watch the show,’ which defeated the entire purpose of the conversation that we had just had, because absolutely no one was aware that I was at the concert until she drew an obnoxious amount of attention to it.” “But like so many things Dolly did, I didn’t understand at the time,” Cyrus said, adding that she could feel Parton’s presence with her during her Hollywood Bowl performance. “Sitting here with you all right now, feeling her all around me, knowing that she’s right here beside me, every day, more than she could be when she was here; I feel her more now than ever,” she said. “Knowing that I get to share this story with you all, it makes that night very worth it. This memory is gold to me. Me and Dolly, we are eternal. Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart, and I’m gonna see her again.” “And I can’t fucking wait because I miss her,” Cyrus said in between tears. “Some of the greatest music that we have today was written, produced, performed by my Aunt Dolly, and this is one of those songs,” she concluded before launching into a rendition of “Jolene.” Parton died Aug. 25, after a “brief battle with cancer,” a rep announced. She was 80. Many celebrities paid tribute to the queen of country music after her death, including Cyrus who penned a tribute , writing on Instagram, “The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share.” “I have an angel by my side. I always have. One of our last conversations was about music and metamorphosis. I will always love her and want to make her proud,” she wrote. “My heart breaks for the world, her family and friends who will miss her deeply. We’re in this loss together and we will see her in all of the most beautiful things.” During Cyrus’ Friday night show, she also clutched a frame in the shape of a heart with an image of Parton during “Wrecking Ball,” as that was one of her favorite songs. The Grammy winner played her first of two shows at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday. Her next performance will be on Sunday. Cyrus recently dropped her 10th studio album Bass Persuades on Sept. 18. THR

articles.title: ‘Perfect Road’ Is a Doc That Follows a Nomadic Cyclist Pursuing Grueling Challenges – and Freedom
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 17, 2026 1:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Perfect Road' Courtesy of Elk Film Years ago, Maximilian Schnell left his job and his life in Paris and began a nomadic lifestyle on his bicycle. The road has given him freedom and adventure. And he has set himself grueling physical and mental challenges. Perfect Road , a documentary from Danish directors and cousins Adam and Christian Bonke, follows him on an extreme journey through some of Europe’s highest mountain passes, while also providing a meditation on modern life and character study. For one, even in an age of digital nomads, Schnell’s lifestyle pushes the envelope. And then, his relationship with his partner Nina makes him question his life priorities. Related Stories Business BBC Asks Judge to Force Trump to Sit for Deposition in His Own Lawsuit Against Broadcaster Movies James McAvoy Reveals Which Film Paid Him "Bonkers" Residuals So, get ready for mountain vistas and exhausting cycling days to take your breath away and questions about your life choices to swirl around in your head! Elk Film and Dogwoof produced Perfect Road , with Andreas Dalsgaard, Anna Godas, Oli Harbottle, Miriam Nørgaard serving as producers. Jonatan Mose served as cinematographer, with editing handled by Martin Anthon. After its Zurich Film Festival world premiere, Perfect Road has been screening at the 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival . THR talked about the film with the Bonkes in London and checked in with Schnell via Zoom in Bolzano. “I had planned the challenge for seven or eight months, maybe a year,” Schnell tells THR . “From what I’ve understood about the film industry, it’s a very long-term process because writing the script, financing the movie, and things like that take a long time, and usually you do that before [shooting] the film.” So when he agreed to the project, he made very clear that the film team had to make things work on his schedule. “I would not postpone the challenge by two years,” he emphasizes. “And I was super clear about that from the first day.” ‘Perfect Road,’ courtesy of Elk Film The film team had to come up with a strategy to capture as much as possible without interfering with Schnell’s challenge. “I always said the same thing,” the cyclist recalls. “‘I’m in my challenge, and I live my life. If you want to do a documentary, it really has to be a documentary. There’s no way I will act anything. There’s no way I will repeat any scene.’ I said, ‘You deal with whatever you can get, but I don’t adapt to you. I don’t want the filmmaking to take a single piece of energy out of me.’ So basically, we’re two distinct entities. They were trying to film something, and I tried to achieve something, and that’s it.” The filmmakers mulled various plans for how to best capture footage. In the process, they embarked on an adventure that involved living three months in a campervan and not only filming technology and nature but also all sorts of other winding roads. “We thought initially that we would have several DPs over the course of three months,” Christian Bonke tells THR . “But then our DP was kicked out by his girlfriend, and he had nowhere to stay. So he said, ‘I’m going to do all three months. This is perfect for me.’ And Adam and I took turns.” You don’t have to worry about the cinematographer, though. “He said, ‘I’ll come back a different man,'” Adam Bonke shares. “And he did. He came back, and he got back with his girlfriend, and now they have twins.” What helped the Bonkes with the planning of the expedition was the man they followed. “Max is very organized. And he is a nerd when it comes to planning and mapping,” Adam Bonke tells THR . “So we did knew pretty much every day where he would be, which peaks he would climb, and we could look 12 days ahead and say, ‘Okay, he’s going to be in Austria on this peak then, and in 16 days he’s going to be there.’ There were some delays, of course, when the weather hit, but he actually stuck to the plan amazingly.” Schnell was adamant that the film crew couldn’t provide any help to him. “At some points, we were thinking that maybe the crew could take a set of tires, so that if my tires wear out, I would have them in their car,” he shares. “But I didn’t want them to take energy from me, and I also didn’t want any advantage.” Christian Bonke highlights how Schnell stuck to his independence and indeed took on the mountain challenge without help throughout the journey. “Many nights, we wanted to invite him inside the campervan and offer him some food,” he says. “But he really refrained from that. He was in the van once for a very short period.” ‘Perfect Road,’ courtesy of Elk Film Adds Adam: “Yeah, we just wanted to show him what we were doing, what we were filming. And he came in for two minutes and then left again.” With Schnell valuing his freedom and nature so much, the filmmaker duo also noticed that at times, he needed more space. “Initially, he was thrilled that we would make the film, but he was so concentrated on the difficult physical task,” says Christian. “So very soon he also became a little tired of the camera being there. One of his core values is solitude, but he had three of us going around with him all the time.” Adds Adam: “I think the worst thing for him probably was this fact that there was a car behind him, because he really loves nature, silence, solitude and just being in that moment. And then there we were in a diesel van behind him a lot of the time.” Concludes Christian: “So, we were focusing on not being too intrusive. I think we let him be in the zone, and I think you can almost feel that sometimes he got so used to us being around that he didn’t even notice us.” That said, the filmmaker duo had to be ready to capture any unusual encounters or special moments. “We quickly learned, and we had predicted this, that, of course, filming a guy going up and down mountains every day is going to get repetitive,” recalls Adam. “It’s going to get boring. So we really needed to be there when he did something else, when he met someone, when he was with friends, when he had conversations with other human beings. We wanted to give him space when we could, but we also really needed to be there when something social happened.” Does the film team feel the camera did have an impact on Schnell? “It’s interesting what a camera does to you in a way. I think you start to reflect somehow,” offers Christian Bonke. “There’s almost a metaphysical element to him sensing our gaze. Early on, he said to us that maybe he was contemplating whether he could continue his whole life like this. So that was something lingering in the back of his mind. He ended up living like that for almost 10 years, sleeping in a tent every night.” 1 Indeed, things have changed a bit since the film shoot three years ago. Asked if he was planning any new big mountain challenges, Schnell tells THR : “There has not been one single idea in those three years since the challenge that really sounded sexy enough to just go for. I mean, I’m in a challenge because I now have a base camp here in Bolzano. It’s quite a challenge to settle somewhere. I create backpacking events, so it’s a different challenge. It’s not a dramatic, sporty challenge, but for me, it’s challenging.” Could people see Schnell in another movie or series? “You never say never, but not a documentary – that’s for sure,” he shares. The cyclist leaves it up to viewers of Perfect Road what they want to or actually do take away from the film experience. The filmmaker duo has taken something with them from those months in the campervan. “We often talk about how we miss those days,” Christian Bonke tells THR . “It was so beautiful, and you felt embraced by nature. After meeting Max, we were completely struck by how conventional our lives at home were and how many constraints they had. So we could get a little glimpse of living differently.” And Adam Bonke shares with THR : “He says he’s trading comfort for freedom. That’s such a nice thing to say. And it really frames things perfectly. We were interested in learning what that price of freedom potentially is. I think we can all somehow relate to what he’s done. We all fantasize from time to time about leaving, about changing things, doing something radical with our lives. But very few of us do anything. Whether you’re interested in cycling or not, this is a guy who actually did something radical with his life.” You have to watch Perfect Road to see how you feel about pushing the boundaries of freedom to their limit. THR

articles.title: Joe Keery On Making His Broadway Debut and Balancing Music and Acting Post-‘Stranger Things’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All October 17, 2026 5:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Marc Piasecki/WireImage Joe Keery is making his Broadway debut in Other Desert Cities this fall, playing a character who at first seems like a smooth Hollywood talker, but ultimately just wants to keep his family together. Or, as he puts it, “My goal, I’ve joked to myself for the next 105 or whatever shows, is to save Christmas.” The play, written by Jon Robin Baitz and directed by John Benjamin Hickey, was an easy “Yes” for Keery, who had been wanting to back into theater after starring as Steve Harrington in Stranger Things , as he had developed a love for the stage growing up and in drama school. What made it easier was the cast members for the play, which started with Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Allison Janney and Ed Harris. “The original reading that I did, it was Julia and Allison and Ed doing that reading. So, yeah, big fans of those three in there. That’s the sort of email you get, and you say, “Holy shit! OK, great. Yeah, I will do that,’” Keery said. Lily Rabe later joined the cast, playing Keery’s sister. She sets the plot into motion as she and Keery visit their conservative parents (Louis-Dreyfus and Harris) for the holidays, and she brings a copy of a new book she’s written that uncovers dirt from the family’s past. Rabe asks for her parents’ blessing to release the book, despite it casting them in a negative light, while Keery’s character acts as the intermediary as tensions erupt, including with Louis-Dreyfus’s sister (Janney). The play opens Oct. 18 at the Hudson Theatre for a run through Jan. 17. Making the show work within Keery’s schedule was a challenge. In addition to his onscreen career, Keery is a musician, performing under the stage name Djo, with songs including “End of Beginning,” which went viral on TikTok and climbed the Billboard Hot 100. In early 2026, he toured Mexico and South America before going on to be the opening act for Tame Impala. And he had been on the U.K. leg of his own tour right before rehearsals for the play began. “It was a rather blunt turnover,” Keery said. “I finished on a Sunday, flew on a Monday, and then started rehearsing on a Tuesday. The first week or two, I was definitely feeling maybe the whiplash of it all, but I just had to make it work.” Amid the starry names on the stage, Keery has one of the standout monologues, in which he points out the love the family actually has for each other, despite the bickering, and how Rabe’s book and overall view on her family may not be entirely truthful and inherently, harmful, despite its artistic value. Preparing for that speech required a deep collaboration with Hickey, as well as learning to internalize the character. “I learned my lines, and then you realize you don’t know them at all, and then you have to learn them all over again. A ton of my work that I end up doing is just trying to, as much as possible, get things into my brain and my body by moving. So, generally, it involves a lot of walking and a lot of talking to myself, and then rehearsing,” Keery said. And despite his initial awe at the cast members, including Rabe, Keery said now that they’re on stage, it feels just like being in a high school play. “There’s something about doing a play that, you kind of have to leave your ego at the door. Everyone’s doing it because they want to do it. Everyone’s doing it because they love it. So, I think it’s kind of this great equalizer,” he said. Keery is one of the latest Stranger Things cast members to come to the New York stage, following Gaten Matarazzo, Maya Hawke and more. He was encouraged to do so by Sadie Sink, who returned to Broadway in 2025 John Proctor is the Villain . Keery appeared in several independent films throughout Stranger Things as well as in the television series Fargo. Going forward, Keery said he plans to continue both acting and performing as a musician, but he doesn’t have an exact calculation on how it will balance out. He adds that post- Stranger Things , he hasn’t planned out any dream roles, per se, but rather continues to look for parts that feel new and challenging. “It’s never really up to you. I mean, it’s not like I have like my pick of the litter of these things,” Keery said. “I’m sort of a big believer in the right things kind of coming my way, and trusting my gut on what I want to be doing, just like day to day.“ THR

articles.title: The Impossible ‘Whalefall’: Director Brian Duffield Wanted a Challenge, So He Discovered a Way to Crush Austin Abrams in a Whale Stomach That Left Onlookers ‘Baffled’
articles.full_text: Dan Doperalski for Variety Turns out that it’s tough to shoot in a whale’s stomach. “ Whalefall ” director Brian Duffield is gleefully outlining some of the biggest hurdles while shooting his new movie. The premise for the film, in theaters now via 20th Century Studios, is simple: A young diver named Jay ( Austin Abrams ) is accidentally swallowed by a whale, ends up in its stomach and must escape before his tank of oxygen runs out. It’s a lean idea, but required an innovative and energetic leader like Duffield to get the claustrophobic shots done on practical sets. Related Stories Danielle Ponder Meshes Old-School Soul With Future Sounds on the Dazzling ‘Everything Has Changed’: Album Review 'Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald' Review: Judd Apatow's Juicy and Haunting Portrait of a Comedy Star as Troubled as He Was Hilarious “It’s such a small space and essentially a 360-degree set,” he says. “There’s a couple portals you can kind of shove a camera through, but it’s also somewhat full of water. All the lighting of the coil is inside the set. Basically everything that you would have on a normal movie set, we’re putting inside of a very small space. It’s also on a gimbal that’s rocking and rolling. So you take your normal film set footprint and then you put it into a bag. And then you also put Austin Abrams into the bag, and then sometimes other animals. If Austin’s wrong an inch, it doesn’t really work. Everyone’s cramped in this little doorway. But he can’t hear us, because the rubber is so thick inside.” Popular on Variety Duffield smiles at the outrageous setup. “I was talking to a director,” he says. “He had a question and I sent him pictures of the set. And he was just like, ‘You’ve got to be joking.’ From when the whale is chewing Austin, it’s just a bunch of big, burly men jumping on the set and crushing down on him. And he’s in there, screaming and drowning with a real oxygen tank. I’m looking at this little monitor and if he needs help, it’s going to sound the exact same. Every time you call cut, you’re just hoping that the screaming stops. We had the studio come to set and watch this thing. From the outside it just looked so silly. I remember Disney safety reps would come and just be watching it, saying, ‘I genuinely don’t know if this is safe.’ But we worked hard, really hard to make sure Austin was safe.” Brian Duffield photographed at the PMC Studio in Los Angeles. Dan Doperalski for Variety Everyone made it out of the shoot unharmed, but the finished product is filled with harrowing set-pieces that are sure to push audiences to the brink. Duffield understood the vision early on, as he reached out to novelist Daniel Kraus on social media when he first heard the premise of the novel of the same name, before it was even published. He read an advance copy of the 2023 book, and was quickly swept away with the cinematic promise it held. Duffield ended up co-writing the “Whalefall” script with Kraus. “You get the initial ‘boy inside a whale’ story, which definitely tickled all the genre parts of my brain,” Duffield says. “The idea of making a movie that had never been made before is always really appealing to me. It’s instantly clear how challenging that was, and I was really looking for a challenge. I was hungry to just keep pushing myself and the crew that I had consistently been working with. I think we just had the appetite at the time to take a big swing.” Duffield is no stranger to ambitious projects. He began his Hollywood career as a writer with a disparate group of scripts, including a big-budget sequel (2015’s “The Divergent Series: Insurgent”), a Western (2015’s “Jane Got a Gun”), a slasher (2017’s “The Babysitter”) and a sci-fi action movie (2020’s “Underwater”). He transitioned into an idiosyncratic directing career with 2020’s “Spontaneous” (logline: a romance is shaded by the fact that people start spontaneously combusting) and 2023’s “No One Will Save You,” a nearly dialogue-free alien invasion movie. Beyond their high concepts, Duffield’s works are marked by an emotional heft, which is no different in “Whalefall.” Jay’s diving trip is prompted by him trying to locate the body of his estranged father Mitt (Josh Brolin) after he dies by suicide. He’d never be able make amends with, or come to an understanding with his father, a theme that resonates through much of the story. “I don’t think I was looking for a father-son story, but I think I needed a father-son story,” Duffield, a parent himself, says. “As soon as I was reading it, I couldn’t stop thinking about … not the whale, but about Jay and Mitt in that relationship. I thought, ‘That was the magic trick of the book.’ You’re forgetting about squids and acid and you’re thinking more about how these two guys are thinking they want nothing more than to spend time together, but they can’t quite express how they need to spend time in a different way.” Brian Duffield photographed at the PMC Studio in Los Angeles in October 2026. Dan Doperalski for Variety While Abrams and Brolin were able to bring the emotional gravitas to flashback scenes chronicling key moments in their frayed relationship, shooting the in-whale scenes was the overarching creative challenge. “I had plenty of directors come and visit and all of them just looked so baffled,” Duffield says. “I had general confusion about how we were doing what we were doing. The thing I’ve learned the most is the joy of making movies for me is the crew and getting to hire a lot of the same people over and over again. I think if I have any gift as a director, it’s hiring people that are extremely talented, Oscar winners and whatnot. I like spending time with them and feel comfortable asking advice. I trust them if I feel like they have a note or an idea — it’s probably good.” It’s part of a larger ethos Duffield brings to every project. “I want to feel the effort, and I want to feel like I’m becoming a better filmmaker because of it,” he says. articles.title: How Netflix’s Messy Transition Will Rock Hollywood: Looking at You, NBCU
articles.full_text: Oct 16, 2026 6:13pm PT How Netflix’s Messy Transition Will Rock Hollywood: Looking at You, NBCU The upheaval of Peter Rice’s appointment and Bela Bajaria’s ouster as chief content officer sets off speculation about the streaming giant’s next moves By Matt Donnelly , Cynthia Littleton , Michael Schneider Add us as a Google Preferred Source Peter Rice, top left, Bela Bajaria, Dan Lin and Jinny Howe Getty It started with a dinner. Peter Rice and Ynon Kreiz met for a meal in late September, days before Kreiz surprised the industry by jumping from the CEO job at Mattel to become co-chief executive of Skydance with David Ellison. The report of the Kreiz-Rice meeting came in the New York Post’s Page Six after Kreiz’s role at Skydance was announced. That set off speculation that he was recruiting Rice for a big role at the enlarged studio. It turns out Kreiz had been trying to persuade Rice to take a board seat at Barbie’s house. Related Stories Linda Cardellini Leads Peacock’s Bold and Bloody ‘Friday the 13th’ Prequel ‘Crystal Lake’: TV Review 'Satoko Always' Review: A Trio of Women Find Their Inner Voice in Shuichi Okita’s Delightful Celebration of the Art of Writing Rice, however, was not destined to advise on matters of Uno and Matchbox cars. The former Fox Searchlight and Fox Networks Group chief — who went to Disney in 2019 as its top TV executive only to be unceremoniously axed during the Chapek regime — has vaulted back to one of the town’s most powerful posts: chief content officer of Netflix . Popular on Variety Media coverage of Kreiz’s courtship of Rice is one of the spurs that pushed Netflix to make the move on a hire that will have ripple effects across its expansive film and TV operations. The ouster of Bela Bajaria from the role that Rice now occupies was messy, and angered many inside and outside of Netflix. “We don’t live in Hollywood right now. We live in Silicon Valley,” said a prominent agent, citing the general mood of the creative community. The brusque treatment of an executive of Bajaria’s stature is a sign that no one is safe from scrutiny, and no one should ever count on making a graceful exit. LISTEN to Variety’s Matt Donnelly, Cynthia Littleton and Michael Schneider break down the shakeup at Netflix “It feels like more of a tech approach than a studio approach to letting someone go. It’s shameful, it sucks and it adds to the feeling that we’re all working by Silicon Valley rules,” the agent said. The source noted the irony of Bajaria getting the ax just two weeks after the executive that she replaced at Netflix — Cindy Holland — was also hastily ousted from her new role at Skydance. Holland’s role was sacrificed to make room for Casey Bloys, the HBO chief who is taking over all streaming now that the Warner Bros. Discovery merger is completed. The bombshell executive upheaval at Netflix, coupled with signals that insiders are reading from the layoffs that Netflix implemented this week, has set off renewed speculation about the streaming giant getting back in the hunt for a major studio or some other significant content assets. NBCUniversal is a logical target, given that the company will be spun out from Comcast next year and thus would make for a much smaller and more manageable acquisition than the entirety of Comcast. The switch to Rice also raises questions about whether Netflix will remain as aggressive in its local-language content strategy as it had been under Bajaria. Rice’s reference in his first memo to Netflix staffers to the need to deliver more buzzy hits for the “UCAN” market (Netflix’s wonky term for the United States and Canada) did not go unnoticed. Bajaria, according to multiple sources, learned the harsh reality of her fate on Wednesday evening when she cornered Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos at the streamer’s offices in Hollywood, just before the screening at a private residence in L.A. for the Season 3 premiere of comedy “Nobody Wants This.” (Notably, neither Sarandos nor Bajaria are seen in any of the publicity photos that have been shared from the event.) Bajaria asked Sarandos point-blank whether there was truth to the rumors gaining stream — and Sarandos, who it’s believed was originally going to break the news on Monday, told her at that moment. Rumors about Bajaria’s fate have swirled in recent months. As the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger saga soldiered on, there was much speculation about HBO chief Bloys jumping ship for a big role at Netflix or to launch a well-funded prestige label for the streamer. But once Bloys was confirmed as the new top boss of streaming for Skydance, the Bajaria speculation cooled off. On Monday, Bajaria was on stage at the Mipcom content conference in Cannes, where she accepted the Vanguard Award for contributions to the global marketplace as bestowed by Variety and Mipcom. But even as top European content industry insiders gathered to hear Bajaria speak, chatter about her future fired back up in Hollywood this week. It turned out to be a perfect storm of events, with Netflix bracing for its largest-ever layoffs and its third-quarter earnings report coming on Oct. 20. The layoffs, amounting to 6% of the company’s workforce, or about 1,000 positions, were implemented Tuesday and Wednesday. That meant Netflix staffers were already on edge when the shock of the Rice news hit just after lunchtime in L.A. on Thursday. Meanwhile, as recently as two weeks ago Rice was telling friends that he had no interest in becoming an executive again — which is a sign that Sarandos acted fast as soon as he learned Rice was available. Bajaria is understood to have received an outpouring of support from her wide network of contacts in the creative community, at home and abroad. Multiple sources say the executive has been telling friends outright that she is shell-shocked, in keeping with her reputation for candor. Bajaria declined to comment. The microscope now turns to Bajaria’s two top vertical lieutenants — Dan Lin in film, and Jinny Howe in original TV series. Lin has been a steady hand in Netflix’s film operations for two-and-a-half years, ushered in to stop the lavish spending of the streamer’s formative Scott Stuber era. Slashing budgets carries an emotional price, though, and Lin has been forced to ensure talent delivers quality product without a widely perceived blank check signed by Sarandos. In addition to making cheaper movies, Lin also backed some high-profile acquisitions (“Emilia Pérez” and Netflix’s current best-hope Oscar contender “La Bola Negra”). Yet, numerous reports have suggested that Lin will exit the company as Rice comes into power. It couldn’t be a more sensitive time, as Netflix will launch Greta Gerwig’s anticipated “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” with a full theatrical release in February. As Bajaria got the boot, the rumor mill instantly offered forth Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy — the ousted Warner Bros. Pictures chiefs — as potential replacements (which actually started a month ago, as Paramount and WBD finally found a path to combine). According to insiders, with Rice likely to kick off his tenure by focusing on the film side of things, U.S. and Canada scripted head Howe appears to be safe in her role. With whispers in Hollywood that Netflix has struggled recently to produce another megahit in the vein of “Stranger Things” or “Bridgerton,” Howe, who took over in August 2025, has a hefty slate on her plate and is just starting to see some of her own development come to fruition. That includes Meryl Streep in “The Corrections,” Adam Driver and Michael Fassbender in “Rabbit, Rabbit,” Martin Scorsese’s “The Roman” and the live-action/CGI “Scooby-Doo: Origins.” “They want her to stay,” said one source. “If she left, that’d be a disaster for them.” Meanwhile, given Rice’s experience, some also wondered whether Sarandos just hired someone who could ultimately be a candidate to replace him — should the stock continue to suffer and the company see a need to make more changes. The week has indeed offered more drama than anything Netflix will put on its service this year.
