articles.title: ‘Renoir’ Producers Join Asia-Europe Co-Production Panel at Tokyo Market as Japanese Accelerator Atmovie Global Track Partners With Ties That Bind
articles.full_text: Oct 16, 2026 10:37pm PT ‘Renoir’ Producers Join Asia-Europe Co-Production Panel at Tokyo Market as Japanese Accelerator Atmovie Global Track Partners With Ties That Bind By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Renoir’ Producers Join Asia-Europe Co-Production Panel at Tokyo Market as Japanese Accelerator Atmovie Global Track Partners With Ties That Bind 7 hours ago Indonesian Zombie Franchise ‘Zona Merah: Dead City’ Unveils Teaser, Takes Outbreak Into the City 23 hours ago Boo Junfeng’s ‘Trinity,’ Sidharta Tata’s ‘Slaughterground’ Among JAFF Market 2026 Selections 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Atmovie Global Track Producers behind Hayakawa Chie’s Cannes competition title “ Renoir ” are among the speakers at a session on Asia-Europe co-production at Tokyo’s TIFFCOM market on Oct. 30, as Japanese accelerator Atmovie Global Track formalizes a partnership with Europe-based workshop Ties That Bind. The open panel, titled “Building Creative Partnerships,” will examine how producers and directors work together to bring projects up to an international level, drawing on case studies of films made between the two regions. It will run in tandem with the Tokyo International Film Festival , and any TIFFCOM badge holder can attend. Related Stories 'Silver Express' Review: Miki Tanaka's Sensitive Debut Feature Explores Asexual and Aromantic Identity For the Love of Television, Please Watch 'The Lowdown' Season 2: TV Review On the panel are Mizuno-Gray Eiko, CEO of Tokyo-based Loaded Films, and French producer Christophe Bruncher of Ici et Là Productions, who both worked on “Renoir,” which competed at Cannes in 2025. Mizuno-Gray’s credits also include Hayakawa’s “Plan 75,” which received a special mention for the Caméra d’Or at Cannes in 2022 and went on to become Japan’s Oscar entry, as well as Kurosawa Kiyoshi’s “To the Ends of the Earth.” She is developing a Poland-Japan co-production from director Ishikawa Kei and a Japan-Philippines project from Hirayanagi Atsuko, and is also a support producer on the accelerator. She also sits on the Tokyo festival’s Asian Future jury this year. Popular on Variety Bruncher, a La Fémis graduate who speaks Mandarin, is head of studies for Ties That Bind. His recent co-productions include Muriel d’Ansembourg’s Berlinale title “Truly Naked” and Kamila Andini’s Toronto selection “Four Seasons in Java,” both of which feature at this year’s Tokyo festival. Joining them are Oh Heejung, the Seoul- and Amsterdam-based founder of Seesaw Pictures, whose films have played Sundance, Berlin, Locarno, IDFA, Rotterdam and Busan, and Moriya Takeshi, the Atmovie CEO who founded the accelerator. Moriya’s producing credits span TV series “Midnight Diner” and Uchida Eiji’s “Midnight Swan,” which was named picture of the year at the 44th Japan Academy Film Prizes. Atmovie Global Track producer Sekiguchi Mio, whose credits include Uchida’s “Fiamma,” curated the panel. Ahead of the public event, Oh and Bruncher will mentor a closed two-day workshop for the accelerator’s fellows on Oct. 27 and 28, built around group sessions in which participants will develop their projects and discuss career paths rather than sit through lectures. The overall program was curated by Alessandro Gropplero, who runs the Friuli Venezia Giulia Audiovisual Fund and co-founded Ties That Bind, which the FVG fund organizes with EAVE and the Udine Far East Film Festival. The workshop brings European and Asian producers together on project development, financing, co-production opportunities and networking. Atmovie Global Track prepares Japanese filmmakers to take original projects into the international co-production market through lectures and mentoring from Japanese and overseas industry figures. Selected fellows pitch at festivals, with milestones including the Japan Pavilion at Cannes in May 2025 and the Japan Pitch event at the Busan International Film Festival in October. The organizers said many creators struggle to build trust across cultures and to communicate outside their native language, and that the open session is meant to share lessons with the wider industry and grow the network of Japanese filmmakers pursuing international work. Support for the program comes from the Japan Creator Support Fund, which the Japan Arts Council created using Agency for Cultural Affairs funding. articles.title: Miley Cyrus Embraces Being the Anti-Pop Pop Star With Her First ‘Bass Persuades’ Concert at Hollywood Bowl: Concert Review
articles.full_text: Oct 17, 2026 12:53am PT Miley Cyrus Embraces Being the Anti-Pop Pop Star With Her First ‘Bass Persuades’ Concert at Hollywood Bowl: Concert Review By Steven J. Horowitz Plus Icon Steven J. Horowitz Senior Music Writer speriod Latest Miley Cyrus Embraces Being the Anti-Pop Pop Star With Her First ‘Bass Persuades’ Concert at Hollywood Bowl: Concert Review 5 hours ago Miley Cyrus Setlist: Every Song Played at ‘Bass Persuades – Live at the Hollywood Bowl’ 9 hours ago Rachel Chinouriri on How Sobriety and Self-Actualization Inspired Her Sophomore Album ‘I Think I Spoke Too Soon’: ‘It Was Like Doing an Autopsy on Myself’ 22 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Vijat Mohindra After she descended from a B-stage in the middle of the stands at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday night, Miley Cyrus sat hunched over on the main stage , visibly sapped by the 200-foot trek back to the spotlight. “You guys gave me so much energy, but you also took a little energy out of me, too,” she said. “It is a lot for me, if you could imagine walking from where I was through each of you and feeling how much passion and how much love each of you radiates to me. And I appreciate you so much. But it is a lot for me and it is a little bit overwhelming.” Related Stories 'Beach Fictions' Review: Utterly Beguiling, Time-Tweaking Korean Romance Shows What a Day a Difference Makes Catherine Zeta-Jones Can’t Save AMC+’s Stylish but Lackluster Thriller ‘Kill Jackie’: TV Review It’s an admission that a seasoned pop star — one of our biggest and brightest, mind you — would rarely deign to make at their first major show in years. And yet, it felt like the thesis for the first of two concerts Cyrus is performing in Los Angeles in support of her latest album “Bass Persuades,” a record with a few bright moments but lacking the singular vision that defined some of her strongest work. Across the nearly two-hour set, Cyrus appeared at odds with the pressures of being a generational talent, proudly chasing her muse with full-throated renditions of fresher, more opaque material while letting the audience carry the vocals on her biggest hits. It was confounding, oftentimes bizarre and, in the end, strangely entertaining, a snapshot of a megastar who, after all this time, is still figuring out what artist she wants to become. Popular on Variety That’s the thrill for anyone who has followed Cyrus’ career since she emerged as a Disney star with “Hannah Montana,” trying on different styles while navigating the mercurial sound of mainstream pop. She’s shape-shifted at a moment’s notice, chasing massive hits with pivots into deeply unconventional genres and sounds, beginning with her reinventive “Bangerz” era in 2013 and its subsequent global trek, her last extensive tour. Since then, she’s remained prolific and expansive, traipsing from psych-pop (“ Miley Cyrus & Her Dead Petz”) to glam rock (“Plastic Hearts”) and, perhaps not accidentally, stumbling into a few massive hits along the way, with songs like “Wrecking Ball” and “Flowers” that she let the audience carry during the Bowl show. Miley Cyrus twerks during “We Can’t Stop” at her Hollywood Bowl show pic.twitter.com/qE3nBto7rG — Variety (@Variety) October 17, 2026 On Friday night, Cyrus hewed closely to her new material with tracks from “Bass Persuades” and a few from 2025’s wildly ambitious “Something Beautiful.” She’s performed so rarely that nearly half the songs on the setlist were live debuts: Over the past few years, Cyrus staged only two fans-only shows in Los Angeles and Paris, appearances that reinforced her strengths as a performer without heeding to the pressures — interviews, TV appearances, radio drops — that come with it. Yet Cyrus was quick to ground the show in her reality, one where she’s learned to balance her public and private lives. “For somebody that likes to keep life fun, and likes to jump out of airplanes and be spontaneous, doing the same thing for your entire life can lose its shine if you don’t continue to give yourself that pressure and polish to create something beautiful, which is the life that I’m living,” she said, leading into the title track from “Something Beautiful.” For Cyrus, that’s meant stretching the boundaries of pop music and, by proxy, pop stardom. All bets were off as she opened with “Orbit,” a very languid ballad about the magnetism of romance. Already the pace was unpredictable, giving way to the zapping synth-pop of “Different Religion” (with featuring and opening act Model/Actriz) and Fentanyl-rejecting “Bass Persuades.” She let her freak flag fly with Flaming Lips’ frontman Wayne Coyne on the B stage for the group’s “Do You Realize??” and their collaboration “Karen Don’t Be Sad,” and strutted across the catwalk at the lip of the stage for “Walk of Fame,” one of the more supermodel songs in her discography. Amid her musings on fame, she struck a truly emotive moment in remembrance of her godmother Dolly Parton, recalling that the only time she had seen her perform was at the Bowl some years back. “Like so many things Dolly did that I didn’t understand at the time, sitting here with you all right now, feeling her all around me, knowing that she’s right here beside me every day, all the time, more than she could be when she was here, I feel her more than ever,” she said, choking back tears as she led into a cover of “Jolene.” “And knowing that I get to share this story with you all, it makes that night very worth it. This memory is gold to me. Me and Dolly, we are eternal. Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart. And I’m going to see her again, and I can’t fucking wait because I miss her.” Miley Cyrus breaks down in tears as she pays tribute to Dolly Parton at her Hollywood Bowl show: “Me and Dolly are eternal.” ❤️ pic.twitter.com/oOmXgsmg8F — Variety (@Variety) October 17, 2026 That’s where she felt most at home, belting out those familiar notes of “Jolene” as she’s done so many times before. So it was strange that she largely held the mic towards the crowd for her bigger hits, “We Can’t Stop” and “Party in the U.S.A.,” where Coyne reemerged with a gigantic assortment of balloons that spelled “Fuck Yeah Hollywood Bowl.” Cyrus seemed removed from those tracks, aware of the power they held over the attending crowd while recognizing they had become so woven into the cultural fabric that they no longer belonged just to her. Perhaps that’s why the first of Cyrus’ shows at the Hollywood Bowl felt so possessive, so intrinsically tied to her recent eras and willing to explore them. There were no traditional dance breaks or wild set pieces to accent the songs; here was Cyrus, 33 years old, coming out on the other end of the hit factory with the freedom to be who she’s meant to be. Whether that’s satisfactory is of little significance when, across two sold-out nights, 18,000 fans are still pining to witness it. articles.title: Coen Brothers Bring Laughs to Lumière Award Ceremony as Javier Bardem Recalls ‘No Country for Old Men’: ‘They Gave Me One Masterpiece’
articles.full_text: Oct 17, 2026 2:20am PT Coen Brothers Bring Laughs to Lumière Award Ceremony as Javier Bardem Recalls ‘No Country for Old Men’: ‘They Gave Me One Masterpiece’ Javier Bardem pays tribute to the Oscar-winning filmmakers with stories from 'No Country for Old Men,' while musical performances and onstage banter mark the Lyon celebration By Lise Pedersen , Elsa Keslassy Add us as a Google Preferred Source Joel and Ethan Coen accept Lumière Award, applauded by Frances McDormand, Javier Bardem, Benoît Magimel Oct. 16, 2026 Courtesy of the Lumiére Film Festival To the sound of the Gipsy Kings’ Spanish-language rendition of “Hotel California,” Joel and Ethan Coen took the stage at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival on Friday evening to receive the Lumière Award, celebrating four decades of filmmaking with a characteristically irreverent tribute to the inventors of cinema. “Thank you to the Lumières for inventing the movie camera, or we’d have been fucked,” joked Ethan, drawing laughs from the audience. Related Stories 'Matchbox: The Movie' Review: John Cena Can't Make This Toy-Car Spinoff Feel Grownup ‘The Table: Day and Night’ Review: Café-Based Korean Romance With Kim Min-ha and Han Sun-hwa Is All Froth, No Kick The musical choice itself was a nod to the Coens’ cult comedy “The Big Lebowski,” featuring John Turturro’s flamboyant bowler Jesus Quintana. Popular on Variety The star-studded gathering included Javier Bardem, Frances McDormand, former Lumière prize winner Wim Wenders, Robert Eggers, Michel Hazanavicius and Bérénice Bejo, Benoît Magimel, Antoine de Caunes and Caleb Deschanel, in town for a masterclass and the premiere of Laika’s upcoming stop-motion animated feature “Wildwood.” Accepting the award, Joel reflected on four decades of filmmaking with his brother. “We did it because we love cinema and we love storytelling,” he said. “We’ve had, pretty much with certain exceptions, nothing but fun making these films over the decades.” Bardem, who won an Oscar for his chilling portrayal of Anton Chigurh in “No Country for Old Men,” delivered one of the evening’s most colorful tributes, recalling how he initially tried to turn down the role despite being a longtime admirer of the Coens. “I sat down with them in New York in their office and I was like, ‘Listen, I admire you, I worship you, you are amazing, but I hate violence, I don’t drive, and I can barely speak English. What the hell am I doing here?’” Bardem recalled. “They gave me no reason whatsoever to do the movie. They were just laughing,” he said. “I thought, ‘I don’t know what this experience is going to be like, but I know it’s not going to be stressful. So yes, let’s fucking do it.’” Bardem also joked about his character’s infamous haircut, which the Coens had spotted in a photograph from the 1960s. “I was single at the time – this is 2006 – and I said, ‘I’m gonna be single until the day I wrap.’” Ethan had another story about Bardem’s commitment to the role. The actor had decided his character needed to be pale, he recalled, so during the largely outdoor shoot, a young production assistant would accompany him to the set holding a light blue parasol over his head. “And he wonders why we laughed at him,” Ethan joked. The actor’s tribute took a more heartfelt turn as he reflected on what working with the brothers had meant to him. “What they gave me was one masterpiece and the gift of a lifetime, personally and professionally,” Bardem said. “They made a dream come true. Ten years after me saying that would never happen, it happened. And it was even better than I would have ever imagined.” The evening also featured musical tributes, with French singer-songwriter Bénabar performing Charles Aznavour’s “Parce que tu crois,” chosen by Joel Coen as his favorite song. Five-time Grammy winner Angélique Kidjo delivered a rendition of Jacques Brel’s “Ne me quitte pas,” one of Bardem’s favorites. Festival director Thierry Frémaux drew laughs by projecting photographs of the Lumière and Coen brothers striking remarkably similar poses, before reminding the filmmakers that, in keeping with festival tradition, they would have to shoot their own version of the Lumières’ first film, “Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory,” on Saturday. After screening one of the original versions, he gave them until the next day to come up with their own take. The tribute also struck a timely note with the screening of Ettore Scola’s 1997 short “1943-1997,” which follows a young Jewish boy fleeing a Nazi roundup in wartime Rome who finds refuge in a movie theater. As five decades of Italian cinema unfold on screen, the boy grows old. The film ends in 1997 with a young African boy fleeing persecution into the same theater, drawing a parallel between past and present. Bardem picked up on the film’s message, stressing its relevance today. “Never again is never again for everybody, from Congo to Sudan to Palestine,” he said. Joel also paid tribute to Lyon’s community of film lovers and the festival’s commitment to the shared experience of cinema, praising audiences who still relish “gathering in a dark room with lots of other people and seeing it on a big screen.” Since making their feature debut with the neo-noir thriller “Blood Simple” in 1984, Joel and Ethan Coen have built one of American cinema’s most distinctive filmographies, spanning the crime comedy “Raising Arizona,” cult favorite “The Big Lebowski,” Depression-era musical odyssey “O Brother, Where Art Thou?” and Western anthology “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs.” Their 2007 thriller “No Country for Old Men” won four Oscars, including best picture, best director, best adapted screenplay and best supporting actor for Bardem, while “Fargo” earned the brothers their first Oscar for original screenplay in 1997. Olivier CHASSIGNOLE At Cannes, their remarkable run began in 1991 when “Barton Fink” swept the Palme d’Or, best director and best actor prize for John Turturro. They went on to win best director for “Fargo” in 1996 and “The Man Who Wasn’t There” in 2001, while “Inside Llewyn Davis” took the Grand Prix in 2013. In 2015, they returned to the Croisette as presidents of the festival’s jury. Friday’s honor makes Joel and Ethan the second filmmaking duo to receive the Lumière Award, following Belgian brothers Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne in 2020. Previous recipients include Clint Eastwood, Quentin Tarantino, Pedro Almodóvar, Martin Scorsese, Catherine Deneuve, Wong Kar-wai, Jane Fonda, Francis Ford Coppola, Jane Campion, Tim Burton, Wim Wenders, Isabelle Huppert and Michael Mann. The Lumière Film Festival wraps Sunday, Oct. 18. articles.title: Taylor Swift Heroine Clara Bow’s Breakout Movie ‘It’ Leads Carlotta Films, Artcraft Pictures French Distribution Deal of Hollywood Classics
articles.full_text: Oct 17, 2026 3:37am PT Taylor Swift Heroine Clara Bow’s Breakout Movie ‘It’ Leads Carlotta Films, Artcraft Pictures French Distribution Deal of Hollywood Classics By Lise Pedersen Plus Icon Lise Pedersen Latest Coen Brothers Bring Laughs to Lumière Award Ceremony as Javier Bardem Recalls ‘No Country for Old Men’: ‘They Gave Me One Masterpiece’ 3 hours ago Yang Li-kuo’s ‘The Dull-Ice Flower’ Set for U.S.-U.K. Release as London-Based Distributor Radiance Films Picks Up Eight Taiwanese Classics 20 hours ago Wang Chao’s ‘A Woman’ Swooped on by France’s Malavida, Which Sets 2027 Retrospective 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Clara Bow in 'It' Paramount Pictures LYON, France — “It,” the 1927 breakout movie of silent film star Clara Bow , to whom Taylor Swift paid tribute in a song named after her in “The Tortured Poets Department,” leads a deal between French classic film distributor Carlotta Films and U.S. restoration company Artcraft Pictures . Under the terms of the deal, Carlotta will represent its Artcraft’s catalogue across all rights in France, bringing a collection of Hollywood classics from the silent and early sound eras to French theaters and home entertainment. Related Stories 'All About Corinne' Review: Isabelle Huppert Stalks Sandrine Kiberlain in a Witty, Deliciously Acted French Industry Satire ‘Other Mommy’ Review: Jessica Chastain’s Doppelgänger Horror Misfires in Every Direction The collaboration is being launched at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival with a newly restored version of Clarence G. Badger’s “It” (1927), the romantic comedy that propelled Clara Bow to stardom and established her as Hollywood’s original “It girl.” The film will screen Oct. 17 at Lyon’s Auditorium, accompanied on the organ by Italian musician Gabriele Agrimonti. Popular on Variety Bow also inspired Margot Robbie’s character Nellie LaRoy in Damien Chazelle’s “Babylon.” Other titles covered by the agreement include Herbert Brenon’s “Beau Geste” (1926), starring Ronald Colman; Cecil B. DeMille’s “The Affairs of Anatol” (1921), starring Gloria Swanson; and William C. deMille’s “Miss Lulu Bett,” adapted from Zona Gale’s Pulitzer Prize-winning play. The slate also extends to early sound films, including Lionel Barrymore’s “His Glorious Night” (1929), starring John Gilbert. Artcraft Pictures was founded by two American film preservation specialists: James Mockoski, a longtime archivist and restoration expert who worked with Francis Ford Coppola’s American Zoetrope, and Robert A. Harris, whose work with James C. Katz includes landmark restorations of David Lean’s “Lawrence of Arabia,” George Cukor’s “My Fair Lady” and Alfred Hitchcock’s “Vertigo.” The company takes its name from the original Artcraft Pictures, a distribution banner established in 1916 that became part of Paramount Pictures and was associated with some of the studio’s biggest silent-era stars, including Mary Pickford. “Artcraft Pictures is thrilled to join Carlotta Films. We share a passion for keeping cinema’s roots alive so new fans can enjoy them,” said Mockoski. “So many wonderful classics could easily fade away, but together with Carlotta, we’re making sure that never happens.” Artcraft is also working with the San Francisco Silent Film Festival, which began collaborating with Mockoski and Harris in 2025 on restorations from Paramount’s silent-era library. The restored “Beau Geste” was presented at the Telluride Film Festival earlier this year. For Carlotta, which has spent close to three decades distributing classic cinema in France, the agreement expands a catalogue that already includes major works of the silent era, from F.W. Murnau’s “Sunrise” and films by Frank Borzage and Erich von Stroheim to G.W. Pabst’s “Pandora’s Box,” starring Louise Brooks. Carlotta plans to release the films in France theatrically and on Blu-ray, with individual release dates yet to be announced. “We’re delighted to represent Artcraft in France and introduce audiences to its restorations of both celebrated and lesser-known American silent films,” said Carlotta’s Vincent Paul-Boncour. “It’s a pleasure to work with James Mockoski and Robert Harris, two seasoned experts in film history and restoration, and to launch this collaboration with the French premiere of the beautifully restored ‘It.’” The MIFC wrapped in Lyon on Oct. 16. The Lumière Film Festival runs through Oct. 18. articles.full_text: Oct 17, 2026 4:03am PT J.K. Rowling’s Agent Slams Trans Rights Protest at ‘Harry Potter and the Cursed Child’ in London: It Put ‘Others at Risk’ By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest ‘The Big Boom!,’ Documentary About Weapons Factory Workers, Picked Up by Lightdox Ahead of IDFA Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Sundance Winners Blerta Basholli and Myrsini Aristidou Compete in Thessaloniki’s Meet the Neighbors+ Competition (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago ‘Women and War,’ About Ukrainian Women Undergoing Trauma Therapy, Acquired by Rise and Shine World Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Photo by Jonathan Brady/PA Images via Getty Images J.K. Rowling ’s agent Neil Blair has slammed the transgender rights activists who staged a dramatic protest before a gala performance of “ Harry Potter and the Cursed Child” on Thursday in London’s West End. The protesters, many wearing masks, hats and goggles to hide their identity, stormed the red carpet as celebrities were arriving for a new shortened version of the show at the Palace Theatre. The activists, one with a T-shirt stating “Rowling money kills,” lay on the red carpet before they were dragged off by security guards. Related Stories 'Between Two Lovers' Review: Nanako Hirose's Contentious Family Drama Examines an Ill-Fated Throuple ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s Latest Animated Feature Is a Giddy Retro-Futurist Noir With More Energy Than Charm In a statement provided to Variety , Blair said, “We respect peaceful activism and the right to express different views. But those rights must be exercised without putting others at risk, including audience members, performers and theater staff, as we saw [Thursday] evening during the protests outside the Palace Theatre in London ahead of the gala performance of ‘Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.'” Popular on Variety He added, “Above all, we want to continue bringing the magic of Harry Potter to the wonderful fans who have supported and embraced this world for so many years. Every fan deserves to enjoy the magic of Harry Potter in an atmosphere of respect and security, and we remain committed to keeping live theater a welcoming and safe experience for everyone.” Local celebrities in attendance for the special performance included TV hosts Vanessa Feltz, Angellica Bell and Richard Arnold, and “The Chase” star Anne Hegerty. The show, originally in two parts, has been reconfigured to become a single-part performance lasting almost three hours. Rowling has been vocal in her criticism of self-declared gender identity, and this has led to allegations that she is transphobic, which she has strongly denied. articles.title: ‘Trust Me, I’m a Doctor’ Review: Kal Penn and Abbie Cornish Star in a Minor Sidebar to the Anna Nicole Smith Story
articles.full_text: Oct 17, 2026 4:31am PT ‘Trust Me, I’m a Doctor’ Review: Kal Penn and Abbie Cornish Star in a Minor Sidebar to the Anna Nicole Smith Story Thane Economou's film follows the Playboy Playmate's physician through the circus of her life and death, but can't persuade us his experience really merits a movie. By Todd Gilchrist Plus Icon Todd Gilchrist Latest ‘Trust Me, I’m a Doctor’ Review: Kal Penn and Abbie Cornish Star in a Minor Sidebar to the Anna Nicole Smith Story 1 hour ago ‘Forgotten Island’ Review: A Delightful Animated Celebration of Friendship and Filipino Culture 3 weeks ago ‘Run Hide Fight: Infidels’ Review: Jonathan Majors Scrapes the Barrel in This Islamophobic Drivel 1 month ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Andy Warhol famously said that in the future, everyone will have 15 minutes of fame. “Trust Me, I’m A Doctor” expands that tally to an hour and 51 minutes for Sandeep Kapoor, the physician who treated Playboy Playmate Anna Nicole Smith and was implicated in her death from a prescription drug overdose in 2007. That’s too long. Though it’s difficult to chronicle any element of Smith’s life without injecting at least a hint of tabloid sensationalism, writer-director Thane Economou (“The Wedding Party”) takes an aggressively cheeky approach to the saga of Kapoor’s involvement, in the process undercutting what he clearly intends to be an empathetic portrait of both the doctor and his patient. Taking the lead in a rare film focused on a prominent Indian American, Kal Penn struggles to wrangle this flamboyant biopic into a serious acting challenge, but he delivers impressive work in its final scenes even if they fail to elevate what came before them. Related Stories ‘14th’ Review: Ava DuVernay's Powerful Sequel to ‘13th’ Turns a Constitutional Amendment into Living History 'The Sea Speaks His Name' Review: Absorbing Indonesian Political Thriller Is an Ode to Disappeared Activists Penn plays Kapoor, a closeted physician who takes over a retiring colleague’s practice, in the process inheriting Anna Nicole Smith ( Abbie Cornish ) as a patient. Like his predecessor, Sandeep agrees to treat Smith under a pseudonym, but she quickly beguiles him with her childlike charm; despite his attempts to maintain a professional distance, he soon becomes a part of her inner circle. Shortly after she invites him to ride in a Los Angeles Pride parade where he participates in a self-described “orgy,” Anna announces that she’s pregnant — with whose baby, he does not know. Even so, he determines that failing to prescribe methadone to curb her festering drug addiction could harm her pregnancy, so he reluctantly writes a big order for her to take with her on a weeks-long trip to the Bahamas. Popular on Variety She eventually gives birth to a daughter, Dannielynn, and just three days later, loses her son Daniel (Jordan Kronis) to an overdose. A few months later, Sandeep learns from news reports that Anna herself has overdosed; he rushes to his office to confiscate her and Daniel’s medical files to protect them from being stolen or leaked, but the media has already staked out his practice. At the urging of a devoted patient, Margie (Jocelyne Zucco), he retains no-nonsense attorney Ellen Garofalo (Linda Hamilton) and mounts a PR campaign to present himself as the upstanding medical professional he claims to be. But when federal investigators discover Anna’s medical records in his underwear drawer, he becomes an official suspect in her death. Eventually, the attorney general working at the direction of gubernatorial hopeful Jerry Brown charges Sandeep, along with Smith’s lawyer Howard K. Stern (David Julian Hirsh) and her psychiatrist Khristine Eroshevich (Virginia Cowan), of criminal conspiracy, with him as the lead plaintiff. As he fights to clear his name, Sandeep unexpectedly discovers that his best ally to win the case may be Harvey Levin (Elon Gold), the TMZ journalist whose photos first incriminated him, even as he reckons with the cost of his relationship with Smith on his family, his practice and his future. According to this film, Sandeep Kapoor was kind of a nitwit regarding his time in the spotlight, but he ultimately occupied only a marginal place in Anna Nicole Smith’s story. His famous patient passes away 25 minutes into the film; the remaining 86 minutes focus on Garofalo’s legal maneuverings and his own incredulity at virtually every part of the process of being put through the public wringer. Given Smith’s celebrity status and the sensational ups and downs of her life, it’s easy for an audience unfamiliar with Kapoor’s memoir, which inspired the film, to assume that he was a sycophant and enabler of this troubled woman. Economou seems to want to do justice to both his and his patient’s lives, but his script obfuscates Kapoor’s involvement in her death more than necessary by jumping back and forth in time, peppering what was already intriguing subject matter with fourth-wall-breaking monologues, montages that meld real and staged footage and at least one sidebar about a character who, though objectively interesting, is more or less totally irrelevant to this story. Events such as his interview with Levin — as Garofalo’s legal strategy or his personal leap into the belly of the media beast — are especially fascinating when we see actual footage of their conversation over the closing credits. But they are unfortunately sandwiched between reams of expository commentary about each participant’s real and imagined motivations, political undertones of the lawsuit brought against him, and Kapoor’s only semi-convincing protestations of his innocence. Understandably, Penn struggles to hold these disparate points of focus together with a performance that vacillates between disarmingly dopey and almost willfully ignorant of the realities of the 2000s media landscape. It does not help that, outside of Hamilton as his tough-as-nails defense lawyer, the rest of the performances are delivered at an almost parodic pitch, led by Cornish with a rendition of Smith that seems pitched more to “Saturday Night Live” than a real film for the big screen. All of which is to say “Trust Me, I’m A Doctor” probably would have worked better as a documentary than as a narrative feature. Even taking Kapoor at his word that he never wanted and was happy to recede afterward from the public eye, Economou clearly possesses an impressive enough archive of material to tell this story with or without his participation, with the same multimedia flair that he deploys here. If nothing else, moviegoers wouldn’t have had to watch Cornish play Smith, an admittedly unenviable acting tightrope that she navigates clumsily at best. Kapoor, meanwhile, seems much more self-possessed in the real footage, making him precisely as sympathetic as the filmmaker intended. Following a handful of genuinely powerful scenes by Penn that sadly come too late to offset the circus-like tone established earlier, the film concludes with a montage detailing what happened to everyone involved after the verdict was handed down in Kapoor’s case. The overarching message of that sequence is that something about celebrity worship seems to drive people crazy, imagining anything connected to it as more significant than it actually is. With respect to Kapoor, Economou should have paid more attention to the epiphanies of his own film; the rollercoaster of Smith’s life will always be a curio, but that doesn’t mean that every passenger on it has a story worth telling. ‘Trust Me, I’m a Doctor’ Review: Kal Penn and Abbie Cornish Star in a Minor Sidebar to the Anna Nicole Smith Story Reviewed online, Oct. 15, 2026. MPA Rating: R. Running time: 111 MIN. Production: (U.S.) A Briarcliff Entertainment release of a Picture Movers, Stadium, RBF Productions Films, Good Good Films, Low Road Films, Spy Films production. (World sales: Fortitude International, Los Angeles.) Producers: Ryan Hawkins, Al Engelmann, Rebecca Case, Geenah Krisht. Executive producers: Kal Penn, Thane Economou, David Gale, Charlotte Ubben, Randy Wooten, Melora Donoghue, Nashwa Krisht, Ali Krisht, Michael Lazari, Tom Ortenberg. Crew: Director, screenplay: Thane Economou. Camera: Bobby Shore. Editor: Brian Berdan. Music: Daniel Stockdale, Niles Hollowell-Dhar. articles.title: Pathé Unveils Sofia Coppola’s ‘Marie Antoinette’ 4K Restoration as Sophie and Jérôme Seydoux Are Feted in Lyon
articles.full_text: Oct 17, 2026 5:07am PT Pathé Unveils Sofia Coppola’s ‘Marie Antoinette’ 4K Restoration as Sophie and Jérôme Seydoux Are Feted in Lyon Speaking at the Lumière Festival's Classic Film Market, Jérôme Seydoux and Sophie Seydoux expressed their confidence in the resilience of cinema, predicted streamers would increasingly release films theatrically and stressed the importance of educating kids about cinema By Ed Meza Plus Icon Ed Meza @edmezavar Latest Apple TV’s Hit German Series ‘Where’s Wanda?’ Returns for Season 2, Again Asking: ‘How Far Would You Go to Save Your Child?’ 3 days ago Going Big in Japan: International French Hit ‘Bright Minds’ Season 7 Heads to Tokyo (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago Louis Malle’s ‘Elevator to the Gallows’ Set for 70th Anniversary 4K Release as Jean-Jacques Beineix’s ‘Betty Blue’ Hits Big Screen After 35 Years 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Marie Antoinette' (Courtesy of I Want Candy, LLC/Columbia/Sony) Sofia Coppola ’s cult classic “ Marie Antoinette ” and three works by Louis Daquin , a champion of the Communist Resistance during the German occupation, are among the latest restored works from French studio Pathé . The company, whose owners Jérôme Seydoux and Sophie Seydoux are being honored at the Lumière Film Festival ’s International Classic Film Market ( MIFC ) in Lyon, is celebrating its 130th anniversary this year, which also marks the 20th anniversary of the Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé Fondation. Related Stories 'Animals' Review: Ben Affleck Returns to the Director's Chair for a Nasty, Compulsive Kidnapping Thriller Catherine Zeta-Jones Can’t Save AMC+’s Stylish but Lackluster Thriller ‘Kill Jackie’: TV Review A bastion of film preservation and the continued transmission of heritage works, Pathé has also been a strong supporter of the Lumière Festival since its establishment in 2009. Popular on Variety The studio is currently marking the 20th anniversary of Coppola’s film with the release of a newly restored 4K version on Nov. 25. The film, which stars Kirsten Dunst and Jason Schwartzman, comes just in time for the recently announced special exhibition at the Chateau de Versailles dedicated to the movie. The 4K restoration is being supervised by Sony Pictures Entertainment in collaboration with American Zoetrope. It follows the late Eleanor Coppola’s new documentary on her daughter’s film, “ Making Marie Antoinette .” Pathé is also celebrating the work of Daquin, described by the Lumière Festival as “a unique figure in French cinema, for whom filmmaking and political commitment were one and the same. A member of the Resistance, a staunch communist and union activist heavily involved in defending film industry workers, he considered his craft to be an extension of his convictions.” Nous les gosses (Portrait of Innocence) Courtesy of Pathé Films Part of a special Lumière Festival showcase, Daquin’s works include his 1941 film “Nous les gosses”(“Portrait of Innocence”), the story of a close-knit group of schoolchildren that can be read as a veiled call for resistance. The fest is presenting the film in its restored 2K version. Likewise screening is 1960’s “The Opportunists” (“Les Arrivistes”), an adaptation of Honoré de Balzac’s book “La Rabouilleuse” (known in English as “The Black Sheep” and “The Two Brothers”); set during the Restoration, it follows a former officer of Napoleon whose greed knows no bounds. The Opportunists (Les Arrivistes) Courtesy of Pathé Films – DEFA Spielfilmstudio The Lumière Festival will present the film in its restored 4K version. Also in the Pathé catalogue is the 4K restoration of Daquin’s 1944 drama “Premier de Cordée” (“First in Line”). Filmed primarily on location in the Chamonix Valley, “Premier de Cordée” represented a remarkable technical achievement during the German occupation of France, Pathé notes. “Directed by a filmmaker involved in the Resistance, the film tells the story of a young man who must overcome his fear of heights to become a mountain guide. Its themes of struggle, perseverance and self-transcendence resonated strongly with audiences in occupied France.” Pathé describes the Daquin showcase as “an opportunity to rediscover a filmmaker who captured working-class France, made films under the very nose of the occupying forces, and helped shape the institutions of post-war French cinema. “Louis Daquin’s career was extraordinary. He directed several feature films during the German occupation while actively involved in the Communist Resistance. His films from this period bear the mark of this paradoxal situation: a left-wing filmmaker, involved in the Resistance, working under the constraints of a fascist regime.” Speaking at the Pathé Bellecour theater in Lyon during the Classic Film Market on Friday, Jérôme Seydoux, chairman of Pathé, and Sophie Seydoux, president of the Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé Fondation, discussed a wide range of pressing issues, from their efforts to preserve, conserve and transmit the company’s century-long heritage to the resilience of cinema, the undeniable power of blockbusters, and the importance of education in cultivating a lasting passion for cinema among young people. Pathé has produced such recent upscale blockbusters as “ De Gaulle: Résistance ,” “ The Count of Monte Cristo ” and “ The Three Musketeers – Part I: D’Artagnan ” — the kinds of films that are necessary to keep cinema alive, according to Jérôme Seydoux. “It is essential that there are films that are called locomotives in France, which Americans call blockbusters. .We at Pathé said to ourselves that we are not going to make cars, we are going to make locomotives. But it’s difficult. It’s difficult because these are obviously bigger risks. These are often bigger budgets. So, you can’t make too many mistakes.” Citing a motto from filmmaker Claude Berri, Jérôme Seydoux added, “When making a film, what matters is not what it costs, it’s what it brings in.” Expressing his confidence in the survival of cinema, the Pathé chairman argued that despite recurring economic crises, technological shifts and the rise of home viewing, people would always seek the shared emotional experience of the big screen. “That cinema is something that would disappear has been said since the Lumière Brothers. The Lumière Brothers, Jean-Pierre Melville, the head of Netflix, and more recently, Sylvester Stallone have announced that the cinema does not exist anymore. “Cinema will resist, no matter what happens,” he stressed. “Cinema has always had crises. There will always be cinema, there will always be crises. And why will there always be cinema? Because today, in a society where people are very individualistic, they still have, at some point, the need to come together, to share emotions together. I am an absolutely unshakeable believer in the survival of cinema.” Cinema will not only resist the dominance of U.S. streamers in France, it is sure to become a significant venue for platforms to launch their productions, Jérôme Seydoux added. The U.S. streamers are also natural partners for Pathé, he stressed. “Today in France, the two main networks for the French are YouTube and Netflix. So these are two American companies. And we are going to work almost automatically with people who have money. The people who have money are the platforms. So yes, we will definitely work with the platforms. It’s mandatory.” At the same time, Netflix will increasingly release films in theaters, he predicted. “I think they will discover that they need, what I call high fashion. When you are in the media business, you need something that shines.” For that reason, “in a short time, in a few years Netflix will make movies that will be released in theaters.” “Not just because of the talents involved, but also for commercial reasons, for reasons that if you want to do something that is truly an event, it is difficult to make an event only on television. It will always be an event whose notoriety will be lower than that of a major film event.” Turning to the company’s film preservation efforts and the use of digital technology, Sophie Seydoux stressed the importance of maintaining film on film. “I am an unconditional supporter of what is called a conservation shoot, meaning that once we have restored a film, digitized it, it goes back to film. We know from here at the Lumière Festival, everywhere in the world, film is preserved for 120 years in an absolutely remarkable way. Currently, for everything that is digital, we do not know the preservation time. And above all, there are a lot of elements that can disappear overnight due to a change in technology. So, we need to be very, very careful. “At Pathé, it’s really a golden rule. We reprint on film for all the restorations we do. There is never the slightest shadow of hesitation about it.” Sophie Seydoux also underscored the importance of education and exposing children to films from an early age to cultivate a lasting passion for cinema. The Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé Foundation conducts specialized educational workshops centered around silent films. “It is very, very, very important to show young people films from early childhood because it will give them this desire to continue to see films,” she said. “At the Foundation we have a very, very important educational program that is focused on silent films, since that is our specialty. We teach them what film is, we let them handle film. Handling is something that is very important. “[Company founder] Charles Pathé was very attached to everything that was manipulation. He thought about it when he built a camera, about the cameraman’s gestures, how it should be done, how it could be improved. And manipulation is very important, so many of our workshops for children involve hands-on activities.” Sophie Seydoux and Jérôme Seydoux Courtesy of MIFC/Bertrand Rindoff/Getty Sylvester Stallone Says Superhero Movie Bodies Aren’t ‘Natural’ and Taking Steroids to Bulk Up Is Like ‘Putting on Part of a Costume’ Loading comments...

articles.title: ‘Crystal Lake’s Gwendolyn Sundstrom On Grace’s Friendship With Jason, “Learning A Lot” From Linda Cardellini & That Killer Twist
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘9-1-1: Nashville’ Pays Tribute To Chad Lowe’s Daughter Fiona With Title Card In Season 2 Premiere KJ Apa Asked ‘Riverdale’ Showrunner Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa For ‘Afterlife with Archie’ Cameo: “I Don’t Know Who I’d Play” Brad Caleb Kane Teases ‘It: Welcome to Derry’ Is “Bigger” In Season 2 With “A Different Kind Of Pennywise” View All October 16, 2026 3:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Gwendolyn Sundstrom as Grace in 'Crystal Lake' Peacock SPOILER ALERT: This post contains details about Peacock ‘s series Crystal Lake . While Crystal Lake revisits several familiar locals from the Friday the 13th franchise, Gwendolyn Sundstrom brings a fresh role to the slasher prequel series. Now available to stream on Peacock, Sundstrom told Deadline that Jason Voorhees’ (Callum Vinson) childhood friend Grace has been her “favorite character so far” to play, filming the Brad Caleb Kane series in New Jersey when she was only 13. Related Stories News ‘Crystal Lake’s Linda Cardellini Used Pam Voorhees’ Grief As “Fuel For Her Rage,” Reveals Her Favorite Kill Scenes: “Feels A Little Too Good” News Brad Caleb Kane On Making ‘Crystal Lake’ A “Small-Town Show” In Same N.J. Locations Where ‘Friday The 13th’ Filmed, “Faithfully” Re-Creating An Iconic Scene & “Twin Peaks-y” Plans For Season 2 “It was fun, ’cause in real life I don’t really relate to Grace that much, but it was fun to try and find things from my life that I could put into Grace and really play her,” explained Sundstrom. “But I had a great day every day on set, it was amazing.” Watch on Deadline As the series recounts the accidental drowning of young Jason that was first mentioned in the original 1980 movie, the opening scene of the first episode reveals Grace throwing a bully’s ball out into the lake after he was teasing Jason. While counselors Claudette (Danielle Kotch) and Barry (Phoenix Parnevik) sneak off to hook up, Jason goes after the ball, only to drown in the depths of Crystal Lake. Jason and Grace’s endearing adolescent friendship continues to play out through flashbacks as she struggles to mourn his death amid the usual complications of growing up. “I think it was really helpful that Callum and I had really good chemistry in real life too, but I think building Grace as a character, she’s also kind of an underdog,” explained Sundstrom. “She also doesn’t have very many friends, so I think we could kind of work off each other and portray that kind of character cause we’re so similar.” With nowhere to put her maternal love after the loss of her son Jason, Pam Voorhees ( Linda Cardellini ) soon takes an interest in Grace, whose own mom appears to be abusive and neglectful. “I loved working with Linda. She was so nice,” Sundstrom said. “I definitely learned a lot from her. I think when Pam takes on kind of this maternal role, I think that’s something Grace, first of all, isn’t really used to, and also doesn’t really want. I think she’s trying to push Pam away, and Pam only wants to get even closer and even more protective, and I think that’s kind of a conflict that the two characters have.” After finding a new “family” in a pack of traveling hippies, Grace ends up on a drug trip that results in a deconstruction of the very first kill in the Friday the 13th franchise. But instead of Pam, it’s revealed that Grace was the person to kill Claudette and Barry in that first-person POV sequence. Callum Vinson as Jason Voorhees and Gwendolyn Sundstrom as Grace in ‘Crystal Lake’ “I had a lot of fun with that scene,” said Sundstrom. “I definitely like filming more dramatic, gritty, emotional things, so that was really fun for me.” And while diehard fans of the franchise might not be down with the retcon of such an iconic kill scene, Kane explained he wanted to “blow people’s minds” and “give the audience something different to chew on.” “You have to re-contextualize it, and you want a shock,” explained Kane. “We come to these movies for the rollercoaster ride of it, we come to these movies for the jaw-drop of it. If you think you know everything from the movie coming into the TV series, and then we just go, ‘yeah, it’s exactly as you thought it was,’ that’s no fun.” Linda Cardellini as Pam Voorhees and Gwendolyn Sundstrom as Grace in ‘Crystal Lake’ Now streaming on Peacock, Crystal Lake stars Cardellini as Pam Voorhees, who struggles to grieve after her son Jason drowned the summer before. As two strangers begin digging into her mysterious past, Pam goes to murderous lengths to keep her secrets buried and find her son, whom she’s convinced is still alive after his body was never recovered. ‘Street Fighter’ Socking Away $30M; A24’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc Eyes $12M J.K. articles.title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Directing Duo Los Javis Reveal How Spanish Sensation Became “The Journey Of Our Lives”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Baz Bamigboye Baz Bamigboye Columnist/International Editor At Large @BazBam More Stories By Baz Sacha Baron Cohen Confirmed To Star In Quentin Tarantino’s ‘The Popinjay Cavalier’ West End Stage Play With Dates & On Sale Window Announced Breaking Baz: Why LFF Opener ‘Elsinore’ Is A Triumphant Epitaph For An Extraordinary Man Breaking Baz: Anthony Mackie Returning To Broadway To Play Macbeth After 16-Year Absence From The Stage View All October 16, 2026 3:15pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Penelope Cruz in ‘La Bola Negra’ Carla Oset/Netflix Penélope Cruz had been a muse to Los Javis — the moniker for Spanish filmmakers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo — for years before they met for lunch to persuade her to play a singer (more a force of nature, really) in La Bola Negra , an electrifying sensation at Cannes that’s now Spain’s entry for best international feature film Oscar . “I saw her in a clip of Jamón Jamón ,” says Ambrossi, referring to Bigas Luna’s 1992 picture, in which Cruz appeared for the first time opposite her now-husband Javier Bardem. “I was young, and I thought, ‘Who is she ?!’ ” Related Stories Reviews ‘La Bola Negra’ Review: Spain’s Javier Calvo And Javier Ambrossi Capture Hearts With Their Unashamedly Romantic Decades-Spanning Drama – Cannes Film Festival Festivals Penélope Cruz’s ‘La Bola Negra’ Lands 20-Minute Ovation From Overjoyed Audience At Cannes Calvo was similarly enchanted when he saw Cruz in Pedro Almodóvar’s 1999 Oscar winner All About My Mother . “She’s got that material of the stars,” he says. “When you put a camera in front of her, she can do anything, and she doesn’t even realize what she’s doing. There’s a power , there’s a force guiding her, and that’s amazing to see first-hand.” Watch on Deadline Los Javis wanted Cruz for a small but pivotal role in their epic tale La Bola Negra , the intertwined story of three gay men who exist in three different time periods in Spain. In 1932, Carlos (Milo Quifes) is a young man in Grenada at a time when Spain is lurching uncomfortably towards an ever-increasing spiteful intolerance of homosexuality. In 1937, against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War, Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) and Rafael ( Miguel Bernardeau ) are soldiers from opposing political divides brought closer by the conflict. And in 2017, Alberto (Carlos González) is a playwright from Madrid who engages with an eminent Federico Garcia Lorca scholar (played by another Hollywood star, Glenn Close , speaking fluent Spanish) in a storyline that links the characters in the prior timelines.

articles.title: How ‘Whalefall’s Director & Author Wove The Closure Of A Father-Son Relationship Into A Survival Tale
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi How ‘Whalefall’s Director & Author Wove The Closure Of A Father-Son Relationship Into A Survival Tale The Smashing Pumpkins Release Latest ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Album Track, ‘Black Stars’ Everything We Know About ‘The Housemaid’s Secret’ Film So Far View All October 16, 2026 4:20pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Director Brian Duffield and Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in 20th Century Studios' WHALEFALL Jennifer Clasen/20th Century Studios SPOILER ALERT: This story spoils the plot of the film Whalefall , now out in theaters, based on Daniel Kraus ‘ novel. A running joke Whalefall director Brian Duffield had going to summarize the film hailing from 20 th Century Studios and Imagine Entertainment and hitting theaters this week was that “men would rather get swallowed by a sperm whale than go to therapy.” Just as Austin Abrams ’ Jay Gardiner finds himself in quite the harrowing predicament trapped in a whale’s stomach after a tangle with a squid, the cast, crew and filmmakers of Whalefall also found themselves in the tricky situation of bringing the premise of Daniel Kraus’ novel to the big screen. Related Stories Reviews ‘Whalefall’ Review: Austin Abrams Wrestles With Grief, Toxic Masculinity & Grotesque Whale Innards In Emotionally Gutsy Body Horror News 20th Century’s ‘Whalefall’ Producers Reflect On Shooting In California: “The Best Creative Teams Are Here” To back up, Jay’s decision to seek out the remains of his dead father Mitt Gardiner ( Josh Brolin ), who has committed suicide by drowning in the Pacific Ocean following a diagnosis of mesothelioma, is what really landed him in this situation. Just as he has to get scrappy and use anything he can find to escape, those behind the making of the movie had to be in constant communication about what it would take to pull off such intense scenes, many of which took place inside a life-sized whale stomach built specifically for the film. Watch on Deadline “It takes a village to build a whale, and I think it takes a really great village to survive it. And that’s been really one of the most gratifying parts of [production],” Duffield said when Deadline visited the set of the movie at Radford Studios in L.A. in September, during an early tank scene where Abrams encountered the whale for the first time. “It’s such a new and unique challenge that I think we hired the right people, because it was a lot of us all banging our heads together trying to figure out how to shoot every day.” Multiple whale stomach models were built by Weta Workshop in New Zealand, with the head, throat, esophagus and larynx constructed in California because they were too big to ship to set on time. The 12-foot-tall, 18-foot-long whale head was manufactured by StudioArt & Technology. Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in 20th Century Studios’ ‘Whalefall’ 20th Century Studios “It’s such an interlocked set. I’ve never made a movie, and I can’t imagine ever making a movie where every single department really has to be talking to each other every step of the way,” Duffield said. “For the stomach, Ramsey [Avery] our production designer [had] to figure out how to build it, and then we [had] to figure out how to put cameras in it, but then also we had to figure out how to light it, and then the lights become bioluminescence. Visual effects supervisor Guillaume Rocheron, who worked on Jordan Peele’s Nope , rigged the LED lighting in the stomach to eventually render as the bioluminescence that then helps illuminate Jay’s environment. “Some colors do not show up the same color in LED lights. So, our costume designer had to build Austin’s costume around what the LEDs would show up with,” Duffield added. “So we would take neoprene samples to New Zealand, where we built the stomachs, to show them under the lights, against the whale skin, to see what colors show up.” Cameras and lenses were broken “nonstop” during filming; the crew ultimately constructed scenes around the one spot the camera could actually fit into the cramped space and worked backwards from that vantage point. If that weren’t claustrophobic enough, Abrams also faced the added challenge of emoting behind a facemask and the diving equipment Jay uses. “We redesigned the regulator to make it as small as possible, because regulators are not really meant to be worn outside of water. And yet, the air inside the whale stomach is toxic. It won’t kill him, necessarily, but it’s full of methane and things that make him a little high,” Duffield said. “So we redesigned the regulator to give him as much mouth shape as possible. He actually does talk throughout the movie to himself or to other characters in the stomach. That has been a challenging learning curve.” Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner 20th Century Studios These formidable aspects of the film’s creation echoe Kraus’ general approach to writing books; he now has 30-plus under his belt. “I like to create new problems and have to fight through the solutions — I try to start with an impossible [conceit] where I just throw hurdles in front of me of things that I don’t know,” Kraus told Deadline on set. “So I have to relearn how to write a book every time.” The impetus for Whalefall came from a viral video in which a kayaker ended up in the mouth of a whale. Once Kraus heard about the clip, it spawned discussions with friends about whether it could actually happen. He could not stop thinking about it. Following an email to author friend Mary Roach, author of Gulp: Adventures on the Alimentary Canal (2013), and correspondence with three whale experts she recommended, Kraus had found the “high concept” hook for the book, which hit shelves in 2023. “I didn’t want to do it if it couldn’t really happen — being swallowed by a whale has been treated like a fable and Biblical stories forever. My interest was, could you do it scientifically accurately?” Kraus said. “And by the end of the day, I was all systems go. All the whale experts were super-excited to help, and they think about whales all day, but never in this context. We were off to the races.” Both Duffield and Kraus drew connections to the science fiction genre in different ways, with Kraus developing an interest in whales during the frontloaded research process for the book, which took about three months. “I became more and more … obsessed, you might say, with whales,” he said. “There’s a lot of what I was doing with this biology of a whale, but I also unexpectedly started to get really enamored of whales as a being, as a force of nature. “Sperm whales are extraordinarily intelligent. They’re one of the most mysterious animals on the planet. Everything about them is strange. They really feel like aliens. Even in the deep ocean, which is filled with alien-like creatures, the whales almost feel like a master alien. They’re not aggressors. They’re very peaceful animals. Sperm whales have been witnessed helping humans many, many times, like divers in trouble.” Experiencing a whale from the inside out adds complicated layers to Whalefall ‘s story, even when it comes to the father-son relationship at its heart. “How do you fall in love with a character through its guts, basically? It’s definitely gross, but what are the ways that we can fall in love with this animal, because Austin is in such a unique situation, and I think there’s something interesting about his character, who is very fond of of animals and nature,” Duffield said. “One of the things that differentiates his character and Josh’s character is Josh is very hard and Austin’s very soft. But they both have this love of nature, and so giving Austin moments that he can really, for lack of a better way to put it, appreciate how cool the situation is — while also being scared sh*tless and thinking he’s going to die pretty much at any given moment — that was part of the craft of it, too.” Duffield evidently shared a similar awe. For him, the trick with the stomach being the setting for a majority of the movie was balancing the claustrophobic feeling of Jay’s plight with breaks from the cramped space. “It’s challenging for a couple reasons. One, it’s such a long stretch of the movie, and quite a lot happens while he’s in in the stomach, but it was also about keeping it fresh and interesting so [that] after 30 minutes, people weren’t just like, ‘Alright, I’m sick of this stomach,’” Duffield said. “[Jay] does have different little side adventures. He spends some time in the second stomach, which is very visually different, and then in the esophagus of the whale as well. Different animals that are also in the stomachs, and different problems he has to MacGyver his way out of, so it’s just trying to figure out how to keep it fresh visually, which Daniel honestly just did a lot of in the book.” Whalefall executive prodcuer Doug Merrifield, whose credits include the Free Willy films, joined Duffield, Kraus and Imagine Entertainment’s Allen Mandelbaum in emphasizing that the whale is not the villain in the movie. It’s orcas that attack Jay’s sperm whale that ultimately provide the antagonists and the catalyst for the film’s climax. “The whale is not a bad guy. The whale is just an animal that’s doing what it’s meant to be doing. The whale is not interested in [Jay]. It’s trying to get a squid, and Austin is in the way,” Duffield said. “The movie makes a very direct correlation, eventually, between Josh Brolin and and the whale, and part of Austin’s journey is making peace with his dad, who is dead at the start of the movie.” L-R: Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner and Josh Brolin as Mitt Gardiner 20th Century Studios One of the main threads of the book that drew Duffield to directing the adaptation was the father-son relationship at its core; his own son was 4 at the time of the set visit. In Whalefall , Mitt and Jay didn’t always know how best to communicate with each other; the ocean is where they find common ground. “The miracle of the book and hopefully of the movie is, when it ends, you primarily are talking about the relationships, and then the whale is third or fourth build, which for a movie that’s set almost entirely inside of a whale feels impossible, but somehow [Kraus] pulls it off,” Duffield said. “As you age up, you start viewing things from different perspectives. I think before I was a dad, I probably would have been firmly in Jay’s point of view, and then now being on the other side of it and having a son — granted, my son just turned 4, so it’s a very different than the relationship between [Jay] and [Mitt] — [I’m] really starting to feel for Brolin’s character, and understand him to some extent.” Kraus, who grew up in conservative small-town Iowa, leaned into the personal when it came to building the tension of Mitt and Jay’s relationship. His father was a hunter, not as extreme as Mitt, but still an inspiration for the character. “I’m a product of [where I grew up], which is to say, I have avoided getting therapy. I’m a product of that culture where you don’t express yourself and you don’t show your feelings when it comes to interpersonal things,” Kraus said. “Mitt is a very emotional guy when it comes to the ocean, like he will fight tooth and nail for every living creature in there. He’ll do whatever it takes to protect the ocean. But when it comes to dealing with his son, he’s absolutely clueless. He would be much better at interacting with a whale than he would be his son. And ultimately, Mitt becomes the whale, in a sense, and through the whale, they are able to have the conversation.” As Jay fights nitrogen narcosis — a condition in divers in which certain gases take on an anesthetic effect in the nervous system, resulting in a kind of high — and the methane in the whale’s stomach, he has flashbacks that help him piece together info he needs for his survival. The memories often involve his father imparting pearls of wisdom, regardless of whether Jay though of them that way at the time. “The challenge really was, the book has probably 50 flashbacks where it’s constantly hopping back and forth. In the movie, [we had] to take all that information that Jay needs to know scattered across all those flashbacks, and find ways to pack them into vastly fewer flashbacks,” Kraus said. “That was really the biggest challenge.” A small creative detail further merges Mitt and the whale, who speak as one character in Kraus’ book. “The whale’s heart is beating, and the stomach is reacting to the beats of the whale’s heart. So that’s sound puppeteering the stomach. There’s water in it, which is moving from that. And then, on top of all of that, just to show how full circle it starts to go, the whale’s heart is Josh Brolin’s heartbeat,” explained Duffield, who came up with the idea. “We’ve recorded Josh’s heartbeat, and then our sound guys made it a whale heartbeat that is playing.” L-R: Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner and Josh Brolin as Mitt Gardiner 20th Century Studios This detail also fits in with Kraus’ thematic vision. “When I came across the concept of a whalefall, which is when a whale dies and its corpse sinks to the bottom of the ocean, and its body, as it decomposes, sets off a shock wave of life, generations of life are born from its remains,” Kraus said. “ I found that very emotional and touching to the idea that when a whale dies, or somebody we know and love dies, that their death sort of begets life, the memory of them, the influence of them. It goes on, and it goes on for generations, and even when I talk about it now, I get goosebumps, it’s just such a beautiful thought.” Sometimes it takes getting stuck inside a whale to provide some perspective. ‘Street Fighter’ Socking Away $30M; A24’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc Eyes $12M J.K. articles.title: Diablo Cody Teases ‘Jennifer’s Body 2’ Explores A More “Sympathetic” Side Of Megan Fox’s Character
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn KJ Apa Asked ‘Riverdale’ Showrunner Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa For ‘Afterlife with Archie’ Cameo: “I Don’t Know Who I’d Play” Brad Caleb Kane Teases ‘It: Welcome to Derry’ Is “Bigger” In Season 2 With “A Different Kind Of Pennywise” Diablo Cody Teases ‘Jennifer’s Body 2’ Explores A More “Sympathetic” Side Of Megan Fox’s Character View All October 16, 2026 6:01pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Megan Fox in 'Jennifer's Body' (2009) Doane Gregory/Fox Atomic/Courtesy Everett Collection As Diablo Cody prepares to resurrect Megan Fox ‘s teen succubus one more time, she’s adding a more human element to the demonic role. While discussing the “imminent” sequel Jennifer’s Body 2 , the Oscar-winning writer explained that the followup will “explore even more about why Jennifer is sympathetic and what she’s been through” after she was sacrificed in a satanic ritual in the 2009 horror comedy, which turned her into the boy-eating entity. “Jennifer is a sympathetic character for me, before and after the transformation,” she explained on the Petticoat Revolution podcast. “I mean, she is very isolated, she’s very lonely, she’s very insecure. Everybody remembers Jennifer when she’s like, ‘I am a god,’ or when she’s at her most radiant and at her most powerful. But people forget about these moments in the movie where she’s like a shell of herself, she’s just exsanguinated almost. And to me, Megan played both of those sides of Jennifer so well.” Related Stories News ‘Jennifer’s Body’ Director Karyn Kusama Teases Diablo Cody’s “Fun & Crazy” Sequel, Recalls Pete Wentz’s Audition, Says Cult Status “Tickles Me” News Amanda Seyfried Teases ‘Jennifer’s Body’ Sequel: “I Didn’t Confirm It!” Cody continued, “And one fun thing—I can’t talk about it too much—but you know we’re doing a sequel to this movie, like imminently, and I felt like in the new movie, I was able to explore even more about why Jennifer is sympathetic and what she’s been through. And there is absolutely, to me, a loneliness and a poignancy to that character that people don’t always recognize.” Watch on Deadline Deadline previously confirmed that Cody is developing the sequel for 20th Century Studios, with the movie’s original director Karyn Kusama teasing that she’s “very excited to hear what comes” of the follow-up, for which Megan Fox and Amanda Seyfried have both expressed interest in returning. articles.title: J.K. Rowling’s Agent Neil Blair Condemns Trans Rights Protest At ‘Harry Potter And The Cursed Child’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Russell Brand Trial: Woman Alleges She Was Raped By Star In Hotel Room After He Posed For Semi-Nude Photos Midjourney: Report Claims AI Model Is Worst Offender For Flouting Hollywood Copyright Russell Brand’s Accusers: Prosecutors Claim ‘Despicable Me’ Star Preyed On Women In TV Industry During “Frenzied” & “Wild-Eyed” Incidents View All October 17, 2026 1:43am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Harry Potter And The Cursed Child' Sonia Friedman Productions EXCLUSIVE: J.K. Rowling ‘s agent Neil Blair has claimed that a trans rights protest at a gala performance of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child put people at risk. During an event celebrating a shortened version of the West End stage show at the Palace Theatre on Thursday night, a number of protesters stormed the red carpet. Wearing masks to conceal their identities, the individuals lay down on the carpet before being removed by security. One was wearing a shirt featuring the words: “Rowling money kills.” Rowling has been staunchly critical of transgender rights activists, funding legal efforts to protect women’s rights and penning X/Twitter posts that are considered to be attacks by the trans community. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News J.K. Rowling To Be Subject Of BBC Documentary Examining Her Rise & Gender Identity Views News 'Harry Potter And The Cursed Child' Rebounds With Tom Felton; Christopher Jackson Keeps 'Hamilton' On Top - Broadway Box Office In a statement provided to Deadline, Blair said: “We respect peaceful activism and the right to express different views. But those rights must be exercised without putting others at risk, including audience members, performers and theatre staff, as we saw yesterday evening during the protests outside the Palace Theatre in London ahead of the gala performance of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child . “Above all, we want to continue bringing the magic of Harry Potter to the wonderful fans who have supported and embraced this world for so many years. Every fan deserves to enjoy the magic of Harry Potter in an atmosphere of respect and security, and we remain committed to keeping live theatre a welcoming and safe experience for everyone.” The new version of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child has been cut from a five-hour show performed across two parts to a single three-hour performance as it is performed on Broadway. ‘Street Fighter’ Socking Away $30M; A24’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc Eyes $12M J.K. Watch on Deadline The new first preview date is Monday, October 19, at Broadway Booth Theatre. Opening night of Sunday, November 15 remains unchanged.
