articles.title: What Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Reveals About Media’s Future (Guest Column)
articles.full_text: Oct 12, 2026 11:00am PT What Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Reveals About Media’s Future (Guest Column) 'You can’t consolidate your way out of disruption,' writes Accenture's John Peters By John Peters Plus Icon John Peters Latest See All Getty Images Paramount Skydance ‘s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery to form Skydance Corp. , which pushes the combined company to second place in Nielsen’s U.S. TV audience share and brings together two major Hollywood studios, has reignited debate about consolidation in media. But the bigger story is what the merger highlights about the pressures reshaping the media industry and the race to reinvent a market where audiences are more fragmented, competition for attention is intensifying and technology is changing how content is created, distributed and monetized. Related Stories Charlie Brooker's New Netflix Series Gets Title, 'Blackmere,' as Rory Kinnear Joins Cast and First-Look Photos Revealed The most interesting thing about this acquisition isn’t merely the consolidation itself. It’s what companies do with the scale after they consolidate. Combining two companies can create scale, but scale alone doesn’t automatically create relevance — much less long-term survival. Media companies now are being forced to take a harder look at their portfolios and determine which assets, brands and capabilities will drive future growth. The real test is whether that scale can be turned into stronger audience affinity, better experiences and new sources of growth. Popular on Variety Competition in an M&A climate Hollywood may be consolidating, but attention is not. There may be fewer traditional media companies today, but there are dramatically more competitors for consumers’ attention. Media companies are chasing the same things: consumer attention, subscription dollars, ad revenue, talent, and data and technology capabilities. And they’re not just competing with each other. They’re competing against some of the world’s largest technology platforms — and the armies of creators that they enable, not to mention the ever-proliferating competitors fighting for attention like video games, music, and even sports betting and AI chatbots. While box office or TV ratings used to be the competitive unit, it’s become clear that the minute is now the competitive unit. Every platform is bidding for the next minute of someone’s attention. The affinity war is on. The Impact on Content So what does consolidation mean for how media companies think about IP? The instinct after consolidation is to assume fewer titles and fewer bets. But technology and AI are simultaneously driving the economics of content creation in the opposite direction. The Paramount-Warner Bros. merger could eventually lead to more content, not less. But that requires a broader view of content, one that extends beyond traditional film and television programming. It’s far past time to stop thinking of content as just “shows” and “movies,” and acknowledge that today’s franchises have ongoing relationships with their fans. Consumers are increasingly moving between long-form video, short-form video, gaming, social communities, merchandise and live experiences. Recent Accenture research found that 55% of consumers want social features within streaming services, while 58% say user-generated video can be just as entertaining as traditional media. The next media battle won’t be held over who has the biggest content library. It’ll be about who’s developed the deepest fan relationship. This is equally appliable in film and TV studios as it is in newsroom, in broadcast trucks outside a sporting event, in record labels and music platforms, social video sites, sports betting apps and AI chatbots. In the affinity war, the future of content may be fewer isolated titles, but infinitely more experiences around the titles and brands that matter. The Audience Is Consuming Everything Streaming is no longer the industry’s organizing idea. The battle has expanded to every channel competing for consumer attention. Audience fragmentation is the new reality, and consumer attention is scattered. Accenture research shows that the number of media types consumers choose most across 10 different entertainment occasions has expanded from just two in 2022 to six in 2025. Streaming remains the dominant source for television content, as it now accounts for almost half of television usage according to Nielsen. Even so, while streaming was once the destination, it’s now just one stop along the way. You Can’t Consolidate Your Way Out of Disruption A merger can make you bigger overnight, but it can’t reinvent you overnight. Accenture research suggests the industry faces a steep challenge: more than nine in 10 media executives expect GenAI and new entrants to significantly reshape the industry within just two years. Meanwhile, 88% of media executives cite rigid technology stacks as a major transformation barrier, and legacy media companies spend roughly 6% of revenue on IT versus 9%-10% for media businesses within diversified technology companies. M&A can create scale, but scale is only valuable if it funds reinvention. The critical question is whether companies will use that financial flexibility to invest in AI, technology, advertising, personalization, new experiences and new business model innovation. The real dividend from consolidation isn’t cost reduction. It’s the ability to build the next generation of media businesses. So the strategic question isn’t “Are we big enough?” It’s “Are we different enough, and can we change fast enough?” The Future of M&A in Media and Entertainment M&A is likely to remain an important part of the industry’s strategic toolkit, although the nature of the transactions may evolve. There is an obvious economic logic to additional consolidation where companies can achieve scale, eliminate duplication or strengthen distribution. However, in the affinity war with audiences fragmenting away from media’s legacy and streaming offerings, scale without reinvention is, sadly, merely increasing the size of the lifeboat drifting helplessly towards the coming waterfall. As the newly named Skydance’s transaction marches toward an increasingly inevitable closure, everyone will naturally ask which big media company will merge next. However, the industry may be asking the wrong M&A question. The key item to consider is which capabilities are media companies missing. For the forward-looking, the next phase of M&A is likely to focus less on scale, and more on acquiring capabilities that create differentiation. In capability-driven M&A, companies are seeking to add AI, advertising, gaming, creator, commerce or data capabilities that can create new growth opportunities and strengthen their ability to compete for audience attention. Roku’s multiyear history of acquiring ad tech fits this model — as does Fox Corp.’s planned acquisition of Roku, which adds not just ad inventory but ad tech, platform and CTV operating-system capabilities. Similarly, Netflix’s recent acquisition of Ben Affleck’s InterPositive accelerates the postproduction AI capabilities they can offer to creatives. Indeed, Accenture research found that 80% of deals that outperformed sector averages saw dealmakers place significant emphasis on technology transformation and technology capability acquisition. The most capable acquirers also get better with every deal. The strongest deals will add something the company lacks. Some of the most important transactions may therefore be smaller acquisitions that bring media companies new skills or technologies. In the war for affinity, legacy brands like Golf Channel and the New York Times are showing what growth and diversification become possible with segment-specific, affinity-targeted acquisition strategies. The rallying cry in corporate development offices across Hollywood should be to stop buying more of yesterday’s media business. Instead, buy the capabilities you need for tomorrow’s. The industry’s future will depend on how effectively media companies turn their portfolios and capabilities into better products, stronger audience relationships, and more engagement experiences. John Peters is Accenture’s global and U.S. media & entertainment industry lead, advising leading media, entertainment and sports organizations on growth, transformation and innovation. Based in Los Angeles, he works with clients across the industry on navigating disruption, harnessing emerging technologies and building new sources of value and competitive advantage. articles.title: Peruvian Filmmaker Sami Hawka Explores Polyamory, Indigenous Rights and Resistance in ‘While Everything Falls’: ’Power Can Oppress People in Different Ways’
articles.full_text: Oct 12, 2026 11:15am PT Peruvian Filmmaker Sami Hawka Explores Polyamory, Indigenous Rights and Resistance in ‘While Everything Falls’: ’Power Can Oppress People in Different Ways’ Selected for VIFF’s Business Hub Co-Productions Forum and the Queer Palm Lab, the film explores marginalized communities and political resistance under a fictionalized dictatorship By Katherine Brodsky Plus Icon Katherine Brodsky Latest Peruvian Filmmaker Sami Hawka Explores Polyamory, Indigenous Rights and Resistance in ‘While Everything Falls’: ’Power Can Oppress People in Different Ways’ 31 minutes ago Beyond ‘Hollywood North’: How Vancouver’s Indie Film Scene Is Building Its Own Ecosystem 3 days ago Jeissy Trompiz’s ‘Three Houses’ Explores a Venezuela Where Afro and Indigenous Communities Sit on the ‘Periphery of the Periphery’ 3 days ago See All Sami Hawka Courtesy of Sami Hawka What happens when the right to love who you want becomes an act of resistance? Peruvian filmmaker Sami Hawka is developing a feature, “While Everything Falls” (Afuera Todo Arde), which explores the fight for personal freedom under a fictionalized dictatorship in contemporary Peru. The story takes place in a conservative rural community where two members of a polyamorous triad marry to keep up appearances. But when their relationship is exposed by their third lover, they flee to the capital, where they become involved in a rebellion against the dictatorship and discover that their fight for personal freedom is inseparable from the struggle for Indigenous rights, the rights of other marginalized communities and economic equality. Related Stories 'Star Trek: Starfleet Academy' Season 2 Adds Bill Nighy, Rosemarie DeWitt in Guest Roles Jason Blum on How ‘Other Mommy’ Got That Controversial Title, Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ and More From Blumhouse at NYCC The Madrid-based filmmaker’s project is gaining momentum after being selected for the Vancouver International Film Festival’s Business Hub Co-Productions Forum and the Queer Palm Lab, an LGBTQ-focused development program associated with the Cannes Film Festival. Hawka is now pursuing international co-production partners and funding for the feature. Popular on Variety “The film follows these characters who are in their bubble,” Hawka tells Variety . “But when they break [out of] the bubble, they start realizing that they have other forms of oppression” beyond queerness and polyamory, and that they share those experiences with other marginalized groups. “In this rebellion, there are also a lot of Indigenous people and Indigenous movements that need vindication of their rights,” Hawka says, connecting the story to Peru’s colonial history and its enduring consequences. “When we as a culture experienced that…It had a very strong impact on our culture and on the lives that we had here.” Peru developed into a country that’s fractured, they explain. “These people still need some sort of citizenship in this new order that’s not organized to fit their needs, or was built on inequality.” For Hawka, the story is also an extension of their own experiences as a nonbinary person with Indigenous roots. They spent a significant part of their childhood in Cusco, in Peru’s Andean highlands, attending an intercultural school where they learned Quechua and developed connections with Indigenous elders and spiritual traditions. Those experiences helped shape both their understanding of gender and their approach to filmmaking. “I think it has helped me situate a place that needs vindication,” they say. “It has helped me look at things from a perspective where rights need to get acknowledged, and where political action needs to start.” Colonialism and cultural erasure, they argue, have also shaped attitudes toward sexuality and gender, leaving a complicated legacy that younger generations are now working to understand and reclaim. “There are documents of many places in the world where societies had more than two genders, and that was sort of erased, and now we are starting to reconnect with that,” they say. In Peru, they point to archaeological ceramics depicting same-sex encounters by shamans in sacred ritual contexts. “Now it’s kind of our work to go back and try to rescue all these things.” For them, reconnecting with Indigenous traditions has also been a way of understanding their own identity. At its core, Hawka says, the film they want to make is about how authoritarian systems restrict people’s ability to determine their own lives. “Power can invisibilize and oppress people in different ways— around class, around gender, around race, around economic privilege,” they say. Eventually, the characters come to recognize that their own experiences of marginalization connect them to a larger struggle. “They realize that they need to join the resistance in order to be free themselves too,” says Hawka. “It’s like a collective thing.” The visual approach will reflect the tensions between the characters’ private lives and the political upheaval around them. Hawka envisions contemplative, quiet scenes in the countryside, with natural light and a documentary-like approach, contrasted with the noise, intense colors, and chaos of the city. They aim to show the “places and spaces inhabited the way they actually ar The film is being developed by Peruvian production company FILMA+ as an international co-production, with casting still open and discussions with potential producers underway. After development had stalled, recently “the project has taken a giant leap,” they say. Ultimately, says Hawka, “While Everything Falls” uses an unconventional love story to explore how people can reclaim the freedom to determine one’s own destiny and fight for what they believe — both individually and collectively — in the face of authoritarianism and oppressive power. Whether it’s about polyamory, or homosexuality — there are a lot of rules that are imposed by power, they say. Social punishment, they note, is also an “exercise of power.” Cynthia Erivo Says ‘Not Enough Credit Is Given to Intimacy Coordinators’: ‘They’re Often Given a Hard Time’ but ‘What They Do Is Important’ Loading comments...

articles.title: How South Africa Rescued Its Rebate and Pulled the Industry Back From the Brink: We’re ‘Back in Business’
articles.full_text: Oct 12, 2026 11:26am PT How South Africa Rescued Its Rebate and Pulled the Industry Back From the Brink: We’re ‘Back in Business’ After more than two years of almost complete paralysis, the country's 25% cash rebate program appears to be back on track By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest How South Africa Rescued Its Rebate and Pulled the Industry Back From the Brink: We’re ‘Back in Business’ 15 minutes ago ‘Mami Wata’ Director C.J. Obasi, ‘Khartoum’ Filmmaker Ibrahim Ahmad and More Take New Projects to Durban FilmMart’s Co-Production Forum 5 days ago Durban FilmMart Head on Why This Year’s Event Is ‘Looking Inward’ as African Screen Industries Strive to ‘Create Solutions’ on Their Own Terms 2 weeks ago See All Courtesy Known Associates Entertainment The long nightmare might be over for South African producers, whose industry has been crippled for more than two years by the paralysis of a rebate program that for all intents and purposes had ceased to function. Speaking this week at the Durban FilmMart , Nelly Molokoane, director of film and television production at the Dept. of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC), insisted that the government body tasked with administering the country’s 25% cash rebate has finally turned a corner. “The department is back in business,” Molokoane said. Related Stories Charlie Brooker's New Netflix Series Gets Title, 'Blackmere,' as Rory Kinnear Joins Cast and First-Look Photos Revealed After months of political pressure from industry bodies that rallied under the banner of the Save SA Film and TV Jobs Coalition, the DTIC is now working through a backlog of applications and rebate claims dating back to 2024, with Molokoane counseling patience as the embattled department attempts to right the ship. Popular on Variety “We know that the industry now is bleeding, but we are doing our best,” she said. The news sparked a collective sigh of relief from the filmmakers and industry groups gathered in Durban, who have locked horns with South African officials over delays in processing rebate claims, bureaucratic bottlenecks, a lack of transparency from their counterparts in government, and overall questions about the future of the once-thriving incentive program. “The worst is over,” said producer Delon Bakker, who serves as chairperson of the Independent Producers Organization. “We’re very confident that we’re now moving in the right direction. We’re not sure at what pace, but we are definitely making progress.” The crisis dealt a devastating blow to a South African industry that was already feeling the squeeze, with the exhibition sector floundering, global streaming networks scaling back their investments in local production and domestic broadcasters — including the struggling public broadcaster, SABC — unable to keep the industry afloat. “We’re talking thousands of jobs. We’re talking hundreds of companies that have suffered losses because of this. We’re talking projects that have made claims that have not been paid two, three, four years later,” said producer Paul Buys, of Rose and Oaks Media. “It’s really pushed everybody to the limits.” The DTIC has made significant strides in paying off most of the nearly 2-billion-rand ($121 million) backlog in unpaid rebate claims and shored up roughly 1.5 billion rand ($91 million) to fund the rebate through 2029. While those producers who spoke to Variety were cautiously optimistic that the industry has finally turned the page, there remains much work to be done. Chief among their concerns is what shape the incentive program will take moving forward, whether it’s a modified version of the existing cash rebate program, a tax credit scheme, or some alternate proposal. Still, after months of often contentious dialogue with government officials, local producers are grateful that both sides have found a way through the impasse. “Ultimately, everyone wants this to work, and ultimately, we want to work with the department,” said Bakker. “We want peace. We want a period of prosperity.” For her part, the polarizing Molokoane — who has faced calls for her resignation from industry bodies — struck a conciliatory tone in Durban. “We’ve been engaging the industry since last year to say, ‘How best can we support this industry?’ And I know maybe the industry has been informed that the DTIC is not on board,” she said. “We are on board…. We would like to work with you in order to ensure that we’ve got a sustainable industry.” For now, local producers are guardedly optimistic that such political goodwill will last, while their foreign counterparts will look for reassurances that the rebate is back on solid footing. “It’s going to take some time to get that certainty back…and build trust internationally,” said Big World Cinema producer Steven Markovitz. In spite of the challenges, South African filmmakers say the rebate crisis has been a wake-up call that has not only galvanized the industry but bolstered their resolve to build a sustainable film and TV business — with or without a functioning incentive program. “There’s a willingness to try and do things in this crisis,” said Markovitz. “I do think that we’re going to come out of it looking at other ways to try and break that dependency on DTI subsidies for every film that we do.” “These obstacles and challenges constantly force us to rethink different ways to do things and different ways to still get our films made and our stories told,” added Yellowbone Entertainment’s Layla Swart. “And I think despite everything, that’s always what we do. We’re fighters and we’re constantly advocating for the things that work with us.” The Durban FilmMart runs Oct. 9 – 12 in Durban, South Africa. articles.title: Tilly Nollywood? African Filmmakers — Ready or Not — Get Set for the AI Revolution
articles.full_text: Oct 12, 2026 11:36am PT Tilly Nollywood? African Filmmakers — Ready or Not — Get Set for the AI Revolution By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest How South Africa Rescued Its Rebate and Pulled the Industry Back From the Brink: We’re ‘Back in Business’ 14 minutes ago ‘Mami Wata’ Director C.J. Obasi, ‘Khartoum’ Filmmaker Ibrahim Ahmad and More Take New Projects to Durban FilmMart’s Co-Production Forum 5 days ago Durban FilmMart Head on Why This Year’s Event Is ‘Looking Inward’ as African Screen Industries Strive to ‘Create Solutions’ on Their Own Terms 2 weeks ago See All "Mystery of Osu Land" (Courtesy Mysterious Tech Studio) The world premiere of what’s been billed as the first photorealistic, AI -generated feature film in the Yoruba language fizzled out last week when user demand overwhelmed the servers of Docuth, the streaming platform that hosted the launch. After months of hype building to the release of “Asiri Ilu Awon Osu” (Mystery of Osu Land), the film’s Nigerian producers, Mysterious Tech Studio, took to social media to apologize for the glitch, telling their followers: “To everyone at home and abroad who has tried to watch and could not get through, please do not be offended or discouraged.” Related Stories Charlie Brooker's New Netflix Series Gets Title, 'Blackmere,' as Rory Kinnear Joins Cast and First-Look Photos Revealed The episode felt somehow symbolic for this moment in the history of AI in Africa, where excitement over the technology’s transformative potential for the continent’s filmmakers often runs counter to the practical realities on the ground. Popular on Variety As African industry professionals convened at this year’s Durban FilmMart , both the potential and pitfalls of artificial intelligence were high on the agenda. Among the chief concerns for many stakeholders are the barriers to entry. AI tools that are widely available elsewhere in the world face unique challenges in reaching African consumers, from high data costs and low broadband speeds to payment-processing headaches. Tamara Dawit, of Ethiopian Canadian production company Gobez Media, noted that those challenges represent significant “systemic barriers” to the adoption of the latest tech tools on the African continent. “How do we address those issues so that everyone is benefitting from the advancements in technology?” she said. “If these are great opportunities for the industry, can everybody actually access them?” Zukisani Karabo Mabece, of media-tech and production company Digicine Motion Picture, agreed. “AI isn’t necessarily a magic pill,” said Mabece, whose Johannesburg-based company has leaned into generative AI with a host of digital tools designed to democratize access to cutting-edge technology for African filmmakers. “It’s very biased. It’s very Western,” he said. “We’re having to build our own language models to accommodate the languages that we have here locally. We took it upon ourselves to build models that serve our market and our geography.” In some instances, the rapid adoption of AI technology has had unintended consequences that aren’t unique to Africa. Earlier this year, the South African government drafted an ambitious AI policy that was summarily withdrawn when journalists discovered that at least six of its 67 academic citations were the by-products of AI hallucinations, referring to journals and authors that did not exist. The drafters appeared to have used a large-language model to compose the policy without verifying its claims. While the blunder was a PR disaster for South African policymakers, Amilcar Patel, who serves as co-chair of the South African Screen Federation (SASFED), noted that there are more pernicious dangers lurking for Africans when it comes to using AI tools developed in the Global North. “We need to be very careful when we’re using AI in our work, especially in our policy and legal work, because we’re infusing a very different culture that doesn’t protect women, that doesn’t protect the poor, that doesn’t protect the vulnerable, into our legislative framework,” said Patel. “And then it becomes law.” For African creatives, there are additional ethical factors to consider. “AI mirrors society,” said Dawit. “Society has a lot of systemic inequities within it, and those show up [in AI models].” “Those that are building AI don’t look like us. Biases are already built into the AI systems,” added Samantha Kaine, of the Independent Media Producers Assn. of Creative Talent (I.M.P.A.C.T.). “When the major AI models are trained largely on Western data and Western culture, what does it take to use these tools without importing someone else’s aesthetic or erasing who we are — erasing our own identity?” Such concerns are likely to be on the agenda next month when Cape Town plays host to the Africa AI Summit, a three-day event that gathers heads of state and global tech and business leaders to draw up a roadmap that will shape the future of AI across Africa and the Global South. Backed by partners including the World Bank, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Nvidia, the event is built around a billion-dollar AI initiative that’s designed to accelerate the deployment of artificial intelligence across the continent. In the meantime, African filmmakers will continue to find uses for AI tools, even as the continent’s digital infrastructure and policy frameworks are forced to play catch-up. One week after the failed rollout of “Mystery of Osu Land,” Kafilat Yusuff, of Mysterious Tech Studio, told Variety that after “viewers experienced intermittent access due to high traffic at launch,” the platform “has now been stabilized.” The film, which incorporated roughly 80% AI-assisted scenes with 20% live-action scenes utilizing real actors and their voices, is now available to stream on Docuth. “Our experience has shown us that AI offers independent African filmmakers new ways to explore ambitious stories and visual worlds,” Yusuff said. “However, it also raises important questions about the role of human performers, consent, compensation, creative ownership and how audiences receive AI-assisted films.” As for future plans, she said that the company is holding off on a follow-up until “Mystery of Osu Land” has had time to enjoy a “full run.” “We spent a lot of time building this, and with the premiere traffic we just saw on Docuth, it’s clear there’s a lot of global curiosity. So our focus now is festivals, wider press and securing a stable global streaming release so everyone who wants to see it can,” she said. “We are documenting everything we learned from this hybrid 80% AI-20% live-action pipeline, which will eventually help us and other African filmmakers make future projects at lower cost.” The Durban FilmMart runs Oct. 9 – 12 in Durban, South Africa. articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Antonio Banderas To Star As Spanish Conquistador Hernán Cortés In Feature From Paul Mignot & Nicholas Kazan ‘FREEAgent:’ Streetwear Pioneer Jeff Staple Among First Guests On Season Two Of Kenny Annan-Jonathan’s Podcast James Gray Says He Considers ‘Two Lovers’ His First Successful Feature: “I Don’t Regard The Films I Made Before This Very Highly” View All October 12, 2026 8:39am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Clockwise from left: Barry Keoghan is Ringo Starr, Paul Mescal is Paul McCartney, Joseph Quinn is George Harrison and Harris Dickinson is John Lennon in Columbia Pictures 'The Beatles – A Four-Film Cinematic Event' Columbia Pictures “We’re on day 180 of the shoot today,” Pippa Harris , the producer behind Sam Mendes ’ The Beatles – A Four Film Cinematic Event, said with a pointed smile this afternoon during a career Q&A at the London Film Festival. “I stepped away for this hour and am going back afterwards. It is a big endeavour,” Harris continued before politely swerving specific questions about the films. Harris did, however, speak about the unique release strategy behind the films. All four of Mendes’ Beatles films will be released in cinemas in April 2028 in what Mendes described at CinemaCon 2025 as the first “bingeable moment in cinema.” Related Stories News Sam Mendes' Beatles Biopic Recreates 'Abbey Road' Album Cover In Behind-The-Scenes Video -- Watch Festivals 'Hamnet' & 'The Beatles' Producer Pippa Harris & 'The Zone Of Interest' Producer James Wilson To Headline LFF's Industry Forum “At the moment, the films will come out in 2028, and we want people to be able to experience them in the cinema at the same time, during the same period,” Harris told the audience at the LFF. Watch on Deadline “Now that doesn’t necessarily mean we’re thinking that people will go and see all four films on the same day. But within the same month, you might see one a week, or you might see one film one weekend and another the next. However you do it, we hope that people will see all four films.” Pippa Harris Photo by Leon Bennett/Getty Images. The Beatles – A Four Film Cinematic Event stars Joseph Quinn as George Harrison, Paul Mescal as Paul McCartney, Barry Keoghan as Ringo Starr, and Harris Dickinson as John Lennon. The films are essentially four separate theatrical biopic films about the iconic British quartet. “They stand alone as individual stories of each of those four men,” Harris said of the four films, “but they have a cumulative power, which I think is greater than the sum of the parts.” Harris added: “They are the greatest band in history, and we’re trying to do our best to do them justice. So hence the four films. I don’t think there’s probably another band that you could legitimately say you wanted to see four films about.” Mendes is directing from scripts written by Jez Butterworth, Peter Straughan and Jack Thorne. A collaboration between Sony Pictures Entertainment and Mendes’ Neal Street Productions, the films are being produced by Mendes, Harris and Julie Pastor of Neal Street, as well as Alexandra Derbyshire, in association with Apple Corps for Sony Pictures. This marks the first time that The Beatles and Apple Corps Ltd. have authorized the use of the band members’ life stories and music in scripted films. articles.title: Director Rory Kennedy On ‘The Trial Of Alec Baldwin,’ And Why ‘Rust’ Star At First Reacted Negatively To Her Film
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Bend Film Festival Prizes Go To ‘Hot Water,’ ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds,’ ‘Kikuyu Land,’ ‘The Lake’ & More ‘14th’ Review: Ava DuVernay’s Impassioned Defense Of Constitution Takes Aim At Trump & Attempted Rescission Of Rights Geeta Gandbhir, Sam Pollard, Alisa Payne Board ICE-Themed Oscar Contender ‘Water Cooler’ As EPs View All October 12, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Alec Baldwin in 'The Trial of Alec Baldwin' Moxie Films/Abramorama Mystery still surrounds the fatal shooting on the set of Alec Baldwin ’s Western Rust , an incident that claimed the life of cinematographer Halyna Hutchins. Did the actor pull the trigger on a prop gun as he rehearsed a scene (he denies that), or did the weapon malfunction and misfire? How did a live round get into the revolver and who brought the lethal ammunition to the set? Why were prosecutors in Santa Fe, NM so intent on charging Baldwin with a crime for what many impartial observers — though not all — saw as a tragic accident? The answers to some of those questions are provided in the new documentary The Trial of Alec Baldwin , directed by Rory Kennedy , which opens in Los Angeles on Friday. The film begins by dispelling one false rumor – that Baldwin initiated the project as some sort of attempt to repair his damaged reputation. Text on screen states flatly, “Baldwin was given no editorial control, nor did he provide any financial support or receive any compensation.” Related Stories News Alec Baldwin Joins Chris Hemsworth, Taron Egerton & Zazie Beetz In Matt Ross-Helmed ‘Kockroach’ News Halyna Hutchins’ Mother & Sister Encourage You To See ‘Rust’ Kennedy underscored that point at the Bend Film Festival in Oregon over the weekend, where the documentary played. At a Q&A that followed the screening, the Oscar-nominated filmmaker told the audience it wasn’t Baldwin who came up with the documentary idea, but the other way around. “I approached him,” she clarified. Watch on Deadline They had met many years before the Rust tragedy. “I have known Alec probably for 20 years,” Kennedy said. “I would say we were friends. We wouldn’t go out and have dinner, but I knew him. Alec is actually a great supporter of documentaries and is associated with the Hamptons Film Festival and also does a summer doc series. And so I’ve been lucky enough over the years to have a number of my films be a part of that. I’ve gotten to know him largely through that.” The documentary project began at a point when it didn’t appear the actor would face criminal allegations. Alec Baldwin in ‘Rust’ Rust Movie Productions LLC “When we entered this story,” Kennedy told the festival audience, “it really seemed like the Rust story was going to be resolved pretty early on and that [the documentary] was really going to be much more of a biopic with the Rust story interwoven maybe as a through line, kind of the backbone of it, but would be pretty thin. And then it just kept coming back and continuing. And we were always there when it had sort of dramatic turns.” Alec Baldwin hugs his attorney Alex Spiro at the conclusion of his trial for involuntary manslaughter in First Judicial District Court on July 12, 2024 in Santa Fe, New Mexico. Ramsay de Give-Pool/Getty Images Those dramatic turns included Baldwin and Rust armorer Hannah Gutierrez-Reed being charged in January 2023 with involuntary manslaughter. A few months later, the charges against Baldwin were dropped. But then in January 2024 a grand jury indicted Baldwin on felony involuntary manslaughter charges and special prosecutors re-filed their case. The prosecution of Baldwin, the film strongly suggests, had less to do with the evidence than with the special prosecutor’s personal animus toward him as a Hollywood star with a history of volcanic behavior. “It just seemed pretty clear that people were going after him and he was being taken to task [for the Rust shooting] in a way that seemed not entirely justified or fair,” Kennedy observed. “And then it started raising questions about how in this day and age with the internet and social media, we hold people to justice outside of the judicial system. Then as the film and the story unfolded, you started seeing how that narrative in social media started impacting the justice system.” Director Rory Kennedy at the Deadline Hollywood Portrait Studio during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival on January 25, 2026 in Park City, Utah. Josh Telles for Deadline Kennedy described the larger concerns raised by the Baldwin prosecution. “You start thinking, okay, how does this kind of [social media] chatter that we’re all doing… how is it affecting our larger institutions? How is it affecting government, for example? …How is it affecting the judicial system? I think it’s an important question that we should be observing and asking ourselves.” Baldwin, it becomes clear, was being tried twice – in the court of public opinion and in a court of law. The film builds to an astonishing crescendo, resulting in the case being dismissed in the middle of the trial (I won’t give away what happened. Close watchers of the case, including my colleague Dominic Patten who covered it for Deadline and appears as an expert in the documentary, know the ins and outs, but they came as a revelation to me). Hilaria Baldwin (R) speaks to her husband Alec Baldwin during his trial on involuntary manslaughter in First Judicial District Court on July 12, 2024 in Santa Fe, New Mexico. Ramsay de Give-Pool/Getty Images There would seem to be plenty for Baldwin to appreciate about Kennedy’s film, given how the court case ended. And yet… “When they [Baldwin and wife Hilaria] initially saw the film, they did not like the film,” the director reported. The cause of their displeasure has to do with scenes woven throughout that illustrate how Baldwin got his reputation for angry outbursts – confrontations with paparazzi through the years, for instance. Kennedy also explores a serious stain on Baldwin’s reputation from 2007 – the infamous voicemail he left for his then 11-year-old daughter Ireland in which he called her a “rude, thoughtless little pig.” That ugly lambasting came in the context of a bitter custody battle over Ireland between Baldwin and his ex-wife Kim Basinger. It’s a crucial piece of background because the special prosecutor referred to that incident in private communications in which she expressed loathing for the actor. “Because the prosecutors were, in my opinion, going after his reputation and not after what he did on the set,” Kennedy said, “we had to show what that reputation was, and we had to show it honestly.” A bit too honestly, perhaps, for Baldwin’s liking. “I think it was just very hard [for him] to see all that… showing his ex-wife in there and then [him wondering], ‘Why are we doing that?’ Well, the only way to really get to the voicemail is to understand that history, to understand what the motivation of the voicemail was. And you can’t get there without having that context.” Baldwin seems to be warming to the film, after hearing feedback from viewers. “I think he’s now come around and is much more supportive of it,” Kennedy noted. “I think there are a lot of people who say… this film is important and in many ways redeems him and also really helps people understand him and understand what he went through and understand the injustice of what happened to him.” ‘The Social Reckoning’ Bombs With $5.5M; ‘Other Mommy’ Rules Frame Catherine Laga’aia & Deacon Phillippe To Lead Disney+ Pilot ‘Spaceship Earth’ ‘Baywatch’ Team On Shooting In L.A.; Prime Swoops For Princess Diana Series 2026 Domestic B.O. Discovery (WBD). As the ink dries on the Paramount -WBD deal, and the newly-minted Skydance plots its vision, the content chief backed up her boss Ted Sarandos in saying that WBD was “always a nice to have at a certain price, not a must have at any price.” Related Stories News Banijay Plots U.S. Expansion As Marco Bassetti Says ‘Peaky Blinders’ Maker Is Not “Jealous” Of Hollywood Studios News Netflix Eyes Major Layoffs – The Dish “We were never going to [spend over the odds],” she told an audience at MIPCOM . “We are financially disciplined. We knew what we had and what the opportunity was.” She was of course referring to Netflix’s eventually failed $83B bid to buy the storied studio , which ended up selling to David Ellison’s Paramount-Skydance for a far superior $110B , creating Skydance. Bajaria said Netflix is now focused instead on the goal of “keeping doing what we’re doing with the same investment, keeping our eye on the ball, making great things that people love around the world.” Watch on Deadline And there’s plenty of room still to grow, she added, pointing out that Netflix occupies around 5% of global audiences’ TV time, leaving a huge slice of the pie. Bajaria was in Cannes talking up Netflix’s global strategy, which goes well beyond huge hits like La Casa de Papel and Squid Game. “There are so many of these titles that go all around the world,” she added, pointing out that Canadian original Below is currently number one in more than 80 countries including France. Bajaria didn’t address the reported layoffs taking place at the streamer but said Netflix will continue to “expand,” something it has always done despite opposing moves from the competition. “When others have scaled back at different times we have continued to be consistent and grow our investment and expand what we do,” she added. “For me that is the most important thing.” She was also robust in responding to the notion that there is too much content out there. “We can see on Netflix our members watch a lot and they have lots of different moods and tastes,” she added. “We don’t programme for a narrow demographic. Apple Original Films on Wednesday released a teaser trailer for Being Heumann , the new film from Oscar-winning CODA filmmaker Siân Heder that is gearing up for its world premiere next week as the opening film of the Toronto Film Festival . Related Stories Festivals TIFF’s 51st Edition Sets Siân Heder’s ‘Being Heumann’ As Opening-Night Film Casting Mark Ruffalo To Star In Apple’s ‘Being Heumann’ From ‘CODA’ Director Siân Heder The film tells the true story of disability-rights advocate Judy Heumann, played by Doctor Who alum Ruth Madeley . Based on Heumann’s memoir, it centers on the year 1977, when Heumann led more than 100 disabled people to take over the San Francisco Federal Building, kicking off a 28 day sit-in — the longest occupation of a federal building in U.S. history. Watch on Deadline The protesters form a tightly bound community, refusing to leave until the government enforces section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which required all federal spaces to become accessible. articles.title: Sean Combs Injured In Prison; Release Date Pushed Back Again Amid Controversies & Violations
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Disney’s Former Top IP Lawyer Sues House Of Mouse For Ageism & Wrongful Termination: “Sleepless Nights & Days” Skydance CEOs Pressed On Layoffs & Donald Trump Interference As They Outline Future At Town Hall ‘SNL’ Cold Open Goes Full MAGA Midterms Desperation With Hegseth’s “Schlong Donkeys”, Trump’s Rambles & A Sad VP View All October 12, 2026 9:37am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sean 'Diddy' Combs Getty Images A trip from prison to the hospital this weekend may be the least of several recent blows to Sean “Diddy” Combs. Amidst tales of high-living indulgences , contraband and other luxuries behind bars at FCI Fort Dix, the much-accused Bad Boy Records founder has seen his release date pushed back by almost two more months. Related Stories Legal Diddy In The Hole As Plethora Of Contraband Violations Revealed; Grammy Winner Faces Delayed Release Legal It’s All About The Release Date: Diddy Gets More Prison Time After Dust-Up With Another Inmate Handed a much-anticipated sanction of over 40 days, Combs now is currently scheduled to walk out of the New Jersey minimum-security facility on March 2, 2028. With a release date that has gone up and down literally since Diddy was sentenced in September 2025 to a 50-month stint (with time served) after being convicted of two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution by a NYC jury in July 2025, the Grammy winner most recently was set to get out on January 21, 2028. At the beginning of October, Bureau of Prisons sources told Deadline that Combs would be facing “serious consequences ” for his violations of sneaking a smartphone into Fort Dix, as well as fine booze and having a paid staff of other inmates. In the immediate aftermath, Diddy was placed in solitary confinement. It was unclear when or if he was placed back in the general population of the generally cushy facility.
