articles.title: ‘Wildwood’ Review: Laika’s Most Ambitious Feature to Date Is a Richly Textured, Transportive Fairytale Epic
articles.full_text: Oct 11, 2026 6:15am PT ‘Wildwood’ Review: Laika’s Most Ambitious Feature to Date Is a Richly Textured, Transportive Fairytale Epic Familiar story elements abound in Travis Knight's film, adapted from Colin Meloy's popular 2011 children's novel, but lavish stop-motion spectacle makes it feel fresh and alive. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Wildwood’ Review: Laika’s Most Ambitious Feature to Date Is a Richly Textured, Transportive Fairytale Epic 2 hours ago ‘The First Taste of Loneliness’ Review: A Sentimental but Affecting Study of Family Life After Bereavement 15 hours ago ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s Latest Animated Feature Is a Giddy Retro-Futurist Noir With More Energy Than Charm 1 day ago See All Courtesy of Laika “Enjoy handmade art before it’s gone forever.” Keen-eyed viewers may read these words fleetingly on screen in the early stages of “ Wildwood ,” amid a wealth of fast-passing sights and sight gags as its young heroine cycles furiously through the homey, bustling streets of Portland, Oregon. Printed on a sign next to the craggly wares of a local ceramicist, the line gently pokes fun at the city’s wholesome, hippy-dippy spirit — but it’s also a sincere advertisement for the predominantly handcrafted virtues of “Wildwood” itself. If the in-joke sounds a little self-congratulatory, director Travis Knight and his team have a right to brag: The sixth feature from independent animation studio Laika is a stunner, a lovingly tactile and thumbprinted feat of stop-motion artistry on a scale rarely seen in the medium, that stands out by a mile in a cartoon marketplace ruled by sheeny, uncanny digital graphics. Related Stories 'Amanda the Adventurer' Video Game Movie Adaptation in the Works From Blumhouse, MatPat and Epic Pictures 'Star Trek: The Next Generation' Star Gates McFadden to Write Dr. Crusher Comic Book Series (EXCLUSIVE) That’s not in itself a revelation. Laika’s pleasingly organic, idiosyncratic (and let it be said, subtly CG-augmented) visual style has impressed from their 2009 debut, Henry Selick’s modern children’s classic “Coraline,” through to the likably goofy comedy “Missing Link” a decade later. Both those films opted for a cozily oddball storytelling style that matched the intimacy of their craftsmanship. In 2016’s historical Japanese adventure “Kubo and the Two Strings,” however, Knight pushed this decidedly miniaturist medium into brashly epic territory — an objective he pursues even more ambitiously in this sprawling 130-minute adventure, which narratively runs the gamut from gothic fairytale to visceral fantasy warfare. Some longtime Laika fans may harbor warmer feelings for the studio’s smaller, quirkier outings, but as both a formal achievement and a generation-crossing crowdpleaser, “Wildwood” is a spectacular success. Popular on Variety If the film is, at a story level, somewhat more generic than we’ve come to expect from the Laika playbook, that also goes for the book it’s adapted from. A 500-page-plus doorstop by indie musician Colin Meloy (of the Decemberists fame) that straddles the border between children’s and YA literature, the novel shows no great originality of prose or concept — fragments of works by C.S. Lewis, J.R.R. Tolkien, Enid Blyton and Kenneth Grahame are all mixed into its narrative and imagery, not to mention a sizable chunk of Jim Henson’s film “Labyrinth” — but it’s an absorbing yarn nonetheless. The same goes for the film, in which the studio’s regular screenwriter Chris Butler perhaps even improves on the source material: The dialogue is sparky, the relationships quick-drawn but genuinely felt. It opens on a sequence of quite frightening, disorienting strangeness that immediately makes sense of the film’s outwardly surprising PG-13 certificate — presaging a degree of bloodshed and emotional intensity not to be ignored by parents seeking an animated film to babysit their little ones. As a thunderstorm rages outside, a young boy in an imposing woodland castle steps onto a high terrace outside his bedroom, and deliberately plunges to his death before his distraught mother can stop him; as crowds gather at the site of the tragedy, it’s discovered that the boy was merely an android, his chest shattered to reveal the metal cogs within. It’s some time before we’re given the context for this solemn, cryptically beautiful opening gambit, as we cut to an altogether more recognizable childhood: that of precocious 12-year-old Prue (voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee), who lives with her bohemian hipster parents (Jake Johnson and Maya Erskine) and baby brother Mac in a tranquil Portland suburb, and who’s just beginning to wish for a life less ordinary, or at least less oatmealy. articles.title: ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight Reflects on Animated Feature’s 16-Year Journey at London Premiere: ‘When We Started This, Barack Obama Was a Fresh-Faced President’
articles.full_text: Oct 11, 2026 7:02am PT ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight Reflects on Animated Feature’s 16-Year Journey at London Premiere: ‘When We Started This, Barack Obama Was a Fresh-Faced President’ By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight Reflects on Animated Feature’s 16-Year Journey at London Premiere: ‘When We Started This, Barack Obama Was a Fresh-Faced President’ 1 hour ago Scarlett Johansson, Sam Rockwell and Brad Bird Sing ‘Happy Birthday’ to Composer Michael Giacchino as ‘Ray Gunn’ World Premieres in London 24 hours ago Danny Boyle Says Third ’28 Years Later’ Is ‘On the Back Burner,’ Explains Why He Put an AI Margaret Thatcher in ‘Ink’ 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Laika Stop-motion animation is a notoriously time-consuming method to make a film, with most features taking several years of painstakingly detailed work by vast teams of creatives. But few have likely taken as long as Laika ‘s sweeping fantasy epic “ Wildwood ,” which had its world premiere at the BFI London Film Festival on Sunday. Speaking on stage at the premiere alongside voice stars Carey Mulligan, Peyton Elizabeth Lee and Jacob Tremblay, director Travis Knight explained the stop-motion process to the audience at the Royal Festival Hall. Related Stories 'Children of Blood and Bone' Author Tomi Adeyemi Quietly Cancels New York Comic Con Panel Magic: The Gathering Reveals New 'Darkhold Destiny' Marvel Set, 'Avengers: Doomsday' Theater-Only Card Giveaway “Basically we build thousands and thousands of this tiny little objects, we put them in front of a camera and set lights and we take a picture, we move them a microscopic distance, we take another picture, we move them another microscopic distance, we take another picture,” he said. “And we repeat that process over and over until either the film emerges or society collapses.” Popular on Variety On “Wildwood,” — which Knight had previously acknowledged was the most ambitious Laika had ever attempted — production started in 2021 in the midst of COVID, but the development had actually begun some 10 years earlier, when Laika optioned the book by Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis. “This movie took us 16 years to make,” Knight explains. When we started Barack Obama was a fresh-faced president in his very first term. I could have become a medical doctor twice in the time it took us to make this movie. A child who was born when we started this could have driven me to the premiere.” Following its world premiere at the London Film Festival, which runs until Oct. 17, “Laika” is due to be released on Oct. 23 by Fathom Entertainment in the U.S. and by Black Bear in the U.K. The film marks the first by Laika to receive a PG-13 rating. articles.title: John Malkovich Says the Oscars Race Was a ‘Different World’ When He Was Last on the Campaign Trail: ‘Now, That’s the Only Way to Get People to Go to Theaters’
articles.full_text: Oct 11, 2026 7:11am PT John Malkovich Says the Oscars Race Was a ‘Different World’ When He Was Last on the Campaign Trail: ‘Now, That’s the Only Way to Get People to Go to Theaters’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest John Malkovich Says the Oscars Race Was a ‘Different World’ When He Was Last on the Campaign Trail: ‘Now, That’s the Only Way to Get People to Go to Theaters’ 1 hour ago ‘SNL U.K.’ Cold Open Sees Reunion Between Prince William and Kate and Prince Harry and Meghan (With Some Help From Former Prince Andrew): ‘They Must Want Us to Be Royals Again!’ 6 hours ago Sofia Coppola on Releasing ‘Making Marie Antoinette’ as a Tribute to Late Mother Eleanor, Even Though She Finds Younger Self ‘Embarrassing’: ‘It’s a Gift’ to See ‘Through My Mom’s Eyes’ 3 days ago See All Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images f John Malkovich has been highly tipped for an Oscar nomination for his performance in Martin McDonagh’s CIA black comedy “ Wild Horse Nine ,” making it his first real shot at an Academy Award in three decades. The 72-year-old actor was previously nominated for best supporting actor in “Places in the Heart” (1984) and “In the Line of Fire” (1993), but never won. Speaking at a London Film Festival Screen Talk on Sunday, Malkovich said he views awards buzz “probably differently than I did then, because the movie business existed.” Related Stories ‘Helluva Boss’ Actor Lashes Out at NYCC Heckler: ‘I’m Going to Jump Over This Fence and End You’ Marvel's 'Zodiac' Sets 2028 Release on Disney+ as New Details Revealed “It maintained an — undeserved, in my opinion, but nevertheless — a very, very high position in the culture. And when I say ‘undeserved,’ meaning there weren’t that many ‘Chinatowns’ or ‘Godfathers’ or ‘Godfathers II,'” Malkovich said. “So now, that’s the only way to get people to go to the theaters, the whole thing. And that’s months and months and months.” Popular on Variety Reflecting on the last time he was up for an Oscar over 30 years ago, Malkovich said the campaigning was not so intense. “When I was nominated for an Academy Award, someone said, ‘You’re nominated for an Academy Award,'” he said. However, Malkovich has never been a huge fan of awards ceremonies anyway, and only attended the Oscars once, when he was nominated for “Places in the Heart.” He told the London crowd that he felt quite overwhelmed by the experience. “I had a manager called Phyllis Carlyle, and we were on our way to the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion, and she was a little bit… bossy. She said, ‘Now honey, when we get there, there’s gonna be a lot of people,'” he recalled. “And I said, ‘OK, but we can just go in a side door, right?’ And she, right in my face, goes ‘Honey! It’s the Oscars, there’s no side door!’ So, I mean, that’s kind of my native personality in the face of that kind of onslaught.” Malkovich acknowledged that Hollywood as a whole has changed quite a lot since the last time he was on the awards trail, with the advent of streaming taking over theaters. Often, he said, campaigning for a film is the only way to make the public go see it in theaters. “Both ‘The Killing Fields,’ which was a 1984 Oscars film I think, and ‘Places in the Heart,’ they’re already been out, they’d already made their money, they were already successful. The same with ‘In the Line of Fire,'” he said. “It was really a different world. Now, that kind of seems to be the only way to get people to actually go to a theater.” He isn’t too bothered by it, though. “I’m 72 years old, things change,” he said. “I don’t really like thinking things aren’t what they used to be. They just change, and you either change with them or die. And I prefer to change with them. I’ll die, anyway.” “Wild Horse Nine,” in which he stars opposite Sam Rockwell as a veteran CIA agent, held its U.K. premiere at London Film Festival on Friday. Set shortly before the 1973 Chilean coup d’etat, the two are dispatched to Easter Island, where they must confront both their dark pasts and present conspiracies. “Wild Horse Nine” first premiered at Venice Film Festival in September, where it received rave reviews and Malkovich took home the best actor prize. At a Venice press conference , Malkovich humbly shrugged off the praise, saying: “That is incredibly kind. I’ve had a long career, and I’ve had spectacular collaborations with writers, directors and actors. I never feel in competition with any of them. For me, it’s a very nice thing. But the nicest thing is the film getting attention. And the film has several terrific performers, and it’s beautifully written and directed. That’s what matters to me.” Vietnamese Supernatural Horror ‘Bloodline: The Curse Within’ Heads to Busan Market With Mockingbird Pictures (EXCLUSIVE) Journalist Massacre Drama ‘Once Upon a Time in the Philippines’ Turns a Bystander Into an Accomplice at Busan Asian Project Market Sci-Fi Thriller ‘Overstake’ Gets Generative AI Rebuild, Boarded by Cappu Films at Busan Market (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Squid Game’ Producer Reads Founding Declaration as Asian Independent Producers Form Cross-Border Alliance at Busan John Rhys-Davies, Diego Boneta Fantasy ‘Starbright’ Boarded by Cappu Films Ahead of Busan Market (EXCLUSIVE) ‘The World of Love’ Producer Kim Sehun Backs Actor-Director Ryu Hyunkyung’s Dark Comedy ‘Dog Fight’ at Busan Asian Project Market Loading comments...

articles.title: DOJ Launches Investigation Of Networks For Suspending TV Pool Amid Trump’s Ban On CNN
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted ‘Saturday Night Live’ Opens With An Overcompensating Pete Hegseth Pumping Up His Plans To Stream A Live Execution DOJ Launches Investigation Of Networks For Suspending TV Pool Amid Trump’s Ban On CNN Donald Trump Picks Katie Zacharia As Next White House Press Secretary View All October 10, 2026 6:05pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump greet President of China Xi Jinping and first lady of China Peng Liyuan. Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images UPDATED: The Justice Department has launched an investigation into whether the five major networks violated antitrust laws when they suspended participation in the White House TV pool in protest of Donald Trump ‘s ban on CNN . Emily Covington, a spokesperson for the Justice Department, said in a statement, “Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.” The New York Times first reported on the investigation. Related Stories News Donald Trump Picks Katie Zacharia As Next White House Press Secretary News FCC Chairman Declines To Say Whether Broadcast Outlets Should Be Allowed To Air Live Execution, But It's Doubtful Networks Would Show It Anyway After Trump announced his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House grounds on Sept. 18, CNN also was restricted from the TV pool. As part of a long-running arrangement, CNN, CBS News , ABC News , NBC News and Fox News rotate pool duty providing technical, video and reporting coverage of the president, with feeds then distributed to other networks and news organizations. The pool is necessary because of the space limitations of areas of the White House, like the Oval Office, or on Air Force One. Watch on Deadline After the CNN freeze out, the other members of the TV pool jointly announced on Sept. 21 that they would refrain from their rotation turn, a move made to protest the White House effort to block the news network. “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” the five networks said in a statement at the time. The suspension lasted for about four days, but it came during the White House visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping. The suspension of the TV pool meant that there was much less video coverage of major ceremonies and other events surrounding his visit. Trump later complained that CNN and MS NOW did not cover Xi’s visit, without mentioning his efforts to ban the two outlets from the White House grounds. ABC confirmed that it has not received any notification of the investigation but it expects to. A CNN spokesperson declined to comment. Other networks in the pool did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The White House has continued to restrict CNN from certain assignments, including flying on Air Force One on presidential trip. After Trump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from White House grounds, those three media outlets sued, claiming violations of their First Amendment and due process rights. A federal judge imposed a temporary restraining order, which last until Tuesday, that has forced the White House to renew access to dozens of reporters. The judge, Timothy Kelly, is expected to rule by then on whether to grant the news outlets a preliminary injunction, something that would prevent the White House from denying access on a longer term. The issue of access to the White House grounds is separate, yet related, to the issue of whether the administration can also freeze out members of the pool because the president does not approve of their editorial decisions. A different case, involving the Associated Press, is on appeal in the D.C. Circuit. The AP was barred from the White House pool because its style guidance did not adhere to Trump’s renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. The investigation has the potential to set up another legal battle against the Trump administration over the First Amendment. Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for the Freedom of the Press, said in a statement that the investigation “appears to be a pretext for seeking records from the networks about how they are covering daily White House events during a media ban the president himself put in place. The decisions news organizations make about coverage are protected by the First Amendment, and summoning antitrust authority, on top of the retaliatory actions the White House has already taken to bar certain outlets, is another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists.” Seth Stern, chief of advocacy for Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement, “The investigation is nonsense. Trump may view the presidency as a business venture, but news outlets’ standing up for their constitutional rights has nothing to do with antitrust law, no matter what Laura Loomer says.” Loomer is the conspiracy theorist and Trump loyalist who posted last month about using antitrust law to punish the networks. The administration has been rebuffed in the federal courts in another effort to seek materials from media organizations as part of an antitrust investigation. Last year, a federal judge barred the Federal Trade Commission from issuing a civil investigative demand to Media Matters for America, the progressive watchdog group, as part of an antitrust investigation of an advertiser boycott of Elon Musk’s X. Media Matters later said that a settlement with the FTC required that the agency forgo issuing such a civil investigation demand. They also said that the “agreement — and the decisions Media Matters won in the district court and the court of appeals — offers a roadmap for other newsgathering and nonprofit organizations facing, or at risk of, government retaliation.” Three advertising holding companies, WPP, Dentsu and Publicis, also reached a settlement with the FTC. A legal battle also would be a test for David Ellison, the CEO of Skydance, which completed its merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. this past week. The Justice Department’s Antitrust Division gave the greenlight to the transaction in June. Vowing to protect editorial independence, Ellison said at a town hall that he backed CNN’s lawsuit over the ban on White House access. ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $28M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted Cold Open Skewers Hegseth’s Live Execution Plan; Shane Gillis Returns ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set Laika’s Stop-Motion Epic ‘Wildwood’; Brad Bird’s Sci-Fi Noir ‘Ray Gunn’ Read More About: 12 Comments

articles.title: Sakha Filmmakers Association & Producers Guild of Korea Pact For Co-Productions
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz AI Productions Require Traditional Skills To Be Cinematic, Say Filmmakers On Kling AI Panel: “You Need Experts To Prevent Everything Looking The Same” Ann Hui, Busan Camellia Award Recipient, Talks Learning From Women Bosses & Hong Kong New Generation Sakha Filmmakers Association & Producers Guild of Korea Pact For Co-Productions View All October 10, 2026 7:18pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source SFA Executive Director Stepan Burnashev & PGK President Lee Dong-ha Sakha Filmmakers Association EXCLUSIVE: The Producers Guild of Korea (PGK) and the Sakha Filmmakers Association (SFA) have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) aimed at creating a direct route to international co-productions and professional exchange between the Korean and Sakha screen production sectors. The Sakha Republic (Yakutia), in Russia’s Far East, has built one of the country’s most procative film industries, making films mostly in the Sakha (Yakut) language and developing a strong local theatrical audience. Its films have been drawing growing attention at festivals and markets across Asia and internationally. Related Stories News Netflix's 'The Blue Road' Director Han Jun-hee On Taking Risks With Stories & Shooting In Japan News AI Tools Bring Efficiencies But Have Limitations, Says Weta CTO Kimball Thurston: "Tech Companies Should Collaborate More With Creatives" The MOU with PGK was signed at the Sakha Filmmakers Association booth during the Asian Contents & Film Market ( ACFM ) in Busan , with the aim of starting a long-term industry partnership between producers from the two territories. Watch on Deadline Under the agreement, PGK and SFA will establish a new framework for co-production between Korean and Sakha producers, aimed at developing projects together and sharing information on public financing available in both territories. The partnership will include project showcases, producer-to-producer meetings and B2B sessions designed to identify projects with international potential and move them towards co-production. The two organisations will also bring the partnership to major international markets, including ACFM, Hong Kong Filmart and the Cannes Marché du Film, creating new opportunities for Sakha projects to connect with the wider Asian and international industry. For PGK, the agreement continues a programme of international partnerships built since the pandemic, alongside MOUs with the Canadian Media Producers Association (CMPA), the Hong Kong Film Production Executives Association (HKFPEA), the Indonesian Film Producers Association (APROFI) and the Brazilian Audiovisual Industry Union (SIAESP). PGK President Lee Dong-ha said: “Sakha cinema is one of the most distinctive voices to emerge in Asia in recent years, and it belongs in the conversation among Asian producers. Through this MOU, PGK and SFA open a direct channel between our two production communities – one that we intend to turn into actual co-productions.” Stepan Burnashev, SFA’s Executive Director, said: “Sakha cinema grew from a small regional community into a strong local film culture because our filmmakers kept telling stories in our own language and from our own perspective. “Korea is an important example of how a strong local identity can connect with audiences around the world. This agreement gives our producers a direct working relationship with the Korean industry. We want it to lead not only to exchange, but to projects developed and produced together, and to a lasting connection between our filmmaking communities.” ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $28M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted Cold Open Skewers Hegseth’s Live Execution Plan; Shane Gillis Returns ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell & Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie & Bacall Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Saturday Night Live’ Opens With An Overcompensating Pete Hegseth Pumping Up His Plans To Stream A Live Execution
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted ‘Saturday Night Live’ Opens With An Overcompensating Pete Hegseth Pumping Up His Plans To Stream A Live Execution DOJ Launches Investigation Of Networks For Suspending TV Pool Amid Trump’s Ban On CNN Donald Trump Picks Katie Zacharia As Next White House Press Secretary View All October 10, 2026 8:52pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Saturday Night Live once again returned Pete Hegseth ( Colin Jost ) to its opener, this time with Donald Trump’s secretary of defense addressing the crew of the beleaguered USS Lincoln. The ship was at sea for 265 days with no port call, and reports of poor conditions and demoralized sailors, but concerns over their plight were dismissed by Donald Trump . Related Stories Late Night TV ‘Saturday Night Live’: Shane Gillis’ Third Time Hosting Is Saved By Cast Newbie Grace Reiter News FCC Chairman Declines To Say Whether Broadcast Outlets Should Be Allowed To Air Live Execution, But It’s Doubtful Networks Would Show It Anyway At one point in tonight’s skit, Jost’s Hegseth tells the crew of his plans to stream a live execution. In reality, the Pentagon confirmed plans to stream the December execution of Nidal Hassan, sentenced to death for killing 13 people and injuring dozens more in a rampage at Fort Hood. “As we get into the Christmas spirit, we’re going to execute a guy on live TV,” Jost said. “Yeah, that’s right. Public executions are back.” Watch on Deadline “And if the guy somehow survives the firing squad, then he’s got to fight Jake Paul. So check that out.” Hegseth’s plans for a livestream of the execution have generated a backlash, with lawmakers in both parties condemning it and the president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops calling it a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death.” Jost has played Hegseth with an ever-present focus on acting tough, yet clearly overcompensating as one of the least qualified individuals to hold the post. Wearing a sash containing small bottles of Fireball whiskey, Jost’s Hegseth told the Navy crew, “I’m wearing an ammunition belt made of Fireball cinnamon whiskey — the only alcohol designed to taste better on the way back up.” Jost’s Hegseth also stood in front of the new logo for the Department of War — the Trump team’s preferred name for the Defense Department — with looks like it has a Third Reich influence. One of the sailors asked, “Sorry, is that a Nazi eagle?” “It’s an American eagle with a Nazi vibe,” Hegseth responded. Last week, after Hegseth gave a speech to the Air Force Academy, there was extensive social media attention to the revised eagle design used as a backdrop and its similarities to one used by the Nazi regime. Tonight’s cold open also featured a cameo by Robert Kennedy Jr, played by James Austin Johnson, who tried to mimic the gravelly voice of the secretary of health and human services. Johnson’s RFK Jr. told the sailors, “Yes, 200,000 pounds of pork, beef and goat meat have been recalled. But I just want to stress that catfish, pony and cricket are viable proteins for any American family.” He added, “But I want to thank you. We were able to spot those recalls early by testing the meats on your ship. The research you provided on Operations Hell Cruise will be vital for many years to come.” Hegseth finished up by quoting Lincoln — actually Linkin Park. “ You strive so hard, and got so far, but in the end, it doesn’t even matter. “ He added, “Thank you for all being willing to go down with the ship — even though it breaks my personal rule of never going down on anyone.” ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $28M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted Cold Open Skewers Hegseth’s Live Execution Plan; Shane Gillis Returns ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set Laika’s Stop-Motion Epic ‘Wildwood’; Brad Bird’s Sci-Fi Noir ‘Ray Gunn’ Read More About: Comments

On this weekend’s episode, the comedian accidentally dropped an F-bomb while playing a defensive son who is suspicious of Sam I Am (Andrew Dismukes) pressuring his dad (Mikey Day) into eat green eggs and ham. “Hey, what the hell is wrong with you? My dad said he doesn’t like them. Walk away,” said Gillis. He said he doesn’t f*cking,” he added, immediately covering his mouth. “Jeez! — like ’em.” Although Gillis moved on in the sketch, Day called back to the expletive later. “Zachary’s the one who’s going. articles.title: ‘Saturday Night Live’: Shane Gillis’ Third Time Hosting Is Saved By Cast Newbie Grace Reiter
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘Saturday Night Live’: Shane Gillis’ Third Time Hosting Is Saved By Cast Newbie Grace Reiter Shane Gillis Drops F-Bomb In ‘SNL’ “Green Eggs & Ham” Sketch, Apologizes Rohan Campbell Teases Directorial Debut Plans: “A Very Personal Story” View All October 10, 2026 10:06pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Grace Reiter and Shane Gillis on 'Saturday Night Live' NBC In his third time hosting Saturday Night Live , Shane Gillis isn’t making the case for a triumphant return to the cast. On this weekend’s episode, which also featured musical guest Rosalía, the comedian delivered several on-brand sketches that featured his signature everyman sense of humor, but no water cooler moments worth meme-ifying. Related Stories Late Night TV Shane Gillis Drops F-Bomb In ‘SNL’ “Green Eggs & Ham” Sketch Late Night TV ‘Saturday Night Live’ Opens With An Overcompensating Pete Hegseth Pumping Up His Plans To Stream A Live Execution Gillis’ opening monologue was a tight five about his Bud Light commercials and getting into shape with workout buddies Joe Rogan and Theo Von, during which he put on his best femme voice to mimic gym gays and complained that “women just dress like whores now” at the gym. The comedian also noted that he’s “balded directly into an Adolph Hitler haircut,” and the only other option is looking gay. “That’s it, you’re either gay or Hitler. And isn’t that where we’re at as a country?” he quipped. Watch on Deadline In the first sketch, Gillis played the host of a cop talk show, in which he just arrested his various guests. Gillis then appeared in a country song music video, playing the father of a bride who imagines what he’ll do with her room when she moves out, only to end up hooking up with Ms. Pac-Man in a cloud of black mold. In a Green Eggs and Ham sketch, featuring Mikey Day as the Cat in the Hat and Gillis as his defensive son who thinks his dad is being scammed, the host made things interesting when he accidentally dropped an F-bomb . A History Channel sketch about WWII-time inventors patenting quiet shoes saw Gillis’ character finding them handy for “sneaking” around his wife, hence the name “sneakers.” Gillis also led a heating/AC commercial that’s honest about how much of a nightmare of a process is, complete with workers making fun of you, smoking in your doorway and staring through your windows. Meanwhile, new cast member Grace Reiter continued to prove her chops as she played problem child Coco in a “Weekend Update” segment in which her mom (Ashley Padilla) can’t find a babysitter. She was a perfect match for Padilla as the bratty daughter publicly embarrassing her mom. Reiter also shared a couple of sketches with Gillis, playing his elderly mother as a hospice nurse (Sarah Sherman) tells him she only has a few days, which conflicts with his plans to see Jelly Roll in Vegas. The sketch also features a cameo from Ben Marshall as Jelly Roll, Marcello Hernandez as Jesus and Rosalía as a horny divorcee, egging him on to make the concert. The final sketch of the episode was set in a kid’s chess tournament, where young TJ (Jeremy Culhane) tries to ignore his parents (Gillis and Reiter) in the stands, where they go from arguing exes to inappropriate flirtation. Saving the best for last, Reiter was certainly a bright spot on an otherwise dull episode. Gillis’ latest hosting gig on SNL comes after he hosted in 2024 and 2025 , following his removal from the NBC sketch comedy ‘s featured cast days after he was announced . The decision came in response to resurfaced videos of Gillis mocking Asian accents, in addition to using ethnic and gay slurs. ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $28M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted Cold Open Skewers Hegseth’s Live Execution Plan; Shane Gillis Returns ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set Laika’s Stop-Motion Epic ‘Wildwood’; Brad Bird’s Sci-Fi Noir ‘Ray Gunn’ Read More About: 4 Comments

articles.title: Ann Hui, Busan Camellia Award Recipient, Talks Learning From Women Bosses & Hong Kong New Generation
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz AI Productions Require Traditional Skills To Be Cinematic, Say Filmmakers On Kling AI Panel: “You Need Experts To Prevent Everything Looking The Same” Ann Hui, Busan Camellia Award Recipient, Talks Learning From Women Bosses & Hong Kong New Generation Sakha Filmmakers Association & Producers Guild of Korea Pact For Co-Productions View All October 11, 2026 12:40am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ann Hui at the 31st Busan International Film Festival Busan International Film Festival Hong Kong filmmaker Ann Hui , who received the Camellia Award at the opening of Busan International Film Festival, shared her experiences of being a woman filmmaker in a male-dominated industry at a festival press conference, along with her thoughts on how Hong Kong cinema has evolved. When asked how other women had helped shape her career, Hui said she’d had five women bosses when she entered the industry back in the ‘70s who had welcomed her and helped her to become established as a filmmaker. “I was lucky because my first five bosses really supported me, gave me freedom and support, and allowed me to do what I wanted with the TV programs I was making. They were only criticizing me to make my work better,” Hui said. Related Stories News Sakha Filmmakers Association & Producers Guild of Korea Pact For Co-Productions News Netflix's 'The Blue Road' Director Han Jun-hee On Taking Risks With Stories & Shooting In Japan “Afterwards I met people who were not so nice, so I really want to talk about these five women in my masterclass. Some were company bosses and there were some actresses as well. It’s true that I seem to learn much less from men. I don’t know why because I’m not unfriendly with them, but perhaps it’s like karma in Buddhism, I don’t work with them as well.” Watch on Deadline Hui started her career working for Hong Kong broadcaster TVB, back then an incubator for Hong Kong’s new wave of pioneering filmmakers, before moving into features, many of which have won awards at major festivals, spanning the ‘80s to the present day. Her body of work includes an early trilogy about the Vietnamese boat people – Below The Lion Rock , The Story Of Woo Viet and Boat People – which was followed by films in a variety of genres including The Romance Of Book And Sword , Eighteen Springs , All About Love , A Simple Life , which won best actress in Venice, and The Golden Era, which won best director at Taiwan’s Golden Horse. Her most recent work, Elegies (2023), a documentary about Hong Kong poetry, opened Hong Kong International Film Festival and was nominated for the Golden Horse Awards. Looking back at developments in the Hong Kong film industry since the ‘70s, Hui also talked about the changing status of female filmmakers. “When I worked in TV in the ‘70s, and later when I made my first film, I tried my best to work on subjects like cops and robbers that men do,” Hui remembered. “I wanted to prove that women can do what men do.” “But once I’d fulfilled that intention, I got back to subjects that really interest me; about the predicament of people in modern-day society, which is also quite a lot about women. It wasn’t intentional to make women’s stories, that’s just the way it turned out.” She also observed that when she started her career, there were many women directors in television, but only two or three in the film industry. Now there are about 10-20 women directors actively working in the Hong Kong industry, she observed (including many that have had films screen in Busan, Hong Kong and Tokyo film festivals, including Norris Wong, Oliver Chan, Heiward Mak, Jessey Tsang and Cheuk Wan-chi). “Nowadays their position has become much better,” she continued. “Back in the ‘70s, I felt under pressure to have very masculine habits and dress like a man. It was almost like pretending to be a man when I’m on set. But nowadays, the female directors do not hide their gender when they’re working, and don’t mind coming across as quite feminine. They’re also much more conscious in the way they’re trying to make films telling women’s stories, which I think is totally legitimate.” While saying that she felt “very jealous” of developments in Korean cinema, Hui said she’s also encouraged by the new generation of Hong Kong filmmakers, who have a different approach to the freewheeling and commercially driven filmmakers of the ‘80s and ‘90s. “Despite the lack of investment, the young filmmakers in Hong Kong are still very dedicated, hardworking, and talented. I feel that if they have an opening, they will be able to make better films than we did, because in the ‘80s and ‘90s it was all about entertainment. There was a lot of volume but very little content. “But now the filmmakers are trying their best, perhaps because it’s so difficult to raise investment, they put a lot of effort into the planning and some of the films are really good.” She also mentioned the big improvements in acting in Hong Kong cinema. “Back in our era, most of the actors and actresses came from soap operas or beauty pageants. Now they all come from the Hong Kong Academy of Performing Arts, so they have a really solid foundation in acting. They also have really professional ethics.” While accepting the Camellia Award at Busan’s opening ceremony, Hui mentioned that it was getting “more difficult” for her to make films as she turns eighty next year. She joked in the press conference about being worried that she’d trip on the red carpet because she’s not so steady on her feet these days. But she also said that she still enjoys making movies and is currently developing some ideas, so she’s not ready to announce her retirement just yet. “My judgment and understanding has not been reduced, in fact experience gives you a deeper understanding. So I still want to make films because I want to convey this new understanding that I have now in my work.” Jointly presented by BIFF and Chanel, the festival’s Camellia Award honors pioneering women filmmakers who advance the role of women in Asian cinema. Previous recipients have included Korean production designer Ryu Seong-hie ( Decision To Leave ) and Taiwanese filmmaker and actress Sylvia Chang ( Love Education , Daughter’s Daughter ). ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $28M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted Cold Open Skewers Hegseth’s Live Execution Plan; Shane Gillis Returns ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell & Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie & Bacall Read More About: Comments

articles.title: AI Productions Require Traditional Skills To Be Cinematic, Say Filmmakers On Kling AI Panel: “You Need Experts To Prevent Everything Looking The Same”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz AI Productions Require Traditional Skills To Be Cinematic, Say Filmmakers On Kling AI Panel: “You Need Experts To Prevent Everything Looking The Same” Ann Hui, Busan Camellia Award Recipient, Talks Learning From Women Bosses & Hong Kong New Generation Sakha Filmmakers Association & Producers Guild of Korea Pact For Co-Productions View All October 11, 2026 2:47am Add us as a Google Preferred Source New Cinematic Possibilities: Reimagining Filmmaking with Kling AI Deadline Is the world ready for a giant worm going to work on the subway? Korean director Kim Sung-soo thinks so and is making a film on this very subject, Worm Train , inspired by Franz Kafka’s short story Metamorphosis . Kim, whose credits include major Korean blockbusters such as Asura: The City Of Madnes s and 12.12: The Day, talked about how he’s using Kling AI tools to make the short film on a panel at Busan ’s Asian Contents & Film Market ( ACFM ) today. Kling AI, which recently released its 4.0 image generation model, also invited Chinese animation filmmaker Li Wei ( Big Fish & Begonia ); Harry Hyun, a director and CEO of Korea’s MooAm Co; and Lee Sang-wook, a producer and team manager at Korea’s MBC C&I AI Contents Lab, to present recent projects made using Kling AI tools, as well as discuss the latest trends in this new mode of filmmaking. Related Stories News Ann Hui, Busan Camellia Award Recipient, Talks Learning From Women Bosses & Hong Kong New Generation News Sakha Filmmakers Association & Producers Guild of Korea Pact For Co-Productions After presenting a teaser for Worm Train , Kim said AI has changed the way he thinks about filmmaking, but that “one thing never changes, which is what makes a film cinematic”. Watch on Deadline “Now everyone has similar tools and anyone can access Kling, but while some will make a masterpiece, others will make a film that is mediocre,” Kim said. “Initially, I thought AI would destroy the industry, but I don’t think so any more, because technology does not replace creativity. The value of images still comes from human intervention.” Hyun, who has made AI films including Crypto Man and Genfluencer , expanded on this topic. “I don’t think AI production compared to traditional production is really that different – the difference is efficiency and simplicity – but if you don’t have experienced filmmakers on set, everything can end up looking the same. “That’s why AI images may look impressive at first, but not later, because everyone is using the same lighting, same everything,” Hyun continued. “You need an art director who can do the fine tuning, a director and cinematographer who have really studied and learned when to use a close shot, wide shot, how to frame an image. These are long discussions we have on set, they’re not random decisions. Only when you’re working with experts will you be able to create something different with AI – not just cookie cutter deliverables.” Li Wei, who is making animated feature Born Of The Tide with Kling AI tools, said one useful aspect of AI filmmaking is that results can be seen right away, so it’s easier to get feedback from multiple people on the crew. “There’s going to be a lot of trial and error in AI filmmaking, but effective communication can be used between the various production members, so everyone has a chance to feed back into the production,” Li said. Lee presented a teaser of upcoming series Rendering Love , produced by MBC C&I and Barunson E&A, which combines live-action scenes filmed the traditional way with AI generated characters to tell the story of a virtual K-pop group. He observed that different roles and ways of working are emerging in AI production crews. “All staff members working on a project must fully understand the technology. That’s the only way to have high quality content. If you’re updating to a new model, the team leaders need to analyse the new features and share that understanding so all staff members are on the same page. The technology is changing constantly and if anyone is lagging behind, overall quality can decrease.” The speakers also discussed whether there was a need to introduce industry standards in AI filmmaking, but Kim suggested it was still too early, at least in South Korea. “Creators in Korea have their own ideas and imagination and want to unleash that using AI tools. We need to see where all this is heading before we start talking about regulations and standards. “But one thing I’m very aware of as a filmmaker is thinking about whether you’re infringing somebody’s rights. That’s something we need to be conscious of from the early stages.” The panel, entitled New Cinematic Possibilities: Reimagining Filmmaking with Kling AI, took place as part of the InnoAsia track at Asian Contents & Market (ACFM), which is running until October 13. ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $28M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted Cold Open Skewers Hegseth’s Live Execution Plan; Shane Gillis Returns ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell & Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie & Bacall Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Shy & Lola’: How Bel Powley, Hayley Squires &  Amanda Coe Brought A Coen Brothers Vibe To BBC Thriller In UK Port Town
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Fox Launching ‘Extracted’ International Production Hub In Malaysia Prime Video Unveils ‘Bloodaxe’ Release Date & Teaser Gerhard Zeiler Officially Exits Skydance To Follow Political Ambitions, Telling Staff In Emotional Missive: “Sometimes We Simply Asked Too Much” View All October 11, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Shy and Lola' BBC/Clerkenwell Films Ltd./Kerry Spicer EXCLUSIVE: What would happen if you took the “visual reference” of the Coen brothers and transported this vibe to the UK’s port town of Grimsby. That question is posed in Shy & Lola, a BBC drama starring Harry Potter’s Bel Powley and The Night Manager’s Hayley Squires , which will be taken to buyers at MIPCOM next week before launching on the BBC. In an interview with Deadline, Powley and Squires stressed the highly original nature of the Amanda Coe -penned series from Baby Reindeer maker Clerkenwell Films, but they did say the work of the Coen brothers influenced its look and tone. Related Stories News Fox Launching 'Extracted' International Production Hub In Malaysia News Disney Heist Doc 'Stolen Kingdom' Heads To Mipcom “The Coen brothers often explore incredibly dark subjects, such as murder, death, blood and guns, but they shoot them in a way that gives the material a sense of levity and lightness,” said Powley. “I think that’s what the cinematographer was looking for visually.” Watch on Deadline Squires said the “Coen brothers’ influence probably comes through in the humor” of Shy & Lola, which also “comes out in the geography where the stories take place and the things that are specific to that place.” Revealed by Deadline several months back , Shy & Lola spotlights its protagonists, two very different women who are forced to become allies when a murder entangles them in the criminal underworld operating in Grimsby. Shy is a cleaner, scraping by and dreaming of a new life in Portugal. Lola is an ex-model-turned-grifter who arrives in town with trouble at her heels. The unlikely pair build an operation that threatens to blow the local bad guys out of the water, as opposing futures beckon. Coe, whose credits include Apple TV’s Dior series The New Look and the BBC’s Apple Tree Yard , was inspired by Fargo. “I love the idea that you can create a world of its own that resonates with the real world but is very heightened and blackly comic,” added Coe. “We use violence sparingly but in an interesting way. There’s a theme of violence going through the show without glorifying it.” Shy & Lola is based on the French show Cheyenne & Lola starring Charlotte Le Bon and Veerle Baetens. BBC Studios approached Clerkenwell with the idea to adapt the French show and the indie immediately saw an opportunity to add its own twist. “It has that mix we love at Clerkenwell,” said Petra Fried, who runs the indie and is an EP on Shy & Lola. “It’s a darkly comic, propulsive story with real emotional depth underneath it. It’s funny and entertaining, but the stakes are very real, so you never stop caring about these women.” Coe, who said she has a track record of making “female-led shows,” noted that there are major distinctions between Cheyenne & Lola and her version. “The French version starts with a character in their underwear looking amazing,” she added. “That is not the vibe of our show.” “I’ve never witnessed that in a chemistry read before” Image: BBC/Clerkenwell Films Ltd./Kerry Spicer BBC/Clerkenwell Films Ltd./Matt Towers In order for this “vibe” to work, the chemistry between the leads had to impeccable. Luckily, they matched perfectly. Powley and Squires are two actors at the top of their game, with BAFTA nominee Powley about to be seen as Aunt Petunia in HBO’s eye-catching Harry Potter, and Squires, who wowed in Ken Loach’s I, Daniel Blake a decade ago , playing a big role in the BBC and Prime Video’s The Night Manager. “I’ve never witnessed that in a chemisty read before where you just go ‘wow’ after 10 seconds,” said Coe. “Together they were more than the sum of their parts.” Squires admired Powley from when she had a small part in one of her breakout hits, Julia Jarrold’s rom-com A Royal Night Out . She said the pair quickly made a “silent pact to find the best version” of the characters they were playing. “We are quite different people but have a real understanding of each other,” she added. “That mirrors the characters of Shy and Lola. They essentially fall platonically in love with each other on screen, which was a beautiful relationship to play out.” Powley also spoke to Shy and Lola’s “unlikely charm” and praised Squires for bringing “such gravity and being so grounded in her performances.” Another “character” in Shy & Lola , according to Powley, is the port town of Grimsby, a place rarely represented in British TV or movies, although it is the home of Sacha Baron Cohen’s ill-fated 2016 comedy that bears its name. Squires, who joked that when she first read the scripts she simply thought to herself, “How am I going to master the Grimsby accent,?” something she eventually did with the help of Grimsby-born Shy & Lola co-star Thomas Turgoose, said the setting brings with it a “sense of community.” “There’s an ensemble of characters who make up the community where they work and live, and it has a real richness to it,” she added. “These aren’t people who despise where they come from or hate where they live. The majority of working-class people actually don’t [hate where they live].” Squires thinks this “richness” has been lost somewhat in the recent depiction of working class communities, as she harks back to successful, multi-faceted 1990s shows like Our Friends in the North. “I feel as though that trend might have changed,” she added. “It’s the same with anything to do with class or culture; if your writer has knowledge of that community then it comes through.” She is enthused by the success of shows like the BBC’s Sherwood, however, and throws her weight behind the national broadcaster as an “organization that has had to battle to hold its ground, and I think it has.” BBC Studios will be selling Shy & Lola at MIPCOM this week. ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $28M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted Cold Open Skewers Hegseth’s Live Execution Plan; Shane Gillis Returns ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set Laika’s Stop-Motion Epic ‘Wildwood’; Brad Bird’s Sci-Fi Noir ‘Ray Gunn’ Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Wildwood’ Review: Carey Mulligan Leads Voice Cast Of Laika’s Ambitious And Visually Stunning Stop-Motion Fantasy Epic – London Film Festival
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Wildwood’ Review: Carey Mulligan Leads Voice Cast Of Laika’s Ambitious And Visually Stunning Stop-Motion Fantasy Epic – London Film Festival ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell And Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie And Bacall In Brad Bird’s Nifty Sci-Fi/Film Noir Mashup – London Film Festival ‘Animals’ Review: Ben Affleck And Kerry Washington Fight A Lot In Netflix Kidnap Thriller That Is Stretched Too Thin View All October 11, 2026 6:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Wildwood' Laika Laika , the Oregon animation house that specializes in stop motion, has a perfect track record of landing Best Animated Feature Oscar nominations for all four of its first films: Coraline, ParaNorman, Missing Link, and Kubo and the Two Strings. With its latest and unquestionably most ambitious project Wildwood , the streak could well continue. This film has been gestating at Laika for 16 years, finally starting production in 2021, and now having its world premiere today at the London Film Festival . It is also slated to open AFI Fest later this month for its North American premiere in Hollywood. For director-producer Travis Knight , who is also CEO of Laika, this adaptation of Colin Meloy’s book has been a personal dream, especially since the setting of the book, and now the film, is right in his hometown of Portland, OR. How could he resist? A sweeping fantasy right in your own backyard featuring a magical forbidden forest of talking animals mixed with humans? It all becomes the center of a truly epic story that feels born to be on the big screen. The painstaking stop-motion animation process applied to a tale on a scale rarely seen on this level is a visual knockout, and the story is a compelling one focused on a scrappy young heroine determined to fight back and save her baby brother after he is harrowingly abducted from the streets of Portland by a murder of crows. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Culture The 30 Highest-Grossing Animated Films Of All Time At The Global Box Office Reviews ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell And Scarlett Johansson Channel Bogie And Bacall In Brad Bird’s Nifty Sci-Fi/Film Noir Mashup – London Film Festival Prue McKeel (nicely voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee) is a loyal and loving teen girl who promises her parents she will take good care of her baby brother Mac on a normal sunny day outing. It turns out to be a frightening one when Mac is snatched up by a menacing swarm of black crows who swoop down in unison from the sky and fly away with him. Her frantic efforts to catch up fail and she sees the birds disappear into the adjoining forbidden forest known to allow no outsiders. Unable to go back home and explain to her parents (Maya Erskine and Jake Johnson), she sets off to find Mac and bring him back. No easy task, but her rather awkward and far less adventurous classmate Curtis Mehlberg (Jacob Tremblay) offers any help he can supply, which isn’t much. Still, he sets out to follow her into the forest where after an encounter with the imposing uniformed coyotes who patrol the place gets separated from Prue. Soon both are swept up, on individual tracks into this world like something out of Lewis Carroll, as they go down the rabbit hole into a society like no other — a land of talking animals, bandits, wise owls, even a loyal rat and more. For Curtis it is meeting the evil Dowager Governess Alexandra ( Carey Mulligan ) who attempts to bring him into her fold. She is a woman devastated by the death of her only son, so much so she can’t function and turns her grief into no good, with the coyote force in lockstep for her dark ambitions. When Curtis sees what she is up to he refuses and is tossed into a prison with other rejects. Meanwhile, Prue, meeting The General ( Angela Bassett ), the wise Great Eagle leader of the Avian Principality, as well as Brendan, the empathetic leader of the outcast Bandits, uses every intuition she has to navigate this dense landscape. Eventually all roads lead her to Alexandra, who lies to her. She encourages her to go home to her parents, saying it is better for a grieving mother to know the truth of what happened to her child. Prue follows the advice, confesses what happened to Mac, and discovers the secret her parents have been keeping from her all along. There is much more to come in this two-hour-plus adaptation including a battle royale that will see Prue returning for a massive fight to the finish, still hoping to navigate a happy ending. With six-time Oscar-nominated cinematographer Caleb Deschanel ( The Black Stallion ) working for the first time on an animated film, the visual palette based in part on the book’s gorgeous illustrations by Caron Ellis is breathtaking. Deschanel makes the stop-motion process feel like live action, the camera picking up character heartache and triumph in ways I haven’t quite seen before in this form. Knight is a born storyteller so the emphasis is always on that, and even though the visuals are quite awesome in their own right, they never overwhelm. Character development is key here, as it was in the book, and each is fully fleshed out. Among them is Bassett’s commanding eagle, the General; Brendan (powerfully voiced by Mahershala Ali ), leader of the Bandits; Maksim ( Tom Waits ), loyal coyote foot soldier to the Dowager Governess; regal Iphigenia (Tantoo Cardinal); bumbling coyote Dmitri (Charlie Day); reclusive aging owl Rex (Richard E. Grant); and Septima, a little rat who rises to the occasion and will break your heart (wonderfully voiced by Awkwafina). There can be no doubt Meloy created this sweeping story in the tradition of other epics like Lord of the Rings and Chronicles of Narnia, and though Wildwood isn’t quite up on that mountain it ably marches to its own drummer, a story of grief, courage, determination and triumph, and yet another Laika stop-motion gem that stays in the heart. Producers are Knight and Sam Wilson. Title: Wildwood Festival: London Distributor: Fathom Release date: October 23, 2026 Director: Travis Knight Screenwriter: Chris Butler Cast: Carey Mulligan, Peyton Elizabeth Lee, Jacob Tremblay, Angela Bassett, Mahershala Ali, Awkwafina, Maya Erskine, Jake Johnson, Charlie Day, Tom Waits, Richard E. Grant, Amanda Stenberg, Tantoo Cardinal, Len Cariou, Marc Evan Jackson Rating: PG-13 Running time: 2 hr 12 mins ‘Other Mommy’ Stalks No. 1 Bow With $28M; ‘Social Reckoning’ Downvoted Cold Open Skewers Hegseth’s Live Execution Plan; Shane Gillis Returns ‘9-1-1’ Stunt Problems Back In Spotlight After Oliver Stark & 3 Others Injured On Set Laika’s Stop-Motion Epic ‘Wildwood’; Brad Bird’s Sci-Fi Noir ‘Ray Gunn’ Read More About: Comments

articles.title: James Gray Says He Considers ‘Two Lovers’ His First Successful Feature: “I Don’t Regard The Films I Made Before This Very Highly”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Siân Heder & The ‘Being Heumann’ Crew On Creating An Inclusive Film & Production Environment — Contenders London Mike Leigh, Marion Bailey & Kate O’Flynn On The Close Collaboration Behind ‘Tender Loving Care’ — Contenders London Society of Composers & Lyricists Opens First International Chapter In London View All October 11, 2026 7:33am Add us as a Google Preferred Source James Gray Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images for BFI. Filmmaker James Gray told a London Film Festival audience this morning during a career Q&A that he believes Two Lovers , his fourth feature, starring Joaquin Phoenix and Gwyneth Paltrow, was the first time he successfully executed his artistic vision as a director. “This movie was very important to me. It was the first time I had creative control. The work took on another character,” Gray said after the LFF crowd was shown a clip from the 2008 film. “I don’t regard the films I made before this very highly. I hope people like them, but I don’t think of them as truly mine. I was still trying to do something. Two Lovers was the first film that felt like who I was trying to be, if that makes sense, because I had total freedom.” Related Stories Festivals 'Wildwood' Review: Carey Mulligan Leads Voice Cast Of Laika's Ambitious And Visually Stunning Stop-Motion Fantasy Epic - London Film Festival News Danny Boyle Says '28 Years Later: Part III' Is Currently On The "Back Burner" Gray added that Two Lovers was a relatively “cheap movie,” costing around $9.5 million. Watch on Deadline “I was left alone. The actors were great. I made exactly what I wanted,” he said. “I don’t know if the film is great, good, or terrible, but my emotional connection to it is profound because it was a beautiful time in my life.” Directed by Gray from a screenplay he co-wrote with Ric Menello, Two Lovers tells the story of Leonard (Phoenix), an aspiring photographer and introvert who has moved back into his parents’ home following a recent heartbreak. His concerned parents try to set him up with Sandra (Vinessa Shaw), the daughter of a family friend. But Leonard meets Michelle (Paltrow), the beautiful but volatile mistress of a wealthy married man who has recently moved into an apartment in his family’s building. He becomes caught between the two women. Gray is at the LFF with his latest feature, Paper Tiger . The film screened last night in London. Adam Driver , Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller star in the pic set in 1986 Queens, NY, in which two brothers become entangled in a scheme that ends up involving the Russian mafia, putting their family at risk. The film premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May. Neon will release the film theatrically on November 13.
