articles.title: Robby Hoffman Snags Stand-Up Sequel at Netflix
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 9, 2026 7:30am Robby Hoffman attends the Vanity Fair Oscar party hosted by Mark Guiducci at Los Angeles County Museum of Art on March 15, 2026. (Photo by Amy Sussman/Getty Images for Vanity Fair) Robby Hoffman is back in the Netflix fold. The Emmy nominated performer, who debuted her first stand-up special on the streamer in December 2025, has struck a deal to return to Netflix with a follow-up. A new one-hour special is set to debut globally on Netflix in 2027. Production company Rotten Science will be producing the outing. No other details have been revealed, like where or when the special will be recorded. As mentioned, it follows the first one, Robby Hoffman: Wake Up, which covered topics like her unique upbringing as part of a large, ex-Hasidic Jewish family, political correctness, gender identity and pronouns, wealth, Hollywood success and more. Also a lot of venting : “It’s a way of going to the gym for me. For me to complain is to enjoy, to understand. It’s a catharsis. If I’m yelling at you, I’m thrilled. I’m happy to be talking to you.” Related Stories Movies 'Animals' Review: Ben Affleck Directs and Stars Opposite Kerry Washington in a Thriller Full of Juicy Elements That Should Be a Lot Tastier Movies 'Cyberpunk 2077' Live Action Film in Development at Paramount Pictures The special had a Hollywood heavyweight behind the camera, too, as it was directed by stand-up superstar John Mulaney . During his Netflix is a Joke appearance with David Letterman earlier this year, Mulaney gushed about Hoffman, calling her a “total original,” and likening her debut to the late and great Sam Kinison, “someone who you’re, like, ‘I’ve never heard of a comedian like this. I’ve never seen anyone this unafraid.'” He added: “When she opened for me in San Diego at an outdoor venue on the water with lots of couples at tables, she never adjusted her act for anyone.” Hoffman works as a writer, actor and comedian. She had a role on the last two seasons of HBO’s Hacks , and earned an Emmy nomination for outstanding guest actress in a comedy series for her work on it. She is currently in the HBO series Rooster opposite Steve Carell, and her credits also include a role opposite Michelle Williams in FX’s critically acclaimed Dying for Sex . Hoffman is developing her own starring vehicle, UnEntitled . THR

articles.title: TV’s Newest Scream Queen Summer H. Howell Has Been Preparing for ‘Carrie’ Her Whole Life
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Howell tackles a new take on the iconic Stephen King character in Mike Flanagan's Prime Video adaptation of the novel. Photograph by JONNY MARLOW Logo text For someone on the precipice of a life-changing moment, Carrie star Summer H. Howell is surprisingly calm. The 22-year-old actress has spent the last year warming up to the idea that she was moving into a new phase of her career with the role as the titular character in Mike Flanagan ‘s Stephen King adaptation. Described as a new take on the iconic horror story, Carrie ‘s a natural progression, as she puts it, in the trajectory her career’s been on. Howell took her first role in a horror film at the age of 8 and hasn’t looked back since. “I feel like I’ve been preparing to be Carrie my whole life,” she tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent Zoom. The show marks her first time leading a television project — or really any major television project. Related Stories TV Karen Read Series Starring and Executive Produced by Elizabeth Banks Ordered at Amazon TV Sam Bankman-Fried Docuseries Set at Amazon (Exclusive) But the show, which premiered on the streamer Wednesday, is exactly what Howell was looking for after gaining years of experience in horror films. “I kind of drew this whole project towards me,” she says. “I’m big into manifesting, and I write things like I have them already.” With this manifestation, it was less about the show itself and more about the environment — she later admits she actually didn’t know much about Carrie going in. She’d seen an image or a GIF here and there, but once she started auditioning, she stayed away from Carrie , both the book and the 1976 film, entirely. It was clear that Flanagan’s version was going for a different take on the story, so it just made sense. No need to worry, she’s since consumed both. Instead, Howell manifested working with “good, genuine people who are kind and want to make real art.” She realized once she was on set that her manifestations had been describing the crew of Carrie perfectly. Howell’s blind faith likely helped, but she also put in hours upon hours to grab the coveted role. She sent in her first tape for the project in January 2025. A month or so later, she sent in the next, new scenes and everything. And so it went for quite some time. While many young actors might’ve found nerves in a lengthy casting process, Howell found herself having a “really good feeling” about her situation. “I started getting deja vu, like I was on the right timeline or something,” she says. “I was telling my friends and family something’s going to happen; they’re going to want to talk to me. And they did.” The actress did a “long work session” with the casting team on a Friday in March 2025. Flanagan wasn’t on the call, something that, at the time, she was grateful for. She needed to focus. She did four intense scenes, including one where she’d have to cry. Finding some boldness within herself, maybe as only an actor with over a decade of experience can, she told the team: “If you want to see tears, it’ll happen on the day.” The call ended, and Howell was told Flanagan would watch over the weekend. “He didn’t,” she explains. “He watched it right away. All of a sudden I was back on a call.” Her manager called her with the request to redo the monologue, this time with tears. “I remember laying on my floor in my room just telling myself all these affirmations and how I’ve come so far,” she says. She did it and went into her weekend anxiously awaiting news. By that next Tuesday, April Fool’s Day of all days, Flanagan, backed with approval from King himself, called to tell her the good news. “The first thing my mom said to me when I got the part was, ‘Your life is going to change forever,'” she recalls. “I feel like I made it happen,” Howell says. “It was meant to be.” Below, the Carrie star speaks with THR about leading the project, why the show gave her hope as a young actor and what a typical day in her life looks like. What was it like for you to be number one on the call sheet and lead this project? That feels like a responsibility. If I hadn’t been acting before I got this job, I would’ve been freaking out the entire time. They probably would’ve fired me because I would not have made the space what I did with all my experience. That was one of the things Mike and I talked about on the first call, [that] he expected me to lead people, lead the actors. Me and Sam[antha Sloyan] were seen as the heads of the department in that way. But it came easier because of my experience. If I was complaining during prom [about] being covered in blood, nobody would’ve had a good time. Howell as Carrie White in Flanagan’s Prime Video adaptation. Courtesy of Prime Having worked in horror since you were very young, were you totally prepared for that day you had to spend prom covered in blood? I mean, you say day, but it was nine days. It might’ve been 11, if we’re including after prom. I was prepared, but I didn’t understand until I was there and I was doing it. A lot of patience required, relying on other people to touch everything for me. I couldn’t really do much because my hands, down to the fingertips, were covered and [they’d tell me] “Don’t mess up the continuity!” When you are stepping into the role of Carrie and you have Mike Flanagan at the helm, are you just trusting that he’s going to lead you in the right direction? What does that partnership look like? Absolutely. I mean, it took time to build that trust, but it came very quickly. It was apparent from the start that Mike… Once you’re chosen by Mike, you’re in this little family. As long as you’re nice to people and you do your job — you show up ready — that’s all he asks of us. He told me right from the start, as much Carrie is his and Stephen’s, she’s now mine, which is unbelievable to think about. He trusted us. I mean, he knows he’s a man and that this is a woman’s story. He made a point to hire women who could shape it the way it needed to be told. We had a lot of powerful directors and powerful women behind the scenes helping us out. It’s just so nice to be given that space and listened to. Did that give you a little bit of hope as a young actress in this industry? Oh, absolutely. You never know who you’re going to have to work with going in, so it was so reassuring knowing Mike is so kind and prioritizes our comfort and our safety. He makes sure we’re happy with the people we’re working with. There were no mean people. We all got along so well, and Mike was pleasantly surprised with that. He kind of paved the way. It gives you hope for sure. Was going back and forth between school and acting something you found difficult as a child? Maybe a little bit. I was the only actor growing up, so I was known for that, and people view me a certain way, I’m sure. It’s made me think back on things. Maybe they saw me a certain way and that’s why we weren’t friends, for whatever reason. It’s strange, for sure. Being a child actor can be very sketchy and weird, but as long as you’re good people… I was very lucky. My mom has always looked out for me and been my rock and stood up to whoever she needed to and taught me how to do that myself. It was awkward sometimes, but… Sloyan, Howell and Flanagan attend Prime Video’s “PROMiere” celebration of Carrie in New York City. Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images for Prime Video What’s something about you that you think people would be surprised to know? The first thing that comes to mind is that I’m 22. When I’m not dolled up, I look very young. It’s funny, I checked into the hotel the other night, and we went down to the lounge. The guy told us to come back at a certain time for the champagne thing. “Not for you, but for you,” [he said] to my mom. I was like, well, I’m 22, but OK. What does your ideal day off look like? Make some good food. I like to cook, so I’ll make something. Spend time outside. Preferably, it’d be nice out and not the middle of winter in Manitoba, which can be awful. Spend time with my loved ones, curl up on the couch, watch some TV with my mom, hug my dogs all day and block out the world. What are you hoping to do next? Are you looking outside of horror? I like to branch out. Not in a leave horror behind way. I still love horror, and I will continue to do horror but it’d be nice to go to work and not cry and scream all the time. I just filmed an action movie called Runaway , so that’ll be coming out sometime next year. I really enjoyed that. Besides all the bruises I walked away with, it was really worth it and fun. I’d like to do some action-adventure or a dramedy or get myself into comedy, maybe. I’d like to do it all. THR

articles.title: $1.1 Billion for Five Warner Bros. Execs: Who Cashed Out From Paramount Sale
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 9, 2026 8:03am JB Perrette, the former CEO of global streaming and games for WBD, saw shares and in-the-money options net him about $157 million, while CEO David Zaslav cashed out $606 million David Jon/Getty Images The sale of Warner Bros. Discovery delivered a windfall for the C-suite of the company, filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission show. Former WBD CEO David Zaslav sold shares worth more than $224 million in WBD on conjunction with the acquisition by Paramount, while options that were in the money netted him an additional $381 million or so. That totals over $600 million, not including any cash severance, a tax benefit or other perquisites. But his top four deputies also sold their shares in the sale, netting more than $500 million between them. That includes former WBD CFO Gunnar Weidenfels and former chief revenue and strategy officer Bruce Campbell, as well as former international chief Gerhard Zeiler, who is now weighing a move to politics in his native Austria. It also includes JB Perrette, the former CEO of global streaming and games for WBD, who is the only member of the WBD C-suite to make the jump to Skydance where he is co-chair & chief business officer for TV and streaming. According to Form 4s that each of the executives filed with the SEC, Perrette’s shares and in-the-money options netted him about $157 million, with Campbell netting $129 million, Weidenfels netting $122 million, and Zeiler netting $92 million. Those are obviously subject to taxes and withholding, and the options are contingent on vesting. The payouts do not include any cash severance, transaction bonuses or other perks. Of course, the top five executives at WBD were not the only employees to own equity. Other top executives, including many who made the jump to Skydance, almost certainly held large equity stakes as well, and Zaslav made it a priority to get employees across the company invested in its success. About half of WBD employees held shares in the company. That means that there are likely other long-time employees who received generous, or at least modest, payouts. The New York Post’s Charlie Gasparino reported that around 500 employees will net at least $1 million, and 1,000 will net at least $500,000. But with Skydance set to drop the axe on many staffers in the coming months as they consolidate, it may not add up to much in the long run. THR

articles.title: Mike Ditka, No-Nonsense Chicago Bears Legend and TV Analyst, Dies at 86
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Ira Kaufman Plus Icon Ira Kaufman View All October 9, 2026 8:28am Mike Ditka Rich Pilling/Diamond Images/Getty Images Mike Ditka, the Hall of Fame tight end, Super Bowl-winning coach of the Chicago Bears and TV analyst whose gruff “Iron Mike” style was parodied on Saturday Night Live , has died. He was 86. “It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather and friend, Mike Ditka,” his family said in a statement. “While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach and leader of the Chicago Bears’ Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever.” Related Stories Lifestyle Serena Williams Says Her New Barbie Doll Proves a Girl Can 'Become Anything She Chooses' General News Michael Kearns, Actor, Activist and 'Jerker' Director, Dies at 76 No cause of death was announced. Ditka had a minor stroke in 2012 and suffered heart attacks in 1988 and 2018. “The thing about me,” he told Rick Telander in April 2019, “is that people didn’t think I had a heart. Now they found out I got one.” Emerging from Carnegie, Pennsylvania, a manufacturing community five miles southwest of Pittsburgh, Ditka coached the Bears from 1982-92, guiding the 1985 team to a Super Bowl rout of the New England Patriots 22 years after winning an NFL championship with Chicago as a standout player. The cigar-smoking Ditka said his “Iron Mike” nickname derived from his upbringing in a steel town, but his brusque manner and short temper contributed to his tough image. He became a larger-than-life character, whether he was sticking a wad of gum on a photographer’s camera lens or berating a referee behind his trademark sunglasses. His persona was so large that he inspired a recurring sketch on SNL in the early ’90s known as “Bill Swerski’s Superfans.” Created by Robert Smigel and Bob Odenkirk, the skit had several Chicago sports fans (played by Smigel, George Wendt , Joe Mantegna, Mike Myers, Chris Farley, et al) sitting around a table at Ditka’s sports bar, drinking, smoking and gorging themselves on assorted meats while extolling the greatness of “Da Bears” and the Windy City’s other teams. The faithful wore dark sunglasses and thick mustaches as a homage to their hero, a member of the College and Pro Football halls of fame. Ditka himself appeared twice on SNL and on other shows including Cheers (he was seen on the bar’s TV in the final episode in 1993), L.A. Law , 3rd Rock From the Sun , Entourage , Becker and According to Jim . And in the 2005 film Kicking & Screaming , he’s asked by Will Ferrell’s character to help coach a kids soccer team. “I eat quitters for breakfast and I spit out their bones,” he tells the youngsters . In a 2015 interview, an amazed Ferrell recalled that during filming, Ditka’s hip “popped out” after recent replacement surgery, but he was able to make it through his scenes with just a couple of Advil. He was born Michael Dyczko in Carnegie on Oct. 18, 1939, the son of a welder. The family’s Ukrainian surname was changed to Ditka. He was recruited by 40 schools coming out of Aliquippa High and chose the University of Pittsburgh to stay close to home and pursue a career in dentistry. He was a three-sport star at Pitt, also excelling in baseball and basketball. (The Panthers retired his No. 89 in football, and he was enshrined in the College Football Hall of Fame in 1968.) The Bears selected Ditka fifth overall in the 1961 draft, and he won Rookie of the Year honors after catching 58 passes and scoring 12 touchdowns, extraordinary numbers for a tight end in that era. Ditka’s signature play as a pro came late in the 1962 season, two days after JFK’s assassination. With the Bears trailing the Steelers 17-14 in the fourth quarter, Ditka caught a short pass and broke eight tackles before collapsing to the turf after a 63-yard gain that set up the tying field goal. After the 1966 season, Ditka was embroiled in a contract dispute with Bears owner/head coach George Halas, whom he publicly ridiculed for “throwing nickels around like they were manhole covers.” Mike Ditka with Will Ferrell in the 2005 movie ‘Kicking & Screaming.’ Courtesy of Photofest Ditka was traded to the Philadelphia Eagles in 1967 before joining the Cowboys two years later. His four seasons in Dallas were highlighted by a touchdown catch against Miami in the 1972 Super Bowl, helping Tom Landry and the Cowboys win their first NFL title. Landry hired Ditka as an assistant coach in 1973, and he spent nine years on Landry’s staff as Dallas captured three NFC titles and won another Super Bowl. Ditka was named head coach of the Bears in 1982, reuniting with Halas. He coached them for 11 seasons, posting a 106-62 record and leading Chicago to seven playoff berths. The 1985 Bears, widely considered among the most dominant teams in NFL history, went 15-1 during the regular season before trouncing three playoff opponents by a combined 91-10 margin. Ditka and defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan clashed often about strategy and which man deserved more public recognition for the team’s success. Quarterback Jim McMahon wore a headband and adopted a rebel stance while Hall of Fame running back Walter Payton led a powerful attack. William “Refrigerator” Perry, a 335-pound defensive tackle, became a household name when Ditka used him as a running back in short-yardage situations. That strategy would soon turn controversial. Perry ran for two scores during the 1985 regular season and bulled over for a 1-yard touchdown in the 46-10 Super Bowl rout of the Patriots. Payton did not score against New England and held a grudge about what he deemed an oversight on Ditka’s part. Years later, the coach said he regretted that Payton, whom he lauded as the best player in NFL history, did not reach the end zone during the league’s showcase game. NBC hired Ditka as an analyst on NFL Live after his dismissal from the Bears following a 5-11 season in 1992. He was lured by the Saints to return to the sidelines in 1997, but that turned out to be a mistake. New Orleans went 6-10 in each of Ditka’s first two years, and he made NFL history by trading all of the team’s draft picks in 1999, plus a first-round choice in 2000, to move up and select University of Texas running back Ricky Williams. Ditka later posed for a magazine cover with the Heisman Trophy winner, who was wearing a wedding dress. After the ’99 Saints suffered their 10th loss in 11 games, Ditka suggested to reporters that the Saints would be better off without him. He stuck it out to the end of a 3-13 season before he was fired yet again. Ditka joined CBS Sports as a studio analyst on The NFL Today following his dismissal from the Saints and later appeared as an ESPN commentator on a variety of platforms. He described himself as an “ultra-ultra-ultra conservative” and was a strong supporter of Donald Trump during the 2016 presidential campaign. Some of his political views espoused while he worked for ESPN triggered controversy as Ditka criticized Colin Kaepernick’s protests and stated his belief that “there has been no oppression in America for the last 100 years.” That remark prompted a rebuke from legendary quarterback Joe Namath, who suggested that Ditka needed to look up the word “oppression.” A columnist from the Chicago Sun-Times labeled Ditka “a white man who is blind to the plight of people of color in this country.” In 2020, he became the owner and chairman of the X League, a tackle football circuit for women that was once known as the Lingerie Football League. Survivors include his second wife, Diana, and his four children, Michael III, Mark, Megan and Matthew. Ditka had little sympathy for players who didn’t work hard enough to reach their potential, a subject he addressed during his 1988 enshrinement speech at the Pro Football Hall of Fame. “In life, many men have talent, but talent in itself is no accomplishment,” he said. “Excellence in football and excellence in life is bred when men recognize their opportunities and then pursue them with a passion.” THR

articles.title: The Most Powerful Women in International TV
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Illustrated by Pixel Pusher As the global television industry heads to Cannes for MIPCOM, which runs Oct. 12-15, scale has become the sector’s answer to survival. Comcast’s Sky has agreed to buy ITV’s broadcasting and streaming businesses for 1.6 billion pounds ($2.12 billion), while Banijay’s $8 billion megamerger with All3Media has created an (even larger) indie production and distribution colossus. But these deals are a response to something bigger: a business whose traditional models, built on linear schedules, scripted dramas and predictable ad revenues, are being upended by streaming, vertical dramas and AI’s ability to automate parts of the creative process. Related Stories Movies U.K. Box Office Back to Full Health -- But What Lessons Do We Learn? Business Skydance's Gerhard Zeiler, Warner Bros. Int'l President, to Depart With Eyes on Politics THR For the women on THR ‘s 2026 list of the Most Powerful Women in International Television, the challenge is to adapt to technological disruption without losing what makes the work worth watching. “You’ve got to continue to invest in AI,” says ITV chief Carolyn McCall, who negotiated the Sky deal. “You’ve got to continue to invest in efficiency, and most importantly, you’ve got to have enough money to constantly invest in content, because content is where it’s at. That’s what makes you all your money.” It’s a sentiment — lean into the technology but keep a focus on the creative — echoed by the execs across this list. Rai Fiction’s Maria Pia Ammirati cautions against “the increasing tendency to delegate creative processes to technology,” while Renata Brandão of Brazil’s Conspiração Filmes wants the industry to trust “producers, creators and instinct over predictive metrics.” Selections were based on an executive’s decision-making authority — the ability to greenlight, commission or finance content — combined with the impact and performance of their work over the past 12 months. Mo Abudu CEO, EbonyLife Media (Nigeria) Abudu has built EbonyLife from a television network into one of Africa’s most ambitious independent media companies, spanning film and television production, talent development and entertainment. She began her media career as the host of pan-African talk show Moments With Mo , launching her own network, EbonyLife TV, in 2013 and film production company EbonyLife Films the following year. EbonyLife was the first African company to sign a multititle deal with Netflix, with Blood Sisters becoming Netflix’s first Nigerian Original series. Abudu has since expanded her international partnerships with companies including Sony, Lionsgate, the BBC and Westbrook Studios. Her brick-and-mortar efforts include the EbonyLife Creative Academy in Lagos, which offers free training on filmmaking and media content production, and the entertainment and lifestyle resort EbonyLife Place. On Oct. 8, Abudu will open EbonyLife Place London, a cinema, restaurant and music/art venue to showcase African talent. Says Abudu: “Talent is everywhere, but opportunity, capital and ownership are not. I think about how we create a future where African storytellers are not just telling our stories but owning them, financing them and taking them to the world.” Maria Pia Ammirati Director, Rai Fiction (Italy) Ammirati has spent more than three decades at Italian public broadcaster Rai, moving from journalism and cultural programming into senior management and becoming one of Italy’s most influential television executives. In a moment when commercial TV is in crisis across Europe, public broadcasters are leading the way both technologically, investing in online and mobile production and distribution, and creatively: Rai Fiction’s fall slate includes an ambitious period drama about the rags-to-riches Panini family publishing empire and the comedy crime series A Small Formality , which is focused on millennials, an overlooked demo in traditional TV. “Audience tastes evolve, as do the social context, technologies and the ways in which people engage with stories,” says Ammirati. “What concerns me most is the increasing tendency to delegate creative processes to technology, with the risk of gradually losing direct contact with the reality we are called upon to portray. It is a challenge we can address and overcome only by ensuring that the human factor remains at the heart of the creative process.” Nadine Bilke Chief Content Officer, ZDF (Germany) A trained journalist who earned her doctorate researching the quality of crisis and war reporting, Bilke joined the German public broadcaster in 2002 and spent much of her early career building ZDF’s digital journalism operation. She became head of ZDFneo in 2018, helping position the channel for younger, digitally oriented audiences, before becoming program director for the parent broadcaster in 2022. Responsible for programming for a nation of 84 million, Bilke says the one thing she worries about “is the growing fragmentation of our societies. We have more content, more platforms and more ways to engage than ever before, yet it is becoming harder to create shared experiences and a common cultural conversation.” Marie-Philippe Bouchard President and CEO, CBC/Radio Canada Bouchard took over CBC/Radio-Canada in January 2025, assuming the tricky role of running Canada’s public broadcaster as linear television shrinks, U.S. streamers dominate Canadian TV, and President Trump’s tariff war and 51st state taunts drive a rise in Canadian patriotism. That’s a bonus for a major broadcaster with a mandate to offer local news, current affairs programming and homegrown TV series coast-to-coast. Bouchard came to the job from TV5 Québec Canada, the French-language broadcaster, where she served as president and CEO from 2016-24. Renata Brandão CEO, Conspiração Filmes (Brazil) Brandão joined Conspiração Filmes in 2006 after studying international relations and communications and completing film-industry studies at UCLA, initially as a production assistant before moving into planning and business management. She became president of business in 2015 and CEO in 2017, helping transform one of Brazil’s best-established independent production companies into an increasingly international operation. Brandão also has expanded Conspiração’s television business beyond Brazil, including into Spanish-language production in Mexico. In 2017, she also founded Hysteria, a Conspiração label focused on stories centered on women. “The obsession with relying strictly on ‘proven IP,’ remakes or hyper-calculated formulas has led to widespread audience fatigue across platforms,” she says. “I would love to see the industry return to trusting producers, creators and instinct over predictive metrics.” From left: Renata Brandao, Mo Abudu and Maria Pia Ammirati Assunta Servello; Courtesy of Subject (2) Amelia Brown CEO, Fremantle U.K. It just made sense when Brown was appointed Fremantle U.K. CEO in 2023: The industry veteran has been with the company for more than 20 years, instrumental in such early hits as Britain’s Got Talent and The X Factor and later Too Hot to Handle for Netflix and Mamma Mia! I Have a Dream for ITV. At the top of the food chain, Brown leads the corporate strategy for one of Britain’s most prolific production outfits and oversees the output of every Fremantle U.K. label. Carol Choi Executive VP, The Walt Disney Co. (Asia-Pacific) Choi’s remit spans both sides of Disney’s Asia-Pacific ambitions: bringing its Hollywood franchises to regional audiences and building a slate of homegrown streaming originals. A Disney veteran since 2006, she previously ran the company’s Japan and Korea businesses and now oversees studios, original content strategy and integrated marketing across the region. With a significant ramp-up of Disney+’s production of international originals now underway, she points to the work of teams in Japan, Korea and Australia as a particular source of pride this year. “From Perfect Crown to A Shop for Killers season two, Battle of Fates and The One Shot , it’s clear that great local stories can stand proudly alongside our most iconic global franchises,” she says. Priya Dogra CEO, Channel 4 (U.K.) Dogra was named CEO of the British broadcaster in December, taking over from Alex Mahon. Her résumé was substantive: She joined Comcast-owned Sky in 2024 as its chief advertising, group data and new revenue officer, having worked at Warner Bros. Discovery and its predecessors for 14 years. At Channel 4, she’s undoubtedly inherited one of the trickiest jobs in the biz — the cash-strapped PSB must adapt or die — and in September unveiled a raft of cuts, she said, part of C4’s “long-term transformation strategy.” Cécile Frot-Coutaz CEO, Sky Studios; Chief Content Officer, Sky (U.K.) The Sky Studios boss actually had her role expanded following Dogra’s departure to Channel 4 and now oversees its advertising division, too. Frot-Coutaz’s remit was already vast — she leads the development, production and commissioning of all of Sky’s original programming, including such record-breaking titles as the Emmy-nominated The Day of the Jackal and the risky SNL UK spinoff. More recently, she’s championed the Dominic West and Sienna Miller-led War , set to dominate our screens this autumn, and played a crucial role in that enormous, billion-dollar ITV-Sky sale. Frot-Coutaz also supervises Sky Studios Elstree, Sky’s state-of-the-art film and TV studio, plus Sky Studios’ global portfolio of production companies that includes Blast! Films, Jupiter Entertainment, True North and Love Productions. Jay Hunt Creative Director of Worldwide Video, Europe, Apple (U.K.) The British Film Institute chair has continued to deftly straddle two enormous jobs in European film and TV. At Apple TV, she’s been pivotal in its transition from middle of the pack to streamer to beat, having championed some of the platform’s biggest global hits, most notably the Emmy-winning Slow Horses , which just scored an eighth season, the BAFTA-winning Bad Sisters and enduringly popular The Buccaneers . Among Hunt’s most anticipated upcoming commissions are Will Sharpe’s magnum opus, Prodigies , and Juno Temple’s starry comedy-drama The Husbands . Jay Hunt (left) and Minyoung Kim Pip/Apple; Courtesy of Subject Angela Jain Head of Content, Disney+ EMEA (U.K.) Jain is overseeing a unit that includes the likes of Rivals , Extraordinary and Stephen Graham’s A Thousand Blows , three huge shows that helped score Disney+ a record 15 BAFTA TV Award nods in March. Before joining the Disney+ team last year, Jain had commissioning stints at E4 and ITV2, where she was responsible for some of the biggest British shows, including Misfits and The Inbetweeners . At ITV Studios, she oversaw big-hitters Love Island and I’m a Celeb . Under Jain, the EMEA team is “ramping up” production across Europe, with regional commissions including the Venice-premiering Oasis documentary and Italy’s Murder on Lake Garda . Ekta Kapoor Joint Managing Director, Balaji Telefilms (India) More than three decades after co-founding Balaji, Kapoor remains one of Indian television’s defining hitmakers. Her revived family soap Kyunki Saas Bhi Kabhi Bahu Thi 2 has topped ratings charts this year, underscoring the enduring pull of her franchises. But the veteran producer also is finding new outlets for her signature serial storytelling. Balaji’s long-term creative partnership with Netflix, announced last year, marked a push to develop projects across multiple formats. In September, she made another significant move: a YouTube partnership for five premium scripted shows spanning 200 episodes. Kapoor will lead the creative direction, with Balaji retaining the underlying IP while tapping YouTube’s global distribution and advertising business — a savvy expansion that doesn’t involve surrendering ownership of her stories. M-K Kennedy Managing Director Worldwide Television, StudioCanal (France) Kennedy has built a career around taking local television production global. A native of Bucaramanga, Colombia, she began in Washington, D.C., producing the Hispanic Heritage Awards before moving to Telemundo, where she helped establish Telemundo Studios Mexico. After seven years at Universal Television and UCP in Los Angeles, she joined Netflix, where she built production teams across Latin America and Europe and oversaw major local-language productions including Money Heist , Dark , Lupin and All Quiet on the Western Front . Last year, Kennedy took charge of StudioCanal’s newly reorganized Worldwide Television division, overseeing the French giant’s international TV drama slate that includes several film-to-series spinoffs drawing from StudioCanal’s vast library. There’s A Prophet (from the 2009 Jacques Audiard prison drama), Apollo Has Fallen (based on the Gerard Butler action franchise) and Army of Shadows , a reimagining of Jean-Pierre Melville’s 1969 film about the French resistance in World War II that is set to star Paddy Considine, Kit Harington, Susan Sarandon and Olivia Colman. Minyoung Kim VP Content, Netflix, APAC (excluding India) For the executive who greenlit Squid Game , Netflix’s most watched series of all time, the bar for a good year is unusually high. But Kim, who is approaching her 10th anniversary at Netflix in November and has overseen the bulk of the streamer’s output in the Asia-Pacific region, has yet another global hit to celebrate. Korea’s Teach You a Lesson recently joined the streamer’s all-time top 10 for non-English television. According to Netflix, APAC content now accounts for more than half the titles in its global non-English Top 10, up from about 30 percent in 2021, while annual worldwide viewing hours for content from the region have quadrupled since 2019. This year’s slate stretches from Thailand’s The Evil Lawyer to Japan’s Plastic Beauty and Australia’s My Brilliant Career alongside a push into live programming with events including BTS: The Comeback and Skyscraper Live . “We’re always looking for the magic of something unexpected that captures the imagination and gets people excited,” she says. “Doing that once or twice is hard work, doing that constantly across nine APAC countries is enough to give anyone insomnia. But, when we get it right, it’s the best feeling in the world.” Anna Marsh CEO, StudioCanal; Member of Canal+ Board; Canal+ Group Chief Content Officer (France) Marsh has spent more than two decades building an international career in film and television sales, distribution and production, rising from international sales at Tele Images and TF1 International to the top of leading French major StudioCanal in 2019. She joined the management board of parent Canal+ in 2022, becoming deputy CEO, and is now also chief content officer for the entire group, putting her undeniably among the most powerful and influential figures in global entertainment with a remit that extends beyond TV to awards-worthy cinema, including this year’s fall festival favorites Elsinore with Andrew Scott and Danny Boyle’s Ink with Jack O’Connell. Under Marsh, StudioCanal has continued to expand its European production and distribution footprint, taking a controlling stake in Italian distributor/producer Lucky Red and Nordic outfit SAM Productions and, at the Canal+ level, signing a new three-year partnership with British pay TV giant Sky that will see the companies develop and co-finance at least two premium English-language dramas a year. Closer to home, Canal+ has announced a French version of Saturday Night Live set to launch this year. Carolyn McCall CEO, ITV (U.K.) Carolyn McCall Courtesy of ITV Has anyone had a busier year than McCall? She negotiated the biggest international TV deal of the year — the 1.6 billion-pound ($2.12 billion) sale of ITV’s broadcasting and streaming business to the Comcast-owned Sky — and handled the aftermath with cool-as-a-cucumber self-assurance. “The announcement of the sale … was a defining moment for ITV,” McCall said on a call with journalists as the company unveiled 2 percent revenue growth in the first half of the year. Unfazed by the prospect of regulatory approval hurdles, McCall (who noted it was ITV who instigated the sale) and her team will be responsible for the most formidable British media group the U.K. has ever seen. Sky would acquire ITV’s networks and streaming businesses (Media & Entertainment) — including the ITV channel portfolio and ITVX — while ITV Studios, the production outfit behind such franchises as Love Island , Britain’s Got Talent and the Netflix hit Fool Me Once , is to be spun off as a standalone listed company, McCall has confirmed. “The competition is ferocious,” she said at a Royal Television Society event in London in September. “It’s not just [being] bigger; it’s also the investment. So you have to invest in technology. You’ve got to continue to invest in AI. You’ve got to continue to invest in efficiency and, most importantly, you’ve got to have enough money to constantly invest in content because content is where it’s at. That’s what makes you all your money.” She has certainly delivered on her promise since taking up the post in 2018, when she vowed to launch a new strategic vision — “more than TV” — in a bid to help ITV adapt to the rapidly evolving media landscape. Her experience spans the top jobs at several of Britain’s leading businesses, including EasyJet and the Guardian Media Group. Beverley McGarvey President, Network 10 (Australia) Twenty years after joining Network 10, McGarvey oversees a portfolio stretching from such free-to-air staples as MasterChef Australia to Paramount+’s full slate of local originals, including NCIS: Sydney and the true-crime series Who the Hell Is Hamish? She says the company’s free streaming service is having its “biggest year yet,” while innovative recent partnerships with such brands as LG and TikTok — the latter aimed at bringing new audiences to Big Brother — have begun to offer fresh avenues to viewers. Keeping Australian production viable amid rising costs and fragmenting audiences remains her priority. “My challenge is creating efficiencies to keep investment flowing into our local content,” she says. One show she wishes she had made over the past year? Disney+’s Rivals . “I just love the escapist, compelling juiciness of the stories,” she says. Anna Marsh (left) and Beverley McGarvey Benjamin Decoin/CANAL+; Courtesy of Subject Anne Mensah VP Content, Netflix (U.K.) Netflix has invested an eye-watering 4.45 billion pounds ($6 billion) in U.K. productions since 2020, creating more than 50,000 jobs in the process. It’s not a stretch to say Mensah and her team have spent well — the buzziest projects among the streamer’s British TV slate continue to overperform across the globe, among them Heartstopper , Adolescence , Black Doves and The Gentlemen . And that’s before you get to the Kate Winslet-Maxine Peake two-hander ( The Unheard ), the untitled Roald Dahl adaptation and the Barry Keoghan-led Top Boy prequel. Cathy Payne CEO, Banijay Rights (U.K.) This year, it was confirmed that Payne would be steering the ship of Banijay Entertainment’s global distribution business following the $8 billion megamerger with All3Media. She’s remained in her post as CEO of Banijay Rights, too, with the Aussie-born executive overseeing the sales of such colossal hits as Survivor , Big Brother and MasterChef , as well as Black Mirror and Peaky Blinders worldwide. Kate Phillips Chief Content Officer, BBC (U.K.) Phillips’ lengthy BBC experience primed her for the CCO role at Britain’s top broadcaster: She was director of unscripted from May 2022 and before that commissioned more than 500 hours of original programs a year, including the still massively popular Strictly Come Dancing and The Graham Norton Show. Now, she’s responsible for all BBC network TV and radio output. Says Phillips, “I’m continually thinking about how we reach audiences who are consuming media on so many different platforms now while still retaining the attribution to the BBC.” Lindsay Salt Director of Drama, BBC (U.K.) Salt is literally behind every single success out of the BBC’s behemoth drama division: Richard Gadd’s Baby Reindeer follow-up, Half-Man ; the long-awaited second season of The Night Manager ; and Sally Wainwright’s Riot Women . She is also the commissioner on some impossibly huge international co-productions, including the BBC and Netflix’s Lord of the Flies and the BritBox phenomenon The Other Bennet Sister (the biggest U.K. drama launch — across all platforms and streamers — this entire year). This is but a fraction of her work platforming original voices, and Salt’s eye for savvy storytelling keeps the BBC’s reputation for prestige drama in tip-top shape. Monika Shergill VP Content, Netflix (India) Netflix’s 10th year in India has given Shergill plenty to celebrate. According to the streamer, India became its largest contributor to non-English film viewing globally in the first half of 2026, while the crime thriller Taskaree: The Smuggler’s Web became the first Indian series to debut at No. 1 on its global non-English TV chart. Her slate’s breadth also is unmatched by global companies operating in the country, spanning the military drama Operation Safed Sagar , the reality series Lock Upp: Sach Ya Sazaa and the Tamil film Made in Korea . “I’m proudest of the range we’ve brought to audiences,” she says. But amid shifting viewing habits, she notes she’s focused most on the nuances within India’s vast viewership: “In a market as diverse as ours, the challenge isn’t scale; it’s specificity for different types of audiences.” Christine Strobl Program Director, ARD (Germany) Strobl has spent her career at the intersection of public service broadcasting and German television drama. A lawyer by training from an impressive family (her father is conservative political icon Wolfgang Schäuble, former president and longest-serving member of the German Parliament), Strobl joined regional public broadcaster SWR in 1999 and rose through programming roles, becoming head of the broadcaster’s film and family programming in 2011. In 2012, she moved to ARD subsidiary Degeto Film as managing director, where she oversaw the development, acquisition and co-production of fiction for the public broadcaster and fought the channel bosses to secure financing for the most expensive German drama of all time: Babylon Berlin . Backed by ARD and pay TV network Sky, Babylon was an early example of Strobl’s push toward cross-channel cooperation, something she’s extended to sports (ARD and streamer Magenta shared rights to matches at this year’s World Cup) and entertainment (the network is seeking a partner to join forces, and share costs, for the broadcast of the next Eurovision Song Contest ). Her favorite non-ARD show of the year was Netflix’s German spy thriller Unfamiliar . “The story itself, with all its twists and turns, is the real star,” she says. “It’s exactly what German fiction can be: high-quality, surprisingly directed and thus internationally appealing.” Christine Strobl (left) and Monika Shergill ARD/Jens Koch; Courtesy of Subject Karen Thorne-Stone President and CEO, Ontario Creates (Canada) As head of the Canadian province’s media investment agency, Thorne-Stone finances everything from feature films to XR content. That role now means navigating industry contraction and uncertainty and ensuring Hollywood producers keep coming to Ontario for tax credits, local talent and varied locations. “There is no end to the talent in our province and country, and we have an extraordinary capacity to fuel growth, jobs and investment if we maintain an environment where creators and businesses can thrive,” she tells THR about her province staying competitive with rival locales. Jane Turton Deputy CEO, Banijay Entertainment (U.K.) Turton is entering a new chapter after steering All3Media for a decade as the company completed its $8 billion megamerger with Banijay this year to create the undisputed indie production and distribution champ. The globe-spanning group with 130 production companies across 25 countries boasts a content catalog that includes The Traitors , Big Brother , MasterChef , Peaky Blinders and Midsomer Murders . The deal marks the end of the All3Media brand, but for Turton, it’s the start of a new chapter. “Leading All3Media has been a huge pleasure and privilege,” she said after the merger closed in July, adding that the combination of the two indie powerhouses would multiply future opportunities “many times over,” bringing together the capacity to deliver “brilliant shows developed and produced by world-class talent” with “the strength of a global distributor, a market-leading digital studio and a growing live events business.” Kylie Watson-Wheeler Senior VP and Managing Director, Disney Australia & New Zealand / head, ESPN APAC (Australia) With The Artful Dodger in production on a third season, Watson-Wheeler, among her many achievements, now has Disney+’s first homegrown Australian streaming hit. She calls the renewal “a rare achievement and a strong marker of the show’s appeal both locally and internationally.” The veteran exec oversees Disney’s Australia and New Zealand businesses and ESPN across Asia-Pacific. After bringing ESPN onto Disney+ in the two countries last year, she has another milestone to celebrate in 2026: the recent successful launch of Disney+ with ads, the streamer’s first ad-supported tier in Asia-Pacific. “Our ad-tier momentum is strong, with sustained acquisition growth and strong engagement,” she says, pointing to opportunities to attract both advertisers and cost-conscious viewers with the platform’s growing mix of live sports, Hulu programming and Disney’s deep library. Profiles by Patrick Brzeski, Lily Ford, Scott Roxborough and Etan Vlessing. This story appeared in the Oct. 7 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Rachel Stockman Succeeds Dan Abrams as CEO of Law&Crime and Court TV

Stockman had previously served as president; Abrams will remain with the company as chairman. Law&Crime has a large online presence in the true crime and legal content spaces. Law&Crime has four FAST channels, millions of YouTube subscribers, billions of video views and more than 700 million hours watched across platforms over the past year, the brand says. Law&Crime acquired Court TV from Scripps in 2026. Just last month, Law&Crime signed with WME for representation, as first reported by THR . Stockman recently oversaw the launch of “Partners in Crime,” a programming initiative featuring six original series developed with popular true-crime creators. Stockman has executive produced dozens of documentaries and series for Netflix, Paramount+, A&E, Fox Nation and ID/HBO Max. “Rachel’s ability to direct the business at the highest level while also making so many smart, granular decisions has helped lead us to where we are today,” Abrams, founder and chairman of Law&Crime and Court TV, said in a statement. “She has truly earned this. I can’t wait to see where she takes us next.” “I’m incredibly proud of our extraordinary team and everything we’ve accomplished together,” said Stockman. “I’m honored to lead this next chapter as we continue to push boundaries, embrace bold ideas and help shape the future of media.” THR profiled Abrams in May . The former court reporter will be plenty busy even with a more passive role at Law&Crime/Court TV. Abrams also serves as chief legal analyst at ABC News, founder and CEO of website Mediaite, host of SiriusXM radio series The Dan Abrams Show (SiriusXM POTUS) and host and exec producer of the cable series Court Cam (A&E) and On Patrol: Live (Reelz). Abrams even owns a winery (Ev&Em) and a Rotten Tomatoes-for-booze company The Daily Pour, as well as popular New York City restaurant Danny’s. articles.title: The Netflix Ax Is Coming as Stock Languishes
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden , Borys Kit October 9, 2026 8:44am Co-CEO of Netflix Ted Sarandos speaks during the Bloomberg Screentime 2026 conference in Los Angeles, on September 30, 2026. Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images For weeks there’s been a steady drumbeat near the halls of power at Netflix over the question of rightsizing, job cuts and a restructure ahead of its third quarter earnings disclosure on October 20. While the streaming giant still lords over its rivals in the subscription space and co-chiefs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters command an annual content spending budget of $20 billion, Wall Street arguably has viewed this as an off year for Netflix. Once a high-flying tech growth story, the nearly 30-year-old company is now the studio establishment as all the attention and investment has gone to AI bets in public markets. The company also has had to fight off an ever-growing YouTube, which is increasingly becoming the dominant platform on TV screens in addition to its video lead on mobile devices. With stock down 20 percent year to date, Sarandos and Peters may unveil a shake up that could be geared in part to showing the Street that it’s ready to accelerate growth in the post-Streaming Wars economy. In the last several weeks, multiple journalists have been hearing that cuts could be in the 5 percent range, or more, at the company. The Hollywood Reporter has been hearing the same from sources about upcoming belt-tightening, and Sarandos himself has been laying those expectations in public settings as well. The company has 16,000 employees, 10,900 of which are based in the U.S., as of the company’s last 10-K filing in December. A reorganization may be undertaken in the next few months. Netflix declined to comment on Friday. “Overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” the co-CEO said at Bloomberg‘s Screentime event on Sept. 30, in a nod to the potential rework to come. He also added, “The business is great and growing fine.” Netflix regularly cuts staff and rehires, that’s been a principle from founder Reed Hastings he even wrote about in his 2020 book, No Rules Rules: Netflix and the Culture of Reinvention . But these pink slips would mark more of a significant mass restructure should they come to pass. Layoffs, if strategically executed with a go-forward plan, can sometimes help boost share price and Wall Street has been valuing austerity at the top publicly traded companies for several years now. The move would be in keeping with layoff season at the other Hollywood majors. Disney, under new CEO Josh D’Amaro, has been in the middle of his first notable round of pink slips while Warner Bros. and Paramount will soon see the ax fall as well as the Skydance team searches for $6 billion in synergies. THR

articles.title: James Bond Comic Book Series in the Works from Grant Morrison, IDW (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Borys Kit Plus Icon Borys Kit Senior Film Writer View All October 9, 2026 9:00am 007 Logo and Grant Morrison Allan Amato Logo text IDW Publishing has acquired the license to thrill and has set Morrison, Grant Morrison , to shake, not stir, things up. Partnering with Ian Fleming Publications, IDW has picked up the license to create all-new comic book adventures featuring the iconic British spy James Bond . The two companies have tapped writer Grant Morrison, the influential and award-winning scribe known for All-Star Superman and his multi-year Batman run as well medium-pushing comics such as Animal Man and Doom Patrol . Related Stories Movies Saoirse Ronan Responds to Rumors That Husband Jack Lowden Will Be the Next James Bond TV Pierce Brosnan and Helen Mirren on Their 'MobLand' Season 2 Return: "Pure Lunacy" “Pairing a renowned franchise like James Bond with the visionary writer Grant Morrison is a perfect example of IDW doing what it does best with licensed properties,” said IDW CEO Davidi Jonas in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter. “Our goal isn’t to simply provide supplemental and optional stories. We strive to take radical swings which celebrate and stay true to the very qualities that make the franchise special while also reinventing it for the modern comic book landscape.” Stated Morrison, “I’ve been a James Bond fan for as long as I can remember and this opportunity to put my own stamp on a British character as iconic as King Arthur, Robin Hood or Sherlock Holmes, was too good to miss.” The comic has no artist on board yet nor does it have a release date. It does, however, have a title for its six-part opening adventure: Sunbreaker . (That is not, however, the title of the comic, which remains at this time for their eyes only.) Morrison is promising new cars, new gadgets, and a new ultimate villain ripped straight from the headlines. “Our opening 6-part adventure, Sunbreaker , attempts to create a definitive Bond story featuring everything fans love about the character and his world, while adding a whole lot more,” Morrison said. “Expect to see James Bond in a few unfamiliar situations, facing unfamiliar foes, in a world very like our own as reflected in a deadly funhouse mirror – a world of intrigue, violence, double cross and deception. A world through which James Bond glides like a killer shark among minnows. Charismatic, ruthless, unstoppable.” A fictional British spy hero, Bond, also known as 007, made his debut in the 1953 with the Ian Fleming-written novel Casino Royale . The first movie, Dr. No , was released in 1962 and starred Sean Connery. Bond movies have been a regular pop culture event since then, with now 25 outings in the film series with another one due to begin production next year. The character’s appearance in comics has been sporadic. Marvel did adaptations of the Roger Moore entries For Your Eyes Only and Octopussy in the early 1980s and new adventures have come in bits, fits and starts since 1989, initially from Eclipse Comics and later from Dark Horse Comics and Dynamite Comics. The license is coup for IDW, which also publishes a slew of Star Trek comics. “James Bond is a character with an incredible legacy across books, films, video games and comics,” said Ian Fleming Publications publishing director Simon Ward. “At Ian Fleming Publications we are always looking for the best medium for each Bond story and there are some adventures that can only be told through comics. The team at IDW wowed us with their vision for the future of 007 original comics and as someone who has been reading Grant Morrison for many years, I think we’re in for something new and very special.” THR

articles.title: ‘Trust Me, I’m a Doctor’ Review: Kal Penn Plays Anna Nicole Smith’s Physician in a Moldy and Misguided Bio-Dramedy
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All October 9, 2026 9:00am 'Trust Me, I'm a Doctor' Briarcliff Entertainment It would have seemed safe to assume that public interest in anything related to Anna Nicole Smith has long since passed its sell-by date. But apparently not to the makers of the too-cutely titled new film about the legal travails of Smith’s former doctor, Sandeep Kapoor, who was charged with multiple crimes related to his treatment of the reality TV star after her 2007 death from a drug overdose at age 39. Based on Kapoor’s self-published memoir (that should have been a clue), Trust Me, I’m a Doctor feels like it’s arriving nearly two decades too late. Written and directed by Thane Economou — whose sole previous feature credit, 2016’s The Wedding Party , is described in the press notes as “a rom-com filmed in one continuous 119-minute take” — the movie stars Kal Penn as the unfortunate doctor who got a bit carried away with his colorful new patient, played by Abbie Cornish ( Bright Star ). He became her friend and confidant, seduced by her fame and lifestyle. Attempting to explain himself, he asks, “Have you ever walked on a red carpet?” Related Stories News TMZ's Harvey Levin Cut Kanye West's Hitler Praise From 2018 Interview, Former Staffer Says Business Harvey Levin's Next TMZ Overhaul: True-Crime, With a Dash of Populism Trust Me, I'm a Doctor The Bottom Line Oy! Release date : Friday, October 16 Cast : Kal Penn, Linda Hamilton, David Julian Harish, Abbie Cornish Director-screenwriter : Thane Economou Rated R, 1 hour 51 minutes Kapoor was often photographed with her at various events and parties, most notably when he rode in her limo as part of a West Hollywood gay pride parade. Beginning the story with a depiction of the police raid on Kapoor’s home that feels more than a little exaggerated in its rabid intensity, the story flashes back to chronicle his relationship with his patient as related during a discovery session with his attorney Ellyn Garofalo (a fine Linda Hamilton ). Economou frequently adopts a decidedly jokey approach, as if he’s aware that it would be hard to take seriously this story involving such outlandish real-life figures as Smith; photographer Larry Birkhead (Ted Jefferies), who filed a paternity suit against her over her daughter Dannielynn; Howard K. Stern (David Julian Hirsh), her lawyer, who co-starred with her in a reality TV show and who also claimed he was Dannielynn’s father; and Harvey Levin (Elon Gold), the founder of TMZ . Penn’s Kapoor narrates the proceedings, often breaking the fourth wall to address us directly. A tired running gag involves Stern’s name (“no, the other one,” characters point out to separate him from the radio show host). Unfortunately, the film lacks the wit that made such similarly stylized true-life films as The Big Short so effective. It’s also very clunky, with background information ladled out via such things as fake TMZ segments and lawyer/client “sidebars” with all the finesse of Wikipedia entries. The tone is maddeningly inconsistent, straining for heartfelt emotion through such maudlin plot elements as Kapoor’s relationship with his parents, who were unaware that he was gay, and his friendship with a dying elderly female patient. The whole story is so bizarre — the segment about Prince Frederic von Anhalt, Zsa Zsa Gabor’s ninth husband, who also claimed to be the father of Smith’s child, could easily be expanded into a feature film itself — that it exerts a certain morbid fascination. But the most interesting character onscreen, Smith, is given short shrift, despite a worthy performance by Cornish, in favor of concentrating on Kapoor, about whom it’s hard to care much about. And though Penn delivers a sensitive turn as the doctor so desperate for attention and validation that he made terrible mistakes in judgment, he’s unable to make the film feel like anything other than yet another sleazy attempt to capitalize on Smith’s notoriety. Full credits Production: Picture Movers, Stadium, RBF Productions Films, Good Good Films, Low Road Films, Spy Films Distributor: Briarcliff Entertainment Cast: Kal Penn, Linda Hamilton, David Julian Harish, Abbie Cornish Director-screenwriter: Thane Economou Producers: Ryan Hawkins, Al Engelmann, Rebecca Case, Geenah Krisht Executive producers: Kal Penn, Thane Economou, David Gale, Charlotte Ubben, Randy Wooten, Melora Donoghue, Nashwa & Ali Krisht, Michael Lazari, Tom Ortenberg Director of photography: Bobby Shore Production designer: Melanie Garros Editor: Brian Berdan Composers: Daniel Stockdale, Niles Hollowell-Dhar Costume designer: Hanna Puley Casting: Anne McCarthy, Kellie Roy, Morgan Robbins, Stephanie Gorin Rated R, 1 hour 51 minutes THR

articles.title: Dawn Porter to Direct Documentary on Pioneering TV News Anchor Max Robinson
articles.full_text: Oct 9, 2026 7:32am PT Dawn Porter to Direct Documentary on Pioneering TV News Anchor Max Robinson By Cynthia Littleton Plus Icon Cynthia Littleton Business Editor @Variety_Cynthia Latest Dawn Porter to Direct Documentary on Pioneering TV News Anchor Max Robinson 1 hour ago Let’s Get Physical: Key Takeaways From The IRL Advantage, Variety’s Experience and Culture Summit 21 hours ago Fox Entertainment Global Keys on Content Creators, Microdramas With Diverse Mipcom Slate 1 day ago See All Variety / ©ABC/Courtesy Everett Collection Dawn Porter is set to direct a feature documentary on pioneering Black TV news anchor Max Robinson for Wise Child Studios . CNN anchor Victor Blackwell is among the producers. “Color Bars: The Story of the Black Journalist Who Broke the TV News Color Barrier” will recount the rise and fall of Robinson’s career in broadcast news for Wise Child Studios. Porter, known for her much-praised docus including 2020’s “John Lewis: Good Trouble” and 2018’s “Bobby Kennedy for President,’ will produce through her Trilogy Films banner. Blackwell, who anchors “CNN This Morning Weekend” and hosts the weekly series “First of All with Victor Blackwell,” will produce through is Fresh Fruit Films. Related Stories ‘Bowie80’ to Celebrate David Bowie’s 80th Birthday With Events, Exhibits, Releases and More Throughout 2027 A Rare David Bowie Self-Portrait — Featuring His Handprints — Is Going on Auction at Sotheby's “Max Robinson was an exceptional journalist by any standard, and he deserves to have a firm place in the history of American journalism,” said Jason Beekman, founder and CEO of Wise Child Studios. “He courageously broke barriers in front of a national TV audience while facing the incredible pressure of simply doing his job. We’re proud to bring his life and legacy to a wider audience, and thrilled to have Dawn Porter’s vision guiding the film.” Popular on Variety Robinson came on to the national scene in the late 1970s as an anchor for ABC News. He gained prominence as an anchor for the NBC and CBS affiliate stations in Washington, D.C. In 1978, Robinson made history by joining ABC News’ national anchor team. He was a founder of the National Association of Black Journalists in 1975. But Robinson’s tenure at ABC News was short-lived as he struggled with alcohol abuse. He died of complications from AIDS in December 1988 at age 49. Robinson is an inspiring figure to a generation of journalists and media business insiders. “I remember watching Max Robinson on television — he was one of the very few Black people on the evening news,” Porter said. “Later I joined ABC News and people still spoke about his impact on the newsroom. At a time when truth and courage in journalism are under assault, everyone should know the Max Robinson story.” Blackwell equated Robinson’s impact to that of Sidney Poitier, Thurgood Marshall and Jackie Robinson. “Max Robinson is my Sidney Poitier. He’s my Thurgood Marshall, my Jackie Robinson,” Blackwell said. “In our current media landscape and social climate, Max’s life and career are more relevant than ever. I’m excited and honored that Dawn has joined the team to tell his remarkable story.” Wise Child Studios was formed in 2023 to develop and package a range of original content. Beekman is a former head of business and legal affairs for RadicalMedia. Wise Child’s investigative docuseries “Reality Check: Inside America’s Next Top Model” debuted on Netflix earlier this year. articles.title: Phoebe Bridgers Reunites Boygenius as Part of Three-Song Studio Performance Video, Directed by ‘Primetime’ Helmer Lance Oppenheim
articles.full_text: Oct 9, 2026 7:44am PT Phoebe Bridgers Reunites Boygenius as Part of Three-Song Studio Performance Video, Directed by ‘Primetime’ Helmer Lance Oppenheim By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Phoebe Bridgers Reunites Boygenius as Part of Three-Song Studio Performance Video, Directed by ‘Primetime’ Helmer Lance Oppenheim 1 hour ago Steve Martin and Alison Brown on Reinventing Lil Nas X’s ‘Old Town Road’ as an All-Star Bluegrass Tune… With Added Lyrics About Buc-ee’s and Sasquatch 23 hours ago Hayley Williams Proves There’s a Lot More to Her Than Paramore in a Galvanizing Solo Show at the Hollywood Bowl: Concert Review 2 days ago See All Phoebe Bridgers fans may not be getting glimpses of her current arena tour, because of the prohibition on cameras and phones, but as far as performance footage goes, she’s given them something better — a three-song in-studio video, shot by her “ Primetime ” director Lance Oppenheim , that features some familiar guests. The filmed performance, part of the “Sound Check at Cherry Lane Theatre” series, has Bridgers singing the closing theme she wrote for “Primetime,” “On Video,” followed by two choice picks from her “Lost Weekend” album, “Haunted” and “Lost Boys.” She’s joined for the last two numbers by Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus , amounting to a Boygenius reunion. The two women also sang harmonies on those two songs on Bridgers’ album, but this acoustic performance provides a much more intimate listen to their vocal interplay. It’s the first time Bridgers, Baker and Dacus have appeared together on camera in nearly three years, specifically since they did “Saturday Night Live” as a group in November 2023. Bridgers and company shot this new footage with Oppenheim following her three sold-out nights at Barclays Center in Brooklyn. The location, Cherry Lane Theatre, is a venerable off-Broadway theater — said to be New York’s oldest — that is now owned and operated by A24, which put out “Primetime,” in which Bridgers has a supporting role, as well as having provided a theme. “On Video” is the first of the three songs in the video, with Bridgers performing in dim lighting in front of a bank of televisions, accompanied only by Jay Gruska, one of the co-producers of the latest album, on keyboards. For “Haunted,” a much jauntier-sounding number with a pronounced country flavor, Bridgers is joined by Dacus, who wields a video camera of her own, and Baker, plus four acoustic musicians. The lineup gets stripped down to just the Boygenius trio for the finale, “Lost Boys,” which has a much softer arrangement than the spirited acoustic version, emphasizing the group harmonies. Bridgers fans will well know that this is Oppenheim’s second time filming a version of “Lost Boys.” He also directed the official music video for the lead single from “Lost Weekend,” with some visual and thematic callbacks to his three-part 2024 HBO documentary, “Ren Faire.” Popular on Variety Related Stories ‘Bowie80’ to Celebrate David Bowie’s 80th Birthday With Events, Exhibits, Releases and More Throughout 2027 A Rare David Bowie Self-Portrait — Featuring His Handprints — Is Going on Auction at Sotheby's Oppenheim is also the co-director of the much-touted upcoming Elizabeth Holmes documentary, “You Can See Everything,” with Nathan Fielder. “Primetime” marks his debut directing a dramatic feature film, dramatizing a story about TV personality Chris Hansen; Bridgers appears in it as a “decoy” attracting potential sexual predators. The “Sound Check at Cherry Lane” installments can be seen on A24’s YouTube channel. Past such performances were provided by artists including Tame Impala and Blood Orange. Merger 19 hours ago Kevin MacLellan, Paramount’s Head of Global Content Distribution and International, Is Leaving Skydance Post-Merger 23 hours ago See All Courtesy of Netflix Netflix is planning a major round of layoffs coming as soon as next week that would cut about 5% of its headcount, according to a new report. The streaming giant plans a significant restructuring that “will impact” about 5% of staffers and “could be announced as early as next week,” according to a report by Puck News, citing anonymous sources. A Netflix spokesperson declined to comment. It’s not clear which departments would be most heavily affected by the reported cuts. Popular on Variety Related Stories ‘Bowie80’ to Celebrate David Bowie’s 80th Birthday With Events, Exhibits, Releases and More Throughout 2027 A Rare David Bowie Self-Portrait — Featuring His Handprints — Is Going on Auction at Sotheby's As of the end of 2025, Netflix said it had about 16,000 full-time employees, which means a 5% reduction in force would eliminate around 800 jobs. Roughly 68% of its workers, about 10,900, were located in the U.S. and Canada as of December. The last major Netflix layoffs came in 2022, when it axed about 450 staffers following the streamer’s net decline of 200,000 subscribers in the first quarter of that year, its first such drop in more than a decade. The company has made additional smaller cutbacks since then, including letting go several dozen members of its global product team earlier in 2026. Ted Sarandos, Netflix’s co-CEO, at last month’s Bloomberg Screentime conference in L.A., said the company is growing — noting that in Q2, it posted double-digit revenue gains in every geographical region — but that “We want to keep growing it faster.” “Yes, overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” Sarandos said, addressing the slowdown in Netflix user engagement (which was up 2% year-over-year in the first half in 2026). He added that the streamer is “also doing things that create a lot of headwind to that number. Meaning, when we do live programming on Netflix, which is a relatively new thing, we spend about 5% of our content budget on live events. They generate about 1% of our watching.” For the second quarter, Netflix posted earnings in line with Wall Street forecasts but issued Q3 revenue guidance below analyst expectations, driving the stock price down. Netflix is scheduled to report third quarter 2026 earnings on Tuesday, Oct. 20, after market close.
