articles.title: HBO Max And Paramount+ Will Eventually Combine After “Short-Term” Bundling Phase, David Ellison…
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Walmart-Owned Vizio Sets Original Film Starring Rachel Bilson And Scott Foley, Adds Film & TV Titles In Big Expansion HBO Max And Paramount+ Will Eventually Combine After “Short-Term” Bundling Phase, David Ellison Says Skydance Chief David Ellison Asks Merger Opponents To “Give Us Time” To “Rebuild Trust” View All October 6, 2026 6:01pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison sees HBO Max and Paramount+ combining into a single service over time after a “short-term” phase as separate-but-bundled services. “Long-term, the plan is basically to bring them together,” Ellison said at a press event held on the Paramount lot to mark the closing of the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. “It’ll take a period of time to do that. So, I think in the immediate [term], you will see them operated separately, with things like bundling or things that you’ll be able to see accelerated in the relatively short term. I can’t be specific about that yet today.” Related Stories News Skydance Co-Boss Ynon Kreiz On When ‘Barbie 2’ Will Be A Go: “Too Early To Talk About That”. However, There’s Hope Executives Skydance Co-CEOs Insist Its Massive Debt Is Manageable And Won’t Shortchange Production Already, the company has managed to bring together the tech stacks of Paramount+, BET+ and Pluto TV, a shift that subscribers and viewers do not notice. Ellison credited “the way AI technology and other things have progressed” for providing a boost to that process. He stopped short of saying outright that those advancements could simplify the cumbersome process of uniting streaming services into a single product. And he also did not address the pricing or strategy for consumer adoption and retention of a single service with multiple branded tiers, a puzzle that general-entertainment services have to solve as they gain scale. Watch on Deadline Ellison said the centralization of tech stacks after the merger close will happen “as quickly as possible,” noting that the project was completed “in record time” after Skydance took over Paramount in August 2025. Sources tell Deadline the consolidation of tech stacks is expected to be complete within a year. Ellison’s projection, which came a few hours after the close of the Skydance merger, seemed to point in a different strategic direction than recent comments by Casey Bloys, head of HBO and HBO Max content. Bloys hinted that bundling would be the focus given the distinct subscriber bases of the two services, which combined have more than 200 million global subscribers. A slide deck released by Skydance earlier this week included images of both streamers, indicating at least they would both continue independently, at least for now. Public statements by Ellison and others have previously suggested that combining the services into one super-app was always the ambition, though getting from today’s setup to a fully integrated future will require a lot of work. Across the streaming landscape, a number of players have found it complex and expensive to meld two services into one. Disney has been chipping away at a long-term positioning of Disney+ as its mother ship, with Hulu programming migrating there behind a home-screen tile. Sometimes, viewer feedback can cause a rethink, as was the case when WarnerMedia merged with Discovery Communications in 2022. Initially, executives pursued a plan to merge unscripted and lifestyle service Discovery+ with HBO Max under the new umbrella brand Max. Warner Bros. Discovery stepped back from that scheme, citing demand for the cheaper (and profitable) Discovery+ as a stand-alone. They also wound up reversing the Max rebrand after two years of viewer and partner confusion and resistance. articles.title: George Cheeks Teases Skydance TV Strategy In Memo To Staff, Exalts CBS, Sports & News
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Peter White Peter White Executive Editor, Television @peterzwhite More Stories By Peter Cable Might Be Declining, But Skydance Sees Value In The Content From Its Core Brands Such as MTV & Food Network George Cheeks Teases Skydance TV Strategy In Memo To Staff, Exalts CBS, Sports & News ‘East Of Eden’ Tops Netflix Charts With Soft Opening View All October 6, 2026 7:34pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc George Cheeks Getty George Cheeks , who has a shiny new role in the Skydance corporation, called the first day of the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery the “start of a new chapter”. Related Stories Executives David Ellison, Ynon Kreiz Praise Staff, Lay Out Priorities For New Skydance: “Getting Here Has Been Quite A Journey” Executives Skydance Motion Picture Group Co-Chairs Josh Greenstein & Dana Goldberg Say In Day 1 Memo That Film Divisions Will Operate Independently In a memo to staff, Cheeks, who is now Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer, Skydance TV, teased the strategy of the new division that now includes CBS, Warner Bros. Television Studios, CBS Studios and Paramount Television Studios, CBS News, CBS Sports, TNT Sports and Warner Bros. Discovery Sports. “By bringing together Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, we’ve assembled a remarkable collection of television brands, networks and studios, backed by some of the most talented teams in the industry,” he wrote. Cheeks did not particularly go into detail on the new structure and his direct reports in the note, but Deadline revealed a few days ago that Channing Dungey, who was Chairman and CEO, Warner Bros Television Group and US Networks, will now also oversee the Paramount cable networks such as MTV, Comedy Central, Nickelodeon and BET as well as VH1, Paramount Network, TV Land, CMT, Pop TV and Logo TV. Watch on Deadline The former NBCUniversal exec, who is also in charge of CBS Studios, run by David Stapf, and Skydance TV, run by Matt Thunell, called the Skydance Television group an “unmatched mix of networks, studios, platforms and programming genres.” He said that the TV studios, which will remain separate, for now, at least, will continue to “create franchises, premium originals and unscripted hits that entertain viewers of all ages and interests”. He also lauded CBS, which he said “remains a cornerstone”. He praised the sports operations, which will now be run by CBS Sports boss David Berson, with TNT Sports chief Luis Silberwasser exiting. Cheeks also called CBS News, run by editor-in-chief Bari Weiss, “one of the most important brands in journalism, delivering national and worldwide news across broadcast, streaming and digital”. The cable side now features more than 50 channels. “There are too many standout shows to name individually, but one thing is clear: the breadth and quality of programming across this group is unrivaled, spanning some of the most watched, most acclaimed and most award-winning in the industry,” he added. Cheeks admitted that staff is eager to hear more about the leadership, structure and strategy and said that more details will be shared soon. “This is a moment of transition. With that comes uncertainty. The stress of this is not lost on me. Expect to hear more on our structure and priorities in the weeks ahead,” he wrote. “The work ahead is significant, and so is the opportunity. I am energized by the possibilities. articles.title: Skydance To Make Paramount & Warner Bros Lots Specialized, Each Housing Film Or TV/Streaming
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Skydance CEOs Meet The Press On Day One Post-Merger With String Of Promises & Few Answers Skydance Co-CEO On Prospect Of TV Studios Merging: “We’re Not Looking To Reduce Output Production” Skydance To Make Paramount & Warner Bros Lots Specialized, Each Housing Film Or TV/Streaming View All October 6, 2026 8:37pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc Getty Images Television and streaming are primed for a major upgrade — getting a whole historic lot all to themselves. The settlement in the state AGs’ lawsuit requires Skydance , the combined company of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, to keep both the Paramount and Warner Bros. lots for at least the next five years. During a press event on the Paramount lot Tuesday, hours after the merger had closed , Skydance CEO David Ellison revealed that the two lots, each historically and currently housing both film and TV, would be organized differently. Related Stories Executives Skydance CEOs Meet The Press On Day One Post-Merger With String Of Promises & Few Answers News Skydance Co-CEO On Prospect Of TV Studios Merging: “We’re Not Looking To Reduce Output Production” “We absolutely will keep both lots, and you’ll probably see us organize film on one, television/streaming on another, and we’ll go back and forth between the two, as well as to the East Coast when required, as well as our Santa Monica offices for animation,” he said of himself and Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz. Watch on Deadline Ellison would not elaborate further but based on the sizes alone — Warner Bros in Burbank being significantly larger than the Hollywood-based Paramount — film would likely be based on the Paramount lot and television and streaming on the Warner Bros lot, I hear. Such delineation would also jibe with Paramount — and its iconic arches — being steeped in movie history and a symbol of the golden era of cinema as the only major studio still located in Hollywood. The division would mean status quo for Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, co-chairs of the motion picture group, who are based at Paramount; and Channing Dungey, head of Warner Bros. Television Group and Skyance’s basic cable networks, who is at Warner Bros.

articles.title: Cable Might Be Declining, But Skydance Sees Value In The Content From Its Core Brands Such as MTV & Food Network
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Peter White Peter White Executive Editor, Television @peterzwhite More Stories By Peter Cable Might Be Declining, But Skydance Sees Value In The Content From Its Core Brands Such as MTV & Food Network George Cheeks Teases Skydance TV Strategy In Memo To Staff, Exalts CBS, Sports & News ‘East Of Eden’ Tops Netflix Charts With Soft Opening View All October 6, 2026 8:57pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc Deadliest Catch Discovery Channel As David Ellison brings together Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery under the Skydance umbrella, series such as Game of Thrones spinoff House of the Dragon, Harry Potter and Taylor Sheridan’s Landman have been in the spotlight. But another swathe of content is driving many of the channels that bring in billions of dollars across the two companies. Comedy Central ’s The Daily Show and South Park, MTV ’s Ridiculousness , Nickelodeon ’s SpongeBob SquarePants and BET’s Sistas will now be placed under the same corporate umbrella as shows such as Discovery Channel ’s Deadliest Catch , TLC ’s 90 Day Fiancé , HGTV ’s The Flip Off, TBS’s Impractical Jokers and Investigation Discovery’s slate of true-crime titles like Ruby & Jodi: A Cult of Sin and Influence. Related Stories Executives Channing Dungey Poised For Expanded Post-Merger Role Overseeing Paramount & WBD Cable Networks – The Dish Executives George Cheeks Teases Skydance TV Strategy In Memo To Staff, Exalts CBS, Sports & News The problem is that while cable is still a high-margin business that throws off a lot of cash, it is declining. Watch on Deadline To paraphrase a former U.S. President, it’s about the content, stupid. At Skydance’s first press briefing following the closing of the deal, Skydance Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz was asked about its cable TV business. “There are many brands within our umbrella, and, ultimately, we’re looking to achieve economic scale, and be productive. We run a business that makes great content that can compete in the marketplace, and ultimately, it’s about investing in content,” he said. The former Endemol and Mattel chief believes that what makes Skydance stand apart is its IP. “The investment thesis is about increasing output and establishing the company as a leading content engine. When you do that, you can then drive growth in your [direct-to-consumer] business. You can continue to optimize linear channels around the world, which is a large business,” he added. Establishing the content engine from the cable side will be a job for George Cheeks , Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer, Skydance TV, and his new report Channing Dungey, who was Chairman and CEO, Warner Bros Television Group and US Networks, but will now also oversee the Paramount cable networks such as MTV, Comedy Central, Nickelodeon and BET as well as VH1, Paramount Network, TV Land, CMT, Pop TV and Logo TV. There are obvious priorities: MTV, Comedy Central, Nickelodeon and BET on the Paramount side and channels such as Discovery Channel, TLC, HGTV and Food Network on the WBD side, which also includes, Adult Swim, Cooking Channel, TNT and TruTV. Some of the brands are already focused on becoming a content engine for a digital world. Jason Sarlanis, President, TBS, TNT, truTV, ID & HLN, Linear & Streaming at Warner Bros. Discovery, told Deadline earlier this spring that Investigation Discovery has become more than just a cable network. “We really have transformed that network into being a content engine for streaming, and so getting those massive documentary ‘docbuster’ events to break through, both on the streaming platform, but using the network as a barker to bring that voracious audience to this new platform has been our strategy.” Paramount has already turned some of its linear franchises into digital properties such as Drunk History, which ran for six seasons on Comedy Central through 2019, which has returned as a series of digital shorts on YouTube . Nickelodeon has also greenlit a number of YouTube originals such as Kid Cowboy and Star Trek Scouts. The idea is that these serve as an incubator for ideas that can then be turned into franchises for its streaming services, which can then be fed back into the linear landscape. MTV seems ripe for this level of experimentation. When Quibi launched in 2020 it ordered a number of reboots of classic MTV series such as Punk’d and Singled Out, so it’s not a stretch to see those types of shows, or other iconic franchises such as TRL and Yo MTV Raps! , go digital. In success, they could be turned into streaming shows that have a second window on the cable networks. It’s not too dissimilar from the MTV Video Music Awards airing on CBS; the show, which featured awards given to the likes of Taylor Swift and Nirvana, hit an 11-year high with 8.43M viewers across CBS and MTV, but only just over 800,000 of those viewers watched on the cable network. Cheeks and Dungey will now be working out what that looks likes for WBD franchises. There is plenty of programming to plunder from Discovery Channel’s Mythbusters , which ran for 17 seasons before ending in 2016, to Ina Garten’s long-running Food Network’s hit Barefoot Contessa , Duff Goldman’s Ace of Cakes, Adam Richman’s Man V. Food and, TLC’s A Baby Story. After Skydance acquired Paramount, Cheeks, who was then Paramount’s Chair of TV Media division, admitted cable was a “super challenging business”. “But, the cable group, the content group, has created these incredibly iconic franchises, and we’re all seeing the pay cable business shifting over to streaming. So, there’ll be a lot of conversations about what iconic franchises we want to continue, shift maybe to streaming,” he said in August 2025. It is a similar message spread by former WBD cable chief Kathleen Finch, who retired at the end of 2024, handing the reins to Dungey. She warned that cable executives should “stop using the word cable” in the future and focus on content creation. “That’s going away at some point, so what we all are is creatives. You make content, then you put it on these different places and the audience chooses to watch it whichever place they happen to prefer,” she said before leaving. Where this leaves the combined company’s cable executives is now one of the big questions; Paramount unveiled its leadership team to run its cable networks in November with Laurel Weir overseeing programming for MTV, Comedy Central and Nickelodeon. Howard Lee has been Chief Creative Officer of U.S. Networks since the end of 2024 as well as continuing to oversee TLC and Discovery Channel, while Sarlanis has been running ID since June 2021 and TNT, TBS, TruTV and HLN since December 2022. Magnolia is run by Allison Page and Betsy Ayala is Head of Content, Food. The cable networks also played a major role in the delay of the deal; California Attorney General Rob Bonta and other AGs filed a lawsuit arguing that the merger would create too much concentration among these channels when it comes to negotiating carriage deals. In fact, the settlement that Bonta and others struck with Skydance meant that the merged company must conduct negotiations for Paramount basic cable channels independently from negotiations for Warner Bros. basic cable channels to “preserve the existing competitive dynamic between the companies”, which the AG would “help to keep prices down for consumers”. If they break this rule, or in fact, break other rules such as the number of theatrical movies it releases per year, it is these cable assets, notably, BET, VH1, Comedy Central, Smithsonian, Destination America, and the Science Channel, that will be in the crosshairs with Skydance forced to sell them. articles.title: Skydance Co-CEO On Prospect Of TV Studios Merging: “We’re Not Looking To Reduce Output Production”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Skydance CEOs Meet The Press On Day One Post-Merger With String Of Promises & Few Answers Skydance Co-CEO On Prospect Of TV Studios Merging: “We’re Not Looking To Reduce Output Production” Skydance To Make Paramount & Warner Bros Lots Specialized, Each Housing Film Or TV/Streaming View All October 6, 2026 10:24pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Channing Dungey, David Stapf, and Matt Thunell Sundance/Courtesy Paramount’s $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery has come without any consolidation of the two companies’ film and TV studios — at least for now. On the TV side, that involves Warner Bros. Television Group, run by Channing Dungey (who also is shepherding the combined basic cable portfolio), CBS Studios , headed by David Stapf, and Paramount TV Studios, led by Matt Thunell, remaining standalone entities within the combined Skydance company, all overseen by George Cheeks, Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer, Skydance TV. Related Stories Executives Skydance CEOs Meet The Press On Day One Post-Merger With String Of Promises & Few Answers News Skydance To Make Paramount & Warner Bros Lots Specialized, Each Housing Film Or TV/Streaming At a press conference held on the Paramount lot Tuesday afternoon, hours after the transaction closed, Skydance CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz were asked how long the three entities will stay separate and if consolidating backend operations is on the table. “When it comes to the TV studios, it’s about scale,” Kreiz said. “We’re not looking to reduce output production. It’s about efficient operation, and we have plans how to achieve that while still maintaining creative labels, creative parts to ensure that creativity still continues to flow, and we attract the best creators.” Watch on Deadline Making operations efficient is important as Ellison and his team at Paramount had promised Wall Street $6 billion in synergy savings post-merger. Later in the press conference, Kreiz elaborated on his comments when he and Ellison were asked again whether departments from the three TV studios may get consolidated en route to a potential full merger and if the studios would compete for talent and projects in the meanwhile. “You need to to keep certain creative parts independent and have them run and operate semi-autonomously,” Kreiz said, adding, “In the sense that the company is still one platform, we would coordinate and align and not compete directly.” Conversations with individual TV studio heads also indicate that they don’t foresee competing for talent or projects and having a collaborative environment where they share information on buyers. “There would still be an element of different teams trying put together great projects and create something that stands out in a crowded market,” Kreiz said. “You cannot aggregate that under one theme in terms of the creative process.” For comparison, it took Disney six years after the acquisition of Fox assets to fully merge the company’s three TV studios — 20th Television, ABC Signature and Touchstone Television — which was done in two stages. articles.title: ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Finale Recap: The Last Match Of The Season & A Shareholders’ Showdown
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi Everything We Know About Prime Video’s ‘Things We Never Got Over’ Adaptation So Far Here Are All The Songs In The ‘Verity’ Film Adaptation: From FKA Twigs To Kali Uchis All The Songs In ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 So Far View All October 6, 2026 11:10pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Abbie Hern, Brendan Hunt, Jason Sudeikis, Tanya Reynolds, Jude Mack and Aisling Sharkey in 'Ted Lasso' Apple TV SPOILER ALERT: This post spoils the Season 4 finale of Ted Lasso , titled “Being Alive.” Another finale episode of Ted Lasso has hit the net, bringing its fourth season, which branched out into the women’s team storyline, to a close. The episode kicks off with a funeral reception for AFC Richmond’s own Mae Green (Annette Badland), owner of the Crown & Anchor pub, at the very pub she helmed for years. The trio of lads who have been around since Season 1 of the soccer comedy, as well as the new trivia opponents who briefly provoked the Lady Greyhounds enough to get them landed in jail, are all at the pub, which is closed for a private event, to mourn Mae. Related Stories News All The Songs In ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 So Far News ‘Ted Lasso’ Pays Tribute To Anthony Head – Here’s Why It Happened In Episode 409 Ted ( Jason Sudeikis ), Michelle (Andrea Anders), Henry (Grant Feely) and Coach Beard ( Brendan Hunt ) are in attendance as well. Michelle questions Beard about his physical transformation, which has become noticeable throughout the season, from his husky-like blue eye contacts to his tan and gray hair, which brings up Mae’s favorite sheep, Doug, who had an ear tag like Beard’s dangly earrings. Watch on Deadline The Lady Greyhounds are there as well, and Niamh Harrigan (Aisling Sharkey) challenges her teammates to split the G, which an older gentleman points out is a tradition that actually started in Britain, not Ireland. He then proceeds to chug just the right amount of Guinness to achieve the feat with the specific beer. Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham) and Higgins (Jeremy Swift) toast to Mae before Higgins gets a call from HR. Keeley (Juno Temple), who we found out was pregnant in Episode 9, runs to her bathroom in a black dress to presumably hurl. Roy looks after her in his all-black suit. He, too, gets a call, but he declines to answer. It’s his ‘Prick Agent’ Patrick calling, which could mean something about his contract at Richmond ending or continuing. Roy voices his concern that, because Keeley is pregnant and they are bringing new life into the world, Mae’s soul had to leave it. This tradition of sharing uncomfortable truths at a funeral stems from Season 2, in which Rebecca’s father died. Weirdness struck at that funeral as well. Keeley points out that things keep changing, like her body, and more. Brett Goldstein as Roy Kent in ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 finale Patrick, Roy’s agent, calls once more, and Roy finally picks up to learn that he’s been offered the head coaching job at Chelsea. He then takes his turn running to the bathroom to puke in the toilet. Ted and Michelle check on Henry, who had grown close to Mae this season, and he wonders what will happen to the pub. As is the theme of the episode, Ted reaffirms that “big changes happen in bunches.” Henry then goes to play darts after sarcastically answering, “I know, I live in London now.” Alice Chilton ( Tanya Reynolds ) framed the team selfie with Mae on the bus. Beard’s ex Jane (Phoebe Walsh) shows up to the private event that has closed the Crown & Anchor in a red dress and hat, calling Mae Meg. One of her rings gets caught on Beard’s earring, and she rips it out of his ear. The Harrigan twins serenade the late Mae with “The Parting Glass,” even though Mae was not Irish. Higgins had something to tell Rebecca before that duet. Henry leaves the pub, and Ted goes to check on him. “I just wish that she could help me with my homework again,” Henry says through tears. Henry then asks Ted how his dad died. Nana (Becky Ann Baker) told Henry that his grandfather fell and hit his head on some stairs, which Ted says is true. Longtime viewers of the show know that that’s not what happened — Ted’s dad committed suicide. He and Beard unpack this later at the office. Here it might be noteworthy to mention that a new voice sang the show’s title theme for the season finale, written by Tom Howe and Mumford & Sons. Could the below be related? View this post on Instagram We meet Lizzie’s (Faye Marsay) co-parent Ben (Simon Lipkin), a rocker man who doesn’t always show up for the mother of his two sons. He says he will try to get the kids the following day, when Lizzie will be part of the Lady Greyhounds’ final match of the season, but he’s a flake. Back to that thing Higgins mentioned, he and Rebecca were summoned to a shareholders’ meeting, even though they don’t know who will show up, because it seems “Rupert” has bought out all the shares, meaning there are no real shareholders anymore. L-R: Tanya Reynolds, Jason Sudeikis and Brendan Hunt in ‘Ted Lasso’ Enter Keeley in some pink pajamas with a new video idea to sell out Nelson Road. It is the opposite of the black-and-white, very serious promo video from the beginning of the season. Keep your eyes peeled, because Nathan Shelley (Nick Mohammed) shows up in a blink and you’ll miss it moment, holding his baby daughter and watching the clip. His and Jade’s (Edyta Budnik) daughter’s name is Athena. Team captain Lizzie is missing in the locker room before the final match. Nate the Great then shows up to say hi to the coaches before their big day. Turns out he’s coaching the Polish national football team — with two other people. Roy interrupts this life update to summon the Diamond Dogs for advice about his predicament. This brings Ted, Beard, Higgins, and Nate to act silly in front of Alice, who takes Ted’s suggestion to act like a cat. Roy reveals Keeley’s pregnancy, and how he’s worried about being a good dad. The Diamond Dogs have some great nuggets of fatherly advice. Beard reveals that Jane faked a pregnancy for 11 months. Alice might drop the biggest piece of wisdom at all: “Don’t disappear when you feel inadequate.” Matthijs (Matteo van der Grijn), who we haven’t seen in a few episodes, calls Rebecca, apologizing that he can’t be there for the meeting. Higgins reveals the Milk sisters have sold their shares, and Zelda Southport (Tracey Ullman) gasps, doing a terrible job of hiding that she now owns those shares. Shannon is in the starting lineup of this final match. Ted gives a simple speech to the women, thanking them. He nods to Mae, who hopefully has good Wi-Fi at the pubs up in heaven. Nelson Road Stadium has been sold out for this last women’s match. Dani Rojas (Cristo Fernández), Isaac McAdoo (Kola Bokinni), Jan Mas (David Elsendoorn), Stephen Manas (Richard Montflaur), Thierry Zoreaux (Moe Jeudy-Lamour), Colin Hughes (Billy Harris), Moe Bumbercatch (Moe Hasim) and Sam Obisanya (Toheeb Jimoh) are in the audience with Roy, clapping for the ladies. Roy asks Sam if he ever questioned leaving Richmond for Man U, and Sam quotes The Wizard of Oz , citing Dorothy and saying that “Sometimes you have to leave to know where home truly is.” This saying ties in with the Wizard of Oz layers in Season 4’s first episode when Keeley, Rebecca and Higgins visit Ted in Kansas City. Turns out Sam was actually citing his Aunt Dorothy, but a story for another time. Keeley gets to watch the game until she yells at the ref. Just as Annette Badland teased to Deadline , Mae’s shares come in clutch from beyond the grave at the Bi-Annual Shareholders’ Meeting, only attended by the three lads from the pub. Zelda, in a black-and-white Cruella de Vil coat, admits that she bought all the shares, making her owner of AFC Richmond with a controlling interest of over 50% of the shares. Her goal all along was to own a men’s Premier League team to make men listen to her. Ted tells Henry the truth about his grandfather’s death. Back at the Shareholders’ meeting, Rebecca and Higgins fake scream at each other and reveal that the Milk sisters didn’t actually sell their shares to Zelda after all. Turns out, Hugo Riddles (Alex Blake) —the HR who called Higgins — teamed up with Rebecca and Higgins, but the math isn’t mathing because now it is 49%-49%. Elaine Pinter (Helen Schlesinger) of Pinter & Sons zooms in to speak on behalf of former client Mae Green to tell Mr. Blumenthal, Mr. La Fleur and Mr. Primrose (the three pub lads) that they’ve become owners and proprietors of the Crown & Anchor pub. Ms. Green’s 2% ownership stake in AFC Richmond goes to Rebecca, as she declared in her will. This puts Rebecca back at 51%. Roy approaches Rebecca to tell her about his decision to go to Chelsea. She does not take it well at first, mocking him and his eyebrows. Roy then mocks her right back. They share a very sweet hug, and she earns her nickname from Roy and Keeley’s future child, Auntie Supreme. Ted asks Rebecca if he can chat with her about the newly opened manager position. Cut to Beard, who is reading how Emma Stone is starring in Jane’s play at the West End, with Richard Schiff starring as the Bearded Coach. Matthijs shows up, points out Beard’s lack of blue contacts, and makes fun of the guinea pig left behind on his head. Rebecca says “Fuck it, marry me” to Matthijs after she’s had a revelation while munching on one of Ted’s biscuits. He says yes! Juno Temple as Keeley Jones in ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Annette Badland’s voice narrates the end of the episode, with Isaac giving Beard a precious haircut, handed an electric razor by Will the Kitman (Charlie Hiscock). Roy packs up his office, and he finds an envelope with his name on it, containing a note from Ted that says he’s going to be a great dad. Ted gives him an army man like Henry gave Ted when Ted first moved across the pond. Keeley comes to walk him out of his office wearing ruby red heels. Alice starts a sticky note countdown of 112 days until the first game of the next season for the Lady Greyhounds. Turns out she’s the one who’s been lowering Ted’s chair this whole time. Ted gives her a going-away present, which seems to be a whistle in a red box, meaning she has been promoted to Head Coach of the Lady Greyhounds. Beard shows up, rocking a buzz cut, wondering if he missed it. A plaque outside their office declares Alice Chilton Manager of the AFC Richmond Women’s team. Willis Beard and Ted Lasso are Assistant Managers. articles.title: Zhang Yimou Teases ‘Three-Body Problem’ At BIFF Opening; Jury Talks ‘The Assassin(s)’ Controversy & Competition Impact
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Michelle Yeoh Talks ‘Blade Runner 2099’ & Return To Asian Cinema – Busan Zhang Yimou Teases ‘Three-Body Problem’ At BIFF Opening; Jury Talks ‘The Assassin(s)’ Controversy & Competition Impact Busan Film Festival Director Jung Hanseok Talks Oscars Pathway, New Competition Section & Korean Cinema Recovery View All October 6, 2026 11:29pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Zhang Yimou, Bi Gan, July Jung, Samal Yeslyamova, Kei Ishikawa, Tran Thi Bich Ngoc, Moon Choi Deadline Chinese filmmaker Zhang Yimou , who is serving as president of Busan International Film Festival’s competition jury, offered some details of his upcoming adaptation of sci-fi epic The Three-Body Problem at the festival’s opening ceremony on Tuesday night. First announced at Shanghai film festival in 2024, there hasn’t been much news about the project recently, but Zhang explained that it’s moving steadily ahead: “ The Three-Body Problem is a great work of science fiction, but it’s hard to photograph, so we spent several years polishing the script,” he said on stage at Busan Cinema Center. Related Stories News Michelle Yeoh Talks 'Blade Runner 2099' & Return To Asian Cinema - Busan News Busan Film Festival Director Jung Hanseok Talks Oscars Pathway, New Competition Section & Korean Cinema Recovery He added that his team has collected around 400,000 online comments from fans of the novel about their hopes for the film: “In this era of AI, with its democratization of images, audience expectation is extremely high so we hope to live up their expectations and make a good movie.” Watch on Deadline One of China’s most acclaimed works of science fiction, Liu Cixin’s The Three-Body Problem is the first book in a trilogy that begins with a scientist who discovers that an alien civilization is planning to take over Earth as their own planet is too unstable. It has already been adapted by Netflix as an English-language series and has had two Chinese-language adaptations – a live-action series produced by Tencent and an animated series from Bilibili. The property has had a colourful history with one Chinese-language feature adaptation left unfinished and an executive involved in handling the rights murdered by a colleague in 2020. Zhang’s version is being produced by Beijing Enlight Media, the studio behind blockbuster animation Nezha 2 , and is understood to involve a significant AI component. One of China’s most acclaimed directors, with a career stretching back to the Fifth Generation, Zhang continues to make hit films in China today, most recently with spy thriller Scare Out over Lunar New Year. The day after the BIFF opening, Zhang gave a typically diplomatic answer at the jury press conference when asked about the controversy that has erupted in Korea over Hur Jin-ho’s political thriller The Assassin(s) . The film, which premiered at Toronto International Film Festival, revolves around the attempted assassination of South Korean President Park Chung-hee in 1974, which resulted in the death of the First Lady. Right-wing groups have attacked the film for lack of historical accuracy, with the issue even being debated in Korea’s National Assembly, forcing the film to cancel its planned promotional activities at BIFF due to security risks. When asked about the relationship between historical accuracy and freedom of speech, Zhang replied: “Creation is creation and sometimes what we create is not historical fact. We may ask ourselves, should this be based on our lives? But often we need to go beyond our lives to make a good film.” He continued: “I haven’t seen the film in question, but we have to respect the creators – history is distant from us, but we can use it to tell stories to audiences living in current times, so in some ways it’s a form of art. What the audience feels or thinks after watching the film is up to them – everyone has different opinions – and this is the charm or beauty of the film.” Korean filmmaker and jury member July Jung ( Dora ) added: “I feel discouraged by this situation as a filmmaker. Due to the way this film depicts certain people, it means that some people could be damaged or hurt by his film. On the other hand, as filmmakers we need to accept that some people will criticize our work and take full responsibility for the worlds we create.” The BIFF jury also debated the impact of the festival’s competition section, now in its second year, which this year has a selection of 13 films, with the jury handing out six prizes. Under new Academy rules, the winner of the festival’s Best Film Award will automatically qualify for submission to the Best International Feature category of the Oscars. Chinese director Bi Gan ( Resurrection ) said: “Busan was already a strong festival without the competition, but it’s now a core component of the festival for filmmakers in China, Japan and Korea because it creates a new trend. It’s not just about selecting prize winners, but it gives people more reason to discuss the selected films. It’s a good way to open the discourse between people.” Vietnamese producer Tran Thi Bich Ngoc ( Skin Of Youth ) said: “Busan has always been a crucial place to discover new talent and New Currents [previously the main competition section at BIFF] did a great job in recognizing emerging directors who needed a platform for us to discover their voices. But Asian cinema is growing fast in terms of quality and the number of great films coming from the region. So the festival’s new competition section matches that growth and demand.” BIFF’s seven-person jury also includes Korean actress Moon Choi, who produced and acted in Bedford Park , which is screening at the festival this year; Japanese director Kei Ishikawa ( A Pale View Of Hills ); and Kazakh actress Samal Yeslyamova ( Ayka ). The jury will be handing out their awards at the closing ceremony on October 15. articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake ‘Doctor Who’ Bids Revealed: Jed Mercurio Leads Pitch To Regenerate BBC Series, As STV Studios Plans To Transport TARDIS To Scotland Jeffrey Archer Dies: Bestselling ‘Kane & Abel’ Author & Politician Was 86 BBC Names Ex-‘Panorama’ Editor Rachel Jupp As Director Of News View All September 17, 2026 9:35am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Doctor Who' BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/James Pardon The BBC has fired the starting gun on the regeneration of Doctor Who . The British broadcaster on Thursday launched a competitive tender for Season 16, in which producers will pitch in a bake-off-style process to refresh the iconic sci-fi series. The tender process follows the BBC announcing a major creative rethink of Doctor Who in June after showrunner Russell T Davies and producer Bad Wolf abandoned ship, and Disney’s co-production deal expired. Ncuti Gatwa also will not return as the Time Lord. Related Stories News ‘Doctor Who’ On Prime Video? Amazon Execs Say They “Welcome Any Conversation Around IP” News Billie Piper Says ‘Doctor Who’ Fans Need To “Chill Out” After Sci-Fi Show’s “Rough Time” In a document inviting submissions ( see it here ), the BBC said producers should detail a vision for Doctor Who that can return to screens in 2028-29 — as predicted by Deadline — and ensures the series remains “relevant, surprising, brave and inspiring for both long-standing fans and new audiences.” Watch on Deadline

articles.title: ‘Doctor Who’ Bids Revealed: Jed Mercurio Leads Pitch To Regenerate BBC Series, As STV Studios Plans To Transport TARDIS To Scotland
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter , Max Goldbart October 7, 2026 12:12am Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Tennant in 'Doctor Who' BBC Studios EXCLUSIVE : Could Jed Mercurio be about to take control of the TARDIS? Deadline can reveal that the Line of Duty showrunner is spearheading a bid to produce Doctor Who after the BBC launched a competitive tender , a bake-off-style process in which producers have put forward plans to regenerate the iconic sci-fi series. We are told Hat Trick Mercurio (HTM), the production company Mercurio runs with Hat Trick founder Jimmy Mulville, has submitted a proposal with Mercurio attached as an executive producer. Mercurio is a sci-fi fan and created BBC series Invasion: Earth in the 1990s. He has since become one of the nation’s pre-eminent TV scribes, with credits including Bodyguard and Cardiac Arrest. HTM declined comment. Related Stories News Katherine Parkinson, Omari Douglas & Toby Stephens Join BBC & BritBox's Poirot Series News Martin Freeman & Jim Broadbent Set For Dickensian Christmas Ghost Story 'The Bride's Chamber' At The BBC HTM is one of several production outfits bidding for Doctor Who. Line of Duty producer World Productions has submitted separate plans to reimagine the Time Lord after CEO Simon Heath recently mooted his interest in the Doctor Who tender. Sources said that World is effectively spearheading ITV Studios’ efforts to land the contract. World Productions declined comment. Watch on Deadline Or could the TARDIS soon be spinning its way to Scotland? Deadline is told STV Studios , the production group behind Blue Lights and Criminal Record , has made an audacious bid to move the show north of the English border for Season 17. Deadline understands that the company has teamed up with Screen Scotland to table the proposal. STV Studios declined comment. We previously revealed that two different BBC Studios labels will likely table bids to make Doctor Who , with scripted boss Jamie Hall animatedly saying the entire BBC group should “reap the rewards” of the iconic sci-fi series. He told Deadline last week “there is an opportunity to get back to what the core offering was” during the era of Matt Smith and David Tennant. BBC Studios runs an in-house drama teams along with majority-owning big beasts of the UK production world like Baby Reindeer maker Clerkenwell Films, Sherwood producer House Productions and Lookout Point. The deadline for Doctor Who submissions was last Friday, meaning the BBC is now considering competing visions for the show, which requires a dramatic refresh after showrunner Russell T Davies and producer Bad Wolf abandoned ship. Peter Capaldi stars in ‘Doctor Who’ BBC A Scotland bid is intriguing. The BBC has stipulated tha t Doctor Who must be made outside of London after Wales served as the show’s home for many years. The BBC came in for some criticism last year for axing long-running Scottish soap River City, although it is worth noting that at the time it said it would spend £100M ($132.3M) on drama in the nation over the next three years. STV Studios also has a connection to the Whoniverse: Peter Capaldi, who played the Time Lord for three years, stars in Criminal Record , the Apple TV series produced by his wife, Elaine Collins, who runs STV-backed Tod Productions. Deadline’s list of bidders is by no means exhaustive and other interested parties may yet emerge. There is speculation, for example, of a second Scottish bid with a well-known native actor thought to be interested in picking up the Sonic Screwdriver. The previous Doctor, Ncuti Gatwa, was brought up in Scotland. Deadline has established that several top producers have declined to throw their hat into the ring, with many citing concerns about the lack of rights and the production contract sucking creative energy away from other projects. Among those not bidding are A24 UK, Playground, Mammoth Screen, New Pictures, Big Talk Studios, Expectation and Quay Street. “Anyone with a pulse knows it will go to BBC Studios,” was the view of one producer. Another seasoned production chief added: “If Jane Tranter and Russell T Davies can’t make sense of that show, then who can and who wants to? It feels like a thankless task.” In a document inviting submissions ( see it here ), the BBC said producers should detail a vision for Doctor Who that can return to screens in 2028-29 — as predicted by Deadline — and ensures the series remains “relevant, surprising, brave and inspiring for both long-standing fans and new audiences.” Interviews with bidders will take place in January, with the BBC awarding a contract in March. The BBC was not prescriptive about budgets but invited producers to propose “third-party investment.” This has raised eyebrows among some producers, who would have liked more detail on the BBC’s funding expectations for the series. The BBC declined to comment. articles.title: Abundantia Entertainment To Turn AI Creative Arm AiOn Into Standalone Studio: “Truly A Confluence Of Technology And Art”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse ‘The Empress’: Trailer For Season 3 Finds Sisi Stuck Between Royal Duties & Her Heart’s Desires Abundantia Entertainment To Turn AI Creative Arm AiOn Into Standalone Studio: “Truly A Confluence Of Technology And Art” Natasha Ofili Signs With Established Artists Management View All October 7, 2026 1:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Subedaar', 'Maa Behen' and 'Daldal'' Vikram Malhotra (inset) Netflix/Prime Video/Abundandia Entertainment EXCLUSIVE: This time last year, India ‘s Abundantia Entertainment launched an AI production division named Abundantia AiOn . Today, we can reveal that is morphing into a fully standalone native AI studio that will seek harness in an influx of ideas from non-traditional sources. “AiOn will develop its own stories, create its own content, produce fully generated as well as hybrid work, and manage the entire ecosystem, just as Abundantia does as a standalone studio,” Vikram Malhotra , Abundantia’s founder and CEO told Deadline during an exclusive interview. Malhotra will remain in charge of AiOn for the time being. “For the moment, it will sit within Abundantia, but we are building it in a way that gives it its own identity and scope,” he said. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Raj Shamani, Indian Content Creator & Host Of 'Figuring Out' Pod, Signs With WME News 'Kaali Kheti', Horror Starring Jackie Shroff, Sharad Kelkar and Neha Sargam, Sets Indian Release Date “Workflows have become hybrid, and production and creative thinking are becoming hybrid. The capability needed to run AI at studio level will not be found solely within the conventional media and entertainment system. It is truly a confluence of technology and art.” Malhotra said the move had been taken after receiving “three times as many pitches from people who have never written, made films or belonged to the conventional filmmaking ecosystem as I have in the past” over the last six months. He cited the rise of directors such as Obsession ‘s Curry Barker and Backrooms ‘ Kane Parsons as evidence of a “democratization” of ideas that would be powered by AI studios in the future. “AiOn defines itself as human-first and AI-empowered, and I’m seeing that happen in front of my eyes in real time,” he added. Earlier in the year, Abundantia announced another AI studio initiative, teaming with AI video tech company InVideo to launch a film studio, which will develop a slate of five films over the next few years. That company is also teaming with Abundantia aiOn. Malhotra, one of India’s most experienced execs and producers, launched Abundantia back in 2013 after exiting a role as COO of Viacom18 Motion Pictures and a shorter spell leading Balaji Motion Pictures. The company has since made films such as Baby , Airlift , T oilet – Ek Prem Katha , Shakuntala Devi , Sherni , and Chhorii and Chhorii 2 . On the series from, it produced Prime Video’s Breathe . This year has seen the launch of Netflix films Maa Behen and a movie and series for Prime Video, Subedaar and Daldal , respectively. The former is an action drama directed by Suresh Triveni and fronted by Anil Kapoor; and the latter an original drama series starring Bhumi Pednekar. Maa Behen , a Hindi-language black comedy starring Madhuri Dixit and Triptii Dimri among others, was well received on Netflix. It became the #1 trending film on Netflix India in the week of its release in June and rose to #2 in global non-English films. Subedaar , meanwhile, was notable for being Anil Kapoor’s first action movie since S. Shankar’s Nayak: A Real Hero , which was released in 2001. Malhotra addressed how he tempted the actor back to the genre (clue: It wasn’t a hard sell) and gave his assessment of the Indian production as we look ahead to 2027 and beyond. DEADLINE: There’s a lot of interesting work going on at Abundantia right now. How has the year been so far? Vikram Malhotra: It’s been an exciting year. We completed 13 years on the 26th of this month, and in many ways this year has been the manifestation of the 12 years that came before it – and hopefully a sign of things to come. The last nine months have been exciting for us on all fronts. DEADLINE: What has happened that really punctuates that progress? Malhotra: When I started building Abundantia in 2013, the fundamental gap I had identified throughout my time in the business, including at Viacom18 and Balaji, was that the supply of high-quality, progressive content for a younger, more evolved audience wasn’t meeting demand. Abundantia was formed and built with studio economics in mind, rather than project economics. I was always focused on building an institution, rather than approaching the business on a project-by-project basis, which is often the short-sighted way demand or opportunity is evaluated in this market. If we use 2026 as a symbol of that approach, the year has included three releases: One film on Prime Video, one series on Prime Video and one film on Netflix. We also have theatrical work lined up, more projects with those two streamers and a number of things in development. The founding philosophy remains the same: Put the customer at the heart of the business, let creativity drive the velocity of the business and continue disrupting the kinds of stories you tell. Whittock: One of the major strategic moves you have made is into AI, including the deal with InVideo in February and your AI studio. There is a lot of discussion around AI, and companies are still working out what it means for them, but Abundantia seems to have moved beyond the theoretical stage. How would you describe the strategy? Malhotra: AI is a strategic priority for us. It is not simply another means of reducing costs and saving time. Throughout our journey, we have factored in technological shifts. COVID taught us how to work remotely, and we naturally began weaving that into our production workflow. When streaming arrived in India, it completely changed how hundreds of millions of Indian consumers experienced content. We were the first company from the film ecosystem to move into streaming. I sense an even bigger opportunity with AI. Abundantia has been working on it in our own way for the past two years. As with streaming, the idea was to first understand what we were dealing with, build capability and build for the long term. DEADLINE: Will AI end up as a positive thing for the industry, then? Malhotra: I look at AI as an amplifier of imagination and an accelerator of growth. More importantly, I see it addressing a fundamental aspect of the content business: Risk. This business has risk built into it because risk comes from the consumer side. It is an intangible reason why people spend time and money on what we offer. Any attempt to eliminate that risk would be futile. So we asked ourselves: Can AI help reduce the cost of going wrong? Beyond the logistical benefits – cost, time and scale – can it improve our ability to understand how and where we go wrong? If we do go wrong, can we learn quickly from those mistakes and build that learning into a replicable model? That is fundamentally how AI is built into Abundantia’s strategy.” We have a dedicated creative division called AiOn, under which we have been doing all our AI work. I’m happy to tell you this today that in 2027 we are launching AiOn as a fully fledged, fully native AI studio. AiOn will develop its own stories, create its own content, produce fully generated as well as hybrid work, and manage the entire ecosystem, just as Abundantia does as a standalone studio. DEADLINE: Will it remain within Abundantia? Malhotra: For the moment, it will sit within Abundantia, but we are building it in a way that gives it its own identity and scope. Workflows have become hybrid, and production and creative thinking are becoming hybrid. The capability needed to run AI at studio level will not be found solely within the conventional media and entertainment system. It is truly a confluence of technology and art. Technology has already disrupted the conventional media and entertainment model in two important ways. First, through funding from technology-native companies; and second, through disruption in distribution, whether via streaming or other non-conventional forms that are now mainstream. This is technology creating a new wave of creatives. AiOn is intended to harness that at a dedicated level as a native AI studio. DEADLINE: Who will lead AiOn? Malhotra: In the immediate term, it will remain under Abundantia’s leadership, with me leading AiOn as well. To clarify, we will continue to call it AiOn – we are not calling it AiOn Studios. I’m using that description for ease. We will draw on Abundantia’s learning and capability across the ecosystem, from creative to screen and everything in between. We will also draw on the networks, knowledge and access we have built, while rapidly creating a similar ecosystem under AiOn. The strategy is based on the fact that we will need new skill sets. The person telling the story will still be human, but that person’s background may be very different from what we have conventionally seen. DEADLINE: What prompted you to make this move? Malhotra: One statistic excites me most. In the last six months, on average, I have received three times as many story pitches from people who have never written, made films or belonged to the conventional filmmaking ecosystem as I have in the past. That is the impact of AI-driven democratization on our business. People can bounce ideas around, refine pitches, create an audiovisual package around the story they want to tell and add music. AiOn defines itself as human-first and AI-empowered, and I’m seeing that happen in front of my eyes in real time. DEADLINE: You have spoken about two films coming out of the studio – Chiranjeevi Hanuman and Jai Santoshi Mata: Sukh Sampatti Daata . Where do those projects stand? Malhotra: Chiranjeevi Hanuman is completing readiness. Jai Santoshi Mata is a hybrid project and is set to go on the floors early next year. The work on world-building and on every aspect of AI generation is already under way. Beyond that, we have accelerated the slates we have been building. Our work with one of our long-standing partners, InVideo, is bearing fruit. Two films are under way, including one that is about to go on the floors, and three other scripts – with defined filmmakers, timelines and budgets – are already in development. My understanding of using AI to create films is that the only way to do it is to get on and do it. We have accumulated significant learning through the production process of Chiranjeevi Hanuman . We are building on that as we take Jai Santoshi Mata and two other films to the floors, as we find new filmmaking voices and as we learn through consumer research. When I say AiOn will operate like a studio, there is a reason I distinguish that from its current form as a creative division. AiOn will leverage AI across the value chain. DEADLINE: You have mentioned the increase in pitches from non-traditional sources. In Hollywood, YouTube creators and people from the wider creator economy are moving into film and television rapidly. Are you seeing the same change in India, and are you looking in those places? Malhotra: It is safe to say that the penetration of AI into daily life, especially among people under 35 in India, is virtually 100%. Anyone with a smartphone is experiencing AI at work. Anyone with a smart device is experiencing AI at work. That gives me confidence and optimism. I no longer have to sell the concept. A year or 18 months ago, I was talking about upskilling writers and directors and asking how people would be able to create. People have moved so aggressively along the learning curve that those challenges are falling by the wayside. Anyone with a story to tell now has the ability to get that story into tangible form. The democratization of distribution through YouTube, Instagram and WhatsApp means those stories can reach audiences. The gatekeepers who controlled which stories were told to the wider public are falling away. As a studio and producer, my ability to access disruptive, non-conventional voices is greater than ever. We are constantly scouting these platforms to see whether there is a distinctive voice, a concept or a story we would otherwise not encounter. It is easier said than done, because much of the time we have to go to those creators rather than simply wait for them to come to us. DEADLINE: So how do you harness all of this? Malhotra: The key issue is mindset. Before you build an AI team, workflow, company or film, you need an AI mindset. I’m constantly telling my team to think about timelines, opportunity and economics as they would in technology, while retaining blue-sky thinking in the way we tell stories. It is happening in real time. The number of pitches I receive from creators, especially those under 30, is phenomenal. Yesterday, my team and I heard a story and looked at one another, saying that it would never have occurred to someone who was native to the conventional system because it was so far outside the usual way of thinking. There has never been a better time to be in the storytelling business. Audiences are more willing than ever to consume and accept differentiated content – look at the success of phenomena such as Obsession and Backrooms . At the other end, creators of all kinds are being empowered to tell their stories better. The challenge is to identify the right voices and build an institution around them, rather than treating them as one-off projects. DEADLINE: Moving back to your traditional business, Abundantia has this year launched films for Prime Video and Netflix and a series for Amazon. Maa Behen performed well on Netflix and charted strongly. Are there plans to expand that universe, perhaps through a sequel or series spin-off? Malhotra: Both films we made this year, Subedaar and Maa Behen , are built around strong central characters and large, expandable worlds. The director they have in common, Suresh Triveni, our partner and collaborator, who imagined these worlds and characters as extending beyond a single outing. Development work is under way, given that both films landed with reasonable success. If the creative interests align, they lend themselves to franchising and future instalments without a doubt. However, a sequel should build on the original and its foundations, and it cannot depend on the original alone for its success. There has to be a solid reason for a second instalment of anything. Whittock: There was a lot of excitement about Anil Kapoor returning to the action genre with Subedaar . Was it an easy sell, or did he need convincing? Malhotra: Anil and I have known each other since 2011, when I was running Viacom18 and we were marketing and distributing Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol in India, which featured him. We have enjoyed each other’s company and shared sensibility ever since. When Suresh was developing Subedaar – a unique mainstream action drama around an older hero, something Hindi cinema and much of Indian cinema is not known for – he had one actor in mind: Anil Kapoor. At the time, Anil hadn’t led an action film for 23 years. I called him and said, ‘Anil, I’m producing this film with the wonderful director Suresh Triveni, who made Jalsa and Tumhari Sulu for us. We’re building an action film about an older ex-serviceman who takes on the system.’ Before I could ask whether he was interested, he said, ‘Done. I’m in. I’ll do the film. When do we start?’ Although it seemed like an instinctive decision, he knew the genre was right for him. He knew his audience and understood that his fans wanted to see him return in that kind of role. He also saw the creative talent involved and committed to it completely. DEADLINE: Looking ahead to 2027 and 2028, what is the plan for Abundantia? There is a lot of money in the market, but some of it appears to be receding and the number of commissions is coming down. It feels like a difficult place to work if you don’t know what you’re doing – commissions and greenlights are no longer being handed out simply to meet the demand created by the streaming boom. How do you read the market? Malhotra: That’s a fantastic assessment. India is an unforgiving market because it is made up of extremely value-conscious consumers. The Indian content consumer wants disproportionately high value for their time and money – in that order: time and money. And 2026 has been a year of growth across content consumption. The overall pie has increased, but the way it is sliced, and where growth and decline are happening, is constantly shifting. This year has seen a major return to cinemas. The habit that COVID disrupted, but which began rebuilding gradually from 2022 and 2023, has demonstrated that people are willing to go to theatres. Films that succeed seem to have no ceiling. We are seeing bigger blockbusters at the level of individual films than ever before. At the same time, we are seeing rejection at an unprecedented level. There is no ceiling to how well a film can perform, but there is also no floor to how badly it can do. Audiences are exercising their choices more decisively. DEADLINE: So how do you meet the challenge? Malhotra: To align with it, you have to keep sight of where the goalposts will be when your film or series is ready to be consumed. Novelty is also being rewarded, and that is something Abundantia has factored in from the beginning. It is becoming a significant moat for us. New worlds, new characters, new forms and disruptive genres are becoming the need of the hour. The market is becoming more challenging, but that does not necessarily mean there is a recession. The kind and volume of content being sought are being defined more sharply. Everyone is focusing more on engagement, return on investment and a forward-looking perspective, rather than simply buying something off the shelf to meet demand for the following weekend. That mindset is gone. This is a healthy correction and a timely rationalisation. It will improve the overall health of the business and allow quality players—and customer-focused platforms, streamers, networks and cinemas – to prosper.
