The first offer was, in the words of one person familiar with the terms, a “lowball.” Ellison had offered a package valued at about $19 per share, with only 60 percent of that in cash, and the remainder in stock. WBD’s board would later write that they felt the offer “undervalued” and “inadequate,” and they unanimously rejected it as they pushed forward with their plan to split the company in two. That’s when the billionaires got involved. David’s father and tech mogul Larry Ellison and Zaslav’s mentor and cable mogul John Malone would enter the picture the following week. On Sep. 24, Zaslav, Malone (then chairman-emeritus of WBD) and Larry Ellison met via Zoom to discuss the first offer, and why WBD rejected it. The next few months saw a flurry of phone calls, Zooms, emails, text messages and in-person meetings, with Ellison raising his offer and reiterating his desire to acquire WBD, at one point floating the idea of Zaslav being co-CEO. WBD, however, remained committed to seeing through the split, with executives there confident that they get more than Ellison was offering if they followed through. They were proven correct just a few weeks later. In October, report leaked that Paramount was actively pursuing WBD, and the floodgates opened. Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos and Comcast’s Brian Roberts reached out to Zaslav, unsolicited, after the media reports, each of them expressing interest in the streaming and studios side of the business. A formal strategic review followed, and the race was on. Comcast proposed an unusual deal, sparked by Mike Cavanagh, that would have seen NBCUniversal spun out and merged with WBD’s streaming and studios business, while Netflix proposed a deal to buy that piece of WBD’s business for $27 per share in a mix of cash and stock. Ellison, meanwhile, continued to up his bid, and began to take meetings with Middle East sovereign wealth funds to shore up the financing for the deal. But as the weeks dragged on, and the talks between the companies continued, Ellison and his team felt that they were not being taken seriously, and that WBD was preferencing other bidders. The Paramount team was flabbergasted: “Every offer [Paramount] made put more money in David Zaslav pocket and put more money to Warner Bros. shareholders, and made it even more certain by going all cash,” one insider recalls. It came to a head on Dec. 4. Sarandos called Zaslav and told him that Netflix was ready to ink its deal for Warners that evening. If they didn’t, the streaming giant would walk away. As the WBD board met to discuss the ultimatum, Ellison sent Zaslav a text message, one that would go unanswered: “Daivd [sic], I appreciate you’re underwater today so I wanted to send you a quick text. Please note when you next meet as a board we wanted to offer you a package that addressed all of the issues you discussed we [sic] me. Those were 1 we wanted to offer complete certainty 2 strong cash value 3 speed to close. Please note importantly we did not include ‘best and final’ in our bid. “Also please know despite the noise of the last 24 hours I have nothing but respect and admiration for you and the company,” he added. “It would be the honor of a lifetime to be your partner and to be the owner of these iconic assets.” Netflix announced its deal the following morning, and the Ellison team went to war. Going to War David Zaslav, Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters as they visited the Warner Bros. Studio lot in December. Warner Bros. Discovery On Monday morning Dec. 8, Paramount announced a hostile tender offer for Warner Bros. At $30 per share, all cash, just hours before Sarandos and Peters were set to take the stage at the UBS building in Manhattan. “Today’s move was entirely expected,” Sarandos told attendees, even as Paramount’s team set up shop just down the hall. “We have a deal done, and we are really happy with the deal for shareholders, for consumers, it’s a great way to create and protect jobs in the entertainment industry. We’re super confident we are going to get it across.” What followed was what one source described as a combination of clever lawyering from Delrahim, and cutthroat dealmaking from RedBird Capital’s Gerry Cardinale, the financial and strategic partner of Ellison. Even as Netflix had a signed deal, Delrahim filed Paramount’s proposed takeover with federal regulators, starting a ticking clock that would prove to be prescient just a few months later. And as WBD’s board continued to rebuff the tender, seeking guarantees from Larry Ellison that he would backstop any deal, the pressure was ratcheted up, with Paramount filing suit in Delaware Chancery Court to gather internal communications about the deal talks, followed by Ellison and Paramount threatening a proxy fight, the financial equivalent of all-out war. But the fight was working. Investors began to get anxious that the Netflix deal might not be as “clean” as the all-cash offer from Paramount. “It’s too complicated. At least I can send a signal that I like cash and the timing of the deal,” said the prominent money manager Mario Gabelli at the time, noting that he was likely to tender most of the Warners shares his funds held. “As far as the attempt by Paramount to have a proxy fight, why not. It’s all part of the smoke signals and mechanics of it.” Regulatory concerns began to rise, with growing uncertainty that Netflix would be able to close its deal in short order. Netflix would go on to change its offer to all-cash offer, and gave Warners a window to negotiate with Paramount. Ellison would revise his offer to $31 per share all cash, paired with a bit of financial engineering that one Wall Street source called a “genius move” at the time, though it would come back to bite them: The ticking fee. The fee meant that every day after a predetermined date (it ended up being after Sep. 30, a small fee would accrue, effectively raising the price for the deal. The fee would add up to $0.25 for every quarter the deal hasn’t closed. It was effectively a way to raise the price without raising the price. If Paramount closed the deal quick, the price would be lower, but the shareholders would be paid out. If it dragged on, they would be compensated for the delay. The Netflix deal unwound even faster than it started. Sarandos was scheduled to meet with officials at the White House on Thursday Feb. 26. Shortly after the meeting, WBD released a statement declaring that the Paramount offer was superior. One executive familiar with the talks at the time said that the company expected Netflix to make a counteroffer. Instead, Netflix released a statement shortly after withdrawing their bid. “We believe we would have been strong stewards of Warner Bros.’ iconic brands, and that our deal would have strengthened the entertainment industry and preserved and created more production jobs in the U.S.” Sarandos and Peters said. “But this transaction was always a ‘nice to have’ at the right price, not a ‘must have’ at any price.” Paramount and WBD sealed their deal, and Ellison had his prize. Or so he thought. The Antitrust Fight California Attorney General Rob Bonta speaks during a news conference at Gemperle Orchard on April 16, 2025, in Ceres, California. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images On Friday Feb. 27, Zaslav and WBD CFO Gunnar Weidenfels gathered staff for a virtual town hall. They took no questions, instead laying out the rationale for the new deal, which Zaslav acknowledged “even for us, the speed feels a little whiplashy.” One WBD staffer said that Zaslav and Weidenfels looked “shellshocked” at the turn of events. The savvy lawyering from Delrahaim had paid off. Regulators around the world, including in tough jurisdictions like Australia, the E.U. and U.K. all cleared the merger, with Delrahim and Ellison taking meetings to figure out how to resolve whatever concerns were raised. Ellison also tried to woo the town, making a surprise appearance at Cinema Con in Las Vegas, where he once again promised to produce at least 30 films per year in theaters. At the same time, the leadership of the company was thrown into some chaos. Jeff Shell, the former NBCUniversal CEO, stepped down amid a lawsuit alleging that he shared company secrets, leaving Ellison without a media veteran at his side. Over the coming months, however, Ellison would connect with Mattel’s Ynon Kreiz, who still held Hollywood ambitions, and would ultimately join him at Skydance. David Ellison and his father Larry Ellison also played their political cards closely, with the tech mogul going so far as to discuss the future of some CNN talent in a White House meeting late last year, according to a report in The Guardian . On June 12, the Department of Justice officially signed off on the deal, and in a move that one observer called “unprecedented,” it paired that sign-off with a document outlining why the merger would be good for competition, a move seemingly meant to preempt any antitrust suit that could come from elsewhere. For example, it noted that linear cable TV is on the decline and converging with streaming, making that market functionally irrelevant. And when it comes to theatrical films. “The substantial body of evidence available to the Division indicates that the transaction is not likely to harm competition in studio development, production, or distribution of films for theatrical release. Instead, the evidence shows extensive competition within the industry, which has generated greater output and diversity of film offerings, and is likely to continue unabated,” the DOJ wrote. Two days later, David Ellison and his streaming chief Cindy Holland sat ringside at the UFC event held on the South Lawn of the White House on President Trump’s birthday. And then the states filed suit. A coalition of 12 attorneys general, led by California’s Rob Bonta, sued to block the merger. The Writers Guild of America did, too. The crux of the antitrust argument was built on the basic cable TV market, i.e. not HBO or streaming, as well as around both wide release theatrical films as well as for “anticipated top-grossing films.” The lawsuit drew some ridicule from top executives, including at other companies, given the decline of cable TV and the rise of streaming, but the theatrical concerns were real. After all, every previous studio merger had resulted in fewer films being made, not more. The states secured some early wins, and Paramount agreed not to close until summer 2027, or until the lawsuit was resolved. Paramount CEO David Ellison Matthew Stockman/Getty Images Ellison wrote an op-ed in The New York Times arguing that the antitrust suit was something of a ruse: “I believe this fight is not really about market share. If it were, it wouldn’t have been reviewed and approved by regulators reflecting 65 countries, including the United States and China, as well as the European Union. I believe a plainer worry sits beneath the briefs and the news releases: the news. The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN. There has been speculation about my politics, my loyalties, my intentions.” It turns out that Ellison may have been on to something. For Bonta, the suit may have been, as he said over and over again a “bread and butter antitrust suit,” but Connecticut AG William Tong said after the settlement that he “wanted and demanded full divestiture of CNN and CBS News. We wanted to save ethical and independent journalism and news. We fought aggressively for that remedy. I am deeply disappointed that we could not do more.” But with the ticking fee looming, Paramount’s pressure campaign ramped up. Ellison floated the idea of having the companies leave California if the suit wasn’t dropped, while states like Texas and Tennessee actively courted the mogul. “His intent is to be committed to California,” Delrahim said a Politico summit, but, he added: “You have to take a look at the business environment and look to see what’s best for not only the community and the business. And ultimately, you know, go to the place where you’re wanted.” Bonta began to feel pressure, publicly and privately. Guilds like IATSE and the DGA released statements urging settlement talks, as did movie theater owners. Former political power players, including ex Los Angeles Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa and former U.S. Senator Barbara Boxer, both working for the public affairs firm Actum, had also backchanneled Bonta to try and help find a resolution to the suit. Boxer says that the settlement was a “win-win for California and American jobs, to ensure a bright future for our iconic entertainment industry that I have supported over many years. “I was pleased to be a part of a team of former elected officials at Actum, pushing for a timely settlement that not only increases jobs and production, but also stops a costly court case that could have dealt a devastating blow to California’s economy,” she added. Perhaps no politician was more instrumental than California Governor Gavin Newsom, who is said to have been spooked by the threat by Paramount to leave, and a recognition that Hollywood was hurting. Newsom is said to have huddled with both sides to try and hammer out a deal. In the end, the “bread and butter” antitrust case was settled without any divestments, instead focused on commitments around theatrical releases and a promise to negotiate cable carriage deals separately. If they don’t follow through on the theatrical front, a $30 million per film penalty comes into play, as is a possible divestment of Miramax. On the cable front, a court could force the sale of BET, Comedy Central and other channels. It was, as one industry veteran lamented, a “fold.” With California out, other states and the WGA followed. In his press conference announcing the deal, Bonta defended it as a “strong” settlement, but even he sounded skeptical. “I don’t think these two companies should merge,” he said. “But that’s not something that we are focused on with our resolution here.” That settlement paved the way for the combination that will now reshape Hollywood. David Ellison unveiled the corporate constellation, with the Skydance title at center. @ellisonskydance/X THR

articles.title: László Nemes Boards Jack The Ripper Series ‘Sickert’ (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All October 6, 2026 8:00am László Nemes and producer Alexander Rodnyansky Neilson Barnard/Getty Images; Aldara Zarraoa/Getty Images László Nemes , the Oscar-winning director of Son of Saul , is attached to co-write and direct Sickert , a historical thriller series set in the world of Jack the Ripper. The limited series is focused on influential German-British painter and visual artist Walter Sickert, suspected by some historical theorists as being the Victorian serial killer. Adam Baroukh will co-write the series. Oscar-nominated producer Alexander Rodnyansky ( Leviathan , Loveless ) will produce through his AR Content production banner. Nemes will also serve as executive producer alongside Rodnyansky, Stuart Manashil, and Michael Kupisk. Related Stories Movies American French Film Festival Lineup Features Int'l Oscar Contenders, "Cinema of Resistance" Movies London Film Fest Gets Concrete - Literally, and More Than Once! “My fascination for the first modern serial killer and for the mystery of the gothic world of Victorian London dates back to my childhood,” Nemes said in a statement. “I have the ambition to tell a story that is both epic and personal, frightening and illuminating, and to immerse today’s viewer in a universe that remains largely uncharted.” Set in London in 1888, a city gripped by panic over Jack the Ripper’s brutal murders, Sickert follows the artist as he straddles both the world of art and high society, and that of the marginalized underclass Sickert is drawn to paint, the very people Ripper is claiming as victims. When Sickert becomes a person of interest in Scotland Yard’s murder investigation, the artist’s grip on reality begins to falter and he starts doubting his own innocence and identity. Nemes says he will base the style of the Sickert series on historical records as well as from the real artist’s own haunting paintings of life in the ghettos of Whitechapel, where Jack the Ripper found his victims. Walter Sickert’s work is credited with influencing artists like Francis Bacon and Lucien Freud, and the artist was a key figure in avant garde movements including the London Impressionists and the Camden Town Group. Nemes won an Oscar for his debut feature, the Holocaust drama Son of Saul (2015). He followed up with the period dramas Sunset (2018) and Orphan (2025). His latest, Moulin , his first French-language film, depicting the story of French resistance leader Jean Moulin , premiered in Cannes competition this year. AR Content produced Orphan , which premiered in Venice last year. The company’s current slate includes Place to Be from Hungarian director Kornél Mundruczó, starring Ellen Burstyn, Taika Waititi, and Pamela Anderson, and Amos Gitai’s documentary The Road to Jericho , both of which premiered in Venice this year. On the TV side, AR Content produced High Value Target: The Hunt for Saddam , a limited series starring Joel Kinnaman, on TNT. THR

articles.title: Ava DuVernay Returns With One of Netflix’s Most Political Docs Ever: “This Movie Kicked My Butt”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close Ava DuVernay in 2023. Gioncarlo Valentine/The New York Times/Redux In an early September morning over breakfast on a restaurant patio in her Eastside L.A. neighborhood, Ava DuVernay is remembering a piece of advice Steven Spielberg gave her more than a decade ago. Around the release of Selma , the fiery 2014 historical drama that received a best picture Oscar nomination, DuVernay attended a dinner at J.J. Abrams’ house and found herself seated next to Spielberg. Her movie was launching her into a new sphere of opportunity — and visibility — in Hollywood, and there, a few inches away, was arguably the most famous filmmaker in the world. She marveled to Spielberg, “Your name is on so many things — even things that you don’t direct,” before asking how he handled the pressure of delivering every time. What if a project left his fans or peers disappointed? Related Stories TV Jamie Foxx Does Not Want to Be Canceled Over New Hulu Stand-up Special: "After That Kevin Hart Roast, I Had to Cut Everything" Beyond the Book Zoe Kazan on Honoring Steinbeck's 'East of Eden' for Netflix Series While Rethinking Its Characters “He said, ‘You make another one,’ ” DuVernay recalls. ” ‘You just keep going.’ “ DuVernay has held that advice close ever since. This morning, she’s only a few weeks from the New York Film Festival premiere of her latest film, 14th , a documentary about the 14th Amendment and its increasingly fraught place in American political life. It’s a companion piece to her Oscar-nominated 2016 documentary 13th , which examined mass incarceration and the prison-industrial complex through the amendment that abolished slavery. The new film also comes on the heels of Origin , DuVernay’s ambitious 2023 narrative drama, which resonated with critics but — like even a few Spielberg movies — underperformed with audiences. “I’ve talked to a lot of fellow filmmakers about that experience,” she says. “Some really famous, well-known guy friends reminded me that everyone has films that are not as widely seen as they should be.” And so, on to the next. The director on the set of her 2023 narrative drama Origin . Neon/Courtesy Everett Collection The idea for 14th came to DuVernay in early 2024, when Donald Trump , campaigning to return to the White House, was promising to challenge birthright citizenship — one of the rights enshrined in the 14th Amendment. At first, that gave her the movie’s frame. Then the frame kept widening. Once Trump was back in office, the amendment seemed to keep turning up in the news: due process, public debt, even its language around “insurrection or rebellion.” What had begun as a film about one contested constitutional guarantee was becoming something larger — and, for DuVernay, harder to pin down while history was still moving beneath her feet. “This movie kicked my butt because it was like building a plane midflight — so much stuff was coming in every day, everything was happening,” DuVernay says. During production, she followed Carla Hayden, the first African American and first woman to serve as librarian of Congress; three weeks later, Hayden was fired. She followed Dr. Lonnie Bunch, the first Black secretary of the Smithsonian Institution who later retired amid speculation of political pressure, which Bunch has denied. “All my feelings about everything happening in the past three years — creatively, politically, socially, culturally — are being put into this film,” she says. “At least I’ve felt productive and not like I was going crazy with worry and fear and anger.” For 14th , DuVernay interviewed more than 50 experts, scholars and politicians, interweaving their insights with vérité interludes and brief snippets of relevant stand-up from comedians like Hasan Minhaj. “Comedians are the last frontier of truth-telling,” she says. The film was made for Netflix , which DuVernay considers her “home studio,” having worked with the Ted Sarandos- and Greg Peters-run streamer on such projects as 13th . But 14th arrives as some of Hollywood’s largest companies have come under scrutiny for their handling of politically sensitive material. Amazon dropped the Sam Altman docudrama Artificial with the statement, “We believe that Artificial will be better served if it were released by a different studio,” after striking a major deal with Altman’s OpenAI. (Neon quickly picked it up.) Apple, meanwhile, pushed the Jessica Chastain political-violence thriller The Savant by more than a year after the assassination of Charlie Kirk; Chastain later said she was “not aligned” with that decision. DuVernay interviews activist and philosopher Angela Davis for 13th. Courtesy of Netflix 14th ranks among the more overtly political projects Netflix has backed, and DuVernay wondered whether the company would stay out of her way. “I was really hopeful that they would continue to support the filmmakers in the way that they’ve established — and they did,” she says. “I was hoping they would hold their stance under what has felt like a lot of pressure to do otherwise. … In this climate, I would’ve expected a little more ‘helicopter mom.’ ” The cancellation of Stephen Colbert’s late night show, the turmoil around Jimmy Kimmel and Paramount’s settlement of Trump’s lawsuit against 60 Minutes all registered with DuVernay as she worked. Most unnerving was the short-lived merger agreement between Warner Bros. Discovery and Netflix, which drew attention in Washington. “I was like, ‘What’s this merger? What’s happening? What’s going on?’ ” DuVernay recalls asking Adam Del Deo, Netflix’s vp docs. “He said, ‘Ava, just keep making the movie you want to make. I can’t tell you what’s going to happen. I really don’t know what’s happening.’ “ She then asked, “Are you guys going to drop this?” Del Deo responded, “I don’t know. Just keep making it.” “I feel like everyone’s afraid, and I’m no exception — I’ve been cautioned about this material and about my points of view on all kinds of things,” DuVernay says. “We’ve seen a total recession in films by certain kinds of people and movies made for certain amounts of money — I think artists and executives feel a lot less free.” A former film publicist, DuVernay broke out behind the camera in the 2010s with the emotional, character-driven indies I Will Follow and Middle of Nowhere . Since then, she has moved across documentaries, limited series and big studio movies. Her 2018 Disney tentpole A Wrinkle in Time disappointed at the box office; a year later came the massively popular and Emmy-winning When They See Us . Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor stars in the film, based on Isabel Wilkerson’s Caste: The Origins of Our Discontents. Neon/Courtesy Everett Collection Over time, she has grown less interested in being one of the industry’s designated spokespeople on representation. “Is Alex Gibney going to get that question? Is Nathan Fielder going to get that question? What are those directors doing from their position for women?” she asks, referencing the men behind other high-profile documentaries this fall, Musk and You Can See Everything . “Until it’s a priority for everyone who says that they care about other people and are interested in a just world, then there won’t be one. “You’re making a choice for the types of films that you make to look a certain way — you’re making all those choices — and so people will make their choices, and I’ll make mine. My choice is just to try to be self-sustaining,” she continues. “I used to be the poster child of talking about this because I felt like it could make a difference — but what I’ve come to realize is it’s too difficult to do if enough people aren’t on board, and there just aren’t enough people on board. It doesn’t mean give up — it means just do it in other ways.” Her work still continues, for instance, with Array, her sprawling distribution and advocacy company for underrepresented filmmakers. One way 14th differs from 13th is in the audience DuVernay imagined watching it — particularly its attention span and knowledge base. Early in the process, she ran an informal poll of people at the Grove in Los Angeles, asking what they knew about the Civil War, who fought it and what it was about. DuVernay with sitting Librarian of Congress Carla Hayden while making 14th. Paul Garnes/Netflix “The answers were startling, shocking, in terms of people not even having an idea,” she says. “But I don’t want people to feel bad about what they don’t know. I don’t want people to feel overwhelmed.” The film features historians, current and former senators and members of Congress, and political operatives, but DuVernay widened the mix to include commentators with big online followings, among them Ringer podcaster Van Lathan Jr. and Hasan Piker, the left-wing Twitch flamethrower who has become one of the right’s favorite media bogeymen. “I would like people to feel like you can enter into this — that this is not going to feel like medicine,” DuVernay says. Sherrilyn Ifill, former head of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and one of the film’s most prominent legal voices, says DuVernay was unusually good at keeping all that expertise from swallowing the movie. “I was routinely stunned by how quickly she seemed to absorb detailed information,” she says. “Ava never loses sight of her audience. I had to trust her to bring me back from the minutiae and to remember the ordinary people she hopes to reach with the film.” As DuVernay puts it, “I wanted different people to be able to see themselves.” Which at times proved to be difficult. U.S. Rep. Charles Rangel in the Oscar-nominated 2016 doc, which explores the amendment that abolished slavery and its connection to the present-day prison system. Courtesy of Netflix Getting Republicans into the film, for instance, proved a considerable challenge. DuVernay says her team approached nearly 300 GOP officeholders, but only a little more than a dozen engaged with them at all. That group included conservative Trump critics like strategist Steve Schmidt and former Sen. Jeff Flake. Florida Rep. Anna Paulina Luna did agree to participate and defends Trump administration policies in the documentary. “Although I am diametrically opposed to almost everything she believes, I had a lot of appreciation for Anna Paulina flying into New York and sitting there with me,” DuVernay says. “No one else would. We asked. I have the receipts.” DuVernay insists 14th is not a Trump takedown. “He’s a small cog in a wheel that’s been rolling for a very, very long time,” she says. “The current administration is embracing tactics that are tried-and-true and have been tested and weaponized in new ways.” She thinks of the movie instead as a record — of the history it recounts and the period in which she made it. “COVID, wars, Gaza — it’s been quite a decade, and I don’t think we, as people who experience it, appreciate what we’re living through. They’re going to study this time,” DuVernay says. “My question is, how are we getting our arms around that artistically? This film is like an essay. We were writing through it, about what we discovered, how we felt and what it means.” This story first appeared in the Oct. 7 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: American French Film Festival Lineup Features Int’l Oscar Contenders, “Cinema of Resistance”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 6, 2026 8:00am 'Minotaur' Mubi The Franco-American Cultural Fund (FACF) has unveiled the full lineup of films and series for the 30th American French Film Festival (TAFFF), which will compete for the TAFFF Awards. The fest, running Nov. 3-8 at the Directors Guild of America (DGA) Theater Complex on Sunset Boulevard, will screen international feature film contenders galore, from Minotaur and Fjord to All of a Sudden . Overall, it will showcase 60 films and series. “Since 1997, the Franco-American Cultural Fund, founder of The American French Film Festival, has brought more than 1,200 French films and series into the Hollywood spotlight and given thousands of French artists, from newcomers to well-known directors, to writers, composers, actors, and producers, the opportunity to present their work before their American peers in the heart of Hollywood,” said director Taylor Hackford, a FACF board member. “This year, there will be another spectacular selection and delegation to celebrate the 30th anniversary event at the Directors Guild of America, making TAFFF the second oldest film festival in the city of Angels.” Related Stories TV László Nemes Boards Jack The Ripper Series 'Sickert' (Exclusive) Movies London Film Fest Gets Concrete - Literally, and More Than Once! François Truffart, executive producer and programmer of the festival since 2004, added: “Supporting filmmakers from their earliest short films to eventual Oscar recognition, creating a platform where both established and emerging talent can present their work, being the first to launch a series competition alongside feature films, and consistently championing female filmmakers are just a few of the many meaningful milestones I cherish with TAFFF.” Anouchka van Riel, TAFFF’s deputy director, described this year’s selection as “a cinema of resistance.” She added: “Individuals stand up to systems that exist to grind them down: a corporate machine in A Good Little Soldier and Minotaur , a courtroom built by men in Women on Trial , an online mob in Forsaken , and an exploitative labor chain in Strawberries . Running alongside that is a quieter thread about care, illness and what we owe one another.” The entire lineup for the 30th anniversary edition of the festival includes 31 fiction features, 11 series, four documentaries and 14 short films, many of which are getting either their North American or U.S. premieres. 58 will be up for The American French Film Festival Awards. Among special events at the fesf are the first U.S. screening of the biopic and box office phenomenon De Gaulle , written and directed by Antonin Baudry, which stars Simon Abkarian as General Charles de Gaulle, the U.S. premiere of the comedy All About Corinne , written and directed by Marc Fitoussi and featuring Isabelle Huppert, the North American premiere of Guillaume Canet’s psychological thriller, Karma , starring Marion Cotillard, and the political thriller Jupiter , written and directed by Alexandre Smia. The list of official submissions for the best international feature film Oscar include France’s entry Minotaur , written and directed by Andrey Zviagintsev, Japan’s All of a Sudden by Ryūsuke Hamaguchi, Belgian submission Coward by Lucas Dhont, Romania’s Fjord , the winner of the Cannes Palme d’Or, written and directed by Cristian Mungiu, and Morroco’s Strawberries by Laïla Marrakchi. The TAFFF program will also highlight French animation with three features: opening film In Waves by Phuong Mai Nguyen, Iron Boy , written and directed by Louis Clichy, and Blaise by Dimitri Planchon and Jean-Paul Guigue. With the festival moving from spring to fall, TAFFF is this year also bringing the best French films from Cannes, Venice and Locarno to Hollywood, including Gentle Monster , written and directed by Marie Kreuzer and starring Léa Seydoux, One Minute to Midnight by Nicolas Pariser, The Green Eyes , written and directed by Fanny Liatard and Jeremy Trouilh. Seven films will compete for the best first feature at TAFFF this year, including Congo Boy , written and directed by Rafiki Fariala, and Cannes Critics’ Week winner La Gradiva , written and directed by Marine Atlan. THR

articles.title: Sam Bankman-Fried Docuseries Set at Amazon (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All October 6, 2026 8:30am Sam Bankman-Fried. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images Logo text Amazon is getting into the crypto game, kind of, though it may have picked the wrong partner. Propagate and Amazon MGM Studios have teamed on the three-part Sam Bankman-Fried documentary series The Boy Who Stole Billions? , which is set for a November release, The Hollywood Reporter has learned. The question mark in the title is doing some serious work here. The Boy Who Stole Billions ? gained access to Bankman-Fried in prison, so you’ll get his side of the story straight from the fraud’s horse’s mouth. The docuseries “delves into one of the biggest frauds in U.S. history with unprecedented access and exclusive firsthand accounts from Sam Bankman-Fried himself from prison,” according to Prime Video . Related Stories TV Emmy Awards Enter Streaming Era: Prime Video, TV Academy Ink Six-Year Deal Lifestyle Prime Big Deal Days 2026: What to Snag (and Skip) During Amazon's 48-Hour Sale It continued: “At 30, Sam Bankman-Fried ran a $32 billion crypto empire until he was convicted of stealing $8 billion in customer funds, one of the biggest frauds in U.S. history. For the first time, he tells his story from prison in this riveting three-part docuseries. Was it fraud, or did his risky bets simply spiral out of control? With never before seen interviews from those who built FTX with him, the series probes SBF’s pressure-cooker world, inner circle, and complicated relationship with his CEO and former girlfriend, Caroline Ellison.” FTX was a major cryptocurrency exchange. It collapsed in November 2022 due to severe fund mismanagement, a massive multi-billion-dollar deficit and, depending who you ask, fraud. Bankman-Fried was in Ben MacKenzie’s ( The O.C. ) crypto-takedown documentary Everyone Is Lying to You for Money (2025). In 2023, he appeared on 60 Minutes in segment “The Rise and Fall of Sam Bankman-Fried.” The Boy Who Stole Billions? is produced by Amazon MGM Studios, Propagate and West Buttermilk with Howard T. Owens, Ben Silverman, Drew Buckley, Isabel San Vargas, Taylor Levin, Nanette Burstein and James Packer serving as executive producers. THR

articles.title: Inside the Shocking Decision to End ‘Young Sheldon’ at Its Peak (Exclusive Excerpt)
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Done Deal: Paramount Completes Warner Bros. Takeover, Creating Hollywood Giant close Sheldon (Iain Armitage) on 'Young Sheldon.' Sonja Flemming/CBS Logo text “One thing about a television show that succeeds is that a family is created over many years, and when you bring it to an end, there’s grieving,“ Chuck Lorre reflected on the ending of CBS hit show Young Sheldon . The series, which premiered in 2017 and starred Iain Armitage, Lance Barber, Raegan Revord, Zoe Perry, Annie Potts, Montana Jordan and Emily Osment, ended in 2024 after seven seasons. And though Young Sheldon was successful, in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic and joint writers and actors strikes in 2023, it became apparent to the show’s creative team that the narrative of the TV show‘s story was leading to an end. Related Stories TV Harlan Coben Previews 'Final Twist' Season 2, "Bonkers" First Episode and How His Onscreen Work Has Evolved General News Joey and Matthew Lawrence on Launching Their New Graphic Novel, '90s Nostalgia and Hopes for an Animated Series Jessica Radloff, New York Times best-selling author and host of The Official Big Bang Theory Podcast for HBO Max and Warner Bros., explores the decision to end the show and more in her upcoming book, Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw’s-Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Comedy , releasing on Oct. 20 from Grand Central Publishing. Through exclusive interviews, Radloff offers behind-the-scenes revelations and heartfelt anecdotes from the show‘s cast and crew as well as the emotional journey that led to the end of the series. Though any end to a show can be bittersweet, Radloff‘s book explores how the cast experienced an array of emotions after learning the show would not be continuing — while on a Zoom call. Four days after the actors’ strike ended, castmembers Barber, Perry, Potts, Armitage, Revord, Jordan and Osment were invited to a mandatory Zoom meeting with Lorre, Steve Molaro and Steve Holland where they would shockingly learn the show‘s fate. Below, The Hollywood Reporter shares an excerpt on the Zoom call that ended it all from Radloff‘s Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw’s-Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Comedy . ***** The spring of 2023 marked the start of a complicated time. Young Sheldon had just wrapped season six and had one more year on a three-season renewal that began in 2021. If Young Sheldon was going to continue past season seven, the main cast would have to negotiate new contracts. The goal is always the same when you’re on a hugely successful show: Get more money. But times were changing in Hollywood, and budgets were starting to shrink post-pandemic. Then there was the fact that Iain Armitage and Raegan Revord were getting older. Time on the show had already been slowed down since it was established that George dies when the twins are 14, so at one point do you totally abandon Big Bang canon? And if you don’t, do you continue a show without the gigantic presence that is and was George Cooper? As if the writers and producers didn’t have enough to think about, a writers’ strike was looming, which had the potential to bring Hollywood to a halt. But if the pandemic taught anyone anything, it’s that you have to take each day as it comes. And so, when the last episode of season six was completed, Lorre, Molaro, and Holland approached the upcoming summer hiatus with the hope that they’d be back in the writers room come June, back in production in late July and on the air in September. Steve Holland: You get to the end of a season, and you’re exhausted and burned out, so the thought of “Let’s start planning for season seven in case there is a writer’s strike” was not really something that was really feasible. Plus, writing that early wouldn’t have really helped anyway, as it takes about six weeks of writing and brainstorming to even get to the point of planning a new season and the first few episodes. And while we did think a strike was likely, we also didn’t think it was going to last that long. Nor did anyone else. But on May 2, 2023, the Writers Guild of America officially went on strike due to labor disputes with the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers. Nearly two and a half months later, on July 14, 2023, the Screen Actors Guild followed suit. At this point, even if the writers’ strike had been resolved, writing teams would already have been behind schedule for their normal September premieres. Grand Central Publishing Lance Barber: My concern was for the future of the business and everybody’s career, which is still playing out. We made strides, but work is so limited in this town. At the time, though, I felt like we were one of the shows that was earning revenue since we were a primetime hit show. But we were all on the picket lines, for sure. Nobody wanted to see a strike happen — and I’ll speak for myself — but I could afford to be on strike, which is not the situation for most actors. And so that wasn’t lost on me that I could fight the good fight because I could afford to. Holly Revord: During the strike, we were with Holland a lot, picketing. We didn’t know what the future of Young Sheldon looked like, but I was always trying to have conversations with Holland about it, like what happens after George dies, and Mary’s a single mom to teenagers. Lance Barber: I think from what I was told secondhand, the producers said, “Yeah, we want to see Missy graduate high school, and we want to take this as long as we can and we can cheat [the timeline].” Iain Armitage: I didn’t expect the show to go on forever. I expected it to go for about six or seven years. Lee Armitage: But I think Raegan felt they were promised like, “You’re going to be doing this show until…“ and Iain never had that conversation. People would say, “Would you do more?” just to find out where he was with it. And I would tell Iain, “Don’t give a yes or a no; take the time to think it through, and talk to your agent, talk to me, think about it.” So all my care was put into how to handle it if that ever came about. Raegan Revord: I definitely thought we had another couple years. At some point, I think business affairs came to us to negotiate about a pickup, so when we were told the show was ending, it was shocking. And yeah, Lance, Zoe and I would be surrounding Holland all the time on the picket line, pitching stories, asking what might happen, et cetera. We definitely asked a lot of questions, but I do know everything was tentative because in this business, nothing is concrete until the episode is out. Still, there were discussions about where the show could go after George’s death, but we weren’t ever told, like, “Oh yeah, it’s happening.” That was never told. But the discussions were there. Steve Holland: The actors joined us a bunch on the picket lines and there was definitely—and understandably—a lot of interest about the future of the show. At that time, we weren’t even sure we were going to get back to doing a season seven or if the strike was going to throw the whole season off. But I certainly never thought the show had four more years left in it. After 148 days, the writers’ strike officially ended on September 27, 2023. While the writers were now free to go back to work, the actors were still on strike. Steve Holland: The fear of the writers’ and actors’ strike was the longer it went on, the smaller you saw season seven becoming. We wanted to make sure we could give it what it deserved if it was going to be our final season, but as the actors’ strike dragged on into the fall, our hope for 22 episodes became 18 episodes, then 16 episodes. We knew basically in season seven that George was going to die, and Sheldon was going to go away to Caltech. Steve Molaro: We held off on those big moments in show time for as long as we could. But we were now approaching them, and I didn’t want to make a show without George and with the main character away at grad school. Steve Holland: Steve was very adamant that he didn’t want to do another season of Young Sheldon after that. I think I agreed with him, but I was more open to seeing what a season eight would look like. Steve Molaro: They could have gone on. There’s a world where there could have been a season eight, and I could have just said, “I wish you all well; I’m going to take a step away from this.” And I would have. I personally did not want to make the show without George. So if everybody wanted it and were excited to do it and had a take on it that they were psyched about, I would have probably consulted, but I was ready to take a step back and think about other things. Steve Holland: Molaro and I sat down at Chuck’s house and chatted about whether there was a world beyond George dying and Sheldon going away. And as we were talking about it, it felt like the story arc that was Young Sheldon was really so much about Sheldon looking back on his relationship specifically with his dad, and realizing and seeing it as a dad in a different light. That wasn’t the thesis statement going in, but as the show went on, it became very clear that the emotional through line was an older Sheldon with kids looking back on his parents, but specifically his dad, and realizing that he had maybe been unfair to him for most of his life. And it felt like that was the end of that show. It also felt like coming back to it without Sheldon there or George there … it would be hard to just to not live in the grief of George being gone. It felt like it was going to be going past the end of the story. Chuck Lorre: I absolutely agreed that we told the story, and once season seven was finished, Young Sheldon had come to an end. Sheldon was now taller than most of the other characters on the show, so the “young” word was kind of looking a little silly. Steve Molaro: Plus, we were not going to go follow Sheldon to Caltech. That was already a show, and it’s called The Big Bang Theory . And I’m not interested in telling the stories in the years before he met Leonard. But based on the ratings, I understand why a season eight on paper would have made sense. I just didn’t think creatively it was a good choice. What Molaro and Holland did think was a good choice was a possible spin-off focusing on Georgie, his wife Mandy, and their new baby, CeeCee. It wasn’t until after the writers’ strike ended that the two started putting more thought into the idea, but the seed was actually planted a year before. Alex Reid: We were on location in season six doing something with Georgie and Mandy, and it was going smoothly and all the jokes were landing. I just happened to be standing there when Molaro said something to Holland and the writers, like, “I could see myself doing five years with these two.” There was always talk or whispers of a spin-off, so at that point, he wasn’t saying that for nothing. Steve Holland: I think it became clear watching Georgie and Mandy together that they were great, and to follow them would be great. What we didn’t know at that point was when that would be. We didn’t know how long Young Sheldon was going to go. Montana Jordan, Emily Osment and Iain Armitage in Young Sheldon . Bill Inoshita/2024 Warner Bros. Entertainment That is until late September 2023, when Molaro and Holland decided to actually present the idea of a Georgie and Mandy spin-off to Lorre, knowing that there would be no season eight of Young Sheldon. Steve Molaro: I called Chuck and said, “Here’s my pitch: we make a show for Georgie and Mandy living with her parents, who we already know and love, but we flip it back to multi-cam.” There was a pause, then Chuck said, “You son of a bitch! Stop getting me excited to do multi-cam again!” He loved it. Chuck Lorre: It made perfect sense. It just felt right. Steve Molaro: We knew that CBS wanted Young Sheldon to keep going, regardless of what the creative was, but we had found this other path where we could potentially keep something going that was related to it but without having the weight of George gone, and Sheldon gone. There wasn’t any joy in that, but by flipping the format to multi-cam and focusing on other aspects seemed to me to be a version where if they wanted to do that, we could keep the comedy and joy going. Alex Reid: Molaro also found the single-camera process completely tedious and frustrating. He could do another single-cam if it was eight episodes, but he can’t do six or seven seasons of 22 episodes a season. It just wore him down. He loved how the episodes turned out, and was very proud of them, but how the sausage was made was really not appealing to him. But the window to bring Young Sheldon to a close with enough episodes to tell that story was getting narrower as the actors’ strike went on. Plus, as soon as the actors’ strike ended, CBS was going to enter into negotiations with the actors since their contracts would be expiring soon anyway. Steve Holland: It was still a big hit, and it’s tricky because financially, things get more expensive as they go on, and if we had done another season of Young Sheldon , they might have had to cut the budget some to do it. Who knows? The shows get more expensive and the return on them gets less. They’re already presold into syndication, so each show that you make becomes less and less valuable at a certain point. So there’s a world where CBS would have said yes to more seasons, but cut the budget for it, and we also weren’t interested in doing a slightly slashed version of the show. So we met with the studio (Warner Bros. Television) and network (CBS) to talk about Young Sheldon , and I think they were probably assuming we were going to talk about season eight. Instead, we told them this was going to be the last season, but we had some good news. I had a picture of Montana and Emily holding the baby on my iPad, and we said, “But we have another show for you, and it’s this one here.” To their credit, they were incredibly supportive, but I think in that moment they were incredibly taken aback because they were not expecting us to say we want to end the biggest comedy on television right now. Connor Kilpatrick: I didn’t think CBS was going to let it be the end, truly. That might have been wishful thinking, but I know they didn’t want it to end. I had always heard the story of when Charlie Sheen left Two and a Half Men , Chuck wanted to end the show, and Les Moonves (then chairman and CEO of CBS) told him something like, “I don’t care if you’re a part of it, but there will be a Two and a Half Men on CBS.” [ Author’s note: And there was, with Sheen being replaced by Ashton Kutcher.] So I had a feeling that CBS was going to be like, “We don’t care if you guys walk away, but we’re going to keep making Young Sheldon .” Iain Armitage in Young Sheldon . Bill Inoshita / 2024 Warner Bros. Entertainment Inc. But that’s not what happened. Given Lorre, Molaro and Holland’s success with The Big Bang Theory and Young Sheldon , CBS trusted their creative instincts and had faith in a potential spin-off. The only problem was that since the actors’ strike was still ongoing, Lorre, Molaro and Holland couldn’t approach Montana Jordan or Emily Osment to even see if they were interested. Steve Holland: We assumed they would all want to do it, but honestly, the one question mark was Montana, because he and [his now wife] Jenna were having a baby. I really didn’t know him well enough to know whether he wanted to keep doing this or go back to Texas, because he really loves being in Texas, and he loves being around his family. I could have seen a world where he was like, “I’ve got my Young Sheldon money and this has been great, but I just want to go back to Texas and raise my baby.” And then we would have no show. We just didn’t know. And we couldn’t ask him at that moment because they were still on strike. Eventually the actors’ strike would come to an end, and on Nov. 9, 2023, 118 days after it began, the work stoppage was over. The cast of Young Sheldon was excited to get back to work but had no idea about the decisions that were already made behind the scenes. Steve Holland: We had to do two things back to back, which was unfortunate, because we were about to start production. We had to inform the cast and tell them this was going to be the last season. We had done it on Big Bang , which was worse, but at least that was in person. In this case, because many of them were out of town due to the strikes, we had to get them all on Zoom. We wanted to tell them as soon as possible because we felt they should know, and didn’t want the news to leak. On top of that, we couldn’t talk to Montana and Emily about the spin-off until we told everybody about Young Sheldon ending, because we didn’t want them to be the only ones who knew this was going to be the last season of Young Sheldon . That didn’t feel fair to them. And so, four days after the actors’ strike had ended, Lance Barber, Zoe Perry, Annie Potts, Iain Armitage, Raegan Revord, Montana Jordan, and Emily Osment received invites to a mandatory Zoom meeting with Chuck Lorre, Steve Molaro and Steve Holland. Lee Armitage: When I got the hint that there might be something more to this meeting, I made it my business to know for Iain. I don’t want anybody sort of timing a surprise, good or bad, like that. I know what’s on his mind, and I know what he needs to know when. And so I found out. I don’t think they handled it perfectly, and I also think there’s no perfect way to handle it. Iain Armitage: I was lucky, because I was not blindsided by their announcement when they told us. Holly Revord: I knew it wasn’t good news because Chuck was also going to be on the Zoom, and Chuck can’t make the decision alone to do more seasons. They would have had to reach out to everyone’s representatives, and then the cast would have to decide to do more or not. So I knew there was a decision made for us, and especially when the email invite said, “Meeting with Chuck tomorrow … you have to be there.” I think we asked if the kids had to be there, and they said yes, which meant that if they were in the middle of schooling, we’d have to get them out of a lesson. Plus, no one’s agent had come to talk to us. So we knew. I didn’t want Raegan to be blindsided, but I didn’t want to tell them either. So I just said, “This is either really good news or really bad news.” Raegan said, “Okay,” but I don’t think they really thought much of it. The show was still doing so well in the ratings, and we were hearing from Warner Bros. business affairs there might be a multiple-season pickup, so in Raegan’s brain, the show was going to keep going. Annie Potts: We were the number one show on network TV. So when they scheduled a Zoom meeting, I thought they were going to say, “Listen, we got a pickup for three years!” Perry and Barber, meanwhile, were less optimistic. Zoe Perry: There was a lot of uncertainty, but once we heard there was a Zoom, I thought, “Okay, this is it, because you wouldn’t normally have a meeting like that.” Lance Barber: I assumed it might be to announce the end, because otherwise they would have to negotiate new contracts and they knew everybody would hold out and go to the table for some big money. But the show already had a natural stopping point coming up that would be appropriate, storytelling-wise. If they continued it, which they did in another way, it would be one that behooved them business wise. So I kind of felt from that three-season pickup at the end of season four that that was where it was headed. But I hoped for myself and everybody else that it would bring us work for longer. On Tuesday, Nov. 14, 2023, the cast logged on for the Zoom meeting and made small talk with each other. Everyone was in a good mood, if a little nervous about what was going to be discussed. There was some teasing about Lance Barber’s beard, followed by everyone congratulating Montana Jordan on the news that he was going to be a dad. “Our baby’s all grown up,” Zoe Perry could be heard saying, with Barber joking he was sick of his real family and ready to be reunited with his TV family on set. Once Chuck Lorre logged on, Steve Holland began by saying, “Hello everybody, it’s so nice to see your faces. And I know some of you have guessed this, but we wanted to get everyone in one place to make it official that this is going to be the final season of Young Sheldon .” He paused, and everyone remained quiet, but their feelings were written all over their faces. A second or two later, he continued: “[This] is incredibly difficult to say because of what an amazing place it is to work, and a lot of that is due to all of you. So thank all of you for being such incredible partners, and friends, and castmates, and family on this run.” Steve Holland: I said, “To us, this just feels like the natural end of the show,” and “We talked about whether there was a version going forward, but this just felt that it was the right time to end it and go out on top.” But there was a lot of frustration and anger on that Zoom, like, we’re still a big hit show, and who walks away from that? Our feeling was, that’s when you walk away, when it’s still great, and don’t let it sort of taper off into mediocrity. But it’s a lot to drop on people. And especially for the kids and their parents, this had been such a huge chunk of their lives. I mean, it’s scary. It was scary for the Big Bang cast, knowing that was ending, but when you’re now 15 or 16, and you’ve been on this show for eight years, it’s what you know. And you’re losing a family. It’s a lot to process. Steve Molaro: It was tough. We’re all a family and we all care about each other. I don’t want to watch anybody be sad or be shocked, but at the end of the day, I still believe creatively, that was the right time to end that story. Steve and I feel the same way about how Big Bang ended. They wanted it to keep going, and yes, there’s a world where it could have, and I’m only speaking from a creative standpoint, but creatively, to us, it’s hard for me to imagine a version of that that wouldn’t have been challenging. Montana Jordan was the first to speak once Holland finished relaying the news. “Well, I wasn’t expectin’ that!” he said, his voice choking up. There was some uneasy laughter, and then, what everyone else was too afraid to say came from the only person who could. Annie Potts: I said, “Well, that sucks! I don’t like that at all!” I felt I had voiced what everybody else was feeling, and I thought, “Well, I shot myself in the foot.” I went full Meemaw on them, I have to say. I mean, what did they think we were going to do? It wasn’t couched in “We know this is going to be upsetting,” so we had a second to collect or read what was happening in that Zoom room. I felt like I had been thunderstruck or lightning struck. It was more than a rumble. It was a direct hit. Holly Revord: I wish we could have all been together. [ Tearing up ] It would have been nice in those moments to hug each other. And especially for Raegan, who literally didn’t say one thing on the call; they were mute. I will never forget Annie’s reaction. I wanted to be in person to hug her because she broke my heart. Montana Jordan: I was in Texas, and just sat there, shocked. I kinda wish they had done it in person because then you can show your love to them, but I understand their reasons. I was just kinda sittin’ there in my own thoughts, like, “Oh, did he just say that?” And then right after, I called Jenna and said, “I better start applying to McDonald’s or something.” Steve Holland: Montana seemed really shocked and upset about Young Sheldon ending, so I immediately thought, “Oh, he’s going to do the spin-off [now based on that reaction].” Montana Jordan and Emily Osment in Young Sheldon . Sonja Flemming/CBS Emily Osment, unaware that she’d be receiving good news soon thereafter, said, “I just got here! This is awful. You guys have been here so much longer than me. That sucks.” Molaro and Holland took a moment to then reiterate that this wouldn’t be so hard if they didn’t all truly enjoy each other, followed by Lorre announcing that the upcoming final season would consist of 14 episodes (shortened because of the length of the strikes), whereas most other shows were only doing 10. Lance Barber: Young Sheldon could have gone on as The Cooper Family , but it still would lack some of the integrity of the show, potentially, if it moved beyond that storyline. So I was grateful, as I was from the beginning, to have the story end there because of the legacy of the character for me as an actor. Selfishly. But it wasn’t the same experience for everybody else and reasonably so. They want to keep working, and it’s a jackpot job. Nobody wants to look for another job. So I felt for everybody. Zoe Perry: But that Zoom afforded Lance and I a chance to express some gratitude to the guys for what we got to participate in all those years. The Armitages took the news as well as you could expect, given that Lee already had a heads-up. But like many people who often turn to humor in uncomfortable situations, Iain attempted to make a few jokes, while Holly Revord remained totally silent. Only at the end did Raegan say, “Sorry, guys, I’m still totally in shock.” Still, the 15-minute Zoom ended on an inspired note, with Osment saying she was going to start making baked goods for everyone to celebrate the final episodes, and Lee Armitage offering up a virtual group hug to everyone. “We’ll see you in a couple weeks,” Lorre said, followed by several “Love you’s” among the cast. Of course, it wasn’t until after everyone logged off that the weight of what just happened started to feel real. Iain Armitage in Young Sheldon . CBS/2024 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. Holly Revord: Raegan just went to their room and cried. I wish that the producers would have given the moms, at least, a heads-up about how to handle it with our kids. I mean, the kids spent half their life on that show. They don’t know another world. Lance Barber: I think we all got together on a call right after with each other [since] the reveal of the news felt informal and impersonal over Zoom. It gave them a buffer of us not being able to come up to them afterward and saying, “What the fuck?” But I realize now, which I hadn’t thought of at the time, that they wanted to tell us right away instead of waiting any longer, and not everyone was back in town yet. Holly Revord: But when we were told it was “a creative decision,” it just felt like bullshit, and something we were being fed. There’s obviously still storylines. The Cooper family is still around a lot. Just on a different show. Annie Potts: I can’t remember what happened after that Zoom. I think I blacked out. I’m kidding. I think it ended with “Thanks so much for the last seven years!” I mean, you couldn’t have just done that for one more year? But I had heard some people saying in season six, “I don’t know, this could be our last year because the kids are grown up now, and he’s going off to Pasadena.” And it was like, “Well, let him go! Let him go to Pasadena!” [ Laughs ] I think the audience would have been fine with letting him go off to Pasadena and hanging with the rest of us. But it wasn’t my call. Connor Kilpatrick: We knew something was happening that day because all the executives showed up at our office building. And when you go to the office and there’s a bunch of fancy cars that are not normally there, and everybody is dressed nicer than normal, we know something’s going on. They had a meeting all morning, we started late, then they were in their offices for a while, locked behind closed doors. Right after they told the cast, the Steves finally came into the writers room and told us, and then they had a bunch of phone calls to make. And I went into my office and cried for 30 minutes. Even when I was told the writers room was regathering, I was like, “I can’t, I’m not ready. I can’t go back in there.” And even when I did, there were still tears in my eyes. It was a hard day. Chuck Lorre: It was heartbreaking. There’s no way around it. One thing about a television show that succeeds is that a family is created over many years, and when you bring it to an end, there’s grieving. But unlike a movie where you work together on an intense experience for two to four months … a television series, if you’re lucky, goes on for years. And it’s very hard to say goodbye. A press release announcing the end of the show was released immediately. Lorre, Molaro and Holland thanked the fans, while CBS president Amy Reisenbach added, “ Young Sheldon proved lightning can strike twice. It set itself apart with a remarkable cast that felt like a family from the first moment we saw them onscreen and brought characters to life with unique heartfelt stories that drew audiences in from the start. We extend a sincere thank you to executive producers Chuck Lorre, Steve Molaro and Steve Holland and the entire writing and producing teams for six wonderful seasons. We look forward to seeing their final season unfold and giving it a proper send off with the best episodes yet for their fans to enjoy.” Not included in the press release was the news that CBS was going to greenlight a spin-off focused on the characters of Georgie and Mandy. And that’s where things got really messy. *** Excerpted from Young Sheldon Copyright © 2026 Jessica Radloff. Published by Grand Central Publishing, a Hachette Book Group company.
