articles.title: Annabelle Wallis on the Defining Question of ‘Unabomber,’ a Potential James Wan Reunion and ‘Peaky Blinders’ What-Ifs
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Brian Davids Plus Icon Brian Davids Writer PickYourBrian Follow Sign Up View All October 3, 2026 2:15pm Annabelle Wallis Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty Images Logo text Annabelle Wallis has long considered herself an outsider, but she still has a knack for getting inside Hollywood’s most impenetrable personas. She may look like she’s from Southern California and sound quintessentially English, but the Oxford-born actor’s heart and sensibility belong to Portugal, where she spent her formative years before returning to the U.K. at 17 to pursue an acting career. That cultural duality made her early casting endeavors more challenging than anticipated. “I was expected to be a very classical, conventional period drama actress, but I had a very Latin life. So it became very confusing for me to understand why casting directors found it so hard to place me in things,” Wallis tells The Hollywood Reporter in support of Unabomber . Related Stories Next Big Thing Alexander Ludwig Was Frustrated by a Lack of Good Roles. Then Mike White Called Movies 'Unabomber' Review: Jacob Tremblay and Russell Crowe in a Facile Rendering of Ted Kaczynski's College Days The end of 2013 proved to be a game-changer when she debuted as an undercover Irish cop named Grace Burgess opposite Cillian Murphy’s Tommy Shelby in Steven Knight’s BBC series Peaky Blinders . Posing as a barmaid at the Birmingham gangster’s favorite watering hole, she soon found herself caught between her assignment and her growing feelings for Tommy, eventually becoming the love of his life. The first season was critically well received, but it wasn’t a ratings juggernaut (yet). Nonetheless, Wallis’ status as an early fan favorite likely helped land her another major role just a couple of months after Peaky Blinders season one concluded. Producer James Wan and director John R. Leonetti cast her as the lead of Annabelle , the first spinoff in the Conjuring universe, which went on to gross $257 million against a $6.5 million budget. Its runaway success paved the way for seven more films, and pound-for-pound and dollar-for-dollar, the Conjuring series might now be the most successful cinematic universe outside of Marvel. It was through her collaboration with the famously introverted Murphy that Wallis began to develop a reputation for working well with stars who have distinct personas. Murphy may be the anti-movie star compared with the larger-than-life personas of Tom Cruise, Russell Crowe , Jason Statham, Sacha Baron Cohen and Jude Law, but Wallis has shown a natural ability to get past each of their defenses. Wallis credits her “tomboy” childhood in Portugal, as well as growing up in a social household where she, her brother and their friends spent a lot of time together. “People say, ‘Annabelle’s great with these big alpha males.’ I want to connect to who they really are in their essence, and you can’t avoid it with me. There’s no escaping it,” Wallis says. “I will etch away at their being until they give me that kernel of humanity. It’s a je ne sais quoi that I’m very comfortable in, and it’s become a niche.” At the start of Peaky Blinders season three (2016), Wallis’ character, the newly minted Mrs. Tommy Shelby, was murdered in heartbreaking fashion. With Tommy being a tormented World War I veteran turned brilliant criminal, Wallis understood that happiness could only be temporary in his cutthroat world. She had also begun receiving other major studio film offers around the same time, including The Mummy with Cruise, so she was already looking ahead. What nobody could have known was that season three would transform Peaky Blinders into a global cultural phenomenon via Netflix. And in the years that followed, Knight came to understand just how deeply audiences had connected with Grace. Wallis would return as an apparition in season five, but she says Knight still has regrets about the decision to kill her off. “Steve and I remain very close, and he has always said to me, ‘I think I messed up with Grace. If I had known Grace and Tommy would be a dynamic that people longed for all these years later, I would’ve perhaps done something very different,’” Wallis shares. In 2019, Wallis reunited with her other The Mummy co-star Crowe in Showtime’s The Loudest Voice , playing Laurie Luhn, the Fox News booker who accused CEO Roger Ailes (Crowe) of sexual harassment over two decades. Wan was so taken with Wallis’ performance that he rehired her to lead Malignant , his bonkers horror movie that became a cult hit despite being released as part of Warner Bros.’ pandemic-era day-and-date experiment, dubbed Project Popcorn. Wallis now says she and Wan might be reteaming on something else soon. “James actually sent me a message the other day: ‘Annabelle, watch this space. I’m about to tell you something,’” Wallis says. “So, for the fans out there, who knows? He might ask me to trust him again, and I bloody will. I cannot wait to see what James brings to me.” Currently, Wallis can be seen next to Crowe for the third time in Janus Metz Pedersen’s Netflix chart-topper, Unabomber . She portrays Christiana Morgan, the co-creator of the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), a psychological test that asks people to interpret ambiguous images. Morgan developed the test with her longtime collaborator and romantic partner, Harvard psychology professor Henry Murray (Crowe). In the late 1950s, they oversaw the grueling and highly controversial personality experiment involving a teenage Harvard student named Ted Kaczynski. The 16-year-old was subjected to severe psychological stress over a series of sessions spanning 200 hours, raising the disturbing question of how much influence Morgan and Murray actually had on the young man who would go on to become the infamous Unabomber. The real Kaczynski has referred to the study as the “worst experience of his life,” but he denied the notion that it helped turn him into a domestic terrorist. Wallis, however, believes the study left a lasting psychological imprint, whether he realized it or not. “In my opinion, I do believe that the study had an impact. Adolescence is such a pivotal moment in all our lives. If you were subjected to that kind of pressure at 16, what would become of you?” Wallis asks rhetorically. “So, of course, he would deny its impact. He became so unwell that how would he even know? How would he be able to reflect and recollect?” Below, in a conversation with THR , Wallis also discusses Morgan’s inner life before remembering her late friend and Peaky co-star Sam Neill . *** You and Russell Crowe share the screen for the third time in Unabomber , but it’s your fourth time in the same cast. The first glimpse of you in a studio movie was Ridley Scott’s Body of Lies with Crowe and DiCaprio. Wow, I had totally forgotten about that. Thank you for the reminder. Body of Lies is interesting. I was cast for this whole other segment of the movie, but then, for either budgetary reasons or so many other reasons that I’m not even aware of, they cut that whole section. I was out in Morocco for a long time, just waiting to be used. ( Laughs. ) I remember Mark Strong. I remember Leonardo DiCaprio. I remember being on that big set, but Russell had fallen by the wayside in my mind. God, I’m going to have to tell him about this. Russell Crowe as Henry Murray and Annabelle Wallis as Christiana Morgan in Unabomber . Philippe Bosse/Netflix The main three projects — The Mummy , The Loudest Voice and Unabomber — each involve monsters in various forms. And like The Mummy , Unabomber has the two of you conducting a study of another monster — teenage Ted Kaczynski at Harvard in the late 1950s. So, to start with the defining question of Unabomber , how much influence do you think that study had on the horrors to come? We’re all born with a bedrock of genetic code, epigenetics, that makes us susceptible to high-pressure situations. There are circumstances in life that one can’t control, and he might have had the bedrock that allowed him to be the perfect candidate to then become the Unabomber. Therefore, in my opinion, I do believe that the study had an impact. When you subject someone to a study like this, you have no idea where they come from, what their epigenetic line is and what cellular trauma can be triggered. So there’s no doubt in my mind that it affected him later on in life. The real Kaczynski said that the study had no bearing on him becoming the Unabomber, but we can’t exactly trust his own self-diagnosis. Can you imagine going to Harvard as a 16-year-old boy? He had immigrant parents, and he was the first in his family to go to such a prestigious school. The societal pressures and the weight that he bore must have made him so vulnerable. And whether or not he was conscious of that, clearly he wasn’t if he denies it. Adolescence is such a pivotal moment in all our lives. If you were subjected to that kind of pressure at 16, what would become of you? So, of course, he would deny its impact. He became so unwell that how would he even know? How would he be able to reflect and recollect? Annabelle Wallis as Christiana Morgan and Jacob Tremblay as Ted Kaczynski in Unabomber . Philippe Bosse/Netflix In her private moments, do you imagine your Christiana Morgan felt guilty about how much she and Henry Murray (Crowe) manipulated and misled this 16-year-old boy? I do. It’s the only way I could relate to a woman who was able to subject a young boy to this. It’s the only way I could empathize with her. There’s no doubt that she felt guilt. How could you not? She led a very unconventional life. She had an open marriage with Henry Murray for more than 20 years while being academic colleagues. She also had a son, and she was perhaps not the most loving mother, from what I’ve read in the family accounts that I was able to get. For a woman in that time to even get to her position at Harvard, you’d have to have been so intellectually savvy and so emotionally intelligent to rise through the ranks within that male-dominated environment. The mercurial aspect of the ego wants so much to be validated, respected and understood for a pursuit. And she might’ve felt like this was her chance to stand amongst the greats. So I have no doubt that in her private moments she wondered about the decisions she made through her academic ego. You are often paired with leading men like Russell who have reputations that precede them: Jason Statham, Jude Law, Sacha Baron Cohen and Tom Cruise. I would also add Cillian Murphy to the list just because his introverted self is the stuff of legend on the internet. ( Laughs. ) Yes. Have you noticed this pattern by now? It’s interesting, because when you bring it up, it makes me reflect on how unconscious it was. I didn’t really think about it much at the time, but I have heard people lead with that line. They’ll say, “Annabelle’s great with these big alpha males.” I think I’m a strong woman, and I always try to be equal to those I work with. And I wonder if it’s the fact that there’s a level ground when you are not overwhelmed by the stature of the person in front of you. When you play the truth so wholly, it allows them to play the truth, and you can both separate the persona that they walk into the room with. I’m always so curious about humanity. I want to connect with the human being in front of me so much that I can’t fake anything. When I meet someone or work with someone, I really want to connect to who they really are in their essence, and you can’t avoid it with me. There’s no escaping it. I will etch away at their being until they give me that kernel of humanity that I’m looking to connect with in the scene. So I treat them nicely, and they feel safe enough to expose something that works on screen. Therefore I get cast onward. It’s a je ne sais quoi that I’m very comfortable in, and it’s become a niche, I suppose. You were able to crack Cruise’s shell in a way that few have. For example, you got him laughing about stories he wouldn’t normally volunteer. Whenever we’d go on a chat show, he’d say, “If you dare say that we did this on set …” And I’d say, “Well, well, Tom, now I’m going to say it.” ( Laughs. ) I’m a contrarian by nature. I’m very mischievous, and so are all these men. I grew up in Portugal, I did motocross. I rode horses. I was a real tomboy, even though my aesthetic is very feminine. I grew up in a house where a lot of kids came over because they perhaps didn’t have as nurturing a dynamic in their home. So we had a lot of other kids around, and it became a lot of boys because I have a brother. But I didn’t realize then what an asset it would be to be able to rough and tumble in this vehicle of femininity. With these big personas, everyone has all these ideas about them, but I’m not interested in the ideas. I’m interested in how they treat me and how they are in the scene with me and how close we can get to the humanity of it. So I’ve been fortunate that the people I’ve worked with have responded, and I’m proud of all the work that we’ve done together. Annabelle Wallis and Tom Cruise in The Mummy Courtesy of Universal Pictures You touched on it already with Christiana Morgan, but you’re often asked to play women in male-dominated arenas. Besides Morgan, Angie Ellis from Mutiny fits that description, as does Grace from Peaky Blinders and Alice from The Silencing . So I wonder if your upbringing is helping influence that in some intangible way. I do think my upbringing informs the work now. Starting out in the U.K., I remember feeling very much like an outsider compared to the classical actresses I was up against because I’d grown up in a Latin country. I was expected to be a very classical, conventional period drama actress, but I had a very Latin movement and passion and life. So it became very confusing for me to understand why casting directors found it so hard to place me in things. That’s still true to this day. And when you look a certain way, they want to cast you in a certain role or certain stereotype, but then you don’t quite fit because of the way you speak or your intellect or the way you see the world. So it’s been a very interesting journey just to observe how people view you in ways you don’t expect. In my mind, I’m a character actor who is longing to be seen as a character actor, but the vehicle that I’m in confuses people. So there’s a pigeonholing that’s forced upon you that you’re constantly up against. But through the vehicle of these men you named, I get to show a different side, a strength, that is innately honest. So I’ve really had to find a little niche for myself. A few years ago, your Mutiny director Jean-François Richet made a film called Plane with Gerard Butler, and he was going to executive produce a sequel called Ship until Butler reportedly dropped out a couple weeks before cameras rolled. Do you know if Richet repurposed that script into Mutiny ? Firstly, I had no idea about that bit of information. It’s been known to happen, especially with Statham. He’s made a couple other movies that were originally designed for Sylvester Stallone. That’s very interesting. Maybe it was fate. But I don’t think so. I think the powers that be at Lionsgate had something cooking themselves, but that would’ve been a good story. We’ve reached the Peaky Blinders portion of the interview. Can I first get your take on The Immortal Man ? ( Wallis breaks the news gently .) I didn’t watch it. What!? You’re Grace Shelby. You can’t say that. ( Laughs .) There were conversations about different versions, and so I know about those films. Obviously, none of them transpired. They weren’t the right directions to take. I’m still friends with everyone from the core season one and two group, and we all have the best memories. But from what I’ve heard and what I’ve sensed from people who’ve watched it is that perhaps they were longing for a throwback to the earlier characters or things like that. Look, Peaky Blinders stands alone. The brand, the IP, can go anywhere. And with Steve Knight at the helm, he’s unstoppable. He’s such a talent. But I did get the sense that people had waited all these years for some answers and perhaps they didn’t get them. So who knows? You never know what Steve is up to. He might feed them to fans later in some other way. Annabelle Wallis and Cillian Murphy’s Grace and Tommy Shelby in Peaky Blinders . Robert Viglasky/Netflix My one hang-up with the movie is that several people, including Ghost Grace, were absent from a particular moment in which they really should have been present. Thank you. It’s amazing when people resonate with a piece of work. I remember being like, Oh, I’ve done this great piece that I love. There’ll be so much more of this caliber. And I’ve had to reconcile with the fact that it’s very rare for things to come together like that. It’s rare that you get actors who are involved in things for the right reasons and with that kind of passion behind it. It was very special for all of us. Cillian calls it the gift that keeps on giving. The seismic loss of Helen McCrory led to the final season being rewritten. Were you slated to come back for that original iteration? Steve and I remain very close, and he has always said to me, “I think I messed up with Grace.” You have to remember, nobody watched Peaky Blinders when it came out on BBC. It wasn’t a popular show, so decisions were made without an understanding of the audience at the time. It took a few seasons to really gain momentum. Once it got bought by Netflix before season two, it was off and running by season three. Steve sent me this video where the public got to vote on their favorite scene of all time, and the “already broken” moment was number one. Tommy and Grace are in the pub, and she stands to sing to him. None of us could have imagined the chemistry and the ease between Cillian and me, considering it was a storyline that was written in the moment. They had no idea what they were going to do with Grace at first, but they responded to the rushes [dailies] so much that they used Grace to propel Tommy’s story. So Steve is often like, “If I had known Grace and Tommy would be a dynamic that people longed for all these years later, I would’ve perhaps done something very different.” But because he did [kill her off at the start of season three], it created a deep longing and a deep wound for the audience and their leading man’s journey. So Grace’s death was a very useful tool for the show. The Peaky family endured another huge loss recently in Sam Neill. You worked together quite a bit in the first two seasons. Do you have a memory that you keep coming back to in recent months? What a life he lived. He was such a lovely man. He nurtured young talent, and he was so generous and so kind. He’d be like, “Annabelle, we’re in Liverpool. Let’s go to a cathedral.” He had an obsession with cathedrals. Then he’d take me to all the wine shops that sold his wine, Two Paddocks, and we’d go in to do our sell-the-wine schtick. He always checked in, and he always stayed connected. It was just a great, great loss for so many people. Every actor that I’ve worked with either has a story about Sam Neill, or they loved him as much as I did. He was a great friend, and he’ll be very much missed. I interviewed him in the summer of 2022, and he was an absolute delight. He cracked himself up numerous times, and he seemed without a care in the world. It wasn’t until months later that we all learned he’d been going through cancer treatment during that exact time period. He didn’t tell any of us — and same with Helen McCrory. She didn’t say a word. God bless both of them. Annabelle Wallis’ Mia in Annabelle Warner Bros./Photofest In 2020, there was a viral news story about the Annabelle doll escaping from the Warren Museum in Connecticut. Many fact-checking websites then sprang into action and traced the root of this obviously bogus story to an interview being mistranslated overseas. There seems to be a lot of that lately. ( Laughs. ) Well, the root cause of that particular Annabelle story was my last interview with you. Stop it! We talked about the Annabelle doll because you starred in the first Annabelle , and then we talked about how Annabelle the actor pulled off the rare feat of running side by side with Tom Cruise. Somehow, those ingredients were garbled up, leading to headlines about Annabelle the doll escaping her museum. So that viral story was partially our fault. We went viral — and I didn’t even know it! Oh my God, that’s wild. That shows you the madness of the time that we’re in. Maybe we’ll start something in another part of the world with this interview. What might the miscommunication be now? Let’s wait and see what France has in store for us. ( Laughs .) Exactly. I’m surprised it hasn’t happened more given the name overlap. There was such a bizarre synergy between that film and being the same namesake as this doll. I’m very spiritual. I like to think there’s a message out there for you in that way. And while I don’t believe in ghosts or negative spirits, bizarre things definitely happened on that film. [ Writer’s Note: Priests started blessing all the future Conjuring universe sets .] We shot in some of Koreatown’s old Art Deco buildings, and someone would say, “Oh, someone was murdered here.” And when we would go over time, these lights would flicker, amongst other things . It’s a testament to James Wan, [director] John Leonetti and the world they created really creeping into your being to where it’s never forgotten. I still hear from people about Annabelle . Around Halloween, around right now, I see the residuals and the appetite for those films. ( Laughs. ) So I like to think I’ve transmuted something terrifying into a blessing. I have to pay my belated respects to your work in Malignant . The pandemic robbed us of many riches, and while I’ll always wish I could have experienced it in a packed house, it was nevertheless one of the few silver linings of that time. That’s really kind of you to say. I remember sitting down with James Wan, and he was like, “Annabelle, do you trust me?” And I was like, “Yeah.” And he was like, “Are we going to go for this?” And I was like, “ Yeah .” And we went wild . There were options for certain moments, and it was always like, “Let’s go for the strongest, most giallo-inspired, most outrageous thing that we can do.” I feel really proud of that fearless expression. It’s so rare, especially now, in the fear culture of Hollywood and the consolidation that’s happening. It’s so rare to ever be in the presence of someone who has the freedom to go wild, and I love that. And for women, we don’t often get the opportunity to play rage and darkness in that way where you’re physically embodying it. It was such a fun riot. James actually sent me a message the other day. He was like, “Annabelle, watch this space. I’m about to tell you something.” So, for the fans out there, who knows? He might ask me to trust him again, and I bloody will. Yeah, we were robbed of an opportunity [for a proper Malignant release], but regardless, I cherish the closeness I have with him, his wife, Ingrid [Bisu], and the whole Atomic Monster team. I love to see them thrive, and I cannot wait to see what James brings to me. Annabelle Wallis in James Wan’s Malignant . Courtesy Warner Bros. Pictures He just regained creative control of the Saw franchise he created, and even though he’s not directing the next one, I wonder if that’s what he’s thinking. I would love to try a bit of everything. It’s important to embrace all the genres. I don’t have that tactic like some other actors who are so clear about the one direction they want to go. I would like to try all of it and then see what lands. If something does, it does. But at least there’s movement, expression and a deep dive into the psyche of all things. I’m not a linear person, so a movie like that really represents the left turn that I can make in a moment. Some people are fearful of that, but I’m not. Not at all. *** Unabomber is now streaming on Netflix . THR

articles.title: Florence Pugh on How Zoe Kazan ‘East of Eden’ Collaboration Helped Boost Her Confidence
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All October 3, 2026 3:06pm Florence Pugh with Christopher Abbott in 'East of Eden' on Netflix. Courtesy of Netflix Logo text When Zoe Kazan set out to adapt East of Eden into what would become the seven-episode Netflix limited series, she only had one actress in mind for the central role of Cathy Ames: Florence Pugh . “I didn’t have a backup,” Kazan previously told Netflix . “I didn’t have another person that I thought would be just as good. She is the exact right person to play Cathy.” Elaborating on what it was about Pugh that stood out, Kazan said the actress embodied how John Steinbeck described the character in the novel. Related Stories TV 'A Different World' Earns Fast Season 2 Renewal at Netflix Movies Ben Affleck Explains His Approach to Using AI Ethically on New Movie 'Animals': "It's Not About Making Fake People or Replacing Anybody, Ever" “The way that Cathy Ames is described in the book is kind of doll-like but with something icy or steely underneath,” Kazan told The Hollywood Reporter at East of Eden ‘s New York premiere Wednesday night. “And I felt in Florence this mix of a very feminine presentation with, in a Jungian sense not in a gender sense, of masculinity to her soul. That she had a lot of raw emotion and agency and action, which is very Cathy to me.” Kazan was also struck by Pugh’s performance in 2019’s Midsommar . “I feel like that performance announced a generational talent,” she said. “I think she’s a genius. It was very clear to me that, even though that character is very different from Cathy, if she can do that magic trick of a performance, she can do this.” Kazan sought to center Cathy’s perspective and understand more of the motivations behind the complicated antihero. Pugh also serves as an executive producer on East of Eden , taking on a central role in the creation of the series since she was brought on in 2020. Pugh “felt very honored” when Kazan approached her. “I couldn’t believe that she was wanting to cast me,” Pugh told THR on the East of Eden premiere red carpet . Beyond that, though, being able to help shape the adaptation through the executive producer role, Pugh said, helped boost her confidence. “She really wanted me to be a part of the process; she wanted to create it with me. And that was just huge,” Pugh said. “At that time in my career and in my life, I was being given an opportunity that was a massive moment for me to step up and to lead in a different way. Those moments in people’s careers are the beginning of feeling truly confident about yourself. This project has meant a lot to me.” Pugh also wrote about her long journey with East of Eden on Instagram , saying of Kazan, “Zoe Kazan has poured her heart and soul into this project, I wouldn’t have been able to do any of this without her. She was my protector, my work wife, my cheerleader, my confidence. She created something so epic we all wanted to work on it.” In East of Eden ‘s stellar reviews (the limited series boasts an 85 percent freshness rating on Rotten Tomatoes), Pugh in particular is praised for her performance. In his review of East of Eden for THR , chief TV critic Dan Fienberg writes that Pugh, “tears into one of fiction’s great and confounding antagonists, a woman so determined and determinedly wicked that she makes Becky Sharp from Vanity Fair look like a Girl Scout. … Having Pugh playing a character who is, by her very nature, hesitant to reveal her truth is an interesting choice that puts the onus on everybody around her who doesn’t recognize what is so obvious to viewers. Cathy is scary when she lies, but she’s scarier when she tells the truth, with an unobscured honesty that is purely Pugh-ian. She’s so good that even in the second half of the series, when Cathy ages past the point at which Pugh is convincing, it still works.” Esquire calls Pugh’s performance a “career best,” with USA Today saying that she makes the show a “must see.” From left: Zoe Kazan and Florence Pugh at the East of Eden NY premiere on Sept. 30. Arturo Holmes/Getty Images THR

articles.title: ‘A Statement’ Review: A Top Ensemble Including Paul Rudd, Amy Ryan and John Turturro Breathes Surprising Vitality Into Dry Docu-Drama
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All October 3, 2026 5:15pm From left: Dylan Baker, Paul Giamatti and Zach Woods in 'A Statement.' Courtesy of NYFF To borrow the title of a vintage Supertramp album that predates the events of this movie by five years: “Crisis? What crisis?” In truth, that’s the attitude of a tiny minority gathered in a Florida hotel conference room for 36 hours in 1980 in Tom McCarthy ’s engrossing verbatim drama, A Statement . But it reflects the frustrating stalemate at which the group of 20 scientists, environmental activists, bureaucrats, academics and policymakers arrive after a marathon session of back-and-forth on climate change. And it typifies where we still are today as global CO2 emissions continue to hit record highs despite growing clean energy adoption. Related Stories Movies 'Behemoth!' Review: Pedro Pascal Hints at Soulful Depths, but the Drama Keeps Stalling in Tony Gilroy's Wan Character Study of a Virtuoso Cellist Movies 'Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall' Review: Paul Thomas Anderson's Effectively Austere Concert Doc Puts You Right in the Room Echoing the methodical approach he applied to investigative journalism in Spotlight , writer-director McCarthy brings exacting attention to long stretches of wonkish process and debate, somehow making the talkathon dramatically and visually dynamic. But the film’s biggest asset is its excellent and uncommonly egalitarian ensemble cast, each of them given moments to shine in sharp characterizations. A Statement The Bottom Line Talky but stimulating and incisively acted. Venue : New York Film Festival (Spotlight) Release date : Friday, Dec. 4 Cast : Paul Rudd, Evan Peters, Amy Ryan, Paul Giamatti, John Turturro, Tatiana Maslany, Nina Arianda, Jason Clarke, Noah Robbins, Zach Woods, Mary Catherine Garrison, Michael Chernus, Dylan Baker Director : Tom McCarthy Screenwriters : Noé Debré, Thomas Bidegain, Tom McCarthy, adapted from Nathaniel Rich’s book Losing Earth: A Recent History 1 hour 51 minutes No one is going to call A Statement an exciting movie; it doesn’t have the stirring emotional pull of another film set in a Florida hotel, Regina King’s One Night in Miami , which imagined a 1964 conversation about the Black struggle between Malcolm X, Sam Cooke, Jim Brown and Cassius Clay, as the boxer was still known at that time. Unlike King’s film, which was adapted from a largely fictionalized play, McCarthy and his French co-writers Noé Debré and Thomas Bidegain took a brief chapter from Nathaniel Rich’s 2019 climate science book Losing Earth: A Recent History as their source, folding in word-for-word transcripts for sections set in the conference room of the Don CeSar Hotel, an imposing pink palace that sits on the beach in St. Petersburg. But A Statement might just as easily have been a stage play; the mere fact of having the entire principal cast in one room for much of the time contributes to the theatrical feel. McCarthy moves through the set-up with admirable economy, conveying in onscreen text that Congress, in response to reports about the effect on the climate of burning fossil fuels, assembled the group of experts with a mandate to write a statement on how best to address the problem. Or whether even to call it a problem. That turned out to be an insurmountable challenge, even if those present, after a day-and-a-half of discussion, debate and compromise, are closer to being on the same page — or at least willing to acknowledge the cause for concern. Early on, one of the participants tells a joke about how many scentists it takes to change a lightbulb: “We don’t know for sure. We need to put more money into research.” That kind of hurdle applies equally to government, chiefly represented by David Slade ( Paul Giamatti ), the cynical director of the Energy Department’s Office of Carbon Dioxide Effects. Slade is by no means alone in questioning the urgency to take action, given the uncertainties of the research; he hammers the view that America’s carbon emissions are small compared to those of other continents. But he indirectly points up the major difference that climate change was a nonpartisan issue 46 years ago, on the eve of Ronald Reagan being elected to his first term, when he observes, “Well, presidents come and go, but if there’s one thing we will always agree on, it’s science.” The presence of a rep from Exxon (Eli Bildner) anticipates the outsize influence the oil and gas industry would have on climate control. While the cast is uniformly strong and clearly bouncing off one another like theater pros, inevitably there are standouts. In addition to Giamatti, they include Paul Rudd as conference moderator Tom Jorling, struggling to keep the conversation productive, to ensure that everyone is heard, and to steer the room toward a consensus statement. Evan Peters is punchy as Rafe Pomerance, a director of Friends of the Earth, simmering with anger that so few people share his alarm. John Turturro injects sly humor into MIT nuclear engineer Dr. David Rose, a superbrain who invokes the Egyptians as a civilization that failed to heed warning signs. And Jason Clarke is amusingly flippant as John Perry, a meteorologist turned government science authority. Despite intimate knowledge of the projected patterns for global warming, Perry maintains that humanity will have roughly a century to adapt once definitive findings are released, blithely suggesting that the American population can be relocated to landlocked states. Theories like that prompt legal scholar Edith Brown Weiss ( Tatiana Maslany ) to comment during a break, “Why is there no agenda? It feels like the blind leading the annoying.” The writing in the non-transcript scenes outside the conference room is expertly chiseled, far more so than in McCarthy’s collaboration with Debré and Bidegain on 2021’s swiftly forgotten cross-cultural drama Stillwater . The women in the room are very much a minority and both Edith and public health official Annemarie Crocetti ( Amy Ryan ) at various points are made to feel out of their depth. But both speak up forcefully as the discussion wears on. Ryan is electrifying when Annemarie cuts in just as time is running out on day two, urging everyone to consider the issue a human problem. The other woman on hand is stenographer Bernadette (Nina Arianda), who becomes cozy during breaks with Robert Cunningham, a young atmospheric sciences expert played with nervy energy by a terrific Noah Robbins. When he asks Bernadette how she manages to remain detached while matters of such gravity are being discussed, the DC veteran calls it a professional necessity. But as she sits off to the side, catching every exchanged glance or nervous silence in the room, the arguments start to inch under her skin. This happens after a wonderful interlude during which Dr. Rose, Bernadette and Robert all crash a wedding downstairs in the hotel ballroom and she takes the perspectives of both men on board. As is to be expected of a meeting that took place relatively early in the climate-science trajectory, discussions of renewables are inconclusive. Dr. Rose grows frustrated when the proposed wording focuses on solar and wind energy but excludes nuclear, with someone inevitably bringing up the Three Mile Island power plant accident the previous year. He seems as surprised as Edith when she speaks up in support of his pushback against the exclusion of nuclear energy. Some will likely question the point of A Statement given that the movie ends in collective failure, with the group unable to formulate a statement. But as a microcosm for the ongoing conversation about global warming, it’s effectively sobering, enhanced immeasurably by Stuart Dryburgh’s nimble cinematography and Bryce Dessner’s appropriately pensive score. At any rate, as a reflection on the climate crisis, it has much more to say than Digger . articles.title: Jeremy Strong Says He Doesn’t “Need to Apologize” for Method Acting: “It’s in Service of the Material”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 3, 2026 5:58pm Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) in Columbia Pictures’ The Social Reckoning Sony Pictures Jeremy Strong says it’s “never my intention to interfere” with the people he works with when method acting, but he doesn’t believe he “need[s] to apologize” for his approach. The Succession actor is a known method actor , which he has led to criticism from his peers in the past. When speaking with David Remnick for The New Yorker Radio Hour podcast, the host asked Strong if he feels his tendency to do research on his characters and bring that knowledge into his performance is “appreciated by the people around you.” Remnick specifically cited his Oscar-nominated turn in The Apprentice , where he added a scene to the film that wasn’t in the original script. Related Stories Movies Aaron Sorkin Made a Movie About Her. She Just Hopes Mark Zuckerberg Watches. Movies Jeremy Strong Treated His 'Social Reckoning' Co-Stars "the Way He Imagines" Mark Zuckerberg Treats People, Aaron Sorkin Says “I think I can’t really speak to that,” the actor said. “Of course, some people seem to have been… it is never my intention to interfere with anyone else’s experience or anyone else’s way of working. First, do no harm, right? But commit to fucking what you’re doing, and utterly.” He was then asked if he gets frustrated by others who are not at the same level of commitment, to which Strong responded, “No, just meaning that I’m just there to commit utterly to serving the material.” “So, if some people feel that I’m taking it too seriously, or it changes the molecules in the room in a way that makes something uncomfortable, I guess that’s something that I don’t feel that I need to apologize for,” he said. “Because I believe, and I think the directors that I work with all believe, that it’s in service of the material, and I personally think that a lot of the reactions to it are of a personal nature.” Strong will next star in Aaron Sorkin ‘s The Social Reckoning as Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. The director recently told The New York Times that Strong treated his co-stars “the way he imagines Mark [Zuckerberg] treats the people around him.” Sorkin explained, “Jeremy does a lot of his own work. He does a tremendous amount of work before he shows up on your set. He did not speak in his own voice on the set or walk the way Jeremy walks.” “I told all the other actors in his scenes: ‘Guys, he’s not going to be hanging out with you at craft service. He’s not going to be yucking it up with you between takes. He’s probably not going to speak to you at all. He is going to treat you the way he imagines Mark treats the people around him,’” he added. “And that’s what happened. You cannot argue with the results.” Brian Cox, Strong’s former Succession co-star, shared his criticism of his method acting in a viral New Yorker profile , where he said, “I’ve worked with intense actors before. It’s a particularly American disease, I think, this inability to separate yourself off while you’re doing the job.” The Troy actor has made many remarks about Strong’s method, saying previously, “It’s not good for the ensemble. It creates hostility. That’s the problem.” Of his reaction to the profile, Strong previously told The Hollywood Reporter , “It was painful for it to be put out to the world, maybe in a less compassionate way than I would’ve hoped.” He added, “I felt that I had a safe forum at The New Yorker . I felt that I had a safe forum to share those things — and ultimately that experience was put in doubt.” When asked if he was hurt by his co-stars coming off as being dismissive of his process, Strong said, “Yeah,” adding, “But a lot of that is just things that are presented out of context or with a certain agenda. I know what everybody said, and there was an angle and a narrative that was being presented. Which is not to say that there was never friction between my co-stars. We’re a family in every sense of the word. But foundationally, there’s deep respect and even love.” THR

articles.title: How ‘Freaks’ Sent Zach Lipovsky and Adam B. Stein to Hollywood: “That Film Changed Our Lives”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 3, 2026 6:18pm Adam B. Stein and Zach Lipovsky Eric Charbonneau Zach Lipovsky has done good business with gory horror movies. Lipovsky and longtime collaborator Adam B. Stein ’s 2018 dark sci-fi thriller Freaks, starring Emile Hirsch and Bruce Dern, was an unlikely box office hit, having made over $375 million worldwide during its theatrical run. “That film changed our lives,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter from the Sony Pictures studio lot in Culver City, California. Freaks effectively transformed the filmmaking duo from B-movie mavens to hot commodities in Hollywood after the dystopian drama world premiered at the Vancouver Film Festival (VIFF). “I grew up in Vancouver. We made the first film in Vancouver. And as a teenager I went to the Vancouver Film Festival, and got a super pass to not only see five films a day, but go to press screenings for three weeks before the festival,” Lipovsky recalled. Related Stories Movies Sony Pictures in Talks to Acquire Michael B. Jordan 'Battlefield' Video Game Movie Movies '24 Jump Street' and Ridley Scott's 'Treasure Island' Get 2027 Release Dates From Sony That festival play gave a young Lipovsky a crash course in world cinema. “I remember seeing filmmakers up on the stage, presenting their films and wishing one day that would be me,” he added. After Freaks – — which featured 7-year-old Chloe (Lexy Kolker) being locked in a ramshackle suburban home by her protective and paranoid father, played by Hirsch — Lipovsky and Stein are returning to Vancouver with their follow-up Freak 2 to screen on Saturday night at the Rio Theatre. “The first film was very much about a girl who can’t leave her house, and really wants a mom. And in the second film, she’s now much older. So she doesn’t want a mom. What she wants is a friend,” he explained. “And how do you find a friend, and how do you build a relationship in a world where society wants you dead,” Lipovsky adds as he teases Freaks 2. Paramount Pictures has already picked up the sequel where Amanda Crew is a mother and Lorelei Olivia Mote plays her daughter, as both look to survive a world that wants to wipe out “freaks” like them as they seek vengeance for their family. Freaks 2 also follows hot on the heels of Lipovsky and Stein directing Final Destination Bloodlines, the sixth installment of the supernatural horror franchise that grossed over $285 million at the worldwide box office. “It’s very hard to believe I’m sitting here on the Sony lot where we have our first look [deal] now. And we have a whole building of people now working with us to make movies, which is very surreal,” Lipovsky adds as he and Stein met nearly 20 years ago as rival competitors on On the Lot , the Fox filmmaking competition series from Steven Spielberg and Mark Burnett. “We didn’t win, and we were off the lot,” Lipovsky recounted. But, two decades later, he and Stein are in-demand movie directors at work on projects like the Long Lost short story adaptation for Amblin and Universal, as writers on Chris Columbus’ Gremlins 3 and for Sony the animated Venom movie and Metal Gear Solid . Getting known around Hollywood still has Lipovsky pinching himself. “Over 20 years of making movies, you get very used to things not happening, and very used to people saying something’s happening, and then it doesn’t happen. So when things start to click into place, your brain has a very hard time trying to accept that it’s actually real,” he added. Lipovsky also puts himself and Stein becoming bankable in Hollywood after Freaks and Final Destination Bloodlines down to the recent summer box office success of breakout horror pics Backrooms and Obsession. “Horror is one of the few genres where it’s normal for audiences to show up in theaters for original movies,” Lipovsky argues. “It’s the voice of the authors that are creating the work that audiences are becoming attracted to, and even more so when the work is original, and Hollywood is definitely starting to pay attention to that.” Lipovsky will be accompanied at the VIFF screenings for Freaks 2 by his mother, who as a single parent cast aside her own aspirations to become a movie director to work as a TV producer at Knowledge Network, a local Vancouver network. “Becoming a director back in the [19]80s wasn’t really a career path for many women, and she’s always been there by my side, and for her to see the kind of levels to which I’ve been able to create movies has been amazing,” he recalled. One of the VIFF screenings for Freak 2 will also be at the city’s historic Park Theatre, an art deco movie house that Lipovsky helped save from closure as a private investor along with Osgood Perkins, Mike Flanagan, Sean Baker and Finn Wolfhard. “It’s very special to be able to do the screening there, with a lot of the people that made the movie and a lot of my old friends in the audience and within minutes of where we shot the movie,” he insisted. THR

articles.title: Taylor Swift Crashes Dakota Johnson’s ‘Saturday Night Live’ Hosting Stint: “My Literal Therapist!”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 3, 2026 8:47pm Logo text Dakota Johnson got a special visit from Patient Zero on Saturday Night Live . Taylor Swift joined the Verity actress during her opening monologue on Saturday night’s episode, marking quite the surprise appearance. Johnson joked about having “two very public, very lame breakups with two very awesome musicians” since she’d last been on SNL , and how she had the most supportive friends who “don’t judge me for dating these men.” Cut to Swift! Johnson joked that the singer was “my literal therapist,” to which the Grammy winner responded, “I’m not your therapist. Actually, you just show up once a week at my house with an empty bottle of wine and ask if I want some.” Related Stories Movies Tom Cruise Stands Up for 'Digger' Amid Tough Box Office: "I'm So Proud of What We Created" Movies Tom Cruise's 'Digger' Plunging at Box Office With Less Than $10M as 'Verity' Leads “Yeah, well I have manners,” the actress said, as Swift continued, “And then you flop on my couch and overshare, and every so often I just say, ‘Damn, that’s crazy.'” “Is that not a therapist?” the Fifty Shades of Grey actress questioned. On Sunday, Swift released the music video for her new single “Patient Zero,” starring none other than Johnson and Colin Farrell. The two debuted the video at the MTV VMAs on Sunday, with the track serving as one of four new songs the musician released as part of The Life of a Showgirl : Encore Edition last Friday. To close out her monologue, Johnson concluded, “Well, just quickly, while we’re on the subject of musicians, I think actually I’m doing a public service by dating them, because ladies, I am saving you a lot of money on Zoloft. So, you’re welcome, America! And also England and parts of Ireland and Cleveland, allegedly,” Johnson said, as Swift added in a quick, “Woo-woo!” “Cleveland” is another new track from Showgirl: Encore , where Swift sings about her husband Travis Kelce and their marriage. “Now I’m wearing white (Yeah), so hate all you like (Uh-huh) / This is the love of my life (Hey, hey, hey),” Swift sings at the end of the song. At the top of her monologue, the Verity actress also addressed the box office bomb Madame Web , while noting that her last SNL appearance was tied to promotion for the film. She joked, “The last time I was here, I was promoting a movie called Madame Web . And tonight, I’m still promoting it. Because the movie hasn’t made any money yet.” Dakota Johnson’s monologue! pic.twitter.com/ZxOi5zVZLF — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) October 4, 2026 The cold open saw a group of “Republican heavy hitters” get together to film ads ahead of the midterms. Among those who appeared were Marco Rubio, portrayed by Marcello Hernández. Mikey Day also joined as Mitch McConnell, and Jeremy Culhane as J.D. Vance. The last guest before James Austin Johnson’s Trump also joined was Pete Hegseth (Colin Jost). He joined the sketch with a Bero in hand, which he described as “Spider-Man’s new non-alcoholic bitch beer.” “Now listen up, OK, ’cause I need all you patriots at home to do the gayest thing ever and vote,” Jost’s Hegseth said. “Thanks to me, the military finally has its priorities — and sexuality — straight.” the Republican National Committee takes on midterm ad campaigns pic.twitter.com/6xn5F75XT1 — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) October 4, 2026 Saturday night’s episode marks Johnson’s third time hosting SNL . She made her debut in February 2015, and returned once more in January 2024. She’s made several appearances throughout the years, including for the 40th anniversary special and a cameo during Josh O’Connor’s hosting stint last December. Season 52 of SNL premiered last week with New York Knicks star Jalen Brunson and Katseye. Later this season, Shane Gillis will host on Oct. 10 with musical guest Rosalia, while Obsession star Inde Navarrette makes her SNL hosting debut on the Halloween episode with Gracie Abrams. THR

articles.title: Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Tries New Marketing Tactic: The French Love It, Americans Don’t
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All October 4, 2026 7:29am Tom Cruise in 'Digger.' Courtesy Warner Bros. Pictures Well, maybe this one will work. Warner Bros. rolled out a new ad for Digger that is trying yet another approach to market the tough-to-sell Alejandro G. Iñárritu film. The online ad (below) shows a series of glowing quotes from critics from various countries and contrasts them with negative reviews from U.S. critics. The sort-of implication: The rest of the world loves this movie — it’s just dumb Americans who fail to appreciate its genius. At the start of the ad, Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell says, “America has stood beside the world in its darkest of hours,” to which Riz Ahmed’s character shoots back, “Not anymore.” Related Stories Movies Tom Cruise Stands Up for 'Digger' Amid Tough Box Office: "I'm So Proud of What We Created" Movies Tom Cruise's 'Digger' Plunging at Box Office With Less Than $10M as 'Verity' Leads Then comes the succession of critic quotes alongside a flag representing the critic’s country. The first is from a Mexican YouTuber who called the film “Epic, Extraordinary and Biting,” followed by a Playlist quote, along with an American flag, which called the film “Grotesque, Deliberately Tacky.” Later there’s a French critic who calls Digger “A Gem of Intelligence” followed by The New York Post calling it “An Unintentionally Bad Movie.” The ad concludes with Cruise’s character declaring, “You decide which!” Digger is expected to gross only around $8 million at the domestic weekend box office, which is even lower than the studio’s meager $12-$15 million prediction, and certainly leagues lower than the film’s $125 million projected budget. Is it actually true, however, that the international press likes Digger more than the American press? There may be a little truth to this. While Rotten Tomatoes has the film at 50 percent positive, French aggregation site AlloCiné currently gives the film an average press rating of 3.2 out of 5 across 30 reviews. The two metrics aren’t directly comparable, but the French score suggests a somewhat warmer critical reception. Several top critics in Britain and Australia were notably warm towards the film, though both countries, certainly, had dissenters as well. The film’s CinemaScore in the U.S. — polled from moviegoers exiting the film on Friday — was a rather brutal C+. Cruise took to social media on Saturday to express his pride and support of the film, writing, “ Digger is officially in theaters and I am so honored to have had the opportunity to create this film alongside such talented artists. Thank you to the entire cast and crew for your dedication, hard work and joy. The experience was truly unforgettable and I’m so proud of what we created.” You decide which. DIGGER is now playing in theaters and IMAX. Get tickets now. https://t.co/oVDCbKhdrU #DiggerMovie pic.twitter.com/p0cHPHqvwe — Digger (@diggerthemovie) October 3, 2026 THR

articles.title: Tony Gilroy Says Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Will ‘Destroy’ a ‘Healthy and Beautiful Business’ in ‘The Name of Venture Capital’: ‘It’s Tragic’
articles.full_text: Oct 3, 2026 12:15pm PT Tony Gilroy Says Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Will ‘Destroy’ a ‘Healthy and Beautiful Business’ in ‘The Name of Venture Capital’: ‘It’s Tragic’ By Antonio Ferme Plus Icon Antonio Ferme Latest Tony Gilroy Says Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Will ‘Destroy’ a ‘Healthy and Beautiful Business’ in ‘The Name of Venture Capital’: ‘It’s Tragic’ 19 hours ago Sylvester Stallone Says Superhero Movie Bodies Aren’t ‘Natural’ and Taking Steroids to Bulk Up Is Like ‘Putting on Part of a Costume’ 5 days ago Chris Rock Says Infidelity and Struggling to ‘Make It’ Aren’t Just Hollywood Problems: ‘If You Got No Love, You’re Broke as F—k’ 7 days ago See All Getty Images for FLC Tony Gilroy blasted the “tragic” nature of the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger at the world premiere of his new film, “ Behemoth! ” Produced on a $36 million budget , “Behemoth!” is representative of the mid-budget, adult-oriented drama that once sustained Hollywood’s theatrical business — and allowed filmmakers like Gilroy to make a name for themselves in the industry. He fears the impending merger (which David Ellison just announced would place both of the historic movie studios under a company named Skydance) threatens to dismantle the very “healthy and beautiful business” he has worked in for over three decades. Related Stories 'Gremlins 3' Delayed to 2028 by Warner Bros. Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta 'Don't You Dare' Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: 'Do Not Cave' “People say the movie business is in trouble,” Gilroy told Variety Friday night at Alice Tully Hall. “You go around, you stand anywhere you want, what do people talk about? Did you see this? Did you see that? What episode are you on? The business is solid, and to destroy the architecture that made it so in the name of venture capital, it’s tragic.” Starring Pedro Pascal as a gifted cellist re-immersing himself in the world of Hollywood film scoring, “Behemoth!” marks Gilroy’s first major project since completing his work on the Emmy-winning series “Andor.” It was also selected as the centerpiece of the 64th New York Film Festival , following James Gray’s star-studded opening-night film “Paper Tiger” and preceding Ava DuVernay’s closing-night documentary “14th.” While introducing his new film, Gilroy praised the festival’s lineup as a bright spot amid an increasingly turbulent Hollywood landscape . Popular on Variety “Thank you for making [the festival] so elegant and glamorous, and for surrounding us with so many amazing films,” Gilroy told the crowd. “The way this is curated this year, this is a freakin’ lineup! Holy sh*t. And everybody knows it. When so many things go to shit in Hollywood, this is like a thank you. Thank you for letting us bring our soufflé to your groovy party.” Gilroy also thanked Matt Greenfield and his partners at Searchlight Pictures, the indie studio owned by the Walt Disney Company, which also produced “Andor.” “This is not an easy movie to greenlight, and it’s not an easy movie to sell,” he concluded. “But here we are. We’re here. We got here calmly, gracefully, no drama, and our joie de vivre intact.” Tony Gilroy introduces his new film “Behemoth!” at its worldwide premiere at #NYFF : “This is a hard movie to green light, and a hard movie to sell. And here we are.” pic.twitter.com/WeHLKyJ8Gc — Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026 Skydance has tentatively set Tuesday, Oct. 6, to close the merger, which will consolidate Hollywood’s traditional Big Five studios (Disney, Universal, Sony, Warner Bros. and Paramount) under just four corporate owners. While Ellison has maintained that Paramount and Warner Bros. will retain their separate studio identities under Skydance, industry figures — including “Behemoth!” producer Sanne Wohlenberg — fear the consolidation will make the “possibilities for a filmmaker alarmingly limited.” “God, it’s certainly turbulent and uncertain times, isn’t it? It never seems to get any easier,” Wohlenberg said. “I do think you have to take a deep breath and keep believing that things will be circular and come back. When you look at history, there have been many, many bad times. Sadly, we are steering into one, which will make the competitive nature of the industry and possibilities for a filmmaker alarmingly limited. And it shouldn’t be like that. I think we will survive it and I hope for better times.” Travis Kelce Speaks Out on Wedding to Taylor Swift: ‘Best Night of My Life’ and ‘It Was Cool to Live Out My Childhood Dream’ of Being in MSG Tom Cruise Says Taylor Swift Was ‘Schooling Me on Football’ at Chiefs Game, Calls Her a ‘Brilliant Musician and Director’ Taylor Swift Announces New Single, ‘Patient Zero,’ Coming This Week Newly Discovered Plant-Eating Insects Named After Taylor Swift Todd Rundgren Slams Taylor Swift, Says She ‘Ruined Music’ and Is ‘the Apotheosis of Mediocrity’ Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Music Video, Starring Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell, to Debut at VMAs Loading comments...

articles.title: ‘RuneScape’-Inspired Animation Series in the Works From Lyrical Animation and Jagex
articles.full_text: Oct 3, 2026 2:00pm PT ‘RuneScape’-Inspired Animation Series in the Works From Lyrical Animation and Jagex By Payton Turkeltaub Plus Icon Payton Turkeltaub Latest Jeremy Strong Defends Method Acting, Says He Doesn’t Feel the Need to ‘Apologize’ to Co-Stars Who May Think ‘I’m Taking It Too Seriously’ 15 hours ago ‘RuneScape’-Inspired Animation Series in the Works From Lyrical Animation and Jagex 17 hours ago Box Office: ‘Digger’ Nosediving With $3.4 Million on Opening Day, ‘Verity’ Lands at No. 1 With $15.1 Million on Friday 23 hours ago See All Jagex Lyrical Animation is developing a new animation series based on “ RuneScape ” in partnership with creator Charlie “MoistCr1TiKaL” White and game developer Jagex, the company’s CEO Jon Bellamy announced on stage at RuneFest in Birmingham, UK, on Saturday. The project will bring the world of Gielinor to the screen, and marks a new step in Jagex’s ambition to expand the “RuneScape” world beyond the gaming ecosystem. Related Stories 'Gremlins 3' Delayed to 2028 by Warner Bros. Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta 'Don't You Dare' Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: 'Do Not Cave' “For 25 years, our players have helped shape ‘RuneScape’s’ extraordinary world, its characters and its stories,” said Bellamy. “When we talk about the future of ‘RuneScape,’ we don’t just mean games. We see huge potential to bring Gielinor to life in new ways, both for the millions who already know and love it and for a whole new audience. It’s early days, but we’re excited to explore that potential with Charlie and the team at Lyrical Animation, and we wanted our players to be the first to know.” Popular on Variety Jagex first released “RuneScape” in 2001, and it has grown into a massively popular fantasy multiplayer online role-playing game. Through quests, combat, exploration and cooperative adventures, players can forge their own paths through the medieval fantasy world of Gielinor. The franchise now includes “RuneScape,” “Old School RuneScape” and “ RuneScape Dragonwilds .” White is a longtime member of the “RuneScape” community and has amassed more than 25 million followers across his channels and platforms. “I’ve been playing RuneScape for 22 years, and it’s one of my favorite IPs ever,” said White. “I’m so excited to be working with the team on this project.” “RuneScape has such a unique storytelling voice, at once laugh-out-loud funny and effortlessly insightful,” said Daniel Dominguez, creative director of Lyrical Animation. “To be allowed to help bring that to life for its millions of fans alongside our dear friend Charlie again is a dream come true.” Lyrical Animation will produce the project alongside White’s Meatier Productions. Development is in its early stages, and the company expects to reveal more details in 2027. articles.title: Jeremy Strong Defends Method Acting, Says He Doesn’t Feel the Need to ‘Apologize’ to Co-Stars Who May Think ‘I’m Taking It Too Seriously’
articles.full_text: Oct 3, 2026 4:05pm PT Jeremy Strong Defends Method Acting, Says He Doesn’t Feel the Need to ‘Apologize’ to Co-Stars Who May Think ‘I’m Taking It Too Seriously’ By Payton Turkeltaub Plus Icon Payton Turkeltaub Latest Jeremy Strong Defends Method Acting, Says He Doesn’t Feel the Need to ‘Apologize’ to Co-Stars Who May Think ‘I’m Taking It Too Seriously’ 16 hours ago Aaron Sorkin Says It ‘Never Occurred’ to Him That Jesse Eisenberg Wouldn’t Play Mark Zuckerberg in ‘The Social Reckoning,’ Claims the Paycheck Was a ‘Disincentive’ 21 hours ago Box Office: ‘Digger’ Nosediving With $3.4 Million on Opening Day, ‘Verity’ Lands at No. 1 With $15.1 Million on Friday 23 hours ago See All Getty Images Jeremy Strong , now infamous for his dedication to method acting, recently admitted he doesn’t feel the “need to apologize” to those he works with who may feel he is taking the process “too seriously” on a recent episode of The New Yorker Radio Hour podcast . The actor, who stepped into the role of tech billionaire Mark Zuckerberg for Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” out Oct. 9, was asked by podcast host and New Yorker editor-in-chief David Remnick how much he feels his method approach is helpful to the director and fellow castmates when filming, or, on the opposite end of the spectrum, how much it might throw them off. Related Stories 'Gremlins 3' Delayed to 2028 by Warner Bros. Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta 'Don't You Dare' Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: 'Do Not Cave' “I think I can’t really speak to that,” Strong began. “Of course, it is never my intention to interfere with anyone else’s experience or anyone else’s way of working. First, do no harm, right? But commit to fucking what you’re doing, and utterly.” Remnick then interjects to ask whether Strong gets frustrated with others on set who may not be so committed, to which the “Succession” actor responds, “No, just meaning that I’m just there to commit utterly to serving the material.” Popular on Variety He continued: “So, if some people feel that I’m taking it too seriously, or it changes the molecules in the room in a way that makes something uncomfortable, I guess that’s something that I don’t feel that I need to apologize for, because I believe, and I think the directors that I work with all believe, that it’s in service of the material, and I personally think that a lot of the reactions to it are of a personal nature.” Strong’s method acting antics have long made headlines. In Sept., Sorkin told The New York Times that Strong was treating his co-stars “the way he imagines” Zuckerberg would treat them during filming. Strong’s “Succession” co-star Brian Cox has repeatedly criticized the actor’s method acting, calling it “ fucking annoying ,” though he also noted in a later interview that Strong “was wonderful to act with.” “I had no argument with Jeremy’s acting,” Cox said. “He would be an even better actor if he just got rid of that so there would be much more inclusiveness in what he did.” Strong, Jeremy Allen White, Mikey Madison, Bill Burr, Betty Gilpin and Billy Magnussen star in “ The Social Reckoning ,” which follows whistleblower Frances Haugen, who teams up with Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz to expose the inner workings of Zuckerberg’s Facebook. articles.title: Paul Rudd Says He Stopped Bringing His Phone to Film Sets Because He’s ‘Addicted Like Everybody Else’: ‘They’re Facilitating Our Own Destruction’
articles.full_text: Oct 3, 2026 4:43pm PT Paul Rudd Says He Stopped Bringing His Phone to Film Sets Because He’s ‘Addicted Like Everybody Else’: ‘They’re Facilitating Our Own Destruction’ By Antonio Ferme Plus Icon Antonio Ferme Latest Paul Rudd Says He Stopped Bringing His Phone to Film Sets Because He’s ‘Addicted Like Everybody Else’: ‘They’re Facilitating Our Own Destruction’ 15 hours ago Tony Gilroy Says Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Will ‘Destroy’ a ‘Healthy and Beautiful Business’ in ‘The Name of Venture Capital’: ‘It’s Tragic’ 19 hours ago Sylvester Stallone Says Superhero Movie Bodies Aren’t ‘Natural’ and Taking Steroids to Bulk Up Is Like ‘Putting on Part of a Costume’ 5 days ago See All Getty Images Paul Rudd plays the moderator of the first-ever meeting dedicated to solving America’s climate crisis in “ A Statement ,” the latest film from Oscar-winning director Tom McCarthy . Set at a Florida beachside resort in 1980, the film follows 20 experts who spend a weekend in a conference room and — analogous to “12 Angry Men” — hash out their differences over how to draft a statement to Congress about the effects of carbon dioxide emissions on the climate. Related Stories Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta 'Don't You Dare' Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: 'Do Not Cave' 'Gremlins 3' Delayed to 2028 by Warner Bros. Rudd found himself more connected to the sprawling ensemble cast, which includes Paul Giamatti, Tatiana Maslany and John Turturro, by leaving his smartphone in his trailer, a practice he claims he’s now followed for some time. “I don’t go to sets with a phone. I haven’t done that for a while now,” he told Variety Saturday evening during the film’s world premiere at the New York Film Festival . “It’s important to put it down. Anytime. They’re horrible things. I’m addicted to it like everybody else. They’re facilitating our own destruction.” Popular on Variety Rudd revealed that McCarthy enforced a “very strict no phones policy” on the set of “A Statement,” which he found brought his castmates closer together and made filming feel more like a play. “The world has changed since cell phones have existed. We don’t look at each other or talk to each other quite the same way,” Rudd said. “Now, [with the phone ban], we were forced to really spend time with each other and talk. Working on a movie set in 1980, we’re dressed in a certain kind of way. It felt like, ‘Oh, yeah. I remember this. This feels like it used to feel when people sat around and spoke to one another.’” Amy Ryan, whose character delivers a sobering wake-up call to the group at the film’s climax, encouraged other filmmakers to follow McCarthy’s lead. The absence of notifications and doomscrolling, she said, “definitely made the work much more rich.” “What happens is there’s a five-minute break and people are connected. ‘Hey, what are you doing? How’s your morning? What do you think of this scene?’” Ryan explained. “I equate it to like when you quit sugar. In three days, it’s out of your system. You don’t miss it!
