articles.title: Why ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Isn’t Live on the West Coast
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 30, 2026 6:53am 'Dancing With the Stars' season 35. Disney/Christopher Willard Logo text Every Dancing With the Stars episode used to begin with the iconic introduction: “Live from Hollywood, it’s Dancing With the Stars !” But for those tuning in from the West Coast, the show isn’t live at all. Season 35 of Dancing With the Stars airs Tuesdays at 8 p.m. for both coasts, simulcasting across ABC and Disney+, streaming the next day on Hulu. New episodes begin filming in Los Angeles at 5 p.m. PT, airing immediately for the East Coast audience at 8 p.m. ET, but not until 8 p.m. PT. for the West Coast audience. Related Stories TV 'Dancing With the Stars' Sets Super Bowl Night TV 'Dancing With the Stars' Caps Yacht Rock Night With a Shock Elimination: See the Scores, Who Went Home The discrepancy in air time is a pain point West Coast viewers who are easily spoiled on social media about how couples fared. Voting also only takes place during the live taping, meaning West Coasters have to “blindly vote” for their favorite celebrities and remember to send in their votes in from roughly 5 p.m. to 6:45 p.m. if they want to be counted. Dancing With the Stars has historically utilized this format for airing the show, but that hasn’t made viewers any less frustrated. Season 31 was exclusively streamed on Disney+, and began at 5 p.m. PT; the show returned to ABC for season 32, though, and has since retained its method of airing at 8 p.m. for both coasts. “I’m angry and sad that The West Coast cannot watch the premiere live!” reads the title of a Reddit thread from 2023 when Dancing With the Stars shifted back to ABC for its 32nd season. The same user wrote, “Please help me understand why The West Coast cannot watch the premiere or future episodes of Dancing With The Stars live on Disney plus? It makes no sense and I’m furious! It almost makes me want to boycott the show.” A recent Reddit thread left another user with the same confusion about the show’s air time: “The show does not air live on the west coast. Not entirely sure WHY, but it doesn’t air live. So the show has happened, you have to vote blind, and you’ll get to watch at it at your appointed time.” The reason Dancing With the Stars doesn’t air live for its West Coast audience stems back to local news and the coveted primetime programming slots. Evening news is a major primetime program, and airing hours belong to differing identities, meaning ABC can’t just shift Dancing With the Stars into that 5 p.m. PT slot. One outlier to this more-often-than-not rule is Saturday Night Live ; the late-night show airs at 8:30 p.m. PT/11:30 pm ET on NBC, also simulcasting on Peacock. However, since it airs somewhat later for the West Coast and on Saturday nights, local news won’t be disrupted by showing new episodes. The Hollywood Reporter recently spoke with showrunner Conrad Green for a DWTS season 34 finale piece , and when THR asked Green why Dancing With the Stars doesn’t air or stream live for the West Coast, he clarified that the question is moreso “a discussion with the affiliates who show the show across the network [ABC] all over the country. “It’s a big issue for them is if everyone starts watching the show at 5 p.m. when it airs. If you’re in L.A. and you watch at 5 p.m. when it airs [at 8 p.m.] on the East Coast, then it’s going to massively affect the people who will watch the show when it comes over to these different territories and those markets,” he said. “The affiliates are hugely important in the bigger picture for the overall economic structure of the show and for the history of ABC and all of those things.” Green said he understands the frustration from West Coast viewers, “but the good thing is, you can still vote. You’re just basically voting blind. But if you love someone, you can set your alarm for five o’clock and vote 10 times for them on both methods and make sure your voice is heard. It just requires a bit of forward planning ( laughs ).” THR also asked if Green knew why every Dancing With the Stars season wasn’t available to stream on Disney+. (As of Sept. 2026, only seasons 31-35 are available to watch.) “I haven’t had that conversation with Disney+, but the rights to restream the show are expensive; the licensing terms for the music we use on the show and all of those kind of things are pretty significant,” he said. “So I guess there’s a calculation to be made about how much interest is there in previous seasons versus the cost of having them on a platform.” West Coast viewers who aren’t able to tune in live can keep up with Dancing With the Stars by following along with THR ’s weekly live recaps . Or wait until 8 p.m. PT to watch — but make sure you get your votes in by 6:45 p.m. PT. THR reached out to ABC for comment, but did not hear back by the time of publication. THR

articles.title: ‘Digger’ Ad Fires Back at Critics With Tom Cruise Character Declaring “F**k Those People”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 30, 2026 7:04am Ross Hatt with Tom Cruise (right) in 'Digger,' a Warner Bros. Pictures release. Courtesy Warner Bros. Pictures Don’t listen to those hoity-toity critics. Go see Digger and make up your own mind . That’s the gist behind Warner Bros.’ online ad for the new Alejandro G. Iñárritu film, which is receiving some scathing reviews (and, to be fair, many rather positive ones, as well). “Decide for yourself,” declares the text introducing the ad (below). The ad then kicks off with a critic quote saying Digger “is an ambitious film sure to polarize audiences,” before Tom Cruise ’s titular character exclaims, “You know what? Fuck those people!” Related Stories Movies Tom Cruise Slams AI, Defends $125M 'Digger' as Reviews Divide Critics: "People Want Real Things" Movies Tom Cruise 'Digger' Reviews Are Brutally Split: From "Insufferable" to "Terrific" Other contrasting critic quote messages flash across the screen, juxtaposing the words “Unpleasant” and “Masterpiece,” and then, “Baffling” and “Brilliant,” and “Insufferable” and “Magnificent.” The ad ends with Cruise’s character saying, “Never be afraid to tell the truth — whatever that is.” It’s a pretty bold ad for a rather bold film, essentially telling moviegoers: “Some people really dislike this movie, so go buy a ticket to find out why and, hey, maybe you’ll agree — or not.” The studio must have had some idea that the film was going to get pilloried in some corners as the ad went live even before the review embargo broke Tuesday. The $125 million production stars a nearly unrecognizable Cruise playing an oblivious oil tycoon whose drilling in Greenland dislodges an ice shelf from a glacier that’s going to cause a global disaster. He must race to prove that he’s humanity’s savior before the ecological accident wreaks havoc on the planet. At least, that’s the film’s ostensible setup. Digger contains a twist upending its narrative that’s complicated the reviews and discussion as critics have been tiptoeing around describing the film’s actual meta storyline. Decide for yourself. DIGGER – in theaters and IMAX FRIDAY. Tickets on sale now. https://t.co/Z1IpSpFnXd pic.twitter.com/e5ID4WUxbL — Warner Bros. (@warnerbros) September 29, 2026 Some critics have praised the film as a bold and timely story with incredible production design and features Cruise clearly giving the role everything he’s got in a bombastic performance. But others have slammed the effort as a pretentious and obnoxious slog. The Hollywood Reporter ‘s David Rooney wrote that Digger is “a climate crisis satire so smug and bombastic it makes Adam McKay’s Don’t Look Up seem almost innocuous. Digger is basically what happens when you put two outsize egos together with nobody holding the reins to keep their most self-indulgent impulses in check … so meta that you watch in excruciating weariness as [the film] disappears up its own ass and then realize to your dismay that there’s another eardrum-shattering hour left to endure … It’s difficult to imagine mainstream audiences ever wanting to be a part of this bludgeoning ordeal.” While reviews are still coming in, so far Digger has a 53 percent positive rating on Rotten Tomatoes across 113 reviews, a split that almost perfectly reflects the polarized response to the film. Digger opens in theaters Friday, Oct. 2. THR

articles.title: John Grover, Film Editor on Six James Bond Movies, Dies at 87
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Rhett Bartlett Plus Icon Rhett Bartlett dialmformovies Follow Sign Up View All September 30, 2026 7:07am John Grover Courtesy of British Film Editors John Grover, the British film editor who helped assemble a half-dozen James Bond movies and spent six long months breathing heavily at the behest of Stanley Kubrick for 2001: A Space Odyssey , has died. He was 87. Grover, a longtime vice chairman of the British Film Editors who received their Lifetime Achievement Award in April, died Monday at his home in Buckinghamshire, England, following a short illness, his son, Tim, told The Hollywood Reporter . Grover served as the film editor on the 007 films For Your Eyes Only (1981), The Living Daylights (1987) and Licence to Kill (1989) and also helped put together The Spy Who Loved Me (1977), Moonraker (1979) and Octopussy (1983) . Related Stories Movies Two-Time Oscar Winner and 'Atonement' Writer Christopher Hampton to Lead Tallinn Film Fest Jury Business From 'F1' to 'Slow Horses' to 'Call My Agent!': Mediawan Executives Take Madrid Spotlight In all, he did six films starring Bond star Roger Moore , including The Wild Geese (1978 ) and The Sea Wolves (1980), and also cut The Final Option (1982), Tobe Hooper’s Lifeforce (1985), the 1984 NBC miniseries The First Olympics and what he said was his favorite film, Jim Henson’s classic Labyrinth (1986). Early in his career, Grover worked as an uncredited assistant editor for Robert Wise on The Haunting (1963), for David Lean on Doctor Zhivago (1965), for John Frankenheimer on Grand Prix (1966), for Kubrick on 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) and for Herbert Ross on Goodbye, Mr. Chips (1969). During a 2016 editing conference, Grover talked about his awful experience dealing with Kubrick, the manically perfectionist director of 2001 . “I spent six months of my life with that idiot,” Grover said. “Although he was a supposedly good filmmaker, he was mad. He’d kill the artist by [saying] keep going again and again and again.” “I think [ 2001 is] a load of rubbish, it’s the most boring, long, stretched out [film]. I mean, OK, it was very clever [with its] use of original music, which we had to get back from Germany, ‘The Blue Danube’ and all that. It’s very ahead of its time; what actually we were doing in imagination actually happened, and the space stations are now up there.” In his 2018 book Space Odyssey: Stanley Kubrick, Arthur C. Clarke, and the Making of a Masterpiece, Michael Benson wrote that Grover accompanied editorial assistant David de Wilde to record Kubrick — battling a head cold — breathing heavily. The audio was then used to accentuate tense scenes featuring astronauts Dave Bowman (Keir Dullea) and Frank Poole (Gary Lockwood). “With Grover’s help, they ran a microphone from the soundboard in the theater and positioned it next to Kubrick’s face, after which he lowered the helmet onto his shoulders,” Benson explained. But Grover claimed that it was he, not the director, who did the laborious inhaling and exhaling that’s heard in the movie. “All I did was breathing for six months,” he said. “[Kubrick] wanted it done with the helmet … He’d sit right at the front … with a notebook, and you’d run the sequence and he’d be writing and he’d come back and say, ‘OK, John, very good, do it again.’ You had to watch [the film] pretending you were doing exercises and straining and moving things.” A spokesperson for the British editors guild said “both Stanley K. and John Grover were recorded for the ‘heavy breathing’ — and it is thought that the recording of John was the one used for the film.” What is known for certain is that the breaths were recorded simultaneously on two rolls of 35mm film, in 10-minute takes, so that Grover could more easily cut between them when removing ambient noise. A decade later, Grover was assembly editor on another space-set adventure, Lewis Gilbert’s Moonraker. Working alongside editor John Glen, they cobbled together the final cut of that Bond movie from 800,000 feet of film. It took 10 months — until the day before the premiere — to be completed. On The Spy Who Loved Me , Grover was tasked with editing the iconic pre-credit sequence that culminates with Moore skiing and then parachuting off a cliff. With Glen stationed with the second-unit team in Switzerland and then in Baffin Island, Canada, Grover waited back in the studio for the rushes. “I was in the cutting room preparing, waiting for film and it didn’t come in, because they couldn’t shoot it,” he said. After a 10-day wait because of atrocious weather, the crew was able to film the spectacular jump during a 15-minute break in the harsh conditions. In his final edit, Grover snuck in a music box he was given on the set of Doctor Zhivago that played “Lara’s Theme” and was used by Anya Amasova (Barbara Bach) in The Spy Who Loved Me . Composer Maurice Jarre received royalties for the brief use of his leitmotif. Born on Oct. 24, 1938, in Barnet, Middlesex, England, Grover enlisted in National Service as a teenager. Upon his return, he started as a numbering boy at MGM Studios, where his uncle was supervising editor, earning 6 pounds 10 shillings a week. Grover said he enjoyed working with Lean, who was opinionated yet open to collaboration. “He’d say, ‘Get everybody in here, let’s have a look at this, what do you think?’ ” he noted. “He’d listen to you, provided you had an answer.” He recalled that Zhivago’s 70mm Los Angeles premiere was interrupted by a loud bang from the projection booth at the first change-over reel. A gear box had exploded, causing the screen to plunge into darkness for eight minutes. A larger disaster unfolded during the postproduction of The Living Daylights when a work print containing dialogue sequences was leaked and circulated on VHS. Grover, who co-edited Timothy Dalton’s 007 debut with Peter Davies, was called into the office of producer Albert Broccoli and associate producer Tom Pevsner. “That was really frightening,” he remembered in 2018. “Of course we were the No. 1 suspects; we were in the cutting rooms, we were the only one who had access to it.” But Grover revealed that whenever parts of the film were sent away, he would mark a single frame with an identifiable symbol and document who it was sent to. “We found out it had been copied and duplicated in New York by the trailer company, which immediately went bust,” he said. In addition to his son, survivors include his wife of 62 years, Jenny; daughter Camilla; five grandchildren; and two great-grandchildren. After his retirement, Grover recalled the formula that Bond producers and directors used that helped make the franchise an everlasting success. “Bad language was unacceptable, but some violence and sexual innuendo was OK,” he said. “Family entertainment was their motto. Grandparents could always take their grandchildren to see the films to enjoy them together.” Moore was his favorite Bond actor, and his favorite 007 scene was the car and circus-train chase on railway tracks in Octopussy , he said. “For God’s sake, we got on those pictures, and for nine months I basically would never go home,” he added. “So you had to have a good family behind you.” THR

articles.title: Two-Time Oscar Winner and ‘Atonement’ Writer Christopher Hampton to Lead Tallinn Film Fest Jury
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 30, 2026 7:15am Christopher Hampton Courtesy of Gerard Philippe Mabillard The Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) on Wednesday unveiled a five-member jury for its 30th edition’s official competition. Two-time Oscar-winning screenwriter and director Christopher Hampton will lead the jury, joined by Lebanese producer Myriam Sassine, U.S. cinematographer and visual effects specialist David Stump, French producer Julie Billy and Estonian actress Tiina Tauraite. Hampton won Academy Awards for best adapted screenplay for Dangerous Liaisons and The Father . His other film credits include Atonement , The Quiet American and A Dangerous Method , while his work for the stage includes Les Liaisons Dangereuses and Sunset Boulevard . He has also written and directed three feature films: Carrington , The Secret Agent and Imagining Argentina . Sassine’s credits include Costa Brava, Lebanon , 1982 , Dancing on the Edge of a Volcano and Diaries From Lebanon . In 2016, she co-founded the Maskoon Fantastic Film Festival, dedicated to genre cinema in the Arab region. Stump is known for his work on Breaking Bad , The Morning Show , Quantum of Solace and the first two X-Men films. His honors include an Emmy Award and an Academy Award for Scientific and Technical Achievement. Billy is a Paris-based producer who founded June Films in 2020 after working with such filmmakers as Jonas Carpignano, Nadav Lapid and Yorgos Lanthimos. Her recent productions include Hafsia Herzi’s The Little Sister , which premiered in competition at Cannes in 2025 and won the Queer Palm and best actress award, and Emma Benestan’s Animale . Tauraite has appeared in such films as Autumn Ball , The Temptation of St. Tony , The Spy and the Poet and 8 Views of Lake Biwa . The 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival will take place Nov. 6-22. It will open with Viesturs Kairišs’ Ulya , a co-production between Latvia , Estonia, Poland and Lithuania that world-premiered in the Un Certain Regard program of the Cannes Film Festival earlier this year. Related Stories Movies John Grover, Film Editor on Six James Bond Movies, Dies at 87 Business From 'F1' to 'Slow Horses' to 'Call My Agent!': Mediawan Executives Take Madrid Spotlight THR

articles.title: Netflix’s ‘Wednesday’ Season 3 Wraps Filming, But Fans Still Have a Long Wait
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 30, 2026 7:45am Jenna Ortega in 'Wednesday' season two. Courtesy of Netflix Logo text A woeful update for Wednesday fans wondering when they’ll get a third season. The good news is the third season of the Netflix supernatural hit has just wrapped production. The bad news is that still means a long wait for the new episodes given the show’s extensive post-production effects work. There was a three-year gap between season one (2022) and season two (2025). The wait for season three will almost certainly be a bit shorter, with a return next fall seeming very plausible given the second season had an eight-month turnaround after filming wrapped. Netflix declined to add any other updates about the show, which stars Jenna Ortega as Wednesday Addams, a dour, sleuthing student at Nevermore Academy. The rest of the season three cast includes Eva Green, Emma Myers, Hunter Doohan, Joy Sunday, Moosa Mostafa, Georgie Farmer, Isaac Ordonez, Billie Piper, Luyanda Unati Lewis-Nyawo, Victor Dorobantu, Evie Templeton, Oscar Morgan, Kennedy Moyer with Luis Guzmán, Catherine Zeta-Jones, Joanna Lumley, Winona Ryder, Chris Sarandon, Lena Headey, Andrew McCarthy, James Lance, and Fred Armisen. The debut season of Wednesday became Netflix’s most-watched English-language original series of all time (the first season of Squid Game holds the top spot among all shows). Season two also performed well, ranking No. 6 among all-time English-language TV seasons. THR

articles.title: San Quentin Film Festival 2026 Lineup Revealed (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 30, 2026 7:57am Prisoners at dinner, Michigan City, Ind. 1907 Library of Congress The Hollywood Reporter can exclusively reveal the official selections for the 2026 San Quentin Film Festival (SQFF26). The third-annual installment is set for Oct. 22–23 at the San Quentin Rehabilitation Center in Marin County, Calif. — SQFF26 remains the only film festival held inside of a U.S. prison. It’s there for good reason: SQFF honors the creative work of current and former incarcerated filmmakers, “spotlighting stories of resilience, redemption and artistic expression from behind the walls, in competition with filmmakers from across the country and around the world,” per the festival. Related Stories Movies Oscar-Nominated Documentary 'Cutting Through Rocks' Among Athena Film Festival Award Winners (Exclusive) Movies A New York Startup Just Threw a Splashy Event to Hail the Future of AI Movies “When this festival began, we dreamed of bringing films from different prisons and countries into conversation with one another, while giving formerly incarcerated artists a place for their voices to be heard,” said Cori Thomas, SQFF co-founder and artistic director. “Filmmakers who explore incarceration through their work are part of that conversation, too. I’m thrilled that artists from Cameroon, South Africa, Italy, Spain, and Germany are joining American filmmakers this year. And it is especially meaningful to present special selections from five prisons, including San Quentin. Together, these films create the vibrant chorus of voices we hoped this festival would become.” The 2026 program has a preview night, Wednesday, Oct. 21, when the first hour of Lynn Novick’s upcoming four-part PBS documentary series Crime and Punishment in America , which features one hell of an impressive voice cast, will screen for an audience of San Quentin residents (we would formerly call them inmates). Directed by Novick ( The Vietnam War , Hemingway , College Behind Bars , The U.S. and the Holocaust ) and executive produced by Ken Burns and Sam Pollard, the eight-hour series “explores the history of criminal justice in America, from the pre-colonial period through 21st-century mass incarceration, examining how the intertwined forces of law, power, race and class have shaped and reflected the American experience across four centuries,” according to its synopsis. A panel discussion with Novick; SQFF co-founder and series consulting producer Rahsaan Thomas, and “survivor advocates” Annie and Jess Nichol will follow. The conversation will be moderated by Kevin D. Sawyer, former editor-in-chief of San Quentin News and recipient of the SQFF24 Best Pitch Award for his documentary project, The History of Prison Journalism . “The San Quentin Film Festival is an incredible event doing vital, transformative work, bridging communities through the profound power of storytelling and film,” Novick said in a statement. “We feel deeply honored and lucky to share our series in such a unique and important space.” Narrated by Keith David, Crime and Punishment in America features voice performances by Samuel L. Jackson, Laura Linney, Bobby Cannavale, Matthew Rhys, Michael Stuhlbarg, David Hyde Pierce and BD Wong. The series is produced by Lucas Frank, Vanessa González-Block, Lynn Novick and Prisca Pointdujour. It will air over four consecutive nights on PBS beginning Nov. 16, 2026, and will stream on all PBS digital platforms for four weeks. Jail Time Records. Courtesy of Jail Time Records The 2026 San Quentin Film Festival received 75 submissions for its 2026 competition. The Short Film categories, open exclusively to currently and formerly incarcerated filmmakers, are judged by SQFF’s Industry Jury, the Feature category is evaluated by an Inside Jury composed of San Quentin residents, and the Long Short category is judged by an Inside Jury of residents at Central California Women’s Facility. (“Long Short” is new this year and is comprised of films running up to 40 minutes — the in-betweeners.) The fest’s pitch competition received an additional 68 submissions from incarcerated writers at 20 facilities across America (and one in Panama — the first ever from outside the U.S.). SQFF’s Industry Jury selects the winners. Nearly 400 people will attend the two-day festival — half entertainment industry professionals and the other half San Quentin Rehabilitation Center residents. Those who cannot attend will be able to screen the official selections from Oct. 26 to Nov. 8 via screening passes available for sale. Incarcerated people in California will be able to watch the films through the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) institutional channel. The SQFF26 official selections are below by category. articles.title: ‘Unmasking a Monster’: Star, EP, and ID President on Using AI Masks to Perfect Their Aileen Wuornos Look
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 30, 2026 8:15am Actress Morag Peacock before an AI mask made her look like Aileen Wuornos in 'Unmasking a Monster: Aileen Wuornos' Courtesy of Investigation Discovery You’ve never see Aileen Wuornos like this. Or perhaps it is more accurate to say you’ve seen her exactly like this. Investigation Discovery’s new documentary series Unmasking a Monster: Aileen Wuornos utilized an AI -mask tool in post-production to make actress Morag Peacock look exactly like the infamous serial killer. The docuseries then did the same with nine other actors and their real-life counterparts. This specific deployment of AI is a first for the industry, the series’ executive producer Stephen Dost told The Hollywood Reporter . The vice president of content at Arrow Media had been “aware” of the digital mask tech, which he describes as “really advanced motion capture” — Dost just needed a use case. “We were asking ourselves, ‘If you could show someone as they were at the time, what kind of story would make sense for that?'” Dost recalled. “I just kept coming back again and again to Aileen Wuornos, and probably the reason for that is that if you’re going to show someone’s face, there’s got to be a reason. It can’t be for the sake of showing off tech.” “With [Wuornos], if you look at her face, you can see the the suffering that went behind it. You can see the abuse that she went went through,” he continued. “It’s a bit like the story of her life you can read on her face, and she went through hell.” There were other reasons. For starters, archival footage of Wuornos is “very limited,” Dost said. Plus, traditional TV reenactments are flawed, ID president Jason Sarlanis told THR . “Audiences want realism and access to the truth behind these stories. Reenactments have been part of this genre from the start, but they’ve also been an obstacle to believability,” Sarlanis said. “By augmenting our actors’ performances with digital prosthetics, we can bring viewers into these key moments with a new level of authenticity.” “In a traditional reenactment, you would actually try to avoid [the actor’s] face. You would try to be abstract,” Dost said. “But this was an opportunity to look right at her — uncomfortably — at the humanity that was there.” Dost just needed a human with a face. OK, it was a bit more than that. The docuseries needed a capable actress that, with 90 minutes of hair and makeup (and one prosthetic tooth), could kind of look like Wuornos. “Where the tech was at the time, we needed someone who had basically the same face shape,” Dost said. Peacock’s face worked for the assignment. It was her eyes that did the heavy lifting. “We would get through a take, and you could hear a pin drop at the end. We’re not seeing any of the VFX — it felt like we were in the room with Aileen Wuornos,” Dost said. Peacock played it as if her own face would make the finished product. “I’m going for as close to her as possible, and then the the technology bit kind of left my head after that. I was like, ‘This is the job that I’m supposed to do. I’ll do mine to the best of my ability, and then after that, it’s over to them. Hopefully, they get what they want, and everyone’s happy,” she told THR . “So, I knew about it — it was probably there in the back of my mind, but it was more about…matching her mannerisms, her quirks, the way she expressed with her eyes and things like that.” Peacock says she was “pleasantly surprised” by the trailer, which is the first time she saw footage from the final cut. “I can definitely recognize myself underneath it,” Peacock said. Her family did too. Aileen Wuornos: The Selling of a Serial Killer, Aileen Wuornos, 1992. Strand Releasing/Courtesy Everett Collection. AI is Hollywood’s hottest-button issue this side of Paramount/Warner Bros., the latter of which owns Investigation Discovery. At first, Peacock had reservations about accepting the Wuornos gig — and not because of the whole serial killer thing. “Probably much like most people, as soon as you see ‘AI,’ you kind of go, ‘Hold on,’ you know? So it was really important that myself, my agent, we discussed it, and we got to grips with what it was that was being asked of me, and what was going to be the end result,” Peacock said. “I’m not redundant in any way, I haven’t been cloned. There isn’t an AI persona that’s being created — nothing like that’s happening,” she continued. “Once I’ve kind of got to, ‘Well, yeah, it’s basically kind of like CGI…and it’s still me.’ Then, yeah, I was comfortable with that.” One thing AI was definitely not was a shortcut. “Anyone who tells you that using AI speeds things up is wrong,” Dost said. “It slows things down by a lot — especially if you’re going to do it the right way.” It took three years to “ethically” use AI to make Unmasking a Monster , Dost said. He shared his ethical roadmap with us: Getting consent from the real people (homicide investigators, defense attorney, private investigator, Wuornos’ friend), as well as from the actors playing them. Not using the tech in cases where we could not get consent, like Mike Joyner, who died after giving his interview, or Tyria Moore, Aileen’s ex-girlfriend, who did not participate in the documentary. Ensuring authenticity throughout our scenes. Everything in the scenes comes directly from the transcripts, police records, and memories of our interview subjects. Nothing is invented for dramatic purposes. Being transparent about the process and the technology used. With interviews like these and behind-the-scenes videos to come, we want to be as transparent with our audience as we can about the process we used to visualize these new stories. Sarlanis said ID takes the “responsibility of every creative choice we make in crafting these complex stories very seriously.” “We knew that these tools, if used improperly, could and should warrant pushback. That’s why we took just as much time and care into developing the guidelines for how we would use the tech as we did in developing the capabilities of what the tech could do,” he continued. “Our focus was always on using these tools to empower the creativity of our filmmakers and in doing so we believe we’ve unlocked a way for the audience to experience this story in a uniquely authentic way.” (L to R) Sarah Paulson as Aileen Wuornos, Jessie Lee as Shelby in episode 406 of Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story. Courtesy of Netflix Dost and Peacock are not the only duo tackling Wuornos this month. About two weeks prior, Ryan Murphy’s Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story premiered on Netflix. Though Borden (played by Ella Beatty) is the star of the show, Wuornos (Sarah Paulson) is a substantial recurring character. The timing is “totally coincidental,” Dost said, but ultimately “a good thing.” Buzz about Monster can only help pique interest in Unmasking a Monster , and the two series don’t really play the same game. “Although they do scenes that are directly pulled from transcripts, they also imagine her as a Lizzie Borden admirer, which obviously she wasn’t,” Dost said. “Probably if she knew anything about the real Lizzie Borden, [Wuornos] would have hated Lizzie Borden. But it’s fiction, so that’s OK.” Between Paulson and Oscar winner Charlize Theron (for portraying Wuornos in 2003 film Monster ), Peacock is in good company — even if she didn’t previously know who Paulson is. (She’s since Googled her). “Everything Sarah Paulson does is amazing, and no, luckily Morag was not aware at the time that she would be up against Sarah Paulson,” Dost said, “because who would want that as a challenge?” Unmasking a Monster: Aileen Wuornos premieres tonight on ID and HBO Max. THR

articles.title: ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Trailer Plunges Ethan Hawke’s Lee into a New Conspiracy
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All September 30, 2026 8:22am Tommy Lee Jones and Ethan Hawke in 'The Lowdown' season two. Share Brown/FX Logo text The season two trailer for The Lowdown suggests Lee Raybon’s ( Ethan Hawke ) circumstances may have improved a little — but also that it won’t last. The critically hailed FX series from creator Sterlin Harjo ( Reservation Dogs ) puts Lee into the middle of a new investigation in Tulsa involving, as he puts it to Keith David’s Marty, “two confirmed murders and the whole sheriff’s department. It goes all the way to the top.” Lee is drawn into the case by Ginger ( Betty Gilpin ), a public defender who’s dealing with a mystery involving one of her clients. Also complicating matters is the return of Lee’s estranged father, Lee Sr. ( Tommy Lee Jones ), who shows up in a red baseball cap that references a Bible verse (Psalms 107:29, “He calms the storm, so that its waves are still,” per the New King James version). Watch the trailer below. Related Stories TV 'American Horror Story' Is Back With 13: Here's How All the Seasons Connect (So Far) TV Ryan Murphy Reveals Ariana Grande's 'Scream Queens' Role in 'AHS' Season 13 That Never Happened (Exclusive) Season two of The Lowdown will also feature Kaniehtiio Horn, Ryan Kiera Armstrong, Killer Mike, Michael Hitchcock, Macon Blair, Siena East, Cody Lightning and Jude Barnett reprising their roles. Martha Plimpton guest stars (season one star Kyle MacLachlan also makes a brief appearance in the trailer), and FX advises viewers to keep an eye out for “a number of familiar faces” from Harjo’s Reservation Dogs . Paulina Alexis (Willie Jack) made a brief appearance in the show’s first season. Harjo is the showrunner on The Lowdown and executive produces with Garrett Basch, Ethan Hawke, Ryan Hawke, Duffy Boudreau and Scott Teems. FX Productions is the studio. Season two premieres Oct. 14 with two episodes on FX and Hulu. THR

articles.title: Tribeca Festival Sets 2027 Dates, Submission Deadlines
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All September 30, 2026 8:41am The Tribeca Festival Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images After celebrating its landmark 25th anniversary edition, the Tribeca Festival isn’t going anywhere. The festival has announced that its 26th installment will take place from June 3-12, 2027. Submissions are now open across the festival’s programming categories: features, shorts and music videos, Tribeca TV, Tribeca digital creators, Tribeca games, Tribeca podcasts and Tribeca X. The 25th anniversary festival, which took place from June 3-14 earlier this year, featured a record 104 feature film world premieres and more than 240 live events. Highlights included Bruce Springsteen receiving the Harry Belafonte award and participating in a conversation and performance with Bono and Patti Smith as well as the premieres of Madonna’s Confessions II cinematic experience , a companion piece to her Confessions II album released in July; Katy Perry’s concert film The Lifetimes Tour: Live From Paris ; the Katie Holmes-Joshua Jackson rom-com Happy Hours , marking a much-anticipated onscreen reunion for the Dawson’s Creek stars; the all-AI Iran film Dreams of Violets ; and the compelling Margo Martindale-led trucker drama The Long Haul . Related Stories Movies David Cross, Thomas Mann, Hasan Minhaj's Comedy 'Lucy Schulman' From Ellie Sachs Lands Release (Exclusive) News Robert De Niro, 9/11 and a Night at the Movies I'll Never Forget “Building on a record year at the box office, we cannot wait to welcome our passionate audiences back to New York City for our 26th year to discover and delight in the incredible stories, creativity, and cultural experiences that make Tribeca so special each June,” Tribeca Enterprises CEO Rebecca Glashow said in a statement. “At its heart, Tribeca has always been about bringing audiences and artists together to experience the new voices shaping our culture.” Festival director and senior vp, programming, Cara Cusumano, added: “Last year’s record-breaking submissions helped make our 25th anniversary one of the most remarkable editions in Tribeca’s history, and we can’t wait to see what comes next. Tribeca was built on the belief that the next great storyteller could come from anywhere, and we look forward to meeting the voices who will define the 2027 Festival.” Festival passes, including for the new Hudson Opening Weekend option, offering access to Festival programming from opening night through its first Monday, and, in its second year, an Under 25 pass, are now on sale. Deadlines for 2027 Tribeca Festival submissions follow: Features: October 21, 2026 (early), November 18, 2026 (official), December 16, 2026 (extended) Shorts & Music Videos: October 28, 2026 (early), December 2, 2026 (official), February 3, 2027 (extended) Tribeca TV: October 21, 2026 (early), November 18, 2026 (official), February 3, 2027 (extended) Tribeca Digital Creators: October 28, 2026 (early), December 2, 2026 (official), February 3, 2027 (extended) Tribeca Games: October 28, 2026 (early), December 2, 2026 (official), March 4, 2027 (extended) Tribeca Podcasts: November 11, 2026 (early), January 13, 2027 (official), February 24, 2027 (extended) Tribeca X: January 13, 2027 (early), February 24, 2027 (official), March 31, 2027 (extended) Tribeca Works in Progress: January 27, 2027 (official), February 24, 2027 (extended). Submissions for the Works in Progress category open January 5, 2027. THR

articles.title: Being Clarissa Ward: CNN Star Speaks on Gaza, Trump — and Her Ellison-Era Future
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All September 30, 2026 8:45am CNN chief international correspondent Clarissa Ward attends the conversation as part of Warner Bros. Discovery WBD at Cannes Lions on June 23, 2022 in Cannes, France. Ward has been on the frontlines of foreign reporting lately, in multiple ways. Arnold Jerocki/Getty Images for Warner Bros. Discovery What’s more scary than being a lead international correspondent at a time of multiple brutal wars and violent online rhetoric? Being a lead international correspondent when the whole future of your network is entering uncertain ownership hands. As CNN ‘s chief international correspondent, Clarissa Ward may have one of the best jobs in all of media. But she also has one of the most fraught jobs in all of media. Dodging explosions in Ukraine, seeking an entree into Gaza, reporting from the Spanish-run city of Ceuta as migrants come pouring in from Morocco — Ward has been in every hotspot and then some recently. And all this before David Ellison got final approval to buy CNN along with the other assets of Warner Bros. Discovery. The Hollywood Reporter met the London-based Ward last week at a midtown Manhattan hotel on a rare recent trip to New York (she was here to see her bosses and meet with the president of Latvia, as one does). Not even 24 hours had passed since California attorney general Rob Bonta and other states settled their case against Ellison, clearing the way for him to own the cable-news giant. She had a few things to say about all of it. First, how are you feeling? About the state of the world but also the state of the news world. Oh it’s all great [laughs sarcastically]. No, I think I’m feeling really good about journalism. It’s hard, but there’s so much great work everywhere. As for the world… One of your biggest crusades has been about a place you can’t report from — Gaza. Are there signs that the Israeli government is changing its stance and will journalists have more access, as you and others have been pushing for? There’s a massive amount of pressure but not really. And we need to. What you can get now just isn’t enough. I don’t want wide shots of rubble — I want an old man in a chair telling me his story. And also I can’t report with the same moral authority if I’m not there. No one can. So that really needs to change. Iran seems to pose similar challenges right now. Totally. We mostly hear what the U.S. or Iran want us to hear, and the people of Iran lose when that happens. Everyone loses when that happens. There’s of course the fear that even if you get in to those places there’s a limit to what we can trust because a lot of Palestinians are still so afraid of Hamas and a lot of Iranians still so afraid of the regime. Does that concern you? Absolutely. In every conflict there’s self-censoring but in these two it’s worse in many ways . As we’re speaking there’s another kind of censoring effort going on right here in the U.S., with Trump banning CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House. How is that landing with you? It’s very concerning. But I think it’s also very encouraging to see the solidarity — look at what Fox News just did [in joining the other networks’ pool boycott]. Media companies realize a threat against some of us is a threat against all of us, even if they don’t agree on much else. What’s one place you’d like to be able to report from that you haven’t been allowed into recently? Sudan. It’s extremely hard, and Darfur is even harder. And the country [in the midst of a brutal 3+ year civil war] is in major crisis. What’s one place or story you have recently reported on that we’re not paying enough attention to? The migrant crisis in Europe. Being in Ceuta and seeing the migrants streaming across the border — this is part of a phenomenon that is going to change so much. Look at what just happened with AfD in Germany [ winning an election in Saxony-Anhalt] and how the migrant crisis plays into it. It’s affecting everything. You’ve tried to mix things up on social media lately, talking about journalism while having tea in your kitchen or pastries in an airport or just dancing through a train station to “Shake Your Groove Thing .” It’s a bit of a different path from what you and frankly many foreign correspondents have previously taken. At the beginning people were saying ‘this is weird’ and ‘what are you doing?’ But I feel we have to meet viewers where they are. Some institutions have become a little bit [pauses]…formal in how they report the news. [Lowers her voice to faux-seriousness for the next phrase] ‘Over these hills behind me, you can see’ — I mean, nobody talks like that anymore. Content creators talk the way viewers themselves talk. [Laughs] No certainly not, though there are some who say foreign correspondents should keep that formal tradition alive. And I get that. I wouldn’t do it if I was, say, reporting from Syria. We have to be careful not to cross any lines. But also I think it’s OK to ask ‘what if we tried something on for size, in the right context?’ ‘What if it feels looser, more like you’re listening to a friend?’ People don’t want to feel like they’re being bullshitted — young people especially but everybody. So I’m trying to do something so they don’t feel that way. Some people will see these videos and also wonder if you’re planning on a post-correspondent life. A few of your CNN colleagues have certainly had success outside the machine — Jim Acosta, Don Lemon. Is that something you can see yourself doing? They’ve done great but I’ve always loved being in the field, being out there reporting, and to do that [for broadcast] you really need an institution like CNN behind you. But nowadays you’d be unwise not to look at other things. I’m not going to pretend I know what that is [at this point]. But you have to look. A lot of tongues wagged when back in the spring you signed only a one-year contract instead of a long-term one. Was that a signal you may be preparing for an eventual life outside CNN, especially with a new owner coming in? There are so many things going on and you don’t want to rush into anything without a clear-eyed view in terms of how much is changing. So that’s where that was coming from. On the subject of that train video, you did get a clapback from the White House social media team, which derided you for doing it and called you a “hot mess,” among other lovely names. What was your reaction to that? I mean, we’re having fun. It’s social media. So much of content is people taking things out of boxes. It’s not like we were on CNN on the front page of the web site. I don’t know, I’m not sure why overt displays of joy make some people feel inadequate. THR
