articles.title: PGA Tour Taps Ryan Holcomb to Lead Original Content (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 29, 2026 6:00am Ryan Holcomb Courtesy of the PGA Tour The PGA Tour is pushing further into entertainment, bringing on Ryan Holcomb to serve as the golf organizer’s senior VP and head of original content. Holcomb was most recently head of development at Box to Box Films, the studio behind shows like Formula 1: Drive to Survive and Faceoff: Inside the NHL , and previously worked in content at World Surf League, Excel Sports Management, STX Entertainment and Lionsgate. At the PGA Tour he will be tasked with helping to develop and drive the Tour’s content beyond the live competitions, including through its PGA Tour Studios content team. Holcomb will report to Luis Goicouria, executive VP & GM of PGA Tour Studios. Holcomb joins the Tour as it leans farther into media, both on and off the course. PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp, who previously led the NFL’s media business, is overhauling the structure of the Tour’s events with future media deals in mind. Rolapp’s media background has been useful as the Tour seeks new ways to engage with fans through premium programming. At the same time, there is a growing awareness that other forms of content are needed to help grow fandom around the sport. That’s where PGA Tour Studios and its original content come into focus, with originals and co-productions like Full Swing , Chasing Sunday , and Truth or Putt . PGA Tour Studios sits within the Tour’s enterprise operations division, led by president Andy Weitz, alongside marketing, technology, investor relations and board administration. “The PGA Tour provides an unmatched opportunity to tell stories that deepen the connection between fans and players, while highlighting the incredible competition that defines this sport,” said Holcomb in a statement. “I’m excited to help build on that foundation by developing original content that showcases the personalities, competition and culture of golf in new and compelling ways, reaching audiences wherever they engage with sports and entertainment.” THR

articles.title: ‘SNL UK’ Season 2: All the Hosts and Musical Guests
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 29, 2026 6:00am Danny Dyer, James Norton and Cynthia Erivo will host 'SNL UK' next month. Michael Shelford/Getty Logo text Saturday Night Live UK is back on our screens. The second season kicked off on Saturday, Sept. 9 with host Jeff Goldblum and musical guest CMAT. It follows a well-received first season for SNL UK (a round-up of the reviews can be found here ), which aired from March onwards earlier this year. The series regulars were all relatively unknown stand-up comedians and social media stars, such as Hammed Animashaun, Ayoade Bamgboye, Larry Dean, Celeste Dring, George Fouracres, Annabel Marlow, Al Nash, Jack Shep and Emma Sidi. Weekend Update presenters Ania Magliano and Paddy Young saw particular breakout success, and both of them scored sold-out runs for their solo comedy shows at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival just last month. Related Stories Business Amazon MGM Execs Tout New Mercedes Ron Hit, How Spain's 'Apocalypse Z' Became a Hit That's Getting a Sequel: "Zombies Have No Nationality" TV Netflix's 'The Eternaut' Effect: Subscriber Impact Estimate Disclosed at Iberseries Joining the cast this season is Freddie Meredith, who most recently featured in Kat Sadler’s twisted female-driven comedy Such Brave Girls on the BBC. Season one’s inaugural host was U.S. star and SNL hall-of-famer Tina Fey, who shepherded the show to a solid start. The Hollywood Reporter ‘s review determined : “Good cast, spotty writing — like the mothership,” about the London spin-off of Lorne Michaels’ long-running NBC sketch show. That first episode on Sky (available on Peacock in the U.S.) was watched by over 220,000 people in Britain, as Jamie Dornan, Riz Ahmed, Jack Whitehall, Nicola Coughlan, Aimee Lou Wood, Hannah Waddingham and Ncuti Gatwa booked season one hosting slots. Some of the group’s best sketches across the season included a spoof skincare advert where the women look so young that their partners were arrested for being paedophiles, a Traitors parody whereby a giant crab goes undetected at the roundtable in a savvy social satire, and “The Prince Andrew Plan,” which saw MI5 staffers confirm that every single royal family snafu over the last three decades has all just been to make King Charles look great in comparison. Season two opened with Goldblum and Irish singer-songwriter CMAT, before actor-comedian Jamie Demetriou took the next hosting gig on Sep. 19, with rock band Royal Blood as his musical guest. Demetriou is best known for roles in Fleabag , Stath Lets Flats and Barbie . The following week, Chicken Shop Date presenter Amelia Dimoldenberg took the reins alongside English singer Rachel Chinouriri. Dimoldenberg’s SNL UK appearance came hot on the heels of her confirmation that she’s bringing Chicken Shop Date to an end after 12 years. On Tuesday, Sept. 29, the SNL UK team confirmed the next three hosts: Danny Dyer ( Rivals ) with musical guest Sasha Keable (Oct. 10), James Norton ( House of the Dragon ) and The Streets (Oct. 17), and after that, Cynthia Erivo ( Wicked ) with Blossoms (Oct. 24). On the production side, Laura Claxton has been promoted to SNL UK co-head writer, joining existing head writer Jonno Johnson. Liz Clare returns as director. Heather MacVean joins as costume designer and Sinead Oldnall is heading up the U.K. talent team as director of on-screen talent. Lorne Michaels serves as executive producer on the show, and James Longman is lead producer. Here, THR rounds up the hosts and musical guests confirmed for season two of SNL UK . Sep. 12: Jeff Goldblum, CMAT Sep. 19: Jamie Demetriou, Royal Blood Sep. 26: Amelia Dimoldenberg, Rachel Chinouriri Oct. 10: Danny Dyer, Sasha Keable Oct. 17: James Norton, The Streets Oct. 24: Cynthia Erivo, Blossoms THR

articles.title: YouTube Exec Sees More ‘Obsession’-, ‘Backrooms’-Style Smashes Hitting Box Office – and Oscars
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 29, 2026 6:16am Inde Navarrette and Michael Johnston in 'Obsession.' Courtesy of Focus Features Curry Barker’s Obsession and Kane Parsons’ Backrooms , two Gen Z creatives-led horror stories, have proven the concept that viral online video creators can conquer the box office. And Pedro Pina , vp, YouTube , Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA), thinks that they will be followed by more successful moves from the online into the cinema world. He shared that forecast on the opening day of the sixth edition of Iberseries & Platino Industria in Spain’s capital, Madrid , on Tuesday in a keynote appearance entitled “YouTube: The Strategic Ally of the Audiovisual System.” “We can see that creators are defining and shaping the culture. As a result, the cultural impact that we have is phenomenal,” Pina touted. “And you also see, from a cinema standpoint, a huge impact. [The creators of] Obsession and Backrooms , as you know, were YouTubers who decided to go into the box office [business] … – and they were a tremendous success this year. And I would expect to see more and more of these examples [at] the Emmys and Oscars” in the coming years. Pina on Tuesday also explained YouTube’s recent focus on positioning itself as a partner to media and entertainment content companies. “The objective of being here at this event, as well as so many others … is to really show up and really explain how our model works,” he highlighted. “The majority of people in the industry, unfortunately, don’t understand it as much, and that’s 100 percent our fault. We never spent enough time explaining to the industry how we work, how you can monetize.” The result? “To a point, a lot of people were afraid of YouTube. They had fear of YouTube mostly because they did not understand how the platform works, how their content could be protected, how it could reach new audiences, and why it works to monetize,” Pina continued. “Once you start breaking down that information and providing examples and showing the way, you see more and more people starting to look at this. So we started this journey roughly three years ago.” And YouTube has seen the benefit of making its narrative heard. “The amount of content uploaded by traditional players is increasing now,” Pina concluded. Earlier in the Iberseries day, Amazon MGM Studios executives discussed the success of the Mercedes Ron young adult novel adaptations and Spanish zombie horror film Apocalypse Z , while Parrot Analytics shared data trends and estimates for the subscriber impact of Netflix’s Argentina hit series The Eternaut . The industry gathering runs through Friday. THR

articles.title: Kyle MacLachlan, Star of David Lynch’s ‘Dune,’ Was the Only One on Set Who Knew What ‘Dune’ Was About
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Kyle MacLachlan Plus Icon Kyle MacLachlan View All September 29, 2026 7:00am Kyle MacLachlan as Paul Atreides in 'Dune' (1984), directed by David Lynch. Courtesy Everett Collection Chihuahua, Mexico Spring 1983 Filming out in the Chihuahuan Desert is actually chilly in the morning, but when the sun comes up, the heat is unreal. Just biblical. With the camera crew setting up in the distance and the wind not cooperating, Patrick Stewart and I sweat in our “stillsuits” and wait. In the world of Dune , the suit transforms the sweat into drinking water; but in the Mexican desert, the sweat just pools, sticks to my skin and runs down my arms. The custom-fit suit is a near-torture device of costuming that severely limits my ability to move. It’s like fighting against a giant rubber band wrapped around my body. When the suit is zipped all the way up, I can’t even raise my arms. Not ideal. The key, I’m learning, is to limit unnecessary movement. Or, really, any. Related Stories Movies Naomi Watts Praises Husband Billy Crudup for Backing Her Menopause Activism: "So Sweet -- and Sexy" TV Hints of 'Sex and the City' and 'Narcos': A Look at Literary Works Being Pitched for Screen Adaptations at Iberseries & Platino Industria Wondering how much longer before we roll, I turn to see David Lynch , the film’s director, up on a desert dune in a yellow hat, white collared shirt, the shortest shorts on earth, and brown loafers with white socks pulled up to his knees. (He has a particular distaste for sand in his shoes.) He’s talking to cinematographer Freddie Francis, shirtless in a boater hat, and to the assistant director, José “Kuki” López Rodero, in a white panama hat. They are huddled together around the camera, looking like a bizarre collection of bandits. Freddie’s crew is setting up big silver reflectors to light the actors’ faces, which bounce the sunlight right into our eyeballs. Brutal. (Now I understand why Clint Eastwood characters are always squinting.) In the distance, across the Samalayuca Dune Fields, men are burn­ing old tires to get the right color and intensity of black smoke. As a key point of the plot, the planet Arrakis, aka Dune, doesn’t have water; thus, it has no blue sky. But of course, Mexico does. Can’t get around that. So, our intrepid director, the 37-year-old for­mer Eagle Scout from Montana, the Oscar-nominated visionary be­hind Eraserhead and The Elephant Man, Lynch has taken on the not-inconsiderable task of blotting out the sky. Those tires are still burning in the distance, but now the black smoke is moving in the wrong direction, away from us. So, we wait. We can blot out the sky, rip up the desert, but we can’t control which way the wind blows. Assuming it’ll be some time, I unzip my stillsuit to down around my torso and tie the arms around my waist, my black T-shirt comically drenched: I’m now half Paul, half Kyle. Both of us carrying a lot on our minds — and shoulders. Kyle Maclachlan ‘s memoir, Fictional Selves (Crown). Penguin Random House Dune is populated by an impressive list of international talent on and off camera: acclaimed actors like Max von Sydow, Francesca Annis, Jürgen Prochnow; up-and-comers like Blade Runner ’s Sean Young and gigantic stars like Sting; top craftsmen like Oscar-winning cinematographer Freddie Francis, Tony Masters (Stanley Kubrick’s production designer), effects wizard Kit West ( Raiders of the Lost Ark ), creature creator Carlo Rambaldi (who also designed E.T.), and famed costume designer Bob Ringwood, whose Batman suit five years later will be modeled on the “fetish industrial” look of Dune ’s rubber stillsuits. In Mexico for budgetary reasons, the day-to-day production has customs issues, technology issues, communication issues, construction issues, electricity issues, on top of the typical challenges that come with a movie of this size and complexity. The power goes out regularly — our home base, Mexico City, has brownouts — and the crew on the soundstages often have to switch to generators. It’s a real roll-with-the-punches situation, an adventure in the grandest sense of the word. When I first arrive, I am wide-eyed, viewing the project as a throwback to the “sword and sandal” movies of the 1950s and early ’60s that I used to watch on TV. Go off somewhere impossible and exotic and come back and hope you have a movie. During the scene Patrick Stewart and I are shooting that day, Paul Atreides, the character I play, has been in the desert for a couple of years. I had petitioned for my hair to go past my shoulders, Jesus style — a sexier and messiah-like Paul — but was overruled. The final decision is a compromise that serves neither side: hair extensions glued to my scalp with a latex adhesive. Taking them off at the end of each day is a painful process that involves rubbing alcohol and a light scalping that leaves behind stubborn balls of latex in my hair. Currently, I am wearing a white hairnet over my perm, to keep it in place before we shoot. Patrick, mostly bald on top, has longer hair extensions, too, given that his character, Paul’s adviser and friend Gurney Halleck, has been in exile as well. We stare off into the distance, catching our breath, saving our energy. The first thing I noticed when I met Patrick was his voice. I went to school for three years to learn how to speak onstage, but I’ll never sound like him. Coming from the prestigious Royal Shakespeare Company, Patrick has the most mellifluous tones, regal and elegant. No one can make the line “Behold, as a wild ass in the desert go I forth to my work” sound correct except for him. He is Gurney Halleck, master swordsman and troubadour. And because he’s also Patrick Stewart, he’s suave and debonair about it. When he puts on the Atreides battle jacket or the Fremen stillsuit, it’s like he’s lived in it all his life. He also has the most marvelously shaped head of any human I’ve ever seen, and I tell him so. He gives me a “thank you, I think” kind of look. Patrick is in his early 40s at the time, but this is only his third film, and he’s a neophyte when it comes to the complicated world of Dune. Because he’s a last-minute replacement — for Aldo Ray, whose struggles with alcoholism have rendered him out of commission — I try to offer assistance. Patrick simply hasn’t had time to soak up the extensive Dune lore I have spent a lifetime accumulating. Still, we are both newcomers to film, so we share a certain awe about the hectic and bizarre world spinning around us. MacLachlan (left), Patrick Stewart (center) and Sting (knife), in Dune . Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection Patrick is a mix of stately confidence and thoughtful inquiry. He regularly leans over and, sotto voce , asks me questions about what’s going on. Though he presents a very cool and collected mien, he is just trying to figure shit out like me. We connect on our theater background — I did Shakespeare the previous summer — and laugh at the exponential difference between simple theater productions and … whatever this is. The size and scope of the film often leave us speechless, and I feel less alone with him beside me. On his first day of shooting, he and I took our seats in a half-built “ornithopter,” which is like a giant, multifaceted bee that flies over the desert. We were seated in front of a gigantic blue screen, where the landscape would be matted in later. I could feel Patrick’s nervousness as we prepared to “fly” over the shield wall and the Great Desert of Arrakis. He leaned forward and quietly asked, “Kyle, what are we looking at here?” I leaned back and spoke in an undertone: “There’s a sandworm down there bigger than a tractor trailer.” “Aha. And there?” he asked, pointing lower down. “It’s swallowing one of the harvesters.” “Harvester?” he asked. “It’s like a large metal factory on wheels.” “Seems like a risky mission,” he said, a trace of somber gravitas. “Tremendous risk,” I said quietly. Patrick’s key line in the scene is “The worm is eight minutes away, sire.” After the first take, he had a question. “Pardon, David?” “YES, PATRICK,” David said in his distinctive honk. “How exactly would I know how far out the worm is?” I’m impressed that Patrick exists deeply enough within his character to ask such a thing. David stopped, re-calculating in his mind. “EXCELLENT QUESTION, PATRICK,” he said, like a supportive teacher. “THANK YOU.” He then dispatched a propman to construct a gauge, with analog hands to be inserted later. Having carried the world of Dune in my head for years, I, too, arrived on set with such inquiries. Carefully and diplomatically, I at first pushed back on some production details. I know the book inside and out — I am likely the only one on set who does — so I feel I carry a responsibility to the story. When I was fitted for the stillsuit, I felt some things were missing: “How come these suits don’t have hoods?” “Where are the capes?” “Will there be a headpiece?” “Wait, where’s the mouthpiece so you don’t lose moisture when you breathe?” I wasn’t trying to be difficult; it’s just that I had absorbed the reality of Frank Herbert’s story so completely. If Paul had to survive in that desert climate, in those bleak conditions, with only this protection, he would die. And if being stranded on Dune wasn’t a life-or-death situation, then that would change a whole series of things that affected the characters’ decisions. There was an internal logic that needed to remain intact. My concerns were never about my ego or vanity, but about the truth of that world. “Kale,” said producer Dino De Laurentiis, still struggling to pronounce my name. “We don’t hire famous actors to cover their faces where no one can see them.” This did have an unavoidable logic to it. He had plenty to worry about already, and often he and his daughter Raffaella De Laurentiis, also a producer on the film, and David were managing a hundred things at once on a scale I couldn’t even conceive. After my third degree about the costume, I made a point to choose my battles more carefully. Still standing around in the broiling desert with Patrick, waiting for the smoke to change direction, we walk over to where Everett McGill is sitting on a chair beneath umbrellas, out of the sun. Everett, who plays Stilgar, a tribal leader of the indigenous “Fremen,” has the calm but commanding presence of an Old West sheriff. He’s got classic movie-star features, a strong jaw and penetrating eyes, but he remains offbeat enough to stay interesting. “Hey, young buck,” Everett says, his nickname for me. “Surviving?” I part my hands, like Take a look , making a dramatic flourish of my current state — hairnet, half-removed stillsuit, sweat-drenched T-shirt. Everett is a different breed of actor, and I’m instantly drawn to him. He’s a taciturn guy who grew up in Kansas, and he has that cowboy feel about him, even down to his badass boots, which I make sure to find a pair of for myself. To protect his vocal cords, he carries a converted soda bottle from which he regularly inhales. It is lined with damp cotton, to hold moisture. He wants Stilgar’s voice to have the deep timbre of a respected elder. Everett is meticulous and thorough, if eccentric, carefully considering all kinds of little details for his character. Patrick, Everett, and I stare at the thick black smoke coming off the burning tires, the most toxic cloud I’ve ever seen. “You think that’s why we couldn’t shoot this in the States?” I ask, and Patrick and Everett laugh. Everett seems more sanguine about our current conditions. He’s been around. “This is child’s play,” he says, “compared to what we went through on Quest. ” He has been entertaining us with tales from Quest for Fire, the historical fantasy film directed by Jean-Jacques Annaud that he recently made with Ron Perlman and Rae Dawn Chong. The film had a legendary shoot, nearly a year long: actors sitting for five hours of makeup a day, learning a completely invented language, dealing with the elements in freezing Scotland and blistering Kenya. “It was grueling,” Everett says, carefully inhaling from his bottle and regaling us like a chieftain before a campfire. He starts enumerating on his fingers. “Ron and I both got frostbite, they had real bears and elephants on set, a volcano eruption we had to plan around, and a set designer got anthrax from animal skins.” He says it all matter-of-factly, a little pride in his resonant voice. “Jesus,” I say. I glance over at Patrick, and he looks mystified . But as a Hollywood veteran, Everett takes things in stride. Assuming the Dune pictures will keep me in the space-fantasy business for a while — after all, I had signed an enormous book of a contract for five Dune (and three non- Dune ) films for Dino’s company — I listen to his stories in a little bit of awe. I’m excited, even gung ho about clawing my way through those kinds of challenges. The exuberance and stupidity of youth have me embracing the idea of testing myself on a film set. I can’t wait to come back with stories. “Yeah, we kept it light, though,” Everett says. “You gotta. Or you’d go insane. Ron and I were always pulling shit on each other. One time, I had to traverse this sandhill barefoot where the ground temperature was nearly a hundred fifty degrees. When it was Ron’s turn, I waved him up without saying a word, and boy he nearly killed me. The bottoms of his feet were bright red! Nearly scorched them off!” Everett laughs aloud in his rich tenor. Between him and Patrick, I’m surrounded by the most melodious sounds. The three of us are becoming fast friends, and though I’m over a decade younger, I feel comfortable with the relaxed camaraderie in the midst of the madness. I’m discovering that friends on a shoot can become a type of family. We few, we happy few, we band of brothers. Everett is playfully envious of my youth — that’s what the whole “young buck” thing is about. “You gotta get out there and graze, ” he tells me. “Everything is out there for you. You can go all night, come to set without sleeping.” I find his words equally inspiring and demoralizing. I’m not great at embracing the moment and a little gun-shy about real-life adventure. But I have always wanted to traverse the country on a motorcycle; for some reason, after time with Everett, I will make a plan to do exactly that when the shoot ends. It goes against all my natural caution, so it is perfect. Suddenly, the wind shifts. Now the black smoke is blowing right across our faces; it is pure poison, lethal in our throats and lungs, a shock to breathe in. It’s like a neck punch, freezing my vocal cords, stopping me from speaking. Again, not ideal. Everett puts his head down and inhales from his bottle. The rest of us just have to breathe as little as possible. “OKAY, EVERYONE.” David’s distinctive honk comes through nearby walkie-talkies. “GET IN POSITION, PLEASE.” Extras spread out across the dunes. Crew members scurry over to the actors with a gardening-type tool, opening the nozzle and blowing a cloud of yellow and red dust onto us. I close my eyes as it covers my hair and face, hold my breath as it gets up my nose and the grit lodges in my teeth. “BOBBY,” David says over the walkie. “WILL YOU HIT KYLE ONE MORE TIME?” Someone from wardrobe runs over and shoots me with the dirt gun again for good measure. Now I’m completely covered in it. When I turn around and face the camera, I notice that every single crew member is wearing a nose mask, face covering, and giant black-framed goggles. I have to keep from laughing. The “dirt” is actually a calcium-based clay called fuller’s earth, a powder that gives images texture and a sense of depth. The effects team has set giant airplane propeller–type fans right off camera. During the shot, they feed fuller’s earth into the fan blades to be blown onto the actors. When I get home that night, I’ll have to rinse out my teeth, spitting red-dirt saliva into the sink. The epitome of Hollywood glamour, just like Cary Grant. I get into position, the fans blowing dirt and smoke across my face. We spent hours waiting for the wind and then create our own. This is madness. This is Dune. Paul’s costume includes a “weirding module” attached to his throat; it sticks out like a giant door hinge. In the scene, he and Gurney recognize each other in the desert after years apart, a heartwarming moment. But as he hugs me, Patrick accidentally jabs the module back into my Adam’s apple. I am stunned as my breath and voice stop sharply. My eyes fill with tears from the pain, and I make a slight grunting sound. I don’t speak because I can’t. The wind shifts again right as we finish, so that’s the take that goes into the film. Moving on. Excerpted from FICTIONAL SELVES: A Memoir by Kyle MacLachlan. Copyright © 2026 by Kyle MacLachlan. articles.title: ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Directors Tease Hulk Return, Say More Secret Characters Coming
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 29, 2026 7:01am Did any of these actors actually meet? Logo text Think the full cast is already known for Avengers: Doomsday ? Think again. Despite containing 31 announced Marvel characters (full list below), Doomsday directors Joe and Anthony Russo say even more characters are appearing in the team-up superhero film — including, quite possibly, the Hulk (Mark Ruffalo). Speaking to Empire Online , Russo said, “[Bruce Banner] is certainly involved in the story that revolves around Doom. We will not confirm nor deny his appearance in Doomsday .” (So that sounds like a yes). Related Stories Movies 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Eyes Rerelease With Unseen Footage Movies 'Avengers: Endgame' Powers $26M Return at Crowded Box Office Anthony Russo then added, “The farthest we can go is to say, there are characters and actors who have not been announced, who are a part of Doomsday .” Anthony recently told The AP : “The MCU is this massive experiment in how vast, how much scope can an ensemble really have?” The duo also confirmed they started shooting Doomsday without a completed script: “We always view the script as a living organism,” Joe said. “We’re improvisation-based, rehearsal-based directors. We like to see what the actors bring to the characters, and sometimes you don’t get the actors until a few days or a few weeks before you shoot them. And a lot of the time, that’s when the magic happens.” The duo are currently promoting the re-release of Avengers: Endgame , which has racked up another $86 million over the weekend. The film grossed $2.8 billion back in 2019 and now includes four new end-credits scenes to help set up Doomsday . Joe Russo has previously called Endgame “required viewing for following the story in Doomsday .” Here’s the full list of confirmed characters appearing in Doomsday: MCU veterans : Steve Rogers/Captain America (Chris Evans), Thor (Chris Hemsworth), Sam Wilson/Captain America (Anthony Mackie), Bucky Barnes/Winter Soldier (Sebastian Stan), Ant-Man/Scott Lang (Paul Rudd), Loki (Tom Hiddleston), Shang-Chi (Simu Liu), Shuri/Black Panther (Letitia Wright), M’Baku (Winston Duke), Namor (Tenoch Huerta Mejía), Falcon/Joaquin Torres (Danny Ramirez). The Fantastic Four : Reed Richards/Mister Fantastic (Pedro Pascal), Sue Storm/Invisible Woman (Vanessa Kirby), Johnny Storm/Human Torch (Joseph Quinn), Ben Grimm/The Thing (Ebon Moss-Bachrach). Thunderbolts/New Avengers : Yelena Belova (Florence Pugh), Red Guardian/Alexei Shostakov (David Harbour), U.S. Agent/John Walker (Wyatt Russell), Ghost/Ava Starr (Hannah John-Kamen), Sentry/Bob Reynolds (Lewis Pullman). X-Men/Fox-Era Characters : Professor Charles Xavier (Patrick Stewart), Magneto/Erik Lehnsherr (Ian McKellen), Cyclops/Scott Summers (James Marsden), Beast/Hank McCoy (Kelsey Grammer), Nightcrawler/Kurt Wagner (Alan Cumming), Mystique/Raven (Rebecca Romijn), Gambit/Remy LeBeau (Channing Tatum). Plus : Doctor Doom/Victor von Doom (Robert Downey Jr.), Cassie Lang (Kathryn Newton), Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell) and Namora (Mabel Cadena). Doomsday opens in theaters Dec. 18. THR

articles.title: How a Microdramas Director Landed Her First Feature Film Gig
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All September 29, 2026 7:30am Kristen Brancaccio Chris Jon Directing a microdrama and directing a feature-length film are very different tasks, typically diverging in budgets, schedules and expectations for a viewer’s attention span. But in an era when more up-and-comers and film school grads are going straight into the verticals business, it’s possible that some of Hollywood’s next big feature directors could emerge from the world of bite-sized entertainment. What exactly would that transition look like? Kristen Brancaccio, who The Hollywood Reporter has learned was just tapped by Graviteur Studios to helm its first feature film Crush Party , has a pretty good idea. Related Stories TV 'The Tonight Show' Is Bringing Back Its Billionaire Microdrama Satire for a Second Season Business Microdrama Producers Voice Cautious Optimism on the Sector Despite AI Worries Brancaccio has an impressive resume in the microdrama world. She’s directed 21 verticals, including one bona fide hit in Screen Time , the first microdrama from Issa Rae’s company Hoorae Media, which earned nearly 75 million views in its first week on TikTok and PineDrama. She also directed one of aTwist’s first projects, Hollywood Starlet , produced by The Bold and the Beautiful producer Bradley Bell, and the Audible vertical Southern Belle Insults starring Keke Palmer. That’s not to mention her work on YouTube, which is how Brancaccio broke into the business, working on the comedy channel The Key of Awesome and then as an independent contractor directly for the platform. Crush Party , beginning principal photography in 2027, will be her first-ever feature. For Graviteur Studios development and production head Emerson Davis, Brancaccio’s non-traditional background was a big draw. The indie studio, which launched earlier this year as a joint venture between Dolphin Entertainment and KYNETIC Media Ventures, is focused on creator-driven storytelling at a moment when next-gen directors like Curry Parker and Kane Parsons are burning up the box office. The Graviteur team found Brancaccio through Screen Time , which they enjoyed, later to be impressed by her range as a director. “With Kristen, she’s shown how exceptional of a storyteller she is across formats and genres,” Davis said in an interview. “Some of our early conversations were both about story but a lot about connecting with an audience and what audience are we trying to reach. She brings that natural ability to think like that.” As her journey may — or may not — be a bellwether for promising verticals directors in the future, Brancaccio was game to discuss how it happened. In an interview, she talked about the evolution of the microdrama industry, transferable skills and staying audience-focused in traditional moviemaking. Let’s start with how you got into microdramas in the first place. What led you to the verticals industry? I have a background in the digital space. I started my career on YouTube and over the years have worked on a ton of projects that met where digital and traditional industry converged. And one of the projects that I did was I wrote and directed a pilot for SyFy that was meant to be a digital show. SyFy never ended up going that route, but that pilot ended up with some producers at ReelShort in very early 2024. And it had a very strong romance element and that’s what they were looking for. I got a phone call and they just sort of explained, “Hey, there’s a new format in town. We’re shooting this movie vertically. Are you interested in directing it?” And the rest is history. Do you have any idea how they got their hands on the SyFy pilot? Yes. The production designer from that pilot is friends with a producer from a microdrama production company that was working with ReelShort. So it was just one of those projects that I had written off as a bummer that it never went further than it did, but then ended up totally changing the trajectory of my career path. And I think there were a few reasons they resonated with it. Obviously, the fact that there was romance in this pilot. The budget level was, I would say, comparable to what a lot of microdrama budgets are. And again, it was made for digital, so it moved pretty quickly. I very quickly understood this [microdrama] format. I was like, “Oh, this is for the people. This is what the audience loves. The audience that is reading Wattpad, the audience that is consuming romance, people that just want certain plot points to be hit at a certain speed, people that are addicted to TikTok, they’re expecting a certain cadence and that’s what these shows deliver.” How have you noticed the microdrama industry changing or evolving in particular ways over the last few years? We’re starting to see different lanes emerge. At first, these apps were interchangeable. Now they’re starting to realize the value in building their brand. That’s something that traditional Hollywood players understand very well. And so the people coming into the space like Issa Rae, she knows her audience inside and out, so she’s going to deliver a really compelling, well-told story, perfectly suited for digital, that is going to be high production value. She’s not going to follow the same cadence or rules that ReelShort follows. It’s just a totally different approach, but it’s very, very successful. The one I did for her has at least 250 million views, if not more. And then we’re also seeing a lot of very talented people [that] really understand the audience they’re going for. They’re not ignoring the work that has been done so far in the microdrama space. I think they’re doing a very good job actually of analyzing that, what has worked so far? Why has it worked? What can we do differently? As you’ve been working on all these microdramas, how did the chance to direct this feature come up for you? This is what I was hoping and praying that this corner of the industry would lead to. For a long time, verticals were in this… almost a silo. It was just shoved to the corner. I don’t know if “stigma” is maybe too strong a word, but there wasn’t an understanding that there was value in what we were doing and in the skills that we were developing. I have a background in producing and I was just consistently blown away by frankly what I could accomplish myself, but also what everyone in this corner of the industry is doing. We’re doing so much in such a fast timeline. We’re doing it consistently. We’re turning out a movie a month, essentially. I was like, man, I hope other industry players notice this. It all starts with a phone call coming out of the blue and [I] found out that David and Bill at Graviteur were…. I think it was Screen Time that had caught their eye. They had this movie script that they developed in-house, they were looking for a director and they really saw the value in somebody with vertical experience, somebody that had all those skills that I mentioned, both the technical and the creative, that comes from just working in digital and specifically working in verticals. I was so excited to get that call because I was like, “Oh my gosh, this is everything. This is what I hoped would happen. People are recognizing the value in these skills.” What are some of the lessons that you’ve learned in the microdrama industry that you’re planning on bringing to your work on Crush Party ? I’ve met some very, very talented, skilled people who can accomplish a lot on a limited budget, both in front of the camera and behind the camera, [and I’m] actually wanting to bring some people with me. Aside from that, I think the aspect that I’m going to bring with me to Crush Party and other projects is I feel like I keep the audience in mind in a different way and meet the audience where they are. And what’s nice about this script in particular is it’s targeting an audience that is thriller and horror. Those are emerging genres in the microdrama space and fans are starting to really respond to them. When you’re thinking about the audience, it causes you to think about the whole project in a different way. So many filmmakers forget that you’re making your movie for an audience and you can make the best movie in the world, but if it doesn’t reach the audience, no one’s going to see it and that’s such a shame. So who is your audience? What is it they’re looking for? What matters to them? That needs to matter to you too. On the flip side, are there any elements when it comes to working on a feature that you feel will really stretch you as a director? When you make a lot of microdramas, you understand the time you have and the decisions you make are usually to meet those demands on time and budget. Unfortunately, time, budget, creative is the order in which you have to think about things. It’s a necessity; thinking the opposite way will make you crazy in the microdrama space. But I think it’s going to be a little bit of a brain rearrangement, a very lovely one, to maybe be able to say, okay, obviously this is not a massive budget studio feature, right? So I’m aware of what this budget is and what it can get me, but it does allow me to think creatively first, and then assess, okay, does this work with the time and budget that we have? In general, what kind of preparation do you think microdramas offer early-career directors for working in other formats like features? I think the value in directing microdramas is learning the skill of shooting for the edit. You don’t have time to find the movie in post. So even if you have time on set, which you never do, at the end of the day, these post timelines are so tight, you don’t have time to try and shape it into anything else. And obviously your scripty [script supervisor] is hopefully there to help you, but as a director, you also need to learn that skill. Working with actors, you don’t have time for a ton of takes. So learning very quickly how to communicate to an actor, how to quickly understand maybe why isn’t a scene working or what could we adjust in this scene to make it better or to change the energy of the scene. You get very quick. So I think overall it’s getting your reps in all these different areas. You’re shooting multi-cam, you have to be able to hold in your head what multiple cameras are doing. I think there’s just so much value in the technical, practical skills of directing when you’re directing microdramas. What are your ultimate aspirations as a director and where do you want to go from here? I’m going to sound like a cliché, but I love telling stories. And so I think I’m very interested in telling stories in lots of different mediums, lots of different ways. I don’t know what the future of my career looks like, but I’m pretty confident that it will involve somehow combining my digital experience with narrative experience. And whether that’s in more digitally focused projects or more films or streaming projects, I don’t know. But that seems to be what my career has flirted [with] consistently, at that meeting point. And I think Graviteur has the right idea in that they’re creating a movie that is a very traditional format, but just the fact that they even hired me, they’re thinking about it also with the eye towards what matters in digital, what skills do people coming from digital bring to the table, which is very cool. I think they’re a little ahead of the curve on that. I mean, we’ve obviously also seen many examples of YouTube creators doing this very successfully, but I think that will stop being an outlier and that will start being a more established pipeline. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. THR

articles.title: ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Author Ali Hazelwood to Release Book Sequel, MRC Developing Film for Amazon MGM
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexy Perez Plus Icon Lexy Perez Senior Digital Editor and Producer View All September 29, 2026 7:52am 'The Love Hypothesis' Philippe Bosse/Prime Video The story of Olive Smith and Adam Carlsen will continue in a book sequel. Author Ali Hazelwood announced Tuesday that she will release a sequel, The Two-Body Problem next February. The sequel is in early development and comes amid the recent release of Prime Video‘s adaptation of Hazelwood‘s bestseller The Love Hypothesis , starring Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman. Sharing the cover on her social media Hazelwood wrote, “‘I wrote a sequel to The Love Hypothesis ‘ is not a sentence I thought I’d say a year or so ago, but now I weirdly can’t imagine a world in which The Two-Body Problem doesn’t exist. I’m really eager to talk more about this book and how it came about in the next few months. For now let me just say that the TLH movie and its cast made me fall for Adam and Olive all over again, that revisiting them was an absolute pleasure.“ Related Stories Lifestyle Kyle MacLachlan, Star of David Lynch's 'Dune,' Was the Only One on Set Who Knew What 'Dune' Was About TV Hints of 'Sex and the City' and 'Narcos': A Look at Literary Works Being Pitched for Screen Adaptations at Iberseries & Platino Industria She continued, “As someone who gets VERY attached to stories and characters, I know that unannounced sequels can be blindsiding, so feel free to skip this book and overwrite it with whatever headcanon you prefer, and I’ll see you on the next one! But if you want to read more about Adam and Olive, The Two-Body Problem spans a couple of years, and it’s a mix of slice of life, postdoctoral turmoil, and unflinching exploration of the hardest challenge one will face in a long-term relationship: deciding what to have for dinner. If you pick it up, I really hope you enjoy.“ Though she prefaced that “nothing is guaranteed,“ Hazelwood also announced, “MRC is developing a film based on the The Two-Body Problem for Amazon MGM Studios.“ Further details were not shared. Since its publication in 2021, The Love Hypothesis has since become a full-blown phenomenon — a New York Times bestseller, a BookTok obsession and a career launchpad, turning Hazelwood into a household name. Her books have sold more than 10 million copies worldwide, several already in the book-to-screen pipeline. The film adaptation, which premiered on Sept. 23 on Prime Video, was directed by Claire Scanlon and produced by Elizabeth Cantillon. The romance , which began as Star Wars ’ Reylo fan fiction (featuring Daisy Ridley’s Rey and Adam Driver’s Kylo Ren ) , follows Olive Smith ( Reinhart ), a graduate student and Stanford Ph.D. candidate who embarks on a fake romance with the notoriously stern Adam Carlsen ( Bateman ), known as “Dr. Evil” to his students. The move is solely to reassure her friend Anh (Rachel Marsh) that Olive’s feelings for her bestie’s current love interest are entirely behind her. The Two-Body Problem book will be published on Feb. 2, 2027. View this post on Instagram THR

articles.title: Jenna Johnson on Her Rich ‘DWTS’ Legacy and How Season 35 Could Become Her “Dream Come True”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 29, 2026 8:30am Jenna Johnson. Carly Sharp Logo text Jenna Johnson has had a fruitful career as a Dancing With the Stars professional dancer. Season 35 with Harry Shum Jr. is shaping up to be another standout season on her résumé. “You know when you look around and you’re like, Oh, I’m exactly where I need to be ? That’s how our partnership feels,” the pro tells The Hollywood Reporter of her collaboration with the actor. “I feel so grateful this partnership happened. That’s the beauty of casting — we have no control over it, but once you’re in that pairing, you realize like, This was meant to be .” Related Stories TV Tamera Mowry-Housley Boards 'Scrubs' Season 2 TV Philo Sets Exclusive Streaming Date for Page Six 'Virtual Reali-Tea Awards' The Emmy-nominated choreographer has won DWTS twice, and could become the most decorated female pro if she won her third mirrorball this year. She’d also tie the record for the second-most wins ever for a pro, evening out with Mark Ballas and her husband Val Chmerkovskiy, who each have three wins. Those are statistics she did not know, and she doesn’t want to think about right now. “I really just want to focus on one week at a time ( Laughs ). But those are incredible facts,” she says, although it’s a reality Jenna could soon face if she and Harry make it to the season 35 finale this fall. Below, Jenna dishes on how So You Think You Could Dance led her to DWTS ; reflects on her niece, Hailey Bills, following in her footsteps being partnered with a woman on the show; what Pasha Pashkov really told her during that internet-breaking Viral Hits Night moment ; and her Broadway aspirations. *** It’s my understanding you were noticed on So You Think You Could Dance and then brought into the DWTS troupe. I also know you come from the interconnected world that is the Utah ballroom dance scene, so can you talk about your journey to getting on the troupe? I did grow up in Utah at the same studio that a lot of the pros grew up at. I was a competitive Latin dancer as well as in the commercial convention circuit for jazz, ballet and hip hop. At the time, So You Think You Can Dance was popping, so I auditioned and I got onto it, which was absolutely incredible. It’s pretty ironic, but So You Think You Can Dance and Dancing With the Stars are filmed at the same studio at CBS Television City, and I guess the producers caught wind of my name, and they asked me to be on the troupe. Growing up at my studio in Utah, I had seen people like Derek and Julianne make it in L.A.; they’re dancing for their careers, and they’re household names as ballroom dancers. It was iconic, so to be asked to join the troupe, I was so hungry and eager to learn as much as I could. At that time I joined, you still had the OG pros on the show. There was Derek, Karina [Smirnoff], Kym Johnson, Maks [Chmerkovskiy], Tony Devolani; it was OG pros that I got to really watch their process and learn from. I’m so grateful for that time period because it gave me the tools to go into my time as a pro and feel like I could have the confidence to navigate it. Your first season as a pro, you were eliminated first, then you took a break for season 24 and came back for season 25 and w o n with Adam [Rippon]. How do you reflect back on your early time on the show? I think timing is everything, and everything happens for a reason. I kind of got to experience this with my niece [Hailey Bills] just barely; she was eliminated her first season as a pro [this season], but there’s such a beautiful journey that’s awaiting you. It was very unique being eliminated my first season, but then getting to be partnered with someone like Adam Rippon the next season and take home a mirrorball; to feel that sensation is one of the craziest moments of my life. But I think that’s the beauty of the show, is getting to be partnered with somebody so vastly different each year. Can you take me through that moment when you learned Hailey was going to be a pro this season? I hate to say this, but I wasn’t surprised, because she is one of the most talented human beings I know. I think she really made a name for herself the first year on troupe; she just has that star quality. Obviously, I wanted it for her, and I know how much she wanted it and how much it meant to her. So when she did get asked to be a pro, it just made sense. I can’t wait to see what she does as a pro on the show. Her journey was cut short this year, but man, it is just getting started for her. I can’t wait to see what she does next in the next upcoming season. Her casting was also monumental in the fact that she was the second pro to be in an all-female partnership, second to obviously you. Do you think the decision to pair Hailey with another woman was at all a callback to your partnership with JoJo Siwa or was done in a way where you could guide her in this second-of-a-kind casting for Dancing With the Stars ? You know, I’m not sure why, but I do think that it made sense: the casting of [Hailey and Sarah Jane Nader] together. They were both young, they looked absolutely stunning next to each other, and their personalities were super fun and playful together. I think that the casting was brilliant, and it made sense. Is it ironic that the two of us are the ones to do it? Absolutely. When she was told that she’d be dancing with a female, I wanted to do that for her, because I have been in that situation before, so anything she needed, I wanted to help her out in any way. It is pretty crazy. Like, we’ll always have that bond that we can share together. There is so much discourse going into new seasons about who is partnered with who, and [your season 35 partner] Harry is obviously an amazing dancer. What would you say to somebody who is critical of pros being partnered with “ringers”? What is your take on that discourse? It happens every year, so I think we can expect it. But I think they do need to know that we have nothing to do with our casting. That is not our decision whatsoever. It’s very much up to the production of it all, and they have a rhyme and a reason for all of the pairings. So when there is discourse and there are lots of loud opinions, [I] totally get everyone having their feelings. But there’s nothing we can do. We are given our partner, and then from then on, it is our responsibility to show up and be there for them. So I understand when there is a lot of talk, and obviously there was this current season. But I’m just doing my job. I’m doing what I’m told. And ringer or not, I think each partnership is going to bring its own challenges. With this quote-unquote “ringer” title, that’s a lot of pressure to live up to. Plus, I’ll just speak for my partnership on behalf of Harry, even though he has some dance experience — yes, we’re not running away from that. But dance is so vastly different. He’s never done Latin. He’s never done ballroom. He’s never done frame. All of this is a new world for him, so I hope people can appreciate the effort and hard work that he does put in because that shouldn’t go unnoticed. Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson on Dancing With the Stars season 35. Disney/Christopher Willard As a viewer, it appears that you and Harry have such similar energies. How has working with him so far this season been? Honestly, literally, since the first day we met, there have been so many synchronicities in our lives. You know when you look around and you’re like, Oh, I’m exactly where I need to be ? That’s how our partnership feels. It’s wild to think that I didn’t know him a couple weeks or months ago, because he just fit so beautifully into my life. It’s been so much fun being paired with him, and I feel so grateful this partnership happened. That’s the beauty of casting — we have no control over it, but once you’re in that pairing, you realize like, This was meant to be . This upcoming week is Yacht Rock Night. What do you have planned for that number with Harry? I’m so excited because we’re doing Jive to a great Hall & Oates song, and it feels very Harry. He’s the epitome of joy and bubbly energy, and that’s what we want to do this week. We just want to put a smile on people’s faces. Jive is one of my favorite styles to do because it’s upbeat and fast, but you want to get up and dance with someone. On last Tuesday night’s episode, there was a clip of you and Pasha after Maura Higgins’ dance that went viral. Everybody was trying to figure out what Pasha said to you. Are you able to share what happened in that conversation? Of course. So before Maura and Mark had come up, we were actually just raving about what an incredible dancer Maura is, and Pasha was telling me while they were talking, and this is kind of what went viral, but he was saying, “I saw them do the cha-cha in the beginning of the week.” I guess he had come in and watched their dance early on in the week, and he was like, “It is incredible, her improvement, she’s just gotten so much better” from that first initial rehearsal that he saw. And so you see me going like, “Wow, that’s awesome.” ( Laughs ) So that’s what he was telling me, and everyone was like, “What are they saying?” But we were really just [going] goo-goo ga-ga about how much we love Maura. That’s the tea. This could be the first year that you and your husband, Val, potentially make a finale together. What would that experience mean to you? There’s so much that can happen from now until then, but I would absolutely love to have that moment together. It’s kind of funny, for the past 10 years that we’ve been competing on the show against one another, we’ve never had a situation where both of us have two capable people. It’s like either one of us is going to the finale, the other one’s eliminated early, or vice versa. So this [year on season 35] was a really unique experience for us navigating it. I’m just always so grateful for his support, and I love cheering him on. It’s one of my favorite things to do in the ballroom, so to be able to share that special moment together would be a dream come true, obviously. We will see what happens. You’re very immersed in Dancing With the Stars right now. What do you see yourself doing next? Would you ever potentially do any other competitive reality TV shows? I really wanted to do Special Forces . I love physical activity, so I feel like that would be fun. Other than that, regarding reality shows, I really just want to be a judge on a baking show. Like, that is my dream, honestly. That’s as dramatic as I want to get in the reality space. But career-wise, I feel so blessed that I get to do my dream job every day. I don’t take that for granted. I would really love to dabble in Broadway. I would love to experience live theater in that sort of a situation. But also, I really love my mentor, Mandy Moore. She has just changed the way that dance has been portrayed in films and in TV shows, so I would love to also really dive into choreography of it all and putting it more into film and TV. I saw a video you posted right before the season started: Y’all were in New York and you were talking about how Broadway was something you wanted to do. Have you heard from anybody from that world yet? I absolutely geeked out because the premiere night there was a producer from Chicago in the audience, and I was just like, What is life right now? That was pretty epic. Jenna Johnson. Carly Sharp What is your favorite part of a full week in the Dancing With the Stars process: choreography, teaching/rehearsing, dress rehearsal or live show day? I really think it’s the rehearsal process. I love watching somebody put in hard work and effort, and seeing it come to fruition. I’m just going to speak on my partner right now, but watching Harry have no ego in the midst of learning something new, that is so fulfilling as a partner, as a choreographer. I think it’s really beautiful, this concept of shared purpose. We go into rehearsal having a combined goal, and to be able to achieve that together of like, “OK, today, let’s focus on getting the routine to count; tomorrow, let’s focus on getting it to music; now let’s add in the performance element,” I love that camaraderie of having a partner that you accomplish goals with and have a shared intention and purpose. I obviously also love the creation of it, although we’re kind of always on a time constraint during the season. That can be a little bit stressful. But I think watching somebody do something scary, put in their whole heart and soul, and effort, blood, sweat and tears and then watching them accomplish it is the best part. What is your favorite style of dance to choreograph? I really love a Tango. It’s the best; it’s sharp, strong, hot, sexy. There’s so much traveling, there’s a lot of power behind it. But also, this week, I’m having so much fun with the jive Do you have a favorite number that you have choreographed on Dancing With the Stars ? Oh man, that’s so hard. That’s like asking to pick your favorite child. One that stands out forever will be the piece that Val and I got to choreograph for Len Goodman, for his tribute . That was one of the most special creations of my life, and to honor somebody who holds so much legacy, it was really special. I also do have to say my dance that I did with Joey [Graziadei] to give up our title — each time somebody wins, they come back the next season and do an honor dance in the finale. The dance that Joey and I got to do last year in the [season 34] finale was one of my top favorite dances ever, ever, ever. Describe Dancing With the Stars season 35 in one word. Mind-blowing. *** Season 35 of DWTS airs Tuesdays at 8 p.m., simulcasting across ABC and Disney+, and streaming the next day on Hulu. Read all of THR ‘s DWTS coverage here . THR

articles.title: Chile’s Sanfic Set to Screen Late Documentarian Antonio Caro’s Swan Song ‘Monguen’ Among Nine Chilean Pics in Competition (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 29, 2026 7:07am PT Chile’s Sanfic Set to Screen Late Documentarian Antonio Caro’s Swan Song ‘Monguen’ Among Nine Chilean Pics in Competition (EXCLUSIVE) By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest Chile’s Sanfic Set to Screen Late Documentarian Antonio Caro’s Swan Song ‘Monguen’ Among Nine Chilean Pics in Competition (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago ‘The Platform’ Co-Producer David Matamoros of Doce Entertainment Spain Boards Matías Rojas’ ‘Dog Legs’ (EXCLUSIVE) 8 hours ago Madrid Audiovisual Cluster Dives Deeper Into New Business Models, AI and Emerging Technologies at Iberseries & Platino Industria 10 hours ago See All 'Monguen' Courtesy of Sanfic Chile’s 22nd Santiago Film Festival ( Sanfic ) features nine pics in its Chile Film Competition this year vying for cash prizes in the best film, director and actor categories. Among them, four are debut features, including “ Erratics” by Thomas Woodroffe, which competed at the San Sebastian Festival’s New Directors sidebar. The lineup also features ‘Monguen,’ the swan song of docu filmmaker Antonio Caro, who died unexpectedly a few weeks ago. “We present his film with special affection, as a way of honoring his work and keeping his perspective present within this selection,” said Sanfic artistic director, Carlos Núñez. Related Stories ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Has Already Made $50 Million in Pre-Sales, Three Months Before Release 'Avengers: Endgame Encore' Adds 4 New Scenes Tying to 'Doomsday': [SPOILER] Fights Doctor Doom, [SPOILER] Travels to the Past and the Multiverse Collapses “This competition reflects a particularly diverse moment in Chilean cinema, with films that engage with our present through very different languages, territories and generations. There are works that cross between fiction and documentary, new voices alongside filmmakers with established careers, and a strong presence of perspectives emerging outside traditional centers of production,” he pointed out. Popular on Variety “We want Sanfic to be precisely that kind of space: a place where Chilean cinema can connect with its audiences while, at the same time, reaching an international stage.” Chile’s film industry has never been more robust, with the 2026-2027 industry catalog reporting a 20.5% surge compared to the last season. The catalog was unveiled at the San Sebastián Festival where eight Chilean titles screened across seven sections. However, the industry is bracing for some belt tightening – and will most likely resort to even more co-productions starting next year – given the upcoming cuts announced by the administration of new President Jose Antonio Kast, who took office in March. Cuts to the Ministry of Culture and various competitive funds for the Arts are forthcoming although the ministry downplayed the cutback, stressing that it would be an overall decrease of 9% next year. However, the Audiovisual Investment Support Fund drops from approximately $586,000 (540 million pesos) in 2026 to $208,000 (192 million pesos) in 2027—a 64% reduction. Speaking to Variety when the news first broke, Alejandra Garcia of Ronda Cine, producer of “The Meltdown,” Chile’s Oscars submission, said: “The recent budget cuts to culture in Chile are deeply frustrating. It’s difficult to understand why a country’s support for culture is still seen as an expense to be reduced, rather than an investment that should be strengthened.” The other nine sections of the festival will be announced on Oct. 20. Sanfic runs Nov. 2 – 6 in Santiago de Chile. Chilean Pics in Competition: “Animals” (Andrés Waissbluth Weinstein, Retaguardia Films, Avispa Cine, Frutacina, Chile, Argentina) In a near future where animals have civil rights, three privileged couples see their lives disrupted by an eerily human quadruped: a sheep running for office, a dog that can sniff out lies and a jealous cat. Produced by Felipe Azúa and Iván Eibuszyc, the Chilean-Argentine Sanfic world premiere was developed through Santiago Lab, BrLab and Guadalajara’s Co-production Meeting, with support from CORFO, Ibermedia and Buenos Aires’ Mecenazgo program. ‘Animales’ “Beat” (“Latir,” Patricio Loutit Azócar, Suroeste Films, Reinos Cine, Chile) Loutit Azócar’s feature debut follows Manuel, a retired university professor who joins a body-percussion workshop during Chile’s 2022 constitutional plebiscite. The experience transforms his life as he confronts his wife’s terminal illness. World premiering at Sanfic, it was produced by Manuel González Llanos and Daniel Rebolledo. The Chilean production received support from the Audiovisual Development Fund in 2024 and participated in Industria FIC Viña’s 2024 business meetings. ‘Beat’ “Black Corp,” (“Cuadro Negro,”Carolina Adriazola and José Luis Sepúlveda, Iglo Cine Chile) Adriazola and Sepúlveda’s film follows Sofía, a young journalist documenting the Chilean army who returns to live with her grandmother after a breakup. She meets María, whose view of the military legacy contrasts with her grandmother’s. Produced by Sofía Paloma Gómez, José Luis Sepúlveda and Carolina Adriazola, the film premiered at Punto de Vista, winning the Grand Prize for Best Film and Youth Jury Award for Best Film. It marks its Latin American premiere. ‘Black Corp’ “Death Brought You Back” (“La muerte te vio volver,” Sebastián Cuevas Barria, Praxia Producciones, Mala Films, Chile; Vert & Bleu Productions, France) Cuevas Barria’s debut follows Silvia, returning to Chiloé after 30 years to claim her dying mother’s inheritance and confront a disturbing family past. Produced by Catalina Alarcón Reyes, it received support from Chile’s Audiovisual Fund and was developed through Sanfic Lab, CCC and the Lebu Film Festival Lab. Selected for Sanfic’s 2024 Ibero-American WIP, it won the Films en Cours Award at Entrevues Belfort and FECILS’ Sound Award. Participated in Ventana Sur in Montevideo. ‘Death Brought You Back’ “Erratics” (“Bloques Erráticos,” Thomas Woodroffe , La Belle Affaire Productions, Un Puma, Chile, France, Argentina) Woodroffe’s debut follows filmmaker Lucien Castelnau’s ghost, played by France’s Denis Lavant (“Holy Motors”), released from a glacier after a century into a futuristic Patagonia where technological progress collides with forgotten histories. A Rotterdam CineMart winner produced by Rodrigo Díaz, Pascual Mena and Jérôme Blesson, the Chilean-French-Argentine co-production was developed through La Fabrique Cinéma, TorinoFilmLab, CineMart Darkroom and Sanfic Lab. Selected for San Sebastián’s New Directors , it received Eurimages’ New Lab Outreach Award and support from Chile’s Audiovisual Fund and TorinoFilmLab’s Co-production Fund. ‘Erratics’ “Floating Population” (“Población Flotante,” Carlos Araya Díaz, Maria una vez, Chile) Araya Díaz’s docu-fiction hybrid follows a filmmaker reconnecting with a childhood friend through an actor’s voice, revisiting his final days as a bus worker. World premiered at Czech Republic’s Ji.hlava Fest and marking its Latin American premiere at Sanfic, the film was produced by María Paz González and developed through Encuentros Australes at FIC Valdivia, where it won Best Chilean Film of the Future (First Cut) in 2023, plus WIP selections at FIC Viña del Mar. ‘Floating Population’ “Inner Rebellion” (“Rebelión Interior,” Sofía Paloma Gómez Vergara, La Jauría Comunicaciones, Chile) Gómez Vergara’s documentary revisits Chile’s social uprising through a health brigade treating protesters injured by police repression, connecting present violence with dictatorship-era wounds. World premiering at Sanfic, it was produced by Catalina Alarcón Reyes and developed through FIC Valdivia’s Cine Chileno del Futuro, where it won Best Chilean Film of the Future (Post-production) and the Sonamos Award. It also participated in WIP FicViña, DocsMX and Fidba’s LINK-WIP and received national post-production funding in 2025. ‘Inner Rebellion’ “Monguen” (“Life,” Antonio Caro, Lemuntu Producciones, Totem Producciones, Chile) The late Caro’s documentary feature follows Fresia, a young Mapuche woman from Alto Biobío who must leave her community to give birth in the city, navigating motherhood between two worlds. World premiering at Sanfic, the film is produced by Michel Toledo and was developed through Conecta CCDoc, Residencia Arca, Nuevas Miradas EICTV, Hot Docs Forum, Cannes Docs at Marché du Film and Encuentros Australes Fic Valdivia. “The Tiger of the East” (“El Tigre del Este,” Jorge Acevedo, Yareta Films, Queltehue Films, Chile; Estudio Churubusco, Mexico) Acevedo’s debut pic follows Andrés, a young Chilean muleteer and self-taught musician who leaves his hometown to pursue his dream of becoming a professional musician in Mexico. His wish to gift an original song to Los Tigres del Norte inspires the journey. Produced by Mixie Araya Soler, the Chilean-Mexican co-production premiered at Shanghai Film Festival. Developed since 2018, the project has participated in international labs and markets including Cannes Docs, DocsMX and FiDocs. ‘The Tiger of the East’ Marvel Launches ‘Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday Official Podcast’ Ahead of Movie’s December Debut Disney CEO Admits ‘Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu’ and ‘Moana’ Underperformed at Box Office but ‘Fueled Other Parts of Our Company’ ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Adds 4 New Scenes Tying to ‘Doomsday’: [SPOILER] Fights Doctor Doom, [SPOILER] Travels to the Past and the Multiverse Collapses Florence Pugh Says ‘I Was Never Scared’ of Publicly Supporting Palestine and ‘I Don’t Know Why It Took So Long’ for Hollywood to ‘Start Talking’ ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Has Already Made $50 Million in Pre-Sales, Three Months Before Release ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer: Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom Faces Off Against Mister Fantastic, X-Men and Avengers With Army of Sentinels Loading comments...

articles.title: Jia Zhangke, Tian Qi’s Unknown Pleasures Lands Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s ‘Jenjira’s Magnificent Dream’ for China
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 29, 2026 7:28am PT Jia Zhangke, Tian Qi’s Unknown Pleasures Lands Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s ‘Jenjira’s Magnificent Dream’ for China By Jenny S. Li Plus Icon Jenny S. Li Latest Lee Sinje Readies Feature Directing Debut ‘Wanita,’ Unveils ‘Dead Tide’ at Pingyao 3 hours ago ‘Light Pillar’ Director Xu Zao Readies AI-Themed Follow-Up ‘Easy, My Friend’ 4 hours ago Jia Zhangke Readies Zhao Tao Road Movie ‘Mamma Dunhuang,’ Rules Out AI in Production (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Unknown Pleasures Pictures Jia Zhangke ‘s Unknown Pleasures Pictures has acquired China rights to Apichatpong Weerasethakul ‘s “Jenjira’s Magnificent Dream,” co-founder Tian Qi has confirmed to Variety . The Chinese art-house distributor is also negotiating to acquire two titles from this year’s Cannes Film Festival. In June, it added Andrey Zvyagintsev’s “Minotaur” and Marine Atlan’s “La Gradiva,” and in January it took Greater China rights to Rafael Manuel’s Sundance title “Filipiñana,” which Jia executive produced and which had its Asian premiere at Pingyao this week. Related Stories Tom Hiddleston Recalls Trekking to Everest for ‘Tenzing’ and Kevin Feige Telling Him ‘Thor’ Wasn’t ‘Going to Be the Only Film’ He Would Play Loki In How Oscar-Tipped Rising Star Anthony Ippolito Turned ‘I Play Rocky’ Into ‘I Play Sylvester’: ‘You Only Have One Chance to Do This’ Named after Jia’s 2002 feature, Unknown Pleasures is run by Jia and distributor Tian, who also founded Hero Films, the distributor of Gu You’s Busan title “The First Taste of Loneliness.” The label focuses on niche international art films, and alongside festival titles, it looks for hidden gems that lack strong international sales backing. Popular on Variety Before the label launched, Tian’s previous company released Weerasethakul’s “Memoria” in China, where it grossed $360,000, a third of the film’s total box office. Jia and Tian say that early success gave them confidence. Unknown Pleasures launched in 2025, with Italian director Paola Cortellesi’s “There’s Still Tomorrow,” one of Italy’s biggest box office hits of 2023. Acquired in 2024, the film screened at the Pingyao International Film Festival and opened in Chinese cinemas on March 8 for International Women’s Day. It grossed $6 million on the back of strong reviews. Later that year, the company picked up four Cannes titles: Joachim Trier’s “Sentimental Value,” Kleber Mendonça Filho’s “The Secret Agent,” Fukada Koji’s “Love on Trial” and the restoration of Charlie Chaplin’s “The Gold Rush.” “The founding ethos was that the world is full of wondrous movies, and among the 1.4 billion Chinese population, these films are bound to find their audience,” Tian says. He adds that not every acquisition has to turn a profit. “Once we acquire a title, we definitely aim to release it with the fastest speed.” Jia says he and Tian agree on keeping the company’s finances stable, but the main mission remains “to distribute films we truly like. If we stand purely from a business point, we wouldn’t start this business anyways.” He wants the company to help grow China’s art-film market. “We operate with a long-term library strategy: these titles should remain evergreen in the coming years. By building our own catalog and taking a long-term financial view, we keep the revenue sustainable,” Jia says. For Jia, movies “that are genuinely interesting, deserve to be shared, and people might easily pass over – those are the ones that really need to be seen in a cinema.” “We can’t help but sigh over some films that were released online – they actually belong to cinema,” he says. articles.title: ‘Sin Filtro’ Producer JK Media Producing First Original Microdramas Shot in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision’s ViXMicrO (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 29, 2026 7:45am PT ‘Sin Filtro’ Producer JK Media Producing First Original Microdramas Shot in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision’s ViXMicrO (EXCLUSIVE) By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest Chile’s Sanfic Set to Screen Late Documentarian Antonio Caro’s Swan Song ‘Monguen’ Among Nine Chilean Pics in Competition (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago ‘The Platform’ Co-Producer David Matamoros of Doce Entertainment Spain Boards Matías Rojas’ ‘Dog Legs’ (EXCLUSIVE) 8 hours ago Madrid Audiovisual Cluster Dives Deeper Into New Business Models, AI and Emerging Technologies at Iberseries & Platino Industria 10 hours ago See All Fernanda Romero in 'Trapped with the Enemy' Courtesy of JK Media JK Media, the producer behind the hit unscripted celebrity show “ Sin Filtro ” and its various iterations, has developed and produced the first original microdramas in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision ’s ViXMicrO. The new Spanish-language microdramas, “Trapped with the Enemy” (“Encerrada con el enemigo) and “Threatened Infidelity” (“Infidelidad amenazada”), were both shot in Los Angeles and are slated to bow in October this year. Each series consists of 60 episodes running 90 seconds each and will be available in Mexico and the U.S. Related Stories Zurich Film Festival Heads on Theatrical-Loving Gen Z, Prioritizing Private Equity and Tilly Norwood a Year Later: This Is the ‘Place Where You Address the Real Hot Questions’ Tilly Norwood Creator Says AI Actress Made 'Many People Realize That AI Is Coming' and 'That Was the Point' “We are excited to dive into the microdrama space for the first time and launching some of the first-ever U.S. produced vertical series for ViXMicrO,” said JK Media Group founder and CEO Sebastian Jimenez. Popular on Variety JK Media Group founder and CEO Sebastian Jimenez The two series are executive produced by Jimenez and Flavio Morales, who was an EP on HBO Max’s global hit “Like Water for Chocolate.” Sergio Jablon (“Súbete a mi moto”) serves as a writer on both series. “We’ve assembled a tremendous team, both in front of and behind the camera, for these two series and we can’t wait to share them with the ViX audience,” said Jimenez. “Trapped with the Enemy” is described as a “romantic thriller that unfolds in real time, within a single setting, where the suspense offers no respite and desire seeps through the cracks of fear.” It follows Clara, who thought her nightmare was over when her abusive ex, Hugo, is sent to prison. But he’s escaped and is waiting for her in the parking garage after work. With her car sabotaged, no phone signal and a dead guard nearby, escape seems impossible — until Leo appears. Mysterious and eerily like Hugo, he could be her savior or her next threat. As the danger closes in, an unexpected connection sparks. “Threatened Infidelity” is “a romantic comedy with teeth — where infidelity is the doorway into a twisty thriller of entanglements, betrayals and desire, in which no one is entirely innocent… but some are far guiltier than others.” It centers on Daniela, who returns home to find her husband, Mario, secretly having an affair with their yoga instructor neighbor, Valentina. When a forgotten watch exposes him, Daniela finds an unexpected ally in Carlos, the handsome new neighbor. But Valentina’s affair is part of a darker scheme: she wants the building Daniela’s father designed — and she’ll eliminate anyone who stands in her way. Fernanda Romero (“The Eye,” “The Burning Plain”) stars in both microdramas while Suanny Serpas (“Eye for an Eye”) and comedian Concrete also appear in “Threatened Infidelity.” Liliana Arriaga (“La Chupitos”) makes a special appearance in “Trapped with the Enemy.” Launched last year, ViXMicrO features the wildly popular short-form scripted series that are designed for vertical, mobile-first viewing. According to research company Omdia, the format, which first originated in China, generated global revenues of $11 billion last year and is expected to hit $14 billion by the end of 2026, with Latin America emerging as a major market. The format is particularly popular with the youth, with politicians turning to it to power up the youth vote, most recently by L.A. mayoral candidate Nithya Raman. Madrid-based confab Iberseries & Platino Industria, running Sept. 29 – Oct 2, has programmed events around the fast-growing format. Specializing in original series and films in both Spanish and English, JK Media recently launched “Ninel Conde: Sin Filtro” with ViX and produced the historic pay-per-view live broadcast of “Gloria Trevi: Live” from BMO Stadium, which was streamed with VEEPS. The company is behind such award-winning titles as “Chiquis Sin Filtro,” “La Trevi Sin Filtro,” “Chiquis’ Foodie on the Go” and “Larrymania,” starring Larry Hernández, among others. The company is set to produce additional PPV events across the globe, including upcoming events in Mexico, Colombia and Argentina.
