articles.title: Madrid’s Iberseries & Platino Industria Bosses Tout Expansion and Innovation: “The Key Is Usefulness”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 28, 2026 5:30am Iberseries & Platino Industria 2024 in Madrid Courtesy of Georg Szalai All eyes on Madrid ! The Spanish capital and film and TV production hub is bringing together media and entertainment industry folks, including producers, creatives and executives from Europe, Latin America, the U.S. and beyond, to discuss Spanish- and Portuguese-language content opportunities and hot industry topics at the sixth edition of Iberseries & Platino Industria this week. Organized by the Secuoya Foundation, Spain’s largest rights collection agency EGEDA, and the Ibero-American Federation FIPCA, the big annual event, which runs Tuesday through Friday, will once again feature keynote addresses, panel discussions, screenings, pitching sessions , and social events, along with all sorts of innovations. AI, microdramas, co-productions, literary adaptations and much more will be in the spotlight during four jam-packed days in Madrid. Among the many high-profile speakers and panelists at Iberseries are the likes of Katina Medina Mora, who has directed such series as Off Campus , The Summer I Turned Pretty , Emily in Paris and Swagger and such films as LuTo , Luis Fernández, chairman of NBCUniversal Telemundo Enterprises, and Pedro Pina, vp, YouTube EMEA. THR caught up with Iberseries & Platino Industria co-directors Samuel Castro , head of Iberseries, Juan Alía, head of Platino Industria, and Adriana Castillo, general coordinator of Platino Industria, to preview the 2026 showcase of the Spanish- and Portuguese-language content industry event and what’s different this year. What’s new for this year’s edition? Could you highlight any new offerings and innovations? SAMUEL CASTRO This year, we wanted to reinforce our commitment to the industry and further establish Iberseries & Platino Industria as a truly business- and networking-driven event. With this in mind, we have launched two new pitch sessions: Euro Atlantic Series Co-Pro Pitch, focused on European series projects seeking international co-production and financing partners; and the Fundación SGAE Pitch Session, featuring outstanding projects from Spanish-speaking showrunners. ADRIANA CASTILLO One of the things we have worked on this year is making Iberseries & Platino Industria useful at different stages of a project’s journey. We do not want it to be simply a place where talent comes together; we want it to be a place where talent finds the conditions to grow: financing, partnerships, distribution and real international opportunities. That has led us to open new doors this year. We created the Literary Works Pitch for Audiovisual Adaptation, strengthened international co-production through the Euro Atlantic Series Co-Pro Pitch and the Co-Production and Financing Forum, and opened spaces to discuss new ways of telling stories, including vertical fiction and microdramas. For me, the important thing is that these are not isolated activities. We are trying to connect the dots. A creator can arrive with an idea or an IP and meet producers, financiers, platforms, studios, distributors, or potential partners. Ultimately, what we want is to shorten the distance between a good story and the people who can help bring it to life. JUAN ALÍA I do not think the novelty lies simply in adding more activities. When an edition ends, we sit down to look at what worked, what we can improve and, above all, what the industry is asking of us. This year, we have opened up more avenues for projects to find financing, partners and buyers, and we have broadened the scope with areas such as literary IP and vertical fiction. For us, the key is usefulness. We want professionals who come to Madrid for four days to have real opportunities to find the content, project, or partner they are looking for. If those meetings lead to synergies, co-productions or new lines of business, then the event is fulfilling its purpose. Why did it make sense to add the first edition of Euro Atlantic Series Co-Pro Pitch to your already busy program? And Sony Pictures Television’s Elevator Pitch will also return. How successful was that last year? CASTRO Euro Atlantic Series Co-Pro Pitch was created with the aim of promoting the co-production and international circulation of European fiction, docuseries and animation projects conceived from the outset to travel across territories and connect with global audiences. It is another reflection of the increasingly international scale of Iberseries & Platino Industria, as we continue evolving from an Ibero-American event into a truly global industry platform. Samuel Castro, co-director Iberseries & Platino Industria Courtesy of Iberseries & Platino Industria The selection committee for this first edition also brings together highly respected professionals from the European audiovisual industry, including Laura Miñarro, vp of international business and co-production at Buendía Estudios (Spain), Diego del Pozo, fiction manager at Atresmedia Televisión (Spain), José Fragoso, programming director at RTP1 and RTP Internacional (Portugal), and Georges Huercano, development and co-productions manager at RTL (Belgium). Can you tell me a bit about why you added the new literary works adaptation pitch event? CASTILLO It emerged quite naturally from what we had been hearing from the industry. In our conversations with [streaming] platforms, studios and producers, IP comes up again and again. Executives are looking for attractive properties, of course, but above all they are looking for powerful stories, distinctive worlds and characters capable of sustaining an audiovisual life. At the same time, there is an enormous catalogue of stories in the publishing world, and there is not always a natural space for the publishing and audiovisual sectors to meet, or even to speak the same business language. We saw a clear opportunity to build a bridge between them. This is not about bringing a book fair to an audiovisual market. It is a curated business space where publishers and literary agencies can present works directly to producers, studios and platforms looking for material to adapt, and then continue those conversations through one-to-one meetings. Literary IP also brings something extremely valuable to the audiovisual pipeline: narrative development and, in many cases, a story that has already connected with a community of readers. But our interest goes beyond a one-off rights sale. We want to foster longer-term relationships between publishers and producers, help those catalogues circulate internationally and identify stories that can genuinely find a second life on screen. In that sense, the pitch [event] also reflects something we are seeing across the industry: the search for IP has become much more strategic. It is no longer simply a question of whether a book is well known; it is about whether there is a powerful story there and what can be built from it. ALÍA In this case, we are not inventing a need; it is something the market has been signalling to us for some time. Platforms and production companies are increasingly looking for IP, while publishers and literary agencies have enormous catalogues of stories. What was missing was a more direct and structured meeting point between the two sectors. If a publisher or agency leaves Madrid having started a real conversation with a production company, studio or platform, then the pitch has already been useful. Everybody is talking about AI in the industry. How important a topic will that be at Iberseries? And what other key themes do you expect to be in focus at this year’s edition? CASTRO AI will have the prominence it deserves, but always from the perspective of understanding it as a regulated tool at the service of creators, technicians and audiovisual production professionals. Among this year’s activities focused on AI, I would particularly highlight the workshop “ Artificial Intelligence for Creators: Enhancing Audiovisual Storytelling,” led by Concepción Díaz, head of AI trainings EMEA at Google, and the conference “AI in Action: New Production Models,” featuring Erik Barmack, founder & CEO of Wild Sheep Content (USA), and Johann Choron, partnerships & Gen AI lead for film & TV at Google EMEA (France). How is attendance trending this year compared to what I think was a record last year? CASTRO It is still difficult to give a definitive answer. The industry as a whole is going through a period of some contraction, and companies seem to be taking a more cautious approach. Against this backdrop, we have deliberately chosen to offer a more disruptive and ambitious program this year. I hope that this will encourage even more industry players to join us. Are there any key new companies or industry sub-sectors coming to the event this year? CASTILLO Yes, and I think what is particularly interesting this year is not only the arrival of new companies, but also the way different areas of the industry are beginning to connect within Iberseries & Platino Industria. We are also seeing very interesting models emerging from the meeting point between traditional audiovisual players and digital communities. Disney+ and Luzu TV are a great example. ‘Somos así, la serie de Nadie dice nada’ comes out of an alliance between one of the leading streaming platforms and one of Argentina’s most influential digital communities. A live-streaming phenomenon is being transformed into fiction, and that raises a very interesting question for the industry: how do you take a community with such a strong relationship with its creators and build a fictional universe around it without losing the authenticity that made it successful in the first place? Adriana Castillo, general coordinator of Platino Industria Courtesy of Iberseries & Platino Industria Then there is the increasingly important role of audience intelligence. JustWatch adds another dimension to that conversation with its session on intent-based marketing: how behavioural signals and audience preferences can help us understand not only what people have watched, but what they are looking to watch next, and how that information can be used to make more efficient marketing decisions. Netflix, for example, is participating through different parts of the programme. One of them addresses an increasingly important challenge for the audiovisual industry: how we train the next generation of professionals, how we reduce access gaps in training and how we build a more diverse, equitable talent base with broader territorial reach across Ibero-America. A panel featuring FORMA, the training initiative promoted by FIPCA [, an intercontinental organization that brings together producer associations and audiovisual companies,] with the support of Netflix, is a good example of the kind of collaboration we want to encourage more and more at Iberseries & Platino Industria: initiatives that not only respond to the needs of today’s productions, but also strengthen the industry over the long term. The platform is also involved in content presentations, so its presence connects training, industry development and programming. ALÍA I think what matters is that we are trying to open the scope as widely as possible. Netflix, Disney+, Luzu TV and JustWatch are very different players, but each represents a very specific change taking place in the sector: training and professionalisation, the transition from digital communities to fiction, and the growing importance of audience data in marketing and decision-making. CASTRO One of our main [goals] this year has been to give the event an even stronger European dimension. We have attracted major companies such as Banijay, Mediawan, Beta, ARTE and RAI, to name just a few. But perhaps even more significant is the growing number of European production companies interested in co-producing with Spain. This is reflected in the participation of leading professionals such as Iris Bucher, Femke Wolting from Submarine and Nathalie Perus from Atlantique Productions, among others. It is not about adding companies simply for the sake of adding logos. We want the event to be the opportunity the producer or executive has been looking for. Which Spanish- and Portuguese-language or -produced films and series have highlighted the global appeal of Iberian content? CASTILLO There are some very clear examples. El Eternauta (series The Eternaut ) from Argentina and O Agente Secreto (film The Secret Agent ) from Brazil have shown, in very different ways, how stories deeply rooted in a specific place and culture can have an international life and reach new audiences. And I think that is very important: global does not have to mean neutral. Very often, the specificity of a story – its language, its characters, its social context, even its sense of place – is precisely what makes it interesting to other audiences. This year, we will present Véspera , HBO Max’s new Brazilian original series based on Carla Madeira’s bestselling novel. It is a complex family story, deeply Brazilian in origin, but built around emotions, relationships and moral conflicts that are entirely universal. For me, Véspera also connects with another conversation we are having this year: the strength of literary IP. It shows how a successful Portuguese-language novel can move into another medium and potentially reach a completely new audience. That circulation between books and screens, between local identity and international audiences, and between Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking territories, is exactly the kind of movement we want to promote through Iberseries & Platino Industria. ALÍA I think Spanish- and Portuguese-language content no longer has to prove that it can travel. Titles such as El Eternauta and O Agente Secreto make that quite clear: they emerge from very specific cultural realities and yet work internationally. Juan Alía, co-director of Iberseries & Platino Industria Courtesy of Iberseries & Platino Industria That is also why we believe it is important to present titles such as Véspera at Iberseries & Platino Industria. A market should not only look at what has already worked; it should also help upcoming projects find partners, circulate and reach new audiences. CASTRO Portugal is particularly important to us this year. We have worked closely with APIT and the Portugal Film Commission to bring a delegation of Portuguese producers to the event, including Nicky Correia from SIC, Bruno Lima from Coral Europa, Pandora da Cunha Telles from Ukbar Filmes and Piet-Hein Bakker from Plural Entertainment, among others. Their participation reflects both the strength of Portuguese production and our commitment to strengthening connections between the Portuguese, Spanish and wider international audiovisual industries. Is there anything else you would like to highlight? ALÍA Ultimately, what matters to us is that all of this is useful. The number of accredited professionals is important, of course, as is the event’s international character, but the real assessment does not end on 2 October. What will truly make us happy is to look back in two or three years and see that projects presented here in a pitch, a forum or a meeting have become reality, have reached a cinema, a television channel or a platform and, above all, have reached audiences. If Iberseries & Platino Industria has contributed to that, then we will feel that we have done our job well. CASTILLO I would certainly highlight Mexico, which is our Country in Focus this year. We were very clear that the objective was to put forward a specific industry proposition. For several years, the conversation around Mexico has focused on its talent, the size of its market and its production scale. These are already recognised strengths. This year, we want to take the conversation one step further and ask another question: why produce in Mexico today? There are new conditions that make this conversation particularly relevant: incentives, such as [the Tax Incentive for Film and Audiovisual Production] EFICA, production infrastructure, specialised technical services, post-production, film commissions and, of course, a production community with enormous experience in both Mexican and international projects. That is why there will be a series of activities designed to position Mexico from different angles: its creators and stories, of course, but also its production capacity, its services and its potential to become a partner on international projects. I think that is the message we want to leave: Mexico has always had stories and talent. What is particularly interesting today is the combination of that creative strength with increasingly competitive conditions for making films and series in the country. CASTRO There are two highlights I would particularly mention this year. The first is Pedro Pina’s keynote, “YouTube: A Strategic Partner for the Audiovisual Ecosystem,” which will explore YouTube’s increasingly important role within the audiovisual industry. The second is the Mediawan Spotlight, featuring Elisabeth d’Arvieu, CEO of Mediawan Pictures and chief content officer of Mediawan, which I believe will be another major moment in this year’s program. THR

articles.title: What Will David Ellison Name His Mega Hollywood Studio?
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All September 28, 2026 6:12am David Ellison already likes the Skydance Corporation name. Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images Bigger-is-better studio merger logic goes back in Hollywood nearly as long as the industry has existed. So, too, do eyerolls about such consolidation. In 1933, for instance, comedy troupe the Marx Brothers unveiled the name of their production company, with a characteristic wink , as International Amalgamated Consolidated Affiliated World Wide Film Productions Company Incorporated, of North Dakota. That name makes saying aloud “ Paramount Skydance Warner Bros. Discovery ” seem like almost like a breeze after the final ink is dry on David Ellison’s $111 billion merger. But, for this day and age, even five words — a mashup of two century-old studio names on each side of an upstart new media company, with a cable channel tacked on at the end — seem like too much. That’s the dilemma facing Team Ellison: What does he name a company that just seemingly vacuumed up half of Hollywood? Up until now it’s been known as WarnerMount, which tellingly leads with the acquired studio, or ParaBros, which is more of a nod to the optics of the C-suite mix of the buyers. But the formal name has yet to be unveiled and Paramount is staying mum, declining comment on that. But the name is no small thing. The decision will signal to both the industry and the Wall Street crowd what its new owner prioritizes. On a big picture scale, you could say it sets the strategic direction. Does Ellison want to look forward, rather than backward, given all of his talk about taking on tech giants in the attention economy? Or does his love of the entertainment industry, and big-budget moviemaking, nod to a nostalgic side? And now, with a rules-of-the-road consent decree to abide by thanks to California attorney general Rob Bonta, he’s got to keep in mind the optics for that crew as well (You can’t look like a monopoly right after closing a deal where the primary complaint from critics is that the merger vaporizes another buyer from the landscape). And the titling will also tip to how Ellison’s own ego plays in to the process, too. The Paramount Pictures logo, circa 1989 when Gulf and Western Inc. changed its name to Paramount Communications. Everett The Warner Bros. logo during its Time Warner days. Everett There’s tradition to think of. The Paramount Pictures name and script typeface conjures up Oscars’ best picture winners like The Godfather or Forrest Gump or Top Gun . That’s the reason why, after Shari Redstone re-merged her father Sumner’s Viacom and CBS empires, she rebranded the robotic and clunkily named ViacomCBS as Paramount Global, alongside christening its flagship streamer Paramount+ (and ditching that CBS All Access name). The Paramount name, Redstone believed, signaled quality and Classic Hollywood, and was a known commodity worldwide. The same could be said about Warner Bros., home of Casablanca and Rebel Without a Cause and countless other classics (many of which we associate with Warners but are actually MGM features, like Wizard of Oz , thanks to Warners buying much of that library and playing those movies on rotation on the Turner Classic Movies channel). It’s the reason why the Warner name has stuck around despite countless mergers and acquisitions. It weathered a merger with then-publishing giant Time Inc and suffered the indignity of having AOL take it over in what’s now regarded as the most disastrous media megadeal of all-time. In what probably should’ve been a tell, when AT&T acquired it in 2018, the telecom swallowed Time Warner whole and there was no trace of the Warner name. Deemed immaterial to AT&T just a few years later, it was spun out to David Zaslav’s cable giant, who — in arguably a nod to his ego — made sure that Discovery was represented in the Warner Bros. Discovery merger. That framing made it seem like Warner Bros. and Discovery were equals, when in reality the assets that were sought after (like the movie studio and HBO) were mostly all on the WB side. Zaslav’s team tried a stab at that Golden Age of Hollywood quality when revealing a truly hideous logo in 2021 alongside a quote from The Maltese Falcon (“The stuff that dreams are made of”). Yes, this was a real logo , circa 2021, for Warner Bros. Discovery. But by the time the company closed in 2022 it was consigned to the trash bin. One clue as to how Ellison may look to go about the naming is what he did when his far-smaller Skydance Media (Est. 2006) merged with Paramount (Est. 1912). Remember, when Skydance first inked a deal in 2024 nearly a year before closing on Paramount it initially redesigned the Paramount logo to look like the Skydance one. As if that Skydance DNA would be what turbocharged the next chapter of Paramount. In an investor presentation , Skydance’s team initially redesigned the classic Paramount logo with the Skydance font. Paramount Skydance That change ultimately didn’t take when the deal closed — why mess with a font synonymous with Hollywood? The Paramount script has been around nearly as long as the company existed. It’s been replicated on venues far from Los Angeles and has been the first thing that audiences have seen on countless titles in theaters (the Indiana Jones movies come to mind as far as how each first scene finds a way to play off the Paramount mountain). There’s an authenticity test here. That Skydance-ified Paramount logo looks just a bit off , especially for a studio that’s been around 100 years. Here’s the Paramount Pictures logo adorning the front gate of the Hollywood studio lot in 1920: The front gate to Paramount Studios in 1920. If you squint, it could be 2026 except for that car driving through the gate. Getty Images While formally the company is now titled Paramount Skydance (i.e. framed as a marriage of equals even though it’s really not), just take a look at the water tower on the lot to see how Ellison is really playing it. The tower has the iconic Paramount mountain, stars and script font with just a small disclaimer underneath that says “A Skydance Corporation.” Should we expect that for the Warner Bros. water tower in Burbank soon as well? It seems like a decent bet. Is “A Skydance Corporation” the biggest hint to how Ellison is approaching these names? Mario Tama/Getty Images In that case, when the deal formally closes, presumably in early October, will Ellison ultimately unveil Skydance Corporation as the new name for his entire holding company that houses dozens of cable channels along with two movie studios and two major news brands? HBO, a Skydance Corporation. CNN, a Skydance Corporation. Paramount has been there before, too, when it was snapped up by manufacturing conglomerate Gulf and Western Industries in 1966 and got labeled “A Gulf + Western Company” underneath its logo. There’s some organizing logic there for synergy when labeling a far-flung empire of assets. There’s a few problems with that. First, Skydance is the least iconic of all the names that Ellison has collected so far. Yes, it’s his own company that he boot-strapped and built himself (well, boot-strapped and built with financial help from his father, Oracle mogul Larry Ellison, who’s worth around $200 billion). But, optically, nothing says “I bought and ingested iconic studios and now they’re just tiles on a screen in my holding company” like wiping out the studio names from the parent company’s business card. Second, this new company isn’t AT&T, which ultimately cared far more about the telecom side of things and was fine jettisoning Warner because it wasn’t a core part of its business. Movies and television shows are the name of the game for this merged company. So you’d guess, then, that you should put your best foot forward by leading with the most recognizable, blue-chip names. Think back to all the handwringing and embarrassing reversals during the AT&T and Warner Bros. Discovery years as to whether the flagship streamer should be named Max or HBO Max. (It started off as HBO Max before turning in to Max and then going back to its original name HBO Max.) Ultimately, the C-suite led with the name that signaled quality to the widest set of possible consumers (even if execs privately fretted about diluting the good name of HBO with a streaming service featuring thousands of shows of varying quality). In this instance, if Ellison does indeed name his holding company Skydance Corporation it may be the Max of all the options, even if it doesn’t tip his hat in favor of any particular studio aside from the one that he started himself. Right now, the company trades as PSKY on the Nasdaq, though it’s set to move to the New York Stock Exchange in early October. (The symbol, SKY, it should be noted, is already taken on the NYSE by a modular home manufacturing company.) If including Skydance Corporation in the main part of the name is indeed the plan, maybe going the Marx Bros.’ “Amalgamated Consolidated Affiliated…” approach with the studio names would’ve been the better call, after all, to keep a piece of Hollywood history preserved. The Hollywood Reporter ‘s front page on March 11, 1933, which included an item about the Marx Bros. naming their company the International Amalgamated Consolidated Affiliated World Wide Film Productions Company Incorporated, of North Dakota. THR

articles.title: Daisy Jelley and Connor Simos Tapped to Lead Netflix Hockey Romance ‘Icebreaker’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All September 28, 2026 8:15am Connor Simos and Daisy Jelley Sally Flegg; Lily Craigen Logo text Netflix has founds the Icebreaker leads. Daisy Jelley ( Poser , How to Have Sex ) and Connor Simos ( Subversion ) have been cast as Anastasia “Stassie” Allen and Nate Hawkins, the streamer announced Monday. The show, based on Hannah Grace’s best-selling romance novel of the same name, centers around the relationship between a college hockey player and a college figure skater. The novel is the first in Grace’s college-set Maple Hills series and is one of, if not the, most recognizable title in the hockey romance sub-genre. Related Stories Movies 'Unabomber' Review: Jacob Tremblay and Russell Crowe in a Facile Rendering of Ted Kaczynski's College Days TV Felicia Pride on Capturing Innocence, Humanity in 'A Different World' Sequel and Revering the Original: "We're Not Replacing It" The show’s synopsis reads, “The upcoming college romance series follows Anastasia Allen, a competitive figure skater with her eyes on Olympic gold. Everything changes when Anastasia is forced to share the rink with Nate Hawkins, a hockey player who’s equally determined to go pro. Despite the cold temperatures on the ice, the heat between Anastasia and Nate is undeniable. Is ambition or attraction the sharper blade?” Amanda Lasher ( Gossip Girl, The Bold Type ) will serve as the showrunner. She’ll co-write and execute produce the series alongside Jade Bartlett, who’s created as the creator. Alex Cooper’s Unwell Productions is executive producing the series with Cooper, Matt Kaplan and Meena Lefevre also serving as EPs. Grace also serves as an executive producer on the project. The greenlight comes on the heels of two successful hockey romance series at other streamers. Crave and HBO Max’s Heated Rivalry kicked off the wave on television (it’s long been popular in the romance novel space) in November. The show, which follows the decade-long romance between two rival hockey players, became a global hit and launched its two stars, Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie, into the spotlight. It’s set to return in 2027 for its second season. Earlier this summer, Prime Video released its foray into hockey romance, Off Campus , which became the streamer’s third biggest debut ever. The buzzy show, centered around a college hockey team and the women in their lives, is currently shooting its second season, which will feature a new couple — played by Mika Adballa and Stephen Kalyn — in the leading roles. THR

articles.title: Fox News’ Latest Digital Expansion Is a Podcast for ‘The Girls’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 28, 2026 9:00am Spencer Platt/Getty Images Fox News Media is building out its portfolio of podcasts with a new panel roundtable conversation series. The pitch? The show will feature an all-female cast, with rotating guest hosts from across the company’s footprint. The new show is called The Girls , and the first episode will feature Fox & Friends Weekend host Rachel Campos-Duffy, anchor Harris Faulkner, Gutfeld! panelist Kat Timpf. It will also include former ESPN NFL Sunday Countdown host Samantha Ponder, who left the sports media giant in 2024. And also featured will be Melissa DeRosa, previously a top aide to former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo. Fox News says that DeRosa has joined the channel as a contributor. Future episodes of The Girls may include those names, as well as others. The first episode debuts Oct. 1 with future episodes dropping every Thursday on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Spotify and Fox News Digital. Fox News has been perhaps the most aggressive cable news channel when it comes to developing a podcast slate, with shows hosted by veteran TV talent, digital creators, and even acquired shows like Ruthless. the company’s slate includes Hang Out with Sean Hannity , Ruthless, Will Cain Country, Planet Tyrus and The Riley Gaines Show , with episodes living on the digital platforms where consumers watch and listen to podcasts, as well as Fox’s own platforms where they can sit alongside TV programming. Fox News has also leaned into the talents of its female hosts on its linear channel, where Outnumbered still holds down the noon to 1 p.m. ET timeslot, with four female co-hosts joined by “one lucky guy.” “ The Girls is a natural addition to our growing podcast portfolio, and we’re thrilled to continue expanding our slate of distinctive shows that complement our existing lineup while creating new opportunities for our audience to engage with our content,” says Porter Berry, the president of Fox News digital and new media. “We’re excited to deliver a no-holds-barred format that captures the authenticity and perspectives of the many dynamic women of Fox News Media and beyond,” added Megan Albano, executive VP of morning programming & program development. THR

articles.title: ‘The Day the Earth Stood Still’: THR’s 1951 Review
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By THR Staff Plus Icon THR Staff View All September 28, 2026 9:14am 1951's 'The Day the Earth Stood Still' Everett In September 1951, 20th Century-Fox ‘s sci-fi drama The Day the Earth Stood Still rolled out in theaters following its premiere opening on Sept. 18 at New York’s Mayfair Theatre (where it grossed $6,500 that day). At the beginning of the month, the film screened at the World Science Fiction Convention in New Orleans, where 250 attendees “universally acclaimed the picture.” The 92-minute feature, directed by Robert Wise, was released as Cold War fears were at the top of the headlines and was intended as a cautionary tale (decades later, the studio remade the film with Keanu Reeves and an aughts sheen in 2008). The Hollywood Reporter’s original review is below: In The Day the Earth Stood still, producer Julian Blaustein and director Robert Wise have a highly exploitable, suspensefully entertaining drama that will ride the crest of the current cycle of science films with the ease of a space ship. Adapted from a story by Henry Bates, the drama is an intriguing science fantasy, made believable by touches of genuine humor and the faint suggestion of a romance between a pretty American widow and a mysterious visitor from another planet. The overtones of social significance are adroitly handled and make real sense in an era of tragic international quarrels. Physically, the production is all science saga should be — Blaustein supervises the special effects with telling results; the Washington locale is excellently fulfilled; and the thoughtful choice of actors accounts for convincing performances throughout. Wise’s direction imbues the narrative with the compelling atmosphere of the documentary; he creates an illusion of presenting the real thing rather than a fictional motion picture. Inevitably, the Wise technique heightens suspense values and writes terrific punch into the action scenes involving a powerful robot who accompanies the human visitor to the U.S. Michael Rennie is the visitor, a man who whirls into the center of Washington in a space ship accompanied by his robot. His mission is one of peace — he wants to talk to the President. An hysterical soldier shoots him, Rennie is carried to Walter Reed Hospital. Here, by administering medicine brought from his outer-planet home, Rennie recovers. He tells the President’s secretary that he wishes to speak to representatives of all nations on earth. The secretary informs him this is impossible. Rennie casually leaves the hospital, takes a room in a boarding house where he meets Patricia Neal and her young son, Billy Gray. His adventures with the lad are amusing; one includes a visit to Sam Jaffe’s home where, by working an intricate scientific problem within seconds, he identifies himself as a super-intellect. Jaffe agrees to bring men of science from the four corners of the globe to hear him speak. Meanwhile the police are searching frantically for him. Though wounded again, he escapes to his ship and before flying off tells those who hear him that the world must solve its petty political problems; otherwise, action by other planets in the universe will destroy the world. Rennie’s quiet dignity in the part of the space visitor brings conviction to the interesting role. Miss Neal is vibrant and lovely as the young widow, and Hugh Marlowe is vigorous as her ambitious suitor. Jaffe’s scientist is portrayed with the actor’s usual resourcefulness. Gray is fine as the youth. Supporting players include some of Hollywood’s best character actors. Commentators Drew Pearson, Gabriel Heatter, H.V. Kaltenborn and Elmer Davis are on deck to implement the air of authenticity. Leo Tover’s work in the trick photographic department is exceptional. Lyle Wheeler and Addison Hehr, allowing imagination to run wild, perform a superb job of art direction. Bernard Herrman’s eerie score and the editing of William Reynolds are other outstanding contributions to the success of the production. — Staff byline, originally published on Sept. 4, 1951. The poster art for 1951’s The Day the Earth Stood Still . The Hollywood Reporter ‘s original review of The Day the Earth Stood Still in 1951. THR

articles.title: Shawn Levy Inks Overall Deal With Disney’s 20th Television
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All September 28, 2026 9:33am Shawn Levy Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images Logo text Prolific producer and director Shawn Levy has a new TV home. Levy and his 21 Laps Entertainment have signed a big overall deal with 20th Television, under which they’ll develop and produce new projects for the media giant’s various platforms. The deal will kick in starting in October 2027 and marks a big move for Levy and his company; he’s been based at Netflix since 2017. “Shawn has a rare ability to tell stories that are wildly entertaining and deeply human, something he’s brought to Disney across two decades,” Disney president and chief creative officer Dana Walden said in a statement. “He moves effortlessly across genres and franchises with a remarkable sense of what captures audiences and inspires passionate fandom. He’s an incredible storyteller and a true creative partner of the highest caliber, and we are thrilled to be building this next chapter together.” Related Stories Movies Lily James Horror Film 'Seasons' Lands Fall 2027 Release From Amazon MGM (Exclusive) Movies Ryan Gosling Shows Off First Footage From 'Star Wars: Starfighter,' About "a Guy From the Wrong Side of the Galaxy" The new deal is also something of a homecoming for Levy: Some of his earliest directing credits were on Disney Channel shows The Famous Jett Jackson and So Weird . “Years before I directed movies, I started my career directing and producing television episodes for Disney Channel, and I’ve always felt a kindred spirit in Disney and their storytelling ethos,” he said. “Having worked with Dana Walden over the years when we were both at Fox, I know her to be a formidable, smart and authentic person, not to mention a force of nature as an executive. Coupled with the amazing Debra OConnell, Disney Television has such an exciting era ahead, and I’m enthusiastic and inspired to produce the next wave of 21 Laps television series with the entire Disney team. I know from experience the passionate creative DNA of this place, and it honestly just feels like home.” Levy also has an existing relationship with the company, having recently wrapped filming on the next Star Wars feature film, Starfighter , starring Ryan Gosling. Levy also directed produced Deadpool & Wolverine for Marvel and 20th Century Studios and is reteaming with Gosling and Starfighter screenwriter Jonathan Tropper on a Ghost Rider movie . “Along with Shawn’s remarkable body of work in film, he’s also been one of the most prolific producers in television over the past decade,” said Disney Entertainment Television chairman Debra OConnell. “We couldn’t be more proud to welcome Shawn and the incredibly talented team at 21 Laps Entertainment.” Levy had a very fruitful tenure at Netflix, executive producing and/or directing Stranger Things (and its animated spinoff Tales From ’85 ), The Perfect Couple, All the Light We Cannot See and Shadow and Bone , among others. “I will forever cherish the incredible ride 21 Laps has had with Netflix,” Levy’s statement reads. “I am deeply grateful to Ted [Sarandos], Bela [Bajaria], Jinny [Howe] and the many talented Netflix execs with whom we have worked over the years and, of course, look forward to continuing our collaboration on the Stranger Things universe from the Duffer Brothers. As 21 Laps fortuitously heads into its 21st year, I remain gratified by all the stories we’ve gotten to tell and as hungry as ever for the ones we haven’t yet told.” Levy and 21 Laps are repped by WME and attorney Wendy Kirk of Johnson Shapiro. THR

articles.title: Neil Patrick Harris, Julianne Hough, Austin Scott to Return to Broadway in ‘Damn Yankees’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All September 28, 2026 9:56am Austin Scott, Julianne Hough and Neil Patrick Harris. Emilio Madrid A revival of Damn Yankees is coming to Broadway starring Neil Patrick Harris, Julianne Hough and Austin Scott. Harris, a Tony Award winner for Hedwig and the Angry Inch , will star as Applegate, alongside Emmy Award winner Julianne Hough ( Dancing With the Stars ) as Lola, marking her first Broadway musical after she appeared in POTUS on Broadway in 2022. Scott ( Hamilton ) will play Young Joe. Further casting will be announced at a later date. The new adaptation features a book by Will Power and Doug Wright, with additional lyrics by Lynn Ahrens, and direction and choreography by Tony Award winner Sergio Trujillo. This is the first Broadway revival of Damn Yankees in more than 30 years. Major League Baseball and its production label MLB Studios will serve as a partner on the production. The musical originally premiered in 1955 with a book by George Abbott and Douglass Wallop, and music and lyrics by Richard Adler and Jerry Ross and direction by Abbott. Bob Fosse choreographed the show, with Gwen Verdon starring as Lola. The story has been updated to the early 2000s, where diehard baseball fan Joe Boyd dreams of his team, the Baltimore Orioles, which has been on downswing, returning to glory. So when a charming stranger and his accomplice arrive with an offer, Boyd makes a high-stakes deal for himself and his team. It comes to New York after an out-of-town run at Arena Stage in Washington D.C. Lia Vollack ( MJ ), Haley Swindal, granddaughter of New York Yankees owner George Steinbrenner, and Julie Boardman are producing the musical for Broadway. The musical will play the Marquis Theatre with its first preview on March 24, 2027 and an official opening April 20. THR

articles.title: Strap-On and All, ‘Rose’ Puts Sandra Hüller Back in the Oscar Conversation
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Seth Abramovitch Plus Icon Seth Abramovitch Senior Writer SethAbramovitch Follow Sign Up View All September 28, 2026 10:20am 'Rose,' Sandra Huller, 2026. The Match Factory/Courtesy Everett Collection The bullet that tore through Rose ‘s face now hangs around her neck. Occasionally, she raises it to her mouth and sucks on it, a small, private gesture from a woman whose survival depends on keeping nearly everything about herself private. As played by Sandra Hüller in Markus Schleinzer’s Rose , she is a veteran of the Thirty Years’ War, which devastated Central Europe from 1618 to 1648. Now she is attempting to settle into a rural German community, acquire land and build a life, all while passing as a man. The trousers grant her freedoms she could never otherwise claim. A marriage to a local woman makes the arrangement considerably more complicated. It is a performance built from watchfulness and restraint, with Hüller allowing glimpses of tenderness, fear and finally fury to emerge from beneath Rose’s carefully maintained exterior. Related Stories Movies 'Rose' Trailer: Watch a First Look at Sandra Hüller's Next Must-See Performance (Exclusive) Music MTV Video Music Awards: Taylor Swift's Record, Madonna's Domination, Snoop Dogg's Dig and More Memorable Moments The role has already earned Hüller the Silver Bear for best leading performance at this year’s Berlin International Film Festival and could bring the Anatomy of a Fall Oscar nominee back into the best actress race. Austria has selected the black-and-white drama as its international feature submission. A new trailer debuted today ahead of the film’s Dec. 11 U.S. theatrical release. In a conversation with The Hollywood Reporter , the two discussed the freedom of leaving several central questions unanswered, the homemade device that helped Hüller find the character’s physicality and why Schleinzer refused to make her undress to prove anything. *** Rose evoked several of my favorite films. I’m very drawn to this genre of hiding within gender. I thought of movies like Yentl , Boys Don’t Cry and M. Butterfly . The tension of wondering when they’ll be found out gives those films a simmering intensity. Were those some of your inspirations, Markus? MARKUS SCHLEINZER I watched all of those films, but that was the second part of the process. The first part of the process was an incident. A friend of mine called me to wish me happy birthday. At the end of the call, she said, “Listen, it’s weird. I just finished reading a book today about a woman who got executed on this very day, your birthday, about 250 years before your birth, because she was wearing pants, because she was trying to live a different life. That’s the reason why she got executed.” This was very touching to me, and it was the beginning of a very long process of research. I started on women in pants: Why had women chosen to wear pants? To gain more freedom. I think it was two to three years, this research process, in which I was able to learn about 300 women across three different centuries. These are the women who got caught, the women we are aware of, so the figures must be much bigger. The reason why these women chose this kind of life was always different. Most of them tried to avoid getting married to someone they disliked. Some wanted to avoid rape or sexual harassment. Some wanted to have access to education, like in one of the films you mentioned, Yentl . Then there were women who wanted to fight for their countries and were not allowed to do so as women, so they chose to live like men. Some women just wanted to follow their husbands into war. There were transgender people or lesbians, I think, of course, but in those days there wasn’t an idea or words for this. All very different reasons, but the goal was always the same: to have more freedom, live more freely, have the possibility to do something which is already allowed to others. And as my first two movies had dealt with the so-called outsiders of society, I thought, OK, why not do it again, proceed with this research and this time talk about the biggest group of outsiders in the world: women. It was very interesting. The interesting thing is, when it comes to cross-dressing movies with men in dresses, what they have to do to reveal their gender is take off the wig. That’s what they do mostly. And what women in trousers always have to do is … SANDRA HÜLLER Completely undress. SCHLEINZER Yeah, completely undress to prove their gender. When we started writing the script, I said, OK, I want to try writing something on this topic without the naked body, because I don’t think a story like this needs to prove it through the naked body. Why? How often do I have to fill out some form on the internet, what’s your gender, male, female, diverse, whatever, and how often have I ticked “male” without sending pics of my naked body to prove it? So this was the beginning of this project. Is it true you wrote a novel version of Rose before you wrote the screenplay? SCHLEINZER I was a casting director for 17 years and I read the traditional scripts, but I dislike the form. As an author, I get much more in contact with a person when I choose to write in prose, like a novel, because writing in that style you can discuss thoughts, you can discuss fears, whatever. This is what I like very much. We started in the early years of Rose, when she was a child, and the novel ends where the film ends. It was about 1,000 pages. And then I thought, “Okay, you idiot, no one is going to give you millions of dollars to make a 45-hour movie.” So we just skipped the first 800 pages and concentrated on the last 200 pages of the novel, because that could survive as a movie by itself. You should release that book. I’d love to see what else happened in her life. HÜLLER Yeah, Markus, just do it. Just release the book. SCHLEINZER I don’t know. I’m not this merchandising guy who does something and then has to shoot out more, more, more, more, keep the money coming. Maybe in some 20 years I will do so. Sandra, how did you approach a character as quietly complex as Rose? Was her facial scarring something you were hesitant about, or something you thought helped you find the character? HÜLLER The script was so poetic, and there was so much information in it about the emotional state of the people. It didn’t have the usual form. It was written like a poem. Even the [stage directions] came in this special [prose] form that Markus had found. So that set the inner tone for everything we did. It gave a certain tenderness to everything we did, despite the brutality of the things that are actually happening. I can only thank Markus that he wrote it in this manner, because it was so rare. It did something very special to the whole work. As for the actual deformation of Rose’s face, it took us some time to find it. I remember, Markus, that you sent me a picture of a woman who had a scar from war, very early on. So I got familiar with the thought of having something put on my face. It was a pretty interesting construction. There had to be some pulling of the face up, and it would be clipped into the hair, like with a rubber band that kept it in place, and above that would be the form of the actual hole in the face, the scar. That’s something I’d never experienced before, and I was curious how it works when you can only use half of your face, and maybe just your eyes, for the things you want to express. I find limitations in acting very interesting. They force you to choose a certain form and help you find the essence of something when you leave a lot out. I found that very, very helpful. And it was, of course, a true pleasure to be in the makeup trailer of Anette Keiser for two hours every day. So that was always a good start. And then there was also the costume, of course. Markus referenced the trousers, the boots. HÜLLER Markus, you remember, you gave me your personal shoes, which I would have loved to keep, but I didn’t. A lot of Markus’ private life is in there, and that’s something you are aware of every day when you wear these things. You’re aware of the details and of all the love that has been put in there. It was meant to disguise something, and at the same time it was meant to give a certain feeling of strength, of course, because wearing armor does something to the body. Then we find out how her “horn” [a homemade strap-on sex device] that we discover later in the film is placed on the body, and that would also help to find out how to move and all of these things. Markus is someone who cares about all of these things. It’s something I would never have had to find out alone. It’s never specified what Rose’s impulse is for passing as a man, beyond the freedom of it. Did you come to a conclusion in your own mind as to whether she was trans, or a lesbian, or just a woman who wanted more opportunities for herself? What was your take on it? HÜLLER It’s part of the story that we don’t know, and it’s part of her personal freedom that she doesn’t tell anything about it, and I respected that. That’s all I can say. And as Markus said before, this character is an essence of hundreds of female characters from that time who chose this exact path, and their choices were very different from each other. So why would we decide on one reason? And yet there is a real love story going on between you and Caro Braun’s character, which is very heartwarming to watch unfold. But one thing you never find out is how she got pregnant with their child. Did you intentionally leave that a mystery as well? SCHLEINZER Well, I did, because I didn’t want to have this. I don’t want to look at people only as victims, and giving her this story might have put her in the victim corner. I think the things that happen to us should not define us completely. HÜLLER Caro said such a beautiful thing about that pregnancy when we were talking about the film in Berlin. She chose, for herself, that it is something that happened with pleasure. And that is something I love so much about her as a person, that she is choosing this story, although we don’t know the truth. We just have to respect it. SCHLEINZER When we were working on this, I went to Caro and said, “OK, I know you cannot play this without knowing how this happened to you, so find your own story.” And the funny thing is that she came back and said yes, now she knows everything, but she didn’t give it away. I asked her, “Who is the father?” She said, “None of your business.” Every time she gets asked in interviews, she always says, “None of your business.” And this I like very much. What do we really have to know about other people? Knowing too much, or knowing something about other people, so very often turns into judging. And is this a good thing? Does judging mean understanding? I doubt it. Was Sandra always the actress you had in mind for Rose? SCHLEINZER The part was written for Sandra. When it comes to a German-speaking part like this, there’s no way not to think about Sandra. So I stalked her. I watched all the movies I could get, to get my impression of how she does it, my impression of her enormous talent. And then I had the joy of acting alongside her in a movie, Sisi & I . I was pretty bad in that movie, because all I did was look at her and try to figure out, OK, [how would she do it?] I never told her this was written for her. HÜLLER It doesn’t always help when you know. SCHLEINZER Someone can write something for you and it still is shit. So I was very, very, very happy that she said yes. Can we talk about the scene when the townspeople confront Rose and you finally lose your cool? They reduce her identity to anatomy, while she’s arguing for her right to exist on her own terms. It brought to mind the trans and anti-trans debates you read every day on social media. What did that scene mean to you when you were making it? HÜLLER Well, we can talk about it on many levels. There’s a practical level: a night shoot in the dark, in the cold, with a lot of people who probably want to go home, so you have to really do it well so you don’t waste everybody’s time. I like the idea that she is going into the confrontation in the first place. She’s not shying away from that discussion, and she’s basically asking, Markus, please correct me if I’m wrong, whether anything she’s done for the community changes if her gender were a different one. And I think that’s fair, because obviously the answer is no. The things she has contributed to the village and to the people there, what she taught them and how she showed up, don’t change in the slightest if people find out she is not a man. It’s heartbreaking to watch you have to even make that case for yourself when you’ve done so much for the community, and they still don’t care. They still want blood. SCHLEINZER You will never fit. Is this how we want to live together as a community on this planet? I don’t know what kind of future mankind has, but this is what I see so very often. This could be a win-win situation. What she’s doing there, she’s saving a life, she’s creating jobs, she’s paying people, they learn how to read and write, things like this. She’s doing what she can, and she just wants to do it within the existing community. HÜLLER But it’s not for her to decide. That’s what we learned there. THR

articles.title: Media Company HardScope Launches With Studio Built Around Creator-Led IP, Sets Digital Series Slate (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 28, 2026 9:00am PT Media Company HardScope Launches With Studio Built Around Creator-Led IP, Sets Digital Series Slate (EXCLUSIVE) By Ethan Shanfeld Plus Icon Ethan Shanfeld @ethanshanfeld Latest Media Company HardScope Launches With Studio Built Around Creator-Led IP, Sets Digital Series Slate (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Michael Che Sets Third Netflix Special ‘Shot in Minnesota’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Tucker Carlson Returns to ‘SNL’ to Review ‘The Odyssey,’ Gender-Neutral ‘Spider-Man’ and Left-Wing ‘Obsession’ 2 days ago See All Courtesy of HardScope A new player has entered the creator economy. HardScope , founded by Matt Kalish, is a media company with an in-house studio built around creator-led IP. The brand is launching its YouTube channel on Sept. 30 with a slate of digital series. The company’s goal is to create original franchises that can be developed into something larger — brand partnerships, live experiences, licensing and distribution beyond HardScope’s own channels. As an incentive to grow the franchises, creators participate as equity partners in the IP they help build. The studio team includes creative executives that helped push FaZe Clan to become a global force in online gaming culture. Related Stories Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban ‘48 Hours’ Expands Use of Video Podcasting With 'Woman in the Woods' “We’re here to bring ambitious projects to life,” said Kalish, who also serves as CEO of HardScope. “We believe that working hand-in-hand with creators as business partners is how the future of media and IP will be made, grown and scaled.” Popular on Variety HardScope’s first batch of series are set to debut between September and November, backed by nearly $4 million in production and development investment. The shows include “R3born With N3on,” which will take viewers inside the streamer’s fitness transformation, and “Unpacked With Matcrackz,” a collectibles-themed project which will see celebrity guests hunt down their most-wanted piece of memorabilia. Plus, there’s “Love & Justice With Zach Justice,” in which the host will hear both sides of a relationship issue and deliver a verdict, and “Small World With Bloody Osiris,” a global travel show that explores “what happens when a New York fashion icon goes on the hunt for the perfect outfit and location for a fit-pic.” “Creators have given the world more great content to watch than ever before, and somehow we’re choosing less of what we actually watch,” said Lars Bengston, chief content officer of HardScope. “As algorithm fatigue sets in, taste and curation start to matter a lot more. We’re building HardScope to give audiences a brand they can identify themselves in, and creators a place to build beyond what they’re already known for.” TikTok Star Chris Olsen on His Memoir Helping Young People Struggling With Substance Abuse Issues Feel ‘Less Alone’ Adam Brody Calls for a ‘Free Palestine,’ Says He’s Never ‘Ducked’ Politics: ‘I Just Answer the Questions I’m Asked’ ‘Minions & Monsters’ Sets Peacock Release Date Korea Box Office: ‘The Assassin(s)’ and ‘Tazza 4’ Dominate Chuseok Holiday Weekend Surge Law&Crime Launches ‘Partners in Crime’ Initiative, Six New Series With Court TV Kacey Musgraves Pays Heartfelt Tribute to Dolly Parton With ‘I Will Always Love You’ Performance at MTV Video Music Awards Loading comments...

articles.title: Jennifer Hudson Thanks Her Talk Show Team at Power of Women: ‘I Could Not Live This Life Without You’
articles.full_text: Sep 28, 2026 9:30am PT Jennifer Hudson Thanks Her Talk Show Team at Power of Women: ‘I Could Not Live This Life Without You’ By Tanya Fedak Plus Icon Tanya Fedak Latest Jennifer Hudson Thanks Her Talk Show Team at Power of Women: ‘I Could Not Live This Life Without You’ 31 minutes ago ‘Minions & Monsters’ Sets Peacock Release Date 2 hours ago ‘Jack & Christine’ Trailer: John Hawkes Turns A Dinner Party Into A Night of Chaos – Film News in Brief 2 days ago See All “The Jennifer Hudson Show” received the Variety Changemaker Award, presented by Waymo, at Variety’s L.A. Power of Women event on Wednesday in Beverly Hills. The award was presented by Waymo’s chief marketing officer Suzanne Philion, honoring the show’s cultural impact. In her introduction, Philion shared that the EGOT winner’s talk show is an example of what is possible when people “lead with empathy, authenticity and heart.” Related Stories ‘60 Minutes’ Notches Ratings Gain Over Last Year, but Cedes Viewers From Season Premiere ‘48 Hours’ Expands Use of Video Podcasting With 'Woman in the Woods' “In a world that can often feel chaotic and overwhelming, ‘ The Jennifer Hudson Show ’ offers that exact same sense of sanctuary,” she said. “Every day, Jennifer and her extraordinary team turn daytime television into a space where people from all walks of life feel seen, feel safe and feel genuinely celebrated.” Hudson accepted the award alongside the team behind her show, saying that the award is “such an amazing representation of 150 producers that are standing right here. I always tell them, ‘I could not live this life without you.’” The singer and actress invited Michelle Salemi, the show’s co-executive producer, to the microphone to accept the award as Hudson joined the team behind her. “At ‘The Jennifer Hudson Show,’ we strive every day to make content that’s creative, joyful and meaningful,” Salemi said. “It makes you laugh. It makes you think. It makes you feel. In a world where our industry landscape is changing every day, we are steadfast in the pursuit of meeting people where they are.” Striving to tell stories that inspire audiences, the show has donated more than $3 million and has reached more than 11 billion views online throughout its five seasons, Salemi shared to applause. “Those numbers are incredible, but what they really tell us is that we’re connecting. And standing up here with me tonight is an incredible group of women who represent the 150 people who come together every day to make this show,” Salemi said. “Isn’t that what our industry is about? It’s about collaboration.” Salemi then thanked Hudson for working alongside the team in creating a show that makes a difference. “From the beginning, Jennifer wanted this place to be where people could come together, be themselves and feel seen. And that’s really the heart of the show,” she said. “Jennifer, thank you for being that north star to us and standing alongside us every day.” “The Jennifer Hudson Show” premiered in September 2022 and has continued to resonate with audiences. Its pre-show ritual, the Spirit Tunnel, went viral on social media and has since amassed more than 6 billion views across social media platforms. In the show’s 2025-2026 season, its followers on social media rose 90.7% to 17.5 million, impressions increased 242.8% to 7.5 billion and engagement jumped 164.1% to 537 million. The series ranks No. 1 among daytime talk shows on TikTok and Threads. articles.title: Shawn Levy Enters Disney Overall Deal After Nearly a Decade at Netflix
articles.full_text: Sep 28, 2026 9:39am PT Shawn Levy Enters Disney Overall Deal After Nearly a Decade at Netflix By Selome Hailu Plus Icon Selome Hailu Latest Shawn Levy Enters Disney Overall Deal After Nearly a Decade at Netflix 33 minutes ago ‘South Park’ Season 29 Premiere Hits 4.2 Million Viewers in Three Days and Jumps 33% in Rating After Renaming to ‘South America’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago ‘Sesame Street’ Movie Set at Netflix, Plus ‘Gabby’s Dollhouse’ Spinoff and ‘KPop Demon Hunters’ Game 4 days ago See All Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images Shawn Levy has set an overall deal at Disney ‘s 20th Television after a long tenure at Netflix that began in 2017 . He and his production company, 21 Laps Entertainment, will begin developing and producing projects at Disney in October 2027. Levy is a powerhouse filmmaker who first rose to prominence as a comedy director, though in recent years, he’s become best known for genre projects. At Netflix , he executive produced all five seasons of “Stranger Things” and directed several episodes, in addition to writing and directing the 2022 Ryan Reynolds-led film “The Adam Project” and executive producing both seasons of the fantasy series “Shadow and Bone.” He will continue collaborating with Ross and Matt Duffer — who moved their own deal to Paramount — on the “Stranger Things” franchise at Netflix. Related Stories ‘60 Minutes’ Season Debut Sees 21% Drop in Ratings: Is NFL or CBS News to Blame? Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban Disney’s relationship with Levy is not new; most notably, Levy co-wrote, directed and produced the 2024 Marvel Cinematic Universe film “Deadpool & Wolverine.” Several of his earliest successes were also at Disney (and companies now owned by Disney): He began his career directing episodes of Disney Channel series including “The Famous Jett Jackson” before going on to helm 20th Century projects such as “Cheaper by the Dozen” (2003) and the first three “Night at the Museum” films (2006-2014). His next two Disney projects are already set: He will direct Lucasfilm’s “Star Wars: Starfighter” and Marvel’s “Ghost Rider,” which both star Ryan Gosling. Popular on Variety Levy is repped by WME and Wendy Kirk of Johnson Shapiro Slewett & Kole. Read his statement about the Disney deal below. Years before I directed movies, I started my career directing and producing television episodes for Disney Channel, and I’ve always felt a kindred spirit in Disney and their storytelling ethos. Having worked with Dana Walden over the years when we were both at FOX, I know her to be a formidable, smart and authentic person, not to mention a force of nature as an executive. Coupled with the amazing Debra OConnell, Disney Television has such an exciting era ahead, and I’m enthusiastic and inspired to produce the next wave of 21 Laps television series with the entire Disney team. I know from experience the passionate creative DNA of this place, and it honestly just feels like home. I will forever cherish the incredible ride 21 Laps has had with Netflix. I am deeply grateful to Ted, Bela, Jinny and the many talented Netflix execs with whom we have worked over the years and, of course, look forward to continuing our collaboration on the ‘Stranger Things’ universe from the Duffer Brothers. As 21 Laps fortuitously heads into its 21st year, I remain gratified by all the stories we’ve gotten to tell and as hungry as ever for the ones we haven’t yet told. articles.title: John Mayer Sets Sphere Residency for Spring 2027, Combining Full Band, Trio and Solo Sets
articles.full_text: Sep 28, 2026 9:41am PT John Mayer Sets Sphere Residency for Spring 2027, Combining Full Band, Trio and Solo Sets By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest John Mayer Sets Sphere Residency for Spring 2027, Combining Full Band, Trio and Solo Sets 33 minutes ago Taylor Swift Still Has Unfinished Business With Her Exes — Thank God! — While Also Mooning Over Her Groom in ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’: New Tracks Review 3 days ago VMAs Producer Van Toffler on Madonna’s Return, the Taylor Takeover and Why He Brought the Show West Again: ‘L.A. and Snoop Is a Lethal Combo’ 4 days ago See All Mark Seliger John Mayer knows his way around Las Vegas’ Sphere , having spearheaded the residencies that Dead & Company did at that venue in 2024 and 2025. That Grateful Dead spinoff group may have reached its natural end with the death of Bob Weir in January of this year, but as it turns out, that did not mean that Mayer has lost his taste for exploring the possibilities of what can be done with the marriage of music and groundbreaking visuals there. He’s coming back on his own — with the various ensembles he leads as a solo atist — for a residency in April 2027. Related Stories Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban ‘60 Minutes’ Notches Ratings Gain Over Last Year, but Cedes Viewers From Season Premiere Only six dates have been announced for Mayer’s spring residency, although if this is like any other Sphere engagement to date, it’s likely more shows will be added as these sell out. The shows he has put on the calendar for now will all take place in short succession on April 8, 10, 11, 15, 17 and 18. Popular on Variety Mayer fans will be pleased to know these are trifold shows, offering Mayer by himself, with his full band and with the John Mayer Trio. Traditionally, these are separate shows and tours, so the so-called triple bill could augur for some epic-length concerts, in the Dead & Company tradition. The general on-sale will begin Oct. 9 at 10 a.m. PT at Ticketmaster. An artist pre-sale will take place two days prior to that, Oct. 7. Registration for the presale is now taking place at JohnMayer.com. A SIriusXM presale will take place Oct. 8. VIP ticket packages will go on sale first, via Ticketmaster on Sept. 30. VIbee packages will also go on sale that day and include stays at the adjacent Venetian Hotel. The announcement said general ticket prices will begin at $129. For the two Dead & Company residencies, Mayer was the artistic director, commissioning and overseeing the highly acclaimed visuals, setting a high bar — after U2’s initial residency — that other artists following in their wake there have had a hard time measuring up to. The setlists and their accompanying visuals tended to have new wrinkles each night. The announcement for the residency promises that he won’t neglect that side of things, saying “these performances will combine immersive sound, visual spectacle, and sensory feedback to make each show a unique, unforgettable celebration.” ‘Minions & Monsters’ Sets Peacock Release Date Jennifer Hudson Thanks Her Talk Show Team at Power of Women: ‘I Could Not Live This Life Without You’ Florence Pugh Speaks Out Over Cornell University Sexual Assault Case: ‘We Need Our Men to Be as Horrified and Sickened as Us’ Law&Crime Launches ‘Partners in Crime’ Initiative, Six New Series With Court TV Taylor Swift Premieres ‘Patient Zero’ Music Video at VMAs, Turning Her New ‘Showgirl: Encore’ Single Into a Dramatic Ghost Story Kacey Musgraves Pays Heartfelt Tribute to Dolly Parton With ‘I Will Always Love You’ Performance at MTV Video Music Awards Loading comments...

articles.title: ‘Crew Girl’ Star Miku Martineau on the Show’s Love Triangle and Her Hopes for an All-Girls Team in Season 2
articles.full_text: Sep 28, 2026 9:45am PT ‘Crew Girl’ Star Miku Martineau on the Show’s Love Triangle and Her Hopes for an All-Girls Team in Season 2 By Isabelle Farina Plus Icon Isabelle Farina Latest ‘Crew Girl’ Star Miku Martineau on the Show’s Love Triangle and Her Hopes for an All-Girls Team in Season 2 32 minutes ago Jeff Probst Says ‘Survivor’ Needs Diversity Despite Paramount’s DEI Rollbacks: ‘All Those Differences Matter in the Story’ 18 hours ago How To Watch Neil Young, Willie Nelson, Dave Matthews Band and More Perform Live at CNN’s ‘Farm Aid Music Festival’ 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Netflix Just like the training their characters had to endure, the cast of Netflix’s latest YA hit series “ Crew Girl ” attended a two-week rowing intensive in Victoria, British Columbia, Canada, before filming. The show’s lead Miku Martineau and her pack of rowers hit the open water to soak up as much information about the sport as possible. In the meantime, they developed the camaraderie and chemistry required to be teammates on and offscreen — and even had some memorable recreational races. Related Stories ‘60 Minutes’ Season Debut Sees 21% Drop in Ratings: Is NFL or CBS News to Blame? Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban In one of these high-speed competitions between co-stars and onscreen love triangle members Kyle Clark and Sam Braun, Martineau came out on top as the duo tumbled into the water repeatedly, struggling to find their seats. Popular on Variety That training has paid off, because “Crew Girl” has sat in Netflix’s English TV Top 10 since its Sept. 10 release, and the coming-of-age sports drama has already amassed more than 16 million views in its first two weeks — a “surreal” statistic, an “ecstatic” Martineau tells Variety . “It’s such a beautiful thing when you get to collaborate with so many people on one project, and for it to finally come out and for other people to enjoy it as well,” Martineau says. “Crew Girl” follows Martineau as 16-year-old Teagan Tao as she adapts to her new life after her father’s financial fraud forced her family to move across the country and back to her mother’s hometown. There, Teagan must navigate the choppy waters of her elite prep school Easton Academy and its all-boys crew team. Unwilling to give up her own rowing dreams, she finds a spot for herself as coxswain, leading the team to victory and falling in love with some of her teammates along the way. Courtesy of Netflix While Season 1 focused on Teagan navigating her place on the boys’ team, Season 2 of “Crew Girl,” which was confirmed on Tuesday , will likely focus on the creation and development of an all-girls team, especially if Martineau has anything to say about it. “I hope there is a strong sense of friendship and teamwork and mutual respect,” she says. “I think, guys aside, the female friendship that she and Brittany could potentially have through rowing could be very special and powerful.” Like her fanbase, Martineau is just as torn over Team Josh or Team Cam — but is ultimately choosing Team Teagan. “I think [Josh and Teagan] developed a very intimate and close relationship,” Martineau says. “However, with Cam, she relates to him because he’s kind of the underdog as well as her. And he’s also just such a sweetheart, but he has his own things as well. So it is like, what’s happening with this girls’ team?” As the lead actor in a YA drama, the 22-year-old felt the responsibility to try and accurately depict teenage hardships and resilience. But she also had the added weight of representing women in male-dominated sports. Courtesy of Netflix “I hope that Teagan represents just how powerful and strong women are,” Martineau says. “I hope it gives young girls who see Teagan onscreen permission to feel like it’s OK to take up space. It’s OK to be competitive and it’s OK to not back down from a challenge, even if you’re underestimated and even if you are the underdog. It’s unfortunate that we have to go the extra mile to almost earn a seat at the table. But if anyone can do it, it’s a woman.” This spotlight on women in “Crew Girl,” especially in less-mainstream sports like rowing, is what drew Martineau to the project. That, and of course, the juicy love triangle. “I love the duality of a really strong-willed woman pursuing her greatest desire while also allowing herself to be human, and that’s OK,” Martineau says. Martineau acknowledges how influential characters like Teagan and the other players on her team can be for young audiences. “When we’re very, very young, all we want to do is fit in,” Martineau says. “The media we consume, we look for things that we can relate to to feel like we’re a part of the community. So that’s why it’s important to represent a lot of communities and people of diverse backgrounds, so that it feels like the world that we are living in.” Martineau appears to be similar to Teagan in her sunny demeanor, passion for her work and determination — but she wants you to know she’s not playing herself. She prefers each character of hers to be distinctive. For her starring role as Yumeko in the 2025 Netflix original series “Bet,” Martineau rocked blunt bangs to differentiate herself from the character and for Teagan, she proposed going fully blonde. COURTESY OF NETFLIX She also had to establish mutual trust and respect with showrunner Vivian Lin and the “Crew Girl” directors. “I want to do my best job to bring the story to life,” Martineau says. “They do as well, so it’s me trusting them and them trusting me.” Before she settles back into her single scull for Season 2, Martineau is taking it day by day just like Teagan, grounding herself with long walks and self-care. “I wish I could say what else I have in store, but it’s been so full of so many blessings and it’s so amazing,” Martineau says. articles.full_text: Sep 28, 2026 10:00am PT ‘Stillwater’: Amazon Series Based on Graphic Novel Casts Ben Hardy in Lead Role By Joe Otterson Plus Icon Joe Otterson TV Reporter joeotterson Latest ‘Icebreaker’ Netflix Series Casts Daisy Jelley, Connor Simos in Lead Roles (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Peter Sarsgaard Joins Kenneth Branagh in Paramount+ Series ‘Laird’ 3 days ago ‘Star Trek: Strange New Worlds’ Star Celia Rose Gooding Breaks Down That Time-Jumping Season 4 Finale 4 days ago See All IONA WOLFF Ben Hardy is set to star in the series adaptation of the graphic novel “ Stillwater ” at Amazon Prime Video , Variety has learned. The series is based on the Skybound graphic novel of the same name and was greenlit at Amazon back in July. The streamer has given the one-hour show an eight-episode order. The official logline states the show is a “mind-bending horror thriller that focuses on ex-con Daniel West (Hardy). When Daniel receives a mysterious letter promising answers about his past and a substantial inheritance in the small town of Stillwater, he discovers a community where nothing ever ages, no one ever dies, and nobody ever gets out.” Related Stories Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban ‘60 Minutes’ Notches Ratings Gain Over Last Year, but Cedes Viewers From Season Premiere “We’ve been fans of Ben’s for a long time, and we’re thrilled to get to tell this story together,” said series writers and executive producers Greg Berlanti and Carly Wray. “There’s a toughness to him, but also something incredibly open and soulful underneath it. Daniel needs both. From the moment we saw Ben in the role, it was impossible to imagine anyone else.” Popular on Variety Hardy is known for his roles in films like “The Conjuring: Last Rites,” “Bohemian Rhapsody,” “6 Underground,” “Only the Brave,” and “X-Men: Apocalypse.” He has also starred in shows like “The Girl Before,” “The Woman in White,” and “EastEnders.” He is repped by UTA, Principal Entertainment LA and Independent Talent Group. The “Stillwater” graphic novel was created by Chip Zdarsky and Ramón K Pérez. Wray and Berlanti co-wrote the pilot episode and executive produce, with Berlanti doing so via Berlanti Productions. Sarah Schechter, Leigh London Redman, and Robbie Rogers of Berlanti Productions also executive produce along with Robert Kirkman, David Alpert, Rick Jacobs, Glenn Geller, and Zdarsky for Skybound Entertainment. Jonathan Gabay also serves as an executive producer. Warner Bros. Television and Amazon MGM Studios will produce. Berlanti and Wray are both under overall deals at WBTV.
