articles.title: Brazil’s Desvia Filmes Enters New Era With Doubled Focus on Indie and Rachel Daisy Ellis’ San Sebastián Co-Pro Forum’s Buzzy ‘The Last Cruise’
articles.full_text: Sep 24, 2026 6:05am PT Brazil’s Desvia Filmes Enters New Era With Doubled Focus on Indie and Rachel Daisy Ellis’ San Sebastián Co-Pro Forum’s Buzzy ‘The Last Cruise’ Veteran British producer Ellis is ushering Desvia into its next chapter following Gabriel Mascaro's exit to launch Trema label alongside Paula Cosenza earlier this year By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Brazil’s Desvia Filmes Enters New Era With Doubled Focus on Indie and Rachel Daisy Ellis’ San Sebastián Co-Pro Forum’s Buzzy ‘The Last Cruise’ 1 hour ago Mauro Mueller’s ‘111 – Echoes From Halifax’ Might Chronicle Tragic 1998 Swissair Plane Crash, but This Is Not Your Regular Disaster Movie 2 hours ago San Sebastian’s Creative Investors’ Conference: 10 Takeaways From AI to ‘Obsession,’ YouTube and Why International Movies Could Dominate the Oscars 6 hours ago See All Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building Courtesy of Desvia Filmes Very few production companies can boast about landing major international festival premieres for every project in their slate. Brazil ’s Desvia Filmes is one of them, with all of its 16 features launching at festivals such as Berlin, Cannes, and Locarno. Founded in 2010 by “The Blue Trail” director Gabriel Mascaro and British producer Rachel Daisy Ellis – who has long been based in Recife – Desvia is behind films such as Bruno Santamaría’s “Six Months In the Pink and Blue Building,” Benjamin Naishtat’s “Rojo,” Manuel Abramovich’s “Pornomelancholia” and all of Mascaro’s films, including “Divine Love” and “Neon Bull.” Related Stories Mahershala Ali Finally Made His ‘Blade’ Film With ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Amazon's Prime Video Is Using AI to Lip-Sync Actors' Mouths in Dubbed Titles, Starting With German Series 'Maxton Hall' Earlier this year, the company underwent a major transition, as Mascaro left Desvia to launch Trema alongside veteran producer Paula Cosenza. Trema will focus on international co-productions, scripted series and auteur-driven cinema with global reach, while Desvia will keep its laser-sharp focus on films, backing auteurs and filmmakers playing with form and genre. Popular on Variety Speaking with Variety out of San Sebastián , where she presented “The Last Cruise” at the festival’s prestigious Europe-Latin America Co-Production Forum, Ellis reiterates how thrilled she is for Mascaro and Cosenza’s new venture and the opportunities it will open up for both companies. “It’s one big portfolio of projects now split between two production companies, and amplified in this sense,” she says. “For many years, Desvia worked almost exclusively on Gabriel’s projects, especially because the two of us had a very strong creative partnership. We’ve reached incredible heights together, but had arrived at a moment when both of us wanted to branch out, so it was an organic process.” The producer says she and Mascaro have “an incredible history together,” with “nothing stopping them” from working together again in the future. “For now, this setup makes it possible for him to work with new filmmakers, and for us at Desvia to bring new creative voices in.” And, while Desvia is indeed bringing in new voices into its slate, it is also currently at full steam ahead with Ellis’s own directorial projects, which include the documentary short “The Book of Colors,” feature docs “Drone” and “The Dream Conference,” and “The Last Cruise.” The latter sees the director step into fiction, mixing doc elements with a fictionalized narrative to tell the story of an elderly couple who decides to forego a retirement home in favor of spending their last years on a cruise. “It’s a project we’ve been researching for over two years, but I had the seed for the idea over 15 years ago,” she says. “I was in touch with someone from the British Council in Recife, who told me a crazy statistic: one of his main jobs was repatriation, and a lot of elderly Brits died on cruise ships, with their bodies being stored under the deck. He also told me a lot of retirees prefer to take one last big trip in life rather than settle into a care home, and many didn’t want to—or couldn’t—fly. So the option was a major around-the-world cruise.” The producer wanted to make a documentary about the phenomenon at first and then, during the pandemic, she read an article about the growing phenomenon of people choosing to live in these lavish boats as it costs less than living in many major cities during a cost of living crisis. “Once I read that article, the original idea came back into my mind, and I was set on making it happen.” “The Blue Trail” Courtesy of Guillermo Garza/Desvia Ellis has locked financing for production in Brazil, which was an important step given it is “not a cheap project.” The film requires her to follow a couple on a cruise for a year, with the subjects also filming themselves and their routine in this very particular environment. “This first-person point of view is very much part of the way I work as a director,” she says of the creative choice. “It’s a way of having access to a layer of intimacy I otherwise wouldn’t be able to capture. I also realized this film is about love and companionship. ‘Eros,’ my previous film, was also about this, and I feel this film is a continuation of my interest in how people communicate with their partners when they live on the periphery of the norm.” With Mascaro gone, long-term producing collaborator of Desvia, Camille Reis, became a partner and is now leading on several projects. Given Reis’s limited bandwidth, Ellis brought in renowned Argentinian producer Gema Juárez Allen (“Reas,” “Plaza Catedral”) to lead on “The Last Cruise,” with the duo seeking a co-production with Argentina. “I worked with Gema before; we worked on ‘Pornomelancholia’ together, and when I invited her to produce the project, she loved the idea,” says Ellis. “It’s been incredible working with her, and this partnership as a producer is beautiful to me, because I know what it feels like to have an incredible producer by your side and how that changes the project. Once she boarded ‘The Last Cruise,’ I knew we would be good to go.” As for the next steps with the company, the producer says they are “very focused on cinema.” “We haven’t had the drive to branch into TV or other formats. When I look back at all the projects I’ve worked on with Gabriel, and all the co-productions we’ve worked on, they are all very daring films, with a latent desire to provoke. This is something that attracts me both as a producer and director, and we want to continue to bring Desvia towards that pathway.” And it is indeed an exciting pathway, with Desvia’s slate including Clarisa Navas’s “They Burn the Same Way,” which was a buzzy project at this year’s Venice Gap-Financing Bridge; Filipa Reis’ “Lontra,” a co-production with Portugal, Spain, France and Argentina; and “Who Named the Earth?” an exciting feature debut by Indigenous filmmaker Wara. ‘Kill Jackie,’ Starring a Glamorous, Lethal Catherine Zeta-Jones, Acquired by Warner Bros. articles.title: Marlene Emilie Lyngstad Addresses First Reactions to Controversial Love Story ‘Cute’: ‘Maybe People Are Confronted by Their Own Monsters?’
articles.full_text: Sep 24, 2026 6:25am PT Marlene Emilie Lyngstad Addresses First Reactions to Controversial Love Story ‘Cute’: ‘Maybe People Are Confronted by Their Own Monsters?’ By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Marlene Emilie Lyngstad Addresses First Reactions to Controversial Love Story ‘Cute’: ‘Maybe People Are Confronted by Their Own Monsters?’ 31 minutes ago In ‘Tenzing,’ Jennifer Peedom Ensures the Iconic Himalayan Mountaineer Is Finally ‘the Protagonist of His Own Life’ 2 hours ago In Docuseries ‘Keinaan, Go Back to Somalia,’ Finnish-Somali YouTube Star Turns Racist Comments Into a Personal Statement 3 hours ago See All Samai Collado, San Sebastian Film Festival Marlene Emilie Lyngstad has ruffled some feathers at San Sebastián with her feature debut “ Cute .” “I find it interesting and exciting that the film creates such strong reactions,” she tells Variety . “It’s never explicit, so the discomfort must arise from the inner battles of the characters. Maybe people are confronted by their own monsters?” Related Stories Amazon's AWS Now Lets Streamers Deliver up to 10 Live Feeds on One Screen Nicholas Sparks’ ‘Counting Miracles’ Adaptation at Amazon to Be Helmed by ‘The Peanut Butter Falcon’ Filmmaker Tyler Nilson (EXCLUSIVE) Her lead, Richard, is certainly used to dealing with his own inner demons. Attracted to his girlfriend’s seven-year-old daughter, he leaves and hides in his old childhood home. There, he meets his mother’s caregiver, Stella, who likes to behave like a little girl. Also in front of the camera. Popular on Variety “I think there’s an important distinction between the guilt of someone who has abused a child and the guilt of someone with an unwanted attraction who’s determined not to act on it. My film deals with the latter,” emphasizes Lyngstad. “Richard is fighting an inner battle that confronts us with difficult but important questions: How can this person forge a decent life while carrying shame that can never be eliminated? Is this person also worthy of love?” “Cute” is a love story, she says. “It asks what love is. It’s about two adults, each broken in their own way, who long to be loved unconditionally.” While the media tends to feed people black-and-white narratives, people watch cinema “because they want more than that.” “I’m not interested in discomfort for its own sake, but I do think that some degree of unsettlement is inevitable when asking questions that might not have answers. I find humans uncomfortably contradictory, and I love it when cinema exposes these contradictions.” TrustNordisk handles sales for “Cute,” produced by Nordisk Film Production A/S (Denmark). It’s co-produced by Nordisk Film Production Ab, Film I Väst (Sweden) and Amarcord (Norway). Jan Gunnar Røise, who worked on her graduation film “Norwegian Offspring,” Karin Bertling, Kitt Maiken Mortensen and Molly Kirk Rasmussen star in the film. As well as newcomer Gina Jaqueline, who plays Stella. “I first met Gina while doing research for this film. She was a collector of the ‘cute’ aesthetic, and I was interested in understanding its appeal on grown-ups. When I told her about Stella, she opened up about her experience with OnlyFans and the online erotic market,” recalls Lyngstad. She asked Jaqueline to join as a consultant when developing the script. “She knew this universe firsthand. When we started the casting process, I decided to invite Gina, even though she had no formal acting training. She turned out to be a raw talent. She had the ability to lift the scenes from the page and deliver performances beyond my imagination.” “She was navigating the line between being exceptionally charming, vital, very vulnerable and haunted. I was very touched by her presence.” Lyngstad found the contrast between Røise and Jaqueline “especially exciting”: “It was Jan Gunnar’s precision and control against Gina’s playfulness and intuition,” she says. As proven by their first responses following the world premiere, cinema audiences have a complicated relationship with sexual imagery these days, even though anything is available online. “It’s hypocritical,” says the director. “That’s why I wanted to deal with the imagery provided by the internet. Images connecting childhood and sexuality are a part of pop culture and even mainstream pornography. A new territory of moral ambiguity has emerged. How should we navigate these blurred lines between fantasy, representation and exploitation?” She adds: “I think we don’t want to look at this. articles.title: Carat Names Sarah Stringer, Brian Meuleman to Global Roles
articles.full_text: Sep 24, 2026 6:37am PT Carat Names Sarah Stringer, Brian Meuleman to Global Roles By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest CNN Chief Says He’s ‘Enthusiastic’ About Staying Under Paramount, but Not Sure He Can 20 hours ago CNN’s Interactive ‘Office Hours’ Has John Berman Testing New Skills 20 hours ago ‘Today’ Snares Top Two Positions in Morning-News Battle for First Time in 14 Years 22 hours ago See All Eleanor Shakespeare for Variety Carat named Sarah Stringer and Brian Meuleman to key global roles aimed at helping bridge gaps between strategic theory and commercial results. Stringer was named global chief strategy and innovation officer. Her remit includes turning strategy into an immediate, actionable competitive advantage. Meuleman was named global chief planning and intelligence officer and will use evidence, behavioral science and proprietary intelligence to shape how media investments are designed and measured. They both will report to Chrissie Hanson, Carat’s global brand president. articles.title: Zurich Film Festival Heads on Theatrical-Loving Gen Z, Prioritizing Private Equity and Tilly Norwood a Year Later: This Is the ‘Place Where You Address the Real Hot Questions’
articles.full_text: Sep 24, 2026 6:52am PT Zurich Film Festival Heads on Theatrical-Loving Gen Z, Prioritizing Private Equity and Tilly Norwood a Year Later: This Is the ‘Place Where You Address the Real Hot Questions’ The festival will also continue to cement its reputation as an awards launchpad with screenings of titles such as 'I Play Rocky,' 'Wild Horse Nine,' 'Tenzing' and 'The Debut' By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Brazil’s Desvia Filmes Enters New Era With Doubled Focus on Indie and Rachel Daisy Ellis’ San Sebastián Co-Pro Forum’s Buzzy ‘The Last Cruise’ 48 minutes ago Mauro Mueller’s ‘111 – Echoes From Halifax’ Might Chronicle Tragic 1998 Swissair Plane Crash, but This Is Not Your Regular Disaster Movie 1 hour ago San Sebastian’s Creative Investors’ Conference: 10 Takeaways From AI to ‘Obsession,’ YouTube and Why International Movies Could Dominate the Oscars 5 hours ago See All Courtesy of Zurich Film Festival If one film could define this year’s Zurich Film Festival , it would be Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” a heartfelt drama about the making of the Sylvester Stallone-starring classic that is playing as one of the festival galas. The film embodies not only the festival’s 2026 motto of “Dream Big,” but also a go-getter attitude that saw CEO Christian Jungen buy out former owner — Swiss newspaper NZZ — and lead the festival alongside an investment team that secured private funds to ensure the event’s continuity and independence. A year on from the bold strategic move, Jungen is confident in its success and the advantages it brings for the future. Related Stories Amazon's Prime Video Is Using AI to Lip-Sync Actors' Mouths in Dubbed Titles, Starting With German Series 'Maxton Hall' Emmys in Talks to Move to Amazon Prime Video Under New Licensing Arrangement, as the Broadcast Wheel Deal Ends (EXCLUSIVE) Speaking with Variety ahead of this year’s edition from an office decorated from wall to wall with prized “Rocky” collector items — think golden gloves, intricate statues and vintage posters — Jungen says the Farrelly film has been a great source of inspiration for this year’s festival. “It’s a film about a big dream. In these rough times, when it’s very tough to finance films, that’s something that is going to speak to everybody in the industry. I am sure it will be embraced broadly in our industry and with audiences. It’s a crowdpleaser.” Popular on Variety Jungen says delivering the festival is now “easier because we are independent.” “In these polarized times, we got caught up in political discussions,” he adds, referring to the NZZ’s right-wing-leaning editorial line. “Now it’s all about cinema again. Not that it wasn’t before, of course, but when you belong to a newspaper, and they have strong opinions, you risk becoming collateral damage.” “We found new partners for the first time in five years, which is good because it’s very challenging to finance cultural events,” he went on. “Most partners want to be part of emotional stories. It’s more about telling stories together than about visibility. Ten years ago, they paid money, and you put their logo on the photo wall. Today, they want to offer their employees or clients an emotional evening, and are very interested in having talent on stage. That doesn’t mean just big Hollywood stars.” But it is indeed a starry roster, with the likes of Martin McDonagh, Anna Kendrick, Jesse Eisenberg, Tom Hiddleston and Naomi Watts all landing in the Swiss city over the next few days. The festival, which kicks off with the European premiere of the Hiddleston-starring “Tenzing,” will host European premieres of several other major fall festival titles, including Chris Rock’s “Misty Green,” Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky” and Lauren Miller Rogen’s “Babies,” starring Kendrick and Seth Rogen. Other major titles such as “Bunker,” “Ink,” “Club Kid,” “The Debut” and “Wild Horse Nine” will also bow at the festival. Jungen remains focused on making Zurich a strong awards launchpad. “After the first premiere, films need a second turf to display their stars and start a conversation,” he says. “The good thing abut Zurich is you have a film-friendly audience and, at the same time, we are the door to the German-speaking world, which is a $100 million market. We are a real test with audiences, and our positioning is glamorous. For us, it’s important to be a platform with a real audience, but also to have an impact with Academy or Golden Globe voters.” “We are at the end of fall festival season, and many of the decision-makers from the industry who were in Venice went over to Toronto and are maybe doing San Sebastián, and have Zurich as their last stop, where they finally have time to watch a movie,” he notes. “It just so happened that, over the last years, films that had their European premiere in Zurich, whether it was ‘Green Book’ or ‘All Quiet on the Western Front,’ were successful at the Oscars. This could be the case for ‘I Play Rocky’ or ‘Tenzing.’” “I Play Rocky,” courtesy of Zurich Film Festival Zurich is also a great city for theatrical exhibition, featuring 63 movie theaters for a population of 440,000, making it one of the strongest exhibition capitals in the world. And the festival has a young audience eager to fill those seats. “Gen Z is reawakening cinema,” says festival director and co-owner Reta Guetg. “That is really cool, and I think only the start of a wave that will keep growing. Our young programming team was raving about Rhys Marc Jones’s ‘Black Church Bay,’ a thriller starring Joe Locke, who is also one of our guests. The film is a world premiere; it has amazing direction, really interesting cast. These kinds of films help shape the program. We try to be at the forefront of discovering new talent.” This interest in new talent doesn’t come only from audiences, but it is also shared by the high-profile executives travelling into town for the festival’s highly prestigious industry sidebar, the Zurich Summit . “They are always asking me: who are the creatives this year? Who is the up-and-coming talent? What should we see? They are actually more interested than you would think in new talent,” says Guetg. “We have a panel this year with the CEO of the Oscars, Bill Kramer, who will sit next to [‘Obsession’ director] Kane Parsons, a 20-year-old still living with his parents in San Francisco, and a sensation who cracked 4 million admissions in cinemas,” she adds. “And they are both eager to hear from each other. It’s a great space to make these connections happen because we have a lot of openness from both sides.” A year ago, the Summit made major headlines when it introduced the market to AI-generated actress Tilly Norwood, launched by AI talent studio Xicoia. Asked about Norwood’s impact — and controversies — in the year since, Jungen says, “Zurich is the place where you address the real hot questions.” Tilly Norwood, courtesy of Xicoia Courtesy of Particle6 “AI is the big game changer of our times,” he goes on. “In my mind, it’s bigger than the introduction of the internet in the late 90s. We didn’t expect the reactions to Tilly Norwood last year, but it proves there is a lot of energy in those questions. The Zurich Summit takes place in neutral Switzerland; it’s where everybody finds common ground, where Americans meet Europeans. We have a tradition of being a platform for exchange and openness.” The festival will also bring back the Film Finance Forum, an event even more exclusive than the already exclusive Summit. The Forum takes place a day before the conference and brings together bankers, investors and major producers for closed-door discussions on film financing. “We want to put our international guests in an exchange with the people from the finance industry here,” says Jungen. “Quite a few companies have found investors for their businesses at the Zurich Summit, and that’s a role we want to play. We want to turn Zurich into a platform where you get access to private equity because this is the way to go, as the pre-sale business is truly challenging.” “With private equity, we can move faster, produce faster, and since Zurich is literally the world capital of wealth management boutiques, I think we have a lot of stakeholders who might be interested in hearing from the lion’s mouth, from people from Los Angeles or New York who can say that investing in film can mean a return,” says the festival head. “Investing in film — it’s not just about supporting the arts; it’s business.” The Zurich Film Festival runs Sept. 24-Oct. 4. articles.title: ECAM Incubator Title ‘Copy’ Pairs a Heartbroken Film Assistant With a Movie Star Accused of Murder
articles.full_text: Sep 24, 2026 6:53am PT ECAM Incubator Title ‘Copy’ Pairs a Heartbroken Film Assistant With a Movie Star Accused of Murder By Callum McLennan Plus Icon Callum McLennan Latest ‘Suro’ Director Mikel Gurrea on ‘Saints,’ Directing ‘The Beloved’ Star Victoria Luengo, Religious-Art Theft and Finding Mystery in Care 5 hours ago ‘200 Lives, Paco Rabal,’ Told in the Spanish Screen Legend’s Own Voice, Boarded by Latido Films 5 hours ago Juan Sebastián Mesa, Tatiana Huezo, Felipe Solari Yrigoyen Triumph at San Sebastián Industry Awards 19 hours ago See All Ángeles L. Guerrero, Miguel Machetti and Tina V. Mollá Courtesy of Gelatina Películas What happens when an emotionally stranded young film worker becomes indispensable to one of the world’s biggest stars who may also be a murderer? That collision drives “Copy” (“El participio del verbo oír”), Miguel Machetti’s feature project, currently in development and produced by Ángeles L. Guerrero and Tina V. Mollá through Gelatina Películas . Selected for the ninth edition of Madrid film school ECAM’s prestigious Incubator, the project was also presented in ECAM Forum’s 2026 Films to Come strand. Related Stories Paranormal Comedy 'Don't F — k With Ghosts' Premieres On Demand, Launches Original YouTube Channel (EXCLUSIVE) Emmys in Talks to Move to Amazon Prime Video Under New Licensing Arrangement, as the Broadcast Wheel Deal Ends (EXCLUSIVE) The story follows Ramón, a film assistant reeling from a painful breakup, who begins working with Camille de Valois, a legendary French actress returning to cinema after two decades away following an accusation of murder. Popular on Variety “One of the most important themes to explore throughout the film was always the extraordinary within the absolute normality of everyday life,” Machetti told Variety. “Everyone has perhaps experienced a painful breakup, but what would it be like to face one alongside a living legend and potential serial killer?” While everyone around Ramón obsesses over whether Camille actually committed the crime, Ramón becomes far more consumed by the attention she gives him. “The fact that the most famous person in the world sees him, recognises him and, in many cases, depends on him, makes everything else fade into the background,” Machetti said. That dependency also attracted Gelatina to the project. Founded in 2025 by Guerrero and Mollá, the young company see in “Copy” both an unconventional first feature and a story they hope will travel beyond its film-industry setting. “You do not have to work for a major film star to recognise yourself in a toxic relationship from which you feel unable to escape,” the producers said. “Beneath its specific setting, ‘Copy’ speaks to something far more universal: the power dynamics, dependencies and contradictions that can shape our relationships with others and with ourselves.” Those power imbalances extend to the film set. Machetti drew on years working in assistant direction, describing the industry as “an extremely hierarchical environment.” The project is now entering its final stages of development, according to Gelatina, with international co-production a priority. The producers are particularly looking toward France and Belgium and envision Camille being played by an established French or Italian actress opposite a largely unknown actor as Ramón. “This echoes the central dynamic of the film itself: a young outsider suddenly sharing the screen with an established star,” they said. “The casting becomes an extension of the story, allowing fiction and reality to subtly mirror one another.” Filmmakers out of the incubator have included Jaione Camborda (“The Rye Horn”), Estibaliz Urresola (“20,000 Species of Bees,”) and Alauda Ruiz de Azúa (“Lullaby,” “Sundays.”) For Machetti, even the title crystallizes the hierarchy. “Copy” is Ramón’s habitual radio response. “It is perhaps the word he says most often throughout the day,” he said, “through a device that seems like an extension of his own body, and through which he only receives orders that he has to carry out.” SND Swoops on Toronto-Bound Bérénice Bejo Starrer ‘Alice: Pioneer of Cinema’ Ahead of Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Kill Jackie,’ Starring a Glamorous, Lethal Catherine Zeta-Jones, Acquired by Warner Bros. articles.full_text: Sep 24, 2026 7:00am PT Tribeca Festival Opens Submissions for Untold Stories Filmmaker Program With $1.2 Million Prize (EXCLUSIVE) By Anna Tingley Plus Icon Anna Tingley Latest The Best Pop Culture Halloween Costumes for 2026: From Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl Shrubs to Taylor Swift’s Knicks Shirt 16 hours ago Los Angeles Lakers Release Official Photo Book Chronicling Seven Decades of Purple-and-Gold History 18 hours ago No, Those Dior x A24 Shirts Aren’t Going on Sale 18 hours ago See All Tribeca Festival and AT&T have opened submissions for the 10th anniversary of AT&T Untold Stories, the filmmaker development program that awards one emerging director $1.2 million to produce a feature film. The production prize, which increased from $1 million to $1.2 million in 2026, is billed by Tribeca and AT&T as the largest unrestricted film production award of its kind in the world. Submissions for the upcoming edition are open through Jan. 18. Lobbying Group Amid Backlash Over Cost of Sports on Streaming Each year, five filmmaking teams are selected to pitch their projects live at the Tribeca Festival, with one winner receiving full production funding, year-round mentorship and support from Tribeca Studios. Popular on Variety The next recipient will be selected at the 2027 Tribeca Festival and will receive $1.2 million toward production ahead of a guaranteed premiere at the 2028 edition. “Tribeca is incredibly proud of our decade-long collaboration with AT&T and the success of the filmmakers who have come through Untold Stories,” said Bryce Norbitz, VP of Tribeca Studios and artist development. “We’ve watched pioneering storytellers take bold new ideas from concept to screen, garner the support of major distributors, and reach the audiences their stories deserve.” Norbitz added that the program’s continued growth is “a testament to the power of investing in emerging voices, especially at a time when independent filmmaking has never been tougher.” Launched in 2017, Untold Stories has awarded more than $9.2 million in funding, supported more than 45 projects and produced eight feature films. Recent winners include David Fortune’s “Color Book,” Lilian T. Mehrel’s “Honeyjoon” and Liz Sargent’s “Take Me Home,” all of which secured theatrical releases in 2026. Other past recipients include Faraday Okoro’s “Nigerian Prince,” Sasie Sealy’s “Lucky Grandma,” Kate Tsang’s “Marvelous and the Black Hole,” Nardeep Khurmi’s “Land of Gold,” So Young Shelly Yo’s “Smoking Tigers” and Sid Gopinath’s 2026 winner “Minnesota Goodbye.” Filmmakers can submit projects through Jan. 18 at Tribeca’s Untold Stories website. articles.title: ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Director Claire Scanlon Talks “Pressure” Of Chapter 16 Scene, “Dynamic” Captured With First Kiss & More
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Director Claire Scanlon Talks “Pressure” Of Chapter 16 Scene, “Dynamic” Captured With First Kiss & More All The Songs In ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Film Adaptation: Gracie Abrams To Haim Streamer Subscription Prices And Tiers – Everything To Know As Costs Rise And Ads Abound View All September 23, 2026 2:26pm Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman in 'The Love Hypothesis' Prime Video SPOILER ALERT: This piece spoils the entirety of The Love Hypothesis movie now streaming on Prime Video . Editor’s Note: Trigger Warning – The following contains mention of sexual harassment. Help is available at the National Sexual Assault Hotline: 1-800-656-4673. The order of several pivotal scenes in Ali Hazelwood’s The Love Hypothesis was switched up for the film adaptation of the bestselling romance novel, which is directed by Claire Scanlon and stars Tom Bateman and Lili Reinhart. The Prime Video film centers on a fake dating ploy that benefits both parties — Olive (Reinhart) convinces her best friend Anh (Rachel Marsh) that Anh should shoot her shot with their mutual crush Jeremy (Nicholas Duvernay), and Dr. Adam Carlsen (Bateman) makes his higher-ups aware that he’s in a serious relationship and in no way planning to leave Stanford University, which has funded much of his research but pulled the plug based on rumors he might depart. What starts out as a simple business arrangement between Olive and Adam develops into real romance, which faces obstacles when a certain Dr. Tom Benton (Arty Froushan) comes to town. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Books All The Songs In ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Film Adaptation: Gracie Abrams To Haim News Everything We Know About ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Movie So Far The very important Chapter 16 sex scene between Olive and Adam was moved up in the film, and Scanlon already felt the “pressure” to get that one right alone. Luckily a test audience of 40% book readers and fans gave the green light. “When we started, there was just a quick paragraph of the sex scene, and then I read the book, and [said to] Sarah Rothschild, who wrote a great adaptation, ‘I think we need to build out that sex scene.’ Then I went on TikTok and I saw everyone [saying] ‘chapter 16, chapter 16.’ I was like, ‘Oh my goodness, this has to be more,’” Scanlon told Deadline. “Translating the book, which is over a chapter, to the screen — you can’t do that long with a sex scene. That would be not right. But just making sure that you got it tonally is always going to be tricky because everyone’s got their own internal dialogue and their own imagination of what it all looks like. We were ready for all the criticism, and then there wasn’t any.” To back up, a chaotic kiss with Carlsen initiated by Olive sets the fake-dating scheme of The Love Hypothesis into motion. Olive panics and smooches the first man she sees — who happens to be the notorious Doctor Evil — to throw Anh off the scent late one Saturday night in the lab. This snowballs into a whiplash of planned PDA and falling in love between the scientists. “We shot the first kiss on the first week. I wanted to make sure we got that dynamic established. And when we got that scene, I was like, ‘We have a movie’ because you just get all of it, watching it, trying to re-create the book cover in the actual scene. Paying homage to the book cover, and just in general, trying to get the tone of that scene, all the elements that were going into it. Anh’s coming up the stairs, [Olive]’s running this way. He’s like, “What?” Scanlon said. “Then he’s pissed because when you think about it from his point of view, he hasn’t been touched for years by anyone. Everyone’s so scared of him. That fact that someone smacked a kiss on him and then immediately rejects him, like that’s gotta suck, you know?” Carlsen quips about filing a Title IX complaint because Olive technically doesn’t wait for him to give consent before she kisses him. Another key moment that brings Title IX into the picture was shuffled to occur after the Chapter 16 scene, compared to book order: At the Society for Biological Development Conference, Carlsen’s colleague and seemingly close friend Benton, whose research aligns with Olive’s pancreatic cancer work, offers her a position on his lab bench at Harvard to continue conducting her experiments. But rather than base it off of Olive’s merit alone, he lays down the ultimatum that Olive must sleep with him in order to use his lab and equipment.

articles.title: Peter Byrne Dies: Naked Eyes Singer Who Scored ’80s Hits ‘Always Something There to Remind Me’ & ‘Promises, Promises’ Was 74
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Peter Byrne Dies: Naked Eyes Singer Who Scored ’80s Hits ‘Always Something There to Remind Me’ & ‘Promises, Promises’ Was 74 Dick Guttman Dies: Longtime Hollywood Publicist To Barbra Streisand, Clint Eastwood, Paul Newman, Gary Cooper & Many More Was 93 Rachel Dratch & Jeff Hiller Join Encores’ ‘You’re A Good Man, Charlie Brown’; Gershwins’ ‘Let ’Em Eat Cake’ Added To Season View All September 23, 2026 2:55pm Pete Byrne of the Naked Eyes Getty Peter Byrne , the singer and songwriter for the band Naked Eyes who scored 1980s hits with “Always Something There to Remind Me” and “Promises, Promises,” died peacefully in Los Angeles, California, on Monday, September 14, after a brief illness. He was 74. His death was announced on the band’s official website . One of the most popular, if fleeting, British New Wave bands of MTV’s golden era, Naked Eyes was founded in 1982 by Byrne and keyboardist Rob Fisher, who had been college friends in their native Bath, England, and had performed together in a band called Neon from 1979 to 1982. (That band also included Curt Smith and Roland Orzabal, who would go on to form Tears for Fears.) Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries Obituaries Duncan Sheik Dies: “Barely Breathing” Singer-Songwriter & ‘Spring Awakening’ Composer Was 56 Within two years Naked Eyes had scored four Top 40 hits on Billboard’s Hot 100. The highest charting was “Always Something There to Remind Me” which peaked at #8 during the summer of 1983. A cover of the 1963 song written by Burt Bacharach and Hal David for Dionne Warwick, the Byrne-Fisher demo of “Always Something There to Remind Me” was strong enough to convince EMI Records to sign the duo that would become Naked Eyes. The band had three subsequent top 40 hits, the most successful of which was “Promises, Promises,” written by Byrne and Fisher and not to be confused with the Bacharach-David song of the same title that was a hit for Warwick. Both songs were included on the band’s debut 1983 album Burning Bridges , as was a third, less successful single “When the Lights Go Out.” DEADLINE RELATED VIDEO: The band’s second album, 1984’s Fuel For The Fire , featured a modest hit “(What) In the Name of Love,” but failed to match the success of the debut album, prompting Naked Eyes to disband (the group never toured). Fisher died in 1999 at the age of 42 following cancer surgery. Born June 9, 1952, in Bath, Byrne continued writing, recording and touring following Fisher’s death, releasing the solo album The Real Illusion in 2001 under Pete Byrne, followed by two albums under the Naked Eyes name: Fumbling with the Covers in 2007 and Disguise the Limit in 2021. A remaster of the original Naked Eyes self-titled album was release in 2025. In 2008 Byrne’s Naked Eyes took part in the U.S. “Regeneration” tour with Belinda Carlisle, ABC and the Human League, and in 2024 joined a similarly ’80s themed tour of the U.S. and Canada with Wang Chung, Men Without Hats and The Motels. Outside of Naked Eyes, Byrne’s work included providing backing vocals on Stevie Wonder’s 1985 hit “Part-Time Lover,” as well as songwriting for film and television. He wrote the song “I Am The Cute One” in 1993 for the Olsen Twins. Byrne is survived by his siblings Eileen, Sandy, Carol and Steve; children Merlin, Dylan, and Chloe; and ex-wife Elena. A private service will be held for the family. articles.title: Ex-Disney CEO Bob Chapek Blames Bob Iger For Ouster In New Memoir
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill Ex-Disney CEO Bob Chapek Blames Bob Iger For Ouster In New Memoir Paramount Eyes Elon Musk For Investment As WBD Deal Nears Finish Line – Report Disney Hikes Price Of Disney+ And Hulu Streaming Plans View All September 23, 2026 3:29pm Bob Chapek Laurent Viteur/Getty Images; Simon & Schuster Bob Chapek , fired as Disney CEO in 2022 after less than three years, lays the blame for his ouster squarely on Bob Iger in an upcoming memoir, according to the New York Times, which obtained a copy. Behind the Castle Walls: My Thirty Years at the Happiest Place on Earth comes out Sept. 29 from Gallery Books, a division of Simon & Schuster. Related Stories Executives Disney Shocker! Bob Iger Back As CEO, Bob Chapek Out Executives Did Someone Save Disney’s Life Last Night? Behind Bob Iger’s Stunning CEO Return & What’s Next For Media Giant “My abrupt dismissal hurt my reputation, leaving those close to me, outsiders and some within the kingdom trying to figure out what I did wrong,” Chapek writes. “The answer, again, is nothing.” Instead, he claims that Iger, who had handpicked him for the job, relentlessly and intentionally sabotaged him. Chapek’s belief on that front is no secret but he lays out his thoughts and defends his tenure publicly at length for the first time in the book. He calls himself a disrupter and writes, “I didn’t get a chance to finish what I started.” Watch on Deadline Iger resigned abruptly as Disney CEO in February of 2020 after an epic run but remained as executive chairman for two years, retaining control over creative endeavors at the company and reporting directly to the board of directors. Chapek reported to both the board, and to Iger. The two clashed. Chapek suggests that Iger believed he could reclaim the job whenever he wanted, the NYT says. Describing Iger’s exit from Disney, Chapek wrote, “I have been told by several high-ranking people both in government and private business that in their opinions, the real reason he left the company so abruptly was his anticipation of the arrival of Covid.” Disney declined to comment. The company has denied the pandemic had anything to do with Iger’s exit. Iger has said he wanted to wind down after a successful run. He felt at the time that Chapek was the right person for the job. “I had been CEO for about 15 years. I started the company in 1974 at ABC. I had been around a long time. There were plenty of things in the world that I was interested in that I either wanted to do or wanted to learn more about. I had not really had a day off in I don’t even remember,” Iger told a NYT DealBook conference in 2023 about his departure. He said he was “disappointed in what I was seeing, both during the transition period when I was still there and while I was out. But I really worked hard at distancing myself from it because one, I couldn’t do anything about. It in a way, it wasn’t my business at all, really. It was his business to run.” Soon after he started as CEO, Chapek was being pilloried on several fronts including management decisions that vexed key executives, and a public fight with star Scarlett Johansson that alienated talent. The company’s response to legislation (dubbed the ‘Don’t Say Gay’ bill) in Florida angered both Disney employees and Gov. Ron DeSantis. His ouster came shortly after Disney reported a greater than expected $1.5 billion streaming loss for its latest quarter. Chapek’s apparent rubber stamp by the Disney board, followed by his rocky tenure, was used as ammunition by activist investor Nelson Peltz in a bruising proxy fight with the Mouse House. Iger returned as chief executive after Chapek was fired and remained in the job through March of this year. Josh D’Amaro, head of Disney’s giant theme parks and experiences business, was named CEO after a considerably more robust executive search process. Chapek, a 30-year Disney veteran, had also been running parks and experiences when he was anointed chief. articles.title: As YouTube Remains Streaming’s Alpha Dog, It’s Adding Even More Unlikely New TV Tricks
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Barry Diller Drops Bid To Acquire Full Control Of MGM Resorts As YouTube Remains Streaming’s Alpha Dog, It’s Adding Even More Unlikely New TV Tricks As Living Room Viewing Booms, YouTube Debuts Live Dubbing, Shorts Series And Raft Of Other Features View All September 23, 2026 4:29pm Neal Mohan at YouTube Brandcast in 2026 Noam Galai/Getty Images for YouTube It’s been clear for a while that YouTube ‘s biggest screen in terms of viewing is the TV – but don’t expect the tech giant to just sit back on the couch. On the contrary, it is embracing the idea of adding more and more counter-intuitive features to the living room experience. At its annual Made on YouTube event Wednesday, the company unveiled nearly three dozen new features for creators, viewers and brands, the latest of what CEO Neal Mohan said were 3,000 new product updates in 2026 to date. Viewers on TVs can now post comments; view “posts” (still images and texts posted to channels by creators); and watch series on YouTube Shorts . Related Stories News Disney Hikes Price Of Disney+ And Hulu Streaming Plans News As Living Room Viewing Booms, YouTube Debuts Live Dubbing, Shorts Series And Raft Of Other Features These interactive elements are a key reason why YouTube has topped the Nielsen charts for three years straight with, as of July, 14.2% of all viewing via a TV in the U.S., executives say. (Of course, being available for free doesn’t hurt either.) Watch on Deadline “Consumption is moving away from being passive, and people want to be engaged,” Kurt Wilms, senior director of product management, YouTube on TV, told reporters after the New York event. Asked to elaborate, he clarified, “I wouldn’t call it passive. I would call it, like, lean back . I’m watching it. Something maybe happens in the show. And then I’m like, ‘Oh, well, I want to read the comments, or I want to leave a comment myself, or, wait, what did she just talk about a different video? I wanna go to her channel and see.’ So now, instantly I become a leaned-in viewer. And so I think it flows, ebbs and flows between two. We don’t think of them as a hard line.” Though its presence on landscape televisions seems counterintuitive, Shorts has been a runaway hit in the living room, with viewers watching more than 2 billion hours of its programming on TVs each month. Even inside the company, the reaction to the notion of adapting features from the mobile and web experience is often, “Is this meant for the TV?” Wilms said. “But we’re hearing viewers ask for it and creators ask for it.” The rollout of expanded capabilities is rooted in a mission to preserve the DNA of the first iteration of the site, which launched in 2005. (The first comment posted on “Me at the Zoo,” the first video ever uploaded, the company breezily noted on Wednesday, was a succinct “Lol.”) “We didn’t want it to feel broken,” Wilms said of the app when it is viewed on a TV. Although Shorts seems like a left-field stunner, in retrospect its success made perfect sense. “The first thing everyone was telling me about Shorts on the TV is there was no good way to watch this content with friends or family,” Wilms said. “The TV unlocked communal viewing for Shorts in a way that just wasn’t possible before.” The strategy of “bringing all these content formats that you might not think would resonate with viewers on the TV” has been a particular focus over the past two years, Wilms said, citing gaming videos, podcasts and shorts. “We saw it again actually around the same time with video comments,” he recalled. Viewers told the company, “‘I want to read the comments on TV,’ and we were thinking, ‘Really?! You want to read the comments on the TV?!'” While YouTube has not put numbers to it, Wilms estimated that the amount of viewers reading comments on TVs rivals the number doing so on the web. Similar to Shorts and comments, the Posts functionality resulted from consumer and partner research. “It’s all born out of creator and viewer feedback,” he said. “And we’ve seen time and time again when we bring [features] to the big screen, they’re successful.” Rather than bucketing viewers according to those who lean back and those who interact, Wilms says the company’s research shows a more blended experience. “One of the things when we talk to viewers that we hear about a lot is, we call it modes – like, a viewer is in a mode ,” Wilms said. “It might be, at night you want to use YouTube on your television as your home stereo and use it for music. Another mode might be you’re with your family and your kids, and you want to use YouTube as a way to watch with them. And so another mode that we’ve heard about is, ‘Oh, I don’t know totally what I want to watch, but I want to sit down and kind of get some quick bites, and so I go into this Shorts mode.” Enter microdramas, the booming sector that has spawned a host of startup studios along with optimism that the major component of the Asian entertainment ecosystem will gain similar adoption elsewhere. Microdramas “have been incredibly successful on YouTube,” Wilms said. “There are more than 6.5 billion views of this content on YouTube already this year. On TV screens specifically, microdramas are growing 90% year over year.” Execs see more upside ahead. “Microdramas in particular, they’re fast paced, they’re action packed, they’re quick, and so in the industry as a whole, I think viewers are resonating to this type of content, so I assume it’s gonna continue to grow,” Wilms added. Overall, we see a lot of success of bite-sized content that could be personalized to your taste. …. People are seeing it as a place to spend breaks in their day.” 150 Tech Roles Set To Go; TV & Radio Network Closures Expected Next Week Trump Ban Temporarily Blocked; CNN Credentials Restored Key Asian Markets Set For $15B Content Spend In 2026 – Study HBO’s Bloys, Par’s Cheeks Fuel Merger Intrigue With Joint Appearance At ‘War’ Premiere Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Trump DOJ Official Minimizes State AGs’ Paramount-WBD Settlement, Says It Yielded No New…
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Judge Says He’ll Rule “As Soon As I Can” On Trump’s Ban On CNN, Politico And MS NOW; Expresses Concern Over Due Process CNN CEO Mark Thompson Addresses Donald Trump’s White House Ban, Pending Paramount Merger In Town Hall Reporters Committee And Dozens Of Media Outlets File Legal Brief Urging Judge To End Trump’s Ban On CNN, Politico And MS Now View All September 22, 2026 3:20pm Story Arc Getty Images A top Justice Department official is minimizing the concessions state attorneys general received in the settlement of their antitrust lawsuit to block the Paramount -Warner Bros Discovery merger. Stanley Woodward , associate attorney general, said in a statement Tuesday, “After a thorough review of the Paramount/WarnerBros deal, DOJ concluded that market dynamics create the necessary incentives to protect competition. Related Stories News Paramount Settlement Terms Laid Out By CA AG Rob Bonta, Who Says Deal Is “Not A Blessing” Of WBD Merger News David Ellison Hopes To Close Paramount-WBD Deal “In Approximately Two Weeks” As He Hails Legal Settlement In Company Memo “The only antitrust related provisions in the States’ settlement require that Paramount honor its already-stated commitments to maintain and grow its movie and TV businesses.” The DOJ signed off on the $111 billion merger in June, with no concessions from Paramount of requirements of divestitures. Merger opponents criticized the DOJ’s review as insufficient amid Paramount’s wooing of the Trump administration, and the next month a dozen state attorneys general sued to halt the transaction. Watch on Deadline But a settlement was announced Monday that includes a set of behavioral conditions to last for five years, including a commitment by Paramount to release 30 films for the first and second years, and 32 films for the third, fourth and fifth years. The consent decree also includes a theatrical release window of at least 45 days. Paramount CEO David Ellison had previously stated he would commit to such windows and to the 30-movies-per-year releases. Woodward said in his statement, “Consumers benefit when transactions close quickly after federal enforcers have concluded a substantive review. Under President Trump’s leadership, DOJ will continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy.” At a press conference Monday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta , who led the 12 states in the litigation, repeatedly said the settlement would be an “enforceable commitment,” including that it would “significantly increase domestic production in the United States, and necessarily production right here in L.A., in Hollywood.” Among other things, he said, Paramount also would spend $300 million more each year in domestic film production, while agreeing to conduct Paramount and Warner Bros cable channel negotiations independently. The settlement also includes an independent monitor to oversee compliance, Bonta’s team noted. Bonta had previously indicated that only a structural remedy — like a commitment to divest assets — would suffice when it came to a settlement. The consent decree does contain requirements to sell off Miramax and selected cable channels if there are breaches of the settlement terms. Just last week, before the settlement was reached, the DOJ sided with Paramount in its motion to require that the state AGs put up a $1.88 billion bond as the litigation dragged on. The trial had been scheduled for March, but Paramount faced having to pay a $7 million-per-day ticking fee to Warner Bros. Discovery for each day that the merger didn’t close after September 30. articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Barry Diller Drops Bid To Acquire Full Control Of MGM Resorts As YouTube Remains Streaming’s Alpha Dog, It’s Adding Even More Unlikely New TV Tricks As Living Room Viewing Booms, YouTube Debuts Live Dubbing, Shorts Series And Raft Of Other Features View All September 22, 2026 4:30pm Story Arc New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani with Donald Trump after their meeting at Gracie Mansion on Monday Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani , a day after continuing his congenial dealings with President Donald Trump, blasted the “federal leaders” supporting the Paramount -Warner Bros. Discovery merger. “America is free only when the media is competitive, independent, and accountable to the people,” Mamdani posted on X Tuesday. “This merger strikes a chilling blow against that freedom – and hands even more power to billionaires like David Ellison to decide what Americans see and hear, all while lifting scrutiny off the federal leaders who pushed it through.” Related Stories News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery News Read The Proposed Consent Decree To Settle The Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger Paramount on Monday reached a settlement with attorneys general from 12 states, including New York, as well as with the Writers Guild of America in dual antitrust lawsuits filed last July. The agreements remove the final barriers keeping Paramount from closing the controversial $111 billion transaction, which will remake Hollywood and likely result in sizable layoffs. Trump has yet to weigh in publicly on the deal, though Larry Ellison, the Oracle billionaire who is a key funder of the deal and CEO David Ellison’s father, is an ally of the president. Watch on Deadline Mamdani in his post saluted New York AG Letitia James “for the protections she secured for workers.” He closed with a withering line about the regulatory process, though he didn’t make the target of his scorn completely clear. “This decision is a shameful monument to corruption and a betrayal that the American people won’t soon forget,” he wrote. The social media missile stood in contrast with Monday’s atmosphere at Gracie Mansion, where Mamdani hosted Trump at the mayoral residence during his visit for the United Nations General Assembly. Their joint news conference showcased their mutually respectful, at times almost playful, dynamic. Behind closed doors, they said they discussed topics like affordable housing and immigration. Trump repeated his hope that Mamdani would be “a great mayor.” Mamdani defended the decision to engage peaceably with Trump despite their many policy disagreements. “I committed over the course of the campaign, as well as while being in office, that I would meet with anyone, work with anyone that could deliver for New Yorkers,” he said. “So having a conversation about potentially building 12,000 homes, about the importance of our Haitian neighbors here in this city, those are conversations that are worthwhile to have.” Even though the president has mounted constant attacks on “radical” and “Communist” Democratic candidates in November’s midterm elections, he has appeared to be charmed by the young mayor of his home town. They have met two previous times at the White House. Presidential visits to Gracie Mansion have been rare, the New York Times noted . Harry Truman attended a luncheon there in 1949 for a ceremony during construction of the UN’s headquarters building. John F. articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Terence Winter To Adapt Jay Stratton’s ‘Out Of The Shadows’ Memoir About Investigating Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena As TV Series HBO’s Casey Bloys & Par’s George Cheeks Go To ‘War’ Together: Execs’ Joint Premiere Appearance Creates Intrigue With WBD Merger Closing ‘A Man On The Inside’ To End With Season 3; Netflix Comedy Starring Ted Danson Sets Returning Cast, Guest Stars & New Mystery As Production Starts View All September 23, 2026 1:12pm Story Arc L-R: George Cheeks and Casey Bloys Getty Images Casey Bloys ‘ social calendar has been getting a lot of attention over the past several months — especially the timing of some of his engagements. The Chairman and CEO of HBO and Max Content is a fixture at all of the streamer’s events, so him attending the red-carpet premiere of the new drama series War in New York on Tuesday night was not a surprise. His plus-one, George Cheeks , was. Related Stories Executives Casey Bloys Celebrates HBO’s 21 Emmy Wins, Congratulates Apple, Gives Updates On ‘Last Of Us,’ ‘True Detective,’ ‘Gilded Age,’ ‘BLL’, ‘Heated Rivalry’ News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Cheeks is Chairman of TV Media for Paramount , a company in the final stages of acquiring HBO parent Warner Bros Discovery. Bloys and Cheeks’ joint appearance was arranged weeks ago, sources said, with Bloys inviting his friend to a premiere of a buzzy new show. They kept the affair relatively private by not posing for photos together. Still, the sight of top Paramount and WBD TV executives together stirred a lot of buzz at the event, coming just a day after a settlement in 12 state attorneys general’s antitrust lawsuit was announced, paving the way for the Paramount-WBD merger to close in the next two weeks after months of uncertainty. Watch on Deadline Bloys similarly got tongues wagging in March when he was spotted lunching with Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos just a couple of weeks after Netflix had walked away from its proposed merger of WBD following the late $111 billion bid by Paramount. The HBO boss’ social engagements are being closely scrutinized because what he will do next is one of the most intriguing questions surrounding the Paramount-WBD merger. Paramount CEO David Ellison and Sarandos have both spoken highly of Bloys, who is coming off another strong Emmy season at HBO where he is under contract through 2027. Bloys is expected to be a key part of Ellison’s plans for the combined Paramount-WBD. It is the way streaming leadership is structured with the planned merger of Paramount+ and HBO Max that would determine whether Bloys and Paramount Chair of Direct to Consumer Cindy Holland both stay or one of them leaves as it’s likely neither would report to the other. Current speculation is that Bloys would stay on, with Netflix chatter remaining in the background. Cheeks, the only Paramount co-CEO to continue after the company’s 2025 acquisition by Skydance, is part of Ellison’s senior management team and is expected to carry on, with his role possibly adjusted post-WBD merger. (Heading into the transaction, Cheeks oversees Paramount’s basic cable networks, while Channing Dungey, Chairman and CEO of the Warner Bros. Television Group and Warner Bros. Discovery’s US Networks, does the same for the WBD ones, raising questions whether the combined cable portfolio will be consolidated or remain split.) So, Cheeks’ visit to the War premiere may have been a precursor, similarly to then-Discovery CEO David Zaslav’s October 2021 attendance of the Season 3 premiere of HBO’s Succession alongside Bloys while the Discovery-WarnerMedia merger was still being finalized. The situation is a little different as Bloys and Cheeks are considered peers with their areas not expected to overlap if both stay on at Paramount, making their premiere date two potential co-workers hanging together. HBO/Sky’s drama War stars Dominic West and Sienna Miller as tech entrepreneur Morgan Henderson and film star Carla Duval in the grips of an acrimonious divorce. articles.title: Sturm Und Drang At Warner Bros Amid Paramount Merger Has Insiders Wondering If The Brand Survives
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony Sturm Und Drang At Warner Bros Amid Paramount Merger Has Insiders Wondering If The Brand Survives ‘Dynamic Duo’ & Untitled ‘Gremlins’ Head To Fall 2028 Amid Warner Bros Release Date Changes UTA Signs ‘Club Kid’ Star Reggie Absolom View All September 23, 2026 4:34pm Story Arc Paramount & Warner Bros water towers Getty Images UPDATED: A Zoom call on Wednesday with 500 senior Warner Bros staffers to discuss Paramount ‘s settlement of the antitrust lawsuit brought by state attorneys general related to its merger with WBD did little to dissipate the gloomy, Mordor-like clouds over the Burbank lot, to use a Lord of the Rings reference. The video call, which has been routine since Paramount won the $110 billion bid for Warner Bros Discovery, was led by WBD Studios Chief Operating Officer Simon Robinson, who is running point on the merger integration; Chief Legal Officer Priya Aiyar; WBD Chief Comms Officer Robert Gibbs; and HR boss Amy Girdwood . According to sources, the four conceded they didn’t have much visibility into Paramount’s plans for a newly combined company, but indicated that the anticipation is for the deal to close in about 10 days, in line with Paramount CEO David Ellison ‘s two-week timeframe he provided Monday. Related Stories News David Ellison Says “We Have Complete Clearance For This Merger” After Settlement With State AGs Over Paramount WBD News Post-Merger Paramount May Overdeliver On Settlement Terms With 36-Film 2027 Slate Amid Speculation About Duplication & WB Leadership The name and the leadership structure of the new company will likely be announced ahead of close, the executives reportedly said, though they weren’t clear as to when exactly that might be. We heard that Girdwood told leaders to take a moment to reflect on the great work accomplished during their tenures. Watch on Deadline “It feels like a scramble,” one source said. To say staffers were surprised by the AG settlement Monday doesn’t really cover it. “It was a big shock,” one person said. “If you were riding the roller coaster, you felt like things were not progressing.” Still, even if the settlement and its timing came as a surprise, the ultimate result seemed inevitable as WBD CEO David Zaslav has been hellbent on selling the studio. Ellison’s takeover of the cinematic institution founded by Albert, Harry, Sam and Jack Warner “was always bound to happen,” one insider exclaimed. Zaslav, who is likely to walk away with more than $600 million from the $110B merger, was not on today’s Zoom, we’re told. The Ellison-run Paramount has said that the Warner Bros acquisition will yield $6B in synergy savings, which don’t necessarily translate into job cuts, but rather by reducing inefficiencies in other structural areas (i.e., real estate portfolios, data servers). But Warner Bros staffers aren’t buying that. “We’ve been here before. We know what it looks like,” said one insider about the changeover in ownership of Warner Bros over the past decade. It was only four years ago that AT&T dumped WarnerMedia into the hands of Discovery. Myriad people inside Warner Bros are cynical about the capping of severances and the fact that only a few at the top are bound for a post-merger windfall. There’s also ire over the pausing of contract renewals due to the acquisition, as well as irritable infighting between departments about theatrical failures this year: No one WB title has cleared $100M at the domestic box office, with the highest-grossing movie stateside being Wuthering Heights at $84M. Home entertainment and data analytics divisions were none too happy about DC’s Supergirl tanking; with its $186M net production cost and a global box office gross of $126.3M, key staffers believe DC Studios chose the wrong comic book character to adapt. On the immediate horizon as the Paramount-Warner Bros marriage comes together is Digger, the $125M political satire starring Tom Cruise, directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu and produced by Legendary. It opens on October 2. While domestic debut prospects are at around $20M, Warners is hoping to get past any sour headlines about box office-to-cost ratios on the film, much like it did on One Battle After Another, as the four-time Oscar-winning filmmaker’s Doctor Strangelove -like epic is being primed as an awards-season contender. It is a chip Paramount really doesn’t have on its year-end schedule. The new Paramount could also inherit another awards contender and its first billion-dollar-grossing title since Skydance took over the Melrose Ave lot with Legendary/Warner Bros’ Dune: Part Three. That opens on December 18. To date, the Denis Villeneuve franchise counts $1.12B at the global box office and eight Oscars. We’ve heard on the Paramount side that it’s still TBD in regards to how the merger will handle duplications in marketing and distribution. Warner Bros international distribution has more of a solid presence in offshore territory offices and staffers than Paramount, which needs to untangle itself from UIP. Paramount could find great muscle in Warners International distribution and marketing infrastructure. While we were told by Paramount sources that the plan isn’t to create two studios, it might be wise for Ellison to keep each respective marketing team at their respective labels if he wants each studio working to the top of their creative merits and box office strengths: former Warner Bros exec Josh Goldstine presiding over global marketing and distribution at Paramount, and the team he built at Warners — Dana Nussbaum and Christian Davin in global marketing along with Creative Advertising EVP John Stanford–exactly over at Warners. Marketing and distribution rolls up and reports into the motion picture heads. During Warner Bros’ $4.38B grossing 2025, the trio of Nussbaum, Davin, and Stanford achieved great innovative marketing efficiencies, we’re told, and yes, those 11 Oscars for the Burbank, CA lot. There’s also a thick fog around those staffers who were bound to decamp from Warner Bros proper in the previously planned Gunnar Wiedenfels-led Global Networks spinoff. Yes, Warner Bros staffers are already putting themselves out there for other jobs. Some of them have already found new gigs: Former EVP Comms Katie Martin Kelly, prized by Warner Bros Motion Picture group co-heads Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, high-tailed it for Netflix as her contract ended, rather than wait for the Russian roulette the new conglomerate could bring. Former HBO Max EVP Originals Marketing Pia Barlow found a new job at Amazon MGM Studios as their Series Marketing VP, a gig that triggered WBD to sue for poaching. The merger closing will likely trigger more voluntary departures as many WBD executives had been waiting to cash out stock options post-transaction, no longer bound by contracts that typically provide a way out in case of change of ownership. “Since David Zaslav took control of Warner Bros, there’s just been thousands of jobs lost,” one former Turner publicist emphatically told us. “Those are jobs that the entertainment industry is never going to get back.” And therein lies the ultimate piercing wound for any Warners or Paramount employee in the danger zone: The fact that there are not a lot of jobs out there is a big deal. What’s more, adds a source, “People are very concerned about the survival of the Warner Bros brand.” Counters a senior ranking insider at the conglomerate: “There’s a feeling of relief from senior executives to junior staff about the possibilities that the new company can bring. They were very excited by David Ellison’s note.” For now, Paramount is inheriting at least 39 Warner Bros theatrical releases on the calendar dated between October 2 this year and the end of 2028. That output reps 56% of what will be a currently combined 70 features between the two studios. During the agita of Netflix and Paramount courting Warner Bros, the studio’s greenlighting of productions has been at a loud hum; assumptions were made by some that Warner Bros Motion Pictures would be in purgatory during merger talk time, and that filmmakers and reps would be wary of taking projects to them. That’s not really an option for content creators at a time when it’s a miracle for any major motion picture to get off the ground. Something to look forward to: While a Barbie sequel hasn’t been greenlit due to ongoing talks with top-tier talent including director Greta Gerwig and stars Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, expect that to be one of the first orders of business for the new Ellison-owned Paramount-Warner Bros. Beams one optimistic Warner exec, “The new merger gives us the all the financial resources to compete on a level with the big streamers.” 150 Tech Roles Set To Go; TV & Radio Network Closures Expected Next Week Trump Ban Temporarily Blocked; CNN Credentials Restored Key Asian Markets Set For $15B Content Spend In 2026 – Study HBO’s Bloys, Par’s Cheeks Fuel Merger Intrigue With Joint Appearance At ‘War’ Premiere More from this Story Arc Paramount WB September 23, 2026 HBO’s Casey Bloys & Par’s George Cheeks Go To ‘War’ Together: Execs’ Joint Premiere Appearance Creates Intrigue With WBD Merger Closing September 22, 2026 Judge Sets Hearing On State AGs’ Settlement With Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery View All Story Arc Read More About: 4 Comments

articles.title: proposal to acquire full ownership of MGM Resorts
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill Ex-Disney CEO Bob Chapek Blames Bob Iger For Ouster In New Memoir Paramount Eyes Elon Musk For Investment As WBD Deal Nears Finish Line – Report Disney Hikes Price Of Disney+ And Hulu Streaming Plans View All June 1, 2026 8:45am Barry Diller Kristina Bumphrey / Getty Images Barry Diller is making his next big move as People Inc. (previously IAC) submitted a non-binding proposal to acquire control of MGM Resorts International . The plan would be to buy outstanding MGM shares that People doesn’t already own and take the publicly-traded company private. People Inc. already holds a sizable 26% stake in MGM Resorts. The proposal, offering $48.30 per share in cash, values the casino giant at $18 billion. “We believe that MGM’s assets and businesses are not currently realizing their full potential in the public markets and that it will be difficult to correct this situation in MGM’s current form as a public company,” Diller wrote in a June 1 letter to the MGM Resorts’ Board of Directors. Related Stories Executives Ari Emanuel Has A Plan To Quell Fears About "Larry Ellison Controlling CNN & CBS"; TKO CEO Follows David Ellison's NYT Rebuke Of ParaBros Suit News Barry Diller Wants To Buy CNN "Before They Ruin It Any Further": "Hopefully Before It's Extinct" “We began investing in MGM nearly six years ago because we believed it represented a rare kind of business: one with real world assets that AI cannot easily replicate or disintermediate and exceptional digital growth opportunities. That conviction has only strengthened over time,” said Diller, who is People’s chairman and senior executive. “We continue to believe the market materially undervalues the power and durability of MGM’s assets. We believe MGM’s management team is superb, and that there is a compelling opportunity to support MGM’s next phase of growth and help unlock its full value.” Watch on Deadline The deal would be financed by a combination of existing cash on hand at People and at MGM and additional debt and equity funding commitments. People would end up controlling the MGM business with about 50.1% of the equity. Other investors, which may include existing shareholders of MGM, may hold minority interests. Diller called the offer a “high certain transaction.” The proposal reps a premium of 24% to the volume-weighted average price of MGM common stock for the 30 trading days ending on May 29, 2026, a more than 30% premium to the stock’s volume-weighted average price for the 90 trading days ending on the same date, and a 10.6% premium to the most recent closing price. Diller’s IAC rebranded to People Incorporated in April. articles.title: Rolf De Heer To Head Competition Jury At Tokyo Film Festival; ‘The Survival Of Kindness’ To Play In Australia Spotlight
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz ‘Bling Empire’ Breakout Kim Lee To Host ‘Rice To Riches’ Reality Show For KC Global Media Asia ‘H Is For Hawk’ Investor Kliff Studios Expands Thai New Talent Slate With Sci-Fi Drama ‘Algo In The Sky’ Canada’s Omnifilm Expands Scripted Slate With English-Language Remake Of Korean Drama ‘The Good Detective’ View All September 23, 2026 5:00pm Rolf de Heer Tokyo International Film Festival Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF) has announced that Australian director Rolf de Heer will serve as president of the International Competition jury at this year’s edition of the festival. De Heer’s 2022 film The Survival Of Kindness , which was selected for competition at the Berlinale, will screen in Tokyo as part of an Australia Spotlight, a special showcase of Australian cinema presented in cooperation with the Australian Embassy in Japan. Based in Tasmania, de Heer has a career spanning more than 40 years and widespread international acclaim, starting with Bad Boy Bubby (1993), which won the Special Jury Prize and FIPRESCI Prize at Venice. Other early career highlights include Dingo (1991) with Colin Friels and jazz legend Miles Davis; The Quiet Room (1996) and Dance Me To My Song (1998), both selected for Competition at Cannes. Related Stories News Stan Sets 'McLeod's Daughters' Revival, Rachel Griffiths-Starrer 'Slander' & Angourie Rice's 'Pride & Prejudice' Reimagining News Netflix NFL Opener In Australia Draws 18.5M Viewers, Extending League's Muted Start To Season In total, four of his films have screened in Official Selection at Cannes Film Festival, including Ten Canoes (2006), which won the Special Jury Prize in Un Certain Regard. Watch on Deadline Mid-career highlights also include The Tracker (2002), which also played in Venice competition and marked de Heer’s first collaboration with Australian Indigenous actor David Gulpilil; Alexandra’s Project (2003), which won best actress at San Sebastian for Helen Buday’s performance; The King Is Dead! (2012); and Charlie’s Country (2013), which won Gulpilil a Best Actor award at Cannes. De Heer said: “For any of us attending the Tokyo International Film Festival, it is a privilege. For me, as a filmmaker, it is even more so. The more films I manage to make, the fewer films I manage to see, especially on the big screen. “But as a part of this jury, I have the duty, the obligation, to see at least 15 films and talk about them with other filmmakers! And not just any old 15 films, but the 15 films in Competition, drawn from films made all over the world by all sorts of extraordinary filmmakers! And to do this in a city that plays host to one of the most formidable film cultures in the world! Can life ever get much better than this?” Tokyo Festival Director Takeo Hisamatsu said: “We are delighted to welcome Rolf de Heer as President of the International Competition jury at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival. With his distinctive perspective and unwavering commitment to filmmaking, de Heer has spent decades opening up new possibilities in cinema. We look forward to the fresh dialogue and discoveries that his wealth of experience and deep insight will bring to this year’s Competition and its diverse selection of films.” Tokyo International Film Festival will take place October 26 to November 4, with the TIFFCOM contents market running October 28-30. 150 Tech Roles Set To Go; TV & Radio Network Closures Expected Next Week Trump Ban Temporarily Blocked; CNN Credentials Restored Key Asian Markets Set For $15B Content Spend In 2026 – Study HBO’s Bloys, Par’s Cheeks Fuel Merger Intrigue With Joint Appearance At ‘War’ Premiere Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Meta Introduces New VR Glasses With Access To Content From YouTube, Prime Video, HBO Max, Disney+ & More
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Tom Tapp Tom Tapp Deputy Managing Editor More Stories By Tom Meta Introduces New VR Glasses With Access To Content From YouTube, Prime Video, HBO Max, Disney+ & More Jalen Brunson Has One Key Problem In New ‘SNL’ Promo 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More View All September 23, 2026 7:37pm Meta VR Glasses Meta Meta today announced a new generation of VR glasses that it promised will “define a new era for virtual reality,” creating an all-in-one productivity and media device. Meta VR Glasses will deliver cinema, TV and sports content in one device with access to Prime Video, YouTube, Peacock, HBO Max, and Paramount+, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, Tubi, the NBA, MLB, ESPN, MLB, NBC Sports, TNT Sports and UFC, some with virtual and 3D enhancements. The frames are set to be released in Spring 2027 at a price point of $1300. Like Apple’s Vision Pro — to which they bear more than a passing resemblance — you can watch movies, TV and sports on “theater-sized” virtual screens, video chat with your friends or work in an app environment similar to that on your phone. Related Stories Legal Rob Bonta Says It's "Telling" Meta Settled With State AGs In The Midst Of Instagram Head Adam Mosseri's Testimony & Before Mark Zuckerberg Took The Stand Legal Meta Settles Landmark Social Media Addiction Case For $17 Billion, Enhanced Protections For Teens Meta VR Glasses will be operated with hand gestures or by moving your eyes to icons on the screen. Watch on Deadline Thankfully, Meta VR Glasses are five times lighter than their predecessor, the clunky Meta Quest 3. That’s primarily because the device is split in two: the frames and a pocket-sized device called a “puck.” The VR Glasses handle sensors and display. The puck, connected by an optical tether, handles compute, battery and storage and can be slipped into (or clipped onto) a pocket or bag. The device’s TV app promises “the best media lineup of any VR device,” plus offerings from the 3D media catalogs of Peacock , HBO Max and Paramount+. Even before the glasses launch, through a partnership with Disney+ , subscribers to that service will be able to stream movies like The Avengers, Black Panther and more in 3D on Meta Quest headsets. There will also be themed immersive viewing environments from Disney franchises like Tatooine and the Avengers Tower. Hundreds of movies will be available to rent or buy later this year on Meta Quest, with thousands of titles available by Meta VR Glasses’ launch next spring. Those will eventually include 3D films from Lionsgate and “first time in 3D” blockbusters from James Cameron and Lightstorm Vision. Sports apps, like NBA, MLB and ESPN will be available on the device, with ESPN offering “Immersive Sports,” billed as “a front-row seat, 8K streaming, and 180-degree views.” Immersive Sports will launch with college football this year on Meta Quest, with more sports to come in 2027.
