articles.title: Bad Brains’ Earliest Studio Recordings to Be Released in November
articles.full_text: Sep 23, 2026 7:03am PT Bad Brains’ Earliest Studio Recordings to Be Released in November By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Bad Brains’ Earliest Studio Recordings to Be Released in November 6 minutes ago Warner Chappell Co-Chair/COO Carianne Marshall to Step Down From Post 2 days ago Sesame Street Transforms Chappell Roan’s ‘Hot to Go!’ Into the Potty-Training Anthem ‘Got to Go,’ With Lead Vocals From Cookie Monster 5 days ago See All As anyone reading this probably knows, the Bad Brains were one of the most important punk-rock bands of all time, Washington D.C.-bred pioneers of the sound that became hardcore. While they were a complete anomaly at the time — four Black dudes in an overwhelmingly white music scene who seasoned their blistering rock songs with impressively authentic reggae — their impact was immediate and immense. While the group was as fractious interpersonally as they were musically — they split up many times, usually when they were on the verge of a breakthrough — their early albums and particularly their explosive live shows contain some of the most powerful rock music of the ‘80s. They are considered by many to be the greatest hardcore band of all time; Dave Grohl has said he learned how to play drums by bashing on pillows along with their records, and a mural of the band was painted in 2024 across the street from the site of their frequent haunt CBGB in New York. Related Stories Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’ A Graffiti Mural incorporating Glen E. Friedman’s artwork celebrating the punk rock band Bad Brains on the corner of Bleeker Street and Bowery is shown in a photograph taken on October 24, 2024 in New York City. (Photo by Al Pereira/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images) Getty Images The group’s catalog is about to get an addition that is both old and new: On November 6, just in time to join the insurrection that will surely follow the midterm elections, a little-known recording of their first session in a proper studio will be released as “Are You Ready: The First Studio Recordings.” While an early demo recording was release in 1996 as the “Black Dots” album, this six-song session, recorded in an hour at Inner Ear Studios in March 1979, predates even that by three months. Popular on Variety The recordings were remixed by Minor Threat/ Fugazi co-founder and longtime friend Ian MacKaye — who has been on an archival binge recently, having worked with Henry Rollins to restore the catalog of psychobilly legends the Cramps — and will be available on vinyl, cassette, and digital. The EP joins the group’s full catalog, much of which was out of circulation for many years but recently got a proper reissue treatment and now is available on streaming services. It includes a previously unreleased recording of the band’s legendary debut single, “Pay to Cum,” which is released today with video footage filmed ay CBGB in October of 1979. “The riff for ‘Pay to Cum’ started as a stream of punk rock vibes fueled by the Ramones, the Damned, and Return to Forever,” says Bad Brains bassist Darryl Jenifer, reflecting the band’s unusual combination of inlfuences. “It was a gift that served as a springboard into our sound – sheer, straight-ahead three-chord mayhem with a few breaks and a stop. The title actually meant nothing to us; it was just a fun-loving play on words.” Listen/share “Pay to Cum” here and watch the video – with footage was filmed by Barry Masterson at CBGB’s October 24th 1979. On November 5, a day before the album’s release, Jenifer and Ian will appear in conversation at the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library, discussing the session and the band’s formative years. From November 6 through the 22nd, an exhibition of archival Bad Brains material will open, featuring contributions from the archives of Darryl Jenifer, Alison Braun, BJ Papas, Lucien Perkins, Alec MacKaye, Roger Gastman, and more. articles.title: Brad Pitt Praises Streamers For Creating Opportunities & Says He Believes The Indie Film Space Is Currently Just As Strong As In The ’90s — San Sebastián
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Brad Pitt Praises Streamers For Creating Opportunities & Says He Believes The Indie Film Space Is Currently Just As Strong As In The ’90s — San Sebastián Creative Risks, AI & Brazil’s Production Boom: Topics From Day One Of The 2026 San Sebastián Creative Investors’ Conference Brixton Community Cinema Creator Abiba Coulibaly On Why She Decided To End The Popular London Film Club View All September 23, 2026 4:09am Brad Pitt and Odin in 'Heart of the Beast' Paramount Pictures Brad Pitt was optimistic about the current indie film landscape during a packed-out press conference this morning at the San Sebastián Film Festival, where he is set to screen his latest feature, Heart of the Beast . “The current setup is really conducive to independent cinema in a really cool way because more eyes are getting on these projects. It even feels as strong as in the ’90s,” Pitt told the audience in San Sebastian when asked about the current film landscape. The veteran actor also spoke positively about what he described as the creative opportunities streaming platforms have added to the movie business. Related Stories News Creative Risks, AI & Brazil's Production Boom: Topics From Day One Of The 2026 San Sebastián Creative Investors' Conference Reviews 'Heart Of The Beast' Review: Brad Pitt And A Soulful German Shepherd Struggle To Survive The Wilderness In An Emotional Journey That Will Have You Sobbing “Streaming has brought us so many more opportunities for actors, writers, directors. And because of that, we have a greater plethora of really interesting stories and really interesting talents, and that’s been amazing,” he said. Watch on Deadline But Pitt added a caution to his comments and highlighted what he described as the tightening space in the marketplace for mid-budget films, which he said were his bread and butter. “Movies got so expensive. We always talk about how the very big tentpole movies are able to recoup. And the more independent, lower-budget, or anything in the middle ground—anything from 30, maybe 40, 60—has a really difficult time getting made, even movies like ours, because it’s very difficult for the studio to recoup that middle budget,” he said. Pitt added: “I’m hoping those movies still have space, because that’s usually where I end up most, in the middle ground.” Heart of the Beast was one of the late additions to this year’s San Sebastián lineup. Pitt is here at the festival with director David Ayer. The film follows a former Army Special Forces soldier (Pitt) and his retired combat dog who battle for survival after a plane crash deep in the unforgiving Alaskan wilderness. The film’s official synopsis reads: After a harrowing plane crash, Special Forces officer James Belmont (Pitt) and his combat dog, Odin, find themselves stranded deep in the Alaskan wilderness. Together, they are forced into a brutal fight for survival against the elements. Cameron Alexander wrote the film. Olivia Hamilton, Marty Bowen, Ayer, and Pitt are producers. Exec producers include Damien Chazelle, Scott Lumpkin, Cameron Alexander, Chris Long, Pete Chiappetta, Anthony Tittanegro, Andrew Lary, Sophie Cassidy, and Zack Conroy. The project reunites Pitt and Ayer for the first time since Fury , their 2014 WWII drama for Sony, and comes following Pitt’s starring role in the Oscar-nominated Apple flick F1 . Paramount debuted footage of the pic at this year’s CinemaCon. articles.title: John Cleese Accuses BBC Of “Social Engineering” After Cutting Blackface Sketches From ‘That Mitchell And Webb Look’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Sacha Baron Cohen’s Character Reinforcing “Harmful” Racial Stereotypes John Cleese Accuses BBC Of “Social Engineering” After Cutting Blackface Sketches From ‘That Mitchell And Webb Look’ Chapter One Producers Complete Management Buyout From Anonymous Content; Take Investment From Former Fifth Season CEO Chris Rice View All September 23, 2026 4:33am 'That Mitchell And Webb Look' BBC Studios John Cleese is unhappy with the BBC for removing sketches from comedy series That Mitchell and Webb Look . The BBC confirmed earlier this week that jokes featured in David Mitchell and Robert Webb’s show had been cut ahead of it being restored to iPlayer for its 20th anniversary. As many as 11 sketches were removed, including a self-referential skit in which Mitchell and Webb joked about the appropriateness of Blackface while in Blackface. Cleese, who is no fan of historical revisionism, attacked the BBC in X/Twitter posts, describing the edits as “social engineering.” Watch on Deadline Related Stories News 'Committed': First Look At Dustin Milligan & Diona Doherty As Transatlantic Lovers In CBC & BBC Sitcom Casting BBC Drama 'Ministry Of Time' Adds Adeel Akhtar, Ciaran Hinds & Eight More To Cast “If the BBC could prioritise making great programmes ahead of social engineering they might be worth the licence fee,” he wrote. If the BBC could prioritise making great programmes ahead of social engineering they might be worth the licence fee https://t.co/hyP6iYHg4M — John Cleese (@JohnCleese) September 23, 2026 In another, Cleese shared a post from James Dreyfus, star of BBC comedies including Gimme Gimme Gimme and The Thin Blue Line . “So, the BBC have decided that 11 of Mitchell & Webb’s sketches are no longer deemed ‘appropriate for modern day audiences,’ despite the fact that ALL their material comes from an intelligent source base, that pokes fun at & ridicules the foolish & ignorant,” Dreyfus wrote. “And people have the nerve to suggest that ‘we’d miss the BBC if it suddenly disappeared’…? Not in its current incarnation, believe me…” Cleese responded: “The BBC knows what’s best for us. And some of us know what’s best for the BBC.” The BBC declined to comment beyond a statement issued earlier this week. “ That Mitchell and Webb Look has been made available on BBC iPlayer. This is a 20-year-old sketch show; in consultation with the programme makers, we have included the ones that still work today and not the ones that don’t,” a spokesperson said. Cut sketches include one in which Mitchell and Webb play English Civil War re-enactors who have grown bored of their roles and recreate a conflict between government forces in the Democratic Republic of Congo and a rebel militia. Mitchell asks: “Are you absolutely sure that this isn’t racist?” They agree to stop the reenactment at the first sign of racism. When one threatens the other with a machete, they halt the reenactment, concluding: “It’s racist. Very, very racist. Shame.” In another sketch, Webb and Olivia Colman parody a makeover show and are confronted by a woman in a burqa. It then cuts to Webb discussing whether the sketch is offensive, with the woman in the burqa removing her garment to reveal Mitchell in Blackface. In 2020, Cleese voiced his disapproval of a decision by BBC Studios-owned broadcaster UKTV to scrub an episode of classic British comedy Fawlty Towers from its back catalog. UKTV removed “The Germans” from its Gold Box Set of downloadable programs, citing the fact that it contained “racial slurs.” UKTV was not specific about the slur, but it is believed to have been uttered by character The Major (Ballard Berkeley), who uses the n-word when referring to Caribbean sportsmen. “The Major was an old fossil leftover from decades before. We were not supporting his views, we were making fun of them,” said Cleese. “If they can’t see that, if people are too stupid to see that, what can one say?” ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Racial Stereotypes MIP London Comes To An End After Two Years; Organizers Plot New Event Judge Sets Settlement Hearing Date; Read Consent Decree; More Reax Tom Cruise Pic’s World Premiere Was A Royal Affair; Recap + Photos Read More About: 1 Comments

articles.title: ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Sacha Baron Cohen’s Character Reinforcing “Harmful” Racial Stereotypes
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Sacha Baron Cohen’s Character Reinforcing “Harmful” Racial Stereotypes John Cleese Accuses BBC Of “Social Engineering” After Cutting Blackface Sketches From ‘That Mitchell And Webb Look’ Chapter One Producers Complete Management Buyout From Anonymous Content; Take Investment From Former Fifth Season CEO Chris Rice View All September 23, 2026 5:00am Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G Amazon MGM Studios EXCLUSIVE : As the self-anointed “voice of youth” in the late 1990s, Ali G was a British cultural sensation, parroted in school playgrounds and quoted in Parliament. But nearly 30 years on, Sacha Baron Cohen has been criticized for “microwaving a relic from a generation ago” with his unexpected decision to reboot the suburban rude boy. In interviews with Deadline, Black British comedians voiced dismay at Amazon MGM Studios ’ upcoming film Ali G: Who Iz I? , arguing that the character is no longer associated with its roots of satirizing white men trying to adopt Black street culture. Instead, they said Ali G perpetuates racial stereotypes, diminishes the Black experience, and appropriates culture in a way that is damaging to the Black community. Related Stories Casting Michelle Rodriguez Latest To Join Amazon MGM Studios' Romantic Comedy 'Egg Baby' Casting Nicole Wallace Joins Josh Heuston In Amazon MGM Romance 'Throttled' Baron Cohen and Amazon MGM Studios declined to comment, but Deadline spoke with Colton Dunn, one of three Black writers who worked on Ali G: Who Iz I? , who said he did not recognize the criticisms. He argued that Baron Cohen remains faithful to Ali G’s origins, adding that the jokes target the movie’s subjects rather than Black people. “From my point of view, Ali G is not a racist character. Ali G is a tool to expose racists,” he said. Watch on Deadline Dunn explained: “He puts himself in the most ridiculous situations, and he doesn’t do that because he’s racist. He goes into these crazy-ass places, places where people would kill him if they knew what was going down. I don’t think he’s doing that from a racist point of view. That’s why I signed on. I wouldn’t sign on to work with somebody that I thought was racist, that’s against everything that I’ve done.” The debate erupted after the trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I? went viral last month. Jack Black, Tom Brady and Diplo all endorsed the character’s return, but it also sparked an online campaign to get the movie shut out of British cinemas because Ali G perpetuates “harmful stereotypes.” The campaign looks set to fail (Vue is among the theater chains planning to screen Who Iz I? when Sony releases it in the UK on October 23), but its message resonated with some in the Black British comedy community. Gina Yashere , a standup who co-created and starred in CBS comedy Bob Hearts Abishola , accused Baron Cohen of ostensibly adopting Blackface and “cosplaying” as another race. “He’s not targeting white people,” she told Deadline. “People watching that character are going to laugh because it’s a caricature of Black people.” Curtis Walker, another standup who starred in BBC series Paramount City , said he found Ali G “degrading” and “disgusting,” adding that it was “sad” that Amazon MGM Studios was backing the character, rather than Black creators. Yashire and Walker first voiced their concerns 26 years ago, when they were interviewed by New Nation , a newspaper for Britain’s Black community. The criticisms then grew louder at the Ali G in Da House premiere in 2002, when protesters demonstrated in Leicester Square, waving placards comparing the comic creation to Al Jolson, the American entertainer who was famous for performing in Blackface. Baron Cohen was aware of the concerns at the time, not least because Walker confronted him at an industry event. Baron Cohen told WTF with Marc Maron in 2016 that he decided not to engage publicly with the critics, even though he considered himself “vehemently against any form of racism.” He has long asserted that Ali G wants to be Black, but his true ethnicity is intentionally ambiguous. “He’s not Black. He is delusional,” he told NPR’s Fresh Air in 2009. Yashire and Walker’s views are shared by younger Black comics in the UK. Dane Baptiste, creator of BBC shows Sunny D and Bamous , said Ali G created a “skewed idea of Blackness” in Britain, and his revival is akin to “microwaving a relic from a generation ago.” He told Deadline: “After Black Lives Matter and the brief humanization of Black people and Black creatives, it seems very dubious that we are now regressing back, not just five years, but 25 years, to bring back a character that was able to flourish because there were no accurate portrayals of Black Britishness on screen.” Mo Gilligan, one of the UK’s most successful comedians, picked up on this theme during a recent appearance on The Louis Theroux Podcast . The BAFTA-winner said the depiction of Ali G became very “normalized” in the UK and there was a sense among some in the Black community that “you were being laughed at, not laughed with.” Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G Athena Kugblenu, a BBC New Comedy Awards finalist, argued that the latest incarnation of Ali G has had to embrace more “acute” racial stereotypes, including dreadlocks and a rastacap, because his costume is no longer unusual amid the assimilation of Black culture over the past 30 years. “He’s an analogue character in a digital age,” she wrote in an Instagram post liked by fellow comics, including Living With Yourself star Aisling Bea. A source close to Baron Cohen denied that Ali G has dreadlocks in the film. Michael Eboda, the former New Nation editor and CEO of Powerful Media, added: “There are far more serious things in the world than Ali G. It’s just something that has had its time. It was there for a minute, and now it’s just a bit sad that he’s having to rehash it.” Colton Dunn, whose credits include Widow’s Bay and Key and Peele , found Ali G “hilarious” when he first encountered the character during high school. “We all felt we knew a guy just like Ali G. I don’t remember it being controversial at all,” he said. “I don’t know what the experience is like for the Black performers in Britain. I’m not going to speak on their experience and I respect their experience, but I also respect my experience.” Dunn declined to comment on specific scenes or storylines, but said Baron Cohen has been working on the movie for years and Ali G’s contemporary relevance has been honed alongside many collaborators. The film is expected to touch on issues including cancel culture and immigration, while also having “ridiculous, silly-ass fun,” according to Dunn. Peter Fincham, the British television producer who first gave Ali G a platform in topical comedy series The 11 O’Clock Show , told Deadline that he was fascinated to see how the character has moved with the times. He admitted, however, that if a young white comedian was creating Ali G today, “questions would be asked” by studios and broadcasters. “The culture has changed. Sacha’s a very smart guy and will be sensitive to that, and I’m sure it will be reflected in the film,” said Fincham, who co-hosts Insiders: The TV Podcast. ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Racial Stereotypes MIP London Comes To An End After Two Years; Organizers Plot New Event Judge Sets Settlement Hearing Date; Read Consent Decree; More Reax Tom Cruise Pic’s World Premiere Was A Royal Affair; Recap + Photos Read More About: 5 Comments

articles.title: ‘Where’s Wanda’ Season 2: Watch Trailer For Apple TV’s Darkly Comic German Series From UFA Fiction
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Tubi’s Brett Takeshita Joins Canada’s Enlighten Content ‘Where’s Wanda’ Season 2: Watch Trailer For Apple TV’s Darkly Comic German Series From UFA Fiction ‘The Masked Singer UK’ Producer Argonon Names New CEO As Founder James Burstall Becomes Exec Chair View All September 23, 2026 5:00am EXCLUSIVE: Here’s the trailer for Season 2 of Apple TV ‘s German dark comedy Where’s Wanda? . The sophomore season starring Heike Makatsch ( Love Actually ), Axel Stein ( The Vault ), Lea Drinda ( The Gryphon ), Leo Simon and and Nikeata Thompson ( Späti ) debuts globally on October 21, and this is the exclusive trailer ahead of the launch. Episodes will drop weekly through December 9, as previous announced. The UFA Fiction German-language comedy-drama picks up after the events of the first season, which saw Carlotta and Dedo Klatt (Makatsch and Stein) searching for their lost daughter Wanda (Drinda). As the season opens, Wanda is seemingly caught red-handed standing over a dead body and is hauled off to jail. Related Stories News Studiocanal Announces Wrap Of Final Film In Ambitious German-Language 'Woodwalkers' Trilogy Casting Janeane Garofalo Reteaming With Ben Stiller On Apple TV Comedy 'Protective Custody' Carlotta and Dedo have to do everything in their power to prove her innocence and avoid losing her again, with their investigation taking them to the heart of their sleepy suburban town, Sundersheim. Watch on Deadline In the trailer we see a shaken Wanda in jail. The scene morphs back to the murder scene, as Wanda finds a body dead backstage at a funfair. As the curtains pull back, she is revealed standing over the corpse with a bloodied trophy in her hands as the audience gasps. From there, her parents hatch their crazy plan to set her free and reveal the killer. “We end Season 1 with Wanda returning to her family, which is a great relief for them,” said Where’s Wanda? exec producer Nataly Kudiabor in an exclusive interview. “We had already announced that Wanda will be in prison in Season 2, and that has a huge impact on the family,” she said. “They have just got their daughter back, and now they have to deal with what this will do to them. “It also affects the family’s position in Sundersheim. What are the neighbours thinking? What do the people in Sundersheim think? Is it right that their daughter is in prison? There are a lot of questions being asked.” Sam Riley, Alexandra Maria Lara, Harriet Herbig-Matten, Gisa Flake, David Schütter, Palina Rojinski Suzanne von Borsody, Kostja Ullmann, Devid Striesow, Frederic Balonier, Sascha Geršak, Torben Liebrecht , Aaron Maldonado-Morales and Anton Dreger are also cast in Season 2. Oliver Lansley created, written and executive produced season 2, alongside UFA Fiction co-Managing Director and executive producer Nataly Kudiabor and Oliver Ossege. The series was co-created and based on a story by Zoltan Spirandelli, though he was not involved in Season 2, we understand. Tobi Baumann and Christian Ditter. We sat down for an exclusive interview with Kudiabor this week, who said Drinda’s titular character would be far more present in Season 2. “We always felt that Wanda was the heart of the show, so we wanted her to return and to give her more screen time,” she said. “Lea Drinda is a fantastic actress, and this time she isn’t hidden away for several episodes – she is there from the beginning.” Kudiabor revealed there would be “surprises” for the audience. “We love our surprises. For example, new neighbours move in: the Kimballs, played by Sam Riley and Alexandra Maria Lara, who are internationally known. They are a couple in real life, and we cast them as a couple in the show, which I think was a great idea. They bring a new layer to the series.” She added there would be “more twists and turns,” saying: “Oliver is very good at leading the audience in one direction and then revealing something unexpected from another side. There are also lots of interesting new characters in Sundersheim whom audiences haven’t seen before.” Kudiabor said that if Season 1 was about “the search, the neighbours and everything people were hiding in Sundersheim,” Season 2 was about “what the crisis is doing to the family and how they rebuild afterwards.” Working with Apple TV Where’s Wanda? was the first German-language original to come from Apple TV, with the likes of Constellation and Berlin ER following later. Prior to the show’s launch, there was a feeling within the German television production community that the global streamer’s future in Germany hinged on its success, with several privately voicing the opinion to Deadline at the time. The Season 2 renewal was validation the dark comedy had cut through, and Kudiabor praised the collaborative nature of Apple’s execs, with UFA Fiction in regular communication with Jay Hunt’s London office throughout the process. She noted that having an English writer in Lansley was “really helpful” to the flow of the development. “We were very excited to make Apple TV+’s first German original,” she said. “It’s great to work for a streamer with so many excellent shows. I’m a big fan of Apple’s productions, and quality is very important to them. “They always challenge us to do our best in terms of storytelling and production value, and it’s a great experience to be challenged and to keep getting better. Sometimes you think you know best, but ultimately it’s teamwork.” She compared the first mover experience to that of Wiedemann & Berg when it made Dark as Netflix’s debut German original. “If you’re the first show in a market for a streamer, you have to learn how to work together,” said Kudiabor. “I imagine it was a similar experience for Netflix when it made Dark . In the second season, the process was extremely nice and easy because we already knew each other and understood how things worked. There was a lot of trust in us, which was really nice.” German market in flux UFA Fiction, known for the likes of the Deutschland and Ku’damm franchises, has been on a roll over recent years, with Wanda? and Prime Video YA smash Maxton Hall – The World Between Us driving its streamer slate, with the likes of Disney+ miniseries Sam – A Saxon and Netflix movie Rising High also cutting through. However, the Fremantle-owned company could be seen as an outlier in the German production market. Last week at Seriesly Berlin, much of the chatter was about a general lack of funding outside of the global streamers, and whether international co-production could fill the gaps. With the likes of Sky Deutschland exiting the originals market in the past half-decade, things remain tough. “Streamers and commissioners are flooded with good ideas,” said Kudiabor. “What do you need to stand out? We’re really trying to work on that. I’m not saying we achieve it all the time, but we’re giving it our best, and perhaps our work shows that this approach is working for us.” She attributed UFA’s hot streak on “a mixture of luck, timing, having the right talent and finding the right story,” and hinted at several upcoming projects. “At the moment, we’re working for Amazon, with two shows launching there,” she said. “We’re working with Disney and have some developments with them, and we’ve just worked with Apple. We’re also working with HBO, so there are a lot of opportunities. “But it’s also about excellence. We’re challenging ourselves to ask, before we go out: Is this really the best story we have? Is this the best talent? Is there something else we can do before we go shopping?” Kudiabor admitted the success of Maxton Hall , which became Prime Video’s most-watched international original series. “The first season was amazing, but I don’t think we expected such sensational success,” she said. “I loved the second season, but wait for the third – it’s even more mind-blowing. The fans are so engaged and give their feedback through social media, which is crazy. Our main actors are now big stars, and it’s really a ride. “It’s a once-in-a-lifetime moment. When you go to the premieres, it feels like a real event: The fans are going crazy and they really want to be part of it.” As for the future, Kudiabor said UFA Fiction will look to work with more production companies across the Fremantle group, as TV consolidated giants look to use their assets to create co-productions. “I’ve been speaking with colleagues in the Netherlands, for example, because our markets are quite similar and they have great shows coming out there,” said Kudiabor. “We recently had a meeting here to look for a project we could make together, so we want to develop something jointly. We’re also speaking with some UK companies.” Meanwhile, UFA Fiction is hoping Apple sees a long-term future for Where’s Wanda? . “Creatively, we have lots of ideas, but of course I can’t speak for Apple,” said Kudiabor. “Right now, we’re just happy to be returning for a second season. We hope to excite the viewers, and then we’ll take it from there.” ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Racial Stereotypes MIP London Comes To An End After Two Years; Organizers Plot New Event Judge Sets Settlement Hearing Date; Read Consent Decree; More Reax Tom Cruise Pic’s World Premiere Was A Royal Affair; Recap + Photos Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Jesse Eisenberg Talks Writing ‘The Debut’ Specifically For His “Favorite Actor And Actress” Julianne Moore & Paul Giamatti — San Sebastián
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Brad Pitt Praises Streamers For Creating Opportunities & Says He Believes The Indie Film Space Is Currently Just As Strong As In The ’90s — San Sebastián Creative Risks, AI & Brazil’s Production Boom: Topics From Day One Of The 2026 San Sebastián Creative Investors’ Conference Brixton Community Cinema Creator Abiba Coulibaly On Why She Decided To End The Popular London Film Club View All September 23, 2026 5:22am Jesse Eissenberg Unanue/Europa Press via Getty Images Jesse Eisenberg heaped praise on Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti, the co-stars of his latest feature, The Debut , this morning during a press conference at the San Sebastián Film Festival, where the musical comedy is set to make its European debut this week. “We filmed the first two days of the movie in one day, and they were big days with musical numbers, because the two actors were just so great,” Eisenberg said of Moore and Giamatti. Eisenberg told journalists in San Sebastián that he specifically wrote The Debut with Moore in mind. The writer-director said he has closely admired her work since the pair collaborated on Eisenberg’s debut feature as a director, When You Finish Saving the World. Related Stories News Brad Pitt Praises Streamers For Creating Opportunities & Says He Believes The Indie Film Space Is Currently Just As Strong As In The '90s -- San Sebastián News Creative Risks, AI & Brazil's Production Boom: Topics From Day One Of The 2026 San Sebastián Creative Investors' Conference “The first movie I did with Julianne was like five years ago, called When You Finish Saving the World . I’m not sure if it ever played in France. It barely played in America. It barely played at my parents’ house,” Eisenberg joked. Watch on Deadline “She’s amazing in it, and she plays this character who is emotionally guarded,” Eisenberg added. “It’s very different than The Debut . But there’s one little scene in that movie where she started doing this unusual voice, and that voice was in my head for two years. And when I started writing this movie, I just thought it had to be that voice and had to be that actress.” Eisenberg continued to say he realized he had written himself into a “big problem” when he finished the screenplay. “If the actress you wrote it for doesn’t want to do it, you’re screwed,” Eisenberg said. Thankfully for him, Moore signed on. Eisenberg later described Moore and Giamatti as his “favorite actor and actress.” The Debut is Eisenberg’s third feature as a director. Oscar-winning Moore plays a shy woman who is unexpectedly cast in a local production of an original musical. Under the spell of the strong-willed and enigmatic director (Giamatti), she loses herself in the role and the high-stakes world of this community theatre production. Moore and Giamatti are joined in the cast by Eisenberg, Halle Bailey, Havana Rose Liu, Bernadette Peters, Colton Ryan, Lilli Cooper, Maulik Pancholy, and Bonnie Milligan. Eisenberg’s last film, A Real Pain , notched two Oscar noms for Original Screenplay and Kieran Culkin in Best Supporting Actor, winning for the latter. A24 has set a Dec. 11 limited opening for the film in the United States. articles.title: French Film & TV Sectors Sound Alarm Over Cuts To State Broadcaster Budget; Say They Are At Odds With Macron’s Lumière Summit Pledges
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie ‘Ray Gunn’ Trailer: Netflix Adds Limited Dec 4 Theatrical Release For Brad Bird’s Sam Rockwell & Scarlett Johansson-Voiced Animated Sci-Fi Studiocanal Announces Wrap Of Final Film In Ambitious German-Language ‘Woodwalkers’ Trilogy Oscars: Italy Submits Paolo Strippoli’s ‘The Spiral’ For Best International Feature Film View All September 23, 2026 6:05am French flag Getty Images France ’s film and TV sectors are sounding the alarm over a proposed €47M ($53M) cut in public funds for state broadcaster France Télévisions in 2027. In a joint open letter published on Wednesday, independent producers’ guilds, Le SPI, l’USPA and AnimFrance accused the government of engaging in “a brutal social plan” which could cause irreparable damage to France’s audiovisual sector. The guilds said the cuts also fly in the face of pledges made by President Emmanuel Macron at his Lumière Summit, unfolding in the South of France on September 7 and devoted to the future of the moving image, and its accompanying declaration highlighting “the vital role of the state” and the “audiovisual industry as an engine for economic growth”. “In the wake of the Lumière Summit, the first international summit dedicated to the future of cinema and the moving image, government decisions are set to plunge the entire sector into deep chaos: after affirming the strategic nature of the image industries and the importance of our cultural sovereignty, the government has chosen to undermine those who create, produce, and distribute these works,” read their letter. The open letter follows in the wake of an interview with France Télévisions President Delphine Ernotte Cunci in the ‘Le Monde’ newspaper on September 18, in which she said the state broadcaster was facing a €90M ($100M) cut in its budget for 2027. This was due, she said, to a proposed €47M ($53M) cut in state funds combined with a fall in advertising revenue and the impact of rising inflation. She noted that the state cut in funds for 2027 followed in the wake of a €80M cut for 2026. She said the funding situation risked destroying France’s cultural model. “I’m pulling the alarm to safeguard our cultural model,” she said. “What’s emerging is that the foreign platforms will soon account for the biggest investments in French creativity. “That means series and films will be greenlighted, financed, cast, written and conceived by the Americans and the Chinese. Do we want to weaken this industry of creation, of freedom, which employs more people than the car industry?” The proposed France Télévisions budget cuts are part of a larger €54B ($61B) package of spending cuts being put forward by the French government to rein in public debt, which it says is poised to hit a record 121.7% of domestic product (GDP) in 2027. “SPI, USPA, and AnimFrance are fully aware of the state of public finances and the need for everyone to contribute to the collective effort. However, this effort must be managed responsibly and be economically efficient,” the guilds said in their letter. “At a time when overall unemployment is rising alarmingly and recession is looming, the state, as shareholder of France Télévisions, has made a harsh and counterproductive budgetary decision: the planned cutbacks in public broadcasting risk producing the exact opposite of the intended result. This move deals a severe blow to the 700 production companies working with the public broadcaster and will inevitably cause unprecedented social damage within the audiovisual sector.” The guilds reiterated Ernotte Cunci’s comments on the audiovisual industry employing more people than the car industry in France. “The audiovisual sector accounts for 260,000 direct and indirect jobs across France and generates over €12 billion in added value, surpassing both the automotive and textile industries,” read the letter. It added that it was wrong to view state funding for France Télévisions uniquely through the lens of budgetary expenditure, saying it was also an investment. The guilds said that every euro in state funding went onto generate €2.40 within the French economy, with €0.50 of that “flowing back into state coffers”. “Reducing public funding will not result in equivalent savings for the state; instead, it will trigger a destructive downward spiral of fewer jobs, lower social security contributions, reduced tax revenue, and higher unemployment benefit payouts, ultimately yielding no real savings while leaving the country culturally impoverished,” read the letter. Related Stories Acquisitions Disney+ Seals EMEA Deal For Season 1 Of TF1 Hit 'Cat's Eyes' As Season 2 Gets October Launch Date News Oscars: France Selects 'Minotaur' For Best International Feature Film Race It added that the cuts came at an already difficult time for the audiovisual sector, due to fewer commissions from private broadcasters, the budgets of which have also been hit by falling ad revenue and inflation. Watch on Deadline “In practical terms, a further drop in orders and contracts resulting from public austerity measures will immediately impact production companies’ ability to sustain employment. Writers, directors, actors, and staff—whether permanent or on short-term contracts—represent a vast pool of skilled, high-value-added jobs that the proposed budget places in immediate jeopardy. This would mean the direct loss of nearly 10,000 jobs, on top of the 10,000 already lost since 2023,” read guild’s letter. In other woes, not detailed in the letter, figures released by film and TV export body Unifrance earlier this month revealed a collapse in international sales for French shows in 2025 to a ten-year low. Le Spi, Le SPI, l’USPA’s open letter, follows a similar statement published on September 18 in the immediate aftermath of Ernotte Cunci’s interview, from nine film and TV bodies including director’s guild L’ARP, distributors’ organisations DIRE and SDI as well as the screenwriters association SCA. They were equally scathing in their criticisms of the government’s proposed cuts, saying it would be a “devasting blow” for both the TV and cinema industries. The letter also took aim at Macron’s Lumière Summit, which gathered a host of U.S. studio and streamer heads and Hollywood stars in the South of France, while much of Europe’s independent international film sector was focused rather on the Venice Film Festival in Italy. Macron hosted the event jointly with Korean President Lee Jae Myung, with their respective countries pledging to invest 1 billion euros ($1.16 billion) in the global screen industries from 2027 to 2031. “While the President of the Republic was rolling out the red carpet for American platforms at the “Sommet Lumière” on September 7 and speaking of a “civilizational issue”, we learned just days later that public broadcasting faces unprecedented peril, and with it, our cultural sovereignty,” read their statement. “It is unacceptable for paid American platforms to become, in the near future, one of the primary financiers of French cinema. Audiovisual and cinematic creation is a strategic asset for France, yet this financial decision demonstrates that our government fails to grasp the magnitude of what is at stake. Worse still, it is undermining a common good belonging to the French people and the production of our collective narratives.” ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Racial Stereotypes MIP London Comes To An End After Two Years; Organizers Plot New Event Judge Sets Settlement Hearing Date; Read Consent Decree; More Reax Tom Cruise Pic’s World Premiere Was A Royal Affair; Recap + Photos Read More About: Comments

articles.title: David Ellison: Me, Move? I Love L.A.
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 3:17pm Paramount CEO David Ellison Valerie Macon / AFP via Getty Images Fresh off brushing past California attorney general Rob Bonta with a settlement in which arguably only minor concessions were made, David Ellison is ready to re-commit to the idea of keeping his Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery empire in Los Angeles. “Now that we reached and announced a settlement, we’re eager to get to work building a stronger Hollywood,” Ellison said in a statement. “Let me be clear: the newly merged company will be headquartered in Los Angeles. We aren’t going anywhere. Our history is here and this is where our future is being built.” This brings the mogul back in line with his tune circa February of this year, when he was making promises to California politicians about how he would boost local production and bring back glory to Hollywood’s hometown. Then California attorney general Rob Bonta and his posse of 12 states filed a lawsuit in July that seemingly had Paramount on the ropes. And then the whispers started. You know, Ellison and his family have deep ties to Tennessee , he could pull up stakes and move Paramount there. Texas officials want the state to be the corporate headquarters capital of the United States, plus they have lower taxes — how does Austin sound for a Paramount base? Even at the time, these hints were chalked up to a game of high-stakes chicken over the summer between Ellison and California. Bonta himself, in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter in August when he struck a more defiant tone about the lawsuit, characterized it as a “ Hail Mary ” move and said “it seems like they’re grasping at straws.” But with each passing day, and with the threat of a $7 million-per-day ticking fee that Paramount would have to pay starting in October, the threat of a relocation kept feeling a bit more serious. Also, other states appeared to start taking the rumors seriously, too, which probably helped kick up the dust even more. Now there’s a legal settlement in place between the 12 states and Team Ellison dictating some terms for what “Stay in L.A.” means. Per the consent decree, the Warner Bros. and Paramount lots in L.A. County can’t be sold during the commitment period, which is five years. (Right now the Warner Bros. lot sits on about 140 acres, including the Ranch, while Paramount’s Melrose Ave footprint is about 65 acres.) It’s worth noting that up until Ellison’s buy, Paramount had been headquartered in New York (Paramount has an office in Times Square), and only last year had moved to L.A. And outside of the studio lot infrastructure itself, there are no commitments in the consent decree for, say, having a new office complex in another market outside of L.A. WarnerMount (ParaBros?) is a sprawling empire, after all. For example, does a combined company that owns both CBS News and CNN need office space in L.A., New York and Atlanta? Paramount owns 14 properties totaling 2.1 million square feet of space while Warner Bros. owns 14 properties totaling around 9.5 million square feet globally, per a June report commissioned by L.A. County. There are plenty of real estate scenarios to walk through that have yet to be sorted. But the question was never really about the fine-print of where the corporate HQ was. It was about intent. Through this summer of leaks, the implied message from Team Paramount was that Ellison would be ready to potentially do damage to the Los Angeles entertainment economy if things didn’t go his way in the court battle. There were plenty of locales that would be happy to greet Paramount and set up a water tower and some soundstages. Just look at the production flight that had been plaguing L.A. for years on individual feature films and television series. Local officials feared that a Paramount move would be the straw that broke the camel’s back, despite California doubling its tax incentive annually to $750 million and pledges to cut red tape and make it easier to shoot in state. Now that things did go the way that Paramount hoped as far as the settlement, it may prove tougher to just hit rewind to when Ellison was writing letters in March to California lawmakers saying, “my expectation that the commitments I have made will preserve and expand good-paying film and television jobs in the area.” But as of this settlement Monday, we’ve now hit full circle in that regard. Next up, if the deal closes as expected in a couple weeks, is the plan to start finding those $6 billion in cost synergies between the companies while fulfilling the rules-of-the-road in the consent decree. If L.A. County’s own commissioned report in June is any indicator, there will be a lot of redundancies up ahead as the studios start integrating. “The merger places about 2,495 jobs in Greater Los Angeles County and about 6,000 globally at potential risk,” it estimates, “mainly in corporate, tech, real estate, and other shared functions due to duplicative roles across the two companies.” THR

articles.title: Clavicular Charged With Rape, Drugging Person for Sex in Massachusetts
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 7:44pm Clavicular Francois Durand/Getty Images “Looksmaxxing” influencer and streamer Clavicular , whose real name is Braden Peters, has been charged with one count each of rape, drugging a person for sex and providing alcohol to a minor in Massachusetts, according to new court documents obtained by The Bulwark . The charges, filed by prosecutors in a Cape Cod courthouse on Sept. 8, are reportedly connected to an incident that happened on May 23, 2025. The 20-year-old’s arraignment is set for Oct. 14. The Bulwark wasn’t able to access additional records on the case, but the timeline appears to match a civil lawsuit filed in April against the streamer in Florida. Related Stories General News D4vd Murder Case: Victim's Family Demands Justice as Indigent Claim Draws Scrutiny Music Tupac Murder Trial Begins as Prosecution Calls Rapper's Death "An Act of Revenge" CBS 4 Miami previously reported that 18-year-old Alorah Ziva, whose real name is Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, accused Peters of battery, fraud and sexual misconduct, according to the complaint. She alleged the influencer injected her with Aqualyx, a fat-dissolving substance not approved by the FDA, during a livestream in 2025 without her consent. The lawsuit also accused Peters of nonconsensual sexual encounters at his parents’ home in Cape Cod while Mendoza, who said she was a minor at the time, was intoxicated. In July, Peters filed a motion to dismiss several counts of the civil lawsuit. In response to The Bulwark report, Peters’ rep wrote in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter , “Clavicular has not been physically served. As usual, the Bulwark is exaggerating the status of a case to boost traffic. We appreciate the Hollywood Reporter for fact checking.” Later on Monday, Peters took to X to share a letter that he claimed Mendoza sent him after the alleged incident, appearing to thank him for “helping me as much as you have been.” The streamer also shared a video of Mendoza, where she appeared to call the Aqualyx injection “fun,” and said Peters was “super nice” and “sent me an Uber home right after.” It’s unclear when the video was filmed. “Trying to get my attention in anyway possible, a lawsuit? Seriously… really petty of you,” Peters wrote in the X post. He added in a separate post Monday, “Lmao was literally trying to work at Bacara as a bottle girl… how about dont finance cars you cant afford. Happens to all successful young men, people try to come for your money. Greed is evil.” In another video that’s been reposted on X , allegedly from the 2025 livestream, Mendoza also appeared to say she was 18 years old at the time. If convicted in the Massachusetts case, Peters faced a maximum sentence of twenty years in prison on the rape charge. This isn’t the first time the streamer has faced criminal charges. In April, Peters was charged with unlawfully discharging a firearm after he was seen in a video shooting an alligator in the Florida Everglades. At the time, Peters’s lawyer Jeffrey Neiman said the group was “following the instructions of a licensed airboat guide.” He added that the streamer “relied on that guidance” and that “no animals or people were harmed.” Earlier this year, Peters was also hospitalized after appearing to overdose during a livestream in April. After being released the following day, he wrote on X , “Just got home, that was brutal. All of the substances are just a cope trying to feel neurotypical while being in public, but obviously that isn’t a real solution. The worst part of tonight was my face descending from the life support mask.” THR

articles.title: Elliot Graham, Oscar-Nominated Film Editor on ‘Milk,’ Dies at 50
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes , Carly Thomas September 21, 2026 8:12pm Elliot Graham Joe Maher/Getty Images Elliot Graham, the film editor who received an Oscar nomination for Milk and cut films including Steve Jobs , Captain Marvel and No Time to Die , has died. He was 50. Graham died by suicide Saturday in Los Angeles, according to the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner. The biopic Milk (2008), directed by Gus Van Sant and written by Dustin Lance Black, starred Sean Penn as Harvey Milk, the first openly gay man to be elected to public office in California. The film was nominated for eight Oscars including best picture and won for best actor and original screenplay. Related Stories Movies Anjanette Comer, Actress in 'The Loved One' and 'The Appaloosa,' Dies at 86 TV James Sloyan, Actor in 'The Sting,' 'Xanadu' and 'Oh Madeline,' Dies at 85 On Facebook, Oscar-nominated Milk producer Dan Jinks wrote that his movie “wouldn’t have come together in the way it did without [Graham’s] amazing work.” Graham then reunited with Van Sant on the romantic drama Restless (2011), starring Mia Wasikowska. Graham also won a BAFTA award (shared with Tom Cross) for editing the James Bond film No Time to Die (2021), directed by Cary Joji Fukunaga in what would be the film editor’s final credit. And he produced and served as film editor on the 2018 FX series Trust , about the 1973 kidnapping of teenager John Paul Getty III. Born on June 8, 1976, in Claremont, California, Graham got his first credit for editing the thriller The Last Minute (2001), directed by Stephen Norrington. Next, he handled additional editing chores on X2: X-Men United (2003), then worked again for director Bryan Singer as film editor on Superman Returns (2006). In addition to Danny Boyle’s Steve Jobs (2015), starring Michael Fassbender, and Anna Boden and Ryan Fleck’s Captain Marvel (2019), starring Brie Larson, Graham served as film editor on Bill Paxton’s The Greatest Game Ever Played (2005), Robert Luketic’s 21 (2008), Stephen Daldry’s Trash (2014) and Aaron Sorkin’s Molly’s Game (2017). He also did additional editing on films including The Amazing Spider-Man 2 (2014), I Am Michael (2015) and Beasts of No Nation (2015). THR

articles.title: New Book on MGM Classic ‘The Women’ Reveals Extent of Joan Crawford and Norma Shearer’s Feud (Exclusive Excerpt)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Illeana Douglas Plus Icon Illeana Douglas View All September 22, 2026 5:00am 'The Women' LMPC via Getty Images Illeana Douglas ’ new book Jungle Red! The Making of MGM’s The Women , published on Sept. 15 by Lyons Press, delves into the titular 1939 classic which boasted an all-star cast of actresses — among them Joan Crawford , Norma Shearer , Rosalind Russell, Paulette Goddard and Joan Fontaine — and provided a template for modern female-driven projects like Sex and the City and The Real Housewives. In the following exclusive excerpt from the book, Douglas makes the case that the greatest Hollywood “feud” of all time did not involve Crawford and Bette Davis or sisters Olivia de Havilland and Fontaine, but rather Crawford and Shearer. Related Stories Movies Ann Blyth, the Evil Daughter in 'Mildred Pierce,' Dies at 98 Movies Casey LaLonde, Grandson of Joan Crawford, Dies at 54 Joan Crawford and Norma Shearer in a promotional portrait for The Women (Screen Archives/Getty Images) If MGM had been primed to sell The Women as “the Catfight of the Century,” they didn’t need to invent antics or drum up stories of feuds. Everyone knew that Norma Shearer and Joan Crawford really didn’t like each other. In March of 1939, before Crawford had even set foot on set, Howard Strickling had approved a Look cover promoting The Women that depicts Shearer and Crawford glaring at each other, with a headline that reads, “They Don’t Like Each Other… Inside Stories of 31 Hollywood Feuds.” On April 25, 1939, MGM’s production, listed as #1091: The Women , began shooting. A movie based on the stories of what happened behind the scenes might make a good sequel. When director George Cukor was asked whether he was fearful that longtime rivals Shearer and Crawford would try to upstage each other, he laughed, saying, “They’re too smart for those antics.” He was being optimistic. The best publicity angle, since there were no men in the cast and no juicy romances, was to exploit their longstanding “feud”. How much each actress fueled their “feud” is a matter of opinion, but since every squabble — the billing, the dresses, the trailers, and their eventual showdown because of Crawford’s knitting needles — was dutifully reported on, you have to imagine someone was spilling the tea. Anita Loos, screenwriter of The Women , said, “Norma and Joan could never have been personal friends— they came from different worlds. Norma thought Joan crude and pushy and Joan considered Norma overbearing and uppity — but they both knew the ‘feud’ was good copy, and so they helped it along.” When Shearer hosted a wrap party luncheon, chiefly to show the press how well they were getting along, Crawford skipped it. She seemed delighted to let the bad feelings percolate, telling gossip columnist Hedda Hopper, who was cast in the film, “So many people say Norma and I don’t like each other. Who are we to disagree with the majority opinion?” Shearer then refused to attend the premiere and penned an open letter to the trades downplaying her role and casting shade on the one actress she had least wanted to work opposite, Crawford. “I’m asked about the so-called power and influence I had at the studio. I don’t think anyone acted more like an employee than myself. Just because of my marriage to Mr. Thalberg, and as a consequence of my friendship with the other executives, there have been any number of times when I did not put up as stiff a fight as another actress would have. I didn’t want to appear to be taking advantage. For instance, I didn’t want to make The Women . I did make it, for the reason I just explained, and partly because I was taught by Mr. Thalberg to think of what is good for the picture as a whole rather than what is good for me as an individual.” Crawford had her reply teed up. She praised Russell for walking away with the film. Of her other co-star, Shearer, Crawford said, “Norma Shearer, as usual, played the perpetual virgin, the wronged wife.” She did give her one compliment. “I love playing bitches, and Norma helped me tremendously with this part.” When Cukor came on board to direct The Women in February of 1939, only one queen, Shearer, was attached, set to play the leading role of Mary Haines. She had seen the play on Broadway in 1936, and it was inevitable she would star in it. But when Shearer spoke to Hopper, who reported on every casting decision — including her own — Shearer distanced herself, saying, “You know, I hesitated a long time before playing this part. Then I decided that fighting to hold a husband is every woman’s problem.” Shearer referencing holding on to a husband when talking to Hopper was significant. After her husband Irving Thalberg’s death, she was in the process of reinventing herself. Doing a comedy about a bunch of bitter, funny wives complaining about men, when her husband was gone, was not in sync with her carefully crafted image of herself as the grieving widow of a man who was already gaining mythological status. She could also read the newspaper. The Women was no longer a Norma Shearer vehicle but, courtesy of Hunt Stromberg, “George Cukor’s The Women .” Every day, names were being mentioned: “Suzanne Kaaren gets a role in an MGM picture on the strength of a single test. George Cukor picks her for The Women ” ( Hollywood Diary ). Shearer waited on the sidelines, nervously wondering who her co-stars would be. The stable of talent at MGM was vast, and with 135 roles up for grabs, Cukor was auditioning all viable options except, it seems, Crawford. In March, the press was reporting that Crawford had been turned down for the role of Crystal, while it was announced that eighteen-year-old Lana Turner had been cast. Hairstylist Sydney Guilaroff wrote, “When Norma was cast as the jilted wife, Joan Crawford set her sights on Crystal. She relished the notion of going head-to-head with Queen Norma, now without the protection of her late prince.” Crawford was resentful that even in Thalberg’s absence, Shearer was still getting all the plum roles. Stromberg promised Crawford that Idiot’s Delight would be her next film, but then Mayer decided to give the part to Shearer. “‘No tits Shearer,’” Crawford complained, “could neither dance nor sing and had no experience playing fast women.” Crawford had been looking forward to working in Idiot’s Delight with Clark Gable, and perhaps rekindling their on-again/off-again romance. Instead, it was Shearer he held in his arms. “She had no chemistry with Gable, and that’s what the picture was all about.” Crawford was envious that Shearer had just received, with the studio’s backing, her fifth Oscar nomination — for Marie Antoinette . MGM consistently threw their voting bloc to Shearer, while Crawford had never even been nominated, despite standout performances in Paid (1930), Grand Hotel (1932) and Sadie McKee (1934). She was not about to let The Women slip through her fingers — even testing for the role, something unheard of for an actress of her stature. Eventually she won over Cukor, convinced Stromberg the picture needed her, and beat out teenager Turner by telling Mayer, “The woman who steals Norma Shearer’s husband can’t be a nobody.” Crawford may have, as she said, “resented the hell out of Shearer,” but playing Crystal only made sense if she appeared opposite Shearer. Without her, Crawford would be left playing a supporting part, a “heavy,” as Mayer called it, and for nothing. Shearer was pragmatic. She may have feared working with Crawford, but she knew The Women would garner more attention if Crawford was in the film, but only if Shearer could control the narrative, like later claiming it was her idea to cast Crawford. In the opening credits of The Women , Cukor had the cheeky idea of depicting each actress on-screen as some kind of animal. Crawford is a leopard. Shearer is a young deer. An innocent little deer does not do Shearer justice. A more accurate representation would be a lioness, for Shearer persevered in the jungles of Hollywood, marrying the boss, becoming “the first lady of MGM,” picking up six Academy Award nominations, even winning Best Actress for The Divorcee (1930). But Shearer was threatened by Crawford from the day she was hired as Shearer’s body double in Lady of the Night (1925). As for Crawford, Shearer’s marriage to Thalberg solidified the rivalry. Less than a year after Shearer’s wedding, Our Dancing Daughters (1928) was released, making Crawford a breakout star in the public’s eyes, but not at MGM, and not with Shearer, who called Crawford “an ambitious upstart” and referred to her as “common.” Crawford’s chief resentment was that Shearer got the best female roles at MGM only because of Thalberg. After Crawford was relegated to a succession of dancing films, like Hollywood Revue of 1929 , and Untamed (1929) — an unhinged, “jungle-themed” musical — Crawford confronted Thalberg. “Why do you save all your good roles for your darling Norma?” she asked. “Don’t you think I deserve some consideration?” Thalberg punished her for impertinence and put her in Montana Moon (1930), a low-grade musical Western. In 1938, after being labeled “box office poison,” Crawford needed a hit badly and lobbied hard for Idiot’s Delight . The part of a former showgirl masquerading as a Russian countess, opposite Gable, seemed tailor-made for Crawford. Stromberg told her that Shearer wanted to play the part. Of all the slights, this was perhaps the biggest grudge Crawford carried into The Women . “I cried buckets over Idiot’s Delight ,” she said. After The Ice Follies of 1939 . Crawford was at a low point professionally. She needed a hit. Her philosophy of going after the role of Crystal was simple. “It’s going to be a good picture. I need a good picture. If I can’t get one of my own, let me sneak into someone else’s.” She convinced Stromberg to talk Cukor into testing her. Though intrigued by the idea of an on-screen rivalry, Cukor was not a fan of Crawford’s acting, which he felt was mannered. After testing her for Crystal, though, Cukor consented and told her the part was hers. What changed? Crawford was not shy about her open and persistent dislike of Shearer. Once, years before, when she was asked what she thought of Shearer, she smiled and said, “Well . . . I’m an actress . . . and she’s married to the boss.” Cukor may have decided, possibly with the influence of Stromberg, that the competition with Shearer would make their scenes sizzle. Crawford was excited, telling the press after she won the part, “Even people who didn’t like me admitted I had intestinal fortitude, taking my career in both hands and gambling.” When Hopper asked Shearer what she thought about Crawford being cast, Shearer graciously said she was looking forward to it, and that The Women was “going to be a fascinating experience for her.” Butter wouldn’t melt in her mouth, as they say, but before shooting began, she made sure her contract stipulated that only she would have top billing, with her name above the title. It was a battle she would later lose, first to Crawford, then Russell. Shearer arrived early her first day to check the set and saw that there were three star trailers parked side by side. In accordance with being number one on the call sheet, Shearer had been assigned dressing room number one, nearest to the camera. It had been redecorated for her in coral, pink and cream. It was also air-conditioned. Inside there was an upholstered floral lounging sofa where she could rest and practice her lines, with fresh orchids on her dressing table. Shearer noticed that one of the trailers — dressing room three — was sticking out one foot further than the other two. When she inquired as to who was in dressing room three, she learned it was Crawford. Russell had been assigned number two. Shearer demanded Crawford’s trailer be moved back one foot in accordance with the others. Crawford’s arrival had been accompanied by glowing stories from reporter Harry Mines in his Raves and Raps column. “ The Women has been before the cameras at MGM,” he wrote, “but not until yesterday did Joan Crawford start work. Joan has a new and fancy portable dressing room, decorated in mauve. It was difficult to get a peek at the quarters, as baskets of flowers took up most of the space. Miss Crawford’s friends have deluged her with posies and telegrams on her first day in production.” Crawford stepped out of her limousine that first day of filming accompanied by her maid. Her uniformed chauffeur carried her record player and records, and one of her beloved dachshunds, Pupchen, acquired during her marriage to Franchot Tone. Crawford had a special clause in her contract allowing her to bring Pupchen to the studio when filming. An insurance policy protected the company in case the dog ever bit anyone or barked during a take. Cukor did not have to worry about a barking dog. It was Crawford’s vocalizing to opera that could be heard loud and clear during Shearer’s rehearsals. Though the set was not far from her dressing room, Crawford insisted she be driven to it via limousine. Shearer later followed suit, always making sure her limousine arrived after Crawford’s. Hairstylist Sydney Guilaroff recalled that Cukor’s greatest challenge was not directing on-screen but trying to keep the peace off-screen. He wrote that one solution was to always keep the actresses busy, separating them whenever possible. If one was rehearsing, then he could send another one to a fitting, or have them get a hair and makeup test. That way they were unlikely to be in the same space at the same time. “This worked well,” he said, “until Shearer and Crawford had their one face-to-face scene together.” To rattle Shearer, Crawford called in sick, and Cukor had to rearrange the schedule. Harry Mines, in the Los Angeles Daily News , ran a story that Crawford was under doctor’s orders not to work, and was ill from a combination of “intestinal flu and arsenic poisoning.” It’s hard to believe Crawford came across arsenic on the set, unless someone slipped it in her tea! (Hmm…) After two days, however, it was reported that she had made a remarkable recovery — or at least was well enough to continue. “On her sickest morning,” Mines wrote, “Joan had to do her most important scenes with Norma Shearer. Despite the tough break, Miss Crawford sallied through, doing such a good job that few realized how bad she was feeling.” The scene in question takes place after the fashion show in Crystal’s dressing room. Mary Haines (Shearer), Sylvia (Russell), Peggy (Fontaine) and Edith (Florence Nash) discover Crystal is trying on dresses and has asked the saleswoman (Frederika Brown) to charge the clothes to Mr. Stephen Haines’s account. Mary crosses the hall to confront Crystal and enters Crystal’s dressing room. Cukor began to rehearse. What happened next has been written about and reported from so many angles it’s like the film Rashomon (1950). Every bystander recalls what happened with slight variations, but all agree on one thing: Crawford, after years of perceived slights at the hands of Thalberg and Shearer, saw an opportunity to get even, and she did. Without Thalberg, there would be no repercussions. Crawford perhaps even sensed there was a bit of schadenfreude from Cukor, the cast, and the crew, knowing this moment would come, and wondering which cat would draw the most blood. THR

articles.title: ‘R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2’ Trailer Teases Cassandra Peterson’s New Role and the Curse’s Return (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Abbey White Plus Icon Abbey White Contributing Writer View All September 22, 2026 6:00am R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2. Tubi Something wicked this way comes in the new look at R.L. Stine ’s Pumpkinhead 2 . Ahead of its Tubi premiere on Oct. 9, The Hollywood Reporter can exclusively debut the sequel’s first full trailer. Helmed by Jem Garrard, the filmmaker behind the franchise’s 2025 installment, Pumpkinhead 2 once again follows kids Sam (Bean Reid) and Becka (Adeline Lo) as a new curse awakens in Redhaven. While still struggling with the fact that his family doesn’t remember him — a consequence of stopping the harvest curse — Sam and his friend Becka begin to notice strange things around town. To get to the bottom of this series of unsettling occurrences, the duo reteams and, in the process, discovers there’s a new crop of cursed pumpkin entities, conjured up by an ancient ritual book, just like the one that nearly took Sam’s brother Finn (Seth Isaac Johnson). Related Stories Beyond the Book Inside 'The Love Hypothesis': How Director Claire Scanlon, Star Lili Reinhart and More Adapted BookTok's Biggest Obsession Movies Nicole Wallace Joins Josh Heuston in Amazon MGM's 'Throttled' Adaptation This time, the friends are facing a series of child-like pumpkin-headed monsters, seemingly victims of the previous curse, called up from the ground of Redhaven. “I would like to go back to when one murderous scarecrow was the problem,” an exasperated Becka is seen telling Sam in the upcoming film’s two-minute trailer. Their investigative trail leads them to the town sheriff (Bob Frazer), who was responsible for keeping the first child-stealing curse alive. He reveals to the duo that he stole the cursed book from a woman named Cassandra, seemingly a local who lives on the edge of the town’s forest. Portrayed by Cassandra Peterson, best known by horror fans as Elvira, this wise witch has powers that may be key to helping the kids stop their Pumpkinhead uprising. “I can end the curse,” she tells Becka and Sam. “The magic is strongest on the harvest moon.” Working with others from the town, the duo once gears up to take on the powerful and deadly Pumpkinhead children to ensure no more kids are forgotten. “We don’t get to forget,” Sams says. Inspired by Stine’s The Haunting Hour , the Tubi film is written and directed by Garrard, and also stars Matty Finochio, Sebastian Billingsley-Rodriguez, and Kendra Anderson. Pumpkinhead 2 is executive produced by James Mattagne, Joan Waricha, Harvey Kahn, Yvonne Bernard, Dan Bernard, Jem Garrard, Allen Lewis, and Rama Diallo, and produced by Front Street Pictures. R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2 is part of the “Terror on Tubi” lineup. Timed to its release, Garrard and Stine will be joined by Tubi Chief Content Officer Adam Lewinson and drag queen and actor Jimbo ( RuPaul’s Drag Race UK and All Stars ). THR

articles.title: VFX House 22Dogs Launches New Facility at Pinewood Toronto Studios (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 22, 2026 6:00am Pinewood Toronto Studios Courtesy of Pinewood Studios 22Dogs VFX, the visual effects studio behind work on Apple TV’s The Morning Show and the Netflix heist thriller Here Comes the Flood, has opened a new base in Toronto as its North American headquarters. The Milan-based international studio, with VFX credits also on Netflix’s Outer Banks, Lionsgate’s Day Drinker and Prime Video’s The Greatest, already has a Los Angeles commercial office in its global footprint. The new North American headquarters at Pinewood Toronto Studios will be the third production studio for 22Dogs VFX after facilities in Milan and Tenerife. 22Dogs VFX joins other global studios in Toronto doing visual effects magic for major studios and streamers chasing digital tax breaks, currency savings and lower labor costs in Ontario. The Pinewood Toronto Studios facility will be led day-to-day by Samara Melanson, head of studio, who will work closely with Andrea Marotti, 22Dogs partner and executive producer, based in the Los Angeles commercial office. “Since founding 22Dogs, our vision has always been to build a studio where creativity, innovation, and collaboration come together to support filmmakers at the highest level. Toronto is a natural next step in our global journey, and we’re excited to welcome new artists, partners, and clients as we continue to grow our international footprint,” Carlo Tosi, founder of 22Dogs VFX, said in a statement. The Los Angeles office will continue working closely with major studios and streamers and international producers, many of which bring film and TV series work to Canada for production and post-production. Pinewood Toronto Studios already serves as a Canadian production hub for Netflix and Amazon MGM Studios. “Toronto attracts leading creative companies from around the world, and we’re pleased to see 22Dogs VFX establish its Canadian home at Pinewood Toronto Studios. Their investment reflects the reputation of Ontario’s screen industry and further enhances the collaborative ecosystem our studios are known for,” Sarah Farrell, general manager of Pinewood Toronto Studios, said in her own statement. THR

articles.title: ‘Heart of the Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt and His Canine Co-Star Earn Your Tears in David Ayer’s Tense, Tender Survival Thriller
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All September 22, 2026 6:00am Brad Pitt in 'Heart of the Beast.' Paramount Pictures If you’ve seen the trailer for Brad Pitt ’s new movie, you probably think that it’s a harrowing tale of survival in a dangerous wilderness. Don’t be fooled. Heart of the Beast is actually a love story, and one of the most moving to come along in a long time. That it’s a love story between a man and his dog doesn’t at all detract from its emotional impact. Indeed, Pitt displays an engagement with his co-star that may be his most resonant yet. Although to be fair, that isn’t really saying much since two of his most notable cinematic romances are Meet Joe Black , in which he played Death, and Mr. and Mrs. Smith , in which his character spent most of the film trying to kill his wife. Related Stories Movies Netflix's 'Cliff Booth' Trailer Has Brad Pitt Taking a Playful Poke at Leonardo DiCaprio Movies 'World War Z' Sequel Back on With Brad Pitt Returning, Edward Berger Directing Heart of the Beast The Bottom Line Packs a surprising emotional punch. Release date : Friday, September 25 Cast : Brad Pitt, J.K. Simmons, Anna Lambe Director : David Ayer Screenwriter : Cameron Alexander Rated PG-13, 1 hour 41 minutes The film, reuniting Pitt with his Fury director David Ayer , features the actor as James Belmont, retired after a 30-year stint with Special Forces that saw him facing combat in Iraq and Afghanistan. Now he lives a quiet, solitary life. Well, not entirely solitary, since he shares it with Odon, his beloved German Shepherd combat dog, with whom he experienced many dangerous missions. Odon bears the physical and emotional scars of his years in combat, sporting titanium teeth and an artificial leg, and suffering from PTSD-induced nightmares. The story begins with James flying his Cessna plane into the Alaskan wilderness (convincingly and gorgeously played by New Zealand) for a few days of camping and fly-fishing. The happy solitude is briefly interrupted by a stranger who happens by and spends the evening chatting away with the mostly silent James before taking off in a canoe early the next morning. He’s played by J.K. Simmons , making a strong impression in a brief amount of screen time and demonstrating yet again that he’s one of the most invaluable character actors in the business. An impending storm forces James and Odon to leave early, leading to the first of several surprises in the screenplay by Cameron Alexander. The plane winds up crashing into the water, not because of the weather conditions but rather James suffering a heart attack that renders him unconscious. Both he and Odon, who was thrown from the plane before it went down, miraculously survive, and when we later see James scarfing down aspirin by the handful we realize that he was well aware of his heart condition. Thus begins the survival part of the story, with James and Odon having to traverse 58 miles of wilderness to reach the nearest road. Along the way they encounter a variety of life-threatening situations, including a massive grizzly bear, a treacherous tree-bridge crossing over a gorge with rapids below, and an attack by a pack of CGI wolves. Both man and beast suffer an array of debilitating injuries along the way. But what makes the film special are not the survival elements, as grippingly and (mostly) convincingly filmed as they are, but rather the relationship between James and the loyal Odon, both of them constantly risking their lives for the other. Pitt makes his character’s feelings for his dog touchingly palpable, most notably in a quiet scene in which he removes Odon’s artificial leg and gently massages his stump. And while Odon doesn’t have much in the way of dialogue (he does have a very expressive bark), the way he looks at his co-star is so adoring and non-judgmental you may find yourself reevaluating the relationships in your life. Odon is mostly played by Uber (we can forgive the name), who would be the instant frontrunner for the PATSY Award if that worthy honor still existed. Credit must be given to his trainers, handlers, and Pitt himself, who reveals so much chemistry with his canine fellow actor that his previous female co-stars might be jealous. For certain scenes Uber is doubled by three other dogs, all of them his sons, which must have made for an especially harmonious set. Heart of the Beast sometimes feel repetitive in its pile-up of perilous moments, but Ayer’s expert direction and the fast-paced 101-minute running time prevent monotony from sinking in. And if the film’s ending leaves you dry-eyed, you’re clearly not an animal lover and someone I have no desire to meet.
