articles.title: ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M From Sale Of Pulse Films
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Princess Diana’s Brother Over “Bulls***” Claim In Bombshell Memoir Tom Cruise Earns Applause With Six-Minute Monologue On Why Art Beats AI In Filmmaking: “There Is Nothing Like Human” BBC Removes Blackface Sketches From ‘That Mitchell And Webb Look’ View All September 22, 2026 3:38am 'Gangs of London' Sky/Vice Studios EXCLUSIVE : Thomas Benski and Marisa Clifford , founders of Gangs of London producer Pulse Films , are suing Vice Media , claiming they are owed more than $20 million. Vice took a majority stake in Pulse Films in 2016 before acquiring Benski and Clifford’s remaining 22% shareholding in December 2021 for $10M in cash and $43.24M in loan notes. Soon after, Vice ran into serious financial difficulty, with Benski and Clifford alleging that the company failed to pay loan notes totalling $20.4M, breaking the terms of their sale agreement. The producers — who exited Pulse in 2022 — claimed that they were persuaded not to exercise their contractual rights by former Vice executives, who they accuse of making fraudulent misrepresentations about the company’s financial health and failed sale to Antenna Group. Related Stories News Could 'Gangs Of London' Be About To Move To Miami Or Johannesburg? Vice Studios Boss Amy Powell Says She Is Mulling Franchise Expansion News Pulse Films Exits TV & Film Game After 20 Years As Vice Makes Layoffs In London Vice Group entered Chapter 11 bankruptcy in May 2023. Three months later, a consortium of former lenders — led by Fortress Investment Group, Soros Fund Management and Monroe Capital — acquired the company after a bankruptcy auction. Watch on Deadline Vice Media’s position is that Benski and Clifford’s allegations are baseless and lacking in evidence. The company intends to vigorously defend its position. Details of the dispute emerged for the first time in a UK High Court ruling earlier this month, during which Benski and Clifford failed in their efforts to get Vice to disclose thousands of documents relating to their grievance. Judge Peter MacDonald Eggers dismissed Benski and Clifford’s pre-action disclosure application, but did not reach any conclusions on the merits of their case. Deadline understands that the producers will continue to pursue action against Vice and are currently assessing their legal options. The duo, who now run Magna Studios, declined to comment. A Vice Media spokesperson said: “Vice Media is pleased to note that the London High Court has dismissed an application for pre-action disclosure by Thomas Benski and Marissa Clifford in relation to allegations concerning events prior to Vice Media’s Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023. “Those allegations are groundless. In dismissing the application, the court relied on the vague, inconsistent and unsatisfactory way in which the allegations have been advanced. We will continue robustly to defend any claim, to the extent it is pursued.” Benski and Clifford’s pre-action disclosure application named four defendants, including Pulse Films and Nancy Dubuc, the former CEO of Vice Media. Pulse Films’ intellectual property, including Sky series Gangs of London , now sits under Vice Studios. Summarizing Benski and Clifford’s claims, Judge Peter MacDonald Eggers wrote that they have “advanced serious allegations of fraudulent misrepresentation and unlawful means conspiracy against the respondents [at Vice]. In particular, the applicants’ case is that they were induced not to exercise valuable contractual enforcement rights by alleged repeated and false assurances by the respondents as to the valuation, solvency and an imminent sale of the Vice Group.” He continued: “Whether the allegations of fraud and conspiracy can be established will be an issue in any substantive proceedings which may be issued by the applicants in respect of their claim and will turn on the respondents’ knowledge about the Vice Group’s financial position and the failure of the sale process at the time they were allegedly giving assurances to the applicants.” The judgment added: “The respondents deny the allegations of fraud and conspiracy, which they state are couched in ‘unacceptably nebulous terms, based on unwarranted inferences, and without any sufficient evidential foundation.'” Vice’s position is that its executives were not obliged to keep Benski and Clifford abreast of the company’s financial position and that they dealt with duo with “honesty and integrity” at “all times.” ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Diana’s Brother Over Memoir Which Midnight Madness TIFF Pic Could Become The Next Box Office Obsession? ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $108M WW Read More About: Comments

articles.title: MIPCOM Bets On Creators, Brands & AI As International TV Business Readies For Cannes Get-Together
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart MIPCOM Bets On Creators, Brands & AI As International TV Business Readies For Cannes Get-Together Dhar Mann, Sean Atkins Set For MIPCOM’s First-Ever Pre-Opening Keynote Princess Diana Documentary Featuring Unheard Tapes Set For International Launch At MIPCOM View All September 22, 2026 5:06am MIPCOM in Cannes RX France MIPCOM boss Lucy Smith wants the world to know that October in Cannes is now about more than buying and selling TV programs. “Our biggest challenge is changing the perception,” she says, with this year’s event just weeks away. “You don’t come to MIPCOM just for your distribution deals anymore. You’re coming because you’ve got to find valuable IP, or you want to find out more about what’s going on in branded entertainment, or you’re looking at what’s happening in vertical drama or AI.” Distribution remains the spine of MIPCOM, but as the international TV industry has changed, so has its biggest annual get-together. “We are a marketplace, but it’s not just a buy-and-sell market anymore,” Smith says. Related Stories News Muse Entertainment Unveils 'Doula: A True Crime' Trailer As Boat Rocker Studios Boards CBC Doc News Dhar Mann, Sean Atkins Set For MIPCOM's First-Ever Pre-Opening Keynote That wider remit for MIPCOM means embracing the creator economy, brand partnerships and tech. Watch on Deadline Put simply, it had to change to stay relevant. Consolidation and industry shifts are impacting its core distribution business. For example, Warner Bros. and Paramount may have separate stands and spaces in Cannes this year, but that is unlikely to be the case when MIPCOM 2027 kicks off. The same is true of Banijay and All3Media. The medium-sized and small distributors, meanwhile, are feeling the pinch. Acquisition execs still attend MIPCOM in healthy numbers, but often with reduced buying power as their budgets come under pressure. Smith’s first MIPCOM was in 2006 and she now runs the market, which is organized by RX France. She says: “We evolve with the changes in the industry. We came out of probably ‘24 thinking, ‘This whole industry is just changing so much, and there’s less funding from traditional sources, so what does all that mean?’” The change under her leadership is visible. First, there was a heavy push into co-production and FAST channels, and then into brands and the creator economy. “We really wanted to make sure we were bringing more of the creative conversations around funding and IP. That was the first step, and then we brought the MIP Innovation Lab, so we could address streaming in a broader way. “And then, the big push had to be the creator economy.” YouTube had its biggest-ever presence at MIPCOM in 2025. It will be even more visible this time. Smith says partnering with the Google-owned company was “the right way to really make a mark and to say MIPCOM would be focusing and pivoting to the creator economy.” This year, Dhar Mann Studios kicks off MIPCOM, with a pre-market headline session on Sunday, before proceedings start in earnest on Monday. Powerhouse digital producer Mann and DMS CEO Sean Atkins will jointly keynote. “We all know that you know creator-led businesses are reshaping the global media landscape and we knew that that was that was something we needed to address,” Smith says. “We were getting calls from studios saying, ‘Hey, we want to meet all these creator-led businesses.’ And these businesses are really at that intersection of creators, brands and branded entertainment.” Having partnered with BrandStorytelling last year, RX France launches MIP BrandWorks this time to cover off its branded entertainment activity, with denstsu the headline partner. “We want to become the home of branded entertainment because we see ourselves as the gateway to the global entertainment content and media business. If you want to be working in content, and obviously brands need to be embedded in content to be culturally relevant, this is where you come and do that.” Artificial intelligence is also on the menu. A new conference and market will run under the MIP AI Entertainment Forum banner, with Versos AI and Protégé the partners. “Companies involved in AI and entertainment have a specific need to be part of the content industry conversations,” Smith says about the reason for launching the new forum. “You’ve got the studios and producers, the production side of things, you’ve got the workflow piece, and you’ve got the licensing part; those will be the pillars.” While the focus is shifting, MIPCOM’s USP remains bringing a critical mass of people together. In a world of Zoom meetings and with pressure on travel budgets, the numbers are not as big as in yesteryear, but no other international TV event gathers 10,000 people. “We know that bringing people together at one time in one place gives them the opportunity to work together on what these new businesses are,” Smith says. “We wanted to bridge the gap in the conversations between traditional media companies, who remain hugely important, and these newer creator-led studios.” Glitz and glamor are in the DNA of Cannes. The film festival and Cannes Lions lean into that with starry photocalls and A-lister parties. MIPCOM has the same setting and its own share of photo moments, but as it expands its focus, the event is still really all about dealmaking. “If you really want to do business and understand these new ways of doing business, this is where it’s going to be happening, and this is where things will start moving forward,” Smith says. ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Diana’s Brother Over Memoir Which Midnight Madness TIFF Pic Could Become The Next Box Office Obsession? ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $108M WW Read More About: Comments

articles.title: ‘Heart Of The Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt And A Soulful German Shepherd Struggle To Survive The Wilderness In An Emotional Journey That Will Have You Sobbing
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Forgotten Island’ Review: H.E.R. And Dave Franco Give Life To Gorgeously Animated And Frenetic ‘Toon ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Oscar-Predictive Toronto Film Festival People’s Choice Award ‘Magazine’ Review: Lily McInerny And Bright Young Cast Give Flavor To Pre-Digital Vanishing Era Of NY’s Literary World – Toronto Film Festival View All September 22, 2026 6:00am Brad Pitt and Odin in Heart Of The Beast Paramount Pictures Going to see Heart Of The Beast is a dangerous proposition if you don’t want to be seen crying uncontrollably in public. This man and his dog story is an emotional roller coaster that lays it all out there, and I lapped it up just like I did in My Dog Skip, Turner & Hooch, K9, Marley & Me, Old Yeller, and countless others. But there was something visceral about this one, a largely dialogue-less film where the story is told in the eyes of Brad Pitt playing opposite a loyal and tough German Shepherd named Odin. This is a story of a 30 year military veteran and the dog who stood with him in Iraq and Afghanistan only to finally find peace in the Alaskan wilderness until the unthinkable happens and it becomes an even greater tale of survival against all odds. It stays with you, won’t let go, and gives you new appreciation for those who serve, whether on two feet or four paws. Related Stories News Post-Merger Paramount May Overdeliver On Settlement Terms With 36-Film 2027 Slate Amid Speculation About Duplication & WB Leadership News Paramount Settlement Protects Pluto TV, Sets BET & Comedy Central As Potential Divesture Targets While Omitting Premium Channels & TV Studios David Ayer who directed Pitt in the terrific 2014 tank movie, Fury, here gets perhaps the most moving performance the actor has ever given. He plays Sgt. Major James Belmont whose military service is behind him and has come to the peace and solitary serenity of the wilderness, flying his plane, his dog, aka Canine Commander Odin by his side. It is as if this pair simply survived hell on earth to one day find heaven together. Watch on Deadline We see them all alone among nature’s wonders, until one day a stranger just appears out of nowhere. James hoists his gun but isn’t necessary. The man, Watkins (nicely played by J.K. Simmons ) is a friendly guy just looking for a little company before rowing off on his boat down the river. It turns out to be a welcome interlude, brief but meaningful. He will be the only human being James and Odin encounter together on their journey. Both suffer from bouts with PTSD, and James comforts Odin after disturbing nightmares shake him. It gets real when James suffers a heart attack and the plane careens out of control, finally landing in the water and sinking. Odin is thrown out before that, and somehow James survives and struggles to go back frantically trying to find his dog. He does even as Odin shows little signs of life, but after a night willing him to live, Odin, who wears a prosthetic leg and has few teeth due to another cruel war injury, clearly has a knack to survive and the next morning he is miraculously back to his old self. Using his expertise with a map and a compass, James and Odin set out to somehow find a semblance of civilization but the trip becomes one harrowing hazard after another including a frightening confrontation with a grizzly bear, a fight with a pack of wolves, James being swept away down the river, and more things most people could never live to tell. This is a pair that survived the worst of war (brief flashbacks briefly show that aspect of their past shared life) and now are unexpectedly in survival mode once again. His heart failing, James inherently knows his own days may be numbered, but he is going to make sure they find the road for reasons he doesn’t share with Odin, or Odie as he calls him. Heart Of The Beast is one of those movies that, with great dignity and little fanfare, shows the true connection between man and animal just as countless movies have done since Rin Tin Tin starred in silent pictures. That Ayer, with a heart wrenching screenplay by first time writer Cameron Alexander, has found a way to make it all feel fresh is why this director should be applauded. The success of the film is also due in no small part to Pitt who makes us believe this animal is his soul brother, much more than just a pet, or even a partner in combat. Odin is all he has left and he will honor him no matter what it takes. No spoiler but Pitt will simply break your heart in doing just that. As for Odin, has any dog ever won an Oscar? Lassie, Benji, anyone? Well, it is high time. Odin delivers one of the best performances by an actor this year, hands down. Actually the truth is he is played by four canines, the main star being Uber, with strong support from his own sons, Ryker, Zika , and Hondo. Give much credit to their trainer, Andrew Simpson. Other than Simmons and of course Pitt, the only other human on board is Anna Lambe as a woman driving her truck when in the distance she sees a dog sitting in the middle of the road. That is the opening image of the film, and then the story flashes back a week. I will leave it at that. New Zealand stands in for Alaska, quite convincingly, with stunning cinematography and camerawork from Mauro Fiore. As pretty as the natural landscape all is to watch it is still the gut wrenching emotional reach of this simple story of humanity at its finest, loyalty and friendship at its most meaningful, and above all the heart of a ‘beast’ and the man standing at his side. There will not be a dry eye in the house. If this one doesn’t move you, there is no hope. Producers are Pitt, Ayer, Olivia Hamilton and Marty Bowen. Damien Chazelle is among the Executive Producers. Title: Heart Of The Beast Distributor: Paramount Release Date: September 25, 2026 Director: David Ayer Screenplay: Cameron Alexander Cast: Brad Pitt, J. K. Simmons, Anna Lambe, Odin. articles.title: Elliot Graham Dies: Oscar-Nominated ‘Milk’ Editor Was 50
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38 Cate Blanchett Asks London Audience To Stop Filming Play, Says Stage Is Place “Where We Can Simply Be Together And Be Present” Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic” View All September 22, 2026 6:53am Elliot Graham (2022) Joe Maher/Getty Images Elliot Graham, the Oscar-nominated film editor for Milk whose credits also included Steve Jobs, No Time To Die, Superman Returns and Captain Marvel , died Saturday, September 19, in Los Angeles. He was 50. Graham died by suicide, according to the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner . Born in Claremont, California, on June 8, 1976, Graham launched his show business career in the early 2000s with the feature film The Last Minute (2001) and the TV series House (2004). He moved into big-budget feature projects with 2006’s Superman Returns . Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries News Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38 Two years later he was hired by edit Milk , the Harvey Milk bio-pic written by Dustin Lance Black and directed by Gus Van Sant. Starring Sean Penn, Milk was nominated for eight Oscars, including for Graham’s editing. (Black and Penn won their categories). Watch on Deadline “The movie Milk wouldn’t have come together in the way it did without the amazing work of our editor Elliot Graham,” Milk producer Dan Jinks wrote in a tribute on Facebook . “He was nominated for an Oscar for his role.” “I have so many thoughts and feelings about this sweet, kind and quirky man,” Jinks continued. “For now, I’ll just say rest in peace Elliot.” After Milk , Graham worked again with Van Sant on the 2011 film Restless starring Mia Wasikowska. He also edited an episode of the Kelsey Grammer series Boss that year. Additional credits include Steve Jobs (2015), Molly’s Game starring Jessica Chastain (2017), Captain Marvel (2019) and No Time To Die , the 2021 James Bond film starring Daniel Craig. Graham and editor Tom Cross shared a BAFTA award for their work on the film. In addition to his editing credit for the 2018 FX limited series Trust , the Danny Boyle-directed project about the kidnapping of John Paul Getty III, Graham also served as producer. Graham also provided additional editing on X2: X-Men United (2003) and The Amazing Spider-Man 2 (2014). articles.title: “It Fills Me With Pride”: How the Basque Country Is Nurturing Its Next Generation of Filmmakers
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 3:00am Nitya López Saitua on the set of 'Family Drill.' San Sebastián Film Festival It’s no longer a secret that Basque cinema is getting some overdue time in the spotlight. Thanks to an almighty production boom in the region, powered by a whopping 60 percent tax rebate (increasing to 70 percent for projects shot in the Basque language, Euskera), the Basque Country’s film and TV output has never looked so healthy. And the proof is in the pudding: The Hollywood Reporter took an in-depth look at the record 45 nominations for Basque projects at this year’s Goyas, also known as “the Spanish Oscars,” after a decade of concentrated investment. Related Stories Movies Red Sea Film Festival Cancels 2026 Edition, Vows to Return Next Year With "Renewed Vision" Movies San Sebastian Winner Yesim Ustaoglu Returns to Competition With 'What Remains' (Exclusive Clip) With San Sebastián’s profile rising exponentially every September, the people working behind the scenes to make sure Basque cinema is capitalizing on every single success are already pushing the next generation of original voices into the festival hot seat. At the 74th edition, a total of 31 titles with Basque production ties — including David Pérez Sañudo’s hotly anticipated competition title The Harvester — will screen across the festival’s many selections. Twelve are documentaries, marking a real moment for Basque docs at this installment. But with award statuettes firmly on the mantel, the Basque region now sets itself the task of sustaining this run of form long-term. The answer? Find and nurture the next generation’s emerging talent. For example, the debut feature from Nitya López Saitua in Zinemira, Family Drill , a project fuelled by word-of-mouth buzz across northern Spain . “He’s been doing great as a first AD and second AD for so many years,” begins Mar Izquierdo, coordinator of Zineuskadi, a non-profit operating at the epicentre of the Basque film and TV industry, “and everyone was like, ‘But he’s got it. He’s not going to be an AD.’ And we really do hope that with this film, everyone else will be able to see it.” Izquierdo’s company works strategically to promote the Basque audiovisual sector, partnering with every production output in the region, working alongside the Basque government’s culture department and public broadcaster ETB Basque to help facilitate co-productions, distribution and sales deals, as well as earning key projects coveted slots at the globe’s biggest film festivals and plotting awards campaigns. One young talent they’ve thrown their support behind is the 30-year-old López, who was in such a hurry to capture the creative process practically spilling out of his head that Family Drill — a co-production with Mubox Studio, who are distributing the film — was shot with just 10 people across three days in his childhood home on the Basque coast. He tells THR : “Iraia Elias and Miguel Garcés [play] my mom and dad and we recreate my parents’ relationship, [leading up to] the last argument that broke the relationship when I was four years old.” It is as deeply personal as it sounds. “This was a way to recreate memories that I didn’t have,” says López, firmly out of AD mode and in full-fledged director mode. “And I think it was very important to free-work on the scenes, without a script.” Family Drill San Sebastian Film Festival López’s determination to start the shoot before he lost that powerful sense of direction in chronicling his parents’ split speaks to the strength of the Basque Country’s storytelling. “We have really great directors here in the Basque Country, and internationally they are [getting] more recognized,” continues the first-time filmmaker. “I have the opportunity of working with many of them, and I love their work, and I’m very proud to be part of the next generation making movies. I think that we are in a great moment [compared to] making movies here 20 years ago.” It used to be the case that, “if [creatives] want to direct, they must go to other places, go to Madrid,” he explains. Here in the region López calls home, there have never been so many reasons to put roots down. One of his countrymen, Javier Giner, also arrives at the San Sebastián Film Festival with his first movie. This Solitude is premiering in the New Directors section. A debut feature it may technically be, but director-writer Giner has known global success with the International Emmy-winning I, Addict series, based on his own life and struggle with drug addiction. With This Solitude , Giner, who grew up in Bilbao, reacts to the unprecedented impact of that show. “ I, Addict was a huge hit in Spain and it dealt with a part of my life where I suffered [with] the illness of addiction,” he says. “After that explosive TV series where I presented myself to the world with no mask, I needed to go back to my childhood, to a very intimate place, a very silent place — much smaller than I, Addict .” Giner suddenly found himself shooting where he grew up, Bilbao, back to the places and locations that he says “have an emotional resonance” for him. The film, starring Oriol Pla, Marina Salas, Gemma Martínez, Kai Etxaniz and Itziar Lazkano, is a Balance Media Entertainment production, with The Embassy TV and Basajaun Filmak as co-producers, and Filmax handling distribution. “We meet two young people who live in Bilbao, Leo and Lorea, and we follow them through the grief process after they break a five-year-long relationship,” Giner explains. “And I use that journey as an excuse to talk about a lot of things like class, the housing [crisis]. […] Those moments in our lives everyone goes through, in a sense of reconstructing yourself because nothing works around you and you don’t quite grasp who you are [or] what you want.” He speaks with as much gusto as López, who also, in some way, depicts his Basque youth on screen — a common theme running through many of these films — and seeing fellow regional filmmakers make a name for themselves in recent years only speaks to the urgency of the stories coming out of the Basque Country, according to Giner. “To be honest, it fills me with pride,” he says. “I think movies and filmmakers, when they’re honest with their upbringing and their roots, there’s something very beautiful in it. As an audience member, I love when I discover London through Mike Leigh’s eyes, for example, or I discover parts of the world that I don’t know about through some filmmaker’s eyes.” Giner says that in the last 10 years, especially, Basque stories have been “very important to tell.” He continues: “I jokingly call This Solitude my very Basque movie, because there’s a reflection of identity in the movie… It tells [you] a lot about the place. And the Basque Country, it’s beautiful. It has beautiful landscapes. It has great possibilities. It is filled with really talented people, both in front of and behind the camera. So, I mean, it fills me with total pride if someone considers me the representation of the Basque Country at this year’s festival.” He is admittedly still pinching himself that he’s here: “It’s incredible. To be honest, a lot of my film education has to do with the San Sebastián Film Festival because when I was a teenager, I used to go from Bilbao to San Sebastián and watch movies.” López concurs that Basque cinema has its own culture, but also lauds the region’s directors for still being able to make “really universal movies.” And Izquierdo says the variation across the projects this year is particularly exciting for her. “The best thing is we are covering every possible subject,” she says. “We have a biopic for a musical group. We have culinary cinema. We have a French co-production, a coming-of-age [film] within a school. We have everything.” Basque filmmaker Javier Giner. San Sebastian Film Festival And naturally, the festival also serves as something of a springboard for those nail-biting awards runs. “It’s the most important film festival in Spain and one of the [category] A film festivals in the world,” says Giner about what a premiere in San Sebastián can do for one’s Goya hopes. “So it’s definitely a great trampoline. But it’s something that I don’t want to think about because I don’t want to get lost in that narrative and it take away from the pure pleasure of putting a film out there and sharing it with the public.” Of course, it’s not just Basque filmmakers travelling to shoot here. Taiwan’s Tsai Ming-liang is presenting Dust in San Sebastián, a short film and exhibition piece as part of his Walker series, which is a Basque co-production. Nanni Moretti made the most of those tempting tax incentives, too, with his last movie It Will Happen Tonight filming in the region before its recent Venice Film Festival premiere, and the Catherine Zeta-Jones starrer Kill Jackie — releasing Oct. 2 — shot extensively across Bilbao. “It’s not only that we continue to have emerging talent, but we are able to co-produce and have A-class films as minority co-producers,” beams Izquierdo. But she maintains that the most rewarding part of her job is platforming the next generation of Basque filmmakers, who are carving out a path by leading with instinct, leaning into personal storytelling, and celebrating each milestone. “The big names know how to [make] their way through the other festivals,” says Izquierdo. “But some of them need this in order to get the next one — it’s a window of opportunity for them, because otherwise maybe their documentary or small film would be just another small fish in the pond. Here,” she adds, “they get the chance on the big screen, where exhibitors and distributors will be able to notice them.” The 2026 San Sebastián International Film Festival runs Sep. 18-26. THR

articles.title: Red Sea Film Festival Cancels 2026 Edition, Vows to Return Next Year With “Renewed Vision”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 3:43am Johnny Depp at the 2025 Red Sea Film Festival closing ceremony Courtesy of Getty The sixth edition of the Red Sea International Film Festival has been postponed, the event’s Foundation has confirmed. A note released to press on Monday explains that this year’s installment, originally set for Dec. 3-12 in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, has been pushed back to the fourth quarter of 2027. It comes as the entire region deals with ongoing military tension amid the U.S.-Israeli-Iran war, with the threat of missile and drone strikes active and Saudi Arabia dealing with targeted attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis. Related Stories Movies "It Fills Me With Pride": How the Basque Country Is Nurturing Its Next Generation of Filmmakers Movies San Sebastian Winner Yesim Ustaoglu Returns to Competition With 'What Remains' (Exclusive Clip) The decision follows “a comprehensive review of a range of considerations relating to the timing of the next edition, including the logistical requirements involved in staging an international event of this scale,” said the statement. “It reflects the Foundation’s commitment to ensuring the Festival takes place at the right time and under the right conditions to deliver the experience for which the Red Sea International Film Festival has become known,” it continued. “As part of this continued commitment, the Foundation will introduce year-round programming at Culture Square in Historic Jeddah beginning in November 2026, establishing it as an ongoing destination for film screenings, cultural events and specialised film-industry programmes.” Organizers have vowed that the festival will return in 2027 with a “renewed vision and a programme that continues to celebrate cinema and filmmakers from Saudi Arabia, the region and around the world.” The Red Sea Film Festival has gone from strength to strength in recent years and funnelled much of its investment into attracting Hollywood A-listers to Jeddah, as well as its Red Sea Fund, Red Sea Labs and wider initiatives, which will continue to operate within the Foundation’s “year-round ecosystem.” Among the attendees last year were Michael Caine, Johnny Depp, Sean Baker, Juliette Binoche, Adrien Brody, Kirsten Dunst, Jessica Alba and Queen Latifah. THR

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico Sue White House for Revoking Press Credentials: “Patently Unconstitutional”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 5:03am The White House Briefing room, on September 19, 2026 in Washington, DC Photo by Graeme Sloan/Getty Images CNN , MS NOW and Politico are suing the Trump administration after the White House revoked their press credentials, effectively banning them from the White House complex and making it a challenge to cover the President and his staff. “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the three news outlets said in a statement early Monday morning. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” Related Stories Business Sylvester Stallone Learned About Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship While Watching TV: "It Won't Work" TV Alan Ritchson Reveals Which 'Reacher' Season Got Canceled After "Someone Got Re-Elected" In fact, CNN had been slated to be the primary TV press pool Monday, a day in which President Trump is slated to fly to New York for meetings with Mayor Zohran Mamdani and French President Emmanuel Macron on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. In a memo later Monday morning, the White House TV pool had been suspended given CNN’s banishment. CNN splits the primary pool duties with ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News. “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government,” a joint statement from TV pool companies said. “No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.” In their lawsuit (led by famed First Amendment litigator Ted Boutrous), the news outlets argue that Trump’s decision was in profound conflict with the law. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the suit states. “Presidents from the earliest days of the Republic have disagreed with and complained about the tenor and content of press coverage of their administrations. But as the Supreme Court has recognized, the First Amendment, including its guarantee of a free press, reflects “a profound national commitment to the principle that debate on public issues should be uninhibited, robust, and wide-open, and that it may well include vehement, caustic, and sometimes unpleasantly sharp attacks on government and public officials.” The suit states quoting a passage from the landmark case, New York Times Co . v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254, 270 (1964). “And the Constitution protects the liberty and property interests that news organizations and White House reporters have in their press credentials and the access those credentials afford them to cover the White House for the benefit of the public,” it continues. “No official can deprive Plaintiffs of those interests on a whim—with no notice, no process, and no warning—as the President did here.” Trump announced his ban in a post Friday , causing some confusion in the White House as crews from the outelts remained onsite. However, on Saturday morning journalists from all three outlets trying to enter the White House complex found that their credentials had been revoked . In an Oval Office appearance, Trump said that the decision followed cumulative coverage over the past few years, and wasn’t driven by any story in particular. “The President repeated his straightforward rationale for targeting these three news organizations, calling it ‘wrong’ to ‘allow people to write purposely negative stories,'” the lawsuit recounts. “The President complained about coverage he considers ‘one-sided’ and ‘never good,’ and at one point even referred to his own unprecedented act as the ‘ban on the free press.'” He also suggested that he knew his move would end up being litigated, suggesting that the outcome would depend on the judge that gets the cse. In his first term the White House banned CNN correspondent Jim Acosta from the White House, but a judge ordered his pass returned, citing First Amendment protections. The AP had also sued after it was barred from covering certain events after its style guide declined to refer to the body of water as the Gulf of America. THR

articles.title: Kit Harington Credits Harry Potter With Helping Him Through Sobriety Struggle
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 6:03am 'Game of Thrones' Courtesy of HBO Logo text Kit Harington is feeling warmer — a bit — towards the idea of reprising his iconic fan-favorite role of Jon Snow, and discussed his return to HBO in the upcoming Harry Potter TV series. The actor first told the Happy Sad Confused podcast Monday that he actually feels more comfortable with the idea of reprising the reluctant Game of Thrones warrior than he did in the past. The topic was raised when Harington was asked about HBO’s Snow spinoff sequel that was developed several years ago and then shelved. Related Stories TV 'A Tale of Two Cities' Review: Kit Harington Has Done Far, Far Better Things Than This Bland MGM+ Dickens Adaptation Lifestyle 'Game of Thrones: The Mad King' Play Sets London Transfer “We developed it two years or so,” Harington said. “I still think there’s a world in which something could work. I wouldn’t have gone into it in the first place if I didn’t. But I was very insistent at the start — as was HBO and George R.R. Martin — of like: ‘If we don’t find the right thing, let’s not do it. It’s much better if we don’t.’ After a little while of of thinking about it — it kind of was me — [I said], ‘This isn’t quite the right [story].'” Continued Harington: “[But] now I’ve gone and done all these other things and now I feel more comfortable with that character and that world again and where it sits in my life.” Yet it was another franchise headed to HBO that helped Harington with his sobriety struggles — Harry Potter . Harington told the podcast that the Potter audiobooks were helpful in the wake of ditching alcohol. “My brain is incredibly busy, especially at night, and I’ve always found going to bed very difficult like and my brain doesn’t turn off,” he said. “When I got sober that got especially bad. So I started listening to Harry Potter audio books, and now they’re the thing I listen to every night.” THR broke the news of the Snow development in 2022. In our cover story profile of Martin in January, we reported the initial idea was a tale of Snow living alone as a broken man with PTSD, having chased off his direwolf Ghost and thrown away his sword Longclaw. Harington wanted Jon to eventually die and to avoid being a hero. The story echoed, in some respects, Harington’s personal struggles — entering rehab following an intense shooting experience on Thrones. Last year, a new writer (Quoc Dang Tran from Drops of God ) came aboard to attempt to revive the sequel idea, possibility shifting the drama to the Mediterranean-like land of Essos. Harington was cast as Gilderoy Lockhart in the Full Cast Audio editions of the Potter books, which were released last year. Last month, Harington was cast to join HBO’s live-action Harry Potter series, where he’ll play the dangerously narcissistic Defense Against the Dark Arts professor in season two. “Lockhart is addicted to himself,” Harington quips. “It’s just a tiny step to my left [for me].” Harington is currently promoting his role in a four-part TV adaptation of Charles Dickens’ A Tale of Two Cities on MGM+, which was released Sept. 6. THR

That job will include all entertainment and sports bookings at the venues (excluding the New York Rangers and New York Knicks), as well as live bookings at the Sphere in Las Vegas. Vaccarello was most recently executive VP of live for MSG Entertainment, where she helped book major concerts and sporting events, as well as residencies like those from Billy Joel and Harry Styles. She joined the company in 1998 as an administrative assistant and has worked in multiple roles since. “Over her nearly thirty-year career with MSG, Josephine has not only been instrumental in growing our live event business but also established herself as one of the industry’s most impactful and respected leaders,” said Jim Dolan, executive chairman and CEO of MSG Entertainment and Sphere Entertainment. “Her deep understanding of our businesses and unparalleled industry relationships will continue to be an asset in this new role as we execute on our strategic vision for the Company, including identifying innovative growth opportunities and furthering our leadership position in live experiences.” “I am fortunate to have built my career at a company like MSG, which has always used the breadth of its portfolio to offer a wide range of events that push live entertainment forward and create unforgettable experiences for millions of fans each year,” added Vaccarello. “I am honored to take on this expanded role and look forward to continuing to work with teams across the MSG Family of Companies to deliver world-class live events that grow our businesses and keep our Company at the forefront of the industry.” THR

articles.title: Netflix’s ‘Cliff Booth’ Trailer Has Brad Pitt Taking a Playful Poke at Leonardo DiCaprio

The new footage (below) has Brad Pitt ‘s former stuntman now working as a Hollywood fixer, while also bartending and working as a projectionist. The trailer also includes a playful joke at the expense of his Once Upon co-star Leonardo DiCaprio . Booth explains he no longer doubles for DiCaprio’s character Rick Dalton because “Rick got too fat.” Related Stories TV 'Sweet Magnolias' Canceled at Netflix After Five Seasons Business Netflix Stock Falls After Wells Fargo Downgrade: "Engagement Trends Look Worrying to Us" The film marks a unique collaboration — written by Quentin Tarantino with David Fincher taking over as director. Here’s the detailed official description and trailer: “Murder, blackmail, theft, extortion — just another summer in Hollywood. It’s 1977, eight years since Cliff Booth (Pitt) encountered the Manson family in Quentin Tarantino’s parallel history of 1969, Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood. In The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , directed by David Fincher from a new script by Tarantino, the fairytale is over. Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s great and, sometimes, not so good.” Continued the description: “He’s curious when he gets a call from talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), on behalf of her client, TV megastar Charlie Peters (Scott Caan) — a man known for doing his own stunts. And he’s further entertained and intrigued when he meets other characters in Charlie’s world, from his knowing wife Toni (Carla Gugino) to pro football champion turned screen star Roderick ‘Hot Rod’ Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II). Then there are the Verdusco brothers (Matt Groove and JB Tadena), mysterious gangsters causing mayhem across the city. What was once a fairytale is now a crime story — a cocktail of violence, ambition, and desire that could only happen in L.A.” THR

articles.title: Movie Theater Advertising Giant Closes $275 Million Deal to Expand to Offices
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 7:12am National CineMedia's Noovie pre-show, hosted by Maria Menounos, features trivia, ads and promo interviews. National CineMedia National CineMedia , the in-theater advertising company that works with AMC Theatres, Cinemark and Regal for pre-show commercials content, has closed a major deal to venture outside of the cinema. The firm, led by Thomas Lesinski, has sealed an agreement to acquire Captivate Holdings, which powers tens of thousands of small screens in office buildings, lobbies and elevators that show short ads and content as people walk by (or when waiting for your floor in an elevator). The deal is valued at $275 million. National CineMedia already has a foothold in this business through all of its screens showing ads in movie theater lobbies (it had 17,000 screens in over 1,300 theaters, as of its annual report). Now it wants to bring that formula to office buildings and residential properties, too. And with Captivate’s platform, the company says it’ll have 48,000 digital screens to do so. Its primary vehicle to sell ads is its Noovie pre-show which is hosted by former Today correspondent Maria Menounos and features movie trivia, junket-style interviews with celebrities and Hollywood flashback moments mixed in with commercials. Since emerging from bankruptcy in 2023 — just as the COVID years were particularly brutal to theaters, they also wreaked havoc on in-theater advertising — National CineMedia has been positioning itself for a rebuild. The company spent $8.2 million last November to buy Spotlight Cinema Network, an ad network which caters to boutique, luxury and drive-in theaters like Cinépolis Luxury Cinema, Landmark Theatres and more. The restructured firm, once co-owned and launched by the major theater chains as a joint venture, also disclosed in its annual report that it now has no ownership interest from AMC and Cinemark as of the beginning of this year. Now it’s looking to become a national player in the advertising game, but is taking on debt to do so in the form of a $275 million senior secured first lien term loan facility. National CineMedia bought Captivate from growth equity firm Generation Partners, which had owned the advertising platform since 2013, when it purchased the company from newspaper giant Gannett. “The acquisition of Captivate is a key step in advancing NCM’s strategy to build a broader premium video and digital out-of-home advertising platform,” stated National CineMedia chief Lesinski on Monday, adding: “With the transaction now closed, our focus turns to bringing these capabilities together and executing on the opportunities we see across the combined business.” THR

articles.title: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Daisy Edgar-Jones and George MacKay Are Standouts in a Jane Austen Redo That’s Fine if Not Strictly Necessary
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 8:00am Esmé Creed-Miles (left) and Daisy Edgar-Jones in 'Sense and Sensibility.' Courtesy of Focus Features Pity any director who undertakes to remake a beloved literary property previously seen on screen in what is widely regarded as an unimprovable adaptation. That’s the daunting task faced by Georgia Oakley, who landed on the map with her assured 2022 debut feature, the politically personal queer character study Blue Jean . But the director’s take on Sense and Sensibility seldom steps out from the long shadow of Ang Lee’s enchanting 1995 retelling of the Jane Austen classic, scripted by Emma Thompson with endless amounts of verve, wit, emotional perspicacity and exquisite romantic yearning. Related Stories Movies Inde Navarrette: I Didn't "Want to Make Any Friends" During 'Obsession' Shoot to Focus on Film Movies Why 'Sense and Sensibility' Star George MacKay Still Hasn't Watched Ang Lee's Oscar-Winning Classic No disrespect to Oakley’s cast, all of whom are more than capable actors, but in almost every familiar beat of the story I found myself thinking back fondly to the actors who filled those roles for Lee — chief among them Thompson, Kate Winslet, Hugh Grant, Alan Rickman, Gemma Jones and the priceless Elizabeth Spriggs. I get it that this is intended as a fresh spin on Austen’s 1811 Regency romance, aimed at a new generation of movie lovers who have no great attachment to earlier versions. But for those of us who adore the 1995 film, unfavorable comparisons seem inevitable. Sense and Sensibility The Bottom Line Glum and glummer. Release date : Friday, Oct. 16 Cast : Daisy Edgar Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe, Bodhi Rae Breathnach, Frank Dillane, Herbert Nordrum, George MacKay, Fiona Shaw, Stacy Martin, Tom Brooke, Turlough Convery, Chloe Pirrie, Eliot Sumner, Bethany Slater, Ceara Coveney Director : Georgia Oakley Screenwriter : Diana Reid, based on the novel by Jane Austen Rated PG, 2 hours 11 minutes One subtle shift in first-time screenwriter Diana Reid’s adaptation is the firmer centering of the quarrelsome but inextricably bonded older Dashwood sisters, Elinor ( Daisy Edgar-Jones ) and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles). Of course this was always the case in Austen’s novel, right down to the way the title reflects the two sisters’ contrasting characters, with Elinor’s rationality and restraint representing “sense” and Marianne’s unguarded passion and unbridled emotionality signaling “sensibility.” Theirs is the paramount love story here, which works well in some ways but less so in others, somehow diminishing the stakes of their respective longing for Edward Ferrars ( George MacKay ) and Willoughby ( Frank Dillane ). Part of the brilliance of Thompson’s screenplay for the 1995 adaptation is that it foregrounded the sisters while also making the world they inhabited and its characters equally vivid. Here, there’s too little relief from the sisters’ downbeat moods to make us care about them. Oakley and Reid lean so heavily into Elinor and Marianne’s crushing disappointments and the forces holding them back in a period of vast gender inequity, that their sorrows shove the characters’ more captivating qualities to the side. Sense and Sensibility is a book with its fair share of melancholy — starting when Elinor, Marianne, their younger sister Margaret (Bodhi Rae Breathnach) and their mother ( Caitríona Balfe ) are forced after Mr. Dashwood’s death to vacate their Sussex home, Norland Park, due to stringent primogeniture laws. But I can’t recall another adaptation, either for film or television, that made the story so overwhelmingly morose and its protagonists such a joyless pair. Casting John (Tom Brooke), the eldest Dashwood offspring, who inherits the estate, as a spineless weasel yields little tension because it’s obvious from the minute we meet his avaricious wife Fanny (Stacy Martin) that she will talk him down on any annual stipend he proposes allocating to his stepmother and half-sisters, in compliance with his late father’s wishes. Austen’s mean-spirited vipers — Caroline Bingley and Lady Catherine de Bourgh in Pride and Prejudice and Mrs. Elton in Emma , as well as Fanny — are as memorable as her heroines. Martin plays Fanny with the right brittle calculation, but she’s a standard-issue rich bitch. I missed the outrageous malice of the character in Lee’s version, hilariously evil in Queen of Mean Harriet Walter’s delicious turn. Humor is often a casualty here, even in the book’s most dependable source, wealthy widow Mrs. Jennings, the mother-in-law of a distant cousin of the Dashwoods, who offers them a cottage on his estate in Devonshire. Sublime English character actress Spriggs made this raucous, gossipy matchmaker a spark plug who brought fresh fizz to Lee’s film every time she appeared, as did a marvelous Imelda Staunton as her complete twit of a daughter, Charlotte. Fiona Shaw ’s work here as Mrs. J is colorless by comparison, loud and abrasive and so unable to read the room that we never get much sense of the kindness and generosity beneath the character’s overbearing manner. She just seems to require an audience. Other characters blend into the wallpaper, among them Mrs. Dashwood, wasting the considerable talents of Balfe (so wrenching as the unhappy mother in Andrew Haigh’s upcoming A Long Winter ); and Lucy Steele (Ceara Coveney), whose confidences are a form of torture for Elinor though here she’s barely around long enough to make an impression. That leaves the men, who fare well enough. Playing Edward as the courtly and compassionate polar-opposite of his awful sister Fanny, MacKay brings a gentle diffidence that syncs beautifully with Edgar-Jones’ delicate reserve. Their climactic scenes near the end, once all the obstacles have been removed, are lovely — and not just because Austen’s prose in their outcome is so indestructible. Dillane, superb in Harris Dickinson’s Urchin , has presence but is somewhat shortchanged by the script’s one-dimensional grasp of Willoughby, the dashing romantic hero revealed to be an opportunistic cad who breaks Marianne’s heart. And as the self-abnegating Colonel Brandon, Norwegian actor Herbert Nordrum (one point of the triangle in The Worst Person in the World ) is touching as he takes several steps back when he sees that Marianne’s affections lie elsewhere, then steps forward with heroic devotion when her health is in grave danger. Nordrum didn’t quite rip out my heart the way Rickman did 31 years ago, but his watchful intensity gives him one of the most moving character arcs. The performance likely to have the most fervent admirers in Creed-Miles’ as Marianne, the reckless romantic who lets her heart lead her, with devastating results. Oakley and costume designer Grace Snell break from the traditional pristine elegance in period films set in this era, making Marianne a free-spirited child of nature whose dresses and hair look consistently bedraggled, starting when she is first seen lying in long grass in the opening scene. The director certainly gets a lot of raw feeling out of the actress, but should the character really seem almost feral? The emphasis on naturalism perhaps removes some of the emotional barriers for young contemporary audiences, but it also gives the movie a low-energy feel and a drab look, with flat light and a dreary color palette. Historical sticklers will roll their eyes at all the free-flowing tresses in place of tidy updos, though the element that made me groan the most was the ball scenes. Does every post- Bridgerton period piece now have to mix traditional dance with expressively stylized modern touches? That kind of flourish has become as much a cliché as the buttoned-up starchiness of old-school costume dramas, especially when it’s as inorganic as it is here. The women just appear to have gotten lost on their way to quadrille practice and stumbled into a Pina Bausch class. Still, I suppose we should at least be grateful that Oakley for the most part held back from the gimmicky Emerald Fennell approach . Full credits Release date: Friday, Oct. 16 Production companies: Working Title, in association with November Pictures Distribution: Focus Features Cast: Daisy Edgar Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe, Bodhi Rae Breathnach, Frank Dillane, Herbert Nordrum, George MacKay, Fiona Shaw, Stacy Martin, Tom Brooke, Turlough Convery, Chloe Pirrie, Eliot Sumner, Bethany Slater, Ceara Coveney Director: Georgia Oakley Screenwriter: Diana Reid, based on the novel by Jane Austen Producers: Tim Bevan, Eric Fellner, India Flint, Jo Wallett Executive producers: Thea Paulett, Angela Moneke Director of photography: Arnaud Potier Production designer: Francesca Di Mottola Costume designer: Grace Snell Music: Roger Goula Editor: Izabella Curry Casting: Kharmel Cochrane Rated PG, 2 hours 11 minutes THR

articles.title: There’s a Deal, Now It’s All About the Details. Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Fight
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Alex Weprin , Winston Cho September 21, 2026 8:03am Paramount CEO David Ellison and 12 states led by California AG Rob Bonta have agreed to terms. Getty Images Logo text They have a deal. After days of marathon negotiations, Paramount Skydance and the state attorneys general have settled the blockbuster antitrust lawsuit over the $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed. The agreement is expected to be announced later Monday (on Yom Kippur, no less). But it also clears Paramount to close the deal, which had a so-called $7 million-per-day ticking fee set to begin Oct. 1. The settlement allows the studio to avoid paying those costs assuming it can close in the next 10 days or so. The agreement comes after months of what has been a bitter and public back and forth, with threats by Paramount to leave the state of California (Texas and Tennessee both courted the company), accusations of antisemitism levied at some critics of the deal and a political undercurrent running just beneath the surface of the whole thing, given the Ellison family’s relationship to President Donald Trump, Rob Bonta’s own political ambitions and the hyper-politicized nature of dealmaking today. The state attorneys general, led by California’s Bonta had sued to block the deal, alleging that the merger would give the combined Paramount-Warners too much control over basic cable TV and the theatrical film business. The Writers Guild of America later joined the fray, with a lawsuit that argued the merger would suppress wages and worsen working conditions for writers by creating a single mega-buyer of film and television programming. Earlier this year, consumers had also filed a complaint challenging the purchase. Ellison, for his part, promised to release a minimum of 30 films per year theatrically, though many in the industry remain skeptical about how long the company can sustain that level of production. Bonta had maintained he’ll only accept structural remedies, which typically involve companies selling off parts of the combined business. It’s believed a sticking point for the states in any settlement involved Paramount operating the two studios as independent businesses and selling off parts of its cable business. For Ellison, parting ways with CNN was a no-go. Still, the specifics of a deal are still TBA, including any potential divestitures. The legal and public message jockeying in the court battle was contentious. Leading up to the deal, Paramount had said it would leave California if an agreement wasn’t struck by Oct. 1, when the so-called ticking fee starts accruing, regardless of the outcome of the lawsuits — a move Bonta had called “blackmail.” This came after the studio came to terms with Bonta and the WGA in a joint agreement to hold off on consummating the merger until a trial had determined whether it violated antitrust laws, though it was scheduled for next year. Across the litigation, Paramount had been rankled that the government and dozens of foreign regulators cleared the purchase. In June, the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division found that the acquisition would actually increase competition across media and entertainment. The decision cleared the way for Paramount to become among the largest theatrical distributors in the country and own a top five streamer by subscriber count, until the deal was challenged by the states. Notably, the green light didn’t require any divestitures, behavioral remedies or concessions. Paramount has framed the merger as one that will boost competition, arguing it’s necessary to compete against tech giants like Netflix, Amazon and Apple. Hollywood will soon see whether that’s true. THR

articles.title: James Sloyan, Actor in ‘The Sting,‘ ‘Xanadu’ and ‘Oh Madeline,’ Dies at 85
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 8:37am James Sloyan Carsey-Werner / Courtesy Everett Collection James Sloyan, the busy character actor who appeared in films including The Sting and Xanadu and played Madeline Kahn’s husband on her short-lived 1980s ABC sitcom, has died. He was 85. Sloyan died July 22 at his home in Sherman Oaks, his family announced over the weekend. Star Trek fans know him for his five appearances as a member of four species across The Next Generation , Deep Space Nine and Voyager in the 1990s, and he served as the voice of Toyota’s luxury brand Lexus in commercials for 18 years starting in 1989. Related Stories Music Chad Gilbert, New Found Glory Guitarist, Dies at 45 Movies Gerrit Graham, Actor in 'Phantom of the Paradise,' 'Pretty Baby' and 'Used Cars,' Dies at 77 In George Roy Hill’s The Sting (1973), winner of the Oscar for best picture, Sloyan helped set the plot in motion with his turn as Mottola, the numbers runner who works for racketeer Doyle Lonnegan (Robert Shaw) and falls victim to a “pigeon drop scam” perpetrated by Johnny Hooker ( Robert Redford ) and Luther Coleman ( James Earl Jones ). And in the Olivia Newton-John musical fantasy Xanadu (1980), he played Simpson, the tyrannical boss of Michael Beck’s artist Sonny Malone at AirFlow Records. Sloyan landed the role of Kahn’s husband, a guy who writes steamy romance novels under the pen name Crystal Love, but the 1983-84 show — the first produced by Carsey-Werner Productions — lasted just 18 episodes. The youngest of four kids, James Joseph Sloyan was born in Indianapolis on Feb. 24, 1941. His father, James Sr., was a construction engineer. When he was 4, he “discovered the delights of the Indianapolis State Fair, wrangling an appearance with [Western movie actor] Lash LaRue and his traveling Western Show,” his family said. After spending time living overseas and in Albany, New York, Sloyan graduated from the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York and served three years in the U.S. Army before returning to New York, where he acted and was a choreographer for fight scenes for Joseph Papp’s New York Shakespeare Festival. He made it to Broadway in Arthur Kopit’s Indians in 1969, had the lead in such off-Broadway productions as Irv Bauer’s A Dream Out of Time and made his onscreen debut in the 1970 film The Traveling Executioner , starring Stacy Keach. Sloyan, who moved to California in 1973, appeared in The Gang That Couldn’t Shoot Straight (1971) and on episodes of The Doctors , The Streets of San Francisco , Kojak and Delvecchio before landing a regular role on the 1977 ABC drama Westside Medical . He played a Romulan admiral and then the son of the Klingon Worf (Michael Dorn) on Next Generation , the Bajoran scientist Dr. Mora on Deep Space Nine and the Haakonian scientist Ma’bor Jetrel on Voyager . His TV résumé also included the telefilms The Disappearance of Aimee , starring Faye Dunaway and Bette Davis, and The Billionaires Boys Club and stops on Wonder Woman , Buck Rogers in the 25th Century , Lou Grant , Falcon Crest , Knots Landing , Cagney & Lacey , Moonlighting , Murder, She Wrote , Quantum Leap , The X-Files and NYPD Blue . “Friends and colleagues remember him always present, always curious, courageous, inventive and loyal as well as brash, mouthy and very urban. He was one-of-a-kind,” his family said. Survivors include his wife, actress Deirdre Lenihan ( Needles and Pins , The Waltons ), whom he married in 1973, and their children, Daniel, a musician, and Samantha Sloyan, an actress ( The Life of Chuck , Dr. Penelope Blake on Grey’s Anatomy ). His brother, author and Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Patrick Sloyan, died in February 2019. THR

articles.title: Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 6:15am PT Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review By Aramide Tinubu Plus Icon Aramide Tinubu Latest Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review 2 hours ago ‘MobLand’ Season 2 Proves the Show Just Wouldn’t Work Without Tom Hardy 3 days ago Netflix’s ‘Monster’ Finally Delivers an Outrageously Engaging Season With ‘The Lizzie Borden Story’: TV Review 4 days ago See All NBC For decades, law-enforcement procedurals have been staples on television, and when they are done well, these series build loyal fanbases that stick with them for years. NBC ’s newest drama, “ Line of Fire ” is from “Quantico” creator Joshua Safran and loosely based on executive producer Jenna Bush Hager’s experiences with the United States Secret Service. The show has all the makings of becoming a classic in the canon of beloved police procedurals. “Line of Fire” follows the Hollingsworth family: Secret Service Agent Mike Hollingsworth ( Peter Krause ); his estranged wife, U.S. Marshal Jane Hollingsworth ( Hope Davis ); and their three adult children, FBI Agent Clare Hollingsworth (Kat Cunning), Secret Service Agent Mike “Micah” Hollingsworth Jr. (Tommy O’Brien) and DOJ analyst Russ Hollingsworth (Taylor Bloom). Mike, Jane and their children try to keep things professional, but continually cross personal boundaries because of their agencies’ proximity. Boasting intense family dynamics and several truly intriguing cases, “Line of Fire” has a depth, intensity and a hint of soapiness that works perfectly within the genre. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony The 10-episode first season (two episodes were available for review) opens in Crozet, Virginia. A U.S. Marshal, under the guise of being a delivery driver, attempts to track down a missing fugitive. Unfortunately, before the morning breaks, both the Marshal and the outlaw lay dead in the woods. The next day, Jane arrives at the crime scene, determined to figure out what happened. Needing a bit more reach than the Marshals can offer, Jane calls in her daughter, Clare, for her expertise and for the FBI’s resources. Though Clare is eager to help, Jane’s team is not exactly pleased that the FBI is encroaching on her territory. For her part, Clare isn’t thrilled when her mother badgers her about bringing her mysterious new boyfriend to dinner to finally meet the family. Popular on Variety Back in Washington, D.C., Mike is set to finish out his final week at the Secret Service Headquarters before retiring. Yet, he’s increasingly concerned Micah is skirting his professional duties for a personal relationship with Sydney (Savannah Lee Smith), the president’s college-age daughter. Elsewhere, Russell is ready to get his feet wet at the DOJ, but his family’s constant requests complicate his role. Chaos and dysfunction are par for the course for the Hollingsworths. But when a seemingly standard case unearths long-buried secrets that threaten the family’s safety, each person must decide whether their jobs are worth more than the people they love. From bank robberies to cartel killings and even contending with the First Family’s drama in the White House, all of the cases the Hollingsworths handle are interesting. Still, the Hollingsworth family dynamic anchors “Line of Fire.” Though they’ve been long separated, Jane and Mike have a solid friendship; one that can only be formed after knowing and loving someone intimately for half your life. Not only do the former couple share children, but Mike and Jane also share secrets — shocking ones they keep close to their chests. The siblings, each with unique relationships with their parents and each other, are also well mapped out. Though only two episodes were available to screen, the family feels well lived-in: a boisterous clan with varied personalities becomes the ecosystem that shapes the series. In the pilot, Mike and the siblings arrive at Jane’s house for a chaotic and hilarious family dinner to meet the beau Clare has avoided introducing them to. Immediately, the audience gets a full sense of who these people are and how this family functions. Yet, that doesn’t make any of the cases sprinkled within the show any less worthwhile. In fact, it makes the conspiracy sitting at the center of “Line of Fire” even more gripping. “Line of Fire” has all of the essential elements that make procedural dramas so fun. With a stellar cast and some detailed mysteries which will likely stretch across the season (and into the next, assuming there is one), changing the Hollingsworth family dynamic as we know it, it’s clear NBC has a gem on its hands. “Line of Fire” debuts Sept. 21 on NBC, with the remaining episodes airing weekly on Mondays. And I do that because my brain is incredibly busy, especially at night, and I’ve always found going to bed very difficult. My brain doesn’t turn off,” Harington said. “When I got sober, that got especially bad. And so I started listening to ‘Harry Potter’ audiobooks, and now they’re the thing I listen to every night. So they have a very special place in my heart.” Popular on Variety Related Stories Chile Film Industry Surges 20.5% Compared to Previous Season, New Catalog Reveals (EXCLUSIVE) Where Is Spain Heading? María González Veracruz, Secretary of State for Digitization, Unpacks Roadmap In fact, Harington was recently part of Audible’s “Harry Potter” audiobooks as the voice of Lockhart — a famous yet arrogant wizard who becomes the new Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher at Hogwarts — before the TV series came his way. “When I knew they were doing this show, I was like, ‘I think that’s a brilliant idea, I think they can really delve into it further than the films did.’ I’m fully supportive of it,” Harington said. “And then I got called to be in it, and that was just a very simple, ‘Yes, please!'” Harington took over the role of Lockhart, who will first be seen in Season 2, from Nicholas Hoult after he exited the series due to scheduling conflicts. articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 7:26am PT Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban 1 hour ago Paramount Settlement Talks With States Progress but Some AGs Push for Tougher Terms 14 hours ago White House Blocks CNN and MS NOW Journalists From Entry and Confiscates Their Badges After Donald Trump Bans Networks 2 days ago See All Getty Images In an unprecedented move, four of the five TV networks that provide White House pool coverage of President Donald Trump — ABC News , CBS News , NBC News and Fox News — have joined in solidarity with CNN , which is the fifth TV pooler, announcing they are suspending coverage of the president because of his ban of CNN. “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government,” the five networks said in a joint statement Monday. “No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.” Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast The blackout of White House pool coverage by the networks comes after the Trump administration suspended CNN as the designated TV pool provider on Monday, Sept. 21 — leaving no TV pooler for the day. It also follows CNN, MS NOW and Politico announcing that they are suing Trump and three White House officials over his unilateral ban of the news outlets, alleging it violates the First Amendment. Popular on Variety The suspension of the TV news pool means that, for the time being, no major television network will provide coverage of Trump’s events, including his scheduled appearances Monday at the White House and his visit to the United Nations in New York City. Bryan Boughton, Fox News’ Washington bureau chief and the current White House TV pool chair, wrote in an email to the other networks Monday, ”This is to advise that, effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President. This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties. There will be no replacement pool put in place.” The White House designates secondary TV news pool providers (as well as those for print, radio and new media outlets). However, the secondary TV networks do not have any obligation to provide content to third parties. Trump said on social media Friday, Sept. 18, that he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico “effective immediately” from the White House , citing his familiar allegation that they propagate “fake news.” The White House barred entry to staffers from the three outlets on Saturday and revoked their press passes. At an Oval Office briefing Friday, Trump indicated that there was no single story that triggered him to ban the news outlets, but was rather a cumulative effect of their “purposely negative” coverage. articles.title: Paramount Settles Antitrust Case With State AGs, Removing Obstacle to Warner Bros. Deal
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 7:56am PT Paramount Settles Antitrust Case With State AGs, Removing Obstacle to Warner Bros. Deal By Gene Maddaus Plus Icon Gene Maddaus Senior Media Writer @GeneMaddaus Latest Paramount Settlement Talks With State AGs Reach Critical Stage as Merger Opponents Rally and Urge Rob Bonta ‘Do Not Cave’ 1 day ago Gavin Newsom Signs Bill Creating $10 Million Post-Production Tax Credit 2 days ago Paramount and California AG Bonta Reportedly in ‘Advanced Talks’ to Settle Antitrust Suit 3 days ago See All Getty Images Paramount has reached a deal with 12 state attorneys general that removes a major obstacle to closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The deal comes just before the company was to begin accruing a $7 million daily “ticking fee” on Oct. 1, which was seen as an important milestone in the case. Bloomberg was first to report the news, followed by the Wall Street Journal. A source also confirmed to Variety that a deal is done. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony The merger was on hold pending the outcome of the states’ antitrust lawsuit, which was set for a trial on March 2, 2027. The $111 billion merger is the largest in Hollywood history. Popular on Variety Details of the agreement have yet to be made public. An official announcement is expected to come later Monday. The two sides spent the weekend in tense discussions over Paramount’s commitments to remain in California and over guarantees for its production levels. The discussions also focused on editorial oversight of CBS News and CNN, a key concern for East Coast attorneys general. Sources said the settlement does not require Paramount to make any major divestitures. California Attorney General Rob Bonta led the 12-state coalition, which sued to block the deal in July despite prior approval from the U.S. Department of Justice. Since then, Bonta has insisted on “robust structural remedies” — which has been taken to mean significant divestitures. Opponents of the deal were quick to blast Bonta for “caving” to Paramount’s pressure campaign. “Today, billionaires have yet again bribed, censored and bullied their way to the top,” said Alvaro Bedoya, a senior advisor at the American Economic Liberties Project, who also expressed disappointment with California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Xavier Becerra, who is running for the governor’s seat. “People want champions who are not afraid of rich bullies. Newsom, Becerra and Bonta did not meet that mark. The people who work in the film and TV industry and the small businesses who support it will suffer as a result. And so will everyone who values dissent in our democracy.” The Writers Guild of America filed a separate suit to block the merger in July, and that case was set to be heard along with the states’ case in March. The WGA is expected to sign on to the settlement agreement. Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin, who is overseeing the states’ antitrust case, granted a 28-day restraining order in July, finding that the states had put forward a strong case that the deal would harm competition in the basic cable and theatrical markets. Paramount then agreed to pause the transaction until a trial on the merits, rather than fight a motion for a preliminary injunction. The states argued that the merger would lead to higher prices and fewer options for theaters and cable and satellite providers, who would in turn pass on higher costs to consumers. Paramount has argued all along that the deal is pro-competitive and will result in more content production as the company seeks to take on streaming giants like Netflix and Amazon. In recent weeks, Paramount has sought to ratchet up the pressure on Bonta to abandon the case, including by threatening to leave California and move to Texas or Tennessee. Paramount has also enlisted state Democratic lawmakers to urge Bonta to settle, while IATSE and the Directors Guild of America have also pushed for a deal. Cinema United, the trade group representing theaters, had initially strongly opposed the merger. But as its three largest members — AMC, Cinemark and Regal — came out in favor of a settlement one-by-one, the group also reversed itself and called for a deal. That left Bonta and the other attorneys general in the position of trying to prove economic harm to exhibitors without the support of many of them.
