articles.title: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Georgia Oakley Puts a Moody, Naturalistic Spin on the Jane Austen Classic
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 8:00am PT ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Georgia Oakley Puts a Moody, Naturalistic Spin on the Jane Austen Classic The British director’s follow-up to her BAFTA-winning “Blue Jean” brings Daisy Edgar-Jones, George MacKay, Esmé Creed-Miles, and a scene-stealing Frank Dillane together in a romantically earthy 18th-century England. By Beatrice Loayza Plus Icon Beatrice Loayza Latest ‘Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ Review: Alex Gibney Profiles the Controversial Author During His Harrowing Hospitalization 3 days ago ‘Hombre al Agua’ Review: Gael García Bernal Directs and Stars in a Sputtering, Screwball-y Dramedy About One Man’s Identity Crisis 1 week ago ‘A Good Little Soldier’ Review: Alba Rohrwacher Goes Corporate Drone in Stéphane Brizé’s Lukewarm Workplace Drama 2 weeks ago See All Screenshot courtesy YouTube/Focus Features It’s been over 30 years since Ang Lee’s “ Sense and Sensibility ” became (for this critic, as for many) the Platonic ideal of the Jane Austen adaptation. Lush but controlled, dryly funny (thanks to Emma Thompson’s Oscar-winning script) in that chatty, cheeky, keenly perceptive Austen way, Lee’s classic also boasted a formidable cast to unleash a floodgate of big, ugly-cry-inducing emotions by its finale. All of which is to say that Georgia Oakley had a tough act to follow in taking on the beloved tale of two sisters navigating matters of the heart in two vastly different ways. Though slightly muted (in both feeling and color palette) by comparison, Oakley’s moody, naturalistic spin on the Austen touchstone is a solid undertaking. It’s also a confident, bigger-budget follow-up to her BAFTA-winning debut “Blue Jean,” a poignant Thatcher-era queer drama; that film’s restrained yet tactile intimacy translates well to a late 18th-century England of stifled desire and pastoral exuberance. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony There’s an earthy romanticism to Oakley’s vision of the times, with shots of quivering cattails, dew-spotted spiders, and floating lilypads complementing the roiling inner lives of sisters Elinor ( Daisy Edgar-Jones ) and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles) Dashwood. The younger Marianne is the more daring and vivacious of the two — a lightly shaky camera is on her heels as she adventures through the forest and receives news of their father’s death — and thankfully Oakley avoids the corny Mother Earth symbolism (à la “Hamnet”) that woodsy women amid sun-dappled pastures can so easily invite. The film’s natural splendor is pleasing, of course, but Oakley makes a point to show the grit and exhaustion of scaling hills and taking multi-day journeys by horse carriage — tough physical realities matched by the cruel social conventions that upend the Dashwoods’ lives. Popular on Variety Hewing close to the novel’s major plot beats, Diana Reid’s script efficiently lays out the stakes, as mother Dashwood (Caitríona Balfe) finds herself penniless and powerless against the takeover of her family’s estate by John Dashwood (Tom Brooke), her dead husband’s only male heir from his first marriage. Before she and the girls relocate to a modest seaside cottage in Devon, they suffer insults from John’s comically stingy wife Fanny (a wonderfully catty Stacy Martin) while Elinor meet-cutes with Fanny’s brother Edward ( George MacKay ), their mutual affection growing over wholesome nature walks and portrait sessions. (In a sweet reversal of the typical gendered gaze, it’s Elinor who draws Edward.) Sadly, Edward is too spineless and, er, sensible to follow his heart and lets a confused Elinor slip away when her family finally retreats to their new isolated home, courtesy of the kindly but coarse Mrs. Jennings (Fiona Shaw). For her part, the blunt and free-spirited Marianne finds her match in the dashing Willoughby ( Frank Dillane , the face of Harris Dickinson’s “Urchin”), brushing off the endearingly awkward advances of Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum, from “The Worst Person in the World,” speaking in a placid baritone). In Devon, Marianne and Willoughby enjoy a rustic romance of piano dueting and cliffside snuggling, and though he makes quite the statement in giving her a white steed, he never commits before heading back to London and remaining there for the foreseeable future. London is where Edward is, too, so when Mrs. Jennings plans a trip to the capital, Marianne and Elinor eagerly tag along. The girls’ weathered white gowns and tousled, stallionesque manes confer a cottage-core modernity that’s set in contrast to the gilded interiors and tightly-wound updos of their London acquaintances. Between the two sisters, Elinor’s prudence and Marianne’s joie de vivre are charted out via Holly Blakey’s enchanting choreography: In the country, Marianne and Willoughby partake in a riotous, rollicking folk dance, while Elinor and Edward cross paths at a buzzy London ball where they dance a comparably restrained, yet slinky, sensual waltz. Oakley’s beautifully textured worldbuilding — of soft, candlelit interiors; hunted game hanging on wall hooks; and so very many neat dogs (pugs, sheepdogs, mastiffs, whippets!) — is paired with a quivering psychological realism. Low-angle close-ups betray the fragility of Elinor’s self-composure when Edward tells her that he is engaged to another woman; and Marianne is a jittery bundle of broken idealism when she finds Willoughby arm-in-arm with a wealthy fiancé. These lovers’ quarrels unfold with a touching sincerity to Roger Goula’s wistful score, though Oakley’s more grounded drama also feels oddly safe, with a seriousness of tone that strips away some of the wit and comedy that makes Austen’s work, well, Austenesque. And though players like Edgar-Jones and MacKay make for perfectly tender lovebirds, they don’t exactly breathe new life into their characters. This might be the difference between being a gifted actor and a real star, which Lee’s “Sense and Sensibility” had across the board. Creed-Miles’ sharp-tongued, twinkle-eyed Marianne comes close to that inexplicable magnetism, though the script, which makes her sound like a broken record with the number of times she goes on about passion and passionate men, renders her a tad clichéd. In terms of casting, what Oakley’s “Sense and Sensibility” does confirm is that Dillane’s recent breakthrough was no fluke. His Willoughby is a slouching, smug-faced scoundrel — a rake all his own, and perhaps the only major presence in the film that brings an unstudied lightness and humor to this world of breath-held decorum. ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Georgia Oakley Puts a Moody, Naturalistic Spin on the Jane Austen Classic Reviewed at Universal Screening Room, New York City, Sept. 18, 2026. MPA Rating: PG. Running time: 132 MIN. Production: (U.K.) A Focus Features presentation of a Working Title production. Producers: Tim Bevan, Eriv Fellner, India Flint, Jo Wallett. Executive producer: Thea Paulett, Angela Moneke. Co-producer: Jane Frazer. Crew: Director: Georgia Oakley. Screenplay: Diana Reid. Camera: Arnaud Potier. Editor: Izabella Curry. Music: Roger Goula. With: Daisy Edgar-Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, George MacKay, Herbert Nordrum, Frank Dillane, Fiona Shaw, Stacey Martin, Tom Brooke, Caitríona Balfe. articles.title: Reza Rahadian, Dian Sastrowardoyo Starrer ‘Descendants of the Sun’ Heads to Busan Market as Barunson E&A Launches Sales
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 8:00am PT Reza Rahadian, Dian Sastrowardoyo Starrer ‘Descendants of the Sun’ Heads to Busan Market as Barunson E&A Launches Sales By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Reza Rahadian, Dian Sastrowardoyo Starrer ‘Descendants of the Sun’ Heads to Busan Market as Barunson E&A Launches Sales 31 minutes ago ‘A Teacher’s Gift’ Lands U.K. Distribution Deal With Peccadillo Pictures (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Bestselling Japanese Novelist Maha Harada Says ‘If This Is a Dream, I Hope I Never Wake Up’ About Her San Sebastian – and Busan – Bound Directing Debut ‘In My Father’s Room’ 6 hours ago See All Barunson E&A Barunson E&A will launch international sales for “ Descendants of the Sun ,” a big-screen version of the landmark Korean series that first aired in 2016, at the Asian Contents & Film Market in Busan, running Oct. 10-13. The Seoul-based company, known for producing Bong Joon Ho’s Academy Award winner “Parasite,” is making the film alongside Dapur Film, Tobali Putra Productions, NEWKO and Barunson C&C, its own subsidiary production arm. NEW (Next Entertainment World), owner of the original intellectual property, has come on board as a co-production company. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony Production has wrapped on both parts of the film, which were shot back-to-back. Part One is aiming for an Indonesian theatrical bow by mid-2027. Popular on Variety The adaptation arrives at the original series’ 10th anniversary, a show many credit with helping bring K-drama to global audiences. The original drew a 38.8% rating in its home market, marked the first instance of a Korean drama airing simultaneously in China, where iQIYI logged upward of two billion streams, and eventually found distribution in more than 30 territories, among them the U.S., the U.K., France, Germany, Japan and Russia. The series was similarly popular in Indonesia a decade ago, fueling anticipation for the new version before any footage had surfaced. The Indonesian film relocates the central romance to a setting and cultural backdrop specific to Indonesia while retaining what the studio describes as the emotional core of the original. Hanung Bramantyo, one of Indonesia’s leading box office directors, helms the project. He previously directed “Miracle in Cell No. 7,” an Indonesian version of the identically titled Korean film that ranks as the country’s eighth-highest-grossing domestic release. Reza Rahadian and Dian Sastrowardoyo lead the cast. Rahadian’s credits include “Vengeance Is Mine, All Others Pay Cash,” which won the Golden Leopard at Locarno, and Sastrowardoyo has appeared in Netflix’s “Cigarette Girl” as well as “The Fox King,” a Toronto Film Festival premiere. “Ten years on, ‘Descendants of the Sun’ is still one of the titles people point to when they talk about the start of the K-drama wave,” said Barunson E&A CEO Yoonhee Choi. “We see the strength of the Korean IP as a starting point, not an endpoint. This adaptation places that globally recognized story under a different sun, in an Indonesian landscape with a local sensibility all its own. It retains the familiarity of a story audiences already know and love, while opening it to a new context and, we believe, audiences beyond Indonesia.” “As the producer behind the original series, I deeply admire how the director has honored its spirit while creating a truly Indonesian story that I believe will translate just as powerfully wherever it’s seen,” added Woosik Seo, CEO of Barunson C&C and an executive producer on the film. “Descendants of the Sun” heads an ACFM slate for Barunson E&A that also includes “Satan’s Slaves: Origin,” a prequel to Joko Anwar’s horror franchise, whose first two entries are among Indonesia’s highest-earning local films; “Stoneborn,” an occult mystery from the “Exhuma” creative team starring Jongseo Jeon of Cannes title “Burning” and Sul Kyung-gu of Venice title “Possible Love”; and “Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng,” a comedy debuting at the Busan International Film Festival ahead of an Oct. 28 theatrical release. ‘The Odyssey’ and ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Power $239 Million U.K., Ireland July Box Office Korea Box Office: Local Comedy Remake ‘The Intern’ Leads Weekend Admissions as ‘The Odyssey’ Retains Revenue Crown Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Eclipses ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Continues Dominance ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day,’ ‘The Odyssey’ Continue Tussle Atop U.K., Ireland Box Office John Carpenter, Colman Domingo and Charlize Theron to Be Honored at Academy Museum Gala Loading comments... articles.title: Carly Rae Jepsen on How Marriage, Motherhood and the Joy of Pop Music Fueled Her Ambitious Double Album ‘Day and Night’: ‘I Knew What Colors I Was Playing With’
articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 8:00am PT Carly Rae Jepsen on How Marriage, Motherhood and the Joy of Pop Music Fueled Her Ambitious Double Album ‘Day and Night’: ‘I Knew What Colors I Was Playing With’ By Steven J. Horowitz Plus Icon Steven J. Horowitz Senior Music Writer speriod Latest Jhené Aiko Scores First No. 1 on Albums Chart With ‘Westside Whimsy’ 20 hours ago Chad Gilbert, New Found Glory Guitarist and Backing Vocalist, Dies at 45 20 hours ago Jay-Z Revisits the Ghosts of Lyrics Past in the Illuminating (and Possibly Too Thorough) ‘Jay-Z in 8’: TV Review 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Mikayla LoBasso It sounds like an obvious approach, but Carly Rae Jepsen began working on her new double album “Day and Night” with a simple ethos: make the type of music she would want to listen to. “Like, what do I have to offer to the musical landscape right now?” the 40-year-old tells Variety over Zoom, just weeks before her sixth album released this past Friday. “And that began with how I always begin every project, which is, what am I attracted to? What music am I listening to that I love?” Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony As evidenced by the album’s two-dozen tracks, split evenly between Laurel Canyon coffee pop and synth-glittered bops, “Day and Night” is an amalgamation of self-professed influences — a “mixed bag of chips,” she says — inspired by artists and styles spanning Blossom Dearie and Minnie Ripperton to ABBA and house music. The “Day” section of the album is decidedly folksy, packed with organic instrumentation across tracks like acoustic ballad “Wild Child” and shimmying “After All,” while “Night” slips into something a bit more mischievous on the smoky “Amalfi Coast” and effervescent “Don’t Leave Me on the Dance Floor.” Popular on Variety For anyone who’s followed her since her explosion into mainstream pop with 2012’s “Call Me Maybe,” it’s clear that Jepsen is a creature of creation, consistently amassing songs until they start to take shape as a project. (She famously recorded 250 songs for her seminal sophomore album “Emotion,” which she recently celebrated with a 10th anniversary show at Los Angeles’ Troubadour.) With “Day and Night,” Jepsen had been working on material and was a quarter of the way through the process when she presented her work to her guitarist, Tavish Crowe, who realized that she was making music in two distinct lanes. “He said, ‘What if it’s like a house party, and as a thought experiment, we make this the upstairs and the downstairs?'” she recalls. “So we started doing that for fun. And then ‘Day and Night’ was born when I was just driving in my car here in LA. I loved its simplicity. It perfectly described this organic kind of dreamy thing, and then the nighttime, you immediately feel things get heightened and a little darker and more experimental. So then I would show up with sessions with a bit more intention and it became really fun because I knew what colors I was playing with.” “Day and Night” is also a diary, of sorts, as Jepsen began to fall in love with her now-husband Cole Marsden Greif-Neill, known to the music world as Cole M.G.N., whose credits include Beck, Wallows and Christine and the Queens. They had previously worked together on “So Right,” included on her 2023 album “The Loveliest Time,” and on “Day and Night,” he contributes to a handful of tracks — some of which are directly inspired by their burgeoning romance. Throughout the record, Jepsen sings of surrendering to this newfound love, of basking in the resplendence and joy that it brings. Mainly, she says, there’s an element of “how shocked I am that this is all happening.” She explains that she’s always thought of herself as an artistic observer of life, as opposed to a participant, and that in the past, she’d written about relationships that may have been doomed because she loved “an impossible situation.” “I think that the idea of really engaging, saying yes to the whole thing — a baby, a child, a family, a forever — that felt like big stuff,” she says. “So it wasn’t until I really met Cole that I — and probably even before I met Cole — that I had done some of my own personal work to get to a place where I was ready to meet a man like Cole, where I was like, okay, this is wild. I want all the things. And even the first time I might have even admitted that to myself was when I was writing ‘After All,’ which is how I decided to open the album so boldly. Like, alright, here we go!” Jepsen lights up when talking about the very first day she met Greif-Neill, when they ended up in the studio to write “Day and Night” cut “No Labels, I Love You.” “I was driving home from that session and I thought, cute guy, but [only] in there. Not gonna touch that hot stuff. And you know, don’t kiss the producer. Rule number one,” she says with a laugh. She pulled to a stop sign and saw he had texted her with questions about the song’s second verse and decided to save his number under a combination of his name and the track they had just worked on. “I put ‘Cole I Love You’ in my phone. Lo and behold, five years later, we’re married with a baby, and I’m like, oh. Well, that worked out. He’s still saved as ‘Cole I Love You’ because of that day.” Shortly after marrying in October 2025, Jepsen and Greif-Neill welcomed their first child in March amid the completion of “Day and Night.” She had been prepping for the baby’s arrival while balancing the demands of being a pop star — at the “Emotion” anniversary show in August 2025, she says she was four months pregnant and wore a dress with “distracting lines” in hopes of making it an “optical illusion” — and is gradually learning how to delineate between family and career. “I’m more of a planner than I’ve ever been before,” she says. “A big part of getting ready for this double album and mixing it and putting the art together and even preparing like what videos were shot when was all around the idea of like, baby’s on the way. It was like a different meaning for the word deadline… And there was a conversation of, am I doing this before the baby comes or after the baby comes? It was like, before, because after the baby comes, I’m gonna be focused. So it’s changed that in a really wild way that I didn’t expect. It was so obvious what the priority was, which was building a career around a life, not the other way around.” That includes making time for the Broadway adaptation of the 1999 rom-com “10 Things I Hate About You,” set for previews in August 2027. Lena Dunham is adapting the musical’s book with Jessica Huang, while Jepsen is writing the music and lyrics with Ethan Gruska, whose credits include Ryan Beatty, Fiona Apple and Phoebe Bridgers. “We wanted to handle with care, but not trepidation,” she says of the musical. “We wanted to feel emboldened to think about what would cause these characters to feel like words are not enough and they need to break into the song. So we began with playlists for each character. Bianca had like her ’90s playlist. And it became really fun to sort of think about, you know, what the message of our show is.” Jepsen stops short of giving too much away: When asked about how she plans to handle the iconic scene where Heath Ledger’s character sings Frankie Valli’s “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You,” she demurs. “That one you’re gonna have to come and see. I know, disappointing answer, but I gotta leave some for the show.” For now, Jepsen is enjoying the spoils of motherhood as she releases one of her most ambitious projects to date. In the past, she’s complemented her studio albums by releasing full companion records of B-sides, something she’s not entirely counting out for “Day and Night. “In a very elusive way, in a very non-sexy way, I’ll say I consider myself sort of like a chipmunk,” she jokes. “I like to store my ideas in my cheeks, save them for later. Who knows.” But, as always, she’s looking for the next spark of inspiration. “A big part of my nature is to be in constant creation. I like to be making things. I don’t find it tiring,” she says. “It fuels and excites me. One of my greatest joys, even when I’m on the road is to pull up with Tavish and be like, hey, like late night tonight, let’s go to like your hotel or my hotel and we’ll get the office space and pull up some sound and just jam. That’s going to be different with a baby, but we’re going to figure out how to make that happen and fit it in between the cracks.” ‘The Odyssey’ Becomes Universal’s Highest-Grossing Film of All Time Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Bests ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Box Office: ‘Practical Magic 2’ Conjures Up $13 Million on Friday as ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Nears All-Time Domestic Box Office Record ‘The Odyssey’ Leaked on X: High-Quality Bootleg Seen by Millions in Hours Before Takedown ‘The Odyssey’ Sets 20,000 Screen China Release, Including Near-Total Imax Commitment (EXCLUSIVE) China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Continues Dominance Loading comments... articles.title: Melissa McCarthy on Getting Serious for ‘JonBenét Ramsey,’ the Psychiatrist on Set and Hollywood’s ‘Bulls—’ Excuse for Why Comedies Don’t Work Anymore
articles.full_text: Ramona Rosales for Variety Melissa McCarthy , one of the most gifted comic actors working today, will soon be starring in a tragedy. In “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” — premiering on Netflix on Dec. 10 — McCarthy plays Patsy Ramsey, the mother of 6-year-old JonBenét, who was killed in the Ramseys’ Boulder, Colorado, home on Christmas night in 1996. Because JonBenét had won several child beauty pageants, images of her in makeup and garish costumes created a spectacle around the case (which is still unsolved), and around the Ramseys. JonBenét’s father, John; her mother, and even her 9-year-old brother, Burke, all became suspects in her murder, and the series examines the fallout from her death. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension Ramona Rosales for Variety Because of the O.J. Simpson trial in 1995, true crime had become a national obsession, and with JonBenét’s murder, newsmagazines, talk shows and tabloids had a field day, inciting the public to rabidity: Today, McCarthy remembers being part of the “feeding frenzy” herself. Clive Owen, who plays John, says McCarthy’s involvement as both an actor and executive producer was a “big part” of the reason he agreed to take the role. “Yes, she’s a brilliant comedic actress, but she’s just a brilliant actress ,” Owen says. Popular on Variety “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” from showrunner Richard LaGravenese (and made without the family’s involvement), was an emotionally wrenching endeavor, and McCarthy and Owen formed a bond. “We have become friends,” he says. “Because it was such a difficult project, just having her alongside as an ally was really, really important. And honestly, after doing this project with her — she can do anything.” And she has. After playing chef Sookie St. James in the beloved dramedy “Gilmore Girls” from 2000 to 2007, McCarthy broke out in film in 2011’s Paul Feig-directed blockbuster “Bridesmaids” as the crude yet earnest Megan. The scene-stealing role brought her a best supporting actress Oscar nomination, a rarity for comedy — especially given that in the film’s famously gruesome food poisoning set-piece, Megan uses a sink as a toilet. McCarthy was shocked when she learned of her nomination, saying to her husband, director Ben Falcone, “I don’t think that’s true,” when he told her. (McCarthy was nominated for an Oscar a second time, for her fearless lead performance in Marielle Heller’s 2018 “Can You Ever Forgive Me?”) Over her career, McCarthy has starred in hit comedies such as Feig’s “The Heat” and “Spy” and Falcone’s “Tammy” and “The Boss” — and as the villainous Ursula in Disney’s 2023 live-action version of “The Little Mermaid.” But with “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” she returns to her earliest training in New York City, when she spent two years studying the Sanford Meisner method of acting. Back then, McCarthy was “carrying folding chairs up to a rehearsal space to do a show and just making enough money to hopefully pay for the space that night.” Despite the different scale of audience, the same passion and community spirit went into “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” McCarthy says in her first interview about the series, with the cast and crew putting in “hardworking days” while suffering through “hard moments.” Wanting to do right by Patsy, who died of ovarian cancer in 2006, McCarthy found people who knew her. “And they were like, ‘Those kids were in jeans riding their bikes. JonBenét wasn’t out in a pageant dress in her front yard.’” Playing Patsy Ramsey is such a heavy thing — what went into your decision to do it? I said, “Oh, no. I have no interest in that.” I didn’t think it was any of my business to do, I guess? But I spent a lot of years not working, and somebody took the time to ask me — I should take the time to look into it. The more I started to, I was really floored by the lack of humanity that had been shown to that family. In 1996, I was 26, and I have a very vivid memory of standing in a grocery store and looking at a tabloid and thinking, “How could you dress a little girl like that?” Because that’s what we were being told. I remember being obsessed. I had never put it together that I was a part of [judging them]. I went willingly. And that’s on me. I just thought if it can make some people realize, “Oh, God. I was part of that — I did that,” it gives us a little of our humanity back. And the hope is not to dredge it up for that poor family again. This might sound nuts: I’m very fond of Patsy. I have so much compassion for them, what they went through, and go through currently. That’s a bizarre thing to have a child’s trauma be like Wimbledon. It was a turning point, being able to watch something like that as sport. And even when I finally decided to do this, everybody said their theory [about the case] as if it was true. People in your life, you mean? People in my life! Very smart people, very open-minded people. I was like, “What is that based on?” Because I’ve now read every police report, every coroner’s report. So we’re still doing that. I said, “You got caught up in the riptide.” I hope with my whole heart that this — I don’t know if “helps” is the right word. Clive Owen and Melissa McCarthy Courtesy of Chris Large/Paramount+ Does the show have a point of view about what happened? This is not a whodunit. It’s not like, “Ooh, there’s a big reveal!” This is a character study of everyone who was caught in the undertow, and a look at all of us — as a civilization, really. Seeing that happen to a child I think breaks everybody. We do show all these different theories. They were all real working theories. Showing the chaos of it is something that we’ve not seen. It’s a new telling of it, because you’re like, “My God, is this really what was happening?” For your performance’s sake, did you decide what you thought happened? Yes. Just my personal feeling. My heart says no one in the family could have done that. I don’t have the ability, or probably the right, to say that, but that’s what my gut says. Which I probably am not supposed to say. But shooting that, I had to pick. I had to have that for myself, if nothing else. It’s such a heartbreaking and very physical performance as Patsy. In the two episodes I’ve seen, you’re crying so much. What was that like? It’s tricky. Luckily, I loved who I was working with. I’d never worked with Clive before — I can’t say enough good stuff about him. What a joy of a human. Everybody in the cast, every single person, they’re fantastic. It just felt elevated. And I felt like everybody knew that we had to do right by the story and not just try to do something that’s going to get a lot of views. That set was so serious, and some of those days were so hard. We had a psychologist on set at all times. You did? And it was needed sometimes, especially during some of the really intense scenes. It would take people down, and they’d just need a minute. I felt obligated to stand up for her, which — maybe it’s none of my damn business, but I feel protective of her. It makes you get up and go to work every day and try to give it your all. This show was filmed in Calgary, far from your home with Ben and your two teenage daughters. After the workday, were you taking Patsy with you? I had rather weird sleeping hours. It would depend on what the next day held, but I called my kids, for sure, and my husband, and made sure throughout the day I talked to them and checked in on days when I could. Some days I couldn’t. I didn’t want them to see me in that state. Sleep wasn’t always great when that’s what was in my head. But I was like, “Well, I bet she wasn’t sleeping great either. So get up! Get up.” As you prepare for the show to come out, what have you been thinking about? I think about the one thing I can’t control, which is how people will receive it. And, of course, you think about the family. My intentions don’t mean anything — their feelings are their feelings, and all I can do is hope that I did right by them and by Patsy. The only people that really get a vote are them. Patsy Ramsey died in 2006. But would you ever be interested in talking to John or Burke Ramsey? I would. Again, I don’t know if I’m supposed to say this: I’ve written John many letters that I haven’t sent. I wrote before we did it. I wrote, during the thing, to him and Burke — many letters — to be like, “I’m doing my best by her. I’m really trying to show who I felt she was.” “Bridesmaids”: Melissa McCarthy, Ellie Kemper, Rose Byrne, Wendi McLendon-Covey, Maya Rudolph, Kristen Wiig Courtesy of ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection You’ve excelled at drama, and this role is as dramatic as it gets. But you came up through the Groundlings, the improv and sketch program, where you met your husband, Ben Falcone, and “Bridesmaids” screenwriters Kristen Wiig and Annie Mumolo, along with so many other people you’ve gone on to work with. How did you get involved with the Groundlings? My very first stuff in New York was stand-up. I did all the free cheap rooms where you got a minute and a half, and you worked your way up to two and a half minutes and so on. But then I didn’t like those rooms anymore — I just found them really misogynistic. There was literally a guy in every room saying, “Show me your tits.” To the point where I was like, “Is it the same guy? The same lonely guy?” He’s not going to stop. The only way to make him stop is to eviscerate him. I was like, “I’m here to try to make people laugh, and now the only way I win is if I actually embarrass you. I see I’ve done that and now you’re quiet. So now I feel terrible.” I love live performance; it’s my favorite. But that realm was not. I didn’t want a fistfight. And then I moved to L.A., and my sister sent me a little magazine story about the Groundlings. I see. I was like, “Oh, there must be amazing theater in L.A.!,” because I’d never been here when I moved here. When I was doing stand-up, I didn’t really know how to write, so a lot of it was improvised. I also had a thing of like, “You’re not a writer unless you’ve been trained to write.” I would always go up with a paper, and I would do my monologue, and Ben was the first person that leans over and he goes, “Why do you always go up with a blank page?” I was like, “What? What are you talking about?” He’s like, “You go up with a blank page, you do a monologue.” I was like, “That’s not writing.” And he’s like, “It is writing.” I was like, “No, it’s not, because I don’t know how to write.” He’s like, “You just did a whole monologue, and then you wrote down what you said.” I had such a weird, I didn’t go to college — I’m not a writer. Groundlings literally taught me to be like, “OK: You are writing, you are doing this.” What was the “Bridesmaids” experience like once the movie came out? The fact that Kristen and Annie let me come in for that truly changed my life. I thought I blew the audition because I got too weird, because I was sitting there improvising with Kristen. I got too comfortable! I said weird things! Before “Bridesmaids” was released, people were like, “The numbers are not looking good.” And I was like, “It’s not out yet.” And they’re like, “We know how to do this, and the numbers are not looking good.” And I was like, “OK, but I’m just saying I think it’s really funny and I think people are going to think it’s really funny.” Opening night, Ben and I were sitting in Paul Feig’s backyard with him and his wife, Laurie, and we’re having dinner and Paul’s like, “Oh my God. Oh my God. I think it’s working! It’s working!” Then all of a sudden he’s like, “Every theater in L.A. is full. Get in the car, get in the car, get in the car!” We went to the ArcLight, I think? We just stood in the back, and it was rolling, crazy laughter. You, Ben, Paul and Laurie? Yes. We were like, “Oh my God, it’s working! What we think is funny is funny!” It was about that group of people; it was about the characters. Just running through theaters, and Paul in his suit — and Ben and I not dressed as nicely. No one does dress as nicely as Paul Feig. No, nobody. It also felt important — a comedy about women becoming such a massive success. Yes. Which is insane, but it did. Two women wrote it; we all felt like this is what’s funny . This is what we as women write about and talk about, and we are this weird. And it wasn’t about, “My dress isn’t perfect!” even though that was part of it. This is what trying on dresses really is like — it’s a bit of a shitshow. Literally. Well-played. As soon as the movie came out, people started saying you needed to be nominated for an Oscar — which you were! But that’s so uncommon for a comedy. What was that like? Disorienting. Now I can’t remember if Octavia’s name was said first or mine. Jim Rash and Nat Faxon were nominated for “The Descendants.” Kristen and Annie were nominated for screenplay — this was, like, our weird ragtag group. And I just kept saying “Octavia’s nominated!” Ben went, “Mooch, you just got nominated.” I was like, “I know Octavia got nominated for an Oscar!” And he was like, “ You just got nominated for an Oscar.” I was like, “I don’t think that’s true.” And he’s like, “We just watched it.” Then I just balled my eyes out. Right! That was the year Octavia Spencer, also your friend since the Groundlings days, won for “The Help.” And Jim and Nat won that year. We were all just there — and we were like, “What are we all doing here? This is amazing!” But our own Academy, our own industry, doesn’t respect comedy. I don’t know when that became the thing to do — and you can call any project a comedy to get into an awards category. Anybody just gets to claim it, because no real comedies are ever going to get awarded. I’m stopped 15 times a day by somebody who says, “I desperately need you to do another comedy.” And I’m like, “We are trying. I’m trying!” And people need it, that’s for sure. “The Heat”: Sandra Bullock and Melissa McCarthy ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection Can you talk about your creative partnership with Paul Feig? Paul should be legally bound to make one comedy at least every two years. His taste level as a filmmaker, his visual aesthetic, is so good — which is important. You have to make a proper film. It has to look good. It has to have great pacing. And he’s just funny as hell. He just wants to lift other people to be as funny and as good as you can possibly be. I miss him doing comedies — for myself, but also as an audience member. We’ve made it so hard to do comedies that we have our best and our funniest people not doing what they do. Why is that? I think the narrative of comedies don’t work anymore is bullshit. I think it’s absolute bullshit. It’s a false narrative. Comedy is like music. It’s a feeling — not everybody can do the same thing. Two equally incredible musicians have totally different styles. You don’t go in and break someone’s style or what they do; you have them do the best of what they can do. I think because people can laugh at a movie, for some reason, it’s less respected. And so they think, “Well, I know what’s funny.” And I always want to be like, “You’ve never been funny to me! You’ve never said anything funny. You’ve never thought of a funny idea.” It doesn’t mean you’re not great at your job — Are we talking about the executive level now? People at all the levels are now like, “Let me tell you who to put in to make it funny…” And I’m like, “Well, those four people aren’t funny.” It’s like Feig putting in Jason Statham in “Spy.” Oh God, yes! Paul and I went out to dinner with Statham, and we were just goofing around the table, and I was like, “Stop talking about it! Just do what you’re doing — it’s so funny.” But Paul had the idea to be like, “What about Statham?” But when you take all of the artists out of it — they start to do the math of it, and that’s not comedy. They want a big premise. But most really great comedies, it’s about the people and the characters and the story, and it’s not like, “And they were both aliens at the end!” But people really think they want that hook, and it’s just not real. Then they say comedies don’t work, and I’m like, “No, bad comedies don’t work.” And I won’t take the fall for that. “Spy” Melissa McCarthy and Jason Statham ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection To me, in a just world, “Spy” would be a franchise. We should be on the ninth “Spy”! Everyone on “Spy” was ready to re-rack immediately. There should be a new villain, new location. Why didn’t it happen? Because you’re a woman? No — well, Jesus, that probably doesn’t help, but I don’t know. It did so well. People can say that doesn’t matter. I think it does. For “Thunder Force,” we were going to roll right into another one. We were like, “It’s so fun. It did incredibly well for Netflix. We already have the idea for it.” If I write something — or Ben and I write something — and it tanks, I’ll take the fall. Which we have not had to take. We don’t make $8 billion. We don’t make those kind of movies, but, I mean, $120 million, I’m not mad at that. The studio’s not mad at that. We want to make a reasonably priced thing that makes you a good profit. For some reason, that model is no longer desirable. I can’t figure out the math of it. For the never-made “Bridesmaids 2,” I’d heard that Kristen and Annie’s idea was that was Lillian gets divorced, and there’s a divorce party. Why did that not happen? And how! That I don’t know. I know that was a hard movie to make. It was, but it was also so fun. Oh my God , it was so fun. Literally laughing on set in such a way that I am shocked that we shot stuff. Rose [Byrne] is such a wonderful, bad laugher. On the plane, her little stick arms are up, and when Ben and I are doing our weird thing, she just laughs out loud . It’s a glorious thing. She just kept putting the magazine up to hide — and it’s in the movie. So that was what shooting was like. It was like you were literally hiding because someone was always like, “Oh, I’ve dropped something,” because they’re under the table laughing. That’s just not a bad day. I don’t know. I think it’s gotten so corporate. I miss the people that work off their gut. When I think about the hellish world that we live in now, I can kind of trace it directly back to the backlash against “Ghostbusters” in 2016. [ Sighs ] What madness. It does really correlate! When people were like, “You’re ruining our childhood,” I was like, “You definitely seem like you had a terrible childhood.” It just had so many cooks in that kitchen. Katie Dippold co-wrote “Ghostbusters” with Paul Feig — for her “Widow’s Bay” triumph. Oh my God , I loved her show. I almost got nervous, like, “It’s so good. Is it not going to do well?” And I ate it up. I couldn’t get enough fast enough. Then I just started hearing person after person be like, “Have you watched this thing?” It is not shocking that Katie Dippold wrote something incredible. I’m just like, who’s the genius that backed off and let her? “Gilmore Girls”: Melissa McCarthy and Lauren Graham ©CW Network/Courtesy Everett Collection Sookie on “Gilmore Girls” was your first big role. It’s not easy to do Amy Sherman-Palladino dialogue! It’s good training, I tell you that! What was that experience like when you look back on it? It was hard! It was really hard. But to me, that was normal, because it was my first show. So I was like, “Oh, our scripts are 93 pages, and you can’t change a contraction, even if you get them that morning and it’s a 10-page oner.” And that’s just what it was. I love that she had her own style, and I love that she built that world. I love that she fought for it, because a woman running that show at that time, I think you kind of had to be like, “It’s my way or the highway.” I think she had to probably fight to keep it the way she wanted to. And I’m glad she did, because it stood the test of time. People really take ownership of that show. So huge with Gen Z. And the fact that they keep re-watching it. I’m like, “Really?” It’s so funny, my kids have not watched it. But Vivian and I were both home with the flu — this is years ago. And it came on and she was like, “That’s your show, right? That was your first show?” I was like, “You’re on the very end of that show when I’m pregnant.” I think I’d had four kids on the show. And then I finally went to Amy and I’m like, “I’m actually pregnant. You can have me have another kid again, and I’ll give you the prop for free.” And she was like, “No, I don’t think so.” So then I had to hide it! I was like, “We already have four kids. I can’t have five?” But we watched just the pilot, and Vivi, my oldest, she kept going, “What are you doing with your voice?” And I was like, “Oh, it’s youth.” She’s like, “That doesn’t sound like you at all.” I was like, “Yeah! I was youthful and I didn’t have kids yet. And now I sound like this grizzled old man.” Courtesy of The CW You did one day on the Netflix revival, “Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life.” It was fun to see everybody again. I still see Lauren [Graham] and Yanic [Truesdale]. We’ve gone on vacation with Yanic. We’re really close. I just wanted to go and see everybody. So it was really nice to do. I always wonder, will something else happen with that? I don’t know anything about it, but — Amy has done a ton, but it’s kind of her life’s work, right? When something catches like that, there’s no rhyme or reason. You have to just love it. I mean, I’m always shocked at all the “Gilmore” comments when I’m out. I’m like, “I’ve worked since then!” But it is nice. And I think we all are very aware of that, or I hope so. But when something catches like that, like “That’s my comfort show,” or, “That’s what I watch going to sleep” — what a thing to get to do something that gives people comfort like that. Totally. It’s the coziest. It’s the coziest! I felt lucky doing it, and I feel lucky to have been a part of it. Courtesy of Joyful Heart Foundation Charity Spotlight: Joyful Heart Foundation Melissa McCarthy remembers meeting Mariska Hargitay the old-fashioned way: through their assistants. Hargitay, McCarthy says, seemed like someone who “probably has her shit together” enough to make recommendations for, say, “a good water filtration system.” Their texting relationship soon blossomed into a real-life friendship, which, McCarthy says, “doesn’t always happen when you meet a new friend in your 50s.” As Hargitay puts it, “When we finally did meet in person, our hearts did a dance.” Their dynamic is a playful one. When Hargitay rolled her ankle and needed surgery in July 2021, McCarthy stood on a Burbank street holding a sign asking drivers to honk to speed up the “SVU” star’s recovery. And earlier this year, McCarthy surprised Hargitay by doing a cameo on “SVU.” (“I still don’t know how they pulled it off,” Hargitay says.) For her Power of Women charity, McCarthy is putting a spotlight on Joyful Heart Foundation, which — inspired by the subject matter of “SVU” — Hargitay began in 2004 to advocate for survivors of sexual assault, domestic violence and child abuse. While other actors might have just said, “This is what I do for a living,” McCarthy says, Hargitay instead embraced it as a responsibility. “Her power is through kindness and consideration and a moral compass.” For Hargitay’s part, she says of McCarthy, “It’s a gift to find someone who’s willing to roll up their sleeves and help bring change.” Styling: Katja Cahill; Stylist assistants: Aliya Iahijani, Tracey Moore; Tailor: Daniela Kurrle; Makeup: Afton Williams; Hair: Mark Townsend/Forward Artists; Dress: L’Academie, Hat: Sadie James, Cape: Viviano; Earrings: KerenWolf, Spectrum Jewels , and Mindi Mond New York; Rings: On Aura Tout Vu, Spectrum Jewels, Le Vian Jewelry and Zales;Necklaces: Zales and Sterling Forever; Bracelets: Zales and Sterling Forever Loading comments... articles.full_text: Sep 21, 2026 8:41am PT David Oyelowo and Nate Parker’s Mansa Studios Partners With Macro Television Studios to Produce Vertical Series By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Executive Editor franklinavenue Latest Sony TV North America Distribution Executive Vice President Flory Bramnick Plans to Depart After 24 Years (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago ‘The View’ Season 30 Launches With Best Premiere Week Ratings in Six Years (EXCLUSIVE) 5 days ago As ‘American Idol’ Leaves Los Angeles for Atlanta, More Concerns Emerge About the State of Local Production 6 days ago See All Mansa Studios Mansa Studios, the media company co-founded by David Oyelowo and Nate Parker, has partnered with Macro Television Studios to develop, finance and produce various vertical series, the two companies announced Monday. Macro and Mansa will develop, market and promote the projects coming out of the partnership, while also share ownership of the intellectual property. “Mansa has developed real expertise in the emerging vertical format, and we see this as an exciting opportunity to pair that experience with Maceo Television Studios’ vast capabilities across genres,” said Macro founder/CEO Charles D. King in a statement. “We are looking forward to learning from the collaboration and seeing how audiences respond and explore innovation opportunities for the format.” Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony Mansa already distributes film, TV and short-form content across platforms including its own free ad-supported streaming service and FAST channels. Popular on Variety “Mansa was created to ensure that culturally rich stories can reach audiences wherever they are,” said Mansa Studios co-founder Oyelowo in a statement. “As viewing habits evolve, we are embracing new storytellers, formats and platforms that allow us to remain connected to our global audience while creating meaningful opportunities for a diverse array of talent.” Macro most recently worked with Oyelowo as a producer on Apple TV’s “Government Cheese,” which starred the actor. Macro TV Studios, a division of Macro founded in 2015, recently produced Netflix’s “Raising Dion” (nominated for a Children’s & Family Emmy) and Netflix’s “Gentefied,” which was nominated for a Peabody Award. The company also produced FX’s docuseries “Dear Mama: The Saga of Afeni and Tupac Shakur,” which was nominated for a Primetime Emmy and for a Grammy Award. Macro is also behind Macro Film Studios, in-house branding and creative agency Brand Macro, talent firm M88 and affiliated venture firm MaCVenture Capital. articles.title: Eagle Eye Drama Acquires ‘The Great Dictator’, Matthew Sweet’s Biography Of Barbara Cartland
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse BBC Drama ‘Ministry Of Time’ Adds Adeel Akhtar, Ciaran Hinds & Eight More To Cast Eagle Eye Drama Acquires ‘The Great Dictator’, Matthew Sweet’s Biography Of Barbara Cartland Princess Di Returns To ‘SNL UK’ As “Deeply Intelligent, Autonomous, Neurokinetic Android” In Cold Open Skewering King Charles, Ed Sheeran & AI View All September 21, 2026 2:29am 'The Great Dictator' ITV Studios EXCLUSIVE: Eagle Eye Drama has acquired the rights to The Great Dictator , Matthew Sweet ‘s biography of the flamboyant and eccentric late Dame Barbara Cartland . Historian, novelist and screenwriter Sweet’s book tells the story of author known as ‘The Queen of Romance’ Cartland, who was one of the UK’s most recognizable figures across the 20th century. She was famous for dressing in pink and taking her Pekinese dogs with her wherever she went. Born in 1901, Cartland was a fixture of British high society, rubbing shoulders with press barons, politicians, the aristocracy and the Royal Family, as step-grandmother to Princess Diana. Related Stories Cancellations and Renewals Mark Gatiss Drama 'Bookish' Returning For Third Chapter & Festive Special Acquisitions HBO Max Buys Mark Gatiss Series 'Bookish' For Australia As Sales Pass The 100-Territory Mark Bookish co-writer Sweet’s book, published this month by Hodder & Stoughton, is the result of years of research into her life. It has been positively reviewed by the likes of The Guardian, The Times and documentarian Louis Theroux, and ITV Studios-owned Eagle Eye will now look to adapt the story of the ‘woman in pink’, whose romance novels sold close to a billion copies in 38 languages. Watch on Deadline Eagle Eye Drama CEO Walter Iuzzolino said: “Matthew Sweet gained unparalleled access to the Cartland family archives, and what he has uncovered is a story more compelling and unbelievable than her most outlandish plots, which will provide a wonderful bedrock to build an unmissable scripted series.” Eagle Eye CCO Jo McGrath added that Cartland was the third-biggest selling author of all time, behind only William Shakespeare and Agatha Christie, adding she would be a “gift of a role for a great actress.” “Known for her outlandish pink chiffon clothes and thick Meltonian black shoe cream mascara, she is a figure who has been loved and scorned in equal measure,” said McGrath. “She was a ferocious champion of romantic love with a less than idyllic and rather scandalous love life of her own. “A friend of Winston Churchill, she dined with Margaret Thatcher – to whom she prescribed alternative remedies and oxygen supplements – and of course the step-grandmother to Princess Diana, who loved her books as a young woman.” Sweet, whose series Bookish is produced through Eagle Eye, said: “I feel like I’ve been caught up in a pink chiffon whirlwind in the last few days, with the reviews and the Baillie Gifford longlist. Now Eagle Eye Drama has acquired the rights to bring The Great Dictator to television. They are the perfect producers and I know they will bring Barbara’s world to life with impeccable style.” Eagle Eye is arguably best known for Bookish , the light crime series in which Mark Gatiss plays a closeted post-war detective. It was renewed for a third season and festive special last month. The production house also makes Channel 4’s The Couple Next Door and the high-rating Patience and Ben Miller drama Professor T for ITV. It is also adapting ITV’s forthcoming Richard Armitage crime series Winter after secured the rights to the book. Tom Perrin, Editorial Consultant, Hodder & Stoughton, noted The Great Dictator had been “a runaway success” since publication and had been longlisted for the Baillie Gifford Prize. Cartland’s life has been the subject of many documentaries, while Anne Reid starred as the author in the BBC’s 2008 telemovie In Love with Barbara . articles.title: BBC Removes Blackface Sketches From ‘That Mitchell And Webb Look’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake David Walliams Fully Dropped By Publisher As It Emerges He Is No Longer Being Actively Repped By TV Agent Tilly Norwood Malfunctions During Piers Morgan Interview: “Seems I Had A Little Hiccup” ‘Doctor Who’ Re-Gen Is Go! BBC Calls On Producers To Pitch “Brave” New Vision For Sci-Fi Series View All September 21, 2026 2:47am 'That Mitchell And Webb Look' BBC The BBC has cut Blackface and other sketches from That Mitchell and Webb Look after making the comedy series available on iPlayer. The British broadcaster recently reinstated That Mitchell and Webb Look online to mark its 20th anniversary, but eagle-eyed Reddit users pointed out that the broadcaster had removed sketches. As many as 11 sketches are said to have been expunged from the BBC Studios-produced series, starring Peep Show actors David Mitchell and Robert Webb . A BBC spokesperson said: “ That Mitchell and Webb Look has been made available on BBC iPlayer. This is a 20-year-old sketch show; in consultation with the programme makers, we have included the ones that still work today and not the ones that don’t.” Related Stories News ZDF Boards BBC Drama 'Shy & Lola' Featuring 'Harry Potter' & 'Night Manager' Stars News 'Doctor Who' Re-Gen Is Go! BBC Calls On Producers To Pitch "Brave" New Vision For Sci-Fi Series Cut sketches include one in which Mitchell and Webb play English Civil War re-enactors who have grown bored of their roles and recreate a conflict between government forces in the Democratic Republic of Congo and a rebel militia. Watch on Deadline Mitchell asks: “Are you absolutely sure that this isn’t racist?” They agree to stop the reenactment at the first sign of racism. When one threatens the other with a machete, they halt the reenactment, concluding: “It’s racist. Very, very racist. Shame.” In another sketch, Webb and Olivia Colman parody a makeover show and are confronted by a woman in a burqa. It then cuts to Webb discussing whether the sketch is offensive, with the woman in the burqa removing her garment to reveal Mitchell in Blackface. British comedian Dom Jolly told The Times of London that the cuts were “hysterical censorship,” but the BBC is being consistent in deleting the scenes. The BBC previously removed Little Britain and Mighty Boosh from iPlayer in similar circumstances. Discovery Read the full story By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse BBC Drama ‘Ministry Of Time’ Adds Adeel Akhtar, Ciaran Hinds & Eight More To Cast Eagle Eye Drama Acquires ‘The Great Dictator’, Matthew Sweet’s Biography Of Barbara Cartland Princess Di Returns To ‘SNL UK’ As “Deeply Intelligent, Autonomous, Neurokinetic Android” In Cold Open Skewering King Charles, Ed Sheeran & AI View All September 21, 2026 3:00am Clockwise Top L-R: Hong Chau, Adeel Akhtar, Tamara Lawrence, Emily Fairn, Josh Finan, Hélène Patarot, Ciarán Hinds, Nahuel Pérez Biscayart, Tawfeek Barhom and Aisling Loftus Chris Pizzello, Sarah Cresswell, Pip, Phil Sharp, Ruth Crafer, Liam Murphy, Roch Armando, Bertie Watson BAFTA winner Adeel Akhtar ( Sherwood ) and Academy Award nominee Ciarán Hinds ( Belfast ) have joined the cast of A24 ‘s BBC drama series Ministry of Time . Also announced this morning are Hong Chau ( The Whale ), Tamara Lawrance ( Get Millie Black ), Emily Fairn ( The Responder ), Josh Finan ( Say Nothing ), Aisling Loftus ( Sherwood ), Tawfeek Barhom ( Cairo Conspiracy ) and Nahuel Pérez Biscayart ( 120 Beats Per Minute ) and Hélène Patarot ( Paris, Je T’aime ). They join Aoife Hinds and Billy Howle in the series, which is based on Kaliane Bradley’s debut novel of the same name. Alice Birch ( Normal People ) is adapting the show, with Aneil Karia ( Top Boy ) is lead director on the six-part series, which is produced by Beef and Dreaming Whilst Black maker A24 for BBC iPlayer and BBC One. Related Stories News BBC Removes Blackface Sketches From 'That Mitchell And Webb Look' News 'You Can See Everything': A24 Solidifies October Release Date For Elizabeth Holmes Documentary The show follows the professional friendship between Sophy (Hinds) and Graham (Howle), which “develops into an intense forbidden romance that reveals the transporting power of love across centuries, just as the sinister nature of the Ministry’s true intentions increasingly puts them in danger.” Watch on Deadline Akhtar will play Quentin Ackerly, Sophy’s ‘handler’ at The Ministry, and while Aoife Hinds’ her real-life dad Ciarán will be Sophy’s father, Peter, with her mother, Patarot playing her on-screen mom Channary. Hong will play Adela, the Vice-Secretary of Expatriation; Lawrance is Simellia, a ‘bridge’ alongside Sophy; Fairn will one of Commander Gore’s fellow ‘expats’, Margaret Kemble; Finan plays Captain Arthur Reginald-Smyth and Aisling Loftus is Anne Spencer. Barhom and Pérez Biscayart also star as the elusive Brigadier and Salese. Filming on the six-part show is currently taking place in and around London, UK. A24 is executive producing alongside Birch, Bradley, Karia and Jo McClellan for the BBC. Frances du Pille is the producer and A24 has international distribution rights. articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival Cancels  2026 Edition
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Dubai Film Festival To Return In December 2027, As 2026 Edition Of Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival Looks Uncertain Israeli Film Council Calls For Festivals To Be Removed From Funding Criteria & Creation Of Strand For Films Celebrating Israeli Soldiers Amid ‘NAZA’ Firestorm Oscars: France Selects ‘Minotaur’ For Best International Feature Film Race View All September 21, 2026 3:00am Alessandra Ambrosio attends the Closing Night red carpet at the Red Sea International Film Festival 2025 Getty images Saudi Arabia ‘s Red Sea Film Foundation has cancelled the 2026 edition of the Red Sea International Film Festival , saying in a statement that the sixth edition had been postponed to the fourth quarter of 2027. The announcement follows weeks of speculation over whether the 2026 edition, scheduled to unfold from December 3-12 in the Red Sea port city of Jeddah, would take place amid tensions across the entire Gulf region due to the U.S.-Israeli-Iran war. Aside from retaliatory strikes on neighboring territories, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman, Iran has also sought to take control of the Strait of Hormuz connecting the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, a key shipping route for their oil and other goods. Related Stories Festivals Dubai Film Festival To Return In December 2027, As 2026 Edition Of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea Film Festival Looks Uncertain News Saudi Arabia To Invest $7 Billion In Three Theme Parks Near Paris Beyond direct threats from Iran, Saudi Arabia is also dealing with a flareup in its conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi group in recent weeks. Watch on Deadline The foundation did not mention the geopolitical tensions saying rather that the decision “followed a comprehensive review of a range of considerations relating to the timing of the next edition, including the logistical requirements involved in staging an international event of this scale.” Since the event’s launch in 2021, in the wake of Saudi Arabia’s lifting of its 35-year cinema ban at the end of 2017, it has grown into the Gulf region’s main film festival with a steady flow of high-profile Hollywood guests, burgeoning industry events, and wide Middle East and international participation. Aside from geopolitical tensions beyond its control, the festival has also been subject to internal debate about its future direction in recent months. In June, the foundation’s longtime Managing Director Shivani Pandya Malhotra, who helped spearhead the launch of the festival having joined the body in 2019, stepped down with a number of her close team members leaving as well. In the backdrop, there are also wider questions around Saudi Arabia’s larger commitment to the film industry, with the country’s entertainment focus shifting to the video game sector and sports such as boxing and soccer. The foundation made it clear in its statement that the festival will be back for sixth edition in 2027 with “a renewed vision and a programme that continues to celebrate cinema and filmmakers from Saudi Arabia, the region and around the world.” It also emphasized that it will continue its year-round mission of supporting filmmakers and strengthening the film industries through the Red Sea Fund, Red Sea Labs and its wider programmes and initiatives. As part of this continued commitment, the foundation said it will introduce year-round programming at Culture Square in Jeddah from November 2026, establishing it as an ongoing destination for film screenings, cultural events and specialised film-industry programmes. “The Red Sea Film Foundation extends its sincere appreciation to filmmakers, partners, guests and audiences for their continued trust and support. We look forward to welcoming the global film community back to Historic Jeddah in 2027 for a sixth edition that celebrates cinema, creativity and cultural dialogue,” concluded its statement. In the meantime, Gulf neighbor the United Arab Emirates announced last week that it is reviving the Dubai International Film Festival following a 10-year hiatus, with a scheduled December 8, 2027 opening date, which could see it clash with the Red Sea. In the backdrop, Qatar’s Doha Film Festival is pushing on with plans for its second edition running this November 19-27, 2026. articles.title: CNN, MS NOW And Politico To Sue Donald Trump Over His White House Ban
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted CNN, MS NOW And Politico To Sue Donald Trump Over His White House Ban CNN, MS NOW And Politico Journalists Denied White House Entry; Colleagues Condemn Trump’s Ban Judge Says Kennedy Center Must Give Court 30 Days Notice Of Any Demolition Plans After Trump Floats Prospect It Could Be “Ripped Down” View All September 21, 2026 3:43am Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images UPDATED: CNN , Politico and MS NOW are suing Donald Trump and other White House officials after the president banned him from the complex. In the lawsuit, the news outlets are asking a federal judge to immediately restore their access, which was denied on Saturday, a day after Trump announced he was restricting them from entry to the White House grounds. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.” The new organizations said in a joint statement, “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” Related Stories Politics Sylvester Stallone Told Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship Was "Impossible" But Was Appointed Anyway: "It Won't Work" News Alan Ritchson On The 'Reacher' Season That Was Canceled After "Someone Got Re-Elected" The White House also removed CNN from the White House pool on Monday, the day it was scheduled to be the primary network for their coverage. As a result, there will be no TV pool on a day when Trump is traveling to New York, signaling that other networks declined to serve as replacements because of the president’s targeting of CNN. Watch on Deadline The news outlets state in their lawsuit, “The President banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and the individual reporters covering the news for those media organizations, in disregard of the most basic guarantees of the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause. He did so expressly for the improper purpose of retaliating against Plaintiffs for past news coverage because he deemed it ‘negative’ and chilling future reporting about him and his administration’s policies and actions. “President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration. But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting. The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained.” The lawsuit claims violation of the Fifth Amendment’s due process clause and First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. The outlets are seeking a temporary restraining order and injunction to prohibit the ban from being enforced and to require that their access be restored, as well as a declaratory ruling. The outlets are represented from Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., who represented CNN’s Jim Acosta when his credentials were revoked in Trump’s first term, as well as others at Gibson Dunn, including Katie Townsend and Patrick Fuster. In addition to the impact of the ban on their own news organizations, the outlets argue in the lawsuit that it “inflicts an injury on all news media organizations—who now risk a similar fate if they engage in reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable. And the public at large suffers for however long the unconstitutional ban restricts access to current and complete information about their government. These irreparable harms should not be tolerated for a day longer. The Court should immediately enjoin enforcement of the ban.” The lawsuit also names White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Secret Service Director Sean Curran and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. Shortly after the lawsuit was announced, Trump posted on Truth Social, “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” In 2018, in the case of Acosta, a federal judge ruled that precedent required that the White House give proper notice of a revocation. In the 1977 D.C. Circuit opinion, Sherrill vs. Knight, the judges ruled that “the protection afforded newsgathering under the First Amendment guarantee of freedom of the press requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons.” The White House has yet to provide a legal justification for revoking the credentials of the news outlets. On ABC’s This Week on Sunday, host Jon Karl pressed House Majority Leader Steve Scalise on Trump’s ban. “Do you support him banning these news organizations because he doesn’t like what they are reporting?” Karl asked. Scalise deflected, pointing to Trump’s accessibility to the media and claimed that Joe Biden removed the press credentials from more than 400 news organizations. In fact, the Biden White House established new criteria for credentialing, based in part on how often holders had used the hard passes and that they had full time employment and residency in the D.C. area. It was not based on a news organization’s viewpoint, although the changes were made after one correspondent had repeatedly interrupted press briefings. Karl told Scalise that they “were not banned from the White House.” He then asked Scalise whether Trump’s ban violates the First Amendment, but Scalise again did not answer. Karl moved on to another topic. Discovery Read the full story By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Movistar Plus Announces 2027 Slate, Including JA Bayona & Fernando León Projects, At San Sebastián Naomi Watts Says She’d Like To Work With Paul Thomas Anderson & Praises The Advancements Older Women Have Made In Hollywood — San Sebastián San Sebastián Opens With Political Declarations And Tributes To Werner Herzog & Outgoing Festival Director José Luis Rebordinos View All September 21, 2026 5:18am We have the first trailer for David Fincher’s latest, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth . Directed by Fincher from a screenplay by Quentin Tarantino , the film will premiere in IMAX on November 25 for a two-week engagement, followed by its release on the streamer on December 23. Pitt, who earned an Oscar for his role as Cliff Booth, returns to play the character, but this time it’s 1977, and Hollywood looks very different. The film is a follow-up to Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood . The film also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, and Peter Weller. Related Stories News JoAnna Garcia Swisher Thanks 'Sweet Magnolias' Team For Giving Her "Somewhere To Belong" News Ben Affleck Nearly Cast Ex Jennifer Garner As His Wife In 'Animals': "You Just Get Baggage" Once Upon a Time in Hollywood premiered in 2019 and was written and directed by Quentin Tarantino. The film featured a cast that included Pitt, Leonardo DiCaprio, Margot Robbie, Austin Butler, Dakota Fanning, Timothy Olyphant, Mike Moh, Margaret Qualley, Al Pacino, Emile Hirsch, Bruce Dern, Luke Perry, and many others. Watch on Deadline Pitt’s Cliff Booth plays a stunt double and DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton’s best friend, driver, and personal assistant. Cliff is a World War II special ops veteran who lives in a trailer with his pit bull. The character struggles to find work following an altercation with Bruce Lee and rumors that he killed his wife. Tarantino’s film went on to win two Academy Awards: one for Pitt in Best Supporting Actor and another for Barbara Ling and Nancy Haigh for Best Production Design. Buzz for Cliff Booth has been building since it was announced in 2024 that Pitt and Fincher were teaming on the project that Tarantino originally wanted to direct. Once Tarantino gave his blessing for Fincher to come aboard, Netflix was the obvious stop given the director’s exclusive deal there. Watch the trailer above. articles.title: ‘Stuff The British Stole’ Producer WildBear Entertainment Reshuffles Top Team To “Get Ahead” Of Industry Transformation
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse ‘Stuff The British Stole’ Producer WildBear Entertainment Reshuffles Top Team To “Get Ahead” Of Industry Transformation BBC Drama ‘Ministry Of Time’ Adds Adeel Akhtar, Ciaran Hinds & Eight More To Cast Eagle Eye Drama Acquires ‘The Great Dictator’, Matthew Sweet’s Biography Of Barbara Cartland View All September 21, 2026 5:36am L-R: Craig Meade, Michael Tear, Harriet Pike, Serge Ou and Alan Erson WildBear Entertainment EXCLUSIVE: Australian factual producer WildBear Entertainment has unveiled a new look for its management team amid “the biggest transformation we’ve seen in decades” for the entertainment industry. A eight-strong team will lead activities the company, which is known for the likes of Stuff the British Stole , Rise of the Dictators and Every Little Thing . WildBear co-founder Michael Tear will remain CEO, and under him will be join co-founder Serge Ou, who becomes Head of Creative Services, leading on production, post-production, design and visual effects. Alan Erson takes on a newly created role as Managing Director of Premium Television, and will oversee the WildBear factual slate and creative strategy. Related Stories News 'Stuff The British Stole' Presenter Marc Fennell To Lead 'Manosphere' Doc 'The State Of Man' For Australia's ABC News 'Stuff The British Stole' Doc Series Adapted As Scripted TV Heist Caper; Wooden Horse, Warner Bros, Anchuli Felicia King & Ben Chessell Attached Exec producer Craig Meade is upped to Head of International TV and Harriet Pike segues from COO to Chief Strategy and Growth Officer, which WildBear is calling a “pivotal new role.” Pike will oversee international activities and expand her to include digital and post services, catalog and rights and commercial opportunities. Watch on Deadline Both Meade and Pike will work with distributor Wild Thring Media on new commissioning opportunities, co-productions and global potential of WildBear’s content. Rounding out the new-look top team are Caroline Nicols, who is Chief Financial Officer, Matt Nightingale, who becomes Head of Production and Miranda Kelly, who is Head of Production Finance. WildBear is one of Australia’s oldest factual-focused producers, having started life more than four decades ago. The company now has around 100 staff across Australia and New Zealand, and it currently produces around 150 hours a year. “Our industry is undergoing the biggest transformation we’ve seen in decades and while WildBear has always quietly weathered every change, the time felt right to really get ahead of things, analyse all the forces at work and decide how we best want to meet the challenges ahead to steer our own future,” said Tear. “The new leadership structure brings together some of the strongest creative and commercial talent in Australia and sends a clear message to the market about our abilities and intentions. It gives us the focus to continue producing bold, world-class factual content at scale – telling ambitious true stories for a range of audiences – while expanding internationally, building new partnerships and creating greater long-term cross-platform value from our intellectual property, rights and creative services.” ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $60M Open Hollywood Turns Out For Opening: Inside The Event, Plus Photos & Video ‘Ride Or Die’ Canceled By Prime Video After One Season, Being Shopped By Paramount ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Oscar-Predictive TIFF People’s Choice Award Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Networks Halt TV Pool Coverage Of Trump In Protest Of President’s Ban On CNN
articles.full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted CNN, MS NOW And Politico To Sue Donald Trump Over His White House Ban CNN, MS NOW And Politico Journalists Denied White House Entry; Colleagues Condemn Trump’s Ban Judge Says Kennedy Center Must Give Court 30 Days Notice Of Any Demolition Plans After Trump Floats Prospect It Could Be “Ripped Down” View All September 21, 2026 7:16am Donald Trump Getty When Donald Trump travels to New York on Monday, there will be no primary TV pool, after major networks declined to replace CNN in the regular rotation after it was banned from White House and other coverage of the president. CNN was scheduled to serve as the pool network, but the White House released a schedule late Sunday showing that was no longer the case. On Friday, Trump announced a ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW from White House access because of their negative coverage of him. The five major networks in the pool — CNN, Fox News , ABC, NBC and CBS — indicated that there would be no such TV coverage as long as the restrictions remain in place. Related Stories News CNN, MS NOW And Politico To Sue Donald Trump Over His White House Ban Politics Sylvester Stallone Told Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship Was "Impossible" But Was Appointed Anyway: "It Won't Work" “This is to advise that, effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the president,” read a message from Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who is currently chairing the pool. “This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties. There will be no replacement pool put in place.” Watch on Deadline He added, “All other pool coverage will continue as normal, including Congress, VIPs, and selected events in Washington and around this country. We will provide further updates as this situation develops.” The network boycott of the pool is taking place during an eventful week: Trump is addressing the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday. Later in the week, he will host Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, including for a state dinner. In a statement, the five networks in the TV pool stated, “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.” The network pool distributes video and audio to other outlets, a system designed to rotate responsibilities and costs while gaining access where space is limited. Earlier today, CNN, Politico and MS NOW announced that they were filing a lawsuit against Trump and other members of the administration, claiming First Amendment retaliation and violation of due process. The lawsuit seeks a restoration of journalists’ access and credentials. Print, photo and radio pool coverage is scheduled to continue, as well as secondary TV poolers.
