articles.title: Alfonso Cuaron to Make First Korea Visit at Busan as Festival Also Spotlights European Women+ Filmmakers
articles.full_text: Sep 17, 2026 11:43pm PT Alfonso Cuaron to Make First Korea Visit at Busan as Festival Also Spotlights European Women+ Filmmakers By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Japan’s Top Broadcasters Unite for First Joint Delegation to MipCancun (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ 2 hours ago ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’ 4 hours ago See All Michelle Quance The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has announced the first-ever Korea visit by Alfonso Cuarón, alongside a dedicated spotlight on nine films from European women and genderqueer filmmakers. Cuarón, who has won the Academy Award for best director twice, for “Gravity” (2013) and “Roma” (2018), also holds the Venice Film Festival’s best screenplay prize for “Y Tu Mamá También” (2001) and a Golden Lion for “Roma.” He first caught Hollywood’s attention with “Y Tu Mamá También,” a portrait of youth and desire, before taking “Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban” (2004) in a moodier, more personal visual direction than the series had gone before, and later used extended long takes in “Children of Men” (2007) to pull audiences directly into a world at war. He is expected to appear at BIFF’s opening ceremony and will sit down for an extended conversation with festivalgoers about the camera language and instincts behind his films. An Imax screening of “Gravity,” co-written with his son, filmmaker Jonás Cuarón, will also be at the festival. Related Stories ‘On Behalf of My Son’ Director Gabriel Martins on Black Brazilian Representation in His Films: ‘It’s a Life Project To Me, Not Just Cinema’ BBC, Bobby Prod, Folivari, Gao Shan Pictures Honored by Europe's Animation Industry at Cartoon Forum Jonás Cuarón’s latest feature, “Campeón Gabacho,” will have its Asian premiere in the World Cinema section, followed by a post-screening Q&A. Since writing on “Gravity,” the younger Cuarón has built his own filmography with “Desierto” (2015) and “Chupa” (2023). “Campeón Gabacho,” starring Juan Daniel García Treviño, Leslie Grace, Rubén Blades, Eddie Marsan, Rosario Dawson and Cheech Marin, follows a Mexican immigrant building a life in the United States, and was produced by Jonás Cuarón alongside his father and Gabriela Rodriguez under their Esperanto Filmoj banner, with Nicolás Celis also producing. Popular on Variety Elsewhere at the festival, BIFF is showcasing “Europe! Voices of Women+ in Film,” a program run with the European Film Promotion (EFP), spotlighting nine officially selected films through targeted promotion and industry networking. The lineup spans period drama, documentary and contemporary narrative work built around questions of freedom, memory and family, with four of the nine as feature debuts. May el-Toukhy ‘s “Woman Unknown,” winner of the Golden Lion at Venice, anchors the group; el-Toukhy became the first Danish woman filmmaker to take that prize, while Mathilde Arcel won the Volpi Cup for best actress in the same film. Also included are Marine Atlan’s debut “La Gradiva,” Pegah Ahangarani’s “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime,” winner of the Un Certain Regard Prize at Cannes, Margherita Ferrari’s debut “Föa – Once Upon a Future,” Isabelle Stever’s “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming,” Marie Kreutzer’s “Gentle Monster,” Shahrbanoo Sadat’s “No Good Men” and Sarah Arnold’s debut “Too Many Beasts.” Judith Godrèche’s “A Girl’s Story,” part of this year’s gala presentations, joins Angela Schanelec’s “My Wife Cries,” Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak’s “Birds of War,” Jacqueline Lentzou’s “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra,” winner of the Horizons Award for Best Director at Venice, and Konstantina Kotzamani’s “Titanic Ocean” among the additional selections. Five directors from the program, el-Toukhy, Godrèche, Ferrari, Lentzou and Kotzamani, will travel to Busan to present their films. Godrèche will also take part in a Cine Class session, “Women, Rewriting the Screen,” and BIFF and EFP will co-host a Talk-to-Talk panel, “Women Directors: Taking the Scene,” bringing together Ferrari, el-Toukhy and Lentzou alongside Iranian director Marjan Khosravi (“Dreams of the Wild Oaks”), Chinese director Michelle Zhou (“Big Little Things”) and Afghan director Zainab Entezar (“771 Days”). BIFF programmer Seo Seunghee said that in reviewing films for this year’s festival, she noticed European women directors becoming more prominent among the strongest titles under consideration, in both volume and quality. “Moreover, the fact that four of the nine invited films are feature debuts is also an indicator of the generational shift taking place in European cinema,” Seo said. “Our ongoing collaboration with EFP has become a reliable channel for discovering and validating outstanding films and filmmakers, and the results are fully reflected in this year’s lineup.” EFP managing director Irina Ignatiew-Lemke said the “Europe! Voices of Women+ in Film” initiative lets EFP and its member organizations “join forces to give distinctive European voices greater international visibility.” She added, “Busan is an important platform for bringing these filmmakers and their works into dialogue with audiences and industry professionals in Asia. By combining the festival’s selection with EFP’s targeted promotion and networking, we are proud to support underrepresented voices and create opportunities for the next generation of women+ filmmakers.” The program runs in collaboration with BIFF, the Sydney Film Festival and Festival do Rio, with support from the Creative Europe – MEDIA Programme of the European Union. This year’s participating national film promotion organizations are Austrian Films, Cinecittà, the Czech Film Center, the Danish Film Institute, German Films and Unifrance, with Cineuropa serving as media partner. The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15 at the Busan Cinema Center and venues throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13. articles.title: ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’
articles.full_text: Sep 18, 2026 1:41am PT ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Japan’s Top Broadcasters Unite for First Joint Delegation to MipCancun (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ 2 hours ago ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’ 4 hours ago See All Netflix Competitive Bollywood fusion dance has thrived on American college campuses for decades, but it has rarely been the subject of a scripted feature film. Lena Khan ‘s “ Best of the Best ,” premiering Friday on Netflix , follows childhood best friends Maya and Anjali as they join UCLA’s competitive dance team, only to discover that the road to the U.S. Championship is far more raucous and cutthroat than they imagined. Related Stories EbonyLife's Mo Abudu on TIFF Premiere 'The Secret Lives of Baba Segi's Wives' and 'the Consequences of the Decisions We Take as Women' TIFF Takeaways: A Chris Rock Crowd-Pleaser, Peter Farrelly's 'Rocky' Standing Ovation and Market Growing Pains Written by Hasan Minhaj and Prashanth Venkataramanujam, who each competed in similar circuits growing up, the script drew Khan in even though she was not initially sure she would take on the project. Early on, she recalls mentioning it to a childhood friend, who was dismissive. “Bollywood competitions, really?” the friend said, and made it seem like it was not that cool, according to Khan, who says the reaction reflects something broader. “I think South Asians, especially in the diaspora, are so used to not even having our own self-respect.” Popular on Variety That realization shaped how she approached the film’s tone. “We have so much respect for the skill sets of other cultures. We’re looking at kung fu, we’re looking at these different arts. But when we look at our own, we’re used to seeing ourselves as Apu or as the funny nerdy side characters,” Khan says. She wanted the movie to carry a different posture entirely. “We can be proud of things that we do as South Asians,” she says. Minhaj and Venkataramanujam drew on their own backgrounds for the script. Minhaj’s wife danced competitively, and Venkataramanujam performed with an a cappella team called Chai Town, giving him firsthand knowledge of how consuming the competition circuit can become. Khan spent time with UCLA’s own dance team and traveled to North Carolina to observe competitions in preparation. Khan’s earlier work directing episodes of Netflix’s “Never Have I Ever” fed into how she thinks about representation. “When you have more than one of a minority character, then there’s suddenly become real characters,” she says, describing the shift that happens once side characters are allowed the same depth as anyone else. “You get to focus on the humanity between them, the things that become relatable to everybody else.” Casting required actors who could carry both comedy and depth, and several, including Maitreyi Ramakrishnan, had never danced competitively before landing their roles. Khan recalls pushing Ramakrishnan toward a specific physical transformation during casting. “I need you to give me some Channing Tatum energy. And then I was like, no, actually, I need you to do a Christian Bale on me. I need a complete athletic transformation,” she says. Ramakrishnan went on to complete months of intensive dance training ahead of the shoot. Khan built the dance sequences with choreographers Phillip Chbeeb and Makenzie Dustman, with Joya Kazi credited as co-choreographer. Each number was approached with a single guiding question, she says: “What is the essence we are trying to bring out in this particular moment?” Where a typical Bollywood dance sequence gets five days to shoot, the production often had just one. The choreography also draws on multiple regional styles, including Kuthu, Bharatanatyam and Pakistani-influenced dance, reflecting the mix of identities on the fictional team. Priyanka Kedia, Lena Khan and Maitreyi Ramakrishnan on the sets of “Best of the Best” Netflix Khan, whose credits include the independent feature “The Tiger Hunter,” says the industry’s relationship to South Asian stories has shifted since that film came out in 2016, even as some structural limits remain. “We still don’t have that many romances or romantic comedies with South Asians,” she says, pointing out that South Asian men are often not given the chance to play the lead. The film flips that dynamic elsewhere in its own casting, she notes: “The nerdy minority character is actually a white guy. Like we have a token white guy.” She also credits a wave of South Asian musicians and actors, including Joy Crookes, whose song she fought to include in the soundtrack, with making the film possible. “And now we’re like, well, we’ve really made it when we make a movie that’s just good,” she says. That philosophy extended to how much cultural context the film explains for a global Netflix audience. Khan says she resisted pressure to over-explain South Asian references, trusting shows like “Never Have I Ever” to have already proven audiences do not need everything spelled out. “At some point this country and the world is just full of people in different cultures,” she says. Working with Minhaj and Venkataramanujam, both first-time feature writers, meant frequent creative disagreements, Khan says, but never without purpose. “There would be such a thoughtful reason that we were always fighting over why we’re doing a certain thing, but it was never for a vapid reason,” she says. “And they’re also just the most gracious people.” Hasan Minhaj – “Best of the Best” Netflix Looking ahead, Khan says she is drawn to projects centered on overlooked people or subjects, alongside a personal passion project already underway. “I’m always on the hunt for that,” she says, describing a search for stories she wishes already existed and a way to make them for a wide audience. “Best of the Best” also stars Lilly Singh, Nihar Duvvuri, Nico Greetham, Amryn Khurana, Tanishq Joshi, Saara Chaudry and Sasha Bhasin. It is streaming now on Netflix. articles.title: Tom Cruise Says Taylor Swift Was ‘Schooling Me on Football’ at Chiefs Game, Calls Her a ‘Brilliant Musician and Director’
articles.full_text: Sep 18, 2026 2:40am PT Tom Cruise Says Taylor Swift Was ‘Schooling Me on Football’ at Chiefs Game, Calls Her a ‘Brilliant Musician and Director’ By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest ‘War’ Trailer: Sienna Miller and Dominic West Endure a Bitter Divorce Battle in HBO and Sky’s Legal Drama 22 hours ago ‘Slow Horses’ Renewed for Season 8 at Apple TV 3 days ago Oscilloscope Lands North American Rights to ‘Game,’ Rave Thriller From John Minton and Portishead’s Geoff Barrow Starring Jason Williamson of Sleaford Mods (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All Getty Images Tom Cruise and Taylor Swift made headlines on Monday when they sat next to each other at the Kansas City Chiefs’ first game of the season. But what were the two megastars talking about? “She was schooling me on football. For real,” Cruise revealed to Jimmy Fallon during an appearance on “The Tonight Show” on Thursday. But that wasn’t the first time Cruise and Swift have had a meeting of the minds — he was spotted at her Eras Tour in London in 2024, and when the pop star married Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce in July, Cruise was in attendance. Related Stories 'Like ‘Amores Perros,’ I Hope My Film Will Also Transcend Time in Some Way,’ Says Gael García Bernal of His Third Directorial Outing, ‘Hombre al Agua’ Heartfelt, Rare Animated Belgian Feature 'Juul' Headlines Studio 100 Film's Expanding Slate at TIFF Market “First of all, she’s a genius. I’ve been following her since she was a kid,” Cruise said of Swift. “Everybody there, all their friends — they’re a beautiful couple and magical in their own right.” Popular on Variety And Swift has real ball knowledge. “Oh, she knows her stuff,” Cruise continued, adding that the singer “knew nothing about football when she met Travis.” Other than Swift coaching him through the game, Cruise said they “talked about music and movies.” “She’s funny, she’s got such a great sense of humor,” he said. “A brilliant writer also, by the way. A brilliant musician and director — very skilled.” Swift has directed many of her own music videos over the years, and delved further into filmmaking with 2021’s “All Too Well: The Short Film,” starring Sadie Sink and Dylan O’Brien. In late 2022, it was announced that she would be making her feature directorial debut for Searchlight Pictures, though her record-breaking Eras Tour that began the next year (and extended through December 2024) seems to have delayed this . Elsewhere in his interview with Fallon, Cruise was asked about rumors that his new film “Digger,” directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu, was actually a musical. “No, but I think it’s a very good idea,” he laughed. “I think we should do ‘Digger’ the musical. Digger down!” Cruise and Fallon then broke out into song and dance in their seats. Cruise’s press tour for “Digger” will also include an appearance on Travis and Jason Kelce’s “New Heights” podcast, releasing on Friday. Watch Cruise’s full interview with Fallon below. articles.title: Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’
articles.full_text: Sep 18, 2026 3:37am PT Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Japan’s Top Broadcasters Unite for First Joint Delegation to MipCancun (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ 3 hours ago ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’ 5 hours ago See All Toronto Film Festival “ The Age of Goodbyes ” begins, in more ways than one, with a curse. In Li Zi Shu’s sprawling Malaysian Chinese novel, a family is said to be marked by early death; in Edmund Yeo ‘s screen adaptation, in the Special Presentations section of the Toronto Film Festival , that curse becomes the hinge on which five decades of Malaysian history swing, carried by a woman named Du Li An and the two men, one thought dead, who share the same face. Related Stories Jordan Firstman, Matteo Lane Lead U.S. Voice Cast of Cannes Breakout Comedy 'Jim Queen’ (EXCLUSIVE) Marie Clements on the Power of Indigenous Women’s Stories and Her Interview With Gloria Steinem: 'We Have More in Common Than What Works To Divide Us' (EXCLUSIVE) Li Zi Shu’s book, which begins on page 513 as a deliberate nod to May 13, 1969, was long considered too structurally slippery for cinema, its timelines folding into one another, its narrators unreliable, its boundary between memory and myth left permanently uncertain. That date refers to race riots that broke out in Kuala Lumpur following a bitterly contested general election, leaving hundreds dead and prompting a state of emergency; the ethnic and political fault lines that hardened in its aftermath still shape Malaysia today. Popular on Variety “I wasn’t interested in taking this very labyrinthine novel and making everything neat and chronological for the audience,” Yeo tells Variety . “I wanted to find a cinematic equivalent for the experience of reading it.” Even the novelist had her doubts. “In fact, when I first met Li Zi Shu to discuss the project, her first question to me was, ‘Are you sure it is adaptable?'” Yeo recalls. He told her then that he knew he could not reproduce the novel literally. At the center of the frame story is Kai (Troy Liu), a boy who stumbles onto a novel titled “The Age of Goodbyes” and finds himself drawn into the world of Du Li An ( Vivian Sung ), whose romance with Lin Sang (Stanley Yau) in Ipoh in 1969 ends when he vanishes after confiding in her about his family’s curse. Years later, a man named Mong Sang, also played by Yau, arrives bearing Lin Sang’s exact face and insisting he is someone else entirely. The film, a Taiwan-Malaysia co-production shot in Mandarin, Cantonese, Malay, Thai and English, marks Yeo’s fifth fiction feature, following “River of Exploding Durians,” “We, the Dead,” “Malu” and “Moonlight Shadow.” Yeo made one significant departure from the source material. In the novel, Lin Sang disappears on the day Du Li An marries another man, Steely Bo; in the film, Yeo tied that disappearance directly to the racial violence of May 13 instead. “They are ordinary people living inside history, and its consequences are felt through fear, absence, separation, rumors, memories and things people don’t say,” he says. That instinct comes from Yeo’s own family. He discovered Li Zi Shu’s novel shortly after a trip to China, where he visited his family’s ancestral shrine in Chaoshan and learned new details about his grandfather’s migration to Southeast Asia. His mother once told him that his great-grandfather was a kung fu master who leapt across a moving train while carrying his infant grandson to safety, a story he has no way of confirming. “I think families are full of stories like this,” he says. “Someone tells a story, someone else remembers it slightly differently, certain details disappear while others become more dramatic, and eventually nobody is around anymore who can tell you what actually happened.” That inheritance runs through the soundtrack, too. Several songs in the film were written and performed by Yeo’s own parents in the 1970s, decades before their son thought to build a movie around a fictional Ipoh where they might have been playing on the radio. “The whole film is about things being transmitted from one generation to another: stories, memories, trauma, myths, even gestures,” Yeo says. “And suddenly my mother’s actual voice, singing a song composed by my father and recorded when they were young, was being transmitted through a film I was making decades later.” For Sung, the challenge was finding continuity in a character who ages from a lovestruck young woman into a wife, mother and stepmother across shifting timelines and an uncertain grip on her own past. “When I first spoke with the director about the script, he told me that Du Li An was a ‘survivor.’ That word stayed with me and became the key to understanding her,” Sung says. Playing opposite Yau as both the vanished Lin Sang and his double, Mong Sang, meant sitting inside uncertainty rather than resolving it. Sung recalls filming Du Li An’s first sight of Mong Sang. “My mind was telling me very clearly, ‘This isn’t him.’ But my body and my memories believed something else,” she says. That confusion is written into the dialogue itself. Du Li An speaks Cantonese at home, Mandarin with Lin Sang and Cantonese with Mong Sang. “Sometimes, when she speaks Mandarin with Mong Sang, it actually reveals that the person she is really trying to speak to is Lin Sang,” Sung says. Sung, who is Taiwanese, spent five to six months preparing the role, working with two language coaches on a 1960s Malaysian Chinese Cantonese and Hokkien accent and living for a month in Kuala Lumpur before joining the crew for pre-production in Ipoh. The costume department let her keep the qipaos she wore in fittings. “There was this strong feeling that I wasn’t simply wearing a costume. It felt like my body had somehow stepped into another era,” she says. Yeo built the film’s structure around a delayed reveal: the title card does not appear until 40 minutes in, marking the point where the novel itself begins. Everything before it, he says, is his own expansion of material only briefly suggested on the page, an approach he traces back to adapting Banana Yoshimoto’s novella “Moonlight Shadow.” “What ‘Moonlight Shadow’ gave me was confidence that adaptation is ultimately a conversation with the original work,” Yeo says. “You have to identify its soul rather than protect every incident.” Sung, who relocated from Taiwan to Los Angeles two years ago, isn’t chasing a specific type of role next. She’s drawn to a story about modern love. “Two people who really like each other, but both come with their own problems, fears, and maybe a little bit of craziness,” she says. Yeo is already developing several new projects, among them a century-spanning vampire story set between Borneo, Macau and Kaohsiung, and a multigenerational drama connecting Malaysia and Japan through a family of filmmakers. “Apparently, after making a film about people being haunted by stories from the past, I responded by developing several more films about people being haunted by stories from the past,” he says. articles.title: International Oscar Submissions: Spain, Indonesia, Hungary, Nepal, Israel and More Join the List
articles.full_text: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection The campaigns for the Oscar for international feature film are gaining momentum, with final submissions due by Oct. 1. The Oscars shortlists will be revealed on Dec. 15, with 15 international films selected to be voted on by Academy members in all branches who commit to watch all 15 films. Oscar nominations will be revealed on Jan. 21. This year’s entries include titles like Romania’s “Fjord,” which won the Palme d’Or at Cannes; Chile’s “The Meltdown,” which screened in Un Certain Regard; and Germany’s “Everytime,” which won Cannes’ Un Certain Regard prize. Meanwhile, a new Academy rule allows any film that wins the top prize at one of the six biggest festivals — Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance, Busan and Toronto — to be entered in the international feature race even without a national committee’s backing. Gondhal (India) Image Credit: Davakhar Films The Film Federation of India has selected the Marathi-language drama “Gondhal” as the country’s entry for the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards. Written and directed by Santosh Davakhar, the drama unfolds over a single night in rural Maharashtra, following a newlywed couple whose traditional wedding ritual becomes the setting where old customs, private desires and hidden fragility all come to a head. The cast includes Ishita Deshmukh, Yogesh Sohoni, Kishor Kadam, Suresh Vishwakarma, Nishad Bhoir, Anuj Prabhu and Vitthal Kale. “Gondhal” picked up a Golden Peacock nomination at the International Film Festival of India’s 56th edition, and Davakhar took home the event’s Silver Peacock for best director. The film later won a Fipresci prize when Bengaluru’s international film festival held its 17th edition, along with best director and best cinematographer honors from Pune’s international film festival and a further best director win at the Third Eye Asian International Film Festival. La Bola Negra (Spain) Image Credit: 'La Bola Negra' “La Bola Negra,” Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s Cannes Festival sensation, is Spain’s international feature Oscar submission. That comes as little surprise Scoring a 16-minute standing ovation at the Cannes Festival, where it shared its best director award “La Bola Negra” again moved waves when Netflix, its U.S. distributor, announced it would give “La Bola Negra” a 47-day U.S. theatrical window the longest for any movie in the streaming giant’s history, a sure indication that the film will feature strongly among the streamer’s awards priorities for the fall. “La Bola Negra” is already being talked up as a candidate for Oscar nomination in multiple other categories. Sweeping, unapologetically passionate and hugely ambitious, “La Bola Negra” braids three connected stories, each shot in different film registers, chronicling the travails and legacy of Spain’s gay experience in 1932, 1937 during the Spanish Civil War, and 2017. It picks up on the first four pages in an unfinished novel by legendary poet-playwright Federico García Lorca plus some of his nearly last poems. The film features a feisty turn from Penélope Cruz as a cabaret dancer and a cameo from Glenn Close as a modern-day hispanist, accompanying Spanish stars Miguel Bernardeau, Guitarricadelafuente, Milo Quifes and Carlos Gutiérrez in lead roles. Four Seasons in Java (Indonesia) Image Credit: Forka Films Indonesia has selected Kamila Andini ‘s “ Four Seasons in Java ” (“Empat Musim Pertiwi”) as its submission for the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards. Written and directed by Andini and produced by Ifa Isfansyah for Forka Films, the film stars Putri Marino, Arya Saloka, Christine Hakim and Hana Malasan. The story centers on Pertiwi (Marino), a formerly incarcerated woman who comes back to a hometown that will not welcome her, pushing her to reckon with a painful personal history set against ongoing silence, violence and social division. Elements of mystery, magical realism and science fiction run through the psychological drama as it examines trauma, memory and what it takes to reclaim a sense of home and identity. The selection extends Andini’s run as one of Indonesian cinema’s most consistent presences on the international festival circuit. Her 2021 feature “Yuni” premiered at the Toronto Film Festival, where it won the Platform Prize, and went on to become Indonesia’s Oscars submission that year. Her film “Before, Now & Then” (Nana) played in competition at the Berlin International Film Festival, where Laura Basuki won the Silver Bear for best supporting performance. “Four Seasons in Java” had its world premiere in the Centrepiece program at the ongoing Toronto Film Festival and is set to screen at the Busan International Film Festival next month. It has also picked up a best cinematography nomination at the 2026 Asian Pacific Screen Awards. Silent Friend (Hungary) Image Credit: Courtesy of Films Boutique Ildikó Enyedi’s “Silent Friend” is Hungary’s submission for the 2027 Oscars in the best international feature film category. Enyedi’s “On Body and Soul,” which won Berlin’s Golden Bear, was Oscar nominated in the same category in 2018. “Silent Friend,” which stars Tony Leung Chiu-Wai, Luna Wedler, Enzo Brumm and Léa Seydoux, is a poetic exploration of the relationship between humans, plants and time. It received six awards at the 82nd Venice Film Festival, and was recently selected as one of five nominees for the FIPRESCI Grand Prix, recognizing the best films of the year. Filipiñana (Philippines) Image Credit: Kino Lorber Rafael Manuel ’s “ Filipiñana ” has been chosen as the official entry from the Philippines in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards. The film is written and directed by Manuel and is distributed by Kino Lorber. The film is set against a backdrop of oppressive heat and drought. The narrative follows Isabel, a 17-year-old from the provinces of the Philippines, who gets a job at a prestigious golf resort. The cast includes Jorrybell Agoto, Carmen Castellanos, Teroy Guzman, Carlitos Siguion-Reyna, Isabel Sicat and Nour Houshmand. Executive produced by Chinese auteur Jia Zhangke, “Filipiñana” bowed in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, where it took home the World Cinema Dramatic Special Jury Award for Creative Vision. The film went on to make its European premiere in the Perspectives section of the Berlin Film Festival. The film’s festival run has continued to build momentum since. It played the San Francisco International Film Festival, picking up the New Directors Award, and the Independent Film Festival of Boston, where it won the Grand Jury Prize for Best Narrative Feature. “Filipiñana” also collected the Luna de València for Best Feature Film at the Cinema Jove International Film Festival. Elephants in the Fog (Nepal) Image Credit: Courtesy of UTN, Les Valseurs, DGS Nepal’s International Feature Film Selection Committee has chosen Abinash Bikram Shah’s “Elephants in the Fog” as the country’s entry for the 99th Academy Awards. The film marks Shah’s feature directorial debut and follows a Kinnar community in a Nepalese village fighting to protect itself. It premiered in the Un Certain Regard section of the Cannes Film Festival in May, where it won the section’s Jury Prize, and also picked up nominations for the Caméra d’Or and the Queer Palm. The cast is led by Pushpa Thing Lama, Deepika Yadav, Jasmine Bishwokarma, Aliz Ghimire and Dura Sanjay Kumar Gupta. The Oscars selection comes as “Elephants in the Fog” continues to expand its footprint in international markets. Sales company Best Friend Forever has closed deals in several territories, including MetFilm Distribution in the U.K., Filmin in Spain, Vedette in Benelux, Trigon in Switzerland, Lev Cinema in Israel, Jayantii in Australia, EFAR Films in India, PT Falcon in Indonesia and the Film Development Council of the Philippines, alongside an inflight deal with Silk Route. Those additions build on earlier deals covering France, Germany and Austria, Brazil and Nepal itself. The film is produced by Underground Talkies Nepal, Les Valseurs and Die Gesellschaft DGS. We Are All Strangers (Singapore) Image Credit: Giraffe Pictures “We Are All Strangers,” written and directed by Anthony Chen, has been selected as Singapore‘s entry in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards. Set in contemporary Singapore, the film centers on family relationships and unexpected life changes. It stars Chen’s frequent collaborators Yeo Yann Yann and Koh Jia Ler, with Andi Lim and Regene Lim rounding out the cast. Earlier this year, it became the first Singaporean film selected for the main competition at the Berlin Film Festival. “We Are All Strangers” completes Chen’s Growing Up trilogy, which began with “Ilo Ilo” in 2013 and continued with “Wet Season” in 2019. The two earlier films have collectively won more than 50 international accolades, including five Golden Horse Awards, along with “Ilo Ilo‘s” Caméra d’Or win at Cannes. Both films previously served as Singapore’s Oscars entries, at the 86th and 93rd Academy Awards respectively. No Paradise if You Are Killed By a Woman (Iraq) Image Credit: Courtesy True Colours Kurdish-Norwegian director Halkawt Mustafa’s “No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman,” a Hollywood-style thriller about a female Kurdish sniper who returns to Mosul to try and rescue her younger sister, has been selected by Iraq as the country’s official entry in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards. “No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman” follows a female sniper named Vyan who returns to the battlefield she once escaped, driven by vengeance and by the desperate hope of rescuing her younger sister who is still imprisoned by ISIS. The thriller launched out-of-competition at the Venice Film Festival and also plays in Toronto. Avan Jamal (“The Exam”) stars as Vyan, alongside Norwegian actor Thorbjørn Harr. The film’s main cast also comprises Kanar Sarchl and Kader Jalal. Mustafa, who was born in Iraqi Kurdistan and fled to Norway as a child, wrote the film that is inspired by his encounter with a female Peshmerga sniper on the front line in 2014, according to a statement from the Norwegian Film Institute which supported the film’s production. The film was shot on location in Mosul, Iraq, “using the city’s real streets and surroundings to create the physical and emotional authenticity Mustafa felt could only be achieved there,” the statement noted. Mustafa previously directed the feature “El Clásico” and the documentary “Hiding Saddam Hussein” that was successfully released in movie theatres across the Arab world. “No Paradise” is produced by Halkawt Mustafa, Janne Hjeltnes and John M. Jacobsen for Hene Films in Norway, in co-production with La Media in Iraqi Kurdistan and The Chimney Pot in Sweden. Italy’s True Colours is handling international sales. Strawberries (Morocco) Image Credit: 'Strawberries' Courtesy Lucky Number Laila Marrakchi’s “Strawberries” (“La más dulce”), about a group of Moroccan seasonal laborers hired to pick strawberries in Spain who decide to stand up to their abusive employers, has been selected by the Moroccan Cinematographic Center as its official entry in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards. Marrakchi, after portraying Morocco’s upper classes in “Marock” and “Rock the Casbah” (2013) – and then veering into TV by directing episodes of Damien Chazelle’s “The Eddy” for Netflix and of several French TV series including “The Bureau” – in “Strawberries” turns her eye to the true story of young women who leave Morocco for a strawberry farm in Southern Spain in hopes of providing a better life for their families, only to contend with harassment and inhumane living conditions. The female-driven drama, which is It is produced by France’s Lumen and Morocco’s Mont Fleuri Production with Spain’s Fasten Films and Belgium’s Mirage Films, launched earlier this year from Cannes’ Un Certain Regard. Lucky Number is handling international sales. Morocco has yet to score an Oscar nomination, though it has made the shortlist three times most recently in 2023 with Asmae El Moudir’s “The Mother of All Lies.” Tell Me Everything (Israel) Image Credit: Ziv Berkovich Moshe Rosenthal’s “Tell Me Everything” has been voted Best Picture at Israel’s Ophir Awards, automatically making it the country’s submission for best international feature film category at the 99th Academy Awards. “Tell Me Everything,” set in the 1980s against the rising HIV epidemic, premiered at Sundance in the world cinema dramatic competition. It is Moshe Rosenthal’s sophomore feature. “Karaoke,” his directorial feature debut, premiered at the 2022 Tribeca Film Festival. “Tell Me Everything” follows Boaz (played by Yair Mazor), a 12-year-old who discovers a devastating secret about his father. Catching up with Boaz as an adult (played by “The Vanishing Soldier’s” Ido Tako), the film delves into their father-son relationship as they attempt to heal wounds and repair bonds. Assi Cohen (“Yossi & Jagger”) stars as Boaz’s father. Fjord (Romania) Image Credit: Courtesy of Tudor Panduru “Fjord,” written and directed by Cristian Mungiu, is Romania’s submission for the 2027 Oscars in the best international feature film category, having been unanimously chosen by the country’s selection committee. The film premiered in the official competition at the Cannes Film Festival, where it won the Palme d’Or for best film, the FIPRESCI Prize, the Ecumenical Jury Prize, the Prix de la Citoyenneté and the François Chalais Prize. Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve star in the lead roles, with cinematography by Tudor Vladimir Panduru, editing by Mircea Olteanu, and production design by Simona Pădurețu. Aontas (Ireland) Image Credit: Púca Pictures “Aontas,” the Irish-language heist thriller from director Damian McCann, has been chosen as Ireland’s entry for the best international feature film category at the 2027 Academy Awards. The film was selected by the Irish Film & TV Academy (IFTA) and a committee including “Evil Dead Rise” director Lee Cronin, “Derry Girls” creator Lisa McGee, BAFTA-nominated director Brian Kirk (“Game of Thrones), BAFTA nominated director Kathryn Ferguson (“Nothing Compares”), Emmy-winning actress and filmmaker Aisha Tyler (“Friends”), actress Fionnuala Flaherty (“Kneecap”) and IFTA chief executive Áine Moriarty. Told in reverse chronology, “Aontas” follows three unlikely thieves, led by a woman on the verge of a breakdown, who rob a rural Irish bank. Opening in the tragic aftermath of the heist-gone-wrong. What starts as a poorly executed robbery becomes a portrait of a wilful woman trapped in her own past. It stars Carrie Crowley (“The Quiet Girl “), Bríd Brennan, Eva-Jane Gaffney, Seán T. Ó Meallaigh, Marcus Lamb and Art Parkinson. The Meltdown (Chile) Image Credit: 'The Meltdown' Courtesy of Mubi Chile’s Film Academy has selected “The Meltdown” (“El deshielo”) by Manuela Martelli, her post-Pinochet mystery drama set in an Andes ski resort, to represent the country in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Academy Awards. Martelli’s follow-up to her acclaimed drama “Chile, 1976” had its world premiere at Cannes’ prominent strand Un Certain Regard this year. “The Meltdown” stars Maya O’Rourke – in her film debut – who plays a nine-year-old at her family’s ski resort who witnesses unsettling events that will test her loyalties. Other cast members are Paulina Urrutia, Mauricio Pešutić, Paula Zúñiga, Marcela Salinas and Lautaro Cantillana. All of a Sudden (Japan) Image Credit: Courtesy of Neon, Cannes Film Festival Hamaguchi Ryusuke‘s “All of a Sudden” has been selected as Japan’s entry in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards, the Motion Picture Producers Association of Japan (Eiren) has revealed. The selection marks the second time a Hamaguchi film has represented Japan in the category, five years after “Drive My Car” won the international feature Oscar and picked up nominations for best picture, director and adapted screenplay at the 94th Academy Awards. “All of a Sudden” is a France-Japan co-production made with backing from Germany and Belgium, shot largely in Paris. The film draws on “When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher With Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist,” a book of correspondence by Miyano Makiko and Isono Maho. It follows Marie-Lou Fontaine (Virginie Efira), who runs a nursing home outside Paris and pushes to adopt a more dignity-focused model of elderly care, and Morisaki Mari (Okamoto Tao), a Japanese theater director undergoing cancer treatment. Nagatsuka Kyōzō and Kurosaki Kōdai round out the cast. Everytime (Germany) Image Credit: Courtesy of The Barricades Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime” has been selected as Germany’s entry for the Academy Award for best international feature film. The film’s synopsis reads as follows: The last photograph Jessie took shows the sun over Berlin. It hangs there as if nothing had happened. But Ella has lost her daughter. What remains is Jessie’s younger sister and a complicated relationship with the boy everyone blames. The unlikely trio ends up on a family holiday that never really existed. Under the shimmering sun of Tenerife, memory and the present become inseparably intertwined. The ghosts are everywhere. “Everytime” celebrated its world premiere at the 79th Cannes Film Festival in May. Wollner’s third feature film, for which she also wrote the screenplay, was selected for the Un Certain Regard sidebar where it won the Prix Un Certain Regard, the section’s top award. Cannes was followed by invitations to the Sydney Film Festival and the Karlovy Vary Film Festival, among others. At the Sarajevo Film Festival, “Everytime” was awarded the Heart of Sarajevo Grand Prize. Its North American premiere will follow in September at the Toronto Film Festival. Other festival appearances include the New York Film Festival. Becoming Human (Cambodia) Image Credit: Anti-Archive The Cambodia Oscar Selection Committee (COSC) has selected “Becoming Human,” directed by Polen Ly, as the country’s official submission for the international feature film category at the 99th Academy Awards. The film follows Thida, the spirit guardian of an aging cinema slated for demolition, as she weighs the choice of rebirth against her existence as a ghost. Her bond with Hai, a living man she meets along the way, pushes her to confront both her spiritual fate and a country in the midst of sweeping social change. “Becoming Human” is Ly’s debut feature. He previously made the short film “Further and Further Away” in 2022 and the documentary “Until the Orchid Blooms,” which premiered at IDFA in 2024 and won the grand prize at the Taiwan International Documentary Festival in 2026. The cast is led by 15-year-old newcomer and dance student Savorn Serak alongside Piseth Chhun, who won the Venice Horizons award for best actor in 2021 for his role in Kavich Neang’s “White Building.” First Light (Australia) Image Credit: International Film Festival Rotterdam “First Light,” the feature directorial debut of Filipino-Australian filmmaker James J. Robinson, has been selected as Australia’s entry in the international feature film category at the 99th Academy Awards, marking the first Filipino-Australian co-production and the first Tagalog-language film the country has ever submitted for Oscar consideration. The film follows Sister Yolanda (Ruby Ruiz), a nun and nurse leading a peaceful, disciplined existence until a young construction worker’s suspicious death draws her into uncovering corruption reaching both the community’s wealthy elite and the church she has devoted her life to. The film premiered at the 2025 Melbourne International Film Festival, where Robinson took home the best Australian director award. It later screened in the main competition lineup at Marrakech and went on to play the New Zealand International Film Festival, the International Film Festival Rotterdam and the Glasgow Film Festival. Possible Love (South Korea) Image Credit: Courtesy of Netflix, Venice Film Festival The Korean Film Council (KOFIC) has selected “Possible Love,” directed by Lee Chang-dong, as South Korea‘s official entry for the international feature film category at the 2027 Academy Awards. “Possible Love” marks Lee’s first feature in eight years, following “Burning,” “Poetry” and “Secret Sunshine.” The film centers on two married couples whose lives intersect after a funeral: Mi-ok and her laid-off husband Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), who live quietly with their young son Cheol, and Ye-ji, a filmmaker making a documentary about workers who lost their jobs, and her husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). When Mi-ok agrees to be filmed by Ye-ji, the two women grow close, while Mi-ok finds herself unsettled by an attraction to Sang-woo. As the two couples’ worlds overlap, cracks begin to surface in both marriages. In its evaluation, the committee cited the film’s polished craftsmanship and the clarity of its directorial vision, pointing to the tone and mise-en-scène that sustain a sense of pressure throughout the story. The drama was described as prompting reflection on gentle forms of violence, incomplete freedom and the nature of true happiness, alongside a labor movement sequence that the committee said captured layered social undercurrents. Like a Limbless Tree (Turkey) Image Credit: Courtesy Tekhne Film “Like a Limbless Tree,” an intimate social drama directed by Tunç Davut, has been selected as Turkey‘s entry for the Academy Award for best international feature film. Davut, whose previous works include the 2015 drama “Entanglement and TV series “Serçe” and “Kinali Kuzular,” delves into the fragility of human existence against a backdrop of the theme of immigration in “Like a Limbless Tree.” The film is produced by Istanbul-based Tekhne Film and stars Ali Ipin, Fayyaz Duman and Selen Kurtaran. Davut’s drama – which won an award at the Bosphorus Film Festival and was selected for the Antalya Golden Orange Film Festival and the Ankara Film Festival – is about a retired engineer named Refik whose life changes forever after being diagnosed with a terminal disease just as his Syrian caregiver disappears while attempting to flee to Europe, leaving him in charge of her two children. Who is Still Alive (Switzerland) Image Credit: Courtesy Swiss Films “Who is Still Alive,” a documentary directed by Nicolas Wadimoff that gives voice to Gaza humanitarian crisis survivors and refugees, has been selected by the Swiss Federal Office of Culture as Switzerland ‘s entry for the Academy Award for best international feature film. The documentary, which looks at the lives of nine Palestinian people who escaped the crisis in Gaza and explores the loss of home against the backdrop of the Gaza War, had its world premiere in Venice at the 2025 Giornate degli Autori, AKA Venice Days, sidebar. For director Nicolas Wadimoff, “Who is Still Alive” is his third film dealing with Palestine, following “Aisheen (Still Alive in Gaza)” about the aftermath of Israel’s 2008 air strikes on the Gaza Strip and “The Apollo of Gaza” in 2018. “Who is Still Alive” was produced by Nicolas Wadimoff, Philippe Coeytaux, and Ketsia Stocker of the Geneva-based production company Akka Films, where Nicolas Wadimoff also serves as founder and producer. Co-producers include Easy Rider Films (Paris), Philistine Films (Palestine/Jordan), Cocoon Films (London), and RTS Radio Télévision Suisse. How to Divorce During the War (Lithuania) Image Credit: Courtesy of New Europe Film Sales Andrius Blaževičius’ “How to Divorce During the War” has been selected as Lithuania’s entry for the Academy Award for best international feature film. Blaževičius’ third feature won the directing award in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at the Sundance Film Festival. The film was picked up for theatrical distribution in North America by Zeitgeist Films, in association with Kino Lorber, and will be released on Aug. 21. Set in Vilnius in 2022, it’s a story of a high-flying executive Marija, who chooses the worst possible moment for an honest conversation with her husband Vytas about divorcing – just one day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine goes into full scale. Now the couple must navigate the process of separation as it collides with a refugee and mid-life crisis. Loading comments... articles.title: Catalonia’s New Generation Raises Its Game as Ambition, Scale and Genre Drive Bolder Arthouse and Crossover Titles
articles.full_text: Sep 18, 2026 4:17am PT Catalonia’s New Generation Raises Its Game as Ambition, Scale and Genre Drive Bolder Arthouse and Crossover Titles Key emerging Catalan filmmakers at San Sebastián – Berto Romero, Mikel Gurrea, Meritxell Colell, Aina Clotet – are raising their game, in larger scale, genre blending, visual ambition and more involved storytelling. They have very good reason By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Catalonia: A Dozen Highlights at San Sebastián, From a Time-Loop Thriller to a Singular Heist Tale and a Potential Arthouse Sleeper 2 hours ago Catalonia’s New Generation Raises Its Game as Ambition, Scale and Genre Drive Bolder Arthouse and Crossover Titles 2 hours ago Oscars: Spain Selects ‘La Bola Negra’ for International Feature Race 2 days ago See All 'Five More Minutes' Courtesy of San Sebastián Film Festival Over 2019-25, annual Catalan government general cinema funding soared from €12.5 million ($14.4 million) in 2019 to €30.2 million ($34.8 million) in just specific support lines. Now, however, the films that are being made are also getting bigger, as a new generation of filmmakers and TV creatives emerged over the last decade raise their game in their artistic ambitions and production values. Related Stories Chase Infiniti on TIFF Breakout ‘The Julia Set,’ Love Bombing and Music Video Stardom Jorge Alonso's Spanish Romance Drama 'All That We Never Were' Sells to France and India (EXCLUSIVE) New movies at San Sebastián from rapidly consolidating Catalan or Catalonia-based writers and directors is a case in point. Mikel Gurrea’s main competition player “Saints,” for example, launches as a mini visual mystery thriller. Distant lights – maybe car lights or fireflies – dance across a pitch-black night scene. They are finally revealed as the head-lamps of a gang of thieves, robbing a church, caught closer up, their faces occasionally emerging from the gloom. Popular on Variety Cleverly, in visual terms, not dialog, Gurrea not just launches the film but anticipates its focus: This is an identity drama, this focus becoming how late-20s Lali establishes her priorities, between a chosen family – an elite band of church artefacts thieves – and her biological family, her dying mother. “Saints’” budget is “roughly twice” that of “Suro,” Gurrea’s 2022 debut which also competed at San Sebastián, says “Saints” producer Laura Rubirola Salas. That budget spike can be put down to spiraling production costs and a film “more complex in terms of locations, number of characters and overall production values,” she adds. Written and starring Berto Romero , “5 More Minutes” delivers a reportedly excruciatingly comedic sci-fi thriller as an on-the-rocks couple are caught in a time loop at a rural getaway. Suddenly, a world of normal multi-shot set-ups morphs into one of millimetrically calculated five-minute sequence shots, film at the same time of 6.35 p.m. to achieve similar light conditions. None of which as an easy task. 2018’s “Land of Loneliness” (“Con el viento”), Meritxell Colell ’s first fiction feature, unspooled in a Spanish village. Her third, “Far From the Trees,” one of Locarno biggest winners this August, begins in the Amazon jungle, so0n moves to Peru’s highlands, following Adela, a sound artist recording endangered languages. The locations can be eye-catching. What quickly dazzles, however, is an intricate mix of present and past, collective and personal memory, of the archive footage of the Catalan diaspora after the Spanish Civil War and scenes of Adela as a child, and a present in a film which speaks about family, forced exile, roots, memory and identity. Why the Step-Up in Ambition? Aiming to raise the ante in style and scale, cineastes are emboldened by success, theirs and of others. Over the last decade, Catalan productions have won Best First Feature (“Summer 1993”), a Golden Bear (Alcarràs,” also from Carla Simón) and Best Leading Performance (“20,000 Species of Bees”) at the Berlin Film Festival. “Sirāt” took a Cannes Jury Prize last year, and two Academy Award nominations. Smaller films have also triumphed: “The Good Daughter,” now playing at San Sebastián, scooped top prizes at Tallinn Black Nights Festival, last year; “Forastera,” directed by Lucía Aleñar Iglesias, won a Fipresci Prize at 2025’s Toronto. In a more commercial way of things, Paramount Pictures is giving a theatrical release to “Tad and the Magic Lamp,” part of the animated movie series, in over 40 international territories, including nearly all major markets around the world, notes producer Edmon Roch. Another film he co-produced, Aina Clotet’s “Alive” (“Viva”), now at San Sebastián, won the 2026 Cannes Critics’ Week’s Louis Roederer Foundation Rising Star Award. “Nobody sets out to make a bigger film, that isn’t the place we create from,” says Colell. So she wrote “Far from the Trees” “freely, without thinking if the film could be made, pouring in cinematographic, emotional and narratives desires.” That said, she is “less afraid of taking risks” thanks to a growing confidence of her own capacities and those of key collaborators, such as editor Ana Pfaff, who has also edited Clara Simón’s films including the sensational short “Flamenco,” set to screen at San Sebastián. “Suro’s”success gave us the confidence to make a film that could once again compete in the Official Selection of a major festival like San Sebastián, and travel internationally without any complexes. I feel this is something we question less and less,” Rubirola Salas says, talking about Gurrea’s debut. Also, the money’s there. In 2025, Spain produced 435 features, more than any other country in Europe. That speaks large, in part, to the emergence of consolidated regional firm industries such as Catalonia’s. But Spain’s regions do not finance films on their own. “Far From the Trees” worked a “fundamental” national-regional axis, says Colell, tapping finance from Spain’s national ICAA film agency and the Catalan Government ICEC. “5 More Minutes” benefitted from co-production by Movistar Plus, the biggest Spanish pay TV/SVOD operator, which set out from its first announced slate in 2023 to make auteur event movies at budgets competitive with similar movies in , say, France. Spain, and most especially Catalonia, which boasts a minority co-production fund, furthermore ranks with Belgium among the easiest of co-producer partner countries in Europe. And success breeds success. The relationship between Lastor Media and Italy’s Kino Produzioni, forged on “Alcarràs,” now both producers on “Saints,” has been “key to expanding our financing capacity,” says Rubirola Salas. Also, in producing more original films, which push the envelope on narrative or visuals, filmmakers are making a virtue out of a market necessity. Bolder films made at higher production standards is one way to stand out from the crowd. “Films have to be very competitive these days. We are releasing them in the same conditions as the rest of the films in the world. Filmmakers realize that it’s not enough to just have good ideas,. They also need great ambitions and to show them,” says Roch. That includes first-time feature directors. Roch cites “Alive” (“Viva”), made by Clotet, bulwarked in confidence by her breakout groundbreaking international TV co-production “This Is Not Sweden.” An issue-blender, it turns on Nora, 40, who plunges into a relationship with a much younger man. Also, she faces possibly recurrent breast cancer and a world desiccated by global warming. Another case in point, Roch says, is “5 More Minutes.” Romero had just made for Movistar Plus the TV series hit “The Other Side,” which confirmed his ability to juggle genre – there horror, comedy and a thriller propulsion. Movistar Plus was “very comfortable with Berto making a first feature, was with us from the very start and made it possible for us to have the elements we needed to make it,” says Roch. “The idea is to get great stories and then just power them up across the board in all their different elements to have international stories that they can travel very well.” Tom Hanks, Ta-Nehisi Coates and More Join Barack Obama’s ‘A Great Book’ Podcast at Audible Like Nastya Signs Content Development Deal With Disney Alfonso Cuaron to Make First Korea Visit at Busan as Festival Also Spotlights European Women+ Filmmakers San Sebastián 2026: ‘Les Mis,’ Los Javis, Brad Pitt, Penélope Cruz and Much More ‘Heated Rivalry’ Star Hudson Williams Sparks TIFF Chaos, Teases Season 2 Rei Ami on Her New Pop Girl Era, and How Feeling Confident Inspired Her New Single ‘2 Loud’: ‘It’s a Clapback’ (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... articles.title: Catalonia: A Dozen Highlights at San Sebastián, From a Time-Loop Thriller to a Singular Heist Tale and a Potential Arthouse Sleeper
articles.full_text: Sep 18, 2026 4:31am PT Catalonia: A Dozen Highlights at San Sebastián, From a Time-Loop Thriller to a Singular Heist Tale and a Potential Arthouse Sleeper Catalan films also take in the latest from Isaki Lacuesta, a double San Sebastián Golden Shell winner, and a chance to catch up on co-productions , such as Berlin title 'Narciso,' and Isabel Coixet’s ’Three Goodbyes’ By John Hopewell , Rafa Sales Ross , Roberto Prieto , Callum McLennan 'Far From Trees' Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Barcelona’s soccer players packed out Spain’s FIFA World Cup winning team. Now Catalonia, the northeast region of Spain counting on Barcelona as its capital, accounts for a very significant chunk of the Spanish films playing this year’s San Sebastián Festival, one of its principal draws. Some 150 Catalan companies, no less, will be in San Sebastián. The bullish Catalan presence can be put down to an exciting new generation of Catalan directors and producers exploding on the scene over the last decade, since Carla Simón’s “Summer 1993.” Related Stories EbonyLife's Mo Abudu on TIFF Premiere 'The Secret Lives of Baba Segi's Wives' and 'the Consequences of the Decisions We Take as Women' Heartfelt, Rare Animated Belgian Feature 'Juul' Headlines Studio 100 Film's Expanding Slate at TIFF Market Key, also is Catalonia’s drive into pan-regional co-production, as many movies tap funding from around Spain. Also at play is a step-up in ambition among Catalan films at large and far larger mobility on the part of talent. So “Saints,” one of the big new Catalan films, is directed by Basque but Barcelona-based Mikel Gurrea , and one of the standout films by a Catalan director at San Sebastián, Carla Simón’s short feature “Flamenco,” is produced by Madrid’s Mamma Team. Popular on Variety Here are just some standouts from the far ranging Catalan presence at the 2026 San Sebastián Film Festival : Main Competition “5 More Minutes” (Javier Ruiz Caldera, Movistar Plus, El Terrat, Ikiru Films, Spain) ‘Five More Minutes’ Courtesy of San Sebastián Film Festival An on-the-rocks couple is caught in a time loop at a rural getaway. Part sometimes excruciating dark comedy, part sci-fi mindwarp and part suspense thriller whose grip bids fair to surprise at San Sebastián. Written and starring Berto Romero , one of Spain’s top stand-ups, playing opposite Belen Cuesta (The Endless Trench”) and an ineffable Javier Camara (“Talk to Her”). Spanish pay TV/SVOD colossus Movistar Plus, El Terrat, a Mediapro Studio company, and Ikiru Films, produce a typical genre cocktail for Romero, much directed with virtuosity by Javier Ruiz Caldera as a series of millimetrically calculated five-minute sequence shots. Filmax handles world sales. JH “Saints,” (“Sants,” Mikel Gurrea, Lastor Media, Nocturna Pictures, Deloris Films, Kino Produzioni, Spain, Italy) Courtesy of M-Appeal Played by Victoria Luengo, who starred opposite Javier Bardem in “The Beloved,” Lali cares for her dying mother Glòria, as she falls in with a gang who steals statues of saints, giving much of the proceeds to the needy and forsaken. Gurrea’ second feature, a step-up in style, shot with a continuous visual pulse, varying in tone from scene to scene. Produced by Barcelona’s Nocturna Pictures, Deloris Films and Lastor Media and Kino Produzioni, the latter two both behind Berlin Golden Bear winner “Alcarràs,” another exploration of an alternative economy. JH Special Screenings “Pray for Us,” (“Ruega for nosotras,” Daniel Monzón, Arcadia Motion Pictures, Ikiru Films, Spain) The latest from the still underrated Monzón, director of the breakout blockbuster “Cell 211” and the memorable “The Laws of the Frontier,” a five-time Goya winner that played out of competition at 2021’s San Sebastián. Set in 1974, after a night on the tiles, Ana, 19, is dispatched by her wealthy family to Spain’s Women’s Protection Board, a Francoist state-backed institution confining young women in the guise of moral “reform.” Arcadia Motion Pictures, behind the Oscar-nominated “Robot Dreams” and Sorogoyen’s “The Beasts,” produces. Picked up by Film Factory Entertainment for international, Elastica for Spanish distribution. JH Horizontes Latinos “Ashes,” (Diego Luna, La Corriente del Golfo, Animal de Luz Films, Inicia Films, Perro Azul) Lauded actor Diego Luna (“Y tu mamá también,” “Andor”) steps behind the camera to helm the adaptation of Brenda Navarro’s critically acclaimed feminist novel “Eating Ashes.” The film stars Anna Diaz (“La Cocina”) and Adriana Paz, who shared the Cannes best actress award with Zoe Saldaña, Selena Gomez and Karla Sofía Gascón for “Emilia Pérez.” The heartfelt drama trails Lucila, a young woman who leaves Mexico with her young brother to reunite with their distant mother in Madrid. Luna also produces via his La Corriente del Golfo label, founded alongside Gael García Bernal. Luxbox handles sales. RSR “Narciso,” (Marcelo Martinessi, La Babosa Cine, Guay Films, Bocacha Films, Pandora Filmproduktion, Bteam Pictures, Oublaum Filmes, Esquina Filmes, La Fábrica Noctura) Paraguay’s submission to the Oscars, the eight-country co-production “Narciso” began its lauded festival journey at the Berlinale, where it won the Fipresci Award at the Panorama section. Martinessi’s sophomore feature is set in 1959, where the charismatic titular performer returns to Buenos Aires at the height of a strict military regime. When the popular young man is found dead after a show, the culprit becomes even harder to find within this regime built on silence and fear. Luxbox handles world sales. RSR Zabaltegi – Tabakalera “Far From the Trees,” ( Meritxell Colell , Allegra Films, EXIT Media, Animalita Cine, Spain) A Locarno 2026 Fipresci Prize winner. Adela, a sound artist recording endangered languages travels to the Peruvian highlands in a film which weaves present and past – collective and personal memory and archive footage of the Catalan diaspora after the Spanish Civil War – speaking about family, forced exile, roots, memory and hybrid identity. “A richly contemplative journey of physical and mental meanderings, beautifully combining 4K digital with Super 16,” says Variety. “Ambitious in scope yet intimate in focus,” Far From the Trees” “could well become an arthouse sleeper,” it adds. JH “Flamenco Sketches,” (“Jaleos,” Isaki Lacuesta , Lastor Media, Goroka Contents, with La Termita Films, Spain) Courtesy of San Sebastián Film Festival Sharing with Francis Ford Coppola the rare honour of two San Sebastián Golden Shells, Isaki Lacuesta returns to the festival fresh from co-directing HBO Max’s acclaimed series “Ravalear.” “Flamenco Sketches” is a restless ride through cinema, machines, Nazism, Civil War, and avant-garde art. The film shows how flamenco has often swallowed disruption whole only to morph itself anew. “Always dying, never dead.” one of the many contributing voices in the doc tells us. CM “Red Rocks,” (Bruno Dumont, Rosa Filmes, Luxbox, Nightswim, Andergraun Films, Tessalit, Pulpa Films, Sula Films) The latest by the Silver Bear winner of “The Empire” premiered at Directors’ Fortnight in Cannes and tells the tale of two gangs of kids who compete in the dangerous game of cliff jumping in the French Riviera. Dumont worked with a cast of non-professional actors, adopting a documentary-like approach to the film, shot against the cliffs and open waters of the Mediterranean. The lauded director won two Grand Prix awards at Cannes for “Humanity” and “Flanders.” Luxbox handles world sales. RSR Made in Spain “Alive” (“Viva” Aina Clotet, Ikiru Films, Funicular Films, La Terraza Films) In the intimate “Viva,” which earned its director-star Clotet the Louis Roederer Foundation Rising Star Award, follows 40-something Nora as she finds a new lease of life following cancer treatment. The heartfelt drama explores relationships, as well as the dilemmas brought in by climate change, with a standout performance by the established Clotet, whose 2024 series “This is Not Sweden” racked up several awards and found great success with audiences. The director produces under her Funicular Films label, alongside veteran Edmon Roch of Ikiru Films. Loco Films handles sales, while Caramel Films distributes in Spain. RSR “The Good Daughter,” (Astra Pictures, Avalon, Krater, Spain, Belgium) The sophomore feature of Julia de Paz Solvas, also a co-writer on Alauda Ruiz de Azúa’s “Querer,” plumbing gender violence from the untutored perspective of Carmela, the daughter of a direct victim. A trenchant portrait of self pitying, violent male narcissism and an uplifting take on teen female friendship which swept the Tallinn Black Nights Festival in November, sweeping its Grand Prix, actress (Kiara Arancibia) and Audience Awards. JH “Sixteen Moments of My Life” (Albert Serra, Idéale Audience, Andergraun Films, Weltfilm, Spain, France, Germany) The latest by irreverent Catalan maverick Albert Serra (“Pacifiction,” “Afternoons of Solitude”) premiered at Locarno. It documents a one-off performance by legendary German film actress and singer Ingrid Caven – known for her collaborations with then-husband Rainer Werner Fassbinder – at the Théâtre des Bouffes du Nord in Paris. Neither a biopic nor a concert movie, “Sixteen Moments of My Life” puts forward a fascinating portrayal of creatives on creatives. Serra’s Andergraun Films label produces and handles sales. RSR “Three Goodbyes,” ( Isabel Coixet , Cattleya, Ruvido Produzioni, Bartlebyfilm, Buena Pinta Media, Vision Distribution, Bteam Prods, Perdición Films, Tres Cuencos, Apaches Entertainment, Spain, Italy) Bowing at least year’s Toronto, a home-run from Isabel Coixet, Adapting a short story collection by Italy’s Michela Murgia, who died of cancer at 51. articles.title: Japan’s Top Broadcasters Unite for First Joint Delegation to MipCancun (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Sep 18, 2026 5:00am PT Japan’s Top Broadcasters Unite for First Joint Delegation to MipCancun (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Japan’s Top Broadcasters Unite for First Joint Delegation to MipCancun (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ 3 hours ago ‘Best of the Best’ Director Lena Khan on Making a Bollywood Fusion Dance Movie for Netflix, Working With Hasan Minhaj and Telling Maitreyi Ramakrishnan to Bring ‘Channing Tatum Energy’ 5 hours ago See All MipCancun Ten major Japanese broadcasters are joining forces for the first time to send a joint delegation to MipCancun , marking the country’s first coordinated television market presence outside Asia. The “All- Japan ” initiative is organized under the Japan Commercial Broadcasters Association (JBA) in collaboration with Japan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC) and the Broadcast Program Export Association of Japan (BEAJ). JBA represents commercial broadcasters operating television and/or radio services across the country, and the initiative is designed to promote Japanese IP and expand business opportunities across the Latin American content market. MIP Cancun is marking its 13th edition this year. Related Stories Richie Mehta on Turning Bandit Queen Phoolan Devi's Story Into a 48-Hour Siege: 'She Was Somebody Who Found Agency' How Irish Indie ‘Lemonade’ Landed Barry Keoghan in Between Beatles Shoots and Gave Him ‘Closure’ About Care System (EXCLUSIVE) The delegation includes Tokyo-based key stations TBS Television, Nippon TV, TV Asahi, Fuji Television Network, Inc. and TV Tokyo, along with Wowow Inc., BS Asahi, Tokai TV, MBS, Inc. and Yomiuri Telecasting Corp. A dedicated Japan Pavilion will be set up within the market’s matchmaking zone, giving each company its own table for meetings with Latin American buyers. Popular on Variety While Japan remains best known internationally for anime, the delegation will emphasize live-action content, particularly television drama, a category the Japanese government is now specifically targeting for overseas growth. “As IP development and co-productions become increasingly vital in the entertainment market, the industry is reaching a major turning point,” said Maria Perez Bellière, director of MipCancun. “We have high expectations for this initiative to introduce the appeal of Japan’s new content and firmly establish the ‘Japan brand’ in Latin American countries, with whom Japan shares a long history. We are deeply honored that Japan has united to leverage the unique Latin American market opportunities that MipCancun has spent 13 years building here in Cancun.” A “Japan Content Showcase” screening event will run Nov. 18 in the Cancun Theater Room, spotlighting programming from the participating broadcasters with a focus on Japanese drama for Latin American industry professionals. A networking cocktail reception will follow, giving the visiting companies and local buyers additional time to talk business. The push into Latin America comes as the Japanese government has named the content industry one of the country’s core growth sectors. Tokyo has set a target of expanding the overseas market for Japanese-origin content from JPY5.8 trillion ($37 billion) in 2023 to JPY20 trillion ($129 billion) by 2033, with a specific target of JPY0.5 trillion ($3.2 billion) for live-action content overseas by 2033. Latin America brings its own long history of serialized television drama, rooted in telenovelas that have been produced across the region since the 1950s and have traveled widely across borders. The continued growth of streaming in the region is also opening new pathways for international scripted content to reach audiences. Organizers frame the delegation as a way for Japanese networks to strike deals with Latin American buyers, distributors and producers when the market runs in November. MipCancun is a content market and conference serving Latin American and U.S. Hispanic television, bringing together acquisition, distribution and production companies to close content deals in the region’s growing TV markets. articles.title: ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators Wanted Green Lantern For Their DC Crossover Episode But Had To Settle For The Flash
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Katie Campione Katie Campione Senior TV & Labor Reporter @katie_campione More Stories By Katherine ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Recap: Season 35 Kick Off Continues With Ladies Night & Another Elimination ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Season 35 Premieres To 24% Audience Boost With Ladies’ First Routines Still To Come ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Season 35 Premiere Recap: The Men Take The Lead In First Of Two-Night Kick Off & Someone Goes Home Already View All September 17, 2026 6:30pm 'Stuart Fails To Save The Universe' SPOILER ALERT! This post contains details from Thursday night’s episode of HBO Max ‘s Stuart Fails to Save the Universe . Related Stories News ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Panel Teases DC Episode, OG Returns As ‘Big Bang Theory’ Franchise Makes Comic-Con Return Cancellations and Renewals ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Renewed For Season 2 By HBO Max As the title of this week’s episode (“Spoiler: We Couldn’t Get Green Lantern”) suggests, the creators of Stuart Fails to Save the Universe really did want the Green Lantern to be at the center of the show’s DC comic crossover. Unfortunately, the man without fear was already booked. “They told us we couldn’t have him because of [HBO’s live-action series] Lanterns , which I understood,” Zak Penn , one of the series’ creators, revealed to Deadline. “Chuck [Lorre] was a little grumbly about it, but Bill and I pointed out to him that Flash was actually perfect. If we needed something that’s going from dimension to dimension, Flash worked even better than Green Lantern.” Like Penn says, the episode ultimately sees Stuart (Kevin Sussman) and his friends stuck inside a comic book, where Mr. Freeze is terrorizing Gotham City. To get out of that dimension, they go off in search of Golden Age Flash for help. Watch on Deadline “It was half opportunity and half what they encouraged us, but Golden Age Flash appealed to us a lot, just because he’s kind of silly. No offense to Golden Age Flash,” Penn said. If it seems kind of backward that the gang would trek all the way to Central City to enlist The Flash to help them take on a villain in Batman’s territory, that’s the point. The writers reveled in the opportunity to poke fun at the more far-fetched notions accepted in comic lore. “Bill [Prady] and I were laughing a lot [about] the whole notion of Gotham City isn’t where New York City is, which makes no sense,” Penn said. “All those things were just kind of built up humor and things that we felt about comic books. So, the next obvious decision was, in terms of a villain, let’s put the villain who seems right and that people know more, and then have our characters comment on the fact that he’s the wrong villain for this piece.” Penn is surely considered the superhero expert of the group as a Marvel vet who also famously wrote a script for a Suicide Squad film that went unused. However, he says his fellow creators Prady and Lorre, as well as several of the other writers, had their own affinity for DC comics to draw upon for the episode. He and the writers thought a commentary on how a layperson would navigate a comic locale like Gotham City “seemed like the perfect sense of humor for our show.” “If you were in the DC universe, it would be pretty boring a lot of the time because you’d just be sitting around waiting for planes,” he laughs, adding that the irony is there’s also a bit about that exact notion in an early episode of Lanterns. That other DC show didn’t steal all Stuart ‘s thunder, though, and in fact there is plenty that the comedy series can get away with that its drama counterparts cannot in that the writers can lean into the quirks of these convoluted superhero universes rather than shy away. “One of the things about this show that’s really fun is that you know when you work on an actual comic book movie, you really have to be rigorous about the consistency of the reality, because people will pick you apart if you’re not, and on this show we kind of took the attitude of ‘we’re going to purposely break things and then have the characters notice that the multiverse doesn’t work as well as it should,'” Penn explained. Similarly, Penn says the episode could adopt a visual style more consistent with comic books without asking the audience to do more work suspending their disbelief. “[Director] Robbie McNeill deserves a lot of credit, because he really added a bunch of stuff, like the way the frames panel at certain points, which is something that I don’t always think is effective. Back in the early days of comic book movies, when people did that, I think it really took you out of it,” Penn told Deadline. “But this show’s sense of humor needs that, so it was really helpful.” The writers worked closely with DC’s Jim Lee to develop the versions of the comic characters that appear in Thursday’s episode. Lee teased the partnership over the summer at San Diego Comic-Con, assuring the audience in Hall H that the DC IP would be in good hands with the Stuart team. “Some of the DC characters they have in it, I think are some of the best versions I’ve seen of those characters, and so I’m super excited for you guys,” Lee said at the time. Penn, who had previously collaborated with Lee and the DC team on Ready Player One , remembered the Stuart reteam fondly: “They were great. They basically said, ‘How can we help? Other than we won’t give you Green Lantern.'” The series has already been renewed for a second season ahead of next week’s Season 1 finale. Penn tells Deadline he “would be shocked” if the writers didn’t once again mine from the DC universe in future episodes, but Season 2 is still in early stages. “The writers’ room hasn’t started yet. Next week, we’re going to get back together and start talking about this,” he said.
