articles.title: The Old & New Hollywood Guard Wielding AI’s Might
articles.full_text: Sep 17, 2026 7:01am PT The Old & New Hollywood Guard Wielding AI’s Might A look at 10 companies that are looking to mold cutting-edge tech into must-have tools for the industry By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest James Cameron’s Lightstorm Scoops Up AI-Powered 3D Tech Company Outsyders 23 hours ago Universal Music Group Sues DistroKid for Deceptive Trade Practices and Building an ‘AI-Slop Pipeline’ 2 days ago Interview With Tilly Norwood Reveals Even Fewer Reasons For the Existence of the AI ‘Actress’ 3 days ago See All ILLUSTRATION: MICHAEL STARBUCK/VARIETY VIP+ The AI gold rush has hit showbiz, even as the tech-fueled race to riches remains fraught. Morphing at a mind-bendingly fast pace, artificial intelligence technology has roiled the entertainment industry, which remains split between those convinced that it can be a powerful tool for creative expression and those wary of i ts potential to introduce “cinema illiteracy” and cut humans out of the equation. Variety takes a look at how 10 companies are taming the AI beast with specific use cases that creatives can get behind in a way that keeps them firmly in control and respects copyrights. Related Stories Filmax Launches Mar Olid’s ‘The Wedding Hustlers’ (EXCLUSIVE) Markus Lehmusruusu’s Finnish Oscar Entry ‘The Squirrel’ Earns Aki Kaurismäki’s Stamp of Approval: ‘He Said It’s Like ‘2001: A Space Odyssey,’ but Better Because It’s Full of Humanism’ Some of the industry’s household names have been at the forefront of AI. This spring Netflix announced the surprise acquisition of Ben Affleck’s InterPositive AI start-up. Amazon MGM and Lionsgate have both appointed AI leaders, and Google, a foe and friend alike to creatives, has partnered with Oscar-winning talent through its DeepMind unit in a bid to strengthen its relationship with filmmakers. Popular on Variety Alongside the old guard, there’s a new one: a collection of companies not afraid to ruffle feathers, promising an unprecedented — and controversial — leap in how films are made. Such is the case with Particle 6 , the brash creator of AI “actress” Tilly Norwood, and the rabble-rousers at Higgsfield . Both upstarts have produced or are producing AI-generated films to showcase their technology. Other creative-minded AI companies include Runway , which is bullish on the democratization of filmmaking, and the Martin Scorsese-backed Black Forest Labs . What’s behind Hollywood’s new AI arms race? “It’s a maturing of some of the tools where it actually can be used now,” says Erik Weaver, the principal of AI and emergent media at the University of Southern California’s Entertainment Technology Center. And at the same time, “a lot of the studios are also seeing that land rush,” he adds — meaning, in other words, that they see the need to get on board or get left behind. Netflix last year said it was “all in” on incorporating AI throughout its business, but it was unclear exactly what that meant. Then it spent nearly $600 million on Ben Affleck’s secret AI company. The purchase of the tools-focused InterPositive in March signaled both the company’s investment in the space — with Affleck’s filmmaking background and film-focused team as the core drivers behind the purchase — and its belief in partnering with creatives as it experiments with the technology. Since then, Netflix has revealed that roughly 300 programs across its library have incorporated generative AI in some fashion, it’s experimenting with AI-animated projects (though none are actively in the works) and it has worked with the AI audio firm ElevenLabs to weave in an AI replica of Gene Wilder’s voice for its upcoming reality show “Wonka’s The Golden Ticket.” For some, the endorsement from the world’s biggest streamer helped validate AI’s presence in entertainment. “We really wanted to help folks contextualize and understand that AI is impacting all different parts of the production chain, and some of the examples from our different filmmakers using it kind of hit at the core of that kind of thesis,” says Girish Balakrishnan, Netflix’s senior director of creative innovation, about disclosing the 300 AI-enabled projects. “But kind of in [how] creator-led, filmmakers leading those productions are doing it, and we just want folks to be aware that that’s the state of things.” It’s an approach adopted by Amazon MGM, the tech giant’s studio arm that has developed its own AI wing. The studio last year appointed Albert Cheng, previously head of Prime Video in the U.S., as its inaugural head of “AI Studios” and charged him with integrating — though not mandating — the technology’s use throughout its production pipeline. Since then, Amazon MGM has hosted its “AI on the Lot” conference to discuss AI’s place in Hollywood, where it announced a slate of AI-animated shows (though one, from “The Book of Life” director Jorge R. Gutierrez, ended after Gutierrez backed out following an outcry over his plans for an AI-animated project). “AI helps the production pipeline move faster, so our customers won’t have to wait 24 months between seasons of a show,” Cheng says. “The goal is to figure out how we can put these tools into creators’ hands to help them make more series, more movies.” Not to be outdone, Lionsgate appointed industry veteran Kathleen Grace as its first-ever chief AI officer in February, tasking her with overseeing the studio’s strategy regarding the tech. The company hasn’t unveiled plans for how it’s using AI with its own IP, but in June expanded its yearslong deal with Runway through acquiring an equity stake to tap into one of its franchises for an AI-generated short-form series. “The thing we’re interested in is how do we use generative AI to find new opportunities and new audiences for the content we own?” Grace says. “New ways to distribute it, new ways to think about it, and that, to me, is the interesting thing about AI. It’s not just an efficiency play. It’s ‘Can we bring new life or new audiences to things by either using the intelligence that it offers us to make us distribute it more effectively or smartly?’ Or use AI and large language models and large amounts of social intelligence data to understand, ‘Oh, maybe there’s a subculture that is really into this movie that we have in our catalog, and we should be marketing it to them.’” Google, meanwhile, has tried to integrate itself into the creative community. The internet company has rankled some in entertainment and media over how it has trained its AI models. But Eli Collins, DeepMind’s vice president of product, says the company helps build custom models for many of its partnerships, such as the AI-powered production of “The Wizard of Oz” at the Sphere in Las Vegas, and will potentially be involved in the upcoming “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” at the venue. That’s helped earn the trust of directors like Darren Aronofsky, whose AI studio Primordial Soup partnered with Google, and director Doug Liman, who helped develop an immersive film, “Asteroid,” for the company’s extended-reality app. “When we work within a domain, we think it’s really critical to work with people in that domain,” Collins says. In video, “we’ve worked with people, industrial designers, we’ve worked with illustrators, and as videos progress, that’s really allowed us to go more into film and storytelling generally as a medium.” Google’s AI entertainment push included a $75 million investment this summer in indie film darling A24, which is researching new tools in partnership with DeepMind. That pact spawned a backlash among those incredulous that A24 was getting in the AI game; responding to the brouhaha, A24 said, “We’d rather have a seat at the table than [sit] on the sidelines.” Collins is tight-lipped about that partnership, as well as the company’s potential involvement in the Sphere’s upcoming production of “The Rocky Horror Picture Show.” As established studios and big tech companies plant their AI flags, a new crop of disruptors has emerged. Particle 6, the U.K. company behind Tilly Norwood, caused a firestorm over the boisterous claim the “actor” would soon be signed to an agency (agencies said “no thanks” ) and stirred fears that Tilly would take actors’ jobs (leading to new SAG-AFTRA guidelines on synthetic performers). CEO Eline Van der Velden says the industry got it wrong. She says Tilly’s whole purpose is to exist for “underserved” audiences and that the AI character was never intended to replace human actors. “Everything would need to be AI,” she said. “That’s where Tilly makes sense.” Van der Velden says the controversial Tilly-led film “Misaligned,” which kicked off an anticipated 12-month production cycle this month, is simply meant for those audiences eager for more “niche” content. She also thinks Tilly herself could be a new model for human actors to work with, akin to motion capture. “In a way, I’m a puppeteer, because especially when I’m doing motion capture, where I’m the creative director of her acting,” she says. “This is what I think actors in the future will be in charge of.” For companies invested in the intersection of AI and entertainment, much of the work to date has been proofs-of-concept. Fountain 0 ’s debut of the docudrama “Dreams of Violets” at the Tribeca Festival in June made it one of the first fully AI-generated films to premiere at a major festival. The company also made a knockoff of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” dubbed “Odysseus: The Fall,” hoping to show how close the technology can get to producing a similar version of a $250 million summer blockbuster. (Unsurprisingly, not everyone agreed that it was in the same ballpark.) Ash Koosha, CEO of Fountain 0, says his goal is to help people execute their own visions for movies, without the dozens of crew members typically needed for a feature film. The company also inked a deal with “The View” co-host Sunny Hostin, who licensed her likeness to the company to help adapt her novels. “I think we’re going to see with AI the power of a $400 million film, the look of it, the reality of it, in the hand of an arthouse filmmaker,” he says. Along those lines, Runway and Higgsfield have made moves to get their respective generative-AI platforms into the hands of aspiring filmmakers. Higgsfield has hosted contests and inked likeness- licensing partnerships , while Runway has held its AI Festival each year since 2022. Both companies have given creators a chance to bring their stories and intellectual property to life, a la the director Kane Parsons’ journey from YouTube creator to theaters with his thriller “Backrooms.” “New technology unlocks new creative formats, and this is just another example of the sort of IP or celebrities crossover, something which they couldn’t do typically,” Higgsfield CEO Alex Mashrabov says. “This is just a great example of how a traditional story, how a traditional script, can be applied to these modern realities.” Runway’s festivals have drawn the likes of director Ron Howard and Netflix’s Balakrishnan. Co-CEO Cristóbal Valenzuela says the company plans to drop “AI” from the title next year in the spirit of its belief that, after this moment of “transition,” the use of AI will be as commonplace in cinema as cameras. A future like that takes the backing of those who know how to make movies — and some heavyweights have come out in support of using AI tools in the craft. “I don’t think there’s going to be a day or a time or a month when someone’s gonna say, ‘OK, this is the day we stop saying this is AI video or not AI video,’” Valenzuela says. “It just happens naturally. It’s a transition, and we’re going through a transition right now.” Scorsese’s backing of the German AI company Black Forest Labs represented the most public endorsement from a film visionary of the technology’s place in the production process. But for the company itself, it was a partnership tied to research and exploration of how the tools could work for creatives. While Scorsese hasn’t commented on the partnership (and the start-up won’t say whether he’s using its Flux models on his next film), the revelation of his participation marked another divisive moment for the industry. “AI in the creative space is an emotive issue,” says Ben Brooks, Black Forest’s head of public policy. “We’re sensitive to the depth of feeling across the community, but at the same time, building these bridges, having this kind of dialogue, is really important to understand how we can make the technology work for the community.” How fully Hollywood deploys AI may be held in check by one key factor: Public sentiment appears to remain strongly against the technology’s use in movies and TV. Social media users flamed the use of AI in Eli Roth’s “Ice Cream Man” and the David Dastmalchian-led “Late Night With the Devil,” among others. Many people fear AI’s societal impact. Director Jon Erwin, who founded Innovative Dreams , an AI offshoot of his Amazon-affiliated Wonder Project initiative that fuses generative technology into its projects, thinks such fears stem from people lumping productive use cases together with forms of AI “slop.” Erwin, who has incorporated generative-AI technology into his Amazon MGM show “House of David” and his Angel Studios film “Young Washington,” says artificial intelligence should be seen as part of the long arc of technology adoption by creators. “There is a collision of technology and art,” Erwin says. “Hollywood has always been an art form that is a fusion of tools that are disruptive and given to artists — and used in ways no one would expect.” *** Amazon MGM Studios AI focus : Company in May greenlit three shows under its “GenAI Creators’ Fund,” including shows from “Book of Life” director Jorge Gutierrez (who backed out) and ex-Nickelodeon president Albie Hecht; the home of Jon Erwin’s shows, adopting the filmmaker’s use of the technology; developed “Project Nara” with AWS, a workspace for creators using AI. Key player : Albert Cheng, head of AI studios Why they matter: The studio arm of the e-commerce behemoth is in pole position among major studios to harness the power of proprietary tech, prodigious computing power and top-tier content production. Black Forest Labs Image and video generator AI focus : Martin Scorsese put the company on the map when he cited it as helping him plot out the storyboard for an upcoming film. Investors include BroadLight Capital and CAA co-founder Mike Ovitz. Key players : David Dorfman, co-founder and managing partner; Kevin Yorn and Rick Yorn, co-founders and general partners Why they matter: Because Martin Scorsese said so. Fountain 0 Filmmaking and streaming platform AI focus : “Dreams of Violets” accepted into Tribeca, a breakthrough for AI movies; recently licensed “The View” host Sunny Hostin’s image for AI movie adaptations of her romance novels. Key player: Ash Koosha, creator and CEO Why they matter: Koosha has an expansive vision of what AI filmmaking can achieve. Google DeepMind AI research laboratory AI focus : Its work with filmmakers Doug Liman and Darren Aronofsky and A24 underscore its pursuit of Hollywood. It’s also focused on AI experiences, like “The Wizard of Oz” at the Sphere in Las Vegas, and its potential involvement in the venue’s “Rocky Horror Picture Show” production. Key player : Eli Collins, VP of product for Google DeepMind, Márcia Mayer, head of production for DeepMind Why they matter: Because they’re part of Google. Higgsfield AI AI video platform AI focus : “Hell Grind” and “Cully Hill Boys” showcased what an AI-generated action-adventure could look like — even if the final product wasn’t great; AI-assisted films and licensing influencers’ likenesses for a project. Key player : Alex Mashrabov, CEO and founder Why they matter: Higgsfield has hosted AI contests and inked likeness-licensing pacts. Innovative Dreams Virtual production studio AI focus : Director Jon Erwin has forged an indie path through his Wonder Project venture, and he’s also been a maverick who has publicly embraced the efficiency of AI tools to enable creatives. The filmmaker’s production technology venture Innovative Dreams launched earlier this year with AI firm Luma. Key players : Jon Erwin, Luma CEO Amit Jain Why they matter: Wonder Project has impressed by building an indie film and TV business in just a few years since its 2021 launch. AI’s potential could turbocharge that growth and Erwin’s experimentation could attract others to his firm’s tech. Lionsgate AI focus : In 2024, the studio set a deal to train an AI model on the company’s film library in order to generate new content. It also hired its first-ever AI division head. Key player : Kathleen Grace, chief AI officer Why they matter: Lionsgate has the kind of huge library that could be attractive to a content-hungry AI firm with deep pockets. The studio is seen as a bellwether for Hollywood M&A. Netflix AI focus : The streaming giant says flatly that more than 300 of its programs use AI in production. It surprised the industry with a $587 million deal to buy Ben Affleck’s InterPositive startup. It’s even bankrolling Joseph Gordon-Levitt’s AI thriller “2034.” Key players: Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters; Girish Balakrishnan, senior director of creative innovation; Ben Affleck Why they matter: Because they’re Netflix. Particle 6 Content studio AI focus : The company is home to the synthetic actress Tilly Norwood, whose debut as a film festival PR stunt triggered fears about AI creations taking the place of human actors. Key players : CEO Eline Van der Velden Why they matter : Love Tilly or hate Tilly, Van der Velden has proven her ability to garner attention and spur outrage among anti-AI purists. Runway AI research, audio and video image generation AI focus : A leader in AI generation and exhibition; expansive partnership with Lionsgate to work on IP illustrates how Hollywood is willing to cede its most valuable assets to AI models; showcases AI films at its annual bi-coastal festival, which this year saw its biggest turnout and included Ron Howard. Key player : Cristóbal Valenzuela, co-founder and CEO Why they matter: The former NYU Tisch researcher has gained the trust of major filmmakers and studios to help them learn how to use AI tools. articles.title: Channel 4 Rules Out Reviewing Record Executive Pay Amid Dramatic Job Cuts
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter , Max Goldbart September 17, 2026 4:00am 'The Great British Bake Off' Season 17 Channel 4/Love Productions EXCLUSIVE : Channel 4 has no plans to review record levels of executive pay in recent years despite the UK network’s ambition to radically reduce its cost base. Deadline understands that Channel 4’s board is not giving active consideration to reducing the pay packets of top executives amid a broader strategic review at The Great British Bake Off broadcaster, which will result in 340 layoffs before the end of the year. Alex Mahon and Ian Katz were the highest-paid CEO and chief content officer in Channel 4’s history, and executive remuneration often became a lightning rod for disquiet about the network’s performance. Related Stories News Channel 4 & Paramount's 5 Make History With Advertising Deal News International Insider: European TV In Peril; Venice & TIFF Latest; Mercedes Ron Interview The pay levels contributed to a feeling that Channel 4 became “bloated” and inefficient under Mahon’s regime, with these concerns resurfacing after new CEO Priya Dogra announced last week that the broadcaster will cut more than a quarter of its workforce. Mahon declined to comment. Watch on Deadline Mahon pocketed total pay of £8.46 million ($11.3M) during her tenure, which was up 33% on her predecessor, David Abraham. Katz earned £4.2M in his first six years as chief content officer, a 34% increase on what Jay Hunt was paid during an equivalent period of time. Channel 4 top brass came in for criticism during layoffs in 2024, when it was revealed its top three earners would accept bonuses . Katz ultimately decided to forego his . Channel 4 declined to disclose how much Dogra will be paid, though her earnings will eventually be published next year in the 2026 annual report. Alex Mahon Will Johnston Photography Channel 4’s remuneration committee considers multiple factors when awarding pay, including remit targets, though overall growth is considered a key metric. Channel 4 posted record sales of £1.16 billion on Mahon’s watch in 2021, but the 33% increase in her pay outpaced the company’s revenue growth of 5.6% during her time in charge. Channel 4 chairs have consistently defended executive pay. Interim chair Dawn Airey said last year that Mahon had done an “extraordinary” job in marshalling the company’s resources towards streaming and growing digital ad revenue. Not all agree with Airey. “Executive pay is a tiny proportion of Channel 4’s overall costs, but it’s a perception issue. It speaks to the psychology at Channel 4. The notion that Channel 4 was in rude health under Alex appears to be deception in the context of Priya’s cuts,” said a senior producer, summing up the sentiment of many. “If you want to judge the mess, look at the cleanup.” Swelling Workforce Channel 4 is slashing its workforce by 28%, with around half of commissioning roles at risk. Channel 4’s drama and comedy teams are being smashed together , with talk of seven roles becoming three, encompassing two genre heads under a scripted chief. Film4 is not part of the changes. Insiders said the mood is grim and chaotic. Some criticized the way in which layoffs were handled, including that two different groups were invited to meetings on the same day and “it became quite clear quite quickly which was for redundancy and which wasn’t,” according to one. But Dogra has argued that the changes are essential to ensuring Channel 4 cuts duplication and spends more money on screen. A senior Channel 4 source added that the need to slash costs has been made more urgent by the ad market taking “a dramatic shift down from where all the projections were.” The redundancies have cast light on Channel 4’s workforce swelling in recent years. The company’s average number of employees increased 50% to 1,276 during Mahon’s tenure, a notable period of expansion compared with the BBC, a fellow public service broadcaster, which cut headcount by 20% under former director general Tim Davie. This period included a plan to cut 200 jobs in 2024 , though Channel 4’s average employee numbers only fell by 67 roles during that year. “You always felt like they were bloated and in the end the previous regime’s inaction has meant the current one is now walking off a cliff edge,” said one regular Channel 4 supplier. A former employee lamented: “They’ve known for ages that having about 50 commissioners was wrong, but weren’t brave enough.” Mahon’s allies said she changed internal metrics to include long-term contractors, forcing employee numbers up. Mahon was also responsible for delivering on government demands to grow Channel 4’s presence outside of London, though critics said she chose to do this by duplicating rather than displacing jobs. “To please the politicians, they’ve built these offices and filled them with people, but they haven’t bitten the bullet on how to restructure the center,” said a well-placed industry source. Others pointed out that Channel 4 has made cuts in London and that its Horseferry Road headquarters — which will be put up for sale amid belt-tightening — has been quieter in recent years. A Channel 4 spokesperson said: “It is important to view past remuneration and workforce numbers in the context of one of the most significant periods of transformation in Channel 4’s history. During this time, the organisation managed the impact of the Covid pandemic, expanded its presence across the UK and accelerated its digital transition to a public service streamer. “The organisational changes proposed last week are the first stage of a transformation strategy to prioritise content investment, grow Channel 4’s impact and secure long-term sustainability, and will ensure that the organisation is in the right shape and size to deliver that future.” Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra Channel 4/Getty Dogra’s willingness to grasp the nettle of change has impressed insiders and Channel 4 observers, even if there are reservations about her decision to carve up the chief content officer role . Interviews have been ongoing for the director of programmes, with frontrunners said to include BBC iPlayer boss Dan McGolpin and Twofour CEO David Brindley. Numerous key Channel 4 suppliers characterized this hire as being one of the biggest decisions in Channel 4’s 43-year history. “The issues facing Channel 4 go far, and it’s going to take time and real creative leadership to turn things around,” said one. Roughcut CEO Ash Atalla, who produces comedies Big Boys and Stath Lets Flats , is among those who have defended Katz’s record , saying he backed “disruptive shows and the troublemaking that is important to Channel 4.” Dogra has made headway in other ways by poaching Paramount’s £300M TV advertising sales business from Sky, meaning Channel 4 now controls ad sales for Channel 4, 5, and UKTV. David Abraham, Channel 4’s former CEO, said it was the “most significant commercial deal” the company had signed in over a decade. “It brings together a block of the UK airtime and streaming market, which combines UKTV, Channel 4 and Channel 5, to a scale that is material and distinctive enough from what will become the Sky/ITV block,” said Abraham. “It’s a major feather in Priya’s cap and a big achievement to have done it because it’s not easy doing these deals.” Netanyahu Moves To Revoke ‘NAZA’ Directors’ Citizenship Audiences Flocking To Anime On Netflix, Report Finds Australia’s Stan Reviving Rural Drama ‘McLeod’s Daughters’ California Exit Plan Takes Shape Amid Antitrust Battle Over $111B WBD Merger Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Pingyao Film Festival Unveils 10th Edition Line-up; ‘Spring In A Small Town’ Set As Opening Film
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz CJ ENM Sells ‘Hotel Del Luna’, ‘Signal’ & Other Hit K-Dramas To CME Slovakia & Czech Channels Zhang Yimou To Head Seven-Member Competition Jury At Busan International Film Festival ‘Possible Love’ DoP Kim Ji-yong, ‘The Blue Road’ Director Han Jun-hee & WETA FX’s Kimball Thurston Among Speakers For Netflix ‘Creative Asia’ At BIFF View All September 17, 2026 4:13am Torino Shadow Pingyao International Film Festival China’s Pingyao International Film Festival (PYIFF) has announced the line-up for its tenth anniversary edition, which will open with a 4K restoration of Fei Mu’s Spring In A Small Town . Good Trip , co-directed by Hong Kong filmmakers Norris Wong and Hoi Wong, will close the festival. Short film Torino Shadow , directed by Jia Zhangke , co-founder of the festival, will be screened on Fenjiu Night, which will also feature a live performance by Chinese rock band Wutiaoren. Torino Shadow has its world premiere in this year’s Cannes Classics. The festival also announced the titles selected for its Crouching Tigers competition, which focuses on first, second and third films from international directors, and the Hidden Dragons competition for films from emerging directors making Chinese-language films. Related Stories Trailers 'Paper Tiger' Trailer: Adam Driver And Miles Teller Are Brothers In Harm's Way In James Gray's NYC Drama News James Gray Talks Dream Quality Of Cinema & Approach With Cast: "I'm Not A Good Director Of Actors" - Locarno Crouching Tigers includes Ben’imana , which won the Camera d’Or at this year’s Cannes film festival; Congo Boy , which won Best Actor in Un Certain Regard; and Filipiñana , which premiered at Sundance and has just been selected as the Philippines’ official entry for the Oscars (see full line-up below). Watch on Deadline Hidden Dragons include Zou Jing’s A Girl Unknown , which premiered in Cannes Critics Week, Dong Jie’s Zoom In, Zoom Out , which premiered in Venice Critics Week and Yeung Leung Chuen’s We Are Born Good , currently premiering in Toronto’s Discovery section. In addition to closing film Good Trip , Gala screenings at the festival include Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster , Na Hong-jin’s Hope , Christian Mungui’s Fjord and Jame Gray’s Paper Tiger , among other films. As part of the festival’s ten-year anniversary celebrations, PYIFF and the Nationwide Alliance of Arthouse Cinemas (NAAC) will mark their shared tenth anniversary with a “NAAC & PYIFF 10th Anniversary Celebration”, looking back at the films and filmmakers the two organisations have supported over the past decade. Also joining the anniversary programme is Slices Of Time: An Electronic Remix DJ Set , conceived by musician Lim Giong, who will perform live alongside film sound designer and musician Zhang Yang, electronic musician Li Yanzeng and DJ Weng Weng, with moving-image works by visual artists Ye Qiusen and Wang Tianyu. Reworking film excerpts through experimental moving images and live electronic sets, the event will bring image and sound together against the historic backdrop of Pingyao, while looking ahead to the festival’s next decade. articles.title: Clare Stewart Steps Down As Rotterdam Managing Director
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Trailer: Joseph Zada Stores Up Fury For The Revolution As Colorful Creatures Attack In The Arena Bonnie Greer Dies: British-American Writer & Cultural Commentator Was 77 Oscars: Spain Selects ‘La Bola Negra’ For International Feature Film Race View All September 17, 2026 4:52am Rotterdam Film Festival Clare Stewart has stepped down as Managing Director of Rotterdam Film Festival . In her role, Stewart jointly led the organisation alongside Festival Director Vanja Kaludjercic. She will remain in post until next year’s edition, her fourth in the role. Stewart, however, will remain involved with IFFR’s Displacement Film Fund, the short film grant initiative founded and led by Cate Blanchett. IFFR’s Supervisory Board has begun recruiting for a new Managing Director. During Stewart’s tenure, the IFFR team has secured several key funding commitments for the festival and its year-round work. This includes 4-year subsidies from both the National (OCW) and municipal (Gemeente Rotterdam) governments, which see the Festival supported up to and including the 2029 edition, and a successful bid from the content team (led by Chief of Content Melissa van der Schoor) for increased 3-year support from Creative Europe up to and including the 2028 edition. Related Stories News Cate Blanchett's Displacement Film Fund To Support Short Films By Mo Amer, Annemarie Jacir, Rithy Panh, Akuol de Mabior & Bao Nguyen News EST N8 Takes Worldwide Rights To Bangladeshi Rotterdam Winner 'Master' “It has been a privilege to share the custodianship of one of the world’s most essential film festivals with Vanja and to back her artistic and cultural vision for the future of IFFR,” Stewart said in a statement. Watch on Deadline “I am proud we have stabilised the business position of the organisation in a very challenging era for film festivals globally, and I truly believe that now is the right time to hand over to a new Managing Director to bring fresh energy and perspective to the continuing work of securing a sustainable future for IFFR. Importantly, this timing will also mean my successor has a decent runway into the next Dutch subsidy cycle.” Kaludjercic said in a statement that Clare “brought exceptional commitment, fearlessness and professionalism to IFFR” during her tenure. “One of Clare’s particular strengths is her ability to open up new possibilities for IFFR and pursue them with clarity and determination,” Kaludjercic said. “This has been especially evident in the way she has helped develop and steward the Displacement Film Fund with such confidence and momentum. While her role at the festival is changing, our collaboration will continue through the DFF, and I look forward to remaining closely connected as we take its next phase forward.” Netanyahu Moves To Revoke ‘NAZA’ Directors’ Citizenship Audiences Flocking To Anime On Netflix, Report Finds Australia’s Stan Reviving Rural Drama ‘McLeod’s Daughters’ California Exit Plan Takes Shape Amid Antitrust Battle Over $111B WBD Merger Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Israeli Film Council Calls For Festivals To Be Removed  From Funding Criteria & Creation Of Strand For Films Celebrating Israeli Soldiers Amid ‘Naza’ Firestorm
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Israeli Film Council Calls For Festivals To Be Removed From Funding Criteria & Creation Of Strand For Films Celebrating Israeli Soldiers Amid ‘Naza’ Firestorm Oscars: France Selects ‘Minotaur’ For Best International Feature Film Race Oscars: Italy Unveils 21-Title Shortlist With Nanni Moretti’s ‘It Will Happen Tonight’ & Venice Orizzonti Prizewinner ‘The House Of The Monkey’ View All September 17, 2026 5:50am Naza co-directors Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham at the Venice Film Festival Aurore Marechal/Getty Images The Israeli Film Council has called for film festivals to be eliminated from a points system used to set film fund budgets in the wake of the Venice Film Festival’s selection of bombshell documentary Naza exposing Israel ’s deliberate targeting of civilian targets in Gaza. At the same time, it has also recommended a new state backed funding strand for films celebrating the “heroism” of Israeli soldiers. The body, which advises the Israeli Ministry of Culture film policy, made the recommendations following an emergency meeting called in the wake of the Naza world premiere in Venice last week where it garnered a 25-minute ovation and won the Special Jury Prize. Related Stories News Ireland Boycotts Eurovision Again Over "Appalling Loss Of Lives In Gaza" News Netanyahu Moves To Get 'NAZA' Directors' Israeli Citizenship Revoked The incendiary documentary, revolving around the testimony of 24 Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers which have since been challenged by the Israeli army, has prompted a political firestorm in Israel. Watch on Deadline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has threatened to strip Israeli co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of their citizenship, while prominent filmmakers Ari Folman, Shlomi Elkabetz, Ran Tal and Michal Aviad have signed a petition expressing their solidarity for the pair. In a note forwarded to Deadline by an Israeli producer, the Israeli Film Council explained the motivations for its recommendations. “The move is meant to counter the smear and defamation campaigns being waged against Israel worldwide, while also strengthening films that reflect Israeli life and the memory of fallen soldiers’ heroism,” it wrote. It said the recommended new funding strand would support films “centered on the heroism of IDF soldiers and veterans of Israel’s wars who fought to secure the state’s existence, in keeping with the spirit of Israel’s Memorial Day Law for Fallen Soldiers.” The removal of film festivals as one of the criteria deciding film fund budgets will likely further isolate the Israeli cinema industry. The industry’s international standing has plummeted in the wake of Israel’s military operation in Gaza, which was in turn triggered by Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. It is a shadow of its former self, battered by boycotts on one side, and pressure from Netanyahu’s nationalist, rightwing government on the other. Under Israel’s complex state film funding system, the budget for cinema, which currently comes in at around 130m Israeli Shekels ($42m), is divided between six funds. They comprise the country’s oldest film fund, Israel Film Fund, which has recently supported films such as Sundance-selected Oscar entry Tell Me Everything ; Berlinale 2026 title Where To? by Assaf Machnes and Nadav Lapid’s Yes !, a satire critiquing Israeli society in the wake of October 7 and the Gaza military campaign, which was considered to hot to handle for Cannes’s Official Selection and played in Directors’ Fortnight instead in 2025. They are joined by more recently created entitles The New Fund for Cinema & Television; The Makor Foundation for Israeli Film and Television; The Jerusalem Film & Television Fund, and The Yehoshua Rabinovich Foundation for the Arts and the Gesher Multicultural Film Fund. The funds put in tenders for state finance, with their eventual award decided on a points system assessing their recent performance in which the number of A-list festival selections for the films they have backed has traditionally been one of the criteria. “The funds are competing between themselves for the funds from the Israeli Film Council, and one of the things contributing to their final grade is if they have A-list festival films,” explained the Israeli producer. “It was an important criterion but it’s not about the films but rather the motivations of the funds. When funds decide to support a film, one of the things that they consider is whether a director is known or not, say like Ari Folman. The likelihood of his films going to an A-list festival is one of the things that might convince the fund to invest. It’s not the only thing, of course, but it is an important factor along elements like the screenplay, budget,” they said. The producer continued that the Israeli Film Council statement was on one level “empty rhetoric” because Naza was not financed with any Israeli state money, or support from local broadcasters. It was produced instead by Guardian Documentaries with JW Films in association with Placeholder Films and Unseen Hand. “ Naza was not funded by Israeli funds or Israeli television, for sure,” they said. “They didn’t approach them, they didn’t apply. “That’s why these recommendations are so funny. Firstly, they want to take away the film festival marks… and then they want to glamorize the IDF. This is really like North Korea. It’s more funny than sad… it idiotic.” In the backdrop, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced on Wednesday that he is fast-tracking two bills through parliament in response to Naza , the first revoking the citizenship of anyone who “defames Israeli soldiers”, and the second ratcheting up potential damages payments in successful defamation cases against bodies or individuals maligning the Israeli military. Netanyahu’s threat to revoke Abraham and Szor’s citizenship follows in the wake of a similar threat by Culture and Sports Minister Miki Zohar, even though he has no legal power to set in motion such a move. If Abraham and Szor, who are both Jewish and born in Israel, were to be stripped of their Israeli citizenship it would unprecedented. While Palestinians with Israeli citizenship have been stripped of citizenship and deported to the West Bank or Gaza, no Jewish Israeli citizen has ever had their citizenship revoked. In the late 1990s, there were calls for the citizenship of Yigal Amir, who assassinated former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in 1995, to be removed. The Supreme Court refused the request. Alongside the political threats, Abraham and Szor have received multiple death threats, with far-right Israeli activists gathering outside the home of the latter’s parents chantings slogans such “death penalty for traitors”. The Brussels-based Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) has condemned the attacks and suggested the government rhetoric is putting the filmmakers’ live in danger. “Israeli authorities must ensure the safety of Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and immediately reject any attempt to use citizenship rights as a weapon against journalists,” it said in a statement this week. “Threats from senior government officials can have a chilling effect on journalists and encourage members of the public to engage in intimidation and silencing against them. These threats cannot be dismissed as political rhetoric. They are a warning to journalists and sources about the potential consequences of reporting critically on powerful institutions—and a dangerous signal to other journalists considering whether to investigate or expose alleged wrongdoing.” Netanyahu Moves To Revoke ‘NAZA’ Directors’ Citizenship Audiences Flocking To Anime On Netflix, Report Finds Australia’s Stan Reviving Rural Drama ‘McLeod’s Daughters’ California Exit Plan Takes Shape Amid Antitrust Battle Over $111B WBD Merger Read More About: Comments

articles.title: San Sebastián Film Festival Director José Luis Rebordinos On This Year’s Line-Up & Why Festivals “Have To Speak About Human Rights”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana José Luis Rebordinos Reflects On His Final Year At San Sebastián: “What Surprises Me The Most Is How Much The Festival Has Grown” ‘Onwards And Sideways’ Team Rhys Ifans, Laura Linney & John Madden On Making A Parkinson’s Story That Finds Laughter & Love In The Unexpected — Toronto Former DreamWorks & MGM TV Exec Brian Edwards Teams With Alpha Film Founders To Launch Time Zone Capital View All September 17, 2026 5:52am San Sebastian International Film Festival San Sebastian International Film Festival With the fall festival season underway, the international film community is now turning its head to Spain’s Basque Coast as the San Sebastian International Film Festival kicks off its 74th edition on September 18. With 263 projects from 47 countries in the official lineup, the program looks set to bring together a mix of established auteurs, emerging filmmakers and star power that continues to make it one of the most interesting European launchpads on the festival calendar. Tomorrow will see the event open with the world premiere of Fatih Akin’s fantasy drama Ghost Song , which will compete for the festival’s Golden Shell award. Further titles in the competition line up include Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut with Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti; Pablo Larraín’s Netflix horror series My Sad Dead ( Mis muertos tristes ); the world premiere of Fred Cavayé’s action-skewed adaptation of Les Misérables ; Mike Leigh’s Tender Loving Care ; Ah Biao’s Chinese-language feature debut Border ; and Nicole Garcia’s Marion Cotillard starrer Milo . The festival will close with Le Faux Soir from Belgian filmmaker Michaël R. Roskam on September 26. Related Stories News 'Club Kid' & 'The Man I Love' Among Titles Added To San Sebastian Lineup News Jesse Eisenberg's 'The Debut' & Fred Cavayé's 'Les Misérables' Among Six New Titles In San Sebastián Official Selection “We are always very eclectic,” says San Sebastián Film Festival Director José Luis Rebordinos about the selection for his final edition at the festival. The well-respected veteran has been running the event since 2011 and is stepping down at the end of the year. Watch on Deadline “This year, we have a mix of commercial and more radical cinema,” he says. “I’m really happy that we have Les Misérables in competition because, for me, it’s a good example of popular French cinema. It’s a very good film and a big production that will be really popular with our audiences. At the same time, we have Border , a very radical, but very difficult and interesting film as well as Pablo Larraín’s My Sad Dead ( Mis muertos tristes ).” This year’s event will also pack star power, with Naomi Watts, Brad Pitt, Penelope Cruz, Cotillard, Orlando Bloom, Rami Malek and Diego Luna among expected attendees. Watts will be the recipient of the festival’s prestigious Donostia Award, and she’ll touch down to screen her latest film The Housewife , the directorial debut of Canadian helmer Ben Shirinian. Director Werner Herzog will also receive a Donostia Award this year, while Pitt and director David Ayer will screen their latest film Heart of the Beast , which is set to play out of competition. It will mark Pitt’s first trip to the festival since 2009, when he and Quentin Tarantino presented Inglourious Basterds there. Ira Sachs will preside over the competition jury this year. “One of the most important sections for the festival is the New Directors section because we are very free and open when we select them,” says Rebordinos. “This year, I think the new directors we have selected in the section are more courageous than ever.” The New Directors strand includes first or second-time directors from Bulgaria, Chile, Germany, Iran, Japan, Kazakhstan, Mexico, Norway, South Korea, Spain, Taiwan, the UK and Ukraine. It will open with The Bad Son ( El mal hijo ), the debut feature from Jaime Lorente. The film’s official synopsis reads: When 11-year-old Ruben’s father mysteriously disappears, the boy has to move in with his grandmother, a woman he barely knows. In a rural setting, where time seems to have stood still, the child will learn that family wounds are passed down from one generation to another and will try to find a way to heal them as he grows. Les Miserables Curiosa Films – Eskwad – Studiocanal – TF1 Films production – Photo by Christophe Brachet “I think it’s a good moment for the new directors,” continues Rebordinos, pointing to Jordan Firstman’s feature debut Club Kid , which premiered in Cannes and saw A24 acquire the title for $17M in a competitive situation. Firstman rose to fame during the pandemic through is viral satirical impression videos on Instagram. Club Kid will screen in San Sebastián’s Perlak strand, which comprises a selection of feature films that have yet to be released in Spain but have had critical acclaim at other international festivals. Further titles in that lineup include Pawel Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord , Na Hong-jin’s Hope , Olivia Wilde’s The Invite and Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine . “The lineup really reflects the situation of cinema at this moment, in that it is very complex and different,” Rebordinos says. “Our official selection is definitely one of the most interesting lineups we have had in years. Cinema tends to reflect the society from which it originates and that’s why this year some titles reflect the way people film for Instagram and TikTok and so on.” Just a few weeks ago at the Venice Film Festival, the Gaza humanitarian crisis became a huge talking point at the festival with NAZA , a documentary about the killing of Palestinian civilians by Israeli forces in Gaza, taking a special jury prize at the festival. That film was directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and just this week , Benjamin Netanyahu has threatened to “revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world.” As a progressive festival, San Sebastián has refused to shy away from the conversation: Last year, the festival issued an open letter calling for an “immediate ceasefire” in Gaza, a unique move for any film festival. It publicly stated its “rejection of the genocide [and] of the unimaginable massacres to which the government of Benjamin Netanyahu is subjecting the Palestinian people since Hamas perpetrated the terrorist attack of 7 October 2023, which, we of course, also condemn.” This year, Rebordinos says its stance remains the same and stresses that festivals and individuals who have a platform should be inclined to use it for speaking about human rights. “I think when you have a possibility to speak to the world, you have to speak about human rights,” he says. “It’s not about taking a position on the left or the right. I have always said that in San Sebastián, all people are welcome. The people who are not welcome are fascists, the people who are against freedom. That is not welcome in San Sebastián. When you are watching Israel kill people – civilian people – I think you have to say something. We can be a small but loudspeaker to the world. “I don’t have anything against the Israeli people – nothing. In fact, this year’s New Directors section has an Israeli member of the jury – Dana Blankstein Cohen. But at the same time, we can’t deny that in this moment, the government of Israel and the military of Israel are killers.” The 74th San Sebastian Film Festival takes place September 18-26, 2026. articles.title: Dhar Mann, Sean Atkins Set For MIPCOM’s First-Ever Pre-Opening Keynote
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart Dhar Mann, Sean Atkins Set For MIPCOM’s First-Ever Pre-Opening Keynote Princess Diana Documentary Featuring Unheard Tapes Set For International Launch At MIPCOM Former Sony, Endemol & Talpa Exec Ziad Kebbi Takes The Reins At MForMedia As Dubai-Based Production Company Refocuses On Originals & AI View All September 17, 2026 6:00am Dhar Mann & Sean Atkins are headed to MIPCOM Cannes Ian Spanier, Justine Knight EXCLUSIVE: Dhar Mann is headed to Cannes for MIPCOM . The powerhouse digital producer will take a headline slot alongside Sean Atkins, CEO of Dhar Mann Studios . The pair will speak on Sunday, October 11, the day before the MIPCOM market opens. It marks the first time MIPCOM organizers have scheduled a pre-opening keynote in this way. The reality of the market is most folks arrive on the Sunday to be in position for proceedings, which start the next day. MIPCOM organizers said Mann and Atkins will break down how an audience-first creator business works. They will also cover how to build IP around communities, work up positive stories, and create new partnerships that link creators, brands and the entertainment business. Related Stories News Princess Diana Documentary Featuring Unheard Tapes Set For International Launch At MIPCOM News 'Killing Eve' Origin Story 'Honey' To World Premiere At MIPCOM Mann majors in uplifting content aimed at a wide audience. DMS has 170M followers and its content registers 300M views every week. It operates out of a 125,000 sq. ft. studio in Burbank. Watch on Deadline It recently partnered with Disney with a deal for original programming and has inked a distribution deal with Fox Entertainment for a slate of vertical video titles. It has also partnered with brands including Adobe, the NFL, Microsoft and Gap. “Creators are building audiences at a scale that used to be possible only through traditional media, but what’s most exciting is when we turn that connection into franchises, new formats and partnerships that can travel around the world,” Mann said. “Sean and I are looking forward to coming to Cannes and sharing what we’ve learned scaling Dhar Mann Studios, and why we believe the future of entertainment will be shaped by creators and the traditional industry working much more closely together.” The MIPCOM activity comes as the event’s organizers, RX France, position it as more than a place to buy and sell TV shows. Under the stewardship of event director, Lucy Smith, it has pushed heavily into digital, branded content and the creator economy in recent editions. “Dhar Mann Studios is a powerful example of how creator-led businesses are reshaping the global entertainment industry,” Smith said. “Bringing Dhar and Sean to our main stage reflects MIPCOM’s role in bringing together the established entertainment business with the creators, platforms and new models shaping its future.” We hear DMS and MIPCOM will also co-host an invite-only dinner on the Sunday evening, bringing together about 25 CMOs and industry leaders for a pre-market get-together. MIPCOM runs from October 11-15. articles.title: José Luis Rebordinos Reflects On His Final Year At San Sebastián: “What Surprises Me The Most Is How Much The Festival Has Grown”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana José Luis Rebordinos Reflects On His Final Year At San Sebastián: “What Surprises Me The Most Is How Much The Festival Has Grown” ‘Onwards And Sideways’ Team Rhys Ifans, Laura Linney & John Madden On Making A Parkinson’s Story That Finds Laughter & Love In The Unexpected — Toronto Former DreamWorks & MGM TV Exec Brian Edwards Teams With Alpha Film Founders To Launch Time Zone Capital View All September 17, 2026 6:13am José Luis Rebordinos San Sebastian International Film Festival As the San Sebastián International Film Festival kicks into gear this weekend, it will be a bittersweet moment for José Luis Rebordinos. The longtime festival director is stepping down after what will be his 17th edition this year with deputy director Maialen Beloki taking over in January 2027. “Maialen is a highly qualified professional with an in-depth knowledge of the festival,” Rebordinos tells Deadline. “She has been part of the team for seventeen years, serving as deputy director for the last eleven of those. I can’t think of anyone better suited to the role.” Related Stories News 'Club Kid' & 'The Man I Love' Among Titles Added To San Sebastian Lineup News Jesse Eisenberg's 'The Debut' & Fred Cavayé's 'Les Misérables' Among Six New Titles In San Sebastián Official Selection While assured the festival is in good hands for its next chapter, Rebordinos says there are three things of which is he is most proud: “First there is the growth we have created in the industry activities, the second is that we have made it into a festival that works all year round with our school of cinema and residential projects and the third is the archive.” Watch on Deadline Indeed, San Sebastián has increasingly ramped up its industry activity during Rebordinos’ tenure and the Spanish event is now considered the premiere hub for connecting Europe’s film industry to Latin American cinema and filmmaking talents. In the past, the festival had supported early works of filmmakers such as Brazil’s Walter Salles to Argentina’s Daniel Burman whose respective early works Foreign Land and A Chrysanthemum Bursts in Cincoesquinas both screened at the festival. Rebordinos has built on that with sections such as its Europe-Latin America Co-Production Forum, which started in 2012, and its Works in Progress LatAm, which was launched in 2020. In 2015, the festival started its Ikusmira Berriak residency program in partnership with the Tabakalera International Center for Contemporary Culture and Elías Querejeta Zine Eskola (EQZE). Filmmakers to emerge from that ecosystem include Chilean filmmaker Diego Céspedes with his feature The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo ( La misteriosa mirada del flamenco ), and Gabriel Azorín with his feature Last Night I Conquered the City of Tebas ( Anoche conquisté Tebas ). Céspedes’ project premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in 2025 where it took a top prize in Un Certain Regard while Azorín’s film premiered at Venice the same year. Since 2018, San Sebastián has also worked closely with EQZE on Artxiboa, a historical digital and physical archive of the festival that is dedicated to preserving and sharing seven decades of the festival’s history. It contains more than 15,000 paper documents, 17,000 photographs, press dossiers, journals and festival posters dating from the festival’s founding in 1953 to the present. San Sebastian’s Creative Investors’ Conference Deadline In 2022, San Sebastián teamed up with CAA Media Finance to launch an annual Creative Investors’ Conference, which runs during the festival and has seen the attendance of major international players such as CAA’s Roeg Sutherland, Goodfellas founder Vincent Maraval, Neon’s Tom Quinn and Mediawan’s Elisabeth d’Arvieu, “We have more and more people attending each year and it’s become incredibly successful,” says Rebordinos. “Business agreements have taken place here and it’s important that we have a relaxed atmosphere to support this. We are a smaller festival for a reason. We don’t want to be a very big festival. We want to be a human festival for industry activities. We are not a market – it’s impossible for us. We are a little city and a little festival but sometimes it’s good to be smaller.” Maraval, a longtime supporter of San Sebastián, notes that Rebordinos helped propel the festival “to another dimension.” “His sense of hospitality and his taste positioned San Sebastián in the top three international festivals,” says Maraval. “He knew how to take advantage of all of the assets of this beautiful city and make the festival unique.” He continues: “I won’t miss him because he became a friend and my friendship won’t stop because he is no longer in charge. We will continue our cinema discussion around a great meal, and I hope I will still benefit from his advice like when he told me to look at Los Javis’ work. His job is perhaps over but his taste remains.” Sutherland agrees noting that Rebordinos “has turned the festival into an international destination.” “Like Venice, San Sebastián is a launching pad for awards pictures, as well as a celebration of Spanish cinema and putting it at the forefront of our minds,” says the CAA exec. “In the last several years, he established a conference that brings together like-minded voices to address the needs of our industry and find solutions for the future and preservation of cinema.” Spanish producer Marisa Fernández Armenteros, whose film Sundays won the Golden Shell for Best Film at the festival last year, says: “Rebordinos is, above all, a hopeless optimist. I still remember the 2020 edition during the pandemic. Everything was being canceled and Rebordinos would call us to say, ‘Between optimism and pessimism, it is better for me to be an optimist. We’ll make it happen. There will be a festival.’ And he did. “I will always be grateful to him for calling me, whether it was to share good news or bad. He has always faced up to things, understanding that it is part of his responsibility. And the longer I work in this industry, the more I value that attitude. I have seen him quietly support directors and producers with their first films, as well as projects from Latin America that were stuck in financing limbo. And always, quietly, behind the scenes.” Rebordinos says he’s not leaving the industry completely and plans to consult with other festivals down the line on “matters relating to Spanish and Latin American cinema.” “But I won’t be on the front line,” he says. “Rather, I will always be working in support of others.” The 74 th San Sebastián International Film Festival takes place September 18-26, 2026. Zac Ntim contributed to this report. Disney/Randy Holmes Rosie O’Donnell is stepping into the role of The Narrator in The Rocky Horror Show for two weeks in October. O’Donnell takes over the role after appearing Off- Broadway this summer at the Daryl Roth Theatre, where she performed her one-woman show Common Knowledge for 12 performances. She then took over Jimmy Kimmel Live! for a weeklong stint in August.
